en: Dharma is the foundation of the entire world;
[this is] the Prājña Pāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala Granthamālā Mīmāṃsā Koṣa.
Seventh Part: (ca-ha) Editor:
Brahmībhūta: Kevalānandasarasvatī;
Mārgaśīrṣa, bright fortnight, 1st day; Tuesday; Śaka year 1888. Table of Contents.

Publisher’s Note … … … Abbreviations for the Text and Other Works, with Explanations … … 1–5 Table of Corrections … … … … 6–8 Mīmāṃsākoṣaḥ … … … … 3633–4542 Publisher’s Note: This is the seventh and final volume of the Mīmāṃsākoṣaḥ.
This *Kopa* was composed by my venerable teacher (*asmad-gurucaraṇaiḥ*), and this section concludes with the letter *ha*.

The editing of this part has been accomplished by Dattātreya Śāstrī, known by the surname Tāmrai, who bears the lotus feet of his guru and is adorned with the title *Mīmāṃsābhūṣaṇa* and the status of an *Āhitāgni*.

Furthermore, the entire undertaking—from the initial compilation through to the printing and publication of all parts—has been carried out by his assistant, the managing editor Śrīraṅganātha Śāstrī, also known as Gadyāsa.

The Ministry of Education of the Republic of India and the Department of Higher Education of the Government of Maharashtra have provided financial assistance for the printing costs of this volume; both deserve our heartfelt appreciation.

As for my venerable teachers, they did not accept any financial assistance from anyone else for the compilation of this treasury. Considering its composition to be a form of austerity (*tapas*) consisting of self-study (*svādhyāya*), they spent many years with their minds fully concentrated on this work.
Having completed the repayment of the debt to the feet of my guru, I consider this treasury to be entirely fulfilled; thus, the circle of our Prājña Pāṭhaśālā has achieved its purpose.

The operation of an injunction (*vidhi-vyāpāra*). For we shall explain in the subsequent section (Vārttika 3.1.6.2, p. 691) that nowhere else does this operation of an injunction exist apart from the extension of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) and the extension of the meaning (*atideśa*). That which is desired by a person even without the operation of an injunction is merely the objective (*uddeśya*) with respect to the means being enjoined; it is understood through the injunction.

In the case of *soma* (as in "He cleanses the cup with the *daśāpavitra* filter," etc.), the extent of contact with the operation of the injunction must be investigated; for there is the determination that whatever is touched by the force of the injunction is to be performed, and nothing else. Vārttika 3.1.7.3, pp. 700–701. It is not an absolute rule that the injunctive power of specific verbal suffixes is obscured by their being used as mantras.
Vārttika 2.1.6.20, p. 439: The power of injunction (*vidhiśakti*) transfers to a subordinate element (*guṇa*).
Sūtra 3.3.10.12, p. 869: The power of injunction does not exist in a nominal word (*nāmapada*).
Sūtra 2.4.3.2, p. 332: The power of injunction is obstructed by the word *yat*, as in "those [worlds] do not perish" (*na tā naśanti*), and so forth.
By means of the vocative case, as in "O Ahibudhnya, protect my mantra" (RV 10.87.22) and so forth;
by means of the first person, as in "I bind, I take hold" (ŚB 3.2.4.15) and so forth;
and by means of the word *yat* (if), as in "If they should carry off the Soma" (TS 6.5.1.1) and so forth.

"Those words which have been handed down in the tradition, whose injunctive power is destroyed by the attachment of particles such as *yat* and the like, are in every respect merely denotative. Vākyapadīya 2.1.6.13, p. 433.

"Because it impels toward the Self, because it is conjoined with yoga, and because it is designated as pure consciousness, the fourfold group beginning with the word *yat* would constitute the power of injunction (*vidhiśakti*).
Whatever is grasped by the power of injunction is indeed intended [by the speaker]. (Page 668)

In the same way, that which is abandoned [as a primary injunction] should be explained as being unintended [for the purpose of prescription]. Vākyapadīya 3.1.7.3, p. 703: "The state of lacking injunctive power is the nature of an *arthavāda*.
Parākrama 5.2: "The injunctive power [is neutralized] by the word *yat*, by the first person [optative], and by the vocative case ending."
In the passage, "If both of one's sacrificial offerings should meet with disaster," there is the word *yat* (the relative pronoun).
In the passage, "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods," there is the first person singular verb (*dāmi*). In the passage, "O cook, distribute the fires," there is the vocative address, "O cook."

That which obstructs the power of an injunction: "Because it manifests [the object] as already established, because it is impossible for the speaker to be directed toward [an action], because there can be no instigation toward oneself, and because it denotes being a cause."
The fourfold set consisting of the word *vat*, the vocative case-ending, the first person [verb], and the word *yadi* would be destroyers of the power of the injunction (*vidhi*).
Even in the case of a yoga of attainment (*prāpyayoga*), some among these might possess the quality of being a destroyer.
Thus, there is this fourfold set: the suffix *-vat*, the vocative case, the first person, and the word *yadi*.

Su. Pṛ. 668: "Indeed, even by a hundred injunctions, a person does not act in the same way as they do out of desire" (Vākyapadīya 3.4.10.28, p. 960). Regarding the statement "And the words of injunction," it was established therein that in mantras such as "O Agni, O householder, O good householder," the portions beginning with "a hundred winters" are supported by supplementary statements (*vākyaśeṣa*) such as "He says this so that you may live for a hundred winters"; these serve as indicative marks (*liṅga*) for the fact that the intended meaning of the mantras is to be expressed.
"Nor is a secondary meaning understood from an injunctive word. (Bhāṣya on PMS 10.2.1.47).
"If an injunctive word were a mantra, its existence would be [for that purpose]; by it there is an injunction.
Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is the statement: "That which belongs to Agni, prepared on eight potsherds, is constant on the new moon and full moon days. (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa).
Agni is the deity of the cake (*puroḍāśa*) prepared on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*).
And for Agni, there are names such as Agni, Śuci, Pāvaka, Dhūmaketu, Kṛśānu, and so forth.

Such being the case, in the deliberation as to which name should be uttered in the mantras of invocation and other rites—specifically in the formula of renunciation, "This is for [so-and-so], not mine"—the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Regarding the phrase "in the case of a mantra," the suffix *sva* is used in its own sense, meaning "in a mantra. In other cases, such as in the *nigada* and in a mantra of renunciation (*tyāga-mantra*), there should be the presence—that is, the pronunciation—of the word "Agni" itself as it occurs in the injunctive sentence; no other synonymous term should be used. This is because the injunction, the impulsion to action, has proceeded by means of that very word "Agni."

Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that in the *tyāga* and in the *nigadas*, the reference must be made by the very word that denotes the deity according to the injunction (*vidhi*).
(Mīmāṃsākośa 459: *vidhiśabdasya*)
The section concerning words expressing injunction (*vidhiśabdādhikaraṇa*):
Being connected with the oblation, a word expressing an injunction establishes the deityhood of the object, and not otherwise.

The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), however, is as follows: the word is entirely subordinate with respect to the object; it is thus connected to the action because of its [the object's] primacy. The word "fire" does not itself enter into a direct relationship with the substance that is the object of the action.
What then? It is conjoined with the meaning (*artha*).
And because the designation is directed toward the meaning, synonymous terms are excluded here.
Furthermore, it is not only that which has the word "fire" as its referent that is conjoined with the substance; rather, [the word] functions precisely because it possesses gender (*liṅga*).
By means of the sentence and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*),
it is not indicated as a separate factor by the instrumental case,
whereby the indicative mark (*liṅga*) would be sublated.
If it were extracted and then combined with the *puroḍāśa*, in that case,
the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) would not arise;
moreover, there would be the definition of a word-meaning within the meaning of a sentence.
The meaning of a sentence is preceded by the meanings of its constituent words.
If the word itself were the deity, then only the word "deity" would be significant;
and since that word would be devoid of meaning, only the meaning expressed by the word "this" (asau) would remain.
In that case, because it would possess expectancy and not have its expectancy satisfied, it would not even constitute a syntactical unit (*vākya*).
But even so, there would still be no connection between synonymous words.
How? The word "Agni" establishes its own meaning as the deity of the *puroḍāśa* cake.
And that divinity, if one relinquishes the substance with reference to the Vedic scriptural statement (śruti), is thereby accomplished, and not by any other means.
In this state, it is the word *ima* alone that revolves in the mind, and no other.
Therefore, for that reason as well, only that which is revolving [in the mind] should be grasped, and nothing else.
And that [word] is verbal.
Therefore, it is that very word which must be uttered at the time of the perception of the expressive sound.
To this, it is replied:
The word "Agni," having fulfilled its purpose by establishing itself as the deity of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) in its own meaning,
has no further function at the time of its utterance;
otherwise, the sacrifice would not take place.
In this state, the word *agni* is not heard;
it must be uttered by some word or other,
and the word *agni* is [unavailable] because it is separated [by intervening sounds].
Therefore, it cannot be restricted that the word "Agni" [denotes the deity].
However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: the word "Agni" itself, when connected with the eight-pot-sherd cake (aṣṭākapāla), establishes the deity-status of the object.
Just as in the case of the injunction "one should recite the verse dedicated to Viṣṇu," the Ṛc being mentioned establishes the meaning of the Ṛc.
Nor is the intended meaning of the *ṛc* verse connected with the ritual action;
likewise here too, it is not intended otherwise by way of connection with the action.
Furthermore, even for one who desires to connect the purpose with the eight-pot-sherd offering (*aṣṭākapāla*), the scriptural text expressing that [purpose] must be recited.

By means of that [word], the deity is brought into connection with the ritual action. In this regard, first there is the status of the object as the deity, and subsequently the utterance of the word is enjoined; thus, two meanings are expressed through both direct statement (*śruti*) and contextual purpose (*artha*).

Furthermore, in a case where the deity itself is already established by the [mention of] the eight-potherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*), then only its utterance is enjoined—namely, "one should offer the eight-potherd cake to Agni and so forth. For that [injunction], this [mention of Agni] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the deity-status.
Just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with the *pūtika* plant," the sacrifice is obtained by implication;
because the injunction for the remaining [deities] is one and the same, therefore it is heard everywhere.
Commentary: Thus, by the word "injunction" (vidhi), the expression must be uttered. Why? Because among the mantras to be known, there is a single word:
that very word which is the injunction is heard everywhere—in the *ayāṭ* formula, in the *ajuhota* formula, and in the *svāhā* formula.
In the case of the *akāra* (the syllable "a"), [he recites]: "May he sacrifice to the dear abodes of Tvaṣṭṛ, to the dear abodes of Soma, to the dear abodes of Agni," and so forth.
In the case of the *ujjipā* (the act of lifting up), [he recites]: "O Agni, I have sought after your life; O Soma, I have sought after your life.
In the case of the *svāhākāra* (the utterance "svāhā"), [he recites]: "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! and so forth.
And thus, even when heard as if they were restrictive rules (*niyama*), they will become non-binding (*apāśika*), just as it was taught in the case of the *assaminī* [verse].
Therefore, there must be the presence of the injunctive word within the mantra.
Śā—In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard: "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni."
Furthermore, there are many designations for Agni, such as "Agni," "Śuci," "Pāvaka," and so forth.
In that regard, within those Vedic texts (nigamas) beginning with "tat" and others, should the designation of Agni be made by any word whatsoever, or must it be made specifically by the word "Agni"?
In this context: "Once the deity-hood of Agni has been established, the application of other words ceases."
At the time of practice, the formal instruction is accomplished by anyone whatsoever.
The injunction means only this much: "the deity must be made the object of the fire.

Since the status of being a deity belongs to that which is designated by a word, the utterance of the word follows from the ritual injunction (*prayogavākya*). However, there is no authoritative evidence for a restriction [on which specific word must be used].
For even when the deity is designated by the word *pāvaka*, the very status of deity expressed by the injunction is successfully accomplished; therefore, there is no restriction.
This being the case, it is true that the injunction declares the object itself to be the deity;
however, its status as a deity consists precisely in its being designated by means of a word.

Therefore, the person’s activity consists solely in the utterance of that word, and he is enjoined with respect to his own activity. Thus, even though the object is said to be the deity, [the result follows] by that alone.
The section concerning injunctive words (*vidhiśabdādhikaraṇa*): An injunction, which consists in the utterance of a word, reaches its completion only after having performed its enjoining function.
And in that state, since there is no reason to abandon the word present in the injunction when it is available, only the utterance of that very word is enjoined, not another word.
Therefore, there is a restriction regarding the injunctive word.

Soma [objects]: Just as in the previous case there was a contraction of both the apūrva and the uddeśya, so too here, because there is no evidence for a contraction such that the designation of the deity must be performed by the injunctive word alone, it follows that the designation of the deity may be performed by any word whatsoever; thus, the connection is established.

As for the connection with the [etymological] definition, it is because of the consequence of contradiction and because of the determination that [the words] are synonymous; this is the remainder of the argument regarding the investigation.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: since in the case of a mantra there is a necessity of uttering the word denoting the deity of the mantra, the "being" (bhāva)—that is, the utterance—of the word *agni* occurring in the injunction (*vidhi*) would take place, because by that injunctive word the offering (*havis*) is connected [to the deity].
As it is said: "Whether by way of synonymy, or by the mention of the deity, or by the very word of the injunction itself..."
The first [type of inference] is due to a difference in meaning; the other is preceded by a word and is concomitant.

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the inquiry whether, in all cases such as "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni" (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ*), the word denoting the deity must necessarily be uttered in its inflected form at the time of the offering, or whether this is not a fixed rule—the first position is that the word itself constitutes the deity. For is this stated while disregarding the object, or while taking the object into account? It cannot be the former; because in both common usage and the Veda, it is well-established that names such as "Agni" denote objects, and if they lacked reference to an object, the nominal stems of words like "Agni" would not exist, resulting in the impossibility of their taking case-endings and so forth. Nor can it be the latter.

If the deity-hood (*devatātva*) of that [word] is established by its being focused upon the meaning, then there is no evidence for the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word itself in terms such as "Agni" and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that deity-hood—in the form of being the object intended (*uddeśyatva*) by the word—is impossible in that case, because deity-hood is a property of the word consisting in being the object of utterance at the time of the relinquishment of the substance (*dravya*). This is because there is no evidence that being the object intended must necessarily involve utterance; rather, since it consists in being the object of cognition (*jñāna*) at the time of the relinquishment of the substance, it is possible even in the case of the meaning. Furthermore, there is no such rule that cognition itself is dependent solely upon the utterance of words.
Since remembrance is possible even through the sight of the proximity of substances and so forth, the utterance of the word itself is the [necessary factor];
thus, in the absence of any other means of knowledge, the restriction to the specific word mentioned in the injunction is indeed difficult to maintain.

Or, let it be that the status of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) is constituted by utterance; nevertheless, since the deity-hood consists simply in being the thing to be conveyed by the mere utterance, there is no impossibility regarding its referent.

Nor should it be argued that, even so, there will be a restriction of the word as it is being uttered based on its specific [context], since the word is already apprehended through direct audition (*śruti*) and other means; for a word whose purpose is fulfilled by enjoining a meaning cannot logically function as a restrictor of the word itself.
This is because the requirement is satisfied merely by grasping the expressive word, regardless of its specific quality.

Otherwise, even in the case of a word denoting a substance—such as in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*) where the mantra "O *medha* of the rice-grains, being well-disposed... occurs and *bṛhaspati* is substituted for Maitrāvaruṇa and others—there would result the undesirable consequence of restricting the word to that which is enjoined by the injunction.

Although there is inherence (*samavāya*) of the substance in the action by way of its own form, whereas for the deity it exists through the medium of the word—this much being the difference between them—nevertheless, since the heard word, having fulfilled its purpose by enjoining [the action], stands in need of a specific word [to denote the deity], it is indeed equal [in authority] regarding that restriction.
Furthermore, in cases where synonymous words are employed, such as "to Agni Pāvaka" and so forth, the use of two words occurs;
how else could this be established?
For in that case, since there is no evidence for a restriction to two specific words, it is logical that the word itself is to be restricted merely by way of requirement (*apekṣā*).

Therefore, there is no restriction of the word belonging to the injunction (*vidhi*) regarding the abandonment (*tyāga*) and so forth. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: the deityhood of the object does not arise through mere cognition alone, independent of its utterance; for if that were so, in cases such as "to Agni Pāvaka," it would be possible to enjoin the object itself by means of the word, because of the *arthāpatti* (presumption) regarding the word and the substance.

Therefore, although the word *pāvaka*— based on the examination of the Purāṇas and other sources— denotes a specific type of fire, nevertheless, because it is possible for that term to stand in grammatical apposition with a word denoting a particular [quality] such as "ignorance" (*avidyā*),
the substitution of the word *agni* itself is appropriate. Consequently, the utterance of the word must certainly be performed in accordance with the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
For this very reason, in such passages as "One should meditate upon Prajāpati with the mind," that state is merely verbal.
Having pronounced the name and lineage, one should speak with perfect faith, having specified the place, time, and so forth, saying: "I bestow this upon you."

"One should also proclaim the cessation [of ownership] with the words 'not mine' (na mama); endowed with faith, one should perform acts such as giving and fire-offerings. This meaning is determined here by the statement established through the citation in Hemādri.

Therefore, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), deityhood (*devatātva*) consists solely in being the object of the utterance of the word prescribed by the injunction, and not in being the object of a separately extracted cognition, nor does it consist in the word as expressed by the utterance at the time of renunciation (*tyāga*), because that would involve excessive complexity (*gaurava*).

Here, the term "prescribed" (*vihita*) is used to prevent the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that would result from taking any random utterance whatsoever. And this very point is the meaning of the word *tadit*.

Therefore, even though [the mantra] does not convey that meaning which constitutes its primary purpose, once the definition of "word" (śabda) is accepted, the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) is enjoined by the injunction (*vidhi*) in that very same way.

Thus, in cases involving two words, the status of both as deities is to be understood through their conjunction (*samuccaya*), based on their inclusion within a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*) and so forth.
As for the meaning (*artha*), however, it is merely incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*).

Section on the Word Denoting the Procedure (vidhiśabdādhikaraṇa): Since the cognition [of the deity] by means of that [word] is necessary, the secondary status of being a deity (*bhākta-devatātva*), which consists in being denoted by such a word, is also established by the sense of the matter; therefore, it is not enjoined by the scripture.

By this, the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) belongs to the pure referent (*artha*). And the status of being a deity consists in being that which is expressed by the word functioning as the object of utterance at the time of renunciation (*tyāga*). Furthermore, in cases such as "to Agni Pāvaka," the duality of deity-status resides in a single referent, just like the duality of the word itself; and since this is obtained from its inclusion within a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*), the objection that there would be the consequence of uttering only a single word therein is refuted. Moreover, [the view that deity-status belongs to the compound] is rejected because it is cumbersome to postulate a linguistic potency (*śakti*) for the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) and so forth for a cumbersome deity-status, and because the aforementioned meaning is obtainable through other means.

By this very argument, the position of the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*, who maintains that "one must accept that the meaning qualified by the word itself is the basis for the *prātipadika* designation, and thus [the deity] is something other [than the word] when it possesses the nature of a deity as defined by etymology (*nirukta*)," is also refuted; for there is excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in the determinant of the denotative power (*śaktatva*) of words such as secondary suffixes (*taddhita*).
Therefore, since the word itself is what connects with the sentence-meaning, there is no possibility of employing another word at the time of abandonment.
As for the mantras used in the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, it is beyond dispute that no other word is employed simply because that specific word has been recited therein.

In that context, in the case of the latter [type of] word, there is no indication by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) nor is there any status as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*); rather, its objectivity (*viṣayatā*) consists in a specific relation consisting of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), and not in the form of something to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*).
— Bhāṣya.

Only the state of being that which is to be enjoined (vidheyatva) should be intended, not the state of being that which is to be adopted (upādeyatva), nor the state of being a qualifier (tadviśeṣaṇatva).
Bāla. p. 13.
[The term] *viśeṣatva* [is used here].
An injunction (*vidhi*) is the statement that something unknown is to be performed; it is a property (*dharma*) conditioned by the word.
In the case of a difference between things to be enjoined (*vidheya*), a difference in the delimitors of the state of being enjoined (*vidheyatā-avacchedaka*) is the general rule.

Consequently, there are universals (jāti) subsumed under "sacrificeness" (yāgatva) and so forth, such as the form of *samid-yāgatva* (the nature of the *samid* sacrifice), *tanūnapāt-yāgatva* (the nature of the *tanūnapāt* sacrifice), and so on.
Having indicated these through the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) occurring in their respective sentences, they are enjoined precisely as belonging to those sacrifices delimited by those [specific names].
(Kauṇḍinya-bhāṣya 2.2.12, p. 151).

By the maxim, "If this [effect] is not accomplished without that," the dedication to the deity (*devatoddeśa*) is established as the essential factor in a sacrifice (Sūtra-pṛ. 802). There is also the maxim: "Without sandalwood from the Malaya mountains, [the fragrance] does not grow. This applies when the intention is to express that a wise person attains elevation by taking refuge in a great individual who possesses the highest virtues, and not otherwise.
[The opponent] objects: "Destruction is absolute non-apprehension; this is observed in the world. [Reply:

Straightforwardly, on page 249, since the Prābhākaras do not accept destruction as being a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), that very non-apprehension of jars and other things—which occurs even when the totality of conditions for apprehension is present—is itself their destruction.
Non-apprehension is also that very same thing for it. (p. 251) This is the principle of the lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*).

The meaning is as follows: *yukti* (reasoning) is that which favors one side; *vinigamanā* is the determination toward one of two alternatives, which is to say, the capacity for ascertainment. *Virahe* means the absence or lack thereof.
For example—some [hold] that the extreme precision found in the *Sūryasiddhānta* is due to its being based on correct principles.

However, others [argue] that since both the observation and the calculation have attained identity, there is extreme subtlety; therefore, because it is highly agreed upon and due to the absence of a deciding factor (*vinigamanā*), the opposite conclusion would follow. Even if the observation-calculation were to serve as the deciding factor, it must be stated that they are indeed extremely subtle; thus, the claim [of the opponent] is empty—this is the sense. (Sāhasī 17) By the one who is employed.

There is no authority whatsoever for the claim that "that which has already been enjoined need not be enjoined again," provided that it possesses its own inherent injunctive power. (Vārttika 2.1.6.30) Otherwise,
there would be the fallacy of enjoining what has already been enjoined (*viniyuktaviniyoga*).

For indeed, refined people do not reuse a plantain leaf that has already been employed for eating. (Vi. 6.1.24) Even the re-employment of what has already been employed is not prohibited, just as the potsherd (kapāla), which was employed for the baking of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), is subsequently employed for the scattering of husks (tuṣopavāpa).
"Another [means of proof] is the applicatory [scriptural statement] (viniyoktrī śrutiḥ). The capacity to apply belongs to the word and to the case-endings (kāraka-vibhakti).
Vārttika 3.1.2.3, p. 700.

*Sudhā*: "Viniyoga" (application) is the cognition of mere syntactic connection (*anvaya-mātra-bodha*); even though it is fivefold, it possesses the character of an applicatory factor (*viniyojakatva*) because it consists in the cognition of a connection expressed by another word.

The *viniyogakatrīśruti* (directly expressive scriptural statement of application) is eightfold: 1. *vidhi* (injunction), 2. *parasmaipada* (active voice), 3. *ātmanepada* (middle voice), 4. that which is characterized by proximity (*upaśleṣalakṣaṇā*) consisting of a single word such as a nominal or verbal ending, so it is said; 5. that which takes the form of a single suffix (*ekapratyayarūpā*); 6. the case-ending denoting a *kāraka* (case-role); 7. among the case-endings used for accompanying words (*upapadavibhakti*), the dative expressing purpose (*tādarthyacaturthī*); and 8. the genitive denoting a residual relation (*śeṣaṣaṣṭhī*). Bālakrīḍā, p. 41. The *viniyoktrīśruti* (scriptural statement of application) is threefold: (1) by means of a case-ending (*vibhaktyā*), as in "one should cause [them] to eat with three" (*tribhir bhojayet*) or "one buys [it] with a red [cow]" (*aruṇayā krīṇāti*), and so forth.

(2) *Samānābhidhāna-rūpā* (based on co-referential expression): In the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), both singularity and masculinity possess the status of a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) by virtue of the *samānābhidhāna-śruti* (the co-referential scriptural statement), namely the suffix *-nā*.
(3) *Ekapada-rūpā* (based on a single word): "One should sacrifice" (*yajeta*). This is a verbal form (*tiṅanta*) consisting of a single word.

In this context, the singularity denoted by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) is subordinate to the sacrifice (*yāga*) by virtue of its being part of the same word (*ekapada-śruti*). According to the view of Bhaṭṭa Gomeśvara, there is yet another type of *viniyojakī* (applicatory) direct statement (*śruti*), namely: the particle *iti*, the suffixes *ṇamul*, *ktvā*, *lyap*, *tumun*, *ṇvul*, verbal nouns (*bhāvavacana*), the suffix *aṇ*, the *kṛtya* suffixes, *suc*, and the present tense marker (*laṭ*).
All of that is considered invalid by Pārthasārathi Miśra (Bāla., p.
46–47). That word from the mere hearing of which the relationship [between the act and its accessory] is understood is the *viniyoktrī-śruti* (the injunctive scriptural statement).
In the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), the instrumental case-ending conveys the relationship of the animal with the sacrifice. [This is] *mīmāṃsā*.
*Viniyoga* (application) refers to the application of the mantra for carrying the fire to the act of spreading the sacrificial grass.

Bhāṣya 3.4.1.10: The application (*viniyoga*) of the mantras beginning with "drunk by Indra" (*indrapītasya*) is to all acts of consumption during the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. See the discussion in the *Mīmāṃsākutūhalavṛtti* (mīko.), page 1050, under the section titled "The Section on [Mantras] Concerning What was Drunk by Indra" (*indrapītādhikaraṇam*), at Bhāṣya 3.4.1.28–29, 39, and 44.

Viniyoga [is determined] by sequence (*krama*, i.e., by the means of knowledge known by that name), Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1059; see the section titled "Kramādhikaraṇa" for the discussion on this topic. Viniyoga: 3|4|1|12; the establishment of the rule of application (*viniyogavidhi*).
Viniyoga: The application of the mantra beginning with "gāyatracchandasaḥ" and so forth is to [rites] characterized by various meters (nānācchandaske).
See the section titled "Chando'dhikaraṇam" on page 1027 of the Mīmāṃsākośa (Mīko.). Viniyoga is the communication of the purpose for which something is intended.
As for the application (viniyoga), however, it follows from the capacity [of the words]. Vā. 3.4.1.4; see Mīko. p. 266, under the section "Prakaraṇādhikaraṇam. One should consult that section.
Viniyoga (application) consists of a property that becomes the object of the knowledge which generates activity; it is common to both optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites.
(Bhāṭṭa 6.1.6).
Viniyoga [is seen] in the *bhakṣānuvāka* [of the Jyotiṣṭoma], where, according to the indicative mark (*liṅga*), [the mantras] are applied to the drawing of the cups (*grahaṇa*) and other such acts.
The application (viniyoga) of the Manotā mantra is [established] through its secondary (gauṇa) meanings.
(Bhāṭṭa 3.2.1).
The application (*viniyoga*) of mantras is to their primary meaning (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2913).
The relevant section should be consulted under the "Barhis-nyāya" (Sūtra 3.4.1.2–9).
The application of the mantra for cutting is to the *barhis* (sacrificial grass) itself, which is its primary sense.
The application [of the mantra] is by means of direct statement (*śruti*). Bhāṣya 3.4.12–2;
Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.4.17–10.
Viniyoga is established by name (*samākhyā*).
In this regard, the section titled "The Section on Name" (*samākhyādhikaraṇam*) should be consulted.
The application (*viniyoga*) of the *sūktavāka* mantra is to the extraction of the essence of the meaning within the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Bhāṭṭa 3.2.6:

The application (*viniyoga*) of the specific *sūktavāka* sentence in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) occurs through the superior force of syntactical connection (*vākya*) over contextual setting (*prakaraṇa*).
The application [of a mantra] is determined by its position; "position" is another name for "sequence. See the section titled "On Sequence" (Kramādhikaraṇa) on page 1505 of the Mīmāṃsākōśa.

Viniyoga: The mantra "O preparer of the oblation, come" (haviṣkṛdehi) is used for the purpose of summoning during the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1022; see the section titled "Āhvānādhikaraṇa"). Between the originative injunction (utpatti-vākya) and the applicatory injunction (viniyoga), the applicatory injunction is more powerful.
Thus, this section (3.1.16) is based on reasoning (*nyāya*).
Vārttika 3.4.19, p. 818:

Just as ritual items (*padārtha*) enjoined by means of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth, are prescribed by the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), so too sequence (*krama*) is prescribed by the injunction of performance because it is enjoined by means of direct statement, purpose (*artha*), and so forth.
Nor is it the case that [the means of proof] such as direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth, are the sole applicators of everything;

for that restriction applies only to the application of word-meanings (*padārtha*). Since there is no contradiction even when the sequence is applied by means of direct statement and the like—such as the order of recitation—it is just as the property of the Veda regarding application is explained in the *Nirukta*.
"Because it indicates [the application] as if by direct audition from the attainment [of the result], it has the purpose of application (*viniyoga*).
For the demonstration of that purpose is indeed the means for establishing the fruit.
(Vi. 3.13.2. Kaṇikā, p. 177). The duty of the *viniyoga-veda* must be performed, not the duty of the *utpatti-veda*."

Vārttika 3.2.1, p. 814: Because the power of application (*viniyoga*) determines only the connection [of a word], it is not possible for there to be a sense of "being something to be done" (*kāryatva*) regarding that connection.

Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 100: An example of an injunction common to the application [of subsidiaries] is: "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) which is used for the *ātithyā* [offering], that same [grass] is for the *upasad*s.

Or, for example, the injunction regarding the sacrificial grass and its properties, as well as the injunction regarding the altar (*vedi*) and its properties, is common to both the subsidiaries and the primary rite.
Vāla-pṛ. 20: *Liṅga* (indicative power) consists of the capacity for application (*viniyoga*).
Vā. 3.3.4.11: The very hearing of a case-ending (*kāraka-vibhakti*) constitutes the cause of application.
Su. pṛ. 1209: There are six means of proof (*pramāṇa*) that effect application. [Note: The word *pramāṇa* here refers to the Vedic means of proof.]

In the case of conflict between two Vedic texts (viprapittau): when there is a contradiction, there would be an option (vikalpa) between a mantra expressing the singularity of the noose and a mantra expressing the plurality of the nooses.

Because of their equality; for in the act of releasing the bonds (*pāśonmocana*), the designation of "bonds" (*pāśa*) as the object (*karman*) remains applicable to both mantras alike. Now, one might argue: "Even so, the plural number (*bahuvacana*) has its purposeful application in a rite involving many bonds; therefore, the plural number should be displaced (*utkarṣa*), and when it is displaced, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) should also be displaced.
If this is said, we reply: no.

However, when a subordinate element (*guṇa*) is the primary factor, it is possible to assume an improper application (*anyāyakalpanā*). Since the singular number of the word "noose" (*pāśa*) is improper, one might argue that the plural number must be disregarded because it is merely a part of the expression.

But since the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is the primary factor, it is impossible to assume an improper application there; therefore, the meaning of the nominal stem must indeed be intended, and thus there is no displacement [of the mantra].

Consequently, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that just as the mantra ending in the singular occurs in the archetype (*prakṛti*), so too the mantra ending in the plural may be applied optionally.
And the context (*prakaraṇa*) is equal.

It has been stated that in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, both the mantra expressing the singular number of the tether (*pāśa*) and the mantra expressing the plural number of the tether are to be applied as alternatives, because they are equal; therein, he establishes their equality:
for both mantras, the context is one and the same.
Thus, due to the specific context—namely, because they belong to a single context—there is equality.
And because of this equality, both are to be included within the context;
furthermore, their application is by way of option.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is no exaltation of anyone;
the reading "due to a specific context" (*prakaraṇaviśeṣataḥ*) is appropriate here, yet it is not found anywhere. Thus, [this] intellectual effort is futile.

"Or [there is] elevation, as in the case of the two sacrifices. In the context of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīyapaśu*), two mantras—one expressing the singular number of the tether (*pāśa*) and one expressing its plural number—are recorded in the scripture without distinction. The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) maintains that both are to be inserted into the context itself; however, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣī*) raises an objection. The word "or" (*vā*) serves to set aside the position of the final view.
It is not a matter of the end; rather, there would be an upward displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the mantra expressing the multiplicity of snares during the ritual procedure involving many snares.

This is like the case of the "Two-Sacrifice" (*dviyajña*): because it is stated that one should perform the *pratipad* verse "For you two are the lords of heaven" (*yuvaṃ hi sthaḥ svarpatī*) for two sacrificers, an upward displacement of this *pratipad* "For you two are... is made in the *kulāya-yajña*, which is a sacrifice of two sacrificers.
However, due to the absence of purpose, it would not be so here; the other [mantra] is merely a subordinate quality (*guṇamātra*).

The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) refutes the doubt raised by the opponent (pūrvapakṣin), who argues that just as the introductory verse (*pratipad*) "For you two are the lords of light" (*yuvaṃ hi sthaḥ svarpatī*) is transferred from the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—which has a single sacrificer—to the *Kulāya* sacrifice, which has two sacrificers, so too the mantra expressing the plurality of nooses, "May Aditi release these nooses" (*aditiḥ pāśān pramumoktu etān*), should be transferred to a rite involving many nooses.

[The siddhāntin replies: Because of the absence of the purpose; since the purpose—the duality of the sacrificers—is absent in the *Abhīdhoma*, the introductory verse "For you two are... would not find application there.
However, this does not mean that the mere quality [of duality] is absent.
The mere quality and the mere plurality of the bonds would not be established as inherent in the archetype (*prakṛti*), nor would there be any transference (*utkarṣa*).
Rather, either the plural number would be unintended, or the plurality of the bonds would be justified as being inherent in the archetype itself through that very lack of intentionality.
As for the other [element], it would be thus: the other nominal stem (*prātipadika*), however, would be established as inherent in the archetype because of its connection with it.
And thus, the rule is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Therefore, there is no extension [of the rule].
If it is argued that [the rule applies] "to both," [we reply: no.

The opponent might argue: "Just as the mantra for the performance of the *dyāvāpṛthivī* sacrifice—'May I prosper in these two worlds, heaven and earth, which are the sacrificial ground of the gods'—is extracted from the archetype (*prakṛti*) and applied to a rite dedicated to those same deities, so too should the mantra expressing the plurality of fetters (*pāśa*) be extracted and applied to a rite involving many animals. This is the construction:
"As with the two [worlds], so with the *pāśa*-mantra.
The term "of the two" (*dyāvoḥ*) means "of heaven and earth" (*dyāvāpṛthivyoḥ*).

Because it is an original statement (*utpattiśabda*). The opponent raises the objection: "The *dyāvāpṛthivyanumantraṇa* mantra, which is recited in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, belongs to the sacrificer; therefore, it should be displaced (*utkṛṣyate*) to a ritual dedicated to those very deities (Heaven and Earth). Likewise, the mantra expressing the plurality of nooses (*pāśabahutva*), though recited in the context of a single animal sacrifice (*paśu*), should be displaced to a rite involving many animals. The proponent of the established view (*siddhāntin*) refutes this doubt: If you say [it should be displaced] because of the words "of the two heavens" (*dyāvostya*), we say no. This is because the *pāśa* mantra is an original statement (*utpattiśabda*), whereas the *dyāvāpṛthivyanumantraṇa* mantra lacks the status of an original statement.

For in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is no deity prescribed for Heaven and Earth by means of the word "vipatti. Furthermore, there is a disparity because the mantra denoting the plurality of nooses is prescribed specifically for the animal sacrifice in the archetype (prakṛti).
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that both mantras are to be employed without any optionality.

In the section beginning with "In the case of a deficiency of priests, there should be an oblation of sacrificial food because of its suitability" (1.3.15), [it is stated]: "Aditi releases the noose. In the case of a deficiency of priests...

Having set aside these two [formulas] containing contradictory properties—namely, the two mantras ending in the singular and plural numbers, "aditiḥ pāśān pramumoktu etān" (May Aditi release these bonds)—which are handed down as alternatives for the act of cutting, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the mantra ending in the plural must be displaced (*utkarṣa*) from its context because its meaning is not applicable (*asamavetārthatva*) to a rite involving a single bond. However, even though the plural form has an inapplicable meaning, one should follow it; for, in accordance with that [plural form], the [mantra] whose contradictory properties have not yet arisen [in conflict]...
In the case of a conflict, [the rule is] "the offering to Indra and that to Prajāpati [follow the New Moon ritual], while the others follow the Full Moon ritual.

In this context, the cake for Indra and the curd for Prajāpati require the characteristics of the New Moon sacrifice because they are modifications of the *aindrāgna* and *āmikṣā* offerings; however, the honey and ghee require the characteristics of the Full Moon sacrifice because they are modifications of the *upāṃśuyāja*.

Thus, when these seven sacrifices have commenced together, the two *vārtraghna* *ājyabhāga* mantras are obtained for the rites of the Full Moon (*paurṇamāsī*), whereas the two *vṛdhanvant* mantras are obtained for the two modifications (*vikāra*) of the New Moon (*darśa*). Consequently, the characteristic of the majority—namely, the *madhu* and other [mantras]—is inferred to apply here.

This is because the rule "In a conflict of contradictory characteristics, there should be conformity with the majority" (12.1.22) belongs to a different section than the rule "Or rather, the primary [should prevail], due to the prior injunction, as in common worldly practice" (12.1.23).

Su. Pṛ. 1173: In the case of conflicting attributes, this very principle of following the majority (*bhūyo'nugraha-nyāya*) applies. Pṛ. 812: Even when a minor element is primary, its conformity to the majority is indicated by this principle.
Oṃ. In the case of a conflict, the instrument [is used] because of a specific connection with the other mantra, since there would be a distinction.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma (Agnīṣomīya).

Regarding the binding of its sacrificial post (yūpa), there are two mantras: one belonging to the Adhvaryu priest, which is an instrument (*kara*), namely "thou art enveloped" (*parivīr asi*); the other belongs to the Hotṛ priest, which is a descriptive reference to the action being performed (*kriyamāṇānuvāda*), namely "the youth, well-clothed" (*yuvā suvāsāḥ*).
Regarding these two [texts], since they both prescribe the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, a doubt arises as to which one is intended.
What, then, is this doubt? Here, the office of the priests is handed down in the rule: "He who is the Hotṛ is the Adhvaryu.

Does this mean that the Hotṛ should perform the duties of the Adhvaryu because of the causal connection, or rather that he should perform the duties of the Hotṛ while reciting the *kriyamāṇānuvākyas*?
This also is examined immediately following the present topic as a secondary consequence (*prasaṅga*).

Herein is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): regarding these two formulas, "Thou art girt about" (*parivīrasi*) and "The youth, well-robed" (*yuvā suvāsāḥ*), which are respectively an injunction (*vidhi*) and a descriptive restatement (*anuvāda*) being performed, and which are employed simultaneously by the *adhvaryu* and the *hotṛ* in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is understood through the statement "He who is the *hotṛ* is the *adhvaryu*" that the duties of the *hotṛ* and the *adhvaryu* have a single agent in the case of the Kauṇḍapāyinas.

In that case as well, since the conflict arising from the priority of application (*prayoga*)—namely, the conflict with the *hotṛ* word—is accepted as primary, the word *adhvaryu*, which appears later and is not [otherwise] applicable, must be described as having the sense of indicating the function (*kārya-lakṣaṇārtha*).
Consequently, it follows that the two mantras—the *karaṇa-mantra* and the *kriyamāṇānuvādin-mantra*—should be recited by the *hotṛ* alone.

However, since a single person cannot perform the recitation of both mantras simultaneously, there is no fixed rule; rather, the *karaṇa-mantra* should be recited by the *hotṛ* at one time, and the *kriyamāṇānuvādin-mantra* at another.

Alternatively, because the statement "he who is the Hotṛ is the Adhvaryu" prescribes the office of the Adhvaryu for one who does not abandon his own duties—that is, the Hotṛ—the Hotṛ, acting as an independent agent, must be employed as the reciter of the *kriyamāṇānuvāka*.
The mantra belongs to the Adhvaryu.
However, its connection with the performance [of the rite] arises from this instruction: "he who is the Hotṛ is the Adhvaryu."
Since direct instruction (*upadeśa*) is stronger than extended application (*atideśa*), the instrument-mantra (*karaṇamantra*) must be employed by the *hotṛ* alone.

It has already been stated that in such cases, the *hotṛ* is connected with the duties of the *adhvaryu* while not abandoning his own specific functions; for the name "hotṛ" does not arise from a connection with the act of reciting (*yoga*), but rather the office of the *hotṛ* (*hotram*) consists of the *hotṛ*'s own ritual duties.
Just as a king’s action is called "kingship" (rājya), but one does not become a king merely through connection with kingship;
so too, by the mere study of the Ṛgveda, one acquires the fitness for the office of the Hotṛ priest,
because it is logically consistent that even one who has abandoned his own specific duties may be appointed to the offices of the Hotṛ or the Adhvaryu.
By the force of the instruction (*upadeśa*), the *karaṇa* mantra must be employed precisely at the commencement of the action;
the *kriyamāṇānuvādī* mantra, however, must be employed while the action is being performed by the person corresponding to the *hotṛ*.

Now, an objection may be raised: according to the principle "the commencement of the rite coincides with the end of the *mantra*" (*mantrāntena karmādisaṃnipātaḥ*, 12.1.125), the employment of a *karaṇa* mantra would result in its recitation after the act of measuring has been completed, whereas the employment of a *kriyamāṇānuvādī* mantra would occur while the measuring is actually taking place.
Therefore, since the two mantras belong to different times, there is no contradiction whatsoever even if they are both employed by a single *hotṛ* priest.
As it has been said: "A contradiction between two mantras would indeed occur if they were used at the same time;
however, one [the *karaṇa-mantra*] stands before the action, while the other [the *anuvāka-mantra*] stands after it."
Thus (Vārttika, p. 1126). It is replied:
for "being performed" (*kriyamāṇatā*) belongs to the preparatory rite (*paricaraṇa*) from the beginning of the Adhvaryu’s movements until its completion.
The time for the proponent of the ritual action (*kriyamāṇavādī*) is when the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) has not yet become part of the assembly and so forth.
Even in the mantra, "Thou art young, well-clothed, and girt about," the word "thou" (*asi*) refers to the sacrificial post present [at that moment].
For that sacrificial post becomes present when it has been brought forward for the purpose of being covered with jewels and for the binding of the rope.
Consequently, due to the movement through the paths and so forth, there is an absence of familiarity with the earth and the present state.
Therefore, because they are simultaneous, there is a contradiction here.
This being the case, it must be employed by the Hotṛ priest for each individual person according to the instruction.

Among individual persons, that one in whom a distinction is perceived—whether by reason of preeminence or by being occupied with the task—should alone be employed. This is the established rule; [it applies] in case of conflict.

It has been recited. Furthermore, the mantra for the Hotṛ priest, "The youth, well-attired, girt about, has arrived," which is a restatement of an action currently being performed (*kriyamāṇānuvādī*), is recited in the Ṛgveda.
In that context, the *karaṇa-mantras* pertain to the commencement of the ritual action,
whereas the *kriyamāṇānuvādī* mantra pertains to the time simultaneous with the performance of the *parivyayaṇa*.
These two mantras reach the Kuṇḍapāyins through a succession of extended applications (*codaka*).
And in the case of the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, it is said: "He who is the Hotṛ is the Adhvaryu;
he is the Potṛ. He who is the Udgātṛ is the Neṣṭṛ; he is the Acchāvāka.
He who is the Maitrāvaruṇa is the Brahman; he is the Pratihartṛ."
He who is the Prastotṛ is the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; he is the Ārdhavṛt. He who is the Pratiprasthātṛ is the Agnīdh; he is the Udgātṛ. The Gṛhapati remains the Gṛhapati.
In the passage, "The characteristics of the Sūtra are the Sūtra-Brahmins," the transposition of the duties of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is heard.

This being the case, it appears that the Hotṛ priest must recite even the mantra that describes the action being performed (*kriyamāṇānuvādi-mantra*), and because of the hearing of the transposition, the Adhvaryu priest must also recite the instrumental mantra (*karaṇa-mantra*).

However, a conflict arises when it follows that the final syllables of the instrumental mantra must be recited at the very same moment that the initial syllables of the descriptive mantra are to be recited. Thus, there is a contradiction.

This being the case, a doubt arises: should only the mantra pertaining to the preparation (*karaṇa*) of the field be recited, or should only the mantra that describes the action as it is being performed (*kriyamāṇānuvādī*) be recited? Thus, since there is no fixed rule here, one might think that either may be recited according to one's preference. To this, the Sūtra states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
In the case of a conflict between two rules of equal force, the *karaṇa-mantra* alone must be recited by the Hotṛ priest.
Why? Because of the "distinction of connection" (*samavāya-viśeṣāt*), that is, a distinction in the relationship [to the action].
The *kriyamāṇānuvādī* mantra is inferential (*ānumānika*) because it is obtained through the general rule (*codaka*).
Furthermore, the *karaṇa-mantra* is directly perceived because of the explicit scriptural statement, "He who is the Hotṛ is the Adhvaryu.
Direct perception is more authoritative than inference,
and direct instruction is more authoritative than extended application (*atideśa*).

On account of this direct scriptural instruction (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), which is a specific teaching based on the reason of a particular connection (*samavāya-viśeṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the Hotṛ priest himself should recite the *karaṇa-mantra* belonging to the Adhvaryu, namely: "Thou art the encircler; I encircle thee. [Objection:
If that is so, then who shall recite the *hotra-mantra*, "The youth well-dressed"? [Reply: He says—it is the other mantra.
Another officiant might recite the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ.

Nevertheless, among those attendants of the Hotṛ, that one who possesses the specific qualification based on the designation "Hotṛ-puruṣa"—namely, the distinction of being free from other duties at the time of the preparation of the sacrificial post (yūpa)—should recite it. Who?
[The answer follows: Ke.
"In case of conflict, the instrument [is determined] by a specific connection, because from that there would be a distinction for the other mantra" (3.8.10.22).

In the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana*, it is heard: "He who is the Hotṛ is the Adhvaryu."

In this context, since the terms *hotṛ* and *adhvaryu*—which denote two distinct persons—cannot be in a primary state of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), one of them must be understood as figurative (*lakṣaṇā*). Since the term *hotṛ*, heard first, must retain its primary sense, the term *adhvaryu*, heard later, is taken as figuratively indicating the duties of the *adhvaryu*. Thus, the injunction prescribes the *hotṛ* as the agent for those duties indicated by that term.

Consequently, between the *adhvaryu* and the *hotṛ* who are both established by the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is the displacement of the *adhvaryu*; the determination is made that even the duties of the *adhvaryu* must be performed by the *hotṛ* alone.

In that context, regarding the time of the binding of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-paricayāṇa*), there are two mantras—"aparivīrasi" and "yuvā suvāsāḥ"—which are recited by the Adhvaryu and the Hotṛ respectively as *kriyamāṇānuvādī* (recitations following the action) during the binding. These two persist from the initial intention for the binding until its completion; thus, they share a single point in time. Since they fall within this interval and coincide with the commencement of the binding, they are *karaṇa-mantras* (instrumental mantras). This same principle applies to the Kuṇḍapāyināmayana sacrifice. However, since it is impossible for one person—the Hotṛ—to perform both simultaneously, and because the Adhvaryu's mantra must take precedence, the *hotṛ-karma* (the duty of the Hotṛ) obtained through the indicative power of the archetypal model (*prakṛti*) is set aside. This is because the duty of the Adhvaryu is directly enjoined by the authoritative scriptural statement (*śruti*). Thus, there is a sublation of the Hotṛ's duty as established by the inferred archetypal rule.

In that context, the application [of the *hotṛ*] is obtained through the word by virtue of its being the archetype (*prakṛti*), because a direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣavacana*) must be relied upon; and since the application of constituent elements (*padārtha*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) occurs by way of their beneficial effects (*upakāra*), the application of the *hotṛ*'s duties is also dependent on the application of the *hotṛ* himself.

In the case of the injunction “One desiring sovereignty should sacrifice with the Vājapeya,” if one holds the view that the Vājapeya is a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) of the sacrifice, two sets of contradictory factors arise regarding the sacrifice.
The triad consisting of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*), being the subject of restatement (*anuvādyatva*), and being primary (*mukhyatva*) is one set;
the triad consisting of being the thing to be adopted (*upādeyatva*), being the thing to be enjoined (*vidheyatva*), and being subordinate (*guṇatva*) is another.

One sentence is "one should effect the sacrifice by means of the *vājapeya*," and another sentence, "one should effect sovereignty (*svārājya*) by means of the sacrifice," is to be supplied. In that context, the three properties beginning with being the object of reference reside in the fruit in the form of sovereignty, while the three properties beginning with being the thing to be adopted reside in the sacrifice which serves as the means.
The sacrifice is undertaken with a view toward the fruit;

The Section on Contradiction.
Regarding the section on contradiction:
if there were a dispute between Smṛti and a directly perceived Vedic statement, the former would be sublated by the latter for the sake of universal prosperity.
Furthermore, because there is no exclusion, the authority [of the Smṛti] is not absolutely negated; rather, it is maintained.
Moreover, even regarding such a basis for Dharma, how is it determined? For instance: "Is it that sometimes the status of being rooted in Śruti is asserted, or is something else excluded?"

If it is asked, "Whence comes this doubt? it is said: because its basis is uncertain. For if [the Smṛti] is established by means of Smṛtis, who—even Indra—could prevent it from being accepted, either for the sake of avoiding contradiction or because its basis is equal [to that of Śruti]?

Whether an action is established by the principle of having a single root— thereby excluding other roots— or whether it is the opposite, it cannot be observed for the sake of removing invalidity when two cognitions that bring about contradictory conclusions regarding the same object are in conflict.

Furthermore, the mutual contradiction between the Śrutis does not result in a relationship of sublation and sublated because of a determination of relative strength and weakness— unless such were the case. If it were so,

then even when there is a suspicion of contradiction between Śruti and Smṛti, the Smṛti that contradicts the Śruti would have to be set aside on the grounds that it has another source, provided that some kind of contradiction between them could be established.

But when the delusion regarding the "already-risen" (udita), the "not-yet-risen" (anudita), and so forth is removed, the systematic arrangement [of the rules] will be established through their having distinct objects of application according to the prescribed method.

Whether in the case of injunctions or prohibitions, since there is no contradiction with even thousands of Śrutis due to the inclusion of both passion and its absence, and because a combination is possible in this matter and place, if certain Smṛtis—though appearing mutually contradictory for the sake of performing a single act—are found to have meanings contrary to the statements of one's own Vedic school (śākhā), then, by accepting their authority on the grounds that they are part of the practical application (prayoga) and thus capable of sublation, there may be a reconciliation of both. Even when such an effort toward optionality is made, a contradiction with the words of other cognitions is observed; therefore, because of the total absence of contradiction, and because the knowledge produced by direct perception and inferred Śrutis are equal in strength for those who engage in all ritual practices—since they are equally authoritative as Vedic—the authority of both must be accepted. Thus, by the mere fact of being established, the Śrutis of another place (purāntara) brought forward through firm recollection are not set aside.

Therefore, it is not fitting to claim that even regarding the subject matter as it has been presented, the authority of Smṛti is non-existent; for one must consider the principle that "two [contradictory] things cannot be prescribed for the same person.

Now, even if one were to exert effort to avoid censure, there can be no restriction established by human agency regarding the authority of the Śrutis toward all persons with respect to their objects—just as there is none regarding their study—nor can there be such a restriction in the case of Smṛti, because of the contradiction with the object of knowledge (prameya), nor through their combination, nor due to the capacity to uphold the Śrutis.

Therefore, just as even in the case of contradiction, [the validity of both] is established through an option (*vikalpa*)— for what else could it be?— rather than from the mutual impairment of both, so too is the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) for those [scriptures] that are recited and whose efficacy is recognized. Let it be understood in this very way, like worldly perception and inference, as a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the ultimate reality.

Furthermore: "In the absence of contradiction, that which is rooted in Śruti possesses no great distinction of strength; for in that case, since there is no other possible source, it is accepted that when such a possibility exists, another source may exist.
