Furthermore, Smṛtis that are free from deceit and possess intrinsic authority can certainly be established as the basis for legal practice (*vyavahāra*), provided that their roots in the Veda and so forth are possible. However, when a Smṛti is contradicted by the Veda, it is not logical for it to be either a contradictory [authority] or a sublater [of the Veda].

If it is argued that there is no validity for these [Smṛtis] due to some pretext such as the contradiction between different branches of the Veda (*dhanaparaspara-vigāna*) or other causes, then when their lack of authority is thus postulated, one would fall into the "old woman's logic" (*jaratīyatā*) which rejects everything— including the various branches, the entire *Prakaraṇas*, and all else— without exception. For the authors of the Smṛtis, who are distinct from one another, know and remember the various *Prakaraṇas* belonging to the many branches of the Veda and their respective contradictions.

In the Vedas, including the *Medastomces* [sic], having abandoned the status of being rooted in the *Upavedas*—which consist of direct revelation (*śruti*), indicative power (*liṅga*), and so forth—some other cause must be sought here. Since the grounds for acceptance or rejection of authority are grasped through hundreds of diverse means of knowledge such as names, regions, and the like, the status of authority would have to be asserted based on those.

Because the instruction consisting of indicative power (*liṅga*) and so forth belongs to us through extension (*atideśa*) by way of names and the like, that [status of authority] would consequently apply everywhere.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "those [Smṛtis] which consist of various portions characterized by passion, hatred, pride, and so forth. From such passion, hatred, pride, and negligence, confusion arises. It is impossible to conceive what kind of Smṛti could be contradictory to which portion of the Veda, or at what time the grounds for the authority of the Smṛti could be inferred.
For this must be inferred by means of a mind that has not perceived [the contradiction].
Therefore, for one who has thus become suspicious, it is nowhere easy to find a virtuous foundation;
rather, the acquisition of a corrupt foundation occurs due to the defect of one's own disposition.
What religious practice is there in which a visible cause is not applicable,
or which is in some way contradictory to direct perception and the revealed scriptures?
For the foolish materialists, no other activity exists at all.
Whatever has a visible purpose, they indeed perform for that visible purpose;
even the rituals of the Vedic followers, they know, have only visible purposes.
And on account of even a slight pretext, they contrive opposition.
And they granted this man named Aprasara, a certain Mīmāṃsaka, [this authority];
for at that time, none of them would have deviated from the path of Dharma,
as long as those monkeys did not obtain any foothold.
Neither hunger nor thirst assails them while they are within their own domain,
for they have obtained their abode according to their own will whenever an opportunity arises.
Who, having fallen of his own accord upon their path, could possibly find the means to live?
Therefore, for those who abide in the Lokāyata system and are bees destroying the Dharma,
the Mīmāṃsaka’s task is not merely to fulfill their desires;
rather, what was initially established through faith is subsequently proven by means of logic.
The fourfold collection beginning with the Purāṇas possesses the authority of being established by scriptural injunction;
this is likewise confirmed in the section concerning non-contradiction.
If there were a conflict in that case, it would result in the sublation of both; thus,
this cognition of a mixture is equal to non-apprehension.

Therefore, because both [scriptures] possess authority, the lack of authority for either one of them is extremely unjust; it is an instability of both. For where a settled determination can be found, it is not right to establish another.
For indeed, when a single nature is maintained everywhere, it is possible to employ a uniform linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*).
Therefore: "That which is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must always remain a means of valid cognition;
likewise, that which is not a means of valid cognition must be called non-valid."

If that very same [cognition] were at one time a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and at another time not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*), there could be no confidence whatsoever. Thus, this leads to an undesirable consequence (*āpatti*), because one of the two—either [the status of being] a means of valid knowledge or [the status of being] not a means of valid knowledge—must necessarily be abandoned. For in that case, there is no fixed characteristic established by which it would be a means of valid knowledge in one instance and not a means of valid knowledge in another.
Furthermore, there are two clear grounds for the distinction between Śruti and Smṛti,
by which the authority of Śruti is established while the lack of authority of Smṛti is demonstrated. First, regarding their intrinsic nature, one possesses authority while the other lacks it.
Consequently, invalidity and validity would both depend upon something else.
For whatever property is established as being inherent in the very nature of a thing is set aside or superseded by a more powerful external cause;
however, a cognition produced by a Smṛti cannot supersede a cognition produced by Śruti.
The Vedic (śrauta) is understood to be the sublater of the Smārta because of its superior strength;
this has already been determined in the case of both direct perception and inference.
Just as the relative strength and weakness of the Vedic text (śruti) and the indicative mark (liṅga) are established by logical principle, so it is here.
In this world, the Śruti and Smṛti relate respectively to proximate and remote objects.
As long as something is cognized through Smṛti, it is not so established by Śruti;
for a single Dharma cannot admit of two contradictory natures.
Furthermore, there is no way for one who arrives late to attain a goal that requires speed;
for who can possibly recover what has been carried off by swift donkeys?
And having grasped the object through memory, before one can apply the hearing (of scripture)...
As long as the cognizer proceeds to infer that object which has already been known from another source, and as long as the agent deliberates, "What should be done?",
so long does the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) operate; [but] that [object] does not become newly cognized (pramita).
If the meaning of both Śruti and Smṛti were to be investigated simultaneously, then,
because no distinction [between their authority] has been grasped, one would have to stop at that point; or rather, as long as the meaning of the Śruti is perceived directly, [the Smṛti must yield].

At that very moment, memory (smṛti) would assume the status of a root source (mūla), namely scripture (śruti). Consequently, even though there is a temporal distance from the object, there would be equality in terms of being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) between scripture and memory,
because the meaning of the memory is derived from the acceptance of scripture.
Since the assumption of a Vedic text arises only after a long time, even when the matter has already been grasped through Smṛti,
that [Smṛti] would be sublated because it remains unestablished;
for a Smṛti that does not depend on a Vedic source is discarded simply by virtue of being a Smṛti.
Furthermore, that [Smṛti] which lacks a scriptural basis is sublated by Śruti.
First, this method of sublation of Smṛti occurs without resorting to the path of optionality (*vikalpa*).
By the second [method], the path of optionality is reached through the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Or rather, when one has fallen [into error], memory is either partially or completely obstructed;
for that purpose,
in the case of the alternative view, one accepts the authority of the Vedic revelation (śruti).
And at that time, the lack of authority of Smṛti follows by implication; for when its lack of authority is postulated, it is superimposed upon it just as [the lack of authority] is upon Śruti.
However, its status as a means of valid knowledge is brought about by its being rooted in Śruti;
therefore, because it has that as its source, it is determined to be authoritative at that time.

Furthermore, after the connection with its Vedic source has been severed, because it is composed by those who have already rejected its basis and who are subject to contradictions and discrepancies, it follows as a matter of course that—due to its lack of a fixed foundation—it possesses a certain degree of instability. Consequently, some single factor such as personal intention (*abhiprāya*) becomes its underlying basis. And when a basis for a Smṛti is postulated elsewhere than in the Śruti, its status as a valid means of knowledge is utterly destroyed by that very act.
For at the time of the adoption [of the rule] regarding rice (*vrīhi*), the invalidity of the Vedic text concerning barley (*yava*) was merely superimposed as something non-existent.

However, upon the occasion of the subsequent conflict, by virtue of being revealed through your grace, and because there is no distinction between proximity and remoteness of meaning, it is once again overcome by the validity of the sacrifice.
But the Smṛti is not capable of reviving its own status as a means of valid knowledge.
Because its scriptural source has been interrupted, the Smṛti is held by reasons such as the Āgneyī [mantra] to have a different basis.

For it is not possible to maintain the contradictory determination that at the time when a single Smṛti is not accepted by a directly perceived Śruti, its basis is an inferred Śruti, whereas upon hearing of its acceptance, its basis is the Āgneyī and so forth.
He says:
If it were true that one who initially forms a conceptual construction regarding the meaning of the Vedic revelation would subsequently grasp a grosser meaning in subsequent applications,
then he would always be obstructed by the previously stated path. However, there is no such possibility for this [Smṛti] when it is accepted as being prior [to the Śruti].

"For indeed, when one who has first heard a Vedic text (*śruti*) subsequently encounters another Vedic text that contradicts it, the inference [of the latter] is based on that [first] Vedic text. Even a Vedic text heard later cannot be an obstacle [to the former],
for even a donkey might [be made to] carry a load out of respect for its master's will."
Nor is there any such rule that those desiring to know [the truth] must first hear only that Śruti which is not contradicted by Smṛti.
For among many who are desirous of knowing, something [contradictory] might occasionally present itself.
This is the section concerning contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*).
The section on contradiction (virodhādhikaraṇa): Due to the distinction from the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there is no equality with that [previous case].
In the first chapter (prapāṭhaka), by which the scriptural injunction regarding rice (vrīhi) is perceived.
In the second [chapter], the *Yavāśāstra* is not at all weak in its essential meaning;
for even regarding matters not prescribed in their own treatise, all the authors of ritual manuals (*kalpakāra*) accept those found in other scriptures that have been duly deliberated.
The withdrawal [of a statement] at all times is approved even by Jaimini;
however, an object already previously cognized is not to be restated after a subsequent injunction.
Therefore, the hearing of the text for that purpose is not meaningless.
And it is not taught for the sake of a single person.

By this principle, those seekers of knowledge—who possess a cognition dependent upon the Vedic knowledge that is eternally established and whose meaning is being constantly clarified with respect to all persons—must accept its authority as being determined solely by the injunctions of their parents and elders, which are based on the power of prior impressions and the influence of past grasping, and which consist of words composed of preceding phonemes. They have accepted its authority as being restricted precisely to this.

Otherwise, indeed: "The validity of what was previously perceived [would be negated] by the subsequent [perception]; this would result in a lack of restriction regarding the determination of the object of cognition. And for this reason, when the possibility of being rooted in error is imagined in the case of memory—"
For even in the absence of contradiction, the authority of [Smṛti] would be difficult to establish;
for either all [Smṛti] would have the Veda as its root, or else all would have error as its root.
Thus, like Smṛti, it would be determined in this way, but there is no confusion of their respective sources.
It is said:

although, when one perceives a Vedic text through a memory of a prior perception, the measurement of that unobstructed Vedic text is established, nevertheless, upon hearing that same Vedic text at a later time, it becomes a subject of doubt due to its nature as a [previously] perceived object.
Because of the affliction of sublation (*bādhā*), there necessarily occurs a shift toward another basis by virtue of the severance of its status as being rooted in the Veda.
"And therefore, reflecting that this prior cognition was false,
one determines at the very outset that memory lacks validity.

For even if someone were to conduct business in the midst of the world for an eon using a counterfeit coin, he should not continue to conduct business in that same manner merely because he has developed a discriminative knowledge [of its falsity]."
Nor [is it the case that] the cognition of the present moment alone sublates even the previous ones,
because they have the same object;
for if those [previous cognitions] were false, the present one could not be true.
"But surely, in the prior state, [the Vedic text] was inferred by means of the Śruti itself;
it is that very same [text] which is now understood to be contradictory, not the Smṛti.
This is not so.
This is because of the examination of the application and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For if, by examining a single application, another application were also inferred—such that, having made the scriptural injunction regarding rice-grains authoritative, one would perform sacrifices only with that [rice] for as long as one lives—then practical activity (*vyavahāra*) would not be established by the two options being alternated according to each individual's absence [of the other].

Therefore, by the force of the observation of the means of knowledge that arises during the preliminary application (*prayoga*), even while not hearing a Vedic text anywhere regarding his own self, he again perceives only a memory; having mentally inscribed what is to be done, he infers a Vedic text. Then, because the perceived Vedic text is obstructed by the mental eye (*akṣisintati*)—that is, by the [contrary] perception—and because it is otherwise untenable, he assumes the lack of authority of the Smṛti. Having thus determined that its basis is indeed non-existent, he arrives at the conclusion that its authority is merely superimposed. This is because its authority is easily understood only when it is not obstructed.

"Just as this infinite regress (anavasthāna) is urged by you against me, it applies equally to you; therefore, it should not be urged from one side alone. For when, at the outset, having heard the scripture, [the Dharma] is well-inferred from the Smṛti through reasoning,"
Then, because it is established that [the later cognition] has another source, it sublates [the earlier one] by its very nature as having an "i" ending.
Furthermore, even when a sublation is clearly perceived at a different time,
that invalidity which was previously produced is thereby set aside.

And in the *Pūrvasmṛti-brāhmaṇa*, it is stated that even for those who do not themselves perceive a sublation, the continuity of sublation persists by the force of attaining the hearing of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
Furthermore, the sublation by another person is certainly not a cause for error;
for the delusion of two moons is not left unsublated by other men.

[Objection: "But then, since the Vedic text regarding *yava* is being accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there would be a contradiction by another person at that time, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its falsity. [Reply: It is said: "Because they are both being recited, their rising and sinking [of authority] are equal for everyone; no other distinction between them is perceived."
Recollection is declared to be invalid because it is always absent for as many persons as it first becomes an object for.
And the status of being invalid is understood from recollection alone at its very first occurrence.
To that extent, since falsity has been established, the Smṛti is capable of subverting the Śruti;
furthermore, falsity would have to be superimposed upon the pure Śruti. Thus, it is assumed that what was already established in the Smṛti is likewise [established] by the Śruti.

For when two conflicting sources, Śruti and Smṛti, result in the contingency of an option (vikalpa), one must postulate the invalidity of one of them. However, as soon as one begins to postulate this based on the Śruti—according to the maxim of covering with a cloth—the very strength of the Smṛti is found to rest upon Varuṇa; thus, once that [conflict] is resolved, it is never possible to postulate the invalidity of the Śruti regarding the *yava* grain. [Objection: "But surely, for a Smṛti that is not contradicted by Śruti, there is certainty that it is rooted in Śruti.
It is obtained even through inference, yet it is obstructed by someone."

Therefore, due to the disparity of causes, uniformity would be established in both cases; for the fundamental determination follows its opposite. Consequently, there is an avoidance of the consequence that the object would appear [as it truly is].

Just as— “Since the status of being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the inferential mark (liṅga) and so forth is established by the earlier authorities based on their being either contradictory or non-contradictory [with respect to one another],
so too here [in this system] there is such an establishment; thus, there is no mutual confusion.”
Due to both prohibition and permission, there is no uniformity in the Veda.

Although that which is connected with the *sūtras*—such as the *Dharmasūtras*, the *Smṛtis*, and the characteristics of direct perception—is included within the Veda according to the rule of "wherever and whatever," it has nevertheless not been cited here like the *Smṛtis*, because it will be discussed later, because it is intended to be of superior authority, and because there is no difference in its being taught by a person.

Although the statement regarding the accentuation of *kītarāja* and others is indeed recorded as authoritative, nevertheless, because that [accentuation] lacks utility in connection with the *āhavanīya* fire, and because it contradicts the prohibition against eating until the conclusion of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice—which is established by the three Vedas (*trayī*) for those who are qualified—Bhartṛmitra cites it [in the *Vākyapadīya*] as an example of the rejection of a Smṛti rule, based on the principle that "due to the specific context, that which is qualified would be contradictory," intending thereby to show the distinction between the relative strength of what is qualified and what is not qualified.

Although the state of having black hair is ambiguous as to its coexistence with the condition of having fathered a son—since it may pertain to any specific stage of life or time—nevertheless, because the injunction "one should seek dharma while still young" and similar Smṛti texts indicate that one must adopt the stage of youth, and because the period of study connected to the student's bath is heard to extend until the end of life or at least up to forty-eight years, and since this period of age amounts to slightly more than fifty-four years, a manifest contradiction is indeed seen due to the unavoidable necessity of following the sequential order.
But surely there is no contradiction, since touching while wrapped is possible, as it was ordained after all the Vedic recitation had been performed by the predecessors.

How can there be no contradiction? For "touching" (sparśana) consists in the perception of the object to be touched through the medium of the sense of touch; and the touch of the Audumbarī post cannot reach it when it is separated by cloth.
And when a garment is touched, the *audumbarī* tree is not thereby touched,
because there is an essential difference between the genus of the garment and the genus of the *audumbarī* regarding the nature of touch.
Now, it might be argued that it is enjoined that one must remain untouched by even a creeping insect.

The touching of the ground would, in that very case, constitute the actual touch. Now, one might object: "Since the *audumbarī* post exists on the ground, yet there is no cognition of it when it is covered, I see that this is not a valid example. For instance, even when the touch of a Caṇḍāla is mediated by a wall, an offense may still occur in some cases."
O Deity, when there is purity through direct contact as if touching,
that bathing which is performed by touching Brahman is considered pure;
for that [other type] is indeed regarded as having an impure cause, like the touch of a Caṇḍāla.

And likewise, when even a garment touched by such a person is defiled by that contact, a fault certainly arises when it is touched again, as it is effectively in conjunction [with the defilement]. But how is this fault— caused by the sight and touch of a Caṇḍāla— determined, even though it is not explicitly recorded in the Dharmaśāstra?

Or how is it that no fault is admitted in the case of wood, clods of earth, grass, and so forth, when they are touched by those [beings] who have been touched by them? Here, logical arguments do not apply.
To this it is said: "Just as the purification of wood, grass, and so forth comes from the wind alone..."
It is not remembered that a garment [is purified] in this way without washing it with water.
But surely, for one smeared by such [an act], that purification is prescribed?
No; the word "smeared" (lipta) does not exist in that ancient reading.
Regarding impurity, they recite as follows:
"One who has been touched by a Caṇḍāla must remain so for three days;
therefore, purification by water and other means exists."

But surely, since the injunction for penance is prescribed for a human being alone on account of contact with a *caṇḍāla*, it follows that impurity consists in the form of invisibility (*adṛṣṭi*) and not in other substances such as cows or horses.

Therefore, when there is doubt as to whether [the object] was burnt by a cow or horse, or seen by a person, it would be proper to determine that it was indeed burnt by a cow or horse. It is replied: "Because bathing is prescribed for a man who has been touched by a dog."
Therefore, it is held to be as clear as a person, and not like a cow, a horse, or similar animals.

For even when a *caṇḍāla* is touched by a pure hand or the like, whereas cows and other such animals touched by a *caṇḍāla* are not understood to be purified because there is no injunction for bathing or washing them, [the former] does not fall into that same category. Consequently, in this manner, the cognition of touching cannot be established through the touching of that which is connected to the *audumbarī* tree.
But when it is said, "one should rise having touched [the *audumbarī*]," because of the nature of the case-ending, only the two [hands] must touch the *audumbarī* pillar;

furthermore, even the position that accepts the act of leaning is established only upon the lack of knowledge regarding the state of being touched, and thus it is not possible [for the rule to apply] when the pillar is entirely covered.
Moreover, even a garment supported by another attains the status of being the instrument of touching.
Therefore,
because there is a contradiction between the touching of all [the posts] and the touching of the Audumbarī post, it is logical to establish the relationship between the sublated and the sublator.
Now, for what purpose are these two injunctions considered as alternatives?
Because memory is not prescriptive and because one's own opinion is not authoritative, this was stated with the intention of including the reading of another scripture inferred from it.
[The phrase] "not when there is a cognition of delusion" refers to the assumption of absolute delusion by the very same path previously described.
In the case of the alternative [interpretation], it is settled that [the term] refers to memory (*smṛti*) which has fallen into error.

Furthermore, "deluded cognition" (*vyāmohavijñāna*) will be understood either as the determination of delusion residing in another cognition, or as the state of being deluded within that very cognition.
Therefore, it should be construed either as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) or as a descriptive determinative compound (*karmadhāraya*).
However, they say that conceptual construction (vikalpa) sometimes interrupts memory and brings about a state of confusion.

And since even a single instance of such scriptural cognition (*śrauta-vijñāna*) is permitted as a superimposition (*adhyāropaṇa*), it never abandons its validity because it is free from contradiction; thus, there is the designation "that which is cooked" (*āpākita*). In this way, the position that [the Smṛti] is entirely non-authoritative is grasped, and its survival becomes impossible; yet, there is the recollection of the Smṛti as being "occasional" (*pākṣika*) for all time. Or rather, he says "and occasional. Just as in the case of the initial optionality of a ritual alternative (*vikalpa*), when one adopts the position of the authority of the Śruti, the assumption of a corresponding Śruti for the Smṛti—being singular—is transferred to another source (*mūla*); consequently, there arises the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would be non-authoritative at all times.

And since the Śruti, having once found an opportunity for its authority, will never again be deluded by a weak understanding, it is argued: "For that which serves as the root for it in one instance [is the same]. Thus he says: "Indeed, it is not possible to assume that the Śruti has fallen into error; rather, Smṛti occurs when it is rooted in a misheard text or a dream-cognition."
By the statement, "Therefore, there is no cognition of this," it is said with reference to valid cognitive awareness (*pramāṇavijñāna*).
By the phrase, "another delusion," he refutes one who has shifted from the conceptualization of delusion to the alternative position that there is an absence of valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*).

When it is understood that the knowledge derived from Smṛti alone has not shifted to the position of being authoritative due to the delusion previously determined, [the author] demonstrates the contradiction with Śruti on the grounds that its source consists of misheard texts, dreams, and so forth, by stating: "Because the causes are equal. Since it is always obstructed by the inference of Śruti—which is more powerful because it is not refuted by a counter-argument—there is no shifting of the Smṛti toward the position of authority.

"And furthermore, because of the determination [of the truth] through mutual dependence. Later, by explaining mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), he states that mutual dependence is indeed a contradiction: "For when two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are seen to be mutually contradictory and non-deviating from their respective objects, the determination therein must be made by another [means]."

Since the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are neuter—either because they have knowledge as their substratum or because they are produced from existence—the words "the Vedas are a means of valid cognition" (*vedaḥ pramāṇam*) and "the Smṛtis are a means of valid cognition" (*smṛtayaḥ pramāṇam*) would necessarily imply delusion regarding their own objects, whether in the sense of being means of valid cognition or in the sense of being Smṛtis.

Alternatively, if one were to follow the gender and number of the denoted object to avoid a lack of distinction, then according to the rule *vyudantād iṣṭāni*, the form *prāmāṇyam* would be obtained; thus it was previously stated that "validity resides in the Smṛti.
Therefore, those who seek to justify this usage of the Commentator—which has fallen away from both [grammatical rules]—should formulate the inference in this way:

"Since the Śruti is the root source, it attains authority; how much more so, then, is the Smṛti said to possess authority when its essence is derived from one or the other? In that regard, although eternality and authorlessness may be primary [in the case of the Śruti],"
Even if it were the case that [the rule] *balādika* applies,
the elision of *y* would not fail to occur on the grounds of the status of being a *varṇa* (vowel). For the elision of *y* by the rule *vyorvali* is indeed [an application of] *balādika*.

Alternatively, by means of a grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*), the *vedha* [prefix] and the *ca* [particle] are elided; thus, there will be an elision of both the letter *va* and the letter *ya*. Once this elision of *ya* and *la* has been performed, the pure vowel *a* remains as a residue.
In the case of *tadantāvadhi* (having that as its limit) and *praśādattadāpikye* (in the context of *praśādatta* and *dāpikya*),
the rule for lengthening a vowel with its homogeneous counterpart (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*) applies to the two subsequent elements because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*).
Having established the authority of all [the rules] in that manner, the correct form is subsequently understood.
"It has been stated that this results in a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*). Alternatively, the authority of Smṛti is desired because the Śruti lacks authority;
yet, once that [Smṛti] is established as authoritative, the assumption of the Śruti's lack of authority follows."

Likewise, because the authority of Smṛti depends upon the authority of Śruti, the determination of Śruti’s authority is established only when the non-authority of that [Smṛti] is proven. Thus, for one who maintains the position of optionality (*vikalpavādin*), there is this mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) between the two; this is not accepted by those who maintain the opposite view.
"In that case, because of the absolute limitation [of the object], another reason (*hetvantara*) is clearly [required].
Since the author of the *Bhāṣya* has stated this here, he has mentioned one of those two [alternatives]:
'In that case, the root of the Smṛti must be assumed to be the same as that of the [Vedic] touch.'"
It is not on account of an intention to introduce an entirely irrelevant alternative reason that [the object] is measured through this determination. Furthermore,
as for the mutual dependence established between the two subjects under discussion, that determination occurs from another source once the additional property has been ascertained.
"Because the Veda possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-sthitaprāmāṇya*), it would have its root in an assumption (*kalpamūlatā*).

Consequently, the Smṛti would have its root in an assumption whose validity is derived from the Veda; and thus, for the sake of assuming the validity of both the Veda and the non-Veda (Smṛti), the validity of the Smṛti [would depend on the Veda], while by that [Smṛti] the invalidity of the Veda would be assumed—thereby making the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) unavoidable.
Nor can this be avoided even by superimposing [the Veda onto the Smṛti]."
There would be a lack of authority [for the Smṛti];
and as long as that [lack of authority] remains unestablished, it is impossible for the Smṛti to possess validity.
He who desires to establish a powerful opponent who has already been defeated—[such an effort is futile].
Like a foot-soldier facing an elephant, he will not stand for long.
Thus, while the authority of Smṛti is being postulated, it is first defeated.

However, when the mutual dependence of the two authorities of Śruti and Smṛti is examined, then even in that case, because its faultlessness is established in relation to the lack of authority of the opposing Smṛti, the maintenance of its authority is proven.
Because it is dependent on another, the authority of Smṛti is established only after [the Veda]; thus I shall attain [my goal]. "The lack of authority of the Smṛti is already established;
having attained its own authority for even a single moment, the Śruti then assumes authority."

Therefore, since it is observed that the Veda possesses no authority at the very first moment when it merely presents itself to memory during the state prior to inference, the Veda— having thereby already acquired its authoritative status—
is always free from contradiction; thus ends the section on the "Topic of Contradiction" (*virodhādhikaraṇa*).
In this case, the self-validity of the scripture is determined;
whereas elsewhere, due to the invalidity of the Smṛti, it is maintained for only a moment. Therefore, the limit is established as being entirely within that momentary duration.
One should proceed in due order until another [point] is clearly established.

He demonstrates this by means of one part: "Because it has a fabricated basis, the authority of Smṛti is not unimpeachable," and so on, up to "the postulation of Śruti based on Smṛti is untenable due to the absence of evidence.
In the second part as well, starting from the demonstration of the authority of Śruti, it should be carried forward until it is established beyond reproach.

However, because the injunctions regarding *brīhi*, *yava*, and *bṛhat* have no other possible recourse, they must be applied exactly as previously taught; for, like words separated by an interval, there is no difference in their position, and due to the power of merit (*puṇya-bala*), one cannot assume an unstable application.
Therefore, the authority of a Smṛti that contradicts direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) is not to be relied upon.
This is also because a motive [for falsity] is observed.

Commentary: Out of greed, some, desiring to obtain [the fruit], covered the Audumbarī pillar with cloth; this is their own tradition based on that recollection. Desiring to eat, some performed the eating of [food] for which a king has been purchased.
Concealing their lack of virility, they performed the *brahma-carya* (celibacy) for forty years;

from this, it is understood that this is a traditional legal text (*smṛti*). [The subsequent portion of the commentary beginning with "Or, this is another topic" has been collected under the heading "The cloth used in the *vaisarjana-homa* belongs to the last person" in a separate section.]
Therefore, it should be examined in that very place.
Or rather: "For this reason as well, there is no status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*), because of the dependence on another fundamental cause;
for when there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*), there is no arising of either perception or inference."

"The Smṛti that gives rise to the delusion of contradiction with the Śruti has its root tainted by the aforementioned reasoning and by the necessity of postulating another source due to the error in inferring the Śruti. [Objection:
"In some cases there is non-delusion, in some cases beauty, and in some cases the construction of logical arguments;
because it takes the form of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*), it cannot be rejected."
Furthermore, for a Smṛti that arises from a misconception of the Śruti, other causes are possible;
however, it is not the case that the Śruti itself [is the cause] when there is a contradiction between them, for in such a conflict, the Smṛti is sublated.
Thus, its being rooted in the Veda cannot be established with absolute certainty.
Likewise, one might suspect that it has another source; therefore, this is said [in response]:
"And this is more reasonable on the basis of Vedic statements and inference.
For when the seen is available, the postulation of the unseen is without authority."
This much must also be stated regarding this section on the marks [of contradiction]:
"Since it has been previously established that the Smṛtis are rooted in Śruti,
how can another basis be known even when a contradiction exists?"

For indeed, Vedic sentences that have become scattered within the range of the sense of smell—perceptible only to other persons, not recited through the sequence of human performance of religious duties, and not preserved in their own form for fear of the destruction of the Vedic tradition—are recovered by means of their connection with the meaning. Being manifested as if they were specific sounds, even though they remain beyond the senses, these [sentences] are recollected by him after being gathered together.

In this regard, just as it has been stated that students understand what is recited, uttered, or even not uttered here—beginning with the *āsaptama* (seventh generation) and so forth—in the same way, the words of the author of the Sūtras, which stand in the place of the teacher’s words, cease their function once they have effected the presentation of corresponding Vedic sentences; therefore, they should not be disparaged as being of human origin, like the prompting of sounds such as *tātyādi*. For it is the Veda itself that is manifested by men here; that [Veda] might be manifested by those who recite it, sharing equally in the object of memory (*smara*), or at the time of performance, it is manifested solely through latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
This Veda also approaches and stands near that very debt created by him;
therefore, since it declares the meaning through that [Smṛti], the Śruti is said to have its meaning already recorded.
By what logic can this [Smṛti], which is equal to the recited [Vedas], be sublated?

Just as the single Smṛti-śāstra is entirely complete in its own right, so too is that [Smṛti] alone liberated; therefore, other [texts] are for the purpose of providing knowledge regarding worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*).
How then could these [other texts] not be rooted in the Śruti, as they are recited in the Āgamas and elsewhere?
Smṛtis are observed in all instances, such as the bringing of auspicious objects and so forth;
at that time, if a single statement among them were forgotten,
we have no tongue to suggest another source for it.
When a certain Smṛti has been sublated by a logician,
and a Śruti belonging to another scripture is heard not long thereafter,
then what preeminence could there be for you who pride yourself on being a Naiyāyika?
An infinite regress of contradiction and non-establishment necessarily follows, as that which is cited as the sound of the *vaiṣṭuta* chant is contradicted by both touch and hearing.

This is evident from the *Chāndogya* and other texts where the *udumbara* cloth is prescribed based on its root in the *Śabdāyani* Brāhmaṇa; and regarding the covering of the *udumbarī* post, the followers of the Śākhā see the cloth in both places, as it is shown that "the *vaiṣṭuta* is indeed the cloth, the cloth is prosperity (*śrī*), and prosperity is the *sāman*. Thus, it is understood that even the cloth for covering the *udumbarī* has the status of being rooted in a revealed text (*prakāśa-śruti*).
The section on contradiction concerns its own nature. And therefore, because it is rooted in scripture, that which is cited as an example is not [an instance of contradiction].

Indeed, logical reasoning (*nyāya*) applies only to those [interpretations] that are of equal status in terms of their means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, there would be contradiction only if the verbal expression were contradictory; however, no such contradiction exists here.
For it is not the mere act of wrapping that is contradicted by the scriptural injunction regarding touch.
If the Udumbara post were wrapped with two or three finger-breadths from the middle toward the upper part, what indeed would not have been accomplished?
The author of the Sūtra did not say that it must be wrapped entirely.
No one should perform a wrapping around the roots of her ears;
even if the garment is loose, one should speak of a complete wrapping all around. When that is accomplished on every side, he indeed becomes possessed of wealth.
And as for that covering of her entire body which is imagined to be rooted in greed,
that greed would be all the more established,
just as the inner and outer garments are to women, since they are both the root and the measure [of her form].
For one born of a noble lineage, there is no exaltation without virtues;
and here, prior to greed, contact is indeed mediated by *kuśa* grass.
Having been first enveloped with *kuśa* grass, it is subsequently wrapped with a cloth.
In the passage concerning the *kuśa*-grass binding, some Vedic vision is observed;
likewise, it is seen even in the case of the restrictive rule (*niyama*), though not in the case of upward breathing (*ūrdhvaśvāsa*).
Furthermore, the eating of the corpse-king (*kītarājaka*) and other such practices are Atharvavedic, found elsewhere [in the Veda].
Furthermore, there is no reason whatsoever for its lack of authority;
if the Atharva Veda has no utility here in this [context of sacrifice],
by what means is its status as a source of knowledge regarding other matters refuted?
For rituals intended for pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), and exorcism (*abhicāra*) are based upon a single sacrificial offering (*havis*);
by these actions, those whose sphere of activity is the sacrificial ground are likewise gratified here.
Moreover, this injunction regarding the knowledge of sacrifice is not like the scriptures on pacification and the other rites.
Therefore, its status as a valid means of knowledge is also set aside by the purpose of man;
for this is not taught for the sacrificer alone,
but rather this state of being fit to be eaten is heard in the scripture as applying to all men.
If the eating of food by one who has performed the *īkṣita* sacrifice is prohibited by other statements,
yet its subsequent permission is heard [in scripture]:
"When the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice is concluded, or when the King [Soma] has been purchased."
This is a variation regarding time;
it may be considered as a means of terminating the period of impurity.
Indeed, even the duration of impurity depends upon considerations such as the severity of the violation of dharma.

Therefore, even for him, the state of being free from conceptual construction is not at all accepted [as the final goal], whether his purification occurs in a short time or otherwise. Why should he, having become purified by that much, resort to a long period of time?
If impurity persists for ten nights even for a pure Brāhmaṇa who has undergone purification after one or three nights,
how can this be so?
For purity is indeed the destruction of evil, or rather, fitness for the Dharma.
How could there be a conception of its existence or non-existence prior to the ten-day period? Likewise, prior to the animal sacrifice, the purity of the initiated seer [is established].
One does not tolerate the dogmatic restriction that "it exists" or "it does not exist.
That time which is grasped beforehand by means of the word "syāt" (perhaps/maybe) belongs specifically to that very oblation, just like the time prior to sunrise.
It is logical that there is an absence of conceptual distinction between the states of having arisen and not having arisen from the wind;
herein, there is no contradiction regarding existence and non-existence as previously stated.
Furthermore, the statement regarding the oblation performed before sunrise is not rendered meaningless by the mention of the oblation performed after sunrise.
There is no difference here at all regarding the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth;
however, while [the path] here [in this system] leads to purity in a short time,
that which requires a long period of time does not increase the number of days [of practice], even if it is obstructed by illness.
No one would ever desire that position, for it is largely composed of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, if that [position] is not accepted, his statement would be meaningless.
Consequently, because there is no other alternative, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not tenable.
And he has been told that there is no increase of days [for the funeral rites] in cases where there is affliction by disease or the like, nor when the name has not yet been assigned;
and for those whose teeth have not yet emerged, for those born after [the naming], and for those who have not had the tonsure ceremony,
the cremation rites are performed respectively in three days, one day, and one day, and in those cases there is no increase of days.

Likewise, it has been stated by Gautama: "For the sake of not interrupting the affairs of kings, and for the sake of not ceasing the private Vedic study of Brahmins. Or else: "If some cause for impurity should occur, purification shall take place there even by means of the remainder [of the period]."
One should not extend the days [of impurity], even if they arrive due to some specific cause;
for by the persistence of that very same prior period,
the duration beginning from the tenth day and so forth remains unaltered.
The impurity that has fallen within he pervades by means of his own status;
for those ten days are established as the limit,
and he is indeed able to distinguish the impurity that has arrived.
For purity and impurity are indeed understood according to scriptural injunction, since they are not perceived by the senses.
But in that case, there exists no restrictive rule regarding food;
for in that context, the injunction for a long duration would be purposeful only by way of permitting a short duration.
Therefore, even in this case, the cause for the inequality between the two limits must be stated.
Even if that [cause] is impossible here, those who have been initiated may still give it.
Once the purchase of the *soma* has been made, that which was given according to the etymological derivation of the term "given" (*datta*) should be consumed.
Just as other rules for times of distress (*āpaddharma*) are caused by the impossibility of following the primary rule, so too is this section on contradictions;
this is the section on contradictions.

Likewise, when there is danger to one's life, one may eat the food of a king who has been purchased [as a slave]. Ah! Thus, another kind of non-prohibition has been stated. For instance, Viśvāmitra, having fallen into a state of distress, accepted the wealth of Śakti.

It is said: "One [act] is performed even without permission because there is no other way; however, another is performed with permission, and between these two, the latter is superior. Since permission is granted in general, it is specified here even in the case of what is desired."

Even a specific [alternative] is entirely free from fault, provided it involves an action accompanied by only minor defects; and thus Manu has also stated regarding one who has entered upon the duties of distress: "At the end of that [period], there shall be purification for the remnants of the sins incurred therein."
"By whatever action here, whether mild or harsh, one should uplift one's own distressed self; once capable, one should practice the Dharma.
Thus it is said.
"First of all, there must be the sequence of expiation (*prāyaścitta*);
thereafter, through that purification, another [sequence] will follow for the sake of the fruit.

As for the statement regarding the edibility of food from one whose king has been purchased, it is understood as being intended merely to indicate the absence of fault when neither of the two [options] is possible."

Furthermore, in that case as well: "He who, being capable of performing a primary rite independently, proceeds by means of a secondary substitute—this is the understanding of contradiction [in the section on contradiction]. (Virodhādhikaraṇa 3666)

The commentators themselves have established the following conclusion: since in every inference the desire to know the object of inference (*anumeya-jijñāsā*) is a necessary cause, and since the *audumbarī* post has already been determined by direct Vedic injunction (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) through the prescription of touching it—thereby being characterized as "already enjoined"—there is an absence of the desire to know; consequently, the inference of a Vedic text prohibiting the touching of the *audumbarī* is impossible.

Likewise, even in cases where there is no contradiction with direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣaśruti*), if there is a motive such as greed—as in "He takes the cloth used for the *vaiśravaṇa* oblation"—there too the [Vedic] text is not to be inferred, because the status of being a source (*mūlatva*) is established by the already existing motive itself. The author of the *Vārttika*, however, maintains that the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) cannot be inferred [as the source], since such a desire arises even when one desires to perform the *Agnihotra* sacrifice; or, even if it were its cause, the Vedic text—which is the object of inference—would still be what is desired to be known. Furthermore, if one were to admit that [Smṛti] is rooted in greed and the like even in the absence of a contradiction with direct revelation, then the same undesirable consequence would apply to the *Ekāha* sacrifices and others as well.

Therefore, even when there is a contradiction with direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), it is entirely appropriate for a Smṛti to possess authority, since its basis in the Veda can be inferred from the fact that it is accepted without distinction by the learned members of the three higher castes (*śiṣṭa-traivarṇika*).

However, the act of wrapping [the sacrificial post] should not be permitted as long as the Vedic text is not observed; for since we see in the Smṛtis instances where what appears to be an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is actually an injunction (*vidhi*), it is possible that the present case is likewise based on such a source.
And since that proposed source may be a fallacious appearance (*ābhāsa*) when it contradicts a directly perceived Vedic text.
And for this reason, he states that the Sūtra intends that non-authoritativeness consists in the characteristic of non-performance as long as there is no observation of scriptural testimony.

Alternatively, since it is possible that even the Śākyas and others perceived the Vedas—which are well-known as belonging to the Kṣatriyas—their composed Smṛtis might also be rooted in the Veda, on the grounds that the Vedic Śrutis which served as their source have perished. To this [objection], the following is established: because there is no reason for the authority of those Smṛtis (such as the presence of seers) as was the case in the previous section, and because they are remembered by the learned members of the three higher castes (*śiṣṭa-trairvāṇika*) as being Dharma, and because their authority is not accepted due to the very reasons used to refute the authority of the Vedas, the assumption that they are rooted in the Veda is untenable; thus, [the Sūtra] means that [the Smṛtis] possess authority.

Maṇḍana: "A Smṛti that contradicts Śruti is not authoritative. Śaṅkara: "That is not so, because of the contradiction with Śruti. Soma: The section concerning contradiction (virodhādhikaraṇa) has as its subject matter the texts of the Śākyas and others.

(According to the Vārtika school): Su. p. 228. In the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*), it is stated that both Smṛti and Ācāra possess authority when they contradict Śruti. Kau. 1.3.4, p. 54. In the section on contradiction, while establishing the authority of Smṛtis that are contradictory [to Śruti], the authority of Smṛtis that are not contradictory is declared to be beyond reproach.
Su. pṛ. 204: In the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*), the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the texts of the Śākyas and others has been established.
Kau. 1.3.13: In the section on contradiction, examples from all the Vedas and Smṛtis have been presented.

Su. pṛ. 227: According to the view of the Vārttikakāra, in the section on contradiction, the lack of authority of the texts of the Śākyas and others is demonstrated on the grounds that they cannot possibly be rooted in the Veda.
That very point was also raised as the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the section concerning the *Kalpasūtras* (Kau.

1.3.6). Since the authority of custom (*ācāra*) has already been established in the section concerning the *Smṛtis*, its authority regarding matters in conflict with the Veda was refuted in the section concerning contradictions (*virodhādhikaraṇa*), on the grounds that it is likewise a *smṛti*.

Su. p. 207. When it is not merely the presence or absence of contradiction that is being examined here (in the section on "Residual Conditions," 1.3.4), but rather—even though a contradiction exists—whether there is an insistence on the superior strength of practices such as ritual sipping (*ācamana*) as *dharma*, or whether there is a sublation (*bādha*) due to the duality of authority, this is investigated for the purpose of providing an exception (*apavāda*) to the section on contradiction.
Su. p. 134. First of all, when there is a contradiction between *smṛti* and *śruti*, the [former] cannot be inferred from *śruti* according to the principle of the section on contradiction.

In the *Bhaṭṭadīpikā* commentary on the *Virodhādhikaraṇa* (Kau. 1.3.17), Tōma states at its conclusion: "The injunction regarding the deity is to be inferred from the mantra, as is the injunction regarding the fruit of giving a horse" (*Bālakrīḍā*, p.

12). On the occasion of refuting the *Bhāṣyakāra*'s *Virodhādhikaraṇa*, the authority of even those *Smṛtis* that contradict *Śruti* was established; however, their authority therein rests on the possibility of performing both [options] by way of alternative (*vikalpa*).
(Ku. 1.3.5–8, p. 64). Thus, the scope of the subject matter of the *Virodhādhikaraṇa* is simply this: whether a contradiction exists or does not exist.
(1|3|4) "Of the locus"—by this [statement], its connection [is established].
*Soma* 1314. There is an apprehension of contradiction.
For the apprehension of contradiction is twofold: either non-coexistence, as in the case of shade and sunlight, or mutual exclusion, as in the case of existence and non-existence.
Kaṇikā, p. 112:

Regarding the contradiction [of the 3667], the seed of the intention [to speak] is the contradictory [element]; there would be a restriction in a single hearing because the grasping [of the meaning] is purposeful, since it is distinguished by its being beyond [ordinary] movement.
Among conflicting items, when one is heard, there must be a restriction— that is, a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi)— must be accepted,
because the hearing of one among them serves a purpose and achieves its fruitfulness.
Since the direct Vedic statement (śruti) is distinguished by being directly stated and enjoined, it would override the authority of the general rule (codaka).

Just as in the Vājapeya sacrifice, by the injunction "the sacrificial post is made of *khadira* wood," there is a restriction to *khadira* wood and an exclusion (*bādha*) of *pālāśa* wood; and just as in the *Maidhātavyā* sacrifice, based on the scriptural statement "the middle cake is made of barley," there is a restriction to barley and an exclusion of rice; and just as when it is said "the sacrificial grass is made of *śara* reeds," there is a restriction to *śara* reeds and an exclusion of *kuśa* grass—so it is in this case as well.
Such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
If it is argued that there is "pervasion of both regions," the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) raises this objection.

Since there is a specific injunction for both *śara* and *pālāśa*, as well as for *bṛhat* and *ratha*, or for *vrīhi* and *yava*, it is not possible for the *pālāśa*, *śara*, and *vrīhi* to be excluded by the general rule (*codaka*) because of this specific instruction (*upadeśa*).
Therefore, there is no restrictive rule, but rather an option (*vikalpa*), even in the case of the *śara* reeds.
The proponent of the established view (siddhāntin) counters the objection raised by the opponent:

"If, because of the instruction regarding both [materials], there is no exclusion of the *pālāśa* wood and others, then there would likewise be no exclusion in the case of *śara* grass; consequently, an option (*vikalpa*) would result even in that instance."
If it is argued that [the same applies] to arrows because of the mention of "contradiction," the proponent clarifies the opponent's position:
there is no fault regarding the arrows.

Because of the mention of "opposition" (*virodha*), there is no apprehension of that which is opposed; for if it were admitted that the *śara* grasses are in opposition to the *kuśa* grasses, then the apprehension of the *kuśa* grasses—which are the opposites of the *śara*—would be possible.
Consequently, the *śara* grasses would thus function as the eliminators of the *kuśa* grasses, and likewise the latter [the *kuśa*] would be the eliminators of the former.
The proponent (siddhāntin) says by way of an objection:

"In that case, if another material such as the *syādi* wood—which is contrary to the *pālāśa* and other materials—is accepted, then the *pālāśa* and other materials, being contrary to the *syādi* and others, could be taken as the constituent parts (*aṅga*).
Therefore, there is a restriction regarding the *syādi* and other materials, and an exclusion of the *pālāśa* and other materials."
"If it is argued that the scripture would be rendered meaningless"— thus the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) objects again. If,

by accepting the exclusion of the *palāśa* and other woods due to the apprehension of contradiction, one were to admit [the exclusion], then the scripture— the injunction (*codaka*)— which prescribes the use of both *śvabhiḥ* (dogs) and *apalāśa* (non-palāśa wood), would result in being meaningless (*anarthakatva*).
If it is argued that, therefore, there is not the exclusion of the *palāśa* and other materials, but rather an option (*vikalpa*), [we reply:
because the act of taking up [the material] serves a purpose, both would be employed.
The proponent (siddhāntin) says:

Because there is the injunction for the inclusion of those [materials] that are contrary [to others], such as "the sacrificial post is of *syādi* wood," "the *pṛṣṭha* chant is the *bṛhat*," and "the middle *puroḍāśa* cake is made of barley," and because this serves a purpose—namely, to establish the fruitfulness [of the rite]—there would be non-application (*apravṛtti*), meaning no application, of both *syādi* and *palāśa*, as well as of both *bṛhat* and *rathantara*, and of both barley and rice.
Rather, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is a restriction (*niyama*) of the *syādi* and so forth, and an exclusion (*nivṛtti*) of the *palāśa* and so forth.
And there is no simultaneous operation of what is contradictory;
because of their contradiction, as in the case of worldly experience. (Bhāṣya 10.7)
Those means which accomplish a single effect through alternative options are mutually contradictory;
there is no simultaneous application of them because of their mutual contradiction.
This is like common worldly usage, as in the injunction, "One should not eat fish with milk," where milk is excluded by the fish; it is just like that.
Such is the principle. According to the Vṛtti,
dissolution (vilāpana) is a property of the intellect (ādhyadharma).
Bhāṣya 3.1.4.7: *Vileśa*. Now, we shall take up the verses (*ṛc*) that consist of a single metrical foot; from that, we shall cause the melody (*gīti*) to be split (*vileśayāma*).
[In the singing of a Sāman over verses of measured length, the non-appearance of the Sāman at the end of the verse is called *vileśa*.]
Bhāṣya 9.2.122: *Vileśaḥ* means smallness or deficiency.

Vi. 9.2.124: *Vileśaḥ* is smallness in comparison to the *ṛc*. If the *sāman* produced for a verse of fewer syllables is sung upon a verse of more syllables, then that small *sāman* would be capable of filling out the *ṛc*.
[This is like] an elixir (*rasāyana*).
