An investigation into the possibility and impossibility of intention (*vivakṣā*) and non-intention (*avivakṣā*) in the Veda—see *Mīmāṃsākośa*, pp. 1629–1631, under the section *grahaṇāgrahaṇādhikaraṇa*. The seed of intention is the very thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), not the status of being something to be taken up (*upādeyatva*) or its being a qualifier (*tad-viśeṣaṇatva*); thus, according to the *Nañvāda*: "The [number] 'two' is not intended."
The commentary (*vārttika*) on the verse "one should drink [the mixture] whether increased or not increased" (pp. 211–213) provides a clarification:
"It is not held that being something to be adopted (*upādeyatva*) alone is the cause for [the speaker's] intention (*vivakṣā*)."
For there must be a great reason for the intention to express a qualification by those who are great.

The intended singularity [is] that of the animal in such [injunctions] as "one should sacrifice the animal" (*paśumālabheta*) and "one should sacrifice with the animal" (*paśunā yajeta*). See *Mīmāṃsākośa*, p. 2494, under the section "The Topic of the Singularity of the Animal" (*paśvekatvādhikaraṇa*). Bāla., p. 13. 4.1.16–16. *Mīmāṃsākośa*, p. 2494. "The Topic of the Singularity of the Animal" (*paśvekatvādhikaraṇa*); this should be consulted therein.
The gender (liṅga), such as masculinity and so forth, intended [to be expressed] applies to the animal.
See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 3354, under the section "Liṅgādhikaraṇa" (Sūtras 4.1.16–18).
If something serves a purpose, it is said to be intended [to be expressed].
Bhāṣya 4.1.511: If one admits a deficiency relative to the intended meaning, there would be the consequence of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) and the fault of sentence-splitting (vākyabheda).
If one admits an excess relative to the intended meaning, there would be the consequence of meaninglessness (ānarthakya).

In that regard, regarding the admission of deficiency in relation to the intended meaning, the example is as follows: "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava" (Viśuddhi, p.
256); this is to be seen in the passage, "In the Atirātra, [the Stoma] consists of twenty-one [verses], etc. (ŚB 4.5.1.1).

In the *vikṛti* sacrifices characterized by increased or augmented *stomas*, there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the extended (*atidiṣṭa*) *sāmans* by those *sāmans* specifically prescribed (*upadiṣṭa*). However, in those sacrifices with increased *stomas*, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of both the prescribed and the extended *sāmans*.

(Vi. 10.4.12) Regarding the sacrifices with increased *stomas*, it is stated: “One desiring offspring should sacrifice with the *Ekaviṃśa* *Atirātra*; one desiring vigor with the *Trivṛt*; one desiring stability with the *Trayastriṃśa*.
This increase occurs only in the *pavamāna* chants.
In the *bahispavamāna*, there are indeed no repetitions (*āvṛtti*) of the *ūrgāna* verses.

Consequently, for the sake of completing the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*ekaviṃśa-stoma*), four *ṛcas* must be introduced; six for the nine-fold (*trivṛt*); and eight for the thirty-three-fold (*trayastrimśa*). These introduced *ṛcas* are to be placed at the end, and not before the *paryāyas*, because their sequence has already been established—this is the incidental conclusion [of the discussion] (5.1.14). In sacrifices where the *stomas* are increased, the *sāmans* that are to be introduced into the *gāyatra* and other *pavamānas* are to be placed within the *gāyatrī*, *bṛhatī*, and *anuṣṭubh* meters, but not at the end of the *ṛca*.
5|1|13-14. Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 260: "In the case of the *atirātra* sacrifice, when there is an increase of optional *stoma*s, [the number] is for the purpose of completing the count.
This should be consulted in this regard.

In sacrifices where the *stoma* (hymn-chants) are increased (*vivṛddhastoma*), there is no sublation of the original *sāmans* by the *sāmans* taught [in the specific context]; however, in sacrifices where the *stoma* is augmented (*abhivṛddhastoma*), there is sublation of the original *sāmans* by the *sāmans* taught [therein].

This is because it is accepted that "when there is an increase in the *stoma*, there should be an addition; when there is an increase, there should be a modification of the substance" (Jaimini Sūtra 10.4.10–12).
Commentary: There exist sacrifices characterized by increased *stomas* and sacrifices characterized by augmented *stomas*.
"One should cause one desiring offspring to sacrifice with the Ekaviṃśanātirātra; one desiring vigor with the Trivṛt; and one desiring stability with the Trayastriṃśa.
Likewise, there are thirty-two Pavamāna chants for the Abhiplava.
Among them are nine Rājasāman chants and eleven Rājasāman chants, [including] those of Bala, Udaśravas, Vasiṣṭha, Janila, and Niti, from the *Sākaṃpravedana* [section].
And [the rules for] *śuddha* and *śuddhī* apply when *saṃśava* follows;
likewise, in the case of the prescription of the *punar-stoma* sacrifice,
[the rule applies] to the *punar-stoma* sacrifice characterized by *apaciti*.
"Furthermore, the midday pressing of the Punahstoma is known as having twelve stotras;
in both pressings of the Kāya, there are nineteen stotras.
Thus it is said.

In this regard, in some cases the number of hymns (*stotra*) has increased, while in others it has decreased. Regarding this, there is a doubt: whether in both cases of increase and decrease there is the cessation of the original (*prakṛta*) *sāmans*, or whether there is cessation only upon decrease and not upon increase? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? There is cessation in both cases.
For that which is obtained through the *codaka* (the general transfer rule) is set aside by what is directly heard in the text (*pratyakṣaśruta*).
Furthermore, the originative injunctions (*utpatti*) of the *sāmans* will thus become purposeful, as they are performed in connection with new rites (*apūrva*).
This being the position reached, we reply:

In the case of an increase in the *stoma*, there should be no exclusion of the additional [verses]. Why? Because it will be stated that the completion of the number of *sāmans* occurs through addition (*āgama*), since there is no scriptural authority for their displacement (*bādha*).
In this way, there will be favor toward the injunction;
however, upon increase, the original [number] should be set aside.
To the extent that the original number is not completed by what has been set aside, to that extent the original should be superseded.
The other would be merely the ordinary [ritual].
Why? Because the other is not heard [in the scripture]. And the other is indeed heard: "The traditional transmission (āgama) must be performed."
Only the number is heard;
therefore, there is no cessation [of the original elements] in those sacrifices where the *stoma* has increased.
In those sacrifices where the *stoma* has decreased, however, they should be omitted as far as necessary.
Now, as for what was said— that the origin of the *sāmans* will be purposeful— it is replied:
let it be set aside by the Vedic injunction (*codaka*).
The term *viśiṣṭaguṇaśrauta* refers to that which is based on the Veda and possesses specific qualities.

Śā—In cases where there is an increase in the *stoma*, such as in the passage “the Pavamāna is thirty-two-fold, to be performed with the Abhipañcanīya,” etc., there arises the question: since there is an explicit Vedic injunction (*pratyakṣaśruti*), are the archetypal (*prakṛta*) elements replaced by the royal *sāmans* (*rājasāman*), or is there a combination (*samuccaya*)?
In that regard, it will be stated later that in those cases where the *stoma* is increased, the required number is completed through the addition of new elements (*āgama*).

In that case, when the extension (*vivṛddhi*) has been fulfilled by means of the traditional scripture (*āgama*), the *rājana-sāmans* heard directly in the sacred texts—which find their place in the extension—operate by subverting the original (*prākṛta*) ones. Therefore, there is subversion everywhere both in the increase (*abhivṛddhi*) and the extension (*vivṛddhi*).
This being the position reached, we reply:
"The impossibility of the modified (*vaikṛta*) [elements] exists only so long as there is no subversion of the original (*prākṛta*) ones."
In those very cases where there would be sublation, there is the possibility [of coexistence] when there is an increase;
therefore, when there is an increase, there is a combination (*samuccaya*).
This is the connection (*saṃgati*) as an exception (*apavāda*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: When there is an increase in the *stoma*, there should be a combination with the original (*prākṛta*) [elements], because the other [new elements] are introduced by way of addition. However, when there is an increase where the original number remains as it was, or where it is reduced—as in passages such as "the middle pressing of the *punarstoma* is remembered as twelve"—in both cases, the original is set aside; for without that [setting aside], the introduction of the modified (*vaikṛta*) elements would be impossible. Vi—[Commentary]: "In the case of an increase or a decrease of two *stomas*, is the original set aside? Or rather, only when there is no increase? The first [alternative] holds, because of its utility for the *sāman*."

It is a displacer (*nivartaka*) of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) [elements] for the sake of utility toward the increase (*vṛddhi*), but it is not a displacer with respect to the increase itself, because it is useful for that increase. The Bhaṭṭa [view]: Where the *stoma* is exactly as in the archetype, or where it is deficient—as in cases such as "the *agniṣṭoma* has thirty-six [verses]"—there, by means of the specifically enjoined *kautsa*-verses...

It has been stated that in the case of sacrifices characterized by increased *stoma* chants (*vivṛddhastomakratu*), there is a sublation of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements by those that are non-worldly (*alaukika*), provided they are equal in number. However, in cases where the sacrifice has an increased *stoma* relative to the archetype—such as in the injunctions, “One desiring offspring should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with the twenty-one-fold *atirātra*, one desiring vigor with the nine-fold [stoma],” and so forth—the *rājasāman*s prescribed therein do not exclude the archetypal ones. This is because the requirement is satisfied by the very mantras prescribed for the specific number of verses mentioned in the scripture.

For this very reason, it will be stated that even when the number is completed by means of scriptural injunction (*āgama*), since the accomplishment of the *āhuti* is established, the number is not completed even by those [substitutes] that are appropriate;
as Maṇḍana says: "There is no sublation (*bādha*) when there is an increase in the *stoma*"; and Śaṅkara says: "In the case of an increase in the *stoma*, there should be no sublation."
The increase [of the number of offerings] due to the differentiation of the ritual acts should be prescribed for each case, like the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*).
In the archetype (*prakṛti*), five fore-offerings (*prayāja*) are prescribed;
however, regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya paśu*), it is heard in scripture: "He performs eleven fore-offerings."
And in the case of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, there is the injunction: "He performs nine fore-offerings.

Regarding this, when the question arises whether the number eleven applies to each individual fore-offering or to the collection of fore-offerings as a whole, the author states the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view:
the increase—the number eleven, which is greater than the original number five—should be prescribed for each and every one of those individual fore-offerings.
"Due to the difference in action" means due to the difference in the primary action characterized as the *prayāja* offerings.
Just as with the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), where it is said, "He sacrifices the *anuyāja*s with speckled butter," a distinct quality is differentiated for each *anuyāja*, so it is here.
And thus, there would be five *prayāja*s in the animal sacrifice, and forty-five in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices.
Moreover, it would be the number of all [the animals], and its modification would be understood.
The word "api vā" (or rather) is for the purpose of refuting the prima facie view.
It is not that each individual has the number eleven; rather, it would be the number of all [the animals].
This number eleven would be a modification (*vikāra*) of all five *prayāja* offerings and all three *anuyāja* offerings. That modification would be of that number five,
and the number eleven would be understood as a modification of the [total] number of friends (*mitra*), rather than being understood for each individual one.
Therefore, the established conclusion is that all [the numbers] apply.
In the animal sacrifice, there are eleven each of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings; in the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices, there are nine each.
Who [holds this view]?
The maxim is: "For those who have fallen away from discernment, there is a downfall with a hundred faces.
[This refers to] the *sāhasī*. According to Haradatta on Pāṇini 2.1.35 (*bhakṣyeṇa miśrīkaraṇam*), the term *viśadam* means "distinctly divided" (*vibhaktāvayavam*).
Due to its hardness, there is clarity as the ultimate synonym...
Bhāṭṭa.
Regarding the subject matter, it is non-worldly (alaukika) because it serves all purposes.

In the context of the *Gārbhira* [sacrifice], with reference to the *Ājyadoha* Sāmans, it is heard in the scripture: "They praise with the *Agniṣṭup* as the underlayer" (*agniṣṭup-upaniṣadāya stuvate*).

In this regard, when there is a doubt as to whether the "underlayering of the *Agniṣṭup*" refers to something worldly or non-worldly, one should employ the non-worldly, that is, the Vedic *Agniṣṭup*, as the underlayer.
Why? Because it serves all purposes; that is, because the Vedic [fire], such as the *āhavanīya*, exists for the sake of all Vedic rites.
This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Regarding this, elsewhere there is a twofold reading—“the worldly” (*laukika*) and “worldly” (*laukika*)—distinguished by gender and by case-ending respectively.
There is no elision of the vowel *a*.
In that regard, according to the first interpretation, the word *syāt* is also recited in the sūtra.

However, in the case of the second interpretation ending in the accusative, the word *syāt* does not exist in the sūtra; rather, there is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the word "one should place" (*upanidadhyāt*).
"Not the Vedic [fire], because of the mention of its purpose.
Regarding the *ājyadoha* Sāmans in the *garbhiṇīrātra*, it is heard in the scripture: "They chant the praise after placing the fire nearby" (*agniṣṭupaniyāya stuvate*).

In this context, having refuted the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that one should place the Vedic fire nearby—by means of the aphorism, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by way of elimination (*pariśeṣanyāya*).
One should not place a Vedic fire nearby.
Why? Because of the specification of purpose. A specific purpose or specific utility for the Vedic fire has been specified.
And in that context, during the recitation of the Ājyadoha Sāmans, the placing [of the fire] is not mentioned.
Therefore, one should not place the Vedic fire;
by process of elimination, one should place the worldly fire—this is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
Likewise, because there is equality regarding the delight in their production from water.
It has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that, since the *ājyadoha* verses are recited at the same time as the *garbhira* verses,
the *agniṣṭup* must be brought forth [from a worldly source] by way of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*).
If it is argued that, by process of elimination, the placement of this particular hearth is impossible for me, [we reply:

the production of the other hearth-fires is likewise [impossible], just as it is with the Āhavanīya and the others. They too are enjoined for specific, non-common ritual functions; therefore, the placement of any one of them is also impossible.
Because of their equality with the Āhavanīya and other fires;
therefore, in the matter of the *pari* [enclosure],
it is non-worldly (*alaukika*).

Regarding the prescription of a qualified object (viśiṣṭārthavidhi): when there is a prescription of a qualified [object]—that is, when the prescription of a qualified object is conveyed through a compound—there is no syntactical split (vākyabheda). Bāla. pp. 109–102. This is the section concerning the status of being the object of prescription as a qualified substrate (viśiṣṭādhānacidheyatvādhikaraṇa).
2|3|34. See *Mīmāṃsākośa*, p. 930, under the section "Ādhānādhikaraṇam.
Since there is no fault in having a qualified object of reference (*viśiṣṭoddeśya*) as in the case of *anumati*, it is the compound word itself that is to be inferred.
*Saṃkarṣa* 2|3.
"The apprehension of the qualified [object] does not occur when its qualifier has not been apprehended; however, no one maintains that there is either expression or non-expression [of the qualifier].
Since a specific cognition does not arise regarding the qualified object if it is not expressed when its qualifier has not been apprehended, the apprehension of that [qualifier] must be respected.

However, nothing is defective by virtue of the qualifier not being previously known. *Vādārtha*, 3.4.4.13, pp. 915–916. Śiromaṇi maintains that the cognition of the qualifier is not accepted as a cause for the cognition of the qualified (*viśiṣṭajñāna*).

*Tattvacintāmaṇi*, p. 28. Some hold that the cognition of the qualifier is not a cause for the cognition of the qualified, because the causal factor for the cognition of the qualified is the sensory contact between the sense organ and both the qualificandum and the qualifier.
Page 21. There is a maxim that in the case of an injunction regarding a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there is a rule that the operation [of the qualifier] is restricted to the qualifier itself.

For example, in such cases as "the one with earrings goes" (*kuṇḍalī yāti*), it is observed that the property of going—which belongs to the qualified entity alone—resides in the qualifier, namely the earrings.
However, in cases such as "the one with earrings eats" (*kuṇḍalī bhuṅkte*), since the earrings and so forth function as a mere indicator (*lakṣaṇa*), their connection is with the act of eating.
[Sāhasrī, 263]: From the negation of the qualified follows the negation of the qualifier.
Negation is an operation that effects the negation of an object.

Bāla. p. 30: Even when there is a mention of a qualified entity, it is appropriate for the body and the person alone to be denoted, because it is possible for the stick—which is perceived through the word "stick"—to function as a qualifier, just as in the case of [the expression] "Kṛṣṇa's staff."
"Like a crow" (*kākavat*) [refers to] Devadatta’s house; "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī puruṣaḥ*).

Vākyapadīya 1.3.1.33, p. 318. Precisely because of the cognition of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*), in all cases, through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), the operation of either one or both of the two components—the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*)—is postulated in the word.
And that [presumptive implication] consists in the impossibility of anything else [accounting for the fact], and it occurs regarding an object that cannot be obtained otherwise.
Vākyapadīya 3.4.4.13, p. 916: "The qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*).

Since a qualified cognition is observed even in the case of words such as *śoṇa* ("red") without a prior cognition of the qualifier, the rule that a qualified cognition is necessarily preceded by the cognition of the qualifier applies only when there exists a pair of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehend the qualifier and the qualificand separately, and not in all cases.
Sphuṭārthā, p. 1408: Because the qualifier and the qualificand possess parts consisting of a qualified form, the cognition of the qualified does not arise without the cognition of those [two].
Su. pṛ. 1409: It is understood that the word *daṇḍa* does not apply to a mere staff [in isolation], but rather denotes something qualified.

Vā. 1.3.133 pṛ. 318: According to the maxim that "a word denoting a qualified whole [is used] with reference to a part when [that part alone is intended]," the consequence of the term being figurative (*lākṣaṇikatva*) would be unavoidable if, in passages such as "having encircled the sacrificial post with the *trivṛt*," only the number nine were taken [as the meaning].
Therefore, in such cases, the meaning of the word *trivṛt* is simply the triad itself (*naiguṇyam*).
Kau. 1.3.15, p. 76. *Viśiṣṭavidhānam* (Injunction of a qualified entity).
When it is understood that there is no [prior] attainment by any means of knowledge whatsoever, then one accepts an injunction of a qualified entity.
Thus, because there is an absence of what is obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*), the heard [text] is accepted as enjoining the subordinate elements (*guṇa*).
Or [it may be said]: PMS 3.5.2.31 states that because it is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), an injunction regarding the pure meaning is more powerful.
As stated on page 768: "In a qualified injunction, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)," as in the example: "One should sacrifice a white horse."
[Objection: But even here, the sentence would be split, because two distinct meanings—"one should make [the offering] white" and "one should sacrifice that"—are being enjoined. [Reply:
We say no.
For it is not too much of a burden for the word *ālabheta* ("one should sacrifice") to express human effort in connection with both the substance and the deity.
For example, when a sentence such as "yoke a red horse" (*raktaṃ aśvaṃ yojaya*) functions as an injunction of a quality, there is a need for two separate sentences to enjoin the two qualities.
However, when it is said, "bring the red one" (*śoṇam ānaya*), the injunction of the quality is already complete within that single sentence;
since the substance qualified by the specific quality is understood through direct audition (*śruti*) itself, there is no excessive burden upon a single sentence to enjoin two qualities.
Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 2.2.124: In the case of an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), there is no split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

As for what was stated—that a sentence is split when multiple qualities are enjoined—if these two qualities were enjoined as qualified by the act of establishing the fire (*ādhāna*), then there would indeed be a split of the sentence.
However, by means of two qualifiers, a single *ādhāna* (fire-installation) is enjoined as qualified [by them].
Therefore, there will be no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). (2.3.134, p. 564).

The impossibility of enjoining a qualified [action] (viśiṣṭavidhānānupapattiḥ). 3677. The determination of the injunction of a qualified [action]: if it is somehow possible for [the sentence] to be a restatement (anuvāda), then the injunction of a qualified [action] is impossible. Vārttika 3.5.1032, p. 1006. The principle of the injunction of a qualified [action] (viśiṣṭavidhānanyāyaḥ).
For where multiple qualifiers of a single action are employed, the injunction of that [action] is easily obtained by means of them;
thus, in such cases, there is the principle of the injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*). What, then, is an injunction of a qualified entity?

"The definition of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) is dependent upon the rule of the absolute injunction (*atiśadvavidhi*); [this is] the specific point regarding the establishment of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*). (Vārttika 3.1.716).

Thus, even when injunctions regarding the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇavidhi*) are postulated due to the impossibility of an injunction for a qualified object (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), although the sacrifice and so forth—which constitute the meaning of the injunction—are indeed qualifiers, there is no injunction whose object is those qualifiers themselves. Rather, it is the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) that transcends the root-meaning which is enjoined by the suffix itself; it is not enjoined in its pure form as something arrived at through another word [2.2.1.9].

For it has been stated therein: "Just as proximity (*sannidhi*) is defined in dependence upon the definition of that which is proximate, and knowledge is defined in dependence upon the definition of the object of knowledge, so too is the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) defined in dependence upon the definition of its limiting factor (*avacchedaka*). (Sūtra-pṛ. 704).

Therefore, that which cannot even be defined without the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is all the more impossible to enjoin when expressed by a suffix alone in its pure form, even without the injunction. Since the injunction is enjoined only as colored by the meaning of the verbal root through the very injunction heard in the text (*śruta*), no separate injunction is postulated regarding the qualifier that is the form of the verbal root’s meaning. Even though the logic of the section on the singularity of the cup (*grahaikatvādhikaraṇa*) was cited, it was stated that the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) delimited by the meaning of the verbal root is the object of the heard injunction.
Thus concludes the exposition of the qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).
Bāla., pṛ.

The Vaiśvadevādhikaraṇa [is introduced] for the purpose of establishing the superior force (*balīyastva*) of that which is taught in the originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), in order to refute the objection that the purpose is the production of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).
The principle of "the injunction of a qualified [object] is clearer than others" (*viśiṣṭavidhirviśadantanyāyaḥ*) applies here:

if, in the case of the rule "(if one should depart from the *satra*, they should sacrifice with the *pṛṣṭhya-anīkā*)," the conjunction were impossible, then—by the aforementioned principle—the injunction of the qualified object would somehow incur the burden of being a qualified injunction even while accepting the injunction of agency as its subject; thus, the conjunction would be clarified. However, since that [conjunction] is obtained as an inherent property through the employment of a single word, it is merely restated and is not intended to be emphasized (*na vivakṣitam*).
It is a rule that a property residing in a qualified entity necessarily resides in its qualifier as well;
for example, in the statement "the one with earrings goes," the earrings themselves indeed go too.

In the case of a cognition of the qualified as qualified (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyajñāna*), the certainty regarding the status of the qualifier-determiner as a mode (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedakaprakāratvaniścaya*) is the cause [of such a cognition].
Maṇi, p. 15.

In the perception of the qualified-qualifier relation (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya-pratyakṣa*), the certainty of the qualifier-nature of the delimiting factor of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka-prakāratva-niścaya*) is the cause;
this is stated in Maṇi, p. 30.
Śiromaṇi, however, does not accept that the certainty of the qualifier-nature of the delimiting factor of the qualifier is the cause for the cognition of the qualified-qualifier relation.
Maṇi, p. 28.
The manifestation of the sentence-meaning in the form of qualified-qualificative relation (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya*) is fourfold.
(1) The qualificative relation of the qualified (*viśiṣṭasya vaiśiṣṭyam*), as in "the ground possesses a man with a staff" (*daṇḍimad bhūtalam*).

(2) A qualifier in relation to the qualificand, and another qualifier in relation to that [qualifier], as in: "The man possesses a blue staff. (3) The qualification of one thing by another when it is already qualified [by a third] (i.e., the qualification of the qualified), as in: "Devadatta, who possesses a staff, also possesses an earring.
(4) Both [qualifiers] in relation to a single [subject], as in: "Devadatta possesses a staff and an earring."
The maxim "women are long-lived, provided they possess distinguished qualities" (Maṇi, p.
"Viśeṣa" (the specific) refers to that which is unique.
*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 8.1.9.16: A specific rule sets aside a general rule when both apply.
A specific rule is stronger than a general one.
The ten-fold nature of the *sāmidhenī* verses is general, whereas the eleven-fold nature is a specific rule for the *vaihārika* sacrifice.
Therefore, by the specific number seventeen, there is a sublation of the general number twelve.
(Vi. 3.6.3) The specific is stronger than the general.
A particular is a specific instance of a universal; 3679: having the form of a particular.
It is possible to enjoin [an injunction] regarding what has already been obtained, and not otherwise.
When a general rule has been obtained, a specific rule is enjoined.
*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 10.1.2.16: For while some particular may exist within a universal,
no particular whatsoever can be established that is devoid of a universal.

"Furthermore, a particular is always held to depend upon the attainment of a universal. (Vākyapadīya 3.2.8.22, p. 778). "Or [it is said]: 'A particular is always desired to be dependent upon the attainment of a universal. (Vākyapadīya 3.4.14.4, p. 182).
The general rule is set aside by the specific rule.
"He offers in the Āhavanīya fire" is a general rule; "He offers on the footprint" is a specific rule.
By the footprint, the Āhavanīya fire is superseded.
The universal is sublated by the particular.

What is the reason? The Dakṣiṇā in the Viśvajit sacrifice (3688). Regarding the Viśvajit, according to the Bhaṭṭa school, there is a discussion concerning the purpose of the dharma: in the Jyotiṣṭoma and its subsidiaries, as well as wherever the giving away of one's entire property (*sarvasva*) is prescribed, the following account has been established.

At the very commencement of the ritual, by virtue of a scriptural injunction, the sacrificer sets aside his own wealth in three portions: for the purpose of consumption (*bhakṣārtha*), for the purpose of the rite (*ṛtvartha*), and for the purpose of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇārtha*).

In that case, because there is no distinction regarding ownership for anything whatsoever, even the *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter) is to be given; however, it is not the case that the "allness" (*sarvatā*) applies to the portion intended for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

Since in the archetype (*prakṛti*), that portion has the purpose of being the sacrificial fee, the injunction to give away one's entire property (*sarvasva*) is an attribute of what is to be enjoined (*vidheya-dharma*).
In its absence, since even the three portions would be indistinguishable, the designation "this portion is for the purpose of the sacrificial fee" would be untenable.

Therefore, due to the direct scriptural injunction (*pratyakṣavacana*) regarding the gift of one's entire property (*sarvasvadāna*), there follows the omission of the remaining ritual acts that would otherwise be obtained by extension (*atideśa*). Since the constituent parts (*padārtha*) are subordinate to the primary act, and because it is illogical—following the principle of the "loss of the object of cognition" (*prameyāvalaya*)—to set aside the primary act for the sake of the subordinate sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that some small amount should be given to the priest and everything else should be bestowed upon others. However, since the designation "for the sake of the sacrificial fee" establishes its connection [to the act], it is simpler to enjoin only the "entirety" (*sarvatā*) itself; thus, the gift of the whole belongs to that [priest] alone.

Nor should it be argued that, because [the rule] applies to the archetype (*prakṛti*) as well, there would be the consequence of giving that [entirety], which would render the injunction useless; otherwise, since it would serve the purpose of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), its status as such would be untenable. This is because, by the statement, "If the priests were not satisfied by this much, but rather by the whole property," even that [entirety] serves the purpose of the sacrificial fee when satisfaction cannot be achieved by the twelve-hundred [cows].

And here, since it is established that only the portion intended for the sacrificial fee is to be given, some maintain that the preceding six topical discussions (*adhikaraṇa*) are to be understood as hypothetical deliberations (*kṛtvācintā*).

In reality, however, since even the father and others possess shares for the sake of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and because their status as protectors makes such deliberation appropriate, one should not treat this as a hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtvācintā*).
Maṇḍana [holds]: "It should certainly not be given for the sake of the ritual. Śaṅkara [holds]: "And everything should be for the sake of the sacrificial fee."
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, at the time of giving the sacrificial fee, one must give away everything that is currently possessed.
That which is one's own at the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be understood as being connected to that gift.

Because the rule for giving applies only to one's own property.
