Therefore, only what is available at the time of the *dakṣiṇā* should be given.

Śā—Is it that wealth which has already become available for use prior to the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇākāla*), yet was not used and was preserved with effort, must be given because it was determined to be given; or rather, is it that only that which exists at the actual time of the fee must be given? In this doubt, [the view is] that for the sake of favoring all those who have faith, there is a giving of both what has already occurred and what is yet to come. Since everything arises at the very time of the sacrificial fee, there is no need for preservation or application [of effort]. Furthermore, since one does not possess ownership (*svatva*) over what is yet to come at that time, its giving would be impossible.
He thought: "That which is to be given must be either what has already occurred, what is yet to come, or what is currently present at that time.
Of these, the first is contradicted by all scripture, and the last is impossible; therefore, [the second remains]."

Bhaṭṭa: At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), only that over which one possesses ownership (*svatva*) may be given; it is not the case that wealth already available for enjoyment must first be withheld through effort and then given.
There is no evidence (*pramāṇa*) to support such a requirement of withholding.
Furthermore, as for future wealth, giving is impossible precisely because at that time there is no ownership over it.
Furthermore, ownership does not arise merely by hearing [the promise] even regarding a future object;

for if that were the case, since giving would be impossible, the injunction "what has been promised must indeed be given" would be rendered meaningless. Moreover, if the root *dā* (to give) signified mere surrender, it would result in a figurative usage (*lakṣaṇā*).

By the act of promising (*pratiśravaṇa*), one merely generates a state of incapacity regarding one's own enjoyment and the giving of the object to others; this is because of the aforementioned rule on giving—"and that which has been promised to another"—which prohibits giving it to anyone else. However, ownership (*svatva*) is not extinguished, as in the case of an oblation (*nirvāpa*).
Maṇḍana states: "But it is given at that very time" (the meaning is:
it is given only when it exists at the time of the gift, and not something that is non-existent at that time, whether past or future).
Śaṅkara: "And as for what may occur at the time of giving [the sacrificial fee]:
one who possesses less wealth than twelve hundred [paṇas] has no entitlement to the Viśvajit sacrifice.
(Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 314). Regarding the statement, "There is no entitlement to the Viśvajit for one whose wealth is less than twelve hundred," one should consult the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*).
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, a Śūdra who serves for the sake of dharma and wealth must not be given away.

"And the Śūdra [is not to be given], because he is a follower of the Dharmaśāstra. The Commentary: This doubt arises specifically regarding the Viśvajit sacrifice: should a Śūdra servant be given as a gift, or not?
What is established? That in the Viśvajit sacrifice, one's entire property is to be given, because it is prescribed as being present for the sake of dharma in the Viśvajit.
This being the case, we reply:
"And a Śūdra is not to be given"—this is a prohibition. Why? Because it is a treatise on Dharma (Dharmaśāstra).
Because it is established by the Dharmaśāstra:
"In this manner, one who is approached by a member of the three higher castes and the like, while serving him, should be supported according to the law.
Thus, even if he is being given away to another, he should not desire it.
And it does not prevail for one who has not ascertained it;
nor should it be accepted by force.
But he who would accept it from another might even have to give it away.
However, it cannot be given merely by [the master's] will alone.

Śā—As for the question of whether a Śūdra who attends upon a patron (*yajamāna*) as a servant for the sake of religious duty (*dharma*) should be given away or not: he may be given, because he can be determined [as property] through the favor of universal faith;
yet he is not to be given, because he lacks ownership and because, being unwilling, he cannot be accepted as another’s property.

But a slave must indeed be given. Soma says: "Since a Śūdra who has come for refuge possesses ownership by virtue of being subject to authority at that time, there is consistency with the direct scriptural statement that 'there should be giving. However, the meaning of the Sūtra is: and a Śūdra is not to be given away, because he is [governed by] the Dharmaśāstra."
This means that he has approached for the purpose of learning the *dharmaśāstra*.
Vi [jñāneśvara] states: "A Śūdra who serves for the sake of *dharma* and wealth—should he be given [in marriage] or not? He is like a slave.
He should be given because he is [the master’s] own; yet he is not given because he lacks independence."

Bhaṭṭa: Even a Śūdra who stands as a servant for the sake of dharma or for maintenance should not be given away, because he lacks ownership over himself and because it is impossible for another’s ownership to be established [over him]. However, those such as a slave from birth (garbhadāsa) may indeed be given away.
Maṇḍana: "One who has come for the sake of dharma should not be given away."
Śaṅkara says: "And likewise Dharmadāsa [states]:
'[The son] born of a purchased wife and so forth shall indeed be [the owner];
in the Viśvajit sacrifice, in the passage 'he does not give to a maned beast,' this is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)."
The meaning is that everything belonging to the horse, except for the horse itself, should be given; however, the horse must not be given. (Vi. 6.7.3)
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, as in the case of the Bhāṣya 10.6.8.24, there is no application of all [the stotras] such as the Bṛhat and others.
In the Viśvajit, by virtue of its name, the precedence of the Āgrayaṇa vessel is obtained in the Gavāmayana.
Dvaidhapūṣā 10.12.15.8, p.

1980: In the Viśvajit sacrifice (in which all [stotras] are performed), one employs the *Rathantara* at the *Pavamāna*, the *Bṛhat* at the *Ārbhava*, and the others in between; the *Vairūpa* is the *Sāman* of the Hotṛ, the *Vairāja* of the Maitrāvaruṇa, the *Raivata* of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and the *Śākara* of the Acchāvāka.
Bhāṣya 7.3.13.
Mīmāṃsākośa 462:
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, the "Vatsa" [garment] and other such items would be brought forth because they serve as a common ritual element (*tantra*).
In the one-day (*ekāha*) Viśvajit, for the purpose of wearing [the garment], it is prescribed: "Having emerged from the *avabhṛtha* bath, he puts on the Vatsa-garment."
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, a new garment is for the purpose of wearing as an undergarment;
in the Aṣṭarātra, both [the new garment and the old] are obtained.
Since these two garments serve the same purpose, a choice between them would normally arise; however, the author states the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position.
On the first day of the Aṣṭarātra, at the Viśvajit, there should be the calf-skin; there is no option. This is because [the calf-skin] is obtained from the one-day Viśvajit by virtue of its name.

Otherwise, in the absence of extension by name, since the Aṣṭarātra is a *tantra* (a composite ritual framework), and since the Jyotiṣṭoma character would apply to the many subsequent days within the Aṣṭarātra system, the calf-skin would be obtained through that predominance of the Jyotiṣṭoma character.
Therefore, in the Viśvajit sacrifice, there should be the possession of a calf-cloth (*vatsatva*) itself, and not its absence;
or rather, there is no contradiction, for the upper garment (*uparivāsa*) is indeed what constitutes the state of possessing a calf-cloth.

When eight nights have passed in the Viśvajit sacrifice, for the purpose of the sacrificer’s wearing garment, the calf-skin is obtained from the one-day Viśvajit, and the unwashed (unhemmed) garment is obtained from the [Viśvajit] lasting ten days. Because of the conflict between these two, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the calf-skin alone should be taken. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:
there is no conflict; nor is there any contradiction between the calf-skin and the unwashed garment.
For this reason— namely, that the calf-skin is the upper garment and the antelope skin is the lower garment because of their suitability—
the combination of the calf-skin and the antelope-skin as garments is the established conclusion (siddhānta).

The word "vā" (or) is for the purpose of refuting the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the alternative view. What [is the correct view]? It is the giving away of only that which exists as one's entire property (*sarvasva*) in the Viśvajit sacrifice.
Furthermore, because it is eternal, there can be no connection with things that are non-eternal.

The Commentary states: Regarding the Viśvajit sacrifice itself, there is a doubt concerning the injunction "he gives away his entire property" (*sarvasvaṃ dadāti*). Does this mean he should give all the implements acquired by him, as many as belong to a human being and as many as he is able to acquire—even those not yet fashioned—or rather, only those which actually exist for him at present should be given, and those not currently in his possession need not be produced? Why is there this doubt? Because the expression of the statement is possible in both ways.
And if it is implied in this way—that all things which are one's own—what are they?
It is enjoined that one should give all those things which are beneficial to a person, such as beds and so forth;
that is, when those things which belong to a person are capable of being given.
In the Viśvajit sacrifice,
[the rule] pertaining to the sixth day applies; in the Viśvajit sacrifice, [the rule] pertaining to the sixth day applies.
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, "all" [is used];
by saying "all those," the state of being "all" is enjoined.
If giving were what is enjoined, then this would be the giving of even those things that are not normally given, such as finished vessels.
Now, if "all-ness" (sarvatva) is enjoined, then it must refer to what is already present.
What, then, is the prima facie position? That vessels already made should be given.
In that way, the direct Vedic statement (śruti) regarding the injunction of giving is upheld.
Otherwise, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*);
and since direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is more authoritative than syntactical connection,
therefore, vessels already prepared should be given.
This being the case, we reply:
because [the self] is eternal, there is no connection with cognitions.
The word "ca" (and) is used for the purpose of restating the point.
It has been stated that horses are not to be given,
and that items already fashioned into objects should not be given.
For in the Viśvajit sacrifice, the act of giving is always restated as being obtained through the general injunction (codaka).
Furthermore, since there are "ready-made articles" (*kṛtabhāṇḍaka*) that are indefinite, it is not possible to include all of them when the Viśvajit sacrifice is being performed.
In that case, for some of those ready-made articles, their production would have to await the gift at the Viśvajit;
thus, that [gift] would be occasional (*naimittika*), whereas [the Viśvajit] is obligatory (*nitya*).
And that [gift] is enjoined by the *codaka* as something permanent, not as being connected with a specific occasion (*nimitta*).

Therefore, this must necessarily be accepted: that completeness is enjoined for the gifts that have already been obtained. Furthermore, when a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is impossible, the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) must indeed be accepted.
Therefore, [the gifts] should be given as finished articles.

Śā—Regarding the statement "he gives his entire property" (*sarvasvaṃ dadāti*), the meaning of the scripture is that he gives everything that is his own property, whether it is fit for enjoyment such as flowers, or whether it is base metal (*kupya*) or non-base metal (*akupya*), or land, cattle, and so forth.

Consequently, even one who does not possess something should acquire it and give it; for when there is the doubt as to whether the meaning is "he gives whatever belongs to him" or "he gives all [that he possesses]," one considers this to be an injunction regarding giving, out of a desire to follow the scriptural injunction that "he gives whatever is his own property."

Since the giving is already established by the injunction [to give], the word "all" (sarva) prescribes that one who possesses something should proceed to give twelve-fold portions of whatever he has, thereby giving everything. Furthermore, because this word "all" is well-established in its application to all things, it does not imply the acquisition of things that have not yet been acquired.
Therefore, what has been acquired through effort must be given.

Soma: As before, there is no exclusion (*paryudāsa*) here; rather, the connection [of the word *sarva*] arises from its position as a suffix (*pratyayasthāna*). The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is this: because giving is obligatory (*nitya*), while the objects to be acquired are occasional (*anitya*) due to the possibility that they may not be obtained at certain times, there is no [permanent] relationship between them.
Viśvarūpa: "Even after having acquired [wealth], should everything be given, or only that which one possesses?"
The injunction of "all" applies only where nothing has been previously obtained; it does not apply when something is already established.

Bhaṭṭa: Since it is the meaning of the scripture that one gives "everything" (sarvam) that belongs to a person as an object of enjoyment—whether it be movable or immovable property, such as cattle and the like—even one who does not possess something must acquire it and give it, because the injunction regarding the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) is obtained.

This being the prima facie view, [we reply]: because it would result in a sixth type of injunction; because, by restating the gift already established by *codaka* (archetypal transfer), the mere state of "all-ness" is enjoined through the measure of one hundred and twelve; and because the word "all" is justified by its well-known conventional sense, it is improper for it to imply the acquisition of what is not yet possessed. Therefore, one should not give after having acquired [new wealth].
Maṇḍana: "And that which is already established is given.
Śaṅkara: "And even that which is brought near should not be given.
[This concerns] the extension (*atideśa*) of the *pṛṣṭha* chants occurring within the six-day period in the Viśvajit sacrifice.
See the section *Atideśaḥ viśvajiti ṣaḍahagatapṛṣṭhānām* (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 220).
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, among the Rathantara and other Sāmans belonging to the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), the Vairūpa Sāman is to be inserted for the purpose of the Hotṛ’s Pṛṣṭha-stotra.
Because the term "pṛṣṭha" implies [all] pṛṣṭhas on every back, there would be a partiality of the pṛṣṭha, since its location has already been established.
The Bhāṣya states: This is recorded in the tradition: "The Viśvajit is *sarvapṛṣṭha*.
In this regard, the meaning is subject to doubt: is the placement of all [pṛṣṭhas] in the place of the pṛṣṭha, or is one [pṛṣṭha] in the place of the pṛṣṭha while the others are elsewhere?
What is established? In this *sarvapṛṣṭha* sacrifice, there is the placement of all the *sāmans* in the region of the *pṛṣṭhas*.
But what, then, is the region of the *pṛṣṭhas*? It is the interval above the *mādhyandina-pavamāna* and prior to the *maitrāvaruṇa-sāman*; this intermediate space is the region of the *pṛṣṭhas*.
That single region alone shall belong to all the *sāmans*.
Why? Because of the word "pṛṣṭha" (back).
And this place is prepared for one who is performing the function of the pṛṣṭhas.
Therefore, all [the pṛṣṭha-stotras] are to be inserted in the region of the back.
"But it would be due to the remoteness of the injunction.
The Commentary: The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
Although this is established by logical reasoning, it must be otherwise because of the explicit scriptural statement.
One should perform the function of the *pṛṣṭha* for a single [stotra], having distributed them completely.

How so? "He performs the *rathaṃtara* on the *pavamāna*, the *bṛhat* on the *ārbhava*, and the others in the middle—the *vairūpa* as the *hotṛ*'s *pṛṣṭha*, the *vairāja* as the *brahman*sāman, the *śākvara* as the *maitrāvaruṇa*sāman, and the *raivata* as the *acchāvāka*sāman.
In this way, the injunction prescribing the function of the *pṛṣṭha* for a single [stotra] will be meaningful.

If the placement were for the purpose of completing the others, then otherwise the prescription of the *pṛṣṭha* function for a single one would not be tenable; let that not be the case. Therefore, we see that the placement is for the *pṛṣṭha* function of one, while for the others it is for the purpose of completion.
Śabara: It is heard in scripture, "The Viśvajit sacrifice has all the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras].
Regarding this, it was established in the seventh book that there is an injunction for the *rathaṃtara* and other *pṛṣṭha* chants belonging to the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*).

In that context, a doubt arises: do all six *sāmans* serve as the means for the *pṛṣṭha* praise, and are they to be inserted at that *pṛṣṭha* location—specifically in the middle of the Mādhyaṃdina-pavamāna, between the Ārbhava and the Vairūpa? Or is it that only the Vairūpa serves as the means for that [praise] and is inserted there, while the others serve as the means for other stotras and are employed at their respective locations?

Regarding this, in the sixth [book], since they serve as the means for the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra] there, and because here too the word *pṛṣṭha* indicates their status as its means, it follows that all [sāmans] should be employed in the very place of the *pṛṣṭha*. To this, we reply: From such scriptural injunctions as, "One should perform the *rathaṃtara* in the *bahiṣpavamāna*, the *bṛhat* in the *ārbhava*, the others in the middle, and the *vairūpa* in the *hotṛ-pṛṣṭha*," it is established that the *vairūpa* serves as the means for the *pṛṣṭha*; otherwise, it would be the means for a different stotra. Nor should it be argued that because they are enjoined again in the praise of the *pṛṣṭha*, they must therefore also be employed in other stotras.
Because it would follow that the injunction regarding the *vairūpa* [sāman] as the *pṛṣṭha* would be rendered meaningless.

Furthermore, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the term "all *pṛṣṭhas*" (*sarvapṛṣṭha*) prescribes the *rathantara* and other *sāmans* belonging to the six-day rite (*ṣāḍahika*) which serve as the means for the *pṛṣṭha*.

Since there is no plurality of praises (*stuti*), the application of the word "all" (*sarva*) is impossible. Moreover, since these *sāmans* mentioned here require a function (*kārya*), and their purpose is already fulfilled by the functions explicitly stated in the text, why should one assume that they all serve as the means for the *pṛṣṭha*? Therefore, their placement is only within the [specific] *ṛc*s.

Soma: In the preceding case, there was an objection raised that while the chanting (*sāman*) is obtained through the force of the general rule (*codaka*), here the *pṛṣṭha* chant—obtained by the natural force of the word *pṛṣṭha*—should not be chanted in the location of the *pṛṣṭha*. This is the connection [of the present discussion]. As for the meaning of the Sūtra: "by all words" means "in the case of the *sarvapṛṣṭha* [rite].

In that context, if there were to be a single location for those *sāmans* which constitute the *pṛṣṭha-stotras*, it would be because of the word *pṛṣṭha*; and because the word *pṛṣṭha* has a fixed location.
Vi— "Does 'sarvapṛṣṭha' mean all [the *pṛṣṭha* chants] in every location, or according to the specific statement? Because of the word *pṛṣṭha*, there is a restriction to the location of the *pṛṣṭha*.

Bhāṭṭa— Regarding the passage "In the Viśvajit, there is the *sarvapṛṣṭha*," it is established that the *rathaṃtara* and other *sāmans* belonging to the six-day sacrifice (*ṣaḍaha*) are enjoined as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the Viśvajit.

In this regard, since it has been assumed that all six [Sāmans] serve as the means for the *rathantara-pṛṣṭha* stotra and so forth during the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) beginning with the *māhendra*, they should likewise be included here by way of combination (*samuccaya*), just as in the case of the *saṃsthā*. This being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), we reply: because of the injunction, "The *rathantara* is in the *pavamāna*, the *bṛhat* in the *ārbhava*, the others in the middle; the *vairūpa* is on the *hotṛ*'s *pṛṣṭha*, the *vairāja* on the *maitrāvaruṇa*'s, the *śākkara* on the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*'s, and the *raivata* on the *acchāvāka*'s," there is an ordaining of their placement within other specific stotras; therefore, they are not all to be placed solely upon the *hotṛ*'s *pṛṣṭha*.

Furthermore, by this statement, there is no re-enactment (*punarvidhāna*) of those [Sāmans] already established therein within other stotras, because that would result in the fault of over-specification (*viśiṣṭavidhi-gaurava*),
and because it would entail the necessity of re-enacting the *vairūpa* Sāman as the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ.

Therefore, since the Sāmans are already obtained by virtue of their connection to the sacrifice, there is— by way of parsimony (*lāghava*)— a sublation even of all those whose relationship is already established, through the mere act of excluding them from the form of the other stotras.
Nor does it follow that, since the properties of the *rathantara* and so forth are already established as means for producing the *pṛṣṭha-apūrva*, they would not apply here in another *stotra*;

for, according to the maxim "when the principal is being led away, it carries the subordinate elements with it," and by necessity in accordance with the *stotra* and its instruments, the *rathantara* is enjoined here itself as a means for the *pavamāna-pṛṣṭha-apūrva* through the word *rathantara* used in a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*), precisely because it must be performed with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*).
Maṇḍana says: "There is no twofold nature every day."

The application of the two-fold *sāman* is the connection [to the rule] that it does not occur every day for all [of them]. Śaṅkara says: "In the Viśvajit sacrifice, that [sāman] consists of all the *pṛṣṭha* hymns."
In the Viśvajit sacrifice characterized by all the *pṛṣṭhas*, the [Lokampṛṇā] bricks should be taken; they should also be taken in the Agniṣṭoma [as the twenty-one-fold Lokampṛṇās].
Saṃkarṣa 1.3.13.
In the Viśvajit with all *pṛṣṭhas*, because it is preceded by that [Agniṣṭoma], the *pṛṣṭhas* belonging to the Agniṣṭoma exist, and the word *pṛṣṭha* is indeed present.
It is heard in scripture: "In the Viśvajit, it is *sarvapṛṣṭha*.

Regarding this, in the deliberation as to whether the word *sarvapṛṣṭha* is a restatement (*anuvāda*) or an injunction (*vidhi*), he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it is a restatement.
Since the Viśvajit sacrifice is already inherently *sarvapṛṣṭha*, it is not possible for all the *pṛṣṭha* stotras to be enjoined there again by means of the word *sarvapṛṣṭha*.

How is there "all-pṛṣṭha" (sarvapṛṣṭhatā) in the Viśvajit? Because it is preceded by that—that is, because it is preceded by the Jyotiṣṭoma, because it has the Jyotiṣṭoma as its archetype—the *pṛṣṭhas*, namely the *pṛṣṭha* stotras belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma, are obtained for the Viśvajit through the rule of extension (*codaka*).
Therefore, the Viśvajit is indeed "all-pṛṣṭha.
And in the Jyotiṣṭoma, there are four *pṛṣṭha* stotras beginning with the Māhendra; those [four] are also [present] in the Viśvajit.
Furthermore, the term *pṛṣṭha* is well-established in the *māhendra* and other stotras as "the seventeen *pṛṣṭhas*.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that in the Viśvajit sacrifice, the expression "all *pṛṣṭhas*" is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
For in that [Viśvajit], there are injunctions based on its being a six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*).

In the case of the statement "In the Viśvajit, there are all the *pṛṣṭhas*," the term *sarvapṛṣṭha* is a restatement (*anuvāda*), as established by the preceding Sūtra which holds that the *pṛṣṭha* stotras are extended to the Viśvajit from the Jyotiṣṭoma.
[In the Viśvajit, there is] everything;
in the Viśvajit, one's entire property [is to be given].
Rejecting the alternative view with the word "or" (vā), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
the extension (*atideśa*) of the *pṛṣṭha* chants in the Viśvajit sacrifice is from the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), not from the Jyotiṣṭoma.

This is because in that six-day period there are injunctions for the six *pṛṣṭha* chants—namely, the Rathantara, Bṛhat, Vairūpa, Vairāja, Raivata, and Śakvara—as seen in such statements as "in that [period] the Rathantara is the *pṛṣṭha*."
Even though there may be *pṛṣṭha* chants in the Jyotiṣṭoma, nevertheless not all of them are used;
however, in the six-day sacrifice (*ṣaḍaha*), all are used.
"In the Viśvajit, indeed all [are used]."
Therefore, in the Viśvajit sacrifice, only the *pṛṣṭha* chants of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*) are extended by analogy.
Consequently, the word "all-*pṛṣṭha*" in the Viśvajit is a rule based on extension (*atideśika*).
This is also because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Regarding the statement, "The Viśvajit has all the *pṛṣṭhas*," the author states another reason for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the extension (*atideśa*) of all the *pṛṣṭhas* in the Viśvajit is from the *ṣaḍaha* sacrifice itself, and not from the Jyotiṣṭoma. The indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the sentence concerned with their arrangement—"He performs the *Rathaṃtara* on the *Pavamāna*, the *Bṛhat* on the *Ārbhava*, and the others in between; the *Vairūpa* is the *Sāman* of the Hotṛ, the *Vairāja* of the Maitrāvaruṇa, the *Raivata* of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and the *Śākvara* of the Acchāvāka"—shows that the *pṛṣṭhas* in the Viśvajit are those belonging to the *ṣaḍaha*.
Therefore, there is an extended application (atideśa) from the six-day period (ṣaḍaha).
The term *pṛṣṭha* has its origin and application (*utpannādhikāra*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma;
specifically, within the Jyotiṣṭoma, the word *pṛṣṭha* has its origin and application in the four [stotras] beginning with the Māhendra.

The injunction "They praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*" is operative with reference to those [stotras] that have already arisen; however, in the case of the *dvirātra*, it is operative with reference to those arising [at that time]. Furthermore, the statement "The *bṛhat* becomes the *pṛṣṭha*" shows that the *pṛṣṭha* actually arises in the *jyotiṣṭoma*, whereas in the *māhendra* and other [stotras], the word *pṛṣṭha* applies there merely by way of a common designation (*chandaḥ*).
Therefore, in the Viśvajit sacrifice, there is an extended application (atideśa) of all six *pṛṣṭha* stotras from the Ṣaḍaha itself;
this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). [Objection: "But there is an injunction for only two."

Regarding the statement, "The Viśvajit has all the Pṛṣṭhas," the opponent objects to the established conclusion (siddhānta) that there is an extension (atideśa) of the six-day (ṣaḍaha) Pṛṣṭhas. He argues that if the injunction of the six-day Pṛṣṭhas were accepted, two injunctions would result: one for the Pṛṣṭhas themselves and another for their "all-inclusiveness" (sarvatva).
Therefore, the extension of the six-day [rite] is not tenable.

Furthermore, since the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* [sāmans] exist as options in the Jyotiṣṭoma, their combination (*samuccaya*) in the Viśvajit would have to be enjoined by the term "all-sāman" (*sarvapṛṣṭha*), resulting in an injunction for both.
If this is argued, it is not so, because the word "all" (*sarva*) would be redundant.

Regarding what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view—that in the Viśvajit sacrifice, the conjunction of both the Bṛhat and Rathantara *pṛṣṭha* chants, which are obtained as options in the Jyotiṣṭoma, is enjoined by the term "all-pṛṣṭhas" (*sarvapṛṣṭha*)—that is not correct.
For the word "all" would be redundant;
it would entail redundancy, since this word "all" has a broad scope and is not applicable to only two things.
However, there is no such fault in the case of the prescription of the six [days] belonging to the Pāḍahika [section].
Therefore, it is indeed the prescription of the Pāḍahika days themselves.
Even in that case, "entirety" (sarvatva) alone is what is to be prescribed; as for the *pṛṣṭha* chants, they will follow by implication.
For it is not possible to achieve the state of "all" (sarvatva) without performing the *pṛṣṭha* chants;
therefore, there is no occasion for two separate injunctions.

Consequently, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the Viśvajit sacrifice, there is an extended application (*atideśa*) of the six *pṛṣṭha* chants belonging to the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), and not those belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma.
And thus, this is the extension of the six-day (*ṣaḍaha*) ritual rules to the *pṛṣṭha* chants;

as stated in [Jaimini Sūtra] 7.3.17: "In the *Viśvajit* sacrifice where all *pṛṣṭhas* are performed, the *pṛṣṭhas* belonging to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* apply, because it is preceded by that, and the word *pṛṣṭha* exists [therein]."

In this context, taking as an example the statement, "The Viśvajit sacrifice has all the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]," one must investigate whether this word *pṛṣṭha* serves the purpose of extended application (*atideśa*) or not. A doubt arises as to whether this word *pṛṣṭha* refers to the *pṛṣṭha* stotras of the Jyotiṣṭoma or those of the six-day sacrifice (*ṣaḍaha*). The prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) argument is as follows: Since the Viśvajit is preceded by the Jyotiṣṭoma, and since in that sacrifice the word *pṛṣṭha* is understood—by virtue of the plural number in the injunctions "They praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*" and "The days of the Sadas are the *pṛṣṭhas*"—to refer to the four stotras beginning with the Māhendra, it is impossible for there to be multiple *pṛṣṭha* stotras [in the Jyotiṣṭoma itself]. Therefore, the word *pṛṣṭha* here is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *pṛṣṭha* stotras obtained through extended application from the Jyotiṣṭoma; it does not serve the purpose of extended application. However, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) will be established by the sūtra, "From the six-day sacrifice, for therein is the injunction" (7.3.318). This is because in the Jyotiṣṭoma, only a single *pṛṣṭha* is prescribed as an option between the Bṛhat and the Rathantara. Consequently, since there is no plurality of *pṛṣṭhas* [in the archetype], the word *pṛṣṭha*—due to its connection with the word "all" (*sarva*)—must signify the extended application of the six *pṛṣṭha* stotras belonging to the six-day sacrifice, namely the Rathantara, Bṛhat, Vairūpa, Vairāja, Śākvara, and Raivata. Thus, the word *pṛṣṭha* is for the purpose of extended application.

*Sūtra-prakāśa*, p. 426: In the seventh section (*adhikaraṇa*), under the rule *viśvajiti sarvapṛṣṭhe tatpūrvakatvāt* (7.3.317), it is explained in detail that in the original model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), there is no plurality of *pṛṣṭha* chants. This is because, regarding the originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*)—"the *rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha*" and "the *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha*"—the word *pṛṣṭha*, which first occurs as the name of the *māhendra-stotra*, is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) in the descriptive injunction (*anuvādavākya*) "the *pṛṣṭhas* are seventeenfold" to refer to the four *stotras* beginning with the *māhendra*.
*Rasāyana*, p. 29: In the *viśvajit* sacrifice, one's entire property (*sarvasva*) must be given away.
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, there is the gift of one's entire property; the section concerning the Viśvajit establishes that "entire property" exceeds [the standard] twelve hundred.
For it remains exactly as it is established in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
And such "all one's possessions" (sarvasva), although obtained through the extended application (*codaka*), is thereby restricted.
Thus, in the Viśvajit sacrifice, "all one's possessions" must indeed be more than one hundred and twelve [cows], and not one hundred and twelve, nor less than that.

VI. 6|7|9: In the Viśvajit sacrifice involving the gift of one's entire property (*sarvasvadāna*), only [one's own] father and other relatives are to be given; a Śūdra is not to be given, because he lacks the status of being one's own property (*svatva*). However, born slaves (*garbhadāsa*) may be given, because they possess that status.
VI. 7|7: In the Viśvajit sacrifice involving the gift of one's entire property, only [one's own] father and other relatives are to be given.

6|7|1|1–2. Regarding the principle of "the gift of all one's possessions" (*sarvasvadānanyāya*), the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted. In the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, when there is a gift of all one's possessions, everything remaining after dividing [the estate] for the sake of dependents and according to actual requirements must be given; and this division is indeed obtained through the force of the injunction (*codaka*). Vi. 6|7|7. In the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, when there is a gift of all one's possessions, the great earth (*mahābhūmi*) is not to be given.

Land should not be given, because it is common to all. The Commentary: Regarding this very matter of giving everything, there is a doubt: should land be given or not? What, then, is intended by "land"? It is that other substance in the form of earth known as the terrestrial globe, and not merely a field or soil. In this regard, what is the prima facie view? That it should be given, because there is no distinction [between it and other things].
For in that case, the word "one's own" (sva) functions by way of a connection with ownership;
and it is possible to relinquish one's own property through a mental act.
This being the position reached, we reply:
"The land shall not be given. Why? Because men are seen to be the masters of specific fields, not of the entire terrestrial globe.
He said: "In that case, whoever is now a sovereign ruler of the whole earth shall give it."
We say that this is not so.
Why?
Because another king possesses as much territory of the earth as a sovereign ruler (sārvabhauma) possesses.
In that regard, there is no distinction whatsoever.

However, for the sovereign of the whole earth (sārvabhauma), there is this additional [duty]: he enjoys a certain portion by means of protecting the rice and other crops produced on the earth, but not a portion of the earth itself.

And as for those people who enjoy that [produce], there is no distinction regarding their lordship over the various activities—such as holding, walking, and so forth—which are performed upon the ground of the earth.
Therefore, land should be given.
Śā—As for this great earth, whether it should be given or not:
considering that even this belongs to the sovereign as his property, he says it should be given; it does not belong to anyone else.

For sovereignty consists merely in the collection of taxes from farmers and others as wages for the protection of one’s own territory and the removal of thorns [enemies], and the imposition of punishment upon those deserving of it; it does not consist in ownership.
Therefore, a universal monarch would not give away the great earth, nor would a regional ruler give away his province.

By the word "wealth" (*dhana*), the connection is indicated: since the father and others do not constitute "wealth," there would be no giving of them; however, because the earth *is* wealth, the objection is raised that its gift should indeed be possible.

Vi— "Should the great earth be given or not? Since it belongs to his own empire, he may give it; for since sovereignty consists precisely in protection, that [earth] is not considered one's own property.
Bhāṭṭa— "As for this great earth, because it is the wealth of a universal monarch (sārvabhauma), its gift is made by him."
This being the case, even for a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*), there is no ownership (*svatva*) over that [earth].
For even in the case of a *jāyā* (conquering king), ownership is produced only with respect to the seizure of wealth belonging to enemies and similar matters.

As for the great earth (*mahāpṛthivī*), however, he acquires only the authority of sovereignty (*rājyamātra*). For sovereignty consists essentially in the protection of one's own territory and the removal of thorns; and based on that, his entitlement is merely the collection of taxes from cultivators and the imposition of punishment upon those deserving of it.
However, ownership does not arise in her merely by that much.

If it were so, ownership would undesirably follow even for grass and such things found in the forest, because that would entail a contradiction with the injunctions regarding the actions that produce ownership;
and furthermore, ownership would also undesirably follow for the house of Prajāpati and other locations situated within her domain.
Therefore, she should not be given; nor should the mandala be given by the local ruler. However, things such as household labor and houses or fields must indeed be given.
Khaṇḍana: "The terrestrial globe (bhūgolaka) is not to be given. Śaṅkara: "Neither is the terrestrial sphere (bhūrmaṇḍala) to be given.
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, the ritual procedure (vidhyanta) belongs to the Soma sacrifice, not that of the Darśapūrṇamāsa.

"That [sacrifice] would have heaven as its result, because there is no distinction with respect to all [people]" (4.3.17.16)— by this sūtra, in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice, the qualification of the result, namely heaven, although not explicitly mentioned, is established through reasoning in order to determine the qualified performer (this is the *pūrvapakṣa*).

Indeed, in the section on the Viśvajit (4.3.15), it is established that all those statements made outside of specific ritual contexts (*anāramyavāda*) which lack a heard fruit and are devoid of evidence for a connection to a particular rite, possess fruitfulness by refuting their state of being fruitless.

In the *Ratnaprabhā*, regarding the sūtra on the established conclusion (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*) concerning the Viśvajit sacrifice (4.3.5–11), the passage beginning with "for because the purposes [of the subsidiaries] possess purposefulness" (*arthānāṃ hyarthavatvena*) is explained as being intended for something else (*anyaparatva*), due to its being separated [from the main topic] by way of conformity to logical fitness (*yogyatā*).
Su. pṛ. [page number].
And [the sacrifice] beginning with the Viśvajit is performed;
however, since there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) when [the result] has become the object of the action, there is no absence of the [desired] fruit.
And the Viśvajit sacrifice does not lack a material substance, because such a thing is not established;
or rather, it is because there is no equality of capacity, meaning that [the opponent's] argument lacks logical force.
The Viśvajit sacrifice, mentioned in the section on the Ekāha, is the example here.

And the meaning of the sentence is like that of an injunction for a subordinate element (guṇa). The Bhāṣya states: "Just as in the case of 'sukaraḥ indrāya rājñe,' where an injunction of a subordinate element occurs by means of an injunctive word situated in another sentence, so too an injunction of a result (phala) ought to be possible."
Just as there is authority even for the assumption of an exclusive restriction (vyavaccheda) in such statements as "Varuṇa indeed seizes him," so too should this [present case] be understood.
Śabara [says]: "In injunctions where no fruit is heard, such as 'One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit,' there is a doubt as to whether a fruit exists or not.
There is certainly no fruit in this injunction, because no fruit is mentioned."
For how could the fruit, which is an object to be reached through words, be understood without that [word]?
Since it is obtained through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*),
this sentence is complete and does not require ellipsis.
"But in the absence of that [an injunction], who could prevent the fact that the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is that which is to be brought about (bhāvya)?
And this being so, the sentence is complete and does not require supplementation.

Thus, when it is argued that "this action is indeed fruitless," it is replied: "An action conjoined with an injunction does not at all leave the meaning of the verbal root as that which is to be brought about."
"Without an object to be accomplished (bhāvya), this sentence would not be complete;

therefore, for the sake of completing the sentence, a result (phala) shall be supplied. Thus, even for those [injunctions] where no result is heard, a result shall be supplied from among those things to be accomplished."
In this context, it is established that all ritual acts possess fruitfulness.

Soma: [The connection is as follows: because no fruit is heard of for the *vratas* (observances), even the *Viśvajit* sacrifice and others are not for the sake of a fruit; thus, they are rejected. Vi: "Is there indeed no fruit in the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, or is there one? It is not so, because no fruit is heard of."

The fruit for the person must be postulated in the case of an injunction where there is an expectation for a verbal suffix (bhāṣyāpekṣā), as stated in the *Bhāṭṭa* [school]: "In the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others—such as the Viśvajit mentioned in the section on one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*) where no fruit is explicitly heard—the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) has an expectation for a fruit. Even though the sacrifice is brought forward by the direct statement within the same word, it cannot be the object to be produced (*bhāvya*). This is because, elsewhere, it is understood that the human goal (the fruit) is what is to be produced, since the injunction functions as an impeller toward that which is a human goal; and furthermore, because the sacrifice is understood to be the instrument (*karaṇa*), due to its grammatical coreferentiality with a name ending in the third case."
Therefore, even though the fruit is not explicitly stated, by supplying a word for the fruit at the end of the phrase "desiring that" (*tadācakṣakāma*), it results in a human goal as its fruit.
And although that word is supplied through ellipsis, because it is supplied due to the Veda's own requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*), it is indeed authoritative.
Or [the result] may be equal to that of the Vedas.

And only one such result is postulated, not all of them, because by postulating just one, the requirement for further results is satisfied. Furthermore, that single result is heaven alone, and not sons, cattle, and so forth; for according to the scriptural passage beginning with "that which is unmixed with suffering," the word *svarga* (heaven) is understood as denoting nothing but a specific kind of pleasure. Moreover, if heaven were the result here, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) regarding the delimiting factor of its being produced (*janyatāvacchedaka*). On the other hand, since sons and the like are desired as means to pleasure, [postulating heaven as the result] ensures that the scope of the scripture remains vast.

Furthermore, even though there is no difference in parsimony (*lāghava*), "being a Sugata" cannot be the delimitor of the effectness (*janyatāvacchedaka*) because it is not present in the context of this [inference], as it is common to both this world and the next. Moreover, by its very nature, what is intended here is pleasure mixed with suffering; thus, being mixed with suffering cannot logically constitute the result. Additionally, when a subordinate property (*vyāpyadharma*) can serve as the delimitor of effectness, it is redundant (*anyathāsiddha*) to use a more inclusive property (*vyāpakadharma*). Finally, because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*), "being a Sugata" cannot be the delimitor of effectness, just as "being heaven" (*svargatva*) cannot be.

Therefore, it is logical that the delimitor of the producedness (janyatāvacchedakatva) as characterized by the unobstructed cause of the Viśvajit sacrifice is precisely the nature of a distinct class of heaven (vijātīyasvargatva).

Furthermore, if liberation (mokṣa) consists of the destruction of suffering, then—just like the destruction of sin—it is not produced by the Viśvajit, due to the excessive complexity (gaurava) of the delimitor of its producedness.
However, if it consists of the attainment of bliss, then because it is produced solely by the [effort] of Śiva, it cannot be produced by the Viśvajit.

Even when, on the basis of the statement "Indeed, Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone," it is held that mere action constitutes liberation, or that the combination of knowledge and action is authoritative, even then—by considering the beginning and conclusion [of the text] starting with "Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action"—it is determined that the word "action" refers to all actions; thus, there is no evidence for the view that it refers only to sacrifices such as the Viśvajit, whose specific fruits are not mentioned in scripture.

Nor should it be argued that even if this were the case, since [the result] could still be logically established for this [act] through its commonality with other acts, the statement regarding the Viśvajit sacrifice would have fulfilled its purpose by merely enjoining the origination (*utpatti*) of the rite, and thus its status as a source of inference (*kalpaka*) would not be figurative. For, by the aforementioned statement—and in accordance with the principle of parsimony (*kalpanālāghava*)—one understands that only those rites whose performance is already established possess liberation as their fruit. If one were to include the Viśvajit and others whose performance is not yet established, a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*) would result; therefore, even in the case of the Viśvajit statement, the postulation of a fruit for the rite is necessary in order to establish the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*).

By this, the view that the Viśvajit and other such sacrifices serve merely the purpose of the desire to know (*viditṣā*)— based on statements such as "one should sacrifice when [the ritual] is defective" (*vidhivipanne yajeta*)— or that they serve merely the purpose of attaining the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*), based on statements such as "by [this] rite, the world of the ancestors [is attained]," is refuted. For this very reason, since there is no need to postulate a separate performance [of these rites for those ends], the *prayāja* and other such auxiliary rites do not [function] according to the principle of the Viśvajit (*viśvajinnyāya*) for the sake of the desire to know.
By this, the view that the Viśvajit sacrifice has the destruction of sin as its fruit— based on such scriptural statements as "by this dharma one dispels evil"— is refuted.

For if it were considered obligatory (nitya), there would arise a lack of uniformity (vairūpya) in assuming that the Viśvajit serves as a motivator (prayojaka) only when performed as a contingent rite (naimittika) occasioned by a specific cause.
Maṇḍana: "The Viśvajit sacrifice is fruitful.
Śaṅkara: "And there is a fruit for the Viśvajit.
[Viśvajin-nāyaka: "(Heaven is the fruit)."
That [result] would be heaven, because it is common to all [persons].
The Bhāṣya states: "In examples of this kind, it has been established that there is a single result.
Now, this is being questioned: is it some unspecified result, or is it heaven?

It follows that it must be "whatever [is available]," since no specific distinction is stated. To this, it is replied: "That [result] would be heaven, because it is common to all without distinction."
For all men indeed desire heaven. Why is this so? Because heaven is pleasure, and everyone seeks pleasure.
What follows from this? If it is so, then a word that expresses without qualification will not be restricted to a specific [meaning], such as "one should sacrifice" or "one should act.
Therefore, [the injunction] must have heaven as its fruit in this manner.
And there is conviction.
The Commentary states: In the world, regarding an action whose fruit has not been explicitly prescribed, there arises the conviction that heaven is its fruit;
it is said thus.
"Devadatta has established a grove; for him, heaven is certain.
Devadatta has constructed a pond; for him, heaven is certain.
What follows from this? By this reasoning, there arises a conviction regarding heaven.
Since they do not explicitly utter a statement regarding the fruit when ritual acts that lead to heaven are to be performed—understanding that it is indeed implied—we maintain this position:
that in such cases, heaven is the fruit.

Śa [objects]: It has been stated that there is a single fruit, yet it is not known what that one is; therefore, once again, either the universal applicability [of the injunction] or its lack of authority would result, because there is no determination of anything else.
This is stated as follows: "Heaven consists of unsurpassed bliss and is devoid of suffering;
indeed, many men desire it, while few desire a trifling pleasure.
When possible, the more extensive statement of the scripture is appropriate, so as to avoid excessive restriction of that which applies without distinction.
And heaven (svarga), being of the nature of supreme pleasure conjoined with suffering, is accepted by all;
yet heaven is sought only by some, as it is accompanied by suffering even among animals and is but meager.
However, the avoidance of suffering is desired by everyone, though it depends upon specific conditions.
Even with some delay, it reaches the heart.
Therefore, the supreme fruit is indeed happiness, which is easily known;
and because it is not subject to diminution, it is established as being superior to heaven.

Soma: The meaning of the Sūtra is that whatever single fruit [of action] there may be, that would be heaven (svarga), because it is common to all men. Viśvanātha: Whatever single thing is fixed as a result is not a restrictive factor;
therefore, heaven belongs to all men, for that [result] is indeed the desired heaven.
Maṇḍana: "Because it is not distinct from heaven itself" (the meaning is: because it is the most desired object by all persons). Śaṅkara: "Even in that case, for us, it is heaven alone."

Regarding the *Viśvajit* sacrifice—as in the section on the *Viśvajit*, where it is said, "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit"—since no fruit is heard [explicitly] stated there, and because an injunction (*vidhi*) cannot be established without a fruit, it is argued that when a fruit must be inferred for what is not heard, heaven (*svarga*) is the fruit, as it is desired by all.
Thus, this is the scope of the present principle: wherever a fruit is not heard in either an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) or an injunctive passage (*vidhi*), heaven is to be inferred.

In this way, it should also be inferred in other primary rites (*prakṛti*). [Regarding] the *Sāhasī* sacrifice, although heaven is not explicitly mentioned, it must be postulated according to the principle of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice (in the case of the study of the Veda).
[This is] because no fruit for the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is heard [in the scripture].
Nor can it be postulated according to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice, since for one engaged in an act for the sake of another, the desire for personal gain is impossible.
10.8.14: Therefore, gold (*suvarṇa*) should be worn.
Since there is no possibility of restriction in the sense that "it becomes *suvarṇa* [merely by being worn]," this wearing is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
Nor is there an absence of fruit here; for, according to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice, heaven (*svarga*) is to be postulated as the result.

The sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]" does not even establish the connection with the fruit, because that has already been established by the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) according to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 4.3.10–15). (Ṭupṭīkā 9.1.1.1, p. 1636)

Following the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), there are two types of sacrificial sessions (*satra*): those consisting of thirteen nights (*trayodaśarātra*) and fourteen nights (*caturdaśarātra*), and so forth; all these are specific varieties.

Generally, such a sacrifice is designated in the singular number by emphasizing the collective whole, as in the expression: "That particular sacrificial session in which there are thirteen nights is a 'thirteen-night session'.
Occasionally, however, by accepting the individual importance of each night that constitutes the whole, a single specific sacrificial session is referred to by the word *rātra* in the plural number.
In such a night-sacrifice (*rātrisatra*), heaven must be postulated as the fruit according to the principle of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice;
this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
According to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice:
in the section concerning Viśvāmitra’s inquiry into dharma, it is not as [the injunction for study] is postulated for the sake of heaven in the case of the Viśvajit.
*Ḍupū*. According to the *Viśvajit-nyāya*, this is the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) view. In *Bālakrīḍā*, page 2: "One who knows the fruit should not eat"—here there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
And for that resolve (*saṃkalpa*) of non-eating, heaven (*svarga*) must be postulated as the fruit according to the *Viśvajit-nyāya* (this is the prima facie view).

Ci. 6.2.5: Regarding such passages as “One should not eat [the sacrificial food] when one knows the fruit,” the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) to abstain from eating is enjoined for the sake of heaven (*svarga*), according to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice.

Bhāṭṭa 6.2.5: And in this case (of the pouring of gold), there is no absence of a fruit, because heaven is to be inferred by way of the Viśvajit principle. Regarding the Upāṃśuyāja sacrifice, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the preceding section, just as there was no restriction regarding the material (*dravya*), might there likewise be no restriction regarding the deity? For since the deity is known solely through scripture (*śāstra*), it is impossible to conceive of one without such scriptural authority. However, because other contextual statements—such as "He performs the Upāṃśuyāja dedicated to Agni elsewhere" and "He performs the Upāṃśuyāja dedicated to Indra elsewhere"—are connected with the terms *Āgneya* and so forth, they are interpreted as injunctions for optional deities. Alternatively, since among those very sacrifices under discussion, some exhibit the characteristics of Prajāpati and the quality of being performed in a low voice (*upāṃśutva*), one might conceive of an injunction for Prajāpati. But this conception of Prajāpati as the deity is untenable; for while Prajāpati is enjoined by the rule "One should sacrifice to Prajāpati mentally," he is characterized by the absence of form (*ūrṇābhāva*), and thus lacks the characteristic of being performed in a low voice. Furthermore, when a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is possible, it is illogical to assume non-restriction. Therefore, based on the principle of primacy, since the term *Āgneya* alone is to be observed, and by way of an option within the general injunction for the Upāṃśuyāja, there is a restriction to Agni. It is with this deliberation that the Sūtra "Or Viṣṇu" adopts the deity based on the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*).

Consequently, since there is no connection with an unrequired benefit to the observer (*draṣṭavya*), its capacity to determine the deity is logically justified; thus, the injunction of the deity is established through the wording of the mantra (*mantravarṇaka*).

The author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
the entitlement to the *sattra* belongs only to those who possess fires, not to those without fires.

Why? Because the Soma sacrifice is preceded by the *iṣṭi*, the *sattra* is preceded by the Soma sacrifice, and the *iṣṭi* is preceded by the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*). Therefore, the qualification belongs only to those who possess the sacred fires (*sāgnika*). Furthermore, because it is prompted by its own purpose.

In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that "the entitlement to the *sattra* belongs only to the masters," [the author] states another reason, indicating a collection of reasons with the particle *ca*:

"One should establish the fires" (*agnīn ādadhīta*). By means of the middle-voice ending (*ātmanepada*), it is stated that the establishment of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) is for one's own sake. Therefore, the accomplishment of another's purpose by means of another's fires is not possible.
By this, what was stated—namely, "because of the lordship over the dwelling" (6.6.5.27)—is refuted. Furthermore, it shows the *saṃnivāpa* (the collective distribution).

In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the right to perform the *sattra* belongs only to Sāmīs, [the author], indicating another reason by means of the word "and" (*ca*), states an additional argument.

The Śruti states, "Those intending to offer the Sāvitra oblations should combine [the fires]," thereby demonstrating the combining, placing together in a single pit, and unifying the fires belonging even to seventeen sacrificers prior to the Sāvitra offerings.

[Objection: Since there are no fires at all for those who possess no fires, how can there be a combining of them? Therefore, those without fires have no entitlement to the Sattra; rather, it is only for those who possess fires.
An expiation may apply in the event of an emergency.

In the sūtra, "And because of the prescription of expiation" (6.6.5.29), the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) states the rebuttal to the reason given in the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) that those without sacred fires (anagnīn) are entitled to participate in a sacrificial session (satra). He says:
the expiation prescribed by the passage beginning with "To Agni Vivici" would apply only in times of distress.

For instance, when people traveling through a forest or wilderness, or while staying there, experience terror due to the threat of bandits or the fear of an enemy, or if their fires should become mixed with a forest fire or with one another—that will be the occasion for the expiation.
But in the case of a *satra*, since the simultaneous pouring of the oblations (*saṃnivāpa*) is expressly stated by the scripture itself, there is no occasion for an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that only those who are *sāmin* (performers of the sacrifice) are entitled to participate in a *satra*.
Ke.
In the southern sacrificial hall (*dakṣiṇa-vihāra*) during the Varuṇapraghāsa rites among the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, there is a separate performance [of the mantras].
(Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 3424; see the section on "In the Varuṇapraghāsa rites in the southern sacrificial hall").
In the southern sacrificial hall during the Varuṇapraghāsa rites of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the Adhvaryu must indeed perform the recitation of the mantras separately from the Pratiprasthātṛ.
12|1|19|12. See the section on the *varuṇapraghāsa* sacrifices regarding the *pratiprasthātṛ* in the southern *vihāra*. This refers to the *vihārādhikaraṇa*. (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 3426)
The *abhimaya* [fire] is for Vedic purposes alone, not for purposes such as cooking the *sthālīpāka* and other worldly tasks.
Worldly rites are not to be performed in the *gārhapatya* fires. The *vihāra* (the sacrificial fire-arrangement) may accomplish worldly purposes because of its inherent capacity.
Commentary: "Vihāra" refers to that which is designated as the Gārhapatya fire and so forth, because it is carried forth (viharaṇāt).

It should accomplish—that is, bring about the completion of—worldly rites such as the Pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka and others, as well as other tasks to be achieved, such as cooking, burning, and illuminating; this is because of its capacity. For fire is indeed capable of casting [oblations] and of performing cooking and the like.
Furthermore, the substance fire is not produced for any specific purpose, as in the injunction, "One should establish the sacred fires in the spring.
By virtue of its inherent capacity, it is employed here and there wherever it is required;
thus is its production brought about.
*Ṭup-ṭīkā*: Should one perform whatever can be accomplished by means of the *āhavanīya* fire and so forth, or should one perform only that which is specifically prescribed?
In this regard, according to the authority of indicative mark (*liṅga*), whatever can be done should be performed—whether it be Vedic or worldly, provided it is achievable through fire.
And the prohibition against cooking meat applies in the same way.
Commentary: The prohibition against cooking meat is likewise. Just as it has been taught in the Nyāya:
"They should not cook meat for their own sake; if they were to cook it, they would commit an act of theft."
For while the preparation of meat occurs in worldly cooking, it does not occur in Vedic [cooking]; the cooking of meat takes place at the *śāmitra* fire.
Because of the specific injunction, this should apply to Vedic rites. The Commentary states: "The sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) should serve the purpose of Vedic rituals, not worldly ones."
Why? Because of the specific instruction (*nirdeśāt*).

The function of the Gārhapatya and other fires is specifically instructed by such sentences as, "When one offers in the Āhavanīya, thereby that fire becomes pleased," and so forth. That requirement for a function belonging to the Upabhṛt is fulfilled by these descriptions.
Therefore, it has been withdrawn for this very purpose.
Consequently, they would apply to worldly [acts].
For those as well, the oblation would necessarily take place only in the Āhavanīya fire.
This is not a fault.

The statement, "One offers in the Āhavanīya," is intended solely as a restrictive rule (niyama). For even without such a declaration, the offering would take place in the Āhavanīya, and elsewhere in the morning.
This is the intermediate position (*madhyāsana*), wherein the scope [of the rule] is understood through the contingency of non-restriction (*aniyama*).
And in the case of Vedic matters, the contingency of non-restriction arises because no specific location has been specified.
But for worldly [rituals], the location has been specified: the domestic fire (aupāsana).

Therefore, those [offerings] would necessarily be performed only in the Āhavanīya fire. This being the position reached, [the author] says: *Ṭup-ṭīkā*: Thus, when this [objection] has been raised, he says:
The fires that have arisen for the Āhavanīya are rendered free of expectancy by the sentence itself:
"He offers oblations in the Āhavanīya," "He cooks the sacrificial offerings on the Gārhapatya," and "He cooks the Anvāhārya rice on the Dakṣiṇāgni.
Furthermore, it is not possible to enjoin these [fires] in a worldly context.
For indeed, the oblations and other rites are performed by means of the great fire-altar,
as in the case of the *padahomas*; moreover, this is because the domestic fire (*aupāsana*) is seen [to be used] when [the altar] exists.

The Commentary states: And while the sacrificial enclosure (*vihāra*) exists, the *aupāsana* fire is prescribed [in the text]: "He who should desire, 'May the kingdom be for his progeny,' should sacrifice, having offered an animal dedicated to Pratiha at the *aupāsana* fire.
This statement occurs when the *rājasūya* ritual has commenced;
at that time, the sacrificial enclosure exists.
And if this very [fire] were to accomplish the purpose of worldly activities, then while it exists, the *aupāsana* fire would not exist because there would be no function for it;
and this is because its absence is observed.
The Commentary states: "It shows the absence of the cooking of meat on the sacrificial fire (*vaihārika-agni*)."

"Indeed, when one offers meat into these fires, the fires of the sacrificer devour it; they meditate upon the sacrificer himself and consume the sacrificer. Others indeed cook meat in the fires in vain; therefore, he avoids offering meat to these sacrificial fires (*vaihārika*).
For this reason also, there is no fire for the sacrificial rite (*vihāra*) among worldly fires."
The cooking of meat would be a case of a prohibition of what has been enjoined, because of its connection with the oblation.
The Commentary states: As for the claim that "the prohibition of cooking meat is like that," it would be a case of a prohibition of what has been enjoined.
The cooking of the omentum (vapā) in the Āhavanīya fire has been prescribed;
this is its prohibition. Why? Because it is already established [as required], and because of its connection with the oblation (āhuti).
Regarding that fire, the supplementary statement is heard in connection with the oblations: "He does not cook meat in that fire in which he offers the oblations.
And since the oblations are offered in the Āhavanīya fire, this prohibition refers to the cooking of the omentum (vapā).

Or rather, it is the remainder of the *vāmī* [cow] that is used for the procedure beginning with the southern fire. The commentary states: "Alternatively, there is this other resolution: the cooking of the wife's vow-food (*vrata*) is prescribed in the southern fire."

When the flesh of the mouth and the lips is taken for the purpose of the vow (*vrata*), then it must be cooked in the *dakṣiṇāgni*; this sentence regarding the cooking of the vow-food in the *dakṣiṇāgni*—"except for meat"—is a supplement to that [rule].
Furthermore, the oblation in the *dakṣiṇāgni* is heard in the text: "She who is Sarasvatī, the one who dwells in the house.
Therefore, it is understood that the intention refers to the *dakṣiṇāgni*.

Śabara: Is the *gārhapatya* fire the locus for all [rituals], both the worldly ones—such as the cooking of the *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka*, the *caru*, the *guḍa*, and the *āhuti*—and the Vedic ones, such as the boiling (*śrapaṇa*) and so forth? Or is it only for the Vedic ones? In this doubt, [the conclusion is: because of its capacity (*sāmarthya*), because it is the occasioning cause (*nimitta*), because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), and because of the observation of the prohibition against cooking meat [only in the *gārhapatya*], it serves all purposes.
It is replied: "He boils the oblations (*havīṃṣi*) on the *gārhapatya* fire; he cooks the *anvāhārya* rice on the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire; he... [The text continues with specific ritual injunctions.]
Thus it is established. However, rites such as the *khālīpāka* are prescribed for the *aupāsana* fire, not for the general fires such as the *gārhapatya* and others.
Therefore, the ritual arrangement (*vihāra*) is an auxiliary only for Vedic rites.

Previously, the common and uncommon [applications] of external consecrations (*saṃskāra*) were examined; by way of that context, the common and uncommon [applications] of the sacred fires (*agni*) were also examined—this is the connection.
Regarding this: "The sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) serves all purposes or only Vedic purposes, because it possesses the capacity [for both].
The first [position holds], because [the fires] have no further requirements once they are satisfied by direct scriptural statements; therefore, the latter [position holds]."

Bhaṭṭa: When the Āhavanīya and other fires, having been produced by the rite of *ādhāna*, stand in need of a purpose, they are—by their very capacity and through the inference that they must be accomplished by means of fire—distinguished from ordinary worldly things. Consequently, sentences such as "One offers oblations in the Āhavanīya," "One cooks the sacrificial offerings on the Gārhapatya," and "One cooks the sacrificial offerings in the Dakṣiṇāgni" are merely partial restatements (*avayutyānuvāda*) of what is already established. Alternatively, even if these sentences were taken as the actual injunctions for their application, nevertheless, because of the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), one should accept only these [fires] for other ritual acts, since activity proceeds toward them alone; for there would be the complication (*gaurava*) of having to postulate other fires.

This being the case, although it might follow from their inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*) that they serve all purposes, their universal application is precluded precisely because the injunctions regarding their specific locations would otherwise be rendered meaningless. Nor is there any extension of their use to other contexts. For this very reason, these [fires] are not included even among those fires unique to other [Vedic] traditions (*āgnyantara*), because there is a prohibition against taking them as receptacles (*āyatana*), and because the Smṛtis record prohibitions against cooking and other such acts in the Śrauta fires; furthermore, among the Smārta rites, the *aupāsana* fire alone is the primary locus.
Therefore, the application of these fires in oblations and similar rites is restricted solely to the Śrauta fires.

For this very reason, it is said: "Truly, for one who performs the *āhuti* sacrifice, the sacrificial fires do not merely consume [the offerings] but meditate upon the sacrificer himself and intend for the sacrificer; they indeed cook even the meat of others in vain, yet for them there exists no other desire for meat than this. Thus, the cessation of the consumption of meat other than that from the animal-sacrifice (*paśubandha*), as well as the avoidance of worldly meat, follows the maxim of the tree and its shade.
This maxim operates when one intends to express the attainment of a goal that is established by itself, without effort.
For example, it is well known that a tree is sustained by water and the rays of the moon;
thus Kālidāsa said: "The livelihood of a tree requires no other means. This is not [an instance of] rashness.
956. When the word "tree" (vṛkṣa) is uttered, only the meaning of the tree revolves in the mind, not accompanied by anything else;
however, when the [compound] word is uttered, a mutual conjunction (itaretarayoga) is perceived, and that is its meaning.

"Of those with qualifiers, there is no [compound] formation," and so forth.
*Maṇi*, p. 146. The arrangement of the recitation as a completed unit (*vṛtta*) occurs either when the sense of the *ṛc*s is not yet concluded, or [as a rule].
2|1|0|25. Furthermore, the narration of another episode is not for the purpose of becoming that episode itself; rather, it is solely for the sake of generating interest (*prarocanā*).

Bhāṣya 2.1.30: "The narration of an untrue event is for the purpose of praise, because praise is what is understood [therein].
