Since that [narration] is neither a motivator nor a deterrent toward the actual event, it is purposeless and thus not intended to be expressed.
Bhāṣya 1.2.120.

Alternatively, the rule regarding the abandonment of one's own meaning (*svārtha*) is not mandatory. Therefore, we describe [the figurative usage] as having its own meaning precisely by means of abandoning the status of being a praise (*stuti*).
It has been stated that all words occurring in a poetic composition (*vṛtta*) are "non-abandoners of their own meaning" (*ajahatsvārtha*). Thus it was said.

Su. Pṛ. 1080: It has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya that all *vṛtti*s do not abandon their own meanings (*ajahasvārthatva*), as in [the discussion on] 1.4.1–3; and it was also stated by the author of the Sūtras in the rule 3.2.19, "Now, because of this being seen elsewhere... (atha etat anyatrāpi dṛṣṭatvāt). Pṛ. 1447: The removal of the *vṛtti* consists of the inclusion of the sense of the causal agent (*āpanna*) and so forth, as formulated by Kātyāyana in Bhā. 12.16.15.2. In the view that there is a *vṛtti*, the compound is not mandatory;
therefore, this restriction for that purpose appears to yield only a very slight result.
pp. 39–40. Furthermore, even according to the established doctrine of others (*pareṣām api siddhānte*), no such false suspicion arises regarding this [point].
For it is maintained that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as cognized by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpakapratyaya*) alone is the object of conceptual cognitions (*savikalpaka*).
And that characteristic exists in reality (*paramārthataḥ*).
However, cognition whose object is accompanied by a mental construct (*sadeṣaviṣaya*) is true and not false, just like non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpakajñāna*).

This much, however, is the distinction: that which was previously apprehended along with the non-conceptual cognition—the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—its subsequent synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*), namely its conjunction (*yojana*) with other objects, through this [synthesis] this conceptual cognition arises. Non-conceptual cognition, on the other hand, arises without such prior synthesis.
Even in this established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the state of being an object cognized by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpakapramiti*) remains exactly the same.

Since the subsequent synthetic cognition (*anusandhānapratyaya*) also possesses the same object, it is not tenable to claim that the conceptual (*savikalpaka*) is false while the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) is true;
thus, such a distinction is non-existent.
For these two [characteristics] do not exist for worldly people.
Therefore, since there is no suspicion of falsity, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) does not exist; thus, the refutation is useless.
(Page 40, *Bṛhatī*): But surely you yourself have stated, "Let there be this much distinction."

By this distinction, it has been stated by others: "The object being synthesized [by the cognition], because it belongs to the domain of the *saṃhitā* (the continuous sequence), is not at all the object of a single cognition; rather, its state of being delimited is not apprehended by that cognition. However, it does attain the status of being an objective support (*ālambanatā*).
(p. 40). [Commentary: "But surely, by you yourself..."—this is the support for the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

It has been stated by others that, through this very distinction—namely, the connection with universals (*jāti*) alone—a thing is born [as an object of conceptualization]. That specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is the form of the external object as apprehended by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*), does not become the object determined (*paricchedya*) by a conceptual cognition (*vikalpapratyaya*), though it does serve as its objective support (*ālambana*).

This is the intended meaning: an external object cannot be conjoined with universals and so forth, because conceptualization is of such a nature [as being restricted to its own internal representation]. Rather, even without grasping that [external object], conceptual cognitions appear as if they possess the conceit of having grasped it.
In accordance with that conceit, they are held to have that as their objective support;
however, in ultimate reality, they are indeed without any objective support.
And thus, falsity has already been stated by the opponents themselves.
Page 40. Bṛhatī: Therefore, they maintain that the synthesizing cognition (*anusaṃdhānapratyaya*) possesses the quality of determinative discernment (*paricchedakatva*), just like memory.

And in this established doctrine (*rāddhānta*) of the Mīmāṃsakas, even conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor is this [the case] for others who assert that the synthesizing cognition is merely conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*).
It is established that there are two [types of invalidating factors], namely sublation (*bādha*) and defects in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣa*).
Therefore, for one who desires this [scripture] to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), this restriction was formulated [in the Bhāṣya].
But how, then, do they consider the synthetic cognition (*anusaṃdhāna-pratyaya*) to be conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)?
(The opponent says:
There is a difference between the universal and the possessor of the universal, because a difference is admitted in the synthetic cognition [of them];
people in the world understand "this is a cow" as "this substance possesses cowness," not as "this is the substance cowness."

But is it not the case that even when there is a cognition of difference, a metaphorical identification (abhedopacāra) is observed, as in "Bring in the spears"? True, there is a metaphorical identification;
however, ordinary people do not have a metaphorical cognition in the case of "This is a cow."
Therefore, it cannot be said that this cognition is merely metaphorical;
nor does this cognition terminate solely in the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because it involves the synthesis of other objects.
Hence, we consider this to be a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
If this cognition were one that apprehends [an object] otherwise, how could it be subverted? (Subversion is a sublating cognition.
It is said:
For where a substance is determined as having the nature of another substance, there subversion occurs.

Furthermore, this "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth is not a separate substance, because it is not perceived as distinct from its particular instances (*viśeṣa*), unlike [colors such as] blue or yellow.

For precisely because these particulars are apprehended by a cognition of a universal, those who understand conceptual construction (*vikalpavidaḥ*) maintain that this and that cognition—which are objects of valid means of knowledge—is a conceptual construction.
By this very same reasoning, the postulation of qualities (*guṇakalpanā*) is also explained, since they too are not perceived separately.
But is it not the case that the name is indeed grasped separately?
No;
for even there, one says, "This is Viṣṇumitra," or "This is Adityapratyaya."

However, there is this distinction: in the conceptualization of genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*), in one case there is the conceptualization of difference between two things that are non-different, while in the other case there is the conceptualization of difference between two things that are different (*i.e.*, between two non-different genera). [Furthermore,] there is the conceptualization of non-difference between two things that are different, namely the name (*nāman*) and the named (*nāmin*).
Therefore, this is a distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), not a distinction of conceptualizations.

But surely, in the case of the conceptualization of action (*karma*), neither of these two is possible; for it is understood and designated that the connection exists only between two distinct things, namely the action and its agent (*kāraka*).
(Answer: It is not so; here too, it is understood that there is merely a metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) of non-difference.

This is because we observe the use of a generalizing suffix (*sāmānyika-pratyaya*) in such expressions as "Devadatta cooks" (*pacati devadattaḥ*). But is it not the case that even grammatical discordance (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is observed, as in "He cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*) and "He cooks with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*)? [And] it is also said, "It is cooked."

[The opponent asks: "By Devadatta"—what is it that is being perceived here? [The answer is: Because of the observation of a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). For a lack of coreferentiality is observed even in the case of universals (*jāti*) and so forth, as in: "the state of a cow is cowness" (*gorbhāvo gotvam*), "the whiteness of the cloth" (*paṭasya śuklatvam*), and "this is its name" (*asyeyaṃ saṃjñā*).
This designation is made with reference to the conceptualization of [the universal] as both distinct and non-distinct [from the individual].
Furthermore, there is no comprehension of a distinct object that is not [already] differentiated.
Therefore, this conceptual construction (kalpanā) is also [of the form] "Devadatta. (p.
40–46). *Ṛju*: Just as grammatical non-co-referentiality (vaiyadhikaraṇya) is observed, so too is grammatical co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).

Furthermore, it is not possible for a single entity to possess both difference and non-difference; therefore, this [entity] cannot be either different or non-different, because these two perceptions are mutually contradictory and thus annul one another.
And a cognition that manifests a non-existent object is nothing but mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*).
Just as a difference in grammatical substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is observed in the case of an action, so it is also in the cases of genus, quality, and name;
yet these are not distinct, because they are understood as non-different.
Therefore, it should be understood that that which is non-existent is sometimes conceptualized as distinct and sometimes as non-distinct.
As stated in the *Bṛhatī*: "The same applies even to a substance; for instance, in the case of 'this man is a staff-bearer,' there is a figurative treatment of non-difference."

Therefore, conceptualization regarding the five objects—[namely, name, genus, quality, action, and substance]—is neither a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor a non-means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). [He begins the formal conclusion: It is said:
Conceptual cognition would exist if knowledge were accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, he will state that knowledge is inferential (*ānumānika*).
Now, in the view that knowledge is not directly perceived, the object of support for knowledge is its form alone; otherwise, the arising of knowledge would not be possible.
What is this "otherwise-being" (*anyathābhāva*)? This is the otherwise-being: for mother-of-pearl is manifested as silver.
That cognition has mother-of-pearl as its objective support (*ālambana*), not silver.
How is this known? Because it is seen when the eye is in contact with mother-of-pearl, and because it does not arise otherwise.
For no one else designates a mother-of-pearl shell as "silver.
Indeed, only one with impaired vision perceives the mother-of-pearl as silver, thinking, "My vision is defective regarding silver.
Therefore, that cognition has the mother-of-pearl shell as its objective support (ālambana), not silver.
And this is not possible on the view that cognition is non-perceptual;
therefore, it must be understood that there exists a cognition even when its objective aspect is non-existent.
This is the fivefold conceptualization.
But surely, on the view that the object of cognition is a non-existent form, it follows that cognition would be entirely without an object (*nirālambanatā*).
Not so;
for on the view that there is no object, the designation of one thing by means of another is not tenable.
Furthermore, this designation "silver" occurs with respect to mother-of-pearl.

For, according to the view that [cognition] is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), what could be designated by what, since the cognition of mother-of-pearl and the cognition of silver are distinct?
(pp. 46–47). *Ṛju*: "But surely... it follows."
The meaning of this is as follows: when a cognition appears in a certain form, that [object] is said to be its objective support (*ālambana*).
However, mother-of-pearl does not possess the form of silver;
therefore, mother-of-pearl is not the objective support for a cognition that has the form of silver.
Therefore, the objection is that this [cognition] would necessarily result in being objectless (*nirālambana*). To this, we say: "It is not so.

The meaning of this is as follows: for if the cognition of silver were objectless, there could be no designation of "silver" with respect to the mother-of-pearl, because the mother-of-pearl and the cognition of silver would be distinct entities.
In one case, the mother-of-pearl is the objective support (*ālambana*), while in the other, it is without an objective support (*nirālambana*).
Yet, this designation exists.
Therefore, this is indeed a single cognition that takes the mother-of-pearl itself as its objective support in the form of silver.
*Bṛhatī* (p. 46–47): [Objection] Even on the view that the object is the support (*ālambana*), it is not tenable that a cognition having one form has as its support an object having another form.
*Ṛjuvimalā*: "Support-cognition" (*ālambanajñāna*) means the cognition of a support.
On this view—that only a support is cognized and not a non-support—it is not tenable that the support has one form while the cognition grasping it has another form.
Page 47. Bṛhatī: This indeed is the "object-nature" (ālambanatva) of an object—that it produces a cognition having the very form of that object.
Otherwise, even if [the object] is present, there would be no designation of it as an "object" (ālambana) in the production of cognition, just as in the case of the eyes and other [senses].
Rju: This indeed is the "object-nature" of an object—that it generates a cognition having its own form.

If, however, the object were merely a causal factor (*kāraka*), then just as the eyes and other sense organs—which are active in the production of cognition—lack the status of being an objective support (*ālambana*), so too would the object lack it.
Therefore, that which is intended to be the objective support must also exist in the form of the cognition;

Prohibition (*niṣedha*) refers to those Vedic statements intended to turn a person away from actions that lead to undesirable results, such as "One should not eat *kalañja*," and so forth.

Just as in that case, the particle *laṭ* expresses the immediate succession of the place [of study] following the study of the Veda, so too here, a thing not stated by any other means of valid cognition [is understood].
It is to be inferred; another [sequence] is [established] by another [text], and therein he speaks of immediate succession (*ānantarya*) from something else.

(Ṭupṭīkā 5.1.91, pp. 1289–90). Regarding the statement "having studied the Veda, [one should remain] at home," this expresses the knowledge of the *adhyayana* (study) and *samāvartana* (graduation) as having a sequential relationship and a common agent;
it does not, however, express immediate succession.

VI. 1.11.9: Just as in the statement, "Having prepared the Veda [altar-ground], one prepares the Vedi [sacrificial altar]," a scriptural sentence prescribes a sequence of performance, so too do such passages as, "Having taken up the *graha* cup or having lifted the *camasa* vessel, one performs the *stotra* chant. Māṭhara 4.4.2: The intention of those Mīmāṃsakas who explain the Veda according to logic (*nyāya*) and tradition (*saṃpradāya*) is now set forth.
They understand the meaning of a sentence by following the power of the words;
therein, that which is mounted upon the power [of the word] is what they intend to explain.
But that which is abandoned by their capacity cannot be explained by them.
Or [as stated in] PMS 3.1.133, p. 709: "And some [hold that] the Vedas are of recent origin, being designated by human names.
Some indeed declare the Vedas to be of recent origin;
that is, they are of a proximate time.

The Vedas are of human origin and are contemporary, because they are designated by the names of persons— for indeed, the Vedas are handed down by persons as the *Kāṭhaka*, the *Kālāpaka*, and the *Paippalādaka*—
and because we observe impermanent things within them.
In the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the Vedas are recent and of human origin, this is the second sūtra establishing the reason:
"The observation of certain men subject to birth and death is found in the Veda;
those men are mentioned in the Veda."
The name "the tradition of Vṛṣa Prāvāhaṇa" implies that those Vedas were produced from that person at a later time;
therefore, these Vedas are recent and of human origin.
But it has been stated that [the Veda] is preceded by the Word.

Refuting as being logical the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) reached through the two preceding sūtras—that the Vedas are recent and composed by persons—the author states the established conclusion (siddhānta):
"The Vedas are not recent."
Because we have stated that for students there is the state of being preceded by the word (*śabdapūrvatva*).
(By "word" here, what is intended is study produced by the word.
For all persons, study is dependent upon [prior] study.)
For all [students] desire to learn exactly as it was studied by their teacher;
indeed, there is no one at all who is an independent first student of the Vedas who could be their author.
Therefore, due to the absence of any recollection of an author, the Vedas are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).
Vaidyanāthī:
Regarding the names [of the Vedas],
in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) that "the Vedas are designated as persons," the designations such as *Kāṭhaka* and *Taittirīyaka* are cited as authoritative evidence.
To this, the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) replies:
The Vedas are indeed authorless (apauruṣeya).
As for the designations such as "Kāṭhaka" and so forth, they must arise from the act of recitation (pravacana).
Because a certain branch was specifically taught by Kaṭha to his disciples, the name *Kāṭhaka* became established for that portion of the Veda.
Similarly, [the texts] proclaimed by Tittiri are called *Taittirīyaka*, and so forth. Thus, these designations are based on the act of teaching (*pravacana*), and not—
The [objections] regarding the Vedas (sūtra 3.1.7) are based on the grounds of the Vedas having an author:
"And some say that the Vedas, being recent, are designated by human names."
According to the rule at *Pāṇini-sūtra* 1.1.8.27, the word *ākhyā* in this sūtra should be in the plural;
however, in the Bhāṣya it is cited in the singular.
Nevertheless, this is merely a commonality of phonetic form (*śrutisāmānyamātram*).

The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) refutes the reasoning of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa). As for the further reason stated—namely, "because of the observation of non-eternality"—that is merely a similarity of sound; there is only a similarity in the word "śruti," but [Pravāhaṇi] is not the offspring of Pravāhaṇa.
Thus, the word *ityārthaka* [is used].
The root *vahati* is established in the sense of "carrying" when preceded by *pra*, and [the root *dā*] is established in the sense of "giving" when preceded by *śabda*;
however, no specific compound of these two is established.
The vowel *i* is established in the same way for the offspring as it is for the agent in the action;
therefore, he who causes to flow is the Prāvāhaṇi, namely Vāyu. The word *vatra* is an imitation of sound.
Therefore, these two words will denote that very object which is eternal.
Alternatively, there may be an application [of the word] based on its connection with the action performed.

But [one might ask]: "How can the authority of Vedic sentences such as 'The cows indeed performed this sacrificial session,' 'The serpents performed a sacrificial session,' and 'He extracted his own omentum' be maintained, given that they appear to be the utterances of those who are negligent?"
On this point, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) says:
the word "dā" (the particle *dā*) serves to dispel doubt.
The suffix *kta* in the word "kṛte" has the sense of either the abstract state (*bhāve*) or the object (*karmaṇi*).
In the case of rituals such as the *satra*, there would be an application (*viniyoga*) or syntactic connection (*anvaya*) for passages such as "The cows performed the *satra*," by way of praise;
for these [passages] are in close proximity (*saṃnidhi*) to the ritual of the *satra* and its like, which stand in need of praise, and thus possess the nature of a *saṃbandha*.

Consequently, those sentences serve the purpose of praising the *satra* ritual and do not have their own literal meaning as their primary referent; therefore, they are not like the incoherent prattle of a madman.
Therefore, the Vedas, being of non-human origin, are the authority for Dharma. For even before the refinement [of the word] by means of the Veda— such as through elision and so forth—
the status of the word as a genus-term (jātiśabda), which is accepted by the world, enters into its formation.

Or [as stated in] Vākyapadīya 1.4.7.10, p. 343: "By the Veda itself, through its context and its instrumental function, the distinction between correct and incorrect forms is established. (3.4.8.20). Now, one might object: since both Vedic and worldly usage are established through the recitation of every word—according to the maxim, "The Vedic forms are established by the Veda, and the worldly forms are established from common usage; therefore, grammar is useless"—there is no need for grammar to determine the expressive power of words. Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Su. Pṛ. 310: "Having known [the Veda], we are capable of performing [its injunctions] accordingly, but we are not able to interrogate the Veda, asking: 'Why does this [Veda] enjoin something useless? or, when it does so enjoin, 'For what purpose is it being preserved with such effort?
(Vākyapadīya 1.2.1.2, p. 106). Regarding the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Veda:
"The defect of having a beginning would attach to the Veda; that is not tenable" (Vākyapadīya 3.1.7.14, p. 825).
Bhāṣya 1.1.8.19: "The Veda has authority regarding matters that are to be accomplished.
Bṛhatī, p. 16: "The Veda has authority only regarding what is to be done.
On this point, others—whose discrimination is obscured by the swelling influence of immature learning—raise an objection.

But how can the meaning of the Veda consist of something to be accomplished (*kārya*), given that the Vedāntas have as their object only that which is already established (*siddha*), as is perceived in such passages as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*Vṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.9.28)?
It might be argued that because those [passages] are incomplete, a suitable injunctive verb is supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).
But that is not so, because of the incompleteness [of such usage] due to the absence of a cause. Or, it might be argued:
the derivation of words in their own meanings occurs only within the linguistic usage of elders.
Furthermore, because linguistic usage consists of engagement and withdrawal, and because engagement and withdrawal are preceded by the comprehension of a task (kārya),
the meaning denoted by every word is necessarily associated with a task. And in this case [of the Upaniṣads], there is no task.
"Therefore, because [a sentence] would be incomplete without a connection to an action (*kārya*), an action is supplied [as the object of the injunction].
This is merely a conceptual construction of one's own school (*svasamaya*).

For even without [an explicit] worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) is possible regarding sentences whose meaning is already established (*siddhārtha*) and which lack a connection to an action, such as "A son has been born to you," and so forth.

[Objection: Is it not the case that "acquisition" (*vyutpatti*) is defined as the determination of a word’s power with respect to its own meaning, which occurs through the word, after one has inferred a cognition whose object is a specific thing?
And yet, without linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), it is impossible to infer the cognition of another person. [Reply: It is said:
The cognition of others is indeed capable of being inferred through signs such as a brightened countenance and serenity, which correspond to verbal expressions of joy and the like.
Serenity and so forth infer joy,
and that joy, in turn, infers its cause.
Furthermore, the comprehension of a desired object is a cause of joy,
and that comprehension is brought about by the utterance of a sentence.
Thus, it is understood that by the statement "A son has been born to you," the comprehension of an object that serves as a cause of joy has been produced.
Realizing that the cause of joy belongs to the person alone, one determines that the word’s capacity has as its object a specific meaning.

Furthermore, through the methods of insertion and deletion (*āvāpa-udvāra*), linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) is established here just as it is in everyday usage for each individual word; thus, this is faultless.
Moreover, even though linguistic acquisition occurs through words accompanied by case-endings, there is also the present indicative form "he cooks with wood-sticks" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*).
One acquires proficiency regarding the word "wood" precisely with respect to that which is devoid of connection to an action.

Furthermore, even if words possess only the sense of being connected [to something else] during the acquisition of proficiency within worldly usage (*vyavahāra*), nevertheless, proficiency does not consist in their denoting what is connected to an action;
rather, it consists in their denoting another object altogether.
For whoever desires that [words] denote [an object] as associated with a qualifier necessarily desires that they denote [an object] as associated with another meaning.
And since the application and comprehension [of words] are accomplished by that much alone, it is not possible to postulate that they denote [an object] as associated with a qualifier.
Furthermore, in common worldly usage, most sentences are seen to have already established meanings, such as "Are you well? or "I am well," and so forth.
Furthermore, that which is called an "effect" (kārya) is precisely that which has a required means (apekṣitopāya).
Therefore, the fact that ritual actions possess a required means is already established and understood from sentences whose primary purport is the effect.
Consequently, the meaning of the Veda is indeed something already established.
This is merely the talk of children, and it is only by children that such a view is held in high regard. For linguistic proficiency cannot possibly arise without the usage of elders;
indeed, comprehension directed toward a specific meaning necessarily depends upon the conceptualization of the denotation of that specific meaning.
Furthermore, joy does not suffice for the inference of a specific cause of joy;
nor can there be a determination of a specific cause through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*),
because it is impossible to ascertain through elimination those causes of joy that exist in the three periods of time, as they are remote and concealed.

Furthermore, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), which perceives only objects qualified by action through direct perception, serves as the cause for postulating that words denote qualified objects; it constitutes the primary path toward the acquisition of linguistic competence (*vyutpatti*).
From the very beginning, all words are understood to denote [objects] as connected with an action to be accomplished (*kāryānvita*).

For this very reason, even in the case of a word denoting the present tense, such as in "he cooks with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*), the linguistic competence acquired is likewise restricted to that which is connected with an action to be accomplished, because it conforms to the internal relationship with an object connected to an action to be accomplished.
The claim that words are understood through usage as denoting merely an object conjoined with something else according to one's whim is also the talk of a child.

Since in all instances of the linguistic practice of elders there is the cognition of an object conjoined with an action (*kārya*), it is impossible to postulate that words denote an object merely conjoined with something else.

If even the conjunction with an action were ever to deviate [from the usage], then one might postulate the denotation of an object merely conjoined with something else; but such a deviation does not exist.

But surely, even without a connection to an action, one who is told "this ground is sinking" engages in activity, and one who is told "this path is obstructed by a thorn" desists; likewise, when these things are taught, activity occurs in one who desires to avoid the sinking, and desistance occurs in one who desires to abandon the obstacle.
To this we reply:
Wherever engagement and withdrawal exist, there exists the comprehension of the effect which serves as their cause;
for those two do not occur without it.
And because the word is infinite, an observer standing nearby infers that it has been understood by means of the word itself.

Nor does the fact that a word intended for a specific purpose is not heard constitute a lack of causality on the part of the word, since there is no contradiction in its being a stable denoter even when there is ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and so forth. Furthermore, because the specific item to be supplied is not established by mere general fitness (*yogyatā*), [the word remains the cause].

Nor can it be assumed that the word is indifferent toward the comprehension of the effect, on the grounds that such comprehension cannot be achieved by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is because we observe the commencement of activity upon hearing the word, and because, through the principle of parsimony (*ānantarya*), it is understood that the word itself is the cause therein. However, if that same object were obtained by another means of valid cognition as well, then the word might indeed be considered a mere reiteration (*anuvāda*) rather than the cause.
Furthermore, being merely repetitive (*anuvādakatva*) is not a defect of human statements.

Therefore, since in all conventional sentences there is no deviation from the connection with an action—whether through direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*), implication (*adhyāhāra*), or otherwise—it is established that there is an expression of what is connected to that [action]; specifically, that verbal suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) express the action itself.
Consequently, all words denote an object only as connected to an action.
Nor is there an absence of an object for every individual word, since its purposefulness is established even through an indirect sequence (*praṇāḍyā*).

And when relying upon such a sequence, the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the apprehension of the mutual relationship between the meanings of the various words. Otherwise, if there were no object for each word, there would be a distinction in experience; consequently, among the distinct purposes of the injunctions (*niyoga*), there would be a lack of integration, due to the difference from the case of being bound by a single [accessory], such as the red rope (*aruṇaikahāyanī*).
Furthermore, the comprehension of mutual relationship would itself be an action;
this has been established more thoroughly by those whose intellects have mastered the *pratipadādhikaraṇa* (PMS 2.1.1).

However, as for that usage in common worldly practice which consists merely of an accomplished fact (*siddhārtha*), it should be regarded as figurative (*lakṣaṇika*) because, being "like worldly usage" (*lokavat*), it is directed toward an object already known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
For the connection with the task (kārya) is subject to deviation from mutual concomitance; thus, the justification for its being figurative is established.
Furthermore, "task-ness" (kāryatā) does not consist in being a means to a desired end.
A task is that which is to be accomplished by an effort of will (kṛti).

The means (*sādhana*) is the instrument (*upāya*). And while the means to that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is distinct [from it], nevertheless, action characterized by affliction (*kleśa*) is perceived as the "thing to be done" (*kārya*) by virtue of being the required means; thus, for the dull-witted, there arises the delusion that the state of being an effect (*kāryatā*) does not deviate from the state of being a means (*sādhanatā*), [taking the means itself to be the end].
And thus, it is easily accomplished by oneself.

Since all words in this way denote that which is connected to an action (*kāryānvita*), if in the Vedāntas a suitable action can be obtained through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and other means, then the Vedāntas would likewise have action as their sole purpose. If, however, no such action is found, then they possess no denotative power at all, due to the absence of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).
Therefore, even the rejection of injunctions does not cause any harm to the Vedāntas.
Consequently, it is established that the authority of the Veda resides solely in the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished). (*Rjuvimalā*, pp. 16–18)

Because the Veda is eternal (vedasya nityatvāt), the activity of persons consists merely in the prohibition of what has already been uttered; thus, the Veda is not subject to questioning as if it were an agent.
(Vākyapadīya 3.1.7.4, p. 723). Since the Veda consists of words (padarūpatvāt) and words consist of eternal phonemes (nityavarṇarūpatvena), they possess no dependence upon a cause.
Because the Veda does not depend upon a source [for its authority], its validity is firmly established. Vaiyānathī. 1.1.2.

Just as the Veda possesses authority because it is free from defects in its speaker, so too does an ordinary worldly word, since there is no difference in their lack of beginning (*anāditva*). Vārttika 3.1.925, p. 884. The [passages] such as "the calf's knee" (*vatsajānu*) in the Veda serve only for human purposes. Bhāṣya 4.1.2.2, Section 2. Because the Veda consists of injunctions and prohibitions, whatever is heard therein is understood as being inherently connected to those [injunctions and prohibitions].

In this regard, it should be applied in every respect according to the manner in which [the Veda] becomes the object of injunctions and prohibitions. (Vārttika 3.1.7.3, p. 703). Regarding the view that the entire Veda pertains to *iṣṭi* sacrifices, *ekāha*, *ahīna*, and *sattra* rites: (Sūtra 3.1.9.1, p. 804). Since the study of the entire Veda is enjoined by the rule of study (*adhyayanavidhi*), it is illogical for it to be purposeless if its meaning were not determined.
Su. P. 774: By the reason characterized as the force of the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi-sāmarthya*), it is determined that the entire Veda is a composed work (*grantha*).
P. 394: It is determined solely by the power of the injunction for study that the entire Veda culminates in a purposeful meaning.
P. 21: Furthermore, if there were an injunction in the case of *itihāsa*, the defect of having a beginning (*ādimattā*) would attach to the Veda.
Bhāṣya 9.1.154: Thus far, the authority of the entire Veda has been stated (in the first and second quarters of the first chapter).
1.3.1.9: For the purpose of that [Veda] is seen to be the comprehension of ritual action;
and the venerable ritualists do not declare that its fruit results from mere study alone.

Furthermore, even regarding that which is common and connected [to the ritual], he will state in Sūtra 4.3.1.1—“In the case of substances, purificatory acts, and rituals, because they are for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit is merely an *arthavāda*”—that such mentions are explanatory praises (*arthavāda*).
Regarding the self-validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) of the Veda with respect to Dharma:

Bṛhatī 1.1.15 states that the very absence of any recollection of an author—qualified by the absence of other means of knowledge proving its being composed by a person—is itself the proof for the Veda’s lack of human origin; thus, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) in this argument.
Bhāṭṭa 1.1.1: "How could all the seasons lie down separately?"—thus the study of the entire Veda is enjoined by scripture.
Bhāṣya 3.8.8.18: Even among the three Vedas, there is in some places a state of being permeated by other meters as a means [of recitation].
Vārttika 3.2.8.43: Although the Vedas are eternal like space, it is logically consistent that they are presided over by the Supreme Self.

Su. Pṛ. 1009: Even in the Veda, due to the force of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), one must resort to figurative interpretation (*guṇavāda*) regarding the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*). Vākyārtha, p. 20: Even in the Veda, many injunctions are indeed prescribed that are touched by or have a scent of perceptible purposes; however, this does not entail a lack of basis in the Veda (*vedamūlatva*). Vā. 1.3.7, p. 206: Even in the Veda, both intention and non-intention are possible in their primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*) alone, given the acceptance that the entire world is presided over by a conscious being.

Just as the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) is possible for those selves (*ātman*) residing in bodies composed of earth, water, fire, air, ether, and the vital breaths, because they possess consciousness and the capacity for knowledge; so too, the intention to speak is possible for those selves residing in bodies such as the *Ṛgveda*, because they likewise possess consciousness and the capacity for knowledge.
Furthermore, this can be known by others through the observation of speech.
Page 1009: In the Veda, action is characterized by the word; in common worldly usage, it is characterized by the purpose.
Bhāṣya 3.1.8.17: In the Veda, the entry of a human agent occurs in three ways.

[The opponent might argue that the Veda is non-eternal] either by way of the relationship between words and word-meanings, or by way of the relationship between sentences and sentence-meanings, or else because it is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*) like the *Mahābhārata* and other such works.
However, none of these three possibilities is tenable, because the relationship between a word and its meaning is eternal (*nitya*). The other [two cases] will be discussed later.

(Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.15, pp. 23–24). [Otherwise] the Veda would be subject to human authorship, because it would be subject to absolute modification—namely, if there were even the slightest deviation from the literal sense of what is heard.
Vārttika 1.2.17, p. 112: In the Veda, injunctions and prohibitions are predominant.

Maṇi, p. 9: Because there is an absence of subverting cognition (bādhaka-jñāna) in the Veda, even the suspicion that it does not touch upon the actual meaning does not exist. Bṛhatī, p. 20: In the Veda, words other than mantras lack the capacity for application by means of indicative power (liṅga).

Su. Pṛ. 1209: In the Veda, authority must be accepted as far as it is observed (*chandasi*); one must not go beyond what is observed. Bhā. 1.3.14: In the Veda, the *liṅga* (indicative power) and so forth alone are the motivators, because of the absence of a person (*puruṣa*).
Bāla. Pṛ. 78: In the Veda, linguistic usage is characterized by the word itself.

Bhāṣya 3.1.8.16: For in the Veda, the relationship between the action and its agent is established from the very beginning; it is only when that exists that the designation (samākhyā) comes into operation. We, however, not apprehending that relationship through any other means of knowledge, apprehend it by means of observing the designation.
From this it is known that the designation comes first and the relationship afterwards;
however, in reality, the relationship exists from the very beginning, even if it is not yet perceived. Its existence—

In the Veda [3620], the author of the *Vākyapadīya* (3.2.6.3) has established the designation [of the Veda] solely on the basis of its being non-human (*apauruṣeya*). For in the Veda, the usage of elders is understood through the relationship between word and meaning, and not otherwise.
*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 255: "When one has studied the Veda, two things present themselves: one must either return from the teacher's house (*gurukula*) or investigate the sentences of the Veda.
In this regard, the instruction [to study] is for the purpose of thinking, 'How indeed might I investigate the sentences of the Veda without returning from the teacher's house?
*Bhāṣya* 1.1.1, p. 5: "Even though this Veda, which has for its object the meaning of the Veda, is without beginning or end..."
An explanation may also occur through the primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*) based on intention (*icchā*) or the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*).
(Vārttika 3.1.13, p. 703). For indeed, certain *kaca* syllables are recited in all three Vedas, as are the *yajus* formulas (3.1.11).
Because it is caused by human defects, the erroneous nature of verbal cognition is untenable in the case of the Veda.
Su. pṛ. 632. Furthermore, in the Veda, which consists of knowledge, human effort is not admitted as a cause for the production of that which is intended for human goals.

"In that case, however, the independence [of the Veda] would mean that the status of being human-originated (pauruṣeyatva) would again apply to sentences such as those found in the Mahābhārata and other works."

Now, if [you argue that] independence from recitation applies either directly or indirectly, then, in your view, since the recitation concerning the Veda lacks a preceding recitation, it must be said to have its basis in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

This being the case, because there is no direct perception regarding the subject matter of the Veda, the object [of your claim] is sublated by the inference that "in the absence of a cause, there is an absence of the effect.

If you say, "This is not so, because there is no absence of a cause, as it is possible for it to be preceded by the knowledge of a Lord who is a yogi," we reply: no, because such a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not established.
If it is argued that "that too is established by this very inference," we say no, because it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Furthermore, the very occurrence of the inference regarding authorship by a person (*pauruṣeyatva*) is not established;
and if it were established, one would act on the basis of these [scriptures] which are themselves doubtful.

Furthermore, there is no doubt regarding the author of the Veda, because its non-existence is ascertained through non-perception, just like the ascertainment of the absence of horns on the head of a rabbit.

Now, if one were to proceed with an inference for an author of the Veda based on the non-perception of something unobservable, then [the following would follow]: "The head of a rabbit and so forth possesses horns, because it consists of four parts, like a cow.
In this case, the exclusion of a nature different from that of a cow is pervaded by the non-difference of the cause; thus, there is a contradiction.
To this it is replied:
Is it being proved that the Vedic sentences were merely composed by a person, or rather that they were composed by an independent (autonomous) person?
In the former case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Indeed, we do not maintain that even if phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal, the words and sentences—being endowed with specific sequences (*ānupūrvī*)—are non-human (*apauruṣeya*). For, since phonemes are eternal and all-pervading (*vibhu*), a sequence cannot exist for them either spatially or temporally; therefore, such sequence must be said to depend upon their manifestation (*abhivyakti*). And since that manifestation has human effort as its source, how could there be human authorship of the words "cow" and so forth, or of Vedic sentences, which have the Veda itself as their established limit? Thus [the objection stands].
Now, [the claim that] the work was composed by an independent person is like the case of the verses of Manu and others.
It is certainly not correct to say that the venerable Prācetas, the first poet (*ādikavi*), was independent, while in the Vedic sentences there is some other [author] such as Īśvara,
because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatvāt*).
Because there is an absence of being composed by an independent person such as Prācetasa.
It might be argued:

let it not be the case that the Vedic sentences have the property of being composed by an independent person as their probandum; rather, let it be that they have the property of being preceded by an independent person.

Furthermore, it might be argued that there is no inconclusiveness [in our reason], because even in specific systems of word-meaning (padārthadṛṣṭi) composed by persons such as ourselves—such as those of Maṇipāda and others—there exists, through tradition, the independence of the ancient poet.
This is untenable;

for since the arrangement of words in worldly compositions is established merely by being produced by a person and due to the non-difference of their causes, it is illogical to postulate the existence of an unprecedented [divine] author in the Vedas, as such a mere person would be irrelevant to the case.
Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever between having an identical configuration and being produced by human effort,

such that one would have to exclude a person from that [state of] identity on the grounds that independent conceptualization is impossible. Furthermore, there is no contradiction between having an identical configuration and being ultimately dependent upon another person.
By means of that [quality], the person—being turned away from absolute dependence on its opposite—is pervaded by independence.

Therefore, just as in the case of mantras composed by Maitrītanaya, the darkness [of their meaning] is due to the specific application of non-recitation (ajapa) and so forth, and belongs only to some and not to all; thus, there can be no inference of darkness based on those respective methods.

Likewise, because the production of a sentence arises from sounds uttered at distinct places of articulation through distinct efforts, if a distinction [in the sentence] is joined with a distinction in knowledge following from non-difference [of the source], it is not possible to make that [distinction] dependent upon the dependence of the person.

Thus, this is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) characterized by an inconclusive exclusion (*saṃdigdhavyatireka*). As for one who, like the author of the *Darśanadhantāsaṃyoga*, might attempt to prove [the Veda's non-authoritativeness] by citing the *Bhārata* and other texts—arguing that those sentences are indeed composed by independent persons because they possess the property of being "sentences" (*vākyatva*), just like the Vedic sentences—he must be addressed as follows: "The study of the Veda under dispute is preceded by a prior study of the Veda, because it is an instance of the study of the Veda, just like our own study of the Veda.
This inference does not apply in the same way to the *Bhārata* and similar works.
In this regard, because it is subject to sublation by inference—following the well-known tradition of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana and others—it should not be accepted as authoritative.

In the case of the Veda, however, since the possibility of a memory of an author is impossible, the designation *Kāṭhaka* and so forth is logically explained as referring to the act of recitation (*pravacana*).
Thus, there arises no application of inference whose object is uncontradicted [by scripture].
Furthermore, your inference has no power regarding its [the opponent's] subject,
because that [inference] is based on what is observed in general (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), and a general rule is weaker than a specific rule (*viśeṣaśāstra*).
Thus it has been said:
"That which is well-known in common usage, or that which is established in a specific [scriptural] remainder,
is more powerful than [an inference based on] the perceived similarity of a factor of the probandum.
Thus [it is said].
It might be argued as follows:

since the communication of meaning by words depends for its production upon human convention (*puruṣasaṃketa*), and because some [person] established the relationship between words and meanings through worldly usage, the Veda was composed by him. Nor is it correct to say that the innate power (*svābhāvikī śakti*) of words to convey meaning is merely manifested by convention.

For if some sound, even when a convention has been established, were not to manifest a certain meaning, then it might be possible for some [other] sound to possess an inherent capacity for denotation that is manifested by convention; however, this is not the case. This is because a sound conveys its meaning even without a convention, whereas when a convention does exist, we observe that the cognition of every possible meaning arises from every sound.
That is correct;

for even without a convention, one observes the usage of words based on mere familiarity, since the comprehension of meaning from words is established through the influence of habitual impressions (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, if one were to postulate a [universal] collection (*saṃgraha*), it would result in the fallacy of argument by implication (*arthāpatti*).
Nor is it correct to say that the observation of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is merely a restriction [to specific instances].

For this meaning is not to be understood through a verbal form such as "this object must be cognized by this word up to this point"; rather, it consists in the appearance of signs for engagement and withdrawal immediately following the utterance of the word.

And that [appearance] serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the word's causality therein, by way of inferring the speaker's intention directed toward a particular object based on one's own engagement and so forth.
Furthermore, those [words] as they arise do not perceive a maker of the convention,
nor does there appear here any impossibility of what is being perceived in the absence of a convention or its maker.
Therefore, it is established that sound itself is by its very nature the cause of the cognition of the distinctions among objects.

Furthermore, it cannot be inferred that words such as "cow" apply to horses and so forth, or that words like "Devadatta" apply to cows and so forth, because the Veda is not of human origin and because the application of words in various instances depends upon convention (*saṃketa*). Even in the case of the universal "cowness" (*gotva*), it can be logically established that words such as "cow" function based on convention.

There is no contradiction between the capacity for self-referential cognition—which is manifested through a beginningless succession of linguistic usage—and the absence of convention, because they can coexist. This can indeed be demonstrated to a person who relies on what is perceived: "The persons under dispute have cognitions of 'cowness' and so forth from words such as 'cow' without recourse to convention, because they possess cognitions of 'cowness' and so forth from words such as 'cow', just like ourselves."
This has been refuted by the eminent scholars; thus, only a mere indication has been provided here. Let the learned forgive this somewhat prolix exposition.
Thus it is established. *Kaṇikā* 235–237: The Vedas have the form of an effect (*kāryarūpa*) [according to the view of Guru].

In both the world and the Veda, the object of communication is one and the same: that which consists of an action.
Therefore, there is no plurality of objects of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti-viṣaya-nānātva*).

Consequently, a collection of words that expresses as many word-meanings as are connected toward a single purpose (*kārya*) shall constitute a single sentence; thus, the unity of a sentence will consist in its being determined by a single purpose (so say the Prābhākaras). *Rjuvimalā* 1.1.5–124, p. 263. In the section concerning the commencement of the Veda (1|3|1|1–8), regarding the passage "The Ṛgveda is recited loudly," it is doubted whether the verb *karoti* signifies "recitation" or "injunction. Because the root *kṛ* has the sense of "producing," and since recitation consists in the expression of sound, the metaphorical application of "production" to recitation is appropriate; whereas if it were an injunction, its meaning would be extremely well-known and thus unfit for such a figurative interpretation. Therefore, the verb *karoti* here signifies "recitation."

Thus, having established the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the following is argued]: because it is impossible for the Veda to be the object of the act of "making" (*karoti*), the word "by the *Ṛgveda*" and so forth is understood through indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For when the verb "to make" requires a specific basis that serves as the cause for engaging in an action, it has been demonstrated that it is unfit to designate a specific Veda, since the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*) must be inferred. Furthermore, because the knowledge of qualification (*adhikāra-jñāna*) depends on the injunction of performance—as per the rule "qualification occurs when the task is ready"—and because the injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*) functions as the ordainer of the injunction of performance by being preceded by such knowledge, it is likewise unfit to directly designate a specific Veda. Consequently, it is understood that one of the two types of injunctions—either the injunction of origin (*utpatti-vidhi*) or the injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*)—is intended. Since the term "makes" (*karoti*) is appropriate in the context of the injunction of origin, and because that injunction comes first, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the word "makes" refers to the objects [of the sacrifice] within the injunction of origin.
Su. Pṛ. 1186–87: By the principle of the section on the commencement of the Veda (vedaprakramādhikaraṇa), there is priority for the former alone.

On account of the instruction in the Veda, as in the previous case, they should be performed exactly according to the instruction. There is a Śyena sacrifice prescribed in the Audgātra section and a Vājapeya in the Ādhvaryava section.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the constituent elements (padārthas) of the Śyena be performed by the Udgātṛ priests alone, and those of the Vājapeya by the Adhvaryu priests; or, in both cases, by various different priests?
Now, by way of incidental discussion, the absence of a specific assignment (*avadhi*) for the two recitations (*samāmnāya*) under consideration is being determined.

Herein lies the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): Since the *Śyena* sacrifice is recited in the first Veda (the Ṛgveda), and since it is a modification (*vikāra*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, its constituent elements (*padārtha*) are obtained through the general rule (*atideśa*) as having multiple performers. Therefore, although the entire procedure (*sāṅkhya*) is enjoined by means of the words of the principal *audgātra* section, the subordinate acts (*ajña*) included therein are also enjoined; thus, they too belong to the *audgātra* group.

Therefore, by the maxim "In the case of a conflict between a subordinate and a primary [element], the primary prevails because the subordinate exists for its sake," the performance belongs to the Adhvaryu alone.
Furthermore, since the Veda of the context is the cause,
the officiating priests are determined solely by their respective titles (sāmākhyānika).
And regarding that, it would have to be performed by the Adhvaryu priest in the modified sacrifices (vikṛti) on the basis of the designation (samākhyā).
This being the prima facie view, it is replied:

"Because of the taking up of that [vessel], it should possess its own specific property (svadharma), due to the force of the entitlement (adhikāra); for the remainder, it is accompanied by the auxiliary rites."
This is the intended meaning: this would indeed be the case if the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) were not weaker than the extended application (*atideśa*).
Nevertheless, the injunction of performance first brings together the *praiṣas* and the *anuvākyās*.
In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the acquisition of the archetypal elements must be stated as occurring through extended application.
Furthermore, because of the extended application (*atideśa*), the ritual items (*padārtha*) are first obtained as being performed by the agents associated with the archetypal (*prākṛta*) name.
Therefore, since there is no requirement for other agents, the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) adopts them exactly as they are.

In that case, what will the name *audgātra* (pertaining to the Udgātṛ) do? Nor should it be argued that because the modified (*vaikṛta*) name is directly perceived, the agenthood determined by the name associated with the archetypal attainment is set aside.
Since the archetypal designation (*samākhyā*) is rooted in the modified scriptural injunction (*vaikṛta-śruti*), whereas the modified one would have to be inferred, it cannot set the former aside.
For this very reason, this case does not fall under the principle of the "conflict between the subordinate and the primary" (*guṇa-mukhya-vyatikrama-nyāya*).
This is because the archetypal performers possess greater force, as they are the objects of the scriptural injunction indicated by the designation.
"One who knows the Veda (vedavit) is not a speaker of the altar (vedi), yet he speaks otherwise regarding all men; he would tell it as it is. (Vākyapadīya 3.17.3, p. 699). One who knows the Veda.

The Commentary states: In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the preparation of the altar (*vedi*) is prescribed as occurring after the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*havirbhivāsana*).
However, on the New Moon day, that [preparation] is drawn forward [in time], according to the injunction: "On the day before the New Moon, one prepares the altar."
But as it is being withdrawn from there, does it also withdraw the objects that precede it? This is the doubt.
It is said: "Because of the connection, it withdraws them.

Likewise, there is the *apūrva* [rite]:
on the new moon day that is not preceded by the *prakṛti*, the construction of the altar takes place on the previous day;
on both [days], however, the spreading of the sacrificial oblations occurs on the following morning.

There is no reason—such as a Vedic revelation (śruti) or any other—to hold that the altar (vedi) must be prepared after the spreading of the grass (abhivāsana) on the new moon day.
