The Principle of the Construction of the Altar (*vedikaraṇanyāya*): 3630. Regarding the characteristics of the altar (*vedidharma*), the *Ṭupṭīkā* states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) as follows: "On the day before the new moon, one constructs the altar" (*pūrvedyuramāvāsyāyāṃ vediṃ karoti*). This statement regarding the construction of the altar does not draw forward (*apakarṣati*) the spreading of the sacrificial offerings (*havirbhivāsanā*), which occurs later. Why? Because the construction of the altar, occurring after the spreading of the offerings, is generally applicable to both the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) due to the context (*prakaraṇa*). However, by means of this specific statement, it is only the altar itself that is drawn forward.
The general textual sequence (sāmānyapāṭha), which is set aside on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), finds its fulfillment on the full moon day (paurṇamāsī).

Regarding the rites such as the adding of fuel to the fires (agnyanvādhāna) and the choosing of the Brahman priest (brahmavaraṇa), there is indeed a general textual sequence; however, for the Veda-recitation (veda-stuti), it occurs later than the general textual sequence (i.e., at a subsequent time).

Therefore, the general understanding—that the preparation of the altar (*vedikaraṇa*) occurs after the placing of the oblations (*havirāsādana*) on both fortnights by virtue of its general application—is set aside by the specific [text] (namely, the statement regarding the displacement).
Śābarabhāṣya: "The sequence [of the altar-preparation] would be a subsidiary element based on general application due to the order of recitation and the context;
however, it is specifically heard from the direct statement (*vākya*) that there is an interval [between the two acts] on the new-moon day."

Soma—The connection with the preceding section (*pūrvaprasaṅga*) is due to the absence of a difference in the mode of performance (*prayoga*), as in the case of the animal sacrifices (*pāśuka-anuyāja*), the cake-offerings (*puroḍāśika*), and the sacrificial fees (*dākṣiṇahoma*). "Covering" (*abhivāsana*) refers to the spreading of embers around the fire (the establishment of the fire along with its accessories). As for the meaning of the Sūtra: by the word *apūrva*, which refers to an action not preceded by a prototype (*aprakṛti-pūrvaka-karma*), the state of being unmanifest and lacking a fixed sequence (*avyakta-akramatva*) is indicated.

Such a preparation of the altar does not entail an incidental displacement [of the ritual acts]. As for the question: "Is there an anticipatory displacement (*apakarṣa*) of the *puroḍāśa* offerings in the *darśa* sacrifice or not?"—[the answer is: No, because the altar, having been displaced [earlier], would cause a deficiency; for it is understood from the sequence that the altar follows the covering [of the sacrificial ground].
The Bhaṭṭa school maintains that the altar (vedi) is already established by the time of the New Moon sacrifice (darśa), due to its displacement [from the Full Moon sacrifice].
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the construction of the altar is prescribed after the spreading of the sacrificial grass over the oblations (havirbhivāsana).

And that [preparation of the altar] is heard as being shifted forward by the injunction, "On the previous day, on the new moon (amāvāsyā), he prepares the altar. This would shift forward even the subsequent acts, such as the spreading of the sacrificial oblations (*havirbhivāsana*), because the sequence of the text is determined by the fact that there is a single injunctive rule for the performance (*ekaprayogavidhi*). Furthermore, since the new moon festival (*amāvāsyāparvan*) refers to the ritual action itself, it would entail a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) if it were taken to refer merely to time; therefore, it is understood as referring to the time. Moreover, the injunction for preparing the altar—which occurs after the spreading of the oblations—is clearly intended to indicate its status as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*), just as the preparation of the altar at the end of the Full Moon sacrifice indicates its status as a subordinate part of the Full Moon sacrifice. Nor does the enjoining of two times constitute a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because of the inherent capacity [of the words]. Since it is heard in scripture that "having made the *veda*, he makes the *vedi*," and because the quality of "being on the previous day" is already established here through its connection with the act of making, it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Because of its proximity to the primary [rite] and because the full moon day (paurṇamāsī) has already passed, this injunction regarding time applies specifically to the preparation of the sacrificial ground and altar for the Daśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice.
Consequently, since the textual sequence must necessarily establish the order of performance by virtue of its commonality with the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice.

For this very reason, since the [sacrificial post] is situated at the time of its cutting, one might initially conclude that the sequence extends up to that point; however, even though the injunction regarding time is subordinate to the injunction regarding performance, it is understood that the preparation of the *dāśika* altar must be performed in that same manner. Furthermore, once that is understood, if there is a requirement for an order of sequence, the textual order (*pāṭha*) can serve as the regulator because it is possible [to apply it], and because there exists another scriptural order (*śrauta-krama*). Therefore, the sequence is not fixed by the connection with the offering (*havirbhāva*). Consequently, by process of elimination, the textual order also pertains specifically to the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*).

If, however, on the fourteenth day of the Maṇḍapa-parvan, at dawn on the day of the anvādhāna, the term *amāvāsyā* were used to denote the ritual action—even by resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the sake of accomplishing the construction of the altar—then this alone would be the injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) for the construction of the Daśapavitra-altar; consequently, the construction of the Daśapavitra-altar would not have its sequence strictly fixed by the spreading of the sacrificial oblations (*havirbhivāsana*).

Nor can there be a connection with the *paurṇamāsī* sacrifice through the context (*prakaraṇa*), because the construction of the altar (*vedi*) on the preceding day is enjoined by the direct statement (*vacana*) as belonging to the *darśa* sacrifice due to its specific timing; and since the altar is common to all sacrifices, the construction of it is also a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to them all. Consequently, it is only the threshing with the donkey-yoke (*gardabhābhidhānī*) that is implied by the requirement [of the threshing] aided by the context of the *paurṇamāsī*.
For this very reason, neither the direct statement nor the explicit text sublates the context or the implication of the purpose in both cases.
Likewise, because the injunction on the preceding day pertains merely to the quality consisting of the time and the mantra, it lacks the character of being an injunction of the action itself.
Therefore, there is no extraction (*utkarṣa*) from that which ends in the original context.
Maṇḍana [says]: "Only the altar (*vedi*) is extracted.
Śaṅkara [says]: "And that alone is desired as the unprecedented (*apūrva*)."
That itself is the reduction.

The purpose of the altar is the placing of the sacrificial oblation (Vi. 3.8.17). The characteristics of the altar apply only to the aggregate of the layers (*citi*), and not to the ground that serves as their substratum.

*Saṃkarṣa.* 2|2|16. See the section in *Mīmāṃsākośa*, p. 34, regarding the statement: "In the *Agnicayana*, the ritual properties of the altar (*vedi*) apply to the aggregate of the layers (*citi*) alone. The ritual properties of the altar and the properties of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are for the purpose of enacting the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*), and not solely for the sake of the primary sacrifice. 3|8|16|13. See the section in *Mīmāṃsākośa*, p. 218, regarding the principle of "the refinement of substances" (*dravyasaṃskāranyāya*).

Regarding the spreading over the altar (vediparastaraṇa): in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, concerning the rule for the sacrificial grass on the altar (*vedibarhirdharman*), it is stated: "He spreads the altar-grass in three layers or five layers.
For each layer, there is a repetition of the mantra.
Ci. 11|4|16. Regarding the sprinkling of the altar, there is a repetition of the mantra because of the repeated performance of the action.

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the sprinkling of the altar is prescribed in the scripture with the injunction, "He sprinkles three times. In this regard, when considering whether the mantra should be repeated for each sprinkling or used only once, the author states the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view.
There should be repetition—that is, recurrence—of the mantra "The altar is for sprinkling; for the sacrificial grass, svāhā!

because the action in the form of sprinkling is performed again. Or rather, there should be a single performance, because the mantra serves as an injunction of a single subordinate quality (guṇa). Therefore, it should be used only once.
He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

For a single act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the word "thrice" prescribes a quality consisting of repetition; there is no differentiation of the action itself. This is because of the duality and unity—that is, because the substance [of the altar] and the vessel are one.
Therefore, there should be a single performance of the mantra.
This is the principle of the sprinkling of the altar (*vediprokṣaṇanyāya*).
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the mantra for sprinkling the altar is to be employed only once.
Regarding the repetition of the mantra during the sprinkling of the altar, [the rule applies] because of the repeated performance of the ritual action.
The Commentary states: The sprinkling of the altar is prescribed in the scripture as "he sprinkles three times.
Its mantra is: "vāṃdarśitaṃ vaḥ haṃta tvā."

In this regard, it is considered whether the mantra is to be repeated or whether it occurs only once. What is the prima facie view? That there is repetition of the mantra in the sprinkling of the altar.
Why? Because of the repeated performance in sequence.
Since it is understood that the mantra stated in a particular ritual application pertains specifically to that purpose, there must be a repetition.

Or rather, because there is a single injunction of qualities for one [substance], therefore there is a single performance. The Commentary: There is indeed a single performance. Why? Because of the oneness of the substance.
That single substance to be known is consecrated once by a single mantra;
there is no further purpose for the mantra therein.
But surely, the mantra consecrates the substance by means of the ritual action?
And that action is distinct.
To this it is said:
this is not distinct.
Repetition is a quality [of the action].
For when there is repetition of an action, the suffix *su* expresses the sense of "having been performed," not a difference in the action itself.
Therefore, the mantra should be repeated.

When a mantra is recited once, it is considered as having been performed according to the rules of the mantra; since the requirement of repetition has been fulfilled, there is no need for further performance. Therefore, the application is performed only once.

Soma: If there is a repetition of the mantra even when the action is perceptible, then what need be said regarding that which is not perceptible? This is the connection [of the topic] arising from such a question. Cidānanda: "Is the mantra for sprinkling the altar for the sake of the action, and should it be recited only once?
The first [position—that it should be repeated] follows from the threefold nature of the sprinkling; [the second—that it should be recited] once follows from the unity of the act of pouring."

Bhaṭṭa: In that very context, regarding the statement, "With the mantra, 'Thou art the altar; for the sacrificial grass, thee,' he sprinkles three times," there is no repetition of the mantra. For in this mantra, there is no injunction of a triad; rather, because the word *tri* is enjoined as a modifier of the action (*kriyā*) through its connection with the suffix *-su* (indicating repetition), it expresses a triad pertaining to the practice of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇābhyāsa*), and not a triad inherent within the mantra itself.

Therefore, there is no distinction of acts (*karmabheda*) here based on number—as in the case of "he offers three oblations"—which would lead to a repetition of the mantra here as well, according to the rule "of the mantra associated with the *āmana* [repetition]."

Furthermore, even in that case, there is no necessity for repetition because the recollection produced by the mantra recited once is not interrupted; for it is established as the purpose of the *avaghāta* (threshing) mantra.

This is because of the scriptural injunction, "The beginning of the ritual act coincides with the end of the mantra," which ordains that the commencement of the prescribed act occurs at the time of the mantra's conclusion, thereby making the distinction between the two clearly perceived.

Moreover, this does not result in the knowledge of the commencement of the act being obtained from the birth and death of the mantra, but rather serves the purpose of prescribing the repetition of the mantra in such instances.

In the present case, however, since there is only one enjoined act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), it follows by implication that there is no repetition of the mantra and other ritual elements prescribed for the sequence, because they all share the same character of being performed once at the time the mantra is recited. Furthermore, since there is no interruption in the production of the mantra, there is no authority for repeating the mantra. As Maṇḍana says: "The mantra is used once in the sprinkling of the altar.
And Śaṅkara says: "In the sprinkling of the altar, [the mantra is used] once."
Mantra.
16. The principle of the sacrificial altar and the grass; the principle of the sacrificial altar and the grass.
Connected with a specific context, [the properties] belong to the primary [rite].

The Commentary states: There are the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; therein are the grass (barhis) and its ritual properties, as well as the altar (vedi) and its ritual properties. In this regard, there is a doubt: do the grass and so forth, along with their properties, belong to the primary rite alone, or to both the subsidiaries and the primary?
What, then, is the established position? [The view is] that they belong to the principal rite because they are connected with a specific context.
These duties belong to the principal rite alone.
Why? Because of the specific context.
For the context belongs to the primary acts, not to the subsidiaries;
and their connection is through the context.
Therefore, it pertains to the primary act.

Alternatively—this [topic] is also introduced under the heading of the application of common and uncommon injunctions, by way of determining the conflict or non-conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*).

The altar (*vedi*) is situated within the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Therefore, for what purpose are the acts such as its preparation (*mārga*), its sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and so forth?

Although the cognition that [the acts] are for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the primary rite arises from unqualified statements such as "he should spread the sacrificial offerings," "the offerings on the *barhis* grass," "he cuts the *barhis* grass," and "he digs the altar (*vedi*"),

nevertheless— since those [acts] exist elsewhere and would otherwise apply even to worldly uses such as roofing a house, resulting in their purposelessness— it must necessarily be admitted that they are prompted by being means to a non-qualitative end (i.e., an *apūrva*).
And since that status of being a means to the *apūrva* is not understood through the power of the sentence itself, it is indicated by the context (*prakaraṇa*).
And thus, by this specific qualification that "the context belongs to the primary substance alone," it is understood that the ritual properties (dharmas) belong to the primary substance alone.

Furthermore, although the context itself is not inherently restrictive, it has been stated that its power to apply [the ritual elements] and its capacity to be restricted arises precisely through the specific form of the "category" (kāṭhaka).

And regarding the term "unconnected" (asaṃyukta), even though there is a connection between the oblation and the sacrificial grass (barhis) by way of syntactical connection (vākya), the intention is that there is no such connection when there is a conflict with the context.
For it is considered that the two terms *havis* (oblation) and *barhis* (sacrificial grass) can be integrated into the context, whereas *anāhitatva* (the state of not being consecrated) cannot.
Or rather, [these duties belong] to all [the rites], because they are subordinate (*śeṣatva*) and are prompted by that [context].
The Bhāṣya states: "Or rather, these ritual duties belong to all—the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary rites (*pradhāna*)."
In this context, there is no status of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) nor a state of being part of a specific ritual section (*prakaraṇatā*).
For that [status] is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*):
whatever assists something else is subordinate to it.
And these properties assist all the subsidiaries and the principal acts.
How is this understood? From the syntactical connection (*vākya*).
In the statement, "He places the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) upon them," it is understood from the syntactical connection that it refers to the sacrificial oblations in general.
The principal oblations [are connected] by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*). And syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than context.
Therefore, one places the oblations upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
He said:
"If the context is set aside by the sentence, then even in common worldly practice these properties would be stated for the sacrificial grass (barhis).
What is the fault in that? It would follow that the properties must be performed everywhere."
It is said: because of the context, it is understood that these [rites] are indeed auxiliaries to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices;
therefore, they should not be performed in worldly (secular) activities.
If this is so, then the fire-altar and other such elements do not belong to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice; therefore, they would not apply even in your view. To this it is replied:
Even though the auxiliary parts (aṅgas) do not themselves bear the designation "Darśapūrṇamāsa," they are nevertheless beneficial to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
The ritual duties (dharmas) performed in these auxiliaries will benefit the Darśapūrṇamāsa;
therefore, those duties must be performed for both the auxiliaries and the primary rites.
Or rather—as has already been stated—because there is no distinction in the connection with the sentence for all [the mantras].
Regarding that which is the context (*prakaraṇa*) as the specific allocator, he says: "Because it is not connected to this.
The meaning is that context does not serve as a differentiator here.

But how is it that the established status of context (*prakaraṇa*) as a means of application (*viniyojakatva*) is set aside, or how can a definition of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) characterized by "assistance" (*upakāra*), which involves many faults and deviates from the definition characterized by "being for that purpose" (*tādarthya*), be asserted?
It is replied: Context has no such power of application with respect to matters of this kind.

For it has been stated: "That which is not connected [to the context] is [excluded] by virtue of the context. As for the claim that there is no contradiction—how can there be no contradiction? When, due to the predominance of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), each individual item is connected with the ritual properties (*dharma*), even the fact that they serve as axle-fittings (*akṣārthatva*) is known to be set aside by the force of the context.

But the opponent argues: "Since the over-extension of the sentence has been refuted by that reason, one now understands the context to be free from contradiction; however, if it were to serve as a mere indicator (upalakṣaṇa), it would apply even to worldly matters, and thus [the Vedic injunction] would be rendered purposeless.
To this, the following answer must be given:
Let the sentence, having proceeded on its own, desist precisely at that point where its meaning is most clearly manifest.
And the purpose of the subsidiary oblations is not like that of worldly [acts];
therefore, it will apply there,
and no over-extension [of the rule] occurs.
With this very intention, it has been stated that "for it is characterized by assistance," whereby its status as being for the sake of that [the principal] is designated as the result.

For when something is postulated for the sake of another, one must determine that it is for the sake of that other thing after ascertaining the assistance required by the [principal] which seeks to be provided with a purposeful means.

As for what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya—that it is due to the context (*prakaraṇa*)—in order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), that should be disregarded for now, as it was stated merely to remove the suspicion of a lack of connection.
If it is argued that [the object] is even at a distance;
Commentary: Even in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, it would be joined with the properties of the sacrificial grass (barhis). That [sacrifice] also takes place upon the sacrificial grass;
and for that too, there is a purpose served by the sacrificial grass.

In that case, it would possess the properties of the sacrificial grass (barhis) used for that purpose. Or rather—if, due to its lack of utility, there is an exclusion of the properties of the worldly sacrificial grass, then it follows that there would be an application [of those properties] to the sacrificial grass used in another rite where that [worldly] utility does not exist.
This consequence arises.
Or, if there were some cause for cessation, that too would be distinguished by the possibility [of its occurrence].

In that regard, in the case of the *sattras* and other such rites, even though the injunction "the sacrifice is indeed dharma" is intended, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*—which is devoid of other injunctions—is the illustrative example.
For this will remain established as being both unprecedented (*apūrva*) and consisting of food (*anna*).
"Therefore, there would be the consequence of an absolutely undesirable result.
[Objection: "That statement is not so, because it has that as its meaning.
The Commentary says: "That is not a property of the object for the sake of the *barhis*."
For the single sentence [enjoining] the ritual details is connected with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices;
therefore, those ritual details which assist the Darśapūrṇamāsa apply only where there is a characteristic of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and not elsewhere.
Consequently, they will not apply to the sacrificial grass (barhis) of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
Or rather—this might be so if this sentence were independent;
however, since it is a sentence concerning those duties that are contrary to the Veda, it forms a single syntactical unit with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices].
The meaning is that it has attained the status of a single sentence with that [injunction] sentence.
Therefore, this acquisition of the property applies only to that *barhis* which is contained within that same single sentence,
and not to that which occurs in a different sentence.
Furthermore, the *barhis* of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is not contained within the sentences of the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
Therefore, it will not be connected.
Now, if it is intended that there be syntactic unity with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, then that cannot be obtained except by means of their context (*prakaraṇa*).
And since that context belongs to the principal acts alone, it follows that [the subsidiary] would have no connection with them.
There is no fault at all.
In every respect, [the words] are able to establish a connection with the primary element— either directly through the limb or by way of the principal act—
wherever they may reach according to the Vedic injunction.
Even for one who is a violator of the Vedas, there is a connection through the placing of the oblation (*havis*).

And that placing of the oblation is understood to be that which is prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, as in the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Likewise, the placing of the subsidiary oblations (*aṅga-havis*) is also included within the ritual framework (*tantra*), because the primary sacrifice constitutes a single performance due to its similarity [to the model sacrifice].

[Objection: Is it not the case that, just as the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—though included by a single injunction for performance—do not attain mutual subsidiarity on the grounds that "subsidiaries exist for the sake of another" (*guṇānāṃ ca parārthatvāt*), so too [the subsidiary offerings] do not attain any connection whatsoever?
[Reply: This is not so.
For just as the placing of the primary oblation is connected as a subsidiary, so too the placing of the subsidiary oblations is connected as a subsidiary.
If it were assumed that one places the *barhis* grass for the sake of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* oblation, then [the injunction] would apply only to that specific instance; however, this is not the case.

Since its [the word's] purpose would otherwise be rendered futile, rather than transgressing its own literal form, why should there be such a transgression? Why should one accept that which merely assists the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, rather than that which is for the sake of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* itself?
If the sense of being "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) is accepted, an excessive restriction would be imposed upon the sentence.
But when the assistance rendered to it is taken into account, there is a much wider range of objects;
and just as he says that, so should it be understood.
Even the subsidiary oblation is recognized as assisting it by virtue of being for its sake.
And that door [of application] is appropriate only to that extent, not to the purposefulness (*tādarthya*) itself;

for he will state later that "the commonality of purpose belongs to another," since even without such purposefulness, the properties of the *praṇītā* water will apply to the curd and milk in the *iṣṭi* sacrifice where they have been brought forth, as seen in the case of the eight-pot-sherd offering (*aṣṭakapāla*).
Therefore, unity is thus postulated for the context: that which, when performed, does not accomplish the *apūrva* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices must be performed in each respective instance.
Furthermore, the primary *apūrva* is not accomplished even by the subsidiary oblations (*aṅga-havis*) when they possess three qualities [of excellence].
Consequently, it is logical that the performance of those very acts mentioned as accomplishing the primary *apūrva* should apply to the subsidiaries as well.
On account of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The Commentary states: An indicative mark exists.

Thus it says: "He indeed first pours butter upon the *dhruvā* ladle, for from that he is about to offer the two initial *ājyabhāga* portions. This shows that the pouring of butter has the purpose of serving as the *ājyabhāga* offerings.

Or—if such a thing as this serves the purpose of both the subsidiary (aṅga) and the principal (pradhāna) rites—then the statement, "He sprinkles the oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*," would serve the purpose of both the subsidiary and the principal.

And in that case, even in the sentence regarding the sequence (*krama*), the sequence established by logic, being stated as an established fact, serves as a valid reason for the meaningfulness [of the text], as in: "He indeed sprinkles the *dhruvā* first.
Why? Because of the statement: "For from that [sprinkling], he is about to perform the two initial *ājyabhāga* offerings."
If the *ājyabhāga* oblations were to be poured over with clarified butter (*ājya*), then it should be stated in that way;
otherwise, there would be a mere pouring over of the *dhruvā* for the sake of the *ājya*,
and in that case, there would be no pouring over at the beginning.
Furthermore, [if it were otherwise], the two initial *ājyabhāga* offerings would not be possible;

therefore, it serves all purposes. Śabara says: Because of the contingency of having both common and uncommon injunctions, through an investigation into the conflict or non-conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), it is considered whether the altar (*vedi*) mentioned in the texts—namely, "he places the oblations on the altar," "he digs the altar," "he places the oblations on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*"), and "he cuts the sacrificial grass"—is common to both the subsidiary and primary oblations of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, or belongs to the primary oblations alone.

In that case, since there would be meaninglessness if the sentence were independent, and because there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if it were connected to another [independent] action, one must necessarily assume syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) within the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Now, while it might be argued that the context belongs only to the principal [rite] and thus the altar (*vedi*) is an auxiliary only to the principal oblations and not to the oblations of the *prayāja* and other such offerings, we reply:

True, there is syntactic unity with the subject matter under discussion (*prakṛta*), but that unity serves as a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) rather than as a means of grasping [the connection].
Because it would entail an undue restriction of the sentence;
for the altar (vedi), being grasped by the primary [rite], must serve that purpose alone.

In that case, there would be an absolute restriction of the sentence, and from that, the meaning of the sentence would be: "One should prepare the altar on the vedi prior to the primary [rite] by means of the offering-materials for the primary [rite]."

What then? That which is prescribed for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice is to be performed on the *vedi* alone. For this is the principle regarding the extension of Vedic injunctions (*vedavikarṣa-dharmanya-ya*): by thus [restricting it], no undue contraction of the scope of the Vedic rule would be made.
Nor is it purposeless;
since even the subsidiary oblation (*aṅgahavis*) is indeed beneficial to the principal rite (*pradhāna*), the altar (*vedi*) should apply there as well.

Alternatively, let the principal rite possess the quality of being the "grasper" (*grāhaka*); however, the door [of access] is not restricted solely to this specific oblation, but rather to any oblation that assists it, in order to avoid a restrictive interpretation of the sentence (*vākyasaṃkoca*).

Moreover, even that which merely provides assistance can function as a door [to the primary action]; therefore, although the altar (*vedi*), the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) are employed for the sake of the principal [rites], they will serve that purpose by way of being the means for the realization of the nature of the *apūrva* of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—just as the *prayāja*s themselves do. Thus, it is established that the altar and other such elements are subordinate (*aṅga*) to the *prayāja*s and so on. Soma: "The injunction regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśuvidhi*) is equal for all"—this is the point of the section (*adhikaraṇa*). Since the investigation into whether the context (*prakaraṇa*) is in conflict or not with the preceding [principles] has already been completed, the connection [of this topic] here is not appropriate because it would involve a conflict between syntactical statement (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) [which is redundant]. (This is the objection; the actual connection follows from this challenge.)

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: whether by way of being a subordinate member (*aṅga*) or by way of being the principal (*pradhāna*), that which is distinguished—such as the sacrificial altar (*vedi*) and so forth—even if it is not explicitly connected [to the principal], would belong to the principal alone; because the context (*prakaraṇa*) pertains only to the principal, and the distinction is established by that [context]. As Viśvarūpa states: "Whether the altar and so forth are members of the principal or members of the *prayāja* offerings and the like, that sentence, when joined with the context, is the indicator of their status as members of the principal."
Even though the object of knowledge and so forth is the primary element, it possesses subsidiarity toward the *prayāja* offerings and the like;
for the *prayāja* and other such rites exist for the sake of the primary element, being mediated by their own *apūrva*.

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there arises a deliberation as to whether the altar (*vedi*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), along with their preparatory rites such as digging and cutting, are for the purpose of placing the oblations common to both the subsidiaries and the principal rite, or whether they are solely for the purpose of placing the oblations that constitute the subsidiaries of the principal rite. In this inquiry, because of the injunctions, "He places the oblations on the altar" and "He places the oblations on the sacrificial grass," the placement on the altar and the grass is prescribed specifically for the oblations; furthermore, since the status of being an oblation is understood even from the context, and since the literal form of "oblation" would otherwise result in meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*), one seeks to ascertain the intended meaning through the indicator of being a means to the *apūrva* (the unseen potency). In seeking that indicator, one finds that the purpose is the possession of a motive known as the qualification for the principal rite which possesses an unobstructed fruit. Since this purpose serves as the indicator of the intended meaning, and since it adopts the relationship of subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*)—which is itself verbal—as the constituent of the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it follows that [the altar and grass] belong only to the oblations that are subsidiaries of the principal *apūrva*.

This being the case, since there is no evidence for restricting the scope of the sentence by means of the context (*prakaraṇa*), just as the intention (*tātparya*) is grasped in the context of the primary rite (*pradhāna*) in order to avoid meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*), so too it is grasped even by the weaker context known as the "qualification of the subsidiaries" (*aṅgādhikāra*).
For this very reason, it has been stated that even the performance of subsidiaries taught outside of a specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*) serves to grasp the intention.
Therefore, these [subsidiaries] apply in every respect.
Or let it be that [the connection] exists in the context of the primary [rite].

Even so, being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is not the factor that constitutes the relationship, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*); rather, it is merely the state of being beneficial (*upakārakatva*), as in the case of curd and milk in the *Abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice, or simply the state of being a means (*sādhanatvamātra*), as in the case of heaven and the like in the phrase "it is unattainable" (*agamya*).

Therefore, since it is understood that the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) merely serves as an auxiliary to the primary *apūrva*, the oblations belonging to its subsidiaries—whether studied outside of a specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*) or within a specific ritual context (*prākaraṇika*)—are for the sake of all [the rites], because there is no distinction in their being auxiliaries to the primary rite.
Maṇḍana states: "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is the remnant of all oblations"; that is, it is the "remnant"—meaning an auxiliary—of all primary rites and their subsidiary oblations.
Śaṃkara:

[In the case of] "He takes the Aindrāgna draught," if one were to enjoin the deity by restating the mere act of taking (*grahaṇa*), then—just as in the logic of the altar and the sacrificial grass (*vedibarhirnyāya*)—it would follow that any substance whatsoever from the context could be taken (which would result in a split of the sentence).
(Kau. 2.2.6.1, p. 229; the *vedibarhirnyāya*).

If, however, by some means—accepting the injunction for consuming Soma common to both the subsidiary and the primary rites according to the principle of the altar and the oblation (*vedir-havir-nyāya*) based on the text "he consumes the Soma"—it is argued that the consumption of Soma, even as a subsidiary of the subsequent rite, is obtained through direct instruction (*upadeśataḥ*), even so [the following applies].

(Sūtra 2.2.16, p. 297). In the *sūtradhaṇyānigada*, there would be the consequence of the redundancy of the statement "āmethī sutrayantrā" if the modification (*ūha*) were established merely through logical inference (*nyāyāt*).

In the archetype (*prakṛti*), because the *savanīya* oblations—like the principal *savana* offerings—have Indra as their deity, the *sūtradhaṇyā* formula of the *nigada* would, by the principle of the altar and the oblation (*vedirhavirnyāya*), result in serving both purposes. Consequently, even in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there would arise the contingency of reciting the *sūtradhaṇyā-nigada* either separately for each purpose or without distinction. [This is the view of] Bhaṭṭa. [The portion of the Veda] is indeed worldly (*laukika*). In the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, it is enjoined that "half [of the post] is within the altar (*antarvedi*) and half is outside the altar (*bahirvedi*) for the sake of the sacrificial stake (*yūpa*); therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
[Vidhi 3.1.6]. Because it is the altar.

Just as in the case of the injunction "On the day before the new moon, one prepares the altar," there is a displacement of the altar alone—and not of the preceding rites—because its sequence remains unbroken, so too there is a displacement of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) alone.

Others, however, hold that the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it must be performed after all the original constituent parts (*prākṛta-aṅga*). Since the consecration is like the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) and other such elements, its sequence remains intact despite the displacement, just as the sequence of the altar remains; for the sequence of the altar occurs on the full moon day.
*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 5.1.1: In the case of the drawing out of the Veda, when using *avakā* plants or *cetasa* shrubs, it is done only once, and not at every layer (*iṣṭaka*) during the piling (*cayana*).

In the Vedavistaraṇa (2735), regarding the section on the Vedas (vedādhikaraṇam): in the Vedavistaraṇa, there is a repetition of the *staraṇa* mantra during the spreading [of the grass] in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices—
this is the *nirvāpa*-principle.
11|4|14|17–48. Regarding the spreading of the sacrificial grass, the mantra is: "Spread the *barhis* grass; enclose the altar; do not harm the kin among these heavenly realms.
Spread it with supple, golden-green blades; let these [blades] be for the splendor of the sacrificer. Thus.

In the case of the injunction, "One desiring prosperity should offer a sacrificial pap (caru) to Māndrā for the sake of prosperity," the modification (ūha), "Strew with red lotuses (puṇḍarīka)," must also be performed here.
VI. 9.3.2: In the spreading of the *veda*, all the *barhis* grass becomes the under-layer (*upaśrī*).
Therefore, it should be performed with the *pavitra*, the *paribhojanīya* grass, and the *idhma*.
The *barhis* is for the purpose of spreading the *veda*.
Bhāṣya 1.2.15–18: The fact that the expansion of the Veda and so forth constitute human goals (puruṣārtha). The *godohana* vessel serves a human purpose;
for whatever brings pleasure to a person, there is a desire for it, because such a goal is not distinct from the definition of "purpose" (*artha*).
4|1|24 Section 2.
Commentary: Or rather, the Sūtra is explained as follows.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is recited: "He spreads [the grass] so that it does not overhang; he thus makes him (the sacrificer) one whose offspring and cattle do not overhang."

Likewise, there are such injunctions as: "One desiring cattle should construct an altar with removable clods," "One desiring cattle should construct an altar with the birth-place of a calf," and "One desiring cattle should fetch water in a milking vessel.

In this regard, a doubt arises: are injunctions of this kind for the sake of the ritual action (*kṛtyartha*), or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)? What is the prima facie view? They are for the sake of the ritual action.
Why? Because a visible benefit to the sacrifice is seen from them: the taking of the earth-clods (*purīṣa*) and the strewing of the altar (*vedi*).
As it has been said: "Bādari [holds that there is a purpose] in the case of substances, qualities, and preparatory acts.
Therefore, the conclusion reached is that they have the status of *kṛtya* suffixes (i.e., they denote a purpose).
This being the case, we reply:
that in which a person finds pleasure is indeed the human goal (puruṣārtha),
for pleasure arises from those [means].
Therefore, these are for the sake of the human goal (puruṣārtha).
Now, it was argued that a visible benefit to the sacrifice is observed; to this it is replied:
It is seen as being for the sake of truth, and not for the purpose of assisting the sacrifice;
for these [rites] are heard of in scripture as having fruits from those aforementioned results.
And that which does not assist [the sacrifice] is a *śeṣa* (subsidiary).

As for that which is heard as being for the sake of something else, that is its subsidiary (*śeṣa*); thus it is said: "The subsidiary is that which exists for the sake of another. *Ṭup-ṭīkā*: Or rather, because [the fruit] is for the sake of the fruit, there is no example, no extension (*atideśa*), and so forth.
The milking vessel and other such items serve the purpose of man according to the scriptural statement, yet they are seen to directly assist the sacrifice.

Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that they should be used in combination. However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is based on the restrictive force [of the scriptural injunction].
In the case of being for the sake of a human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), [the status of] being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) is defined by being for that purpose.
From this text, it is inferred that Bādari’s opinion constitutes the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) in that context (at 3.1.3).

Even though the *godohana* vessel and so forth serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), because there is no impulsion (*prayukti*) by the sacrifice itself, and because the fruit is desired by the person, the impulsion comes from the fruit more rapidly; since the benefit to the sacrifice is accomplished by that which is impelled by the fruit, the sacrifice remains indifferent regarding its own impulsion.

And thus, in both the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final (*siddhānta*) positions, the *godohana* vessel is prompted solely by the result (*phala*), and not prompted by the sacrifice (*kratu*). Therefore, this detailed deliberation is not particularly relevant here. [The Viśvaprakāśa states: "The *godohana* would serve two purposes; its dual purpose is established by authoritative evidence."
Otherwise, since the sacrifice is accomplished even without it, that [result] belongs solely to the person.

Bhaṭṭa: Alternatively, although the status of the *godohana* vessel and others as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is established by the direct statement of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-śruti*), they are nonetheless subsidiary to the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*) due to the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Otherwise, because the act of fetching water (*praṇayana*) would lack its subsidiary element—the cleansing of the *camasa* cups—it would be defective; and consequently, a result could not arise even from a quality based on a defective performance of the fetching.
Therefore, because it is that which must be relied upon (*upajīvya*), even though it is weak, the context (*prakaraṇa*) is the means of application (*viniyojaka*).

Alternatively, the genitive case-ending denotes mere relationship; thus, in accordance with the context, the *godohana* vessel is enjoined for the sake of the animal sacrifice—specifically in the form of being the producer of the water-carrying (*praṇayana*) that serves as the purpose for the animal sacrifice as obtained from all the sentences concerning optional desires (*kāmya*)—but not directly.

This being the case, since there is no evidence for a mediated relationship based on following a weaker means of cognition—and because, unlike the case of the *hīpa* and other such items, there is no simplicity in the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*)—the animals themselves are directly the objects of the injunction. Furthermore, since any deficiency in the act of leading forth (*praṇayana*) merely subsists upon the benefit provided by the *godohana* vessel employed by another, and since the *praṇayana* is not a subordinate part (*aṅga*) in that specific performance (as it is not grasped by the *camasa*), such a deficiency is not even to be suspected; thus, the *godohana* serves solely the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Consequently, the *godohana* is prompted solely by the animals, and therefore it must be performed only when those [animals] are independently prompted.

1. Maṇḍana: "The *godohana* vessel is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice. 2. Śaṅkara: "A quality intended for a specific desire (*kāmya-guṇa*) is not for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).
3. The placing of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) upon the altar serves the purpose of providing a surface for the spreading of the Veda."
Bhāṣya 1.1.4.14.44. The Section on the Non-Difference of the Vedas:
"Because there is no difference in the Vedas" (Sūtra 3.1.8.25).
Text.
Is it not the case that the principle of optionality (*vaikalpikanyāya*) is the subject matter of the section concerning the existence of apprehension (*prātiśaṅkā*) and its piercing (*tadvedha*)?

If it is asked, "How can the commencement of the section on piercing (*vedha*) and so forth be firmly established when speaking of the distinction between the two states (*bhāva*)," it is said: the primary resolution is simply that there is no tautology (*paunaruktya*) because of the difference in the scriptures (*śāstra-bheda*).

(Parimala 3.1.14–25). According to the Vārttika (3.1.51), because of its connection with the *vaiśvadeva* [offering], this [passage] has the form of a restatement (*anuvāda*), namely: "These indeed are the ten sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*)."

P. 672. The *vaikkṛta* sacrificial vessel (*yajñāccara*) is not restricted solely to the *pavamāna-havis* offerings; rather, by virtue of the scriptural statement (*vākya*), it is included in all sacrifices, such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. Vi. 3.1.12: The *dhruvā* vessel is modified (*vaikṛtī*). In this case, the mention of a fruit is not an actual result; thus, no fruit has been stated. 4.1.19–3. See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2469, under the "Parṇamayī-nyāya."

The application of modified vessels (*vaikkṛtapātra*) is in all sacrifices, such as the *darśa* and others. (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 3498; see the section titled "Vāraṇādhikaraṇa"). By "modified" (*vaikkṛta*), one refers to a large, mature piece of meat from the side.
Sāyaṇa on Aindra 3.1.12:
All optional [alternatives] are determined from the very beginning from another source, and then the performance is commenced.
Vārttika 3.1.8.46: However, between two optional [alternatives], there is no mutual exclusion because no single cause for one is heard [to exclude the other].

*Ḍupa* 6.5.19.54: Since optional rites (*vaikalpika-karma*) are accepted from the very beginning, the rule for expiation (*prāyaścitta-vidhi*) in the event of transgressing the established order becomes logically consistent.
*Vārttika* 2.4.2.23: For indeed, there is a simultaneous availability of all optional alternatives;
as long as no decision has been made regarding one [alternative], they remain equally available.

For one who is capable of study, that alone should be performed, while there is cessation for others. As it has been said: "In the case of an option, that which was undertaken [continues] because of the specific instruction" (6.3.12.18).
And when one has engaged in that, one does not engage in another, because it is not so prescribed.
Ḍupa. 10|1|2|18. The Principle of Optionality:
When the substance already selected has been lost, another optional substance does not function as a substitute;
that is, an optional substance cannot serve as a substitute.
Regarding that which has proceeded from the explanation concerning conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*), the commentary states:
"In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal to be sacrificed for Agni and Soma, according to the text: 'When one who is consecrated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma.
In that regard—
It is heard in scripture: "One binds the sacrificial animal with *khadira* wood; one binds it with *pālāśa* wood; one binds it with *rauhitaka* wood.
In that regard, suppose a ritual performance has begun using *khadira* wood as the prescribed quality, and the *khadira* is destroyed.
In this situation, there arises a doubt: should an alternative material be adopted, or something similar to *khadira*?
What is established? That it is optional.
Why? Because that is what is heard in scripture;
a wood similar to khadira is not heard of there.
Therefore, there is the taking up of an optional [alternative].
This being the case, we reply:
that substance which is seen in the case of an option is what should be taken up.
That which is prescribed for a particular performance in which it has been introduced is an auxiliary (*aṅga*), specifically an optional auxiliary (*vaikalpikāṅga*).
When the performance relies on *khadira* wood, the *pālāśa* and *rājavṛkṣa* woods— which are not auxiliaries in that context—
cannot be employed at the very time when the *khadira* is being used.
And what has not been heard is impossible [to perform].

Therefore, when the *khadira* tree is employed as the substratum (*āśrita*), the other two [trees] are not to be adopted, because they do not constitute constituent parts (*anaṅga*) [of that specific injunction],
whereas the *khadira* possesses an inherent relationship [with the ritual act].
"If it is argued that it is not based on scripture":
the Commentary says— if one perceives that "that which resembles the Khadira tree is to be adopted," then it becomes something that is not established by scripture at all.
Therefore, because it possesses the nature of sound, it should be accepted as being subject to conceptual construction;
not because of its lack of cognition.
The Commentary states: This is not so.
In that application (*prayoga*), the absence of the *anaṅga* (the non-limb) is optional.
For that application which has been specified is indeed dependent upon the *khadira* tree; because of that specification, there is no hearing of the other [tree].
But surely, in the absence of such a specification, there would be no distinction regarding the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*)?
"Therefore, [it is] in the hearing. What follows from this? If it is so, then when there is the absence of what has been grasped, there is hearing.
This is not so.
For it is thus that the contingent (naimittika) is asserted:
when the stated condition exists, but the *khadira* wood is absent, the other two [materials] are heard in the scripture.
What is the fault in that? That very thing which is required would become a contradiction with the non-required scripture.
And the ritual preparations (saṃskāras) must be performed upon a *khadira* tree;
when something resembling a *khadira* is grasped with the cognition that it is one, they become as if performed upon a *śrū* [sacrificial ladle].
However, they remain unconnected to the optional *śrū* mentioned in the scripture.

Therefore, that which is similar to what has been accepted (*upātta*) is the object to be grasped (*grāhya*). Śabara says: Among optional alternatives (*vaikalpika*), as long as one [alternative] has not been commenced, there is the acquisition of the others; but once that specific performance (*prayoga*) has been commenced, only that becomes a constituent part (*aṅga*), while the other is simply not a constituent part. For instance, one who, having resolved (*saṃkalpya*) to use rice (*vrīhi*), performs the rite with barley (*yava*), would transgress the prohibition "one should not speak untruth," which is a constituent part (*ṛtvaṅga*) of the sacrifice. Therefore, since only the rice is a constituent part, only that which is similar to it should be adopted.
The principle of optionality (*vaikalpikanyāya*): The connection [of this section] is due to the objection that there is no similar material for the *vaiguṇya-soma* here.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: whatever substance is similar to that which is required here should be accepted as a substitute, because it is prescribed as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) for one who has proceeded to employ the primary substance. Vi— "Are barley-grains, used as substitutes, for the purpose of rice-grains because they are similar to them, or is the former [the case] because of the attainment of the primary? The latter is the case, because when the primary is available, the other [substitute] is not; just as in the case of the injunction regarding the cooking of rice."

Bhaṭṭa: In the case of optional alternatives (vaikalpika), such as "he binds with *tvāstra* wood" or "he binds with *pālāśa* wood," if one has commenced a performance using one [alternative] and then there is an obstacle to it, then another alternative must be adopted; however, it need not be another alternative similar to the one previously employed. This is because even the other alternative is the intended object (*uddeśya*). How then could there be a lack of fitness for being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) in that performance for what was prescribed in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? For, while it is possible for the genus (*jāti*), the individual (*vyakti*), and the constituent parts (*avayava*) to function as the means (*sādhana*) by virtue of their primary status, there is no evidence for adopting only that specific material which was the starting point of the previous undertaking.

This being the case, even in that performance, since the other [alternative] would necessarily result in a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) due to its absence as a constituent part (*aṅga*), one must inevitably accept in a case of optionality that which is similar to what was previously employed; for in each specific combination, because the performance consists solely of those respective bases, the other lacks the status of being a constituent part (*aṅga*) in that particular conjunction. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Kaustubha* that in the case of the Āgneya sacrifice and others, rice (*vrīhi*) and the like possess causality individually, uninterrupted by the internal [classification].

In this regard also, if the principle "the determination [of the substitute] is from the very beginning based on a non-volitional name" is authoritative, then the substitution occurs only after the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*); however, in its absence, it should be understood that the substitution occurs immediately after the taking up of a single material.
Maṇḍana states: "The optional is not to be accepted.

The meaning is: "The optional"—that is, a substance prescribed as an alternative to the primary—"is not to be accepted," the remainder being that it is not to be accepted as a substitute (*pratinidhi*).
Śaṅkara: "Where there is no commencement with *vrīhi* [rice]. Regarding the optional *vāghamedha* sacrifices, see Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2960;
they should be consulted under the entry "vāghamedanirūpaṇam."
The optional performance of eating raw grain (*adhaśana*) or cooked food (*vṛtāśana*) at the end of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* in the *Gavāmayana* sacrifice.
(Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1552; see the section on "at the end of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* in the *Gavāmayana*").
There is an absence of the optional purification rite involving the eating of *medha*.
VI. 12|419: The absence of the *vaikārika* fire as the *āhavanīya*.

12|4|18: The modified (*vaikkṛta*) comes at the end and the original (*prākṛta*) comes first; for example, in the *nakṣatreṣṭi*, the *nāriṣṭha-homas* come first and the *upahomas* later. This is the principle of the *upahoma*.

Bhāṣya 5.2.19.17–20: A modified *tantra* is extended into the archetype (*prakṛti*), but an archetypal *tantra* is not extended into the ectype (*vikṛti*) [when the archetype shares a common *tantra* with the ectype].

12.1.133: That which is modified (*vaikkṛta*), depending on the beginning of the injunction up to its end, shall also form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) through inference with the Vedic injunction that is present in the performance. 8.1.12: An injunction not stated in a specific context (*anārabhyavidhi*) is not connected with a modified ritual action (*vaikkṛta*).
3|6|14|18. The archetypal (*prākṛta*) is set aside by the modified (*vaikkṛta*), provided there is no prior existence [of the latter].
For where there is the possibility of both the archetypal and the modified being applicable, there the archetypal is set aside by the modified.
There is an exclusion of the two *pārvaṇa-homas* from the modified (*vaikkṛta*) rites.
See Mīmāṃsākośa, page 2547, under the entry "Pārvaṇa-nyāya" (The Principle of the Full-Moon Sacrifice), sections 9.2.1.50–55.

Because the modified (vaikkṛta) sentence is expectant [of completion], the performance must be carried out through extended application (atideśa), and thus there is no connection with the archetypal (prākṛta) elements. (Dharmamīmāṃsā-nyāyamālā-vistara 9.1.1.1, p. 1637).
The pouring out (nirvāpa) is to be performed for the very deities of the modified rite, even if they are not explicitly mentioned.
6|5|14; 16–17. See the section *Abhyuditeṣṭiḥ darśaprakṛtyuttarā* at Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 589.
In all modified (vaikṛta) injunctions, the entire collection of archetypal (prākṛta) properties is required as a supplementary part of the sentence.
Bhāṣya 10|1|1|1.
Only the chanted (*pragīta*) verses possess the quality of being the means for accomplishing the *apūrva* of the modified sacrifice (*vaikkṛta*).
"The *Vaikhānasa* Sāman belongs to the Aṅgirases in the first [day] of the Dvirātra," Bhāṣya 10.1.13.53.

This is a restrictive statement (*niyamavāda*) regarding the injunction of the *Vaikhānasa* Sāman; the phrase "in the latter [day] there is the *Ṣoḍaśin*" (which would otherwise be established by default) serves as a prohibition of other injunctions in the Aṅgirases’ Dvirātra.

10.1.2.13–54, Section 2. See the section on "The Two-Night Sacrifice of the Aṅgirases" at Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 181. Expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) for the remediation of defects are as follows: "If the sacrifice should suffer a failure (*ārti*) due to the *ṛc*, one should offer an oblation into the Gārhapatya fire with the mantra 'bhūḥ svāhā'.
Then, if [the failure is] due to the *yajus*, one should offer into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with 'bhuvaḥ svāhā'."
"If he says, 'bhūḥ svāhā,' [he offers] into the Āhavanīya; if he says, 'bhuvaḥ svāhā,' [he offers] into the Āhavanīya; if he says, 'svaḥ svāhā,' [he offers] into the Āhavanīya;
if it is unknown, he says, 'bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā,' [and offers] into the Āhavanīya itself. (Bhāṣya 12.1.15–16). There is an option among the expiations for the remediation of defects.
VI. 12|1|15. Vaitānika [3738]: Regarding the Vedic, it is called *vaitānika*—*vitāna* being sacrifice (*yajña*).
The term *vaitānika* refers precisely to the *vitāna* (sacrificial rite), as stated by Vinayāditya; it is with reference to that very rite that the three Vedas (*trayī*) proceed,
because they expound the sacrifices beginning from the *darśapūrṇamāsa* up to the *viśvasṛjām ayana*.
Vedic ritual action is twofold: for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

However, in the first interpretation of the *Lipsā-sūtra* in the *Tantraratna*, a threefold classification of Vedic rituals is stated: for the sake of the sacrifice, for the sake of the person, and that which consists of experience (*anubhavarūpa*).

Study and the establishment of the sacred fires are neither for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) nor for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). However, in the *Śāstradīpikā*, at that very same point, it is stated in the passage: "That which is enjoined as part of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) for the sake of a non-existent [result] or for the sake of the person is for the sake of the sacrifice; otherwise, the instrument and the result are for the sake of the person. Thus, a twofold classification alone is taught.
This is also accepted by the teachers (*guru*).
That opinion is indeed stated there in the *Tantraratna*: "The fact that study has human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) is accepted.

However, regarding the threefold nature [of the Veda], in the root text itself, within the section on the acquisition of wealth (*dravyārjana-varṇaka*), the *Vārtika* provides a fivefold explanation of the *Bhāṣya* passage (p. 1197) which states, "And it cannot be like the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*)," concluding with the final *Vārtika*: "Just as the fire-consecration is neither for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) nor for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)."

This was explained in the *Tantravārttika* with the intention that "the acquisition of wealth is understood to serve as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) through each individual [injunction], whereas the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) is not.
Therefore, there is no basis for a threefold classification in the *Vārttika*;

rather, the basis for a twofold classification is the very sūtra: "Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into what serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*)."
For here, indeed, only a twofold classification of actions has been stated, not a threefold one;

the Bhāṣya also speaks in this very way, stating that "the subsidiary (aṅga) serves the purpose of the sacrifice (kratvartha), while the principal (pradhāna) serves the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha)," and so forth.
However, the other [threefold classification] should also be investigated in the *Śāstradīpikā-prakāśa* from the perspective of the threefold classification found in other texts.

He is indeed deluded because he clings to the literal signification [of the text].
