But under the view that it serves both purposes, since the other [the incorrect forms] are established simply through following the former [the correct ones], it is not logical for them to be the object of a prohibition.
Even from the perspective of grammar, this [principle] can somehow be considered a summary, because it is based on following a single [rule].

But surely, injunctions and prohibitions cannot be applied to every individual word, because it is impossible to recite an infinite number of sentences. In this regard, the absence of a possible meaning was stated in the *Holākādhikaraṇa*: "Therefore, it is not logical that [the Veda] expresses a generic form (*ākṛti*). Nor...
The section on grammatical derivation (vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa) [states]: "It is the denotation of the individual."
Therefore, because it is rooted in impossibility, it is mere tradition (*smṛti*).
Now, whatever matter might be reached [by such means], that is not within the scope of the scripture;
for the established usage of words and their definitions of meaning are derived solely from common worldly practice.

"Now, even if the treatise has wealth as its characteristic, since there is a restriction on application for the sake of dharma by means of the scripture, it would follow that the scripture is one concerning the origin of application. That is untenable,
because a restriction cannot be sublated."
"That whose acquisition is optional is restricted by the grammatical rule;
however, a word whose usage is eternally established is not the subject of a restriction.
Furthermore, that which is absolutely established cannot be restricted by another. [Page 255]
And since I have attained the ultimate limit of that [knowledge] and so forth,
a restriction is untenable in either of the two cases. Furthermore, what kind of restriction could possibly be postulated here?

Is it that one must speak only what is correct, or that one must speak only what is correct? If it were the former—that one must speak only what is correct—then this would not follow from the context. If speaking were mandatory, then the fault of silence would result.
"For if correct and incorrect words were synonymous and obtained as optional alternatives, there would be a prohibition against the correct word.
But according to that view [of ours], however, because it is absolutely incapable of expressing meaning, an incorrect word does not even arise;
thus the restriction of the correct word, which has the result of excluding [the incorrect], becomes purposeful."
Now, if through negligence there is a lapse in the application of the mind, one should employ the restrictive rule (*niyama*). That is eightfold.
For even by means of the scripture, one does not act otherwise due to negligence.
It is observed that practitioners are turned away from [literal] application.

If it is argued that even here, application is seen in the expression of objects through gestures (*dāma*), it is replied: "Application in respect to objects is also seen through other means, such as the contraction of the eyebrows (*ajñi*) and so forth."
No specific restriction (*niyama*) is observed that has the cessation of that [fault] as its result;
nor is the cessation of opposing factors the purpose of restrictions,
because their purpose lies in exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*).
Nor is this restrictive injunction (parisaṃkhyāvidhi) appropriate,
because there is no simultaneous possibility [of multiple options].
Nor indeed is it tenable, since this performance has a visible purpose.
For even that which is unseen is not understood when there is no expectancy for what is seen;
indeed, such presumption (arthāpatti) has no power to postulate an unseen [result] because the fruit is for the sake of another. Thus, it is an explanatory passage (arthavāda).

And when there is no fruit, it is not possible to postulate an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Nor is this "unseen force of restriction" (*niyamāpūrva*) accepted by anyone as being understood within the scope of the word's meaning, its direct audition, the cognition thereof, conceptual construction, or non-articulation.

First, since the word is entirely for the sake of another, it provides no assistance whatsoever through the *apūrva*. Furthermore, even though the meaning (the object) holds primacy because it is the object of expression, in worldly transactions involving perceptible objects, there is no requirement for an *apūrva* because there is no deficiency of constituent parts (*aṅga*) even without it; thus, the *apūrva* serves no purpose regarding the meaning. As for the hearer, however, because he is not included within the scope of the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), he is not the locus of an unreal effect (*asatkārya*).
Furthermore, because cognitions are momentary, it is impossible for them to serve as the substratum for an apūrva that persists over time.
As for the speaker, in the act of speaking, he is always subordinate;
there is no determination of him as being the object of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), an apūrva, or a sanctification (*saṃskārya*).
Furthermore, no principal term (pradhānapada) exists here as there is in the case of "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*).
Nor is there primacy by virtue of ownership through a relationship expressed by the genitive case.
As for that which was postulated in connection with eating and other acts preceded by the restriction of direction (*diṅniyama*), [it does not apply here].

Because it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), it is understood as being for that purpose. And here, there is no utterance by which one might attain something equivalent to eating and so forth;
rather, since it exists in its own form, like the intellect (*buddhi*), it is devoid of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

"Thus, because it has the Veda as its source, it is logical that the traditional grammar (śabdasmṛti) serves the purpose of regulating dharma; yet it is not logical for it to be an independent scripture (śāstra) in its own right.
As it has been said: "If it is argued that [grammar] is a scripture for usage, no, because of the [author's] intention."

"For grammar and the like possess no independence by virtue of being Veda; and because their operation depends on persons, they lack authority when they are dependent. For in all cases other than those [revealed texts], the cognition is 'this person knows this'; thus, since grammar serves to manifest the intention of its author, it is through that very [intention] that the distinction between correct and incorrect forms residing in words is understood."
"And no other Smṛti is observed whose scope does not extend to that same effect;
therefore, it would constitute a firm inference from Śruti, just like the *upanayana* and other rites.
For the most part, the compendiums of Dharma composed by Manu, Gautama, Siddha, and others, exist in agreement regarding identical matters."
Because there is no disagreement even among them, their purpose is the same.
"The teachers stand with mutually conflicting statements in the Sūtras, Vārtikas, and Bhāṣyas; what, then, should be determined therein?"
The author of the Sūtras has not stated any purpose whatsoever. And how could there be such a lapse of memory regarding the purpose in a work of this magnitude?
For even in those other works of his, [the purpose] was clearly stated from the very beginning.
The section on grammatical derivation concerns a certain conformity to the meaning of verbal roots,
by which even that which is employed as such is determined to be a corrupt word (*apaśabda*).

Furthermore, as for the statement, "Having used a word on the path of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), one should perform the expiatory *Sārasvatī* sacrifice," this too must be understood as referring specifically to the employment of untruthful speech or words that violate Vedic usage, and not to the use of words other than those found within the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). For it is said: "How indeed might all those who have maintained the sacred fires [be saved] from this transgression?"
And how may he proceed so that he is not censured by others as being like the learned?
For generally, among the learned whose minds are directed toward righteous conduct, only some lapse occurs due to negligence or oversight;
however, in the usage of words such as *gādhi* and others, no one's purity of conduct is ever seen to be impaired.
Nor is any doubt or censure observed, as in the case of the churning of the *kalpa* and other texts (p. 259).
Furthermore, among thousands of Āhitāgnis, no one else is seen conducting their affairs using only those words considered "correct" (sādhu) by you;
for the learned (śiṣṭas)— those who have composed the Kalpasūtras, Smṛtis, Mīmāṃsā, and Gṛhyasūtras— are observed using incorrect words (apaśabda).

For indeed, all the capacities [of the *ṛc*] are successively excluded as they are not followed by the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) therein; thus, because the accomplishment of the entire capacity is achieved, there arises a state of being free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*). And there is the scriptural injunction regarding the Brāhmaṇa: "The application of the definition consists in the fivefold division of the *ṛc*s intended for recitation—namely, the *prastāva* and so forth."

However, by means of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), whose function is limited merely to following the words, one sees that even those who possess superior vision—though they may be unable to provide logical reasoning regarding the nature of collections of sentences that are not [ordinary] sentences—have protected the truth as it were with weak effort. As it is said: "He who would perceive many sequences of roots, suffixes, compounds, and sentences through the method of perception, he would perceive very little of what lies beyond the sequence of roots and suffixes. Furthermore: "If the gods and others were to consider grammar to be protection..."
In the houses of grammarians, doubts regarding the Vedas are severed.
Who indeed would carry a water-pot constantly suspended from his armpit?
Having brought it, he ought to perform purification elsewhere.

In this world, whatever purpose a thing serves, and whatever qualities are attributed to it by whomsoever, that object is understood exactly as it is through those [qualities] and by that person. Āyurveda is generally employed for medical treatments.
The instruction of reality is obtained from a physician and is acquired from physicians;

however, even for one who is most diligent, grammar or a grammarian are not required for the removal of doubt and error regarding the meaning of Vedic sentences beyond what is gained through the assistance of fellow students.
Therefore, it is by means of fellow students alone that the Veda is preserved in its entirety.

Even though the Veda has perished in terms of its vowels and syllables, it is brought forth again through intense aversion [to its loss]. Therefore, by those compassionate ones—such as Kātyāyana and others—who have taught the treatises on phonetics and so forth, the Veda is not subject to destruction; rather, it is preserved by them.
Therefore, the Vedic scripture—namely grammar—must first be studied.
In the world, however, meanings are established through grammar by means of all languages;
and through linguistic usage, works such as poetry are undoubtedly accomplished.

[Page 263] However, if it is argued that grammar should be studied for the sake of employing correct Sanskrit words—even if they are not immediately useful in everyday discourse—according to the principle seen in treatises on poetics (*kāvyalakṣaṇa*), Prakrit grammar, and the *dvipadī-rāsaka* and so forth; even so, since it would be possible to pose questions regarding even those words whose application is useful in poetry, there would be no fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) among these [works].
It is said: "Even for the sake of poetic beauty, this [grammar] is useful right here;
yet even a grammarian employs difficult words only with great effort."
And it is illogical to assert that "there is no defining characteristic" (lakṣaṇa). For if usage were already established by the world, a defining characteristic would be useless.
Therefore, even in the world, grammar is never for the purpose of protecting words.

"Since even what is to be inferred (*ūhya*) is established from another source, it is like the distinction between the inferred and the non-inferred. And likewise: "Mantras employed in the archetype (*prakṛti*)—by virtue of their primary meaning, their perceived meaning, their own literal meaning, or their inherent meaning—proceed [to the ectype] through the extension of function (*kāryātideśa*)."
The prohibitions concerning modifications apply to those things that have undergone transformation in five ways. When the meaning shifts,
our understanding proceeds toward the modification by means of either a partial or a complete change in the original sense.
How could one whose downfall would occur without grammatical analysis not obtain a worthy place therein?
For the Veda alone stands as the eternal mirror for all.
From that [meaning], the employment of words will become possible.
Alternatively, even that which is employed by people as *gāvī* and so forth for the sake of communication—even that has attained its employment by way of the meaning; who can prevent it?

Regarding the words for the deities (*devatāpadāni*), according to the principle stated in *Mīmāṃsāsūtra* 10.4.23–24—"If a mantra were a prescriptive word (*vidhiśabda*), its meaning would be [subject to modification]," one must set aside all synonymous terms—whether correct, incorrect, or intermediate—and employ them solely in accordance with their usage within the prescriptive texts (*vidhi*). For in those cases, they are employed precisely for the purpose of denoting the ritual action (*karma*), and thus they possess the status of being beyond the scope of ordinary grammar (*atiśāstratvam*).

However, regarding those words denoting substances (*dravya*) and qualities (*guṇa*) which enter the scope of the entire injunctive statement through the completion of the proximate meaning—in these cases, even when other [words] are employed as remembered for the sake of fulfilling the expectancy of the mantra-sentence that was left incomplete by the words whose meanings were not proximate, it is said that there would be no fixed restriction because they are taught for the purpose of the origin of the performance (*prayoga*).

For in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the origin of the performance of mantras is governed by the scriptural injunction; but in the ectype (*vikṛti*), it occurs by virtue of the sense (*artha*) and does not remain restricted merely by following grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), which lacks any conceivable foundational scripture, which is characterized by an instability of authority due to the application of *apasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary rules) and *apavāda* (exceptions) to what is prescribed as artificial, which is beset by defects such as the dimensions of bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) as they are postulated, and which is dependent upon the settled views of Pāṇini and others—it cannot be established that the usages of the world, such as "neva" and so forth, are innate (*autpattika*). Therefore: "For those who possess skill in understanding the meaning through inference, through the knowledge of grammatical rules and their commentaries, and through usage in both the world and the Veda—what is the use of grammar? (Vākyapadīya 1.23)

Furthermore, considering that it is simply impossible for the *ūha* (adaptation) to be accomplished through grammatical analysis, the commentators rightly stated: "The ignorant person, the one who fancies himself wise, the individual soul, and the sense organs—these do not undergo *ūha*, for that [process] is as difficult as fire.
However, that which is designated as the *āgama* (the source text) is intended for a specific purpose."
In that case, it is not said [by us] that the fruit is the study of the Veda through action;

for indeed, the scripture (*āgama*) is declared to be the root of everything that is to be performed, not as its purpose (*prayojana*). "Now, by this very [argument], it would be proper that the scripture has no purpose."
That too is incorrect, because it lacks a valid basis;
moreover, by citing the study of the five Vedas as being without cause, the prohibition of grammar is rendered even more clearly established.
Furthermore, tradition (*āgama*) is said to be nothing other than the words of the Veda.
And how could a rule for those things that have a beginning be established by means of something beginningless?

Therefore, the injunction "One's own Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*), which is observed in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* and other texts, is logical as a prescription for the study of the Veda alone, because it has an eternal purpose as its basis.
However, an injunction for the study of grammar and the like is not heard in any Śruti at all.
Nor does this [grammar] obtain the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the existence of the Veda, because it depends on the eternity of the Veda;
nor does it possess such status even as a subsidiary limb (*vedāṅga*) of the Veda with respect to grammar,
because there is an absence of its being for that purpose (*tādarthya*), just as in the case of the words of the Buddha and others.
First of all, its subservience to that [purpose] is not understood through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth;

nor how could there be any artificial component in that which is itself non-artificial? Therefore, this must be described as referring only to the components [of the Veda]: "The Veda has six ancillaries" is stated with reference to *śruti*, *liṅga*, and the rest.

For, being divided by those six [factors], it is indeed the awakener of karma. Now, if there is no dependence on external knowledge, one might see the qualification as useless in view of the *śruti* contained within the very nature of the Veda. To explain: "The possibility of a qualification arises here through the presence of both possibility and deviation."
"But since there is no deviation from the Veda and other sources, what is distinguished by those [auxiliaries] which are themselves unborn?
It is said in reply: "He who, having understood those [auxiliaries] as distinct through their respective causes, forms, and fruits, studies them—only he makes this injunction meaningful for us."

It is said that "the reality has been realized" and "this is to be meditated upon. Therefore, the Veda, which possesses direct revelation (*śruti*) and other means of knowledge, is to be known through injunction (*vidhi*).
The form [of the deity] is to be meditated upon by means of revelation; this is based on the statement "it is to be meditated upon."
"He, in whom all matters are entrusted by the Śruti, is to be meditated upon constantly by the twice-born.

Consequently, it is understood that this is indeed an injunction for the performance of Vedic study through the medium of the Bhīmāsādva (the terrifying [commentary]), and not an injunction for the study of grammar.
"For us, grammar and other such sciences exist as internal components within the Veda itself."
Or rather, that intention might be the Smṛti rule regarding the study of the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

For, since [works] such as the *Nirukta* and *Vyākaraṇa* are included within the beginning and end of Vedic recitation—as in the statement, "The end of that is the curd-offering" (*tadanto dadhitavaḥ*)—the meaning of the Smṛti would be that the Veda, together with those [auxiliaries], is to be studied according to the injunction.
Or else, it refers to those *Prātiśākhyas* which are studied just like one's own Vedic branch (*svādhyāya*).
Because they are apprehended as having that [Veda] as their object, the term "that" (tat) refers to them;
for it is possible to determine their meaning through indicative mark (*liṅga*) only in those cases where they appear to have the operation of the Veda as their very purpose.
If it is argued that the *Prātiśākhyas* of Pāṇini and others are indeed works on usage (*prayogaśāstra*) merely by virtue of citing a few clear Vedic sentences—[we reply: no.
No;
for their function consists precisely in the nature of the words themselves.
For in the grammatical systems of Pāṇini and others, it is only the words—excluding the Vedic forms—that are refined, and once refined, they are employed.

Furthermore, the Vedic nature [of the tradition] remains uninterrupted because one follows the explanations arising from the knowledge of the application of vowel-sandhis (*svarasaṃdhi*) acquired through the study of the *saṃhitās* of the various Vedas according to the *Prātiśākhyas*.

"According to what was stated previously, there is no [need for] synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) for you who rely on scripture (*āgama*). Scripture consists primarily of study (*adhyayana*), whereas the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*) existed previously."

When it is enjoined that "the Veda with its six auxiliary limbs is to be studied as a duty (dharma) for a Brahmin without [other] motive," and that "prosperity results from the application [of words] preceded by knowledge of the scriptures," then to state this is contradictory.

Furthermore, as for the claim that facility in knowing correct and incorrect words is taught as the purpose, it is truly said that for one whose other purposes have been refuted, only mere facility remains;
or rather, it is as if the very weightiness [of the study] has turned into lightness.
By teaching through inversion, it is like the word *kātaras* used for an arrow.

Having reached the end of exhaustion through investigations into the established doctrines of grammar—which involve the instruction of inverted rules applied to words well-known in the world by means of extremely difficult groups of verbal roots (*dhātugaṇa*), sūtras, paribhāṣās, and the expanded formal derivations (*prakriyā*)—one merely performs a restatement of things as they truly exist (*yathāvasthitānuvāda*). Even therein, the capacity to apply a rule is seen only in some cases, and not in examples outside of those [specifically cited].
Therefore, that which is extremely heavy is metaphorically designated as "light" when it serves as a means to resolve doubt.
As for what was said by someone— that "the comprehension of the true nature of words does not exist apart from grammar"—
that was intended to mean that [grammar] is merely another means of connection.
"For who that knows the nature of the world, being aware of an object accessible through direct perception, would speak thus on the basis of scripture?
For this very reason, the latter half of the verse will be stated:
"There is no comprehension of the meanings of words apart from the faculty of hearing."
Thus [it is said].
For no one here understands [this], because there is no such lack of understanding among the deaf.
And since there is no doubt regarding the meaning of the Veda, that which is stated as the purpose is improper.
Even that [grammar] is not true; therefore, the determination of the meanings of words and sentences does not arise from it.
Since there is doubt regarding the meaning of words, the section on grammar [concludes] that they are established solely through the usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*).

And the remaining [Vedic branches], including the Nigamas, Niṣkās, and Kalpasūtras, are indeed joined with [the purpose of] meaning, because they are all intent upon the exposition of meaning. Grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), however, when explaining the mere form of words without taking the sentence-meaning as its basis, is far removed from the knowledge of meaning. For it has been said: "When [words] are derived from verbal roots, no connection with action is perceived."
Furthermore, at the time of its denotation, there is not even the slightest cognition of that [individual].

For one who follows the etymological derivation from the rule "from the root *gam*, with the suffix *ṅeḥ*" (Uṇādisūtra 235), would conclude that the mere act of going (*gantṛ*) alone is what is denoted by the word "cow" (*go*).
And this is a genus-word (*jātiśabda*), established in the usage of elders, because it is well-known therein through the absence of any other explanation.
Likewise, it is not the case that the meaning of a word follows only from its literal sense, such as "excellent" (*udāra*) or "unwholesome" (*akuśala*).
The established usage of a word's meaning does not rest upon that alone.
This is because, for instance, when there is the application of a compound in words such as *akṛṣṇakarṇa* ("one who is not black-eared"), [the meaning is determined by convention].
An object whose specific qualification has departed is seen [by its name], just as in the case of the word *vṛtta* (fallen).
Likewise, from the word *rājanya* (king), there is disregard for anything other than that;
even when contrary to etymological derivation, it remains established through worldly convention.

Likewise, if the grammatical instruction (*śabdānuśāsana*) were observed to have a meaning contrary to the Vedas, and if it were accepted as such, then its status as being known from the Veda would be contradicted. For instance, a grammarian acquires the understanding of the technical names for compounds seen by Kali and Vāmadeva, according to the rules *kalerḍak* (Pāṇini 4.2.8) and *vāmadevāḍḍyaḍyuḍyau* (Pāṇini 4.2.9). [Page 267]

However, the understanding that follows grammar—which perceives meanings such as "therefore this is called *vāma* because it is excellent wealth" (*tato vasu vāmaṃ saddhamaṃ tasmādvāmedamya*) and "that which belongs to the *kāleya* [period] is the state of being *kāleya*" (*yatkālayattakāleyasya kāleyatvam*)—sublates the [literal] perception of the Veda. Likewise, since the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* provide explanations of words such as "black" (*kṛṣṇa*) by stating, "the blackness is in the skin of the antelope," the meaning is understood through such traditional instruction; thus, the meanings of words like "Yuga" found in the sequence of Vedic sentences are explained according to the tradition of those seeking the Veda's meaning.

Just as in the case of words such as *naivādi*, the comprehension of the meaning without doubt occurs independently of grammar, so too in the case of words like *sthūlapatra* and others, it is only a succession of commentaries (*vyākhyātat-paramparā*) that is capable of providing a definitive determination; thus, grammar is not required.
Furthermore: "Regarding the meanings of sentences, thousands of doubts arise;
yet among these, not even a single prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) can be understood through grammar."

If grammar were intended for the purpose of removing doubt regarding the meaning of the Vedas, then it would resolve such doubts as: Do the *arthavādas* (explanatory passages) convey some independent meaning, or are they merely subordinate to an injunction (*vidhi*)?
Likewise, is the "being made of *udumbara* wood" the actual result of the "upper enclosure," or is it mentioned solely for the sake of praise?

Furthermore, it would dispel uncertainties in cases such as the threefold nature of reasons, the application of *arthavādas* and mantras, the visible purposes of *arthavādas*, and the singular number in the phrase "the cup is one" (*grahaikatva*).

Furthermore, since such matters as these are established by Mīmāṃsā, there is no need for grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) to provide a path [to their understanding]; therefore, it is even more unnecessary to rely on it for the purpose of determining the meaning of a few broad categories of terms established by the statements of the authors of the Kalpasūtras.
Moreover: "Even when doubt arises regarding the definition [of a word], the determination comes from the commentary itself;
even in the case of Vedic words, the commentary cannot be stopped by force."

"Specific understanding [of a rule] is obtained through its explanation" (Mahābhāṣya on the *Prahāra* etc. rules)—by this very maxim, one cannot say "it is the cause of doubt" just as one might say "it is the cause of certainty. Furthermore, the Veda cannot be explained by those who have not grasped the meaning of words; since that is so, certainty must arise from grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).
Just as the Veda exists, so too must its interpretation always be;
therefore, the interpretation of [texts like] the *Sthūlapatra* and others is defeated by grammar.
Furthermore, no accentuation is observed for words used in common worldly speech.
The determination of meaning is based on accent because it arises from linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).

Through the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), the retention of words is established; however, in that context, due to the absence of distinctions such as compound accents, acute (*udātta*) tones, or the original accentuation of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtasvara*), no specific determination of meaning is effected by them.
But where there is knowledge of accent—as is well-known in Vedic sentences—[the meaning is determined].
In that case, it is simply not possible to determine the meanings of words. Even where a determination might occur through factors such as the context of the meaning (*arthaprakaraṇa*),
since that is already established by those very factors, the accent does not possess the capacity for denotation (*abhidhājñatā*) therein.
Therefore, this recitation of the accents is understood to be invisible (adṛṣṭa) at all times,
both in the Brahma-yajña and in the Japa of sacrificial materials (dravya-yajña).

Furthermore, even if its conformity with grammar (*vyākaraṇānugama*) were somehow to exist, it would be solely for the sake of understanding the meaning, not for the sake of common usage (*laukikaprayoga*).

Because it is never actually employed [in that sense]. Furthermore, the meaning is not determined by the accent prescribed in grammar; for this is an instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*), not an instruction on meanings (*arthānuśāsana*).

Therefore, grammar should not be studied even for the sake of removing doubt; for this treatise on the production of specific accentual features does not arise from the ascertainment of word-meanings alone. Furthermore, as for those [purposes] which have been set forth thus, "These, moreover, are the purposes of the instruction of words," some among them are simply incapable of being purposes, some are mere semblances of purposes, and some lack authoritative basis.
Regarding the section on grammatical derivation (vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa):
Furthermore— "If the meaningfulness [of words] is not understood through their primary purposes..."
His hope regarding the incidental [arguments] is as fragile as clinging to *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass.

In that regard, where [the opponent claims] "the *aṅgarā* [is used]," and so forth, the sequence of *arthavāda* passages from the *Upapurāṇas*—which serves as the purpose for [establishing] the absence of corrupt words (*apaśabda*) and the prohibition [of them]—has been stated previously exactly as it stands.

Furthermore, in the statement "a corrupt word" (*duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ*), by inserting the word *śabda* while extracting the mantra-padas recited by the author of the *Śikṣā* as they are well-known among the people, he has merely demonstrated his partiality for his own position.

The application of a defective mantra is indeed written down for the sake of the sacrificer's conviction, as in such passages as: "When the *hotṛ* priest omits [the mantra], he thereby omits the sacrificer. Thus, because all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) see that defects resulting from the destruction of mantras fall upon the sacrificer, a defect is cited specifically regarding the failure in the application of the mantra: "Indra’s weapon, strike him down."

As for what is stated in the *Nirukta*: "That which is studied but not understood is merely recited as a verbal formula" (*anadhyāpitaṃ śuṣkendhano na taj jvalati kathaṃcit*—the remainder being supplied), that has already been explained by us as an *arthavāda* in the very first sūtra, described as the reason for the transgression of the traditional rule regarding ritual bathing (*snāna*).

[The Nirukta continues: "Not transgressing [the tradition], we would otherwise conceive the Veda—which is actually meaningful—to be meaningless; for its purpose is seen to be the instruction of ritual action."
Furthermore, it was stated that because no seat was prepared for the purpose of experiencing [the sensation], "it does not burn anywhere.
This is indeed true;
however, there is no utility for the grammatical analysis in that regard.
The application and origin of ritual action are established through direct perception.

If it were argued that this [grammar] is a science of words (*śabdaśāstra*), then even that would not be firmly established due to its lack of a human author (*apauruṣeya*) and thus its lack of a foundation. Therefore, the application of words as described in the *Kalpasūtras* is logical, but not that of grammar. As it is said: "He who, being skilled in the distinctions [of speech], employs words at the time of conventional usage according to their true nature..."
"He who knows the application of speech (vāgyoga) is victorious in the hereafter as one whose range is infinite; he does not falter through corrupt words" (*Mahābhārata*, p.
269). This too is understood to mean that there is mastery only through the correct application of the words of the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*; for it is said:
"One does not deviate from what has been traditionally handed down, yet one falters through corrupt words."

Even the destruction of Vedic sounds during private recitation, formal study, teaching, sacrificing, or officiating at sacrifices is addressed by the passage, "Whatever [sound] has perished there where it met with distress.
From this statement, it is understood that there is also a restatement of the defects already known from other sources.

Regarding the phrase "one who knows the application of speech" (*vāgyogavit*), the meaning of the words is connected as follows: it refers to a person who, having observed the extensive worldly usage [of language], understands the relationship between words and their meanings; who, among Brahmins, is distinguished by the qualities and attributes prescribed for those being initiated or instructed; and who, through the mantras, possesses the knowledge of the purpose—that is, the capacity to illuminate the intended meaning of what has been enjoined or recited. It is such a person who is called "one who knows the application of speech," not merely a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*). This is because for a grammarian, the science exists solely for the sake of producing such linguistic usage. As it is said: "Those ignorant ones who do not know the protracted vowel (*pluti*) at the end of a name when returning a greeting... (*avidvāṃsaḥ pratyabhivāde...*).
"However, there is indeed a distinction among them; one should speak this [distinction] regarding women.

(This is a verse cited in the *Mahābhāṣya* for the purpose of explaining that the study of grammar has the purpose of avoiding errors concerning gender. Thus, regarding the response to a greeting (*pratyabhivāda*), there is no censure of the protracted (*pluta*) vowel in a name; since such a protracted vowel consisting of three morae (*trimātra*) is well-known in common usage, once the application of names as taught in the Mantras and other sources is established, the production of that [protracted form] in ordinary speech is not prohibited by scripture.

Nor, by this cited verse beginning with "mantra" and so forth, is it intended that there be a knowledge of the discrimination between words and the analysis of their constituent parts—such as roots and suffixes—or that such knowledge be of any utility.

As for the statement that "the *prayāja* offerings must be performed with their case-endings," since this is already established by direct instruction (*upadeśa*), and because we observe the use of various case-endings in the Brāhmaṇa texts—such as "agnirvavrāṇi jaṅghanat," "agniṃ vo vṛtrahantamam," and "agnināgniḥ samidhyate"—grammar is not required even for the mere observation of case-endings, as the performance of the *prayāja* offerings with their case-endings is accomplished through those very [Brāhmaṇa] passages alone. Thus, grammar is useless.

"He who arranges these [verses] word by word or according to their accents when reciting becomes a living seer" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 2.1.22)—by this, the one who studies the Veda correctly is designated.

Likewise, regarding the statement "Speech is measured in four quarters," those [meanings] which are established through etymological analysis (*nairuktya*)—in accordance with the application and arrangement of words known by the learned among the followers of the *Kāraṇas* and others—do not fall within the domain of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). This includes the distinctions between nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*). In that regard, grammar has no authority whatsoever.

As for that which follows the grammarians' doctrine consisting of the fourfold division into nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*), even that is not overly dependent on grammar, precisely because it is established by direct perception and worldly convention.
Furthermore, when this [fourfold division] is being described, it serves as the fourth part of speech, meaning "to be understood" (*mantavya*).
Furthermore, from among the six means of valid cognition (*ṣaṭpramāṇī*), two are extracted because they consist of sentences (*vākya*).

First of all, non-existence (*abhāva*) cannot be a sentence simply because its object is non-existence. Moreover, since scripture (*āgama*) consists of speech, it is a means of valid cognition; however, it is illogical to rely on a word that depends upon that [scripture] as its basis. [Page 270] Fifth.
Because it is included within the category of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is mentioned separately.

As for the meaning of the verse beginning with *catvāri śṛṅgā* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.8.10), which is employed in the *vipruṣvatī* *hotṛyajña*, that has already been explained in the section on mantras (*mantrādhikaraṇa*).
Nor does this require any dependence upon grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).

As for the description of the application of the mantra based merely on a commonality of number—such as "the four classes of words are the horns" and so forth—that is nothing more than a display of skill in grammar.
Since such an interpretation can also be applied by those proficient in it to the Vaiśeṣika and other systems, it is to be disregarded.

Furthermore, even the mantra "uta tvaḥ paśyan" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.2.23) is understood only through a mastery of the world, Nirukta, Kalpasūtras, Mīmāṃsā, and the meaning of the sentences in Vedic texts, and not through grammar or any other such means.

In this way, just as in the previous case, [the purification] is to be described through the clarity of knowing the meaning of the Vedic syllables resulting from the study of the sacred texts (*svādhyāya*) that have been cleansed by the *upaveṣa*, according to the verse: "Like flour through a sieve" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 8.2.22).
As for the statement, "One who has maintained the sacred fires might use an incorrect word" (*Mahābhāṣya*, *Paspaśāhnika*), this has already been explained.

Furthermore, regarding the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), [it is said]: "The first and last [syllables], like the *yoga* [of the name], [are established]; likewise, that which stands beyond the three ancestors becomes firmly established"—this is the remainder [of the sense].

(Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśāhnika): The mention of [words] consisting of two, four, or more syllables, as well as those ending in *kṛt* suffixes and those produced by *taddhita* suffixes, does not establish that Grammar is a science for the production of usage. For even though the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of *kṛt* and *taddhita* are mentioned there, they are merely introduced based on what is already previously established; furthermore, the specific form and measure [of words] are preceded by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Moreover, since properties such as being voiced (*ghoṣavat*) and so forth are enumerated in the treatises on phonetics (*śikṣā*), and since names are assigned to all sounds through their characteristics by means of the sense of hearing, Grammar is not distinct even as a science for the production of usage.

In the passage "sudaivo asi varuṇa" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.5.7), although the case-endings themselves are explained as "the rivers have come together," nevertheless, their designation as "case-endings" is either established by grammar or accepted as already well-known.

As for their actual forms as they appear in usage, these are directly perceived in both common speech and the Veda according to their respective divisions; thus, this statement is not made in dependence upon grammar.

Furthermore, when the rivers are equal— whether the praise is applied to the sacrificial ritual (*yajña*) being performed, or to the words belonging to the *hotṛ* priest, or to the tones of the *sāman* chants, or whatever else is encompassed therein— then grammar indeed has the Veda as its domain, because it falls within the scope of both historical tradition and sacrificial practice. And when the correctness (*sādhutva*) of refined words (*saṃskṛta-śabda*) has been established...
It must be explained how *saṃskāra* [is] and how it is further performed.
When words are being refined by grammar, it is not known what entity is being acted upon, nor what that refinement (*saṃskāra*) is. [The answer is:
it is performed as the production, modification, acquisition of prior means, and the bestowal of capacity.
First of all, there is no refinement (*saṃskriyā*) of the individual manifestation (*vyakti*) of sound as being its own phonetic form (*varṇatva*);
for if that were so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) everywhere, and thus no fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) could be established.
If it were the "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) that was refined, then even the sounds of a dog's barking (*vidhvani*) would possess grammatical correctness (*sādhutā*).
Even among those of the same phoneme, there is equality with words such as *gāvī* and the like.
By this, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the individual phonemes is refuted.
"In words such as *go*, the letter *ga* and so forth, having been refined once somewhere... [p. 271]
In the case of words such as *gāvī* and the like, it would follow that they possess the status of being correct (*sādhutā*), since they are identical to that [correct word].

Thus, if each individual [phoneme] were to undergo grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*), nothing at all would be incorrect. Furthermore, for you, there is no such thing as a "collection" (*samudāya*) [of phonemes], because such a collection is not admitted by you.

"For those [entities] which are by nature perishable, it is impossible for impressions (*saṃskāra*) to be produced in them once they have perished and been reborn. Even while existing, that which is being impressed does not remain stable;
it would perish at the very moment it is intended to be impressed."

Furthermore, no one anywhere will ever see that [consciousness] again once it has been refined. Just as the refinement of groats by means of an oblation results in their being reduced to ashes, so too, if one accepts that consciousness is an object of refinement—as indicated by the accusative case—then because it is impossible for those groats to be seen or employed again, it would follow that all [words such as "groats," "oblation," and "refinement"] would be rendered meaningless; thus, one does not resort to the theory of refinement. In the same way, on the view that consciousness is refined, since it is momentary, there would be the undesirable consequence that it could perform all functions simultaneously.

Furthermore, as for that which was stated previously—that just as a word is established, so too must it be applied in both ways, and thus the definition applies to each individually—this is intended merely to reveal the nature of the logical analysis, or perhaps to avoid confusing the students; it is not appropriate to accept [the literal restriction]. For a restrictive rule applies only to an object that is neither too distant nor too remote.
What conscious person would state a restriction regarding the coldness or heat of fire?
Furthermore, this [notion of] production and refinement would belong to the side of the effect;
consequently, it follows all the more clearly that the scripture concerning its application and production is untenable.

"When correct words (*sādhuśabda*) are produced by a grammarian aided by the process of grammatical derivation (*vyākaraṇaprakriyā*), the rejection of their being eternal, Vedic, and authoritative is brought about by [the grammarian] himself. Now, if the Veda too were constructed from words produced by grammar,
then grammar itself— and likewise the Veda— would lack authority."
If sound were the means of comparison, then because it lasts for only a moment, it would exist in one moment and not in the subsequent moment;
furthermore, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of such a thing is neither possible nor useful.
Therefore, if that which is imperishable is refined while remaining unchanging,

then no refinement— which by its very nature implies modification— could possibly occur for it. Without grammar and the like, [the word] is already established as perfected through the focused operation of the auditory organ.
In this context, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that which has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) is understood through the nature of the injunction;
however, in the case of words whose purpose is seen (*dṛṣṭārtha*), there is no need for an unseen result.
For indeed, no fruit is desired from the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of rice grains intended for food.
The rule for grammatical derivation is not taught in the section on ritual action (karmaprakaraṇa),
by which there might be the refinement of words employed for the first time [in a ritual].
Even though the injunction regarding "one should kill" and so forth is understood, the rule for grammatical derivation is possible [only] as something occurring [subsequently].
How could a person understand a matter through faith?

Therefore, even in the case of an *anārabhyavāda* (unconnected statement), there is no such injunction (*vidhi*). And if it were an unconnected injunction, its application to a specific ritual action would be impossible.
For that which is to be refined must be invariably connected to the sacrifice, like the *sūtra* and so forth;
through that [refinement], there is attainment of the sacrifice, not for that which deviates from worldly usage.
And because words pertain to both the world and the Veda, they are subject to deviation.
Therefore, the grammatical operation (*vyākriyā*) should not apply to the *ṛtu* sound produced by that [articulation];
for how can a sound, which resides in space (*ākāśa*), be said to be "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*)?
It is like the eternal final phoneme (*antyavyākhyā*) or like the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) residing in the ether.
If grammar were merely for the sake of the refinement of phonemes (*varṇa*),

then since that would be accomplished by the *pratyāhāra* [sūtras], there would be no need for the subsequent ones. For it is the aggregate (*samudāya*) itself, as the established principle, that deserves refinement.
And if each [letter] were to possess the nature of fire,
there would be no production of any sound by means of the phonemes as there is in the case of a physical object;
for that [theory of] refinement (*saṃskṛti*) has already been refuted previously.

The postulation of a "word" (pada) in cases such as the cognition of the sphoṭa or the word "cow" is refuted precisely by means of the explanation that it consists of the phonemes beginning with *ga*. Furthermore, a collection of all the phonemes can in no way be that which is to be refined (saṃskārya).
There is no meaningful application for that [word] because it expresses a dense mass [of sounds].
Furthermore, if only three or four phonemes were refined at every step,
then correctness would belong to the mere number [of phonemes], and that would apply even to [corrupt forms like] *itih* and so forth.
If you maintain that this sequence is a property of the sound (*śabda*) and is not cultivated [as a property of the articulation],
and if you consider that only the uttered sounds themselves are to be refined (*saṃskārya*),
then it would follow that an action is accomplished by another action.
For it will be stated: "But when [the qualification] pertains to the agent, there would be a syntactical split because of the lack of inherence in the object" (3.1.10.19). Furthermore:
"The purification of the palate and other organs of hearing does not arise from grammar, because it is determined that they are to be purified by the purificatory rites taught by the Grammarians."
Whether it be the mind (*manas*) or the person (*puruṣa*), if these are held to be the locus of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*),
then the definition of a treatise (*śāstra*) as "that which instructs by means of words" would be rendered meaningless;
for it is precisely the quality of instructing disciples that constitutes the nature of treatises.
For the teaching of grammar is indeed the instruction regarding words;
however, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the word *sphoṭa* is even more untenable.
For in that case, both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) would be non-existent.
For those who maintain that the *sphoṭa* of the sentence is devoid of all constituent parts—
whereby the term "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes nouns, verbs, and particles— that linguistic unit (*śabda*) is what is to be refined.
Where refinement is accepted as occurring through analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra*), [that is the object of refinement].
Having extracted the horn from a rabbit, why is it not slightly fashioned?
If the extraction of other parts is desired because of their similarity in form and so forth,
then why is that [rabbit] not [the word] for the word, due to its similarity with a part of it?
The similarity among those who are ignorant regarding the gavaya and other such animals, which was pointed out,
is likewise explained as being due to the commonality of parts;
however, this has been refuted in detail in the section concerning the sentence (Vākyādhikaraṇa).

Therefore, even the postulation of an analytical extraction (*apoddhāra*) and its grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) is not tenable. If the treatise were to explain [the words] as they appear in common usage, then by this very fact, its lack of authority would be established— like Indra’s net of illusions.
Or rather, because it is not intended for students, this treatise has thus far not provided instruction on individual words nor on sentences; rather,
it provides the refinement (*saṃskṛti*) of those words employed according to their meaning.

A sentence of this kind is desired [as the primary unit of meaning], for individual words lack meaning; just as there is no such thing as "non-Brahmin" apart from a Brahmin, or as there is no such thing as "non-cloak" apart from a cloak,
so too the words "Devadatta" and the like would be meaningless within the sentence.

Having spoken thus at great length and having refuted the claim that grammar is merely for the sake of usage (rather than for the sake of the meaning), it would have been more appropriate to explain grammar itself as being intended solely for the purpose of explaining sentences (*vākya-anvākhyāna*). However, by not adopting that approach, even the authors of the *Sūtra*, *Vārttika*, and *Bhāṣya*—despite their efforts—have demonstrated all the more clearly that grammar was not composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*), as they have stated things that are mutually contradictory. "Therefore, because it is full of contradictions, because it lacks a foundation in either perceived or desired examples, and because it is fruitless, there can be no authoritative instruction (*anuśāsana*) regarding words based upon it."
And therefore—
the section concerning grammatical exposition—
is established as non-dispersal for those who are proficient and who practice [the discipline].
And this is directly perceived: that which is being recited is not heard [in its correct form].
Therefore, when those who are experts teach that "this alone is correct," it is understood to be correct.

Or—if it be argued that it is impossible to determine one or the other among forms that are equally employed and understood—then he says: "In that case, the truth [is determined] because of the specificity of usage."

What, then, is application (*abhiyoga*), or what is its excellence? And how is the status of being a signifier (*vācakatva*) determined by it? This is explained: "Application proceeds through the repeated hearing of definitions and so forth;
through that, there arises knowledge of other definitions, which is designated as its excellence."

For in the case of reciting every single word (*pratipadapāṭha*), it would be utterly impossible; therefore, in the absence of such a method, it is determined that one must follow the grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇa*) alone, since they possess the capacity to characterize all linguistic forms without exception.
Thus: "Therefore, no one can know from worldly usage or the Veda alone how words are correctly used or what constitutes their corruption; [this can only be known] through grammar."
Since their commonality is not fully understood, and because they are defined through the method of elimination (pāriśeṣya),
the determination of ungrammatical words (apaśabda) by means of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) is not tenable.
But there are many sections concerning grammar (vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa) that follow the characteristics [of the subject matter]. Section concerning grammar. Section concerning grammar.
Likewise.
Just as the characteristics of the genuine and the spurious are established in the examination of gems,
so too is the determination of correct words established through grammar.

Furthermore, in the tradition of human grammatical expositions (*pauruṣeya-vyākaraṇa-paramparā*), because one observes other instances of correctness following that [tradition], or because it aims solely at the discriminative knowledge of what was previously observed, there is no consequence of the logic applying to the words of other traditions.
Whatever here has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) is established solely through the two—Vedic injunctions and prohibitions.

For the sake of establishing that, the knowledge of the forms of words—which is easily obtained through the practice of grammar that accords with the usage of Vedic students—is immediately fruitful; thus, there is no consequence of defects caused by human agency.

As for the objection that, because the purpose is already seen and because it is established by its own inherent capacity—according to the principle "the scripture is meaningful where [the matter] is not otherwise established" (6.2.14.19)—the injunction regarding the use of expressive words is untenable, the answer to that will be given by this very section itself in the statement: "Or rather, the Vedic text is said to be for the sake of restriction" (4.1.15.14). And that [restriction] would be impossible if there were no objects to be excluded, such as unexpressive words or mere corrupt speech (apaśabda).
To this it is replied: "Restriction is exclusion... (niyamaḥ parisaṃ...).
[Page 286] "Furthermore, even if the word *smṛti* does not denote [works of] ignorance,
even so, there is no refutation of their status as scripture (*śāstra*) or their validity (*prāmāṇya*).
The *Mānava-dharma-purāṇa* [is such a work]."
"The treatise is the Veda; medical science is [the treatise].

Thus, indeed, there is equality in terms of authority. For it is said: "Or rather, because the author is the same, the principle established for the Smṛti regarding its status as a means of valid knowledge is understood to apply equally to the other branches of the Veda as well."

Furthermore, it has been demonstrated previously that these [scriptures] are rooted in the eight means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since they possess both visible and invisible fruits, there is no lack of authority (*apramāṇatā*) in them.
And when the fact that even a single one among them is well-founded has been established through reasoning, [the rest follow].
It is also accepted that [the Veda] has as its source either a human being or something else;
for when it is said that a human work has an impossible source,
its root is unestablished, and its form is subject to alteration through birth.
In this case, however, because they possess their own foundational sources (*samūlatva*), the absolute validity of the Smṛtis is established.

As for the objection that they lack authority because the authors of the Sūtras, Vārtikas, and Bhāṣyas speak in mutual contradiction—that is addressed as follows: "The lack of authority of the Smṛtis is not caused by such contradictions."
Indeed, a great deal of censure is observed even regarding the Vedas.
If those [Smṛtis] that are based on Vedic statements were themselves subject to censure,
then they would lack authority due to the subversion of their source.
"For the authority of the Smṛtis depends upon their conformity with the root [Veda]; therefore, in the absence of such contradiction, mutual disagreement is not a defect there.
Disagreement and the like may result in doubt, but this does not constitute a lack of authority.
Furthermore, regarding the aspect of being a means for accomplishing Dharma, no disagreement whatsoever exists."
However, a contradiction in the explanatory statement (*anvākhyānavigāna*) is flawed due to a difference in the illustrative examples (*lakṣyabheda*).
For when there is an explanation of a sūtra that involves [charges such as] redundancy (*punaruktatva*) and so forth, and then a subsequent resolution of that [charge],
nothing at all is flawed, because that [resolution] is rooted in the beginning [of the tradition].
And as for the phrase "ye cāpi" (and those also), these are based on other Smṛtis;
nor does the addition of further [authorities] render that which has been set forth invalid.
For example:
Since there are many [passages] in the Vājasaneyi Śākhā, the Ātharvaṇa, and the Caraka Śākhās, they do not disregard those of limited scope on that account;
therefore, this too is not a fault.
As for the objection regarding the statement of the purpose by the author of the Sūtras:
[Page 287] "Since it is established by Śruti and Smṛti, it does not deserve censure.
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the work, its purpose is stated to be that easily understood knowledge which is self-evident.
And speaking the truth is invariably prescribed in all Śruti and Smṛti as a means for attaining heaven and as a means for performing sacrifice."
Truth is twofold: verbal truth and objective truth.

In this regard, just as speech that is not deviant from the state of things as they are is a means to the highest good, so too is speech that is verbally true to the state of things; and just as objective truth serves the purpose of generating conviction through its application, so too does the expression of the reality of words through direct perception.
And it has been stated that the knowledge of the correctness of words arises from a specific application to grammar:
"Therefore,
because it is being produced [from that], the author himself declared that the purpose of the treatise is the grammatical exposition of all words."
And no one speaks with regard to the intended purpose of grammar itself;
rather, this internal discussion concerns whether that very purpose is logical or not.

The author of the *Vākyapadīya* has stated the purpose [of grammar] as "the restriction of *dharma*" (meaning: while word-usage is based on worldly convention, the restriction of *dharma* is established by the scientific treatise).
In that regard, one [purpose] is rooted in the Veda, while the other is for the sake of grammar. Grammar is employed for two rules:

the attainment of the knowledge of correct words, or the accomplishment of assistance toward heaven through yoga preceded by that [knowledge]. And this [latter purpose] is not rooted in the Veda, because it lacks any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, in this case, the restriction of his [speech] to what is Dharma is established by the scripture alone. Likewise, the correct form is restricted by grammar;
otherwise, there would be success [in usage] without distinction, in the absence of the grammatical tradition.

Therefore, when employing words known to the learned and understood by the assembly as recorded in the Vedas, I have stated that one must establish a rule for the knowledge of the forms of words that eternally express meaning, which is to be investigated through the grammatical system (*vyākaraṇaprakriyā*).

And as for what was stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya* regarding Kātyāyana’s view that "dharma is knowledge," whether by way of a *tantra* (a common rule) or a *prasaṅga* (an incidental discussion)—having set aside the position that dharma consists in the knowledge of words because [such knowledge] is not the cause of prosperity (*abhyudaya*) when the means for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) has been determined—it was further said by the *Bhāṣyakāra*: "Or rather, let it be granted for the sake of argument that dharma is knowledge; this was stated according to the logic of 'deliberation regardless of the final conclusion' (*kṛtvā-cintā*), merely to demonstrate the capacity for refutation."

In the ultimate sense, however, since the purpose of the [Vedic] injunctions is understood through the fact that they serve another (the person) as established by the principle of "one of the two," the scriptural mention of results (*phalaśruti*) is not understood to be a means for the actual attainment of those results.

For example, regarding the statement, "He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice, and he who knows it thus," if even the mere knowledge [of the rite] were sufficient to accomplish [the removal of] sins such as Brahmin-slaughter, then who would ever perform the Aśvamedha—which is difficult to achieve due to the labor of preparing the sacrificial materials?
Furthermore, the injunction of that rite would become entirely meaningless.
Thus, who indeed would experience exhaustion from the study of the *Pārāyaṇa* based on the statement that "the cessation of verbal cognition is accomplished"?

Therefore, just as in the case of [the text on] knowledge (*jñāna*), the fruit of the prior yoga is metaphorically attributed to its cause as if it were the effect— just as in the example "the god rains rice" (*devo varṣati taṇḍulān*), where the word "rice" is used metaphorically for rain— the mention of "dharma" is intended solely to demonstrate the capacity to express the avoidance of previously acquired *adharma*, and not to establish that it is the actual fruit.

By the principle stated in [PMS] 6.1.12, "In the case of preparatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*), because they exist for the sake of another," knowledge—being a purification of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*) and thus having no further expectancy—is incapable of being connected with a fruit. For it is said: "Everywhere indeed, knowledge is understood as a purification;
and it is a subordinate limb (*parāṅga*) until the realization of the Self, since elsewhere it is restricted [to that]."

For knowledge of the undertaking is indeed an attachment because it is not distinct [from the action]; it is understood as being for the sake of both the ritual act (*kratvartha*) and the person (*puruṣārtha*), since without it there would be no possibility of engaging in or desisting from rituals that have their fruit in the next world.

Likewise, in such specific scriptural passages as "That Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—that is what is to be sought, that is what is to be desired to be known," and "It is to be reflected upon, it is to be understood," and "One should meditate upon the Self"—there is a connection with the fruit consisting of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*), arising from the attainment of success through the authority of the sentences required for the injunction of the clear knowledge of reality, which culminates in the awakening to the knowledge of the Self, accompanied by the desire to know, and which is established by the context of the Vedic declarations and worldly sayings.

"He attains all worlds and attains all desires; he crosses over sorrow, for he is a knower of the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2). By such passages as "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere will the fathers arise for him; having attained that world of the fathers, he is magnified," the fruits of Brahman characterized by qualities such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and the rest are described.

Likewise, the statement regarding the state of attaining the Supreme Self—known as non-return—is found in: "Indeed, living thus for the duration of his life, he attains the world of Brahman; he does not return again. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1)

In this context, because [knowledge] is not an instrument [of action], its connection with non-conclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) is like the mention of results in passages such as "the unborn" and so forth; it is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
Nor does the injunction of knowledge preclude the connection with ritual action.

Indeed, even the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites prescribed for each stage of life (āśrama) and caste (varṇa) must be performed for the purpose of destroying previously committed evil and for the purpose of avoiding the sin incurred by their non-performance.
Furthermore, because their purposes are distinct and their paths are different, it is impossible for those who are intent on conceptualizing Brahman to be ignorant of one another.

However, since verbal knowledge is invariably preceded by practice and occurs prior [to realization], it is impossible for it to have a separate connection with a distinct fruit; thus, it is determined that its fruit is simply the result of yoga preceded by knowledge.

As for the objection that a connection between the fruits of knowledge—whether at the beginning, middle, or end—and the practice preceding it cannot be conceived as being rooted in an eternal injunction (*anādividhi*), [that is not so].
In this regard, there is no objection, just as in the case of the preparation of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the sequence of sacrificial acts.
Furthermore, by the statement "therefore, this [speech] was articulated," the eternity of the linguistic usage of articulation is declared.
Nor is it maintained that "this [speech] was articulated through a traditional lineage."
In that regard, it is sufficient to say simply "it is explained"; to add "it is explained" is fruitless.
Furthermore, Manu, among those who purify the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*), mentions one who learns from the Veda itself:
"He who explains speech and he who investigates the sacrifice."
"Both of them are performers of meritorious deeds, the purifiers even of those who purify the assembly.

By this statement as well, since it concerns a subject other than the investigation of the Vedic glory—which transcends all desire—starting from the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is established that this very grammar must be resorted to as a limit;
for it conforms to the capacity of those [who are unable to master the Veda].
Commentary: As for what was stated—that meaning is understood from words such as *gāvī*—and therefore their connection with the meaning is also beginningless;
that is understood to be due to their incapacity [to denote directly].

When someone, due to incapacity, utters "gāvī" instead of the correctly pronounced word "go," another person understands that the intended object is the one possessing a dewlap and other such features; desiring to utter the word "go" for that very object, he utters "gāvī.
Because they have been trained in this way, others also utter "gāvī" when they intend to refer to the object possessing a dewlap.
By means of that [corruption], an animal possessing a dewlap and other such features is understood from words such as *gāvī*;
for *gāvī* is indeed a form corresponding to the word *go*.
And because it shares a portion [of the original], it would also function as a case-ending in the three genders.
Commentary: For this very reason, even when there is a triad of case endings (*vibhakti*), the suffix occurs.
When a portion of the word *asmaka* is perceived—as in "I am coming from *asmaka*" (*asmakerāgacchāmi*)—the complete form *asmakebhyaḥ* is what is remembered.
Consequently, even the form *asmakebhyaḥ* is perceived.
Just as there is no fault in the perception of words such as *gāvī* [as denoting a cow], so too is that which possesses a dewlap and other characteristics understood from the word "existent" (*sat*).

Regarding the conflict between Smṛti and Ācāra, it is established that Smṛti is more authoritative; even among Ācāras, the practice of those who are highly learned (*abhiyukta*) is more authoritative.

Now, with respect to the domain of linguistic expertise, it is considered whether the grammatical Smṛti and the practice of those who have mastered it are more authoritative than the common usage of the world.

Therefore, in this context, having cited words such as *go*, *gāvī*, and *goṇī*—which are applied to a single meaning and are either in conformity with or not in conformity with grammar—it must be considered whether all of these are correct (*sādhavaḥ*) and may be employed for that single meaning, or whether only those in conformity with grammar are correct while the others are incorrect and should not be used.
For that purpose, it must be considered whether all of them have an uninterrupted traditional usage (*avicchinnapāraṃparyaprayoga*), or whether some are corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*) due to incapacity.
And for that purpose, it must be considered whether grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is authoritative (*pramāṇa*) or non-authoritative (*aprāmāṇa*).

To establish that, one must consider whether it has a foundation or not. Since the authoritative grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛtiśāstra*) possesses superior force and because the conduct of persons authorized by it overrides the conduct of ordinary people, words such as *gāvī* and the like are considered incorrect (*asādhutva*). Conversely, if it were rootless (*nirmūlatva*), it would lack authority; consequently, all specific worldly usages would have to be employed as correct (*sādhutva*). Therefore, in this context, it is precisely the authority or lack of authority of grammar that must be investigated.
"In that regard, because it lacks a foundation, because it is merely a song, because it is fruitless, because it causes distress,
and because it contradicts what precedes and follows, there is no possibility of its being authoritative.
Therefore, the usage of words is not regulated by it."
Therefore, because the meaning is understood [from any word], there would be no restriction on what should be employed.

Thus, when it is argued that "grammar is an authoritative means [of knowledge] and therefore every word that ought to be spoken [should be regulated]," the following is stated in reply: "Indeed, both the usage and the comprehension [of meaning] are possible even from words that are not denotative [according to grammar].
Furthermore, it is logical for a single meaning to have only one word; it is not right that there be multiple words for a single object."
In this regard, for one who holds that [the Veda] is authoritative, there would be the determination of the remainder:
another Smṛti is the source for the Smṛti in the determination of correct forms;
it possesses equality with a sentence whose words are mediated by perception.

The root of the restriction regarding usage is the Veda; therefore, it possesses authority. [Objection: "Regarding the correctness or the usage of words such as *gavi* and the like, there is no restriction whatsoever, nor is there any absence of restriction, because grammar lacks a foundation."
Only words such as *gavi* and the like would be employed as correct (*sādhu*).
This restriction exists because of the root-nature of each preceding form;
for otherwise, there would be the possibility of the rule for the suffix *-tva* applying to the word *aśvālambhana*.
To determine what is other than this, [the author] states: "By the force of the form arising from the *rāśi* (collection).
Although the authority of grammar is already established by the logic of the *bhāṭṭa-smṛti-adhikaraṇa*, it is here challenged;
for that [grammar] serves the purpose of two-fold restriction (*niyamadvaya*).
"One [view] holds that only what is grammatically correct (*sādhu*) should be employed, and not what is incorrect (*asādhu*);
another holds that only words such as *gavya* are correct, and not words such as *gavī*.

However, a basis for these two rules is not possible, because it is impossible to cite numerous Vedic passages for every individual word, and because it is untenable to postulate a single underlying Vedic text based on a uniform tradition of correctness, given that such correctness would be undermined by its own internal contradictions."

For correctness (*sādhutva*) does not consist in being a cause for the comprehension of meaning, nor in being denotative provided it is beginningless; because even corrupt forms such as *gāvī* possess these qualities, and since corrupt words lack denotative power in some instances, they cannot even be considered figurative in relation to words like *go*. Therefore, since correctness is not established by being denotative, no restrictive rule can be derived from grammar.

This being the position reached, since the usage and comprehension [of meaning] regarding words such as *gāvī*—which depend on the knowledge of correct words (*sādhuśabda*)—are accounted for through the mediation of the presentation of the correct word, they do not possess denotative power (*vācakatva*). Nor is it necessary to postulate multiple denotative powers. Furthermore, the usage and comprehension of modern speakers arise from a misconception (*bhrama*) regarding that power.
Moreover, there is no beginninglessness (*anāditva*) for these words, as is the case with words like *ghaṭaka* (a pot-shard) and the like.

The grammar composed by Pāṇini and others possesses the nature of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Nor is it baseless, for its foundation is the single Vedic revelation (*śruti*) contained in the injunction: "In the restriction of usage, one should employ only what is correct (*sādhu*). Furthermore, correctness (*sādhutva*) is either the state of being a denotative word from time immemorial, or the state of being non-corrupt; or else, it is a universal (*jāti*) produced by the proficiency born from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) generated by the study of grammar. Moreover, its status as a means of valid knowledge (*pramitatva*) consists in its capacity to convey meaning; all this has been established in detail in the *Kaustubha*.
The absence of that [correctness] is ungrammaticality (*asādhutva*).

And the direct scriptural authority (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) is the source, such as: "One should not speak like a barbarian; one should not converse like a barbarian; for this which is an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) is indeed a barbarian.
Furthermore, this prohibition is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, due to the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Furthermore, there is a prohibition even regarding sacrifice itself, according to the Mahābhāṣya: "In sacrificial rites there is a restrictive rule, whereas elsewhere there is no such rule.

Moreover, the attainment of fruit results specifically from the correct usage of words, as stated in the scriptural passage: "A single word, correctly understood and properly employed, becomes a cow of plenty in the heavenly world.
For here, the restrictive rule concerning the correctness (*asādhutva*) of usage is enjoined with a view toward the attainment of a fruit.

Even for one who has attained passion (*rāga*), the status of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) for correct usage (*sādhuyoga*) is established by the statement, "Therefore, this speech is called *vyākṛtā* (grammatically formed). This is clear in the *Kaustubha*. As for the restriction regarding the nature of correct words—namely, that "only *go* and so forth are correct, not *gāvī* and so forth"—the root source is simply the beginningless succession of usage. Therefore, grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, as for the theory of *sphoṭa* and the like which is based on mere logic (*nyāyamūlaka*), it is stated [by us] to be contrary to the revealed scripture (*śruti*). When there is a conflict between logic and scripture, let the authority of the Blessed One (*bhagavat-pramāṇa*) prevail.
Maṇḍana: "Words such as *gavya* are beginningless because of grammar (*vyākaraṇāt*).

The construction is as follows: by virtue of grammar—that is, by the rules established in the science of grammar—words such as *gavya* are correct words (*sādhuśabda*), and they are indeed beginningless, having their specific forms established through usage since time immemorial.
Śaṅkara: "The authority of grammar is established by tradition (*smṛti*)."
In the section on Grammar (Vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa, 1.3.8), the state of having multiple words for a single meaning is subsumed under the principle of having a single word.

Bāla. p. 110. Furthermore, in the section on Grammar, by asserting that the traditional rule (smṛti)—"One should employ only correct words, not incorrect ones"—is rooted in the Veda, the authority of the usage of correct words as eternal denoters [of meaning] is established as a means of knowing Dharma.

Kau. 1.3.18, p. 54. For in the section on Grammar, under the auxiliary aphorism (guṇasūtra) stating "It is improper that there be multiple words [for one thing]," the multiplicity of words for a single referent is refuted.

Ku. 2|1|8|22. In the section concerning the non-transmigrating [Self] (asaṃsāri-vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa), verse 3787: "The sustaining"—namely, that the texts teaching the qualified and unqualified Self have as their primary purpose their own literal meaning, yet serve as causes for worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) because they are required by the injunctions for both types of meditation—will be demonstrated in the *Vārttika* within the section concerning grammatical derivation (*vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa*).

Kau. 1.2.17, p. 29: Furthermore, in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), the exposition of the distinction between correct words (*sabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*) is rooted in the usage of the elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*).
