That the employment of correct words serves both the purpose of the sacrifice (*ṛtvartha*) and the purpose of man (*puruṣārtha*), whereas the employment of corrupt words results in a deficiency in the sacrificial purpose (*ṛtvartha-guṇāpādakatva*), is based on the Veda; and that one is ignorant of the Veda is indicated by the mention of the corruption of Vedic words and so forth—this we shall explain in the section on Grammar (*vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa*).
1.3.12, p. 10: The etymological derivation (*yoga*) supported by grammar possesses greater force than mere usage (*kevala-prayoga*).
Soma, 2.1.4, p. 109: Since grammar and the other [sciences] are useful for the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas, their status as auxiliary limbs (*vedāṅga*) is established.

Maṇi, p. 2: The authors of grammar—Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali—are equal in authority to Manu and others. Vi. 1.3.9: In the philosophical system of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-darśana*), a sentence (*vākya*) is that in which the division into constituent parts has vanished.

Nor does that [sentence] have a relationship characterized as signifier and signified with its own meaning; rather, there is only identity (*tādātmya*). It is the sentence itself that evolves (*vivartate*) into the form of the sentence-meaning, just as a rope evolves into the form of silver through delusion. In this regard, although the meaning of a Vedic sentence has not had its relationship [with the word] grasped because it is to be understood through other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), nevertheless, since the Vedic sentence evolves into the form of the meaning, positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding the status of the material cause (*prakṛti*)—which is superimposed [upon the sentence]—serve merely as a means. (Ṛjuvimalā 1.1.24, p. 266). The tradition of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-paramparā*) is beginningless (*anādi*).

Or [as stated in] Vākyapadīya 1.3.27, page 288: The authority of grammar is declared in the Veda: "Two kinds of knowledge are to be known," so indeed say those who know Brahman—"the higher and the lower.

Therein, the lower consists of the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvaveda, phonetics (śikṣā), ritual (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), prosody (chandas), and astronomy (jyotiṣa)," thus say the followers of the Atharvaveda (*Muṇḍakopaniṣad* 1.1).

"Speech, indeed, was unmanifested and spoke away [from the gods]. Those gods said to Indra, 'Make this speech of ours manifest. Indra, having stepped into their midst, made it manifest; therefore, this speech is called 'manifested' (vyākṛtā)," so says the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa.
Furthermore, the meaning must be determined from the verbal root by means of grammar, etymology, and philology, as in the case of "suṇyeva jarbharī" and similar passages.

The Bhāṣya states that the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*) is preceded by words (*pada-pūrvakatva*). (Su., p. 260). The subject matter (*viṣaya*) of the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇa-smṛti*) is: "Among those [words] joined with a single meaning, which is correct (*sādhu*) and which is corrupt (*apabhraṃśa*)?"
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 3.4.13, p. 922: "The grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) has as its sole object the mere distinction between correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*).

Nor does the function of the tradition consist in intending to establish for which [word] what etymological derivation (*yoganimittatva*) is the cause; nevertheless, since it provides the formal exposition (*anvākhyāna*) solely with the aim of determining correctness (*sādhu*) and incorrectness (*asādhu*), the status of being the cause is understood.
(Commentary on 2.3.13, p. 586).

"Therefore, even though there are paths of experience both extensive and concise, they are employed in the commentary for the sake of utility; thus, something is provided here and there. (Vākyapadīya 3.4.12, p. 651). For while explaining, one attains specific understanding; indeed, it is a logical principle that "there is no definition [of a thing] arising from doubt."

The meaning of this is as follows: "Understanding" (*pratipatti*)—that is, ascertainment (*niścaya*)—results from the explanation (*vyākhyāna*) of the form of either the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) or another [element], which serves to eliminate doubt (*chidra*). For, because of doubt, that which is not a definition (*alakṣaṇa*) cannot be a non-defining characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*), nor can that which is a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) be so; this is because it is appropriate for a treatise (*śāstra*) to produce a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*). In other words, it should be understood that in order to establish certainty from what is incorrect, the treatise requires no cause beyond the removal of doubt regarding the usage of teachers (*ācāryavyavahāra*) whose words may be ambiguous. This principle is stated for the most part in the *Mahābhāṣya*.
In the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*, the "mouth-binding" (*mukhabandha*) itself is stated in the form of a *paribhāṣā* by Nāgeśabhaṭṭa.

[Sāhasī 583]. Regarding the principle "while explaining, there is the understanding of the specific," by this very *paribhāṣā*, one cannot say "there is no doubt regarding the Veda," just as one cannot say "there is no rule [of grammar] due to doubt. [Vārttika 1.3.24, p. 267]. It is proper to determine the meaning according to an explanation whose authority is established; for this is well-known from the maxim: "while explaining, there is the understanding of the specific."
Parākrama 6: The pouring (vyādhāraṇa) with clarified butter (ājya) occurs only at the third pressing (tṛtīyasavana) during the Yoni-homa.

See Saṃkalpa 3|1|7; Mīko., p. 1801. Regarding the statement "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the pouring with clarified butter occurs only at the third pressing," one should consult that specific section (adhikaraṇa).
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the pouring may be performed with either clarified butter or Soma during the first two pressings.
Saṃkalpa 3|2|18. Vyāghāraṇa:
pervasion (vyāpti) 3790; the doctrine of pervasion (vyāptivāda).
In that context, the relation delimiting the probandumness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) is the relation of identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

By means of that [relation], the locus of the non-probandum (*apratiyogi-adhikaraṇatva*)—namely, the absence of the absence of everything characterized by existence in the preceding moment—is present in the locus of the reason (*hetvadhikaraṇa*).
However, in the third [definition], there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as "the self possesses the absence of conjunction with a monkey, because it is a self."

If it is argued: "The absence of the absence of the conjunction with a monkey (*kapisaṃyoga*)—which is the self-residence-conjunction—is itself the conjunction with a monkey; since this [conjunction] is a quality (*guṇa*), its counter-correlate-delimitant (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) is the general absence of qualities (*guṇasāmānyābhāva*). Furthermore, the state of being the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) delimited by that [absence] exists within the locus of the reason (*hetvadhikaraṇa*).
This is not so.
For what is intended is the delimitant of such a counter-correlatehood as the locus delimited by which is possessed of the reason.

Now, an objection is raised: in the inference "Time possesses a jar, because it has temporal magnitude," there is the problem of the non-establishment of an absence that is non-co-referential with its counter-positive (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*). This is because the Great Time (*mahākāla*), which is the locus of the reason, serves as the substratum for the entire universe; thus, all absences are non-co-referential with their counter-positives by virtue of being temporally qualified (*kālikaviśeṣaṇatva*) through the relation that delimits the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedakasambandha*). On this point, some say:
The absence of a pot qualified by the difference from Great Time (*mahākāla*) is non-co-referential with its counter-positive (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*) therein;
for although Great Time is the locus of the pot, it is not the locus of a pot qualified by the difference from Great Time.
[This holds] in Great Time.

Regarding the theory of pervasion (*vyāptivāda*), although they maintain that the mind (*manas*) is a substance that is all-pervading like space, they nevertheless assert that the mind functions as a sense organ only when delimited by the cavity of the ear and by the body; therefore, its conjunction with external objects is impossible.
Otherwise, since inference and other means of knowledge would also have as their objects things conjoined with the mind, it would follow that they too are forms of perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is indeed only fourfold, then how is the perception of sound possible? For conjunction is not possible between the auditory organ—which consists of one or another of ether, ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), and so forth—and sound, since both are inactive (*niṣkriya*), and because conjunction is produced by action (*karmaja*).
It is replied: the contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) between these two is indeed conjunction itself.
And this [conjunction] is not produced by action (*karma*), because there is a deviation in the case of a conjunction produced by a conjunction (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*).
Nor is it produced by conjunction, because there is a deviation in the case of that which is produced by action.
Therefore, the cause residing in the substance is simply proximity (*nairantarya*) common to both.
And that [conjunction] is possible even for two all-pervading entities.

Or rather, let there be conjunction; since there is no evidence for a "conjunction-born conjunction," let conjunction be produced by action (*karmaja*), because it is never found to deviate from that.

For indeed, the conjunction with the shuttle occurs in the yarn, and even when the yarn is absent, it occurs in the jar; yet no other kind of conjunction exists there. Thus, conjunction belongs to all-pervading things.
The theory of pervasion (*vyāptivāda*):
Pervasion is a relation and a rule, yet it is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of smoke and so forth.
And since that [object] is present, it is logical that it is graspable by perception.

For it is not the case that the possibility of its being in another location and so forth must be grasped in order to grasp the [object's] necessary connection, as is the case with the stable form of walls and such things.
Indeed, the fact that their connection to another time is imperceptible does not mean that their form is imperceptible.
Likewise, the subsequent cognition "this is silver" would not be a sublater of the prior cognition, because of the difference in their objects.
For at the earlier time, silver was presented by the cognition of silver;
and at the later time, that [silver] is absent. Since the objects differ, how could there be sublation? Therefore, it must be said that the silver was indeed apprehended as something stable.
And it has been said: "For silver, when being perceived, is understood to be long-lasting.
Thus, since it is perceived as having an indefinite form, its status as direct perception (pratyakṣatva) is logical.
What, then, is this nature of smoke and the like? It is "restriction" (*niyama*), meaning that it is invariably connected [to fire]. That is to say: wherever there is smoke, there is fire.
Therefore, it is established that restriction is an object of perception.
In this regard, the following must be stated:
Is perception the apprehension of only that which exists, or is it also the apprehension of that which does not exist?
First of all, what is called "perception" cannot possibly be the apprehension of only that which exists.
Because it is established that perception occurs through the existence of an object by virtue of being produced in conjunction with it,
there is thus an impossibility of [the rule] being the object of a restriction,
since such a rule would have to pervade all places and times.
For this indeed is the necessary concomitance (*niyama*) of smoke with fire: that it must pervade the same or even a greater range of space and time without delay.

As it has been said: "Whatever is equal to or even greater than another in terms of space and time, that is the pervaded (*vyāpya*); the other is its pervader (*vyāpaka*), being either equal to or even greater than it."
Thus [it is said].

As for what was stated regarding the restriction of the nature of smoke—that even its nature consists precisely of that which is the essence of concomitance (vyāpti) with fire—what is this non-deviation? It is nothing other than the fact that, throughout all space and time occupied by smoke, there is no absence of connection with fire.
And thus, when that [invariable concomitance] is being perceived, the existence [of fire] in another place and so forth would necessarily become perceptible.

However, one perceives directly a form of certainty regarding the smoke—distinct from its connection with those [other places] and like its "whiteness" and so on—and this is firmly established in consciousness.

For if this distinct form were, like whiteness and the like, separate from the pervasion of all [instances], then even when it is grasped through perception, the pervasion of fire across all places and times of smoke would not be established.
For when one thing is apprehended, another is not thereby apprehended, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

And if the non-deviation from place and time is unapprehended, how can there be the arising of inference? When this other form is being apprehended by perception, it is apprehended only as existing in a proximate place and time; thus, no rule regarding another time could be established.
As for what was shown—that the form exists "like that of walls and so forth"—that too must be examined.

What is intended here? Is it that "duration" (*sthāyitva*) itself is apprehended; or rather, that which is the actual nature of the object is apprehended; or perhaps the "fitness for duration"? The first alternative is not tenable. Duration is persistence over multiple points of time; how could that be apprehended by perception, given that perception has only the present as its object?
If this [duration] were indeed apprehended by perception, then the emphasis on recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) for the sake of establishing duration would be useless.

In the second case, however, that [cognition] would have the form of a wall alone and nothing else; likewise here too, if the nature of smoke were restricted by its very essence (*vastutaḥ*), then it would be established as capable of being perceived.
Yet there is no purpose served by that much; for the capacity (*yogyatā*) of all entities is to be understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and thus its perceptibility is untenable.

As for the conviction among common people regarding the stability of jars, walls, and so forth upon merely seeing them, that is non-authoritative, because such stability has already been sublated previously.
Moreover, its inferential nature is evident because its essential character has been described as such.
For instance, this cognition takes the form: "If this object were not perceived through the senses due to sound or other factors, it would persist for some time.
In the same way, even in the case of silver and the like, the persistence of that form is purely inferential.
With this very intention it was said: "For silver, when being perceived, is perceived as something that lacks a substratum.
This alone is the true nature of the sublater (*bādhaka*) as well.

For it is understood through inference that for existing silver, its non-existence as such [silver] cannot occur through direct perception; thus, whether it be "not-that" or "that-form," since both alternatives are established as having one and the same form at the two times, the silver previously apprehended pervades the subsequent time, because it is apprehended at the subsequent time, and the subsequent time pervades that prior time.

Therefore, by the principle of equal necessity (*samānaniyatyā*), there occurs a sublation (*bādha*) of the previously apprehended silver by the [subsequent cognition] "this is not silver," which arises at a later time.
However, where the single nature of an object is not apprehended through inference at both times, no sublation occurs at all;
as, for example, in the case of a jujube fruit, the perception of blackness [is not sublated] by the cognition of redness arising at the time of baking.
But if permanence were perceived directly, O Agni, there would be a contradiction even in that case;
therefore, permanence is not determined by perception. Likewise, "invariable concomitance" (niyama) consists in the pervasion of all places and times.

And it might be argued: "But surely the necessity of a relation consists in its being inherent (*svābhāvika*), not in its connection with another time; and since that [inherence] exists only in the present, it is logical that it is apprehended by perception.
What, then, is this 'inherent' nature? It cannot be eternality, for that is impossible in the case of something that occurs only occasionally."

Now, if it is argued that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the cause [of the cognition], then even in the case of smoke, its own nature would be the cause for its connection [with fire]; thus, this is the doctrine of pervasion (*vyāptivāda*).
The doctrine of pervasion.
For that [fire] as well, the connection with smoke would be necessary.

Now, one might object: "The connection of this [fire] with smoke is caused by wet fuel and so forth, not by its own essential nature. This is true; however, even the essential nature, which has wet fuel and so forth as its cause, is indeed a cause.
For a connection does not exist when the essential nature of the connection is absent.

If it is argued that [inherence] is a property of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), that is the very same fault. Even for fire, conjunction is indeed a property. Now, suppose it is held that a relationship based solely on the essential nature is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*); whereas in the case of fire’s relation to smoke, factors such as damp fuel—which transcend the essential nature—are the cause, but in the case of smoke’s relation to fire, the essential nature itself is the cause and there is no other cause.
If that were so, then inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) would be accessible through perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For it is not possible for perception to cognize the absence of another cause, because perception has only positive existence (*bhāva*) as its object.
However, since the absence of another cause is cognized from the observation of an effect, its accessibility through perception is untenable.
Furthermore, in the case of smoke’s connection with fire, its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone is not the cause, since other factors such as fuel and moisture are also causes.
Therefore, being natural (*svābhāvikatva*) consists precisely in the non-deviation of the essential nature.
And since non-deviation is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) across all places and times, it cannot be apprehended through perception, because perception has only the present as its object.

Moreover, even if [the relation] were intrinsic (*svābhāvikatva*), it could be ascertained only for that which is present and proximate, not for those that are past, future, concealed, remote, or unrelated.

For there are many individual instances of the relation between fire and smoke; how then can perception—which has only a conjoined object as its domain—comprehend that the essential nature of smoke alone is the cause of all those [relations]?
If it is argued that the cause is the generality (*sāmānya*) of the relation, no; because that [generality], being eternal, lacks a causal basis.
Moreover, this same objection applies equally even to the position that [perception] occurs through a single momentary contact;
for in that case as well, it is understood that the conjunction currently in contact is the cause for the cognition of the absence of smoke, and not past conjunctions and the like.
Since that [past conjunction] has perished at another time, the inference at a later time must have as its cause the form of the conjunction that was present in perception.
Therefore, it is established that the restriction (niyama) cannot in any way be an object of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Others, however, consider the restriction to be cognizable through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
When one hears this—that these fires are seen together with smoke, and there is no instance where smoke is not seen—this [fact] would be inexplicable if there were no restriction of smoke by fire.
For it is argued that what is indeterminate might sometimes, in some place, pass away even without fire;
but that too is untenable.
First of all, its non-perception is accounted for simply by its absence.
However, one cannot conclude on that basis alone that fire exists everywhere, for there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Even the mere observation of smoke there is possible due to the presence of fire; yet, by that much alone, one cannot reach the certain conclusion that "there is smoke" in the same way as one concludes "there is omniscience."
Therefore, there is absolute authority for this restriction.
It is said:
What more need be said here? For the author of the Vārttika himself has demonstrated the authority.
For it is stated that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed to be understood through repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*).

In this regard, those who have ascended to inference by relying on great effort regarding the prior portion [of experience] have resorted to a single cognition merely for the sake of avoiding futility.

This smoke is necessarily [concomitant] with fire; indeed, because it relies upon the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) established in consciousness as the nature of the characteristic of knowledge, this restriction (*niyama*), which is to be reached through repeated observation, is established by both [means].

What, then, is this means of knowledge called "repeated observation" (*bhūyodarśana*)? It cannot be said that there is any single fixed rule. Rather, whichever among perception and the other means of knowledge apprehends the frequent coexistence (*sāhitya*) of the mark (*liṅga*) with the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), that very same [means], aided by the observation of the rule, becomes possible as the means of knowledge for the rule itself. Now, one might object: in those specific instances, coexistence is indeed apprehended through repeated observations; however, it is not apprehended everywhere, because all observations terminate within their own respective objects. For the concomitance (*sahabhāva*) existing everywhere is accessible only to infinite perception, and such [perception] is difficult to obtain while one is alive.

Even from the observation of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the absolute absence [of the reason] in the counter-example is understood as being merely proximate; however, its exclusion from *all* counter-examples is indeed difficult to establish, because there is no means of perceiving the non-perception of everything that is a counter-example.

Since non-existence is not established by mere non-perception, how can the necessity (*niyama*)—which consists in pervasion across all places and times—be understood through repeated observation? This very point was raised as a doubt by the Teacher himself, as he said: "For the concomitance (*anvaya*) of the pervader is not seen in every instance of the pervaded."
"For that [object] can indeed be obtained through infinite [perceptions] arising from direct perception and so forth.
Likewise: "For the status of being a logical reason (hetu) is understood through its absence in the counter-example (vipakṣa)."
And thus:
"The state of being free from all contrary instances would not be obtained"—this is the meaning.
And here the justification has been stated: "In that case, [the reason] indicates the concomitant merely by its non-perception."
"Thus.

Here, "therein" means "in the case of the counter-example (vipakṣa). This is what is being said: let us grant for a moment that the absence of the probans from all counter-examples might not be established; however, the non-perception of the probans in the counter-example constitutes its non-existence there. And by that much alone, smoke and the like, when observed as concomitants, become indicators of their concomitants, such as fire.

As for the statement that "coexistence is also seen to be difficult to find everywhere," the answer to that has already been stated: "It is said that coexistence is difficult to find everywhere; indeed, it is not the case that it is never seen anywhere, for it is certainly observed in two or three instances. In the case of fire and smoke, their coexistence is established because they occupy a limited space."
"And because the absence [of concomitance] is not observed, the state of being a *gamaka* (probans) is postulated.
This is the meaning: let there be no observation of coexistence everywhere; however, let there be an observation of a sublation regarding those two specific locations.
However, as long as no deviation is observed, inference does indeed occur.

For if a rule consisting of a pervasion across all places and times were understood through the property that serves as the basis for inference (*liṅga*), then there would be a valid objection. But we do not say this; rather, the cause for the acceptance of inference is simply this: wherever smoke and the like are seen, there it is invariably accompanied by fire and the like, and their non-accompaniment is never observed. It is precisely this much that leads ordinary people to understand that smoke indicates fire.

However, it does not depend upon the comprehension of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) regarding the entire class [of objects], by which the means of knowledge would become difficult to obtain.

Therefore, the statement of the restriction (*niyama*) is not made with reference to all places and times; rather, the restriction is said to be precisely that necessity of the concomitance of the mark (*liṅga*) with the marked (*liṅgin*) in such places and times as are perceived.
Consequently, that alone is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of inference.
And since that is easily understood through repeated observations, there is no need for a restrictive rule regarding the concomitance of the sign (*liṅgin*) with the sign-bearer (*liṅgi*).
As it has been said: "The indicator of a concomitant is merely its co-occurrence.
But what, then, is inference based on a restrictive rule of concomitance? Indeed, in that relationship, one cannot say that it is observed as many times as it is doubted.

As for those who say that the rule (*niyama*) is cognizable through perception aided by repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), and those who say that even when the rule has been grasped through all-encompassing observation (*sakaladarśana*), one seeks further repeated observation to eliminate possible adventitious conditions (*upādhi*)—even they do not require [repeated observation] in this way, just as we do not; thus, there is no fault in our position.
Now, must the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke across all places and times be understood by one who desires to infer? True, it need not be understood.
But if so, how can the general relation of positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*) be said to be established by a hundredfold connection in a single part of the subject (*pakṣa*)?
It is not the proponent of the thesis (*pakṣadeśin*) who is designated by this term, but rather the proponent of the instance (*dṛṣṭāntaikadeśin*).

Therefore, this is the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*: when the relationship between smoke and fire has been ascertained through their respective parts in one and the same locus, such as a kitchen (*mahānasa*), then that part which is the smoke is inferred elsewhere—on a mountain or the like—or at a later time in that very same kitchen. This is because such is observed in the world.

Thus, having stated that the word "ascertained relationship" (*jñātasaṃbandha*) refers to the knower (*jñātṛ*), [the author] says: "Alternatively, it is not a designation of the knower, but rather a designation of some object of knowledge (*prameya*); the meaning is 'not of the knower'."

In response to the question "Of whom [is this] the proponent of a single part of the object of cognition (*prameyaikadeśin*)?", it was stated: "the proponent of a single part of the example (*dṛṣṭāntaikadeśin*). As they have said: "Someone who has cognized the relationship through a single part [of the subject] and a single part [of the example], or another person similar to him, infers [the whole] by means of those two parts through their distinction."

Thus [it is said]. The phrase "he indeed by those two" intends a different time. And speaking in this way, he states that by the term *jñātasaṃbandha* (one who knows the relationship) and the term *ekadeśin* (one who possesses one part), there is the designation of the *ekadeśin* of the example.

Let it be so; let there be inference based on the rule of concomitance (*sāhitya-niyama*) in those places where [the connection] has been observed, such that "wherever there is smoke, there is fire. This is the understanding derived from repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*). How is this? It is not non-existent, nor is it invalid, because it arises with firmness for everyone at all times.
Therefore, it must be stated upon what basis this [inference] comes to have the suffix *ṇic* (i.e., becomes a causal operation).
It is said:
This scripture is inferential (*ānumānika*), because it arises for one who has already known the relationship [between the sign and the signified].

Furthermore, it is not sensory (*aindriyaka*) because it is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), as that would contradict its nature as a specific form of consciousness (*saṃvid-viśeṣa*) characterized by direct manifestation (*sākṣātkārin*).
For, since smoke is observed to coexist with fire in many places and times, there arises an inference:
"All other things—whether past, future, or remote—that possess smoke must possess fire, because they are characterized by smokeness, like the kitchen and so forth which have been directly perceived.

Thus, having understood that from the subject (pakṣa) one follows a general rule of valid cognition regarding the necessity of coexistence with another property, there occurs an inference of that other property.
And it is said: "Therefore, among other phenomena, whatever [light] of whatever kind belongs to someone by means of whatever [cause],
and to whatever extent it is pervaded in a place or at a time—
of that [person], there shall be a corresponding [light] of that same extent in another lifetime, provided the conditions of the present life remain the same."
In the same way, it establishes the pervading factor of the pervasions.
Thus,

by the two terms "of such and such a kind" (*yādṛśatādṛśa*), it is shown that the nature of the example consists in the fact that for a deficient form, there is neither the status of being a logical mark (*liṅgatva*) nor the status of being the possessor of the mark (*liṅgitva*).
For ordinary people do not infer fire from door-panels and the like merely because of a pale garment, in the absence of its being smoke.

Nor is it produced by hot fire; for the transformation of grass is indeed observed [to occur] because its specific properties are known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Since it possesses heat, it is inference alone that leads one to infer the presence of fire.

And just as the course of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the world must be followed by investigators, not by such [fallacious] means, so too has this demonstrated the fallacious nature (*ābhāsatva*) of all non-probative reasons (*aprayojaka-hetu*).
A reason that lacks the form observed in the example is called "inconclusive" (*aprayojaka*).
It is distinct from [the other types] merely by its connection with the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*),
since such [a deficiency] is seen in all inferences.
However, you have accepted a conceptualization of form (*rūpa-vikalpa*) that exceeds that [of the opponent].

By means of this, having observed the concomitance of the prohibited nature of harmfulness (*hiṃsatva*) with unrighteousness (*adharma*), one is able to infer unrighteousness in the harming of living beings (*prāṇī-hiṃsā*) based on the mere fact of its being harmful—even in cases such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa—without [the specific condition of] being prohibited.

Since the state of being prohibited is observed to coexist with unrighteousness even without the quality of being harmful (as in the case of knowing what was previously unknown), it serves as the inferential mark (*anumāpaka*).
Just as it is understood that a student who possesses the capacity for study and so forth must be accompanied by a teacher, and thus is not taught merely by virtue of being a student;

likewise, the coexistence of darkness (śyāmatva) among the sons of Devadatta is established through the pervasion of the food consumed during the transformation of the embryo. This is the demonstration of pervasion (vyāpti).
Since [the color] yellow and so forth are the causes for its perception, in their absence, one could not infer the blackness of that very object merely by virtue of its being Devadatta’s son.
By this, the inference that [substances] such as the body, fire, and so on possess the nature of being perceived due to their being qualified by conjunction—just like a jar—is refuted.

For instance, it is only in the case of objects such as jars, cloths, and houses—which can be constructed through specific manual operations of the hands and so forth—that their lack of an agent is observed. In the absence of such [manual operations], how could there be an inference of an agent based on a specific configuration for things like mountains and bodies, which are products of transformation (*pāriṇāmika*)? Such an inference would be like inferring fire from white clouds and the like. Furthermore, the concomitance between a specific configuration and having an intelligent agent endowed with a body, sense organs, and so forth has been observed; however, that [concomitance] is excluded from sprouts and the like due to the non-perception of such [an agent].
When that [specific instance] is excluded, one should understand that the inference is based on the mere presence of intelligence (*buddhimat*), with the door and so forth as the initial examples;
it is an inference from perception, like the inference of fire from grass and the like.

Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence of the abolition of all inference; for, having set aside the specific particulars, the concomitance of the universal "being an element" (*bhūtatva*) with the universal "fire" was apprehended, and since its non-deviation is observed on the mountain, an inference of that [fire] there is logical.

The universal (*sāmānya*) is inferred, not the particular (*viśeṣa*), because the former is what is followed [by the cognition]. Even though the universal has already been apprehended in the kitchen and so forth, it is recognized through perception or inference in another place or at another time; thus, your argument does not suffer from the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Furthermore, since the universal also possesses distinctness—its relation with the mountain being one of inherence in that which is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*)—its cognition there is indeed appropriate.

But surely, even within a specific location, the nature of things may vary; for in some places death occurs from the sting of a scorpion and the like, while in others it does not. Similarly, there might be a suspicion of the deviation of smoke from fire in another region.
True, such a suspicion arises, but it is mentioned here so that, having come from those respective regions and heard [of these cases], one may refute it; thus everything is clear.

Therefore, when a certain universal or particular, or a certain particular, is perceived as having a necessary concomitance with another through some relationship whatsoever at observed places and times, that very thing—when seen again in another place or at another time—is the indicator of that [other] precisely because of that rule of concomitance.

In observed locations, the rule of concomitance (*sāhityaniyama*) between smoke and fire and so forth can be understood through numerous observations aided by companions; thus it is established that the relationship of the mark (*liṅga*) with the marked (*liṅgin*) is indeed of the nature of a rule (*niyama*), and that this is based on the means of valid cognition consisting of repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*).
The *Vyāptivāda* (Treatise on Pervasion) in the *Nyāyaratnamālā* composed by Pārthasārathi Miśra is completed. *Nyāyaratnamālā*, pp. 56–62. *Vyāptisamarthana*.

Now, it is established that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is to be understood through a single observation. There is no dispute that there exists the cognition "there is smoke because of fire" with respect to things such as those in contact.

And in this case, the object is not perceived as qualified by space and time through the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because qualities have the inherent nature of residing in a substance (*dravya*).
As it has been said: "And because qualities are [already] word-meanings.
If it is argued that this [inference] concerns objects other than the word-meanings—just as in the case of words—[we reply: no, because that too is rooted in perception.

For in the world, in whatever manner the mutual connection of word-meanings is determined through perceptions, in that very same way the word expresses them; otherwise, in the Vedic sentences, the practice of abandoning the literal meaning and describing another sense through figurative (lakṣaṇā) or secondary (gauṇā) functions would be improper.

Therefore, logic (*nyāya*) has as its object only that which is not [already established] by mere [perception], and not that which is verbal (*śābda*). For conjunction (*saṃyoga*), neither space nor time is perceived as a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) of the substance; rather, they are understood through the persistence of the conjoined objects. Thus, one understands: "Now there is the relation of fire and smoke," and not "Now there is the conjunction of fire and smoke. Otherwise, why would one not accept that conjunction itself possesses the specific qualities of space and time? Consequently, since conjunction is perceived as persisting as long as the substance exists, the relation of smoke to fire is established as being purely adventitious (*aupādhika*)—namely, that wherever there is smoke, there is fire—by the observation of a single instance alone.
And the demonstration of the pervasion of conjunction is the non-occurrence of pervasion.

Regarding the doubt that there might be a limiting condition (*upādhi*), that doubt is dispelled simply by observing the conjunction [of smoke] in other individual instances as well. Now, one might object: "But surely there is also a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) for smoke-origination in every individual instance. This is not so; if the apprehension of individuals could occur even without a universal (*sāmānya*), then the universal would indeed be subordinate. However, such is not the case.
Furthermore, there is never any cognition of a particular without a universal,
for it has been stated that no cognition of form exists that is devoid of form.

Therefore, because the particular qualified by the genus is primary, and because through it the connection [of the genus] is present, the existence of fire is grasped all at once in every instance of smoke.

As it has been said: "And this being so, it is only the existence of smoke in another place or at another time that requires a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and when that [existence] is established, there is no [need for] contact with fire.

Thus, even when the absence of limiting conditions (*anaupādhikatva*) has been grasped, if someone should have a suspicion of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), then by means of repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) alone, the mere removal of that suspicion is effected, but not the grasping of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

[Objection: But surely, even when a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is not perceived, the perception [of the relation] must itself be capable [of establishing it], simply because the capacity [for such a perception] has arisen. [Reply: If that were so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); for even in the apprehension of a jar or the like, there would follow the consequence that the apprehension of the jar is also non-conclusive, due to the suspicion of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*).
[Objection: But surely, since the connection with the object of desire is seen once, the inference of smoke from fire is established by a single observation.

[Reply: It is not so; by that very single observation, it would follow that the connection of fire with smoke is also free from limiting conditions (*anaupādhika*). However, at a later time, upon perceiving limiting conditions such as being produced by fire (*āgneyatva*), the certainty of its being conditioned (*aupādhikatva*) is reached.

Furthermore, when the certainty that something is conditioned by a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) arises from the observation of such an adjunct, it does not follow that the thing remains connected to that adjunct even when the adjunct is no longer observed.
Therefore, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs through a single observation alone.
Nor can multiple observations compensate for the incapacity of a single observation, because each individual observation among those many is itself merely a single observation.
Nor does multiplicity of perceptions constitute a grasper [of reality].

If it is argued that this is seen to be the case in the apprehension of the nature of a jewel, it is not so; for even there, multiplicity of perception is not the grasper. Rather, it is engaged in the apprehension of a distinguishing form, and because that form is extremely subtle and because of the absence of mental concentration, it is unable to grasp the reality; it grasps only the jewel in its generality.
Thus, when multiple perceptions have arisen, the reality is grasped through the force of the availability of the causal complex, such as mental concentration.
Therefore, repeated observation has no utility in the apprehension of reality.

If repeated observation were accepted as the cause [of such apprehension], then, just as in the case of the contact of the sense organs with their objects, there would have to be a rule that everyone must possess repeated observation;
yet this is not seen to be the case, for one person grasps reality from a single observation, while another does so even after a hundred observations.

Therefore, the apprehension of the internal reality [of pervasion] does not arise from repeated observation alone. As for the argument that even if a single observation lacks the capacity [to establish pervasion], it is possible for a single instance of a similar class of observation to possess such capacity—just as a single sting by a scorpion can be a cause of death, or a single date-palm fruit can be a "ball" (piṇḍa), and so forth—that too is incorrect. Even in those cases, the capacity must be postulated through a distinction in error or a distinction in location; it is not the case that a single object possesses two distinct powers.
Thus, pervasion is to be understood through a single observation.
Prakaraṇa 20: For that which is pervaded (the *vyāpya*) makes known that which pervades it (*vyāpaka*).
Bṛhatī, p. 71.
The non-establishment of the pervasion and the locus is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). See "fallacious reason" in the *Bindu*.
Maṇi, p. 41.
For the relationship of pervaded and pervader is established between two positive entities;
therefore, between the absences of those two, the opposite is understood.
*Stotrānumāna*, 111–122:
"That which is pervaded by the pervader is all the more pervaded.

When, by the force of an injunction (*vidhi*), it is intended that something is to be pervaded, then according to the principle that "that which is pervaded by the pervader is all the more pervaded," it is understood that [the duty] belongs to Maitrāvaruṇa alone, and to him alone.
"A staff for the Maitrāvaruṇa. (Bhāṭṭadīpikā 4.2.6).
The number residing in the object being pervaded is not intended to be significant.

The notion that the number perceived in the injunction "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) is not intended to be significant in its aspect as a subordinate factor (guṇabhāva) would not be possible unless this principle were stated; and the principle has indeed been stated in the verse beginning with "vyāpyamāna.
Even though it has been established in that manner, [the number] is not intended to be significant.
(This refers to the prima facie view.
Confused.
Human effort is not capable of counteracting delusion; therefore, one should remain indifferent toward such [arguments].
*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 95.
Delusion (*vyāmoha*).

The cause of a false cognition regarding an object is delusion (*vyāmoha*, i.e., error). For that perception which lacks a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is a delusion, such as the perception of silver in mother-of-pearl.
(Bhāṣya 3.8.2.24; Ṛjuvimalā p. 55).
The *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* composed by Vyāsa, consisting of four chapters (*caturlakṣaṇī*), is indeed a distinct scripture [from the *Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa*], as stated in *Saṃkarṣaṇa* 4.4.10:
"Divinity is intended to have a distributive occurrence (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) in both [the individual soul and the Supreme Self]."
Saṃkarṣa. 4|4|6: "Pervasive occurrence" (*vyāsajyavṛtti*). For a pervasive cognition does not occur through the pervasion [of its object] by a single [entity].
When [the ritual] is expanded,
it is designated as such;
it is said that neither the Ādhīyomīya nor the Āgneya [is performed].
Or [it may be said]:
"In the case of a property that exists by way of collective inherence (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), the perception of all its substrata is not a cause [of its own perception].
(Maṇi, p. 16).
The sequence [of the vyāhṛtis, the syllable *haṃ*, the daśahotṛ formulas, and the sāmidhenī verses] follows from logical principle.

The meaning is that, since there is no rule determining the sequence for the *daśahotṛ*, the *vyāhṛtis*, the *hiṅkāra*, and the *sāmidhenīs*—which are enjoined by such rules as "one places these *vyāhṛtis* before the recitation of the *sāmidhenīs*"—they would occur in an indefinite order.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhāntin replies]: because the gerund suffix (*ktvā*) in the statement "having uttered the *hiṅkāra*, he recites the *sāmidhenīs*" expresses a time prior to the action already mentioned, the *hiṅkāra* occurs before the *sāmidhenīs*.

Furthermore, because the recitation (*anuvacana*) is prescribed as being "before" [the *vyāhṛtis*] through the mediation of the Vedic text (*āmnāya*), and because the *hiṅkāra* is not so mentioned, the *hiṅkāra* occurs before the *vyāhṛtis*.
In the case of the *daśahotṛ* and likewise in the *śravaṇa*, because they are manifest from the mantra, their placement occurs earlier;

since the study [of the order] applies everywhere, where the logical possibility arises through the intervention of the sun, the sequence of the *praiṣa* (directions) is established as it is improper for there to be a gross intervention.
— *Saṃkarṣa*.

**Vyutpatti (Acquisition of Meaning):** Having inferred a cognition directed toward a specific object, the determination of a word’s own meaning—which resides in the substance of the word—is called *vyutpatti*. (*Rjuvimalā*, p.
16). Furthermore, this acquisition of meaning pertains to the word together with its object, and not to the cognition which is its effect, because [cognition] is infinite and subject to deviation.
Kaṇikā, p. 268. Etymology:

For in the linguistic usage of the Buddha, etymology is said to be simply the determination of the relationship between the signifier and the signified—that is, the understanding that "by this word, this meaning is expressed. Ṛjuvimalā, p. 164.
It is precisely the connection between action and its factors (kriyākārakānvaya) that brings about grammatical proficiency, and not the relationship of subordinate and principal (śeṣaśeṣibhāva).
Nevertheless, the relationship of subordinate and principal is included within that connection.
A word that is *vyutpanna* is expressive;
*vyutpanna* means having its denotative power (*śakti*) grasped. (Ci. 3.1.1)
*Vyutseka* means throwing out (*kṣepaṇam*).

*Vyutseka* is the pouring out of water in all directions during the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, using mantras such as "May the gods and the officiating priests purify themselves in the eastern direction."
There is a sublation of the act of drawing out [the grains] in the case of the *saurya* oblation of cooked rice.
10|2|20: 61. Regarding the statement "In the case of the *saurya* oblation of cooked rice, there is a sublation of the act of drawing out," the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted.
The separation and the placing [of the cake] are not prescribed in the archetype, because they are not mentioned in the original text.
The separation of the sacrificial cake from the potsherds and its placing upon the sacrificial grass within the altar are performed;
however, both the separation and the placing are not heard of—that is, they are not mentioned—in the archetype.
And that [substitution] should not be performed in the case of the *saurya* oblation of cooked rice;
this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Who [holds this view]?
The Dvirātra sacrifice named Vyuṣṭi;
in that [sacrifice], the subsequent day is an Atirātra.
Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 10.5.10.48.
The *vyūḍha* (expanded) sacrifice.

There are two kinds of *dvādaśāha* (twelve-day rite): the *vyūḍha* and the *samūḍha* (contracted). In the *samūḍha*, the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* days have the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyavāgra*), as does the tenth day; then, among these nine days, the first day has the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu, then those beginning with the *śukra* cup, then those beginning with the *āgrayaṇa* cup, then those beginning with the cups for Indra and Vāyu, then those beginning with the *śukra* cup, and then those beginning with the *āgrayaṇa* cup. In the *vyūḍha*, however, the sequence is different.

Now, regarding the expanded (vyūḍha) arrangement: the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* days have the cups dedicated to Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyava*) first; then, among the remaining ten days, the first day has the *aindravāyava* first, then the one with the *śukra* cup first, then two with the *āgrayaṇa* cup first, then one with the *aindravāyava* first, then two with the *śukra* first, then one with the *āgrayaṇa* first, and then two with the *aindravāyava* first. In this expanded arrangement, there are six days with the *aindravāyava* first (at positions 1, 2, 6, 1, 1, and 12), and three days with the *śukra* first (at positions 1, 3, and 8).
The three [soma-pressings] beginning with the Āgrayaṇa are [performed in the order] 4|5|9 (Bhāṣya 10|5|24).
[The sequence] 5|12|6|88 [is established].

According to the Siddhānta, wherever there is an explicit scriptural statement (*vacana*) or an indicative mark (*liṅga*), the *vyūḍha* (extended) arrangement prevails; elsewhere, in the absence of such specification, the *samūḍha* (contracted) arrangement applies.
The *vyūḍha* (extended) twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *samūḍha* (contracted) one.
(Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2186). Regarding this, the section titled "The *vyūḍha* twelve-day sacrifice is a modification of the *samūḍha*" should be consulted.

In the *vyūḍha* twelve-day sacrifice, a transposition of meters (*chandovyatikrama*) is prescribed: "The meters indeed run after one another’s place—the *gāyatrī* after the *triṣṭubh*; the *triṣṭubh* after the *jagatī*; the *jagatī* after the *gāyatrī*."
In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is a transposition of both the words and the meanings contained within the mantras. [The siddhāntin replies:

There is no transposition of the meanings; rather, the word *jagatī* is to be employed in place of the word *gāyatrī*, and the word *gāyatrī* is to be employed in place of the word *triṣṭubh*; [this applies] in the case of the *vyūḍha-jagatī*.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the section concerning the vows (*vratādhikaraṇa*) and in the case of the word *triṣṭubh*, only the transposition of the words themselves must be performed (Vi.

10.5.26). In the *vyūḍha* twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), there is a transposition only of the words such as *gādhya* found in the mantras pertaining to the *bhakṣa*, *pavamāna*, *paridhi*, and *kapāla*, and not of the objects (*artha*) themselves.
See the section on *mīko.* pṛ. 2209, regarding the *bhakṣapavamāna* in the *dvādaśāha vyūḍha*. In this context, the term *vrata* is a name for a ritual action (*karman*).
*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 6.2.5.20: "Vrata" refers to a mental act; [the *Prajāpativratas*] consist of the resolve, "I shall not do this.

*Bhāṣya* 6.2.5.20: In the statement, "He releases his speech by saying, 'Perform the vow' (*vrataṃ kuruta*)," the connection [between the words] serves the purpose of indicating time regarding the performance of the vow.
See the section titled "The Section on Rising and the Fire" at *Mīmāṃsākośa*, p. 1102.
The *vrata* (vow) in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice during the latter part of the night is not obligatory.
