3|3|6|23. The identity of word and meaning in both worldly and Vedic usage.

1|3|9|30–35. The doctrine of the eternity of word and meaning, and the doctrine of the eternity of the relationship between word and meaning. (3830) The doctrine of the eternity of the relationship between word and meaning.

From the rule *radābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.2.42), which falls under the governing rule *kartari* (Pāṇini 1.4.54), it is understood from the rule *vṛddhirasyācāmādeḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.1) that [the suffix] applies when there is an agent (*kartṛ*).
For this reason, we conclude that the Vedas were not composed by anyone through conventional usage, even though such a connection might otherwise be forgotten;
nevertheless, we do not accept the meaning of such a connection without authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*).
Just as something may remain unperceived even while one is looking for it, we do not, on that account alone, accept the horn of a hare in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the relationship between a word and its meaning is non-human (*apauruṣeya*).
[Objection: But surely we understand the meaning of the relationship through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

For we do not observe people understanding a meaning from a word when they have not previously formed a mental impression (*saṃjñā*) of it. If they were indeed to understand it, they would understand it even upon hearing it for the first time.
If it is argued that because such understanding is not observed, there must necessarily be a relationship [between word and meaning], [we reply:]...
No;
because the instruction is given as an established fact.
If the meanings were not necessarily perceived due to the absence of a relationship, then we would infer the existence of a relationship through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
However, there is another way:
we observe that children first acquire meaning through the observation of elders engaged in practical affairs for their own purposes.
Those elders, when they were children, likewise acquired it from other elders, and those others from yet others; thus, there would be no beginning to this process.
Alternatively, suppose that not even a single relationship between a word and its meaning ever existed, and that the relationships were subsequently established by someone.
In this case, given the existence of the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), there could be no remover of the agent of the relationship from the matter of the meaning.

Furthermore, those who know linguistic usage point to [the relationship] as being perceived directly (*pratyakṣa*); others merely postulate an agent of the relationship. And when there is a direct perception standing as an adversary, a postulation is not tenable.
Therefore, there is no [need for] a creator of the relationship [between word and meaning].
(He applies the words of the Sūtra: "And because of non-difference.
Just as in this region the word 'cow' applies to that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, so it is in all inaccessible places as well.
How can many relations be produced? A single [agent] would not be able [to do so].
Therefore, there is no creator of relation. Another says: "And because of non-difference."
Indeed, there is no time apart from the relationship [of word and meaning] in which not even a single word was related to any object.
Why? Because the very act of establishing a relationship is impossible.
For one who establishes a relationship must necessarily do so by means of some word.

By whom was that by which [an action] is performed itself produced? If it were produced by someone else, then by whom was he produced? And by whom was he? Thus there is no finality. Therefore, one who establishes this relationship must accept that certain words, being unproduced (akṛtasaṃjñā), are established through the usage of the elders (vṛddhavyavahāra).
If the establishment of linguistic usage exists, then there is no presumption (arthāpatti) that a relation must necessarily exist.
It might be argued: "How do children, whose relations are not yet established, learn from the elders?
There is nothing impossible in what is observed.
It is observed that children learn from their elders;
yet they do not grasp the relations of the one who establishes those relations. Therefore, there is an inequality.
When the object is unperceived:
and when an object such as Devadatta is unperceived, the creation of a name is both purposeless and impossible.
For names are created in order to communicate specific distinctions, having designated a specific object as their referent.
Since both [the universal and the particular] are unestablished in the case of specific objects whose songs are unknown,
the relationship between a word and its meaning is therefore non-human (apauruṣeya). And for this reason, it is a means of valid cognition because of its independence.
And this being the case, no other person or another means of knowledge is required.
Therefore, dharma is characterized solely by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) and not by any other characteristic.
The mention of Bādarāyaṇa has already been explained.

*Bhāṣya* 1.1.5, pp. 52–58. *Bṛhatī*: "Now, what is this relation (*saṃbandha*)? [It is that] when the word is cognized, the object is cognized. But what is this relation that has been presented as something distinct? We reply: it is precisely what was stated previously. [Objection:
But surely that relation is characterized by the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*); therefore, one might think that this alone is the relation. That is not correct.

Nevertheless, this very relationship characterized by the signified (pratyāyya) and the signifier (pratyāyaka) has been described as the relationship characterized by the denoted (jñāpya) and the denoter (jñāpaka), namely, the relationship characterized by the name (saṃjñā) and the named (saṃjñin).

Now, one might object: "By stating that the relationship between the signified and the signifier is characterized by the name and the named, and by using the dual expression 'of the signified and of the signifier,' another distinct relationship is being asserted.
This is not so.
Thus, it has been explained by way of the fivefold [analysis] that this very relationship between the signifier and the signified is characterized by the name and the named.
Why is this so? Is it not the case that the genitive case expresses distinction (*vyatireka*)?
Indeed, in this instance, there is a distinction based on the relationship of cause and effect.
The relationship characterized by the name and the named is the cause for the designation of the "signifier" and the "signified.

Otherwise, the utility of the signifier and the signified would be purposeless. You must state that single thing which is the relationship characterized by the name and the named, yet you do not designate it.

By the passage, "For this very reason, it was previously established that [the relation] is produced," he demonstrates that even what was stated earlier is being restated. Regarding the doctrine of the eternity of the relationship between word and meaning:

what is the reason for restating the question? This is the reason here: for in the case of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta-vāda*), as raised by the Grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*), one cannot assert the independence of two things that are separately established; thus, the question is posed by one who reflects upon this.
For it is possible to assert the independence of the usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) on the grounds of its beginninglessness; thus, that alone is put forward.
However, the statement that "it [the Veda] is produced" is made with the very same intention previously described.

Therefore, the proponent of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavādin*) concludes its dependence by saying: "We believe that some person, having established the relationship between words and their meanings, composed the Vedas as the cause for that relationship. Thus, its dependence is summarized.
This is now stated: "Because the relationship is non-human (apauruṣeya), it is established"—this is an introduction of the beginninglessness of the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*).
What, then, is this question and answer? When asked "How?", the answer "Because of the absence of a person who establishes the relationship" is inappropriate.
This is stated here in order to refute that very position.
But how is this suspected as being a counter-argument? It is suspected from the perspective of external [scriptural authority].

Even though the understanding of word-meanings is established through beginningless linguistic usage (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), in cases where an author is perceived, there necessarily follows the status of having a beginning (*ādimattā*), just as in the case of the rule "vṛddhir ādaic" (Pāṇini 1.1.1).

(Ṛju: Although the comprehension of meaning from a word is possible even through the usage of elders and so forth, nevertheless, because it is directly caused by convention (*saṃketa*), its beginninglessness cannot be asserted with respect to the object; thus, [the argument] regarding the perception of the relationship constitutes a counter-position. Therefore, the perception of an author must be refuted.

How, then, is this answer—"Because perception lacks intrinsic validity (*prāmāṇya*), and because these [other means of knowledge] are preceded by it"—appropriate to the question "But how is there no relation? How is it not appropriate? Because it is admitted that inference and the others also possess validity.
(By that [answer], the mere rejection of perception does not entail the non-existence of the relation.
Furthermore, being "preceded by that" is untenable [in the case of verbal testimony], as it would entail its dependence on something else.
Furthermore, because [the meaning] is not inferred from the action,
and because the word would be dependent [on something else], it follows that its innate nature (*autpattikatva*) is lost; thus,
it becomes as if one has forgotten the horse while saying the word "horse."

(Ṛju:)—That which is heard in the world from those whose minds are elsewhere during conversations, such as: "Ghoṭārudra has forgotten your horse (*ghoṭa*)," where "forgotten" means "departed from the mind.
This form [of the verb] is used with the intention of expressing both the object and the agent of the root *smṛ*.

This is appropriate for one who lacks specific intention. For the time being, it is possible for [these two] to function as means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through inference alone, provided there is no opposing party in the beginningless linguistic usage of the elders; that is, they are independent of the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Let it be understood, therefore, that they do not constitute a relationship [of contradiction].
Because the nature of the cause is inferred from its effect through pure inference,
and the cognition of meaning from a word is itself an effect;
moreover, that [cognition] is not necessarily capable of inferring another distinct relation, as it is also established by the beginninglessness of the linguistic usage of elders.

Likewise, scripture (*āgama*) also, like independence (*svatantratā*), is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing a relationship, because its object is something to be accomplished (*kārya*).

If it must be preceded by perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), then even in the case of being preceded by inference, since it is possible to comprehend the beginningless conventional usage (*anādivyavahāra*), there is no such thing as "pure" inference; thus, dependence on perception is not possible.
Therefore, both perception and the scripture-inference preceded by it must be rejected.
Therefore, the reply is established.
Now, for what purpose is the plural used in the phrase "because the others are preceded by that"? It should have been stated as "of the others" (*itareṣām*).
(The answer: Because two [cases] are presented as being subject to doubt.
The plural number is justified by the fact that [the ancestors] are entirely non-existent.
But does he not state its lack of proof by saying "because they have long since passed away"?
How is there a lack of proof? Because it is possible for the ancestors to have been objects of direct perception.

The intention is that it is not the case that because something occurred long ago it is not remembered; thus, even for previous cognitions, it is not possible for them to be mere direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If they were [perceptible], they would be remembered like Pāṇini.
Furthermore, non-remembrance cannot occur as it does in the case of Himavat and other such great beings.
In that regard, a reason for non-recollection is established, such as the particularity of the person (*puruṣaviśeṣa*) and so forth.

What is intended by the statement, "And there is no particularity of persons regarding words"? The intention is this: if [words] were produced (*kṛtaka*), then their authority would depend upon that [person]; however, because they are not produced, there is no interruption [of their authority], and thus recollection is possible. [Objection:

If the relationship were dependent on a person who could be perceived directly, then it would have to be understood through the apprehension of that person's convention (*saṃketa*). However, since that is not the case, [the relationship is eternal].
For there could be no linguistic usage if there were a failure of convention regarding the first and last [sounds] of the word *kali*.
Therefore, for the sake of the mutual understanding of the convention, a person must be remembered;
and this has been made manifest by Pāṇini’s citation of the verse.

Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "Even though we... understand," what is the object of this mention of forgetfulness? If it refers to the subject matter to be proven (*sādhyaviṣaya*), then the very possibility of forgetfulness is itself the proof.
And as it was stated in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa*: "Forgetfulness is possible.
Likewise, the claim that "we do not understand the meaning of the relationship without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)" is not a valid reason (*ahetu*).
Regarding the doctrine of the eternity of the relationship between word and meaning:

even if it is argued that "just as something may exist yet not be perceived, we do not on that basis alone accept a rabbit's horn in the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)," that too is incorrect.
If there were non-perception of only what actually exists, by whom could it be said that "a rabbit's horn does not exist"?
Now, if the intention is this:

"Even though the occurrence of forgetfulness is observed elsewhere, one cannot on that account assert the occurrence of a different property (vidharma) elsewhere," this is an incorrect intention. For it is said that what is seen in one place occurs in another.
For this indeed is the domain of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*).
To this it is replied: neither this forgetfulness nor non-perception is established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

However, this [statement] is also uttered for the purpose of eliminating defects in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣa*) regarding that which has been apprehended. But here, since both [parties] agree that this is established by non-apprehension alone, it was stated to be "incoherent" (*asaṃbaddha*).

[The Ṛjuvimalā states: "Since the connection with all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed through non-apprehension alone, this presentation of forgetfulness is incoherent; it was stated that even by way of eliminating defects in the cause, it does not connect."
Just as there is a non-apprehension of an apprehended object such as a jar, one cannot on that account assert the existence of a rabbit's horn;
for the non-apprehension of an object requires another cause.
Furthermore, the non-apprehension of non-apprehension is simply non-apprehension itself (there is no postulation of another cause therein). Therefore, this is well said.

[Objection: "But [you spoke of] 'by means of presumptive testimony' (arthāpatti)"—is this being presented as a name for a distinct means of valid cognition? [The proponent of the partial view replies: Yes, it is so stated.

(The Siddhāntin: What, then, is it that is not logically possible here, such that it is grasped by [the opponent] with such a misguided understanding? (The Ekadeśin says: But surely there is an author of the relationship. (The Siddhāntin:

How, then, is it that this is not logically possible [and thus so grasped]? (The Ekadeśin: Because the meaning is not understood upon the first hearing. (The Siddhāntin: If one does not comprehend the meaning upon the first hearing, what does that have to do with an author of the relationship? There is no logical inconsistency whatsoever in that regard.

(The Partialist: In that case, if Devadatta is not perceived in his house even though he is a well-known person, what does that have to do with the existence of fire? (In that instance as well, there is no inconsistency in the existence of the fire, which is the object to be inferred.

(The Proponent: We do not say that the existence of fire is inconsistent. What then? It was stated in the definition of *arthāpatti* (presumption) that his "presence" (*vidyamānatā*) is inconsistent [with the fact of his not being found at home].
"That very consciousness [which perceives] 'this exists externally'—therefore, in that case, it is precisely what is logically untenable that is being perceived.

But here, since the meaning is not understood upon the first hearing, one might ask: "Who is the maker of the relationship? What kind of relationship has been observed? [To this we reply: No such logical inconsistency arises. Now, this thought occurs to the mind: "It is not understood from the first hearing, yet it is understood from the second hearing onwards."

"Therefore, another cause distinct from the word must be sought. [The opponent] refutes this: "In that case, it has been stated that the inference of a cause is based on the effect. [The proponent asks:
How then is the Bhāṣya passage 'by presumptive testimony' (arthāpatti) to be justified?"

(The Siddhāntin: "From the meaning" means from inference; that is, from the effect (since presumption is characterized by the effect). Why? Because it has been stated [in the section on the rejection of the relation] that [presumption] is defined by the effect. But surely even inference is not tenable, because the cognition [of the object] occurs upon the first hearing [of the word], and because [the object of] cognition is manifold.

Because the meaning is understood from the Vedic sentence itself upon its first hearing. (The proponent of a partial view [ekadeśin] objects: "But surely this reflection concerns only words; it is with reference to words that this is said, namely, 'because there is no understanding of the meaning upon first hearing. And since no word whatsoever conveys its meaning upon first hearing, there is no fallacy of being unestablished in part (bhāgāsiddhatā)."

(Proponent: What is this thing called a "word" (*pada*)? (This is the thought you are considering. (Partial proponent: Well-known [words] such as "cow" (*go*) and so forth [are the words] in sentences such as "Devadatta, bring the cow.

(Proponent: Are they well-known solely by virtue of being something to be accomplished (*kārya*), or is there an action for the sake of comprehending the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*)? (There is no other function of words than the comprehension of the sentence-meaning.
To the extent that there is comprehension of the sentence-meaning, that occurs even upon the first hearing.)
For that [cognition] arises from a sentence;
[the opponent claims it arises] from a word. And a sentence does not depend on a second hearing.

(An Ekadeśin: [Words] are well-known only as having action (*kārya*) as their purpose. (For, through insertion and deletion, the understanding of the mere meaning of words is grasped only as being for the sake of action.

(He asks: "In what [are they well-known]? (The Ekadeśin: "In linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), by means of which elders engage in communication. (By the etymology "that by which one communicates," *vyavahāra* is indeed the sentence itself. "With what do the elders communicate? (The answer: "With such [utterances] as 'Devadatta, bring the white cow,' and so forth."
(Siddhāntin: In that case, then, linguistic usage [is established] through the sentence.
For an object that is well-known through linguistic usage cannot be said to have some other purpose.
(The partisan [of the Ekadeśin] states the contradiction with the text: How then [do you explain] "What is the meaning of this word 'cow'? and "The dewlap..."?

Regarding the doctrine of the eternity of the relationship between word and meaning: [Objection] How can this relationship be described as innate (*autpattika*) on the basis of the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*)? [If you think that this text does not fit with Mammaṭa’s work, then even in your own view, the description of this relationship as innate on the basis of the linguistic usage of elders is untenable.

For when the usage of elders is examined, it is the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) alone that appears as the effect (*kārya*), not the comprehension of the word-meanings (*padārtha*).]

Therefore, this text should be explained in such a way that there is syntactic unity between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the proof (*sādhana*). That [unity] is indeed explained by the Commentator himself in the section on *tadbhūta* (JS 1.1.25), which is appropriate. But then, how is the avoidance of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) fallacy achieved? It is stated with reference to the cause (*nimitta*).
One who has not previously apprehended the sign does not comprehend [the meaning] from hearing it for the first time;

therefore, the intention is that there must be another sign distinct from that word. Alternatively, the sign—which consists of the word-meanings—is what brings about the comprehension of the sentence-meaning. (Ṛjuvimalā)
The intended meaning is stated as follows: why does that which is heard for the first time not cause comprehension?

A word heard for the first time does not convey its object (padārtha), which serves as the basis (nimitta) [for understanding the sentence]. And one who has not grasped the basis does not comprehend even the meaning of the sentence from a word heard for the first time. Thus, it is established that even in the Veda, that which is heard for the first time is non-conveying.

What, then, is the distinction between the denotative word (*vācaka*) and its cause (*nimitta*)? It is precisely for this purpose that the section on *tadbhūta* (the "become-that" [words]) is commenced; so, enough of this digression.

According to the view that the cause is the word (*nimittapakṣa*), words, while operating toward their own individual meanings, bring about the comprehension of the sentence-meaning; they do not, however, express the sentence as a mere syntactic connection in which the division of words has vanished.
When it is explained in this manner, the distinction between the denotative word and its cause is indeed stated.
"Because the instruction is not like that of one who [already] knows the result" (*na siddhavad-upadeśāt*, Bhāṣya, pp.

55–56). [The author of the *Rjuvimalā* explains: Having transformed the word "instruction" (*upadeśaḥ*), which appears in the nominative case within the *Autpattika-sūtra*, into the ablative case and having supplied the word "as if it were already established" (*siddhavat*), the author of the Bhāṣya stated this.
Its meaning is as follows: "This is established"—that is to say, the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the relationship [between word and meaning] is established.
"From instruction" means from the instruction of elders;
therefore, the postulation of a relationship [between word and meaning] is untenable. What is this "instruction as an established fact," etc.? It is: "This is thus."
In this matter, an author cannot be postulated because the usage of the elders is beginningless.
Therefore, it is established that the relationship [between word and meaning] is innate (*autpattika*). (pp. 131–143)

[Page 153] "What is this? It has begun in one way and concluded in another. It was begun with the claim that 'the meaning is not understood from the word,' yet it is concluded with 'from the linguistic usage of elders.
Thus, this has fallen out quite differently.
When the meaning is understood from the linguistic usage of elders, the meaning is certainly not understood from the word itself, just as in the case of hand gestures and the like."
Even in the case of hand gestures and the like, these are merely well-established through the conventional usage of elders; they are not connected by means of linguistic convention (*śabda*).
For it is linguistic convention alone that brings about the comprehension of meaning, not hand gestures and the like;
for those [gestures] are dependent upon linguistic convention.
Therefore, the word is merely an adventitious condition (*upādhi*) and not the cause of the comprehension of meaning;
it is like the strike of a goad or a whip.

For this very reason, it has been stated by those who maintain the nature of words (the Grammarians)—those proponents of the theory of differentiation—that "only the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) must be accepted."

To this it is replied: What is the use of this partiality for the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*)? This has already been refuted, because oneness is not perceived—that is, because the oneness of word and meaning is not perceived.
If that is so, then the prior authority of the Veda has been refuted.
To this it is replied:

When the meaning of a word is understood through proficiency in the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), what other cause for that word do you consider it to have? Surely you consider proficiency itself to be the cause.
Not so.

For the acquisition of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) occurs through the mode of the relationship between a word and its meaning; it is not the case that the relationship between the word and the meaning arises from the acquisition of usage, because [the relationship] is the object (*viṣaya*) of that acquisition.
Therefore, it has been correctly stated: "Not because of an instruction as if [the relationship] were already established.
Now, one might object: even if the relationship is something to be accomplished (*kārya*), the emergence of the usage of elders is indeed conducive to the understanding of children.

How is this [eternal relationship] suspected to be a counter-argument? True; for linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) pertains to the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*), which is determined by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). There is no contradiction with proficiency in grammar and the like; however, who could possibly postulate that something produced (*kṛtaka*) is free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhi*)?

And it has already been stated that there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) in this case. (The *Ṛjuvimalā* states: Where the relationship is understood through another means of valid cognition to belong specifically to an effect, let there be "being an effect" (*kāryatā*) there.
Furthermore, where there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its being an effect, there its status as an effect must be inferred;
and that [status] is established from the effect characterized by the comprehension of meaning.
If this effect is already accounted for by the very perception of proficiency in the linguistic usage of elders, then an inference based on its being an effect is not possible.

For when another cause is directly perceived, it is not possible in every case to infer that [the word] alone is the cause. Therefore, by means of the mode of apprehending the object, one cannot assert the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatā*) of the relationship.
However, where it is directly perceived, it is accepted exactly as it is.
And it has already been stated that there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this [connection].
Furthermore, if the connection were something produced, there would be no purpose for an author in creating that connection among the words;
for the creation of a connection is dependent upon a pre-existing connection.
For one situated in a difficult position, the application of linguistic usage is not possible.
(If it is argued that there is a relation between word and meaning— this is the theory of the relation between word and meaning.)

If a single person were to compose the Vedas after establishing a relationship between words and their meanings, then he would have to establish that convention only among those who deal with the objects of Vedic knowledge, and not among Mlecchas and others residing in inaccessible regions, because there is no such usage of Vedic objects among them.

Yet, it is observed that even in the lands of the Mlecchas and others, the word "go" (cow) is employed for an animal possessing a dewlap and so forth. Therefore, it is not logical that the very author of the Veda should also be the creator of the linguistic convention.
Because the one who establishes the relationship is the person to be enjoined;
for it is the users [of language], such as those following Pāṇini, who establish the convention.
Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever.
By this, the first explanation of the phrase "and there is no non-exclusion" (*avyatirekaśca*) has been shown. [From Bhāṣya, p. 56, l. 10 onwards, they describe the second:
Furthermore, a relation that is produced is not tenable apart from the word "relation."

If the relationship is accepted as being for the sake of the effect (*kārya*), then the effect is already accomplished [by the relationship itself]. [The *Ṛjuvimalā* states: "The relationship must be established in this manner: 'this meaning is to be conveyed here by this word.
And that cannot be done."

If it is accepted that certain words are established for those undergoing linguistic instruction solely through the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), then these—being connected to the learners by means of prior words—are indeed capable of conveying even the meaning of a sentence. If some words already established in the usage of elders are accepted for the sake of those being instructed, then what is the point of further establishing a relationship [between word and meaning]? Let the usage of elders alone be the means of linguistic instruction.
But surely, even linguistic instruction depends upon the status of something as an action to be accomplished (*kāryatā*)?

How so? [If one were to say], "This is the denoter here," then this understanding of the meaning from the word—namely, that the word possesses the nature of denotation—would not be established. For indeed, nothing is impossible when a perceptible fact is present; for it is observed that children acquire understanding through mere linguistic usage alone.
Therefore, since the means for understanding the meaning of words is directly perceived (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭa*), when the matter is established in this way, the postulation of an author is not tenable.

(He explains the meaning of the phrase "when the object is not apprehended"): This other [point] is also useless for linguistic practice (*vyavahārānaupayika*). For once a relationship has been created, there would be the creation of a relationship for an unseen object such as a deity and so forth.
Incapacity has indeed already been described [in the Bhāṣya].
Therefore, because of its innate nature (*autpattikatva*), its independence is established. (pp.
153–156). For the sake of establishing the eternality of the relationship between word and meaning, there is a requirement for that very basis for the application of a word which is fixed.
Su. Pṛ. 101. The Theory of the Relationship between Word and Meaning. Commentary:
This might be so;
however, there is no relationship whatsoever between a word and its meaning. How, then, could it have either a human or a non-human origin?

How so? This might indeed be the case if one intends to refer to a connection characterized by mere conjunction—that upon the utterance of the words "dhura" and "modaka," there should be the splitting and filling of the mouth.
However, other types of relations, such as those of cause and effect, motive and consequence, or substratum and dependent, are simply untenable in the case of a word. To this it is replied:

For you do not point out that single relationship which is to be designated here—the one characterized as the relationship between the designator (*saṃjñā*) and the designated (*saṃjñin*), namely between the signifier (*pratyāyaka*) and the signified (*pratyāyya*).
He asks: "If the word is the signifier, why does it not signify when heard for the first time? It is replied:
"In all cases, our observation (i.e., worldly usage) is the authority."
We understand that [a word] is a communicator (*pratyāyaka*) by observing its cognition (*pratyaya*), not upon being heard for the first time.

For at the time of the first hearing, since no cognition has been observed, one must wait until—through repeated hearing—it is determined that "this is the name" and "this is the named object. It is from this [repeated hearing] that the comprehension of the meaning arises.

Just as the eye, though seen, does not illuminate [an object] without external light and thus is not itself unperceived—[for it must be admitted that the knowledge of its capacity requires auxiliary factors]—so too [is the case with the word]. (p. 43–44). Śrotra: "In the act of denotation, the status of being the object consists in the connection with the thing to be expressed."

The status of words as either instruments (*karaṇa*) or agents (*kartṛ*) has been defined. He now demonstrates their nature as the expressed (*vācya*) and the expressive (*vācaka*)—starting with the term "abhidhāna" [in the verse].
The operation of a word that results in the comprehension of meaning is the act of expression (*abhidhāna-kriyā*), and that is simply the cognition of the word itself.

The status of an object (*karmatva*) belonging to a meaning by virtue of its participation in the fruit of the action to be accomplished is its "denotability" (*vācyatva*); and the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*) belonging to a word—determined by the speaker's intention—is its "denotative power" (*vācakatva*). "When comprehension [of the meaning] is the objective, and their coexistence is intended, that relation which is restricted to a single [action] belongs to both the meaning and the word."

It is logical that those which are *uddeśya* (the subjects to be indicated), acting independently of one another, do not connect with each other because they govern the action [of the verb] separately.

However, for those which are *upādeya* (the things to be enjoined), since they govern the action through their own means, there exists a mutual restriction (*parasparaniyama*) and connection (*saṃbandha*) by way of that [action]. Likewise, there is also a coexistence (*sāhitya*) between the *uddeśya* and the *upādeya*.

For a designation (*uddeśa*) draws forth an action, and that [action] takes up its own constituent part, the object to be accomplished (*upādeya*), thereby proceeding with itself as the primary element. Thus, in this context, the meaning (*artha*) is the primary element; even for its own establishment, it depends upon the operation of denotation (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*).
And that [operation] takes up its own constituent part, the word (*śabda*); thus, there exists between word and meaning a relationship governed by a single action.
In that regard, although there is no mutual relationship between the factors (kārakas) themselves as related to the son of Pṛthā (Arjuna),
nevertheless, they stand in a relationship of mutual assistance toward that action; it is only after their connection with the action that this relationship between those two is said to occur.
And it has been established that even in this case, inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is not useful.

[Objection: "Granted that there is a restriction regarding a single action; nevertheless, since the actions themselves constitute the connection between mutually related causes, how can there be a connection between word and meaning? To this, he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*).

A word becomes an auxiliary by effecting the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of an object that is useful for linguistic practice (*vyavahāra*) and capable of being understood; and the object is the beneficiary. Thus, there exists between word and object a relationship characterized as benefactor and beneficiary, mediated by the act of denotation (*abhidhāna-kriyā*); this is the relation of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*), which is synonymous with "restriction" (*niyama*) and so forth. [Objection: But if it is produced by such restriction, then verbal cognition would be nothing other than inference (*anumāna*). To this he says: "And not... It has been stated that this restriction occurs after the cognition [of the word] and is therefore not useful for the cognition itself.
If it is argued that "name" (*saṃjñā*) possesses the capacity to convey meaning, then this [name] would not be a constituent part [of the word].
For it is only after observing the *śruti* (the actual phonetic form) conveying its meaning through linguistic usage that the name is postulated.
However, this [name] does not convey the meaning, nor is there any relationship established for it when it is uttered.
Therefore, the capacity to convey meaning arises later, just as it does in the case of smoke and the like.
That [capacity] would be non-essential; this is not the same as the case of smoke and so forth.
(The words *iyam*, *eṣā*, and *iyam* indicate the name. This is stated in two verses and a quarter, beginning with "nodyati-saṃjñā."

For the very nature of being a signifier (*gamakatva*) is what constitutes being a name (*saṃjñātva*); and since that [nature] occurs at the time when the object to be understood is apprehended, it cannot be known beforehand.
Therefore, another relationship must be stated;
for in the absence of a relationship, a name does not cause one to understand the named object.

The meaning is that the capacity to convey [the object], which arises only subsequently, is not even a factor for the denotative power (*vācakatva*) of "smoke" and so forth. He refutes this with the words: "Not this," because "once the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) has been determined, it is that [concomitance] which performs that function [of conveying]."
Because it is indicative, and because [the word] does not arise there previously;

for here, the denotative [words] possess the aforementioned state of being inseparably connected (*avinābhāvitva*). And at the very moment one understands the relationship here from those who have been questioned, [the cognition arises].
At that very moment, [the cognition arises] that "this is the indicator," and not from any other nature.
By stating "this is not similar," he demonstrates the dissimilarity with the words beginning with "nirupite" (when determined).

In the case of smoke and so forth, once the connection is understood by way of place, time, and so on, its status as an indicator exists precisely through that connection; it is not grasped as such at the very first moment.

However, in the case of a word (i.e., a name), its capacity to convey meaning is first apprehended, not any other relation; and it is precisely through the non-apprehension of such [other] relations that its status as a conveyor of meaning arises.

Nor is there the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatā*), because the capacity to convey meaning is established for subsequent individuals based on the apprehension of that capacity in preceding elders.
Thus they say: "O teacher, this person should be understood by us."
In some cases, it is said that "this is the denoter" and "this is the denoted"; in other cases, having observed an action directed toward an object after a word has been uttered,
the status of being a cognizer in those [persons] is understood through inference.
By this very fact, since this word has been determined to be such from this [source], it follows that these two—the world and the expressive power—are established.
This is the method: "From this word, this meaning is to be understood."
"This word is the signifier; this object is its signified"—this is the second [point].

Having observed the cognitive activity directed toward an object arising from a spoken word, the status of being a cognizer (of the meaning) and a signifier (of that meaning) is known by certain pure individuals through inference regarding that object.
And that inference has been demonstrated by the verse.
The meaning is that [the word] is "capable" (śaktikaḥ) or "expressible" (vācyaḥ).
Thus, the threefold understanding from the elders has been shown.
"In this way, denotative capacity is established, even though it is intermingled; thereafter—"
Having extracted the meaning through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), [the word] is restricted [to that meaning].

In this way, the denotative capacity of a word—whether with respect to the genus (jāti) or the individual (vyakti)—is established. However, once the meaning has been extracted in the form of the genus alone, it is subsequently restricted.
Therefore, the capacity to denote is indeed non-inherent;
rather, the relationship characterized by the status of signifier and signified (saṃjñā-saṃjñitva) is caused by that [capacity].

Once this power of comprehension (gamakatva) has been grasped, one subsequently understands the word-meaning through that alone—even in the absence of any other relationship—and thus determines a power of comprehension consisting in the nature of denotation, which is distinct from the mark (liṅga) or the sense organ (indriya), and is synonymous with "name" (saṃjñā). This is the relationship of the union between name and named.

This restriction of the relation, which is called "invariable concomitance" (*avinābhāvitā*), is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as a limitation of the scope of that very relation of being an indicator (*gamakatva*) when it is perceived in its mixed form: "this is the indicator of this," and "this is the indicator of this. Therefore, that alone is the relation.
He states the meaning of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "If the word is the communicator... (Bhā. p. 44): "Therefore, whatever [object] it indicates prior to the grasping of the relation..."
Just as the word *devadatta* does not possess the denotative power (*abhidhāśakti*) for [the meanings] "cow" and so forth,
the *Parihārabhāṣya* states:
"The cognition of the word."
The eternity of sound. The eternity of sound. The eternity of sound.
Knowledge derived from words—specifically worldly verbal knowledge—is not a valid means of cognition (*pramā*), because it lacks the capacity to apprehend an object not already known.

Regarding the conventional usage of the term "validity" in respect to worldly speech and the knowledge produced by it, that usage is merely figurative, based on the assumption that such speech performs the function of a valid means of cognition to a limited extent.
The experts in the science of words have stated that this very essence of sound (*śabdatattva*) manifests itself in the form of objects (*artharūpatayā*).
(Bṛhatī, p. 111). Regarding the eternity of sound (*śabdanityatva*), [it is said in] *Nyāyaśuddhi*:
"In the case of a non-human (divine) relationship, the word attains the status of a valid means of knowledge."
And since that [capacity] would be established only if permanence were proven, it is now demonstrated:
if sound were to perish immediately upon being produced, then its innate capacity to denote its own meaning—which is grasped through the linguistic usage of elders—would be impossible to perceive.
For it is by observing repeated usage that one discerns the capacity to denote its own meaning, having extracted it from the various states [of the sound].

Furthermore, the repeated observation of the use of a word by those belonging to a class who have merely uttered it would not be possible [if the word were eternal]. Now, since space is unitary and that [space] is the auditory organ (*śrotra*), when it is refined, all auditory organs would be refined; consequently, everyone would perceive the sound.
This is not a fault,
because the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*) is indifferent to merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*).
For the refinement of the ear consists in the refinement of the cavity, and since the cavities differ for each person, one whose cavity has not been refined does not perceive sound.
Furthermore, one perceives sound from a great distance when it is carried by the wind,

because the force of the air in the ear, aided by the impulse of the gentle breeze, becomes the cause for its travel over a long distance. However, according to the view that sound initiates another sound [in succession], the wind serves no purpose whatsoever.
"Sound appears as if manifold due to the diversity of its manifestors,
just as the moon appears as if diverse by those [beholders] through the different movements of their eyes."
When that [word] is clearly grasped, the perception of it as manifold is indeed established in the case of sound.

However, by means of various manifesting agents— the internal winds— which are mutually independent and produce distinct refinements of the auditory organ, those who perceive the cognition of the word "existent" (bhūta) as if it were divided, speak of the word as if it were manifold,
just as the moon appears divided by the functions of eyes split by cataracts.
"For they are supported by sounds located in various places, nor do the sounds reside in other things; therefore,
they are supported separately and possess separate movements."

And even if sounds were impermanent, the relationship [between word and meaning] would still be established in this way: let it be that the expressive power belongs to the sound itself, provided its specific nature is not negated; thus, because the expressive entity is eternal, its capacity to convey meaning is indeed established.
To this, he replies: "But the [theory of] sound has already been refuted" (in the section on the refutation of *sphoṭa*).

But surely there are other [factors] such as *gata* (the act of going) which are undesirable [as denoters]; therefore, let only *gata* and the like be the denoters, for they are logically established. And since individual instances of the word "cow" (*go*) are impermanent, they are distinct with each pronunciation, just as the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth are perceived—this is not so. Why? Because no specific difference in the letter *ga* is perceived. For a universal is admitted only where there is a perception of non-difference following upon the apprehension of difference, as is the case with *gata* and the like.

Furthermore, where there is no apprehension of difference (*bhedagraha*), the designation "this is non-different" based on the apprehension of difference—as in the case of mother-of-pearl and silver—is not possible as a definition of a universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). [Objection: If there is no perception of the specific differences of the objects to be understood, how then is there the cognition of difference among mother-of-pearl and humans? [Reply: Precisely because there is a cognition of difference through the distinction of mother-of-pearl and so forth, for that very reason no specific difference is perceived *in itself* (*svataḥ*).
For it is only specific individuals, such as parrots and humans, who attain the status of qualifiers (*viśeṣa*) in that context.
And thus worldly people express these distinctions, saying, "This parrot is reciting," or "This human is reciting," but they do not say, "This particular cow, this particular cow.
Therefore, the fixed nature of the relationship is established.
Therefore, the eternity of the word must be asserted.
This is stated, preceded by an objection: "Some [hold] it to be produced, because it is seen [to be so] in that case.
But if this were so, no relationship whatsoever would be possible.
(The objector asks: What follows from that? (The challenger: There would be the abolition of worldly convention.
(The respondent: And what follows from that? (The challenger: The thesis of impermanence is not tenable;
because it contradicts worldly convention, permanence would result.

(The Partial Mediator: "Let there be no impermanence because it would contradict worldly convention; what follows from the consequence that permanence [would result]? (The Objector: "This follows: namely, the very impossibility of worldly convention. (The Mediator: "That is true, provided that the conventional agreement has ceased [to apply] (the past participle suffix *niṣṭhā* refers to the state).
The meaning is that the conventional agreement is the cause of worldly convention."

(What, then, is the object of the convention (*samaya*) that serves as the basis for linguistic usage? It cannot be the word (*śabda*), because for Bhaṭṭaguru, there is no application of conventional usage to that [word]. To this he says: There is indeed no object that is not the domain of convention; this convention removes all logical impossibilities. (The intended meaning is: This convention has as its object the delusion of non-difference, which—based on the non-apprehension of difference—is produced even though the phonemes (*varṇa*) are distinct at each utterance.
Nor is there a lack of non-contradiction in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), because there is no contradiction with illusion or magic.

For, having cognized an object through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), persons employ words—though they are rooted in error—with the intention of communicating that object, under the conceit that they have correctly produced them. The listener, too, cognizes the object through that very conceit, by means of a falsehood consisting in the non-existence of that [speaker's] intention. Thus, the success of the object is due to the non-deviation of the intention, and from that arises worldly transaction.
But Vedic usage is based solely on the verbal testimony [of scripture]; therefore, it is not dependent upon convention as its cause.
Thus he says: "Therefore, for those who hold verbal testimony to be the means of valid knowledge, authority is established merely through the observation of usage.
Consequently, an effort must be made toward the eternity of the denotation."
And this [objection] has been raised:

"But even if sound is momentary, why should its authority regarding objects not depend solely upon human intention? For instance, why is it that the eyes and other senses, though impermanent, possess authority? To this he replies: because the relationship [between word and meaning] is preceded by the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), and because the understanding of the meaning is preceded by the knowledge of that relationship.
Furthermore, the establishment of authority for the eyes and other senses does not occur despite their momentariness, because they do not yield comprehension upon being heard for the first time.
In the statement, "Some [say] it is produced because it is observed there," the producedness (*kṛtakatva*) of sound is asserted.

What is this producedness? (If producedness is said to mean artificiality with reference to all sounds, then the reason—"because it is observed following effort"—is partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*), since it is absent in the case of the roar of the ocean and the like.
Furthermore, the subject (*pakṣa*) would be contradicted by other means of valid cognition.)

Now, if "being produced by effort" is being proved by taking as the subject (pakṣa) that which has the nature of denotation, then the "producedness" (kṛtakatā) of those things which do not denote would not be established.
[The answer is: "Producedness is said to be origination through human effort.
But surely, even in the case of sounds such as *challaccha* (i.e., *jala*), the production of sound is observed to occur from the clapping of hands.
This is not a fault, because the context concerns denotation.
Furthermore, this denotation is not observed to be devoid of effort.
Therefore, since it is perceived as occurring through another action, we consider that it belongs to those two alone.
How then is it in the case of clay, non-difference, and so forth? (The resolution here is: because their existence is understood from other sources.
In the case of sound, however, there is perception only immediately following effort.
Therefore, it cannot be said that effort is a manifestor of something already existing.
But surely this is a proof for the prior existence of sound through effort.
[He asks: What is this? Let that proof be demonstrated.
Regarding this, he says: "This perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) along with its capacity.

[The objector] asks: "How can there be recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) here? [The answer: "Because there is no apprehension of difference. For recognition occurs only where there is a cognition of non-difference preceded by an apprehension of difference;
however, when there is no apprehension of difference, the delusion of a single determination is based solely on the non-perception of distinction.

[The Objector: Is there not some cognition of difference for one who maintains impermanence? [The Proponent: Why is there no such cognition [of difference]? [The Objector: Because there is a perception of particularity. [The Proponent: [No,] difference is not apprehended; for between the existing and the produced, there is only the difference of the individual [manifestation]. [The Objector: Because of the grasping of specific qualities.
[The Proponent: [Thus,] difference is not understood.
The Supporter: Is recognition based solely on the non-apprehension of specific differences? The Objector: What do you think? [The meaning is: "It is exactly so. The Supporter:

Then recognition would also apply to action (*karman*). The Objector: This is said with reference to the apprehension of the essential nature (*svarūpa*); it has already been stated that action is known through inference (*ānumānika*).

(The Supporter: What is the news regarding flames and the like? (For the nature of flames and so forth is grasped through perception, yet their difference is not apprehended; therefore, do you perhaps intend that there too, for you, there is recognition? The Supporter himself anticipates the intention of the Objector: (If it is argued that) "the eternality of flames and the like contradicts inference," [the Supporter replies:
"The same applies even when they are expressed, because of their non-abiding and so forth."
(He concludes: Therefore, even when the specific difference is not perceived, since perception occurs after another effort [and] otherwise, the production of sound by effort is established;
because it does not persist.
The Commentary: Furthermore, we do not perceive a sound even for a moment after it has been uttered; therefore, we understand that the sound has perished.
Nor is it perceived while existing, because it is not perceived even when there is an absence of causes for non-perception, such as obstruction.
Nor does it fail to reach its object, because it is incorporeal like space, since it is not perceived even when the ear is intact.

Bṛhatī: What is this "immediate apprehension" (attapatti) mentioned in the Bhāṣya? [Answer: If it is argued that even though it does not persist, the capacity to grasp the form is not at all obstructed, and the same applies to the word as well—[Answer: This has already been refuted by the fact that [the word] is understood upon the first hearing. [For] perceptuality depends upon the grasping of a continuous presence, and that cannot be momentary. Therefore, "because it does not persist" (asthānāt) is indeed the reason; it serves to exclude the idea that the relationship [between word and meaning] is adventitious. If it were to remain for another point in time, then it might indeed be established through usage; [the author] demonstrates this with the word "darśayati."
Furthermore, since it lacks stability, it must be maintained by convention alone; thus it is said, "because of its lack of stability.
This follows from the use of the word "to do" (*karoti*).
The commentary states: Moreover, in common usage, one employs such expressions as "Make a sound" and "Do not make a sound."
"It is not that they do not go; rather, this very same sound [is what is meant].
Bṛhatī: A common worldly expression follows this very same principle.

What here is the following of the principle? It is the primary meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do), as in "make a sound," "do not make a sound," and "this boy is a maker of sound" (where the meaning of *karoti* is the production of something that was previously non-existent).
[This applies] to the two primary positions regarding the non-eternality [of sound]:
because [sound] occurs simultaneously in different substances.
The Bhāṣya states: "And we perceive sound simultaneously in various locations."
Therefore, its being one is incompatible with its being eternal;
for if there is no distinction, there can be neither eternity nor multiplicity.
However, in the case of many effects produced in various locations, a connection with multiple places is logically possible.

Therefore, there is no exclusion [of the reason from the contrary]. [Question: What is this "impossibility" (*anupapatti*) mentioned in the *Bhāṣya*? [Answer: This impossibility is that the simultaneous perception of many [parts] by a single [perceiver, such as Devadatta] is not observed.
[Question: What follows from that? [Answer: This follows from it: distinctness (*anyatva*)—namely, the simultaneous perception of many [parts] as excluded from one [part]—establishes distinctness.
But surely there is a difference in meaning [and thus no tautology]. True, it has been established; however, it is demonstrated here by means of a formal reason (*hetu*) and an effort.
What is the benefit? Indeed, none at all.
If there is no one [to refute it], what is the use of the effort of providing reasons? It is true as you have said.
However, this very point implies the rejection of the King's position.
(Someone might have the misconception that "this point, being unrefuted, implies the established doctrine. Therefore, having set aside that [misconception]...
This is the beginning [of the objection]:
for it is not possible to speak of an error regarding that which has not been perceived;
and as long as its status as an error is not established, this [objection] will remain unrefuted by some person of dull intellect.
Furthermore, this entire treatise has been demonstrated by the author of the Bhāṣya under the rule *mandaviśeṣaṇe*.
The Bhāṣya states: "In the absence of a distinction, there is no multiplicity for that which is eternal.

[The opponent] objects: What is meant by this statement, "in the absence of a distinction, there is no multiplicity for the eternal"? Is it possible to say, "in the absence of a distinction, there is no plurality," whether referring to the eternal or the non-eternal?
The inclusion of the term "eternal" (nitya) is not redundant.
If there were multiplicity even for the non-eternal despite the absence of any distinction, then it would be appropriate to say "of the eternal.
Therefore, this passage must be explained.
(Answer: Then it follows that [the reason] is contradicted; for just as a single entity such as a cow is produced simultaneously in many places, so too would it be for that which is eternal.
Therefore, by this [argument], the charge of "unestablishedness" (*asiddhi*) against the [reason] "because of existence in another [place] and because of simultaneity" is raised.
To this, the reply is: "Because there is no distinction.
(The opponent objects again: Is there a distinction between a cow and others? For even that [the universal] is one and undifferentiated;
it is not as if one were a descendant of Cāleya and another a descendant of Bāhuleya.

For you, as one who maintains the proof by means of a reason, speak thus: "This perception of a single entity in multiple locations due to its permanence occurs when there is a particularity, as in the case of cows and the like; however, there is no particularity in the case of sound. Therefore, this perception in one place is not due to permanence, but rather due to the specific effort applied in each respective instance.

When you speak in this manner, your intention is clearly perceived to be that "a particularity exists in cows and the like. Yet this intention of yours is untenable; for even in the case of cows and the like, there is an absence of particularity.

Now, if this is your intention—that "there is no distinction in the universal 'cowness' even when there is no distinction in its substratum, but when there is a distinction in the substratum, there is also a distinction in the cowness"—this intention of yours is indeed untenable.

For, in that case too, it is only the substratum that possesses plurality; what has come of the substrate? (For the substrate does not differ because of a difference in its substrata, since they are distinct). Therefore, even for a single eternal entity, there is simultaneous manifestation in multiple locations.
Therefore, since the simultaneous production of one thing in many places is established even by its permanence, simultaneous perception is not a reason for [its] multiplicity.

Now, this is the view: "The simultaneous perception of a cow or the like does not occur in multiple locations; rather, it is only the individuals (*bhedāḥ*) that are perceived there as being in multiple places, not the universal 'cowness' (*gotva*). (With these words, the proponent of the prima facie position [pūrvapakṣin] anticipates a different intention from the defender [samarthanavādin]).

[Objection: But how then does the cognition "cow, cow" arise with respect to all [individuals]? [The proponent of the theory says: For this very reason—namely, because of the cognition "cow, cow" everywhere—the universal cowness (*gotva*) has no spatial location.
Otherwise, if the individual were perceived as the locus of cowness, there would be the perception, "Cowness is here; cowness is here."

(Objection: How then is inherence established from the cognition "here" (*ihapratyaya*)? (Regarding the statement "inherence [is known] from the cognition 'here,' which is the extraction of this category among the categories of entities—how is that so? The answer is: That refers to a category consisting of a single substance; it does not refer to substances [in general]. (That which is a single-substance category is called the category of action by the word "category.")

The category of action (*karmapadārtha*) alone possesses a single substance; that very [action] has a single substance as its substratum, and not the category of substance (*dravyapadārtha*) or the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*). Therefore, because there is no other way to establish it (*anyathāsiddhi*), the simultaneous perception is the reason for others. The commentary’s statement, "in the absence of a distinction," is appropriate for the purpose of excluding *anyathāsiddhi*. But surely, even for an impermanent thing, there is no difference [between them] when a distinction is absent; therefore, why specify "of the permanent" (*nityasya*)?
The reply: Certainly; even in the absence of a specific distinction, multiplicity exists in cases such as flames, and there is no difference because they are effects.
However, for that which is eternal, since it is not an effect, multiplicity is contradictory; thus, the reason—“because of simultaneity in other existents” (sattvāntare ca yaugapadyāt)—is valid.
This also applies to the relationship between the material cause and its modification.
The Commentary states: Furthermore, regarding the word "daśca," they teach that "the letter *i* is the original form (*prakṛti*), and the letter *y* is the modification (*vikṛti*).
Whatever is modified is impermanent. Moreover, the co-occurrence of the letter *y* with the letter *i* is observed.
By this as well, the relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) between the two is indicated.
Furthermore, grammarians record that words [function] according to the relationship of material cause and modification;
and this [relationship] is not possible for that which is eternal.
Therefore, since we perceive that even the tradition (Vyākaraṇa), by means of the qualities and defects of the previously mentioned causes,
possesses a similarity that is consistent with those [causes], its being an effect is established;
and the intellect is its agent.

The Commentary (Bhāṣya): Furthermore, a great sound is heard when it is uttered by many people. If that sound were merely manifested [rather than produced], it would be perceived even when uttered by a single person, simply because it is being uttered. Therefore, we consider that surely some part of it is produced by each individual, whereby this great sound is perceived.
[The commentators] say: We consider [the atom] to be an effect because we perceive it to possess an increase in its constituent parts, just as in the case of flames and the like.

Therefore, even when its state is not being perceived, an increase in its parts is inferred; the example of the three flames is given. However, in that case, the observation is equal [to the case of the atom].
Commentary: By the word "but" (tu), the position is reversed.

As for what was stated—that because it is perceived at a time subsequent to effort, this [sound] is produced—if we are able to state the eternality of sound through a clear reason, then, by the force of the cognition of its permanence, it will follow that it is manifested by effort.
If [the sound] was unmanifest prior to its utterance and is manifested by effort, then this is the same for both positions.
In the *Vṛtti*: "What is this 'equal view'? This is that equal view: that the reason is the same whether [the sound] is an effect or not an effect."
What is equality? It is the state of being a co-resident (*sāṃvāsikatā*), meaning that which arises from being properly and correctly established together;
it is like placing [the matter] in one's hand as if it were principal capital.

What is established here? This is established here: if we shall state that [the word] is perceptible by a cognition distinct from effort (*saprayatnabhinna-pratyakṣagrāhyatā*), [then it follows that if the word were perceptible by a cognition distinct from effort, then the observation following effort would mean that effort is its manifester; however, if the word were not perceptible by a cognition distinct from effort, then effort would simply be its producer]. But has that [perceptibility by a cognition distinct from effort] not already been stated?
And just as in the case of flames and the like, it is not possible to assert identity when an effort is made through inference;
this is true.
If it were said that recognition is based solely on the perception of difference, then it would be established (as will be demonstrated) that its basis is actually the perception of that [identity].
Therefore, it is established that "the perception there is indeed equal.
As for the non-perception of an existing thing, it is due to the non-arrival of the object.
The Commentary states: as for the other reason mentioned—that [sound] perishes as soon as it is uttered—[it is not so].

In this case as well, if we are able to state clearly that [the word] is eternal, then—by the force of the cognition of its eternity—having observed that there is sometimes perception and sometimes non-perception of the insentient [word], we shall postulate that something is perceived which is mixed with the object of conceptualization (*kalpa*).
And since that occurs when conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) exist, we shall maintain that conjunction and disjunction alone are the manifesters (*abhivyañjaka*).
If it is argued that [the word] is heard even when conjunction and disjunction have ceased:
This is not so;
conjunctions and disjunctions do not cease immediately.
For:
"The sound is perceived"—for these [conjunctions and disjunctions] are not themselves perceptible.

If conjunctions and disjunctions alone manifest the sound and do not produce it, then because sound has space as its locus and because space is one and the same, that which is the auditory space is indeed the same in other locations; thus, would it not follow that the sound manifested by the conjunctions and disjunctions reaching the ear would be perceived even in Pāṭaliputra?
Furthermore, as for that [sound] which they produce, its conjunctions and disjunctions will produce it only in the air, because they reside in the air—
just as threads produce a cloth only within the threads themselves. Thus, its perception in Pāṭaliputra would also be logical, owing to the extreme clarity [of the medium].

Even for one who holds that [the sound] is manifested, this fault does not apply. For the conjunctions and disjunctions do not assist the ear-cavity located at a distance; therefore, what is distant from the auditory organ is not perceived by it.
This is not so.
If the conjunctions and disjunctions [of air] were to assist the auditory organ without reaching it, then two people situated in near and distant locations would perceive the sound simultaneously;
yet they do not perceive it simultaneously.
Therefore, they do not assist [the organ] without reaching it.
If they do not assist [in this way], then conjunction and disjunction would not be the cause for the perception of sound.
This is not so;
for the air-currents impelled by the impact, striking against the still air-masses, produce conjunctions and disjunctions extending in all directions.
They proceed as far as the location [of the sound].
And those conjunctions and disjunctions of the wind are not perceived;
the sound is perceived only while they are still occurring, not when they have ceased.

Therefore, there is no fault. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Vṛtti*: "The non-perception of that which exists [is not a proof of its non-existence], because of the non-arrival of the object [to the senses]"; likewise, it has been said that the perception of inconclusiveness (*anekāntika*) is also [not a valid proof].
But surely this is not tenable: [the non-perception of that which exists].

What is the cause for its constant perception? If you say it is simply the arrival of the objects [of sense], that too is untenable. [The opponent] objects: "Let it be so! [The author] retorts: "In that case, that very thing is difficult to obtain here. Why? [The dull-witted one] states the reason: "For, according to the eternalist position, sound is something to be manifested (*abhivyañjaka*)."
Furthermore, this sound is single and has a single object, because its object is space (*ākāśa*). And since space itself is its perceiver, how can there be such a non-arrival of the object?
Therefore, it is only for that which has been destroyed that non-perception is possible.

[Objection: Why is it not logical [to say] that [the self is perceived] by something else? For if that [perception by another] were accepted, it would follow that this [self] is non-logical (*anyāyyatā*) in every respect; for this very reason it was stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "If [it were] of the word... [Reply:
But even if that [perception by another] is accepted, here [in this context] the self does not obtain its nature as being devoid of obscuration and so forth.
Why? Because of contradiction with what was stated previously.

What is to be said? Space is the sense organ (*indriya*), and it is one. Therefore, even though conjunctions and disjunctions act as manifestors, it follows that all sounds would be perceived by everyone. For all sounds occupy the same location; thus, when one is manifested, all would be manifested, just like a jar or similar objects.
The opponent objects: It may well be that there is apprehension by all [senses], but it is not tenable for all sounds [to be apprehended by all], because they are manifested like [their] causes.
(Just as, due to the diversity of causes, a certain sound is produced by something, so too a certain sound is manifested by something.)

Furthermore, the apprehension by all [hearers] is exactly the same even in the case of an effect [such as sound], because sound arises from the very same auditory organ (*rāvendriya*). And as for a defect that is common to both [the proponent and the opponent], one should not direct it against only one. This objection is refuted, for the author of the *kārikā* has not raised the challenge regarding [sound's] eternity and so forth without having stated a specific distinction.
(Proponent: There is this distinction:

would the manifestation belong to the sound or to the sense organ? Regarding the manifestation of the sound first: since all sounds have the same object, would there be a cause that delimits the object, as is the case with jars and other things? For one who intends to determine the manifesting refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ does not, however, lead to the understanding of any difference among the sounds themselves.

(Objection: But has it not been stated that if conjunctions and disjunctions do not produce a refinement (*saṃskāra*) in the auditory organ capable of perceiving sound, they would necessarily be the producers of the sound itself; and furthermore, there would be a difference [between the sounds]? (Reply: How does this negation imply that another [sound] is produced? (Objection: Because otherwise, their operation would be untenable.

(Objection: If the producers [of conjunction and disjunction] do not effect a refinement (*saṃskāra*), what else could they do other than produce the sound? (Respondent: Must that which cannot logically function as a refiner necessarily be a producer? (Objector: If it is not a producer, then it would be entirely devoid of activity; otherwise, it is observed to have the very nature of producing conjunction and disjunction. And since its status as a refiner has been refuted, it is indeed of the nature of producing what is perceived.

[The opponent] replies: True; let those things which have that [word] as their object be the producers (*utpādaka*) or the manifesters (*saṃskāraka*) [of the word], but not the sound itself, because it lacks that status as an object.
[The proponent asks: "In that case, how is it so? [The opponent] says: "Just as in the case of conjunction and disjunction, it is established for another. [That is to say:

"Let the other person perceive the sound"—let that [status of being a producer or manifester] be postulated for those two [conjunction and disjunction] with respect to that [perception], but in the case of a different object [namely, the word].

Error is said to be like [the perception of] parts [of a whole]. (Or rather: many air-currents, impelled by the same place of articulation and instrument, independent of one another, simultaneously reaching the entire circumference of the ear-cavity, cause the sound to be perceived without interval in the very region of the auditory organ; thus, O Great-souled One, they present the sound as a single entity.
It has been stated that cognition occurs through the capacity [of the sense-organ] in accordance with the refinement (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, this too is an error based solely on the non-apprehension of the differences between mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Consequently, since recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) as a form of perception is established, the previously stated collection of reasons for impermanence is rendered conclusive. (By the term "recognition" here, the graspability of the object by means of the attributes of cognition—namely, the recollection of a previous experience and the reflective awareness "this is that very same one"—is expressed, not the cognition itself.)

The *Nyāyaratnākara* states: Let it be that "soundness" (*dhvanitva*) is a sub-class of "word-ness" (*śabdatva*), just like "letter-ness" (*varṇatva*). And because of those distinctions, words such as the letter *ga* and so forth are ultimately real. Since these [sounds] are audible, by virtue of their contact with them, even the appearance of distinctions among letters—such as nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*) resonance—is easily accounted for; thus, there is no fault whatsoever in the path of the non-eternality of words.

Thus, this difference in effect—where in some cases there is the perception of phonemes (*varṇa*) and in others the perception of mere sound (*nāda*)—leads to the postulation of a difference in the power of the sounds (*dhvani*). Consequently, some manifest phonemes while others do not. Whether these *dhvanis* are air-currents (*vāyu*) or a specific distinction within the genus of sound (*śabdajāti*), one should not be dogmatic on this point. Furthermore, in the case where they are considered sound (*śabda*), since that which is formless cannot undergo increase, the term "sound" (*nāda*) in the *Nādavṛddhi-sūtra* indicates by implication (*lakṣaṇā*) the air-currents whose quality is sound.
(Śloka 228)
"But it must be eternal, because its manifestation is for the sake of another.
Commentary: Sound ought to be eternal.
Why? Because its manifestation is for the sake of another.
The utterance of [words] is for the sake of another, in order to convey the ultimate meaning (paramārtha).
For if a word were destroyed immediately upon being uttered, it would not be able to convey anything else;
therefore, one would not utter it for the sake of another.
Now, it is not tenable to claim that the comprehension of meaning arises because [the word] is perceived many times without having perished.
If it is argued that the comprehension of meaning arises from similarity with a meaningful [word], we say no; for nothing whatsoever is meaningful, since all [words] are non-eternal.
If it is argued that someone might develop an artificial familiarity with the former [term],

it has been said that once [the correct term] is understood as "sahasa," the cognition [of the incorrect term] ceases due to delusion, just like the cognition of the word *mālā* [ceases] upon hearing the word *śālā*.
If it is further argued that, just as the cognition [of the meaning] does not cease when the word *gāvī* is heard because it refers to the same object [as *go*], so too here...
For there is no desire to utter the word "cow" as a reality;
nor here is there a desire to utter another word;
nor by a single utterance—
Since it is possible to establish that [the word] exists for the sake of practical usage through effort, therefore, because perception is for the sake of another, the word is eternal.
