The cognition of "existence" (*sat*) and so on is merely conditional (*aupādhikī*).
The word "existent" (*sat*) is conditioned by the fitness for being apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, the term "sound" (*śabda*) implies something that is not grasped by the ear.
Now, one might object: even a word (*pada*), which is distinct from individual phonemes (*varṇa*), is indeed grasped by the ear.
For instance, in cases such as *nadī* and *dīna*, although there is no difference in the phonemes, a difference in the words is perceived.
Nor should it be said that the word is merely the phonemes themselves,
and that the cognition of a difference between words— such as in the case of *nadī* and *dīna*— arises from a difference in their sequence;
for phonemes are devoid of sequence.
The sequence [of letters] might arise either from their spatial location (*deśina*) or from their temporal occurrence (*kālina*).

However, neither kind of sequence finds a place among the phonemes (*varṇa*), because they are all-pervading (*sarvagata*) and eternal (*nitya*). Therefore, let it be that the cognition (*buddhi*) regarding them possesses sequence.
In accordance with that [perception], the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves also appear as possessing a sequence when each is heard individually.

However, in the case of a single cognition of a word (*padabuddhi*) occurring in a single moment, even a sequence existing within a single cognition is not tenable; how, then, could the appearance of difference be established by means of that [sequence]? Furthermore, since there are many phonemes and the cognition of a word does not have a single [phoneme] as its object, the word is distinct from the phonemes.
Furthermore, if a word does not appear as something distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), then the cognition of meaning from them is simply not possible.
For there is no comprehension of the meaning upon the perception of each individual phoneme;
nor is the simultaneous apprehension of all the phonemes possible, because phonemes are uttered in a sequential order.
Because we perceive the hearing of sounds that follow upon the pronunciation [of letters],
if the letters themselves were the denotators, there would be comprehension of meaning even when the order is different or when the speakers are different.
Therefore, since the comprehension of meaning is impossible based on the letters alone, it leads us to the cognition of a word-entity (*padapratīti*) distinct from them.
It is replied: there is no appearance of a distinct entity over and above the phonemes, such as the "nadī" or "dīna";
for it is only the phonemes, beginning with the letter *n*, that are perceived.
The distinction between cognitions, however, is based on their sequential difference.

This [unitary] cognition is not one, because if it were, there would be no sequence even for the cognitions of the phonemes. For indeed, the distinct cognitions whose objects are the distinct phonemes attain, as it were, a state of uninterrupted unity.
For instance: the cognitions associated with the production of phonemes, which are dependent upon the auditory faculty, arise differently according to the difference in their utterance.

Likewise, memory—which arises through the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) produced by the perception of each individual phoneme—is not conceived as being a single entity whose object is the whole, because the cultivations themselves are distinct.

The cognition of a single word, however, is based on its being the means for conveying a single meaning; and in this case, the apprehension of that meaning cannot be postulated as the cause [of the word-cognition], because it is impossible for it to function as a cause.
It does not serve as a cause by its mere existence.
Because the cognition of the meaning would occur at all times [simultaneously].

It has already been stated that perception does not manifest as distinct words; therefore, since the comprehension of the meaning occurs within the perception of the phonemes themselves, it is appropriate to rely on some specific distinction residing in the phonemes.
This is because [the cognition] depends upon the apprehension of all the preceding phonemes.
And since perception, being momentary, cannot produce a distinction by itself, one must rely solely on the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the previous perception of the phonemes;
and that [impression] is indeed distinct from the impression that is the cause of memory.

The latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is the cause of memory; that which is manifested by a particular perception is capable of producing another perception of that very same object, and not of a different object. Therefore, a cognition whose object is an external thing is untenable [if it arises from such a latent impression alone], which necessitates the postulation of a latent impression distinct from that [perception]. Since this [latent impression] is to be inferred from its effect, when there is no perception, the production of the latent impression is inferred precisely from the absence of perception. Thus, because the latent impression does not arise when there is a reversal of sequence, a difference in the manifesting individuals, or an intervention, there is an absence of the cognition of the object due to the non-appearance of its effect.

Whichever phoneme serves as the cause for the cognition of whichever meaning, it possesses by its very nature the capacity to produce a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) conducive to the comprehension of that specific meaning. However, due to the absence of auxiliary factors, the effect does not arise; yet when those auxiliaries are present, the effect is produced. Therefore, the cognition of the meaning arises from those [phonemes] alone.
Consequently, neither through perception nor through inference is there any establishment of a word (*pada*) distinct from the phonemes; thus, the word consists solely of the phonemes.
What, then, is the meaning? It is the denotable object (*abhidheya*).
And what is this very denotable object? It is that with which the word has a non-human (eternal) relationship.
Now, what is this relationship? It is the state of being the cognizer and the cognized.
That connection is not authorless (apauruṣeya), because by its very nature, a word does not produce cognition [of its meaning].
For if a word produced cognition of its object by its very nature, then why would it not produce cognition when heard for the first time? Therefore, we understand that a word requires something else.

Furthermore, since it is observed that the cognition of meaning in words such as "Devadatta" arises from human convention, the same dependence on convention is accepted even in the case of words like "cow.
If the understanding of meaning depends upon that [convention], then this very [dependence] constitutes the word's nature of producing cognition.
It is said in reply:

Although people do not comprehend the meaning from a word heard for the first time, nevertheless, the capacity of a word to produce the cognition of its meaning is indeed innate; it merely requires a convention (*saṃketa*) [to be manifested]. For instance, when one person hears a sentence—the cause of the cognition—and another person proceeds to act upon it, [the listener] infers the speaker's intention through that cognition.
And immediately after hearing that sound, he first ascertains that the sound is its cause;

however, when those learners standing nearby subsequently attain the cognition of the meaning from that sound on their own, a doubt arises in them: "If the word is indeed expressive, why does it not convey the meaning to me?
Or, if it is not expressive at all, how then does it cause even an elder to understand?"
For those very people who have attained discernment, this further conceptualization arises:
"Surely there exists some excellence or growth of the [cognition] by which the object is apprehended.
Let it be determined: what is that excellence?

Furthermore, when hearing a word, because one observes the comprehension of its own meaning through the mere cognition of the object as understood from the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), it arises for the purpose of determining that the specific feature [of the word] is simply the tradition of causing the cognition of the object; however, it is impossible to postulate that the specific feature for an elder is the cognition of a convention (*saṃketa*), since at that time the convention itself is not being cognized. For one who has mastered the meanings of other words, while understanding the meaning from a sentence expressing a convention, understands it by means of that convention, and not otherwise.
[Objection: But surely, since the convention is observed at a later time, why not simply accept that the capacity to convey meaning (*pratyāyakatva*) consists precisely in that convention?
[Reply: No, because the effect in the form of the cognition of the object is established by the very nature of the word itself.

For if the cognition of the object were not admitted to arise from the word alone, then one might postulate that the convention occurs at that time; otherwise, it would not be possible. However, comprehension is indeed established from the word alone through the aforementioned path.
[Objection: If this is so, how can convention (*saṃketa*) be the cause [of linguistic usage] even in the case of Devadatta and others? [Reply: It is said:
in that case, the convention is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and it is not something to be merely postulated.
Therefore, in the case of Devadatta and others, that very [word] possesses the capacity to produce the cognition of its meaning;

however, in the case of cows and such, there is no room for the assumption of a [causal] function based solely on the observation of an effect. Thus, it is established that the relationship between these [words] and their meanings—characterized as the relation between the signifier and the signified—is non-personal (apauruṣeya).
What is this "not proximate" (*asaṃnikṛṣṭa*)? It means not cognized by any other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

If this is so, how is it that this [object] is made known by words? It has been stated that a word is a means of cognition when its relationship [to the object] is understood through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*).
[Objection: If the object is not apprehended by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can the linguistic usage of elders regarding that object be determined?
Or how can the cognition having that as its object be inferred?
Or rather, how is the expressive power of a word to be postulated?
The answer is: let the repeated practice of the sentence-meaning alone be enjoined.
Furthermore, that proximate meaning is precisely the meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*).
For it has been stated in the *Mīmāṃsā-ślokavārttika* that an injunction (*niyoga*) indeed conveys as the sentence-meaning an unprecedented object not known through any other means of knowledge.
Nor is the injunction itself the indicator of this [object], because it is not perceived apart from its constituent parts (*vigraha*).
Since even the other words have their conventional meaning (*vyutpatti*) as being related to that [injunction], the meaning of the injunction is understood by that very sentence.
In this regard, the cognition of the verbal suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth expresses the very body of the meaning of the mandate (*niyoga*), as intended by the verbal root.
And the other words—denoting the specific object (*viṣaya*), the name (*nāmadheya*), and the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*)—are operative in the cognition of the meaning of the mandate.

Although, according to the principle of the "auxiliaries acting in proximity" (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), they are devoid of any further mandates, nevertheless, because they express their own meanings as connected to the primary mandate, they participate in the cognition of that very mandate just like the other words.

Even though a mantra shares the commonality of being enjoined (*viniyukta*), the collection of substances that constitute it is exhausted solely within the context of the injunction (*niyoga*) by being offered through the knowledge of that injunction; for the knowledge of the injunction, however, at the time of performance, consists in the recollection of the ritual acts and their means as required by the injunction, which is accomplished by the class of mantras through their inherent fitness (*yogyatā*). Furthermore, even restatements (*anuvāda*)—by generating praise for what is to be enjoined—are intent upon the comprehension of the injunction regarding the object of that praise. Thus, the entire Veda is an authority (*pramāṇa*) regarding the *apūrva*, whose nature is the task (*kāryatā*) to be performed.

For this very reason, in order to dispel the doubt as to what the meaning of the Veda might be, the *codanāsūtra* declares that the meaning of the Veda consists of that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*).
Now, an objection is raised: even an established entity (*siddha*), such as Brahman, is perceived as the meaning of the Vedāntas. To this it is replied:
A word conveys its meaning by depending upon linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), and such usage is found in the linguistic behavior of elders; furthermore,
that behavior is based on the comprehension of something to be accomplished (*kārya*).
The acquisition of linguistic proficiency (*śabdavyutpatti*) occurs only through the communication of something to be accomplished (*kāryapratipādakatva*).

Even in that regard, some words are acquired through their direct communication of what is to be accomplished, while others are acquired by virtue of being directed toward their own meanings as conjoined with what is to be accomplished.

Now, one might object: even without linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), there is indeed the comprehension of an already established fact (*siddhārtha*) in the world; thus, proficiency is simply the understanding of a meaning already known.
For example, in the case of the statement, "A son has been born to you.
Here, indeed, the arising of joy in the listener is inferred from worldly signs such as the word "son";
and the arising of joy would not be possible without a cause for that joy.

The fact that even "dearness" (priyatva) is a cause of joy is perceived within one's own self; therefore, it is postulated that by the sentence "A son has been born to you," a dear object is communicated.

Since the dearness of the statement "A son has been born to you" is understood through other means of knowledge, it is postulated that the sentence possesses the very capacity to denote that meaning. Just as in linguistic usage, through the process of insertion and deletion (āvāpoddhāra) for each word, there is a determination of the specific relationship between the word and its own particular meaning.

Likewise, even in the case of the present-tense sentence "he cooks with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*), where the meaning of the case-ending is not explicitly expressed, one understands that what is conveyed by the word "wood" (*kāṣṭha*) is the cause [of the cooking]; thus, perceiving the causal status of the wood through direct perception, they acquire proficiency (*vyutpatti*) in the word "wood.
Furthermore, proficiency is also observed in the form: "this is the meaning of this word.
In that case, it cannot be asserted that the meaning of a word consists solely in its connection with an action (*kāryānvaya*).

Moreover, since the fact that words denote non-actional entities (or established facts) is sufficient to account for their denotation of actional entities as well, one cannot postulate a capacity for them to denote entities as related to a specific [action].
Furthermore, in common worldly usage, sentences are mostly seen to consist of questions and answers concerning established facts, such as "Are you well? and "I am well."
To this it is replied:
For all persons, the very first acquisition of linguistic proficiency is brought about through the usage of elders alone.
Indeed, proficiency in the grammatical analysis of established forms cannot be conceived apart from such usage.

Although it may be inferred through causes such as the primary temple and so forth, and although the cause of joy is understood through the arising of joy and the word’s being its instrument, nevertheless, the capacity of the sentence "A son is born to you" to convey the cause of joy known as the birth of a son— namely, that the cause of joy is otherwise [than what was previously suspected]— is difficult to infer.
Nor can there be a determination of its conveying that [specific cause] by means of elimination (*pariśeṣa*),
because it is extremely difficult to determine through elimination among past, future, and present causes, whether they are proximate or remote.

Furthermore, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), which pertains to objects qualified by perception and is observed there, is capable of serving as the means for learning the relationship between word and meaning by attributing denotative power to the word itself in accordance with that [perception]. And since linguistic usage is the means for learning, who could possibly bring about the theory that words denote only what is conjoined with a task (*kāryānvita*)? For it has been stated in the *Vākyārthamātṛkā* that linguistic usage is not possible without the comprehension of a task.
Thus, that usage of words in the world which has as its primary purpose the accomplishment of an action (*kārya*) will be *lākṣaṇika* (indicative).

For the connection with an action (*kāryānvaya*) is intended as being non-deviant from the mutual connection of word-meanings; yet, even with the intention of expressing the mutual connection of word-meanings, people employ words in the world to express a connection with an action.
And by the force of the speaker's intention, the state of having that [action] as the primary purpose is also accomplished there through indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In the Veda, however, since there is no possibility of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or conceptual construction (*vikalpana*), it cannot be argued that its inherent purpose is not directed toward action (*kāryaparatva*).

Thus, even the linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) that occurs regarding sentences containing established entities (*siddhapada*) does not undermine the fact that [the Veda] is directed toward action.

For all words alike, the inherent direction toward action is established through the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), while the direction toward established entities is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*).

Since in all linguistic transactions there is an invariable concomitance with a purposeful action (*kārya*), one cannot abandon the theory that words denote things as connected to such an action; therefore, it is impossible to rely upon the general view that words denote things merely as connected to some other entity.

Consequently, even in the case of the Vedāntas, one must describe them as having the nature of a purposeful action (*kāryatva*) by relying on their syntactic unity with the injunction traditionally handed down as "The Self is to be known."

Furthermore, because there is an absence of linguistic proficiency regarding the apprehension of established entities (*siddhārtha*), and because it is impossible for words—whose meanings are understood through the usage of elders—to denote [objects] as already connected (*anvitābhidhāna*), they must be described as being solely directed toward action (*kāryaparatva*), even when restating a nature already known through other means of knowledge. Moreover, even if a word were directed toward an established entity, the authority of the Vedāntas over Brahman, who consists of supreme bliss and so forth, would not be tenable; for in that case, one would have to assume an injunction regarding the nature of Brahman by way of restating its essential form.
Furthermore, the nature of Brahman must be accepted as already established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

This is because, in common worldly usage, the word "Brahman" is established as referring to an object already known through other means of knowledge; therefore, even in the Veda, it possesses that same meaning.
Such being the case, an injunction whose form is eternal, all-pervading, and consisting of supreme bliss would contradict all established modes of understanding.
For in all practices, the Self, which has become the means of valid cognition, shines forth;
yet in that state, supreme bliss is not experienced as an object of consciousness.
Nor is its non-manifestation due to being overwhelmed by the sufferings of saṃsāra, because such overwhelming is logically impossible.
For suffering is limited, whereas knowledge-bliss is unlimited; thus, it is not possible for the latter to be overwhelmed by the former, which is so insignificant in comparison.
Furthermore, for that which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), it is simply impossible for there to be suppression or obscuration;

and it has been stated in the *Tattvāloka* that even the demonstration of the realization of the true nature of the Self (*abhijñātmatattva*) is contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Since the state of being devoid of all modifications (*vikāra*) is also contradicted by other means of valid cognition—given the arising of modifications such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth—the mutual compatibility of these [attributes] does not result in their having bliss (*ānanda*) and the rest as their ultimate meaning.

As for the two [qualities] of being ageless and immortal, however, the authority of the statement is merely that of a restatement (*anuvāda*), since they are established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Now, is there not also worldly verbal testimony (*śabda*) that is non-scriptural? Why has that not been defined?
It is said:

in reality, there is no scripture, nor is there any word; for that cognition which arises from a word and is free from affliction would be "verbal" (śābda), and such is not possible apart from the Veda.

For worldly speech does not itself produce certainty regarding its object, because worldly words do not have that [certainty] as their domain, since there is suspicion of their deviation from the actual object.
Now, it might be argued that even so, Vedic speech would likewise not be determinative of its object, because an object presented by a word is seen to deviate from the facts in the world.
To this, it may be replied: from Vedic speech, certainty arises intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
But doubt does not arise subsequently regarding that [object], because it lacks its objective domain;
for example, when a post standing nearby has been determined to be a post, it no longer gives rise to a doubt as to whether it is a post or a person.
Indeed, doubt arises only while the state of perception persists.
And when the object is ascertained, its apprehension occurs; therefore, doubt is not tenable.
Furthermore, the word's capacity to produce ascertainment is not preceded by an ascertainment of non-deviation, such that there would be no ascertainment in the case of deviation.
Rather, it is the word itself, when free from error, which is the cause of ascertainment for the senses.
In this regard: having observed that the certainty produced by a word occurs in both ways, the doubt that arises cannot be suppressed by that very certainty;
for only a doubt caused by another statement is contradicted by certainty.
Furthermore, it is said that its very existence is what is negated by that [negation].
To this we reply: doubt may indeed be appropriate regarding worldly speech.
For people are generally seen employing words that denote related meanings due to a defect in their intention, or through error, negligence, or incapacity.

Consequently, even though the words spoken by them possess the capacity to denote related meanings (*anvitābhidhāna*), the syntactic relation is not ascertained because of the suspicion that the meaning might be unrelated.
How, then, does the engagement in worldly activity proceed from such ordinary sentences? It is said in reply:
People engage in worldly affairs even when there is doubt regarding the purpose; having seen something uncertain, they proceed to actions whose results are objects such as rain and so forth.
Alternatively, this very [investigation] is the means for reaching certainty.
For when a person is thus determined to be neither incapable nor negligent, and is one for whom the means of valid cognition regarding these objects are possible,

and who is free from all defects of intention— since he does not employ words without having understood the meaning and its connection— it is first inferred that there is knowledge of another [person] based on the fact that his speech is preceded by such knowledge.
And from the knowledge of the connection, the connection itself is also inferred.
For knowledge, being invariably concomitant with the object of knowledge, certainly serves as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the inference of that object.
Thus, from the worldly word—which has become a logical mark—the cognition of the speaker is inferred;
from that, a determination regarding the object arises, and linguistic usage proceeds.

And when the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has been thus ascertained, the certainty regarding the meaning of the sentence arises once the suspicion concerning the absence of concomitance (*nivṛttānvaya*) has ceased.
However, at that stage, [the sentence] functions as a restatement (*anuvādaka*).
For this very reason, in ordinary worldly speech, there is no verbal authority (*śābdapramāṇa*).
The word is the mark for the intention;
the intention, too, is a mark.
However, the word is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) with respect to the object, because it produces a subsequent ascertainment due to its nature as a restatement (anuvādaka).

Now, one might object: since words uttered by those who are incapable, negligent, or deluded are seen to have unconnected meanings, a suspicion arises regarding the connected meaning even in the speech of other persons; therefore, let the knowledge of the speaker's capacity, freedom from negligence, and absence of delusion—which serve to purify [the speaker]—be made pervasive only with respect to that [trustworthiness].
However, the ascertainment of the meaning must arise from the sentence itself, for that is the means; let it be so here.
Let there not be the status of a mere restatement of the sentence once the ascertainment of the meaning has arisen from the inferred knowledge of the speaker.
It is said:
here, "finality" (antatva) refers to the person's possession of knowledge corresponding to reality;
"freedom from defects of intention" refers to having as its object that which has already been known.
Capability (*śaktatva*) is the fitness for employing words as intended.
Even in one who is capable, negligence regarding the subject matter as intended is possible; he who possesses this fourfold set is trustworthy (*pratyayita*).
This is understood from the context here.
The employment of his speech is restricted to right knowledge;
therefore, upon hearing his words, a certainty regarding that right knowledge indeed arises.

This knowledge is called "correct" when it is non-discrepant with its object; for one who holds that an object exists exactly as it is perceived, a correct ascertainment necessarily includes the ascertainment of the object itself. Thus, the knowledge of a specific person does not extend merely to the removal of doubt, but rather to the ascertainment of the object itself. Therefore, when the object has been ascertained and doubt has ceased, a statement that produces an ascertainment of the meaning of the sentence is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is a subsequent restatement (*anuvādaka*).

[Objection: In that case, let a human statement (*pauruṣeya-vākya*) which makes known the speaker’s cognition—otherwise unapprehended—be likewise a verbal means of valid cognition (*śābda-pramāṇa*). [Reply:
No, because in that case it is an inference (*anumāna*).
For a statement from a trustworthy person (*pratyayita-vacana*) is [in fact] a cognition of the speaker’s cognition in which the relation [between the word and its object] has been ascertained.
The speaker, however, is the subject (*dharmin*). The specific cognition and the application of the word "fire" are two parts of that [subject].

For this very reason, the venerable Kāśyapa, considering the Vedas to be of human origin, stated that verbal testimony is included within inference; having said that "this is its cause" and "this is its effect" is inferential, he added, "by this very [principle], the verbal is also explained."
For the speaker’s cognition is the cause and the sentence is the effect;
for this very reason, it has been stated by another as well:
"But it [the sentence] indicates the speaker's intention."
That very [object], being presented in such a manner, is the locus (*āśraya*).

Now, if the cognition of the speaker is inferred from the sentence, and the object is inferred from the speaker’s cognition, then once the object has been apprehended, how can a specific feature of that cognition be inferred?
For there can be no specific feature of a formless cognition; nor does an unascertained object impart a specific feature to the cognition.
It is said:
when an object is not yet understood, a specific cognition can indeed be inferred.
Based on the fact that words have been employed which are capable of conveying a particular kind of meaning, a cognition having that very kind of object as its domain is inferred.
But in that case, the authority of the Veda would be discarded.
For the comprehension of meaning from a word in the Veda depends upon linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), and such usage occurs in the linguistic practice of elders (*vṛddha*).
If the utterances of elders function merely as inferential marks (*liṅga*), then there can be no acquisition of usage regarding their own meaning as a source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
It is said:
for as long as the capacity of words to denote specific meanings is not accepted, the specific cognition of the speaker cannot be inferred either;
indeed, it is from a qualified sentence that a qualified cognition must be inferred.

And since there is no other distinction of a sentence than its capacity to convey a specific meaning, one must admit that these [words] possess the power to convey a specific meaning. Indeed, "mastery" (vyutpatti) consists precisely in the possession of this capacity to convey meaning, and from that arises the comprehension of the meaning. Furthermore, even in the case of a restatement (anuvādaka), it is the words themselves that are the conveyors of meaning.
And once comprehension of the meaning has arisen through proficiency in the Veda, its status as a valid means of knowledge is indeed established.
Now, it was argued that doubt must also exist regarding the Veda;
this is true that it was said, but it is incorrect.
First of all, the impossibility of establishing certainty regarding another [source] does not apply to the Veda.
In the world, the use of words for eternal objects is observed to be subject to defects such as the incapacity of the author;
however, there is no human author in the case of the Veda.

Therefore, the faults dependent upon that [human agency], which serve as the reasons for your statement that the Veda does not convey a connected meaning, do not even enter into the word [of the Veda]; thus, the determination of its meaning is known to you.

Nor is it appropriate to suspect that the certainty produced by a Vedic statement might be fallible because of the fallibility of certainty produced by human sentences, for suspicion is rooted in observation.
For whatever is observed in a certain state will lead one to suspect that very same thing in that same state again.
Moreover, even in the case of ordinary worldly people, there is no deviation [from this rule].

When someone, failing to distinguish the statement of a trustworthy person from that of an untrustworthy person, recalls that the statement of a trustworthy person is preceded by perceptual knowledge, yet fails to perceive that recollection as distinct from the original perception, proceeds to act upon it as if it were a direct perception;
in such a case, there is no fault whatsoever.

But surely, since they consist of collections of words, even the Vedas must be of human origin; for collections of words are indeed seen to be of human origin, like the *Mahābhārata* and other such works.
Furthermore, designations such as "Kaṭhaka" and so forth are applied to the Veda as well.
Nor is it reasonable to assume that this designation is based on the *pravacana* (the teaching),
because the *pravacana* is common to many; for many indeed could have proclaimed it.
Furthermore, the agent is unique because of the impossibility of performing what has already been done;
designations occur by way of uniqueness.
Just as there is the *Bhārata-saṃhitā* composed by Vyāsa;

therefore, because the Vedas are of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), and because their authority depends upon the speaker’s reliability and the coherence of their meaning, who can prevent [the same] from applying to those [other works] that are heatedly debated?
It is said in reply:

To begin with, the fact that the Vedas were created by a person is directly perceived from [the mention of] authors such as Aṭṭa and others. As for the traditional designation (*samākhyā*), however, being of human origin and following other means of knowledge, it is not capable of establishing the meaning by itself.
If, upon investigation, we determine that they are indeed composed, then the designation will be based on their instrumentality.
But if, despite our efforts, we do not find evidence of human authorship, then we shall say that it is based on oral tradition (*pravacana*).
For even that would be a unique [reason].
Indeed, the speech under discussion—which consists of a collection of words in a specific context—is not sufficient to infer human authorship.
Because it is impossible for there to be the capacity to compose sentences whose subject matter is the meaning of the Vedas;

for it cannot be said that the Vedas were composed by a madman simply because they are interconnected with one another. Furthermore, how could the initial study of such a vast mass of literature, composed by a madman, ever have come about?
For who, being possessed of consciousness, would—with great hardship—study, retain, and master such a vast mass of texts as this, which is like that of a madman?

Nor would they, even if encouraged by an intelligent author, engage in such a massive composition as the works of the Buddha and others do; therefore, even those acting with intelligence are not capable of composing the Vedas.
This is because their subject matter [is the nature of] the Buddha...
Because it is impossible to superimpose [a meaning upon it];

for the subject matter of the Veda, which consists of the *apūrva*, is the object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). That [subject matter] would have to bring about its presence in the intellect prior to the Vedic statements.
Nor can it be established at a later time,
because for those [entities], the relationship of probandum and probans is not ultimate;
even though the relationship of probandum and probans is conceptual, it is possible to superimpose it upon the intellect.

The fact that [rites] such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* are observed to be means for attaining heaven can be superimposed upon [acts] such as bowing to a stone pillar; however, the *apūrva* (unseen potency), by virtue of its being unprecedented (*apūrvatvāt*), cannot even be superimposed.

Now, if the application of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is identical in both cases, why is it that the words of the Buddha and others do not convey a relationship between a goal and its means, whereas those spoken by the Veda do?
It is said:
First, verbal expressions of cognition have a person who has directly perceived them as their author.
Therefore, it is determined that whatever persons are capable of establishing through other means of valid cognition, all such things are expressed by words.
Furthermore, a person is not capable of introducing something entirely unprecedented into the intellect;
rather, they are able to compose [an injunction] by taking as a basis the relationship between the goal and the means as observed elsewhere and established in the intellect.
However, in the Vedas, no direct author is perceived.
Therefore, one should understand the meaning to that extent according to one's own capacity;
and that [meaning] is perceived as being of an unprecedented nature (*apūrva*).
Once that has been perceived, the capacity for composing sentences concerning it belongs to those whose intellects act with deliberation; thus, its human origin is inferred.

For it is only in those collections of words that can be composed by human beings that authorship is observed; therefore, the inference of authorship does not apply to those things which cannot be constructed.
Nor is the nature of being a collection of words untenable without authorship, for words come to form a collection only by virtue of being uttered.

Furthermore, that [recitation] must either be preceded by another recitation or originate from one's own intellect. For it is observed that what was uttered by one person is studied by another, as in the case of the *Mahābhārata* and similar works; just as people today study the *Mahābhārata* and so forth following a prior recitation, so too do all persons [study] the Vedas—what is there that is untenable?

Therefore, it is established that they are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). And because they are not of human origin, they require no dependence on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Therefore, it has been stated that [Vedic injunction] is a means of valid cognition because it is independent. Now, one might object: injunctions such as "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā" convey an object that is subsequently connected with a fruit.
Furthermore, the fruit is not perceived immediately after the action,
nor is it possible for the fruit to arise at a later time,
because the action would have ceased to exist.
Therefore, because it is sublated by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the scripture (*śāstra*) is not authoritative.

To this it is replied: First of all, the result is not heard to be produced immediately after the word [is uttered], such that there would be a sublation based on the non-perception of an immediate result.
Nor is it impossible for a fruit to arise from an action after a lapse of time,
because it is understood that the fruit arises precisely from the *apūrva* (unseen potency) which persists until that later time.
Nor does it subvert the status of [the sacrifice] as a means to the fruit by demonstrating another cause for its acceptance at a later time.
Let both, being presented by two means of valid cognition, be the means to the fruit as you wish;
however, the scripture has made known that the *apūrva* is the means to the fruit.
Receiving gifts and so forth are established through perception and other means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, it is not untenable for the agent to be the enjoyer of a fruit that arises at a later time,
because [the self] is eternal.

For the *puruṣa* is distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*), the senses, and the body; he is the agent of actions, and because he is eternal, he exists even at a later time, being thus capable of experiencing the fruits [of those actions]. Therefore, the authority of the scripture cannot be challenged on the grounds of contradiction by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In this context as well, the term "scripture" (*śāstra*) refers to that which is known as such by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Etymologically, however, it is derived from the root *śās*, meaning "that by which one is taught. Furthermore, it is of two kinds: perceptible and inferable.
Furthermore, what is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for verbal inference? It is the statement: "The *Aṣṭakā* sacrifices are to be performed.
How so? This tradition (*smṛti*) has been accepted without dispute by the grammarians themselves.
Furthermore, the acceptance of that which is rootless is not tenable;
nor is a root possible through perception and the other means of knowledge,
because they lack both the nature of being an effect and the capacity to have it as their object.

And since in the case of *smṛti* (tradition) an unprecedented action (*apūrvakārya*) is understood, it is possible for the *śāstra* (Veda) to be its source. But [an objection may be raised]: even that [Veda] cannot be established as the source, because it is not perceived despite being sought with effort.
And a word that is not perceived does not cause the meaning to be understood;
nor can it be without a basis when its meaning is not being comprehended.
It is said in reply:
True;
like us, Manu and others also do not perceive that scripture through direct perception.
However, inference is possible for them just as it is for us.

For, having seen another Smṛti that is accepted by the great multitude of people, they too are able to infer that the scripture which is the source of that [other Smṛti] is its root. Thus, because there is the possibility of an infinite succession of Smṛtis serving as the inferential mark (liṅga), there is no subversion of inference, just as in the case of the relationship between a word and its meaning.

For just as, by observing the linguistic usage of an enlightened person (*buddha*), one conceives of that person’s comprehension of meaning; and since that comprehension occurs immediately after hearing the word, one infers that the word is its cause. Then, having reflected—“How is it that this word, which does not itself communicate, communicates this meaning?”—and further determining for oneself that “the word, being understood as a communicator, makes the meaning known,” one postulates the capacity of the enlightened person to comprehend the meaning. Having determined, “By what means was this word ascertained to be the communicator of meaning for the enlightened person? one concludes that surely, for him too, just as for me, the observation of another instance of the enlightened person’s linguistic usage is the very means of acquisition (*vyutpatti*).

Even for another person, it is simply the observation of yet another linguistic usage by an elder; thus, the world acquires proficiency by postulating an beginningless succession of the Buddha’s (or the Sage’s) linguistic usages.
Likewise, by postulating nothing more than a succession of memories, they also perform inference based on scripture (*śāstra*).
Nor is it untenable that what is inferred should serve to establish the meaning of the scripture.
It is like the inference from a mark (*liṅgānumiti*).
It is not [the case that it is] always so, because there is no absence of hearing it.
If it is asked: "Why is there indeed no recitation? [the answer follows].
Because it is not the name of the teacher according to the [respective] teachers.
If it is asked, "How so?
there is no fault, as it is because it is not the name of the teacher according to other teachers.
Nor is it the case that this [word] lacks the nature of sound, because it consists of phonemes;
and each individual phoneme is perceptible by the auditory faculty.
And its status as Veda is non-human (apauruṣeya) because it consists of sentences and is nothing other than that; such is the case for the word "Veda" itself.
Therefore, scripture exists even as something inferable.
Furthermore, some scripture is perceptible, depending on verbal expression, such as the scripture concerning the Piṇḍapitṛyajña and other rites, as well as the Vedic scripture.
For sentences such as the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* [offering to the ancestors] are incomplete because they do not contain a word for the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).

Now, since linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) consists in the denotation of related meanings (*anvitābhidhāna*), when a single word is employed, there is a dependence on other related meanings; thus, if that [denotation of the relation] is not established, the sentence is incomplete.
But when multiple words are employed, since the denotation of the related meaning is established, what basis is there for calling it incomplete?
It is said:
here too, because the expressed meaning is untenable, there is indeed an incompleteness.
Here also, by means of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, a certain aspect of the nature of the task (*kārya*) is denoted.
Furthermore, the nature of being an action (*kārya*) cannot be established without performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), nor is performance possible without an agent (*kartṛ*).

Nor do [the elements] attain the status of an object (*karman*) or an agent without first apprehending the qualification (*adhikāra*). And qualification with respect to an action is possible for one who is enjoined (*niyojya*) within the injunction (*niyoga*).
For he who understands "this is my task" undertakes the action that accomplishes his own task as being for his own sake.

Even though there is no mention of a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) in the form "he shall be an eligible person," the incompleteness [of the sentence] is justified because the status of being a task (*kāryatva*) cannot otherwise be established.
Therefore, the *adhyāhāra* (supplying of an ellipsis), which is determined in worldly usage to complete an incomplete sentence, is also resorted to in the Veda.
What, then, is this so-called *adhyāhāra* (supplying an ellipsis)? It is the introduction of something additional into the mind.
A word being heard when [the required factor] is already present in the mind denotes its own meaning as connected [with that factor].
In this case, the cause is [the presence of] a qualifier, compatibility (*yogyatva*), and parsimony (*lāghava*).
To explain:

although [the qualification] is eternal and independent of living, nevertheless, when that is adopted as a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), one must assume that it implies the performance of the action by another who desires it; however, when it is a qualification of the entitled person (*adhikārī*) in the case of a rite for a specific desire (*kāmya*), since the engagement in the primary act occurs precisely because of the desire for that result, one need not assume that the injunction implies the performance.
Although the destruction of accumulated demerit is also desired by persons, nevertheless, because that depends upon the existence of present demerit, it is cumbersome.

Therefore, that which is desired by all persons—a happiness free from the accumulation of all suffering—is postulated as the qualification of the person enjoined (*niyojya*), denoted by the word "heaven" (*svarga*).
But how is the denotability of such a happiness attributed to the word "heaven"? It is said:

In scriptural injunctions such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," we observe that ritual action (karman) is praised by explanatory passages (arthavādas) as being the means for attaining a very long-lasting happiness brought about by a desire free from all suffering and distress.
Furthermore, the word "heaven" (svarga) is seen in common worldly usage to be employed in reference to some particular object according to its conventional meaning.

As for its application to sandalwood and the like, even that is merely figurative (lakṣaṇā), because when the pleasure has ceased, the word still applies to that very object; and since it is not heard to denote pleasure itself even as a denoter of the means of pleasure, its application to the means of pleasure is possible through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of that which denotes pleasure alone.

In this regard, if the word "heaven" (svarga), having been understood in its primary sense, is applied to the mouth, then the application of the explanatory passages (arthavādas) would likewise be to the mouth.

Since it might also apply to praise, the word *svarga* is accepted as denoting such pleasure; even the figurative usage of the term for sandalwood and the like is explained solely by its being a means to that kind of pleasure, all the more so because of its excellence. Thus, the word *svarga* is not applied to every means of pleasure, but rather to that which generates an extraordinary degree of joy. Furthermore, when such pleasure denoted by the word *svarga* is possible, the aforementioned principle (*nyāya*) itself is the authority; and since its primary meaning would otherwise be untenable, there is no inconsistency regarding the body, location, and other factors suitable for its enjoyment.

Inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*), however, is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for postulating an agent to be enjoined (*niyojya*), because it is seen to be fallacious in the case of teaching and similar activities. Furthermore, since the performance [of a rite] occurs through the impulsion of another Vedic injunction (*vidyāntara*), there is no deficiency [in the ritual procedure]. This is because in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), there is the recitation of sets of items that produce assistance to the instrument (*karaṇa*); since no assistance is possible apart from those, if they were absent, the capacity of the instrument to bring about the result would fail to establish the necessity of the action. Thus, when there is a deficiency, the completion must be achieved through *adhyāhāra* (supplying the missing element).
Furthermore, the supply (*adhyāhāra*) of an independent word-meaning is not tenable, because there is no reason for the introduction of a specific [meaning] not previously mentioned.

Even if one were to supply an auxiliary function of the instrument (*karaṇopakāra*), since that would involve supplying a function not conceived as belonging to the *prakṛti* (the base), it would again be impossible to accomplish the result in the absence of the word-meanings; therefore, the supply of an auxiliary function belonging to the *prakṛti* must be performed.

In that case, since there are many *prakṛtis*, it is logical to supply the auxiliary function of whichever one comes to mind due to its proximity by virtue of the commonality of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the injunction (*codanā*).

If that [word] were supplied, the sentence would likewise remain incomplete; therefore, when there is a requirement for the meaning of a word (*padārthākāṅkṣā*), the determination of the word occurs through the presentation of what assists it, and the expression of the related word-meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*) follows.

Although this assistance (upakāra) was previously understood in the archetype (*prakṛti*) as being produced for that purpose [of the sacrifice], nevertheless, because the ritual elements (*padārtha*) are connected with the *apūrva*, those elements are the producers of that very assistance which is related to the archetypal *apūrva*, and not of one related to another *apūrva*. Now, since this assistance—which serves as the means (*karaṇa*)—is understood as having entered into a connection with the archetypal *apūrva*, it is no longer determined as being produced for that specific [archetypal] purpose; thus, there remains a requirement for those elements that produce it. Consequently, the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*), conjoined with the ritual elements presented by way of the assistance established through its previously perceived connection, is expressed by its own word.
Analogy, however, is not a means of valid cognition regarding the connection between a word and its primary meaning;

One understands the mandate (niyoga), and through that, one apprehends the *apūrva* as something to be accomplished by human effort (*kṛti*). Furthermore, there is a distinction in the effect (*kārya*) due to the distinction in the effort;

Therefore, since even the distinction between injunctions (*niyoga*) must be determined by the distinction between scriptures (*śāstra*), it is precisely through those respective distinctions that the distinction between scriptures is designated.

In the world, the activity of an independent person is seen to be of two kinds.
Sometimes one engages in a good purpose for the sake of one's own desire;

Although even a teacher or similar authority cannot compel one who lacks the desire, nevertheless, even in the case of a disciple or others who lack spontaneous desire, the teacher impels them toward the means by generating a desire through the force of his own instigation. In this regard, the causal efficacy (*pravartakatva*) of the teacher and others—who act immediately after the hearing of a word—is determined by their production of the cognition that prompts one's own activity.
What, then, is this "prompting" (*pravartanā*)? It is a property (*dharma*) of the prompter that serves as the cause for activity.
For, in the absence of such a property of the prompter, the distinction—"this word prompts me in this way, but Devadatta does not"—would be untenable.

However, the status of being the cause of engagement (*pravṛtti-hetu*) is established by way of its being an instigator; for instance, in the statement "Devadatta instigates you," since it makes known the act of instigation (*pravartanā-jñāpana*), it follows that even the word *yat* would possess the quality of being an instigator.

Likewise, it would follow that even the worldly optative suffix (*laukika-liṅ*)—which makes known the command and so forth residing in a teacher or other authority—is an instigator. Furthermore, in the world, the property of being an instigator belonging to a teacher or similar figure is perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣa*) as the thought "I am instigating this person," and it takes the form of a command (*preṣa*) and so on; yet this [application to words] cannot be maintained.
In the Veda, however, since there is an absence of a person, the property of being an instigator must be admitted to belong to the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth themselves;
that alone is the injunction (*vidhi*).
Among these, the highest form of instigation is entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇa*).
An invitation (*āmantraṇa*) is for all [classes of persons];

For in that case, by virtue of the original characteristic mark, the ladles made of *śamī* wood or gold are to be wiped; there is a connection with the word "barhis" (sacrificial grass).
Therefore, there is the exclusion of the original [grass].
This is the established conclusion regarding the *varaṇapraghāsa* sacrifices.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, [it is argued] that in all the extensive texts and so forth where various objects are indicated, this second sūtra has accepted the very section (*adhikaraṇa*) concerning the second [offering], on the grounds that the *saṃmārga* (cleansing) is for the purpose of the offering. [The Bhāṣya states:
"The third [item] mentioned in the Bhāṣya is the *śamyā*, a sacrificial implement (*yajñāyudha*)."
(Regarding the statement, "They cleanse the sacrificial implements," the second alternative interpretation of the second section has been accepted:
One places the *śamyā* upon the grinding stone (*dṛṣad*).
Vi. 3.1.5. Śā—Since both the *kuśa* grass and the *śara* reed are known from authoritative sources regarding their measurement, the property of being a *paridhi* (enclosing-stick) belongs to both.

VI. 1.2.12. Accumulation; cessation [of the *kuśa* grasses] because they serve the same function as the subject at hand. Since the *śara* reeds are prescribed for that function indicated by the word *barhis*, they supersede the *barhis* which is obtained as a secondary element (*pṛṣṭhabhāvena*), by establishing a dissimilarity with the *śara* mentioned in the preceding section.
[The form] "the *barhis* made of *śara*" is derived from the rule *vṛddhaśarādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.144).

Bhāṭṭa 10.4.1: Since *kuśa* grass is also obtained [as an option], it was stated in the section on relative strength (*balābala-adhikaraṇa*, 3.1.7) that because the suffix *mayaṭ* in the sense of a modification (*vikārārtha*) is explicitly prescribed for *śara*, the [use of] *kuśa* is indeed sublated. Therefore, this *mayaṭ* has the sense of a modification; consequently, there is a sublation of the *kuśa* grass by the *śara* grass, which serves as the material for the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Bhāṣya 3.6.18: [The *śara* grass] sublates the *kuśa* grass.

Because it is a modification of *kuśa* grass, that [grass] indicates its effect, namely *śara* grass, because of the injunction regarding it (*su-pṛ*, 883). In the case of an explicit statement (*pratyakṣavacana*), the sublation of the effect is also logical, as in the case of *śara* grass and so forth. Since the order of the primary [elements] (*mukhyakrama*) is based on the application prescribed by direct instruction—[whereby *śara* replaces *kuśa*]—and because it is prescriptive insofar as it is inferred from an injunction, even though it follows the extended application (*atideśa*), there is no sublation; rather, there is a combination: "The *śara*-made [sacrificial seat] is combined with the *kuśa*-made one. Thus, it is a sublater.

If it is argued: "Since sublation (*bādha*) is possible in the case of blackness [of the grains]—just as in the case of *śara* grass and so on—the primary order (*mukhyakrama*) is stronger; therefore, the injunction of abundance (*prācurya*) comes first. Do not say that, for it is established by the explicit statement (*pratipadokti*). [The reply is: Even though the performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*) is based on direct instruction (*aupadeśika*), in its essential form, the Bhaṭṭa school holds that after the injunction "One should offer a *caru* of black rice to Soma-Rudra," there follows the injunction "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is made of *śara*."
Regarding the *śaraṇyāya* (3885): the body is [composed of] reeds (*śara*), but the arrows are merely external materials.
Nor does the maxim apply that "the person made of reeds consists of stone."

The term *kuśa* [is used] because the suffix *mayaṭ* is frequently prescribed to denote the connection with that [material], as in the expressions *kākatālīya-vat* and *bhūmī-vat*. For example, when it is said, "A man has emerged from the reed-fenced enclosure," there is no occurrence of sublation; rather, since it would otherwise follow that the purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*), the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) must be made of reeds themselves. Thus, by means of that [reed], the phrase "belonging to the reed-man" (*śarapuruṣīya*) is equivalent to "by the hand. This is because it is prescribed with reference to the specific object. (Sāhasī. 679)
And yet, even so, the *barhis* consisting of reeds (*śaramaya*) does not exclude the *barhis* for the purpose of the ritual act of recollection;
for it is impossible for the reeds to be the *kuśa* grass itself,
and it is impossible for the suffix *-maya* to be a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to signify a modification (*vikāra*).

Dayana (Bhāṣya 10.4.1.1): "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara* reeds. In reality, because the substance qualified by the preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) has *kuśa* grass as its archetype (*prakṛti*), the archetypal function is obtained in the ectype (*vikṛti*) through the word for the substance which bears the mark of the archetype.

In the ectype, because it has *śara* grass as its material, there is the statement: "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is made of *khadira* wood" (12.3.1.8), and likewise, "the sacrificial grass consists of *śara* reeds."

For in that case, there would result the undesirable consequence of the suffix *mayaṭ* being a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of modification. However, since verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is secondary, even a subsequent means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that has already been established can be possible; just as in the case of the scriptural statement, "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara* grass," which—through a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the remembered ritual requirement—enjoins "only *śara* grass" for the purpose of the sacrificial grass. Therein, no weakness [of authority] exists. Since it is merely to be inferred (*kalpyatva*), the sublation of *kuśa* grass by the injunction is entirely appropriate.
And yet, there is no weakness in the injunction [of the *codaka*].

According to Ratna. 5|1|10|18, because the effect (*kārya*)—as qualified by its own constituent objects—is already obtained previously, it possesses the status of being the subject (*pakṣa*). Just as, for fear of the redundancy of the statement "the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara* reeds," the mutual expectancy is supplied; and since the *śara* reeds possess authority as they are being connected [to the rite], the *kuśa* grass is set aside by the *śara* reeds.

It should not be argued that because [the rule] connects [with the grass] only in the absence of contradiction with *kuśa* grass (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 10.3.1.19), and because it functions as a substitute (*pratinidhi*) in the absence of *kuśa* (10.3.1.15)— just like the *śara* grass— therefore, since the connection "the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara*" is logically established, it cannot be a sublater (*bādhaka*) of *kuśa*. For a scriptural injunction (*śāstra*), which is established by syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), operates by sublating the previously obtained *kuśa* grass.

In the *Adhvarakalpā*, after the requirement for action arises in its proper sequence, the sequence of the performance-injunction (*prayogavacana*) is established precisely upon the attainment of those constituent elements that produce it. Therefore, since the application of the extended injunction (*atideśika-vidhi*) is accepted as a factor in the operation [of the rite], and since that requirement is satisfied by the *śara* grasses alone, the sequence applies to that very function. Thus, according to the words of Bārhaspatya, the sowing (*avāpa*) of the *bārhaspatya* vessels occurs first; thereafter, because the *kuśa* grasses possess the specific characteristics of the *sārasvata* vessels, the properties of the *sārasvata* vessels are in fact obtained by the *kuśa* grasses through their location. (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra-bhāṣya 5.1.10.17–18)
Because [the *barhis*] exists in its functional role (*kārya*),
it is precisely for this reason that there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the extension-rule (*codaka*) by the very first [elements] established by the logicians (*tārkika*).

Although the extension-rule is dependent upon [the archetype] for the purpose of obtaining the function of the *barhis* in order to enjoin the *śara* grass, the *śara* grass is nonetheless grasped only as something not desired by the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), because of the latter's requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*).
Furthermore, there is the sublation of the *kuśa* grasses already obtained by those obtained through the *codaka* (transference).

Or rather, let it be that when the requirements for the producers of the effects first arise through transference (*atideśa*), the word "reeds" (*śara*) is seen to be applied to the *kuśa* grasses as well, because the objects denoted by the term "reed-thicket" (*śaravaṇa*) are perceived separately in different locations.
Consequently, [the conclusion is] that this "thicket of *kuśa*" consists precisely of the effects obtained through transference.
Bhāṣya 8.3.1.33: "In that case, because the injunction of *śara* grass applies specifically to that location, there is no assumption of an extended application (*atideśa*) for the *kuśa* grass.
It has been established that the word *śara* is used figuratively (*bhakti*).
This is because, due to their length and breadth, it is impossible for the forms of the substances themselves to occupy separate locations and so forth."
This statement regarding similarity—"This thicket of *kuśa* grass is indeed a thicket of *śara* grass"—is merely a figurative expression (*pratyāhāra*).
Therefore, its sublation (*bādha*) in its own primary sense is appropriate.
Thus, this is nothing more than a figurative designation.
2. That which exists [in its primary sense] conveys similarity; how could it convey it while abandoning its own meaning?
Maṇḍana says: "The word *śara* denotes *kuśa* grass.
Therefore, in that context, the word *śara* is used only for arrows, not for *kuśa* grass.

Śaṅkara: "Let the *kuśa* grasses be pierced here with arrows. (2.8.3.1.34). The principle of the arrow (*śaranyāya*): among the stars, the subsidiary offering (*upahoma*) by the northerners consists of the *nāriṣṭha*, the arrow, and so forth, for the Vaiśya. One should establish the sacred fires (*agnim ādadhīta*).
Bhāṣya 1.1.3:
"The sublation of the extended homas is like that of the *śara* grass.
This being the prima facie view, [the sūtra states]: "In autumn, one should initiate a Vaiśya. 2.2.2.
6|1|7|33. Since the attainment of even the *nāriṣṭha* oblations is possible through the location by virtue of the observed state of the ritual action, [the rule] applies to the *śara-śarāva*.

In such cases as "one should offer five *śarāva*-measures of cooked rice," the mere fact of being in the same location is not the determining factor due to the difference in the underlying logic (*nyāya*).
This is because we observe the use of words such as *śarāva* to refer to that which is measured by it.

Su. Pṛ. Since the *śara* grasses are prescribed for the purpose of the *barhis*—which is indicated by the word [itself]—it is logical that they set aside the *barhis* as it is obtained through the mediation of that purpose (926). Bhāṭṭa: A so-called "subtle body" (*ātivāhika-śarīra*) is postulated to exist in the interval between the previous and subsequent bodies for the sake of maintaining the continuity of the stream of cognition; however, even though Vindhyavāsin maintains that the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*) is directly taught (*aupadeśika*), he has refuted the primary order (*mukhya-krama*) in its essential form.
Furthermore, an intermediate state body (*antarābhava-deha*) is denied by Vindhya because it is merely postulated, and thus the logic of the *śara* [grass] analogy does not apply.
Bhāṭṭa 5.1.10:
By means of the [logical] mark;
for there is indeed no proof by which anything is understood.

Regarding the body: in the *Ātmavāda* (Maṇiprabhā, p. 46), it is stated that the body is of four kinds—namely, the womb-born (*jarāyuja*), the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), the soil-born (*udbhija*), and the sweat-born (*svedaja*). However, there is no reason whatsoever for the mention of the "body" [in this context] other than its being the unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*).

Therefore, it should be understood as follows: from an action that has the attainment of cattle as its fruit, there arises as a result a specific body, sense organs, and so forth, which is capable of being connected with cattle.
Bhāṣya 4.3.127, Section 2: The configuration of the body is the subject matter of *sāmudrika* (physiognomy).

Su., p. 130. Regarding sugar (*śarkarā*) [in the fire-sacrifice]: it is to be offered with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), not with oil or other substances. Ci., 1.4.19: The maxim of the emergence of pebbles (*śarkaronmajjanīyanyāya*).

Just as when sugar is scattered [into water], it causes a person to emerge; that which is similar to this is called "the emergence of sugar" (*śarkaronmajjanīya*). *Sāhasī* 680. The word *śalā*, signifying the splashing of fire, indicates the complete extraction [of the embers]. *Mīko.* p. 341. Regarding the phrase "from the splashing of fire," one should consult the section concerning words such as *eṇaśalā*.
9|7|29–27. *Mīko.* p. 341. "From the splashing of fire"—in this context, the section on words beginning with *eṇaśalā* should be examined.

Because he is known as one who possesses "thorns" (śalyaka), his desire for the welfare of the world has been cast far away; therefore, it is not logical to infer that his teaching is rooted in a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). [Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 172] Thus, the texts of the Śākyas and others lack authority.

(This is the second exposition of the section concerning contradiction [Virodhādhikaraṇa]): Those works which are not accepted by those learned in the three Vedas (*trayīvid*); which fall into some minor category of mantra, tantra, or narrative; which are intent on the purposes of winning over the world, gain, honor, and fame; which rely on reasonings consisting mostly of perception, inference, and presumption (*arthāpatti*) that are contrary to and unconnected with the three Vedas, such as the *Upaniṣads* and so forth; which establish dharma and adharma based on the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, Pāśupata, and Śākya texts; which display occasional success through the power of seeing certain mantras and medicinal herbs capable of neutralizing poison, subjugating others, causing expulsion, inducing madness, and so forth; which, by virtue of being consistent with the Smṛtis regarding the perfection of non-violence, truthful speech, self-restraint, charity, compassion, and the like, are permeated by the mere scent of the meaning of the Vedic word and provide internal instructions; and those even more external ones which are based on the practice of Mleccha customs and mixed dietary habits—it is for these very reasons of contradiction with the Śruti that their lack of authority (*anapekṣaṇīyatva*) is established by the two sūtras (3.1.4–5).
And this has not been established by anyone in another treatise (*vṛtti*).

Nor can it be said that [the Veda] is simply inexpressible, because the cognition that words such as *gāthā* and so forth denote [their respective objects] would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For if one were to disregard [this], then the status of being a means of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) could not be postulated for the [Vedas].
Thinking that it is impossible, others may come to hold an impartial view.
Or else, by means of the power of speech which is the cause of beauty, happiness, and eloquence,
he attains the worldly success of being honored, as well as renunciation and the final state.

Alternatively, since there is no distinction in being composed by Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, even those possessed of intelligence, by relying on the fact that [the Smṛtis] have the Veda as their source—just like the *Mānava-dharmaśāstra* and others—would accept them as being optional alternatives alongside what is enjoined in the Śruti. Thus: "Therefore, even if some contradictory Smṛti were found to be stated in the Mantras and so forth, nevertheless, in this matter, only this [Vedic injunction] is applicable."
For as long as those things which are utterly opposed to the established path of the Three Vedas have not been refuted, the understanding of Dharma cannot be attained.
In that regard, even they [the proponents of other systems] speak of things such as the "path of entry" (āyana) which are accepted by the great multitude;
indeed, in their own philosophical systems, they describe these in relation to other continents.
In this regard, faith alone is the sole basis for establishing [the authority] everywhere, because [the Smṛtis] follow the conduct of one's father, grandfather, and so forth.

Furthermore, since even those who accept that the Mānava and other Smṛtis are rooted in the Veda as it exists, it is all the more possible for the Śākyas and others to claim that their own works are likewise rooted in that same [Veda].
For who could possibly establish the identity of these [Smṛtis] with the Vedic texts when those texts have been lost?

Furthermore, for some time, whatever [tradition] is being brought forward by certain people—even if it is well-known—may appear to possess a status equal to direct experience (*anubhava*) despite its lack of consistency with the established scriptures (*pratyakṣa-śāstra*), because it remains rooted in lost scriptures (*utsanna-śāstra*).
Therefore, he says: "But in case of contradiction, it should be disregarded" (and also "because of the observation of a reason").

Indeed, their dependence is acknowledged by those very [proponents] because they were composed by specific authoritative persons; furthermore, it is known even by bystanders from their respectful presentation of such [doctrines] as the producedness of sound (*śabda-kṛtakatva*).
Furthermore, because they share the same status as a root source, people do not accept the Veda out of shame, just as one would not accept the words of one's mother, father, or eldest son.
Moreover, a single statement from the Smṛti might contradict only a single scriptural (Śruti) passage;

however, all the words of the Śākyas and others—such as their teachings on self-restraint and charity—are in contradiction with the entirety of the fourteen branches of knowledge, and were composed by Buddhas and others who have strayed from the path of the Three Vedas.

Since these [works] were handed over to those outside the Trayī (the three Vedas)—to outcasts who are for all practical purposes of the fourth varṇa—they cannot be considered to have the Veda as their source.
Furthermore, what confidence can there be that a man who, while being a Kṣatriya, took up the role of a teacher by transgressing his own duty, would teach the Dharma without corruption?
And it has been said: "One should avoid from afar one who performs actions contrary to the next world."
How can he who deceives himself be beneficial to another?
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, this very transgression resides within the Buddha’s own perception of ornamentation;
for which reason he spoke thus: "Whatever sins caused by the defilements of the Kali age exist in the world, let them fall upon me, and let the world be liberated."
Thus it is said.

It is indeed for the sake of the welfare of the world that he, having transcended the duty of a Kṣatriya and assumed the role of a teacher like a Brāhmaṇa, was praised in such a manner—having been instructed by Brāhmaṇas who were incapable of transgressing prohibitions, he taught the Dharma to those Brāhmaṇas, accepting even personal suffering for the sake of favoring others. He is praised because, while instructing those he had instructed, he did not cause all those who act by transgressing the Dharma prescribed by Śruti and Smṛti to be known as practitioners of contrary conduct.
"Therefore, when there is a contradiction with direct Vedic revelation (śruti),
the claim regarding the authority of the texts composed by authors— such as the Mahābhārata— is [invalidated]."
"Indeed, these [Smṛtis], being already bound by the Veda according to the reasoning stated previously, lack the capacity to infer a foundational Śruti.
Furthermore, the destruction of other Vedic branches (śākhās) never occurs;
and because they have been shown to be non-blue in nature as previously argued, their basis is seen to be [the Veda itself]."

For there is no agreement between the Smṛtis concerning the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and so forth, and the texts of the Śākyas and others which are not seen in other Vedic branches; nor, in the same way, is an agreement possible regarding the construction of *caityas*, their veneration, or gifts bestowed by Śūdras and the like.
Furthermore, the postulation of a separate root [cause] has already been refuted previously.
Moreover, in this case, greed and other such causes are perceived in great variety;
when these are present and observed, there is no inference of another root cause.
And the Śākyas and others, while teaching the Dharma everywhere,
never do so free from the web of logical reasoning.
Nor do they claim to have the Vedas as their source, like Gautama and others;
rather, they are designated as "those who state reasons," standing far removed from Dharma.

And these very ones, who do not perform worship even with the protection of sacred speech— namely the heretics (*pākhaṇḍins*), those established in violence, and the rationalists (*hetukas*) as proclaimed by Manu— are indeed [excluded].
Indeed, their very books are declared to be avoided by means of mantras and other such measures:
"Those Smṛtis which are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—
all those are declared to be fruitless, for they are said to be rooted in darkness."

Thus, it is established that for this person, authority of such a kind as is outside the Trayī would be entirely disregarded. Vārtika 13.2.4, pp. 194–196. Śāstra: Those pseudo-dharmaśāstras which have not been accepted by those learned in the Trayī but were composed by the Śākyas and others (the word "others" includes the Pāśupatas and so forth mentioned in the Vārtika—Soma)—their lack of authority is stated here by way of an illustration of the commonality of their authors, as mentioned in the previously cited sūtra.
For their authority, being based on perception and so forth, has already been refuted in the *Pratyakṣa* [chapter].
Here, their authority based on the Veda—as in the case of mantras and the like—is being refuted.
For even though there is no commonality of authorship with well-known Vedic rites such as the *agnihotra*, the Vedas will serve as their source, since they follow different systems.

Just as the *Atharvaveda* exists in a form that constitutes a distinct system separate from the three [other Vedas], so too there may have been other Vedas of a different form than the [current] four;
and those have now perished.
For some indeed maintain that even certain mantras and other texts are rooted in lost recensions (*śākhās*); therefore, the same will apply here as well.

And since validity (*prāmāṇya*) is established in this manner, it is not logical for invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) to apply; thus, this section is intended to refute the objection raised by some, which must indeed be rejected according to the "method of the dull-witted" (*mandipanyāya*).

As for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): although the Veda is not perceived in the *mantras* and other such portions, it is inferred on the basis of the uninterrupted acceptance (*parigraha*) by the Vedic tradition and through logical reasoning.

Among the Śākyas and others, the learned (śiṣṭas) remember that this [system] is utterly contrary [to tradition], non-Vedic, and lacks authority; out of hatred for the Vedas and Vedic teachings, they nevertheless accept its authority. A conceptual construction follows what is observed, not the opposite of it.
Therefore, the hypothesis of a Veda [composed by them] is even more remote; thus, they lack authority precisely because they are rooted in what is non-existent.

(13|3|13, p. 27). Bhaṭṭa: Since it is well known that the Śākyas and others were Kṣatriyas, it is possible for them to have seen the Vedas; therefore, the Smṛtis composed by them are also rooted in the Veda, though the Veda that served as their source has now been lost.
