This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the conclusion is as follows]: Since there is an absence of the reason stated in the preceding section—namely, that the acceptance by cultured *traiṇikas* constitutes a matter of duty (*dharma*)—and since, on the contrary, they are remembered as being non-authoritative (*aprāmāṇya*), and since those who deny the authority of the Veda accept their lack of authority therein, it is impossible to postulate a Vedic basis for them; therefore, they are non-authoritative.
1.3.2. Śaṅkara: "And here is the section concerning the Śākyas and others" (this is a refutation composed in the *Vārttika*).
Refutation of the treatises of the Śākyas and others.
The second exposition of the section concerning the Kalpasūtras:
"Once the pseudo-dharmaśāstras composed by the Śākyas and others have been rejected..."
The status of being a treatise on the application of the Dharma, the refutation of the treatises of the Śākyas and others,
the refutation of the treatises of the Śākyas and others.
Just as the Śākyas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others who fear the Mīmāṃsakas say,
"Our scripture is indeed eternal," they speak thus with empty minds.
Out of malice, they somehow desire the Veda to be their authority;
yet even in that alone, they most intensely desire to be speakers of truth.
Because the words of the Buddha and others are for the most part outside the Veda,
those who pride themselves on logic say that non-violence and the like were not preceded by [Vedic] authority.
Furthermore, because it is of human origin, its authority regarding supersensible matters is [unfounded];
thus, people are deluded by the previously mentioned fallacious arguments for the eternity of the Veda.

Furthermore, since even the Mīmāṃsakas have rejected the authority of statements regarding flowers in supersensuous realms, their determination that [the Veda] is authorless has been refuted. Considering the establishment of its authority—which is free from suspicion of causal defects and beyond reproach—to be unassailable, they are rendered speechless. Though their hearts are being torn apart by their own words, which resemble the imitation of children, they have exhausted their web of arguments and respond like a fool asked about his lineage when seeking a bride: "Whatever is your lineage, that is ours as well."
Those who merely repeat the words of others say that the nature of things is eternal.
When urged with the words, "This statement of ours belongs to you," they prattle back, "This belongs to us alone"; having heard this, it must be investigated by the Mīmāṃsakas.
For one who, having abandoned all shame, utters words that are logically inconsistent and devoid of purpose.
Who, tirelessly practicing deception against others, ever comes to grief?
In that regard, even though the Śākyas are renowned for their doctrine of universal momentariness,
they abandon it by prattling with scriptures that are themselves non-momentary, in accordance with the tenets of the Vedas.
This Dharma was taught by him: "All that is conditioned is impermanent;
all conditioned phenomena are momentary. How can there be action for things that are unstable?"
That which is to be known by the intellect is other than the triad; it is conditioned and momentary.

Likewise, because the cognition of sound is restricted [to specific instances], manifestation (*abhivyakti*) cannot be the cause, as there are faults [in such a theory]; since [the Mīmāṃsakas] thus always establish the non-eternality of the relationship between words and their meanings, their acceptance of the opposite—namely, the eternality of the *Āgama*—would result in nothing more than a target for public ridicule. For instance: "He who, having taken up a shuttle, would strive to weave a cloth without using any warp-threads, would be striking at empty space with his fists."

As long as the permanence of the soul is maintained through such conceptualizations as "I" and "mine," it is difficult to overcome that [permanence] once it has been obstructed by fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).

The meaning is that, even if the eternity of scripture (*āgama-nityatva*) is postulated in such forms as "as far as the word [extends]" and so forth, it is difficult to establish its form, like a house.
(Sūtra-pṛ. 235). The term "eternity of linguistic usage" (*vyavahāra-nityatā*) is a synonym for the "eternity of action" (*kriyā-nityatva*).

If the relationship between words and their meanings were impermanent, upon what basis could the permanence of the linguistic usage dependent upon them rest? This is extremely difficult to establish. Furthermore, for those who maintain that the collection of words, meanings, and their relationships is immutable, the permanence of linguistic usage cannot be conceived as being without a foundation.
When sounds and other objects perish, how could linguistic convention continue?
Therefore, the statement that "their nature remains" is devoid of meaning.
This [moment], perishing in an instant, cannot even be pointed out as "this is it";
how much less so when it exists together with its own state of being expressed as "this"?

Because the eternity of the Veda is untenable given the impermanence of words and so forth, and because a text concerning supersensible objects cannot function as a manual for practical application, it is said: "Not [so], because of the absence of a fixed connection" (*nāsanniyamāt*).
"The scriptures of the Śākyas, Jainas, and others consist mostly of ungrammatical words; and because they lack a real basis, their status as scripture is not recognized."

"For you, indeed, the composition of correct words is based on the Māgadhī shadow-language and its various Apabhraṃśa dialects. For it has been said by me, O monks: 'The word of action is the authority for all;
when one is thus suspended, there is no ground for reproach.'"
In the wind there is no cause;
in the non-existent, there is a cause.
These phenomena that belong to the sphere of the Sakka-possessors arise with a cause and perish without a cause.
"the cause of non-arising," and so forth. "For even for me, monks, all action indeed exists.
Thus, when a clod of earth is thrown upward, there is a cause;
in its falling, there is no [separate] cause."
The phrase "there is no cause for non-arising" is to be supplied.
These conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) arise with a cause; they perish without a cause.
"Non-arising cause"—this is the Sanskrit term.
"Since those words are likewise unreal, how can there be any reality in their objects? Furthermore, since their forms are seen to be subject to change, how could they possibly be beginningless?"

Even when something in the texts of the Śākyas and others is employed with the intention of using correct words (*sādhuśabda*), such as *abhinadhruvā*, only a very small portion is found to be worthy of praise because it consists mostly of usage that is merely commendable, clear, and complete.
How much less so those forms like *bhikkhave*, which are even more corrupted than the well-known regional dialects (*deśabhāṣā*)?
For a Prākṛt word ending in the vowel *e* is seen in the place of the second-person plural, but not in the first-person plural, nor even in the vocative.

Furthermore, in Prakrit and Apabhraṃśa, it is observed that when the word *saṃskṛta* occurs, there is the doubling of the letter *k*, the elision of the *anusvāra*, and the substitution of the vowel *ṛ* with *ā*; however, the production of the letter *ḍ* is not seen.
Thus, this [argument] is a refutation of the treatises of the Śākyas and others.

By the statement "conditioned phenomena [are] Śākyan," destruction—which is itself prohibited at all times—is nonetheless effected; thus, because it is based on incorrect terminology, the suspicion that this might be another unauthored scripture (akṛta-śāstra) like the Veda is dispelled by the reason ending with those words.
This applies to whatever mass of words (śabdarāśi) is unauthored and indestructible.

Only its grammar has been found, and the form characterized by it is not found in the speech of the Śākyas and others as it is found in the Veda; because there is an absence of restrictive rules for its usage, for this reason also it lacks scriptural authority.
The meaning is: "because of non-proximity," that is, because there is no rule [of authorship] established by grammar.

Or, it is stated "because of non-proximity" with the intention of referring to a text whose internal structure is pervaded by a permanence established through a permanence that excludes momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*)—[that is, a text for which impermanence is established by a permanence that has excluded momentariness].

Alternatively, it refers to the fact that there is a rule of demonstration by means of fallacious reasons (*asaddhetu*) for non-existent doctrines such as the theory of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga-vāda*) and the doctrine of non-oneness (*anekatva*); therefore, even the words on dharma uttered by those same authors lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*).
"Furthermore, because the remembrance of an author is firm, these [scriptures] are not considered to be unauthored.
Therefore, regarding an object that lacks even the scent of being unauthored, they possess no authority due to their independence."
Or [the Śākvara] is the *acchāvāka*sāman and the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra] in the Viśvajit sacrifice. (ŚB 1.3.6.12) Page. Śākaraṃ acchāvāksāma pṛṣṭhaṃ viśvajiti.
Bhāṣya 7.3.138: The Śākara is the Maitrāvaruṇa-sāman in the Viśvajit sacrifice when all the Pṛṣṭhas are performed;
the Śākara is the Pṛṣṭha on the sixth day of the Ṣaḍaha, as it is to be produced by the Śākara-sāman.
In the Viśvajit, this [sāman] is obtained from the Ṣaḍaha.
The branch is the motivator for the act of cutting and so forth; the *upaveṣa* (wooden splinter) is not.
See the section titled "The Section on the *Upaveṣa*" (*upaveṣādhikaraṇam*) at Mīmāṃsākośa, page 1104, verses 4.2.318–319.
Even when being cut down by one who strikes the branch, the branch does not accomplish the sacrifice.
[Duh. 4.2.4.11] The branch is prescribed for the purpose of separating the calves.
Bhāṣya 6.4.14.44: The branch is for the purpose of the *sānnāyya* offering;
it is called an *upaveṣa* when it is brought near.

Branches such as the *Kāṭhaka* and others are established as synonyms for "branch" because they constitute certain limbs, flowers, and fruits of the tree known as the Veda, which possesses a specific form.

Just as for a single tree, the trunk—which has a single root and serves as the support for all branches—is metaphorically designated as "the tree" because it constitutes the very root called "branch" and takes the form of the trunk known as "injunction";

so too, since the flowers and fruits [of the Veda] do not exist in their entirety within each individual branch of a tree, the term "branch" is used metaphorically for each individual Vedic branch (*veda-śākhā*), because the flowers and fruits—namely, the various recensions such as the *Ṛgveda* and the ritual duties such as the *Adhvaryu* and *Hotṛ*—do not exist in their totality within each single branch. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 991–992)
The Śākhās [of the Veda]: for these are like branches (śālā). Just as there are branches of a tree, so too here are there branches of the Veda, which stands in the place of a tree.
What is the similarity to a house? Just as [the parts of a house] are situated separately,
and the entire flower or fruit is not contained within each individual part,
so too here, the entire section on qualities (guṇakāṇḍa) is not contained within each individual [part].
Bhāṣya 2.4.128: Regarding the branch, the statement "he brings the eastern [branch]" is a designation for the sacrificial shed (*śālā*), not a designation for a direction (*diś*).
However, ritualists (*yājñika*) maintain that it is a designation for a direction.

"With a branch he drives away the calves" refers to the morning of the day of preparation (*aupavasathya*) for the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*); specifically, when one drives away the calves with a *palāśa* branch.
VI. 4.2–1: The "throwing away" (*praharaṇa*) of the branch means its relinquishment (*tyāga*) into the *āhavanīya* fire. The throwing away of the branch is a disposal act (*pratipatti*).
Regarding the various recensions (*śākhās*):

since it is impossible for persons who are prone to error to travel to all the different regions where these recensions are studied, it is possible that they do not perceive the scriptural texts contained therein.

Furthermore, even regarding scriptural texts located within a single recension but situated in various contexts, it is impossible for persons prone to error to determine whether they pertain to the duties of those [recensions] or to the duties of human beings.
The possibility of *smṛti*, *mūla*, *nirūpaṇa*, *pūla*, and *dhī* [arises].
Su. pṛ. 123.
Even though there are many *brāhmaṇas* in a single *śākhā*, that [action] is one *karman*.
When the *udgātṛ* and others [perform the rites] according to the *Ṣaḍviṃśa-brāhmaṇa*, there are twelve [stotras] for the *Jyotiṣṭoma*;
this is because that [text] is the primary authority for that branch (*śākhā*). (Vārttika 2.4.129, p. [page number]).
This portion of the subsequent sūtra, being treated as a separate unit, has been explained in the Bhāṣya as constituting a distinct topical section (adhikaraṇa).
In reality, however, it is certain that the very portion situated in the eighth sūtra was extracted and explained as the first member of the varga (prathamavarṇaka).
This is the sūtra of the established conclusion (siddhāntasūtra).

Regarding the *palāśa* branch used for the purpose of separating the calves during the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "He brings one facing east," "He brings one facing north," and "He brings one facing northeast.
If it is argued that here the words "east" and so forth refer to the cardinal directions themselves, this is not the case;
rather, the words "east" and so forth are employed to denote a branch that is contrary to the direction of the respective quarter—such as the eastern direction and so on.
Because that [house] is primary, and because the word "eastern" and so forth has the house as its primary referent by virtue of being the maker of the house;
therefore, this is a discourse concerning the house, not a discourse concerning the direction.
Ke.

The Section on Different Branches (Śākhāntarādhikaraṇa). Regarding different branches: because that [rite] is the primary focus within the branch, there would be a division of the *paveṣaṇa* (the act of spreading); that would constitute a discrepancy.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "Having trimmed the shed from its base, he makes the *upaveṣa*. "From its base" means having cut from the root. Here, a deliberation arises as to whether both the shed (*śālā*) and the *upaveṣa* are the motivators for the act of cutting, or whether the shed alone is the motivator while the *upaveṣa* is merely produced as a byproduct thereof. The following is the aphorism of the final conclusion (*siddhānta-sūtra*).
The term "having trimmed" (*parivāsya*) refers to the branch (*śākhā*).

This is because the branch is the primary object; for by the use of the accusative case in the word "the branch" (*śākhām*), the primacy of the branch is understood, and thus the trimming has the branch as its primary object.

However, in the case of the *upaveṣa* (the wooden chip), it would be a mere separation resulting from the trimming and not an integral part of it, since that [the *upaveṣa*] is construed with the verb "to do" (*karoti*).

This is the difference between the *śālā* (wooden frame) and the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick): it is caused by the presence or absence of a syntactical connection (*anvaya*) with the act of trimming (*parivāsana*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *śālā* is the primary motive for the act of trimming—which is synonymous with cutting—whereas the *upaveṣa* is merely a by-product.
This is also because of the departure from the direct Vedic text (*śruti*).
Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "Having trimmed the hall from its base, he makes the *upaveṣa*.
"From its base" means from the root, at a distance of one span (*prādeśa*). "Trimming" means having cut off.

In this regard, the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) stated in the preceding sūtra that the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is with the *śālā* (branch) itself, not with the *upaveṣa* (the base of the branch). To this, an objection is raised: "But since the root (*mūla*) is also a constituent part of the branch, it possesses primacy just like the branch; therefore, the syntactic connection should rather be 'having trimmed from the root' (*mūlataḥ parivāsya*). If this is argued, the answer is: no, because of the exclusion by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). There is an exclusion (*apāya*) of the root—which is a constituent part—from the word *śākhā*, which denotes the whole (*avayavin*) and is restricted in its denotative power (*śakti*) to the branch alone. Thus, the root is excluded from the scope of the term *śākhā*.
The word "avayavin" (the whole) does not apply to its parts by way of primary denotation (*śakti*).
Consequently, the root cannot be grasped by the word "branch," nor can it be connected with the act of perfuming (*parivāsana*).
Therefore, only the *śālā* (the sacrificial shed) is the motivator for the perfuming, not the *upaveṣa* (the fire-stirring stick).
The *upaveṣa*, however, is produced subsequently from that [branch].
Ke:
There is no fixed sequence of priority or posteriority among the branches.

Furthermore, there is no sequence therein by which it could be known that, once a rite has been enjoined by one branch, a repetition in another branch would function as a restatement (*punaḥśruti*) and thereby annul it.

As it has been said: "The simultaneous occurrence of various schools precludes the assumption of a restatement; for in that case, unlike a single school, study does not proceed according to a fixed order."
Or [it may be] so. (Vārttika 2.4.216, p.

638): *Śālādhyayana* (study of the school). Since it is impossible to study another school while abandoning one's own, it is logical to study another school only after first studying one's own, provided one possesses the requisite intelligence.
Su. Pṛ. 190:
Other branches [of the Veda].
"Because it provides some small fruit from the single tree of the Veda..."

In this way, the branches are established, like a tree with many branches. If there were a difference of ritual action (*karmabheda*) for each branch, then— because they would lack a single root and because they would be differentiated from the very beginning and possess distinct flowers and fruits of all their rituals— they would be called different Vedas (*vedāntara*),
not different branches (*śākhāntara*).

Since they all possess the same fundamental form as injunctions (*vidhi*), yet there are certain additional elements of procedure (*itikartavyatā*) in some cases, the designation of "different recensions" (*śākhāntara-bheda*) is justified on the basis of such similarities and differences.
Vārttika 2.4.18, p. 639.
Other recensions include the Kāṭhaka, Kālāpaka, Paippalāda, Taittirīyaka, Tāṇḍaka, and so forth;
as well as the Maitrāyaṇīya (Bhāṣya 2.4.18).
These various recensions possess purposefulness through their presentation of the teachings to different individuals.
Or [it is said]: "For even in another Vedic branch (śākhā), the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that there is a single scripture (śāstra). — *Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 271. *Vārttika* 2.4.13, p. 475.
The section concerning different recensions:
Even when there is a difference in recension, there is no difference in the ritual action.

There would be a difference in the ritual acts (*karma-bheda*) across different recensional branches (*śākhāntara*) due to the observation of differences in name, form, specific details, repetition, censure, incapacity, commendation, expiation, and the logic of purpose.
Commentary: Here, the various recensional branches—such as the Kāṭhaka, the Kālāpaka, the Paippalāda, and so forth—are the examples.

In this regard, there is a doubt: whether the ritual act such as the *agnihotra* that is heard of in one branch remains the same when it is heard again in another branch, or whether it differs? We see that it must differ.
Why? Because of the difference in names.
One is named Kāṭhaka, and the other is named Kālāpaka.
Thus, there is a distinction due to the difference in names.
Is this not merely the name of the book?
True; we say it refers to the actions as well.
By means of these actions as well, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) and the state of having the same case-ending (*ekavibhaktitva*) for such [terms].
This is due to a difference in form (*rūpabheda*).
For instance, in one recensional branch (*śākhā*), they prescribe an eleven-potsherd offering (*ekādaśakapāla*) to Īpa, while in another, they prescribe a twelve-potsherd offering.
In this way, since their forms are distinct, how could there not be a difference in ritual action (*karmāntara*) here?
[This is] because of the specific characteristics of the *dharma*.
The Taittirīyas, having studied the *Kārīrī* section, [perform it] on the ground.
The Section on Different Branches (Śākhāntarādhikaraṇa). Regarding the section on different branches: some followers of a Vedic branch perform a particular ritual act, while others do not.
Likewise, among those performing the Agnihotra sacrifice, some bring water-jars for their preceptor while others do not;
among those performing the Aśvamedha sacrifice, some bring fodder for the horse while others do not;
and others practice different religious duties.
The Aśvamedha and other such rites require the assistance of some among these [auxiliaries],
while they do not require others.
Why should that very same rite not require [the rest], or why should it require something else?
Therefore, it is understood that [the ritual action] is different.
Furthermore, because of the consequence of tautology:
if the ritual action cognized by all branches were one and the same, then the mention in another branch of a ritual action already enjoined in one branch would be a useless repetition.
But this fault does not exist in the view that they are distinct;
therefore, for this reason as well, there is a difference between the actions.
Furthermore, it is because of the statement of censure.

"Every morning they speak untruth, those who offer the *agnihotra* with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) while it is not yet dawn; they proclaim what is to be proclaimed by day while it is not yet day; Sūrya is their light, yet that is not their light. Thus some followers of a Vedic branch (*śākhin*) censure the *agnihotra* offering before sunrise.
Others, however, censure the offering after sunrise:

"If one were to offer when the sun has risen, it would be as if one were to bring food for a guest who has already departed. This contradiction exists within the consensus of all branches regarding the ritual procedure, but not regarding a difference in the essential nature of the act itself.
For this reason also there is difference;
and because of incapacity.
They would not be able to synthesize even the slightest portion of what is known from all the recensions.
In that case, it would have to be asserted that a purpose not previously commenced is being enjoined;
however, this is possible only when there is a distinction between ritual acts.
Therefore, there is a distinction between the ritual acts.
And because of the statement regarding completion:
even when not yet finished, there is a statement of completion.
Some say, "In this place, our fire-sacrifice is completed."
Others point out that there is a completion [of the rite] elsewhere;
that is not tenable if it were a single action,
for it would not be completed there while remaining incomplete elsewhere.
But it is reasonable that there is a distinction; therefore, there is a difference.
And because of the prescription of expiatory rites.

Some authorities prescribe an expiation for the transgression of performing the oblation before sunrise (*anudita-homa*), while others prescribe it for the transgression of performing the oblation after sunrise (*udita-homa*); and they also prescribe an expiation when the order is inverted.
However, a dual inversion is not possible if there is a difference in the ritual acts.

For if there were a difference in the ritual acts, then that act which is performed before sunrise would be subject to inversion when performed after sunrise, and likewise that act performed after sunrise would be subject to inversion when performed before sunrise.
Therefore, there is also a difference.

Furthermore, because another purpose is observed, this is heard in scripture: "If they have previously consecrated themselves for the Soma sacrifice, and if their householder (gṛhapati) desires them, or the fellow-sacrificers (anusatriṇaḥ), they should resort to this very sacrifice characterized by the Bṛhat-sāman; the Rathantara is already attained."

Now, the observation in the *Dvādaśāha* sacrifice that "those who have not been consecrated" applies both to those who have performed the *iṣṭi* and to those who have not previously performed it; this is possible only if there is a difference between the rites.
It is not tenable if there were a single rite.
How so?
In the *Tāṇḍya* it is heard: "This indeed is the first of sacrifices, namely the Jyotiṣṭoma; he who, having not sacrificed with this, should sacrifice with another, falls into a pit or perishes.
That [rule] would apply everywhere.
In that case, the observation of the twelve-day period for those who have not yet been initiated would not be possible.
For this reason also, there is a difference in the ritual action (karma).
Now, this is an observation of an indicative mark (liṅga):
"If one were to measure [the post] equal to the wing [of the altar], he would approach a smaller chariot, a smaller wagon, fewer cattle, and less food; he would become more wretched."
Now, if one measures out the altar, then—since measuring the sides has been prohibited—there is the observation of one who measures the altar.
This is possible only if there is a difference in the ritual acts.
How so? For some measure them equally, saying, "The intervals between the sacrificial posts are the size of a chariot axle."
That would apply everywhere;

and in that case, there would be neither the measuring of the sacrificial mound (*pakṣasaṃmāna*) nor the measuring of the altar (*vedisaṃmāna*). Thus, the observation of the measuring of the altar would be untenable.
Therefore, there is also a difference in the ritual action (karma).
Furthermore, there is another observation of an indicative mark (liṅga):
"For some, in the Jyotiṣṭoma, two [verses] are desired for those who are consecrated, measured by the Virāj."
Others maintain that three *saṃsthās* are intended for the *virāj* measure. If they constitute a single ritual act (*ekakarmatva*), there is a contradiction;
if they are distinct ritual acts (*nānākarmatva*), then two would apply to one *jyotiṣṭoma* and three to another.
Therefore, there is a difference of ritual action.
Moreover, it is heard in the Sārasvata [sacrifice]: "Those who offer the *puroḍāśa* fast;
those who offer the *sāṃnāyya* keep away the calves."
For one who performs the *sāṃnāyya* sacrifice, [the sequence] begins with the *iṣṭi*;
for one who performs the *puroḍāśa* sacrifice, it is the reverse. The observation regarding both types is possible only if there is a difference in the ritual acts (*karmabheda*).
If all [sacrifices] were of a single nature of action (*ekakarmatva*), then all would have the *Jyotiṣṭoma* as their archetype (*pūrvatva*).
In that case, the observed textual evidence (*darśana*) would not be tenable.
Furthermore, it is heard in scripture: "The *Upahavya* is an *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice, having the *Rathaṃtara* as its *sāman*, performed on the new moon day."
A dark-grey horse is the sacrificial fee.
It is heard [in the scripture] regarding others:
"The Upahavya sacrifice, performed without the Nirṛt-offering, is an Ukthya with the Bṛhat-sāman; a white horse with a golden plate on its forehead is the sacrificial fee."
Thus, if there were a difference in the ritual action, the quality of being "Bṛhat" would be redundant— just as in the case of the Rathantara—
because it is known through both recensional branches.
He may be one who has the Bṛhat-sāman or the Rathantara-sāman;
this characteristic is obtained from the archetype itself.
However, if there were distinct rituals, it would be appropriate for one to have the Bṛhat-sāman and another the Rathantara-sāman.
Therefore, a difference in ritual action must exist between different recensional branches (*śākhā*).
Or rather—this [section] is commenced for the purpose of refuting causes of difference other than the eight previously mentioned causes of difference;
therein, certain doubts are rejected by means of another method.
And we shall apply that counter-example while entering into the discussion.
But why, in this case, are other Vedas not cited? [The answer is: because it is something that ought to be done.
In that case, if there were identity [of the texts], it would follow that contradictory properties are co-inherent [in a single entity].
Some say:
"Those [contradictory passages] are also cited by the word 'etc. from other recensions (śākhā)."

But in the case of diversity, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Even by way of incapacity, it would not be a merit; why? Because, just as a rite is presented in one recensional branch (*śākhā*), it is understood that the merits belonging to other branches are to be combined within that same single rite.
The mere name [of a rite] is not a ground for non-connection with the action because it possesses some common qualities;
even a difference in the mode of performance is merely a quality.
This is established through censure regarding other Vedas.
For where a rite is enjoined as being independent of further requirements, even though it has already been mentioned, a specific expiation is presented again;
and sometimes, there occurs the comprehension of that particular expiation in that context.
Just as one might state the avoidance of optionality regarding the *sarvasvadakṣiṇā* (the gift of all one's possessions) to the *adhvaryu*, that is accepted.

In the various Vedic branches (*śākhā*), in rites such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and *jyotiṣṭoma* which involve complete sets of materials and deities, there is no deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) regardless of which method is followed. However, in this case, because the expiations (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth are prescribed as being mutually independent, a deficiency is observed in both instances due to the application of different rules.
Furthermore, they do not tolerate that [action] being a mere ritual act (*karma*), whereas this is not the case with respect to the other Vedas;
for in those [other Vedas], it is possible [for an action] to be devoid of a material substance (*dravya*) and a deity (*devatā*).
Therefore, there is a distinction [between them] as well.

By means of the introductory sūtra, having introduced the mere ritual action of the five [officiants], only the stotra, śastra, yājyā, and vākyā, etc., are enjoined; this is seen in accordance with the traditional interpretation.
If they have already been consecrated (dīkṣita) previously, then the Bṛhat-sāman is employed.
Yet, by that much alone, its requirement for further specification is not satisfied.
Indeed, the meditation is not directed toward the object of comparison,
because the *rathaṃtara* was employed in the previous initiation;
thus, there is an absence of name, substance, deity, and purificatory rites.

As for the statement there, "If they have not been initiated, then they should resort to the Rathantara-sāman," that which is recited as being endowed with a specific substance and deity is, in the Atharvaṇa, merely an injunction of an accessory (guṇa). In the case of a difference in ritual acts, the condition of having performed no prior sacrifice (*aniṣṭaprathamayajñatva*) applies to the Dvādaśāha.
There is a state of expectancy due to the *tāṇḍaka* [text].

And so he will say: "When, by means of the word 'furthermore' (*bhūyas*), there is the predominance of another *jyotiṣṭoma*, this [word] by its own power [indicates] the hearing of both" (A. 3, Pā. 3, Sū. 10).
This is because there is no restrictive rule regarding what has been approached.
But if [the sacrifice] were one and the same across all branches, then it would be the *Agniṣṭoma* in every branch;
therefore, other branches must indeed be cited as examples.
And in that case, there would be no observation of those who have not yet been initiated, such as the *Prāyaṇīya* and others.
Likewise, in the case of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), a difference in name is seen to be the cause [of a distinction between rituals].

For example, in the *Kāṭhaka* version of the *Agnihotra*, regarding the *Ekādaśinī* sacrifice on the two sides of the year, after one [version] has been censured as being according to its own [standard], the other is read in the *Taittirīya* *Agnihotra*, and so forth.
Similarly, the adoption of a specific form indicates the existence [of the rite] as established by another scriptural statement.

For indeed, in another scriptural passage, there is the offering on eleven potsherds and so forth; and in the Vaiśvānara [passage], there is the twelve [potsherds] and the eight [potsherds]. When one is clearly enjoined, what is the purpose of censuring the other? Nor is there a mutual praise between the twelve and the eleven, as in the case of the *vadābhi* and the *kṣāyija*. Therefore, it is logical that the deficiency in one branch is merely a transfer into the interval of another; thus, this difference is simply a matter of quality (*guṇa*).
There is no injunction for these [rites] belonging to the Kārīrī;
therefore, there is a difference in the ritual acts (*karmabheda*).

Even in the case of the Aśvamedha, there are two *stotrīya* verses. Furthermore, since the accessories—such as the eating of the earth, the water-pot, and the *śrāddha*—are indeed present, the statement "ten [verses] exceed the *virāj*" and "three [verses] exceed" constitutes the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for this [rite], because it is stated as something distinct from the previous one. And this is appropriate when the Jyotiṣṭoma is an *atirātra*.
They have been mentioned.
As for the contradiction [suggested by the statement] that "others practice a different dharma," there is no contradiction because it occurs according to the prescribed rule.
This is for the purpose of demonstrating the internal distinctions among the portions of the *puroḍāśa*.

The term *aśvapādāse*, ending in the ablative case, is seen in the middle; it is understood as having been passed over due to the doubt regarding whether [the horse] is initiated or not initiated. It is read at the end of the method of refutation and connects with both [the preceding and following sections]. First, by the former [section], [the horse] is not taken because it is other than the *daśaśāsa* (ten-fold share) and so forth.

Furthermore, there would be an option regarding the substance of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra], because the prohibition of the *adhaḥśāsa* (lower share) and so forth by the latter [section] requires assistance, since there is the injunction of another sacrifice such as the *Aśvamedha*.
And that [action] is obtained by its very nature through the status of being an object (*karman*).
Because it would be a mere repetition, the repeated mention is said to be a differentiator;
[otherwise], it would be in vain due to censure.

In the case of the Upahavya sacrifice, however, because it is for the purpose of restriction, the difference in the connection with the times of "sunrise" and "after sunrise" constitutes a distinction of quality (*guṇa*) alone;
since this is not heard [as a primary element] in the original Vedic text (*śruti*),
there is therefore also a distinction of ritual action (*karmabheda*).
For those who advocate for the offering after sunrise (uditahoma) censure the offering before sunrise (anuditahoma), considering it to be a false statement.
Indeed, when the sun has not yet risen, the mantra recited is: "The Sun is light, light is the Sun; Svāhā! Therefore, the offering after sunrise must be performed.
Others, however, say:
he who rises first after having already accepted the honor from the one worthy of honor is virtuous;
but he who offers honor only after [the time] has passed and [the other] has spoken out against him is not a proper worshiper.
Therefore, the oblation must indeed be offered before sunrise, because there is no distinction in the connection, the form, or the injunction.

The Commentary states: This is not so; that which was asserted, namely, "there is a difference of ritual acts in different recensions," is incorrect. A single ritual act is recognized by all recensions and is indeed one and the same, because there is no distinction in the connection with the purpose.
We recognize that very same purpose for which it is intended;
we recognize that very same form, namely its substance and deity;
and such a human effort is enjoined as well.
And the designation by name is also non-distinct;
therefore, that very same ritual action is established as residing in all the recensional branches (śākhās), since an option is established by virtue of the number [of texts].
And for this reason, one who is indeed unlearned—
who, due to his dull-wittedness, studies only a single Veda while neglecting other branches— being thus deficient, might even mix rice with barley. Therefore, the ritual action is one and the same.
Or rather: "Because of recognition everywhere, there is no injunction by name through names, forms, qualities, and so forth;
for the cognition of a single action does not depart from the scripture."

The Commentary states: As for what was said regarding "the difference in names," that has been refuted by the principle that [the ritual] is recognized across all recensional branches (*sarvaśākhā-pratyaya*), since it is the same even within a single branch according to the name of the Brāhmaṇa text.
Now, as for what was said regarding the ritual action (*karman*)—namely, that even when there is a commonality of names, the intention is that it is one and the same ritual action.
In this regard, as for the statement "because of the observation of the context," this is not a fault;
because of the connection with the text, the ritual action is [included] in the twenty-fifth and twenty-ninth chapters from the Jyotiṣṭoma onwards.
The connection [in terms of] the *Kāṭhaka* and so forth is not due to a connection with the action; rather, the text is called *Kāṭhaka*.
How so? Because of its predominance, there is a mention of the connection with the fruit.

As for "the form"—is it recognized? That action which is connected with the *Kāṭhaka* and so forth is designated by the word *Kāṭhaka* and so forth, provided that it possesses the substance and the deity.

Regarding the term "injunction" (*codanā*): it refers to that which has the *bhāvanā* (productive activity) as its object for all purposes. What follows from this? Even if a ritual injunction were restricted to a specific recension (*kāṇḍa*) due to its connection with a particular text, the name of the rite—such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and others—is declared to be identical across all recensions. Thus, the action itself is said to be undifferentiated throughout all branches of the Veda.

Even though [the Veda] is one, it is seen as the "Kāṭhaka" due to its connection with the Kāṭhaka recension; likewise, from this collection of causes for recognition starting from the beginning, it will become the "Kālāpaka" due to its connection with the Kālāpaka recension. This is established.
Nor is there any other cause for this;
if it is argued that there is a mutual proximity among different recensions (śākhās) similar to that found in different contexts (prakaraṇas), we say no,
because by that very fact [the name] would apply to the others as well— even if the name were indeed "Kāṭhaka" and so forth, since it is grasped in that manner.
For in another instance, an action is grasped as something distinct because of the absence of a connection with the conventional usage [of the name] established previously.
However, this is not merely an action; rather, one who perceives that very same thing as similar to another is able to apply the name.
This is because of the maxim, "It is improper for a single word to have multiple meanings," and because of the indeclinability [of the term], it follows that this is something other than that.

Furthermore, since all [the texts] would be names of books within the scope of a single *śākhā*, their usage as [names of] rituals is justified only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This occurs precisely upon the study of a *śākhā*. However, in another *śākhā*, there are others [of the same name]. How, then, is it understood that these are names of books rather than names of rituals? For, unlike the case of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other rites which are studied differently in various recensions, no reversal of the cognition of difference arises regarding them.

To this it is replied: "Because of the connection with a single branch (*śākhā*), much is produced. Therefore, when one studies two scriptures (*śāstra*), there is an understanding of rituals belonging to a different section (*prakaraṇāntara*); this is logical because of the plurality of rituals.

According to the principle of a single branch, there must be unity; however, this applies to those [rituals] contained within a single branch, whereas in the case of different Brāhmaṇas [within the same branch], [the distinction remains]."
This is not an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa).
For terms such as *Kāṭhaka* and the like involve a fault in their mutual relationship.
Indeed, it is not even accepted that [the text] known from another recension belongs to a single person;
how much more so when it is employed in various ritual acts?

If that [term] were the name of a ritual action (*karman*), what would be the reason for its occurrence within the *tvā*-affix? For by the mention of "Vedic study" (*svādhyāya*), only a single recensional branch (*śākhā*) is grasped;
indeed, a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not applicable there, as no connection [to other branches] is established.
And there would be a conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) among words that have a single referent, because [the action] is one;
however, the denotation of all [synonyms] is difficult to establish, just as it is with etymological derivations (*vyutpatti*).
Therefore—
Just as a universal form (ākṛti) inheres in each individual instance, so too are the rituals characterized by the branch (śākhā) alone, and not the branches by the rituals.
Consequently, one's own study (svādhyāya) pertains to a single branch.
Therefore, although the branches may indeed be differentiated by the designation "one's own study," the rituals themselves are not.
The *Saṃbandha* [section] is not to be studied, because it is presented merely for the purpose of making known the ritual action (*karman*), and thus lacks the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*).
Therefore, the very same *Agnihotra* and other rites are to be studied under different names in a single branch (*śākhā*) due to differences in connection.
But surely, in this way, the Vedas themselves are designated differently?
It does not follow that meditation is [the only means].
No;
for it is established by another scriptural statement: "By this *ṛc*, by this knowledge."
Likewise, in the statement "one who has studied the Vedas or is a knower of the Vedas," the status of being an authority [is established];
because of the mutual expectancy [of the texts], all the various Vedas would constitute a single ritual action, as they are not distinct from one another.
Therefore, because they are effects [of the same action], their combination is understood.

However, in other recensions (*śākhā*), as stated in the Commentary: "If [the rites] were identical even when there is a difference in words, then—due to their independence from the specific words and because the form of the Jyotiṣṭoma and so forth is established as being the same—the identity of the ritual would result from their having the same purpose. In that case, because they are designated by the word 'Kāṭhaka,' there would be identity; [otherwise,] there would be an option (*vikalpa*)."
And precisely because of this expectancy, there arises the inclusion of other Brāhmaṇas found within the same Śākhā;
for the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is recourse to such accumulation.
Now, one might object: "But since these are a single action, there would be an option (vikalpa) between them, due to their being the same action and having the same word."
But this is not so;
therefore, there is no difference.
Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
No;

or, [if you argue] that recognition establishes identity—since, as a general rule, the opposite of the effect is observed in the case of the cause—it would follow that the Agnihotra and other rites found in a single recensional branch (śākhā) are one and the same, simply because they bear the same name, such as "Kāṭhaka" and so forth.
This is the fallacy known as *arthāpattisama* (balancing the presumption), employed by disputants based on the property to be proven and so on.

The *jāti* (futile rejoinder) has been mentioned solely for the purpose of demonstrating the perception of the unestablished nature (*asiddhatva*) of the reason in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Furthermore, it is accepted by some that *jātis* serve as a response (*uttara*) whenever the prima facie argument is flawed;
and [the term] "formulation" (*abhidhāna*) is used in the sense of being produced (*kṛtaka*).
Commentary: This present designation would not have existed previously;
it has been in use only from the time that the relevant statement was committed to memory. From that point onward, it has come into circulation.
It is contradictory to say that this difference did not exist previously but exists now.
Or rather—as it is said: "The Kāṭhaka and other [recensions] are artificial, because they are based on the oral teaching (āsyapravacana).
Nor can beginningless actions be differentiated by something that has a beginning.

Although the *Kāṭhaka* and other such texts are designated as "eternal" because their composition is eternal, nevertheless, this designation is remembered as being based on the act of recitation (*pravacana*), and yet the ritual actions themselves are not being recited.
This is because recitation has sound as its object.
Therefore, for this reason as well, there is no differentiation of the ritual action (*karman*) by means of its name.
Even when there is unity, there is further [distinction].
The Commentary states: Even when there is a single action, a distinction in form arises from the scriptural statement.
And when there is a distinction in form based on the scriptural statement, even if the difference in the action itself is not explicitly present, a distinction between the actions is determined.
Or rather— not [as suggested] by the passage beginning with "nor the number of skull-bowls" and so forth—
because the distinction between different means (dvāra) connected to that [single rite] is not admitted.
Therefore, there will be an option regarding the means within the very same ritual action.
But has it not been stated that there can be no option because [the two] are enjoined by their respective originative injunctions?
This is not a fault;
for since both are equally enjoined by their originative injunctions, they possess equal force.
But how, then, is the oneness of that which has begun with this statement understood? We shall state the resolution to that in the subsequent sūtra:
"In the case of knowledge, the authority is the Dharmaśāstra."
Commentary: Now, that specific quality which was mentioned for the purpose of acquiring knowledge does not assist in ritual action.

How is this known? Because of the absence of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof, and because superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is impossible, it is not prompted by ritual action.
Its re-statement is like that of the *Āgneya* sacrifice.

The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): Now, as for what was stated—that just as in the case of the *āmāvāsya* sacrifice, the middle position [that it is a preparatory act] was rejected due to the fault of redundancy (*punarukta-doṣa*), so too this [position that it is a ritual action] must be rejected for that very same reason—this is the introductory statement (*ābhāṣya*) of the Sūtra, which is to be refuted. [The word] "Vā" indicates that this is a Sūtra of restatement (*anubhāṣaṇa-sūtra*).
Alternatively, this is precisely for the purpose of avoiding the charge of tautology;
for the repetition [of the scriptural statement] serves the purpose of indicating a quality (*guṇa*) and thus has a different meaning.
Or rather, there is no redundancy because the connection with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is indistinguishable.

Commentary: Indeed, this is not a mere repetition of that same statement; rather, it is the very same matter, such as the Agnihotra and so forth, being repeated by many persons. And a single thing, when spoken of by many, does not become a tautology.
If it were so, then [the Veda] would exist as being spoken by many within a single Veda;
therefore, this is a collection of many rituals, and thus there is only one Veda and one ritual.
Or— according to the second explanation, the word "or" (*vā*) serves to exclude other possible solutions.
In that context, a repetition of a scriptural passage occurs for another purpose when either only that much is heard,
or when there exists another element to be enjoined within a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*).
But here, not even one of those [characteristics] exists; for we hear a repeated mention of the principal [element], which is endowed with both totality and singleness.
He considers this very lack of distinction in the connection with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
Furthermore, this is not a case of "repeated hearing" (punar-śruti). Why? Because "repeated hearing" is recognized only for those [teachings] bound within a single branch (śākhā);
however, for the followers of the Kāṭhaka and other schools, there is only a single hearing for each respective branch.

For it has been stated previously that, due to the optionality of studying different Vedic branches (*śākhā*), one who has heard the *Kāṭhaka* version of the Agnihotra never hears the *Taittirīyaka* version; or even if he does hear it, because he perceives it as belonging to a different branch, he assumes it is merely for the sake of the *Arthavāda* (explanatory passage) recited in the *Taittirīyaka*, and thus does not consider it a repetition of what was already heard. Likewise, others do not consider other versions to be repetitions. Consequently, all [practitioners] undertake the Agnihotra and other rites based on the lack of distinction in their connection to a single [universal] revelation (*śruti*).

Furthermore, there is no sequence of priority and posteriority therein by which it could be known that this is merely a restatement from another recensional branch (*śākhā*). As it has been said: "Because the branches exist simultaneously, there is no assumption of a restatement; for in that case, study does not proceed according to the order of a single branch."

Therefore, just as the ritual action belonging to a single recension (*śākhā*), even when heard again in other regions, among different persons, and so forth, does indeed become redundant because the object to be established (*pratipādya*) is not different, so it is also with respect to another recension.
Now, one might object: "If all persons are already established by means of even a single recension, then another recension is surely useless.
It is not useless.
For no one studies [the entire] scripture,

nor does the effort of one person become purposeful by means of teaching that which resides in another person. As for the intention that those who are indeed scholars study and understand it in that very same way, that is due to the fixed nature of the Veda and because its study is not subject to interruption.

This is untenable. Furthermore: "Unless one has abandoned the branch that has come down through tradition and is governed by its own designation, it is not proper to study another branch when the effort required is equal."

Therefore, even in the study of the branches belonging to others, the effort of these persons is directed toward this very [Veda] alone; thus, the study of the branch exactly as it exists is what is required.
Furthermore, the Veda does not deserve to be subjected to criticism regarding defects such as redundancy, because there is no composition of sentences [by a human author].
Or—herein, in this interval, the author of the Bhāṣya has lost the sūtra "vākyāsamavāyāt.
It should be explained as follows:
the statement of another recensional branch (śākhā) does not coexist within a single person.
"And because of the non-proximity of the object.
Commentary: And because of the non-proximity of the object, the designation "branch" (śāstra) will be appropriate.
For these [Vedic texts] are indeed like branches.
Just as there are branches of a tree, so too here the Vedas are like the tree and [the recensions] are its branches. What is their similarity to branches? It is their existence in various locations.

Furthermore, because the entire section on qualities (*guṇakāṇḍa*) is not present in each individual [branch], and due to this non-proximity of the object, it is logical that [the rite belongs] to the branch and so forth;
therefore, for this reason as well, the ritual action (*karman*) is one.
Or: "Of the single tree of the Veda, [this is established] from the basis of certain fruits of ritual action."
In this way, the branches will spread out like a single tree with many branches.

If there were a difference in ritual action (*karma*) for each branch, then—because they would diverge from the very beginning due to the absence of a single root, and because they would possess entirely different flowers and fruits of all ritual actions—they would indeed be distinct Vedas, like separate trees;
they would not be different branches of the same Veda.

The injunction regarding the single performance of the ritual (*ekakarmatva-vidhi*)—along with its procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—is established by some [author] who, having reflected that "this is such-and-such," has formulated an instruction in another recension (*śākhāntara-bheda-upadeśa*) that is consistent in form and other respects.
Alternatively, the Sūtra exists precisely for the purpose of avoiding redundancy (*paunaruktya-parihāra*).
In that case, there is indeed redundancy where the previously stated matter is present to that very same person.
However, in this case, there is no proximity to what is contained in another recensional branch (*śākhā*), and thus it is not redundant;

nor is it taught for the sake of a single person. The Commentary states: "And that *Agnihotra* which is in the *Kāṭhaka* [recension] is not prescribed for a person who belongs to both the *Kāṭhaka* and the *Maitraka* [recensions]."
For the Taittirīya as well, it is indeed a secondary derivative (taddhita),
because there is no mention of a specific person.
And whatever is prescribed for the Agnihotra, that applies to the Agnihotra in all its states.
And that which belongs to the *Kāṭhaka* Agnihotra is the same as that of the *Taittirīya*,
because there is no statement specifying a distinction. (Mīmāṃsākośa 488)

Therefore, it is said that a single ritual action is completed by all the recensional branches (*śākhā*). Alternatively—this is a concessive argument (*abhyupetyavāda*). Even if there were a difference in the rituals, those auxiliary elements (*śeṣa*) connected with the [principal] injunctions, being enjoined by the mere direction of the *agnihotra* and so forth, are understood to serve all purposes; thus, because they are grasped through their essential nature (*svabhāva*), no distinction based on a specific recensional branch can be obtained.

Furthermore, not even the authors of the Sūtras remained content with merely summarizing their own specific recension (*śākhā*), such that one could maintain a restriction of ritual acts (*karma*) to each individual recension.

Even the principal [texts], regarding the primary injunction for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), do not have the power [to restrict]; rather, through their designations (*samākhyā*), which enjoin matters directed toward the general purpose, they apply to a single person present in all recensions.
In that regard, it is stated that when a result is accomplished by any one [of several means], there is the consequence of the other [means] being rendered useless, as they share a single fruit.

Now, if their meaningfulness is due to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then, O friend, one must likewise postulate the non-confusion of those very other recensions (*śākhāntara*) which are established as being understood; thus they are not redundant.
And the conclusion is through conjunction (*saṃśreṣa*).
The Commentary: "In this regard, we too shall conclude," so say those who have reflected upon this.
Regarding the *anvāroha* offerings, [the objection is raised that] for the Maitrāyaṇīyas they are completed, whereas for us they are not completed in those [offerings].

If these [offerings] were indeed different for the Maitrāyaṇīyas alone, how could they say, "For us they are not completed"? Unity [of the ritual] is also logical, for they too possess those [offerings].
Or rather, there is a word-break as "asamāpti" (non-completion).
For if the *karmaitapakṣa* were the case, they would not say, "It is not completed for us," implying that it is completed for them exactly as much as it is completed for others.
Indeed, the *anvāroha* are the mantras for the daily gathering of grain.
Among these, for the Maitrāyaṇīyas, [the ritual] concludes; it is understood that even for us, the *iti-mithunādi* sacrifice is established as a complete rite (*karma*).
Although they are one and the same, there are subsequent statements regarding censure, incapacity, and completion.
The Commentary states: "For censure is not employed for the sake of censuring."

What, then, is the case? It is for the purpose of praising that which is other than the censured. In that context, a prohibition of the censured is not understood; rather, there is an injunction for the other.
Thus, regarding a single *agnihotra* sacrifice, two times are enjoined as alternatives.
Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Likewise, since those who are incapable are unable to collect even the subsidiary elements of a rite prescribed in a single Veda,
whereas those who are capable possess the power to collect the complete injunctions even from all the various recensions (śākhās), it is not contradictory for the ritual act to be one and the same.
Likewise, even with respect to a single action, the word "completion" (*samāpti*) is employed on the grounds that something has been finished;

for example, when the portion belonging to the *adhvaryu* priest is completed, it is said, "The Jyotiṣṭoma is completed. Or rather—since the two alternatives, namely performing at dawn and after sunrise, which serve the same purpose, are mutually exclusive and each is prescribed as an option, there will be an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the ritual act.
Even in your own position, this [distinction] regarding the fruit of the two actions is not distinct;
likewise, the capacity and incapacity of all persons are undetermined.
Furthermore, among all the branches [of the Veda], the injunctions of the specific branch do not differ significantly from those of other branches.
Some who seek the literal meaning describe it thus:

"Only those injunctions belonging to other recensions that are connected with the specific sentence are indeed mixed together; however, for those that belong to the context (prakaraṇa), there is a fixed restriction. Why? "Injunctions pertaining to a single ritual act are optional alternatives for persons."
That which is recited in proximity to it should be accepted as belonging to the context.

When there are alternative options among different recensional branches (*śākhā*), just as the primary act is enjoined for the seeker, its requirement of "how-to-being" (*kathaṃbhāva*) applies only to that specific branch and not to other branches. Consequently, the subsidiary elements (*guṇa*) belonging to another [branch] are not required by the "how-to-being," and since they are not brought forward by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), they do not become constituent parts (*aṅga*); thus, they cannot be admitted.
Therefore, because those connected by syntactical unity (*vākya*) are already present, there is no power to incorporate what is absent.
But this is not as it has been stated. For it is said: "If a ritual act established in one Vedic branch exists [as such], its same nature is obtained elsewhere too; by whom can that be prevented?"
Furthermore, in each and every section, it teaches the duties (dharma) of a person.
Nor is that [teaching] located in another Veda and thus a primary authority; the same should be understood regarding other recensions (śākhā).
These are understood as being based on the duties of ritual action (karma-dharma).

And that ritual action is indeed the same even in other recensional branches (*śākhā*); thus there is no distinction. Although these duties are distinguished from those included in their own specific context—because of the determination that they are grasped through the principle applicable to other branches, such as being contained within a mantra situated in a particular context—nevertheless, even across all branches, the additional injunctions cannot in any way be limited by capacity; therefore, there is no lack of capacity. Furthermore, since the conclusion [of the ritual] is justified in relation to what has been studied, it does not imply a difference [in the ritual act].
Expiation is determined by the occasion.

Commentary: As for what was stated—that the exclusion of expiations applies both to the case of one who has offered the oblation after sunrise and to the case of one who has not—this is not contradictory.
"It is not contradictory in the case of diversity"— this must be refuted. This is a sutra that has been reached through reasoning.
Or—the *anubhāṣaṇa-sūtra* or the *sāmānyaparihāra-sūtra*. Or, by virtue of the context, it is mandatory. The commentary: the word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the previous position.

This is not a fault. A fault occurs when one has commenced with the thought, "I shall offer after sunrise," but then acts otherwise; in that case, it will be the subject for expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Thus, even if there is a difference in the ritual action (*karmabheda*), there is no fault.
Or rather—since optional alternatives (*vaikalpika*) are accepted from the very beginning, the rule for expiation is appropriate when there is a transgression of the sequence thus undertaken.
Completion is understood through superimposition, as before.
The Commentary states: "In the case of that which possesses the prior [action], there is a statement of completion;
that which was begun is brought to its conclusion."
In that regard, "our [desire] is completed" means that which is sought by us is brought to completion;
it refers to the intention for the undertaking of what is beneficial (*śreyaḥ*).
Or—[it may mean] even in the case of oneness, solely by way of its being a completion.

Regarding the phrase "the expectation of a statement of completion": although there is multiplicity [of instances], the statement of completion therein supports only oneness, because it conforms to logical principle (*nyāya*).
That statement—
"This is contradictory regarding the ritual acts.

By that [statement], when it says "with the *sāṃnāyya*," the intention is as follows: in the Sarasvata Sattra, which has the chariot-horses of Mitra and Varuna as its model, just as there is an *atirātra* on the new moon day, so too should they undergo initiation.

Having concluded the Atirātra sacrifice on the new moon day, they should drive away the calves on that very same day. Having moved toward the east for a fortnight until the new moon, they should bring the cows back on the full moon day.
Having moved toward the east after the full moon sacrifice, they should bring the cows back on the new moon day.

By the statement, "Thus turning, they should proceed," since the performance of the *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* rites is prescribed for one side [of the moon] in each month, it must be stated that in both cases: the word *puroḍāśa* is intended to indicate the fortnight suitable for the essential performance of the *paurṇamāsī* rite, and the word *sāṃnāyya* is intended to indicate the fortnight suitable for the performance of the rite called *amāvāsyā*. This is how it is postulated.
Or rather—since, according to the principle of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), both sides [of the lunar fortnights] are preceded by the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it must indeed be stated as follows:

when the *puroḍāśa*-offerers [perform the sacrifice] on the full-moon day, then they "set out the fires" (*uṣanti*); when the *sāṃnāyya*-offerers [perform it] on the new-moon day, then they "drive away the calves" (*vatsānapākurvanti*).
For even due to a difference in time, there occurs a figurative designation of a difference in the performers; therefore, there is no fault.
"Regarding the sublation, there is a counter-exception.

Commentary: Now, as for what was stated—that the injunction regarding the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans] at the Upahavya sacrifice is already obtained by the original model (prakṛti), and that because they constitute a single action, a counter-exception is impossible, so that the second measurement would be purposeless—[this is the point to be addressed].
That must be avoided.
The sūtra ends with the word "ābhāṣa.
Or—"vā" means either "reiteration" (anubhāṣaṇa) or "general refutation" (sāmānyaparihāra).
Or rather, the repetition [of the mention] is for the purpose of specifying a quality (*guṇārtha*).
The Commentary states: "When it has the *rathaṃtara* as its *sāman*, then the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a horse; when it has the *bṛhat* as its *sāman*, then it is a chariot.
Or—alternatively—the repetition of the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* will serve to establish a restriction regarding their number.
And he also shows the evidence.

The Commentary says: If it were not the case that the same ritual action is present in all recensional branches (*śākhā*), how could it be fully enumerated in one branch while its subsidiary qualities (*guṇa*) are enjoined in another?
For example, among the Maitrāyaṇīyas, the *samit* and other such offerings are not fully enumerated.
Moreover, certain qualities are heard: "The seasons, indeed, are the progeny; having brought them together, they are to be offered.

Likewise, even for those followers of a recension (*śākhin*) who do not have the mantra for taking up the fire-wood (*araṇi*) prescribed as "Thou art a fire-wood (*kuṭū*)," it is observed that they say, "He places the fire-wood while reciting either 'Thou art a cock (*kukkuṭa*)' or 'Thou art a fire-wood (*kuṭū*)'.
Therefore, we conclude that it is a single ritual action (*karman*).

Or—by mentioning the oblation together with the *prayāja* offerings prescribed in another recension (*śākhā*), and by prescribing the mantra "kuṭū asi" for the taking of the food in that other recension, [the scripture] demonstrates that the knowledge derived from all recensions is authoritative.
Or rather, due to the connection with a specific sequence, the injunction would be restricted to one [recension].
The Bhāṣya states: For he who compiles the injunctions established in another recension necessarily adopts the sequence prescribed in his own recension.

Therefore, there is a difference of ritual action (*karmabheda*) among the various recensional branches (*śākhāntara*). Or rather—alternatively—the status of being an injunction (*vidhitva*) would be restricted to each individual branch. For if that were the case, the rites prescribed in one's own branch would not undergo differentiation from those of other branches.
And that [measure] does not attain any otherness;

however, because there is no conjunction of contradictory [factors], when there is a single action, due to the conjunction with that, there would be the cognition of all actions regarding the injunctions.
The Bhāṣya says: It is replied.
This is not a case of conflict between contradictory injunctions regarding actions prescribed in different recensions (śākhās) when they constitute a single ritual act;
for sequence is not enjoined by the direct statement (vākya),
as sequence is indeed weak.
The statement is authoritative,
and by that statement there is a synthesis of [details] belonging to other recensions (śākhās).
Therefore, it is established that a single ritual action is enjoined as being recognized by all recensions and recognized by all Brāhmaṇas.
Or rather—where these matters are not sublated by constraints of sequence, time, or measure, there is no annihilation of other recensions (*śākhāntaroccheda*).

This will be explained in the section on different recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*): that [annihilation] occurs only when, after the connection with the entire collection of subsidiaries prescribed in another recension—which possesses weaker authority—is established, the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) is directly perceived as having commenced. Thus it will be stated in the section on different recensions.

Regarding the two offerings prescribed in different recensions—the offering performed after sunrise and the one performed before sunrise, and the cake on eleven potsherds for Indra-Agni and the cake on twelve potsherds—the Vārtika in the *Śākhāntarādhikaraṇa* states that there is an equal option (*samavikalpa*) for all; however, this is the opinion of another (the opponent) and not his own view.

Bāla. p. 91: There is no fault in accepting a restrictive application (*viśeṣopasaṃhāra*) even when a general statement is clear, provided that [the general rule] would otherwise be rendered meaningless.
And in the present case, because the general statement belongs to another recension (*śākhā*), it is not purposeless.
Otherwise, what would be the recourse for explaining the injunctions for the *agnihotra* and other rites found in various recensions?
This has been explained in the section on different recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*) with the words, "Or rather, there is no repetition."

This has been explained and clarified by us in detail during the commentary on the group of five sūtras beginning with "ityādi" (on *Kuśumāñjali* 3.1.15–24). [Now follows] the determination of the essential conclusion regarding the section on different Vedic recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*).

In the *Vārtika* on the section concerning different recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*), it is stated that there is an equal option (*samavikalpa*) for all regarding the offerings made either before or after sunrise, as well as between the eleven-potherd and twelve-potherd cakes dedicated to Indra-Agni prescribed in different recensions (2.4.2). That, however, is the opinion of another [author] and not his own view; for in the section on Direct Assertion and Indicative Mark (*śrutiliṅgādhikaraṇa*), while defining the various types of sublation (*bādha*), the author of the *Vārtika* himself states that what is prescribed in another recension is sublated by what is prescribed in one's own recension.
And this is logical.

Because that which is prescribed in one's own recension (*svaśākhā*) and produced through the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) constitutes an auxiliary part of the ritual (*karmāṅgatva*), when such [auxiliaries] are available, [the requirement] is fulfilled by those belonging to other recensions.

Even for those [auxiliaries] belonging to a single ritual manual (*ekakalpika*) that are not prescribed in one's own recension but are not contradictory to it, their presence as similar qualities (*sādṛguṇyabhāva*) is implied.

However, for that which belongs to a single ritual manual and is both not prescribed in one's own recension and contradictory to it, even that which is produced by studying another recension is indeed implied for the sake of providing similar qualities to the ritual.

This statement from the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* is indeed rooted in this very principle: "Whatever is not prescribed in one's own *śākhā*, but is found in another and is non-contradictory, that should be performed by the learned, just as in the case of the *Itihāsas* and other such texts."
Thus [it is said].

According to the principle of the section on different Vedic branches (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*), even though there is no difference between the *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka* and other rites performed at home, it has been stated in the *Nyāyasubodhinī* that, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the fundamental basis is established through the systematic arrangement of the recitation of injunctions in those respective locations, it is necessary for these to be injunctions for human ends (*puruṣārtha-vidhi*). This is because they are obligatory (*nitya*).
Kau.

1.3.179: (Regarding the passage "abhiprāyeṣu meṣapattiyāṃ meṣapatye," there is no difference in the mantra due to a difference in Vedic recensional branches; for even when there is a discrepancy in a single part, their identity is understood through the principle of the section on different recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*), because they are mixed together at the beginning.
Bhāṭṭa. 1.3.12.

At the conclusion of the section concerning different recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*), by means of the sūtra: "Because of the connection with sequence, there is a distinctness of injunctions established in one [text]" (2.4.2.32), the non-inclusion of ritual elements belonging to other recensions is established due to the contradiction regarding sequence, time, and measure. Subsequently, by the sūtra: "Because of the connection with contradictory matters, there is unity of the substrate; because of that connection, there is the cognition of all rituals as being enjoined" (the Bhāṣya reading is: "Because of the connection with contradictory [matters], there would be unity; because of that connection, there would be the cognition of all rituals as being enjoined"), it will be stated that the ritual elements override sequence and the like.
Su. Pṛ. 104.

A rule serving as an alternative method for the performance of rites, based on the synthesis of the omniscient [Vedic corpus] established in the section concerning other Vedic branches (Śākhāntarādhikaraṇa): "Whether much or little is prescribed according to one's own Gṛhya-sūtra, when that much of the meaning of the Śākhā has been performed by someone, everything [of that Śākhā] is considered performed."
Thus [it is said].

Here, because the *Gṛhyasūtra* is qualified by its own specific term (*svaśabda*), there is the understanding of a rule regarding the study of a single *Gṛhyasūtra* transmitted through tradition (Kau.

The study of multiple Vedic branches (*śākhā*) is not enjoined for a single person. What is the reason? "In the undertaking of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*), only a single branch is indeed grasped. Just as a universal form (*ākṛti*) inheres in each individual instance, so too does the nature of being one's own Veda (*svādhyāyatva*) reside in each individual branch.

Since the injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied" is employed here with reference to the comprehension of ritual action (*karman*), the branch to be studied must be understood as having a singular number intended (*vivakṣita*).
But in that case, would it not follow that the study of another Veda is also precluded?
No, because there is a counter-exception by another statement:
"By this fourfold knowledge."
Likewise, there is the Mānava text: "Having studied the Vedas, or having become a knower of the Vedas.
Because of this expectancy, it is understood that there is a combination (samuccaya) based on the fact that the various Vedas do not perform an identical function.
And precisely because of this expectancy, there is no mention of a combination of other [mantras] contained within a single recensional branch (śākhā).
Or rather: "Indeed, no one studies two treatises simultaneously, except for their own [tradition], which is bound by its own specific designation. (Vārttika 2.4.12.9)
It is not fitting to study one Vedic branch after another when the effort required is the same.
Thus, it is precisely the study of one's own branch as it exists [that is required].
(On this point, there is a Sūtra: "Because of the non-coexistence of sentences. A sentence from another branch does not coexist within a single person.
The destruction of other Vedic branches:
"And the destruction of other Vedic branches never occurs,
because [the Vedas] are eternally fixed as previously stated, nor do these [Smṛtis] have a perceptible basis."
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 1.3.2.4, page 195:
"The principle of other recensions (śākhāntaranyāya): the throwing of the branch is authoritative by way of remainder, because it is not a restatement (anuvāda) in the ritual manuals (kalpa)."
And the principle of different recensions (*śākhāntara-nyāya*) does not apply here, because of the fact that the students are equal.

Or rather, according to the principle of other Vedic branches (*śākhāntara-nyāya*) [as discussed at *Tantravārttika* 2.4.2.8–33, page 241], the single Viśvajit sacrifice is enjoined by two distinct sets of sentences; thus, there is no difference between this [Sābhyutthāna-Viśvajit] and the [ordinary] Guṇaviśvajit.
(*Bhāṭṭadīpikā* 6.1.7).

By the principle of different Vedic branches (*śākhāntara-nyāya*), since the non-difference of the *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka* and other rites is understood, they are recognized as being governed by all ritual injunctions.
(Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 1.3.17–16).

Likewise, because the non-difference of study (*adhyayana*) and the initiatory rites (*upanayana*, etc. is understood through the very same principle of different Vedic branches, it is established that the knowledge thereof is common to all [recensions].

1|3|17|16. Since it will be stated in the twelfth [book] that the rites such as initiation (*upanayana*) and the knowledge thereof serve no purpose in the mere form of the Vedic branch (*śākhā*), but rather find their utility in the act of study itself—whereby that [injunction of study] is understood to be one and the same across different branches, and thus there is no apprehension of difference—and since there is an absence of indicators such as the *vāgṇeṣṭhī* and names, the logic applicable to other branches does not apply to the Maitrāyaṇīya branch.
(Bhāṭṭa.)
