If the proponent (siddhāntin) were to say: "Having made the *veda*, one makes the *vedi*"; thus, when there is a conflict between the scriptural injunctions of the learned regarding ritual items such as the making of the *veda* and *vedi*, and a Smṛti statement such as "Upon hearing [a sound], one should sip water," even the Smṛti statement is indeed an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is not contradictory; for after the making of the *veda*, if a cause for sipping water such as hearing a sound should occasionally occur, that which is prescribed by Smṛti—namely, the sipping of water—must certainly be performed. To this, [the opponent] replies:
No, because the extent of the scripture is limited (*śāstraparimāṇatvāt*).

When the opponent asserts that "once the Vedic injunction has arisen during the performance of the Veda-recitation, the sipping of water (ācamana) prescribed by Smṛti must be performed because Smṛti is an authoritative source," the proponent replies:
"A Smṛti-ordained act should not be performed in the midst of a Vedic act,
because the constituent elements prescribed by Śruti are limited in scope by the scripture."

By means of the scripture—namely, by the scriptural injunction "Having made the *veda*, one makes the *vedi*," and other such texts that convey the sequence—it is understood that there is a specific measure consisting of the delimitation of time and so forth, characterized by the absence of interruption and the like. Thus, because it would result in the sublation of the sequence established by direct revelation (*śruti*), a Smṛti statement such as "One should sip water when the [name] is heard" is not authoritative.
It is measured—that is, understood—by means of the scripture.

Thus is the measure of the scripture (*śāstra*). [The term *śāstraparimāṇa*] is derived from the sense of "action" (*karman*). Alternatively, the meaning of the compound is: because the sequences, times, and measures that contradict the Smṛti rules for sipping water (*ācamana*) and so forth constitute the measure of the scripture, as they are understood through direct revelation (*śruti*).

The meaning is that the specific number (*parimāṇa*), which is a particular count, belongs to that collection of items to be performed (*anuṣṭheya-padārtha*) as understood from the scripture (*śāstra*) and the injunction regarding performance (*prayoga-vidhi*). This is because the injunction regarding performance has restricted this ritual action by stating, "In this rite, so many items are to be performed. Therefore, the intent is that if one were to perform an additional item prescribed by the *Smṛti* in the midst of these, it would result in a contradiction with the scripture.
Alternatively: "Or rather, when no specific cause [for deviation] is perceived, those things employed [by the scripture] should be recognized [as binding]."

Alternatively, the sūtra may simply be: "Or rather, those [practices] employed when no [Vedic] cause is perceived should be recognized [as authoritative]. Or, according to the statement of the Vārttika, the sūtra may be: "Or rather, those [practices] employed when no cause is perceived should be recognized, because no fault is observed in them. This is the sūtra of the established conclusion (siddhānta) regarding the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) that such practices of the learned (śiṣṭācāra)—such as "one must perform [acts] having sipped water" or "one must perform [acts] wearing the sacred thread"—should not be performed as dharma. The word "or rather" (apivā) serves to set aside the prima facie view.
They are not [actions] that ought not to be performed; rather, they are indeed to be performed.

When there is no apprehension of a cause—that is, when there is a non-apprehension, an absence of perception, or an absence of knowledge of any visible means of proof for their being "not to be done"—those actions which are employed and practiced by the learned (*śiṣṭas*) should be understood and known as having the very nature of *dharma*.
This is because no contradiction with the Veda is observed in them.
The meaning is that, provided there is no conflict with the Vedas, the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is also a source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And the commentators on the Vārttika have already stated the meaning of the Sūtra as follows:
"Those actions which have visible causes and are performed by the virtuous..."
"Those [practices] which are performed by the learned (śiṣṭas) should be understood as having the nature of dharma. Whatever practices are performed by the learned as having the nature of dharma,
their status as dharma is accepted because of the commonality of the agent with those who follow the Veda."

Thus, when there is no apprehension— that is, no observation— of a cause of contradiction, namely the subversion of performance (*anuṣṭhānavādha*), then acts such as sipping water (*ācamana*) employed by the learned would be understood as not being in conflict with the Vedic sequence and so forth.
Consequently, since the sequence, time, and measure [of the rites] proceed from the wheel of time that governs the performance of all Vedic and Smārta elements, there is no contradiction.

And because there is no contradiction, the traditional rule (*smṛti*) regarding rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) and so forth when prompted by causes such as hearing [the sound of a Veda-recitation] during the midst of a ritual action is authoritative; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). As stated in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra* (1.3.13): "When a weak means of knowledge has a powerful support... [and in the commentary: "...[then that weak means is not sublated]. The meaning is as follows: When one is engaged in a ritual action, if the sound of a Vedic recitation or the like is heard, the traditional rule (*smṛti*) which prescribes the performance of *ācamana* and other purificatory acts is authoritative. This is because it does not contradict the direct Vedic injunction (*śruti*) governing the ritual; rather, it serves as a supportive factor for its proper execution. Therefore, the traditional rule is established as valid. Furthermore, the principle is illustrated by the following: "When a weak means of knowledge has a powerful support... [and so on]. This indicates that even a weaker authority is not set aside when it is backed by a stronger foundation. In this case, the traditional rule is supported by the very purpose of the ritual, ensuring its flawless completion; thus, it remains uncontradicted and is accepted as authoritative. (Note: The phrase *ke. ' śiṣṭākope* appears to be a fragmentary reference to the *Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra* 1.3.4, *śiṣṭākope*, which deals with the non-sublation of traditional rules by direct Vedic statements.)
Even then, there is the state of being contrary [to Smṛti], as stated under the rule "where there is no contradiction by the learned" (Vārttika 1.3.14, p.
the section concerning non-contradiction by the learned (*śiṣṭākopādhikaraṇa*).
The section concerning non-contradiction with the learned (Śiṣṭākopādhikaraṇa). The principle of the relative strength of the objects of knowledge (prameyabalavattva-nyāya).
Regarding what has been prescribed here at the outset, the Smṛti is the authority.
If it is argued that this is not contradicted because it does not conflict with the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭa), the Commentary states:

"Examples characterized by such [injunctions] as 'it must be performed by one who has sipped water,' 'it must be performed while wearing the sacrificial thread,' and 'it must be performed with the right hand in front' [are to be cited]."

If you consider whether these [Smṛtis] are not to be performed because they contradict the Śruti, or whether they are to be performed despite being untrustworthy, [the answer is]: since nothing Vedic is subverted by their performance, they are therefore non-contradictory. Or rather—thus has been determined the authoritative and non-authoritative status of Smṛtis concerning human goals, both in cases of non-contradiction and contradiction with the Śiṣṭas (the cultured).

At present, however, only the question of whether there is a contradiction or no contradiction between the rules concerning the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), sipping water (*ācamana*), and using the right hand (*dakṣiṇahasta*)—which are prescribed for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*)—and the Smṛti rules that apply to many Vedic injunctions, is being investigated. Once that determination is made, the establishment of the authority or lack of authority of the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*) will follow.
But how can they be considered contradictory, or how can they be considered non-contradictory?
It is accepted [as a contradiction] on account of being contrary to the meaning of the Śruti, or by its absence.

If the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) and other such items, when being introduced as part of the performance, are neither included nor even rejected by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) and the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance), then there is a contradiction.

However, if—because they are consistent—they are introduced as part of the performance through their connection with the eternal Smṛti inferred from the context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, just like those items explicitly mentioned in the texts, and nothing previously accepted is thereby impaired, then they are not contradictory.
There is, however, another view:
even when there is a contradiction, doubt arises because of the lack of non-contradiction regarding the relative strength of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For it is said: "When there is a conflict between *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, the relative strength [of each] is indeed already known."

And when there is a conflict between a property (*dharma*) and its substratum (*dharmī*), the substrata are more powerful. For [the author] will state: "In a conflict between the quality of a subordinate element and [another], the former prevails because it exists for the sake of that" (JS 1.3.12). Nor is any sublation of a scriptural (*śrauta*) item suspected here on the basis of a Smṛti rule; rather, sequence, time, and measure are determined as properties belonging to all the items collectively.

In this regard, if the strength of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is more powerful, then because they are to be known through a stronger Vedic revelation (*śruti*), acts such as sipping water (*ācamana*) would be set aside by the sequence and so forth, even though [the latter] are weak in their own nature. However, if the strength of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is more powerful, then acts such as sipping water are stronger than the sequence and so forth—which are properties of the ritual acts—by virtue of being the primary acts themselves. Thus, even though the means of knowledge called "Smṛti" is weak, it will set aside only the sequence and so forth, which are weak in their own form despite having a strong basis.
What is correct? That there is no contradiction, for how could there be a contradiction even with a Smṛti that has a purpose?

For indeed, nothing heard regarding that purposeful action is lost. Just as even by the Vedas and other means of knowledge—though they possess infinite power and are themselves limitless—all remaining elements that are cognized are grasped through their status as auxiliaries to the primary rite (*śeṣikārtha*), together with the manner of performance (*itthambhāva*), because they are not explicitly stated in the direct revelation (*śruti*) and so forth;
in the same way, they are offered by Smṛti, by commendatory passages (*saṃstuti*), and by the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).
The apūrva is grasped through the entities of the meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) by means of the instruments of accomplishment (sādhana).
How so? Because the apūrva, which is dependent on the "how" (katham-bhāva), has its dimensions unknown; therefore, whatever is obtained by any means whatsoever becomes known [as part of it].
Consequently, even acts such as sipping water (ācamana) are included within the knowledge of the performance of the sacrifice.
Not so, because of the fixed extent of the scripture.
The Commentary states: This is not so;
for they would contradict the sequence determined by the scripture.

How so? Because of the scriptural injunction, "Having prepared the *veda*, one should prepare the *vedi*," which prescribes the performance of the *vedi* after the *veda*—that is, between these two acts of the person following the Veda.
Furthermore, when ritual items are being performed with only the right hand, the primary rite might occasionally be delayed beyond its proper time.
By performing with both hands, however, one will ensure that the time for the primary rite is maintained.
Or—this being introduced—it is stated:

"Because the scripture is the authority, there can be no category of meaning exceeding [the six]; for who is able to transgress the measure established by the scripture? (Śāstra-parimāṇatvāt). This means: because those [categories] have the scripture as their measure; indeed, who is capable of overstepping the measure prescribed by the scripture?
For in the scripture, the measure of categories is established as threefold;
here, that form consisting of the sequence of creation and so forth is sublated.
By two means—the fivefold methods beginning with direct revelation (śruti)—the determination of time and sequence is established.
For ritual elements (padārthas) entering [the procedure] would indeed cause obstruction, whether they be based on Smṛti or worldly custom.
Indeed, it has been established by the injunction of performance (prayogavacana) that "all ritual elements must not be separated from the time of the principal rite.

In that context, there would be the consequence of failure due to the specific performance of elements based on Smṛti, traditional verses, and custom, as well as due to the delay inherent in performance dependent on the right hand, and because of the excessive exertion required for the principal rite.
Furthermore, the entire time for the performance would have to exceed the prescribed periods such as the morning and midday.

Moreover, the sequence—which is understood through the means of order such as direct statement (*śruti*), meaning (*artha*), textual recitation (*pāṭha*), position (*sthāna*), primary function (*mukhya*), and actual practice (*pravṛtti*)—is established upon Vedic matters and its extent is determined by the authoritative means of knowledge; thus, it would have to be set aside on account of the connection with other causes such as direct statement.
This same logic should be applied even to the effort involved in the repeated making of the sacred thread (*upavīta*).
"For when that internal ritual element which is based on Smṛti is performed at that time,
there is the section concerning the non-contradiction of the learned (śiṣṭākopādhikaraṇa)."
The section concerning the non-conflict with the learned (Śiṣṭākopādhikaraṇa):
Indeed, the authority for the sequence is not understood through direct statement (śruti) and so forth;
nor can any other means of proof be conceived for a sequence of the dimensions already described.

Likewise, the magnitude of the constituent parts (padārtha) as understood through the Veda and other means must necessarily be determined by those such as Aśvalāyana for the sake of constructing the entire ritual without forgetting any part.

Consequently, when performing the ritual acts according to memory after they have been initially conceptualized, there arises the possibility of a deficiency because the previously determined sequence is only partially fulfilled; thus, due to the suspicion of an unaccomplished defect (*vaiguṇya*), there would be no receptacle for the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) caused by the purpose of having performed the rite correctly, leading to the undesirable consequence of a diminished fruit due to the absence of *apūrva*.
"In this way, everything belonging to the group of two [the Sāṃkhya and Yoga] beginning with Sārthadāsa is possessed of excellence."
Due to the inability to tolerate deficiency, [Smṛti] necessarily sublates what is contradictory.

Because the instruction of the limited Śruti and so forth has no further expectancy for a remainder, and because it is not of unlimited extent, there is no perception of anything beyond that. And when the objects have been understood in their entirety, even by the thousands... [it is] in every respect.
In logic, contradiction is the cause for two things that produce the same effect to be obtained simultaneously;
but here, both of these conditions are met, and therefore there is an extreme contradiction.
For it is held that the attainment of all the stages of the Kalās occurs at the very end;
even an object of the most minute measure is not heard [perceived] beforehand.
(Regarding the refutation of the contradiction concerning sequence: For when objects have already been apprehended, sequence is required subsequently;
since it is established [only] after they have been apprehended, by whom could it be characterized as having five or more forms?
(Thus, he himself resolves the apparent contradiction: "But even the [fixed] size is for the sake of the object, in order to ensure that it is not forgotten."
It is deliberated upon by the wise themselves; that is accepted by those learned in the Smṛtis.
The number of words is not determined by any means of valid cognition (*māna*).

In that regard, if there were no other causes for the recollection of all the constituent parts of the words, then this [number] might also be established as a single cause, and thus even the measure (*parimāṇa*) would be fixed.

However, even in that state, just as the mere measure of purity is not completed but rather the designation (*samākhyā*) is invoked—which depends upon the maintenance of the measure pertaining to those parts whose attainment has not yet occurred—so too will the measure according to the Smṛtis and traditional practice (*ācāra*) be adopted; thus, there is no fault.
(The section concerning the non-contradiction of the learned; the section on the non-contradiction of the learned.)
"Tara" refers to the transgression of dharma resulting from engaging in sexual intercourse with those who are forbidden.
Regarding Indra as well, there was a transgression of dharma because he, while occupying that very position, committed adultery with another's wife; and the same applies to Nahuṣa.
Likewise, there was the rash act of suicide by entering the water due to grief for his son committed by Vasiṣṭha;
and the officiating at a sacrifice for a Cāṇḍāla performed by Viśvāmitra. The application [of these cases] is like that of Vasiṣṭha and like that of Puruṣavasu.

There is the instance of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, who had taken a vow of lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*), engaging in the procreation of offspring through the wives of Vicitravīrya; and Bhīṣma’s remaining outside the duties of all the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*) while being childless, yet performing the ritual union during the fertile period (*ṛtu-prayoga*) like Rāma;
likewise, the case of the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and so forth—these are instances of actions not sanctioned by those [scriptures] excluding the *Pāṇḍu* [lineage].
Likewise, there is the marriage of Yudhiṣṭhira’s younger brother to his elder brother’s wife; the acquisition of wealth for the sake of dharma and artha by means of the preceptor and others;

the marriage of Vāsudeva and Arjuna to Subhadrā, the daughter of their maternal uncle, despite it being forbidden; the practice of drinking liquor by both [Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa] under the pretext of "the two of us are horses and kine";
and even Acyuta’s drinking of liquor along with the inhabitants of Ahicchatra and Mathurā.
From the hermitage of Kairavya, [the following practices arose]: for those of the North, the paths of lending, receiving, selling, and trading on interest, as well as eating together with outcasts;
for those of the South, the giving away of a maternal uncle’s daughter in marriage, the eating from the same wooden board (*āsandī*), and so forth;

and for both groups, the eating of the remnants of friends and kinsmen, the mutual touching of betel, food, and water by all castes, the wearing of garments grown upon darbha grass that have been washed only once and are not purified by rinsing after use, and the avoidance of the excessive consumption of food and drink beyond what is necessary for the householder's duties.

However, since there are infinite variations in the transgressions of subtle dharmas pertaining to each individual, caste, and family, and since instances of disagreement regarding the causes for such transgressions generally occur everywhere, it is impossible to establish a fixed rule that such [transgressions] constitute a mixture of good conduct and dharma.

Furthermore, as for the question, "Who are the cultured (śiṣṭas) who possess good conduct, and who are those whose actions constitute good conduct?", no definitive conclusion can be reached because their determination is mutually dependent upon one another.
Now, [it may be argued]: "The authority of the conduct of the virtuous (sadācāra) has indeed been recorded by Manu and others;

likewise, self-satisfaction (ātmatuṣṭi) has been recorded by others. But that [self-satisfaction] is unstable, for self-satisfaction arises according to one's habitual practice, due to the diversity of internal dispositions, regarding the performance of good or evil actions."
For instance, someone may feel satisfaction even with such an action, just as the Śākya felt satisfaction in his refutation of the Brāhmaṇas by means of fallacious arguments. Likewise:
"Just as the twice-born feel satisfied when there is a connection with the slaughter of animals and the like."
For it is from those very sacrifices that the Śākyas, being oppressed, revolt.
Likewise, some twice-born ones are satisfied even by eating the food of a Śūdra,
while a Southerner is satisfied upon obtaining the daughter of his maternal uncle.
But others do not perform that [action] with a mind full of hypocrisy.
Consequently, because of this lack of consistency, how else could the clear statement "but one's own satisfaction alone" be interpreted?
Likewise, so too is the statement "and the conduct of the virtuous."
"Even those authors of Smṛtis, who claim that the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is authoritative when its root is unknown to themselves, do not shine as superior [authorities].
For it is the conduct of the learned that must be followed by the authors of Smṛtis, because they themselves are learned."
For otherwise, those who act independently without regard for them would be considered corrupt, not cultured. Furthermore, no basis in Śruti for these [usages] is observed;
if there were such a basis, even if it were remote, it would certainly be remembered as a Smṛti.
"Therefore, there is no disregard for the practices of the learned (śiṣṭas) when it comes to uprooting [the Veda].
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"Or rather, when the cause is not perceived, those [practices] should be understood as being prompted by [an unseen purpose]."
Those actions which are performed by the virtuous for visible purposes and so forth, and which are recognized here as being in accordance with dharma— those too [are included],
as well as those which are employed for the maintenance of the body or for the sake of pleasure.
Alternatively, it may be that those cultured persons (*śiṣṭas*) have no cognition of dharma;
rather, whatever certain things are accepted as having the nature of dharma by the cultured persons who follow the Vedas,
their status as dharma is asserted on the basis of the commonality of the agents [with those of the Vedic tradition].
Giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, the Mātṛyajña and other rites,
and the great festival of the banner of Śakra for the assembly of deities.
(Mahaḥ means a festival.)

And for all unmarried girls, there are fasts on the fourth lunar day; the offering of lamps on the first day [of the fortnight], as well as sweetmeats, cakes, and milk-rice. (The offering of lamps occurs on the first day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika.)

The giving and eating of *modaka* and other such items; the period beginning from the full moon of the month of Māgha, the first day (*pratipad*) of Phālguna, and the Spring Festival (*vasantotsava*), during which there is a rule against eating uncooked food;
the ritual duties to be performed on the seventh day and the full moon of Māgha;
and the Spring Festival observed on the first day following the full moon of Phālguna—regarding these, there is no authority for the performance of such rules other than the scriptures.

The authors of the *Smṛtis* also generally accept the authority of practices (*ācāra*) that are not contradicted by the Veda, stating: "The conduct of the virtuous," and "Local and family customs are authoritative when they are not opposed [to the Veda].
Likewise, there is the section on non-study periods (*anadhyāya*), such as "after eating" or "while facing the north," which establishes the authority of regions, cities, and festivals.

Furthermore, in the Veda itself, within the *Mahāvrata* ritual, following the statement "The Hotṛ priest recites the *preṅkhaṇa*," it is heard in the remainder of the passage: "When indeed the people... [and so forth].
The section concerning the non-conflict with the learned (Śiṣṭākopādhikaraṇa). In the passage, "They enter the swing; then they mount it," the well-known usage of the word *mahaḥ* has been stated.

As for what was stated—that "because dharma and adharma are objects of knowledge defined by limited treatises, and because such [limitation] is impossible here"—that must be rejected in the same manner as the inference regarding the Vedic basis [was previously refuted] (according to the principle in *Vākyapadīya*, p. 163: "due to an erroneous experience").
Furthermore, a tradition (*smṛti*) is not without a foundation, since even extensive discourses are concluded merely by reciting a single chapter, let alone a concise statement.
Moreover, it is possible to infer the words of the Veda in accordance with tradition (*smṛti*).

For instance: "The scripture is purposeful insofar as it makes known the connection with results—which was previously unestablished—for those virtuous acts being performed by the learned, just like the *godohana* vessel and other such things."
"For that [scripture] is not authoritative in such a manner; its very nature must also be understood from that [scripture] alone.
For when an object of knowledge possesses many aspects, it is apprehended by some particular means of valid cognition according to one or another of those aspects."

In that regard, even though the form of conduct is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), its connection with a specific result is understood through scripture (*śāstra*), just as in the case of curd or a cow-milking vessel (*godohana*).

Even in the case of sacrifices and the like, scripture is not required for the knowledge of their essential nature (*svarūpa*); rather, it is required solely because the connection with a result is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). Therefore, although scripture proceeds by means of another indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), the learned (*śiṣṭas*) do not act [merely on that basis]; for there is no separation between the conduct of the learned and scripture at any time, and thus certain acts are restricted as means to attaining heaven and other ends precisely through such conduct.

And since these [people] are employed by the learned inhabitants of Āryāvarta, this very fact serves as an indicator that can be inferred here from the Veda as well—through such passages as "the disappearance of the Sarasvatī" (*sarasvatī-vinaśana*) and "the source of the Sarasvatī" (*sārasvata-prasavaṇa*).
(The "disappearance of the Sarasvatī" refers to its vanishing;
this is an indicator for the region of the Sarasvatī and the Sārasvata country.)

"Now, if it is argued that their status as *śiṣṭas* (the cultured/authoritative) is understood from their acting according to the meaning of the scriptures, and that the teaching of the scriptures is established by their status as *śiṣṭas*, then there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatā*).
This is not so; for their status as *śiṣṭas* is not considered to be caused by their good conduct."
Because they act according to what is directly enjoined, their word constitutes *śiṣṭatva* (the state of being an authoritative person).

For those who perform the duties prescribed by the direct Veda obtain the designation of *śiṣṭa*; likewise, whatever else they do—whether it has been obtained through tradition or not—if they do it with the intention that it is dharma, that too is indeed dharma, just like [the pursuit of] heaven.
As it is said: "The learned one who desires to hear and the Vedic scholar who recites..."
"Furthermore, it is observed that in the Veda itself, regarding killing, eating, and so forth [there is no fixed order].
Therefore, just as there is no fixed sequence between day and night, because [the Veda] is beginningless, there is no contingency of depending on a different basis for the purpose of the Veda.
Having perceived Vedic statements regarding Smṛti and traditional practice, they proceeded solely for the sake of granting permission; thus, there is no fault."

"As for the argument that, having observed other causes [for human activity], one rejects the Veda as the source [of Dharma], even when a visible Vedic source is present— such as the case of bricks seen being used for a desired purpose—
even though many injunctions in the Veda itself are indeed based on visible purposes, their status as being rooted in the Veda does not thereby cease to exist."

However, regarding those activities which are common to barbarians and others—namely, constant and fixed secondary actions such as agriculture, service, and trade for the sake of acquiring wealth; and well-known practices such as fine food and drink, soft beds, pleasant dwellings, domestic music, dance, song, perfumes, flowers, and so forth—in these there is no suspicion whatsoever that they constitute *dharma*.
Thus, by analogy with these, the exclusion of other [practices] is established.
Since only some [of these] are accepted as being *dharma*, the essence of *dharma* does not apply to all of them indiscriminately.

However, "whatever [actions] such as the worship of gods and Brahmins are performed by them, even those do not constitute dharma; for that is considered the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭa), which is like a mere cloud [of appearance]. For in the world, a certain conduct is distinguished by the quality of being 'learned'."
But some [dharma] is common even to all living beings; therein,
that which is practiced by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) in the form of an action—
that alone is dharma, and not anything else merely because it is done by all living beings.

By this, it is established that for those whose selves are refined by the cognition of the infinite dharmas of the Veda, "self-satisfaction" (*ātmatuṣṭi*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the purification of dharma. Likewise, it is stated that for those who possess the impressions (*saṃskāra*) resulting from long-term study and the observation of the meaning of the Vedas, and whose intuitive flash (*pratibhāna*) follows the path prescribed by the Veda, such intuition cannot arise without [the authority of] the *Ṛṣis*: "Whatever a reciter of the Veda utters without remembering [its source], that is considered the word of an *Ṛṣi*."

Thus, it is precisely because it is produced by Vedic impressions (*vaidikavāsanā*) that it becomes such. For instance: "Just as salt in water, or gold on Mount Meru, or a jewel on the ground of Ujjvalakaru, becomes identical with that [in which it is placed], so too should the satisfaction of the knower (*veditṛ*) arise."
"Thus, that which has emerged from the words of the wise is established in form as described by poets;
for the inclinations of the inner hearts of the virtuous are the authority regarding matters that are subjects of doubt.
(By Kālidāsa in the *Śakuntalā*).

Indeed, because of the long-term practice of dharma, it is not possible for the self to act otherwise than through the traditional succession of performing dharma; thus, it is authorized as dharma. Alternatively, "The status of being dharma arises simply from the word of the learned (śiṣṭa).
Therefore, that same [status] applies to the conduct of those who are meritorious and wealthy."
Or, for example, when a boon is granted or when a deity is propitiated,
if a person is addressed with the words, "If you are such-and-such, then this mantra is yours," that person remembers that mantra during the removal of poison and other such occasions.
Or as it is said in the doctrine of snake-charmers: "Whatever medicinal herb a mongoose seizes with its teeth, they call that [herb] the remover of all poison."

Or just as when someone who has performed meritorious deeds dwells upon the earth, that very ground becomes an object of service because it is purified by contact with him, serving as a cause for merit.
Having ascertained that conduct such as the view of a self is righteous for those whose nature consists of dharma,
because it is declared in the Vedas, he obtained a son endowed with dharma.
"Either because of a commonality of scriptural reference (*śruti-sāmānya*), or because of the [mention of] a measure (*mātra*), there will be no fault here;
or because of the exclusion of humans, or by virtue of its brilliance, power, and strength;
or it will be accepted as a property (*dharma*) of that subject in such a way that it is not contradictory."
Prajāpati is so called because he holds the office of protecting his subjects, as it were, from the moment of their birth.

He approached the Dawn at the time of her becoming a *caṇḍālī*; she arises immediately upon his arrival, and thus she is designated as his daughter. Furthermore, due to the casting of the seed by him, whose rays are ruddy, there is a figurative application of the union of man and woman.

Thus, although the Sun possesses all splendor and cannot be designated as Indra by reason of the Supreme Lord, he alone is called "the paramour of Ahalyā" because, by dissolving during the day, he is the cause of the fever consisting of decay for that which is denoted by the term "night" (rātri) and "day" (ahaḥ)—as in the passage beginning "he decays, he does not eat," and so forth—and not because of adultery with another's wife.
For by this [etymology], his own wicked conduct is not established merely through the subsequent attainment of his own essence after the interval caused by another's wife.
And the Śākya [the Buddha] is indeed well-known for having attained the power of a dwelling that destroys [afflictions], produced by a preeminent merit born of devotion to his wife.
As for the conduct of Vasiṣṭha, which was characterized by the delusion of grief for his son—
that too cannot be doubted as being Dharma, because it had another cause.
For that conduct which is performed with the intention of merit proceeds from dharma and so forth;
however, that which is perceived as having its cause in desire, anger, greed, delusion, and the like, will be governed by injunctions and prohibitions according to their nature.

Therefore, even in the case of Viśvāmitra, those unprecedented acts [performed] at the beginning through the power of austerity—such as the conduct of Rudra—are [neutralized] by the maxim "everything is wholesome for one who possesses strength," provided he brings them to exhaustion after performing great austerities.
Or, for one who performs purification through penances (*prāyaścitta*) at a later time, even a sin may be digested;
however, for those of weak austerity, consuming large *vaṭaka* cakes and the like would be like eating ore from a mountain, leading only to self-destruction.

Even in the case of Dvaipāyana, the procreation of a son upon the wife of his maternal uncle’s brother (*mātṛsaṃbandha-bhrātṛ-jāyā*)—that is, upon the wife of Vicitravīrya, who was his brother through his mother—was not excessively difficult due to the power of the asceticism he performed both before and after the act, having transgressed under the command of his guru and being urged by the god Agni.
Anyone else who possessed such power from asceticism could certainly have done so;

however, in the cases of Rāma and Bhīṣma, it was due to the influence of affection and filial devotion respectively. Thus, the accomplishment of the sacrifice occurred for these two—Vidhi and Dharmarāja—who were directly present as the fathers, even though they had not been physically brought there, and because they were free from sin. Furthermore, the fashioning of a golden Sītā was intended to dispel any suspicion of cruelty toward Sītā, which might arise from the fear of public scandal regarding her abandonment.
And Bhīṣma said: "Among brothers born of one father from the same womb, one may have a son;
Manu declared that all [the brothers] become possessed of sons through that very son."

Thus, although not explicitly stated, it is understood that his connection with a wife was solely for the purpose of sacrifice, as he had already obtained sons born from the field (kṣetraja) through various wives. Furthermore,
it is implied that "he who did not offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) into the hand of his father, even though [the recipient] was known."
Since they are taught in sequence according to the meaning of the scriptures, how can they be called "identical"?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, too, by the grace of Vyāsa, saw [his son] at the time of conception just as he had seen the description of the marvel;
for it is heard that great sages are capable of both cursing and bestowing grace.

Likewise, from his words it is understood that Agha was born; and since it is so stated regarding the performance of the sacrifice, it is easily known through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) that he saw him at the proper time.

Since the root *yaj*— in the sense of "worshiping the gods, forming an alliance, and giving"— must here mean "giving," and since gifts, austerities, and sacred recitations are heard in scripture to be equal to the fruits of sacrifices (*kratu*), the term for sacrifice is used metaphorically for those acts. Furthermore, that contradiction regarding the Pandavas having a single wife—
which was raised— was also resolved and established by Dvaipāyana himself.
For Kṛṣṇā herself arose from the middle of the sacrificial altar while still in her youth;
she is Śrī, and Śrī, being enjoyed by many, is not defiled.

And for this very reason it has been said: "This was the supreme wonder there: that the world-renowned sage, who transcends the human condition, and that lady of great majesty and slender waist, remained indeed a maiden day after day as the days passed."
Thus it is said.
For human majesty is not possible [in this case];
therefore, there is a transcendent, non-human nature.
For this very reason, Vāsudeva said to Karṇa:
"And on the sixth day, Draupadī presented herself [to you].
Otherwise, how could one who is an authoritative person speak in such a manner?
Alternatively, it is understood through the presumption of the linguistic usage (*vyavahārārthāpatti*) that there were indeed many Draupadīs of identical appearance who were treated as one;
or else, [the possession] will not belong to Arjuna alone.
Common consensus has been shown [here] because it is refuted by well-established [evidence].

Just as, at Yudhiṣṭhira’s instruction, she suddenly assumed the guise of a menstruating woman while being led into the midst of the assembly, in order to bring infamy upon Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his son and to cast blame upon herself.

Draupadī acted [in such a way] so that the truth—that it was solely through the illusory power (*māyā*) of Arjuna—remained unknown to the people; furthermore, she employed a common pretext to demonstrate that there was no opportunity for the application of deception regarding their mutual agreement. Because this is easily refuted by such considerations, there is no valid objection to what has been stated: namely, that a legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) brought about by passion or greed is not accepted as righteous (*dharma*) even by the disciples themselves.

Likewise, regarding the false testimony concerning the killing of Droṇa and others, it is stated at the end [of the legal treatises]: "Some hold that there is an expiation even for an intentional lie. Thus, since the Aśvamedha is indeed performed as an expiation, its status as a practice of the virtuous (sadācāra) cannot be admitted.

As for the instance cited of Vāsudeva and Arjuna drinking liquor between them and marrying their maternal uncle’s daughter—which is contrary to the Smṛtis—it should be understood that the prohibition of *surā* (fermented liquor) applies to the three twice-born classes (*traivarṇika*) who consume intoxicants; for it is said: "Surā is indeed the dregs of food, and sin is called the dreg;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink *surā*."
Thus [it is said].

However, there is no prohibition at all regarding humans and others who are Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas, because this refers exclusively to Brāhmaṇas, as indicated by the statement: "This is always [forbidden] for the Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, as for this: "Sura is to be known as threefold: that made from molasses (gauḍī), that made from flour (paiṣṭī), and that made from honey (mādhvī)."
Just as one [woman] is, so are all; they must not be approached for drink by those who proclaim the Brahman.

Thus, because the word *brahmavādin* (one who speaks of Brahman) is based on the grounds of habit, duty, or excellence in performance, and because the roots *pra-vac* (to proclaim) and *brū* (to speak) have the same meaning, there is the restrictive rule: "Among these, the Brāhmaṇa alone should proclaim [it]. Therefore, he alone who possesses the proclamation is one who has that habit, that duty, or that excellence; consequently, only a Brāhmaṇa is a *brahmavādin*.
Furthermore, this is beneficial even for the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) censuring birth, as it serves to prohibit the general [misuse] of the term:
"A Brāhmaṇa, deluded by intoxication, might indeed do something else un-Aryan."

Thus, what is meant by this is as follows: "Just as one [woman] who has been approached is not to be drunk from by three [men], so too all [women] are not to be drunk from by those who discourse on Brahman.

Otherwise, both the phrases "just as one" and "by those who discourse on Brahman" would be entirely redundant, since the connection with the three castes is already established by the reference in the subsequent verse.

Therefore, both [the arguments] are contradictory because they belong to the intermediate state (*madhyāsva*). Likewise, there is a scriptural passage showing another meaning that expresses permission: "The garland that was on him was also drunk; the garland is indeed *surā* (wine); from that he attained sovereignty. Therefore, when the daughter-in-law and the mother-in-law have drunk *surā*, they remain lamenting together. The garland is indeed evil (*pāpman*); therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not drink *surā*, lest he be united with evil. Now, a Kṣatriya might say to a Brāhmaṇa: 'Wine thus drunk does not harm one who, knowing this, drinks non-wine (*asurā*)’."
This is due to the confusion regarding the objects [of desire], such as honey-wine (*madhuśīdhu*).

As for the marriage between mother and daughter, that is not contradictory because it is observed in common practice even when there is an intervention by the bond of defects such as being the wife of one’s mother;

for although Subhadrā is known as the sister of Vāsudeva, she is nevertheless said to be the wife of Baladeva and Vāsudeva’s own sister (Ekānaṃśā), since she is described as the daughter of his maternal uncle and paternal aunt, and this is understood from the permission for their marriage.
And [the fact] that he was unknown to Vasudeva contradicts [the status of] Kaunteya; however, there is no contradiction in his being a descendant through a remote relationship.
"By which [path] it is right and fitting that men follow my path in every way, O Pārtha;
for whatever a great man does, other people do that very same thing. Whatever standard he sets, the world follows that."
Thus, being a mirror for all the worlds, how could he promote the conduct of the learned?
By this, the marriage with Rukmiṇī is explained.

As for that which was cited as being contrary to the Smṛtis—such as the drinking of liquor by the Āhicchatrakas, the Ādharas, and others who lack a [proper] abode, or the marriage with the daughter of a maternal uncle among the Southerners.

Regarding this, some say: "Since Smṛti and Ācāra possess equal authority—each being rooted in the Veda independently of the other—there is no fault in adopting either the prescribed or the prohibited option according to one's stage of life (āśrama). However, that view is inconsistent with the distinction between strength and weakness that will be explained later.
Others, however, say: "The rule for 'all sins' and similar cases is determined by location."
Āpastamba, having compiled [the rules], has relied upon both the faulty and the faultless.
Those people who have inherited practices handed down through tradition and performed by their ancestors would not be at fault for practicing them among men.
Likewise, it has been stated by Manu: "By that path which one's fathers have traveled, and by which one's grandfathers have traveled, one should travel;
traveling by that path of the virtuous, one does not incur sin."
However, those for whom a certain practice was not performed by their ancestors and so forth, yet is prohibited by another Smṛti, certainly avoid it.

Or, if they do not avoid it, they are avoided by their own kinsmen and others. But has it not been stated that the authority of practices whose names and customs are contrary to the lineage (gotra) is invalid?
(The proponent of the rebuttal raises an objection: He says, "If there were a contradiction with the Veda, that alone would constitute its lack of authority;
however, the term 'Smṛti' is not used here as a synonym for the Veda."
(He refutes this: But even this is not tenable, because the word *āmnāya* is employed even in the context of the *smṛti* texts.

For, in the section concerning the duties based on *smṛti*, Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated: "The *āmnāya* is that which upholds the *smṛti*. The study of the *smṛti* text—which consists of the recitation of the *smṛti* originating from another source—is stated to be for the purpose of upholding the *smṛti* by those who study the *smṛti* texts.
(He concludes his own position: Therefore, it is impossible to deny the authority of those practices established by the statements of Manu and others.
As for the statement of Āpastamba, however, it has been refuted by Baudhāyana, who cited examples of corrupt practices that contradict the Smṛtis.
Furthermore, because other causes such as clear desire are observed, it is not tenable to claim that either the contradictory practices or the statement of Āpastamba are rooted in Śruti.

(He raises an objection—) He asks: "By whom has the drinking of *surā* by Brāhmaṇī women been prohibited? (He offers a reply—) It is said: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya shall not drink *surā*, nor a Vaiśya. (The objector states his own view—) "Because of the masculine gender used in the reference, it is not prohibited for women."
Therefore, the drinking of liquor does not here contradict either the Smṛti or established custom.
Pārśvaka says: It is argued that even in the prohibition against killing, the masculine gender might be intended to be significant;
likewise, the intention to signify singularity would also follow as a consequence, such that one would achieve the purpose of the injunction only by not killing some [of them] alone.
And when the drinking of intoxicants is prohibited by the word "one," it is as explained before.

(He removes the suspected fault: It is said that whatever is stated based on the intention to express singularity—whether through the connection with each individual instance or through the universal (jāti)—that is not faulty.

(He explains this very point: For since there is a prohibition against the killing or the marrying of even a single Brāhmaṇī woman, it is possible—even if intended—that [the word "one"] might be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) or an adverbial modifier of another action, because it is being restated; how much more so when this is understood as a restatement of the oneness belonging to the genus (*jāti*).
(First, he avoids the over-extension [of the argument]—) He says:

In the prohibition of killing, the Brāhmaṇa is intended as the object (*uddeśya*) of the action, whereas in the drinking of *surā*, he is mentioned as the agent (*kartṛ*). Consequently, because there arises the possibility of similar intentions or non-intentions—as in the case of the sacrificer who desires heaven or the measuring out of the *udumbara* post—there is a disparity between the two examples.

(The following explains how, in the prohibition of killing, the gender of the Brāhmaṇa is not intended to be significant: For instance: "When it is stated, 'He who [is] a Brāhmaṇa,' in the prohibition of killing, or in the prohibition regarding the Brāhmaṇa, no other gender is prescribed."

(He explains the verse: For a prescriptive statement is the opposite of a prohibition; since a prohibition of killing in general is possible, it prescribes a prohibition of killing qualified solely by the Brāhmaṇa caste. If, however, for the sake of [ensuring] cessation, it were to further enjoin either the person (liṅga) as the primary factor in relation to the Brāhmaṇa, or the prohibition itself in relation to the act of killing, then there would follow the fault of syntactical split (vākya-bheda), characterized by the repetition of the suffix.

Thus, first of all, regarding a word accompanied by the negative particle (*nañ*) in a prohibitory injunction (*niṣedhakalpa*), since there is no cognition of an impulsion (*pravartanā*), there is an absence of the goal (*sādhya*) implied by it. Because a Brāhmaṇa is useless [in that context] and therefore not a fit recipient for the rite (*asaṃskāryatva*), even though there is a real status as the objective (*uddeśyatva*) through the exclusion of others (*anyavyatireka*), it has been stated that the gender is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*) because it is merely heard from the words (*śabdaśruti*).

But when it is accepted that since the negation is established by the negative particle (*nañ*) alone, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) serves merely to restate what is already understood from the context of aversion, then—given that the killing (which is the object of refinement) is logically possible as it is conducive to accomplishing the desired end through the instigation of the agent who has learned the command—it is all the more so that the gender is intended to be significant, because it is in fact the objective (*uddeśya*). However, for those [Mīmāṃsakas] for whom both injunction and prohibition are not considered to be the meanings of Vedic sentences in themselves, [the following applies]: even though the gender is heard in the text, because it is not utilized for the prohibition and is not grasped by it, it is unintended (*avivakṣita*). This is another point. Due to its conformity with the proximity of the suffix, and because it does not denote a meaning that is absent, the other negative particle (*nañ*), by means of a further secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), refers to the act of killing—which, though contrary in nature, is obtained through aversion—as qualified by the previously mentioned logic and qualified by the Brāhmaṇa. Thus, the purpose is the meaning of the prohibition. Since the negative particle, while recurring, cannot negate the injunction to kill a Brāhmaṇa, the gender, although heard in the text, becomes unintended because it is not utilized for the prohibition.

For here the explicit mode of expression is: "One who, under the influence of anger and so forth, should kill a Brāhmaṇa," or "A Brāhmaṇa is not to be killed. However, in the view that [the negative particle] is connected with the verb, the construction of the sentence is as follows: "That which is the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, one should not do it," or "He who is a Brāhmaṇa, one should not kill him. Thus, there arises the possibility of inferring another source for the Smṛtis, namely, that this is either an injunction prohibiting the killing qualified by the status of being a Brāhmaṇa, or an injunction prohibiting the killing of a pure, ordinary Brāhmaṇa.
And just as we shall accept these spies,

being merely the observers of those things expressed by words, so too are the authors of the Smṛtis; therefore, because neither the individual nor the generic form is possible [in this case], [the Smṛtis are not authoritative].
"For as far as the practice extends, so far is the perception of the source understood.

For if they had heard the original sources—the Vedic sentences—then the Veda alone would have to be inferred by those who infer [them], just as these [Smṛti texts] were composed, so too would these have been composed;
and for this sentence, there would not have been any other [source]."

However, since [the validity of conduct] can be established through one's own perception and inference— as well as by being expressed as having limited scope— and since people engage in practices [only] when there is conviction in others, they say that "good conduct is authoritative only through the conviction of others. Therefore, it is not possible for the authors of the *Dharma-sūtras* to determine that very [conduct] as being based on the authority of [perceived] practice (*ācāra*),
because it would follow that it would be based on logic (*nyāya*) rather than being recorded as equal to the statements of other *dharma-smṛtis*.

Regarding the statement, "The investigation [concerns] whether the correctness [of usage] is established by logic (*nyāya*)," it is not the case that the *smṛti* (tradition) which operates at a later time due to non-perception [of usage] is being investigated as the source for those [rules].

For if one were to investigate the source [of the *smṛti*], there would be the undesirable consequence of a reversal of strength based on the authority of the source, [which would lead to] the negation of the meaning found in the *pūrvapakṣa-sūtra* after having established the doubt.

(He begins with the third point, the established conclusion [siddhānta]: In this regard, he explains the Sūtra in the same manner as the substance of the preceding section: "Therefore, the authority of the scripture is not even asserted to be limited, because one is able to infer the author. Nor is the root of those practices [the scripture], since they are generally free from contradiction with the injunctions and the Smṛtis.
For there is no such thing as being rooted in many [individuals]."
Nor is consciousness merely of the nature of memory; good conduct (*sadācāra*) is not in contradiction with what is taught in the Śruti and Smṛti.
Therefore, a Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is inferred here [as the source].
Because these conducts have no prior origin and because they are performed by all equally, they are determined to possess authoritative validity.

[This is] due to the reversal of the suffixes *ghañ* and *ac*. For, since it is stated in the Veda that "the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is an authority," by deriving the word *kāra* from the root *kṛ* as signifying "activity" (*vyāpāra*), the conduct of those being measured [as authorities] would first be established; and preceded by that [conduct], there is the word *kāra* ending in the possessive suffix *matup*, meaning "those who possess this activity," which refers to the agents (*kartṛ*). It is not the case that the Vedic and Smṛti [injunctions] lack a foundation because conduct is their root; rather, the agents of these [Vedic and Smṛti rules] are equal. Furthermore, [it is said]: "The conduct of the learned is an authority. Thus, having derived the word *kāra* from the root *kṛ* as signifying "activity" based on the scriptural statement that "the conduct of the learned is an authority," the word *kāra* ending in the possessive suffix *matup*—meaning "those who possess this activity"—refers to the agents (*kartṛ*). It is not the case that the Vedic and Smṛti [injunctions] lack a foundation because conduct is their root; rather, the agents of these [Vedic and Smṛti rules] are equal. (He states the fourth method of exposition: "The analysis of the treatise (*śāstra*) should be performed.

Or rather, [the treatise] operates within a limited scope because it is authorized by the authors of the *Smṛtis* and because there is another great cause. An unlimited [treatise] would not function as a means of instruction.
"Since their root is unknown, no authorization for them is possible;
because practices are limited in number, they would lack scriptural authority.
Thus ends the fifth explanation.

He states the reason: "Because the scripture has a limited scope regarding its objects, the scripture is purposeful even where [the conclusion] has not been reached" (6.2.14.169). [To explain that which is seen to have a finality, he completes the sense by supplying the ellipsis: "Since it acts as the cause, the authority here belongs to the scripture. Therefore, because of the pleasure associated with the object, these [rules] do not depend on the scripture for the determination of dharma and adharma. (6.2.15.170). Because the scripture has a limited extent, these [rules] do not depend on the scripture for the establishment of dharma and adharma.
"In this regard, there is a principle concerning conduct:
the refined customs of Vaiśyas, even when devoid of [Vedic] verbal authority, attain the status of valid evidence—
whether those of the Kānvas or other Vaiśyas in their cities."

Just as the fact that conduct (*caritra*) is measurable by the scriptures is designated by the term "means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇa*), so too let it be here that [conduct] is a constituent part of dharma, adharma, artha, and pleasure. (He concludes the prima facie view: "Thus it is established for both. (He explains otherwise: "And they are limited. Therefore, only the Śruti and Smṛti are the means of valid knowledge regarding the domain of dharma."
The scriptures refer to the Vedas, Upavedas, and so forth.

Among these, there is no comparison between the conduct of the virtuous and the conduct of those who follow the rules of discipline on the one hand, and social gatherings, jesting, and the like on the other; for such [degenerate] conduct does not exist within the scriptures.

Nor does good conduct (*sadācāra*) itself initiate the composition of a scripture (the systematic presentation of tenets or aphorisms), nor is there even the observation or performance of such [conduct] based on a scripture, because the series of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) is entirely dependent [on other means], and because of this very point, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) must be explained. Furthermore, it has already been stated that the Smṛti lacks a foundation regarding this subject matter.

(He composes the formal argument [adhikaraṇa]: Here, having cited the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭas) residing in Āryāvarta—(in the third section, he refutes the alternative view while explaining)—and as before, when there is doubt regarding validity or invalidity, the learned [state]: "Furthermore, it has been considered whether the source would be one or many;
since it is not contradicted even in the case of [multiple] sources, he begins with the established conclusion (siddhānta).
For instance, it is certainly not possible to infer that it is of two kinds."

"As long as that which remains [uncontradicted] by the Śruti and Smṛti is not opposed by it, so long is the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭa)— which possesses various names and forms due to differences of region, caste, and family— not understood as an authoritative means of knowing Dharma, even if it differs [from the scriptures]. If..."
The objection that "the disciple might become angry" is a matter of providing proof; thus, those two [texts] are studied.

However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is this: the performance of rites by followers of the Veda is based on the recognition of them as Dharma; yet, even in the absence of anger, there is no contradiction in the authority of such conduct.
This is untenable in the case of [actions] belonging to the Vedic ritual (*vaidhikatva*).

However, the observation of transgressions and acts of violence—such as the injunctions "one must perform [the rite] having sipped water" (*ācāntena kartavyam*) and so forth—is not based on the notion of *dharma*, because they originate from attachment, aversion, and the like.
The examples of those who possess the notion of *dharma* include the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and those who have died.

There is an inquiry into the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) as to whether it is authoritative or not, because neither a traditional text (*nibandhana*) nor established practice (*ācarita*) serves as a cause for its performance.
For that purpose, one must determine whether [the practices] are contradicted by direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣaśruti*).
Furthermore, because contradictions with Smṛti are observed, there is a deviation from their being indicative marks of Dharma (*dharmaliṅga*).

Even for the sake of those [injunctions] beginning with Manu, which are performed by certain individuals during the course of a ritual through these [practices], there may or may not be a contradiction regarding the general meaning of the scriptural text concerning sequence (*krama*) and so forth, even if it were to be established in its own form.
Alternatively, it has been stated that the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in its own right;
it is not merely by this much that one investigates whether a particular [practice] is a valid or invalid means of knowledge when it contradicts [another authority].
And for that reason, there is a fault [in the opponent's position].

Therefore, just as with the Smṛtis, the authority of customary practices (ācāra) regarding Dharma is established as valid. Now, it must be considered which among these [authoritative sources] are stronger or weaker, and by how much. This is proven.

The question of whether there is indeed a contradiction regarding Soma, or whether there is none, constitutes the subject matter of the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*); thus, its connection with that [section] may be understood in this alternative way.

As for the immediately following section on the observation of a reason (*hetudarśanādhikaraṇa*), since it too is a branch of the section on contradiction, it does not require a separate connection with it.
However, according to the alternative view introduced by "Or rather" (*athavā*), the connection is one of application (*āpādika*) with the section on contradiction.

In the section concerning the lack of authority of traditional conduct (*sadācāra*), however, it is stated that conduct is also lacking in authority, just like the Smṛtis of the Śākyas and others; this constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*). "This is not a Smṛti [to be followed] by one who has sipped water (*ācānta*); let it not be so, because it contradicts the Vedic sequence expressed as 'having performed the Veda [rite]'."
"In this context, the sequence of ritual elements such as the sipping of water (ācamana) is a property (dharma) residing in those elements;
because a property depends upon its substratum (dharmin), it possesses validity through that discourse."

(Now, as for the section concerning the authority of the Smṛtis of Śākya and others composed by the author of the Vārttika: "Is the non-violence taught by Śākya Dharma or not? It is Dharma because it is heard [in scripture].

It is not Dharma, for cow's milk would not be pure if it were held in the Śruti. (Now, as for the section concerning the authority of the conduct of the virtuous: "Is the conduct of the virtuous authoritative or not? It is not authoritative due to its lack of a foundation."
"Because this [Smṛti] concerning the Aṣṭakā and other rites possesses a foundation, it is authoritative.

Thus, for the followers of Bhaṭṭa and the Smārta tradition, when there is a conflict between practices such as ritual sipping (ācamana) and others prescribed by Smṛti on one hand, and the sequence, time, and measure prescribed by Śruti on the other, the latter—namely the sequence and so forth—prevail due to their being based on Śruti; consequently, the Smṛtis concerning those [Smārta] matters lack authority.

For it is not possible to perform the sequence prescribed by the Veda— namely, "having made the *veda*, one makes the *vedi*"— in place of the sequence of stepping [onto the altar] enjoined by Smṛti as "when the *śruti* has been heard, having sipped water," because the items prescribed by Smṛti are numerous; thus, the time of the forenoon and the extent required for the completion of the performance do not fall under the scope of the *Śiṣṭākopādhikaraṇa*.
The censure of the learned can be accommodated;

nor does the fact that sequence and so forth are scriptural (śrauta) entail their weakness relative to the ritual acts (padārtha) such as sipping water (ācamana), since they are properties of those acts.

Since the cognition of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is preceded by the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the relative strength or weakness of the object of knowledge depends upon the strength or weakness of the previously apprehended means of knowledge. This being the case, since sequence and the like depend upon the attainment of the meanings of words, they must be postulated only insofar as they do not contradict the meanings of words as understood through the primary means of knowledge; thus, they do not contradict the meanings of the words themselves. However, *parimāṇa* (measure) does not belong to any scriptural injunction (*śāstra*); therefore, it lacks the status of being directly stated in scripture (*śrautatva*).
Even in cases of contradiction, since acts such as sipping water (*ācamana*) are ritual items (*padārtha*), they remain objects of knowledge (*prameya*).

For there is no contradiction among means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in their own nature; rather, contradiction is based solely on the contradiction between their objects of knowledge (*prameya*).

Thus, as soon as a contradiction with the object of knowledge (*prameya-virodha*) is observed, and the meaning of the scripture has been determined by the relative strength or weakness of that [contradiction], it is not the case here that the very means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—namely, that Smṛti—is the regulator of the strength or weakness of the means of knowledge.
Or rather, let there be authority for that scriptural statement concerning giving and so forth which, among other things, is not contradicted by the Vedas.

This being the position reached, [it is countered by the following]: "One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied"; "The entire Veda is the root of Dharma"; "And that [Dharma] consists of Smṛti and conduct (*smṛti-śīle*); and "The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, together with the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga-miśritāḥ*)."
"Vedas are the fourteen sources of knowledge and of dharma.

According to such scriptural statements, dharma is understood precisely as that which is to be propounded by these fixed authorities; since anything known through other means lacks the capacity to be a means for attaining the fruit [of dharma], those [other means] lack authority.

(Or rather, [the view] beginning with *kāraṇa*: Even though there is no doubt regarding the authority of uncodified customs such as the Vasantotsava and others, if these were rooted in the Veda, they would have been codified by Manu and others—just like the Aṣṭakā rites and so forth—even though they were included in a general manner under the rule "And this [is established] by Smṛti and conduct" (*tad idaṃ ca smṛtiśīle*). Since they are not specifically codified, and because there is no observation of their basis in Śruti, they lack authority. This being the prima facie position, [the reply is: Because they are performed by those learned in the Veda with the understanding that they are Dharma, they possess Vedic character just like Smṛti. As for the specific lack of codification, it is not a defect, as it may arise from a desire to avoid prolixity.
However, the observation of transgressions and acts of violence is Vedic because it is performed by those following the Vedas with the conviction that they are dharma;
yet, this does not imply that everything [in such practices] is non-Vedic.
Therefore, even among customs (ācāras), there is authority regarding both dharma and adharma.

Because it is produced from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the Veda, it is indeed the Veda itself. (Vārttika 1.3.1.7, p. 207). [This is not subject to] the censure of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).

But was it not stated previously (6.2.3) that the censure of the learned (*śiṣṭagarhā*) constitutes the completion [of the rite]? And yet, the learned do not censure [the act] even when it is not completed at home.

So how can there be completion here? This censure of the learned does not exist; nevertheless, despite the contradiction with the previous section, the censure of the learned is not itself an authority, but rather functions as such by way of inferring a Vedic text.

§ Section on Censure by the Learned.
A rite performed for a specific desire, once commenced, must necessarily be completed.
For, due to the commencement, there is a restriction [to finish it], since the action itself is what is subject to that restriction.
Commentary: Rituals such as "One desiring offspring should sacrifice" and "One desiring a village should sacrifice" are recorded in the tradition.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: must that which has been commenced be completed as a matter of necessity, or may it be performed according to one's desire, or even abandoned? What is the prima facie view? It must be completed as a matter of necessity.

Why? Because it is heard thus: "One desiring this should sacrifice. In this way, they teach the meaning of that verb, stating that it expresses [the action] from its commencement until its completion.
The meaning of this [verb] is a specific sequence of activity (vyāpāraviśeṣa) beginning from its commencement until its completion; it is not like "cooking" or "giving.
For in those cases, only the mere existence of the action is indicated, not that it must be commenced and brought to completion.
And thus even ordinary people in the world understand verbal roots (ākhyāta) in this way.
In this regard, it is understood that human effort applies to the commencement [of a rite] only when it is enjoined by Śruti;

for while [rites] are not necessarily commenced because they are enjoined, they are necessarily brought to completion. Therefore, neither commencement nor completion constitutes the literal meaning of the word [enjoining the rite].
What then? Completion is the meaning of the word. Since it has reached its object that is to be completed, it possesses an "undertaking" (ārambha).
Therefore, it is understood that completion is the meaning of the word.
If that [obligation] were the meaning of the word, it would be enjoined as something to be performed throughout its duration;
however, at the very commencement, there is no sense of it being "to be performed.
Therefore, the commencement does not follow from a mandatory injunction.
Completion, however, is mandatory.

Therefore, if one has begun a ritual action, even if the desire for its fruit has ceased or if the fruit has already been obtained, in that state as well, the completion of what was begun must certainly be performed.
It is enjoined that it "must be performed" if it is to yield the desired result.
But surely, that object which is the primary wealth is what is stated here as something to be performed.
This is not so;
for it constitutes the meaning of the entire sentence.
However, the necessity of performing the sacrifice is understood by hearing [the injunction].

Therefore, once a sacrifice has been commenced by one desiring a village or the like, it must be brought to completion. At that time, the mention of the desire for a village and so forth serves as the occasion [for the performance].

It is stated that whatever must be performed when a specific occasion (*nimitte*) arises should indeed be performed on that very day; since it is enjoined that the commencement already undertaken must be brought to completion, it must likewise be performed even when the occasion falls on that same day.
For that day does not become unarisen;
rather, it is the arising [of the action] that is the cause, not its mere existence.
Therefore, once an undertaking has been begun when there is a desire for the fruit, it must be brought to completion.

For the undertaking of an action is indeed the cause for its performance, and that [undertaking] is for the sake of its completion. Therefore, even when the desire for the fruit has vanished, the ritual act must certainly be brought to completion.
Why? Because the undertaking is the occasion for the desire.
Therefore, just as one must perform it when the desire exists, so too, since the undertaking remains even when the desire has passed, the completion based on that occasion must be performed;
that [completion] is enjoined with respect to the fruit.
When the commencement is enjoined, then the completion must necessarily follow because it is implied by that injunction;
for when the completion is enjoined, the commencement is obtained as its prerequisite.
Therefore, since completion is ordained by the scripture, it must be performed even when the desire for the fruit has ceased.

There is no restriction because of the desire for the fruit, as in the case of the *ānuṣaṅga* [mantras]. The Bhāṣya states: The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the previous position; rather, there is no restriction.
Why? Because of the desire for a result.
For one who desires a result and wishes to bring that result about, this means is enjoined as a method, not as a duty in itself.
For if it were enjoined as a duty, it would have to be either a duty regarding the result or a duty regarding the sacrifice.

First of all, there is no postulation of a fruit [in this case]; for it is not the case that one who desires something is enjoined to perform that very act by thinking, "I must do this. Rather, he thinks, "This must be done by me according to the Veda."
But one does not know the means; therefore, one desires it.
This is taught: that sacrifice is the means, and that [the result] is accomplished by means of sacrifice. And yet, there is no obligation to perform the sacrifice itself.
Because it contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For this sacrifice is indeed directly perceived.
If the duty were to be performed by means of another sacrifice, then there would be no contradiction.
If the performance of the sacrifice were mandatory, a result would have to be postulated;
yet there is no means of valid cognition for that which is being postulated. Furthermore, an injunction regarding what ought to be done applies only to things that are possible and so forth.

Therefore, the sacrifice is not something that must necessarily be performed. Rather, having referred to whatever is desired by one who seeks a result, the injunction prescribes the sacrifice as the means for achieving it according to what is already established. Consequently, it does not necessarily have to be brought to completion.
Just as that which has been commenced need not necessarily be undertaken, so too that which has been commenced need not necessarily be completed.
As for the claim that "the meaning of a sentence is sublated by direct statement" (śruti):
it has already been stated that where the meaning of the direct statement is impossible, there the meaning of the sentence is accepted.
Therefore, there is a restriction:
for one who desires a result for oneself, sacrifice is prescribed as the means;
even when that desire has ceased, it does not cease to be the means.
Since it lacks the nature of a means, how could it be performed? Nor is the undertaking itself the cause,
because of the absence of both that which has occurred and that which exists.
Nor is the undertaking indicated by any word whatsoever.

Since "instruction regarding what is to be done applies only to what is possible," it is only in the case of the thought "the sacrifice can be performed" that one can conceive of an injunction to act;
however, it is not the case that "his specific sacrifice must be performed."
The performance of the conduct of the learned.
Since it is caused by that [conduct], the conduct of the learned— whether as a practice or as a rule— should be the cause for the agent.
Commentary: For the undertaking is indeed the cause of completion.
How so? Because it would be the cause for the agent [to achieve his goal].
What is the reason? It is the power of true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpatā*).
For the learned censure one who does not complete an undertaking of such a nature, saying, "This man is a mere initiator; he is not to be trusted. And the censure of the learned is a fault.
Therefore, an undertaking must be brought to completion.
He asks: "But for what reason do the cultured (śiṣṭas) censure [this]? It is said in reply:
"They censure it, saying: 'What is the use of our knowing the underlying cause?'"
Ḍuṇḍa:—They do not censure out of their own arbitrary will;
they would indeed be unrefined (aśiṣṭa) if they were to censure without a scriptural basis.
Therefore, there is the Smṛti based on the conduct of the refined (śiṣṭācāra), and from that Smṛti, the Śruti [is inferred].

Furthermore, there is a statement among the Taittirīyas that has another purpose: "He who, having said 'I shall sacrifice,' does not sacrifice, incurs the wrath of the deities; he should perform the Traidhātavīya sacrifice, and thus he does not incur the wrath of the deities.
