We do not perceive any difference in form between the object and its cognition;
moreover, our cognition is directly perceived.
Thus we see that there is nothing whatsoever called the "form of the object" that is distinct from the cognition itself.
Furthermore, cognition is momentary; it is known even while it is arising, and it makes another object known, like a lamp.
That is not so.
[Bhāṣya] (Vṛtti text): 1.2.15, p. 21. Śūnyavāda.

Thus, when inference as stated by the opponent has been refuted by contradiction with perception, that same proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādin) now rejoins by means of the aforementioned objection, namely, that inference lacks the very capacity to function outside of perception. The subsequent text is for the purpose of refuting that. Vaidyanātha, pp. 30–31: "When the refutation of inference has been stated thus, based upon its cognition..."
But regarding direct perception through knowledge (*jñāna-pratyakṣa*), another [opponent] objects:
"Since it is incapable of operating toward external objects, there is no contradiction of inference by it" (Ślokavārttika 1.1.4).
"It is possible" means that an objection is raised by way of resolving the aforementioned contradiction.
(In the *Śūnyavāda* [section],) Ratnākara: The Commentary—How can there be emptiness?
(He asks the proponent of emptiness [śūnyavādin]: "How can that which appears externally in the form of 'this is blue' and so forth be a form of cognition?
We do not perceive any difference in form between the object and the cognition;
moreover, our cognition is directly perceived.")

Therefore, we observe that there is no such thing as a name whose form is the object. This might be so if cognition possessed the form of the object; however, for us, cognition is formless, while the external object possesses form.
For that [cognition] is perceived directly as connected with an external object;
indeed, perceptual cognition has an external object as its domain, not another cognition as its domain.
For it is momentary and does not persist until the time of another cognition.

(The proponent of emptiness says: "It is said that this [cognition] is known precisely as it arises, and it makes another object known, like a lamp. (The proponent of the established doctrine says: That is not so.
For no cognition is perceived when its object is unknown;
rather, once the object is known, one understands [the existence of the cognition] through inference (namely, by means of the inference characterized by the state of being known).
In that case, simultaneity [of the object and its cognition] is untenable.
(The Śūnyavādin says: But surely it is said that "the object is known" only when cognition has arisen, not when it has not arisen;
therefore, cognition arises first, and subsequently the object is known.
(The Siddhāntin states his intention: True, cognition arises first, but it is not known first.
For it sometimes happens that an object, though existing, is said to be "unknown.
Moreover, the form of cognition cannot be perceived apart from the designation of the object.
Therefore, cognition is not designated [by the object], and that which is expressed by another word is not perception.
Consequently, cognition is not perceptible.
Furthermore, even if it were of a single form, there would simply be an absence of cognition itself, not of the object which is actually perceived.
Nor is there identity of form; for we determine that cognition is indeed formless (anākāra), whereas we perceive the object as having form through direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Therefore, cognition has the object as its objective support (ālambana).
Moreover, it has a fixed cause: the cognition of a cloth arises only when threads are being employed.
Otherwise, even when taking up a thread, a person with unimpaired faculties might occasionally have the cognition of a jar;
but this is not the case.
Therefore, cognition is not without an objective basis (*nirālambana*).
Therefore, perception does not deviate [from its object].

Thus, when perception is being examined, since it possesses the capacity for external engagement, an inference favored by the Buddhists—such as that [perception] is without an objective basis (*nirālambanatva*), which contradicts such a perception of an external object—is untenable. For, while a cognition in which there is a defective instrument or a subsequent subverting cognition may be incorrect, a valid cognition consisting of perception in which neither of those two exists does not deviate at all; therefore, perception is certainly not something that requires examination.
Vaidyanātha, p. 35: Vṛddhatī—But surely, by stating that "it is indeed void," you have already presented that very lack of support for the cognition, asserting its emptiness of an object;
and that [lack of support] has been refuted by the statement that it is equivalent to the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
(The answer: That same refutation is being raised once again.

How [is this] established by reasoning? Because consciousness has an object of cognition as its domain. And that [consciousness] is a property either of the self, or of the intellect (the mind), or it is a property residing in knowledge itself.
That alone is logically its object.
Therefore, that [cognition] is consciousness itself;
and thus it follows that it is the very same thing that is the object of cognition.
Consequently, it is not capable of cognizing another object [due to its dependence on its own substrate].
The nature of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell must be understood as belonging either to the self (*ātman*), to consciousness (*vijñāna*), or to the intellect (*buddhi*).

Is it intended that the word "cognition" (*jñāna*) is meant merely for the sake of illustration, on the grounds that "we do not perceive any difference in form between the object and its cognition"? No;
for when the object of experience rests within the locus of consciousness, only cognition remains, since the intellect and the self are identical in their possession of sound and the other qualities.
And consciousness is inseparable from knowledge;
for in the state of deep sleep, consciousness is not perceived in either the self or the intellect.
Indeed, sleep is the withdrawal of knowledge.
Having considered this, it was said: "We do not perceive any difference in form between the object and its cognition.
But what is this that has been observed? That the object alone is perceived by consciousness.
For we understand that it is indeed being perceived that constitutes its perceptibility; we do not understand it as being an object.
(Reply: Who has ever said that "the state of being cognized is not apprehended as something cognized"?
Rather, because consciousness is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) and because it consists of cognition, we consider that its very nature is that of sound and so forth.
For who indeed would conceive of both consciousness and sound etc. as being [simultaneously] directly perceived?
Therefore, the established conclusion is that the collection of objects such as sound and so forth is of the very nature of consciousness itself;
nor is there anything that exists apart from "I.
But [an objection may be raised]: does this not result in consciousness being non-correspondent with reality (ayathārtha)?
For if consciousness were to possess the form of sound and so forth, the perception of the grasped and the grasper would not be possible;
therefore, it must be understood that this is a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

Nor is it logical that all worldly linguistic usage consists of conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) regarding objects; nor is anything in the world observed to be designated by the word "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*) when it conforms to the apprehension of another object.
Therefore, both [the cognition and its object] possess the status of perception (*pratyakṣatā*); there is no denial of what has been understood.
For at that time, it is consciousness alone that is established; to what, then, does this form of sound and so forth belong?
(The resolution here is: It would be logical if the cognition of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject occurred by means of a different form.
But we do not perceive any other form; for both appear only as the form of blue and so forth.

And the manifestation of both [object and cognition] is of a single form; what else could this manifestation be? Thus it has been said: "We do not perceive even the form of either the object or the cognition.
By the statement, "And our cognition is perceptible," this is what is meant: "And our consciousness is perceptible.
This form of blue and so forth is indeed perceptible.
Therefore, consciousness bearing that form appears in both ways.
Consequently, it is established that this consciousness is devoid of an external object;
thus, the claim that "from its contact with that [object], there arises the cognition of it" is mere idle chatter.
Is this a Yogācāra who asserts [the existence of] mental content (*mātrāvādī*)?
But for the Śūnyavāda, there is no external object existing apart from cognition.
The object is merely a form (*ākāra*) of cognition and consists of nothing other than the very nature of cognition itself, like a dream-eating experience.
Therefore, determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) is not valid knowledge (*pramā*).

To explain: what constitutes the status of being an object of cognition for blue and so forth? It cannot be "being an entity" (*padārthatva*) or "possessing existence" (*sattāvattva*), because that would entail the consequence that yellow and other things would also be objects [of the cognition of blue].
Nor can it be the state of being a cause of knowledge, for that would entail the same status for the sense organs and so forth.
Nor can it be the state of being the locus of the production of knowledge, because in the case of the cognition of color, touch would then result in being its object.

Nor can it be the state of being a cause qualified by similarity, because since the cognition of the qualifier is itself a cognition, it would share similarity [with the qualificand], and since it is a cause, it would consequently result in being the object in the qualified cognition.

Furthermore, absolute dissimilarity is not what is intended here, nor is it [dissimilarity] in terms of being cognition (*jñānatva*), because that is common to both. Rather, it is [dissimilarity] in terms of being the object of the same cognition.

And this is tenable as the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*) because, in the case of a perceptual cognition consisting of the "three-fold circle" (*tripuṭī*), the cognition and the object are the objects of the same cognition and stand in a causal relationship. Thus it must be stated.
In a series of successive cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*), the preceding cognition would result in being the object of the succeeding cognition due to their similarity;
furthermore, since it is impossible for a cognition to be its own cause with respect to itself, its status as an object is untenable.
Nor can it be argued that a cognition possesses causality only when it imparts the form of blue or other objects, and that this occurs through proximity, as in the case of a *japā* flower.
There is no evidence for the external object's capacity to impart its own form, such as blue and so forth, to the cognition.
If it is argued that the diversity of cognitions is the proof [for the existence of objects], we say no; for we observe a diversity of cognitions even in the absence of an object, as in dreams.

Nor can the fact of a cognition being subject to practical activity—such as acquisition or avoidance—be the definition of being an object of cognition (*jñānaviṣayatva*); for if that were so, the atoms (*dyaṇuka*) of a jar would absurdly become objects of the cognition of the jar, and pleasure and other internal states would absurdly fail to be objects of their own cognitions.
Nor should it be argued that the linguistic usage consisting in the employment of words such as "happy" with respect to pleasure and so forth constitutes [the proof of] the object;
for the employment of a word does not itself determine the object of cognition.

Since the employment of a word is preceded by the determination of the object of cognition, if the word were to determine the object, there would result the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

Nor is that [objecthood] a non-reality of cognition, because it is impossible for past and future things [to possess it], and because there is no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for its existence therein.
Therefore, that [objecthood] is simply the nature of cognition itself. Furthermore, the object consists of cognition, because it is perceived together with cognition, just like cognition itself.
The observation of the difference between a jar and a cloth, which are not perceived simultaneously, constitutes the supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*).
Nor should it be argued that "simultaneous perception" is unestablished because the cognition "this is a jar" does not have another cognition as its object;

for, since we observe the recollection of the cognition "the jar is known" at a later time, a prior experience is necessary, and thus one must admit that the cognition "this is a jar" has a cognition as its object.
He refines his own position by asserting that, just as cognitions such as dreams possess a form, all [cognitions] possess a form, and thus there is no object external to cognition.
(In reality, this is not the view of the Śūnyavādin,
but rather that of the Yogācāra, the Vijñānavādin.)
That is questionable;
for there is no evidence that blue and so forth constitute the nature of cognition, nor that cognition possesses the form of its own object,
and because the aforementioned inference is inconclusive.
Furthermore, there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*), because there is no identity between a jar and a cloth when they are perceived together.
Moreover, the object is not of the nature of cognition (*jñāna*).

This is because in a cognition whose object is the absence of cognition, it is impossible for that absence of cognition to be of the nature of cognition; because in a cognition whose object is persistence—as in "this is that very same thing"—it is impossible for that persistence to be of the nature of a momentary cognition; and because in a variegated cognition such as "this has many forms," it is impossible for multiple forms to exist in a single [cognition].

Furthermore, if the object were of the nature of cognition, then since there is a rule that the cognition of its being of the nature of cognition must be immediate (*aparokṣatva*), it would follow—just as in the case of inferential cognition—that its mediacy (*parokṣatva*) would be untenable.

Moreover, it is impossible for the past temporal relation, which is the object of an inference regarding past time, to be of the nature of a present cognition. Nor can it be argued that in that case, the object is simply a past cognition itself.
Since it is impossible for the state of being past to be a form of cognition,
one must necessarily state that the object of cognition is distinct from the cognition itself.
It was stated previously that this status of being an object consists in either being the recipient of the fruit produced by the cognition, or being eternally distinct [from it].
Furthermore, the example of one's own dream is not appropriate, because that too consists of external objects.
Therefore, since it is impossible to deny the external objects being experienced, there is no falsity regarding those objects at the moment they appear;
rather, it is [the cognition] produced by a defective cause that is sublated.
Maṇi, pp. 24–26.

Bālakrīḍā, p. 141: In the Śyena, it is stated, "The priests proceed wearing red turbans, red garments, and with the sacred thread suspended around the neck (nivīta).
On this point, there is the position that the archetypal upavīta is sublated by the nivīta.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the original (*prākṛta*) and the modified (*vaikṛta*). Vi. 10.4.1. [This applies] to what is accomplished by means of the *śyena* sacrifice;
or rather, it is a consideration of the *kura*.
And thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself becomes the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Vi. 10.4.1. In the *Śyena* sacrifice, the red turban and other such items belong to all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), not to the *udgātṛ*s alone.
Mīko., p. 3389; see the section titled "The Section on the Red Turban" (*lohitoṣṇīṣādhikaraṇa*).
In the Śyena sacrifice, the rule "the sacrificial grass (barhis) is made of śara-reeds" sets aside the kuśa grass.
Bhāṣya 10.4.1.9. Regarding the Śyena, it is heard in scripture: "The officiating priests proceed wearing red turbans, red garments, and with the sacred thread suspended around the neck (nivīta).

The Commentary states: In the archetype (prakṛti), there is the rule: "The nivīta is for men, the prācīnāvīta for the ancestors, and the upavīta for the gods; he suspends it over the left shoulder (upavyayate); thereby he makes it a state belonging to the gods."
Thus, it is obtained here by the rule of extension (*codaka*).
In this regard, there is a doubt: is there a cessation of the *upavīta* (wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder), or is there no cessation, but rather a combination?
What is the prima facie view? That there is its cessation; for the directly perceived *nivīta* (wearing it around the neck) sets aside the inferred *upavīta* obtained through the rule of extension.
Moreover, there is also a connection with the natural gender, as in the statement, "They proceed wearing the sacred thread around the neck" (*nivītāḥ pracaranti*).
This being the position reached, we reply: there is no exclusion; rather, there is a combination (*samuccaya*).
There is no connection with the indicative mark (liṅga) of the archetype (prakṛti) here.
Since the wearing of the sacred thread (upavīta) serves an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), how can it be understood that its function is fulfilled by the "suspended" mode (nivīta)?
Therefore, there is no connection with the indicative mark of the archetype.
Therefore, such a ritual refinement (karmasaṃskāra) would be additional in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti).
[This concludes] the Śyena section; the Śyena-nyāya is as follows: the statement "the priests are girded with the cord around the neck" (nivītā ṛtvijaḥ) is not an example [of this principle].
How so? Because there is no *upavīta* (sacred thread) in the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
It is neither directly perceived nor established by the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) that the *upavīta* applies to the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
Therefore, since the *śyena* sacrifice is not modeled upon the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it does not possess that [thread].
The maxim "Because it would be purposeless, [it applies] to its subsidiaries" (2.1.9.18) does not apply here. For the principal [act] is performed in the subsidiaries by implication;
and in this case, the *nivīta* is possible for the principal act itself.
Therefore, because their objects are distinct, there is a fixed rule for the *nivīta* and the *upavīta*.
Furthermore, no contradiction between the *nivīta* and the *upavīta* can be maintained, since both are possible through two garments. Therefore, they are to be used in combination.
Or let there be reflection.

Bhaṭṭa: As for the point raised here by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) regarding the *śyena* sacrifice—where, having raised the objection that the *nivīta* (worn around the neck), prescribed as a refinement of the agent who is a constituent of the performance (*prayoga*), might sublate the *upavīta* (worn over the left shoulder) which is obtained through extension (*atideśa*) and enjoined as being for the purpose of all rites, he established the conclusion (*siddhānta*) that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) because they serve different purposes—that [conclusion] is required [only] if the term has the sense of "beginning with this" (*asyādi*). Otherwise, since even in the case of *śrāddha* and other rites, there would be the possibility of combining the *upavīta* with the *prācīnāvīta* (worn over the right shoulder), and because it is impossible to combine the specific modes of wearing the three-stranded, nine-threaded sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) throughout one's life—which are enjoined as constituents of their respective rites under the names *upavīta*, *nivīta*, and so on—the [Commentator’s] position must be understood in the sense of "beginning with this."
In the Śyena sacrifice, one sacrifices the animals together;
and that coexistence resides only in the Savanīya animals belonging to the time of the Soma-pressing.
(Vi. 3.8.25). In the Śyena.
On the day of the Soma pressing (sutyā), all [rites] beginning with the offering of the *amiṣomapra-yana* are performed on that very day;
this is due to both direct scriptural statement (*vacana*) and extended application (*atideśa*).
Bhāṣya 5.1.6: In the Śyena sacrifice, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the Soma sacrifice applies, because the injunction is unmanifest (*avyakta-codanā*).
Bhāṣya 8.1.9.16: There is no connection between the Śyena sacrifice and the establishment of the fires (agnyādhāna).
The establishment pertains to the fires, and the fires pertain to the Śyena.
Bhāṣya 3.8.20.38: The Śyena rites have clarified butter as their primary substance.

VI. 3.8.21: Regarding the *haviḥ-navanīta* clarified butter used for the limbs of the Śyena sacrifice, it should be understood that it applies not only to the animal and cake offerings (*paśu-puroḍāśa*) belonging to the time of the Soma extraction (*sutyā-kāla*), but to all [rites] including the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and others.
3.8.22: The principle of the Śyena section (*śyenādhikaraṇa-nyāya*).
Sāhasrī, p. 847. The shape of the hawk (*śyenākṛti*): it is purely optional (*kāmyā*) in the Abhiplava sacrifice.

*Saṃkarṣa.* 2.1.40. See *Mīmāṃsākośa*, p. 48, for the section on the statement: “In the *abhimayana*, the falcon-shape is merely optional (*kāmya*)”; this section should be consulted. Because the various elements in the *śyena* sacrifice and others are obtained through extended application (*atideśika*), that which is established by the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) via extended application possesses greater force.

*Bhāṭṭadīpikā* 5.1.10: In the *śyena* and other sacrifices, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the *upavīta* (wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder) obtained through extended application with the *nivīta* (wearing it around the neck) prescribed as a direct injunction (*upadiṣṭa*).
10|4|1|9–2. See the section at Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2327, under the heading “of the Nāriṣṭha-homas and others which are extended by analogy” (ātideśika).

In the Śyena and other such sacrifices, the agent obtained through the designation (samākhyā) of the Audgātra and so forth has as its object the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), just like the archetypal subsidiaries.
Su. p. 1181. In the Śyena and other such sacrifices, there is a plurality of agents regarding the archetypal subsidiaries.

7|1|2|150-51. Rituals such as the Śyena sacrifice are not presented by injunction as things to be performed; for one engages in them solely out of a desire for the result. Indeed, their instruction is that "this is the means for one who desires to kill [an enemy]. (Ṛjuvimalā, p. 29). Because the Śyena and other malevolent rites have harmful results and consist of harm, they do not possess the nature of Dharma.

VI.1.12: Since there is no instruction regarding ritual details (*dharma*) within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Śyena and other sacrifices, those details are obtained through extended application (*atideśa*).
VI.7.1.9: Words such as "Śyena" are the names of sacrifices (*yāga-nāmadheya*).
VI.1.4.15: The maxim of the hawk and the pigeon (*śyenakapotīyanyāya*).
Just as a pigeon was caught by a hawk that had been watching it without being noticed, so too [this occurs] by chance, like a "hawk-and-palmyra" coincidence.
*Sāhasrī* 688: "One desiring heaven should pile the Śyenacit.
This is an injunction for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), based on the assumption of a subordinate quality (*guṇakalpanā*).
Bāla, p. 27: "One desiring heaven should pile the Śyena-cit" (Śyenacitaṃ cinvīta svargakāmaḥ).
Thus, the act of piling is for the sake of the fruit [of the sacrifice].
Saṃkarṣa 1.1.5: There is an extension (*atideśa*) of the properties of the Śyena [sacrifice] to the Iṣu sacrifice.

7|1|2| 13–16. See the section on *mīko.* p. 196, ‘*atideśaḥ iṣau śyenīyadharmāṇām*’. The collection of Śyena-ritual characteristics is extended (*atidiśyate*) to the sacrifice named *iṣu* by the rule: “The rest is the same as the Śyena” (*samānamitaracchyenena*). Vi. 7|1|2. The Śyena-principle: (1|4|15).

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, when various methods of chanting (svaras) from different Vedic branches are applicable according to the injunctions for the Agnihotra, those are set aside by the natural (prakṛta) accent in matters concerning the injunctions obtained from the Darśapūrṇamāsa, according to the Śyena-nyāya.
(Kāśikā 3.12.19, p.
324; Mīmāṃsākośa 496). [This refers to] the fruit of the Śyena sacrifice, and [the comparison] between the Śyena and the Vājapeya.
Since the fruit of the Śyena sacrifice, namely malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), is prompted by passion (*rāga*), it falls within the scope of the prohibition "one must not kill" (*na hiṃsyāt*).
(Bhāṭṭa 4.1.2, Section 2).
The Śyena sacrifice is not *dharma*.

If *niyoga* (the mandate), even when having desire as its governing factor, were to state the duty (*kartavyatā*) of the sacrifice, and that sacrifice—being a means to a result—could not be performed if the result were itself not a duty, then by implication *niyoga* itself would state the duty of the result as well. Consequently, regarding the result too, there would be an "implicative" (*aupādānikī*) activity prompted by the injunction; thus, the violence which is the result of the *śyena* sacrifice could not be prohibited by the rule "one shall not kill," because that prohibition pertains to the person's welfare (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, if one were to prohibit such implicative activity, there would follow the contingency of it being a duty, just as in the case of the rule "one shall not speak untruth."

Likewise, because its result is desired by persons who are not prohibited and is achievable, the injunction regarding the Śyena sacrifice and the like would not be for a non-beneficial purpose (*anartha*).
For that injunction is non-beneficial which has a prohibited result.

Furthermore, in the context of one who possesses a desire (*kāmādhikāra*), the injunction does not state that the sacrifice is something to be performed; rather, its status as something to be performed is established solely through the result itself.

Although the injunction (*niyoga*) is understood as that which is to be performed, and the sacrifice as its means, nevertheless, in the context of a desire-based entitlement (*kāma-adhikāra*), because the scripture culminates in the attainment of the desired fruit, it is not the injunction alone that impels the person toward action for its own sake. This is because the activity is prompted by passion (*rāga*), and the accomplishment of such activity is achieved through the result itself.

And thus, since the engagement in both the sacrifice and its fruit is not based on mere acquisition (*aupādānikī*), the prohibition of that [engagement] would not need to be made; therefore, the prohibition of the fruit of the *śyena* sacrifice is not untenable. Consequently, because it has a prohibited fruit, the injunction for the *śyena* and other such rites—though characterized by a Vedic command (*codanālakṣaṇa*)—is not Dharma; thus, nothing is established. (Ṛjuvimalā, p. 29). Even though the *śyena* sacrifice is prescribed in the Sāmaveda, it is not performed by the Udgātṛ alone; rather, like the Jyotiṣṭoma, various officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are its performers.
Ci. 3.1.23: In the Śyena sacrifice, twelve *mānas* of gold is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* rite, and twenty-four *mānas* at the *prāyaṇīyā*.

In the passage concerning the Śyena, the word "Śyena" is accepted as the name of the sacrifice—just like the name "Jyotiṣṭoma"—by resorting to a figurative application (*gauṇavṛtti*) based on the similarity indicated by the supplementary portion of the text (*vākyaśeṣa*), since it requires a basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
Parākrama [on Jaimini Sūtra] 4.1.23–52:
Regarding the Śyena and Vājapeya sacrifices, they are to be performed by all the officiating groups, beginning with the Adhvaryu.
In the Śyena and Vājapeya sacrifices, there is a plurality of performers with respect to the archetypal injunctions.
As before, due to the instruction of the Veda, they should exist at the end of the Veda according to that instruction.
Commentary: There is the *Śyena* sacrifice prescribed in the *Audgātra* section, and the *Vājapeya* in the *Ādhvaryava*.

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the constituent elements (*padārtha*) of the *Śyena* be performed by the *udgātṛ*s alone, and those of the *Vājapeya* by the *adhvaryu*s alone; or, in both cases, should they be performed by various [priests] according to their respective designations? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It is that they should be performed according to the Vedic instruction, which means according to the specific designations (*samākhyāna*).
As before:
just as the Adhvaryu performs the constituent acts because of the designation "Ādhvaryava," so too at the end of the Veda, they should be according to the instruction;
whatever act is taught in whichever Veda by its designation, that act must be performed by that very [priest].
It is taught there [in that Veda] along with its auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).
Therefore, the ritual acts (*padārtha*) must be performed by the *udgātṛ* priests in the Śyena sacrifice, and by the *adhvaryu* priests in the Vājapeya.

Or rather, this has been explained under the sūtra "In case of conflict between the subordinate and the principal, the connection is with the Veda of the principal because it exists for its sake" (3.1.19), wherein it was stated that the auxiliaries receive their designation according to the Veda of the principal.
Therefore, in the Śyena sacrifice, all the constituent elements (padārthas) that have been prescribed must be performed by the Udgātṛ priests.

Alternatively: "Because of the mention of 'that' (tad), it would be its own duty (svadharma), as manifested by the force of the qualification (adhikāra); [this applies] to the remainder along with the subsidiaries. Commentary: Because of the mention of "that" (tad)—meaning the adoption of the archetypal (prākṛta) duties—it would be connected with its own duties (svadharma) as they are obtained through the *środa* (the specific injunction). These are the duties associated with the Udgātṛs. In the case of the remaining rites, these duties are manifested together with their subsidiaries.
By the force of the injunction, it is heard [in scripture] that "one should perform [the rite] together with its auxiliary parts.
And those auxiliary parts are required in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
In that regard, there are no separate officiating priests (ṛtvij) for the Jyotiṣṭoma; rather, it forms a single syntactical unit with them.
But is it not the case that the designation is based on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), whereas the injunction (*codaka*) is inferential (*ānumānika*)?
It is replied: True, the designation is based on direct perception.
But that [inference] is worldly;
in that case, having inferred the Vedic word, there would be syntactic unity with it.
In the case of the *codaka*, however, there is syntactic unity with the directly perceived procedure (*itikartavyatā*), despite the remoteness [of the inference].
Therefore, the injunction (codaka) is more powerful.
As for what was said regarding "on account of the designation" (samākhyāna),
to that it is replied:
The unmanifest remains; it will be determined by the name (*samākhyā*).
Regarding that ritual act which is not obtained through the extended application (*codaka*), there will be a restrictive rule based on the name.

For example: in the *Śyena* sacrifice, "the *kaṇṭhakavita* [priests] pierce," meaning they will pierce the *udgātṛ*s; and in the *Vājapeya*, "the *upaṇa* [priests] cook," meaning the *adhvaryu*s will cook.

Or rather—it has been stated (at 3.1.29) and will be stated (at 5.1.10–18) that because it pertains to a later time, the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) is weaker than the extended application (*codaka*).
Furthermore, the primary designation (*pradhānasamākhyā*) depends upon the injunction of performance; thus, even though it is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), it is weak.
Moreover, as long as the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) have not been obtained through extended application, for what [action] would these [designations] determine the performers?

But when [the application] is already established, then since their connection with a specific performer is already determined and there is no further requirement for it, what will the name (samākhyā) accomplish?
Furthermore, in this case, there is no sublation of what is already established, because the name is more remote [from the object], as it requires the postulation of a scriptural basis (śruti).
For it has been stated that among means of knowledge whose source is already established, there is sublation of what is already established, but not for those whose source is yet to be postulated.
Therefore, by the mention of the "archetypal" (prakṛta), by virtue of its governing authority, it must have multiple performers just like the Jyotiṣṭoma.

And although even in the archetype there are multiple performers solely on account of the name (samākhyā), nevertheless, because the relationship is already established, the scriptural statement (śruti) of the injunction is equal [in force].
We show that whatever archetypal element arrives, its performer shall be determined by the names of the primary acts, according to the rule: "In the case of the remainder, it is unmanifested."
Because its state has not been established, the connection with the agent of the injunction must be something other than what is already established;
however, its object is not for the sake of right vision.
This is because [actions such as] piercing the throat and so forth are seen in the Veda designated as primary, or in another Veda.
If, first of all, that [action] belongs to that very [Veda], then their connection with the agent is established by the specific name alone, not by way of the primary sacrifice.
If, on the other hand, they are seen in another Veda, then even though they are directly perceived there, the same must hold true: the specific name is more powerful.

In this case as well, the principle from Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.12—that "there is another [rule] when there is a conflict between the subordinate and the primary"—is invoked. Consequently, since the Stotras, Śastras, and so forth are designated by the name *ādhvaryava* (pertaining to the Adhvaryu), it would follow that they must be performed by the Adhvaryu priest.
However, there is no such indicative mark here as there is in the case of the injunction "the morning pressing is slow" (*mandaṃ prātaḥsavanam*).
Therefore, in the case of the subsidiaries of the principal rite, one's own designation (*samākhyā*) is set aside.
However, that [name], being applied by way of connection with the agent as a mark of such a kind, grasps the primary act.
And it is not appropriate for the subsidiary acts to have names such as "Adhvaryava" through the medium of the primary act;
for they are not performed by means of the names "Adhvaryava" and so forth belonging to the primary acts, because they are to be performed by those who are subordinate [to the primary].
And how is it that that [activity] which is not engaged with the primary member (pradhānāṅga) abides in the subsidiary members (aṅga) by means of that [primary member]? [The answer is:

Because the designation (samākhyā) such as "Ṛgveda" applies without interruption even to the subsidiary members of the primary, and because there is the conventional expression therein that "it is performed by that."
And that [action] is indicated as being subject to the injunction by the mention of the primary yoga;

furthermore, there is the designation of "Adhvaryu" and so forth based on the order of recitation (*pāṭhaka*). Nor does anything arise here through any other [principle] than the subordination of the subordinate to the principal (*guṇamukhyavyatikrama*).
The birth of [the names] such as Kaṇṭhakāvita and Udana should be understood as being equal to that of the primary Veda.

And it is possible to say "the unmanifest is the remainder" by way of that very essence; for there is no designation (samākhyā) derived from the Pradhāna itself, as in the case of the Śyena and Vājapeya sacrifices, where words such as "Śyena" and "Śalā" [apply].
Because of the designation [of the Veda], when there is a difference from the primary Veda, the performers of the ritual elements appear according to their respective designations.
Vi— "The Śyena is stated in the Udgātṛveda; the Vājapeya is [stated] in the Yajurveda.
Should it now be performed by the Udgātṛ and others, or should the former [the Śyena] follow its original model?"
In the case of specific names and so forth, the injunction (codaka) indeed precedes the name;
here, the agents established in the archetype (prakṛti) are determined to be the reality.
Bhaṭṭa: In the Sāmaveda pertaining to the Udgātṛ, the Śyena sacrifice is heard of as possessing the characteristics of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

Therein, although various priests are obtained through the general injunction (*codaka*) of the archetype, they are set aside by the direct designation (*upadeśa*) of the name "Udgātra. Thus, among those [priests], the Udgātṛ alone is the performer.
For the name indeed serves to designate the performer.

Furthermore, the agent is a constituent part of the performance (*prayoga*), and the performance is enjoined as a single unit by the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) for the sake of the scripture; thus, even regarding those [subsidiaries] not explicitly mentioned, there is an injunction of the agent through the teaching [of the primary act].

Consequently, just as in the case of "they move about in water," where because water is the location, it is understood that the entire *bhāvanā* (productive operation) including its subsidiaries is the object [of the injunction], and thus sprinkling (*abhivāghana*) applies to the archetypal *prayāja* offerings and so forth, so it is in the present case as well.

Nor should it be argued that because the designation (*samākhyā*), even when heard in reference to the primary act alone, must have its scope extended to include the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) since it depends on the performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*), and because that injunction depends on the subsidiaries obtained through extension (*atideśa*), there can be no sublation of the plurality of agents established by the original injunction (*codaka*) which is the basis for that dependence. For even if the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is indeed heard, the water (*āpaḥ*) must likewise have its scope extended to the subsidiaries; thus, according to the reasoning stated above, it cannot be considered a sublater.

For the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) does not have the power to denote the substratum of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) along with the whole (*sāṅga-adhikaraṇatva*); rather, it denotes only the instrumentality of the principal action (*pradhāna-karaṇatva*). Since that [instrumentality] is untenable without being qualified by its constituent parts, the application to the constituent parts must indeed be inferred. Consequently, as in cases where the instruction regarding the *śara* grass and so forth is already established, it must be stated that even an inferred instruction sublates the extended application (*atideśa*). For this very reason, in cases such as the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns belonging to the primary sacrifice itself—which are found in another Veda—the attainment of a different performer occurs through the instruction in the form of a specific name (*viśeṣa-samākhyā*); there, the principal name (*pradhāna-samākhyā*), which would otherwise have to be inferred for the constituent parts, is sublated.

For this has indeed been described in the section concerning the transgression between the subordinate and the principal (*guṇamukhyavyatikramādhikaraṇa*, 3.1.2): "In the present case, because it is based on extended application (*atideśika*), the designation based on the principal (*pradhānasamākhyā*) alone possesses greater force. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the reply is as follows]: Here too, since that [designation] which relies upon the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) must be postulated with respect to the subsidiaries, it depends upon the extended application (*atideśa*) as its source of support (*upajīvya*). Furthermore, because the agent is already established by that [extended application] as qualified [by the action], there is no further need for an agent; thus, in the absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), the designation cannot give rise to a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). Even if it were to be postulated, since there is no production of new archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries, the designation does not have the power to sublate the archetypal agents.

Nor does it follow that [the injunction] would apply in that manner even in such a case; for [the connection] is directly perceived as being inseparable, and because the connection of those [subsidiaries] with the meaning of the verbal root is untenable, since through the instrumental case-ending one understands their connection with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) which has the whole (*avayavin*) as its instrument. Furthermore, since the *bhāvanā* lacks the quality of being produced (*utpādyatva*), it cannot be connected with that [instrument]; and since the performance (*prayoga*) is common to both the subsidiaries and the primary rite, there is no distinction in the subsequent requirement of place (*deśa*) via the medium of the *bhāvanā*. Thus, by the very teaching, just as in the case of the primary rite, there is no intention to connect [the place] with both [primary and subsidiary], and consequently, there is no sublation [of the place] even in the case of the subsidiaries.

For this very reason, in cases where there is no hearing of the instrumental case—such as in "yajñārthāḥ paśavo vai kāmyā iṣṭayastā upāṃśu kartavyāḥ" (the optional sacrifices for specific desires are indeed for the sake of sacrifice; they are to be performed in a low voice)—there is a syntactical connection with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of the principal action itself. And since that [instrumental] functions according to the principle of being a subordinate element (*aṅga*), it sublates the original accent (*svarādi*) and so forth only in the principal action.

In the present case, however, since the name (*samākhyā*) has as its object only the primary act (*pradhāna*), and since that [primary act] cannot be rendered meaningless because it is performed by the master (*svāmin*), its lack of an object would otherwise be untenable; thus, even if one were to somehow assume—by the principle of "uselessness leading to its subsidiaries" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*, 3.1.9)—that it refers only to the subsidiaries, there is no evidence for assuming that its object consists of those subsidiaries whose agents are already established by other means. Rather, on the strength of its capacity to produce such an assumption, it is concluded that the name refers only to those subsidiaries that are directly taught (*upadeśika*).

In reality, even for those [mantras], since their specific performers are established by their own individual designations (*samākhyā*), they fall within the scope of the primary designation; however, it should be understood that this [designation] applies to those mantras enjoined in the Veda and those mantras enjoined in the Smṛti inferred from the Veda, but not to others.
Therefore, there are indeed multiple performers in the case of the *prakṛta* (archetypal) rites.

Furthermore, since a designation is based merely on the fact of being recited [in a particular Veda], and lacks the basis of an injunction such as "the Ṛgveda is recited loudly" (*uccairṛcā*), and because the *prakṛta* mantras are recited in the Sāmaveda, they do not fall within the scope of that [designation].
Maṇḍana: "In the Śyena sacrifice, the ritual action belongs to all the officiating priests.

The application of the Śyena is characterized by the injunction (codanā)."

Because it has that as its object, because it is an object of knowledge, and because the injunction for the Śyena sacrifice has the prohibited act of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) as its fruit, it is established as a counter-example that [the Śyena] is harmful. (Ṛjuvimalā, p. 32) The word "Śyena" denotes a desire for victory.

It expresses the whole, not a part. Bhāṣya 9.4.25–27. Words such as *śyena* (hawk) and *śalā* (a type of wooden peg), when used in the sense of "to cut out," indicate the manner of extracting the whole.

The words *śyena*, *śalā*, and so forth [refer to the act of cursing]. See the section on the rule "The words *śyena*, *śalā*, and so forth, when used with the verb *abhi-gṛ* (to curse), denote the action" on page 341.
[Pāṇini Sūtra 9.4.25: "In the case of *śyena*, *śalā*, *kaśyapa*, *kavaṣa*, *seka*, and *parṇa*, there is the expression of the form [of the object], because of the proximity of what is well-known."
"May he seize him; make his breast like that of a hawk, his arms like those of a porcupine, his thighs like those of a tortoise, and his knees like those of a frog.
In this context, regarding those [objects] such as the hawk and the porcupine, there must be a reference to their form (*ākṛti*).
By these words, that respective form is expressed, because of the well-known proximity [of the word to its meaning].
The meanings of these words are well-established;
therefore, it is the form (*ākṛti*) that should be understood [by them].
For example, as in the statement, "Let these balls of flour be made into lions," the meaning is that they are to be given the form of lions.

In the same manner: the chest is to be made in the shape of a hawk; the two forearms and the two lower parts of the arms (prakoṣṭhas) are like sticks or rods; the two shoulders and the two upper parts of the arms (aṃsau) are shaped like tortoises; the two thighs (ūrus) are shaped like door-panels (kavaṣā); the two *sekaparṇas* are shaped like *karavīra* leaves; and the two knee-caps (*aṣṭhīvanta*) together with the shanks (*jaṅghe*)—this is the meaning.
Such is the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*).
Or rather, [the sacrifice] must be the whole [animal], because it exists as such.

For it is recited: "Fashion his breast like a hawk (śyena), his forearms like śalā [reeds], his shoulders like kaśyapas [tortoises], his thighs like kavaṣas [door-leaves], and his knee-joints like sekaparṇas [karavīra leaves].

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that these words—*śyena*, *śalā* (meaning reeds), *kaśyapa* (meaning tortoise), *kavaṣa* (meaning door-leaves), and *sekaparṇa* (meaning karavīra leaves)—convey the respective shapes [of those parts].
Setting aside that [view] with the word "but" (vā), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
words such as "hawk" (*śyena*) do not denote a shape (*ākāra*), but rather denote "entirety" (*kārtsnya*), the state of being complete.
The meaning of "Make his breast like a hawk" is: "Make the breast of this sacrificial animal entirely [like a hawk]," and so forth.
This being the case, if the objects such as the breast and so forth were [denoted] by their own nature, then they would have to be extracted exactly as they are shaped;
however, if the words denoted the shape, there would be a distortion of the breast and other parts, and thus a contradiction of the injunction (*codanā*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that words such as "śyena" denote the whole [of the sacrificial act].

(Question: "But what is the fault in performing the ritual action according to the principle that 'those two shoulders which have the form of a hawk [are to be removed], those two shoulders which have the form of a dart [are to be removed]'? (Answer: Because the *abhigū* [mantra] has that as its purpose.
He states another reason for this very point:
because the *abhigū*, i.e., the *abhigū* mantra, has that as its purpose, meaning it is intended for the removal of all the limbs."
For this very reason, at the end [of the section], it is stated: "Make every limb of this animal complete; no limbs should be left deficient.

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that words such as *śyena* (hawk) and others denote the entirety of the breast and other parts. This is discussed in the section beginning with "The hawk, the *śalā*, and so forth" (9.4.25), where it is explained that through the carving of the breast and other procedures, a resemblance to a hawk must be produced by means of the mantra: "Make his breast a hawk," and not otherwise.
The *śravaṇas* (mixings) [number] 3966; the *Śrīsūkta*.
Regarding the *śravaṇas*, since there is no visible benefit, an invisible refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *soma* through its mixing with *soma* is accepted.
Bhāṣya 9.4.12.47. "But because the *śrayaṇas* (pourings) are something unprecedented (*apūrva*), their injunction must be for the purpose of offering."

In the Agniṣṭoma, it is heard in scripture: "He mixes the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa with milk, that for the Aśvins with groats, that for Hariyojana with parched grains, that for Śukra with gold, and that for Pālīvata with clarified butter.

Since the mixing (*śrayaṇa*) of milk, groats, parched grains, and so forth in the Soma sacrifice is *apūrva*—that is, not established by any other means of knowledge—it must be enjoined as an act of offering (*pradāna*). And because they are to be offered, the ritual properties (*dharma*) pertaining to an offering must be performed.
Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that the acts such as separating the calf [from the mother cow] and so forth must be performed upon the milk used for mixing (śrayaṇa).

However, the words "or it is a subordinate factor (guṇa), because it is for the purpose of mixing" refute the prima facie view that "since it is stated in the Agniṣṭoma, 'He mixes the cup for Mitra-Varuṇa with milk,' the properties of the material to be offered (pradeyadharma) must be performed upon the milk, because it is intended for offering."
This milk is not a substance to be offered; rather, it is for the purpose of *śrayaṇa*, that is, for the purpose of mixing.
Since the milk serves the purpose of mixing with the Soma, it is merely an accessory (*guṇa*).
Therefore, the ritual properties pertaining to the offering (*pradāna-dharma*) should not be performed upon this milk.
And because [the mixture] is not specified as such.

Regarding the statement, "In the Agniṣṭoma, one mixes the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa with milk," the author states another reason for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the ritual properties (*pradeyadharma*) pertaining to the sacrificial substance (*pradeya*) need not be performed upon the milk.
When milk is mixed with Soma, it serves as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the Soma.
The milk is subordinate in the act of mixing;
because it is not designated as being connected with a deity, there is an absence of such designation.
That [milk] is what is designated in the mixing.

Therefore, that milk is connected with the properties of the substance to be offered (*pradeyadharma*), because of the primacy of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). In the passage "In the Agniṣṭoma, he mixes [the offering] for Mitra-Varuṇa with milk," the accusative case-ending in the word *maitrāvaruṇam* indicates its primacy; thus, it has the cup for Mitra-Varuṇa as its primary referent, which in turn has the Soma as its primary substance.
In the mixing with milk, Soma alone is intended;
the milk is for the sake of Soma;
Soma is the primary element.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the ritual duties pertaining to the offering—such as the driving away of the calves and so forth—should not be performed in that milk.
Furthermore, this is because of the explanatory passage (arthavāda), since that is its purpose.

When it is stated in the Agniṣṭoma, "He mixes [the Soma] for Mitra and Varuṇa with milk," he states another reason for the conclusion that the offering-related duties should not be performed in that milk.
"He, Mitra, said, 'Mixing Soma for me with milk alone,'" is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the mixing (*śrayaṇa*), because that [milk] is for the sake of that [Soma].
The ablative case is used with the elision of the suffix *lyap*.
This occurs with the intention that "being for the sake of that" means "being for the sake of the Soma."
It was not stated by the mixed [text] that "milk may be my light," but rather that they should prepare the Soma with milk.
Therefore, the mixing (śrayaṇa) is for the sake of the Soma;
consequently, the ritual properties pertaining to the offering (pradāna-dharma) should not be performed upon the milk.
Furthermore, because it exists for the sake of a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), it should therefore be subordinate.

Regarding the statement in the *Agniṣṭoma*, "He mixes the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa with milk," the author states another reason for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the ritual properties of the offering (*pradāna-dharma*) are not to be performed upon the milk.

Because this statement—"He mixes the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa with milk"—exists within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Soma-preparatory rites, it is understood that the mixing with milk is a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the Soma.
For this reason, as well as for the reasons previously stated, milk and Soma should be subordinate and auxiliary.
Therefore, the ritual duties pertaining to the offering (*pradāna-dharma*)—such as the driving away of the calves and so forth—should not be performed with that milk.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
In certain cases, such as "he mixes the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa with milk," the properties of the material to be offered (*pradeyadharma*) do not apply.
Bhāṣya 9.4.145–50. When a cognition has been produced once by a single hearing, a second hearing occurs for the purpose of [conveying] a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).
Bhāṣya 3.1.1.0. The ancestral rite (*śrāddha*).
"Just as eating at the home of one who lacks faith, or likewise abstaining from meat,
is prescribed for the sake of spiritual welfare and is consistent with dharma, it is not prohibited in all circumstances."
Indeed, within the ten-day period, the ancestral rite (śrāddha) is strictly prohibited;
however, according to some, the single-offering rite (ekoddiṣṭa) is always permitted, but never the ancestral rite (pārvaṇa).

In that regard, the rule regarding eating at the houses of those who lack faith is understood to apply specifically to one's own kin (svagotra). (This applies always, both before and after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite; *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* is the ancestral rite.)

Vākyapadīya 1.3.4, p. 191: The prohibition of sexual intercourse during *śrāddha* ceremonies, vows, and the like pertains solely to the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*); the prohibition found in the Smṛtis and other texts regarding the ritual context (*ṛtvartha*) is distinct.
Bālambhaṭṭī, p. 31: "For even one who is weak attains equal fortune if he is constantly industrious"—this is the maxim cited by Bhāravi.

Therefore, whether a substance is explicitly mentioned in the scripture or not is not the determining factor for its inclusion in the injunction.
(Regarding the acceptance [of a term] according to its etymological derivation):

Vārttika 3.1.7.14, p. 709. When both the etymological meaning (*yaugika*) and the conventional meaning (*rūḍha*) are obtained through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the principle is that the conventional meaning takes precedence.

Whatever fault there is in the abandonment of what is heard (śruti), that same fault exists in the postulation of what is not heard.

(Śābarabhāṣya 3.3.7.14, p. 846; 3.4.17.50; 10.1.6.15, 16). Regarding *śrutārthāpatti*—as for the distinction between "presumption from what is heard" (*śrutārthāpatti*) and "presumption from what is seen" (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*), see the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* (Mīmāṃsākōśa, p. 663) and the Śāstra texts.
*Śrutārthāpatti* never occurs among animals, because it is dependent upon the acquisition of linguistic convention (*śabdanyutpatti*).

*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 89: Presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) is of two kinds: worldly and Vedic. *Bālapriyā*, p. 8: Presumption based on what is heard is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," the relationship between the goal and the means for the one desiring heaven is heard [in the text]; this cannot be established without postulating the *apūrva*. (Ke. The direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is unable to bring about what is to be accomplished [since origination (*utpatti*) is required]. (Ṭup. 9.1.1751). The direct Vedic statement, which is denotative, is fivefold, according to the distinction between verbal roots (*dhātu*), nominal stems (*prātipadika*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*).
Bāla, p. 41. Śruti:

"There is a certain *śruti* that is denotative (*abhidhātrī*), another that is applicatory (*viniyojakī*), and likewise a third called the injunctive (*vidhātrī*); the actual usage [of words] is based upon these."
The hearing of the root and the suffix possesses the capacity to denote their respective meanings;
the word and the case-endings possess the capacity for application (viniyojakatva);
and the optative (liṅ), the injunctive (leṭ), the gerundive (tavya), and the fifth tense (the imperative) possess the capacity for injunction (vidhi).

Vārttika 3.1.7.13, p. 700. 🔗 *Śruti* has been stated in the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) sūtra of the *Graha-adhikaraṇa* as the specific cause for the application [of mantras] to acts such as threshing, according to the rule: "The one [mantra] is to be used for the one [act], because of its connection with the *śruti*" (3.1.7.13).
Su. p. 1191. 🔗 *Śruti*.
Direct *śruti* is stronger than indirect *śruti*.
For example, the direct statement regarding ghee (*ghṛtaśruti*) is stronger than the direct statement regarding axle-wood (*akṣaśruti*).

Vārttika 3.1.7.4, p. 840. Direct statement (*śruti*) is stronger than established practice (*ācāra*). Kaṇikā, p. 405. Even an inferred direct statement is stronger than a perceptible indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Or [as stated] on page 841, Vārttika 3.1.7.4: "Indeed, in this context (among *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth), *śruti* alone is the primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); the validity of the others, however, is like that of *smṛti*, being mediated by inference from *śruti*.

That [*śruti*], moreover, is established as sixteenfold in accordance with the factors constituting the means of apprehension" (page 830). The *śruti* is the accusative case ending in the phrase "the *gārhapatya* [fire] for Indra."
The cause of application (*viniyoga*) has been stated [at Bhāṣya 3.4.14.11]. Direct statement (*śruti*) is stronger than order (*krama*). [Vārttika 3.17.14, p. 836].
Direct statement (*śruti*)—which is the primary among the means of proof for indicating order—is the authority regarding order.

*Bālakrīḍā*, p. 8: Direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is the authority that indicates the sequence [of performance]. *Arthasaṃgraha*, p. 13: In cases where there is a conflict with meaninglessness (*ānarthakyapratighāta*), direct Vedic statement is set aside by the context (*prakaraṇa*).
*Bālakrīḍā*, p. 145: Furthermore, direct Vedic statement is stronger than the general injunction (*codaka*).
"One should perform [the rite] by means of the characteristic mark" is the direct Vedic statement (*pratyakṣā śrutiḥ*);
"One should perform it by means of the name" is the extended application (*codaka*).
Bhāṣya 10.4.12, Section 2. It has already been established that the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) overrides both indicative power (*liṅga*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*).

10|6|13. Śruti is fourfold: injunction (*vidhi*), prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), denotative (*abhidhātrī*), and applicatory (*viniyoktrī*). Bāla. p. 9. Śruti is threefold: injunctive (*vidhyātrī*), denotative (*abhidhātrī*), and applicatory (*viniyoktrī*). Mīmāṃsā. Śruti is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the knowledge of Dharma [as one of the various sources].
Maṇi, p. 13: *Śruti* (as a means of proof for order) is a conventional word that conveys sequence through its function;
it consists of words such as *atha*.
Bhaṭṭa, 5.1.2, p. 154: *Śruti* is an independent utterance.

That verbal cognition which, being independent and not contingent upon anything else, generates a cognition of an object, is the *śruti* (direct statement) with respect to that object. *Śruti* is more powerful than *prakaraṇa* (context).

For example, the recitation (*anuvacana*) enjoined by the rule "One desiring stability should recite twenty-one [verses]" is part of the context of the Darśa sacrifice; however, it is set aside by the status of "stability" made known through the genitive *śruti* in the phrase "of one desiring stability" (*pratiṣṭhākāmasya*), which applies specifically to the *sāmidhenī* verses.

"In the case of two sacrificers, one should employ the *pratipad* [verse] beginning with 'For you two are the lords of heaven' (*yuvam hi sthaḥ svarpatī*),"—by this, the status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Jyotiṣṭoma, which is established by the context (*prakaraṇa*), is set aside because it is understood from the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) that the verse is to be recited for a pair. Direct scriptural statement is more powerful than context. (Mīmāṃsā-bhāṭṭālaṃkāra, p. 153). Śruti is stronger than context. (Bhāṣya 2.2.12, 2.4.12, 3.1.17–19, 3.4.14–15; Vārttika 3.17.24, p. 835; 3.9.19; Sucaritamiśra, p. 1296; Vivaraṇa 3.14). This is Śruti.
Those syllables which are perceived directly and are employed [in a ritual application] are called *śrutiśruti*.

However, where syllables that are not themselves injunctive (*aniyojaka*) are perceived directly, and injunctive syllables are inferred through the force of the sense (*arthāpatti*), there the [inferential means such as] *liṅga* and so forth come into play.
Vārttika 3.1.7.14, p. 830. By the power of the *śruti* of the suffix (*pratyayaśruti*), the *śruti* of the word (*padaśruti*) is sublated.
Su. 1.2.130, p. 92. Direct Assertion (Śruti). That meaning of a word which is understood from the mere hearing of the word itself is understood through direct assertion.
Hearing is *śruti*.

Bhāṣya 3.17.14, p. 825: Direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is stronger than indicative power (*lakṣaṇā*). Bhāṣya 1.2.1, p. 23; Duṣaṇa 7.1.11, p. 129; 10.1.12: Direct Vedic statement is not to be set aside by indicative power.
Bhāṣya 7.2.136: Direct Assertion (śruti) is more powerful than Indicative Power (liṅga).

Regarding the statement, "One worships the Gārhapatya fire with a verse addressed to Indra," the verse "kadācana starīrasi" is [addressed] to Indra by way of Indicative Power; however, it serves for the worship of the Gārhapatya fire by way of Direct Assertion, not for the worship of Indra.
Mīmāṃsā: Direct Assertion is more powerful than Indicative Power.

The lack of authority of *liṅga* (indicative power) results from its intervention between the communication of its own denotation and its application, due to the operations of determining its capacity and postulating a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
This is because such intervention does not exist in the case of a directly perceived *śruti*.
[Vi. 3.17] *Śruti* is stronger than *liṅga*.

Bhāṣya 3.1.7.14, p. 823: A *śruti* inferred from an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is understood—by virtue of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)—to be employed solely for the purpose of manifesting the action (and not for the sake of a result). Vārttika 3.1.4.135: *Śruti* is more powerful than syntactical connection (*vākya*). The fact that redness (*āruṇya*) is subordinate to the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*)—which is established through syntactical connection—is set aside by the direct *śruti* [indicating] its subordination to the purchase (*kraya*).
"He buys Soma with a ruddy, one-year-old [cow]. (Mīmāṃsā-bhāṭṭālaṃkāra, p. 152). Direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is more powerful than syntactical connection (*vākya*).

For an injunctive *śruti*, being unimpeded by anything else, establishes its status as an injunction precisely within the *bhāvanā* of the verbal root-meaning due to their proximity, since it finds scope there where [the action] has not yet been established. This *śruti* sets aside the incidental character (*prāsaṅgikatva*) produced by the authority known as "position" (*sthāna*)—as in the cases "he sacrifices the *samidhs*" and "he sacrifices to *tanūnapāt*"—and postulates a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) characterized by being something to be enjoined. If that injunction follows the *śruti*, it determines a distinct ritual act; if, however, it follows proximity (*saṃnidhi*), then it is not a distinct ritual act.
Vārttika 2.2.12, p. 470: *Śruti* consists of injunction (*vidhi*), application (*viniyoga*), and direct denotation (*abhidhāna*).

Or [it may be said]: *Śruti* (direct statement) is more powerful than *samākhyā* (name/designation).

In the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is a mantra recited first which, because it lacks a clear indicative mark (*liṅga*) as a qualifier of the action, has its application determined by the independent sequence and context. Regarding the statement, "One worships the Gārhapatya fire with [the verse] addressed to Indra" (*aindryā gārhapatyamupatiṣṭhate*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because the *taddhita* suffix occurs in the initial word (*upakrama*), it possesses greater force than the *kāraka*-case ending. However, even though predominance (*prādhānya*) is the meaning of the *taddhita* suffix insofar as it is what is to be manifested, this predominance—being a qualifier—is not presented by the *taddhita* suffix itself; therefore, that entity does not possess a distinct status characterized by being a primary scriptural mention (*mukhyaśruti*). Furthermore, predominance is not the meaning of the suffix in the sense of being the desired object (*īpsitatva*) that constitutes a subordinate factor (*aṅga*); rather, like the *bhāvanā*, it is merely the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the verbal cognition produced by the words.

Therefore, since [the object] is desired as the primary factor according to what has been stated, its application (*viniyoga*) would be understood through the direct statement of the nominal suffix (*taddhita-śruti*) by characterizing it as such; thus, the direct statement of the *kāraka* (case-role) is weaker.

Furthermore, other causes for weakness have already been examined in the section concerning Indra (*aindrādhikaraṇa*)—they are largely established here because they are clearly similar to those cases.
Thus, it is established that when there is a conflict with a direct statement (*śruti*), the direct statement of the *kāraka* is stronger.

Even when there is a conflict between two *kāraka-śrutis* (grammatical indications of case-role), their relative strength—such as that based on the relationship between the general and the particular—must be understood from examples such as "He divides the *āgneya* into four parts" and "He divides the *puroḍāśa* into four parts.

Likewise, regarding subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*), even when there is a conflict with a *vijātīya-śruti* (a scriptural indication of a different class), the weakness of the *kāraka-śruti* compared to the *pada-śruti* (the syntactic word-indication) in cases such as "One should sacrifice with Soma" has been explained in the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, because both are singular.

When there is a conflict with a *samānajātīya-śruti* (a scriptural indication of the same class), in the very same *padahoma*, the *āhavanīya* fire is set aside by the *pada* through the force of the locative *śruti*.
Thus, the relative strength and weakness [of conflicting authorities] in the face of a contradiction with *śruti* has been described (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad 3.2.7–14, pp. 250–251).

Regarding a contradiction with a *śruti* of a different class, in cases such as "one should sacrifice with *soma*," even though there is a *śruti* of syntactic relation (*kāraka-śruti*) based on the unity of the case-role, it is weaker than the *śruti* of word-order (*pada-śruti*).
This is because the inference of a *śruti*—namely, the tradition (*smaraṇa*) of the learned three *varṇas*—is characterized by its dependence on the impossibility [of the meaning otherwise].
Or rather:

The sequence of the primary order of the section on ritual performance (*pravṛttikāṇḍa*) consists of the sequence of extended application (*atideśa*), direct statement (*śruti*), purpose (*artha*), and textual recitation (*pāṭha*).
This is an investigation of the six means of proof, beginning with direct statement (*śruti*).

The objects of the senses (*viṣaya*) are also primary entities (*pradhāna*), while the agent (*kartṛ*) is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). For one who performs the performance according to each primary entity, the sequence (*krama*) is indeed established.
Therefore, even those [factors] need not be considered;
rather, the rule of sequence is what is being considered.

*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 5.1.2.12: Because of the remoteness from the direct Vedic statement (śruti) and its meaning, each subsequent factor among the indicators such as direct statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), and so forth, is sublated by the preceding one.

Or [as stated] at Vārttika 3.1.7.14, page 830: "For that which is understood through direct audition (śruti) is understood from the hearing [of a word], whereas that which is understood through a sentence (vākya) involves the connection with another word. And direct audition is more powerful than a sentence.
Also, Bhāṣya 6.1.5.22: "And when direct audition is possible, one should not resort to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā)."

Vārttika 1.2.120: "When direct statement (*śruti*) is possible, syntactical connection (*vākya*) does not apply; it applies only when direct statement is not possible. Bhāṣya 3.1.7.14, p. 714: "Direct statement and the other [means of proof] are the applicators (*viniyojaka*) of the subordinate (*śeṣa*) by means of establishing its subservience to that purpose (*tādarthya*); therefore, a definition must be commenced for the sake of distinguishing them. Vārttika 3.1.2.14, p. 658: "In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), only the first three—direct statement and the others—are the causes for application by way of establishing subservience to that purpose."

Su. Pṛ. 1192: Direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof, having been extended [from the archetype] by transfer (*atideśa*), are sublated in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) by direct *śruti* and the others that are explicitly present. Vā. 3.1.7.14, p. 841: Direct statement and the others, establishing a relationship through their own inherent capacity, fix the injunction upon the specific details of the ritual elements already established;
they are said to be the authority regarding the fact of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*).
Kaṇikā, p. 384: By means of direct scriptural statements (*śruti*) and the like, there is the sublation of inferential [indicators] by other inferential [indicators].

For example, in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), by means of the direct scriptural statements and the like that employ the *prayāja* and other offerings through inference, there is the sublation of the inferential scriptural statements and the like that would otherwise employ them in the *paśupuroḍāśa*.
Bāla, p. 146: By means of direct scriptural statements and the like, there is the sublation of inferential scriptural statements and the like.

Just as in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice and others, by the direct Vedic text (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) "the sacrificial grass is made of reeds" (*śaramayaṃ barhiḥ*), the inferred Vedic text (*anumānika-śruti*) "he places the oblations on the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣi havīṃṣyāsādayati*) [is set aside]. (p. 146) Furthermore, the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) is determined solely by means of proof such as direct Vedic text; the principal element (*śeṣin*) is indicated by a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), and not by the word "internal" (*antrīya*).
(That which occurs in the absence of something else is not invariably concomitant with it.
Vārttika 3.1.1, p. 652. The capacity of *liṅga* (indicative mark) and the others to be sublated by *śruti* (direct statement) and the rest.
Viśeṣa 3.1.12. [The conflict] of *śruti* and the others, which are inferential, with *liṅga* and the others, which are perceptual.

Bāla, p. 146: Among the means of proof such as direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest, each preceding one operates independently of the subsequent ones and is therefore stronger; however, each succeeding one, whose authority depends upon the preceding, is unable to sublate that very [preceding] one.
For the authority of indicative power (*liṅga*) and the rest is not determined by inferring a direct statement.

Vārttika 3.1.7.14, p. 830: Regarding the relative strength and weakness of direct statement and the rest: "That which is to be attained through the pursuit of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) and that which is established merely by its own presence..."
When two people both ascend to attain one and the same fruit,
yet one stands upon a staircase while the other remains on the ground—
and the obstacle for both is equally real and there is no difference between them— [then the result follows].

For when there are two contradictory means for attaining a single result, once that result has been secured by the first, the latter becomes redundant. Therefore, although the capacity of each [means] is established individually, otherwise [it would not be so].
"Nevertheless, in the case of the simultaneous occurrence [of multiple means of proof], there is the rejection of the weaker one.
(Thus it occurs regarding application through *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth.
3|1|7|14, p. 834. Now, the relative strength and weakness of all six—*śruti* and the others—is being investigated.

Page 822, 3|1|7|14: It is accepted that when all [means of proof], beginning with direct statement (*śruti*), are obstructed by purposelessness (*ānarthakya*), they may be sublated even by weaker [means]. For example: although rice (*vrīhi*) and other grains attain the status of being subordinate (*śeṣitva*) toward acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) by virtue of direct statement, this is set aside; rather, there will be a connection based on their being means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*), which takes precedence over the context (*prakaraṇa*). Page 833, 833: Sublation of what has not yet been established (*aprāptabādha*) regarding direct statement and the others.
Vārttika 3.1.7.14, p. 861: Direct perception (pratyakṣa) based on scripture (*śruti*) and so forth is sublated by inference (*ānumānika*) through indicative marks (*liṅga*) and other means.
Vārttika 3.1.7.14, p. 841: An investigation into the conflict or non-conflict between the triad beginning with *śruti* and the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Vārttika 3.4.11 and 3.4.12: The section (*peṭikā*) concerning *śruti* and the other means of proof.
3|1|7|14. Subservience (*śeṣatva*) will be established solely through the means of valid cognition such as direct statement (*śruti*).
Vārttika 3|1|7|14, p. 716. An investigation into the six means of valid cognition, such as direct statement;
therein, the investigation of context (*prakaraṇa*) is treated in detail.
In that very context, the determination of the six types of doubt is presented.
Furthermore, scripture (*śruti*) is fourfold: injunction (*vidhi*), prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), denotative (*abhidhātrī*), and applicatory (*viniyogī*).
Indicative power (*liṅga*) is twofold: the capacity of the word (*śabda-sāmarthya*) and the capacity of the meaning (*artha-sāmarthya*).

The capacity of the word (*śabdasāmarthya*) is also twofold: the capacity of a mantra to manifest a meaning inherent in the ritual action (*karmasamavetārthaprakāśanasāmarthya*), and the capacity to enter into a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyopagamanasāmarthya*). Of these, the latter was treated by the author of the *Bhāṣya* in the section on the conflict between *liṅga* and *vākya* (3.1.7–14, p. 847), while the former was discussed in the section on the conflict between *liṅga* and *vākya*. [Regarding the former, he said: "Now, just as there is an investigation into the six means of proof—beginning with direct statement (*śruti*)—concerning the mantra ‘*syone te*’ [in relation to the act of spreading the sacrificial grass]... (3974).
The capacity for syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with what follows is precisely the capacity for connection (*sāmarthya*). And this capacity is called an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Therefore, when the sentence is split, it is the indicative mark itself that becomes sublated. This is true.
This also is an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Indeed, this very indicative mark, characterized as such, pertains precisely to a remote object.
Because of its syntactic unity with the indicative mark, it therefore possesses the capacity for denotation.
Then follows the meaning of the scripture, according to the passage: "Thus, there is remoteness of meaning" (Bhāṣya, p.
850). Furthermore, a sentence is of two kinds: the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) and the intermediate sentence (*avāntaravākya*).
As it has been said: "In the cognition of their own meaning, compounds have no need for words such as *ahni* or *gvi*;
however, the status of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) arises again through their conjunction."
Thus [Vārttika 3.4.134, p. 366].

In that context, this refers to the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*), because it is distinct from the permanent injunctions (*nitya-vidhi*) due to its being constructed; for, according to the statement of the Vākya, the principal injunction itself is the injunction of performance.

The second [type] consists of such [injunctions] as "He offers the *samidh* oblations" (*samidho yajati*) and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta*).
