Even the intermediate sentence (*avāntaravākya*) is of two kinds: injunction (*vidhi*) and mantra.

As for the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), although it lacks [independent] purport, it is designated separately merely by virtue of its capacity to convey the sentence-meaning through the indication of praise (*stuti*).
Context (*prakaraṇa*) is also of two kinds: the major context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) and the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).
In this regard, the first [type of injunction] pertains to the primary [act], while the second pertains to either the primary or its subsidiary.

Likewise, the first [type] pertains to both the original material (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*), and the same applies to the second. Among these, that which belongs to the original material is one whose procedure is not transferred [from elsewhere], such as the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and other such sacrifices.
However, the context of the modification (*vikṛti*) occurs both through explicit indication (*saṃdarśana*) and through non-indication (*asaṃdarśana*).

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Śāstradīpikā* (p. 246) in the section concerning the relative strength of the order (*krama*) and the procedure (*prakaraṇa*), as follows: "In the *Rājasūya*, [it is said] 'For one who has consecrated himself for the *Rājasūya*... and 'One who performs the *Rājasūya* attains a full lifespan'"; thus, it arises from explicit indication.

Even in the absence of a direct statement (*asaṃdeśe*), the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) prevails over modification (*vikṛti*). For example, where something is enjoined in a modified rite (*vikṛti*) by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of an archetypal (*prākṛta*) action, that is taken as belonging to that [archetype’s] context, such as: "At each *prayāja* offering, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* grain. Likewise, for the *Ahīna* sacrifices and the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), there is the number twelve, as in: "There are twelve initiations (*dīkṣā*) and twelve *upasad* days. This has been stated in the section on Direct Assertion and Indicative Mark (*śrutiliṅgādhikaraṇa*): "Thus, by means of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) [of the archetype], the action of the *upasad* is intended..."
It is grasped as the manner of performance by virtue of being an injunction for twelve-foldness.
Thus (Vārttika, p. 136).

And here, because it is stated "with reference to an action," it is said that in the case of a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) where a genus (*jāti*) or other property is enjoined with reference to a substance—as in "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is made of *udumbara* wood"—the context (*prakaraṇa*) is not sublated.
For this very reason, it was also stated in the *Citrā-adhikaraṇa*: "Without connection to an intermediate action [as provided] by the sentence..."
The qualities, substances, and modes of being are understood as the actions under discussion.
Thus [it is stated in] Vārttika 1.4.2.2 (p. 139).

Nor should it be argued that in the sentence concerning the *audumbara* wood, the connection with the implied tying (*niyojana*) is established by the syntactical force of the sentence (*vākyīya*), because the avoidance of meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*) is accomplished through proximity (*saṃnidhi*) alone.
Furthermore, the tying of the *audumbara* species for the purpose of fashioning the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is established through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*).

Otherwise, even acts such as threshing would result in being enjoined by the sentence for something other than the sacrifice indicated by the *vrīhi* grain (such as another substance). However, in cases where the connection with an action is established through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), only there will the injunction be stated to extend as far as the connection with the action indicated [by the substance], as in the case of the *parṇamayī* sentence.

Thus, it should be understood that in the Vārttika and other texts to be cited later—where it is said that "that which is enjoined by way of reference to a primary act" and so forth—the word *aṅga* refers exclusively to the action.

Regarding the "enclosure" (*saṃdaṃśa*), the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*)—as in the case of the *rājasūya* sacrifice—is not merely a matter of explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*) for the sake of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*); rather, because the enclosure is of many kinds, it is manifold.

For instance: [1] even that which is heard in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) as unconnected, yet enjoined by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of an archetypal injunction (*prākṛta*), is also grasped within the context; this is because, due to the inclusion of the context between two preceding and subsequent archetypal injunctions, there is no interruption of that context in the interim.

[2] Likewise, when something unconnected is enjoined prior to a modification (*vikṛti*), and then something else is enjoined by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to the archetypal (*prakṛta*) elements before that [unconnected item], that which was previously unconnected is understood as belonging to the context of the modification.

[3] Similarly, when something unconnected has been enjoined immediately after a modification, and then something is enjoined by way of reference to the archetypal elements, that which was previously unconnected is understood as belonging to the context.

These three types of *meda* (separation) are stated in the *Balāmalādhikaraṇavārtika*: "But in that modification (*vikṛti*) where some archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiary (*aṅga*) is mentioned and a modified (*vaikṛta*) subsidiary is enjoined either before or after it, there [the latter] will indeed become a subsidiary grasped by the requirement of 'how' (*kathaṃbhāva*), as it is understood from its recitation within that context" (2.3.7.14, p. 852).
This very *vārtika* has been interpreted by Someśvara as referring to the subsequent type of *meda*.

Similarly, if something previously enjoined as unconnected [to the archetype] is later enjoined by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the modified rite (*vikṛti*), that which was unconnected is taken as belonging to the context of the modified rite. Likewise, if after the modified rite some unconnected thing has been enjoined, and then something is enjoined by way of a restatement of the modified rite, that which was previously unconnected is taken as belonging to the context.
These two types of cases are stated implicitly, having already been considered regarding the inclusion within the context of what is enjoined by way of a restatement of the modified rite.

An investigation into the six means of valid knowledge, such as direct audition (*śruti*), etc., [is presented]. [The conflict] occurs between the order of direct audition (*śruti*) and the order of sequence (*krama*). Examples for these two types of conflict, as well as for the three types previously mentioned, are to be sought. For instance, after prescribing the *Sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice, and having prescribed the three modified (*vaikṛta*) mantras beginning with "Thou art firm" (*dhruvo'si*) for the laying of the original (*prākṛta*) enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) which are its subsidiaries, the *Āmana-homas* are enjoined as unconnected [rites] by the rule: "He offers three oblations with the verses beginning 'O gods, of him who is mindful and of him who is not mindful' (*āmanamasyāmanasya devāḥ*)."

Then, regarding them, the sequence is prescribed along with the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings as follows: "If one were to offer before the *prayājas*, one would place one's kinsmen outside the sacrificial ground; if after the *anuyājas*, one would not reach the heavenly world; he offers in the middle, and thus he places his kinsmen right in the middle of himself.
Because they are enjoined as being connected to the archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries, the *āmanahomas* are understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*) to belong to the *sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice.
This very point was stated in the *Caturthatantrasāra* under the section [4.4.14.7] beginning with "Because it is the cause of that which possesses fruit, it should be primary":

"In the case of the statement 'It is known in relation to the Māhendra-stotra,' even though the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and so forth are enjoined as being connected to the archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries of the *Abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice, it is not possible for the context (*prakaraṇa*) to be extended [to them] such that the consecration and so forth enjoined within it would be grasped; for there is no injunction of the consecration and so forth within that [specific] context. This was explained in the preceding section.

For this very reason, the Miśras also state in the *Nyāyaratnamālā* that the *āmanahomas* are understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*), with the following passage: "Even in the case of modified sacrifices (*vikṛtis*), that which is recited in the midst of the archetypal subsidiaries (*prākṛtāṅgas*)—such as the *āmanahomas* and so forth—is included within the context.
(See *Liṅgavākyaprakaraṇasthānasamākhyānāṃ vicāraḥ*, *Mīmāṃsākośa*, p. 3362).

Bhaṭṭa Someśvara, however, in the section on *balābala* (relative strength), maintains that even though there is a sequence, because the *Sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice and others can be construed as a single syntactical unit with such injunctions as "he offers three oblations," he asserts that the *Āmana-homas* are subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) precisely due to their sequence.
That too should be understood as being stated merely for the sake of argument (*abhyupeyavāda*).

Furthermore, what was stated by the Miśras in the *Śāstradīpikā*, in the fourth [chapter], under the sūtra "Because it serves as a cause for that which possesses a fruit" (*phalavaddhītikartavyatātvena*), regarding its being grasped through proximity (*saṃnidhi*), that too is merely a statement made for the sake of argument.

For this very reason, in the *Tantraratna*, it is stated that even by means of proximity (*saṃnidhi*), the establishment of that [contextual] locus is achieved, without having to explicitly mention the grasping of a context (*prakaraṇagrāhatā*).

Thus, it is established that where there is an injunction of twelve *upasads* by way of a reference to the archetypal rite (*prākṛtānuvāda*), or where there is a "sandwich" (*saṃdaṃśa*) of the aforementioned form, only then is context (*prakaraṇa*) the applicator in the modified rite (*vikṛti*); elsewhere, it is proximity alone.

In this manner, the "great context" (*mahāprakaraṇa*) of the primary rite has been defined as arising from the absence of a "sandwich" in the archetype, whereas for the modified rite, it is also defined as arising from a "sandwich."
The intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), however, arises solely from the "enclosure" (*saṃdaṃśa*); and that does not exist at all in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Regarding the *prayājas*, which are to be supplied [from elsewhere], it was stated in the section on the "stepping forward" (*abhikrama*) (3.1.10.19–20).
But for the ectype (*vikṛti*), the intermediate context arising from enclosure was stated in the first topic of the seventh book (7.3.8.20–22) concerning the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices.

For in that context, it has been stated that because of the force of the explanatory exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—"They do not scatter [the earth] on the *uttaravedi* in the *vaiśvadeva*, nor in the *śunāsīrīya*"—which is recited within the intermediate section (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the Varuṇapraghāsas, namely "They scatter [the earth] near the vessels," this statement overrides the intermediate section and refers to the Cāturmāsyas as a whole.
Sequence (*krama*) is also of two kinds: sequence by position in the text (*pāṭhādeśaya*) and sequence by position in performance (*anuṣṭhānadeśaya*).
Sequence by position in the text is also of two kinds: sequential order in the text (*yathāsaṃkhyapāṭha*) and proximity in the text (*saṃnidhipāṭha*).

Name (*samākhyā*) is also of two kinds: worldly (*laukikī*) and Vedic (*vaidikī*). Furthermore, name is again twofold: general name (*sāmānyasamākhyā*) and specific name (*viśeṣasamākhyā*). *Vārttika*, pp. 9–12. Consideration of the conflict or non-conflict with direct assertion (*śruti*) and the other means of proof: it should be understood that this applies to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) just as it does to the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*); *Vārttika* 8.1.5.120. Since they assume a word based on the assumption of a direct assertion (*śruti*), the term "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) is postulated.
Just as in the case of the *kāśika* [region], where *śāli* rice-grains are eaten and cows are milked (*gopyante*). Bhāṣya 9.1.2.16. [This refers to] the postulation of a Vedic text (*śrutikalpanā*).
For it will be refuted that the eternal Vedic texts are to be postulated through the memory of an uninterrupted tradition (*anadhaparaṃparā*) of offspring...
Su. P. 918. *Śrutikrama* (Order based on Direct Assertion): Order prescribed by an individual injunction is *śrutikrama*.

As for order based on meaning (*arthakrama*) and so forth, it is prescribed solely by the general injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), because there is an absence of individual injunctions [for those cases].

*Soma*, 5.1.1, Section 3: Where a sequence (*krama*) or another distinct entity qualified by that sequence is enjoined, there it is "sequence by direct statement" (*śrutikrama*). However, where the word [itself] is subordinate to the sequence, there it is not "sequence by direct statement. *Soma*, 5.1.1, Section 3: The letters, being apprehended through direct audition (*śruta*), convey a particular sequence; because that very sequence is what is being enjoined, it is designated as "sequence by direct statement. *Ṭup-ṭīkā* on 5.1.1: Regarding conflict with sequence by direct statement—it is said that the properties of the *raśanā* (rope) [apply].
For she who is heard to have been arranged for this cake-offering and so forth goes along with the ritual duty (dharma) and gradually reaches the state of being a sacrificial animal.
Vākyapadīya 1.3.748, p. 836.

However, some argue that because the twelve [upasad days] belong to the *ahīna* sacrifice—as in the rule "there are exactly three upasads for the *sāha* and twelve for the *ahīna*"—and since they are not to be performed [in the *agniṣṭoma*], they lack the nature of a duty (*kartavyatā*). Consequently, it is impossible for them to be grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*) which consists of the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*) requirement. Therefore, due to the contradiction between direct statement (*śruti*) and position (*sthāna*), it is proper to cite this as an example where the connection is established through mere proximity (*sannidhi*) alone, following the construction of a context. To this, [the author replies]: (Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.7–14, pp.
And this is on account of its being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*).
However, when there is a plurality of subordinate elements, as in the case of the performance for one desiring cattle, there is a sequence of using the *camasa* vessel and so forth;
therein, the *camasa* is set aside in favor of the *godohana* vessel, which is based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Thus [ends the section]. Page 838. Exposition of the Śruti.

Now, what is this so-called *śruti*? It cannot be merely a capable word (*śaktaśabdamātra*), because the property of being *śruti*—which serves as the defining characteristic (*vibhājakopādhi*) for the means of proof regarding subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*)—must necessarily be pervaded by the aforementioned nature of being a means of proof (*pramāṇatva*). Furthermore, the property of being *śruti* in the form of the defined word is not pervaded by that [means of proof]. For a mere word is not a means of proof for subsidiarity, as seen in the case of the word "sāhasra" (thousandfold) in the phrase *jyotiṣṭomād vā etad ahar sahasrasaṃpannam*, where the word is connected to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice through its qualifying adjunct (*upapada*); it is not, however, a qualifier of the objective (*uddeśya-viśeṣaṇa*), because that would be redundant (*vaiyarthyāt*).

And for this reason, even in the case of the twelfth [day], that which is enjoined under the heading of the *upasad* is indeed placed within the archetype (*prakṛti*); the term *ahīna*, through the etymological derivation "that which is not abandoned" (*na hīyate*), is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, because other sacrifices do not abandon it due to its being the archetype.

Because the rule *ahnaḥ kratoḥ*—together with its continuation *tasya samūhaḥ*—prescribes that the word *ahan* takes a suffix denoting a collection of seasons (*kratu*), and because it further prescribes the substitution of *īn* for that [suffix], the word *ahīna* is derived; nevertheless, since the quality of being a collection of seasons accomplished by days—which is the denotative delimitor (*vācyachedaka*) of the term *ahīna*—is present in the Jyotiṣṭoma consisting of a collection of repetitions, its restatement (*anuvāda*) is justified.

Having thus presented the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the author] states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): Since the injunction of "twelve" would result in an option between eight and ten if it were merely a subordinate instruction (*upasaṃmādeśena*) regarding the number, and since accepting that would lead to a lack of syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*) due to the absence of any other means for those other numbers, and because it would render the terms *sāhna* and *ahīna* redundant; therefore, based on Vedic usage, the injunction of "one hundred and twelve" is connected with the *ahīna*—which is a collection of specific sacrifices to be accomplished—as the term *ahīna* excludes the *sāhna*. This is the conclusion reached.

But others say: because of the rule that there is no difference in the meditation (*bhāvanā*) other than the mere excellence of the *Sudharma* [sacrifice], even in the sixth section (*ṣaṣṭhakhaṇḍa*), since a mutual connection arises, it is not possible to enjoin the number twelve by means of the reference (*uddeśa*) to the *upasads* connected with the *Ahīna*. Rather, by means of the reference to the *Ahīna*, the very fact of having twelve *upasads* is enjoined through extended application (*atideśa*) due to its prior occurrence, just as in the case of "that [is done] with four. They say that the result [of this injunction] lies in the injunction of the number twelve itself.
We, however, say:

In the case of the statement "The *ājya* offerings are fifteen," since the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the twelve constituent parts and the constituent parts of the *upasad* is not already established, it is impossible to enjoin the number twelve for one or the other by means of the location of the *ahīna*. However, in the case of "That [cup] with four," because the taking up (*ādāna*) and pouring out (*āvanā*) are enjoined as the very objects to be performed due to their prior occurrence and because they are obtained through the force of the sense, there arises the distinctness of the four constituent parts; thus, there is the power of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) resulting in a cumulative effect (*samuccaya*). This is the point of difference.
Therefore, the injunction of the number twelve is indeed made with reference to the *upasad* itself.

Furthermore, since it would follow that the *upasat* itself is purposeless, and because the principle of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*—which establishes the restrictive rule—is weaker as a determinant of intention (*tātparya*), one accepts the indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the *upasat* as a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the *ahīna*. Then, accepting the syntactical connection (*vākya*) consisting of the co-occurrence with the word "ahīna" as the determinant of intention, the indirect indication of the *upasat* as a means to the transcendental result of the *ahīna* is admitted.

However, where there is a conflict with the sentence as a whole according to the principle of the restriction on the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offerings and so forth—as in the case of the sentence containing the word "sāhna" within the *trirātra* injunction—there is no sublation by that [prior] principle.

Furthermore, the relative strength between the two indicators of *tātparya* (intentional focus) has been explained in various places. For instance, regarding the passage "He performs the *abhikramaṇa* [stepping forward] and offers the oblation" (*abhighrāṃ juhoti*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established as follows: since the stepping forward would otherwise be purposeless (*ānarthakya*) with respect to the location of the oblation—given that its nature is merely to bring about the oblation—it must, by virtue of being indicated by the *tātparya* indicator in the form of the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, be understood through an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of that which is a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the primary oblation. However, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) established in the third book (*Bhāṭṭa 3.1.10*) is that, by the force of the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the *prayāja* offerings—which is stronger than the great context—the stepping forward is understood through an indication of that which is a means to the transcendental result of the *prayāja* oblations, due to the power of this *tātparya* indicator.

Although the words *juhoti* and *upasad* occurring in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) serve as indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparya*)—namely, that [the sacrifice] is the means for accomplishing the *apūrva* in general, precisely because there is no deviation from the *apūrva*—nevertheless, the introduction of the principle of "restriction by the proponent" (*vādyaniyamanyāya*) and others serves to indicate the intended meaning that it is the means for accomplishing a specific *apūrva*.

Alternatively, the injunction regarding the number twelve for the *upasad*s and so forth is made in relation to the *ahīna* sacrifice, because the *upasad*s and so forth are presented as the objects to be qualified (*uddeśya*) in the preceding sentence; thus, they alone possess the status of the substratum (*āśraya*).
Even in the absence of the referent of the word *upasad*, this [interpretation] alone is logical.

In every respect, since there is no direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) regarding the genitive case, this is an example of a contradiction between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*).
Furthermore, that [contradiction] is a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintā*) based on the assumption that there is no sentence enjoining twelve *upasad*s.

In reality, however, such a sentence does exist there; therefore, just as in the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) consisting of a *sattra*, it is possible for that [number of *upasad*s] to apply to the twelve-day sacrifice consisting of an *ahīna* as well. Consequently, the phrase "of the twelve-day *ahīna*" is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the three types of [twelve-day sacrifices].
The number twelve is great for the Mahā-dvādaśāha sacrifice, whereas for the Jyotiṣṭoma, because it is small, the number three alone is praised; this is the eulogy.
According to the view of the ancients, the usage of the genitive case here is figurative.
For this very reason, they present this as an example of a contradiction between direct statement (*śruti*) and context (*prakaraṇa*).

In reality, it has not been stated otherwise; even the example given for the contradiction between sentence (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) is incorrect. To explain: is the contradiction of the sentence here intended with respect to the context as a means of application (*viniyojaka*), or with respect to the context as a grasper of the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*) characterized by being a means to the *apūrva*? Furthermore, regarding its status as a means of application, does this belong to the great context (*mahā-prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, or to the intermediate context (*antar-prakaraṇa*) of the Upasads? It cannot be the first, because the great context of the Jyotiṣṭoma cannot possibly grasp the "twelvefoldness" of the Upasads, as that would result in the Jyotiṣṭoma itself having to be performed twelve times.

Not the second [alternative], because there is no evidence for an intermediate context (*antaraprakaraṇa*) consisting of the "sandwiching" (*saṃdaṃśa*) of the previously and subsequently stated subsidiary elements; because in both positions the number twelve is already established; because it would follow that the number twelve would not be the purpose of the context; and because, given that the syntactical connection (*vākya*)—in the form of the co-occurrence with the word *upasad*—is equally capable of being the applicator (*viniyojaka*) regarding the element of "twelve" as it is regarding the element of "three" (since there is no factor of determination to the contrary), the context itself cannot be the applicator.

By the logic of the restrictive rule regarding the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice and its subsidiaries, it is simply not possible for the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma to function as a pointer toward the intended meaning (*tātparya*) when [the term] is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to denote being a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the *upasads*. This is because that [context] can only point toward the intended meaning by virtue of being the context of the other *upasads* themselves; furthermore, since the non-deviation from the transcendental result of the *upasads* is itself the pointer toward the intended meaning, the [great context] is set aside. For the context can point toward the intended meaning—namely, the figurative indication of being a means to the transcendental result—only when the subject matter does not deviate from the transcendental result, as in the case of "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), and so forth.

For this very reason, in the section on the *ādhāna* (fire-laying), regarding the statement "the *vāraṇa* tree is a participant in the sacrifice," since trees such as the *vāraṇa* are mentioned as means for the sacrifice, they cannot be directly applied to the *ādhāna* itself—which is not of the nature of a sacrifice. Therefore, by the principle of "uselessness [otherwise] leading to application elsewhere" (*ānarthakyatadanyāya*), their application is restricted solely to the *iṣṭis* known as the *ādhānāṣṭakapavamāna*.

Anticipating this objection, the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) according to the view of the *Bhāṣyakāra*: since the *pavamāneṣṭis* are subsidiary to the fires (*agni*) and so forth by virtue of the statement within their own context, "When one offers in the *āhavanīya*," they lack subsidiariness to the *ādhāna* (fire-laying); thus, what scope is there for the principle of "uselessness" (*ānarthakya-tadanyāya*)? However, according to the view of the *Vārtikakāra*, such a statement is not admitted. Consequently, even if the *pavamāneṣṭis* are subsidiary to the *ādhāna* by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), the *vāraṇa* wood and other materials are prescribed for the sake of the sacrifice. Since the sacrifice does not invariably produce the *apūrva* (transcendental result), and because here the status of being a means to the *apūrva* is understood [only through the context], there is no entry into the context for that purpose. Therefore, as there is no evidence for the *vāraṇa* wood and others to be subsidiary to the *ādhāna*, they do not descend into those *pavamāneṣṭis*.
Thus, the omniscience of Śākalya and likewise the established conclusion [are discussed] in the third [chapter] (Bhāṭṭa 3.1.12).

Therefore, since there is no operation of *prakaraṇa* (context) in the deliberation regarding the application (*viniyoga*) of the number twelve, this is neither an example of a conflict between *śruti* (direct statement) and *prakaraṇa*, nor an example of a conflict between *vākya* (syntactical connection) and *prakaraṇa*; rather, it is an example of a mutual conflict between two *vākyas*.

In the view of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the *upasad* offerings actually belong to the Jyotiṣṭoma, the number twelve is included within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma; this is not the case in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Therefore, the truth is that this is cited as an example of conflict with context (*prakaraṇavirodha*) by both ancient and modern scholars.
We shall, however, demonstrate the example of conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context on its proper occasion.

Thus it is established that, since the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) lacks the status of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), there must be the inclusion of a specific qualification (the qualifier being: "being the relator of a power that is not delimited by a relation residing in any one of the aforementioned [types]").
However, this must be understood:

since words such as *kartṛtva* (agency) and *karmatva* (objecthood) are not denotable when they function as parts of a sentence (*vākya*), even if there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in those cases, it is difficult to avoid the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) with respect to words like *kartṛtva* and *dādi*. Nor can it be argued that the definition is "the state of being the designator of a power (*śakti*) not delimited by being any one of those [categories]—having unified agency and so forth by way of their being any one of them (*anyatamatva*)"; and that for words like *tad* (that), the definition is "the state of being the designator of a Vedic usage residing in any one of those [categories] as delimited by being an object of cognition (*buddhiviṣayatva*)," and thus there is no fault. [For this would fail to account for the specific linguistic behavior of such terms.]
This must be stated:

even in the initial [definition], since it is accepted that there is a "status of being a relatum of a power delimited by a specific form" with respect to that [suffix] in accordance with the objects to be understood as specific causal factors (*kāraka*), the term "primarily for the purpose of excluding over-extension" (*ativyāpti-vāraṇa-prādhānyena*) would be redundant. This is because, in the case of the suffix *kap*, the status of being a delimiting factor of the delimiting factor of the denotability (*śakyatā’vacchedakatā’vacchedakatva*) does not constitute the status of being a delimiting factor of the denotability (*śakyatā’vacchedakatva*). Furthermore, even if the accusative in *saktūn* were to have a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), there would still be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because in reality the status of being a relatum of a power delimited by such a finality (*antyatva*) is not lost.

Therefore, we conclude the following here: *Śruti-hood* (the nature of a Vedic injunction) consists in being a cognition whose intentionality (*tātparya*) is delimited by any one of the properties such as *kartṛtva* (agency) that delimit its own denotable capacity (*svaśakyatāvacchedaka*).

In sentences such as "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), the definition is applicable because it has been established in the section on the locus of relation (*saṃsargādhikaraṇa*) that the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) and others possess an intentionality delimited by their own denotable capacity, namely *karmatva* (objecthood).

Regarding the word *saktūn*, since it has been refuted that the genitive case (*dvitīyā*) has an intentionality delimited by the property of "objecthood" (*karmatvatva*), which is its own delimiting factor of denotability (*svaśakyatāvacchedaka*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). In this context, because the genitive of relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) would over-extend to cases where the sixth case does not intend to express its own denoted agency (*kartṛtva*),
[the definition specifies] the experience of being the delimiter (*avacchedakatva*).
The inclusion of "being a suffix" (*pratyayatva*) is for the sake of [excluding] those beginning with *tad* (i.e., pronouns) from being [considered as such].

To exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to forms like *saktūnām* (where the second case ending does not denote the instrument but something else), the phrase "whose own denotable property-delimiter" (*sva-śakyatāvacchedaka*) is used.

This is precisely why, in the expression *prokṣitānām mūlalulitasulabhā*, there is no over-extension; for although the suffix *kapratyaya* has its denotative power (*śakti*) residing in that which is qualified by the objecthood (*karmatva*), the property of "objecthood-ness" (*karmatvatva*) is the delimiter of the delimiter of the denotable property (*śakyatāvacchedakatāvacchedakatva*), and thus lacks the status of being the denotable property-delimiter itself (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*). Therefore, there is no over-extension.

In the case of [the word] ‘āgneyaḥ’ and so forth, where the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) constitutes the denotatum (*saṃjñāyatva*), the property of being a deity (*devatātvatva*) must also be accepted as being included within the category of being one of the [meanings such as] agency (*kartṛtva*) and so on.

Nor should it be argued that because the deity-status is the delimiting factor of the denotability (*śakyatā’vacchedakatva*) for a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) denoting a substance qualified by deity-status, deity-status itself cannot be the delimiting factor of denotability.

This is because, according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the secondary suffix resides in the deity-status alone, while its application to the substance is accepted as being figurative (*lakṣaṇā*).

Nor is there an over-narrow definition (avyāpti) regarding such injunctions as "A king desiring self-sovereignty should sacrifice in the Rājasūya," because the nominative case following words like "king" serves only for grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) and lacks the meaning of any specific *kāraka* such as agency; furthermore, according to the view that "the nominative expresses a *kāraka* already denoted [by another word]," the nominative itself possesses the meaning of agency and so forth, which are the meanings of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), and thus there is no conflict with either [of the two definitions].

This is because of the maxim "the uselessness [of what is already established]," and because there is no deficiency even if the nominative case is held to serve only for grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), since in cases such as "A king should sacrifice with the Rājasūya," the connection of the king [to the action] is appropriately accounted for by being based on the authority of the sentence (*vākya-pramāṇaka*).

Nor should it be argued that, although the nominative following the word "king" is devoid of meaning, the king's status as the agent is nonetheless established by the authority of a *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) whose purport lies in the verbal suffix expressing agency;
for the verbal suffix lacks the status of a *śruti*, since its capacity to denote agency and so forth has been refuted in the section on the "Agent" (*kartṛ-adhikāra*).

It should not be argued that if the agent (*kartṛ*) and the first-person suffix (*ākhyāta*) were not included [in the denotation], then because they would possess agency (*kartṛtva*) as indicated by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the inclusion of "possessing the nature of holding" (*dhāraṇatvatva*) and "possessing the nature of desiring" (*iṣṭatvatva*) would be redundant; for the agenthood and so forth are indeed included. Nor should it be argued that such an inclusion is impossible because, since the agenthood, objecthood, and so forth are relational properties, the property-limiters (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the respective potencies must be the very factors constituting those—namely, the effort (*kṛti*), the result (*phala*), and the desired state (*iṣṭadharma*)—and thus agenthood itself cannot serve as its own property-limiter.

Since it is precisely a definition involving two properties—the state of being [the denotatum] (*bhūtatva*) and the state of being a duality (*dvitvatva*)—that is intended as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatā’vacchedaka*), and since agency (*kartṛtva*) is an impartite adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) such that agency itself serves as the delimitor of denotability, there is no defect even in the aforementioned definition.

Now, one might object: since it was established in the fourth [chapter] (*Bhāṭṭa* 4.2.6) that in cases such as "He gives the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa," the Maitrāvaruṇa is the intended recipient (*bhāvoddeśya*), the staff is understood as an unintended object (*anīpsitakarma*). Therefore, the accusative case-ending following the word denoting an unintended object would lack validity regarding the status of the staff as the primary object (*karmatva*), and thus, lacking the status of *śruti*, it would be merely indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*) in that context.

To this we reply: the accusative case-ending possesses its primary denotative power (*śakti*) precisely in the sense of objecthood (*karmatva*) common to both intended and unintended objects. This is because the accusative in "the staff" (*daṇḍam*) has as its intended purport (*tātparya*) that very [objecthood] delimited by [the status of being an unintended object].
If this is argued, we say no.

According to the maxim "that which is pervaded by the pervader is even more pervaded," since the *maitrāvaruṇa* priest is [already] the object of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), if the staff (*daṇḍa*) were also construed as an object, it would lead to the erroneous conclusion that the productive operation has only a single object. Furthermore, if one accepts that the accusative suffix following the word "staff" indicates instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then it lacks the intentionality (*tātparya*) to denote an objecthood delimited by its own nature.
For this very reason, in all cases, the accusative suffix following a word denoting an unintended object (*anīpsita-karman*) indicates instrumentality through metaphorical indication.
In the case of the word *saktūn*, there is also the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the modification of the application (*viniyogabhaṅga*).

For this very reason, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) results in expressing instrumentality (*karaṇatva*); for if it were to result in expressing an undesired object (*anīpsitakarmatva*), then even that which is desired would have to be the end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*), leading to the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*).

Furthermore, if the accusative expressed an undesired object, what proof would there be that the groats (*saktavaḥ*) are subordinate to the oblation (*homa*)? It cannot be direct statement (*śruti*), because the accusative lacks the capacity to denote instrumentality, which is the factor that necessitates subordination to the oblation.
Nor can it be a sentence, because it lacks the capacity to indicate the stated instrumentality (*karaṇatva*).

For neither by primary denotation (*śakti*) as the state of being an object (*karmatva*), nor by secondary indication (*lak�ṣaṇā*) as the state of being an unintended object (*anīpsitakarmatva*), does the mention of an unintended object imply that the groats (*saktu*) are subordinate to the oblation (*homa*). Furthermore, any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is simply impossible regarding their subordination to the oblation.

Nor should it be argued that, just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with soma," although both direct statement (*śruti*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*) could potentially serve as the means of knowledge regarding the status of *soma* as the instrument—either through the power of the word itself or through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) involving the possessive sense (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*)—it is nevertheless accepted that the authority belongs solely to the direct statement (*śruti*) postulated by the injunction of the qualifier; so too should it be here.

By the force of the indicator (*tātparyagrāhaka*) consisting in the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word *yajati*, there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *soma* either as "that which has soma as its instrument" or as "that which possesses soma through the relation of instrumentality. This is because the sentence consisting of the word *soma* co-occurring with the word *yajati* serves as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the injunction regarding the proximity of soma; for the operation [of the injunction] occurs precisely in the case of an injunction of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇavidhi*). Therefore, from the heard sentence, there is the comprehension of any one of the agenthoods and so forth as defined by the state of being an accessory (*aṅgatva*), whereas the comprehension of the connection with the injunction arises from the injunction of the qualifier.

For when there is an injunction regarding a qualifier—in the case of an efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) whose instrument is *soma*—there is an understanding that the connection with the injunction is qualified by the injunction itself, through the relation of being the delimitor of the delimitation of the particularity (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by its own mode-ness (*prakāratā*).
However, because it is an instrument, the injunction regarding the qualifier is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), just like the essential nature of the *soma* itself.

In the present case, however, since the flour (*saktu*) is construed as an unintended object (*anīpsita-karman*), the status of being the agent or the instrument—which would necessitate the knowledge of the act of offering—is not understood from the heard sentence.

Therefore, since there is no evidence even for postulating a restrictive rule (vidhi) involving the qualification delimited by instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), and since that [rule] likewise lacks the status of being an authority for the flour (*saktu*) being subordinate to the oblation (*homa*), the subordination of the flour to the oblation is indeed devoid of any proof.

For in the injunction of what is heard (*śrutividhi*), whichever [factor] such as agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth is understood, an injunction qualifying that initial factor and its two [adjunct] words is postulated. For example, in the case of "one should sacrifice with *soma*," it consists of the word ending in the third case; in "they perform the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* in the afternoon on the new moon day," and in "he offers on the footprint," it consists of the word ending in the seventh case. However, in the *soma* sentence, it does not consist of a word expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇatā*), nor in the footprint sentence, does it consist of a word expressing the instrument (*karaṇatā*).

Likewise, in the sentence regarding the barley-meal (*saktu*), since the meal is understood to be an unintended object (*anīpsita-karman*), a restrictive injunction (*viśeṣaṇa-vidhi*) consisting only of words such as "beginning with that" (*tad-ādyakṣa-pada*) would have to be postulated, rather than one consisting of a word expressing instrumentality (*karaṇatā*). Therefore, ignorance (*ajñatva*) is not established by that [sentence] as its authority. Consequently, we understand that the final conclusion of the Siddhānta results only from the syntactical split (*viniyoga-bhaṅga*) when the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) has instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) as its figurative meaning (*lakṣaṇā*), and thus the sentence serves as the authority. Hence, [the status of] the unintended...

Since the accusative case following a word denoting an object signifies instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), and thus lacks the intention (*tātparya*) to denote the state of being an object (*karmatvatva*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the definition of direct statement (*śruti*).

Examples of direct statements expressing agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth, in their respective order, are as follows: "The rite must be performed by one who has sipped water" (*ācāntena karma kartavyam*); "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*); "One should sacrifice with rice-grains" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*); "He gives a cow to a Brahmin" (*viprāṃ gāṃ dadāti*); "He cuts [the portion] for Sviṣṭakṛt from the northern half" (*uttarārdhāt sviṣṭakṛte samavadyati*); and "Whatever he offers in the Āhavanīya fire" (*yad āhavanīye juhoti*).

In such passages as "One desiring cattle should fetch water with a milking vessel" (*godohanena paśukāmasya praṇayet*), the milking vessel is the subordinate factor (*guṇa*) because of the genitive hearing (*ṣaṣṭhī-śruti*). One should note, however, that the designation of the genitive as "hearing" (*śruti*) in this context is figurative.

Some, moreover, maintain that there are three kinds of *śruti* which serve as the means of knowledge for subordination (*aṅgatva*): the declensional (*vibhakti*), the denotative (*abhidhātrī*), and the applicatory (*viniyoktrī*).
The *vidhātrī* (prescriptive) is the scriptural mention of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth; the *abhidhātrī* (denotative) is the scriptural mention of *vrīhi* (rice) and so forth.
The *viniyogakṛt* (applicatory) is threefold: consisting of case-endings (*vibhakti*), consisting of identical words (*samānapada*), and consisting of identical verbal roots (*samānābhidhāna*).

Regarding this, the common maxim "Śruti is an independent sound" means that when the cognition of a word produces the cognition of a meaning without depending on the prescription of another syntactic connection, it is Śruti with respect to that meaning.

Nor should it be suspected that, in the context of discussing the *viniyojaka* (the applicator), the description of the common characteristic shared by both the prescriptive (*vidhi*) and the denotative (*abhidhātrī*) [powers], as well as their definition, is intended for the *arha* (the capacity) alone;
for since both [the denotative and the applicative powers] are equally auxiliary to the prescriptive power through the establishment of the prescriptive applicator (*vidhi-viniyojaka*),

that cognition produced by the knowledge of a word which, depending on an intervention, brings about the understanding of the relationship between two things regarded as the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*) while they exist in their respective forms, is the *viniyokrī* (the applicator).

And this relation— whether it be understood as the state of being an object of ignorance (*ajñatva*), as the state of being a means (*sādhanatva*), or as the state of being a relation (*saṃbandhatva*)—

no distinction between these is perceived in the definition. Therefore, they say that [the definition] includes "the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice" and so forth, as well as the inclusion of the scriptural mentions of the instrumental and genitive cases.
That [position] is extremely weak;

for since the state of being an expressive agent in the form of *śaktatva* (denotative power) does not pervade the aforementioned *śruti* (direct Vedic statement), it is untenable for it to be a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the case-ending delimited by that [power]. Nor should it be argued that because the direct statement within a single word—such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*)—is a *śruti* in its sense of expressing the relationship between the sacrifice and the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), yet lacks the state of being an expressive agent in the form of *śaktatva*, it cannot therefore be a pervader of *śruti*-hood.

Nevertheless, since denotative power (*abhidhātrītva*) can possibly be a differentiator of that [direct assertion] by virtue of being co-referential with other qualifiers that differentiate direct assertion, and because the knowledge of the meanings of the constituent words must be required when producing the knowledge of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal—which is the meaning generated by the direct hearing of a single word (*samāna-pada-śruti*)—it is easy to maintain that the "status of being a direct assertion" (*śrutitva*) as you have defined it lacks pervasion over denotative power even in the absence of the direct hearing of a single word.

For this very reason, since the definition of direct assertion is under-pervasive (*avyāpti*) regarding the direct hearing of a single word, it is also inconsistent to claim that such a case is a thing to be defined (*lakṣya*).

Nor should it be argued that the requirement of dependence on an additional *vyapadeśaka* (designator) for the presentation of the word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*) is not part of the definition [of a subordinate element], and thus there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).

For even a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) that appears through the force of syntactic connection (*saṃsargamaryādā*) in a sentence such as "The Ṛg-veda is recited loudly" (*uccairṛcā kriyate*) would result in over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*) within that related sentence.

Furthermore, in the case of the word "saktūn" (barley flour), although the knowledge of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) to be produced depends on intervening factors such as the knowledge of the primary denotation (*śakyopasthiti*) and the knowledge of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the dative case ending (*dvitīyā*) [is still considered *śruti*]. This is because, when the knowledge of instrumentality is to be produced by the knowledge that [the dative] possesses instrumentality through its connection with the primary denotation (*śakyasaṃbandha*), there is no dependence on any other intervening factor; thus, the dative would incur the status of *śruti*. Otherwise, the principle of "independent application" (*anapekṣānvaya*) would be rendered useless. For it is more appropriately stated that whatever produces the knowledge of a word-meaning through its primary denotative power (*śakti*), and whatever is capable of expressing something in a particular sense, that is *śruti* in that regard.

Furthermore, since "being a *śruti*"—which is the object of the linguistic usage of those who know the *śruti*—is common to both that which expresses an injunction (*vidhi*) and that which expresses a noun-base (*abhidhātrī*), even in cases such as "He offers groats" (*saktūn juhoti*) or "A cow is the sacrificial fee" (*dhenurdakṣiṇā*), where there is a cognition of an injunction belonging to a sentence (*vākyīya*), the noun-base expressing the injunction and the word expressing the injunction act as auxiliaries by presenting the item to be enjoined. Therefore, "being a *śruti*," which is the delimitor of the validity of being an injunction, must be stated as being pervaded (*vyāpta*) by the injunctive noun-base and so forth.

Thus, in order to include cases of co-reference (*samānābhidhāna*) and co-occurrence within the same word (*samānapadaśruti*) as defining characteristics of the *viniyoktrī* (the enjoining power), it must be stated that the cognition of a qualifier occurs even when there is an intervention distinct from the presentation of the meanings of the words constituting its own [compound].

Consequently, there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to sentences such as "A cow is the sacrificial fee" (*dhenurdakṣiṇā*), where even though the remainder [of the meaning] appears through the relation of syntactic connection (*saṃsargamaryādā*), it pertains to the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*śeṣaśeṣiṇvaka*).

In the case of the statement "He offers the groats" (*saktūn juhoti*), since the instrumental sense is indicated by the accusative suffix according to the second rule [of Pāṇini], there arises the contingency that the accusative and other such cases would be *viniyojaka* (determiners of application) based on the cognition of a relationship in the form of instrumentality, which requires mediation by the knowledge of the accusative. Therefore, this objection is of no consequence.

Consequently, having accepted that the designation of "direct assertion" (*śruti*) in the case of "direct mention" (*samānābhidhāna*), "single-wordness" (*samānapada*), and so forth is merely figurative, it is appropriate to define direct assertion solely by the characteristic of being the unique function of a case-ending (*kārakavibhakti*).
Enough of this prolixity.
(Thus ends the determination of direct assertion.
Murāri, pp. 1162–1171.
Determination of Direct Assertion (*śrutiliṅga*).

In that regard, scripture (śruti) is divided into three types: that which effects injunction (vidhi), that which effects reasoning (yukti), and that which effects application (viniyoga). That which effects application is further divided into three types based on the distinctions of identical words and so forth. Among these, the injunctive [scripture] consists of the optative suffixes (liṅ) and the like.
The denotative [direct statement] is the Vedic text concerning rice and other such items.
The applicatory [direct statement] is threefold: single expression, a single word, and a case-ending. This is the definition of direct statement (*śruti*).
The definition of *śruti*: That verbal expression (*śabda*) by the mere hearing of which a relationship is understood is *viniyoga-śruti*.

This occurs where multiple meanings are denoted simultaneously by a single word, just as case-endings (*vibhakti*) denote gender, number, and other factors. In such cases, there is the denotation of those meanings only as already related (*anvita*), because it is impossible for a single word to denote these multiple unrelated meanings simultaneously without the operation of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from among several identical words).

By the word *akṣa*, [the exclusion of] dice-shaking (*videvana*) and so forth is intended. Otherwise, when one is commanded with "Bring a cow," one brings some particular individual; but when commanded with "Bring an *akṣa*," one would be uncertain whether to bring any one of the items such as dice-shaking or the like. And being thus in doubt, one would wonder: "To what end was this [word] employed? Therefore, there is the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*).
Even in that case, by the force of conventional usage, the *kāraka* is primary while gender and number are secondary.

Thus it has been said: "When the object (*karman*) and so forth are the meanings of the case-endings, then oneness (*ekatva*) and so forth are their qualifiers. By this, the view that number is a qualifier of the specific *kāraka* through its connection with the case-ending is refuted.

Even when unconnected [words] are denoted, number is conjoined only with the *kāraka* (grammatical participant) which is introduced by the first word, which is primary (*pradhāna*), and not with the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), which is remote and subordinate. The claim that "number is denoted as conjoined with the meaning of the nominal stem, but not as a *kāraka*-status" is merely a matter of faith for those who have fabricated their own consistent doctrines regarding the true nature of meaning; it is not authoritative, because there is no difference in the cognition [of the two]. Just as when it is said "by means of an animal" (*paśunā*), the animal is cognized in a certain way, so too is "one instrument" (*ekaṃ karaṇam*) cognized in exactly the same way.

Nor is it observed that a single denotation denotes another meaning already connected with other meanings; for this is because the cognition of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and the cognition of the performed action (*kṛta*) are accepted as means restricted by what has been performed. And how is there an implication of an injunction? If it is argued that it is "because of being for that purpose" (*tādarthyāt*), [we reply:]...
No;

for it is impossible for that which is a qualifier with respect to either the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) or the grammatical factor (*kāraka*) to serve as the object of the injunction while disregarding those very things.

Or, if such were possible, then even the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), the "offering" (*havis*), and so forth would have to be objects of the injunction; and since that would be the case, one would have to assume that the wind (*vāyu*)—as the deity—is qualified by the quality of being swift (*kṣipra*). Thus, the deity would be the wind specifically characterized by the quality of speed, rather than the essential nature of the wind itself. Enough of this frivolous dispute.

Thus, in this manner, the connection with the factors of action (*kāraka*) occurs through direct audition (*śruti*), characterized by the employment of the word "eye" (*akṣa*) for number and the rest; however, the connection of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) occurs through syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). For the relationship between the meanings of the base and the suffix is understood from their mere hearing and does not depend upon the consideration of two words; thus, even the word is determined to fall under the category of direct audition. Consequently, there is a mutual restriction among the genus (*jāti*), gender (*liṅga*), and number (*saṃkhyā*), which are each connected to a single factor of action, according to the principle of the red cow and the one-year-old heifer (*aruṇā-kaṇhāyanī-naya*).

The case-ending (*vibhakti*), however, by expressing either the state of being an end (*sādhyatva*) or the state of being a means (*sādhanatva*), serves as the cause for application (*viniyoga*). In this regard, the accusative case expresses the state of being an end, while the instrumental and other cases express the state of being a means. Thus, in the injunction "one threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), the accusative expresses the rice-grains as the end, thereby becoming the cause for applying the act of threshing to them. How then is it that the oblation (*homa*) is not applied to the *śukus*?
Because those [grains] are not what is intended;
for while rice grains (*vrīhayaḥ*) are not intended by their own word,
they are intended as means to the *apūrva* (the unseen potency).

For although the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is obtained as denoting the "thing to be accomplished" (*sādhyatva*), it does not [thereby] obtain the status of being the desired end (*samīhitatva*). Indeed, the accusative does not express the state of being desired; rather, it expresses only the state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*). Consequently, observing that the status of being the primary object (*śeṣitva*) is not possible for the *saknu* (flour-cakes), the efficient force of the oblation (*homabhāvanā*) requires another purpose (*bhāgyantara*). However, in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*), there is no such restrictive cause. To explain: [The text continues: For instance...

The efficient force (*bhāvanā*) of threshing, seeking what is desired by the agent and not being presented as something else to be accomplished, accepts the rice-grains (*vrīhīn*) as its object of accomplishment. It is directed toward them because they are not desired in their own form [as ends].

In this regard, if it were somehow possible for them to be desired—as they are in the case of flour (*saktu*)—then, having turned back, it would require another object of accomplishment. However, it is indeed possible for them to be desired in the form of specific means for the production of the transcendental result (*apūrva*) under discussion. For instance, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice-grains," the rice-grains are prescribed as the means for the sacrifice.
Nor is their status as direct means of the sacrifice established by an originative injunction, for threshing is prescribed [only] for the *puroḍāśa*.

Therefore, their status as means is through being the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the *puroḍāśa*; thus, they are intended in that form, and in that very way they become the ends to be accomplished (*bhāvya*).
And the word *vrīhi* (rice) is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for that [grain in general].
In this way, threshing is established as being directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*) even with respect to barley, because its form is no different in them either.

Thus, the application of threshing is determined by the scriptural statement (*śruti*) conjoined with the context (*prakaraṇa*), since the indication of the means to the transcendental result (*apūrva-sādhana-lakṣaṇā*) is dependent upon that [scriptural statement].

For instance, since the threshing (avaghāta) prescribed for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices does not reach its purpose through the mere rice-grains (vrīhi) connected by direct scriptural statement (śruti), the sentence "one threshes the rice-grains" remains expectant (sākāṅkṣa) and attains syntactic unity (ekavākyatva) with the contextual Darśapūrṇamāsa injunction itself, in the sense that "one threshes the rice-grains related to the Darśapūrṇamāsa. And that connection [with the sacrifice] brings to mind its own objective—the purpose—which is invariably concomitant with that [connection].

When that [purpose] is present, they effect the threshing’s status as being for that purpose by setting aside its status as being for the sake of the rice-grains; thus, the word "rice-grains" comes to signify that it serves as a means for that [threshing].

[Objection: But if this were the case, then because the statement "he measures the sacrificial grass" (*barhir mīnāti*) would also form a single syntactical unit with the sentence concerning the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the cutting of the grass would be enjoined for the sacrificial grass itself as its own means, and its status as serving both the subsidiary and the primary rites would not be established.
[Reply: You have not correctly understood our position, O long-lived one.
There is no defining of scripture; there is no defining of scripture.

For indeed, rice, barley, and so forth are specified for the sake of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices by means of that [sacrifice], as in "rice for the *darśapūr�āpūrṇamāsa*"; however, this is not so merely by virtue of a general connection. Even for those things that are not directly mentioned, such a connection certainly exists because they are contributory (*upakāraka*). When a new transcendental result (*apūrva*) is established following the primary transcendental result (*pradhānāpūrva*), the threshing and other acts—designated by words such as "rice" and "barley" in their capacity as means to that [result] and being enjoined therein—become auxiliaries (*aṅga*) to all of that.

Therefore, even though the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is specified by the exclusion of the *amīkṣā* sacrifice from its very position, the properties of the rope (*raśanā*) and its subsidiaries, which are enjoined for that post, do not belong solely to the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the primary *amīkṣā* sacrifice and its subsidiaries; rather, they also constitute subsidiaries of the *saṃnīya* sacrifice accomplished by that post.
Consequently, the rope and its properties are directly taught (*aupadeśika*) even for the second encircling (*pariṇyāṇa*) of that [post].

If it is argued that these properties apply even to the subsidiaries of that [sacrifice], then by the same logic, the properties of rice (*vrīhi*) would have to apply to the *vaimṛdha* and other offerings by direct injunction alone.
No, because that is absent.

For rice (*vrīhi*) is not directly enjoined for the *vaimṛdha* sacrifice; rather, when they are obtained there through the rule of extension (*codaka*), they are obtained along with the threshing (*avaghāta*). Thus, since they would be stated twice, a direct injunction (*upadeśa*) is impossible.

For this very reason, in the case of the *savanīya*, the injunction regarding the girth-rope (*raśanā*) and other items occurs only at the second binding (*pariṇyāṇa*), and not elsewhere, due to the fault of being stated twice.
Thus it is established that the application (*viniyoga*) of threshing (*avaghāta*) and other such acts is determined by direct statement (*śruti*) through the power of context (*prakaraṇa*).
In this regard, by virtue of the context, it is assumed that the very word heard [in the text] has the purpose of indicating a specific meaning.

However, in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and others, it is the form of the word itself that is assumed to be the applicatory factor; thus, there is no contradiction here, as its dependence on context is not different from the former.

However, for that which has an established non-deviation [from its purpose], such as *khādiratva* (the quality of being made of khadira wood) when it is enjoined as belonging to the *sruva* (ladle) and so forth, even though the *apūrva* (transcendental result) was not previously present in the mind during the inquiry into its purpose, that very *apūrva* comes to the heart by means of that non-deviating indicative mark (*liṅga*). Thus, even in the absence of *prakaraṇa* (context), the application is possible through the indication of the form of its instrument.

Where both [indicative mark and context] are absent, the indication of the instrument is not possible; therefore, *śruti* (direct statement) accompanied by *prakaraṇa* is the cause for the application of the act of threshing (*avaghāta*).

It might be argued: "The second [word] merely expresses that the rice (*vrīhi*) is the object to be accomplished; however, its being accomplished by threshing (*avaghāta*) follows simply from the expectancy arising from the co-occurrence of those words. Therefore, how can it be said that the threshing is for the sake of the rice by virtue of direct statement (*śruti*)? True, as you have said; however, the application (*viniyoga*) occurs precisely through direct statement. For application is indeed a relationship.
And that [relationship] consists of the nature of the means and the end between what is desired and what is undesired.

In that context, the accusative case-ending, by establishing the status of the desired rice grains as the end (*sādhya*), implies their status as the primary object (*śeṣin*) and requires a sentence to specify its particular application; therefore, in both cases, it is said that the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) alone is the cause of application.

Furthermore, in cases where the relationship of principal (*śeṣin*) and subordinate (*śeṣa*), or the relationship of the end (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*), is not explicitly heard [in the text], but must instead be inferred by considering the application of the status of principal and subordinate based solely on the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of two words—as in "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*)—there the application (*viniyoga*) occurs through the sentence itself. For in that case, neither the status of being the end nor the status of being the means is expressed for either the one desiring heaven or the sacrifice; rather, they infer a connection based solely on the co-occurrence of the two words. By the principle stated in the rule "but that which is not a means [is subordinate] because it exists for the sake of that," the primacy of the one desiring [the result] and the subordination of the sacrifice are inferred.
He says: "How is it possible for one who already exists as a seeker of heaven (*svargakāma*) to be something that is yet to come into being (*bhāvya*)?
For it is the agent of becoming who is the *bhāvya*, and becoming does not occur in things that already exist.

Since the agent of becoming is one who is yet to be produced—given that 'becoming' is another name for 'coming into existence'—the seeker of heaven, being [already] existent, is not capable of coming into existence; thus he would not be a *bhāvya*. To this, it is replied:"

Even for that which already exists, there is the status of being the "thing-to-be-accomplished" (*bhāvya*) by way of its own nature for one who desires heaven, as in the case of a sacrifice, rice, and so forth, when they are qualified by another property (*dharma*). From the sentence, it is understood that the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is subordinate to one who desires heaven; and this subordination occurs in two ways: either if [the agent] accomplishes the desired end through its very own nature, or through some property belonging to that [nature]. In both cases, the thing to be accomplished is the principal (*śeṣin*), as is the case with the efficient force of the *prayāja* offerings and the like.

For the *ṛtu* (sacrificial season) is established in its essential form by means of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth; it is precisely their assistance (*upakāra*) that is accomplished. Furthermore, we shall explain that the *prayāja* offerings and others are connected [to the sacrifice] as being for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*).

Just as rice grains, even though already produced, become the *bhāvya* (the thing to be brought about) of the threshing, there is no absolute rule that a *bhāvya* must be something produced in its own essential form (*svarūpa*);
for the status of being a *bhāvya* is possible even through a form distinct from other properties (*dharmāntara*).

In that regard, although it has been determined that the "end" (śeṣitva) consists merely in being something to be brought into being (bhāvya), when there arises an expectation for a specific detail—namely, "by performing what kind of assistance does this [means] become subordinate to this [end]?"—is it the production of its own essential nature (svarūpa), or is it some other form of assistance?—that specific detail is postulated through the force of the context (sāmarthya).

In this case, since it is impossible for a person desiring heaven (svargakāma), who already exists, to be the "thing to be brought into being" (bhāvya) by way of his own essential nature, he can be the "thing to be brought into being" only by way of a specific result (phalaviśeṣatva).
For this very reason, the term *svargakāma* is interpreted by the Mīmāṃsakas as referring to the result.

Just as in the case of the injunction "the staff-bearer recites the *praiṣas*," since the person qualified by the staff is enjoined as the one who knows how to recite, and because the substratum (the person) is already established as the beneficiary [of the action], it is possible for the statement to be intended to establish that the qualifying attribute— the staff— possesses the status of being known for the purpose of recitation; likewise, through the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," the scriptural determination of the sacrificial *bhāvanā* as having human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) is established.

Since it is not possible for a person to possess the status of being a subordinate (*śeṣitva*) in their essential nature (*svarūpa*), one who desires some qualification [for that status] understands through implication that the status of being a subordinate is due to a specific attribute. Thus, when the status of being a subordinate is stated for "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), it refers specifically to the qualification called "heaven. Therefore, the person's status as a subordinate is established by way of heaven being the means. As they say: "Because the goal (*bhāvya*) is what is required, words expressing desire (*kāmaśabda*) are intent upon that;
the predominance of the qualification is demonstrated in cases such as 'the man with a staff' (*daṇḍin*)."
Thus it has been stated very clearly by the Blessed Lady herself, along with her reasoning, in the eleventh chapter.

Indeed, having first raised the objection that no word expressing a fruit is heard here—starting with "Is it not the case that heaven is not heard as the fruit here?"—and having stated, "By this word *svargakāma* [it is expressed]," he then refutes both the view that it refers to a specific person and the view that it refers to a fruit, while raising further objections such as "Is it not [merely] a qualifier of the person? At the point of demonstrating the alternative view—that the number of the agent is conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)—the Sūtrakāra himself clearly determined the matter, stating: "If it is argued that one who desires the fruit is the *nimitta* (condition), no, because of its obligatory nature (*nityatva*). Having thus established through elimination that this is indeed a connection with a fruit, he asks: "But how can this [word] denote a fruit? He then presents two possible syntactical interpretations (*vacanavyakti*), showing that the person is construed as the primary beneficiary (*śeṣin*)—as in the expression "one who is dirty should bathe"—demonstrating that "the sacrifice is taught for the sake of one who desires heaven," and finally concludes that in this context, the intent is simply to convey a specific benefit known as heaven.
Even previously, by that same purpose, it was understood from the very mention of "a man" (*puruṣamātra*) that [the result] comes from that; thus, this statement is simply "heaven comes to be.

Therefore, in cases where there is an absence of case-endings (*vibhakti*) that express merely the relationship between the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*), as in the word *vrīhīn* (accusative plural), and in the remaining case where there is a case-ending expressing the status of being a means, as in *somena yajeta* (instrumental singular), there is application (*viniyoga*) based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

Even in cases elsewhere where the genitive case expresses mere relationship—such as *dabhrendriyakāmasya* (of one desiring strength of sense) regarding the principal (*śeṣin*), or *yājyāyāḥ* (of the *yājyā*) regarding the subordinate (*śeṣa*)—there too, by observing the fitness of the elements, that very case functions toward a specific relationship; thus, it is application by direct statement (*śruti*).

Even where the dative occurs in relation to the principal, as in *maitrāvaruṇāya daṇḍam* (the staff for Maitrāvaruṇa), there too, since the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is clearly intended by the object (*karman*), the direct statement of its status as the goal (*sādhyatva*) is manifest.
When the dative is used for that purpose, the application by direct statement is even more evident.
For example: "If one should vomit *soma*, for him one should offer this *śyāmāka* oblation to Soma and Indra; [one should perform] the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices for the sake of all desires.

However, where there is a conflict between the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and the syntactical connection (*vākya*), as in "On the previous day of the new moon, [one prepares] the altar" (*vediṃ*), where the locative case indicates the substrate (*śeṣin*), and "He offers the flour-meal" (*saktūn juhoti*), where the accusative case indicates the subordinate element (*śeṣa*), there the status of being the end to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) must be conveyed through the power of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) signifying the means (*sādhana*), and the status of being the means (*sādhanatva*) must be conveyed by that which signifies the end.
And since indication is everywhere caused by the sentence, this is called "application by syntactical connection" (*vākyaviniyoga*).

Thus far, the application through direct statement (*śruti*) has been explained in detail. An objection is raised: "How, moreover, can there be an application based on what is not directly stated? For [the text] shows that there are only two ways [of application]: the application of a word joined with an injunction, and the application of case-endings (*kāraka-vibhakti*).

[The author replies: There is no fault here, because the mention of the "word" (*pada*) is intended to indicate that this also includes the application through the direct statement of synonymous expression (*tulyābhidhāna-śruti*).
And thus: "Because it is grasped by the *kāraka*, oneness and so forth serve the purpose of the action;
because it is understood through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) in relation to the *kāraka*, it becomes subordinate to the substance.
Likewise: "Just as oneness in the fifth case is perceived through the direct statement of the word (*padaśruti*)."
"By the more powerful direct statement of common expectancy, there is the cognition of the action.
In this regard, he demonstrates the direct statement of common designation.
Therefore, it is well said that the applicator is threefold;
*Ratnamālā*, p. 123:
"The principle of scripture."

For even in the case of a worldly designation (*samākhyā*), although it may serve as a basis for inferring a root-Vedic text (*mūlaśruti*) through the logic of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), it does not have the power to infer [the application of] place (*sthāna*) and so forth;
in the case of a Vedic designation, however, it does not even possess that much. (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad Bhāṣya 3.3.6.13)
In the case of a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and context (*prakaraṇa*):

if "Ahīna" is the name of a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), then because it is connected by direct statement, there is no inclusion [of other elements] through context due to the absence of such connection; for in that case, there is indeed a conflict between direct statement and context.

(Vārttika 3.3.8.15). When there is a conflict between direct statement and context, since the twenty-one recitations would—by virtue of context—be understood as auxiliary to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the context is set aside because the direct statement determines them to be for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), such as for one desiring stability (*pratiṣṭhā*).

Because the *anuvacanas* (recitations) constitute the commencement of an action and take the form of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), they are to be understood as part of the context; therefore, due to that contradiction, there is no extraction [of them from their original place].
This applies when there are multiple subsidiaries (*śeṣya*).

In the case of the *ekādaśinī* (the group of eleven sacrificial animals), when the performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is intended for the purpose of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), the number fifteen is suggested as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*). However, by means of a direct statement in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-śruti*), the injunction of twenty-one recitations (*anuvacana*) is established.
This is the example cited by the author of the *Vārttika*. (Kau. 1.3.7.14, p. 354)

When there is a conflict between direct statement (śruti) and context (prakaraṇa), because direct statement possesses greater authority, the status of being for the sake of the person (puruṣārthatva) is established by the genitive direct statement.

In the case of the *śeṣanekalava* (the remaining single portion), however, when the performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is undertaken with the desire for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), the recitation fifteen times (*pāñcadaśya-anuvacana*) is prima facie applicable as a subordinate element due to the context (*prakaraṇa*).
