[However,] by means of a direct scriptural statement (*ṣaṣṭhī-śruti*), the injunction for reciting twenty-one times (*ekaviṃśaty-anuvacana*) is established. This example was stated by the author of the *Vārttika*. (Kau. 1.3.7.14, p. 354)
The types of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

Eight types of scriptural statements that possess extreme weakness were refuted by the author of the Vārttika in the section on the Ādhāra-Agnihotra (Su. p. 495). Some demonstrate eight types of scriptural statements that possess extreme weakness: 1. The injunction of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), as in "One performs the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*).

1. *Saguṇa-dhātvartha-vidhāna* (Vārttika): An injunction of the verbal root's meaning as qualified by an accessory (*guṇa*); i.e., an injunction of the verbal root's meaning qualified by an accessory (Sudhā).

2. *Kiñcid-vidhiṣya-dhātvartha-vidhāna* (Vārttika): An injunction of the verbal root's meaning after having enjoined something else; i.e., an injunction of the verbal root's meaning elsewhere (Sudhā); for example, "He sprinkles the rice grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*). 3. *Viśiṣṭa-vidhāna* (Vārttika): An injunction of a qualified verbal root's meaning elsewhere; i.e., an injunction of a qualified verbal root's meaning with reference to something else (Sudhā); for example, "He cleanses the cup with the *daśāpavitra* [filtering cloth]."

5. The prescription of another [element] with reference to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—this is "prescription of another in the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthe anyavidhi*). For example: "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*). 6. The connection of two [elements] with the meaning of the verbal root—this is "prescription of the connection of another in the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthe anyasaṃbandhavidhi*). For example: "He gives two mirrors to the Adhvaryu priest" (*prākāśāv adhvaryave dadāti*). In this case, the connection between the two mirrors and the Adhvaryu is prescribed within the meaning of the verbal root. 7. The connection of two [elements] with the suffix as qualified by the meaning of the verbal root—for example: "One should sacrifice a white animal dedicated to Vāyu" (*vāyavyaṃ śvetam ālabheta*).

8. Apart from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), there is a connection between two other things, as in: "One desiring sensory power should sacrifice with curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya juhuyāt*).
Vārttika 2.1.5.16; Sūtra-pṛ. 767–768. Direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is more authoritative. Bhāṣya 10.8.8.16; p. 2073.
Smṛti originating from direct scriptural statement overrides that which originates from indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, as well as that originating from explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
There is no sublation [of what is] unattained.
Vārttika 3.3.7.14, p. 860. For Vedic matters have scripture as their authority;
for these, there is no other means of knowledge.
Bhāṣya 5.1.2.16: "Because of the authority of the Vedic revelation (śruti), when there is an absence of the prescribed [material], there is no introduction of another, because that would be improper.

In the case of obligatory rites (nitya-karma), when there is an absence of the prescribed material—due to its unavailability or other reasons—and in the absence of the material enjoined for the learned (śiṣṭa), there should be no introduction, i.e., no taking up, of another material serving as a substitute.
Rather, the rite should be abandoned at that very point."
Because it is improper, since no other substance has been prescribed;
because the Veda is the authoritative source, the primary substance alone is supported by the authority of the Veda, whereas the substitute is not supported by the authority of the Veda.
Therefore, in the absence of the primary substance, there is the abandonment of the ritual act.
Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Furthermore, because of the injunction regarding certain cases:
even when the primary substance is available for a compulsory rite (*nityakarman*), a substitute (*pratinidhi*) should not be accepted.
Thus, regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states another reason by way of an indicative mark (*liṅga*):

"If one should not find *soma*, one should press *pūtīka* plants. From this injunction of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) in certain cases, it is understood that where no such injunction exists, there is no substitute.
The word "ca" (and) is used for the purpose of connecting [this] with other deities.
"Or rather, there is scriptural authority [for a substitute], because the purpose of the injunction remains the same.

Regarding the deliberation as to whether a substitute should be accepted when the prescribed substance is lost during rituals such as the Agnihotra, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—established by two preceding sūtras—is that it should not be accepted; for when the scripturally enjoined substance is destroyed, the performance must be abandoned at that point. Against this, the following is the sūtra of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The word "vā" (or) is for the purpose of setting aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
One must bring about the acquisition of a substance that serves as a substitute;

for there is no distinction—meaning no difference—between the primary substance and the substitute regarding the object of the injunction, that is, the fact of being the subject matter of the injunction.
Even in the case of accepting a substitute, there is no contradiction with the injunction for sacrifice;
this is for the purpose of restriction,
because it is prescribed in certain instances.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that for a permanent rite (*nitya-karma*), when the prescribed substance is unavailable, it must be performed with a substitute.

In this regard, the present sūtra is intended to refute the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) raised in [Jaimini Sūtra] 6.3.4.14, which states: "And because there is an injunction in certain cases.
The injunction found in the passage, "If one does not find *soma*, one should press *pūtīka* plants," is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*).

The injunction that "in the absence of Soma, only Pūtīka plants are to be taken and nothing else" is for the purpose of restriction; it is not an indication of the status of a substitute. For that [restriction] is constant, as it is the desire to perform that very rite. In a permanent (nitya) rite, a substitute should be taken when the prescribed substance is unavailable.
The Siddhāntin has stated that the prescription of *pūtīka* [leaves] when *soma* is unavailable is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*).
In that regard, how is its status as a restrictive rule understood? To this, he says:
because the desire to perform that sacrifice is constant; therefore, that *pūtīka* substance is obligatory (*nitya*) in the absence of *soma*.
The injunction regarding *pūtīka* plants is to be accepted as being for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).
Alternatively, the meaning is that "desire to perform" (*cikīrṣā*) implies similarity.

For since the desire to perform that [Soma sacrifice] is observed to have a similarity to Soma in the *pūtīka* plants, when Soma is unavailable, the application of those [plants] occurs; nevertheless, because the *pūtīka* substance is enjoined again, one must set aside any other substance—even if it resembles Soma—and take only the *pūtīka* substance. Thus, that *pūtīka* substance is the restriction.

Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that when the prescribed substance is unavailable, substitutes (pratiniyama) are permitted. It is a matter of curiosity that this sūtra does not appear to reflect the perspective of the Vārttika.
Because the authority for the subsidiaries is derived from scripture, when there is a distinction between the primary acts, their application should be according to their respective spheres.

When a distinction among the primary acts—the *apūrvas* (transcendental results) or principal rites—is established through means of proof such as "difference of words" (*śabdāntara*) and so forth, the existence—that is, the presence—of the subsidiaries should occur according to their respective spheres; that is, without overstepping the sphere or context (*prakaraṇa*).
Whatever is enjoined within the context of a particular *apūrva* should belong to that very *apūrva* alone.

Because of the authority of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). This [text] is the subsidiary (*śeṣa*) of this [principal], and that of this; in such cases, direct scriptural statement alone is the authority.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the determination of subsidiaries is according to their respective contexts (*prakaraṇa*).

Alternatively, due to the distinction between the purpose of the originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*) and the purpose of the application injunction (*viniyoga-vākya*), there would be a unity of properties among the constituent parts, just as there is among the substances themselves.

Regarding the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) stated in the Sūtra—namely, that "for those who are ignorant [of the specific application], the determination is according to the context"—the opponent, rejecting that by means of the word "or" (*vā*), says: the determination is not according to the context; rather, there would be a single set of properties. That is to say, even for principal rites such as the *aindrāgna* sacrifice, there would be a commonality of properties with the principal rites of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.
All dharmas would be for all purposes, because there is no distinction in their origin. By "origin," we mean the sacrifice.
Based on the etymological derivation "that by which something is produced," since the *apūrva* is produced by the sacrifice,
we refer to the *apūrva* as the "purpose" (*artha*).
"Origin" (utpatti) and "purpose" (artha) constitute "origin and purpose. Because of their non-separation— that is, because of their inseparable connection—
all ritual properties (dharmas) mentioned in connection with the sacrifice would apply to all sacrifices that possess the unseen potency (apūrva).
Like "existence" (sattvavat). By using the word "existence," every phenomenon (sarvadharma) is to be understood;
or rather, the reading is simply "like the phenomenon of existence" (sattvadharmavat).

Just as the property of "absence of touch" belongs to the individual being (sattva) named "cow" and so forth, so too it is with this case. Just as the property heard in the injunction "A cow is not to be touched with the foot" is understood—by virtue of its connection with "cowness" (gotva)—as applying to the cowness itself and to the individual bodies (piṇḍa) connected to cowness, so it is here.
Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that all [words] denote all meanings.

"Or rather, because they are supplementary to the injunction (*codanā*), they are restricted according to their specific differences; for [the other elements] are subordinate due to their non-arising [as primary acts].
By the word "or" (*vā*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that all ritual acts (*dharma*) serve all purposes—is set aside. He then states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
"Because the remaining [elements] are supplementary to the injunction."

That which impels is an injunction (*codanā*), namely, the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). And the ritual factors (*dharmas*) are subordinate to that productive operation. Those factors, according to their distinctions—that is, according to the distinctions of the productive operations—should be established, meaning they remain fixed, in accordance with their respective contexts.
Since the origination of the sacrifice—which generates the *apūrva*—is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), the ritual properties (*dharma*) should be restricted according to their respective contexts.

Because they are supplementary to the injunction (*codanāśeṣatvāt*), there is a restriction of properties when there is a difference in the injunction; because the origination is subordinate, there is a restriction of properties. Therefore, the restriction of properties follows the respective context.

The proponent [of the prima facie view] stated that "in the case of *sattva* (the genus 'being'), because of its connection with the characteristic, it is perceived as universal" (*sattve lakṣaṇasaṃyogāt sārvatrikaṃ pratīyate*). The proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) refutes this example by pointing out its dissimilarity: It is logical that the collection of properties heard in relation to *sattva*—such as the generic form (*ākṛti*) of cowness (*gotva*), for instance, when one hears "A cow should be touched with the foot"—is perceived as universal, that is, as residing in every individual cow.
Because of the connection with characteristics: because all individual objects are connected—that is, related—to the characteristic of "cow-ness.
But in the present case, it is not so.
Therefore, the determination of properties is according to the context.
"But this cannot be so because of indivisibility.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) establishes that the properties [of the sacrifice] beginning with the *prayāja* are prompted by the root *yaji* (to sacrifice).
By the word "but" (*tu*), he excludes the view that they are prompted by the *apūrva*.

Thus it would not be so; there would be no application of the ritual properties (*dharma*) to things that have not been previously enjoined. Because the ritual properties are inseparable and the sacrifice is inseparable—since some ritual properties are heard in relation to the substance, some in relation to the deity, and some in relation to the mantras.
Sacrifice (*yāga*) is the relinquishment of a substance with a mantra directed toward a deity;
therefore, the ritual properties (*dharma*) are inseparable from sacrifice. Because they are for the sake of sacrifice, all properties serve all purposes.
Furthermore, the state of being for the sake of a purpose is contradictory.
If all ritual elements (dharmas) were for all purposes, then only on that basis would the observation of the *prayāja* offerings in the *saurya* rite be logical, as in the injunction:
"At each *prayāja*, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* grain."
Otherwise, the *prayāja* offerings would have to be performed differently, and a *kṛṣṇala* weight of gold would have to be used in the *prayājas*.
Furthermore, the scriptural injunction "At each *prayāja*, he offers a *kṛṣṇala*" would become meaningless. And this meaninglessness [would follow].
This is contradictory. Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is once again that all ritual duties (dharmas) enjoined by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) serve all purposes.

Alternatively, because there is no injunction regarding their origin, the application [of the duties] would occur only upon a specific injunction; consequently, there would be a distinction between the rituals (*karmabheda*).
The word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of refuting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that these properties (*dharmas*) are enjoined in relation to the sacrifice.
Because there is no injunction regarding their origin, there is no injunction of the properties in relation to the sacrifice.

Even though they are heard in connection with the sacrifice, nevertheless, their application is directed toward the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) as the cause, being prompted by the injunction of that *apūrva*.
The ritual properties (*dharmas*) pertain to what is not previously established (*apūrva*).
Consequently, because they pertain to what is not previously established, there is a distinction between rituals, and from that distinction of the ritual, there must be a distinction of the *apūrva*.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the determination of ritual properties is according to each respective context (*prakaraṇa*).

Alternatively, even as in the case of the name (*abhidhāna*), all ritual elements (*dharma*) would apply by virtue of their commonality. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) raises the objection: "Even though the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) is the motivator for the ritual elements, they must still serve all purposes. Or rather: even if the *apūrva* is indeed the motivator for the ritual elements, nevertheless, every ritual element would apply to every purpose.
First of all, the designation is the same, namely "apūrva" (the unprecedented).
Just like the designation, its property (dharma) must also be the same.
Furthermore, it is like the designation; for example, [the term] "vāhīka" is like a designation.

Just as when it is said, "A Vāhīka guest has arrived; let barley-water be prepared for him," the term "Vāhīka" refers to the person (the guest), and barley-water is prepared for that specific individual;
so too here, the ritual properties (dharmas) heard in connection with one *apūrva* ought to belong to all *apūrvas*.
Therefore, even though the properties are prompted by the *apūrva*, all properties serve all purposes—this is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) once again.

However, because the purpose (*artha*) is indivisible, it would be so in the case of the designations; for the performance follows the model, since the ritual action is to be accomplished through the word, and because the remaining elements do not apply due to their division.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *prayāja* and other ritual duties are obtained from the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*).
The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that they belong to both the model and the modification (*vikṛti*) universally.

The proponent (pūrvapakṣin) has stated that, in the case of having all things as its referent, it is like the word [‘vāhīka’], using the example of the Vāhīkas. The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin), indicating the dissimilarity of that [example] by means of the word ‘but’ (tu), establishes his own position:

because the connection of the object with a specific region is undivided, pervasive, and common to all Vāhīkas, it would be so in the case of designations—such as the words "Let barley-gruel be prepared for the Vāhīka"—whereby the barley-gruel would have all Vāhīkas as its referent; thus, it would be applicable to all.

For all those residing in the Vāhīka region consume only what is called *yava* (barley). Since the usage— that is, the consumption of what is called *yava*— is established as prior among all [people],
and since the meaning is undifferentiated and the usage is as before, it should be so in the case of denotations.

In the present case, however, because the *prayāja* and other such rites have the verbal expression itself as their objective (*śabdabhāvyatva*), and because they are enjoined by the Vedic word alone, there is a distinction; since the *apūrvas* (transcendental results) are known to be distinct, there would be no application—meaning no extension—of the remaining auxiliary elements of the archetype (*prakṛti*) to other modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the *saurya*.
Therefore, all ritual properties (*dharmas*) serve all purposes;
nevertheless, their arrangement is determined according to the specific context (*yathāprakaraṇam*).

Regarding the objection concerning curiosity (*kutūhala*): in the case of designations such as the instruction "this is a Vāhīka," because the object—the quality of being fond of barley—is undifferentiated and common [to all], it would follow that the serving of barley would occur even for another person who is not a Vāhīka.
Why? Because the usage—such as the usage "this is a Vāhīka"—is preceded by the same [quality], namely, the prior existence of the commonality of being fond of barley.

However, since the ritual action is established by the authority of the word, there is a distinction between them; due to this difference in action, those remaining elements taught in one context would not apply elsewhere. Thus it has been explained.
If it is argued that this is based on *smṛti*:

when the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) asserts that the ritual properties (*dharma*) such as the *prayāja* offerings in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices are prompted by the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) and not prompted by the root *yaji* (the act of sacrificing), the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) raises an objection.

In the texts known as *paricchedas* belonging to the school of the Aruṇaparāśaras, there exists a Brāhmaṇa in the form of a *smṛti* which states: "Whatever properties belong to the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, they all belong to the *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice] as well."
If it is argued that, by this [reasoning], all ritual elements such as the *prayāja* offerings are established as being for the sake of all [results], we say:
no, because they are like the preceding case.

Regarding the statement by the followers of Aruṇaparāśara Śākhin that "whatever ritual properties (dharmas) belong to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, they all belong to the Agniṣomīya and to [the other] sacrifices," such that all properties serve all purposes—the opponent's prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is not tenable. This is because [the modified sacrifices] are preceded by the archetype (prakṛti); the modified sacrifices (vikṛtis) are preceded by the archetype.
For all [sacrifices], the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice] is the archetype for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices when they are not directly perceived;
and the properties of the archetype are extended to the modified sacrifices (vikṛtis) by means of the injunctional transfer (codaka).
Thus, the modified sacrifices are preceded by the archetypal sacrifice.

Furthermore, the fact that the *Smṛti* of Aruṇa and Parāśara is based on an original archetype (*prakṛti*) is established by the logic of the *codaka* (transference rule) and is merely restated there; it is not an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhāna*).
Therefore, all ritual duties (*dharma*) are enjoined for the sake of all [rites], because they are based on the authority of the *Śruti*. Thus, there are no divisions of *Śruti*.

Since the purpose (artha) is brought about by the word (śabda), and because they are recorded in their respective contexts (prakaraṇa), the application [of the ritual elements] must be from the word itself and not elsewhere.

In the inquiry as to whether the *dharmas* such as the *prayājas* are enjoined for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices alone as being prompted by the *apūrva*, or whether all *dharmas* are enjoined even in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛtis*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "everything is for the sake of everything" is refuted; the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is summarized as having established that they are prompted by the *apūrva* and are restricted according to their respective contexts.

Since the category of dharma has its manifestation in words and since words are its sole means of knowledge, there would be a restriction [of application] based on the fact that it is bound to each respective section within each section. The meaning is that those dharmas which are enjoined in a particular section should belong to that section alone.

If it is objected, "In that case, then the *prayāja* offerings and so forth would not occur in the *saurya* sacrifice and others," the answer is: no. Because of the word "like the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*) in the injunction "the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) is to be performed like the archetype," there would be the presence [of those elements] even in other modified sacrifices such as the *saurya*, because they are enjoined and thus permitted.

Furthermore, because of the scriptural injunctions, "He offers these Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations" and "He offers the Aṃyatāna oblations," their existence would occur elsewhere even in the absence of dispute.
From the word itself, their existence would occur elsewhere; however, without a specific statement, there would be no existence elsewhere at all.
Who [are they]?

The impossibility of setting aside that which is established by scripture (śruti) by means of a restrictive rule (niyama). Vākyapadīya 2.13.18, p. 564. The section concerning the superiority of scripture (śrutiprābalyādhikaraṇa). Viṣaya 1.3.2. Sublation of scripture (śrutibādha) by indicative mark (liṅga) in certain cases.

Bāla, p. 145: Those [indicative marks, etc. which are sublated by indicative marks (liṅga) and so forth that are themselves sublated by direct statement (śruti) are sublated by direct statement. Vārttika 3.3.7.14, p. 823: The different types of direct statement are now being described. Direct statement that expresses [the meaning] is fivefold.

A root (dhātu), a nominal stem (prātipadika), an affix such as a kṛt-affix, a prefix (upasarga), and an indeclinable (nipāta) constitute the categories; furthermore, among roots, there are two kinds: those designated as "roots" by the rule "bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ" and those [designated as roots] by the rule "sanādyantā dhātavaḥ."

The nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is also of two kinds: that which has been designated by the rule "A meaningful element that is neither a root nor an affix is a nominal stem" (*arthavad adhātu-pratyayaḥ prātipadikam*), and that which is designated by the rule "Kṛt derivatives, taddhita derivatives, and compounds [are also nominal stems]" (*kṛt-taddhita-samāsāś-ca*).
The suffix (pratyaya) is of four kinds, distinguished as nominal endings (sup), verbal endings (tiṅ), primary suffixes (kṛt), and secondary suffixes (taddhita).

One position is that prefixes (*upasarga*) and particles (*nipāta*) possess denotative power (*vācakatva*). This is because, in the case of *nañ* (the negative particle), its expression of exclusion (*nivartanā*) has been stated; and in the case of *paryudāsa* (exclusion by implication), the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of *nañ* has been stated. Furthermore, since figurative indication is appropriate when the primary meaning is absent—just as in the case of words such as *gāvī*—it follows that these two [prefixes and particles] possess denotative power.
Another position is that these two possess indicative power (*dyotakatva*).
As stated in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*: "Regarding that which is denotative—whether it be the genus (*ākṛti*) or the individual (*vyakti*), that is what is being deliberated.

Even in the case of the term "denotative" (*vācaka*), since the *cola* (the individual) is included within "that other than it" (*tadanya*), both possess the very nature of being denotative; thus, there is no contradiction with the Vedic text (*śruti*). This is because even in the view that the word denotes the meanings of the stem and suffix as unconnected, the word itself functions as the *viniyojaka-śruti* (the injunctive text that assigns application).

The scriptural indications (*śruti*) that effect application (*viniyojaka*) are eightfold: 1) injunctive scriptural indication (*vidhiśruti*); 2) scriptural indication of the *parasmaipada* (active voice); 3) scriptural indication of the *ātmanepada* (middle voice); 4) that which consists of a word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*), characterized by proximity (*upaśleṣalakṣaṇā*), so it is said; 5) the state of having a single suffix (*ekapratyayatva*); 6) the case-ending denoting a factor of action (*kārakavibhakti*); 7) the case-ending of a subordinate word (*upapadavibhakti*), specifically the dative used in the sense of "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*); and 8) the genitive of remainder (*śeṣaṣaṣṭhī*).

In this regard, the scriptural injunction (*vidhiśruti*)—as in "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) and so forth—directs the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), which is its own object, toward a result such as heaven that constitutes a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), having regard for the sacrifice itself, which is not a human goal.

However, the *śruti* in the form of a *parasmaipada* verb was stated by the Miśras in the third [book], in the section (8.1.13–14) beginning "The desire is not [for the agent] because of the connection with the purpose," as establishing the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Because of the *parasmaipada* *śruti* in the word "he should measure" (*minuyāt*), the activity of the Adhvaryu priests is heard to be for the sake of another; due to the contradiction with that *śruti*, the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the passage "If he should desire that Parjanya be rainy, he should measure the *sadas* high" applies to the word "he should desire" (*kāmayeta*). Thus, the desire belongs to another.

By the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) of the *ātmanepada* ending in the rule "āda-bhīta" (Pāṇini 1.3.5), it is stated in the sixth book, in the section titled "In the performance, there is the mention of the person" (6.1.2), and in the *Tantraratna* on the sūtra "The connection with the name is for another purpose" (sūtra 9), that the results of the rites accomplished by the *ādhāna*—such as the *āmiṣṭut* sacrifice—belong to the performer (*āghātṛ*) himself; as it says: "But in the case of the *Saurya* and other such rites, the result is produced solely by the *ādhāna* through the *ātmanepada* ending used in the context of the *ādhāna*," and so forth.

The *viniyojikā* (the indicator of application), consisting of a single word in the form of a direct enunciation (*sūcanā*) and in the form of a single suffix (*pratyaya*), respectively functions as the sublated and the sublator when stated [as follows]: "In this way, the singularity of the fifth [offering] is understood through the direct audition of the word (*padaśruti*);
however, by the audition of the common suffix (*samānapratyayaśruti*), which is more powerful, it belongs to the action."
Thus (Vākyapadīya, p. 840).

The *śruti* that enjoin[s], consisting of a single word in the form of a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), such as the *śruti* "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) and so forth, establishes the status of the root-meaning as the instrument (*karaṇatva*) within the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).

However, as previously stated in the Sūtra, the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) consists of a single form of cognition, such as "with an animal" (*paśunā*), and it also possesses a dual form, such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*).

The *śruti* that enjoin[s] by means of the case-inflection of the grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is now defined. Now, an objection is raised: "Is there not a distinction between the nominal suffixes (*sup*), the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), and the case-inflections of the grammatical factors, such that the latter should be defined separately? It is replied: The *śruti* consisting of the nominal suffixes (*suv-ādi*) applies only to nouns (*sloka*).

The case-ending of the agent (*kāraka-vibhakti*) is the allocator of meanings among themselves; however, the distinction is that while the nominal stem-meaning and the action are both the substrata [of the relation], the case-ending of the agent is what allocates them.

In that regard, the case-ending of the agent is manifold. Among these, the second case in the sense of the object (*karman*), as prescribed by the rule "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), is exemplified in such instances as "he threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn avahanti*).

The instrumental case in "yavāgvā juhoti" (he offers with barley-gruel) and similar instances is the instrumental of the object (*karmaṇi tṛtīyā*), as prescribed by the rule "And the third [case-ending] is used in the Veda."

The dative case is prescribed for the object of a verb meaning "to go" when there is physical movement, as taught by the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi dvitīyā-caturthyau ceṣṭāyāmanv-anasi*; thus, in examples such as *grāmāya yāti* ("he goes to the village"), the dative is used for the object.

Regarding the rule "the third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument," examples such as "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*) and "the Veda, along with its six limbs, should be studied and known by a Brahmin without [specific] motive" (*brāhmaṇena niṣkāraṇaḥ ṣaḍaṅgo vedo'dhyeyo jñeyaśca*) illustrate the use of the third case for the instrument and the agent respectively.
Regarding the rule "saṃho-'nyatarasyāṃ karmaṇi," when it is stated that "he recognizes his father as father" (pitaraṃ saṃjānīte), and so forth, the third case ending is used for the object.

Having stated "the fourth case-affix [is used] in the sense of the recipient" (*saṃpradāne*), [the rule] "he gives a staff to Maitrāvaruṇa" (*maitrāvaruṇāya daṇḍaṃ prayacchati*) and so forth illustrates the fourth case-affix in the sense of the recipient.

Having stated, "And [the fourth case ending is used] for that which has a word denoting purpose as its upapada, when it stands in the sense of the object," the fourth case is employed in the object [as in] "He goes for the sake of fruits" (*phalebhyo yāti*).

The fourth case ending is prescribed for the object of a verb expressing "disregard" (*manyakarma*) when used with reference to non-living beings, according to the rule: *manyakarmaṇyanādare vibhāṣāprāṇiṣu*.

Having understood the rule "the fifth case-affix is used for the ablative (apādāna)," [one applies] the fifth case-affix in examples such as "he gathers grass from the fire" (agner agni-tṛṇāny acinoti).

The ablative case (pañcamī) in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*), as prescribed by the rule "and [the ablative is used] for *stoka*, *alpa*, *kaṭipaya*, and *asūya*," is seen in examples such as "he was released by a little" (*stokena stokād muktaḥ*).

The genitive case in "he plays for a hundred" (*śatasya dīvyati*) and so forth, as prescribed by the rule *divastadarthasya*; the genitive in "he bets against a hundred" (*śatasya pratidīvyati*) and so forth, as prescribed by the rule *vibhāṣāpasarge*; the genitive in "O priest, announce the offering of the forepart of this oblation's omentum and fat" (*agre chāgāyā asya haviṣo vapāyā medasaḥ preṣyānubrūhi*) and so forth, as ordained by the rule *preṣyabruvorhaviṣo devatāsaṃpradāne*; and the genitive in "he sacrifices with clarified butter" (*ājyasya yajate*) and so forth, as ordained by the rule *yajñeśakaraṇe*—these are instances of the genitive used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe ṣaṣṭhī*).

In accordance with the rule "In the Vedic language, the dative sense is frequently expressed by the genitive," the genitive case is used in the sense of the recipient (saṃpradāna) in such passages as: "The man-deer for the moon, the iguana, the kālakā bird, the bear, and the tiger—these are the names of the trees."

When used in connection with words expressing the sense of "times" (kṛtvas), the sixth case is prescribed for time when it is not a verbal root (aḍi-karaṇe), as in the example: "He eats five times a day" (*pañcakṛtvo divo aho bhuṅkte*). In this instance, the sixth case is used for the locus (*adhikaraṇe*).

The genitive case prescribed by the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti" (Pāṇini 2.3.65)—as in examples such as "kṛṣṇasya kṛtiḥ" (the act of Kṛṣṇa) and "jagataḥ kartā" (the creator of the world)—is used for both the agent and the object.
The genitive case in the sense of the object (karma-ṣaṣṭhī), as in "the milking of cows by Citramagopa," is prescribed by the rule "ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi."

The locative case (saptamī) is taught [by the rule] "samam-y-adhikaraṇe ca" in such instances as "one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa on level ground," where it denotes the locus (adhikaraṇa).
Thus has been described the Vedic revelation in the form of case-inflected words.

The dative case in the sense of "being for the sake of that" (tādarthya) is seen, for example, in such expressions as "the Jyotiṣṭoma [is for the sake] of all [desires]" and "the Darśapūrṇamāsa [are for the sake] of all [desires]," and so forth.
The remaining genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is of two kinds: that of quality (*guṇatva*) and that of predominance (*prādhānya*).
Of these, the first is, for example: "One should sacrifice for us in a low voice, as it were, with clarified butter at the full moon," and so forth.

The genitive is used in the sense of predominance (*prādhānya*), as in "There are exactly three *upasads* for the one-day sacrifice (*sāhasya*), twelve for the twelve-day sacrifice (*ahina*)," and so forth.
In the opinion of Bhaṭṭa Someśvara, however, there are other means of application as well.
Thus, the *itikaraṇa* (the use of "iti") refers to [injunctions] such as, "With the words 'For food, thee,' he cuts the branch."
Likewise, the suffix *ṇamul* prescribed by connection with a verbal root is seen in examples such as "he offers oblations toward the village" (*amigrāmaṃ juhoti*).
The suffix *ktvā* is likewise exactly the same.
In that case as well, there are two possibilities: either the former is for the sake of the latter, or the latter is a constituent part of the former.
Regarding this, the first example is as follows: "Having trimmed the grass from its base, he makes the *upaveṣa*.
Here, the trimming is performed from the tip of the *upaveṣa*.
An example of the second type is as follows: "Having sacrificed with the Vālakhilyas, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava."
Thus, that which is inappropriate in speech begins with "Therefore, [he is] the teacher" and so forth.
Thus, the suffixes *tumun*, *ṇvul*, and *aṇ*—prescribed respectively by the rules "tumun-ṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām," "bhāvavacanāśca," and "aṇ karmaṇi ca"—are examples of such suffixes.
Thus, the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is prescribed by the rule "after a numeral, [the suffix] *kṛtvasuc* is added in the sense of a collection of repetitions of an action."

Similarly, the suffix *suc* in the rule "after two, three, or four, [the suffix] *sun*" is also illustrated by such examples as: "He sprinkles the threefold [altar] with the formula, 'Thou art the altar; for the sacrificial grass, thee! and so forth.

Similarly, in the case of the injunction, "One who is beginning the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Āmāvāyava," the *luṭ* suffix— taught as occurring when another action is the purpose (*upapada*) of the first action— indicates by direct audition (*śruti*) that the commencement [of the sacrifice] is the primary factor, overriding the indications of syntactical connection (*vākya*) and so forth.

Regarding the matter of the *itiharaṇa* (the carrying away of the grass-bundle), however, in the section concerning the naming [of the sacrifice] (*tathāhvānam apīti cet*) at 3.1.15–19, the *Śāstradīpikā* establishes the final view (*siddhānta*) that it is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

Regarding the suffix *-ktvā*, however, the *Tantraratna* states that its status as a subsidiary is established through syntactical connection (*vākya*), saying: "And because it is mentioned in the same sentence as the *vājapeya*—which is fruitful—it is a subsidiary of the *vājapeya*.
Likewise, in the section on the *upaveṣa* (the fire-stirring stick) at 4.1.38–39, it is established by means of the dative case itself.

390. A difference in scriptural authority (*śrutibheda*): The definition of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) has been stated [in the following]: "And it is not for the purpose of making a *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick) because of the established conviction that 'one should not pare,' [but rather] it is enjoined [for another purpose]."

In the *Tantraratna* as well, it is stated that there is no "cooking" (*parivāsana*) because of the communication by another; for in the fifth book, section on syntactical connection (*vākya-saṃyoga*), it is said that the accusative case is stronger [than the locative], as in the passage beginning with "to Agni and Viṣṇu.

When there is co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word *dīkṣiyamāṇa* in the sentence, the purpose is initiation (*dīkṣā*). As for the statement: "And a *kṛt* suffix prescribed in connection with a verbal root [is used] in the case of the Vājapeya... [this refers to the rule governing the formation of the term].
Thus, regarding the statement,

"One intending to sacrifice with Soma should establish the fires," the claim that it expresses only the connection between the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) and the subsequent period is the opinion of others;

for the status of the time following the establishment as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the Soma sacrifice is derived from syntactical connection (*vākya*), since the fact that the present tense (*laṭ*) conveys a connection with an action is established as the meaning of a sentence, and thus it constitutes a syntactical whole.
Precisely because it is not found in the revealed scripture (*śruti*).

The rule "suffixes [are applied] when there is a connection with a verbal root" (*dhātusaṃbandhe pratyayāḥ*) is merely a statement intended to establish grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). Even though the *Tantraratna* states that "the suffix *ṇamul* and others are correct only when there is a co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with another action, as in the case of 'one who is about to sacrifice' (*yakṣyamāṇaḥ')... [and so forth].

Just as in the case of [the rule] "being performed" (*kriyamāṇaḥ*), when one action is the subordinate element (*upapada*) for the sake of another action, among the means of proof such as direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth—[as stated in the *Tantravārttika*]: "Direct statement (*śruti*) and sentence (*vākya*)... (p. 859), and regarding "direct statement, indicative mark, and so forth"—it is established that, because of the remoteness of the meaning (*arthaviprakarṣāt*), each subsequent [means of proof] is sublated by each preceding one.

And it is said (in five verses): "When both [the practitioner of yoga and the one who has attained the fruit] ascend toward the attainment of the single fruit—that which is to be reached as the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) and which arises from its own immediate cause—then..."
One [runner] is on a single flight of stairs, while the other stands on the ground;
the speed of both is equal, and there is no obstruction between them.
For the fruit of those two conflicting [deeds] would be obtained in this very life;
since the first has already been taken up, the latter would descend in vain.
Therefore, although its capacity is established individually at other times,
nevertheless, when they occur simultaneously, that which is weaker is set aside.
For indeed, even by those who are weak, the Vedic texts are understood in one way;
yet by those who are powerful, they are understood in another way, since everything remains within the scope of their power.
Therefore, it is logical that something should be relied upon in such cases where the validity of subsequent [cognitions] is accepted;
consequently, there must be sublation by that [subsequent cognition] even when there is a strong contradiction.
As for the claim that "it is a pseudo-means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) that is sublated, not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)," to that we reply:

This too is merely a semblance of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*). How so? "These [means of cognition] never possessed the status of being valid cognitions here; this [status] was seen elsewhere and is imagined through superimposition."

It is not the case that these [cognitions] possess the status of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) wherever there is a sublation of the object. What then? That which was perceived elsewhere as a pure [independent] cognition appears here too in the form of an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*). However, because its object has been seized by a stronger [cognition], it is set aside; subsequently, it is determined to be an error (*bhrānti*).
Alternatively, the very same operation that it had there is also undertaken here;
however, when it does not reach its object because another [cognition] with greater speed has already occupied the field by cutting off its root, what can be done?
Therefore, like a mirage and the like, it is sublated even before reaching its object, and thus remains a non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).

Furthermore, since there is no scriptural authority for it here, the subsequent cognition—which is as yet unarisen—is sublated by the assumption that the intervening cognition was false; thus, they do not possess equal strength merely by virtue of both being cognitions.

Consequently, one should not even suspect a sublation consisting of the destruction or contraction of the cognition. And as for that sublation which occurs after a cognition has arisen, we shall demonstrate that it consists merely in the dissociation from its result.

Page 834–835, line 313/7/24: Regarding *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth—in all cases, it is impossible to apply a subsequent [means of proof] after having inferred the application by means of a prior one.
However, once the application has been established by the prior [means], the subsequent one is understood merely as being necessarily present.
It is said: since *śruti* is perceptible, it is logical that it possesses greater force than *liṅga*.

Now, since indicators (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), and so forth, are not distinct from direct assertion (*śruti*) insofar as they are themselves to be inferred, by what is their relative strength or weakness determined? To this it is said:
"The disparity among indicators and the rest with respect to the meaning of direct assertion is held to be caused by the intervention of one, two, three, four, five, or six [steps]."

Among direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*), each preceding one is a stronger means of proof than each subsequent one. For this [preceding] origin, when examined, there exists no other cognition that sublates it; therefore, in their conjunction where there is conflict, the subsequent ones are weaker due to the remoteness of the purpose (*arthaviprakarṣāt*).
Bhāṣya 3.3.14, p.

862: "In the case of a conflict among direct statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), syntactical connection (vākya), context (prakaraṇa), position (sthāna), and name (samākhyā), the subsequent ones are weaker because of their remoteness from the purpose. That is to say, when there is a conflict—meaning a contradiction regarding a single object—among these six means of knowledge that convey application, it should be understood that each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding.

The state of being weak is "weakness" (*daurbalya*); the weakness of another is "another's weakness" (*paradaurbalya*), which is precisely "supreme weakness" (*pāradaurbalya*). It should be understood that as each subsequent factor becomes weaker, each preceding factor becomes stronger, because of the remoteness of their application (*arthaviprakarṣāt*).

Because of the remoteness—that is, the intervention—of the purpose and the application, the indicative power (*liṅga*) is unable to enjoin its own meaning without the postulation of a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*); thus, the application by indicative power is established through the postulation of a *śruti*. Furthermore, syntactical connection (*vākya*) effects the application after having postulated both the indicative power and the *śruti*.

Context (prakaraṇa) becomes an applicator only by postulating a sentence (vākya), an indicative mark (liṅga), and a direct statement (śruti), and not otherwise. Position (sthāna) also becomes an applicator by postulating context, a sentence, an indicative mark, and a direct statement.
Likewise, name (samākhyā) becomes an applicator by postulating everything from position down to a direct statement, and not otherwise; thus it is considered the fifth [means of application].
By this reason of intervention, each subsequent [means of proof] becomes weaker.
The definitions of direct statement (*śruti*) and the others, along with examples of their mutual conflict, have been explained at length elsewhere; therefore, there is no detailed treatment here.
Ke.

In the section concerning the non-contradiction between direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by considering the inherent power of the mantra's accent; however, in the section concerning [the verse] addressed to Indrāṇī (*aindrī*), the prima facie argument is established solely by considering the direct statement (*tadit-śruti*). This is the nature of the *upaniṣad*.
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1086). It is not proper for the word of direct revelation (*śruti-vacana*) to be sublated by the word of traditional scripture (*smṛti-vacana*).
If, without citing a scriptural statement, one were to say "it exists in another scripture," then whatever anyone desired would be established. (Su.)
Regarding the two statements of the *śruti*: [the word] "ear" (*śrotra*) on page 655;
because it is not cited as an example, it is indistinct. Having stated this, nothing would remain unachievable.
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 2.2.4.10, page 495:
"In a conflict between direct scriptural statement (śruti) and syntactical connection (vākya), the direct scriptural statement is more powerful" (Bhāṣya 2.1).
The properties such as *śruti*, *viniyoga*, and *śruti* themselves are connected with what precedes them.
They do not permit a sale recorded in the *smṛti* that contradicts the *śruti*.
Bhāṣya 6.1.13–15: A Smṛti that contradicts Śruti is not authoritative. 1.3.1.3, p. 185:
The lack of authority of [Smṛtis] concerning women that contradict Śruti.
Bhāṣya:
"There is no interruption whatsoever in the very nature of the Śruti and Smṛti; nor is there an examination of their relative strength, for that [examination] pertains to the objects of knowledge."
"Or [it is so], because the learned (śiṣṭas) are the authority on the basis of the Śruti and Smṛti. — Bhāṣya on Vākyapadīya 1.3.1.7, p. 199.
"Dharma is that which is ordained by Śruti and Smṛti; in the absence of those, the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra) is the authority," so says the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti (Su. p. 213).
"In the case of a scriptural statement being heard, to conceive of it as deficient or excessive..."
In the case of inference, there is the absence of defects such as secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) and syntactical split (vākyabheda).
(Vārttika 1.4.13):
If one accepts that [the number] is deficient relative to what is intended to be expressed, there would be the faults of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
However, if one accepts it as being in excess, then the words beginning with "ten" (*daśa*) would be rendered meaningless.

Alternatively, the meaning is that if one assumes that what is deficient [in the text] has a greater scope of application, there are the defects of *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication), *vākyabheda* (splitting the sentence), and the introduction of *gauṇatva* (secondary sense). That is to say:
if there is deficiency, there are *lakṣaṇā* and *vākyabheda*; if there is excess, there is *ānarthakya* (pointlessness).

Or else, it may be construed as follows: if one assumes something different [from the literal], there are the defects of *vipariṇāma* (modification), *vyavahitakalpanā* (assumption of the remote), and *vyavahārakalpanā* (assumption of conventional usage).
But when there is an inference, since it is precisely that which possesses the capacity to express the intended meaning that is inferred, there is no fault whatsoever. (Su. pṛ.
417–418) "Regarding the conceptualization of deficiency or excess in a sentence being heard..."
In the case of inference, there is the absence of defects such as [the need for] indication (lakṣaṇā) or syntactical split (vākyabheda).

This is the Vārttika regarding the Citrā-adhikaraṇa. According to the logic stated in that Vārttika (on 1.4.13), the accusative case in the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*)—in the phrase "one's own Veda" (*svādhyāya*)—indicates precisely its status as a subordinate factor (*guṇatva*). Otherwise, there would arise a discrepancy (*vairūpya*) in the injunction of a subordinate factor regarding the *svādhyāya*, similar to the case of the sacrifice in the Vājapeya sentence. This is the resolution according to the statement of Bhavadeva; Bālakrīḍā, p. 2.
The maxim from the Mīmāṃsākośa (500) states: "Even for the great, many obstacles arise even toward auspicious goals.
This applies wherever there might be some slight hindrance, such as physical obstruction, to a virtuous deed; even in such cases, [the effort] persists.
Sādṛṣṭī. 534 | Śreyaskarabhāṣya.
Like the *codanāsūtra*, the *Śābarabhāṣya* states: "In that case, that which brings about the highest good (*śreyaskara*) is what ought to be investigated," and so forth.
Bāla, page 1:
[The work] named Śreyaskarabhāṣya.
Therefore, that which is characterized by Vedic injunction (codanā) is the object that brings about the highest good (śreyaskara).
"In that case, then, it is that which brings about the highest good (śreyaskara) which ought to be investigated—namely, the inquiry into Dharma (dharmajijñāsā).
It is replied: that very thing which brings about the highest good is what is denoted by the word 'Dharma'. — Bhāṣya 1.1.12.
If it is asked how the state of being the object of activity entails being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*), [the answer is: in the case of a word.
First of all, the instigation (*pravartanā*) is everywhere understood as having as its object the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) in the form of effort.

When it is said, "Bring the cow," even if the bringing of the cow fails for some reason while the person has directed their effort toward it, we observe the linguistic usage [of the speaker] as "He has carried out my command. Conversely, when it is said, "Move away from here," even if movement away occurs because someone was forcibly moved by another while the person themselves had not directed their effort toward it, we observe the linguistic usage of the commander as "This person did not carry out my command. Furthermore, since instigation (*pravartanā*) is that which prompts a conscious being, and since such instigation is never observed elsewhere than as having effort as its object, it is established that [the meaning of the optative suffix] is the object of effort.

And effort (*prayatna*), because it is produced by desire, is not possible without that [desire]. And that [desire] occurs naturally toward human ends (*puruṣārtha*) such as heaven and the like; since one who knows [the end] lacks a means, for the sake of accomplishing that [end], the desire transfers to the means for its accomplishment. Therefore, since sacrifice and the like—which are not themselves human ends—cannot be objects of desire without being means to a human end, and since activity toward them would otherwise be impossible, the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth could not function as motivators. Consequently, in order to justify that [motivation], it is established that the word implies being a means to a human end.

Even when the means to the highest good (*śreyas*) has been understood, because one observes that it requires great expenditure and effort, aversion arises; since this cannot be dispelled without praise, the desire for praise is difficult to ward off.
The position is that the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is space (*ākāśa*). [From] *Bṛhatī*, p. 202: "The auditory organ is space.

It is true that space is one everywhere; however, its state as the auditory organ exists only in the location of the ear, because it functions as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) through its connection with an agent (*kartṛ*).

Since agency belongs only to the specific location of the body, which serves as the locus of experience for the agent, there is no equality with the manifestation of sound. (p. 217) [The ear is] space; "I" [is the self]; "auditory" [is the faculty].

The meaning of the words must be determined; one [meaning] is established by its own nature, while another is established by something else. In this context, the word *atha* expresses immediate succession (*ānantarya*), just as in the expression "having studied the Veda.

Now, does this passage enjoin the initiation itself, while the sequence is obtained from the order of the text, or is it rather the sequence that is enjoined, such that this is a sequence based on direct scriptural statement (*śrutikrama*)?

Since a single chapter, which consists of a collection of various topics, possesses unity precisely by virtue of its being directed toward a single purpose,

it is logical that even the beginning of such a chapter serves as the cause for the qualification [to perform the rite], because it presents what is to be performed, thereby bringing about that unity.

In this regard, first of all, the existence of the qualification (*adhikāra*) is established by way of introduction; for only when that exists can the inquiry "To whom does this [injunction] belong? arise, and not otherwise. In this context, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) expressed in the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" requires an object to be brought about (*bhāvya*). By means of a direct statement (*śruti*) characterized by the co-occurrence within the same word, it accepts the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—which is subordinate—as the object to be brought about, while grasping the specific person introduced by another word as its agent. This is because direct statement is more authoritative than syntactical connection (*vākya*) and other means. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is: "One should perform the sacrifice with the substance, such as heaven."
Furthermore, the word "desire" (kāma) pertains to one who is performing an action;

therefore, even in the absence of wealth, a desire certainly arises for its attainment, and thus [the mention of desire] is a restatement (anuvāda). Having stated that—according to the sentence-meaning derived from the direct Vedic statement (śruti)—the sacrifice would be subordinated as a secondary element while some other fruit would be the goal to be accomplished, and thus there would be no qualification (adhikāra) for the rite, the final conclusion (siddhānta) is set forth by the force of the injunctive text (vidhi-bhūti).

For an injunction (*vidhi*), having first delimited the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) by drawing it from the verbal root within its own word, leads it toward a human goal because its very nature is that of an instigation (*pravartanā*). Since a person cannot be instigated toward an activity that does not serve a human purpose, it is precisely through this nature as an instigation that it requires the efficient force to take on a desirable form; only its specific details are then understood from the sentence. Once that [desirable end] is known, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) expressed in the same word is accepted as the instrument (*karaṇa*) due to its proximity, while substances and so forth are accepted as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
He said: "The connection with the injunction (*vidhi*) occurs first, because of the initial conjunction with its constituent parts;
subsequently, for those [parts] being connected, there would therefore be no status as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*).
Alternatively, if the entire *bhāvanā* in its complete form were the object of the injunction..."

Consequently, an action devoid of an injunction would not yield the fruit of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). If, first of all, because it possesses the three factors [of the object, means, and manner], only the bare efficient force (*bhāvanā*) were enjoined, then—even though the efficient force subsequently connects with those [factors]—the bare [force] alone would possess the status of being enjoined (*vidheyatva*), due to its direct contact with the injunction. However, since this [efficient force] is not yet fully realized, the connection with the injunction occurs prior to [its full realization]; thus, being devoid of the injunction, it relies upon the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as the objective to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) due to proximity. Consequently, the status of the human purpose as the objective to be accomplished would not be established.
This is not so.

"The connection between the injunction and the productive operation (bhāvanā) is first understood through direct audition (śruti). At that time, because of their incompatibility, they do not at all attain fulfillment."
And because of the attainment of connection, it is understood in this way:
by whatever means the cultivation attains connection with the injunction when complete,
it is fulfilled by those very same means in that same manner.
The human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*), and it is also that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

First of all, the relationship between the injunction (*vidhi*) and the productive urge (*bhāvanā*)—both denoted by a single word—is expressed through direct audition (*śruti*). In that arrangement, because the productive urge alone cannot be performed, its connection, though perceived, is not yet fully established. Even while that [connection] remains unestablished, through the cognition of it, the person at that very moment determines: "This [productive urge] must indeed be connected with the injunction."
Therefore, the injunction should be fulfilled by those [means] which are connected with the *girimara* [grains] and possess the same sequence;

nor can it admit anything else that does not have human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) as its fruit. Consequently, having determined that it must have human purpose as its fruit, and requiring a specific detail for that, it finds the verbal root-meaning situated within the same word to be unsuitable because it lacks human purpose, and thus looks toward what is expressed by another word.

In that context, since a specific [result] such as heaven is understood through words like "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) connects with it. Being thus connected and requiring an instrument (*karaṇa*), it—by virtue of proximity and according to the principle of the section on the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārthādhikaraṇanyāya*)—adopts the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) presented in the same word as its instrument. Then, when there is a requirement for the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāva*), it takes the sacrifices understood from direct audition (*śruti*) as its purposeful elements (*arthabhāva*). Thereafter, the efficient force, qualified by all these factors, is enjoined.

At that very moment, the cognition of the connection with the injunction occurs for the first time, and the status of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) as the end to be realized (*bhāvya*) is established.

Moreover, since even in the case of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the fulfillment of the sequence of injunctions occurs only after the acquisition of knowledge, it is established that even those who are ignorant are subject to the injunction;
therefore, there is no fault whatsoever.
Let us return to the subject at hand.

Thus, when it has been determined by the force of the injunction (*vidhi*) that the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*), then—given the requirement for its specific nature—the heaven and other results, whose predominance is understood from their connection with desire (*kāma*), become the *bhāvya* as subordinate to the person; they do not, as in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), constitute the means (*sādhana*).

For even in the prima facie view, the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) does not refer primarily to the person, but rather aims at establishing that heaven is the means for accomplishing the action through this [person] as a substance.
But how is it determined that the word "person" (puruṣa) refers to that [action] by both the proponent and the opponent? It is said:
First, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) thinks as follows: "The person is merely subordinate (guṇabhūta), being [merely] equal to the action.

Furthermore, in that context, no specific person is presented by the word 'desirous of heaven' (svargakāma), as a specific substance is presented by the word 'king' or the word 'rice' and so on; for whoever is desirous of heaven is also [at another time] not desirous of heaven."
If it were taken as "one who desires that" (*taskāmaḥ*), then the same fault would apply whether [the desire] is understood as a temporal factor (*kāla*) or as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*).
Therefore, there is no syntactic connection here of the person qualified by the desire for heaven as a subordinate element (*śeṣatvena*).

In this regard, since the substantive portion (*viśeṣya*) is already established [by other means], the word refers to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), just as in the case of "one whose turban is red" (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*) and so forth.
Even in that case, if the desire for heaven were taught as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*), it would result in an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*).
For no visible benefit to the ritual action is possible through the desire for heaven.
Moreover, there would be excessive complexity (*gaurava*) for the injunction if it were taught that the desire qualified by heaven is a subordinate factor.

Since heaven, being of the nature of a substance (*dravya*), has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) by virtue of being the object (*karman*) of the means of action, and because there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in enjoining the mere [act] itself, this is indeed an instruction regarding the substance. Furthermore, the suffix *aṇ* expressing the agent is a restatement (*anuvāda*) along with the verb *kāmayati*. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that the fact that the activity—the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—is for the sake of the person is understood solely through the power of the injunction (*vidhi*). For no one engages in an action toward another [object] without the absence of some subordinate purpose (*śeṣābhāva*).

And this "being for that purpose" (*tādarthya*) arises because [the sacrifice] is a means to accomplish a benefit required by that [person]. Thus, once it is established through investigation that the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) has the person as its goal by virtue of being a means to accomplish a required benefit, then—by way of requiring a specific benefit—the word *svargakāma* (desirer of heaven), according to the previously stated logic, functions to designate a specific person for whom the [sacrifice] would otherwise be unestablished. Consequently, the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) of such a person, who requires [the sacrifice] as a qualification, comes to have the purpose of conveying a specific benefit consisting of the qualification itself, namely heaven and so forth.
For this very reason, even when it is used in the sense of a bird (*pakṣin*), the word *svargakāma* does not refer to the person.
However, heaven is the primary goal;
the dispute concerns only the relative status of the subordinate and the principal.
Therefore it has been said: "Is heaven subordinate and the ritual act principal, or is the ritual act subordinate and heaven principal?"
Now, how is it that the person desiring the fruit (*phalakāmin*) is connected as a subordinate element (*śeṣitva*)?

Certainly [he is]. But then, how is there grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word "desire" (*kāma*) and words such as "king" (*rājā*) in passages like "A king desiring sovereign kingship should sacrifice with the Rājasūya," where the word "king" and so forth denote a subordinate element?
It is said: because both [the injunctions] have the agent as their primary referent.
For, by virtue of being the agent, there is indeed an association with the one desiring the fruit, just as in the case of a king.

But that connection [of the person] with the action is for the purpose of showing how it serves as a benefit to the person—just like the statements "one who is dirty must bathe" or "one who is hungry must eat.

For in those cases, although the status of being the agent is clearly expressed by the direct mention of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*), the "subordinate status" (*śeṣitva*) belongs only to the dirty person and so forth; why then should this not also apply to one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) and the like, whose agency is merely inferred through the syntactic connection (*adhyāhāra*) with the result?
Indeed, the connection with agency is not an obstacle to being a subordinate element (*śeṣin*).
For it has already been demonstrated that all grammatical factors (*kāraka*) can potentially be subordinate elements, as in the case of the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.
If this is so, then how is it that the accusative case-ending is a marker of the subordinate element?
But as for the third case and the others, they are established as specific [syntactical relations] because they are the remaining case-terminations (*vibhakti*).
It is said:
the distinction is justified by the demonstration of the relationship between the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

For the accusative case (dvitīyā) indeed conveys the state of being an object (*sādhyabhāva*), and the status of being an object is closely related to the status of being the principal (*śeṣitva*). Indeed, it is not possible for that which is not an object to be the principal; therefore, through its presence, the accusative brings about the cognition of that [principal status]. As for the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*) and other cases, they are said to be the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the status of being a subordinate (*śeṣabhāva*) because they express only that [subordinate status] and nothing more. However, where the status of being the principal belongs precisely to that which has been established as the means (*sādhanabhāva*) by those [other cases], there the status of being an object—though not explicitly stated—is to be inferred; thus, the specific distinction is established.

Therefore, between the two connections—of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) and of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*)—the one who desires self-sovereignty (*svarājyakāma*) possesses the status of a subordinate by the force of the injunction, while the king (*rājan*), by virtue of the principle regarding the connection with substance and action (*dravyakarmasaṃyoganyāya*), possesses only the status of a subordinate because his role is consistent with being a means (*sādhana*).

As for the claim made by some that the one desiring the fruit is connected as the person to be impelled (*niyojya*), even upon analysis, that too results in the very same connection of subordinacy (*śeṣitva*) as previously stated;
otherwise, there would be no distinction from the connection of being an agent.
For it is thus: "The one to be enjoined (niyojya) is he who accepts [the task] as his own duty;
and the fact that the task belongs to him consists in its being pervaded by his performance.
For whatever is pervaded by the performance of someone, and whatever is certain to be performed, that indeed has that person as its agent."

The status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) and being one who is enjoined (*niyojyatva*) is caused by the relationship between the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*). Regarding the view that the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣī*) asserts the connection of the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) as an agent,

while the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) asserts it as one who is enjoined— even he is unable to state a difference in the nature of the connection apart from the relationship between the subordinate and the principal.
For instance: he who understands "this is my duty" is the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).
And therefore, by the [injunction] "one desiring heaven should sacrifice,"...
It must be established that "this is to be done by one who desires heaven";
the meaning is that it is to be pervaded by the activity (*kṛti*) of the one desiring heaven.

For when this is so, he understands, "This is my duty (*kārya*)," and whatever is pervaded by someone's activity is precisely that person's agency (*kartṛtva*), just as in the case of the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*).

Therefore, since it is illogical for both the king and the one desiring sovereignty to be the agent [simultaneously], this distinction must be justified as follows: the one desiring sovereignty is the *niyojya* (the person to be enjoined), whereas the king is the agent (*kartṛ*).
Furthermore, even though he is the agent, the one desiring sovereignty is the *śeṣin* (the primary beneficiary) with respect to the task, while the king is the *śeṣa* (the subordinate).

Now, an objection is raised: "The status of being a *niyojya* consists in being the cognizer (*boddhṛ*), not in being the *śeṣin*. What, then, does the word 'desire' (*kāma*) signify? Does it denote the state of being a cognizer of the task delimited by the object of desire on the part of the desirer? How so? [In the form: 'How indeed is such a task delimited by sacrifice?'"

If this were so, because there would be no poem for one who lacks the capacity to understand it, then the desirous person would understand only that specific meaning intended by the author as "this is what must be done," but not "this is my duty. This is because there is no self whatsoever for whom the relationship denoted by the word "mine" exists in connection with the injunction. Consequently, the status of being a "person to be enjoined" (*niyojyatva*) would be impossible.
For one who merely understands "this is a duty" is not a person to be enjoined; rather, it is one who understands "this is my duty" who is so.
Furthermore, no engagement in action would be established;
for no one engages in an action merely because it is a "task" (*kārya*), but rather because "this is my task.

Moreover, the word that conveys the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) would be purposeless, since even without it, a person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) who is already proficient [in the meaning of the injunction] would certainly understand it through the attainment of the pure self alone.
In that case, there would be a restriction (parisaṃkhyā):

namely, that only one who desires heaven, being competent, would understand [the injunction], and no other. That doubt must be refuted; for even when [the injunction] is being recited, since there exists a person to be enjoined (niyojya) characterized by the capacity to understand among those who are competent, its utterance would occur. Therefore, it must be stated that because there necessarily exists a person to be enjoined—characterized by the capacity to understand—in the form "This task is mine to perform" for one who desires heaven, this very injunction must necessarily establish that "this is indeed the task."

And thus, there would follow the consequence of their being distinct by virtue of being agents. As for the argument that "even though they are identical, this one is indeed different," even so, there is no confusion between the status of being an agent and the status of being subject to an injunction.

"For agency belongs to the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*) due to the difference in their objects, whereas the state of being enjoined (*niyojyatva*) belongs to the injunction (*niyoga*). [To this, the opponent replies: "That is not correct; for no *kārya* (task) whatsoever is established apart from the verbal root-meaning, since that [status of being enjoined] is established only when the state of being enjoined exists."

For it is precisely within this very context that the connection of the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled) is established; it arises from the assumption that [the word] denotes an effect distinct from the action itself.

Therefore, since that [connection] has not yet been established prior [to this], one cannot claim that there is no confusion due to a difference in scope (*viṣayabheda*). Furthermore, because such [a connection] is absent in common worldly usage, even when the vocative case-ending is present in sentences such as "Devadatta, bring the cow," the status of being a *niyojya* would not exist.

Therefore, it must be stated that being a subordinate (*śeṣitva*) with respect to the task (*kārya*), as well as being one who is enjoined (*niyojyatva*) and being an agent (*kartṛtva*), are indeed identical.
As for the one who says: "It is true that the agent is enjoined through the distinction between the subordinate and the principal;
however, there is a distinction for him with respect to the activity (*kṛti*), whereas with respect to the task (*kārya*), both possess the status of subordinates."

Although there is indeed a distinction between the agent (*kartṛ*) and the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) based on the difference between being subordinate (*śeṣa*) and being the principal (*śeṣin*), nevertheless, the person to be enjoined does not possess the status of being the principal (*śeṣitā*) with respect to the injunction (*niyoga*), because that [injunction] is the primary element in all cases.

As it has been said: "Who would not accept that when the injunction is accomplished, everything else is subordinate to it? What, then, is the status of being the person to be enjoined? It is the status of being the principal (*śeṣitva*) with respect to the effort (*kṛti*).

And with respect to that [activity], being subordinate (*śeṣatva*) is the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*); therefore, even one who understands the task to be accomplished as something to be brought about by an activity for his own sake is called "the person to be impelled" (*niyojya*), but not because the task itself is for his sake. Thus, what is the meaning of the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice"? The meaning is: "The task to be accomplished, which is delimited by the sacrifice, is to be brought about by an activity for the sake of one who desires heaven. Consequently, since both the agent and the person to be impelled are subordinate to the task, there is no confusion regarding the relationship of subordinate and principal with respect to the activity.
That too is performed in two ways; for instance: "An activity indeed attains the status of being subordinate to another because it is subordinate to the task."
This [result] would come about through that [means], since it is a subsidiary part of that which is the task.

Indeed, an activity (*kṛti*) that is understood through verbal expression alone as being subordinate to an injunction (*niyoga*) cannot possibly become subordinate to the person (*puruṣa*). For otherwise, its status as being for the sake of something else would be untenable.

However, if the purpose of the injunction were to be subordinate to the person, then—just as the ritual refinements (*saṃskāra*) are subordinate to the person by way of their effect—the activity too would be subordinate to the person by way of its effect; it could not be otherwise.

Now, one might argue: "Even for this *niyoga*, since it is subordinate to the person (*puruṣaśeṣatva*), the fruit is also subordinate to it; and because that [fruit] is likewise pervaded by the action (*kṛti*), the action will be subordinate to the person by way of that [fruit].
