What then is the status of occasional rites (*naimittika*) and prohibitions (*niṣedha-adhikāra*)?
For in those cases there is no other fruit by way of which the action could become subordinate to the person.

Moreover, since it serves as a cause even there, how could that person—who is enjoined to the proliferation of activity consisting of prohibitions—know the task to be something to be accomplished for his own sake?
Therefore, even in the case of the *niyoga* (injunction), it must necessarily be admitted that the task (*kārya*) has the person’s welfare as its purpose.
And this is logical.
For no one can understand that something is to be done (*kārya*) unless it is for its own sake.

If this were not so, then even the fruit (*phala*) would not be established as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), because even in its case, this very same [cognition]—namely, "this is my task"—would persist.

Therefore, even in the case of desire, there must be a distinction such that the person is the principal (*śeṣin*), the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*), the subordinate (*śeṣa*), and the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to the task itself.
Thus, it is incorrect to say that [the Veda] is an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when it is directed toward an injunction for the sake of instruction.

This is because, in cases such as "O Agnīdh, spread the fires," the Agnīdh and others are not persons to be enjoined (*aniyojya*), since they possess the status of being the primary beneficiary (*śeṣin*) with respect to the action (*kṛti*) or the task (*kārya*).
He says: "In the sense of an injunction, which consists of the form of a task (*kārya-rūpa*), there would be the status of being enjoined by virtue of being the primary beneficiary."
But if its nature were that of instigation, then its status as something to be enjoined would be lost.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that an injunction (*vidhi*) has "instigation" (*pravartanā*) as its essence, because it is rooted in the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) of the form, "I shall do this.

And that [instigation] requires one who is being instigated (*pravartya*), as well as an instigator (*pravartaka*), who is the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). In this regard, does the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) provide the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*) required by the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), or rather the person to be enjoined required by the injunction? Since it is impossible for it to be intent on both simultaneously, and because one is established through the other, [it must be one or the other]. For indeed, if the action has heaven as its fruit, a person who does not desire that [heaven] cannot be the person to be enjoined; thus, the person to be enjoined is established by means of the fruit.
Furthermore, for one who desires heaven and is enjoined to an action that has another fruit, there would be the attainment of a specific fruit for which he is neither qualified nor enjoined.
In that case, since the word "one who desires heaven" denotes a person, it is logical that he alone is the one to be enjoined. To this, it is replied:
It is true that the person to be enjoined (niyojya) is required by the injunction; however, at that time, he cannot be determined, for the fitness for the fruit is immediate.

Although an agent who desires the fruit is required [as the *niyojya*], nevertheless, he cannot be determined prior to the apprehension of half the syllables of the category of things to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*).
For the status of being the *niyojya* does not belong to one who merely desires the fruit;
rather, it belongs to one who possesses the capacity for performance.
Furthermore, that [injunction] is defined by its dependence upon the comprehension of what is to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*).

And it is only an action conjoined with a primary element (*pradhāna*) that is to be performed; and for such an action, the injunction occurs only after the relationship [of the action] has been established, not at first, because of its initial unfitness [to be enjoined]. Likewise, the person to be impelled (*niyojya*) is also [defined later]. However, the result (*phala*) can be understood even before the internal relationship [with the action] is established; therefore, this [injunction] is directed toward that [result].

Once that [injunction] has been understood and that other factor (the qualification) has been determined, the injunction enjoins the person—who desires its fruit and is capable of performing it—with respect to the *bhāvanā* as qualified by all its attributes.
And it is said: "The enjoining of the person occurs simultaneously with the *bhāvanā* consisting of both the subsidiary and the principal elements.

Furthermore, even though another person is sought to be enjoined, the word expressing desire (*kāma*) does not have the person as its primary referent; rather, it has the specific fruit as its primary referent.

For it is understood precisely from the injunction (*vidhi*) that there is indeed someone who is to be enjoined (*niyojya*) regarding this activity; and he is the subordinate (*śeṣin*) of that which is fit [for him], for no one can be enjoined to an activity that does not serve his own purpose. He alone is the subordinate who desires to enjoy a specific result (*phala-viśeṣa*) to be brought about by that activity. When this is understood, the word "one who desires heaven" (*svarga-kāma*) refers solely to that specific result. In this regard, *Mīmāṃsā-kośa* 502.

In considering whether the other [the Veda] expresses its own meaning by way of being something to be enjoined (*niyojyatva*) or by way of being a subordinate element (*śeṣitva*), it is better to establish its status as a subordinate element whose comprehension is possible, rather than abandoning the enjoined person whose comprehension is impossible. For while the status of being a subordinate element belongs to that which is qualified by capacity, the status of being a subordinate element is not useful for the performance [of the act]; rather, it is the performer alone who possesses the status of the subordinate. Thus, those who lack the capacity have no entitlement, just as a non-king has no entitlement to the Rājasūya sacrifice.

For in that case, since the status of being a king is not an inherent qualification, it is impossible to determine the character of the subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) prior to determining the form of the qualification itself—due to its entry into the state of the qualification as "not being a non-cultivator" (*atad-acchettṛtā*). Therefore, the connection of the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) is solely by way of being the principal element (*śeṣitva*). And since that [connection] is intended for the cognition of a specific result, heaven and so forth are established as the results. Otherwise, a person’s qualification for the ritual action that accomplishes them would not be established; therefore, the determination of those specific [results] must now be undertaken.

In that regard, since all [persons] possess the qualification for the primary injunction without distinction, and because the ignorant are enjoined in accordance with it, one should do whatever can be done.
For example: "In the case of cutting portions from liquids and solids... [Sixth Adhyāya, Topic 10]. Sixty.

Because they are enjoined as meditations (*bhāvanā*), it is understood that all of them—just like the *āgneya* and other sacrifices—are means to a single beneficial result (*upakāra*). Thus, the status of the *samid* and other subsidiary rites as means to the fruit is established. Since it is the case that where there is a single purpose, there is no independence (*nairapekṣya*), and where there is independence, there is no single purpose, an option (*vikalpa*) is not possible here.

In the case of rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*), however, because both serve as the material for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and thus have a single purpose, an option is appropriate, as their independence is understood from two separate scriptural statements.
Therefore, since the capacity for the result arises directly from the meditation itself, eligibility (*adhikāra*) belongs only to one who possesses the power of exhalation (*udghāna*).

As for the claim that since all [classes] are understood to have entitlement (*adhikāra*) in the principal statement (*pradhānavākya*), the objects of knowledge must accordingly be within the capacity of all—this is incorrect, because there is no contradiction. For it is not by the principal statement that the entitlement of all is definitively established; rather, it is understood only in a general sense. Consequently, the entitlement of all would only follow if there were a specific means of valid cognition (*viśeṣapramāṇa*) [to that effect].
Due to the requirement of ignorance (of the full procedure), it does not apply to everyone, because of the specific scriptural injunctions.

However, where there is a conflict with the principal statement regarding a conditional entitlement (*naimittikādhikāra*), it has been shown in the *Śaktinirṇaya* that there is a partial adoption [of the ritual] according to one's capacity.

Therefore, there is no entitlement for those of small means such as widowers and the like who have not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) due to a lack of assistants or sacrificial fuel, nor is there an entitlement for Brāhmaṇas and others in rites such as the *Rājasūya*.
However, since the *avadāna* (cutting) of the fat and other parts is prescribed there in a specific form, there is no restriction on the statement regarding the substance itself.
Therefore: "The application of the subsidiaries is not described according to their respective qualifications;
rather, the description of the qualification should follow the application."
*Ratnamālā*, pp. 156–168. The sixth and final section [of this chapter]:

Regarding the injunction "one should sacrifice an animal" (*paśumālabheta*), although the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) generally applies to all animals, its scope is restricted by the wording of the mantra, "Recite for the omentum and fat of the goat" (*chāgasya vapāyā medaso 'nubrūhi*). This is because the injunction (*vidhi*) and the mantra must have the same object. Furthermore, since there is no contradiction in applying the general rule to the goat as well—given that the whole is present within the part—and because a restrictive rule (*niyama*) cannot be established where there is no possibility of non-restriction, this will be explained in the sixth and final section.
Su. Pṛ. 525.
The principle of the sixth chapter (ṣaṣṭhādhyāyanyāya).
This principle is illustrated in the Nyāyaprakāśa.

For instance, in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), the objective productive energy (*ārthī bhāvanā*) is expressed by the verbal suffix as "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*). This [productive energy] requires three factors: (1) what should one bring about? (2) by what means should one bring it about? (3) how should one bring it about? Among these, in response to the expectancy for the object of the productive energy, it connects with heaven according to the principle of the sixth chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*], resulting in "one should bring about heaven" (*svargaṃ bhāvayet*).
The *sāhasrī*. 850.
The logical principle of the established conclusion (*siddhāntanyāya*) of the sixth chapter:

Since the word *paśukāma* (desirous of cattle), being employed as denoting a fruit, is taken up [in the injunction], and because it functions as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of one who already possesses the desire for cattle [as understood from the context], the person desiring cattle—by virtue of the word *paśukāma*—is to be designated as "one desiring cattle" according to the logical principle of the established conclusion of the sixth chapter, with the quality of being a cow (*gotva*) serving as the fruit.
Su. Pṛ. 421:

The genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) [applied] to non-living beings (*aprāṇinaḥ*) occurs in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamy-arthe*), sometimes in the sense of the instrumental (*tṛtīyā-arthe*), or in the sense of the accusative (*dvitīyā-arthe*).
Bhāṣya 4.2.13; see the index entry "aprāṇinaḥ ṣaṣṭhī" on Mīko. p. 538.
The sixth [case-ending] is the non-case-inflection (*avibhakti*) expressing a relationship of quality (*guṇasaṃbandhin*).

Vārttika 3.1.6.12, p. 687. The "sixth *citi*" (*ṣaṣṭhī citiḥ*) refers to a performance consisting of a single layer (*ekacitika*), which occurs subsequent to the performance of the *sāsicitya* and possesses a fruit mentioned in the explanatory passages (*ārthavādika*); it is an occasional (*naimittika*) distinct performance, and not a performance consisting of six layers (*ṣaṭcitika*).
Bhāṣya 4.4.7.14–18. The sixth [layer] (pertaining to the gems).

According to Pāṇini 6.3.159, *ṣoḍa-śavidaryasya karaṇe*, the genitive case is used for the instrument (*karaṇa*) when the verb *jñā* (to know) is employed in its sense of "knowing. For example, *sarpiṣo jānīte* means "he consumes [it] by means of ghee" (*sarpiṣā upāyena bhakṣayati*). According to Pāṇini 2.3.52, *adhīgarthadayeṣāṃ karmaṇi*, the genitive case is used for the object (*karman*) when the verb *dhā* is employed in the sense of remembering (*smṛti*).
He remembers his mother; he bestows [a portion] of gold; he rules over the quarters.
Regarding the rule *kṛñaḥ pratiyatne* (Pāṇini 2.3.53), "pratiyatna" refers to the imparting of a new quality to something already existing.
He improves the water with a potsherd.

According to Pāṇini 2.3.54, *rujārthānāṃ bhāvavacanānām ajvareḥ*, [the genitive is used] in connection with a word expressing the agent when it denotes an action meaning "to cause pain" (*ruj*), provided that the action is distinct from "fever" (*jvara*). For example:
*duṣkarmaṇo rogasya rujā* ("the causing of pain by a disease of evil conduct").
According to Pāṇini 2.3.55, *āśiṣi nāthaḥ*, [the genitive is used] for the object when the root *nāth*, which signifies "blessing" (*āśis*), is employed.

The word *nāthate* is used in the sense of "king" (*rājñaḥ*). According to Pāṇini 2.3.56, "the roots *ji*, *nigraha*, *nāṭ*, *kvath*, and *piṣ* [take the genitive] when meaning violence (*hiṃsā*)," provided that they are not used with an object (*akarma-sataḥ*), and specifically regarding the roots *han* and *pat* preceded by *vi*, *asa*, *sam*, or *ni*, as well as in connection with *nāṭ*, *kvath*, and *ghāt*. Thus, it occurs in the context of these verbal forms.

One shouts out for a thief (*caurasya ujjāsate*), one strikes down, smites, or strikes at a thief (*caurasya nihanti*, *prahanti*, *praṇihanti*), one causes to dance (*nāṭayati*), one causes to buy (*krāyayati*), or one grinds (*pinaṣṭi*). According to Pāṇini 2.3.57, "vyavahṛ-paṇoḥ samarthayoḥ," when two verbal roots having the same meaning—namely, those signifying a transaction involving two parties—are used in conjunction, the term [denoting the object] is placed in the instrumental case. For example: *śatasya vyavaharati* (he deals with a hundred) and *śatasya paṇate* (he bets a hundred).
Legal proceedings consist of the non-payment of debts and gambling. According to Pāṇini 2.3.58,
*divaḥ tadarthasya*, the verb *div*— when it signifies legal proceedings or gambling— is used in conjunction with its object.
"He plays for a hundred.

According to Pāṇini 2.3.61, *preṣyabruvorhaviṣo devatāsaṃpradāne*, when the words *preṣya* ("send") or *brūhi* ("speak") are used in conjunction with a word denoting an oblation (*havis*), that word is in the accusative case when it is intended for a deity as the recipient.
"Prompt for the fat," "Recite for the fat";
"Prompt for the oblation," "Recite for the oblation.

[This applies] to words denoting an oblation that are uttered in conjunction with the root *yaji* (to sacrifice), according to Pāṇini 2.3.63: "In the sense of performing a sacrifice (*yajña-karaṇe*)."

One sacrifices to Soma. According to Pāṇini 2.3.64, "In the case of a complete action, when time is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the sixth case is used for a word denoting time that is co-occurrent with a word expressing a number ending in the suffixes *suc*, *kṛtvas*, or *ūn*. For example: *dvir aho bhuṅkte* ("He eats twice a day").
The meaning is: eating, which has the day as its locus and a dual number [as its subject].

Regarding the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65), it applies to words denoting the agent or the object that are co-occurrent with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix. For example: *kṛṣṇasya kṛtiḥ* ("the action of Kṛṣṇa").
The hearing of the *Bhārata*.

According to Pāṇini 2.3.66, "when both [agent and object] are possible, [the genitive is used] for the object," when both agent and object are mentioned together with a *kṛt* suffix, the genitive is used only for the object. For example:
*gavāṃ dohaḥ agopena* ("the milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd").

According to Pāṇini 2.3.69, *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛṇām*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not used for the agent or the object when they occur in syntactic proximity with the following: the substitutes *śatṛ* and *śānac* (the present participles), the suffix *u*, the suffix *uka*, the suffix *adhyaya*, the *niṣṭhā* suffixes, the suffix *khal*, suffixes having the same meaning as *khal*, and those included in the *tṛn*-pratyāhāra such as *śānan*. For example:
*ariṃ jigīṣan* or *jigīṣamāṇaḥ* (desiring to conquer the enemy); *papivān somam* or *papiṣaḥ* (having drunk the Soma).
Desiring to prepare the Soma;
Hari, the slayer of the Daityas;
having conquered the enemy.

"He has eaten the Soma. [This is an example of] Pāṇini 2.3.70: "The sixth case ending is not used after an action noun ending in *aka* or *an*, when it refers to the future or to eating. "The cooks go for the rice. [This is an example of] Pāṇini 2.3.71: "Optionally [the sixth case ending is used] for the agent of roots ending in *kṛ*. Following the connection with a root ending in *kṛ*, there is an option regarding the sixth case ending which would otherwise be obligatory for the agent.

"bhavataḥ kartavyam" (to be done by you), "bhavatā kartavyam" (to be done by you). This sūtra is the result of a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to the third case ending. According to Pāṇini 2.3.72, *tulyārthair atulopamābhyāṃ tṛtīyānyatarasyām*, when words having the sense of "equal" (*tulya*), "similar" (*sadṛśa*), or "like" (*upama*)—excluding the words *atula* and *upamā*—are used in apposition, the third case is optionally prescribed in place of the sixth case that would otherwise be obtained after the object of comparison (*upameya*), provided there is a connection with the status of being the standard of comparison (*upamānatva*).

For example: "The moon is equal to the face," or "by means of the face. Regarding this, some maintain that there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) because of the status of the third case ending as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*);
others hold that it is a conventional power (*anuśāsanikī śaktiḥ*).

Regarding the rule *caturthī cāśiṣyāyuṣyamadrabhadrakuśalasukhārthahitaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.73): when words such as *āyuṣya* (long-lived) and others are used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*) in conjunction with verbal suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, the fourth case (*caturthī*) is optionally prescribed alongside the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) which is obtained through general relation. For example: *devadattasya āyuṣyam* or *devadattāya āyuṣyam bhūyāt*. In all such instances, since the sixth case denotes mere relation (*saṃbandhamātra*), the resulting cognition has relation as its mode (*saṃbandhaprakāraka*).
However, defects such as [the word being] an agent or an object arise by virtue of grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*);
elsewhere, even figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) does not exist— this is the truth.

*Maṇi*, pp. 126–128. The genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not a case-ending (*kāraka-vibhakti*) prescribed by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* (Pāṇini 2.3.50). The meaning of that sūtra is that the genitive occurs when there is a mere relation (*saṃbandha-mātra*) with the meanings of the second case (*dvitīyārtha*), such as the aforementioned status of being an object (*karmatva*), which constitutes the "remainder" (*śeṣa*).
Thus, the genitive has its expressive power (*śakti*) in relation to this relation.
The property of being a relation (*saṃbandhatva*) is the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).
In expressions such as "Caitra’s wealth," the cognition has precisely a relation as its mode (*prakāra*).

However, regarding specific instances—such as the state of being owned and owning, the state of being the object and the subject, the state of being the goal and the means, or the state of being the produced and the producer—the term functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Thus, in cases such as "he knows [the use] of ghee" (*sarpiṣo jānīte*) and "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*), the cognition is indeed one that has the relation as its qualifier.

According to the elders, the specific cognition [of the object] arises either through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or mentally (*mānasa*), depending on the apprehension of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*).
However, others hold that the primary denotation (*śakti*) of the genitive case is ownership (*svatva*) and the like.
In the expression "Caitra’s wealth" (*caitrasya dhanam*), the cognition has as its qualifier (prakāra) precisely the relation of being determined (*nirūpitatva*) or ownership (*svatva*).
Similarly, in "Caitra’s wealth," the cognition is that "the wealth lacks the state of being determined by Caitra.
Furthermore, ownership is the meaning of the genitive case.
The cognition [arising from] "the wealth characterized by ownership residing in Caitra" is as follows:
in cases such as "Caitra's wealth does not exist," the cognition is that "the wealth lacks the property of being the characterizer of ownership residing in Caitra.

Similarly, in cases such as "the absence of a jar," the relation of counter-correlativity (pratiyogitva) and so forth is understood; the cognition is that "the absence has the jar as its counter-correlate."
Thus, they say that there is a conventional (ānuśāsanikī) power [of words] with respect to specificities such as ownership (*svatva*).
That is not so;
for it would involve the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating multiple powers.

For grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*) can be justified even as being based on figurative indication (*lakṣaṇika*). Figurative indication occurs in specific instances of co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*), and the rules serve to restrict it.
Therefore, even where figurative indication might otherwise apply, there is no usage [of the word].
Maṇi, p. 125:
Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita, however, maintains that even the meaning of the genitive case relates only to the *bhāvanā* (efficient force);
and this [genitive] is taught by the rule "The genitive is used in the sense of the residual relation" (*ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*, Pāṇini 2.3.50).
For instance, the "remainder" (śeṣa) is that which is other than what has been mentioned.
And previously, [grammatical relations] such as "objectness" (karmatva) and so forth were mentioned.
Relations such as the "owner-and-owned" (svasvāmibhāva) and others, being different from those, are of the same class (sajātīya).
The meaning of the sūtra is that the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) should be used in relation to them.
Furthermore, there is not a separate power for each of them, as that would entail the fault of postulating multiple powers;
rather, they possess it by virtue of being a "relation" (saṃbandhatva).
And "relationality" (*saṃbandhatva*) is a specific property evidenced by the cognition "this is a relation.

Thus, since relationality—which is the delimiting factor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*)—also exists in [grammatical relations] such as agenthood (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*), these too indeed possess the status of being the meaning of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyarthatā*) in their capacity as relations.

For this very reason, we have examples such as *satāṃ gatam* ("the going of the virtuous"), *sarpiṣo jānīte* ("he knows [how to use] clarified butter"), *mātuḥ smarati* ("he remembers his mother"), and *edho dakasyopaskurute* ("the fuel improves the water").
The genitive [case] is seen in such usages as "I worship the feet of Śambhu" (*aśaṃbhor bhaje caraṇayoḥ*) and "satisfied with fruits" (*phalānāṃ tṛptaḥ*).

For this very reason, the meaning of the term *śeṣa* (remainder) is precisely a relation that is delimited by a delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) other than the aforementioned delimitor of denotability.
And just as in expressions such as "the king's man," there is the relation of owner and owned, so too in expressions such as "gone by the virtuous" (satāṃ gatam), there is agency and so forth.
Furthermore, the property of being a relation (*sambandhatva*) is the delimiting factor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) in all cases.
For this very reason, it will be stated later that there is no secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for its specific varieties, such as agency.

Nor does this result in an inconsistency with the statement of the author of the Mahābhāṣya, "The [meaning] is not destroyed because of the relation," on the grounds that relations are capable of being denoted by their very nature as relations.

This is because that statement is intended to indicate that, just as the word *pārtha* primarily denotes Arjuna due to its frequent usage, when the apprehension of that specific relation is possible, it is improper to apprehend any other relation.
Thus, in the present case of "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), servitude is the meaning of the genitive case.
In that context, the king is construed with [the action] through the relation of being the qualifier (*nirūpakatā-saṃsarga*);
and he is construed with the man through the relation of being the locus (*ādheyatva-saṃsarga*).

In the expression "he knows [the way] by means of ghee" (*sarpiṣo jānīte*), the meaning of the genitive case is, according to the method to be explained, the meaning of the genitive as a relation (*saṃbandhatva*).
In that case, the genitive is used for the meaning of the verbal root itself, as in "he dwells for the sake of the cause."

Although this *vārttika* is recited by the author of the *Vṛtti* in the rule *sarvanāmastṛtīyā ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.27), it was recited by the author of the *Bhāṣya* under the rule *hetau* (Pāṇini 2.3.23).

The inclusion of the term *prāk* (before) is intended to convey that the first and second case endings do not occur after a non-pronoun (*asarvanāman*); therefore, the usage *acaṃ kāraṇaṃ vasati* (he dwells for the sake of food) is incorrect.
(However, such a usage would indeed be permissible if one were to supply [the ellipsis] *acaṃ kāraṇam* [as the object] in the sentence *vasati*).

Thus, according to the rule *ṣaṣṭhyatasarthapratyayena* (Pāṇini 2.3.10), the suffixes expressing the sense of *atas*— such as the suffix *atasuc* prescribed by rules like *dakṣiṇottarābhyāmatasuc* (Pāṇini 4.3.28)— govern the genitive case when used in conjunction with them. Consequently, in examples such as *grāmasya dakṣiṇataḥ*, *uttarataḥ*, *grāmasyopari*, and *grāmasyoparistāt*, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is employed.
In this context, the meaning of the genitive case is counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) [as in the verbal cognition: "in the southern direction having the village as its counter-correlate"].
The separate mention of the quality (*guṇa*) is for the sake of making it understood as such, and not as an exception to the ablative case, as in the example "to the south of the *cintya*."
The genitive case.
Because of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the phrase "the mat was made," the occurrence of the accusative case is justified.

Similarly, in the case of "he has attained grammar" (*vyākaraṇa-prāptaḥ*), since the primary suffix (*taddhita*) is prescribed in its own sense (*svārtha*), its connection there is established even when it is included within the meaning of a *kṛt* suffix.
For this very reason, it was stated by Bhartṛhari: "Then there occurs the connection of actions with those possessing action;
[this connection] is without a physical body (*avigraha*), just as the action of going and so forth is [connected] with the objects of the *ām* suffixes."
"Action is connected [with the suffix], as it resides in such forms as *kṛtapūrvī*.
This means that it is "without a formal body" (*avigrahā*), in the sense that it is not presented as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

The grammarians’ attempt to justify the verbal cognition of forms such as *gata* (gone) by taking them as having an *ādi* (beginning with) sense—thereby establishing the connection of the meaning of the root (*dhātvartha*) with the action—is indeed inconsistent, because the connection of *kārakas* (syntactic factors) with the meaning of the root is nowhere logically tenable.
Now, one might object: "In cases such as *odanasya pākaḥ* (the cooking of rice) or *kṛṣṇasya kṛtiḥ* (the action of Kṛṣṇa), how can there be a connection with *kārakatva*?"

It cannot first be in the sense of the verbal root, namely "cooking," because that [cooking] is not possible even there [in the case of "milk"]. Nor can it be in the sense of the *ghañ* suffix, because that is dependent on a gender marker (*liṅga*).

Furthermore, if there were a connection with those things dependent on a gender marker, it would follow that there must also be a connection with the referent of the word "substance" (*vastu*), which is denoted by the word itself.
If this is argued, [we reply:

even in that case, just as in the expression "the cooked [rice]," the action qualified by the effort (*kṛti*) is denoted independently for the sake of its connection with the factors of action (*kāraka*), or else the effort and the cooking are denoted through direct denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, how could the connection with the factors of action not be established? Furthermore, the resulting cognition is: "the cooking is that which is to be accomplished by an effort conducive to cooking."
However, some maintain that there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the action (*kṛti*) by the suffix *ghañ*;
and when that [suffix] is employed, the genitive case is not intended to express a *kāraka* (participant in an action), but rather is simply the "residual" genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*).

Furthermore, even this [genitive] connects with the primary action in the form of the verb *as* (to be) which is supplied [by ellipsis], through an indirect relationship; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

And thus, even in the case of "kṛṣṇasya kṛtiḥ" (the act of Kṛṣṇa), this understanding [of the genitive] arises. Nor is the rule prescribing the sixth case (genitive) on account of a *kṛt*-affix rendered redundant; for that [rule] is justified even by taking *kṛt* as a specific type of suffix beginning with *t*. So they say. Therefore, it is established that the sixth case is used for the agent and the object only in connection with a *kṛt*-affix, and not in connection with a meaningful secondary derivative (*taddhita*) or in connection with a second case expressing a grammatical relation (*kāraka*). It is for this purpose that the term *kṛt* is included [in the rule].

For this very reason, in the case of *kṛtapūrvī* (one who has previously made), since there is dependence [on an object], one might accept its connection with the meaning of the suffix; thus, let the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of "the mat was previously made by him" (*kṛtapūrvī kaṭaḥ*) also arise. However, the purpose of the mention of *kṛt* [in Pāṇini 2.3.65] is precisely to indicate that when such a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is employed, the case-factors (*kāraka*) do not connect with the verbal root (*kṛt*).

Therefore, it is established that the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs only in connection with a *kṛt* that is not co-occurrent with such a secondary derivative, and not even in connection with such a secondary derivative itself.
Both types of agency are intended here: independent agency (*svatantra-kartṛtva*) and causative agency (*prayojaka-kartṛtva*).
Consequently, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs in both instances in examples such as "the king's priest" (*rājño yājakaḥ*) and "Caitra's cooking pot" (*caitrasya pacanī sthālī*).

However, in the case of verbs with two objects (*dvikarmaka*), the genitive is obligatory for the primary object (*mukhya-karman*), while it is optional for the secondary, subordinate object (*guṇabhūta*).
For this very reason, both constructions—"netā aśvasya grāmam" and "netā aśvasya grāmasya"—are used.
This is explained in detail elsewhere.
Furthermore, this rule for the genitive case is not mandatory, as evidenced by the grammatical indication in Pāṇini 5.1.117: "tadahaṃ".
For this very reason, Bhaṭṭi says: "Therefore, one should slay Rāvaṇa for the sake of supreme joy.
Thus say some.

Similarly, based on the rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.66)—which means that when a *kṛt*-suffix occurs where both [agent and object] are eligible [for the genitive], the genitive shall apply only to the object, while the agent takes only the third case—the genitive does not occur for the agent in examples such as *āścaryo gavāṃ doho 'gopena* ("The milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd is wonderful").
In this context, the term *doha* is a *kṛt* suffix used in the sense of the action (*bhāve*).

Furthermore, it is common to both transitive and intransitive verbal roots, and unlike the *l*-suffixes (tenses/moods) or the past participles (*niṣṭhā*), it does not apply exclusively to intransitive roots. Therefore, in that case, there is the possibility of both [the agent and the object] being expressed.
Consequently, the understanding of the *kṛt* suffix therein should be considered according to the method previously stated.
However, it should be understood that the proponent of the residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) holds that [the genitive] occurs only in cases such as "the work of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇasya kṛtiḥ*).

Alternatively, in all instances where a *ghañ*-affix is used, the object is construed with the meaning of the verbal root itself. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of such a construction everywhere, because it would require assuming a more complex grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) than those already established.

This is because, in cases such as *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam*, it has already been demonstrated that there is no connection between those [two meanings]. Nor is it necessary to assume a more complex grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*); for that [connection] is established by a single principle: namely, that the cause for the cognition produced by a word is the relation of "being the qualifier of the same substratum" (*ekasādhāraṇya*) between the meaning of the nominal suffix and the meaning of the verbal root, through the relation of "not being distinct from the state of being connected with gender and number."

And just as that *pada* [the verbal base] is [a word] due to its being a verb (*ākhyāta*), a primary suffix (*kṛt*), or a secondary suffix (*taddhita*), so too is a verbal root ending in the suffix *ghañ*; thus it is logical. Therefore, the connection with the object (*karman*) applies to that [verbal base] as well.
For here, the word denoting the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) refers to an activity distinct from the factors (*kāraka*) that bring about the fruit.
Therefore, there is no occurrence of a distinction between the *laḍ*-suffix (present indicative) and the *liṅ*-suffix (optative), as they both involve the same process.

This process (*bhāvanā*), in the case of finite verbs (*ākhyāta*) and the like, takes the form of an effort (*kulyādi*), whereas in the case of nominal forms ending in *ghañ* and the like, it is simply the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), because both serve as the instigator of the result.

By the inclusion of the phrase "distinct from the *kāraka*," where the status of the verbal root's meaning as a *kāraka* is not established by analysis—such as in finite verbs where it is distinct from the *kāraka*—there is an exclusion of the syntactic connection of the status of a *kāraka* with the meaning of the verbal root.

In that regard, concerning the *ananvaya* (non-correspondence), the reason why the word *odana* in the second case (*dvitīyā*) is construed with the meaning of the verb *karoti*— in the analysis of "he cooks rice" (*pacaty odanam*) as "he produces rice by means of cooking" (*pākenaudanaṃ karoti*)—
is precisely because the meaning of *karoti* has been established as the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

Here too, if there were a construction with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*) would mean "he performs the cooking of rice" (*odanasya pākaṃ karoti*).
The sixth [case].
By the very rule "the sixth," there arises the undesirable consequence of [the word] being explained [as a genitive].
Furthermore, in the case of a word ending in the *ghañ* suffix, since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is not itself a *kāraka* (participant in action) and lacks gender,

even though that meaning— being expressed by the *ghañ*— possesses both natures [of being a root-meaning and a *kāraka*], its connection with a *kāraka* is not contradictory when it is expressed by the verbal root.
This is because the cognition arising from both the root and the suffix is "cooking that is non-different from the act of cooking."

Therefore, in accordance with experience, since the application of case-role (*kāraka*) relations is established through a single grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*)—whether in the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) or in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—the connection of case-roles to the meaning of the root is unimpeded even in the sentence "The milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd is wonderful. In reality, however, being connected to a gender-mark (*liṅga*) does not enter into the defining scope of the causal factor; rather, it is the state of being presented by the cognition produced by the suffix. Consequently, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that the case-roles connect only with the "making" (*kṛti*) which is the meaning of the *ghañ* suffix, and that they connect with that which is denoted by the word "thing" (*vastu*).
And this prohibition of the sixth case (genitive) in the agent when both [agent and object] are possible applies specifically to the suffixes *aka* and *akāra*.

It does not apply in connection with suffixes having the marker *ṅit*, because of the statement: "It should be stated that there is no prohibition when the suffixes *aka* and *kāra* are employed" (a *vārttika* on Pāṇini 2.3.66). For example: *medikā bibhīr asā vā rudrasya jagataḥ* ("the one who cuts, the one who fears, or the one who is—these belong to Rudra, the world").
*Medikā* means "breaking.
The suffix *aka* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).
In the rule "of that which is prescribed" (*vihitasya*), the suffix *aka* is used in the sense of an abstract state.
"The *yāmuṭ* does not subvert the *suṭ*"—so says the *Kāśikā*.

In that [statement], the word *suṭā* is in the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) because it functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Regarding the two types of suffixes mentioned above, when both [the *suṭ* and the *yāmuṭ*] are applicable, there is an option (*vikalpa*) for the agent (*kartṛ*), according to the statement "there is an option in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe vibhāṣā*; see the *Bhāṣya* on Pāṇini 2.3.66).
The composition of Pāṇini’s grammar is excellent, whether [the name] be derived from *pāṇi* (hand) or *pāṇina*.
This [rule] applies specifically to the domain of the *ṅīp* suffix;
however, some maintain that there is an option without such distinction.
The instruction of grammar belongs to the Teacher (*ācāryasya*) or by the Teacher (*ācāryeṇa*).
In his view, it should be noted that the forms *āścaryo gavāṃ dohaḥ agopena* or *agopasya* are also possible.

Similarly, from the rule *kasya ca vartamāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.67), which means that the genitive case is used in connection with a word having the sense of the present tense, the genitive occurs in the example *rājñāṃ mato buddhaḥ pūjito vā*.
In this context, by the rule *amatibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 2.3.188), the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the present tense.
Consequently, in the expression *rājñāṃ yogaḥ*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the agent (*kartṛ*), because the object (*karman*) has already been expressed by the suffix *ka*.
Furthermore, in the neuter gender when expressing the abstract state (*bhāva*), as in *rājño matam*, the genitive case is likewise employed by this very same rule.

Nor is this [usage] covered by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65), because the upcoming rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā...* (Pāṇini 2.3.69) provides an exception (*paryudāsa*) regarding the scope of past participles (*niṣṭhā*), and this [present rule] serves as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for specific past participles. Furthermore, in such cases as *pūjito yaḥ surāsuraiḥ*, there is no occurrence of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*).
In this regard, the suffix *kta* is justified by its denoting a past state (*bhūtārtha*),
for the suffix *kta* does not occur only in the present tense after roots meaning "to think," "to perceive," or "to honor.

Since we observe in common usage the employment of words ending in *kta*— such as *kānta*— to express meanings that are past, it is impossible for such usage to invalidate the fact that the suffix denotes a past state.

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that the genitive case would not apply in examples such as *achātrasya hasitam* ("the laughing of the student"), where the suffix *kta* is distinct from the *kta* suffixes used in verbal roots like *man* (to think) that denote present time;
for that [genitive] is properly accounted for as a "residual" (*śeṣa*) genitive.
For this very reason, when agency (*kartṛtva*) is intended to be expressed as such, only the instrumental case is employed.

Even when the *kta* suffix has the sense of a fact (*bhūtārtha*), if it denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), there is a reinstatement of the genitive case as before, according to the rule "And [the genitive is used] after that which denotes the locus" (*Pāṇini* 2.3.68). In that case as well, the genitive is applied after intransitive verbs to denote the agent, as in "this is their place of rest" (*idameṣāṃ śayitam*).
Here, "rested" (*śayita*) means the locus of the act of lying down.
Because it has already been expressed by the *kta* suffix, the word "this" (*idam*) takes the nominative case.

However, when the *kta* suffix is applied to transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*) to denote the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the genitive case applies to both the agent and the object, because they have not been previously expressed; specifically, as in:
"This [place] is where the rice was eaten by them" (*idameṣāṃ bhuktam odanasya*).

*Bhukta* refers to the place where eating occurs; it does not refer to the object [of the action] itself. This is because, when both [agent and object] are possible, the rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.66)—which is taught subsequent to *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65)—restricts [the application of the genitive] specifically to that genitive prescribed by the latter rule. Thus, in all instances involving a connection with a *kṛt*-suffix, although the genitive would generally apply by *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*, its exclusion is effected by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām* (Pāṇini 2.3.69).

The substitutes for *la* are termed *kṛt*. Only those beginning with *śatṛ* and *śānac* are understood here, because verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) have already been excluded by the very mention of the term *kṛt*.
Therefore, in expressions such as *odanaṃ pacan* or *pacamānaḥ*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not occur, but rather only the accusative (*dvitīyā*).
Furthermore, by the mention of the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix marker), its substitutes (*tatkāryāṇām*) are also included.

Consequently, although *ki* and *kin* are not substitutes for *lakāra*, they are nevertheless included because they serve the same function as *liṭ*, and because when there is a specific transfer of properties (*viśeṣātideśa*), a general transfer of properties (*sāmānyātideśa*) is necessarily required. Thus, those two (*ki* and *kin*) are also included.
For this very reason, even such usages as "babhrivartman" and so forth are consistent.
(Under the suffix) Ṅa: "kaṭaṃ cikīrṣuḥ" (desiring to make a mat); "kanyām alaṃkariṣṇuḥ" (desirous of adorning a maiden).
(Under the suffix) Uka: "daityān ghātukaḥ" (intent on slaying the Daityas).
"There is no prohibition [of the application] when there is the sense of *kāma* (desire).
(Alternatively, the reading of the Vārttika in the rule *na loka-* is "no prohibition of *am*"). Who? [The author of the Vārttika.]
Because of this statement, however, the genitive case is used in the example "hariḥ lakṣmyāḥ kāyukaḥ" (Hari is the one who desires Lakṣmī).
Regarding the indeclinable: "having made a mat" (*kaṭaṃ kṛtvā*).
There is also a prohibition [of the genitive] after the suffixes *tosun* and *kasun*: this is a Vārttika on the rule *na loka-* (Pāṇini 2.3.69).

And because of the statement "kam" (Pāṇini 2.3.43), the sixth case is used in examples such as "purā vasantām apākartuḥ" ("before the departure of spring") and "purā kuruṣva visṛpo virapsin" ("before you act, O loud-sounding one"). As for the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), examples include "odanaṃ bhuktvā vrajati" ("having eaten rice, he goes") and "caitreṇa kṛtam" ("done by Caitra").
As for words having the sense of the suffix *khal*, examples include "sukaraḥ" ("easy to do") and "prapadyo hariṇā" ("attainable by Hari").

*tṛn* is a pratyāhāra (a grammatical abbreviation). It begins with the word *tṛ* from the rule *śatṛ-śānac-au* (Pāṇini 3.2.124) and extends up to the letter *n* (Pāṇini 3.2.155); by this, it includes *śānac* and the others as well (*śānac*, *śatṛ*, *tṛn*).
The suffix *śānan*: *somaṃ pavamānaḥ* ("purifying the Soma").
The suffix *cānaś*: *ātmānaṃ maṇḍayamānaḥ* ("adorning himself"). The suffix *śatṛ*: *vedam adhīyānaḥ* ("studying the Veda").

In the case of *tṛn*, as in "the creator of the worlds" (*lokān karttā*), however, when used in conjunction with the suffix *śatṛ* following the root *dviṣ*, the genitive case is optional. This is according to the statement from the Vārttika on the rule *na loka* (Pāṇini 2.3.69): "The agent of *dviṣ* [is optionally in the genitive]."
"Or hating Mura, the enemy.

In all these cases, this is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the *kāraka-ṣaṣṭhī* (the genitive of grammatical relation), and not of the *śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī* (the genitive of residual relation). This is logical because it forms a single syntactic unit with that [preceding rule] through immediate proximity (*ānantarya*).

For this very reason, even usages such as *brāhmaṇasya kurvan* ("acting for the sake of a Brahmin"), *narakasya jiṣṇuḥ* ("conquering Naraka"), and *chātrasya hasitam* ("the laughing of the student") are consistent [with the rule].

Similarly, based on the sūtra *akenorabhiviṣyādarthayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.70), which means that the genitive case is not used in connection with a future *akan* suffix or a future *in* suffix having the sense of "speaking" (*ābhīkṣṇya*), in examples such as *edhānāharako vrajati* ("he goes to fetch fuel"), *vrajaṃ gāmī* ("going to the cow-pen"), and *śataṃ dāyī* ("giving a hundred"), only the accusative case is used, not the genitive.

In this context, because only the suffix *aka* prescribed for the future tense (*bhaviṣyat-kāla*) is taken, the accusative case does not apply in instances where *aka* is prescribed for time in general, such as in "the cooker of rice" (*odanasya pācakaḥ*). Furthermore, here, by virtue of the commentary, there is no application according to the respective order of the rules; rather, *aka* applies only to the future, while *in* applies to both [the present and the future].
In the word *gāmī*, the suffix *ini* will occur; in the word *dāyī*, this suffix *ṇini* occurs in the sense of indebtedness (*ādhamarṇya*).

Thus, because the author of the Bhāṣya on the rule *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā* (Pāṇini 2.3.71) performs a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*), the phrase *kṛtyānām* is understood as a distinct sūtra. Furthermore, since the two words from the preceding sūtra—*ubhayaprāptau na*—are drawn over into that [new] rule, when neither the agent nor the object is expressed, the genitive case would otherwise be applicable; however, by the meaning "the genitive is not used in connection with kṛtya-affixes," in the example *netavyā vrajaṃ gāvaḥ kṛṣṇena*, there is no genitive, but rather the accusative and the instrumental.

For here, because this [verb] has two objects (*dvikarmaka*), the primary object (*mukhya-karman*) is expressed by the *kṛtya* suffix; therefore, the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used for "cows" (*goṣu*).
However, because the secondary object (*amukhya-karman*), namely "the pen" (*vraja*), is not so expressed, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is used there.
But where...

Since one of the two—the agent or the object—is expressed by the *kṛtya* suffix when used with these [verbs], there is no possibility of the [genitive] applying to both. When such a *kṛtya* suffix is employed, because the genitive caused by the connection with the *kṛtya* would necessarily apply [to both], the rule "the agent of *kṛtyas* is optionally [expressed] by the genitive" (*kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā*) prescribes an optional genitive for the agent, as in: "this must be done by Kṛṣṇa" (*kartavyam idaṃ kṛṣṇena kṛṣṇasya vā*).

Nor can it be argued that since *kṛtyas* are prescribed only for the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), and since the object is already expressed by the *kṛtya*, the genitive does not apply there; for by process of elimination, the prescription of the optional rule is justified only for the agent.

It should be stated that the mention of the *kartṛ* (agent) is redundant; however, this is not the case. Since the suffix *kṛtya* is prescribed for the agent as well by the rule *bhavyageya* (Pāṇini 3.1.68), when such a suffix is used, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply to the object because it remains unexpressed (*anabhihita*). Therefore, the mention of the *kartṛ* is justified in order to exclude that option [of using the genitive].
For example: *geyo māṇavakaḥ sāmnām* ("The boy is to sing the Sāman hymns").
In this context, the suffix *kṛtya* in the word *geyaḥ* denotes the agent; thus, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is that "the boy is the agent whose object is the singing.

Similarly, according to the rule *tulyārthatulyopamābhyāṃ tṛtīyānyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.72), which means that when used in conjunction with words having the sense of "equal" (*tulya*) or the words *tulya* and *upamā*, either the third case (*tṛtīyā*) or the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) may be employed, as in the example "equal, similar, or same to Kṛṣṇa" (*tulyaḥ sadṛśaḥ samo vā kṛṣṇena kṛṣṇasya vā*), where the sixth case optionally occurs. Here, the dual number in the compound *atulyopamyā* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a plural ending due to the word being a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, this rule—which, by means of "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*), establishes the optional nature of the residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) alone—does not apply to the genitive of grammatical relation (*kāraka-ṣaṣṭhī*). This is because the word *tulya* ends in the suffix *taddhita*, and thus the genitive of grammatical relation is not applicable here.

However, when used in conjunction with the words *tulya* and *upamā*, only the genitive of the residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) applies. For this very reason, in the expression "There is no equal or likeness to Kṛṣṇa," the genitive alone is used; since the third case is not prescribed for these [words] in the sense of the residual relation, the third case does not occur. If it is asked: "How then is the third case used in connection with words such as *tulā* and *upamā* in poetic usage, as in 'When Dantavāsas ascends the scale' (*tulāṃ yadārohati dantavāsāḥ*) and 'Clearly comparable to Śambhu white with ashes' (*sphuṭopamaṃ bhūtisitena śambhunā*)? [The answer follows: The rule Pāṇini 2.3.72, *tulyārthair atulopamābhyāṃ tṛtīyā anyatarasyām*, prescribes the third case optionally after a word expressing comparison when used with words having the meaning of "equal" (*tulya*), provided that the words *tulā* and *upamā* are excluded. This optionality is intended to allow the third case even in the absence of the word *tulya*. Therefore, in the examples cited, although the word *tulya* is not present, the third case is employed by virtue of this optional rule. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the use of the third case here is not based on the rule governing the agent (*kartari tṛtīyā*), because the action of ascending the scale is not performed by the subject (Dantavāsas) himself, but rather by the weight of his own body. Consequently, the third case is correctly established through the aforementioned rule of optionality.
This is because it is logically established as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the verbal root-meaning consisting of weighing, measuring, and so forth.

Alternatively, this third case ending is conditioned by its connection with "concomitance" (*sahayoga*). And concomitance is the state of being a qualifier (*nirūpakatva*); and there is a cognition of that [concomitance] as such from the third case ending.
In the present context, however, there is no contradiction, as the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is excluded when it signifies a remainder (*śeṣa*).

Here, since the inclusion of synonymous terms is already established by the mention of the plural number itself, the explicit mention of "meaning" (*artha*) is intended to indicate that which conveys the meaning independently of any other word.
Consequently, in examples such as "the *gavaya* is like a cow" (*gaur iva gavayaḥ*) or "as is a cow, so is a *gavaya*" (*yathā gaus tathā gavayaḥ*), the genitive case and others do not apply.
The cause for the initial production [of the grammatical operation] has already been stated previously.

Regarding the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*): the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is formed because of the rule *caturthī cāśiṣyāyuṣyabhadrabhadrakuśalasukhārthahitaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.73), which means that when used in conjunction with words having the sense of *āyuṣya* and so forth, the fourth case (*caturthī*) shall be used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), and the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall also be used as a remainder; thus, in the expression *āyuṣyam astu te*, the fourth case is employed, while in the alternative, the sixth case is used.
*Āyuṣyam* means long life.
Although *mada* and *bhadra* are synonyms, both are employed here in order to establish that the words *āyuṣya* and the others refer to their actual meanings.

As for what Kaiyaṭa stated—that since the meaning can be understood from the commentary in all cases, either *mada* or *bhadra* need not be recited—that was required because the author of the Bhāṣya provided a different explanation for this sūtra.
*Kuśalam* means free from disease; *sukham* means tranquility; *arthaḥ* means purpose or motive; and *hitam* means wholesome or beneficial.
Nor is the inclusion of the word *hita* in the rule redundant, for its necessity is established by the Vārttika itself: "The dative case should be prescribed in connection with *hita*.
This is because that restriction applies when there is no benediction (*anāśiṣi*), whereas for this [present rule], it is appropriate as a provision for an option regarding benediction (*āśiṣi*).
For this very reason, in cases such as *āyuṣya* (long life) where no blessing (*āśis*) is intended, only the genitive case is used, as in: *caitrasya āyuṣyam asti* ("Caitra has long life").
Thus it is established that, in every respect, every meaning of the genitive case relates to the meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārtha*).
Rahasya, pp. 126–142.
The sixth [case-ending] is that which completes the number six. (Mahābhāṣya 4.3.148). The sixth occurs when there is a relationship (*saṃbandha*). The sixth.

Grammarians record that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is prescribed after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when mere relationship (*saṃbandhamātra*) is to be expressed. As stated in the *Bṛhatī* (p. 72): "The genitive, by virtue of expressing mere relationship, denotes even a mediated connection—such as a connection involving an intermediary—as in the expression 'the grandson of Devadatta. Likewise, in the statement 'the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of the Vājapeya [sacrifice] is seventeen cubits long,' the connection with the Vājapeya belongs to the height of the post through its being an accessory (*aṅga*) to the animal sacrifice."
VI. 3|1|9: The meaning expressed by the genitive case is exclusively an immediate relationship; however, when that is impossible, a mediated relationship is somehow accepted.
3|1|5: Since the genitive is not a kāraka-case, the traditional doctrine (*saṃpradāya*) holds that its referent connects with the *upapada* (governing word) or similar element.
Others, however, maintain that it is more logical for the connection to occur primarily with verbal nouns (*bhāvākhyāta*) through either a direct or mediated relationship.
*Maṇi*, p. 113: "And for the genitive case, a relationship such as that between owner and owned, or modification and so forth, is to be expressed.
*Vārttika* 3.1.12, p. 674: "The genitive case [indicates] that the *cit* (piling) is occasional and has the purpose of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

The word ending in the sixth case (genitive) qualifies the meaning of another [word]. Bhāṣya 10.3.3: Even for a relation presented by the genitive, the means of cognition is precisely the sphere of syntactic connection (*saṃsargamaryādā*).

For the relationship conveyed by the genitive and locative cases is one in which [the possessor] is the primary element and is non-substantial (asattvabhūta), whereas such is not the case with a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*).
Vārttika on 3|1|12, p. 676.

It is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Nor is there a fault of definition (*lakṣaṇadoṣa*) in the case of a genitive compound, because there is no evidence for such a fault. Furthermore, the identity of meaning between the analytical expression (*vigraha*) and the compound is established by Pāṇini’s introduction of the rule *vibhāṣā* (P. 2.1.11); otherwise, even without the introduction of *vibhāṣā*, the expanded and compounded forms would already be established for the purpose of conveying their own respective meanings.
Otherwise, the distinction [between the two] would be purposeless.

If, however, they have the same meaning, then the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) would be rendered redundant by the compound; thus, there would be a lack of truth [to the claim that the compound conveys something new].

Consequently, since the relationship is understood from the analysis "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), it is logical that there must be a secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) even in the compound in order for that relationship to be understood.

In a *karmadhāraya* compound, the relation of non-difference (*abheda*) is established through the very nature of the expressed meaning of the words themselves. Now, if it is argued that even in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) of a *karmadhāraya*, non-difference is understood as the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) because there is no word expressing non-difference therein; whereas in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the relation is not the sentence-meaning in the analytical sentence, but rather the word-meaning itself due to the hearing of the genitive case—yet the relation, which is not a word-meaning, is the sentence-meaning [in the compound]. [This is the core argument: in a *karmadhāraya*, non-difference is the sentence-meaning; in a *ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*, the relation is the sentence-meaning.]

Therefore, in that case, it is the relation-of-relations itself that is perceived as the sentence-meaning, and not the relation itself. Thus, just as in a *vigraha* (analytic expansion), so too in a compound (*samāsa*), there must be *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in order to establish the cognition of the relation-of-relations. Furthermore, if it is argued that because the connection between the meanings of two nouns occurs through the medium of the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), the relation of the case-ending must necessarily be indicated—[we reply: even so, as in examples such as "look at the curd" (*dadhi paśya*), the cognition of that [nominative] meaning is established by the case-ending itself, even when it is elided.

In the sentence "The jar, the objectness, the bringing, the effort," since there is no other [relation] than that of action and object (*kriyā-karmabhāva*), it is established by the case-ending itself—just as in the case of being the motivator (*prayojakatva*)—that [the relation] is understood. Likewise, in cases such as "Look at the curd" (*dadhi paśya*), if one accepts that the case-ending itself conveys its own meaning (*svārtha*), then in the present case as well (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), since the relation is also presented by the case-ending due to the absence of any other [relation], it must be accepted as such.
Nor is it the case that the elision of the case-ending (*vibhaktilopa*) in a compound is unestablished.
For it is the primary established doctrine of the Grammarians that "eternality is not tenable when there is a modification of a single part.

Thus, one must argue that the elision of the case-ending (*vibhaktilopa*) occurs only in the *prakriyāvākya* (derivative analytical sentence) which is constructed for the sake of instruction according to the maxim of the "line-drawn cow" (*rekhāgavaya*). Consequently, since the genitive case-ending (*ṅas*) itself is absent in a compound (*samāsa*), it cannot serve as the indicator of the relationship.
This being the case, by parity of reasoning, [the same applies to] "dadhi..."
Regarding the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*): even in cases such as *ṣoḍaśī padyaḥ*, since the elision of a case-ending is impossible, there would have to be figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

And if, in that instance, figurative indication is not required because a supplied case-ending is possible despite the absence of an elided one, then let there be only a supplied case-ending in the compound as well.

Even by virtue of the word *ca* (and), which expresses conjunction—as in "it is blue and it is a lotus"—conjunction elsewhere results in non-difference (*abheda*). Thus, even in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) of a *karmadhāraya* compound, non-difference is indeed the meaning of the words.

This is because, although the particle *ca* is non-denotative due to its status as a *nipāta*, when it is employed, the other word co-occurring with it must necessarily relinquish its power [to denote its own primary meaning] in that context.

In cases such as "The mountain possesses fire" (*parvato vahnimān*) or "A man with a staff" (*daṇḍī puruṣaḥ*), since the meaning of the possessive suffix (*matvartha*) can be present [in the compound], it is also logical that the relation established by the genitive case in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) appears through the very limits of the semantic connection (*saṃsargamaryādayā*). (Soma. 6.1.13). Here, the "Principle of the Niṣāda Chief" (*niṣādasthapatinyāyaḥ*) should be consulted in the *Bhaṭṭa* treatise under the entry in the *Mīmāṃsākośa*, page 2312.
This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsaḥ*).

Where there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the sense of the genitive case, there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). However, where there is coreferentiality even without the indication of the sense of the genitive, there is a descriptive compound (*karmadhāraya*).
(Soma. 6.1.13). The descriptive compound is stronger than the genitive compound.

Śā— There is a doubt regarding the *ṣoḍaśin* cup itself: should it be drawn from either the *āgrayaṇa* or the *ukthya*, or only from the *āgrayaṇa*? In this regard, because of the statement, "He draws from the *āgrayaṇa*; he holds back from the *ukthya*," and because the drawing from the *āgrayaṇa* alone is heard in the scripture as a constant rule for one who has performed the bath (*kṛtasnāt*), it is not proper to set that aside; therefore, there is neither an option (*vikalpa*) nor a combination (*samuccaya*).
Should that [Soma sacrifice] be from both the Ukthya and Āgrayaṇa, or from the Āgrayaṇa alone?
It is the first [option], because the beginning and end of the Ukthya are characterized by its subsequent presence.

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the inquiry whether, in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice itself, the drawing [of the cup] is from the *āgrayaṇa* alone or from the *ukthya*, [the conclusion is as follows]: because of the statement "he draws from the *āgrayaṇa*," just as the *āgrayaṇa* possesses the status of the source (*apādāna*), so too because of the statement "he draws from the *ukthya*," the *ukthya* is heard to possess the status of the source; therefore, the drawing occurs either optionally or by way of combination.

Nor should it be argued that in the case of "he draws [the cup] from the Ukthya" (*ukthyād gṛhṇāti*), because the meaning of the form is "he draws [it] after the Ukthya," this merely prescribes the sequence following the Ukthya and does not prescribe the *apādāna* (ablative) relation. For if the fifth case (*pañcamī*) were caused by connection with a direction (*digyoga*), it would be a "case ending of a subordinate word" (*upapadavibhakti*), and since a "case ending denoting a grammatical relation" (*kārakavibhakti*) is stronger, it follows that the meaning must be *apādāna*. Furthermore, in the absence of connection with words such as "from" (*parasmāt*) which denote direction, there is no possibility for the fifth case to be caused by connection with a direction.

Since the rule *anyārāditarartedikchabdāñcottarapadājāhiyukte* (Pāṇini 2.3.29) prescribes the ablative case (*pañcamī*) only when there is a connection with these specific words, this [objection] might arise. However, this is not an ablative used in the sense of "bringing about" (*āpādana*), because if it were so, it would result in the fallacy of eight defects (*aṣṭadoṣa*) and because [the meaning of] conjunction (*samuccaya*) would be lost due to the lack of mutual dependence.

Rather, by virtue of its syntactic unity with the statement in another treatise, "He who takes [the bride] while she has her face turned away," this is indeed caused by connection with a direction (*digyoga*); for there is no obstacle to accepting that even in the case of an expectancy for an option (*vikalpa*), it is a case of a case-ending based on a subordinate word (*upapadavibhakti*).

Nor is it the case that this [ablative] occurs only when there is connection with a word (*śabdayoga*), because we observe it even in the absence of connection with a word—as in "I shall speak after a month" (*māsāt pravakṣyāmi*)—merely through connection with a time (*adhvayoga*).

For this very reason, the usage in the *Bhāṣya* on such rules as "from a nominal stem ending in *ukthya*" (*ukthyāprātipadikāt*, Pāṇini 4.1.1) and "of that which is internal to the *dhṛta*" (*dhṛtādantaratasya*) is also consistent.

And therefore, just as even in the case of the *sahasradakṣiṇā* sacrifice, the instrumental case is used—as seen in the usage "the *ṣoḍaśin* [cup] with the youth" (*ṣoḍaśī yūnā*)—due to the intention to express the meaning of the *amā* (concomitance) and so forth;
likewise, there is no inconsistency in the use of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) precisely because of the intention to express the meaning of the *dvi* (two).

Nor does the objection apply that, by the mere mention of "that *parāṅk*," there would result a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) between the restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *ṣoḍaśin* and the injunction of the meaning of the word *parāk* (which is the meaning of the word *ukthya*).

For even in the case of the *ukthya* vessels, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is indeed used in its own sense as an ablative (*apādāna*). As for the term *parāk*, it should be understood as a restatement of an established fact (*anuvāda*) because it signifies non-repetition—just as in the injunction "one should recite the *sāmidhenī* verses facing away" (*parācīḥ*). This is because, in cases involving words used as adjuncts (*upapada*), the mutual connection [of the case-ending with the verb] is well-established according to the grammarians of the East; furthermore, since the word *parāk* functions as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*), the fifth case itself conveys that meaning, thus precluding any syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Moreover, if the *ukthya* vessel were the single-pointed ablative (*ekavacana-apādāna*), the plural number (*bahutva-vacana*) would be untenable.

Therefore, because there are many procedures for the Ukthya cups, the ablative case in the fifth case-sense (*pañcamyartha*) is prescribed by this [text] as referring precisely to the time of the preceding [cup]. Since this [passage] is syntactically connected with that [preceding rule], it is established that the drawing of the Ṣoḍaśin cup has the Ukthya as its source (*upādāna*). Furthermore, the utility of the statement regarding the Āgrayaṇa cup should be understood as being for the sake of an alternative view, since it is set aside in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Maṇḍana says: "It is drawn from the Āgrayaṇa, but from the Ukthya."
Śaṅkara states: "And that [cup] is known from the Āgrayaṇa.
Regarding the *Ṣoḍaśin*: its extraction (*grahaṇa*) occurs only at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice (Mīmāṃsākośa, p.
1809). One should consult the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) concerning the statement: "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the extraction of the *Ṣoḍaśin* occurs only at the third pressing."

(Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2311; see the discussion under "nānā'hīneṣu pratyahīne").
The *ṣoḍaśin* concludes at night.
B. The *ṣoḍaśin* is a modification (*vaikṛta*) because it is prescribed there in its entirety.
With reference to the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the cup named *ṣoḍaśin* is recorded in the scripture: "He who, knowing thus, draws this *ṣoḍaśin*, prospers in himself and his enemies perish."
In the discussion as to whether that [cup] is to be taken at the modified sacrifice (*vaikṛta*) or at the archetypal sacrifice (*prākṛta*), he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

the cup for the *ṣoḍaśin* should belong to the modified sacrifice. This is because it is prescribed there in its entirety within the modification, so that it may be complete in itself, as stated: "They take [it] on the middle day of the three-night rite."
According to this statement, the injunction "at the Atirātra for a Brāhmaṇa" is understood to refer to the modified (vaikṛta) Atirātra.
Therefore, the Ṣoḍaśin cup belongs to the modified sacrifice,
because its absence is observed in the archetype (prakṛti).
He states another reason for the *ṣoḍaśin* cup being a modification (*vaikṛta*):
because the absence of the *ṣoḍaśin* is observed in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

This is described in the second chapter, under the sūtra "Because of the prohibition of what has been enjoined" (2.4.27), in the passage: "'Two [verses] exceed the *virāj* among the *saṃstutāḥ*'; when the *ṣoḍaśin* is absent, two *stomīya* verses exceed the *virāj*."
Therefore, the *ṣoḍaśī* is a modification (*vaikṛta*).
Furthermore, because it is not mentioned as a sacrifice:
"They say that there is no sacrifice named *ṣoḍaśī*"—this is the statement regarding the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *jyotiṣṭoma*.

Thus, because of the statement that it is not part of the sacrifice (*ayajñatva*), the *ṣoḍaśī* cup belongs only to the modified sacrifice (*vaikṛta*). The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)— established by three sūtras— that the *ṣoḍaśī* cup belongs to the modified sacrifice, on the grounds that it is taught in the context of the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*).

The *ṣoḍaśī* cup is not a modification; rather, it is original (*prākṛta*), because it is taught and prescribed in the archetype, the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, by the injunction "he takes the *ṣoḍaśī*. Furthermore, it is because the archetype is observed [in its context]. For this reason also, the *ṣoḍaśī* should be original, because an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is observed: "In the case of three *saṃsthās*, three *virāj* verses remain over" (this should be consulted under Sūtra 2.4.27, *vihitapratiṣedhāt*). This is because the indicative mark is observed in the archetype, that is, within the context of the archetype itself.
The scriptural statement is for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*).
The following demonstrates the interpretation of the statement asserted by the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "It is taken on the middle day of the three-night rite.
This scriptural statement would serve as an exclusion.

In the injunction "One should take [the cup] for a Kṣatriya at the Agniṣṭoma," the status of the Ṣoḍaśin as being contingent upon a Kṣatriya is stated; and by the force of the *codaka* (archetypal rule), that same contingency upon a Kṣatriya would apply when the Ṣoḍaśin is extended to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). The scriptural text "It is taken on the middle day of the three-night rite" serves precisely to exclude that [contingency].
Consequently, the Ṣoḍaśin would indeed belong to a Brāhmaṇa as well in the archetypal sacrifice. This is the observation of its occurrence in the highest [status].

Regarding what was stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)—namely, "And because non-existence is observed in the archetype" (10.5.12.135)—he says this in response: the observation of non-existence has been refuted; therefore, on account of that observation of non-existence, the *ṣoḍaśī* cup is optional.
Because of the prohibition of what has been prescribed, there is an excess of hymns in certain cases (this should be seen in the sūtra *vihitapratiṣedhāt* at 10.2.4.27).
The *ṣoḍaśin* cup, due to its specific qualities, is not part of the sacrifice.
As for what was stated by the opponent, "Because of the mention of non-sacrifice" (Sūtra 36), that too is understood to have been answered.
Since the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is optional, its status as "non-sacrifice" in one alternative case is merely figurative, based on the quality [of its absence].
Therefore, the *ṣoḍaśin* is archetypal (*prākṛta*), being established by the general rule (*codaka*).
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). What [is the nature] of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice? It is that it possesses both the *stotra* and the *śastra*.

Bhāṣya 10.5.2149–52: Regarding the Ṣoḍaśin and the Atirātra, there is the statement heard in connection with the offering to the Pitṛs: "They modify the consumption mantra [to read] 'the metre is the Anuṣṭubh.
Bhāṣya-Ṭippaṇī 3.2.11.29, p. 788: In the Ṣoḍaśin, the third [cup] is for Indra-Vṛṣṇi;
there are three animals belonging to the seasons (ṛtupaśu).

In the Agniṣṭoma, there is a goat for Agni; in the Ukthya, a second one for Indra; in the Ṣoḍaśin, a third, a bull for Indra. (Bhāṣya 3.6.16.42, 3.6.7.18). In the Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice, there are three seasonal animals:
one for Agni, one for Indra, and a bull for Indra.
9|1|16| 45. In the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, all the stotras consist of twenty-one verses. (Tup. 9|2|5|24, Section 2). In the *ṣoḍaśin*, there are animal sacrifices (*paśu*) for the *savana*s.

This is because of the injunction: "The *paśupuroḍāśa* dedicated to Agni is to be offered first; the second is the one dedicated to Indra at the *ukthya*; the third is the bull (*vṛṣṇi*) dedicated to Indra."
In that regard, although there are three Savanīya animals at the Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice, there is no modification (ūha) of the formula "pra asmai agne" into "pra ebhyaḥ agne" in the case of the Agniṣṭoma.
This is a hypothetical consideration (kṛtvācintā); in reality, however, the modification must indeed be performed. (Vi. 9.3.18).

Regarding the statement, "The *atirātra* is taken by me," one might suspect that this very rule applies even to the archetype (*prakṛti*). Anticipating this, [the text states]: "One should take it in the *agniṣṭoma* for a Kṣatriya; in the *atirātra* for a Brāhmaṇa. Since this is a modified form (*vikṛti*), one might suspect that by the force of this specific injunction, it would apply to the *atirātra* in the modified ritual. However, because it is recorded in the archetype and because the *atirātra* exists within the archetype, the suspicion arises that it is indeed archetypal (*prākṛta*).
Therefore, there is a doubt. What is the prima facie view? That the *ṣoḍaśin* should be a modification (*vaikṛta*). Why? Because it is prescribed in its entirety therein.
The entire [ritual] is prescribed as modified in this context.
How so? Having stated, "He who, knowing thus, draws this *ṣoḍaśin*," it is further prescribed that "it is drawn on the middle day of the *rātri-satra*.
And a direct statement (*vākya*) is more authoritative than the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Thus, when the context is set aside by the direct statement, the injunction "at the Atirātra for a Brāhmaṇa" is understood to refer to the modified (vaikṛta) Atirātra.

Therefore, although this [Ṣoḍaśin] is not fully prescribed in the modification because it was prescribed as part of the archetype (prakṛti) in the Jyotiṣṭoma, nevertheless, it becomes fully prescribed in the modification itself.
Consequently, the Ṣoḍaśin is to be taken in those modifications that are specifically enumerated, but not in the archetype.
*Ṭup-ṭīkā*: "He who, knowing thus, takes the *ṣoḍaśin* [cup]"—this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
By the direct statement, "It is taken on the middle day of the three-night sacrifice," there is a connection with the modified form (*vikṛti*).
In the case of the archetype (prakṛti), there would be a connection by means of a sentence based on the authority of context;
and that [sentence] is weaker than a directly perceived [textual] statement.
Furthermore, because its absence is observed in the archetype.
Commentary: And for this reason also, it is a modification (vaikṛta).
Why? Because its absence is observed in the archetype (prakṛti).
How so? "Of the Saṃsutas, two exceed the Virāj."
It has been explained in the second chapter (2.4.27) that in the absence of the *ṣoḍaśin*, two *stotrīya* verses exceed the *virāj*;
therefore, the *ṣoḍaśin* is also a modification (*vaikṛta*). Furthermore, it is because there is no mention of it as part of the sacrifice.
Commentary: For this reason as well, it must be a modified form (*vaikṛta*).
For there is indeed such a statement: "They say that there is no such thing as the *ṣoḍaśī*.
It is not, however, that the *ṣoḍaśī* does not exist at all.
