In the archetype, the Jyotiṣṭoma, this statement occurs:
"If it does not exist in the Jyotiṣṭoma, then it is established in this way.
Therefore, for this reason as well, it is understood to be a modification (vaikṛta).
The *ṣoḍaśin* [cup] belongs to the archetype (*prakṛti*), because it is taught therein. Commentary: The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the alternative position.
This is not the case; the *ṣoḍaśī* is archetypal (*prākṛta*). Why? Because it is prescribed in the archetype, namely the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
And by virtue of the context, there would be syntactic unity with the Jyotiṣṭoma;
this [unity] does not depart even when [the rite] is performed as a modification (vikṛti).
For this statement is not a prohibition regarding the archetype (prakṛti).

What then? It is the mention in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). Therefore, because there is no prohibition of what has been taught in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), the *ṣoḍaśin* ought to be present.
Moreover, its context (*prakaraṇa*) alone is its proof.
What then? It is also a sentence:
"In the Agniṣṭoma, one should take [the cup] for a Kṣatriya; in the Atirātra, for a Brāhmaṇa.
And since this is not possible in the archetype (prakṛti), it cannot be assumed to apply to the modified (vaikṛta) Atirātra.

Therefore, the *ṣoḍaśī* is natural (*prākṛta*). [The opponent] says: "In this way, there is no fulfillment of the 'what' (*kim-aṃśa*) by means of the sentence here, such that there would be an extraction (*utkarṣa*) from the context."
Therefore, its placement is within the context itself. And because it is seen in the archetype. The Commentary: There is a mention of this *ṣoḍaśin* in the archetype.
"Among those that are sung together, three exceed the Virāj.
This has been stated (at 2.4.127): when the Ṣoḍaśin is being taken up, the observation of three stotrīyās becomes possible.
Therefore, the Ṣoḍaśin is archetypal.

The recitation is for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*). The Commentary states: Now, as for what was said—that "in that case [the modified sacrifice], it is because of the complete prescription"—it has been stated that the mention of that [prescription] does not constitute a prohibition regarding the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*).
Now, if [the rule] is already obtained through the general injunction (*codaka*), for what purpose is it stated again?

For that statement was made without distinction after having prescribed it for the archetype (*prakṛti*); then, by the sentence "for a Kṣatriya at the Agniṣṭoma and at the Atirātra," it follows that this is a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) intended to limit its application. It is stated [again] for that very purpose.

How could it be grasped even in the *Anatirātra* and even in the *Anagniṣṭoma*, given that [the rule] says, "It is grasped on the middle day of the three-night sacrifice"? [This is so] because of the observation of its presence in the final [day]. Commentary: Now, as for what was said—that the *Ṣoḍaśin* is not seen in the archetype (*prakṛti*), since "of the *Saṃsutas*, two exceed the *Virāj*"—[this objection is addressed].
As it has been said: "Because the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is seen, the *ṣoḍaśī* is optional; because of the prohibition of what was enjoined, there is an excess in the six.

[Regarding] the status of being a non-sacrifice due to its qualities: The Commentary states—now, as for what was said, that "the *ṣoḍaśī* is not in the archetype (*prakṛti*) because of the mention of it as a non-sacrifice," that has already been addressed.
Because it is prescribed, it is understood as belonging to the archetype (prakṛti).
But how can it be called "not a sacrifice" (ayajña)? Because it is optional; since that sacrifice does not exist in one alternative, it is figuratively called "not a sacrifice."

Therefore, the *ṣoḍaśī* is archetypal (*prākṛta*). The purpose [of this discussion] is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is not included in the archetype, whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is included.
Knowledge: there exists the *ṣoḍaśī* in the *jyotiṣṭoma*.

And although that *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice has been enjoined for the sake of the person by the rule, "One desiring vigor [should take] the *ṣoḍaśin*," it is further heard as being for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*) in the injunction: "It should be taken at the Agniṣṭoma for a Kṣatriya; even at the Ukthya for a Vaiśya; at the Atirātra for a Brāhmaṇa; it is taken on the second day of a two-night sacrifice; it is taken on the fourth day of a *hīna* sacrifice.
Regarding that *ṣoḍaśin* intended for the ritual, there is a doubt: should it belong to the archetype (*prakṛti*), or should it be displaced (*utkṛṣṭavya*) to the ectypes (*vikṛti*) alone?

Regarding the statements such as "On the following day, [the cup] is taken for one who has performed the Dvirātra," and because of the statement "In the Agniṣṭoma, for a Rājanya," which expresses a connection with a modified (vaikṛta) sacrifice, it might be argued that—since these refer to the modified Agniṣṭoma—the general context (prakaraṇa) is set aside by the syntactical connection (vākya) and the rule is displaced (utkarṣa). To this we reply: since the words "Agniṣṭoma" and so forth, which are taught in the context of the archetypal (prakṛti) sacrifice, can apply right there, why should the modified sacrifice, even though not present in that context, be denoted? Therefore, by the very force of the syntactical connection, the rule should apply to the archetype itself.

In this context, that which was prescribed for the *rājanya* and other [classes] on account of a specific occasion (*nimitta*) is enjoined as non-occasional (*anaimittika*) in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), according to the rule: "On the following day of the *dvirātra*.

Regarding the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, they say that the connection is not between the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*), but rather a connection with the modifications alone; this constitutes the "arising" (*utthiti*) of the logical connection (*saṃgati*).

Furthermore, because of the possibility of sublation (*bādha*), it is considered whether or not the connection of the *ṣoḍaśin* with the archetype is sublated; this is the "narrative" (*ākhyā*) connection.

Vi—‘It should belong either to the modification (*vikṛti*) or to the archetype (*prakṛti*); because of the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *ṣoḍaśī*. However, since there is no displacement due to the non-contradictory statement, it belongs to the archetype. Bhaṭṭa—In the context of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, there arises the inquiry: does the *ṣoḍaśī* conclude within the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, or not? In this deliberation, by the statement ‘One desiring vigor should praise with the *ṣoḍaśī*’, its status as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is understood; therefore, like the *godohana* vessel and others, it is not a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* because of its [separate] context.

Nor should it be argued that, by the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), the statement "one should take [the draught] for a Kṣatriya at the Agniṣṭoma" serves as a rule for the archetype (*prakṛti*);

for that statement refers specifically to the modified (*vaikṛta*) Agniṣṭoma, since it is taught in the context of modifications such as: "it is taken on the second day of a two-night sacrifice, on the middle day of a three-night sacrifice, and on the fourth day of an Ahīna."

In reality, however, because the terms *agniṣṭoma* and so forth exclude other numbers, it is impossible to enjoin the *ṣoḍaśī* sacrifice within the *agniṣṭoma* form—whether in the archetype (*prakṛti*) or the ectype (*vikṛti*). Therefore, in the case of the *dvirātra* and similar rites, this [passage] is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Where even in other forms (*saṃsthā*) it would be appropriate to accept this as a sixth [element] by way of supplementing the preceding form, what need is there to mention the *dvirātra* and others which are devoid of such contradictory forms?
Thus, since there is no evidence to include it in another archetype, it does not belong to the archetype.
This being the case, although words such as *ṣoḍaśin* and others are applied to many things, they are capable of denoting number alone.

Therefore, in the case of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, [the term] functions through conventional indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*), while in other sacrifices it functions through current indication (*sāmpratikalakṣaṇā*), and likewise in the case of the *aṇe* and the *stotra*; this has been thoroughly discussed in the section on number (*saṃkhyādhikaraṇa*) and in the second book of the *Kaustubha*.

Thus, here in the passage "He who, knowing thus, takes the *ṣoḍaśin*," because of the writings of the Commentator and others, it is the sacrificial session (*saṃsthā*) itself, qualified by the taking of the cup, that is enjoined.

By the word "sixteenth" (*ṣoḍaśin*), even though it is a term expressing a number, because it does not apprehend its qualifier [in isolation], it brings to mind the sacrifice qualified by that [number]; thus, from the comprehension of the sentence-meaning as "one should perform the sacrifice characterized by that number," the number indeed becomes connected with the drawing (*grahaṇa*) [of the cup] through the medium of purifying the substance that serves as the means for the repetition of the sacrifice. Consequently, in that context, the completion (*saṃsthā*) is described as being distinguished by the drawing.

It is improper to accept that the word *ṣoḍaśin* refers merely to the act of taking [the cup], for that would result in the fault of *lakṣaṇā* (figurative indication), as it would refer only to that specific qualification.
For this very reason, the injunction regarding the *saṃsthās* (ritual terminuses) is for the sake of their potency (*vīrya*), and not for the sake of the *stotra* (hymn).

This is because the *stotra* is already established by the scriptural statement, "The *stotra* becomes twenty-onefold for the sake of stability," and the present text is merely a reiteration (*anuvāda*) for the sake of its propriety.

For this very reason, the *stotra* and the *grahaṇa* are indeed subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of that [saṃsthā] because they bring about its numerical fulfillment and by virtue of the scriptural statement; it is beyond dispute that they are not subsidiaries of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

And thus, since the *saṃsthā* is for the sake of a result, neither the context (*prakaraṇa*) nor the statement "there are four Soma-saṃsthās" and so forth is capable of establishing subsidiariness, as these are justified solely on the basis of [the saṃsthā] being the substratum (*āśraya*).

Nevertheless, by means of such scriptural injunctions as, "One may draw [the cup] for a Kṣatriya even at the Agniṣṭoma; one may draw it at the Ukthya; one may draw it for a Brāhmaṇa at the Atirātra," its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma is established through the principle of the distinctness of connection (*saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya*).
For these are not merely explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), because indicative marks (*liṅga*) are heard therein and because there is no other determining factor [to the contrary].
Furthermore, the mention of the term "Kṣatriya" and so forth would be useless if they were intended merely as praise.
The meaning of this statement will be explained further on, and has also been explained in the *Kaustubha*.

Furthermore, because these [rules] are restorative injunctions (*pratiprasava*) for occasional rites (*naimittika*), their inclusion in the section primarily dealing with modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) is irrelevant.

Alternatively, let it be that by the "Injunction of the Learned" (*vidvadvākya*), there is merely an injunction for the taking up of the cups (*grahaṇa*) according to the number eight; nevertheless, since the status of that number as a subordinate element of vigor (*vīrya*) is established by the aforementioned statement alone, its application to the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*) is established by that very statement. As for its form as a specific ritual conclusion (*saṃsthā*), that is established through the injunctions for the taking up of the cups and the well-known consensus of the ritualists (*yājñika*); thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Therefore, it is established that this is an occasional (naimittika) subsidiary of the archetype (prakṛti).
Consequently, there is a sublation (bādha) of the permanent form of the rite for a Kṣatriya in the archetype; thus, its utility lies in its application to sublation.

Nor should it be argued that the re-statement [of the rule] in certain modified rites (vikṛtis) is therefore redundant, because its purpose will be explained later as being for the sake of making it non-occasional.
Regarding the *ṣoḍaśī* sacrifice (4027) and the *ṣoḍaśī* hymn, Maṇḍana states: "The *ṣoḍaśī*, however, should be [performed] in the application of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Śaṅkara states: "The *ṣoḍaśī* is [to be performed] only in the archetype."
The view of the Vṛttikāra (the author of the Vṛtti) is that there is an inclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup in the *dvirātra* sacrifice of the Aṅgirases.

The view of the Bhāṣyakāra (the author of the Bhāṣya) is that the phrase "the *ṣoḍaśin* is in the latter [day]" (*ṣoḍaśy uttare*) functions as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for the injunction regarding the *vailakṣaṇa-sāman*. (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 181).
One should consult the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) under the heading: "Inclusion of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup in the *dvirātra* of the Aṅgirases. (Mīko. p. 181; MīmSū 10.1.13–54).

The displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup must indeed take place when there is a displacement of the *ukthya* cups and the deities, etc., because of the injunction "He draws that [cup] away from those who have turned their backs," which prescribes the *ṣoḍaśin* subsequently. (Vi.
5.1.18) The primary *ṣoḍaśin* cup, in order not to subvert its time following the *ukthya*s, must be displaced along with its stotra, thereby subverting the time of the subordinate stotra.
5|1|18: When the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is drawn at the *agniṣṭoma* and other sacrifices where the *stotra* and *śastra* have been performed, it would constitute a numerical count.
However, according to the scriptural statement (*vacana*), when it is drawn at the *agniṣṭoma* or the *ukthya*, it does not effect a numerical count.
(Bhāṣya 10|1|21)
There is a prohibition of the drawing of the ṣoḍaśin cup in the Atirātra sacrifice.
(Bhāṣya 10). The prohibition of the drawing of the ṣoḍaśin cup in the Atirātra is of the nature of an option.
VI. 10|8|3. In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the vessel for the *ṣoḍaśin* is made of *khadira* wood and is elevated.
Bhāṣya 3|1|918. The time for the performance of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice is after the performance of the *ukthya* sacrifice.

Vārttika 5|1|18|35. Regarding the *ṣoḍaśin* recitation (*śastra*), it is stated: "He recites the *ṣoḍaśin* in an inverted order"; by this, the inverted sequence is the Vedic order (*śrauta-krama*) in the *atirātra* sacrifice.
Bhāṣya: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice when it concludes with the Ṣoḍaśin, the performance of the *pratihomas* begins from the morning *agnihotra*.
Bhāṣya 6.5.14.44. The piling of the fire-altar (*cayana*) becomes the food for the Ṣoḍaśin-sacrifice.
(“It does not exist,” according to the reading of Satyāṣāḍha—Ke.).
Vi. 2|1|10. In the *ṣoḍaśi-saṃsthā*, there is the *ukthya-stotra* and the *ṣoḍaśi-stotra*, but not what follows that, such as the *atirātra* and so forth.
Bhāṭṭa. 10|1|12.
In the Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice, the performance of the subsequent oblations begins with the morning Agnihotra. However, regarding the Ṣoḍaśin:

when the Jyotiṣṭoma is concluded as a Ṣoḍaśin, there arises a doubt concerning the omitted oblations—whether their status as "subsequent oblations" (pratihoma) is determined by the evening Agnihotra or by the morning Agnihotra.
What is established? It was stated in the preceding section that [the rule] applies to the evening *agnihotra*.
By way of general principle, it is established that this applies everywhere.
This being the position reached, it is replied:

But in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, [the rule] "one should pass over the morning fire-oblation (*prātaragnihotra*) and so forth" means that the rites should be commenced starting precisely from the morning fire-oblation. (For further details regarding the various commentaries on the Soma sacrifice, such as the Mīmāṃsā-kośa, page 2740, and the section on the "option of performing a substitute oblation" (*pratihomapakṣa*), where it states "the performance begins with the evening fire-oblation," one should consult the relevant entry.)
Maṇḍana: "In the case of the Ṣoḍaśin, the morning rites [are performed].
Since the conclusion of the Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice occurs at night, therefore, in the event of its transgression, the morning oblation (prātarhoma) itself is the first [to be performed]."
Therefore, even in the case of the *prati-homas*, the morning oblation (*prātar-homa*) alone must be performed first.
Śaṅkara states: "In the *ṣoḍaśin* [rite], it begins with the morning.
In the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, it is prescribed as a permanent rule that "the *saubhara* becomes the *brahmasāman* of the *ukthya*s."
Furthermore, in that very same context, it is stated that *saubhara* is enjoined as a fruit by means of the passage beginning, "He who desires prosperity [but] does not desire the *ṣoḍaśin*," etc.
(Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 2.2.12–7). Regarding the subject matter of the *ṣoḍaśin* chant, the injunction for *saubhara* is obligatory.

(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 873). Among the times—namely, the time subsequent to the *ukthya*, the time of "having stayed until the appointed hour" (*samayādhyuṣita*), and so forth—for the *ṣoḍaśin* stotra, the primary time to be adopted is specifically that which follows the *ukthya*; any other time, however, is to be set aside.
Therefore, the *ṣoḍaśin* is to be recited as an *ukthya*.
(Duṣa. 5.1.18.135). Regarding the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *ṣoḍaśi-stotra*, when there is a displacement of the *ukthya-stotras*, there is also a displacement of the *ṣoḍaśi-stotra*;
this point should be examined in the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*).
The time for the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) of the *ṣoḍaśī* stotra is when the sun has risen over the "time" (*samaya*).
"Time" (*samaya*) means sunset; having risen over that [sunset] in the morning is "risen over the time" (*samayādhyuṣita*).
In the Saṃhitā 4028,
that [verse] is "asaṃ. Kātyāyana assigned the designation "saṃ" to the Sāman that follows the Gāyatra belonging to the Ārbhava-gāyatrī.
Vārttika 1.3.6.11, p.
231: Where there is a *sāman* following a *gāyatrī* verse in the *ārbhavapavamāna*, it has the designation "saṃ. Sūtra, p. 230.

In cases such as “*saṃ te prāṇe vātena*,” since there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), only the supplying of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣāpyāhāra*) should be performed, and not *anuṣaṅga* (the carrying over of a word from a preceding context), because [the required word] is separated by intervening elements. This applies to the *abhīṣomīya* animal sacrifice. (Vi. 2.1.18)

In the mantra, “May your [limbs] go together with the wind; may the limbs [go] together with the sacrifices; may the lord of the sacrifice [go] together with his blessing,” the word *gacchatām* (“may they go”) does not apply to the phrase “may the lord of the sacrifice [go] together with his blessing” because it is separated by the plural-ended phrase “may the limbs [go] together with the sacrifices.
Rather, the completion of the sentence occurs through a worldly ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).
(Bhāṣya)
Kneading (*saṃyavana*) should not be performed for the *caru* offering, but it should be performed for the *puroḍāśa* cake for the sake of forming a lump.
Bhāṣya 10.1.13.51. Kneading is the mixing of the flour with water.
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the kneading of the flour is performed [with the words]: “Mix the rice with the *praṇītā* waters.

The fetching of the *praṇītā* waters is for the purpose of kneading the flour; however, their pouring out is a disposal (*pratipatti*). "He fetches the *praṇītā* waters at the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
This [fetching] is set aside in the case of the *saurya* oblation of cooked rice.

In this regard, one should consult the section [of the *Bhāṣya*] concerning the case of the *saurya-caru*, where it is stated that the mixing [of the grain] is set aside: "In the *saurya-caru*, there is a sublation of the mixing"; here, the *praṇītā* waters used in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are prompted by the act of mixing.

The two *triṣṭubh* verses used as *saṃyājyās* are both optional (*kāmya*) and obligatory (*nitya*) in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), due to the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktva*). See Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa 4.3.2; see also Mīmāṃsākośa, p.
2045, under the entry "The two *triṣṭubh*s in the Darśapūrṇamāsa. One should consult that specific section (*adhikaraṇa*) for further details.

According to the principle that "things joined together are to be completed by one [act]," the *vihavyā* and the *anvādhāna* should be performed together with the principal rite alone. (Satyāṣāḍha Śrautasūtra 1.2.6, Vaijayantī commentary:
Because of the connection with the word 'meaning' (*artha*), the purpose of that [connection] follows from the direct Vedic statement.)
Regarding the *agnicayana*, after stating, "There is a *caru* of wild rice (*nīvāra*)," the texts record, "That which he places [on the altar].

In the inquiry as to whether this *caru* is for the purpose of sacrifice—meaning it is to be placed on the altar after the sacrifice has been performed—or whether it is intended solely for the purpose of being placed there—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, because of its syntactic unity with the supplementary statement, "Wild rice is indeed the food of Bṛhaspati," the *caru* is connected with a deity and is therefore for the purpose of sacrifice. The word "but" (*tu*) serves to set aside this prima facie view; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The *artha* (purpose) is the act of placing (*upadhāna*).

A *caru* (oblation) connected with a word denoting that purpose, which is the act of placing, must be for that very purpose—namely, for the sake of placing—and not for the sake of the sacrifice; this is because of its connection with the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). For, having heard the injunction "he places," there is a direct relationship between the *caru* and the act of placing.
However, there is a connection between the *nīvāra* grains and the deity Bṛhaspati through indirect indication (*parokṣā*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the entire *caru* is intended solely for the purpose of placing [the potsherds].
Ke.

In the section [Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 2.3.7] stating "The meaning of that [word] is connected with the word whose meaning it signifies," the initial statement’s lack of expectancy is established by rejecting the view that the supplementary passage (vākyaśeṣa), "Nīvāra grains are indeed the food of Bṛhaspati," serves to designate a deity. Instead, by accepting that the word *bṛhaspati* refers to Brāhmaṇas, it is described as being intended for the praise of Nīvāra as the food of sages (*muni*). Consequently, in the context of the fire-piling (*agnicaya*), regarding the injunction "He places a vessel of Nīvāra rice," which is already satisfied in its expectancy by the prescription of placing a vessel characterized as *caru* for the purpose of preparing the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one does not accept that it enjoins a sacrifice based on the supplementary passage, "Nīvāra grains are indeed the food of Bṛhaspati," which merely establishes a connection with a deity for a subordinate act (*guṇakarma*) related to the placement.
Valor (parākrama) [is the means]. For the separation of that which was united is "severance" (apaccheda).
But when [the acts] are conjoined, it should be by way of their constituent parts (aṅga) because the other is for the sake of that;
since it is prescribed in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices that "one cuts with a long blade," there is a single cutting characterized by the number two.

Thus, having performed the double cutting for the Āgneya offering, one should perform the double cutting for the Agnīṣomīya offering even before its oblation; therefore, the *anusamaya* (consecutive performance) should be done by means of the cutting alone. With the word "but" (*tu*), the author refutes this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) which stands outside the Sūtra, and states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The act of giving, ending with the dedication, constitutes a single ritual element;
therefore, it must be performed consecutively,
according to the principle of "separateness despite connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya*) regarding what is connected [to the same purpose].
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: when the oblation (*homa*) connected with the fourfold cutting (*caturavatta*) is being prescribed, because of the commencement—that is, because of the initial undertaking—with the fourfold cutting, and because the other portioning (*avadāna*) is for that purpose, namely for the sake of the oblation, that [portioning] should end with the oblation; thus, [as the reading here is *tadantaṃ* rather than *tadaṅgaṃ*,] it would constitute a single ritual act (*padārtha*) ending with the oblation—so says the Vṛtti.

Regarding the combined [rite] associated with the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) in the oblation (*homa*): because of the commencement of one after another portioning (*avadāna*), and because they are prescribed as the initial constituent parts; or, since that [fourfold portion] is for the sake of that [oblation]—meaning the fourfold portion is for the purpose of the oblation—the entire sequence ending with the oblation (*homānta*) constitutes a single ritual act (*padārtha*). Alternatively, when the oblation associated with the portioning is being prescribed, since each subsequent portioning is for the sake of that [preceding one], meaning for the purpose of the oblation, and because the oblation commences precisely with the portioning, the entire sequence from the portioning up to the end of the oblation would constitute a single ritual act. This is the point of inquiry.

When the *avadāna* (cutting-off) is prescribed in connection with the *homa* (oblation), because the *avadāna* serves the purpose of the *homa*, and since the commencement of the *homa* is by means of the *avadāna* itself, the *avadāna* must extend until the end of the *homa*; so says Someśvara.
In the *Vṛtti*, the *Kutūhala*, and the *Someśvara*, the reading is precisely "tadantam" (ending with that).
And the reading is likewise in the *Tantraratna*.
In the root text of the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated that "it is its limb" (tadaṅgam), but this has not been explained.
In that context, "its limb" refers to the *avadāna* (cutting-off) as a limb of the *homa* (oblation)—that is, the first part of the *homa*.
Therefore, it should be explained that the *avadāna* extends until the final offering (*pradāna*).

In the passage *saṃyukte tu prakramāt* (5.2.4.6), it is stated that because the "fourfold portion" (*caturavatta*) is prescribed as a constituent part of the "two-fold cutting" (*dvyavadāna*) in the injunction "he offers the fourfold portion," it does not constitute a separate ritual act (*pṛthakpadārtha*).
Conjunction is produced by the action of one [of two bodies], by the action of both, and it is also produced by conjunction.
(Ṛju-pṛ., p. 242)
Conjunction.
Even when there is conjunction with only one part, the designation "conjunction" is established. Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 531.
Conjunction among atoms is accepted as being all-pervasive (vyāpyavṛtti).
Since it is possible for each respective location to serve as its delimiting factor (avacchedakatva), there is no inconsistency even in the case of a non-all-pervasive conjunction;
so say the Vārttikas.
Maṇi, p. 46:
"For a conjunction that is already established becomes the cause [of grammatical operations]. Vārttika 3.7.9.140.
By the maxim that "all conjunctions end in separation," the state of being produced and impermanent is established.
(Upadeśasāhasrī, Pañcama, 16.62, Rāmatīrtha).
According to the sequence of conjunctions, the fixed arrangement of the *sphya* and other implements is demonstrated in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Conjunctions and the like, which involve a second entity, do not apply to a single [atom] when it is unperceived, nor do they reside in a collection.
Furthermore, for you, there would be neither the cognition nor the designation "a collection of conjoined [atoms]."
Furthermore, it is either "this is conjoined with that" or "these two are conjoined.
However, for conjunction and the other [relations], there is inherence in a single object within a composite whole (*samudāya*).
— *Kaṇikā*, p. 416.
Like conjunction and so forth.
Although individual entities do not possess sequence, when they are combined with one another, they bear a sequential form, just as in the case of conjunction and so forth.
Bhāṣya 5.1.12.
A conjunction produced by a conjunction (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*) is not accepted [by the Mīmāṃsakas]. (Maṇi, p. 20).

Because there is no distinction in the nature of the conjunction, and because of the specific context (*prakaraṇa*), the injunction regarding the clenching of the fists (*muṣṭīkaraṇa-vacana*) and the joining of the hands (*hastānv-ejana*) are established as belonging to the entire context; this is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Because of the principle of "separateness despite connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), just as recitation (*smaraṇa*) serves as an external purificatory rite (*bahiḥsaṃskāraka*), so too does it have the fruit of purifying the altar (*vedi*).
Bhaṭṭa 1.1.14.
The principle of conjunction and separation (saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya); the principle of the *khadira* tree and so forth (khādiratvādinyāya);
the principle of curd (dadhinyāya).

The principle of distinct conjunctions (*saṃyogāntaranyāya*). In the Agnihotra, the obligatory nature and the optional nature of the curd are established through the distinctness of their respective injunctions. For a single thing, when it possesses both [natures], there is a distinctness of conjunction.
Commentary: In the Agnihotra it is heard: "He offers with curd. And again: "One desiring sensory power should offer with curd.

Likewise, regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, it is recorded: "He binds [the animal] to a post made of Khadira wood," and again: "One desiring vigor should make the sacrificial post out of Khadira wood."
In this regard, there is a doubt:
is there also something else here for the sake of what is eternal?
This being the position reached, we reply:
When a single act possesses both characteristics—being obligatory (*nitya*) and being conditional (*naimittika*)—the principle of "separateness despite connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*) is the cause.
This principle of separateness despite connection exists here:
one injunction is "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), and another is "For one desiring sensory power, [he should offer] with curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya*).
Likewise, one [text] says, "He binds with a khadira [wood]," while another says, "For one desiring vigor, [he binds] with a khadira.
Therefore, the curd and other such substances serve both as a constant (nitya) requirement and for a specific desire (kāmya).
Indeed, the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*) is the reason why a single thing can possess both forms.
Therefore, regarding such a meaning:
if it is argued that "it is a remainder" (śeṣa), the Commentary states: "If you see it thus, why is there not also a remainder in the preceding case?"

Regarding what was stated—"He offers with curd"—this is the principle of the distinctness of conjunctions (*saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya*). [This occurs] when there is a direct perception of two separate conjunctions, such as "He binds [the animal] to a *khadira* post.
For that very curd, however, the fruit is sensory power (*indriya*), and likewise for the *khadira*, the fruit is vigor (*vīrya*).
"And this is the statement":

[Duh]—just as there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) even when the *camasa* cup is prescribed after the act of carrying has been restated, so too is there unity in the case of "that which one offers, that is for one desiring sensory power.
And thus, because the expectancy is satisfied, there is syntactic unity between both parts.
Not so, because the objects are distinct.
The Commentary states: This is not the case;
these two objects are distinct—namely, that which is the connection of the curd with the oblation, and that which is the connection of the curd with the sense-faculty.
Likewise, there are two purposes in the case of the *khadira* wood: its connection with the act of binding and its [connection] with vigor;
both of these are intended to be enjoined.
And because there is a single purpose, it is understood that this constitutes a single sentence (2.1.14).
In this case, the sentence may be divided according to two distinct meanings.

How so? When the injunction manifested by the verb *juhoti* (he offers) cannot possibly enjoin the primary act of offering itself, it must enjoin the quality (*guṇa*) mentioned in close proximity; and when even that is impossible, it enjoins the connection between that quality and a specific result.
For in those instances, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is set aside in favor of the requirements of another syntactical unit (*vākya*).
How could association be recognized?
Because it deserves prohibition;
therefore, one should avoid association with a woman in her courses.
Or—another statement, "One should not eat from this [vessel]," has also been cited together with it because it serves as a means for seeing another meaning.
A "malavadvāsā" is a woman in her menses.
Even regarding the prohibition of speaking the truth, those same positions apply.

In this regard, since there is no word serving as a similar source for the sound produced by the recitation, and because the possibility of concordance arises without distinction both in the sacrifice (*kratu*) and in the person (*puruṣa*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—following the logic of the prohibition against speaking untruth when it has already been stated—is that there is a prohibition of the concordant speech "O wife, this is your world," which serves the purpose of the sacrifice. To this, the following objection is raised: "This prohibition is preceded by a prior attainment, and that attainment resides in the person; for there is no attainment of [speaking] with respect to the sacrifice for one who has not previously been excluded."

Regarding the injunction "one should sacrifice after having asked her permission," this [prohibition] excludes [the act] from all sacrificial performances (*kratu*) in general; how then could it be understood as applying specifically to a conversation?
Since a person possesses autonomy, the prohibition would be meaningful when applied to conversations at all times.
Furthermore, if the Smṛti enjoins it in this manner, then even in this case, the relationship between the root text and its commentary must be accepted as such.
Indeed, no one has stated that this is a restatement (anuvāda) based on a victory [in debate].
Regarding the prohibitions concerning food:
the Commentary states— "There is a prohibition concerning food: 'One should not eat her food; for a woman's food is indeed ointment. This is a rule enjoining the prohibition of sexual intercourse."
And since that [quality] is not applicable to the specific context (*prakaraṇa*), it is determined that this is a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*) which transcends the context.
Or rather—for the following reason as well—it is a property of every person.
Why? Because "an object in doubt has been described by means of a decision based on a general statement."
(2|16) Furthermore, the duty of a man is beyond doubt, according to the Smṛti statement, "One should not eat her food.
This refers to the prohibition against approaching her, as derived from the refinement of the sentence "one should not eat her food.
For instance, among the Lāṭas, it is well known that "approaching" (*upagamana*) is synonymous with the term for "anointing" (*abhyañjana*).
And that [prohibition] has never been applied to the Vedic sense derived from words;
rather, it is universally established among all living beings as pertaining to human aims.
And it has been stated that the purpose of a prohibition is the same as the purpose of the attainment [of the object prohibited].

Furthermore, because of the injunction regarding celibacy (*brahmacarya*), even though it serves a human purpose, it is prohibited at its own time [of occurrence] due to the possibility of its application;
therefore, by overriding that [prohibition], it remains a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*) for as long as the ritual purpose (*kratvartha*) lasts.
And thus, by analogy with that, the same status applies to other cases; this is the establishment of the meaning through corroboration.
Śabara: Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "One should not converse with a woman who has not bathed after her menses.
Is this a prohibition for the sake of the sacrifice (kratvartha) or for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha)?
Since it would prima facie apply to the sake of the sacrifice due to the context (prakaraṇa), it is now stated [in reply].

Because of the scriptural injunction, "One should sacrifice after having spoken to her," the woman who has menstruated is excluded from all ritual activities; therefore, there is no possibility of conversation with her.
Furthermore, since there is an absence of engagement [in the ritual], a prohibition is untenable.
For it is only when a man is acting independently that conversation with a menstruating woman could occur.
Therefore, since there is a prohibition wherever there is an injunction, this pertains to the purpose of the person (*puruṣārthatā*).
[Soma: "By one with soiled garments" means by one who is menstruating.

The connection [of this discussion] is established because, as before, there is an objection that even here, due to the absence of a specific fruit, the act must serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: the prohibition of conversing with a woman in her menses is for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha), because she is already excluded [from ritual participation] prior to the commencement of the performance.
Vi— "One should not converse with a woman in her menses," this too is like the previous case;
it is for the sake of the person, since there is no possibility of conversation occurring in any case.
Bhāṭṭa: Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices themselves, it is heard in the Śruti: "One should not converse with a *malavadvāsas*. A *malavadvāsas* is a woman in her menses (*rajasvalā*).
Since the fruit of this prohibition is explicitly heard in the scripture, there is no inconsistency in its being for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*).

Nor should it be argued that a prohibition is impossible because the injunction, "If one whose animal sacrifice has been interrupted for three days should find her [the wife] after she has become menstruating, he should sacrifice having removed her," prescribes the performance of the sacrificial application through effort in the rite following the onset of menstruation in a woman who is not currently sacrificing; for neither the sacrificer’s nor the officiating priest’s (ārtvijya) conversation with a menstruating woman—which are incidental to the rite or worldly—could possibly occur. This is because, even though such a conversation does not occur otherwise, it could occur in the form of consent when the woman is in charge of common property.

Since even inference can be employed through a traditional chain to ascertain [the truth], there is no occasion for corroboration. However, regarding a woman other than the wife who is menstruating, although she might be approached out of passion during the ritual season (*ṛtu*), such an act falls outside the scope of the prohibitory injunctions pertaining to the sacrifice. Even though such an act is prohibited in the Smṛti, its prohibition is for the sake of the sacrifice itself, because it is a prohibition similar to that against eating meat. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the Siddhāntin replies]: Manu, having begun with "A menstruating woman and a eunuch... and so forth, states: "In the offering into the fire (*homa*), in giving, and in eating—whatever is desired by these [persons] in a rite for the gods or the ancestors, that becomes fruitless. Thus, the prohibition is indeed for the sake of the sacrifice.

Having said this, by the statement "and them [the women] also elsewhere," which refers to any woman in her menses, the context of the *śrāddha* is set aside; furthermore, because of the injunction regarding the removal [of impurity], there is no possibility of conversation with her, and thus it serves the purpose of the ritual (*kratvarthatva*).
Nor is this very *śruti* the source for that [rule], as it is a *smṛti* concerning the *daiva* [rite].
Section on Concordance 4033: The luminosity of consciousness is of a general nature because its object is merely the action [itself].

Nor is the statement regarding exclusion (aparodha-vākya) redundant even for one who is menstruating; for the statement of exclusion serves the purpose of the injunction to perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), since the husband’s entitlement is only in conjunction with his wife, and in the absence of the wife—who lacks entitlement due to her menstruation—the sacrifice cannot be performed. Thus, the statement is intended to ensure the performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* when she is not present.
For this very reason, the statement "even that which occurs therein is high" (*ucca*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Consequently, since it is not [otherwise] applicable, this prohibition pertains solely to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). However, it should be noted that one can also say it is for the purpose of obtaining the scripturally prescribed expiation (*śrautaprāyaścitta*).

Maṇḍana: "The state of being for all purposes is not contradicted by the Mallikā. The meaning is that "the state of being for all purposes" (*sarvārthatā*) refers to being a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) common to everyone.
Śaṅkara: "And there is the avoidance of the speech of a menstruating woman (*udakyā*)."

"Correspondence" (saṃvādatva) means having as its object that which has [the previous cognition] as its object. This is the principle of the "confusion regarding correspondence" (saṃvādābhrama-nyāya). Maṇi, p. [blank].

Just as someone who perceives the luster of a gem with the notion that it is the gem itself is indeed mistaken, yet at the time of grasping it, he obtains the gem; thus, that error is a "concordant error" (*saṃvādābhrama*). In the same way, for one who engages in worldly activity while contemplating the referent of the word *tvam* (the individual self) as being the referent of the word *tat* (Brahman)—which is like the luster of the gem—he is indeed mistaken; nevertheless, at the time of its direct realization, the direct realization of the referent of the word *tat*, which is non-different from that [self], arises according to the principle of concordant error. This is the view of Nīlakaṇṭha. "Concordant" (*saṃvādinī*) means similar.
An error belonging to that [similar cognition] is a "concordant error. This is the meaning.
The rash one [says]:
921. Consciousness (*saṃvit*): For consciousness is perceptual with respect to an object, not with respect to a cognition (*buddhi*).
*Bṛhatī*, page 128: Consciousness (*saṃvit*). Indeed, consciousness is one only when its object is cognized as a single unity;
it is not [consciousness] if it lacks an object.
And for what purpose is consciousness? We do not say that consciousness is not cognizable;
rather, consciousness is cognizable precisely by virtue of its being consciousness, not by virtue of being an object of cognition (*saṃvedyatayā*).
On page 64: in the Vijñānavāda, it is consciousness itself that is experienced in this or that form, and nothing distinct from it exists.
*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 165: Consciousness (*saṃvit*).
And consciousness is not itself unperceivable, because the state of being perceivable for all entities is rooted in it. *Bṛhatī*, p. 64: Consciousness.

Since consciousness (*saṃvit*) is of the nature of self-luminosity and its manifestation does not depend on anything else, it does not possess the status of an object (*karmatā*). Furthermore, the term "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) applies to cognitions by virtue of their immediacy (*aparokṣatā*), and not because they are objects known through sensory cognition. (Ṛjuvimalā, p. 64: the direct perceptibility of consciousness.)
*Bṛhatī*, page 26: "The luminosity of consciousness.
Self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) means independence from any other consciousness with respect to the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) connected with itself.

Now, one might object: linguistic usage regarding consciousness consists in the employment of words; since such usage depends upon the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*vācyavācakasaṃbandha*) involving the word "consciousness," this definition is impossible.
The meaning is that in the linguistic usage connected with the ether (the void), there is no such independence from a further act of apprehension.
However, the linguistic usage of consciousness (*saṃvit*) does depend on the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācaka*).

Furthermore, the dependence on apprehension is for the sake of recollection; for even when the relationship has been apprehended, if it is not recollected, there is an absence of the employment of words.

Therefore, because both the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) depend upon consciousness (*saṃvid*) for their own empirical functioning, they possess self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*); thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition].
And the proof (*pramāṇa*) is either inference (*anumāna*) or presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
As for the inference: "The empirical usage regarding the cognition of a jar and so forth is based upon that cognition of the jar and so forth."
Because it arises immediately after that [cognition], like the conventional usage of the word "jar.

As for the argument from presumption (*arthāpatti*): the non-usage of the cognition of a jar cannot be accounted for without the existence of a cause for the knowledge of the jar; thus, the cognition of the jar is established as being none other than the cognition of the self. Nor can any other explanation be stated.

[Objection: Is it not the case that everywhere usage is seen to be based precisely on what is known through consciousness that transcends [that] usage? How then can it be established here that in the case of consciousness itself, usage is based precisely on what is known through consciousness? [Reply: It is not so. If the state of being a cause distinct from usage is accepted solely on the basis of observation, then since the fact that usage belongs to a class distinct from [its own] usage is firmly observed, let that too be accepted. And for this reason, even if [consciousness] were known through consciousness, there would still be no usage regarding consciousness itself.

For those who abandon the reason that [cognition] is of a different genus from what is subject to empirical usage (*vyavahārya*), what is the ground for such partiality? Since the phenomenon is accounted for by an established cause, it is improper to postulate "consciousness" (*saṃvit*) as an additional factor. Alternatively, the inference is as follows: consciousness does not depend on another thing of its own kind to produce the effect consisting of its own manifestation in empirical usage, because it produces an effect of that nature which depends on another; for whatever produces an effect of a certain nature that depends on another, it does not depend on another of its own kind regarding that specific effect—just as color does not depend on another color, or dimension does not depend on another dimension.

Is it not the case that there is an absolute certainty [of inference] through a mark (liṅga) by means of a mark? For example, fire is inferred from smoke, and heat from fire; in that case, fire performs the function of being the object of inference for another, and that inference depends upon smoke. This is not so, because even in that case, there is dependence upon a mark of a different class.

For by the term "homogeneous" (*sajātīya*), an absolute universal (*atyantajāti*) is not intended. If it is argued that, in that case, a cognition of a jar does not depend on another cognition of a jar even when one is nearby—since it depends only on the cognition of the object of knowledge—and therefore this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), we reply: it is not so. All cognitions belong to a single genus; the distinction between "cognition of a jar" and "cognition of a cloth" arises from the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhibheda*). Wherever a distinction can be determined through its own nature alone, independent of such adjuncts—as in the case of the self-luminous nature of consciousness (*saṃvittiprakāśatā*)—there the admission of distinction is possible. Therefore, there is no proof of what is already established.

Is it not the case that [the argument] is inconclusive because of the finger? Just as a finger produces the effect of touch directed toward another object, yet requires its own state of being a finger for the touch directed toward itself;
and as it has been said: "Just as this finger is not able to touch itself by its own name, so too cognition is not able to know itself by its own part."

It is not so. For whatever entity has a specific, unique effect (*asādhāraṇa-kārya*), it is to be proven that such an effect, in its own production, depends upon another of its own kind. However, in this case, the effect of touch is not unique to the finger, since it is possible to touch [an object] with other parts as well. But the effect consisting of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) belongs to cognition; the exclusion of color (*rūpa-vyavaccheda*) belongs to color alone; and the usage regarding measurement (*māna-vyavahāra*) belongs to dimension (*parimāṇa*) alone. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever.

Regarding the inference for [the property of] being manifested by another—such as "because it depends on another," "because it is a quality (*guṇa*)," "because it is an object of linguistic usage," "because it is a primary quality (*ādimaguṇa*)," and so forth—all of this has a sublated subject (*bādhitaviṣaya*), because it contradicts the means of valid cognition that apprehends the property [of self-manifestation]. This is because it has been stated that the establishment of cognition occurs through itself alone, not by means of another cognition. How so? Because it is said: "That which arises through itself does not depend on another," and "One must accept the established nature of the act of cognition; even if its establishment were sought through another, it would still be established as such."

Even in the refutation of the theory that consciousness is illuminated by another, there exists an inference in the form of a negative concomitance (*vyatirekin*): because it is an experience, because it is luminosity, and because it is knowledge, it must be established as something distinct—neither that which has been previously perceived nor that which has not been perceived.
(Bhāṣya 10.1.5–6; 59–61). In the *saṃvāda* sacrifice, where both [sāmans] are equal, the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* sāmans are to be employed together specifically in the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*.

In the case of a rite having both sāmans, there should be a division of the *vidhā* (the introductory verses). The Bhāṣya says: There are seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtu*) that have both sāmans; [it is said] "one should perform both *saṃkhye*, and one should perform both *apavitrau* on a single-day sacrifice (*ekāha*)."
In this regard, there is a doubt: do the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans] function separately, or together?
Why are they understood as combined, or why as separate?
It is said in reply:
This very statement indicates that it consists of both [parts].
How so? The sacrifice (kratu) must be connected with both.
Whether those two are taken together or separately, in either case, the sacrifice becomes connected with them.
In this regard, since both alternatives appear possible regarding the statement, which is the correct one?
That they are separate.

Why? Because in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *pṛṣṭha* stotra was accomplished by either one of the two, the Bṛhat or the Rathantara; here too, it is understood that it must be accomplished by either one, in order to maintain conformity with the injunctions of the archetype (*codaka*).

And thus, if the connection with the *pṛṣṭha* were established through the performance of the actions in their entirety, the *codaka* (the rule of extension) would be favored; however, since both [the *rathaṃtara* and the *bṛhat*] serve as the means for the *pṛṣṭha*, they would be mutually contradictory, resulting in an impossibility: namely, that "neither the *rathaṃtara* is the *pṛṣṭha*, nor is the *bṛhat* the *pṛṣṭha*.
Since the meaning of the scriptural statement is established in either case, there is no reason to subvert the *codaka*.
Therefore, just as in the *viśvajit* sacrifice all [melodies] such as the *bṛhat* do not find a place together in one location, so it is here as well.
"Or rather, it is for the sake of the *pṛṣṭha* [laud], because it does not have that as its purpose.
The Commentary says: "This is not so; [it applies] when they are separate.
What then? They should both be in the *sāman* when they are combined."
Why? Because in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *pṛṣṭha* stotra is accomplished by means of the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* Sāmans, which are optional alternatives.

Now, in this ectype (*vikṛti*), since those two have reached their respective places and are obtained as options, this statement exists solely for the purpose of prescribing their simultaneous performance, namely: "One should employ both the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara*.
And thus simultaneity (*sāmastya*) occurs only if those two Sāmans do not abandon one another.
Furthermore, since these two are heard [in scripture] as being means (*upāya*), both the mention of their duality and the mention of their compound form are indeed intended.
Therefore, wherever there is the *Bṛhat*, it is accompanied by the *Rathaṃtara*, not alone. To this, one might object:
The concomitance (*sāhitya*) of these two is in relation to the principal action.
In that regard, their concomitance is not contradicted even when they perform the action separately;
just as in the case of Devadatta and Yajñadatta cooking together, even though they are joined, when the act of kneading is being performed, one does something and the other also does something.

What has been performed by one is not performed again by another; thus, one *sāman* will accomplish a particular *stotra*, and the second [sāman] will likewise accomplish another. Since their association (*sāhitya*) depends upon the assistance rendered to the primary act (*pradhāna*), the connection with the whole is not contradicted.
To this it is replied: Where there is a conjunction of two things in mutual dependence, it is only in that case that this [distinction] is logical.

For when there is a connection with a constituent part of an action—whether by way of its commencement, its middle, or its conclusion—it is not possible for those two [parts] to exist separately from that [action].
Why? Because just as it is understood that "it must be assisted by this [factor]," so too is it understood that "it must be assisted by the other [factors] together.
As for the claim that in common worldly experience, even when the totality of causal factors is mentioned, their functions are seen to be distinct—that is impossible in the present case.

For in this case, once the [oblation] has been placed upon the fire, it is not possible to perform the act of placing it on the fire again; thus, one performs it because there is no contradiction, but it is not enjoined there by the word itself.
Whatever is to be performed must be done together with the [act of] placing, and not otherwise. However, in this instance, there is no impossibility.

For the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are enjoined by way of being metrical hymns (ṛk), and these two, when combined, are capable of consecrating the Pṛṣṭha [Stotra]. Therefore, their conjunction alone is logical.
As it has been stated: "When both possibilities exist, it is logical to favor the *codaka* (the general injunction).
Thus, there will be neither a deficiency in the ritual properties (*dharma*) nor a violation of the causal conditions (*nimitta*).
In that case, since the *codaka* is set aside by the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the complete injunction, no fault arises.
"And because of the observation of an indicative mark.
Commentary: An indicative mark also shows that the two are used together, not separately.
What is the indicative mark? It says this: "The two great trees (mahāvṛkṣau) indeed complete the *nidhana* in the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*; for the two great trees are combined."
For here, it is not by dividing [the two] that one says "the radiance.
From the mention of a difference in the *nidhana* (concluding chant), their location in a single place is understood.
If they were in different places, then this very difference in the *nidhana* would be established there.
But if they were combined, then the statement regarding the difference in their final notes (*nidhana*) would be meaningful.
Therefore, for this reason as well, there is no difference.

Likewise, there is another indicative mark (*liṅga*): "The *rathaṃtara* is indeed in the forenoon; the *bṛhat* is in the afternoon. This shows that they move together on a single day and occupy a single location.
Therefore, both [sāmans] are to be placed in the *pṛṣṭha* position.

Śa: Where, as in the *saṃvāda* and other rites, it is heard in the scripture, "Both the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara* are used," there arises a doubt: do both serve as the means for the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, or is one to accomplish the *pṛṣṭha* while the other accomplishes a different *stotra*? In this doubt, since the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) provides the *pṛṣṭha* through an option (*vikalpa*), in order to favor that [injunction], only one serves as the means for the *pṛṣṭha*, while the other serves as a supplement (*saṃstava*) in the *saṃvāda* and similar rites.

The *sāman* might belong to the *viśvajit* even in other stotras; however, this is not the case here, for there is no scriptural injunction (*vācanika*) regarding the placement of the *viśvajit* in another function. Indeed, there is no such statement here by which it could be placed in another function. Therefore, since the two *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] are obtained as options, the statement merely effects their conjunction (*samuccaya*). As for the sublation of the general rule (*codaka*), that is equal even if they serve as the means for other stotras. Consequently, the placement is indeed within the *pṛṣṭha* itself.

Soma: Since, as previously stated, those two [the *Ṣoḍaśin* and the *Vaiśvadeva*] are merely modifications of the number [of cups] due to the favor of the *codaka* (archetypal injunction), and since in the case of other substances the favor of the *codaka* which brings about the number applies here as well for the sake of that same favor, it has been stated that both are not the means; thus, there is a connection. Vi: "When two [verses] are in conflict, one becomes the *pṛṣṭha* [chant], while the other is joined with the archetype; when there is a division, the other [applies]."
By virtue of the scriptural statement, these two *sāmans* are separated for the two *stotras*;
here, there is no such conjunction as there would be for a subsequent injunction in the case of the *pṛṣṭha*.

Bhaṭṭa: In cases such as the *saṃsava* sacrifice, where there is an injunction for the simultaneous performance (*samuccaya*) of both the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* sāmans, the question arises: are both to be inserted into the original *pṛṣṭha-stotra* itself, or is one to be placed in the *pṛṣṭha* and the other in a different stotra? Upon reflection, since the simultaneous performance of the two sāmans—being heard as connected to the sacrifice—is logically consistent even without being inserted into a single stotra, it is understood that they must be inserted into distinct stotras in accordance with their independence as established by the archetype (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, since the insertion of even one of them is possible through its established connection to the *pṛṣṭha*, there is no evidence for both being so [inserted] in that manner; therefore, one is inserted into the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* and the other into a different stotra, and even there, specifically into the *pavamāna*.

This being the case, there is no injunction here for the simultaneous performance of both Sāmans; this would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Rather, it is an injunction for their combination (*samuccaya*) by way of restating the Sāmans already established by default.
Since that establishment occurs through extended application (*atideśa*) specifically in the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, the combination applies only there.

However, according to the view that in the archetype (*prakṛti*) there is only a single *pṛṣṭha-stotra* accomplished by two *sāmans*, even in that view, since the two *sāmans* have distinct functions in the archetype and are thus independent (*nairapekṣya*), it is the two *stotras* themselves that are the means of accomplishment through an option. Consequently, because there is no evidence for subverting the intermediate function of both *sāmans* as belonging to a single *pṛṣṭha-stotra* understood from the original injunction, there must be an injunction of two *sāmans* characterized by their combination (*samuccaya*) within that very single *pṛṣṭha-stotra*. Otherwise, one would incur the fallacy of postulating an intermediate function for the other *sāman* by way of its being a different *stotra*.
Therefore, according to both views, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of two *sāmans* and their respective bases within a single *pṛṣṭhastotra*.

In that regard, although the injunction "The first three verses are for the *rathaṃtara*, the latter nine for the *bṛhat*"—based on the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating "The forenoon indeed belongs to the *rathaṃtara*, the afternoon to the *bṛhat*"—would suggest using the *sāmans* as they appear in the *ṛc* recitation, one should understand that for the sake of fulfilling the *ṛc*-reading, the *rathaṃtara* is applied to some [verses] in the first position and the *bṛhat* afterwards, by means of alternating turns (*paryāya*).

The authors of the *Kalpasūtras*, however, prescribe that even in the *saṃsava* and other such rites, when there is a single *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, the *viśvajit* should be placed in the *pavamāna* of the other; and in certain other seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtu*), they understand it as follows: "In one case, one [stotra] is on the *bṛhat* and the other on the *rathaṃtara* by way of alternating turns. In others, they understand it as a combination: "In a single *bṛhat*-womb or *rathaṃtara*-womb, the former is in the first half and the other in the latter half.
Maṇḍana states: "Both are declared to be dual."

"In a sacrifice where both [Sāmans] are prescribed—that is, a sacrifice with both Sāmans—the term *dvaiṣṭham* means 'two Pṛṣṭhas'; the intention is that there is a combined performance of both Sāmans, not by way of option (*vikalpa*).
Śaṅkara says: 'In the Saṃsava sacrifice, both [are used] as the Pṛṣṭha.'"

In the *saṃsava* sacrifice and other such modifications (*vikṛti*), there is no performance of the original (*prākṛta*) *pṛṣṭha* and *pratipad* verses, which are contingent (*naimittika*) upon the presence of the *upatiṣṭhat* and *vala* mantras. (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1164; see the section under "upatiṣṭhat-vala-naimittikayoḥ"). Saṃsāra is beginningless (*anādi*).

Mīmāṃsā, Ratnākara, in the *Ātmavāda*, p. 89: "Oṃ. Because the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is beginningless, it is impossible for anyone to conceive of a beginning or an end. Bṛhatī, p. 238: "Moreover, even merit (*dharma*) indeed envelops a man dwelling in the cycle of existence;
for a man is not covered by a body consisting of pure evil alone."

"Or [as stated in] Vākyapadīya 3.4.10.29, p. 162: 'The causes of saṃsāra are the misconceptions that are established as the causes of worldly existence—namely, the notion of permanence in the impermanent, the notion of happiness in what is not happiness, and the notion of a self in what is not the self.
Bṛhatī, p. 49: 'The so-called Saṃsṛp offerings consist of ten oblations in the Rājasūya.'"

Among those, the eighth, ninth, and tenth [offerings] are prescribed to be performed at the beginning, middle, and end of the *upasad* rites; nevertheless, they do not constitute part of the *upasad*, but rather are primary acts (*pradhāna*) within the *rājasūya*, just like the *anumati* and other offerings.
The *saṃsarpa* consists of ten *iṣṭi* offerings in the *rājasūya*.
vi.

Regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), there is the principle: "In this case, ownership over the conditioned ceases merely by entering the intermediate state (*antarāyagāma*), but not without [the performance of] the sacrifice (*ayāga*). (4038) *saṃskāraḥ*.

For this very reason, the agency of the husband and wife in performing acts such as giving is a collective function (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), because their property is held in common and because the cessation of ownership over that which is held in common depends upon both.
Soma-saṃskāra: the piling of the fire-altar (*agni-cayana*).

"He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar"—here, *cayana* (piling) is a consecratory act (*saṃskāra*) for the fire, not a separate ritual action named "piling. This is understood from the world as well; for instance, when men have arrived from another village, the performance of the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire) is spoken of as the "performance of the *aṣṭakā*. (Bhāṣya 2.3.1.21–23). A consecratory act is also known to exist in common usage. For example, when men have come from another village, the performance of the *paryagnikaraṇa* is said to be the "performance of the *aṣṭakā*."
And there is no non-arising in the world.
A *saṃskāra* (consecration) can also be one that produces eight types of assistance (such as the preparation with fire, salt, and so forth for those who have arrived from another village;
this is well known in the vernacular as *ḍhakkana*).
Su. pṛ. 633 | Formative impression (saṃskāra): Recollection occurs only with respect to an object that has been experienced, not with respect to one that has not been experienced.

In this regard, if experience were not to produce some excellence (*atiśaya*) within itself, then, because there would be no distinction between what has been experienced and what has not, memory would arise with respect to both.
Yet it does not arise with respect to both.
Therefore, this restriction—that memory arises only in certain cases—leads us to postulate a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by that experience.
If that [cognition] were also momentary as it is being experienced, then recollection at a later time would not be possible.
Therefore, it is understood that there exists a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) which persists over a period of time. (Ṛjuvimalā, p. 114)
The *saṃskāra* (consecration) is also a subsidiary element.
That which, upon its occurrence, renders a thing fit for some purpose is called *saṃskāra*.
Since it also serves a purpose when an action is to be performed, it too is for the sake of another (*parārtha*).
Bhāṣya 3.1.3: This preparatory act, such as the equipment and so forth, is prompted by the animal sacrifice;
it is not prompted by the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Saṃskāra (consecration): it is prompted by a purpose.
Saṃkarṣa. 2.2.6.
Saṃskāra refers to acts such as threshing, sprinkling, and so forth.
And that is a subsidiary (śeṣabhūta). [Cf. Ci.

3.1.3] *Saṃskāra* (preparation) refers to threshing and so forth. Since rice and other grains, which are enjoined for the production of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and the like, are not fit in their raw state, whereas they become fit once threshed, the act of threshing serves as a *saṃskāra* by bringing about the fitness of the threshed grains.

Or [it is so] because, in the context of consecration (*saṃskāra*), it is not a word denoting the ritual action itself. Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard in the scripture: "One should immolate a ewe," and "One offers four handfuls."
The *ipā* is a certain component of the *śakti* (in the vernacular, it is called *purāṅkhya*). The touching or grasping of the *ipā* is the *ālabhana*.
At the time of the offering,

it is heard in a general injunction (anārabhya): "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," and "One desiring spiritual luster should offer an oblation of cooked rice (caru) to Sūrya."

And thus [it is asked]: regarding this, is it that in the sentence concerning Vāyu, the *ālambha* (seizing) belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is restated (*anūdya*) and the quality of whiteness is prescribed for the *īpā* (the animal), and likewise in the sentence concerning Sūrya, the *nirvāpa* (offering) belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices is restated and the quality of being cooked in four vessels (*caturguṇa*) is prescribed; or rather, are two distinct rituals (*karmāntara*) prescribed—namely, a seizing and an offering characterized by the qualities of whiteness and cooked rice, and having Vāyu and Sūrya as deities, with results consisting of prosperity (*bhūti*) and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and possessing the entire procedure (*itikartavyatā*) as far as stated; or finally, are two sacrifices (*yāga*) prescribed as qualified by the aforementioned qualities and results? Such is the threefold inquiry. Among these, the first position is as follows:
In this sūtra, the second position (*pakṣa*) will be stated in the sūtra "yāvaduktaṃ" (13), and the third position in the sūtra "yajati tu" (14) as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Furthermore, the word "ca" (and) in the present sūtra serves to exclude the restrictive application (*vyavasthā*) of the Dākṣāyaṇayajña and others mentioned in the preceding section.

When a sentence concerning Vāyu is heard outside of a specific context (*aprakaraṇe*), having begun a particular context for something else, the touching (*ālabha*)—which is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the pole (*īpā*)—and the pouring out (*nirvāpa*)—which is a refinement of the rice (*vrīhi*)—are restated (*anūdyate*) in order to enjoin qualities characterized by whiteness and cooked rice (*caru*) respectively, according to their sequence.
Because they lack words denoting an action, in the two sentences concerning Vāyu, there is no mention of the actions of "sacrificing" (*ālambha*) and "offering" (*nirvāpa*).
Since there is an absence of words denoting the actions of unprecedented sacrificing and offering,
it is more appropriate to regard them as mere restatements (*anuvāda*), rather than as injunctions of specific qualities (*guṇavidhi*) that would require a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).

Therefore, by way of restating the touching (*ālambhana*) and pouring out (*nirvāpa*) belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapaurṇamāsika*), there is an injunction of the qualities consisting of the white color and the *caru* (rice-porridge).
This is the first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Regarding this, the Vārttika states: "Just as in the case of the *ayana* sacrifices, where in a sentence intent upon connecting a quality there is no word enjoining a ritual action, and thus it is not a separate rite, so it shall be here as well"—this is what is indicated by the word "and" (*ca*).

And what is this injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*)? The term "outside of a context" (*aprakaraṇa*) is used for the purpose of determining its scope. (The *Sudhā* commentary explains otherwise to dispel the doubt: "Since these are studied as unattached (*anārabhyadhīta*), how can the scriptural mentions of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) and touching (*ālambha*) be for the sake of a quality, given their difference from the *ayana* sacrifices?"—thus it interprets the word *aprakaraṇa*. Alternatively, even if they are heard outside of a context by virtue of this distinction from the previous case, nevertheless, because they are not subsumed under an injunctive word for a ritual action, the repeated scriptural mention is indeed for the sake of a quality.
[Sudhā:

The word "enjoyer" (*bhoktṛ*) is used to indicate that the nature of a deity—which consists in being the recipient of the oblation through the exclusion of others, and which is characterized by being the enjoyer of the oblation—is what brings about the inference of the sacrifice.
Thus [it is said].

The established conclusion (siddhānta) is stated by this Sūtra because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). Regarding the injunctions "One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu" and "One should offer a caru-oblation to Sūrya," a sacrifice is enjoined through the verbs *ālabheta* ("should sacrifice") and *nirvapet* ("should offer") by means of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). In this context, there is the indicative mark found in the sentence "One should cause the sacrifice to be performed in an enclosed space," which follows the introductory statement "One should offer a caru-oblation to Soma-Rudra. Since this sentence is intended to enjoin the enclosure (*pariśrayaṇa*) for the Soma-Rudra caru, the mention of the sacrifice (*yāga-anuvāda*) therein serves as the indicative mark.
In the section concerning the *saṃskāra* (purificatory rites),

in the second [adhikaraṇa], regarding the passages "One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu" and "He offers four handfuls," the white color and the fourfold quantity are determined here as belonging to the animal and the offering, because that which comes from the *īśā* tree is [the sacrificial post], and the tree is connected with Vāyu.

Regarding the term *carum*, [the opponent argues] that because it refers to the vessel (*sthālī*) for the *caru* offering, it can somehow be taken as a restatement (*anuvāda*) due to its proximity; this constitutes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). In response, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) states that since the acts of touching (*ālambhana*) and offering (*nirvapaṇa*) exist even in common worldly practice, there is no necessary restriction to those acts belonging specifically to the *Dārśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. Anticipating the objection that this fault does not apply because of the qualification "those two acts of touching and offering which are enjoined by the indicative mark (*liṅga*"), he replies: such an indicative mark cannot be obtained as a restatement because it functions as an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*); furthermore, if both were accepted simultaneously, there would be a contradiction between injunction and restatement. Thus he answers.
*Saṃskāra* is the sacrifice of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for the deity of the animal sacrifice.
This is the *paśupuroḍāśanyāya* (see *Mīmāṃsākōśa*, p. 2518).
Consecration (saṃskāra) is appropriate for that which has become a subordinate element (śeṣa), and not otherwise. Bhāṣya 4.4.8.12. Consecration possesses an object (saviṣayaka).

Otherwise, if an experience regarding a cloth were the cause of its recollection through its relation to the latent impression (saṃskāra) produced by itself, it would follow that a recollection having "cloth" as its qualificandum could arise from an experience having "pot-ness" as its qualifier.
Therefore, because a latent impression possessing the same qualifier and the same qualificandum is the cause of such a recollection, there is no such undesirable consequence.
(Maṇi, p. 13)
The *saṃskāra* (consecration), namely the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice, is not a separate ritual action from the principal oblations (*pradhānahavis*).
Bhāṣya 2.3.13.16: For that which produces a capacity for its own effect is indeed called a *saṃskāra*.

*Bṛhatī*, page 207: Regarding the touching (*ālambha*) of the calf after the *agnihotra* has been extinguished, [the author states] that the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are for the sake of the purpose [of the sacrifice], because the time is determined by the purpose.

In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, there is a discussion as to whether the purificatory rites such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) intended for the animal sacrifice should be performed separately according to each distinct occasion (*pratipanna-bheda*) or collectively (*tantra*). [The author] here states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The consecrations of the sacrificial post, such as sprinkling and so forth, are to be repeated;
because they occur at the time of the purpose. The "purpose" is the tethering of the animal; these consecrations are performed at that time.
And thus, because of the difference in the time of binding for the three animals, there must be a repetition of the purificatory rites for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to show the distinction from the sacrificial post itself: the post is not repeated, but the purificatory rites are to be repeated.

However, those [rites] belong to that specific time because they constitute the ritual action of the post; because its properties are prescribed [for that time]; and because of the scriptural statement, all paths have a different time.
He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The word "but" (*tu*) excludes the view that the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are for the purpose of joining [the sacrificial post].

Purificatory rites such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth should belong to that time; "belonging to that time" (*tatkālāḥ*) means those whose time is the same as the time of that sacrificial post (*yūpa*), namely, the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*).

And likewise, the times for initiation and the consecrations of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) are [included]. Because they constitute the ritual action regarding the post, it is said "it is performed"; thus, "action" (*karman*) refers to that which is to be done.
Those consecrations for which the sacrificial post is the object of the action are "the consecrations of the sacrificial post" (*yūpakarma-saṃskārāḥ*).
