Because they belong to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), they share its time: that is, they have the same time as the post—the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Alternatively, "having that time" (*tatkālāḥ*) means those consecrations (*saṃskāra*) whose time is precisely the time of that *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice]; thus, all of them proceed by way of a single performance (*tantra*).

Because their ritual properties (*dharma*) are prescribed for that post—because the properties are enjoined, because they are enjoined as being the properties of the post—they do not possess the properties of the tethering (*niyojana*).
Therefore, the consecration times (*dīkṣākāla*) are the times for the preparations of the sacrificial post (*yūpasaṃskāra*).

From whatever time belongs to all purposes—that is, to all matters—even if they were to occur at other times, that would be so by virtue of a specific scriptural statement (*vacana*), through the force of that statement. However, in the absence of such a statement, it is logical that they should occur at the same time as the whole.
And it shows that the measurement is performed only once.
If it is argued that this is for the sake of immediate succession (*ānantarya*),
the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says:
If it is argued that simultaneity is not established by the sequence of the *parivyāṇa* (encircling),

and that the sequence of the *parivyāṇa* exists for the purpose of ensuring immediate succession between the *parivyāṇa* and the *upākaraṇa* (dedication) such that the *upākaraṇa* would follow immediately after the *parivyāṇa*.
It is not so, because it is established by its very nature.
One need not establish a sequential order for immediate succession,
since such immediacy is already established by its very nature.

In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma as well, the dedication (*upākaraṇa*) occurs immediately after the sprinkling (*pariṣyāṇa*). That [dedication] is already obtained by extension (*codaka*) for the *savanīya* sacrifice;
therefore, the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) also constitute a single performance (*tantra*).
But as for the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), they would be restricted according to each Veda, like the ritual acts themselves, based on the capacity of the person.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the purificatory rites such as shaving and so forth—expressed as "he shaves his hair and beard, he cleans his teeth, he cuts his nails, he bathes"—are prescribed with the capacity of the person as the occasion, for the purpose of enabling the performer, the person, to achieve fitness for the ritual act.
These would be restricted according to each Veda, following the injunctive statements, by means of their respective designations (*samākhyā*).

Just as with ritual actions (*karmavat*): those rituals which are prescribed in a particular Veda are performed by a person associated with that very same Veda—such as the *ādhvaryava* rites by the *adhvaryu* priest and the *hautra* rites by the *hotṛ* priest, and so forth.
The term "just as with ritual actions" (*karmavat*) is derived from the nominative case.
The word "but" (*tu*) serves to indicate a distinction from the inquiry raised in the preceding section.

In this case, for the *sudhā*-offerings made by the performers, since they must produce the capacity to bring about the *apūrva*—just like the *sugā* and other offerings—there is a requirement for a consecratory rite (*saṃskāra*) in order to generate that capacity.

However, the rites performed by the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) are governed by the principle "like the ritual act," because he is the primary agent. This is the sūtra of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the prima facie view.
The term "saṃskāraḥ" (purificatory rite) is understood to carry over [from the previous sūtra].

Purificatory rites such as shaving and so forth, in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, should be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*)—that is, they have the sacrificer as their agent—and not by the officiating priest (*adhvaryu*).

Because that is primary—that is, because the fruit of the action is primarily for the sacrificer—and because among the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), the sacrificer alone is primary since the fruit goes to him;
it is like the ritual acts (*karman*): just as the acts involving the relinquishment of substances, which constitute the primary elements, have the sacrificer as their agent, so it is here.
Alternatively, "action" (*karman*) means the fruit of the action—what is accomplished.

Just as the fruit belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), so too do the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) intended for that fruit belong to the sacrificer. Regarding this, the *Sudhā* commentary states: "Since the purpose of the purificatory rites is to generate the capacity to receive the fruit, and since it is the sacrificer alone who requires the generation of that capacity, their purpose is determined by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the fact that they fall to the share of the one who enjoys the fruit; therefore, it is not possible to suspect that the name (*samākhyā*) indicates that these rites belong to the *adhvaryu*."
And because of the designation [of the agent].

This sūtra provides another reason for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as shaving and the like belong to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and not to the Adhvaryu priest.

Because in the cases of "he anoints him" (*tam yajñam anakti*) and "he anoints with a reed-shaft" (*śareṣīkayā anakti*), the act of anointing and smearing belongs to the sacrificer while the Adhvaryu is the agent, as indicated by the use of the *parasmaipada* (active voice); whereas in the cases of "he shaves" (*vapate*) and "he cleanses his teeth" (*dato dhāvate*), the use of the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) indicates that the purificatory rites such as shaving and the like belong to the sacrificer.
The word *ca* (and) has the sense of collecting other reasons (*hetvantara-samuccaya*).

Here, because *sudhā-dhāvana* (plastering with lime), *atitapana* (exposure to heat), and *kuntīnām* (of the *kuntī* plants) are *svarita*-accented, and because the results of the actions of tooth-cleaning and so forth are intended for the agent (*kartṛ-abhiprāya*), the *ātmanepada* [suffix] is used. Furthermore, since it is well known even from common worldly usage that tooth-cleaning is performed by oneself, and likewise that bathing is also performed by oneself; and since it is well known as a rule that shaving and clipping the nails are performed by a barber—[these are included] among the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the sake of purification.

It is understood from the *Saṃkarṣa* (3.2.9) that the persistence of these [substances] lasts only as long as their purpose exists—just as it is understood from the text: "With the *śākhā* at the midday libation (*mādhyandina-savana*), and with the *saugandhika* at the third libation (*tṛtīyasavana*)".
This is because purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are dependent upon their purpose.
And in the archetype (prakṛti), there is anointing with butter during initiation;
here, even such a connection with the modified rite (vaikṛta) must be inferred.
(Bṛhatī, p. 121).
In the discussion as to whether there is a combination (*samuccaya*) or a sublation (*bādha*) of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
In the *sādyaska* sacrifice, there is no performance of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the marking (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth;
however, regarding the purificatory rite of anointing (*abhyañjana*), there is a combination with the archetypal one in the *vālakhilya*.

It may be that, due to a connection with something else at another time for the sake of a specific purpose, there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the ritual properties such as carving and sprinkling in the case of the *khalevālī* (the threshing-floor post).
This is because of the connection.
In the initiation (*dīkṣā*), [the anointing] is with fresh butter; at the pressing (*savana*), it is with *guggulu* and so forth.
The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) should be examined.
There is no extension (*atideśa*) of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
"Butter is for the purpose of lubrication, and substances such as guggulu are for the purpose of drying; this is stated in the *Upaśaya* section of the eleventh book [of the *Bhāṣya*],
Therefore, the conclusion is that there is a combination [of both].
34. Mīko. p. 248: "There is no extension [of the rule] to the *upaśaya* [fire-wood], if it be argued that it is like the *prayāja*s."
Regarding the phrase "of the consecrations of the sacrificial post" (*yūpasaṃskārāṇām*), the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted.

As for the consecrations— such as smearing (*paryuhaṇa*), sprinkling (*secana*), strengthening, and anointing the axle (*akṣan*) and so forth— at the *Añjana* sacrifice within the *Satra*, these are performed with the substance used for anointing and rubbing at the three pressings (*savanatraya*).

Regarding the performance of the ordinary fresh butter (*navanīta*)—which is obtained through the force of the *codaka* (archetypal injunction)—in the case of the *sādyaska* sacrifice involving a threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*), the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) states that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) [of the two types of butter]. To this, the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) raises an objection: "In the case of the *khalevālī*, the purificatory rites such as *paryūhaṇa* (sprinkling around)... [Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, *Tantravārttika*, p. 1536].
Even at other times, the substance is intended solely for that purpose.
Regarding the statement "the performance [should follow] the time," the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) should be examined in the section concerning the purificatory rites (*saṃskārāṇām*).
[The opponent] thinks: "But the object remains the same;
for example, in the case of [the injunction] 'they stand while offering the animal sacrifice,' acts such as shaving and so forth belong to the sacrificer" (Bhāṣya 3.8.2).
Regarding the ritual acts (*saṃskārāṇām*):

thus, while the animal sacrifice remains, there is indeed the omission of the primary acts such as shaving (*vapanādi*) under the view that the bones (*asthiṣu*) possess the qualification for the rite. Therefore, there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the archetypal *prayāja* offerings by the *pāśuka-prayāja* offerings [Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 760 (4), under "asthiṣu"].
There is no combination [of the two].
Likewise, even in the case of the substances *aja* and *anādi*, there is no combination under the view that they are intended for different purposes (*muktādhikāritva-pakṣe*).
In this regard, the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted.
Thus,
[the performance] of purificatory rites (saṃskāra), such as husking and so forth, upon a single substance like rice and the like,
is not for the sake of the purpose [of the final result], because that purpose is constant.

The state of having a single action (*ekakarmatva*) was explained [in the commentary on *sūtra* 4.2.6], namely that there is a single completion (*nirvṛtti*) until the rice is finished; this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) reached by the opponent through the *sūtra*: "If it is argued that it is like the *prayāja*s" (*bhāṣya* 11.4.14.2).
No;
he dispels the doubt:
it cannot be like the *prayāja* offerings.
For indeed, because they share the same substratum as the substance (*dravya*), all [subsidiary elements] possess primacy;
this is due to the distinctness of the purpose— that is, the difference in the objective—
and because even the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), though being subordinate members by virtue of their nature as *saṃskāras*, serve the primary purpose of providing moisture.
Fresh butter [is used] during the initiation for the sake of easy movement;
when the ritual activity has commenced at the Soma-pressing, its status as a substance is established.
Vārttika 3.1.4.7, [concerning] the sacrificer—

The anointing with guggulu and other substances is for the purpose of drying [the body]. Thus, it is evident that there exists a distinct function for the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) in the form of the acquisition of the fruit, which exceeds their status as mere subordinate qualities (*guṇa*) of the sacrifice; therefore, there is no sublation of the original butter (*navanīta*).
Because it is performed by qualified persons, the sacrifice is also applicable to those who have fallen under a curse regarding their status as enjoyers;
this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
This will be explained [in Sūtra 3.7.2].
Regarding the rule *saṃskāre cānyasaṃyogāt* (10|4|6):
"Just as a girl who has bathed but is not yet adorned is [adorned] with a garland, ornaments, and so forth..."

10–12) In this context, regarding "anointing with *guggulu* in the morning," it is stated that one is "refined" (*saṃskṛta*) by even a single part of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). Thus, the anointing with *guggulu* prescribed for the *savana* is described as a hyperbolic praise (*ati-stuti*).

Bhāṣya 7.3.13.34: It is stated that there is a conjunction with the application of fresh butter (*navanītābhyañjana*) by means of one [act]. Even when the consecration (*saṃskāra*) has been performed by one part, the second [part] is also [required] on the authority of the scriptural statement.
p. 178. It may be so. *Oṃ*. And because that is predominant in the case of the consecration (*saṃskāra*); and because of the connection with another [element] in the case of the consecration.

In the forty-nine-night sacrificial session (*sattra*) named *Ajanābhyañjana*, there is the injunction: "They anoint [the sacrificer] with *gavīdhuka* grain at the morning pressing, or they anoint him with *pailudāru* wood.

This is an extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual procedure (*adhikaraṇa*) from the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), where it is said: "They anoint [the sacrificer] with rice flour at the morning pressing, or they anoint him with *pailudāru* wood."
It is heard in scripture: "He threshes the rice" and "He grinds the rice.
Here, the prima facie view is that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of threshing and grinding, since these are already established by worldly practice.
And because it does not conflict with common practice;
this is the position. Just as with threshing, even in the case of splitting, grinding, and so forth, [the rule] follows worldly usage according to the occasion.

In the *saumika-cāturmāsya* sacrifices, regarding the injunction "they place the *vājina* on the *utkara*," the scriptural mention of threshing (*avahanana*) serves to restrict what is already established;
it is like the case of grinding (*peṣaṇa*). Similarly, it is heard in scripture: "They bind the animal to the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*)."
This laying down [of the animal] is also obtained from worldly practice even for the purpose of slaughtering; therefore, the scriptural injunction is for the sake of restriction (*niyama*).
Furthermore, the tying (*niyojana*) is enjoined as a distinct ritual act that is merely a religious duty (*dharma*).
Consequently, this is not an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*), but rather a restrictive injunction (*niyama-vidhi*); such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

This being the case, because there is no obstruction of the archetype (*prakṛti*), [the rule applies] to both the archetype and its derivative (*prākṛta*). As for the meaning of the words of the Sūtra: the word "and" (*ca*) is intended to indicate extension (*atideśa*).

"Obstruction" (*uparodha*) means obstruction of the archetype; it does not mean non-obstruction of the archetype. Regarding the ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*) consisting of threshing and so forth, the Vedic text (*śruti*) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārthā*). That is the primary [point].
Therefore,

because of the statements "He places the sacrificial oblations" and "They bind the animal to the sacrificial post," and because the restrictive rule regarding threshing and so forth is subordinate to the sacrifice,
there is no contradiction with this archetypal [injunction].
Therefore, there is curiosity regarding the subject at hand:
that a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is possible for a substance,
because acts such as placing [the vessel] are accepted as being distinct actions.
Thus ends the *Subodhinī* on the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
That [scriptural] statement in which that restriction is the primary factor is the *śruti*.
Another reason has been stated.
That [action] is primary because the scriptural injunction regarding the preparation (*saṃskāra*) has the restriction of that preparation as its primary purpose.

Since the injunction exists there, the word is the object of doubt; for when something is already established in one alternative by worldly practice, the scriptural mention of threshing and so forth has the purpose of establishing a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
It may be so.
It is clearly perceived. By whom?

In the Saumika Cāturmāsya sacrifices, it is stated: "They place the whey (*vājina*) on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*)," and "And [the act] is for the sake of refinement, because that is the primary purpose" (4.2.11.26).
It is also heard in scripture: "They bind the animal to the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*).
Here, since acts such as threshing and so forth are already established as having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), they are not objects of injunction.

Having raised the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument that "slaughtering and tying are merely ritual acts (dharmamātra) and constitute separate functions," [the author] states the established conclusion (siddhānta): it is an injunction for the sake of restriction (niyamārtha), like the [injunction regarding] place and so forth. He sets aside the objection by means of the word "su" (well/properly) and says:
"It will be stated that this pertains to the original (prākṛta) injunction."
Su. Pṛ. 539:
And because the injunction for the offering and the binding of the modified [animal] pertains to that very context of the Cāturmāsya refinements as its primary focus;

since there is doubt due to contradiction arising from the presence [of these acts] within the ritual section (prakaraṇa), the word of which refers to the offering of the entrails (*guda*) as a disposal (*pratipatti*) among the animals of the Ekādaśinī set.
Whatever purpose for which an injunctive word exists, that shall be its meaning; such is the nature of that purificatory act (*saṃskāra*).
In that case, regarding the *upayāja* oblation, which is a purificatory act, the word whose primary focus is that [act] must have that very thing as its meaning.
And thus, because the *upayāja* oblation serves as the placement of the horse-flesh (*vājina*) and because it is primarily a consecration of the substance already employed,
there is an injunction of the quality in the form of the *utkara* with reference to that [oblation].
In this way, there would be a combination (*samuccaya*) of the original (*prākṛta*) rectum portions, not an option (*vikalpa*).
This is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
Some maintain that, with reference to the tethering of the animal, there is an injunction for an accessory in the form of the enclosing-stick (paridhi); this is how it should be understood.
Therefore, in this case, because the acts of placing and joining are primary with respect to the natural [intestines], as stated in *Sūtra* 1.2.14.8,
the conclusion is that the injunction of qualities regarding the *utkara* and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) serves only a visible purpose.
Here, what is heard in the text— "he performs the *upayaj* with the tail"— is a disposal (*pratipatti*) in the case of a group of animals.
Due to the efficacy of the *saṃskāra* and because of the connection with the qualities (*guṇa*), the conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the *guda* [mantras] has been stated. Bāla. pṛ. 178.

In the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices belonging to the Soma rituals, it is said: "They place the whey (*vājina*) on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*). However, this refers to a distinct ritual act because it prescribes a specific preparation.
Furthermore, it is heard in scripture: "They tie the animal to the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*).
[This is discussed in Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 10.2.13–18.]

In the Saumika-Cāturmāsya sacrifices, where the *utkara* (mound of earth) and the *paridhi* (enclosing sticks) take the place of the ordinary *āsādana* (placing) and *niyojana* (tying), it is stated in the Siddhānta that the injunction "they place the *vājina* on the *utkara*" is a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*) for the purpose of fixing [the substance]. But is it not heard in scripture that "they tie the animal to the *paridhi*"? [And thus, how can the *utkara* be a substitute for the *paridhi*?]
This is the placement [of the horse].

There is a heap of clay for the purpose of inspection; therein, the placement of the horse and the tethering are merely ritual acts (dharmamātra), not a separate action for the sake of the sacrifice—this is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
He says that it would be possible [to perform them] in this way, because they serve to prevent the animal from wandering away, even though it is not tied with a rope.

Since the *āsādana* (placing down) must be performed upon the sacrificial post (*upaśayana*) once the consecration of the horse-sacrifice animal has been completed, it would be impossible to carry out [the original procedure]. Therefore, this injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*)—being impossible to apply—would constitute a different action from the original *āsādana* and so forth.
Thus [it is argued].
To this it is replied: because of the connection with a quality, due to the capacity of the ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*), and because that aforementioned sentence possesses injunctive force,
an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is possible.
When there is a conjunction with such a quality,
it is possible to perform the placing on the heap and the binding to the enclosing-stick as a consecration.
We shall prepare the mound (utkara) and the enclosing sticks (paridhi), which possess such qualities as to awaken the latent impressions (saṃskāra).
We shall prepare the mound with its tip pointing toward the earth.
And we shall make the enclosing-stick (paridhi) thick.
Due to its connection with such a quality, the capacity for the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) consisting of placing and binding will belong to both the mound (utkara) and the enclosing-stick.
Therefore, this is not a separate ritual action, but rather merely an injunction regarding a quality.
"Because of contradiction, the action should belong to the context.
Regarding the Soma-related Cāturmāsya sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "They place the whey on the rubbish heap (utkara)" and "They bind the animal to the enclosing stick (paridhi).

Here, the established conclusion (siddhānta) stated is that the meaning is an injunction of accessory details—namely the form of the rubbish heap and the enclosing stick—with respect to the very same acts of placing and binding that already exist in the archetypal ritual (prakṛti).

If it is argued that, just as in the section on the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice it is said, "He places [the cups of] *surā* upon the head of the Brāhmaṇa," and thus there is merely the placing of the ritual substance (*dharma-mātra*), so too should it be here—[the author] replies: No, because in that context, namely the section on the *Caraka-sautrāmaṇī*, there is a contradiction; for it is impossible to place the vessel of *surā* upon the head of the Brāhmaṇa until the point of its offering (*homaparyanta*). Therefore, the action would be a mere ritual act (*dharmamātra*) performed for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
In the present case, however, it is not possible [to assume a new action];
therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that this is indeed an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi).
Regarding the mention of a fruit in connection with a preparatory rite (saṃskāra), there is the text: "When he recites, having placed [the fire] four times, he recites the Bṛhatī."
This is the declaration of the fruit [of the ritual], which is as follows:
"In the case of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), that which is enjoined for those [rites] should be prompted by them, because it is for their sake.

Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard in scripture: "One threshes with the two mortars and pestles that have been sprinkled," and "One grinds with the two millstones that have been sprinkled."

In this regard, when considering whether the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is prompted by the acts of threshing, grinding, and so forth, or rather prompted by the transcendental result (*apūrva*), the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Regarding the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*), the properties such as sprinkling that are employed in threshing, grinding, and the like, would be "prompted by those"—
meaning prompted by the preparatory rites— because they serve that purpose, namely, because they are for the sake of the preparatory rites of threshing and so forth.

If that for whose sake something is to be performed is its *prayojaka* (instigator), then, consequently, acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) are instigated by acts such as slaughtering (*hanti*) and grinding (*piṣati*). Alternatively:

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard in scripture: "One should recite for the Dīkṣaṇīyā with as much voice as one desires; softly for the Prāyaṇīyā; more softly for the Ātithyā; and in a whisper for the seven [Sāmidhenīs].

Regarding this, in the inquiry as to whether these are prompted by the *paramāpūrva* (the ultimate transcendental result) or prompted by the *dīkṣaṇīyāpūrva* (the intermediate transcendental result), the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Since they are connected to a refinement (*saṃskāra*)—namely, because the duties connected to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are for that purpose, meaning they serve the purpose of the *paramāpūrva*, they must be prompted by that, i.e., prompted by the *paramāpūrva* alone.
For the supreme *apūrva* possesses a fruit, whereas the *apūrva* of the injunction does not;
this is the second interpretation (*varṇaka*).

Because of the connection of the sacrifice with that purpose, there is a relationship with the *dharma*; therefore, it should be prompted by the sacrifice, since the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) exists for the sake of that [sacrifice].
The word "tu" (but) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
As for what was stated—that the acts of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth are prompted by the acts of threshing (*avaghāta*), pounding (*peṣaṇa*), and so on—that is not correct.

Because that threshing and so forth are connected with the *apūrva* of the sacrifice, and because threshing belongs to the context (*prakaraṇa*) as being for the sake of the *apūrva*, the connection with the ritual property (*dharma*) belongs to the threshing by virtue of its being a means to the *apūrva*. Thus, there is a connection between the act of sprinkling and the property [of threshing] through the medium of the *apūrva*.

Therefore, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) performed upon the fingernails during the *nakhanirmit-caru* sacrifice would be prompted by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), because a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) such as sprinkling is for the sake of that [result], namely, for the sake of the *apūrva*. Consequently, the conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that a purification of substances and so forth is not prompted by acts such as threshing (*avahanana*), but is indeed prompted solely by the *apūrva*.
Thus ends the first section. Alternatively:

"One should recite at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* with as much voice as one desires; softly (*mandra*) at the *prāyaṇīyā*; more softly (*mandratara*) at the *ātithyā*; and in a whisper (*upāṃśu*) during the seven [offerings]. This refers to the specific modulation of the voice (*svara-viśeṣa*) in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and subsequent rites.

Regarding the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), it is heard in scripture: "The *upaśaya* becomes a sacrificial post. Eleven sacrificial posts are to be erected.
This twelfth [post] is called the *upaśaya*. It is not erected; rather, it is called *upaśaya* because it lies (*śete*) near (*upa*), that is, close by to the south.

Regarding the discussion of whether this *upaśaya* material should be consecrated with rites such as *joṣaṇā* (approval) and so forth, or indeed remain unconsecrated, the author states the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) view.
The substance for the *upaśaya* should be consecrated by means of consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the cutting of the *jīva* (the living part) and so forth.

The Sanskrit [text], 4048, states that one should recite in the Sanskrit language with devotion, either because it is not a remnant of a sacrifice (*ayajñaśeṣa*) or because it denotes qualities (*guṇābhidhāna*).
Regarding the set of eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), it is heard in scripture: "The *upaśaya* becomes a sacrificial post."

To the south of the sacrificial posts (*yūpas*) lies on the ground that which is called the *upaśaya*, the twelfth post. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), obtained through the Sūtra, is that this [post] should be consecrated (*saṃskṛta*). Rejecting this with the word "or" (*vā*), the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by implication: it is unconsecrated. Although the word *yūpa* is used for the *upaśaya* as denoting a consecrated object, nevertheless this word *yūpa* is used figuratively (*bhaktyā*) for the purpose of praise.
Because this [animal] is not a remnant of the sacrifice;
for no animal is bound to this [post], therefore this is not a remnant of the sacrifice.
How then is the word "yūpa" (sacrificial post) used there? He says:
Because it is the designation of qualities (*guṇa*).
"Designation" (*abhidhāna*) means that which designates (*abhidhatte*).
This word *yūpa* is the designator of only certain preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as cutting and so forth.
Because it denotes qualities, the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) is transferred [to this object].
However, since it is not a remnant of the sacrifice (*ayajñaśeṣatvāt*), this is a "post" only figuratively.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that, like other sacrificial posts, this one is not consecrated by the mantra.

Regarding the question of whether ritual acts (*karmāṇi*) are to be performed upon fires consecrated merely by the *ādhāna* rite, because the *saṃskāras* (consecrations) are for that purpose; or whether they are to be performed upon fires consecrated by the *pavamāneṣṭis*— in this deliberation, the conclusion is that the ritual acts, such as the *agnihotra* and others which are obligatory, as well as the *aindrāgna* and others which are non-obligatory, are to be performed upon fires consecrated merely by the *ādhāna*.

Just as the vows of one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), such as "one who has established the fires should not place wet wood [on the fire]," belong only to that very person who has established the fires, so it is in this case.

Having thus presented the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) which deviates from the Sūtra, he states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "In consecrated fires—that is, in fires consecrated by the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices—the rituals, such as the *agnihotra* and those dedicated to Indra-Agni (*aindrāgna*), proceed."
Why? Because the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as the Pavamāna-iṣṭis and others, exist for that purpose—that is, for another purpose, namely for the sake of the ritual acts (*karman*).

Ritual acts take place once the Āhavanīya and other fires have been established; and the establishment of the Āhavanīya and other fires occurs through the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) and the Pavamāna-iṣṭis.
Therefore, the ritual acts are performed in fires consecrated by the Pavamāna-iṣṭis.
The vow follows immediately because it has become that [state].
Having performed the Pavamāna-iṣṭis at the establishment of the fires (ādhāna), one should perform the Agnihotra and other rites.

"One who has established the fires (āhitāgni) should not place wet wood [into the fire]"—wet meaning moist; "wood" means fuel-sticks; "one who has established the fires" should not [place] wet [wood] into the fire.

However, regarding the passage ending with "he should place," one should accept [the performance] immediately thereafter—that is, even prior to the Pavamāna offerings—following the very establishment of the fires (ādhāna).

This is because the sacrificer becomes that [state] only when the fires have been established, having been perfected as an *āhitāgni*. Furthermore, this is supported by the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the preceding [text].

When it has been stated as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that rites such as the *agnihotra* are to be performed in fires consecrated by the *pavamāneṣṭis*, but not prior to those *pavamāneṣṭis*, the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The word "and" (*ca*) serves the purpose of providing an illustration:
just as the rites would occur after the *pavamāneṣṭis*, they might also occur before the *pavamāneṣṭis*.
"Indeed, they run after Agni with the Agnihotra when he has been well-established"—this indicates that the Agnihotra is to be performed as soon as the fires have been installed.

Because this indicative mark (*liṅga*) is observed, the rites should take place prior to the Pavamāna-iṣṭis. Or rather, it is a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), since the matter [of the Agnihotra] already exists [as a requirement].

Immediately after the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires), or after one year, or after twelve days, the *pavamāneṣṭis*—which constitute an integral part of the *ādhāna*—must be performed.
During the intervening period, the *agnihotra* and other rites must be performed in the form of silent oblations (*tūṣṇīṃhoma*).

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), however, maintains that even prior to the *pavamāneṣṭis*, the primary *agnihotra* oblation as well as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices must be performed.
And he cites "prior to the iṣṭis" as the authority for that [position].
This sūtra belongs to the Siddhānta (concluding) side for the purpose of refuting that.
The word "vā" (or/but) is for the purpose of refuting the doubt.
However, since there exists a purpose consisting of a *tūṣṇīṃ-homa* (silent oblation), the statement "prior to the *iṣṭis*" must be understood as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
Therefore, the primary rites such as the *agnihotra* and others should be performed only after the *pavamāna-iṣṭis*.
This is also because [otherwise] there would be a contradiction with logical reasoning.

If the Agnihotra and other rites, as well as the Aindrāgna and other sacrifices, were to be performed in the fires consecrated by the mere act of establishment (*ādhāna*) prior to the Pavamāna offerings, then there would be a contradiction or conflict based on the principle stated in the sūtra: "Or rather not, because those [offerings] are for that purpose" (3.6.14.12). Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the rites must be performed in the fires consecrated by the Pavamāna offerings. [End of section] Ke. Saṃskṛtavāca.

In the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is maintained that the subsidiary rites (*śeṣakāryāṇi*) must be performed from only a single oblation (*havis*). This concludes the section.

Just as in the case of the husks (*tuṣa*), the *upavāka*, and the *kapāla*, although the remnant (*śeṣa*) is obtained for another purpose, it is intended here as something to be taken up (*upādeya*) with respect to the subsidiary rites; thus, the singular number is significant, and the term "prepared" (*saṃskṛta*) is used because the [remnant] has been consecrated. 4049. [The rites] are completed.
Since the primary sacrifice has already been assisted by the remaining rites performed with the entire [animal], no further rites need be performed from the other remnants.
Such is the meaning of the Sūtra according to the Bhāṣya.

Alternatively, because the remnant has already been consecrated by the *paryagnikaraṇa* and other such rites, and because the subsequent rites for the remnant are themselves consecratory (*saṃskāra*) in nature, it is illogical for all the rites to be performed from all [the parts] for the sake of perfecting the quality of the whole; thus is the explanation of the Sūtra provided by the author of the Vārttika through the connection of the remaining words of the preceding Sūtra.

This explanation is offered by way of refuting the objection that "even for the *śeṣa* (the remainder), this consecration is not contradictory, as it serves to purify the substance for the purpose of the *pratipatti* (disposal), since it is already purified by the purification of the primary means (*pūrvasādhana-yogyatā-jñāna*). [The response is: because it would result in the uselessness of purifying a substance whose purpose has already been fulfilled, and because the opportunity for such purification has already passed. (One may also explain it as "because the opportunity for purification has elapsed";
the meaning of this is: "because there is no purpose in purifying a substance whose function has already been accomplished.")

1063). For *saṃsthā* is either indifference toward an action, or the performance of another activity after the completion of a previous task.

Or [as stated] on page 1063, line 42 of volume 3:
"The forms (saṃsthās) are four: Agniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, and Atirātra.
As for the other three mentioned in the Smṛti, such as the Agniṣṭoma, Vājapeya, and Atyagniṣṭoma, they are included within these very [four]."

Bhāṭṭa: In the section [sūtra] 3.6.16, "And the terminuses (saṃsthās) have common injunctions because there is no distinction in context" (3.6.16.41), the context of the terminuses such as the Ukthya and others is refuted.
If this is so, it is true.

For in that case, because the *agniṣṭoma* configuration (*saṃsthā*) is obligatory (*nitya*), those duties (*dharma*) enjoined without distinction within its context are indeed grasped as being permanently prescribed. However, because the *ukthya* and other configurations are optional (*kāmya*) and thus non-obligatory (*anitya*), their duties are not grasped; this will be stated [later] under the principle of "the conjunction of the obligatory and the non-obligatory" (*nityānitya-saṃyoga*).
"But the terminuses (saṃsthās) have the same injunction because there is no distinction in the context;
four terminuses of the Jyotiṣṭoma are traditionally taught."

The Agniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśī, and the Atirātra. Its ritual duties (dharmas), such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā and others, exist. Regarding these, there arises a doubt: do they belong to the Jyotiṣṭoma in all its forms (saṃsthās), or only to the Agniṣṭoma? This is the sūtra of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).

The word "tu" (but) serves to indicate the entire variety of results mentioned in the thirteenth section. The *agniṣṭoma* and other terminuses (*saṃsthā*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, as well as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, should be subject to the same injunction (*samānavidhāna*) because they are characterized by specific materials; they are not, however, subject to different injunctions (*asamānavidhāna*) like the *phalacamasa*.
Why? Because there is no difference in their context (*prakaraṇa*).

The term *prakaraṇaviśeṣa* means a distinction (*viśeṣa*) of the context (*prakaraṇa*). There is no such distinction of context; therefore, because there is an absence of a difference in context, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are prescribed for all four *saṃsthās* alike, and there is no relationship of archetype (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikṛti*) among them.
And the designation is equal.
The Jyotiṣṭoma has four terminuses (saṃsthās): the Agniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśī, and the Atirātra.
And the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites are the ritual duties (dharmas) therein.

And those *saṃsthās* have identical injunctions; there is no relationship of *prakṛti* (archetype) and *vikṛti* (modification) whatsoever. This sūtra serves to strengthen the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) position. The term "tulyavat" means "exactly equal";
the suffix *-vat* is used in its own sense, as in the rule "asiddhavadatrābhāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.22).

The designation—that is, the instruction of specific details within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma—is common to all its forms (saṃsthās). For example: "If it is an Agniṣṭoma, he anoints the middle enclosing-stick"; "If it is a Ṣoḍaśin, he touches the Droṇakalaśa vessel"; "If it is an Atirātra, he enters the Havirdhāna shed with the Yajus formula. This designation is logically consistent only if the ritual procedure is uniform across all forms.

Likewise, the following designation should also be understood: "In the Agniṣṭoma, one sacrifices a goat as the Savanīya Āgrayaṇa; in the Ukthya, a second, an Aindrāgna [bull]; in the Ṣoḍaśin, a third, an Aindra [bull]; and in the Atirātra, a fourth, a ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī.
Therefore, all the *saṃsthās* (concluding forms) are governed by the same injunction.
However, when there is a connection with a specific desire (*kāma*), they become modifications (*vikāra*) of the obligatory (*nitya*) rite.
There will be desire, and by that much alone there is no certainty of freedom from obstruction,
because of its very nature.
Therefore, the ritual requirements such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others belong to the archetype; they are prescribed for the four terminuses (*saṃsthā*) of the archetype,
the Jyotiṣṭoma— namely, the Agniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśin, and Atirātra— and thus they must pertain to the Agniṣṭoma alone, not to the modified forms (*vikṛti*).
For that [sacrifice], the *dīkṣā* and so forth,
as well as the *sphya* and other ritual duties (*dharmas*), are prescribed by means of the *codaka* (extended application).
And all those ritual forms [are to be performed] together, because of the scriptural statement.
When the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "they have the same injunction" has been reached, this is the sūtra of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*):

"The *agniṣṭoma*, the *ukthya*, the *ṣoḍaśī*, and the *atirātra*—these are the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifices. The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of setting aside the prima facie view. The *saṃsthās* (termini) do not have the same injunction.
The four *saṃsthās* (termini) of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice are governed by the same injunctions; however, the *ukthya* and others are optional modifications (*vikāra*) of the *agniṣṭoma*.

When there is a connection with a specific desire (*kāma*), one should, in the case of the *agniṣṭoma*, offer a goat dedicated to Agni, and a second [goat] dedicated to Indra-Agni for the *ukthya* and subsequent forms. Regarding the scriptural authority (*śruti*) of the *ukthya* and others...
The section on the *saṃsthā*:
since it arises for one who has completed [the sacrifice], there is a designation based on that completion (*saṃsthā*).

For although the Jyotiṣṭoma also possesses the quality of being the "grasper" (grāhaka) with respect to the *uktva* and other [stomas], nevertheless that [quality] is manifested [in the Agniṣṭoma] because its state of being characterized by the *uktva* and so forth serves as the means (*dvāra*) for this [Jyotiṣṭoma] to become the instrument for achieving its own fruit.
Furthermore, the Agniṣṭoma *saṃsthā* is its inherent limb (*nijamaṅga*).
Therefore, it is precisely when it is in that *saṃsthā* that it can be grasped and can be said to be the grasper.
Therefore, it has been correctly stated.

Furthermore, since the commonality of ritual properties (*dharmasādhāraṇya*) is indeed accepted in both positions through the methods of direct injunction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*), the term "prescription" (*vidhāna*) is employed. What is the conclusion? The prescription of ritual properties for the *saṃsthās* (concluding rites) is the same as that of the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Why? Because of the specific context (*prakaraṇa*).

For the Jyotiṣṭoma, because it possesses a fruit and is the primary subject, takes up those ritual details (*dharma*) that are mentioned in close proximity to its connection [with the sacrifice], not merely by virtue of being the Jyotiṣṭoma.
And in these very ritual details, everything—including the *ukthya* and so forth—is without distinction.
Since extension (atideśa) occurs only when direct instruction (upadeśa) is impossible,
it follows that direct instruction alone is common [to all].
And the designation is likewise equal.
Commentary: In this context, the designation is equal [for all].

It is understood from the specific statement regarding every state: "Whether it be a *jyotiṣṭoma* where one offers oblations, a *ukthya* where one anoints the enclosing sticks, or an *atirātra*, one should employ this very same sacrificial food (*havirjana*).
Even that which is general applies only to every state.
For if the procedure were not common to the Agniṣṭoma form, the Agniṣṭoma would not be mentioned here.

Even though it is not explicitly mentioned [in every instance], there is a connection with the ritual details (dharma); because it is mentioned in all its states, we understand that the context (prakaraṇa) pertains to the sacrifice in all its forms.
Moreover, it is heard in scripture: "One should offer an animal to Agni at the Agniṣṭoma; a second one to Indra-Agni at the Ukthya; a third, a bull, to Indra at the Ṣoḍaśin."
In the case of the second and third [sacrifices], they are joined with the same interruption.
For in the Ukthya, there are two causes: the state of being an Agniṣṭoma and the Ukthya-stotra.
Therein, there are two contingent rites: the animal sacrifice for Agni and that for Indra-Agni.
Therefore, a second observation is appropriate in that case;
likewise in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* and the *atirātra*.

However, when there is a relationship between the archetype (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*), the *āgneya* [offering], which is obtained through the general rule (*utsarga*), is set aside by the specific [texts] such as those concerning the *aindrāgna* and others that are directly perceived in the scripture.
In that case, the performance of the second and subsequent [sacrificial days] would not be possible;
yet it does occur.
Therefore, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are the characteristics (*dharmas*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma in all its stages.

Or rather—[the author] mentions the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the remnant of the clarified butter (*ājyaśeṣa*) as being connected to the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *saṃsthā* (ritual terminuses) such as the *vidvaddakṣiṇā*.
[He says]: "If it is an *agniṣṭoma*, he offers an oblation; with that very remnant he anoints the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
If it is an *atirātra*, this is the same oblation; reciting the mantra, 'Ask Yama about the mortal,' he should enter the *havirdhāna* shed."
Therefore, it is understood that the entire rule regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga-vidhi*) is common (*sādhāraṇa*).
What was stated [previously] is as improper as a mere general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*);

for if, by virtue of the syntactical connection (*vākya*), something intended for the performance of the primary acts is connected with the terminuses (*saṃsthā*), then how could it be proper for it to be connected even by a lack of such a connection?
For in cases such as "of the twelve-day sacrifice" (*dvādaśāhina*), there is no difference among the remaining properties (*śeṣadharma*) caused by the meat and so forth;
rather, he explains it thus because statements are limited to what is expressed.
For if that which is prescribed generally were to belong only to the *agniṣṭoma* form, then even by taking up [the term] "day," its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) would not be established.
One should not mention the Agniṣṭoma here.
For if one were to mention it, then certainly the unqualified Agniṣṭoma would not be obtained;
and that [unqualified Agniṣṭoma] would not be obtained if the context were common even to the sacrificial terminuses (saṃsthās).
However, if [the injunction] were situated within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* alone, then this repeated mention would not be purposeful.
Likewise, if there were a context for the *Ukthya* and other sacrifices as well, then the inclusion of the term "ten" (*daśa*) for the sake of determining one or the other would be appropriate.
But if they are not part of the primary context (*aprakṛta*), then—as in the case of the expression "of the twelve-day sacrifice" (*dvādaśāhasya*)—there would be a connection with the "ten" itself.
For it is not logical that this statement applies only to that which stands within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma—
namely, "If it is the Jyotiṣṭoma, then this [is the rule];
if it is the Dvādaśāha, then such-and-such."
For this very statement occurs in many Saṃhitās;
therefore, the context is the same.
There is also this further indicative mark: "One should sacrifice an animal to Agni at the Agniṣṭoma," "A second one to Indra-Agni at the Ukthya," and "A third, a bull to Indra, at the Ṣoḍaśin."

If there is a common rule (*samānavidhāna*), the observation of the preceding and preceding-most [rites] is justified. However, in the view that they are distinct, these [later rites] would everywhere sublate the *aindrāgna* and others based on direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣaśruti*). Now, even if there is direct scriptural statement, because other terminuses (*saṃsthā*) are possible, the preceding one does not apply due to the absence of its specific occasion (*nimitta*).
That which is completed at the Agniṣṭoma-stotra is the Agniṣṭoma-saṃsthā, and not that alone (the word *mātra* being used in the sense of totality).
Therefore, it should be understood that the Ukthya and other saṃsthās do not possess the status of the Agniṣṭoma-saṃsthā even though they include the Agniṣṭoma-stotra.
Furthermore, that which is completed in the Ukthya and subsequent saṃsthās is not completed in the preceding one.

Therefore, because it is observed a second time, perception is equal in both positions. It is true that they are equal if the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is the cause; however, if the hymn (*stotra*) is the cause, there is a combination (*samuccaya*).
And likewise,
the section concerning the sacrificial terminuses (saṃsthādhikaraṇa).
The author of the Bhāṣya says: "For there are two causes therein—the Agniṣṭoma-stotra and the Ukthya-stotra"—thus he states the established conclusion regarding that Vedic passage.

But how is it that, when the mention of the *agniṣṭoma* and so forth is equally common to both the *saṃsthās* (terminuses) and the *stotras*, only the *stotra* is accepted as the cause (*nimitta*) and not the *saṃsthā*?
For since those [terminuses] possess fruit and are thus purposeful, they are themselves understood to be the cause by virtue of their very designation.
Regarding this, some say:
even though there is a commonality of sound [between the two words], because the scripture has a vast scope and great significance, it is appropriate to rely on the basis for the praise.

Alternatively, since the *saṃsthā* (concluding rite) itself is qualified by the praise and is denoted by the word "thus" (*evaṃ*), it is not proper to assume that the cause for the secondary qualification is something other than the cause for the previously perceived primary qualification.

Alternatively, according to the principle of the *ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* (JS 1.3.9), the word is primary with respect to the hymns (*stotra*) and figurative with respect to the sacrificial terminus (*saṃsthā*). Since a direct denotation (*śruti*) is impossible, one must resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, the hymn itself can function as the occasion (*nimitta*) because of its mention in the locative case; and it is accepted that even the *niṣṭhā*-suffixes in words such as *medita* function as occasions by virtue of the force of the scriptural statement.
Alternatively, there is recourse to the *stotra* based on the principle "In cases where there is no doubt, [the decision is] from the remainder of the sentence" (1.4.23–24).
Or, even though the *saṃsthās* are primary, the *stotra* is accepted through the remainder of the sentence for the purpose of establishing conventional usage.
For it is thus heard in scripture: "One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni at the Agniṣṭoma," and "The Agniṣṭoma is dedicated to Agni."
In which *iṣṭi* is this [portion] found? It is in that which belongs to the *āgneyī*;

for this exists as a portion of praise (*stuti*) belonging to the hymn (*stotra*), and not to the ritual conclusion (*saṃsthā*), since the latter consists in the relinquishment of activity and is thus devoid of manifestation.
Furthermore, there is no function for a deity in the case of a non-existence (abhāva).
For even when a sacrifice is repeated, the deity that exists therein performs the *āgneya* [offering] at that very moment, not at the conclusion (*saṃsthā*).
And that [deity] itself is not the conclusion.
Because the preceding [verb] "tiṣṭhati" expresses indifference toward the time subsequent to that,
there is no designation of this [offering] by means of a deity belonging to another. Likewise, the Ukthya and Ṣoḍaśin [offerings] are also distinct from the Daśarātra.
Moreover, in the expression "the *ukthya* rites for Indra and Agni," the mention of the *stotra* (hymns) is explicit.

For the term *ukthyāni* does not denote the *saṃsthā* (ritual terminus); [this is because] the singular form *ukthya-saṃsthā* would contradict the plural number (*bahuvacana*), as the word implies the remainder [of the ritual context].
Therefore, since the *stotra* is the determining factor, their combination is appropriate.

But surely, even on the view that [the Atharva Veda] is a modification, the combination [of all four Vedas] is indeed possible, since for those who follow the *Atharvatantra*, the purpose of the final [Veda] is achievable. For it is said: "That which is merely inferential is not sublated by what is found there [in scripture]; for sublation occurs only when there is a contradiction, and contradiction pertains solely to objects of the same scope."

For if only that which is directly heard in the Vedic text (*pratyakṣaśruta*) were the cause of sublation (*bādhaka*), independent of contradiction, then nothing whatsoever would be sublated—whether it pertains to another ritual, whether its purpose is visible (*dṛṣṭārtha*) or invisible (*adṛṣṭārtha*), or whether it belongs to the same or a different ritual cycle (*tulyakalpa* or *atulyakalpa*). And this is not desired.
Therefore, the observation of the combination (*samuccaya*) of both options is justified.
And so he will state: "Because of the connection with the characteristic of the material cause" (10.4.9).

Likewise, in such passages as "And because they are prescribed among the Prājāpatya offerings" (10.4.14), he will state that there is a combination [of options] due to the absence of contradiction in various instances of this kind.
Regarding that very point, they state the resolution:
In this case, the connection with the natural gender of this very [term] is caused by the designation of the number of the *savanīya* offerings;
for all these have been described by means of the *savanīya* sacrifice.
Therefore, since there is equality of function due to this commonality, it follows that a contradiction exists—this is what must be stated.
Since this is so, even though they share the same ritual procedure (*samānavidhāna*), there arises the contingency of sublation based on the distinction between the general and the particular.
For each preceding [rule] is established as general because it has a wider scope (*mahāviṣaya*) regarding the animal sacrifice;
whereas each succeeding one is established as particular because it occupies a narrower scope (*alpāvakāśa*).
Furthermore, a general rule (*sāmānya*) is sublated by a particular rule (*viśeṣa*), whether that particular rule has scope (*sāvakāśa*) or lacks scope (*niravakāśa*).
However, some say:
because a solitary [general rule] in all its states lacks scope due to the existence of other particulars, it would be sublated by the two middle [particular rules].
Even though there is a difference in the scope of their objects, the operation of the means of knowledge is equal.
Just as this [term *agniṣṭoma*] applies to the common case because its object is the equality of the concluding rites (*saṃsthā*), so too the term *agniṣṭoma* is common to all three concluding rites.
And to whatever extent that [latter] is obtained through effort, to that same extent the former is also obtained.
However, there is no fault even if the *meṣī* sacrifice serves as the occasion [for the application of the rule],
for that specific *saṃsthā* (concluding rite) does not exist within the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Therefore, there is sublation (*bādha*).
It is said:
although there is no sublation, nevertheless, an alternative (vikalpa) results for you;
for a conjunction of things that serve the same purpose is never observed anywhere.
This is a rope with nooses on both ends.

If, first of all, even a slight connection with a ritual action (*kārya*) can be established for the sake of proving their combination (*samuccaya*), then there is combination even in the view that they are modifications (*vikāra*).

On the other hand, if one assumes the status of being a ritual action (*kāryatva*) in order to justify sublation (*bādha*) in that case, then, even though the general rule (*sāmānya-vidhi*) is set aside (the meaning of *sāmānyavidyaṃ* is "even in the prima facie view"), there is a combination like that of rice and barley.

And this is not merely the statement of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*); for even in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), having accepted that view as a necessary course of action, he will state their combination [of meditations] in the sūtra: "But there is a combination because of the scriptural statement" (3.3.64).
To that end, he will state a distinction.
That is now being stated.
"O all you who exist in equal and opposite paths, by virtue of attaining that which arises from every limb,
let the designation [of the cause] be set aside."
For all animals are applicable everywhere because they do not cease based on the instruction [of a specific rule], since that [instruction] is merely the cause [for restriction].
However, by means of the direct perception [of the rule], each preceding animal obtains the status of being the primary subject in the sentence.

In this regard, should one assume a single function by postulating a common basis for both the annulment (*bādha*) and the option (*vikalpa*), or should one postulate a plurality of functions in accordance with the conjunction (*samuccaya*) obtained through syntactical connection (*vākya*)? Since syntactical connection is more powerful, there must be conjunction.
Thus, even though the *prayāja* and other such rites share a single name (*samākhyā*), they have distinct functions and a conjunction [of performance] due to the force of syntactical connection.

Furthermore, in the case of extended application (*atideśa*), there is a single function by virtue of the name, whereas the plurality of functions [and thus conjunction] arises through the extended application itself.
This is included within the instruction regarding that [substitution] (the meaning of "therefore" being "in view of the assumed extended application").
Since designation (*samākhyā*) alone is more powerful, the contradiction would be avoided by relying on the unity of the function produced by it.

And in the case of a modification (*vikāra*), since it is enjoined through connection with the characteristic marks of the archetype (*prakṛti*), the meaning is that there is an attainment of the function (*kāryāpatti*).

However, there is no connection with the gender of the archetype (*prakṛti*) in a case of identical injunction (*samānavidhi*), by which the transference of function (*kāryāpatti*) could be established.

Some say: "In the case of an identical injunction, a difference in ritual acts is determined by the conjunctions with two deities, which are independent of one another. In the case of a modification (*vikāra*), however, only a subordinate element (*guṇa*) is enjoined by way of restating the sacrifice already obtained through extension (*atideśa*)."

Consequently, there would have to be only one sacrifice, and not a second. However, in this case, where Indra and Sarasvatī appear as distinct through their respective qualities (*guṇa*), there is necessarily a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*) because the injunction of multiple substances and deities would otherwise result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

Therefore, it must be established in this way: when this distinct action is being enjoined, does it attain the status of being a means for a separate *apūrva* (unseen potency), or is it rather a means for the very *apūrva* of the archetypal *saṃvanīya* animal?

Since it is possible to assign its function to an *apūrva* already established previously, it is not proper to assume a new *apūrva* and determine that it is a means for that. Likewise, even the *apūrva* of the *saṃvanīya* animal obtained through extension (*atideśa*) does not, at the time it requires a means, abandon the directly present *saṃvanīya* and take up another *saṃvanīya*.

Since, among all requirements, that which is not part of the archetype is adopted due to the impossibility of its inclusion in the archetype, the operation proceeding from the sacrifice is already established as having a relationship with the archetypal *apūrva* (transcendental result); it cannot therefore be understood as having a relationship with another *apūrva*.
If it is asked, "How can an archetypal *apūrva*, whose capacity is not established for this purpose, accomplish another *saṃnāyya* (curd-mixture)?"—the answer is:
just as in the case of another field, the operation belonging to the sacrifice accomplishes another *apūrva*; thus there is no fault.
What, then, is the distinction between these two? It is said:

when the *apūrvas* (unseen potencies) require the operation of the sacrifice itself, at that time the *apūrva* of the modified *saṃnāyya* offering is not powerful enough to cause [the milk] to fall into that [specific vessel].

When, however, an unprecedented (*apūrva*) result is required, then the mind, perceiving that there exists another action already established which is connected with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being the archetype (*prakṛti*) for the *saṃnayya* offering, sets aside the archetypal [action].

And since the state of postulating an unprecedented result does not yet exist in the archetype, fourfold unprecedented results are postulated for the satisfaction and non-satisfaction produced by the enjoined *saṃnayya* offering.
For it is not known therein which other previously established [result] would have a relationship of being the means (*sādhana*).
For at the time of the examination of the ritual acts (*karmālocana*), it is indeed the forms of the acts themselves that are perceived.
Even the conceptualization of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) occurs simultaneously; thus, no distinction is observed [between them].

However, in the view of modification (*vikāra*), it is understood that the archetypal (*prākṛta*) form is established earlier. Consequently, when one of the two acts is remote, the archetypal form must be abandoned, which results in the contingency of sublation (*bādha*).

But surely, under the view that these are modifications (*vikāra*), the subsequent forms (*saṃsthā*) are modifications only of the *agniṣṭoma* form and not of one another; thus, since the original *āgneya* alone would be superseded by the subsequent ones, one would never observe a second [form] anywhere. Why, then, is it said that "the observation of a third does not obtain"? This is not a fault.

For if he were to speak of the observation of sublation (*bādhadarśana*) regarding the *aindra* and other forms already obtained here, then he would be speaking without any basis in authority (*niṣpramāṇaka*).
But this [objection] speaks merely from the perspective of not seeing [the full context].
And that is indeed appropriate because, due to the sublation (*bādha*) of the *āgneya* [offering], it would otherwise apply to the two middle ones.
He states that the *āgneya* is sublated by that very [reason]: "The earlier one is not [sublated] by the later."
Therefore, they are of equal injunction;
however, there is a modification when there is a connection with a specific desire, because that [desire] is equal to the permanent [obligatory rite].
Commentary: This is not so; they are of equal injunction.

What then? The *saṃsthās* such as the *ukthya* and others would be modifications (*vikāra*). Having accepted the *agniṣṭoma* *saṃsthā* as the basis, the ritual duties (*dharma*) beginning with the *dīkṣaṇīyā* are prescribed.
Why? Because the *ukthya* and the others are heard of in connection with specific desires (*kāma*).
"One desiring cattle should take the Ukthya cup";
"One desiring vigor should praise with the Ṣoḍaśin"; "One desiring progeny should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with the Atirātra.
A quality heard as being for a specific desire enters into the permanent rite.
How so? Because in such optional rites (*kāmya*) characterized by specific qualities, the accomplishment of the fruit results from those very qualities.
"One desiring cattle should take the *ukthya* cup," or "one desiring the *jyotiṣṭoma*, or desiring the taking of the *ukthya*.
The meaning is: "He should take it in such a way that cattle come to be."

How is this so? In that regard, since there is necessarily an expectation for a procedure (*itikartavyatā*), it is understood from proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) that the procedure belongs to the obligatory (*nitya*) rite.
But how is it determined that the substance is the procedure for the purpose of the obligatory rite alone, and not for this optional (*kāmya*) rite, or common to both?
It is said in reply:

Wherever there is a desire for a quality, it occurs only when that action is being accomplished, and not otherwise; that procedure which presents itself at the very end is the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance).
Since it is doubted whether this belongs to the means (*sādhana*) or to the goal (*sādhya*), it must belong to the goal.
This [agent] is not connected with the means for the sake of the goal to be accomplished;
for in this way, that specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is heard [in the injunction]:
"by this, the means [is to be employed]."
"One should make it an instrument" (sādhakaṃ kuryāt). Yet, there is no such manner by which, while the action itself remains unaccomplished, one could thereby become its instrument.

Therefore, even for one who accepts that the object to be accomplished (sādhya) possesses a specific mode of performance (itikartavyatā), it must be admitted that this [mode] belongs to the object to be accomplished as well.
And the Jyotiṣṭoma is the object to be accomplished (sādhya), while the *saṃsthās* are subordinate to it.
Therefore, it is established that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) belongs specifically to the Jyotiṣṭoma. Now, why is it not common [to all]?
Because it is prescribed as being constant:
that which is the Jyotiṣṭoma is itself the initiation (dīkṣā).
However, when one desires cattle in the Jyotiṣṭoma, then there is the Ukthya-termination.
The ritual duties (dharmas) must always be performed in the Jyotiṣṭoma;

yet, the claim that they are for the sake of the Ukthya and other terminuses contradicts what was previously stated by the subsequent [argument]. If it were "always," then there would be no application of the names "Ukthya" and so forth; if it were by means of the designations "Ukthya" and so forth, then it would not be "always. Thus, both positions are mutually contradictory.
Therefore, it is common [to both].
And as for that which is a constant injunction (*niyatāmnāna*) regarding the permanent [rite], because of that constant injunction, it is established as non-permanent;
therein, the constant injunction is sublated.

Therefore, the *saṃsthās* such as the Ukthya do not belong to the Jyotiṣṭoma as its constant form; rather, they belong to the desire [for specific results]. Or rather: the Ukthyas and so forth are specific modes of completion (*samāpti-viśeṣa*) enjoined as means to a result. Since they require a substrate for their completion, they resort to the Jyotiṣṭoma under discussion; by displacing its own inherent *agniṣṭoma* mode, they take their place. Thus, they are designated by the term "modification" (*vikāra*).
But surely, once it is established that the Ukthya and other [sacrifices] are terminuses (*samāpti*), there must be a requirement for something to which they belong as terminuses.
However, this is not established prior to their being the terminuses of the Jyotiṣṭoma, because the application of the term "terminus" depends upon the existence of a beginning and a middle.

If, on the other hand, they were first connected to that [Jyotiṣṭoma], then, since their purpose would have been determined as belonging to the ritual (*ṛtu*) first, they could not subsequently be connected to a result; thus, by the principle "that [is] for the permanent [rite], because of its equality," there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that they constitute a qualification (*adhikāra*).
Furthermore: "When two distinct results are being enjoined, how can the connection of the *saṃsthās* with the result be determined?
Regarding this, some say:

The discussion regarding the connection of the *grahaṇas* and other elements with the fruit indeed proceeds as a formal topic (*adhikaraṇa*)—meaning that the investigation of the topic is entirely consistent. [The question is: "Are the *dharmas* prescribed by the injunctions for the Jyotiṣṭoma alone, or do they also apply to the *grahaṇas*?

If it is asked how the word *saṃsthā* (conclusion) applies here, it is because those *grahaṇas* and so forth are enjoined at the end; thus, there is a connection with completion, and therefore the term is used.

"One desiring cattle should draw the Ukthya cup"; "one desiring virility should praise with the Ṣoḍaśin"—these [injunctions], being enjoined after the conclusion of the preceding [rite], possess the character of being a location for another completion. Others, however, say:

since the drawing of the cup and so forth are already established here as having results, they are merely brought forward to be offered in a sentence whose purpose is to enjoin the relationship between the means and the end.
Why? Because: "When the capacity for the ritual procedure has been transferred to the suffix, it is called a verbal root;
therefore, the fruit [accrues] to the agent, as in the case of the Hotṛ, the Veda-study, and the desire for sense-organs."
But surely, because of the usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "one should draw the *ukthya*," it would apply only to the drawing of the cup and so forth?
This is not so.
Because the *ukthya-stotra* and its constituent parts are completed, the word *ukthya* refers to that very completion; and when a primary sense is possible, a figurative one is not accepted.

However, the employment of the *ukthya* and other such rites is constantly seen in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "sacrifice" (*yajña*), as in: "One should sacrifice with the *ukthya*; the *ukthya* is a sacrifice," and likewise, "One sacrifices with the *ṣoḍaśin*; the *ṣoḍaśin* is a sacrifice.
Indeed, there exists a sacrifice named the *ṣoḍaśin*.
And that [term] is appropriate as a statement regarding the absolute and ultimate completion, but not as a statement regarding the cup (graha) or the hymn (stotra).
Furthermore, the word "ṣoḍaśī" is masculine;
it is only as a statement of completion that this becomes logically consistent.
Because the neuter gender refers to the hymn (*stotra*).
As for the masculine usage that is occasionally observed in the hymn, such as "the twenty-first is the *ṣoḍaśī*," it should be understood as figurative (*gauṇa*).
In this supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), the masculine form *ṣoḍaśī* is perceived; thus, it is a designation for the *saṃsthā* (the completion of the rite).
In the statement, “With the *atirātra*, [one should sacrifice] for one desiring progeny,” its status as a designation for the *saṃsthā* is quite clear, for no other action is mentioned therein.

Even if [the result] were heard as being subordinate to the *vyathopasarva*, yet by making it the primary element through the *kleśa* (effort), therefore the completion belonging to the *ātrīmatī* is connected with the fruit.

And if there were a connection with the fruit for both the *grahaṇa* (taking) and the *stotra* (praise), then, because those two are actions (*kriyātva*), they would have no requirement for a substratum (*āśraya*); consequently, their performance would follow as being entirely independent.
Furthermore, in that context, neither the specific occasion nor the purpose for employing terms such as *ukthya* would be known.
Therefore, the completion [of the rite] itself must be the fruit.
But how can there be a completion prior to the connection with the sacrifice (*kratu*)?

Some, however, have said (first stating the view of the Yājñikas): "There are seven Soma-sacrifices: Agniṣṭoma, Atyagniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśin, Atirātra, Vājapeya, and Atirātra. Since it is established that these terms denote the completion of the Soma [sacrifice], and since they do not refer to separate rites, the status of the Jyotiṣṭoma as the archetype is established for all Soma sacrifices required by the context. Others, however, think differently.

Section on *Saṃsthā* (4060): In the case of groups of sacrifices (*saṃsthāgaṇa*), even though there is an injunction that makes known the possession of a fruit, the requirement that the substrate (*āśraya*)—which is distinct from what is to be accomplished by human effort (*kṛtisādhya*)—must necessarily be stated prior to the connection with the property (*dharma*) [of the sacrifice] remains. For this very reason, the traditional doctrine of the root-text (*mūla-pravāda*) holds that the expectancy for the substrate is more extensive than the expectancy for the instrument (*karaṇa*), because the substrate is that which brings about the form of the quality as the instrument, or rather, it is included within the delimitation (*avacchedaka*) of the quality’s status as the instrument.

Therefore, it is established that the *dharmas* (subsidiary elements) possess only the status of being dependent (*āśrayāṅgatva*). However, regarding the cultivation of qualities (*guṇabhāvanā*), there is an extension of the *dharma*s based on their dependence [on the archetype].

Although the purpose [of this rule] cannot consist in the attainment of the desire for qualities (*guṇakāma*), even though the *saṃsthās* (concluding rites) are modifications (*vikṛti*), because the Jyotiṣṭoma—which serves as their substrate—is the archetype (*prakṛti*), one obtains the desires for qualities dependent upon the measuring of the *sadas* and so forth; or alternatively, one obtains the desires for qualities dependent upon the drawing of the cups (*grahaṇa*) which serve as the substrates for the repetition of the *ṣoḍaśin* and other rites.

Nor does the nature of the *udbhid* and other sacrifices consist in having an optional *saṃsthā* (concluding rite) as their archetype (*prakṛti*), for—just like the *yāga* itself—their having the *jyotiṣṭoma* as their archetype is established through mere association (*sāhacarya*). Nevertheless, it should be understood that in cases such as "Now this is the path of the gods," where there is no mention of a qualifying term [indicating a specific sacrifice] as in the case of the *yāga*, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that they have an optional *saṃsthā* as their archetype; whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), they have the *jyotiṣṭoma* alone as their archetype. Furthermore, according to the prima facie view, there would be differences in the ritual properties (*dharmabheda*) due to the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) to the *saṃsthā*, as well as the application of rules pertaining to the Yajurveda and so forth.
In the Siddhānta, however, even the inconceivable [is to be modified].

Likewise, in the mantra "May I obtain the prosperity of the sacrifice" (*yajñasyāśīr vacyamaśīya*) and others accompanied by *praṇava*, the word *adrik* (unexhausted) is to be supplied according to the Pūrvapakṣa, because its omission occurs at the conclusion (*saṃsthā*).
In the Siddhānta, one must substitute accordingly as "the prosperity of the sacrifice's conclusion" (*yajñasya saṃsthāyā āśīḥ*).

Here, it is argued that a combination (*samuccaya*) of substances qualified by their respective deities is enjoined; otherwise, because they would be understood as having a single purpose due to the common designation (*savanīya*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the previously established animal dedicated to Agni being superseded (*bādha*) by the animals dedicated to Indra-Agni and others taught for the modified forms (*vikṛti*) of the subsequent concluding rites such as the *ukthya*.
