In the case of groups of sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthāgaṇa*), the repetition of those [terminuses] is understood from the inclusion of specific characteristics (*kṛtalakṣaṇagrahaṇa*).
Groups of terminuses are heard in such scriptural passages as: "There are five *ukthyas*," "It becomes a hundred *agniṣṭomas*," and "It becomes a hundred *atirātras*.
In these cases, within each respective group of terminuses, the repetition of that particular terminus—that is, the repetition of each individual terminus—is understood.
In the performance of the Ukthya sacrifice five times, it would be a "five-Ukthya";

likewise, in the repetition of the Agniṣṭoma one hundred times, it would be a "hundred-Agniṣṭoma," and in the repetition of the Atirātra one hundred times, there would be a group of terminuses called a "hundred-Atirātra.
This is because the designation is taken based on the specific characteristic [of the number of repetitions].
The Agniṣṭoma and the Ukthya among the groups of sacrificial terminuses (saṃsthās)— that [last one] is the Atirātra; the characteristics of these have been established by their very names.

And thus, those sacrifices for which characteristics have been established are "kṛtalakṣaṇāḥ" (those whose nature is known). It is precisely these sacrifices, whose nature is already known, that are referred to by the terms *pañca-ukthya* and so forth.

Because they are referred to as having their characteristics established, it is understood that there is a repetition (*abhyāsa*) of those [sacrifices] such as the *agniṣṭoma*, and not an extension (*atideśa*) of the twelve-day rites; this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
Or rather, by virtue of the context, the archetype (*prakṛti*) should be qualified by that [term], because the designation is based upon it.

It has been stated [in 8.1.10.17] that "the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is the archetype of the *gaṇas*."

Therefore, in this context, the word *prakṛti* refers to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*). By the pronoun *tat* (in the compound *tadviśiṣṭāḥ*), the *ukthya* and other forms belonging to the subject matter under discussion are indicated.

The *prakṛti* is the twelve-day sacrifice; ten days of the twelve-day sacrifice, characterized by those [forms]—namely, distinguished by the *ukthya* and other terminuses (*saṃsthā*)—are operative in the five *ukthya* sacrifices and so forth.

In the case of the *saṃsthās* (concluding rites) of the *gaṇas* (groups of sacrifices)—namely the five *ukthya*, the *śatastokya*, the *agniṣṭoma*, and the *śatātirātra*—there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), yet in each instance there is that specific *saṃsthā*.
The completion of the Vedic core (*vaidikamarma*) occurs through the recitation (*japa*) of the *saṃsthā*.

In the case of the explanations of the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice, a formal configuration (*ākāra*) might be postulated due to the adoption of earthly substances, but not independently; however, for space (*dik*), time (*kāla*), the self (*ātman*), and the mind (*manas*), as well as for qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*), no configuration whatsoever is possible.
(Vārttika 1.3.1.30, p.
295). Configuration (*saṃsthāna*) means termination (*paryavasāna*), the ultimate limit of activity.
Furthermore, one who is performing [an action] is not said to have ceased from that activity;
for cessation (saṃsthā) with respect to an action consists either in indifference toward it or in performing another action subsequent to the previous one.

Bāla, p. 21:
"Oṃ, it should be [performed] with a skull by nature, because there is no scriptural statement to the contrary for another [vessel].
It is heard in scripture: 'One desiring spiritual luster should offer a caru-oblation to Sūrya.'"

In that case, since it is not heard [in scripture] that the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) should be cooked on anything other than a potsherd (*kapāla*), it should be cooked on a potsherd according to its nature, following the model of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*);
for there is no scriptural statement regarding any other substance serving as the locus for cooking.
That which has no such scriptural statement is "unheard" (*aśruti*).

The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that since there is no scriptural injunction for anything else and since the potsherds (kapāla) are obtained through the force of the extended application (codaka), the sacrificial pap (caru) must be cooked on the potsherds themselves.
Furthermore, the number [of potsherds] is also like the potsherds;
just as the potsherd is obtained for the purpose of cooking the caru by the codaka, so too the number of potsherds is obtained for an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭa).

But if it is argued that the number [of potsherds] is set aside because a sacrificial oblation (caru) can be cooked even on potsherds whose number has not been seen, then the potsherd itself must also be set aside; for both are expressed by a single word. This is the objection.
Or rather, because of the contradiction in a single instance.
It was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) that the *caru* mentioned in the injunction "one should offer a *caru* to Sūrya" must be cooked on a potsherd (*kapāla*).
In that case, just like the potsherd, the number eight would also necessarily apply.
If it is argued that since the number [of potsherds] is sublated, the potsherd itself should also be sublated—this doubt having arisen, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) dispels it.
The word "or" (vā) is intended to set aside this doubt.
The caru-offering is to be cooked on a single potsherd alone.
The number eight, however, is set aside due to contradiction;
for it is not possible to cook a *caru* offering in eight potsherds (*kapāla*).
Thus, because of the conflict, the number is sublated, but the potsherd itself must not be sublated due to the lack of contradiction.

Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the *saurya* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) should be cooked on a single potsherd (*kapāla*). The word "or" (*vā*) is used for the purpose of refuting the prima facie view that the *saurya caru* must be cooked on a potsherd. [The siddhāntin argues: It is not so, because of its connection with a different purpose; since it is not yet cooked, the vessel connected to the cooking process serves the purpose of holding it, and in that case, the acquisition of a vessel would occur naturally as a matter of course. Since there is no specific distinction [stated], there is no restrictive rule. Thus, the *saurya caru* need not necessarily be cooked on a potsherd.
The *caru* for Sūrya is not to be cooked on a potsherd (*kapāla*).
A *caru* is a distinct category from a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
Because it is connected with the act of cooking, and because the cooking of a *caru* is impossible on a potsherd, the *caru* is not to be cooked on a potsherd.

In the case of the *apūpa* and the *puroḍāśa*, however, a potsherd (*kapāla*) is used for the purpose of baking; that is, the *apūpa* can be cooked upon a potsherd. But in the case of the *caru* which is to be boiled, a potsherd must be employed for the purpose of holding water.
That is not possible; therefore, for the purpose of holding water, there would have to be the acquisition of a vessel for that *caru*.
Some kind of vessel must simply be obtained.
And regarding that vessel, since there is no distinction—meaning there is no specific requirement for the cooking of the *caru*—there would be no fixed rule [as to its material].

There would be no restrictive rule that "only a specific vessel must be used"; rather, any vessel suitable for the cooking pot of the *caru* may be used without restriction. Or rather, [the specific vessel] is required because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) regarding the *caru*.

It has been stated that the *saurya* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) is to be cooked in some kind of vessel, not on a potsherd (*kapāla*). If one asks what kind of vessel it should be, [the answer is]: that *caru* is to be cooked in a *caru*-vessel; it is not to be cooked in any other vessel.

In this context, the word *caru* denotes the cooking vessel (*sthālī*). The indicative mark [found in the text], "Those vessels in which the Soma juices are contained are *carus*," shows that the Soma-vessel is intended for the cooking of the *caru*. Indeed, the cooking of the *caru* is most excellent when performed in a shallow pan (*khalyā*).

Therefore, the established conclusion is that the *caru* is to be cooked in a pot (*sthālī*). Thus, the *caru* is a modification of the injunction [itself], not a modification of the potsherds (*kapāla*); and the *saurya-caru* is denoted by the word "boiled rice" (*odana*), not by the word "pot. Furthermore, it is established that the cooking of the *caru* must be performed in a pot, not on potsherds.

Oṃ. He [the substitute] should possess those duties because of his connection with the ritual action.

Regarding a sacrificial session (*sattra*), when any one of the sacrificers has departed, another person who is appointed in his stead should possess those duties—that is, the duties of the master (*svāmin*)—and not the duties of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).
Due to connection with the ritual action and connection with the master’s duty:
whichever person is appointed to a particular task becomes connected with the duties pertaining to that task.
Therefore, it is the established conclusion (siddhānta) that he possesses the qualities of the master.
He whose very nature consists of those qualities alone, whose very nature consists of those qualities alone—he is "taddharmā.
The suffix *an* is applied at the end of the compound.
He is that.
In the *Kutūhala*, the reading for "saḥ karmasaṃyogāt" is "tatsaṃyogāt".

The meaning is that only when the representative possesses the status of an owner (svāmin) is there a possibility of connection, because of the connection with the purificatory rites for the fruit (phalisaṃskāra) belonging to the others.
The reading in the commentary (vṛtti) is "tatkarmasaṃyogāt" (due to connection with his [the owner's] actions);
its meaning is "because of being connected with the actions of the owner."
Some [hold]: "Oṃ, 'That [is for the purpose of the deities], because of its connection with them.

That *sūktavāka* is for the purpose of designating the deities, because it is connected to the *praharaṇa* (the throwing) by way of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*)—such is the literal meaning of the words."

Although Agni and the other deities are individually the deities (*devatā*) in the Āgneya and subsequent sacrifices, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), one should postulate a single deityhood that resides collectively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) as determined by the purpose (*uddeśa*) within these sacrifices.

Consequently, the renunciation (*tyāga*) of this single principal substance is postulated as being performed by means of that single deityhood which inheres in Agni and the others through the instigation of another [sacrifice].

And for the sake of establishing the verbal nature [of the act], the status of being a *homa* (oblation) is established through the term *praharati* (he offers), which indicates it by means of *ajahatsvārtha-lakṣaṇā* (indication without abandoning its own primary meaning), just like the term *ādhārayati*.

Regarding the third [point]: (*"He offers the *prastara* with the *sūktavāka*"). Because of parsimony (*lāghava*) and because of its utility, it is possible to accept that the *sūktavāka* functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*). Furthermore, according to the principle to be stated in the subsequent sūtra, since the *praharaṇa* (the act of throwing) is secondary, there is no fault in taking the indicative mark (*lakṣaṇā*) of "offering" (*homa*) as the result. (Kau. 3.1.5.12–13). "*That [is] for the permanent [rite], because of its equality*" (3.1.6.143). Once it has first been determined that [the *sūktavāka*] serves the purpose of the *kyava*, and because of the absence of a connection with a [separate] result, there arises the contingency of non-modification (*avikāra*)—namely, "*that [is] for the permanent, because of its equality*"—in the case of the *ukthya* and other such rites.
Or [it may be]. Pāṇini 3.1.6.143, pp. 1065–66.
*Oṃ*. That [five-platter offering] should exclude the bath.

Regarding the statement, "If both sacrificial offerings (*havis*) of one who performs the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) should be ruined, he should offer a five-platter rice-oblation (*pañcaśarāva-modana*) to Indra"—that five-platter offering, which constitutes a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*), should exclude the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*).
It would be a substitute for the New Moon sacrifice, but it is not itself the New Moon sacrifice;
because one bathes [after it],
and because the five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*) is prescribed in its place once the sacrifice has been completed.
Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
Because of the connection with a cause, there would be the futility of the injunction for the subsidiary (*aṅga-vidhi-vaiyyarthya*).

Regarding the statement, "In the *darśa*, if both sacrificial offerings (*havis*) should be spoiled, one should offer five-platter rice (*pañcaśarāva-modana*) to Indra," the prima facie view—attained through the sūtra—is that the five-platter offering is a distinct ritual (*karmāntara-rūpa*), not a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā-yāga*), but rather a substitute (*pratinidhi*). This is set aside by the word "or" (*vā*) in the sūtra, because the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is a replacement (*pratyāmnāya*).
The five-portioned oblation (*pañcaśarāva*) is a modification of the constituent parts (*aṅga*),
as it is connected with the *darśa* sacrifice by way of a specific occasion (*nimitta*).

Because of the connection—that is, the prescription of a relationship—of the sacrifice with the occasion in the form of the "overflowing of the oblation" (*havirāti*), the *pañcaśarāva* offering is therefore an occasional subsidiary (*naimittika-aṅga*) of the rite. Who [says this]? [The Mīmāṃsakas].
"Oṃ! That [rite] would be worldly (laukika), because its performance is based on what is already perceived [in common experience].
It was understood in the preceding section that even for rites such as the *saurya* sacrifice, where no specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*) has been prescribed, some form of procedure must exist.
Now, in response to the inquiry as to what that specific procedure is, he says:"
That specific procedure (itikartavyatā) would be worldly (laukika).
By "worldly," what is stated in the Gṛhyasūtras is meant.

Consequently, in rites such as the Pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka, that specific procedure which is observed to be in practice would be the one prescribed in the Gṛhyasūtras, because its application is seen, as in the case of the Saurya sacrifice and others.
For that [fire] is established as the means for accomplishing results such as the *sthālīpāka* and so forth; therefore, it is fit to be taken even in rites such as the *saurya*.
Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is a worldly fire.
However, on account of the scriptural injunction, it is different from that.
It has been stated that in rites such as the Saurya sacrifice, the specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*) required is to be taken from worldly practice;
the word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction from that.
However, where there is a specific scriptural injunction regarding a particular Vedic procedure, then by virtue of that injunction, the specific procedure is distinct from the worldly one.
As in the case of the *upasads* and the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice;
however, in the absence of any scriptural statement, it would be worldly (*laukika*).
Or rather, it should be restricted by the indicative mark (*liṅga*), because that indicative mark possesses those specific qualities.
Even where the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is not explicitly recited, it must nevertheless be adopted from some source;
and it has been stated previously that in some cases this [procedure] is derived from a scriptural statement (*vacana*).
Therefore, the word "or" (*vā*) indicates a distinction.
Or, in some cases, the Vedic procedure may be restricted by an indicative mark (*liṅga*), as in the case of the *saurya* oblation of rice: "At each *prayāja*, he offers a *kṛṣṇala*.
Here, "*kṛṣṇala*" refers to gold weighing one *māṣa*.
"In that [rite] dedicated to Indra and Bṛhaspati, one cuts half of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and not the other half; one makes half of it self-broken and not the other half.
Likewise, in the Pitṛyajña, "one does not choose a Hotṛ priest, nor does one choose the *ardheya*.
From these indicative marks (*liṅga*), it is known that this is the Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
Because the indicative mark (liṅga) possesses that quality;
for instance, the "ajā" and others are indeed qualities of that Vedic *apūrva*. Therefore, in some cases, there is a restrictive rule based on the indicative mark.
Alternatively, because it would be preceded by an improper method, where there might be statements that are merely restatements (*anuvāda*),

the Siddhāntin has stated that the Vedic procedure is restricted by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) as in the case of the *saurya* sacrifice; the word "or rather" (*api vā*) is used here to set aside that [position].

In the case of the *saurya* sacrifice and others, the Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is not established by means of indicative power (*liṅga*), because it would be preceded by what is improper; here there is no basis in reason, as there is an absence of logical justification. What, then, is the application of these indicatives? It is said:

Where there would be statements that are restatements of the blue—wherein a restatement of the established [quality] "blue" is observed—there something might be understood by means of the aforementioned indicative marks;
those [statements] have that as their purpose.
For example:

Since the *pādyas* are established [in the model sacrifice], the injunction regarding the *kṛṣṇalas* is made by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to them; thus, the sentence concerning the *kṛṣṇalas* is displaced from the *saurya* sacrifice.
Alternatively, this is an injunction for the *prayājas* qualified by the *kṛṣṇalas*.

As for the statement "he does not hear the *ārṣeya*," it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is constant, just as in the case of "not in the intermediate space, nor in heaven, [O] Agnīdh! and so forth.

And the sentence beginning with "He cuts half of the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣaḥ*) must be displaced from the *aindrābārhaspatya* sacrifice to wherever the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is already established.
Therefore, in the *saurya* and other such rites, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is purely worldly (*laukikī*) and not Vedic.
This is the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*).
Furthermore, because the qualities are mutually contradictory, there would have to be a conceptualization [of them] according to their actual purpose.

Regarding the *saurya* and other such sacrifices, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) has stated that the worldly procedure (*itikartavyatā*) should be adopted. Someone might say: "Well then, let both the worldly and the Vedic procedures operate.
To this, the proponent of the prima facie view replies:
The simultaneous operation of both worldly and Vedic [injunctions] with respect to a single action is impossible due to their mutual contradiction.

Therefore, there should be a conceptualization of the subordinate factors (*guṇas*) that does not deviate from the actual purpose—that is, without overstepping the purpose established by the original context (*prakṛti*).
There should be a conceptualization according to the actual purpose; thus, the operation should belong to only one procedure (*itikartavyatā*) which produces the result.

And when there is only one [alternative], then because it proceeds from what is already perceived, it is restricted by virtue of its being a participant; for qualities are denotations, and through their connection they function like denotations, just as in the case of "dhenu" (a cow) [referring to] a "kiśorī" (a young female).

Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that in the *saurya* and other such rites the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) would be worldly (*laukikī*), the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) says:
Because of its participation (*bhāgitvāt*), that which participates in the *apūrva* is a participant (*bhāginī*); thus, even the Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is a participant.

Although both the worldly and the Vedic [procedures] are equal in their status as participants, because the qualities such as the *prayāja*s—which are Vedic—are what designate [the action], [the term "designation" (*abhidhāna*)] refers to those that "designate" (*abhidadhati*). Thus, "abhi-" [is used].
The grains [are mentioned] because they are expressive.
How are the qualities expressive of Vedic [rites]? Because of their connection; for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are connected only with the Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
Indeed, the *prayāja* offerings do not exist in worldly rites such as the *sthālīpāka*.

Just like a name (*abhidhāna*); for example, just as the name "Agnihotra" in the *Kuṇḍapāyināmayana* sacrifice brings along the ritual details (*dharma*) associated with the permanent Agnihotra, so too—by virtue of sharing [the same] name, that is, by virtue of the connection of the ritual details with the name—the Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is restricted.
Here, the principle is "by virtue of sharing [the same] name."
The other is the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
For example: "the cow is the young female," or likewise, "the black young female is the cow."

In this context, although the word *dhenu* has its observed application (*dṛṣṭapravṛtti*) in a cow that suckles, nevertheless, due to the commonality of denotation, it partakes in [the meaning] even of a mare that suckles. For the word *kiśora* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) only for the young of a horse.

Likewise here, although the worldly application is observed, nevertheless, because of the participation through the commonality of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), there is a distinction based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Since the originative injunctions (*utpatti*) are equal, the performance should occur according to the respective qualification (*adhikāra*).

The proponent has stated that in rites such as the Saurya sacrifice, the Vedic procedure is established by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in the *prayāja* offerings and the *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces; however, the opponent objects once again.
The word "or" (*vā*) indicates a reversal of the position.
Alternatively, it is not at all determined by the indicative mark.
Because those [subordinate elements] are produced as a complete whole, all of them— including the *prayāja*s and other ritual properties—
are common to the *āgneya* and other primary rites by virtue of their very production.
Therefore, only the *prayāja*s could be inferred as possessing those properties, but not the other subordinate elements such as the *anuyāja*s.
Therefore, not all Vedic *itikartavyatā* (procedural details) can be adopted in rites such as the *saurya*.

For this reason, the existence (*bhāva*) or presence of those specific properties (*dharma*) that are heard [prescribed] in whichever context they belong to, according to their respective eligibility (*yathādhikāram*), shall apply; but not others.

Consequently, there would be the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatvam*) for all those [properties] merely heard in that context, such as the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, in the *saurya* and other rites.
Furthermore, the statement regarding the origin and the remaining [details] would be contradictory in a single case.

When the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) asserts that "the worldly procedure (*itikartavyatā*) and the Vedic subsidiary (*aṅga*) in the form of the *prayāja* offerings would both apply to the *saurya* oblation," this doubt arises: "Surely the procedure would be common to both the subsidiary and the primary; however, the primary is defined by its own procedure, and thus the injunction for the primary itself is what determines it.
Therefore, since the *saurya* sacrifice, along with its subsidiaries, is enjoined by the Veda, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) in that case must be exclusively Vedic.
"It is not worldly.
To this, the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) replies:
"The word 'ca' (and) indicates the exclusion of [the objection regarding] words."
The term "origination and statement of subsidiaries" (*utpatti-śeṣa-vacana*) refers to the combination of these two: origination (*utpatti*) and the statement of subsidiaries (*śeṣa-vacana*).
Within a single sentence or word, the origination of the primary element and the statement and injunction of the subsidiary elements are mutually contradictory and incompatible; they cannot coexist.

For if, in the case of the injunction "One should offer a cake to Sūrya," the subsidiaries were also enjoined by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in the same manner as the primary, then those subsidiaries would also have a connection with the fruit, just like the primary.

Consequently, its status as a subsidiary (aṅga) would be contradicted. Therefore, there is an injunction for both. And thus, in the case of the Saurya and other such rites, the procedure (itikartavyatā) is indeed that of the worldly [sacrifice].

"The injunction proceeds according to the model of the archetype, for there is an indicative mark [to that effect]. By the word 'vā' (but/again), [the author] sets aside the prima facie view—that in the case of the *saurya* sacrifice and others, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) should be taken from common worldly practice—and restates the established conclusion:

when there is an expectancy regarding the "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*) in the injunction of the *saurya* and other such sacrifices, the "how"—that is, the procedure—is indeed Vedic, proceeding according to the archetype, just as in the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*)."
For instance, the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) arises only when there is an expectancy regarding the Vedic procedure (*kathaṃbhāva*).

And since the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), the *anuyāja* offerings and so forth must also be excluded; thus, the observation of the *prayāja* and other elements serves as an indicative mark for the attainment of the Vedic procedure.
Therefore, in the *saurya* sacrifice and others, the procedure is indeed Vedic.
"Because it has the characteristic as its cause, the worldly [usage] would apply to the characteristic.
Thus says the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin).
The statement "That indeed should be so" is a declaration of established knowledge (*prājñitavāda*) regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
See Saṃkarṣa 2.2.21, Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1830: "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the section [beginning with] 'That indeed should be so' is to be consulted."

“Indeed, having sacrificed with the full-moon oblation, one should subsequently offer the *vaimṛdha*”; by this statement, it is understood that the *vaimṛdha* is to be performed at the same time as the performance of the full-moon sacrifice (*pūrṇamāsa*).
*Saṃkarṣa*, 1.2.6. “He indeed does not invoke the *vājina*s”;
[this refers to] the *vaiśvadeva* festival.
That [action] would be a *khaga* (a single, unified act), because it is non-distinct with respect to all [its constituent parts].

For it was understood in the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*) that a ritual action—such as "Therefore, one performs [the sacrifice] for the ancestors on the previous day," "He who consecrates himself for the *sattra* should sacrifice with the *viśvajit*," and so forth—accomplishes only a single result.
What indeed is the name of that single [result]?

In this investigation, that which is the single fruit would be heaven (*svarga*). The masculine gender in the word "that" (*saḥ*) follows the grammatical requirement of the predicate. Why is it specifically heaven? To this he replies: because heaven, consisting of unsurpassed bliss, is uniform for all persons, one desires the happiness of everyone.
If this were accepted, specific scriptural injunctions such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) would not be established as referring to specific [results].
Furthermore, because of the [use of the] suffix:
in cases such as "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) states that heaven alone is the fruit; regarding this, the Sūtra provides another reason.
The particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
In the world, regarding an action that has an eternal fruit (*anādi-phala*), there arises the conviction that heaven is its fruit.
For instance, when someone says, "Devadatta has built a grove," another person replies, "Heaven is certain for him."
When it is said, "Devadatta is the maker of the tank," another says, "Heaven is certain for him.
It is the same here as well.
Who? He would be the owner because of his connection with it.
It is understood that when one of the sacrificers in a sacrificial session (sattra) has become incapacitated, a substitute must be appointed in his place.
And this substitute would be another owner, because of his connection with ownership— that is, because of his connection with the status of being an owner.
For that other person who is brought in is made to perform the ritual action;
therefore, the substitute should be the owner—this is the prima facie view.
Or rather, he is merely a laborer, because he is hired for wages.

Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that when one of the sacrificers in a *sattra* sacrifice has failed, another who is appointed as a substitute (*pratinidhi*) should be considered the owner (*svāmī*), [the author] refutes this with the word "or" (*vā*) in the sūtra and states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). That person being substituted shall not be the owner, but rather a ritual agent (*karmakara*), just like the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in the *darśa* and other sacrifices. Why? Because of being hired (*bhṛtatvāt*), that is, because he is engaged through the payment of wages.
And one who is being hired does not become the owner;
he certainly does not obtain the fruit of the Satra sacrifice.
In the *Kutūhala*, instead of the reading "abhṛtatvāt" (because of not being hired), the reading "akṛtatvāt" (because of not having performed it) is found.

Because the ritual action was not performed by him from the very beginning as a representative, and because the action was thus unperformed, he would not obtain the fruit of the *sattra* sacrifice; therefore, he is not the master (*svāmin*).
Alternatively, there is a word-division (*padaccheda*) as "because it was performed" (*kṛtatvāt*).
The meaning of that [sūtra] is "because of being appointed.
The commentary states: "Because of being purchased," that is, because of having been hired by the giving of wealth.
In that regard...
The meaning of the *saktvadhikaraṇa* is that when a conflict arises, that which is once sublated must be understood as being sublated for good.

If the *paribhāṣā* "in the case of the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), [the substitute applies] to what is explicitly mentioned" were to apply here, then in the form *tisṛṇām*, one might suspect that after the substitution of *tis* (by P. 7.2.99), the substitution of *tray* would follow by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva* because it is subsequent; however, this would result in an inconsistency with the *bhāṣya*, which provides a resolution based on the maxim of "that which has occurred once" (*sakṛdgatanyāya*).
The maxim of "once gone" (*sakṛdgatanyāya*) is found on page 59 as a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*). It states:

"When there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) regarding what occurs once, that which is sublated is indeed sublated for good. On page 154, it is explained that when two rules apply simultaneously to a single instance where both would have their purpose fulfilled (*caritārtha*), there is no sublater (*bādhaka*) because both cannot operate at once. Consequently, since the two grammatical rules (*śāstra*) would otherwise apply alternatively (*paryāyeṇa*), the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedhasūtra*) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). Thus, the establishment of the maxim of "once gone" is demonstrated.

When the referent (*padārtha*) is an individual (*vyakti*), because the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) applies to every instance (*pratilakṣya*), both rules—whose objects are the instances to be defined (*lakṣyaviṣaya*)—would apply alternately since neither has fulfilled its purpose. To establish the restriction that "only the latter [rule] applies," this [sūtra] exists; thus is established the maxim of "once [a rule has applied, it does not apply again]" (*sakṛdgatanyāya*).
So say Kaiyaṭa and others.
(Śekhara, pp. 154–155).
Regarding the word *tisṛṇām*, the Bhāṣya aims to prevent the substitution of *traya* by means of the maxim of "once-occurrence" (*sakṛdgatanyāya*).
This maxim is stated at page 62 as: "What is the use of a veil for that which has already acted once?
Now, the word itself first denotes [the root-meaning] as the object (*viṣayatayā*), and then it also denotes it as the instrument (*karaṇatayā*).
How could that which is uttered once express it twice? Or, if it were to express it [twice], it would likewise express its state as something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
For there is no restrictive rule stating that it expresses it twice and not three times, according to the maxim:
"What is the use of a veil for that which has already functioned once?"

(The meaning of the maxim is: if a woman has once proceeded onto the market road and such places without a veil, she need not put on a veil again when going out; it is as in her first proceeding. This is the *nyāya* "What is the use of a veil for one who has already set out? (*sakṛtpravṛttāyāḥ kimavaguṇṭhanena*). By its connection with an action, even the word *ekahāyanī* loses its independence. ŚBh 4.1.4.4, p. 68. The maxim: "What is the use of a veil for one who has already set out? (*sakṛtpravṛttāyāḥ kimavaguṇṭhanena*).
Even the word *ekahāyanī*, due to its connection with an action, has its independence removed.

In that case, even when there is a connection with a word at the end [of a compound], the rule *śraṇīpāḍā* applies for the sake of that [connection], according to the maxim: "What is the use of a veil once [the action] has already occurred? (Vārttika 3.1.6.12, p. 689). This is the maxim: "A word that requires a complement can be connected with what is present in the intellect."
"This is not so; for that which, when not connected, would be meaningless, is what is connected, and nothing else," says the Bhāṣya.
Regarding this, the Vārttika states: "To the extent that a word-meaning is qualified, to that same extent there is a disruption of the natural flow (*svarasa*) of the direct audition (*śruti*).

Therefore, one must accept that once [the word] has functioned once, it should be qualified by another as well, according to the principle: 'What is the use of a veil for that which has already acted?'"

For a woman who has once engaged with another man will engage again; since this is so, why should she cover herself with a veil so that people might not see her? The meaning is that there is no purpose for the veil. As it is said: "Once the meaning of the scripture has been seen, what need is there for further effort? (Ke.).

Since the substance is one, the rule that "it should be done once" (*sakṛt*)—as in the case of the *aindrī* [verse]—would imply that the consumption should be performed only once; however, because of the scriptural statement, "He consumes the *aindra* twice," there is a double consumption. Vārttika 3.5.5.18. Regarding the argument that "or it should be once, because of the connection with the commencement" (*sakṛdvā''rambhasaṃyogāt*, 9.1.10.135), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the *Ārambhaṇīyā* rite, performed at the beginning for the sake of the lifelong performance already undertaken, [should be performed only once].
In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the ritual properties (*pradeyadharma*) are not to be performed in relation to the flour-offerings (*saktu*), such as milk-flour (*payas-saktu*) and parched grains (*dhānā*).
(Mīmāṃsā-kośa, p. 1824; see the section under "In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, regarding the [meat-portions] for Mitra-Varuṇa and others," Jaimini Sūtra 9.4.12.45–50).
This is the *Saktvadhikaraṇa*.
The principle of the groats (*saktunyāya*):
In the injunction "He offers groats" (*saktūn juhoti*), the accusative case does not indicate predominance.
If it is argued that this is an instruction regarding a substance (*dravyopadeśa*), [the reply follows].
Commentary: If you hold the view that, because a second [entity] is not perceived, substance (*dravya*) is essentially primary (*pradhāna*), this is not so;
for the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) occurs even when [the object] is secondary (*guṇabhūta*).

For instance, it is observed [in scripture]: "He offers the flour-meal," "He offers to the Maruts," and "He offers the cake on one potsherd. But the opponent (the proponent of the prima facie view) says: "The status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) follows from the benefit [conferred] as established through positive and negative concomitance; however, the accusative case-ending is inconsistent with predominance (*prādhānya*)."

Likewise, it is logical that the instrumental case is used when there is exclusivity (*ekāntika*). However, the accusative case is seen even when a substance is taught as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*) rather than as the primary object, as in "He offers the groats" (*saktūn juhoti*).
Similarly, in the injunction "He sprinkles the oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*," the primacy of the clarified butter (*ājya*) is observed even without the use of the accusative case.

Therefore, in the case of "one threshes the rice," even though both [the substance and the action] are possible, the primacy of the substance is established solely by the observation of its utility (*upakāra*), and not by the accusative case-ending, as was the case in the *Saktu-adhikaraṇa*.
And since that [purpose] does not exist in the case of sweeping, sprinkling, and so forth, one might argue that here too the accusative case should indicate the substance alone.
This is not so, because [the action] is for the sake of that [substance], as in common worldly usage, and because that [substance] is a subordinate element (*śeṣabhūta*).
Commentary: The accusative case is not used even when [the object] is a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*).
For those who are learned teach thus: "The second case ending is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), and "the object is that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*).
Furthermore, we do not observe the use of the second case ending for anything that is merely subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) in common usage.

As for the expression "Cook rice-grains for porridge" (*taṇḍulan odanaṃ paca*), it means "Prepare the rice-grains for the sake of porridge"; thus, the rice-grains themselves are indeed what is intended to be attained (*īpsita*).
The intention [of the speaker] in saying "make *balvaja* grass into tufts" (*śikhaṇḍaka*) is that it is the *balvaja* grass itself which is intended in that form.
Furthermore, worldly usage is the means for determining the meaning of words, not Vedic usage.

Regarding the worldly usage "he offers" (*juhoti*), where the accusative case occurs, one can say that the usage refers to that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*): "Offer the rice-grains" (*taṇḍulān juhudhi*), meaning "connect the rice-grains with the oblation."

In common worldly usage, there are indeed many types of intended meanings (*vivakṣā*), and it is improper for a single word to have multiple referents; therefore, while the accusative case is established as denoting the primary status (*pradhānabhāva*), it is here conceived as denoting the subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*). But how can there be a subordinate status in the Veda when the accusative is prescribed? From the prescription of the accusative, we understand precisely that there is primary status.
Thus, once primary status has been understood, it is realized that this primary status does not exist because of a more powerful reason.
Why? Because the status of the flour (saktu) as being for the sake of the oblation cannot be established in any way. Why? Because the flour has no purpose [other than that].
Neither is a final purpose for the flour seen nor is it heard in scripture.
If it were a *homa*, then even that *homa* for its sake would be purposeless. Alternatively, if the *homa* is an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), then it possesses a purpose;
for since it is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, its purposiveness is understood, and it cannot be said to be purposeless.
For that [purpose] is required by the injunctive statement of the performance (*prayoga-vacana*).
Now, one might object: "But surely even the groats will have a purpose through the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Who says they do not? They indeed have a purpose; however, their having a purpose consists in their accomplishing the oblation (*homa*), and not in any other manner.
The substance is not required by it;
rather, the procedure (itikartavyatā) is what is required.
And the oblation (homa) is the procedure, not the substance.
But surely, in the case of the oblation, an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) is produced from the flour-grains.
There is no proof for this.
But surely the accusative case-ending is the proof.
No;
the accusative case-ending indicates that the oblation has the groats as its purpose,
not that the groats themselves possess a purpose.
The oblation would have the flour-meal as its purpose; that is, the flour-meal would be for the sake of encompassing the oblation.
Thus, the flour-meal exists in the oblation as something produced by the oblation.
However, it is not tenable that the oblation has the flour-meal as its purpose when the flour-meal itself serves no further function.
However, the act of consuming the groats does not benefit the person, nor does it benefit the sacrifice; thus, it would be entirely purposeless.
Furthermore, nothing else can be inferred from that act of consumption.
It is that very accusative case ending which establishes the relationship between the groats and the oblation.

And since a relationship exists, by virtue of the rule "when substances are connected with an action, they are related as subordinate factors" (Pāṇini 2.3.19), and because they stand in the state of being subordinate, the third case ending [would apply].
Therefore, it is said that "the second case ending occurs in place of the third.

Consequently, because they are for that purpose—that is, because the groats (*saktu*) are for the sake of the oblation—they do not possess primacy, even though there is a connection with the second case ending.
This being the case, the statement is meaningful;
and since it serves that purpose, it is not meaningless.

Furthermore, that sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) possesses the status of a subordinate element (śeṣabhāva) in relation to the sacrifice and other rites; therefore, they possess a purpose, and in that regard, the consecration (saṃskāra) is not purposeless.
If that [benefit] does not manifest as a visible aid, it will be an invisible one.
It is understood from common worldly experience that there exists an invisible refinement (*saṃskāra*);
for example, it is said that when people arrive from another village, an invisible benefit is produced by the act of fumigation (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
And it does not attach itself to the world.
Furthermore, a purpose is heard in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices: "The ladles are made of *śamī* wood, or they are made of gold.

Since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the transcendental result (*apūrva*) is accomplished by the wiping with flour of various trees, the flour of various trees is used for the purpose of wiping; such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
According to the established conclusion (siddhānta), however, only those made of *śamī* wood or those made of gold are to be cleansed.
Likewise, even in cases where the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are equipped with arrows, *pālāśa* wood must be produced [for them].
This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In the established doctrine (siddhānta), only those [cakes] possessing handles are to be cleansed;
water is to be used for the cleansing.
Likewise, it is heard in scripture regarding the thirty-six-year sacrifice: "The sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) to be offered at the Soma-pressing are made of meat."

In that case as well, a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) made of flour should be prepared for the purpose of the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*); however, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is the meat itself that must be subjected to the *paryagnikaraṇa*.
Or rather, let the practical application (*prayoga*) be set aside for a moment.
What is the reason? Because it is a matter of custom; indeed, the practical application is everywhere superseded by the traditional law (*smṛti*).
"In this context, there is a multiplicity of intended meanings, whereas in the case of memory, there is a single form.
For if the teacher’s intention were uniform, the traditional texts (*smṛtayaḥ*) would certainly not need to be preserved with such effort; [this is discussed] in the section concerning *saktu*.
The section concerning the flour-meal (saktvadhikaraṇa):
that very [point], however, which was unclear due to the confused discussion, is established by means of the traditional interpretation (saraṇa).

The capacity of the second case is its primary meaning, as established by the rules "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) and "the object is that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*).
Thus it is employed in both common usage and the Veda, as in "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*) and "he threshes rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*).

As for those instances in poetry where a doubt regarding deviation [from this rule] might arise, the author of the Bhāṣya cites them: "Cook rice-gruel," "Make the peacock crests strong," and "Offer the rice-grains into the fire."

When the accusative case is employed in such expressions as "taṇḍulaiḥ" (with rice) and "balvajaiḥ" (with balvaja grass), it is understood that it certainly has the same meaning as the instrumental case.
All things such as rice, in their relation to cooking and so forth, possess two aspects; there, the accusative case will reside by taking up the aspect of predominance.

When the grains of rice (*taṇḍula*) are qualified by being the means for producing a crest of boiled rice (*odanaśikhaṇḍaka*), which is a distinct entity, then they take the form of words ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*).

But when rice grains are seen in the form of unspoiled food fit for eating, and when they are pounded with a pestle called a *śikhaṇḍaka* for the sake of producing softness— and likewise, when those [grains], whose status as subordinate factors (*guṇa*) is understood from Vedic sentences, are intended by some Brāhmaṇa woman for connection with the oblation in the *agnihotra* sacrifice performed with material substances (*dravyasādhanaka*), because of their loveliness and her desire to display the excellence of her own work— then she issues such an instruction as, "O sacrificer,
bring the rice grains and offer them," at which point it takes on the character of the accusative case.
"For in the world, there are many kinds of intentions to speak (*vivakṣā*).

Even when a thing is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), some aspect of its predominance may be intended to be expressed for some reason; likewise, even when it is predominant (*pradhānabhūta*), an aspect of its subordination may be intended. Sometimes both aspects are intended, and sometimes neither.
Furthermore, there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to suggest that a thing must be denoted by a word exactly as it appears [in reality].
The reality of the speaker's intention, however, involves resorting to other means such as indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth; it does not involve the abandonment of the primary meaning.
Therefore, primacy alone is the meaning of the accusative case.
(Thus concludes the investigation of the accusative case.)
) (Now, the principle of the groats: How, then, can there be subsidiarity (*guṇatva*) in the case of the groats and so forth? To this it is replied:
"Even there, the accusative case-ending itself expresses primacy (*prādhānya*)."
Due to contradiction, a connection with that [object] is indicated as being subordinate;
for the accusative case expresses primarily the status of being an object through its own power,
and since that is here opposed by a stronger alternative cause, it is not accepted.

However, because it consists of a specific factor of action (*kāraka*), that which is perceived as invariably concomitant with the general nature of a factor of action is intended [as such], since there is no contradiction.
In this regard, the meaning understood is simply this: "The groats are the factor of action for the oblation."

Furthermore, a universal devoid of particulars cannot serve as a basis for linguistic usage; thus, with respect to the particulars, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) will arise, according to the principle of the co-utterance of the already existent and the yet-to-be-existent, as in the rule: "In the case of substances [being] in conjunction with an action" (Pāṇini 6.1.1).

But how can there be an intention to express the predominance of the barley meal (*saktu*)? To this he says: "For a substance intended to be refined is held to be that which has utility in what is already existent or what is yet to be; but the barley meal will not be used by me, nor has it been used anywhere."
For when it is determined that a certain substance will have some utility at some point, it attains primacy with respect to the ritual action because it is worthy of being prepared (*saṃskāra*).

However, for that which has not been used or will not be used, preparation is purposeless; thus, there would be the consequence of such a statement being a rule for its [useless] preparation. And these parched grains (*saktu*) are not used prior to the oblation (*homa*), nor after the reduction to ashes, because there is no scriptural injunction regarding the employment of the ashes.

In this regard, since it has been established that either the entire sentence would become meaningless, or else there must be a secondary figurative function (*lakṣaṇā-vṛtti*) [of the word], one must accept *lakṣaṇā* for the sake of the authority of the Veda. For the primary sense (*mukhyārtha*) is the general rule (*autsargika*), and it is only through the observation of an exception (*apavāda*) that it is understood to be erroneous. Thus, the recourse to *lakṣaṇā* occurs everywhere as a consequence of the contingency of meaninglessness; otherwise, the primary sense would be logically consistent.
Because of that contradiction, the injunction for an oblation prepared with groats (*saktu*) is understood as being connected to the context.

[The Bhāṣya] says, "But surely, even the groats... (referring to the Pūrvapakṣa), meaning that even the groats, when accompanied by an oblation, will have purpose (*arthavat*) by being employed in the Jyotiṣṭoma.

However, the proponent of the Siddhānta [responds] through a quibble, asserting that only those things which serve as the means for the oblation possess purpose, as [the Bhāṣya] says: "Who says 'no'? (referring to the Bhāṣya).

And in all cases, there is no other purpose for substances than the accomplishment of the action connected with the sentence, because they lack connection with the "manner of performance" (*kathaṃbhāva*) and so forth. For example, since the oblation (*homa*) consists of an action, it requires [an answer to] "how? and is thus grasped by the primary manner of performance as a means of assistance; a substance, however, is not like this.
Therefore, there is no assumption of an unseen result (*ad�ष्टकल्पना*), because substances are brought about by action.

Even in cases where a substance is mentioned directly as the fruit, such as "for one desiring cattle, [the ritual] with the milking of cows," even there the *apūrva* will arise only through the mediation of another action that has a specific purpose; how much more so when the groats (*saktavaḥ*) are not heard of as being the object to be qualified? Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such an assumption.
If it is argued that the accusative case [indicates predominance], the answer in the Bhāṣya is "no" (*na hi*).

For the accusative, by declaring the predominance of the barley meal (*saktu*), would make the oblation (*homa*) for its sake; it does not, however, establish the barley meal as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) [of the action] as in the expression *saktum pibet*.
The flour (saktu) is the locus for the disposal;
therefore, by virtue of the accusative case ending, the oblation would be for the sake of the flour.

"How indeed might the groats (*saktu*) be for the purpose of the oblation?"—it is not for any other purpose, because none is heard [in the text]. And these [groats], as it is said in the *Bhāṣya*: "When the oblation has been performed, the groats become the remnants of the oblation" (*homavadāḥ*), have already reached their final status through the attainment of a purpose; thus, even though they are themselves without further purpose, their status as an object (*karman*) is established by virtue of mere primacy (*prādhānya*) with respect to the oblation.

Once the meaning of the sentence is thus established, one subsequently realizes that they are of no use either to the person or to the sacrifice; consequently, either an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) must be postulated on account of that statement, or the cognition of their primacy must be understood as an error.
Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "And it is not possible to assume anything else on the basis of that statement.
In this context, it is only logical to intend the primary status [of the agent].
Thinking that the instrumental case is thus established, the author of the Mahābhāṣya (Upavarṣa) stated: "The accusative is used in place of the instrumental" (Su. p. 632).

Therefore, there is indeed a disparity between the oblation (*homa*) and the cleansing (*saṃmārga*): because the groats (*saktu*) serve that purpose by being devoid of any other utility, whereas the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth, by virtue of being subordinate to another, have their function exhausted in the preparation of the offering and the like.
And when the meaning of the scripture is firmly established, even in the absence of a visible benefit, an invisible result (*adṛṣṭa*) will be postulated.

In the world as well, unseen effects (*adṛṣṭa*) are understood from established practice (*ācāra*), as for example: "for those who have performed the *śrāddha* at the edge of the village" (as stated in the Bhāṣya), where for the sake of peace, there is the circling of salt, curd, unbroken rice, and so forth, above the head, and their placement in a pure location (which is called "visible wood" in common parlance).
Nor is this untenable, because of the authoritative status of practice (*ācāra-prāmāṇya*).
Therefore, since even those things whose purpose is unseen are based on equal scriptural authority, the subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) of the groats (*saktu*) is established.

Now, if this were the case, then in all instances the predominance of the substance would be established by its purpose alone; thus, it would not be necessary to state "because of the equality of the verbal suffix" (2.1.4.10), or one would have to demonstrate that in those cases the predominance is established by the accusative case-suffix independently of purpose, or that the subordinate status is established solely by the instrumental case-suffix. To this, it is replied:

To begin with, regarding predominance: in the case of the injunction, "He worships with the verse addressed to Indra [using] the Gārhapatya fire," since there is a possibility of worshipping Indra by means of that [verse] due to its indicative power (*liṅga*)—as it is intended for Indra—and because of the syntactical connection (*vākya*) with the Gārhapatya, the predominance of the Gārhapatya is established solely by the presence of the accusative case-ending alone.

Similarly, in the case of "The *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *saktuvāk* [formula]," since both [the *prastara* and the *saktuvāk*] are equally purposeful, the fact that the *saktuvāk* exists for the sake of grasping the *prastara* is established solely by the presence of the instrumental case-ending alone.

Therefore, when the relationship of principal and subordinate is expressed by the case-endings themselves, the absence of a purpose constitutes an exception; however, the distinction is that the status of principal and subordinate is not determined by the mere presence or absence of a purpose.
(This is the *saktu-nyāya*).
As for the purpose of the topic (*adhikaraṇa*), they do not fully accept it.
For instance: "By restating the mere *śūla* (spit) and so forth, the *śamī* wood and other materials are enjoined;

it is understood from the previous established conclusion (*siddhānta*) and the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that these are for the sake of both the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*) rites.

Indeed, since [the subsidiaries] are known from their originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*) as being solely for the sake of the principal, it is logical that they do not occur in the *agra* offerings."

However, the use of *śamī* wood and so forth, being enjoined as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the ladle (*sruva*) and other implements in general, is understood to pertain to both the subsidiaries and the primary rite. This is because, according to the principle "Or rather, [the injunction] applies to all, since the status of being a subsidiary is not restricted in that way" (3.7.12), the strength of syntactical connection (*vākya-saṃyoga*) overrides the fact that the purpose would otherwise be understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*) as belonging to the primary rite alone.

Furthermore, no qualifying attribute is mentioned here by which there could be an understanding of the ladle and other implements as pertaining solely to the primary rite; even if such a qualification existed, it would not be intended (*avivakṣita*), as it would merely serve as a qualifier for that which is being referred to (*uddiśyamāna*).

Therefore, even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), those things connected with the primary sacrifice, such as the ladles (*sruva*) and so forth, as well as those means for the remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) such as the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) and so forth—all these are prescribed as being made of *śamī* wood; thus, the cleansing with flour from various trees is established.

It might be argued: "Or rather, it refers to the primary meaning, because the subsidiary is not enjoined" (*3.8.19.36*). Since the specific details of the modified sacrifice (*vaikṛta*) serve only the purpose of the primary, there will be no application here to both the subsidiary and the primary. That is incorrect.
"Where a connection with the primary meaning conveyed by the sentence is perceived, there this [principle] is stated; but here such a thing is not perceived.

For it will be stated [at 3.8.19.35–36]: "The optional sacrifices (*kāmyā iṣṭayaḥ*) are indeed for the sake of the sacrifice; they are to be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). Indeed, the quality of being performed in a low voice, when connected with the primaries denoted by the word "optional," is not enjoined as belonging to the subsidiary (*aṅga*).
And there is no such connection with the primary [act] here; thus, there is a disparity.

Now, one might object: since it is extended by analogy (*atideśika*), when the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) are in a state of not yet being established, the quality of being made of *śamī* wood and so forth, which is being enjoined, must be for the sake of the primary act alone. This cannot be so.

For it would be thus: "The modified [elements], having their requirements for assistance already met by the archetypal [elements], first connect with those archetypal elements that are proximate and enjoined;
and since it is impossible to enjoin multiple matters simultaneously, the ladles and other items are merely restated."
Therefore, although it is directly perceived, the instruction awaits the extended application (atideśa) for the time being; therein,
for as long as it takes for the primary offerings such as the Soma and others [to be established],
this is the section concerning the flour-meal (saktu-adhikaraṇa).

By that alone, even finger-rings and the like would be obtained; thus there is no distinction. Furthermore: "If the connection with the *śamī* wood and so forth were established by the primary [sacrifice] alone, then the archetypal [elements] such as the *prayāja* offerings would necessarily follow in the modified [sacrifices]."
For if the very same means used for the exclusion of the *samāṅguli* were to apply here, then by that same means the exclusion of the *prayāja*s and other elements would also follow;
however, this is not desired because there is no logical justification for it.

Furthermore, even if something were to occur due to its connection with the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*) alone, nevertheless, since its accomplishment would occur through *prasaṅga* (incidental benefit) according to the principle of the Soma-altar and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it is not appropriate to include the archetypal (*prākṛta*) expiations.
Furthermore: "The nature [of the paridhi] is indicated by its very function;
how could there be a wiping of that which has no function, namely the paridhi?"
The term *paridhi* refers to a substance intended for the purpose of encircling;
likewise, the *juhū* and other vessels are intended for the purpose of offering oblations (*homa*).

In that regard, it can also be argued that the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*) is not a motive (*aprayojaka*), according to the rule: "And [an action] whose purpose is already expressed [is not a motive]" (PMS 4.1.1.126).

And therefore, regarding the scriptural injunction for the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) as in the case of the recitation (*vācana*): if one were to rub [the sticks] while they are still unenclosed—such as the *palāśa* wood and others—they would be rubbed while remaining unenclosed. If, on the other hand, one also encloses them, then the rule for the *arvā* (the horse) with its qualities is established; thus the number [is determined].

The rule regarding [marriage] with one of the same lineage (*sagotra*) is a direct injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*). Bālakrīḍā, p. 22. "One of the same lineage (*sagotrā*) is not to be married"—this is to be inferred from the *Smṛti*.

Bālakrīḍā, p. 29. Furthermore, it is recorded in the *Smṛtis* that even among those born of mixed castes (*saṃkara*), through successive improvement of status, they attain the rank of one of the [four] primary castes in the seventh or fifth generation.

In this matter, however, one must rely on this much which is based on scripture; for this lack of restriction regarding human effort is not something accessible through worldly means of valid cognition.

In the *Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa* (1.2.1.2, p. 109), having cited the sentence, "Having sacrificed with rice (*vrīhi*), one should sacrifice with rice until [the next] *Āgrayaṇa*; having sacrificed with barley (*yava*), one should sacrifice with barley until [the next] *Āgrayaṇa*," a doubt is raised as to whether this prescribes a repetition of the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice or a restriction of materials for the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*. Having deliberated thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by the sūtra: "Because it is read in the context of the *āgrayaṇa*, the injunction is for the repetition of the *āgrayaṇa*: 'having sacrificed at the rice-āgrayaṇa, one should sacrifice again at the rice-āgrayaṇa'; thus, 'having sacrificed with rice, one should sacrifice with rice until [the next] *āgrayaṇa*' is a rule for the repetition of the *āgrayaṇa* due to the context. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is established by the sūtra: "'Or rather, [it applies] to the Darśapūrṇamāsa, because of the connection with the interval; it enjoins what was not previously perceived. Since, if it were a rule for repetition, there would be the fault of *vākyabheda* (splitting the sentence) due to enjoining multiple qualities—namely the repetition and the material—at a ritual action already established; and since, if it were a rule for a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*), there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*); and since rice and barley are already obtained as optional alternatives for the ritual called Darśapūrṇamāsa by virtue of being the archetype (*prakṛti*) of the current *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice; therefore, this sentence is for the purpose of prescribing a restriction regarding the sequence of barley and rice during the performance of the *āgrayaṇa* within that context. Thus, it will be concluded that this sentence enjoins a restriction on the materials for the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* itself, based on their connection to the intervening period.
Su. Pṛ. 145–146: As he will state in the *Saṃkarṣa* that "the wife is heard of as being equal [to the husband]," (Bhāṣya 1.2.1.12);
and as he will state in the *Saṃkarṣa* under the section on the purification of women that "[the Vanaspati offering] belongs to the woman," (10.4.16.32).

By the principle of the fourth chapter, second quarter, first section of the *Saṃkarṣa*—"The [quality] is to be understood from the archetype" (*prakṛtitaḥ*)—because of the commonality of being an *anuvacana* (recitation), there is the application of the *ṛc*s (verses) obtained through the *codaka* (transference rule) when the *kāmya-anuvacana* (optional recitation) possesses the same nature as the obligatory (*nitya*) recitation which serves as its archetype.

Ku. 3|1|1|122: The *saṃkalpa* (solemn resolve) pertains only to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, not to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other preliminary rites. Ḍupū. 10|1|2|4: In the *saṃkalpa*, one must mention the possibility of optional alternatives (*vaikalpikatva*). Su. p. 996:

Because of the rule that, according to the sequence of the synonyms for *saṃkalpa*, one should perform exactly that which was resolved among the optional elements—even if they are unknown—one incurs an indistinct expiation (*prāyaścitta*) even for the ritual act itself if there is a transgression of that [resolve].

... because at the very time of undertaking the ritual action (*karmopakrama*), optional rites (*vaikalpika*) whose names are known must be accepted with the thought, "I shall perform this very one"; therefore, when there is a transgression of a subsidiary (*aṅga*) that has been so accepted, the rule for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed. (Su. p. 996). That which has been resolved upon once cannot be resolved upon again. (Vārttika 3.2.1.132). For those who have performed the resolution once, a second performance is not required.
bhā. 6|6|1|14. vā. 1|3|7|17. *Saṃkoca* (contraction) means the fixing of a specific cognition produced by a scriptural statement (*śruti*) upon that very particularity.
soma. 3|1|10. A contraction that is inherently required [by the context] does not constitute a sublation (*bādha*), even if it is carried out in accordance with another [text].
parākrama.: 29|1. *Saṃkramayajña* (the transference sacrifice).
"One desiring food should sacrifice with the *saṃkrama* sacrifice"—this refers to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) themselves as qualified by a specific accessory (*guṇa*).
The result arises from that accessory of those very two sacrifices, not from a separate ritual action.
(Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 2.3.14–19). Summary.

"Therefore, for the sake of both detailed exposition and concise summary, even the subtlest portions of the path are employed in the commentary; thus, this or that has been composed. (Vākyapadīya 3.2.1, p. 651). Number, when expressed by a verbal suffix, is perceived as the agent alone, and not as any other *kāraka*.
Number is understood as being inherent in the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-vacana*).
For example, when it is said, "Bring the animal" (*paśum ānaya*), only one is brought;
when "the two animals" (*paśū*) is said, two are brought; and when "the animals" (*paśūn*) is said, many are brought.
Bhāṣya 4.1.5.13: There is a doubt as to whether the number of that which is being pointed out (uddiśyamāna) is intended to be significant (vivakṣita) or not.
The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that it is not.

Vārttika 1.3.12.13–16: In the case of the "upādeya" (that which is to be taken up), the number is intended to be significant, as in "one should sacrifice with an animal" (paśunā yajeta) and "one should immolate an animal" (paśum ālabheta).
VI. 4|1|5. Number alone is the qualifier of the agent.

Since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is characterized by a sequence of prior and posterior [moments], and since even in the case of a word (*pada*) there is an absence of the action characterized as being conducive to the acquisition of another [object], it does not imply the agent. Or, even if there were such implication, because the number denoted by the suffix (*pratyaya*) is understood only after the meaning of the verbal root has been known, and because the knowledge of the agent occurs at the same time as the knowledge of the number—being separated [from the root-meaning] by the recollection of the *tiṅ* affix and its meaning—the status of being a qualifier of the agent would be untenable due to occurring at a later time than the knowledge of the number. If, however, one were to admit the knowledge of the agent prior to the number according to the logic of number [as applied here]:

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, since the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is understood to belong to an agent who does not depend on a specific number, it is logical that even the singularity [of the agent] may be abandoned—just like other subsidiary elements—in the event of incapacity by one person. Furthermore, because there is the possibility of multiple sacrificers, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *pratipad* verses associated with duality and plurality would otherwise be undermined. Therefore, the number alone is the qualifier of the agent, and the agent is not the qualifier of the number. (Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 1401). Number is a means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for the differentiation of ritual acts; Vedic instruction is verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*). (Bālakrīḍā, p. 8). Number is the differentiator of ritual acts.
"And because it inheres in a plurality [of substrata], number is distinct from other qualities.
Number, which inheres simultaneously in multiple [substances] as they arise, is distinguished from other qualities that do not exist previously. Vākyapadīya 2.1.126, p. 620. Number.

Just as there is a fixed rule that in some cases the agent (*kartṛ*) is the expressed meaning (*vācya*) of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), while in others it is the object (*karman*), so too it is logical—by virtue of the power of words—that in some cases number (*saṃkhyā*) associated with the agent is expressed, and in others it is associated with the object. (Sphuṭārthā, p. 1400). It should be understood, however, that when the production [of an action] is understood through one or another of these five factors [such as other words, etc. via an injunction (*vidhi*), then number—which makes known the multiplicity of productions belonging to that injunction—brings about the mutual distinction between the actions themselves precisely by being enjoined within its own sentence.

Śā. 2|1|1: Number, however, because it subsists by way of inherence in a plurality (vyāsajya-vṛttitva) and lacks residence in a single [substratum], is capable of arising even in actions that are already occupied by another number, through its appearance and disappearance; thus, being unable to project the production of an action qualified by itself, once the production of the action has been determined by another means of knowledge, it merely conveys multiplicity. Su. p. 541. Number is a substance-property; it is fulfilled only by distinct substances and not by subsisting in a single substance. Vi. 10|1|56: Number, such as duality and so forth, is of a collective nature (vyāsajya-vṛtti).
Su. pṛ. 164: Number is the means of proof for the distinction between properties.

Maṇi. pṛ. 12: Number resides in separateness (*pṛthaktva*). In that regard, number is applicable to substances that possess the nature of being distinct and which are the substrata of a single action, as in the expression, "Let ten jars be brought."

Or [as stated in] Śābarabhāṣya 5.3.12: Just as number is non-restrictive (aviśakta) in the case of "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), so too is gender non-restrictive in the case of "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*) according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Śābarabhāṣya 6.1.3: Number, when being enjoined, is enjoined as a delimiting factor due to its suitability.
Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 96: Because number is the meaning of the word, it is intended to be significant in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*).
Bhāṣya 4.1.6: One number does not exclude another number.
Within the syllables delimited by the number eight, there are two constituent parts consisting of the number twenty-four.
For one who has ten cows, he has two groups of five cows.
Therefore, one number excludes another number. Bhāṣya 8.1.15. Number:
by means of indication (lakṣaṇā), it functions in connection with gender for all [entities].
Ḍupū. 12|1|11: For a number functions by means of some connection with a particular subordinate property;
10|7|12|11. Even when a specific grammatical number is not intended to be expressed, whatever number follows must be conveyed by that very expression.
For example, even when stated as a defining characteristic, "one born of the Brāhmaṇa caste is not to be killed," [the singular number is understood].

The designation is not made by means of a dual ending, as in "two Brāhmaṇas are not to be killed" (Bhāṣya 10.3.1.140). For number serves to distinguish the origin [of the action], as in "three oblations," and so forth (Vārttika 2.1.5.16, p. 507). In the verb, only the number residing in the agent is understood, not that residing in anything else.
Su. Pṛ. 1399: And the agent implied by that [action] is also [denoted]; with respect to the determination [of the action], number is intended [to be expressed] as the means of determining it.
Soma. 6.1.2: It has been stated that number is not capable of implying specific distinctions between actions and their factors (kārakas).
Vā. 3.4.1.3, p. 929: Furthermore, the acquisition of its own nature by number is not possible without [the notion of] separateness (pṛthaktva).
Furthermore, a number that has been fulfilled by repetition does not become a distinct [independent] number;

for it is resorted to only as referring to specific elements such as the *prayāja* and *upasad* offerings which have a fixed measure. (2.1.7.21, p. 522). Moreover, one number does not reside within another number.
For number is a quality (guṇa), and qualities do not reside in qualities.
Bhāṣya 8.1.6.14; for number resides in separateness (pṛthaktva).

As in the case of "eight jars" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.17), if one and six were to produce a different number, namely the number seven, through aggregation (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.29). For the number that belongs to the word *juhoti* (he offers) will indeed pertain to the agent, and not to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) or the objects.
Vārttika 2.1.7.21, p. 522: For those things that have a connection with some one [factor], the number enters into that single factor of connection.
In that case, that single related factor must be mentioned, or it should be understood from the context, or that which follows from the sense of the matter should be adopted.
Bhāṣya 10.3.1.144: Number, while delimiting the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), becomes subordinate (*aṅgī*) to the action (*karman*).
8.16.15: By the principle stated in [PMS] 2.1.7.21, "Number causes a distinction in the action," these are twelve sacrifices (*dvādaśayāgāḥ*).
Ḍuṣpūra 9.1.8.32: "Number causes a distinction in the action" (2.1.7).

By this principle—that the word "number" [indicates a distinct action] according to the rule at Sūtra 2.2.1—"the number twelve" denotes twelve sacrifices in the context of the *dvādaśāha* (twelve-day rite).
(1.4.5.18) Number constitutes a distinction of actions, as in: "He offers three oblations."

Vārttika 2.2.5.16, p. 507: There is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the mantras prescribed by number (*saṃkhyā*) in the *Abhicayana* sacrifice. See the section (*adhikaraṇa*) on "Number in the *Abhicayana*" at Mīmāṃsākośa 1.3.14.30, p. 51. And here, the [mantras] under discussion belong to various classes (*nānājātīya*).
Among these, there would be a connection with number,
as in "Let a hundred be given," where a hundred of things belonging to a single class is meant, not things of different classes—
as in the case of substance, quality, action, part, and so forth.

Mā [on Jaimini Sūtra 10.3.1.144]: It is understood from another means of knowledge that the injunction, being an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), possesses multiple objects; this much alone is understood from the number.
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 561). This is the very inherent nature of number: that it resides in distinct things that are mutually connected.
Any other quality is brought under control by each [quality] independently of the others;
and for one who does not understand the attainment of number therein, there will be ten of its own kind for each, such as cattle, horses, and so forth.
Therefore, there are seventeen sacrifices.
But surely, in a single sacrifice, one will sacrifice with seventeen groups of portions (avadāna), because of the scriptural statement;
for that number is heard in reference to the animals, not to the groups of portions.

The portions (*avadāna*) and the oblations (*havis*) are the means of accomplishing the sacrifice, not the animal form itself. That [animal form] qualifies the substance which is the original material for the portions, just as it assisted the primary rite in the archetype (*prakṛti*); likewise, in the ectype (*vikṛti*), it will assist the primary rite by qualifying the substance which is the original material for the portions.
