And in that case, the number seventeen modifies the animal, not the group of portions.
Therefore, for a single set of portions (*avadānagaṇa*), only one animal is to be obtained;

in that case, the number seventeen would not be applicable. It would only be possible [to maintain] this [number] if the terms were intended to refer to horns, colors, or forms—such as "seventeen animals: white, black, red," and so forth—and any one of these were selected.
Alternatively, one of those such as the *tuṣpara*, the horned, or the single-horned is taken;
for they are indeed firm in nature and are heard of in scripture as being uniform in form.
Therefore, this [number] applies to many sacrifices, not to a single one;
thus, there are seventeen sacrifices. The practical implication is that if a single cup (*graha*) is defiled, the entire group of animals (*paśugaṇa*) must be repeated.

If one animal were being sacrificed while another were not being sacrificed, it would serve an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha) in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa). In the established conclusion (siddhānta), however, there is only a single animal;
for when there is a difference in ritual acts, one animal does not require another animal.
Or rather— having already discussed the non-distinction [of action] from the word through repeated practice,
the distinction of number is now being considered.

In this regard, examples of its own number are provided by such [injunctions] as "he offers three oblations" and "he offers twelve sets of twelve," which are enjoined in grammatical apposition with the actions arising [from them].

Since the injunction is heard as "he offers once," and since the act is a single action, it might be argued that the requirement for the number [eleven] will be fulfilled through repetition; however, this must be refuted.
Here, the connection with the number is heard in relation to the oblation as it is being produced, not after it has been produced—as in the case of "eleven *prayāja*s.
Furthermore, a number cannot attain its own existence without distinctness.

Nor does a number that has not been manifested [by a word] become connected [with the action]. For that [number], being restricted to a specific measure, must be resorted to as referring to the *prayāja* offerings, the *upasad* rites, and so forth.
And in this case, since no other number has been previously determined, the distinction exists by its very nature.
Therefore, this [number] must be understood as residing in the distinctness of the actions themselves, and not based on the distinctness of repetitions.
As he will state later: "Or rather, in the case of coming, because repetition is not heard" (10.1.16).
But surely, since a single oblation is first determined by the word *juhoti*, it follows that the completion [of the number] must occur through repetition?

No, because the action denoted by the word *juhoti* (he offers) is of the nature of a non-substance (*asattvabhūta*) and therefore lacks number. Whatever number is present there in the word *juhoti*, it will indeed belong to the agent, not to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) or its substratum. In that case, while one might be about to infer a single offering based on the scriptural mention of "once" (*sakṛt*), one is restrained by the number heard as an inherent property of the word itself; accepting only what is delimited by that [inherent] number, one recognizes a difference in the essential form in every instance.
Therefore, there is a difference of ritual acts (*karmabheda*).

As for the example cited by the author of the Bhāṣya, "seventeen [animals] dedicated to Prajāpati," he intends to demonstrate by this very instance that even a number residing in the substance (*dravya*) effects a difference of ritual acts, thereby establishing what has not yet been seen.
Why is there doubt? It is said: [the reason follows].

"Is the *taddhita* suffix applied first and then the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) performed, or is the *ekaśe� Prajāpati* the deity of these [animals], then the *taddhita* suffix is applied to that which has been indicated by the *sarvanāman* (pronoun) through *ekaśeṣa*. In that case, there is only a single relationship between the seventeen substances and a single deity; thus, there is a single ritual act (*ekakarmatva*)."

Now, if one were to apply the rule of *sarūpaikaśeṣa* (retention of a single form) by first uttering "Prājāpatya" seventeen times—meaning "this has Prajāpati as its deity" (*prajāpatir devatāsya*)—and then forming the compound "Prājāpatyāḥ," then there would be seventeen distinct substances-deity conjunctions as separate entities; consequently, because of each such conjunction, there would be a difference in the acts of sacrifice (*yāga*).
What, then, is the prima facie view? That it is a single act.
Why? Because the plurality of the meaning of the suffix is directly perceived;
and since the formation of the *ekaśeṣa* (single remainder) is caused by that [plurality], it would not occur in the base form (*prakṛti*).
For he who performs the *ekaśeṣa* as "prājāpatyaḥ prājāpatyaḥ" (offspring of Prajāpati, offspring of Prajāpati) thereby accepts that [operation] for both the base and the suffix.
And the reason for this is that the plural expression would otherwise be inexplicable. Nor is it impossible to demonstrate the meaning of the suffix without *ekaśeṣa*,
because at the time of analysis (*vigraha*), [the compound] can be expressed by means of a pronoun.
Therefore, Prajāpati is connected with many deities even when heard only once.
Furthermore:
"The actions not explicitly mentioned [in one context] and their corresponding transcendental potencies (apūrva) are here [to be supplied from elsewhere]."
They will not be subject to further conceptualization, because when the purpose is accomplished, only a minimal conceptualization remains.
For even after forming a *ekaśeṣa* compound ending in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), that alone is not what is expressed;
subsequently, they will not conceptualize the examples as having ritual actions (*karman*) as their antecedents.
And it has been stated in the *Śabdāntarādhikaraṇa* (2.1.1) that those [factors] cannot be postulated according to one's whim;

only that much may be postulated by means of the subsequent hearing of the meaning— namely, just as much as is necessary for the connection between the enjoined substance and deity to be established— and nothing else.
Nothing more than that can be obtained.
One must postulate seventeen primary acts (*karmapūrva*) through the sequence of cutting and so forth.

In that regard, since at the very first moment all substances become possessed of sacrifice (*yāgavat*) by virtue of being performed as a single act and because there is no distinction in their nature, it is not possible for them to proceed further.
Furthermore: "The differentiation of one thing cannot occur through the differentiation of another;
the ritual action does not differ merely because of the differences among the heart and other portions.

For if the differentiation of actions were to arise from the differentiation of substances, then there would likewise have to be a differentiation [of the action] due to the differentiation of the substances offered, such as the heart and so forth.
And it cannot be so;
for [the author] will say: "Or rather, because of the unity of the substratum and the non-distinction of the word 'animal'" (6.3.12).

Furthermore, since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the entire animal serves as the means of sacrifice, when the question arises as to how this is so, it is understood from another scriptural statement that the sacrifice is to be accomplished by means of the animal through its being the source of the ten portions, such as the heart and so forth.
Therefore, that [quality] belongs to the substance (*dharma*), not to the sacrifice.

Here too, once it is understood that seventeen [animals] are the means of accomplishing the sacrifice, all properties (*dharma*) apply to each one individually; thus, even a single animal is taken as being like the group of seventeen sacrificial portions (*vadāna*) by extension (*atideśa*), and consequently, it is impaired.
When it is thus argued that "it is a single action" (*karma*), the following is said in reply:
"In the view that there is a single action (*ekakarmatva*), there would be only one *codaka* (archetypal injunction) here;

consequently, because only one group (*gaṇa*) would be obtained, there would be no inclusion of all the animals. For this sentence, 'the animals dedicated to Prajāpati' (*prājāpatyān paśūn*), does not terminate in [denoting] deityhood; rather, the remainder of the sentence has the purpose of indicating the archetypal model (*prakṛti*)."
And since there is a single action here, the *savanīya* would be the archetype;

and in that case, it follows by necessity that a single group of portions (*avadānagaṇa*) was the means for the sacrifice. Since that too was based on the quality of the desired singular number, it must be performed in exactly that same way.

Furthermore, since the rite is accomplished with a single animal, the other animals are connected to Prajāpati; thus, neither the plurality expressed by its own word (*svapada*) nor the number seventeen obtained from the sentence (*vākya*) is performed.
However, when the understanding arises that there are seventeen sacrifices, then sets of sacrificial portions (*avadānagaṇa*) with unmixed deities are obtained for each ritual act.

For the sake of accomplishing this, even though they are not explicitly mentioned in the text, seventeen additional animals are brought in; how much more so, then, regarding the inclusion of those that are actually mentioned?

But surely, it is not proper to abandon the oneness of the sacrifice established by direct perception (pratyakṣa) and instead postulate multiplicity merely to conform to the inferential injunction (codaka). Observe:
"At the time of the instruction regarding the sacrifice, there arises the conceptualization of it as being either one or many."
And by virtue of that, there is extension (*atideśa*) and not instruction (*upadeśa*), for it is upon that [instruction] that the latter depends.
For the determination of whether actions are one or many occurs at the time of their origination;
and origination is understood through direct instruction, not through extension.
For when there is inequality, the existence of the ritual action does not occur; and while that [inequality] exists, the extension [of the ritual rules] does not proceed.
Therefore, because the distinction [of the ritual] arises from the knowledge of the difference [in the procedure], it is not logical for the distinction to be established through extension.
To this it is replied: "When there is doubt, the determination [is made] from the remainder of the sentence; this was established previously [at 1.4.13].
And because of semantic competency (*sāmarthya*), both of those causes for determination are present here."
"In this case, we have not determined a difference in the ritual action (*karma-bheda*) by means of extended application (*atideśa*).
By what, then? By the direct instruction (*upadeśa*) regarding the *prājāpatya* offerings.
That [instruction], however, is determined solely in the form of the principle concerning the material, the deity, and the sacrifice."

The measure [of the potency] is a specific capacity mixed with effort; being directed toward the meaning presided over by that which remains from the doubt previously taught, it is determined by a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) consisting of an extended application (*atideśa*), as well as by a capacity corresponding to the apprehension of that [meaning].

And although that extended application occurs later, nevertheless, having understood that it will indeed occur here—as in the case of "it shall be so"—one concludes that the teaching possesses a meaning not inconsistent with it.

Consequently, even though the meaning of the sentence is concealed by the status of being related to Prajāpati and another procedure is commenced, nevertheless, because a contradiction is observed at the end, one does not conclude with full awareness that "I have grasped [the meaning] correctly from the beginning.

Nor is there any such mode here—such as the form of a conflict consisting in doubt regarding the application of the original injunction in accordance with the extended application (atideśa)—by which the extended application itself would proceed in conformity with the prior cognition.
For this [text] is not capable of enjoining seventeen groups of portions (*avadāna*) for a single ritual action as they are recited in the archetype;
nor is it capable of bringing seventeen archetypal substances into another group. Furthermore, there is no doubt here by which it might be set aside on account of a direct instruction (*upadeśa*).
Nor does there arise a contradiction of the extended application (*atideśa*) due to the absence of doubt, by which the attainment of a single group would be obstructed;
for a single ritual action has not been taught.
And wherever non-contradiction is possible, contradiction is not to be resorted to.
Furthermore, in this case, the lack of distinction can be established by accepting a multiplicity of ritual acts (*karma*).
Therefore, the statement of the instruction is expressed in this way:
the analysis of the compound is "Prajāpati is the deity of this," and there is a simultaneous utterance (*tantram*) of the seventeen [offerings].

And therefore, up to the seventeenth [chapter], this very [work] concerns the various forms of the primordial deity through their conjunction with other deities, insofar as they serve as the substrata for sacrifice.
As it has been stated: "In the ritual of the animal sacrifice, there is that which is called the 'eleven-fold cutting' (ekādaśāvadāna);
and although the rite is a single action, it is performed for each individual animal."
The claim that [the details] are transferred is incorrect. Why? Because "in this case, transfer based on the manner of the substance (*dravya-kathaṃbhāva*) is not possible."
The state of being produced by action (*karmodbhūtaḥ kathaṃbhāvaḥ*) receives the properties of the action.

For it is required [by the question], "How should one effect [the result] through the *prājāpatya* animal sacrifice? and not, "How with the animal?", because the substance, being directly perceived, has its manner of being already known.

Furthermore, even in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the property of the sacrifice consists in being accomplished by the group of eleven cuttings (*avadāna*) residing in a single animal, and not a property of the animal itself.
Because it would be fruitless.
For if that were its nature, the single [grain] would be refined by the purifications;
yet there would be no purpose served by it, because it has already been destroyed.

Once the sacrifice is established, it follows by implication that it must be accomplished either by means of a living being or by means of the *apūrva*; thus, all of this is adopted as the manner of its accomplishment.
Therefore, a single sacrifice is not capable of accepting multiple groups, nor, in the absence of such acceptance, can multiple animals be accepted.

Even though, in the case of the *avadāna* being the primary substance, one might think that it is sublated by a similar configuration and thus conceive that a single group produced from various animals should be taken;
nevertheless, eleven animals are required here, not seventeen. Not [seventeen].

Section on Number (Saṃkhyādhikaraṇa) 4082: The Established Conclusion (Siddhānta) regarding Number. And because of this, since [the number] is the correlate precisely when it is not delimited by a Bahuvrīhi compound, and since the delimiter of that correlativity resides in each individual [member], there is the cognition of a difference in the correlates; and through that difference, the difference in the relation is established.
Nor does the unity of the sacrifice persist despite a difference in the relations,

because the relationship— whether singular or plural— is established as a regulating factor by virtue of its scriptural authority and its superior strength according to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*).
Therefore, it is established that in accordance with that [scriptural evidence], there is a difference in the sacrifices and a difference in the productive operations (*bhāvanā*) everywhere.

And the purpose [of this discussion] is that, if there were only one sacrifice, then even upon the release of a single animal, since that [sacrifice] would have been completed, there would be no need to perform the sacrifice again;
such is the conclusion in the Siddhānta.
Maṇḍana [states]: "The number seventeen belongs to those who sacrifice with the Maitrī."
Śaṅkara: "This is a distinction of ritual acts based on number.
This refers to the *Saṃkhyādhikaraṇa* (Sūtra 4.1.16.1–16).
In the injunction "the animal for Agni-Soma," the singular number is intended to be significant.
The same applies to such cases as "He joins with non-marriage" (*anudvāhaḥ yunakti*) and "He sacrifices the Kapiñjala birds" (*kapiñjalān ālabhate*).
The section on number (*saṃkhyādhikaraṇa*) serves as a counter-example to the section on repetition (*abhyāsādhikaraṇa*). (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Bhāṣya 2.2)
The mantra for the number [of handfuls]:
4024. Regarding the number of handfuls:
in the Vājapeya sacrifice, for the *caru* consisting of seventeen *śarāva* measures, there is the inclusion of the number four by means of the smearing of the handfuls.
"But because it is subordinate to that, there should be an omission of the number due to the smearing with the fist.
Bhāṣya: There is the Vājapeya sacrifice, [enjoined] thus: "One desiring self-sovereignty should sacrifice with the Vājapeya in autumn.
Regarding this, it is heard: "There is a sevenfold measure of wild rice (naivāra), milk, and a skin."
However, in the archetype (prakṛti), there exist both a number and handfuls, as in the injunction: "He offers four handfuls.
Both of these are obtained through the extended application (codaka).

In this regard, a doubt arises: is it the favoring of the number with the omission of the handfuls, or the favoring of the handfuls with the omission of the number, or is it the omission of both the number and the handfuls, or the omission of one or the other?
What is established? That there is the elision of one or the other.

Whether it be in the case of the handfuls (*muṣṭi*) or in the case of the number (*saṃkhyā*). Why? Because a restriction (*niyama*) occurs only in the absence of a word that would effect such a restriction.
This being the case, we reply:
there should be the "clinging of the handful" (muṣṭilepa), and there should be the favoring of the number.
Why? Because the number is primary.
For the number falls first;
having understood that very number beforehand, one points to it as "endowed with the number" (saṃkhyāyukta). 4086–4087.
It is not untenable.

Therefore, since number is perceptible, its dimension is established through direct perception; having raised the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it is pervaded by both [dimension]—which is extended by analogy from the two dimensions—the refutation of that very [prima facie view] is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). It is precisely the existence [of number] that is the final position.
But the truth is known only to the Lord.
Maṇḍana says: "The number would be the smearing of the fist. Śaṅkara says: "The smearing of the fist is not the number."
29. In reality, however—the numbers co-referential with the word *muṣṭi* ending in the accusative case are intended as the objects of reference.

(10|2|8|65–68) The word *pada* refers to a heap of rice (*vrīhirāśi*) qualified by a specific measure (*parimāṇa*), as it is understood as the subject [of the injunction]: "The sacrificial oblation (*caru*) for Bṛhaspati consists of nine measures (*navāra*) and seventeen *śarāva* measures. Although the measure does not hold primary importance with respect to the number, since the four handfuls (*caturmuṣṭi*) prescribed for the pouring of the original oblation (*prakṛta*) apply to the modified oblation (*vikṛti*) by virtue of the extended application (*codaka*), nevertheless—because the number serves to delimit the measure, and because the measure, being more intimately related (*antaranga*) as the delimiter of the substance, cannot be set aside when the oblation filling seventeen *śarāvas* is obtained through those four handfuls—it follows that the number must be intended as the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) therein.
In the case of the number 4088, when it has been accumulated,
there is a connection with the gender of the base in that enumeration;
for it is not possible to enjoin a quality upon a mere number.
For there is no one for whom some number does not exist.
Bhāṣya 10.4.47.
This is the principle of the excellence or defect of the connection.
This is analyzed according to its states (*paya*).
To explain: "When it is merely existing and merely situated, even its name as 'milk' is not known; yet that very same substance, when placed upon a lotus stalk, shines with the form of a pearl.
Having fallen into the belly of a sea-oyster in the ocean, it becomes a pearl; generally, its quality—whether inferior, middling, or superior—is produced through association."
Thus [ends the section on] rashness. 635.
Association.
"In this chapter and likewise in this section, the logical connections (*nyāyasaṃgati*) have been severed;
once the connection with the treatise (*śāstra*) is understood, the connection with reality (*tattvasaṃgati*) is stated.
Thus, the connection is threefold: the connection with the treatise (*śāstrasaṃgati*), the connection with the chapter (*adhyāyasaṃgati*), and the connection with the section (*pādasaṃgati*).
VI. Introduction, Verse 10:

"Having carried over the general connection (*saṃgati*), one should carry over the intermediate connection (*āvāntarasaṃgati*), as well as the refutation (*ākṣepa*), the method (*paddhati*), the application (*prayoga*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), and so forth."

When a topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) is applied by virtue of its connection to the subject matter expounded in the scripture and so forth, that topical section is designated as "connected to the scripture" (*śāstrasaṃgati*). [For example:
Jyotis, Viśvajyotis, Sarvajyotis...

Because of the difference in names—such as "the *triṣṭubh* and other *stomas* of this [sacrifice]" as indicated by the scripture, and the name "*jyotis*"—there is a difference in the ritual acts (*karmabheda*).

The commentary states that by another means of knowledge, namely the form of verbal co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the word "light" (*jyotis*) [is understood]. It is heard in scripture: "Now this is the Jyotis, this is the Viśvajyotis, and this is the Sarvajyotis;

one should sacrifice with this [rite] which has a thousand-fold sacrificial fee. The meaning is that [the term] expresses the *stoma* figuratively, not through the primary power of the word itself. 1) It is not by the word alone that [it denotes] "all light."

But where that other means of knowledge does not exist, there it cannot increase [the application]. Here there is a doubt: is the original Jyotiṣṭoma mentioned by these names—as in "Devadatta is a lion," where the word "lion" refers to Devadatta, and therein qualities such as a thousand-fold sacrificial fee are enjoined—or rather, is it [the sacrifice] to be described later?
It is not by another means of knowledge; rather, where it is said "one should wear a lion's skin," there indeed other specific rites are enjoined.
What is the conclusion?
There is no other means of knowledge [to establish this].

Therefore, because of the inclusion within the context (*prakaraṇa*), "Viśvajyotis" and "Sarvajyotis" are not injunctions of qualities for the sacrifice under discussion; rather, they are names of the Jyotiṣṭoma. However, [one might object] that this is contradicted by the syntactical connection (*vākya*). But [the reply is] that it is indeed the Jyotiṣṭoma that is being spoken of.
If it is argued that these qualities are not enjoined for the Jyotis and other [sacrifices] by virtue of the Jyotiṣṭoma’s capacity, this is not so;
it is stated that all [these] are distinct rituals.
This is the fault: these are expressive of the Jyotiṣṭoma;
[namely], "jyotis" and so forth.

Or rather—because of the extensive deliberation and with reference to the distinction between the sections on the subordinate qualities (*guṇa-prakaraṇa-bheda*), the name "Viśvajyotis" is employed as a designation for the Jyotiṣṭoma;
this much is cited as an example.
In that context, in the passage beginning with "Now this is the Jyotis," the *triṣṭubh* and other meters are mentioned in the supplementary portion of the text (*vākyaśeṣa*) as its "lights."
These [terms]— *śabda*, *adayaḥ*, *pūrva-prakṛta-apekṣatvāt*, *prakṛta-hāni-aprakṛta-prakri*, *sarvāṇi asya*— are all [to be supplied].
Therefore, this is the Viśvajyotis, the Sarvajyotis, the Jyotis...
Due to the weakness of the name and because even a single [element] [is present], as in the case of the Dākṣāyaṇayajña and others, it follows that this is indeed an Agniṣṭoma.
This being the position reached, we reply:
for there are three names.

Because, through the connection with qualities (*guṇa*), it is established that there are multiple names for the same [sacrifice] in the *māna* [section]. Nor are those [names] merely indicative of qualities or results; they are [the names of sacrifices] such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
For these [factors] pertain to the originative injunction (*utpattikāvya*).

When there is a sentence focused on a connection, another action and a new transcendental result (*apūrva*) are heard from that other action; these, however, are not mere restatements (*punarśruti*) of them.

Therefore, for that purpose, this [passage]— along with the injunctions for rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, whose performance is otherwise not explicitly heard— is postulated as the sentence enjoining the ritual action known as the Jyotis. Anu-...

They will exist. And with respect to the state of being [thus], the Jyotiṣṭoma— since there is indeed a statement regarding a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)— would have its purpose fulfilled by producing a specific modification of the performance of the archetype (*prakṛta*).
If one were to accept [the former view], it would be contradicted;
nor would there be an option between the injunction of another action and the injunction of a quality. Therefore, in that case, there would be sublation.
Nor is there any purpose served by the word "va" (or) referring back to what precedes;
for the seasonal sacrifices such as the Jyotis and others are not illuminated by the Jyotiṣṭoma.
There are other composite wholes; they depend upon another result. Furthermore, we shall explain later that there is no specific sequence among the seasons.
Nor does another whole [word] consisting of a part identical [to the first] have that same meaning;
therefore, even in some cases, there is no hearing of the word *nātha*.
It occurs [thus].
Just as the word *śālā* denotes a house, so too the term *saṃjñā* does not express cultivation (*bhāvanā*), nor does it denote the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Furthermore,
because of their commonality with words such as *yajati* (he sacrifices), even words like *mālā* (garland) do not come to denote a house.
It does not enter into the substance [of the rite], by which there might be a cognition of its difference [from the Jyotiṣṭoma].
Nor is this [name] injunctive, since it is merely taken as a symbolic designation (*pratīka*) for the Jyotiṣṭoma, such that "Jyotis" refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma.
If it were injunctive, it would urge a person toward a different ritual action (*karmāntara*) prescribed by the Vedic revelation.

Nor is there a distinction [of the sacrifice] for a single person indicated there by the word "Jyotiṣṭoma" through indirect indication (*parokṣa*), as is the case with the singularity of the cup (*grahaikatva*);
for that would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in that context.
That [injunction] is of one kind with the word "light" (jyotis) as a perceptible [object];
it falls upon the form of the action which implies qualities and so forth.
Nor is the syntactical unity (vākyatā) sublated;
and this is not reasonable,
for the sentence [depends on] the context (prakaraṇa).
If it were dependent on the sentence of the *ced*-clause, then the distinction would arise only from repetition; however, [the direct statement] is stronger.
Furthermore, it is so because of its illuminating nature (*dyotanārthatva*) or because of its being the "Light" (*jyotiṣṭamatva*).
Furthermore, the connection with the fruit will reside in a distinct ritual action according to the principle: "But [the connection with the fruit occurs] in proximity because there is no separation.
Just as in the case of the *triṣṭubh* and other meters in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, that [connection] does not produce the notion of a separate ritual action.
If it is argued that, like the "milk-pail" (*dadhi-doha*) and other such offerings, the terms *viśvajyotis* and *sarvajyotis* denote the entirety [of the sacrifice], we say: no.
For we shall explain that the fruit resulting from the thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*sahasradakṣiṇā*) and so forth—which belong to the context of the primary rite—is indeed intended.
Furthermore, the word *jyotis* is not well-known in the sense of the *triṣṭubh* and other meters.
Thus,
there is a difference in the ritual procedure (*karmāntara*) for the *sānnāyya* offering.
However, in the case of the *jyotis* and other sacrifices, there is this further distinction.
If one were to speak [of it as such], one would contradict what is well-known.
As for the claim that the word "light" (jyotis) [refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma] because of the supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa),
that is merely a means of bringing about the cognition [of the sacrifice] by virtue of its being a part of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

"Likewise, in the statement regarding the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and so forth": it is understood through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that in that very same sentence, that [term] is employed there [in that specific sense], as in "Every spring, with the *Jyotiṣṭoma*" (*vasante vasante jyotiṣā*), where its employment in that context is perceived [through the supplementary passage]: "These indeed are those *jyotiṣas*..."
It is observed.

Therefore, since there is an absence of a subsequent word, a number, a prior action, connection, a quality, or a different context, it follows that there is non-difference; yet, this being the prima facie position, it is stated: "When a ritual term is not accompanied by a [prior] injunction, whatever name is first applied..."
And because they have the same object, there would be an option (vikalpa), and that is improper;
for that [notion] cannot be removed in any way by the cognition of another entity distinct from the action.
But this fault does not apply in the case of an interval [of time].

Nor is the result derived from a secondary quality (*guṇa*), for that technical designation (*saṃjñā*) which operates once the previously uttered verbal form (*ākhyāta-śabda*) has arisen is possible because it lacks an interrupted substratum.

When, prior to the connection with the action being introduced, a determination has already been made— either toward difference or non-difference— by means of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) regarding the connection with the action, or by means of the sentence (*vākya*) regarding the name, quality, fruit, and so forth, then a subsequent [element] arising later would not cause a division. This, however, is the case for that which is being introduced...

On account of the context, it is therefore also a separate ritual action. Furthermore, the name [Jyotiṣṭoma] applied to the Jyotis and other [forms] does not, like the name "Saṃyukta," reside in a sense of distinctness.
How so? In every case, it is a constituent part of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
For it is improper for two words—such as *ṛk* and *antara*, or *rathantara* and *bṛhat*—which denote multiple meanings, to function as names [of specific rites], since such usage is not observed.
It is established as such.
As for the statement, "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma in spring," it requires another [contextual factor].
Furthermore, because a different name is observed, there is a difference in meaning; thus, both [conditions] apply.

Thus, since the application [of the rule] is observed, it is sublated by the recognition that sublates it, because its strength is derived from being understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This is how it should be viewed.
And there is no such other means of valid cognition here by which this cognition of fatness— unsublated for as long as the cognition of the body does not exist—
is understood to have that [body] as its object;
it simply remains.

Therefore, in this context, the application of the term *jyotis* (light) to the *triṣṭubh* and other meters—which immediately follows the interrupted discussion of the *jyotiṣṭoma*—is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), because it occurs within the same syntactical unit (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as the subsequent mention of another name, "Now this is the *go*" (*athaiṣa gauḥ*). Since that [figurative usage] does not produce a mental impression there, it does not apply to all instances; rather, it serves only to convey a meaning that pleases one's own mind.
It is so obtained;
for instance: "The word 'lion' produces a cognition of some internal quality.
In that case, that designation would apply to this object even before it has arisen."
Because it is a measure (māna), it has been determined [as such].
Even though it is heard in the context of non-existence (asat), as many *yajati*s as were previously uttered in the measure are all understood as being for the purpose of the Jyotiṣṭoma;
thus, its meaning is fully grasped.

Therefore, because it functions within a single, uninterrupted stream of consciousness by adopting its primary meaning, it is established that this is not a distinct technical term (*saṃjñā*), as it is determined to have that very [consciousness] as its object; and from being a distinct technical term, its distinctness [as a separate entity] is obtained.
As it is being introduced,
that [sacrifice] is designated as the *medha*.
Although the *Jyotiṣṭoma* is the archetype (*prakṛti*), even if the injunction is occupied elsewhere with the fruit or the accessory (*guṇa*), it does not [apply] by way of that [archetype].

It is heard [in the scripture]: "Now this is the Jyotis; now this is the Viśvajyotis; he is thus established. Even so, because of the improper application of the word *go* (cow) in the preceding context, and because the cognition of that [previous] sacrifice does not arise when the context has been interrupted, [it is said]: "Now this is the Sarvajyotis; one should sacrifice with this [rite] which has a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*sahasradakṣiṇa*).
Thus, [the new rite] is born as distinct from the context.

In this regard, since *jyotis* and the other terms are grasped by the word "desire" (*etac-chanda*) and are co-referential with the sacrifice (*yajin*), it is established that they are names of the sacrifice, because they fall within a cognition constructed from a different meaning and are separated from other designations. In that context, there arises a doubt: for one unable to reach the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the connection [to the original] is severed due to the intervention of another meaning.
Does the very same *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice that is under discussion here recur [in the subsequent passages] by means of the words "Jyotis" and so forth, accompanied by a thousand [cows]?

For it is thus: when the sacrifice previously mentioned is not interrupted by a new name and so on, is a quality characterized by the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) being enjoined, or do distinct rituals indeed proceed under such names?
Nor can it be said that, as in the case of the *pūrva-stomā*, another distinct meaning is established by force [of the context],
such that the southern [altars] would be enjoined in this manner;
for in that regard, the matter is determined by the context (*prakaraṇa*).

This being the case, the word *atha* is understood as introducing a new topic (*adhikāra*) concerning another action— the accumulation of the requisites for the final goal— because it refers back to what has been previously mentioned, because the Vedic text expresses what is under discussion, because it stands in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that, and because it does not merely signify a sequence. This—

It is better to assume that *jyotis* and the others refer to what has been previously introduced rather than to something not previously introduced; for the word itself, being used in close proximity, denotes the immediately preceding subject just as it did in the prior context.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: when another name is heard, there is a difference in meaning because it is a distinct designation; this applies equally to the subsequent [name] being introduced, so there is no distinction. Thus much is understood.

Because there is no powerful sublation, the state of being a common [subject] is established; for when the context is interrupted, and in the present case, the direct scriptural statement (*saṃśruti*) is resorted to, it follows accordingly.
Therefore, these are distinct rituals.
[The Sūtra says: "In the absence of defects, these are not merely restatements (punarśruti) of those [previously mentioned]."
First [the opponent says]:

Soma—the meaning of the sūtra, however, is this: even a name is a differentiator; because it has been uttered, it is stated that it does not sublate the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), since it resides in distinctness.
The intention [of the opponent] is that even in the *pūrvapakṣa*, words such as "Jyotis" and so forth are not heard again with reference to an action already produced.
It is taken as a whole.
Even though they are names (*saṃjñā*), they nevertheless denote an action that has been produced.
And the statement "Now this [is] Jyotis" would be meaningless;
because of the absence of connection, it is not such [as that].

Section on Designation (Saṃjñādhikaraṇa) 4092: When there is a conflict—regarding the passage "Now this [is] Jyotis," whether it denotes a quality (*guṇa*) or a distinct rite (*karma*)—it is treated separately because the subject matter of the previous context is possible [therein], yet it establishes a different subject matter for its own connection.
For the quality consisting of the gift of a thousand [cows] is indeed already included within the Jyotiṣṭoma.
The distinction is based on the authority of the name (*saṃjñāpramāṇaka*).
(This is precisely the principle of the section concerning names [*saṃjñādhikaraṇanyāya*]: "Now, when the context has been interrupted, this word should denote the subsequent [element]").
Kau. 2|2|8|21, p. 251: Or rather, here [the term] "other action" (anyakarma) is used by way of a new designation.

The Bhaṭṭa [school] maintains that even as a different name is being uttered, it is understood through the assistance of its prior connection: "With reference to the Jyotiṣṭoma, [the text says], 'Now this is the Jyotis; this is the Viśvajyotis; this is the Sarvajyotis; one should sacrifice with this [rite] which has a thousand-fold sacrificial fee. Thus, it produces an understanding in the mind regarding a distinct entity corresponding to itself.

[Śabarabhāṣya on Jaimini Sūtra 2.2.8.22, p. 529]: "In all cases" means that since words such as *jyotis* (light) are well-known in the Vedic texts to denote specific qualities, and because it is improper for a word with multiple meanings to have more than one primary sense, and because there is no other [established] meaning, the justification for their being established as denoting the nature of illumination (*dyotanātmatva*) is seen even in the case of ritual action (*karman*). Therefore, another name (*saṃjñāntara*) is required.

This is because another name is observed, and because of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Furthermore, if that [quality] were enjoined by this very word, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) and so forth; thus, there is a difference [of status]. And both of these [reasons] are stronger [than the prima facie view].

First, its status as a name that sublates [the generic name] is beyond dispute. And that [sublation] does not apply to the sacrifice under discussion, because the name *Jyotiṣṭoma* exists; for as long as such a subverting cognition is absent, the general principle of difference remains unrefuted, since the practical function of a name is accomplished by a single one, and any other would be redundant. (Vārttika)
Nor can there be an option (vikalpa) due to the absence of a determining factor (vinigamakābhāva).

[This is stated] in *Athava* 2.2.8.22: "That which is designated by other technical terms is the non-intended object (*anīpsita-karman*), because the word [denoting it] serves as a regulator that interrupts the governing scope of the preceding term 'object' (*karman*)."

Therefore, just as in the case of "he milks the cow" (*gāṃ dogdhi*), or as in "one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring" (*vasante vasante jyotiṣā yajeta*), no other word is required for the apprehension of the form; for there is no doubt regarding its being a modification (*vikāra*) based on the Vedic text itself. (Maṇi, p. 130). Thus, it is not a matter of grasping a name (*saṃjñā*).
Since its continuity within the context is established by the traditional recitation (*samāmnāna*), it is understood as having a complete meaning;
therefore, the word expressing the name (*saṃjñāśabda*) is determined as such because of this acceptance.
Nor, in the absence of an interruption of the context, should it be considered [a mere] *udbhid* [name].
The very name "Uttara" [the latter] implies that it takes up [the ritual].
For there is no possibility of a distinction among names based on properties such as the prefix *dā*.
When the Jyotiṣṭoma is being grasped by its name at the point of origin (*utpatti*), the proximity of other words must be taken into account.

It should not be argued that, due to the absence of authoritative prescription (*śiṣṭatva*), there might be an option (*vikalpa*) between the two or even a reversal [of the rule] (see Bhāṣya on 9.2.1.23, p. 1711). This is because the application of the names [in the case of] *homayāga* is restricted by the difference in ritual properties (*dharma*) based on the occasion of the ritual procedure (*kalpaprāsaṅga*). For instance, when the name *jyotiṣṭoma* delimits the context, the name *udbhid* cannot in any way be applied as a subsequent mention (*anuvāda*). Furthermore, [the rule] "the sacrificial session (*satra*) is dependent" serves to exclude the name *jyotiṣṭoma*. Thus, how could the name *udbhid* ever find a place there?

Just as [the terms] "Brahmin," "wandering mendicant," and "forest-dweller" [are distinct], because they possess different meanings (bhāva) and because they function as differentiators (bhedaka). Bhāṣya. Because of the difference in their nature. Likewise, because of their differentiating character.

Therefore, there is nothing that serves as a substratum [for the name] (na kiñcinnidhāmakam asti). In that regard, concerning the conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth, there is only an option (*vikalpa*) between the two names.

Because even existing things are obstructed in the present context, because of the absence of another cause, and because of the interruption indicated by the word "atha," the name itself possesses the quality of differentiation (*bhedakatva*).
Alternatively, since it is established from elsewhere, there is no contradiction in its not initiating a new effect.

Or rather: "One should sacrifice with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee" (sahasradakṣiṇena yajeta)—this much alone [is the case] by way of a restatement (anuvāda) of the sacrifice under discussion (pṛ. 929). And thus, since the injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi) is established through the mention of the learned ones (vidvadvacana), the form of the sentence beginning with *jyotis* and ending with *etad* has been determined by the wise as being well-known.
For otherwise, there would be the contingency of meaninglessness (*vaiyarthyaprasaṅga*) regarding points of doubt for those who are wise.

Therefore, the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇabhūtakaraṇa*) perceives that the designations *jyotis* and so forth apply to the entities by virtue of their connection with illumination (*dyotana*) and the like, even if they are not [otherwise] perceived.
Thus:

the three rites characterized by many days, having the *Soma* sacrifice as their archetype, possess the status of being denoted by that [same] word; for that purpose, which consists of the attainment of the *Āruṇāka* heaven, is not established in any way other than as a religious duty (*dharma*) through the sentence "He who desires prosperity should sacrifice with this," and thus it is permitted as a duty.
Since it is enjoined as such, it is established that there is a distinction between the rites based on their names. (*Bhāṣya* 1.3.7)

Page 207. Even though there is a difference in the injunctions (*vidhi*), there is no difference in the essence [of the sacrifice]. Maṇḍana says: "Even starting from the *Jyotiḥ* [sacrifice], it would be the same *Iṣṭi*, because it is enjoined as a constituent part. Thus, despite the multiplicity, there is no difference in name. Śaṅkara says: "In the *Rājasūya*, the various seed-sacrifices (*nānābījēṣṭi*) are intended by that [single] name, extending from the spreading of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina-staraṇa*) up to the making of the sacrificial post firm (*dārḍhyakaraṇa*)."
The word "saḥ" (that) refers to a single ritual act; therefore, it applies to the mortar and other such items. This constitutes a distinction in the injunction (*śāstrabheda*).
Even though there is a connection between the cause and the effect, this primary [act] alone is the basis for the designation. This is the section concerning names (*saṃjñādhikaraṇa*).
The acceptance [of the rule] arises from the certainty that it is possible because its scope is different [from the previous].

Bhāṣya 6.3.18.38. In the state of existence (*bhāvadaśā*), the status of being a name (*saṃjñātva*) was previously established; remaining firm due to the absence of any sublater, [it applies] when there is *satobṛhatī*. 4093. *Satobṛhatī*.
The maxim "there can be no painting without a wall" is clear;
it is not [otherwise].

Furthermore, no *parāsu* (subsequent results) are perceived immediately after the *paśukāmeṣṭi* sacrifice. [This is because] there is a rule that valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) apprehend only what exists.
However, in the case of sound, it is not logical to abandon the effect once its cause has ceased to exist.
vi. "Because it perceives only what is already existent, it is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)"—this is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
"When the causal factors are complete, the effect necessarily comes to be"—this is the Bhāṣya.
Page 92.

Regarding the sense organs, when there is contact with an existing object (*sat-saṃprayoga*), the other scriptural authority (*śruti*) supported by logic is indeed stronger. (Nyāya: *satā* meaning "with an existing [object]"; *saṃnikarṣe* meaning "upon contact with the object")—Brahma Sūtra 3.3.16–27: When such contact exists, the production of a person's cognition constitutes the arising of perception. That perception, in the presence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), forms a non-contradictory connection with proximate properties; it does not serve as a cause for the dharma, nor as that which establishes its essential nature.
Why? Because [the details] exist in the archetype (*prakṛti*);
