The sacrificial cup for the Brāhmaṇas consists of Soma;
for the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, it is a fruit-cup (phalacamasa).
Likewise, the Brahmasāman is the Bārhadgira for the Brāhmaṇas, the Rāthovājīya for the Kṣatriyas, and the Ānājīya for the Vaiśyas.

Therefore, there is no application for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya even in the office of the *gṛhapati*. As for the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) regarding the others due to their status as masters: in the *Sadasasūtra*, for the purpose of demonstrating the entitlement of the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya to the *satra* sacrifice, there is an indicative mark stating, "One should perform the *Bārhadgira* as the *brahmasāman* for a Brāhmaṇa, the *Pārthudrama* for a Kṣatriya, and the *Rāthovājīya* for a Vaiśya. That observation of indicative marks would apply to those who are subordinate.

In the *satra*, however, because the other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) possess the status of masters (*svāmin*), and because it is impossible for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas to serve as such priests, they have no entitlement.
In the *ahīna* sacrifice, on the other hand, Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas do indeed have entitlement.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the entitlement to the *satra* belongs only to Brāhmaṇas, and not to Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas.

The *satras* are modifications of the *soma* sacrifice. (Vi. 5.1.14). The *satras* have themselves as their performers. (10.6.15.1–59). "One who intends to undertake a *satra* should sacrifice with the *viśvajit*"; this is an injunction for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) regarding the state of being [the performer].
Bāla, p. 20:
For one who has merely set out for a sacrificial session (sattra), there is a division [of the merit] upon its completion; it is twofold.
Regarding the *sāmyutthāna* (rising together), it is divided based on the connection with partitioning after purchase.

The commentary states: "They recite this: 'If those who have been consecrated for a *sattra* sacrifice should rise together, they should divide the *soma* and sacrifice with a *viśvajit* *atirātra*, consisting of all *stomas* and having all their possessions as the sacrificial fee (*sarvavedadakṣiṇa*)'.
In this regard, there is a doubt: does the *viśvajit* apply to the rising of one who has purchased the King Soma, or to [the rising] of all?
What is established? The Viśvajit sacrifice should take place upon the completion [of the Soma purchase].
Why? Because of its connection with the distribution [of the Soma], as it is said: "Having divided the Soma, they should sacrifice with the Viśvajit."

Those who, having purchased [the Soma], desire to follow the conduct of a Kṣatriya, would incur a deficiency because of their lack of a share in the Soma. Therefore, those for whom the King has been purchased, upon rising, should perform the Viśvajit sacrifice.

Or rather—this Viśvajit is for the sake of the fruit of the Sattra, or for the purpose of counteracting the defect of the Sattra's incomplete performance; it is not, however, for the sake of every possible fruit, as in the case of the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
Or [it occurs] because the cause has been set in motion.
The Commentary: The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position.
It would apply to one who has merely set out.
Why? Because the occasion has been obtained.
The occurrence of the *samya* is the occasion for the *viśvajit*;
and that has been obtained.

And it is not possible to qualify that [rule] by saying, "If the rising occurs after the purchase. The scriptural statement is for the purpose of an injunction; it is not a restatement of something already known.

Commentary: Now, as for what was said—"In the case of one who has not purchased [the Soma], the Kṣatriyas, while standing, should perform the ritual with qualities such as the absence of division"—[that is now addressed].
That must be avoided. To this it is replied: no division is being enjoined.
For the statement is thus limited:
"At the Sāṃnyūti rite, they should sacrifice with the Viśvajit, having divided the soma.
Therefore, the word "having anointed" is a restatement (anuvāda).
If it is asked, "How is this obtained?"—by implication, a division of wealth arises.
This division of all substances is indicated by the division of the Soma.
By dividing the Soma and [mentioning] other substances, the other scriptural statement serves the purpose of an injunction.

Therefore, [the question arises]: "Does the Viśvajit sacrifice belong to those who stand up [and leave] when the King (Soma) has been purchased, or to those for whom the King has not been purchased? Śabara states: "If, among those initiated for a Sattra, there should be a departure together, one should perform the Viśvajit after distributing the Soma. The inquiry is whether this Viśvajit applies to the departure of one whose King has been purchased, or to one whose King has not been purchased.
In that regard, [the opponent argues]: "This is a contingent rite (naimittika) based on the distribution of the Soma..."
This is specified for the *sattra* sacrifice;
it is not possible [to perform this] where no king has been purchased, therefore it must occur when one has been purchased.

It is said: "If this division of the Soma were enjoined as a subordinate element (aṅga), then it would indeed be so; however, since it is obtained through the sense of the context, it is not enjoined."

Therefore, this is merely a statement regarding the distribution of substances obtained through passion; however, the mention of *soma* is for the sake of illustration, and it is the *viśvajit* sacrifice alone that is enjoined. Thus, it would apply even to one who has not purchased a king (Soma). This is the connection [of the argument], because of the counter-objection: "Just as the *abhyudayeṣṭi* occurs even for one who does not possess *soma*, so too the *viśvajit* occurs for one who has not purchased a king. Vi— "If there is a request from those consecrated for a *satra* sacrifice who have risen together..."
If [the Soma] has been purchased from a Kṣatriya or even a Vaiśya,
the first [verse] applies because of the mention of the Soma-share; since that [share] is impossible if it has not been purchased,
the last two [verses] would be a restatement of the division which follows from the sense.

Bhaṭṭa: It is heard in scripture: "If those consecrated for a sacrificial session (*satra*) should rise together and, having not yet shared the *soma*, should perform the *Viśvajit* *atirātra* sacrifice with all its *stomas*, all its *pṛṣṭhas*, and with the entirety of the *Veda* as the sacrificial fee.

In this regard, there arises the inquiry: does the *Viśvajit* occur after the purchase of the *soma*, or would it also occur upon rising before that? Although mere rising—which is synonymous with abandonment—is the occasion (*nimitta*), neither the state of being denoted by the word *sāmi* (half-finished) nor the purchase of the *soma* is a qualifying condition (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Nevertheless, because even the division of Soma is subject to the injunction by the inclusion of the Viśvajit sacrifice, and considering its nature as a contingent rite (naimittika), it is prescribed only after the purchase of Soma.

For there is no Soma prior [to that point] by which the division of Soma could be performed in its unbroken form. Nor can the possibility of division be established prior [to the purchase] by considering the period beginning with the awakening [of the sacrificer], since at that time there is still no Soma.
If the sacrificer desists even before the purchase of the Soma from the seller, he has no ownership over it;
therefore, the Viśvajit sacrifice is to be performed only upon desisting after the purchase of the Soma.

This being the position reached—[we reply]: there is no injunction for partition here, because when those who have combined their substances desist, the partition of the substance is already established by the requirements of the situation.

For this very reason, the word *soma* refers merely to that which is mixed [with water]; furthermore, because the phrase "having divided the soma" is a restatement (*anuvāda*), the mere act of division is a contingent rite (*naimittika*). Since the condition for the ritual suspension (*vyutthāna*) exists even prior to the purchase of the soma, the division itself is the occasion. Moreover, even if the division is enjoined, nevertheless—just as in the first *Viśvajit* sacrifice—it is not the division of the purchased soma or one's own soma that serves as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka-aṅga*), but rather the division of any ordinary soma belonging to the *satra* sacrifice.
Each division is distinct; therefore, there is no difference in the possibility of such an occasional rite even prior [to this].
This Viśvajit is a separate ritual characterized by its specific qualities (guṇātma-karmāntara), both in relation to the [original] Viśvajit for its own sake and in relation to the Āgūraṇa-Viśvajit.
However, in comparison to those two, their status as distinct sacrifices is established through a different basis.
Furthermore, the subsequent context (*prakaraṇāntara*) should be understood as a means of proof.
The result [of this] should be considered as being like the *āgūraṇa-viśvajit*.

In reality, however, because it is impossible to define a difference in the occasioning cause (*nimitta*), the single sacrifice named *viśvajit* is enjoined by both [texts] according to the principle of other scriptural authorities; thus, there is no distinction between this [sacrifice] and the *āgūraṇa-viśvajit*.

The deliberation as to whether the Viśvajit sacrifice applies to one who has already commenced [the Soma sacrifice] or to one who has not commenced it should be understood as a *kṛtvācintā* (hypothetical inquiry) made in the absence of that [commencement].
Maṇḍana states: "The rising together [of the priests] should take place even when the [Soma] has not been purchased.
Śaṅkara states: "And the Viśvajit occurs even when the [Soma] has not been purchased."
For one who has merely commenced a Sattra—whether he has purchased the King Soma or not—the Viśvajit sacrifice is prescribed as a simultaneous rising [from the session].

In the section (6.5.17–27) beginning with "In the case of an early termination [of a *satra*], at the *Viśvajit*, because of the connection with distribution," the following is cited: "If, among those initiated for a *satra*, there is an early termination, one should perform the *Viśvajit* after distributing the *soma*. Having raised the doubt as to whether this *Viśvajit* applies only when the *rājaka* (the purchased *soma*) has been acquired, or even when it has not been acquired, and having further doubted whether the injunction "after distributing the *soma*" is a mandatory rule (*vidhi*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*), the conclusion is reached: it is a mandatory rule; therefore, being a conditional rite (*naimittika*) qualified by that [distribution], only one who has acquired the *rājaka* is able to perform it, not one who has not acquired it—thus, the *Viśvajit* does not apply to the latter.
This being the case, the statement "having divided the Soma" is a restatement (anuvāda),
because it is established by the sense of the matter itself.

For when those who have pooled their wealth for the purpose of a Sattra sacrifice proceed to perform the Sattra, the taking of the sacrificial fee (dākṣiṇā-dravya) by dividing it— just as in the case of the Soma— is already naturally established.
It is not an injunction.
Consequently, the Viśvajit sacrifice itself is merely occasional (naimittika).

And since that can indeed be performed by one who has not purchased a king [as a priest], it is established as a settled conclusion that such a person also possesses the qualification [to perform it].

*Bāla*, pp. 115–116. In the *Satra* known as the *Ajñanāmyajñana*, anointing (*abhyañjana*) is performed with oils such as *guggulu* and others. According to *Bhāṣya* 12.1, in the *Satra* known as the *Ajñanāmyajñana*, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the anointing prescribed by traditional rule (*prākṛta-nīti*) with the anointing and other rites mentioned in the recensional text (*samāmnāta*).

10.4.6.10–12. In the *satra* sacrifice known as the *Ajñāna*, there is indeed *kāṇḍānusamaya* (sequential performance by sections), because it is prescribed that each respective consecration (*saṃskāra*) must occur subsequent to the initiation (*dīkṣā*). Bhāṣya 5.2.3: In the *satra*, the consecrations such as the *ājñāna* pertain to all [participants].

14. Eligibility for the *sattra*: Only those who possess the same ritual procedure (*kalpa*) as the Vaiśāmitras [are eligible]. Mīko., p. 304: "Regarding the section [on] eligibility for the *sattra*, only those who possess the same ritual procedure (*kalpa*—meaning the *prayoga*, not the *sūtra*) as the Vaiśāmitras [are eligible]"—this section should be consulted. Eligibility for the *sattra* belongs only to those who possess the same ritual procedure (*kalpa*). (Note: *Kalpa* refers to the practical application or performance manual, not the aphoristic *sūtra*.)

6|6|11-12. See the section (adhikaraṇa) at Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 305, under the heading: "In a *sattra*, the qualification belongs only to those of equal status. It was shown in the third [book] that the *adhvaryu* and other priests exist in a *sattra*.

Śābarabhāṣya 5|1|1, Section 3: In the *sattra*, regarding the mantra for the offering of the *iṣṭi*—specifically in the phrase "and those who have increased the lord of glory" (*ye ca yaśapatiṃ varṣān*)—the word *yaśas* should not be treated as plural because it is intended as a praise (*praśaṃsā*).
VI. 9.2.14: In the *sattra* sacrifice, the selection of the *ṛtuyājyā* priests and the giving of gold must be performed according to Ātreya.
Bhaṭṭa 10.2.25: In the *sattra*, there is no fault in the omission of the daily performance of the selection of the *ṛtuyājyā* priests and the giving of gold.

10.2.26: See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1246, under the section titled "In the *sattra*, the omission of the daily performance of the selection of the *ṛtuyājyā* priests and the giving of gold does not constitute a fault."
In a *satra* sacrifice, since the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) themselves are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*), no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) whatsoever should be given.
As it is said: "They say that *satras* are without sacrificial fees; for in this case, neither a cow, nor a garment, nor gold is given" (Vi.
In the *sattra* sacrifice, there is a sublation of the purchase of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij-parikraya*).
And the purchase [is sublated] because it is for that purpose.

The Commentary: Furthermore, the purchase is prescribed in the *prakṛti* (archetype), the Jyotiṣṭoma: "A cow, a horse, a mule, a donkey, a goat, a sheep, barley, sesame, and beans—these constitute the one hundred and twelve sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)."
In that case, since the hiring of services (*dakṣiṇā*) is obtained through the extended injunction (*codaka*) in the *sattra* sacrifice, there arises a doubt:

should it be performed or not? What is the prima facie view? The hiring should be performed, in order to uphold the extended injunction. Moreover, in that context, cows and other items are prohibited: "For here no cow is given, nor clothing, nor gold."
In that case, it is appropriate [to understand] it as a purchase.
This being the position reached, we reply:
"And the purchase is for that purpose."
And hiring (parikraya) should not be performed.
It was stated above that in satras, officiating (varaṇa) should not be performed;
by the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "and hiring," it is indicated that another point is being made—that hiring also should not be performed.
Purchase:
Why? Because it is for the sake of oneself;
no one purchases oneself.
"And the prohibition is like that of the object.
Commentary: That which was stated—that a prohibition is possible only when there is a prior application—must be refuted;
for [the suffix] beginning with *sva* (the genitive case) is merely a property (*dharma-mātra*) of that which is already obtained.
Commentary: The meaning is that the prohibition is logically consistent.
Of what? Of the gift that has been obtained through extension (*codaka*).
For in the *satra* sacrifices, that is merely a duty (*dharma*) obtained through the rule of extension.
Therefore, that [objection] is refuted. Consequently, the prohibition is logically established.
It is not from the word "dakṣiṇā" [that the prohibition arises]; therefore, it must be a permanent restatement (nityānuvāda).
Commentary: This is not a prohibition against one who has already received the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). For the word *dakṣiṇā* occurs here; indeed, the word *dakṣiṇā* is present in this context.
"They say that sacrificial sessions (satra) are without sacrificial fees (adakṣiṇa),
for in them neither a cow, nor a garment, nor gold is given. And the word *dakṣiṇā* has the meaning of "purchase-price" (*parikraya*).
For it is heard there: "Cows, horses, mules, donkeys, goats, sheep, barley, sesame, and beans—his sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of one thousand two hundred [of these].

The *dakṣiṇā* is the gift to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), not that which is obtained from the *ṛṣika*. This prohibition applies to that [gift to the priests] alone, not to that which is obtained from the *ṛṣika*.
Therefore, this is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already permanently established; it does not mean that there is no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in *satra* sacrifices.
Śabara says: It has been stated that the giving of the sacrificial fee is for the purpose of hiring (*parikraya*), and not for the sake of maintaining the day [of the sacrifice].
Now, the doubt arises as to whether hiring itself should be performed in a *satra* or not.
Because it involves bowing down (*ānamanāt*), the act of hiring (*parikraya*) is excluded, just as in the case of the *varaṇa* (choosing).
Regarding the meaning of the Sūtra on Soma: "And hiring is not to be performed in a *satra*, because the *satra* is for one's own sake.
Cī: "In the *satra*, should the purchase be performed or not? Because of the prohibition, there is the assumption of a [different] action."

Just as the selection of priests (*varaṇa*) for a sacrificial session (*satra*) is not performed because it is established by a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*), so too, according to the Bhaṭṭa school, the selection is not to be performed at all, since it is equivalent to the hiring (*parikraya*). For that [selection] does not serve another purpose when it is already established by the daily maintenance (*ahardhāyya*); this is because it was proven in the third book (*adhyāya*) that there is no evidence for the priestly office (*ṛtviktva*) having a visible form (*dṛṣṭarūpa*).
Nor indeed [is it] like the appointment of the *ṛtuyājyā* priests in a *satra*, for that would serve an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), as there is a lack of evidence [for such a claim].
Furthermore, although matters such as this are already established, they are stated here under the heading of "sublation" (*bādha*) for the benefit of the students; such is the distinction.
Maṇḍana [says]: "In *satras*, there should be no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)."
Śaṅkara: "In this case, there is a sublation of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
In the Sattra sacrifice, the sequence of the eleven animals is as follows: those dedicated to Agni, Sarasvatī, Soma, Pūṣan, Bṛhaspati, Viśvedevas, Indra, the Maruts, Indra-Agni, Savitṛ, and Varuṇa."
Saṃkarṣa. 1|4|24:
In the *sattra* sacrifice, the touching (*samāna*) of the *audumbarī* post is performed by only one sacrificer, not by all; for this is not a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificers.
The same applies in the *ahīna* sacrifice.

In a *satra* sacrifice, because there is a plurality of performers (*kartṛbheda*), a collective agency (*vyāsajyavṛtti kartṛtva*) is not accepted; therefore, for the sake of justifying the plural number [in the injunction], it is held that in the case of "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the single agency belonging to both husband and wife is collective (*vyāsajyavṛtti*).
(Bhāṭṭa 6|1|4).

In the case of a sacrificial session (*sattra*), if any participant rises after the purchase of the *soma*, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) should consist of the *viśvajit* sacrifice performed with the *soma* already divided and set aside;
however, if he rises before that, it should be performed with newly purchased *soma*.
In a *satra* sacrifice, if one of the masters dies, there is a substitute;
however, if many have already commenced, one should wait for another to arrive, as otherwise there would be a deficiency.
The Commentary states: "The example from the *satras* is: 'At least seventeen should sit for the *satra*.'"
Regarding some of those masters, when one acts improperly, there arises a doubt: does another person serve as a substitute in that case, or not?
What is the prima facie position? That there is no substitute for a master.
This being the position, we reply:
When a ritual has commenced for many sacrificers and one of the masters has passed away, they bring in another.
Why? Because in this way alone does the deficiency [of the required number] cease to exist;
the number seventeen and so forth residing in the master is an auxiliary element (*aṅga*) in that context.
Without her, the ritual act is deficient;
therefore, another must be brought in to complete that deficiency.
But will you not say that the number resides in the owner [the sacrificer], and not that the owner is the measure of the renunciation?
Therefore, it is impossible for that number to be grasped. It is said: "For it will not belong to the owner."
For that [specific number] cannot be established;
however, this can be established:
that those items belonging to the masters must be performed here by seventeen or more [priests]. This will be demonstrated later.
Therefore, there is a substitute.
Or rather: the number pertaining to the agent, which was obtained without restriction by the [general rule] "they should sit," is restricted by the [specific rule] "at least seventeen.
The agent is that which is pervaded by the fruit.
In that case, another [agent] being brought in is not connected with the fruit of the action;
therefore, due to the absence of such a reality, there is no completion of the number of agents.
Moreover, this number pertains to one who performs the relinquishment of a substance for the sake of a deity.
And the priests would not perform the relinquishment of the substance (*dravyatyāga*),
because the sacrificer alone is the primary agent from the very beginning. Therefore, while being brought [to the priests], it pertains to the owner.

Since it is incapable of fulfilling the number pertaining to the agent as well as the number pertaining to the object, there can be no substitute. Furthermore, there is the completion of what has been commenced by means of specific details.
This being the case, we reply:
the completion of the commenced sattra must be exactly as prescribed in the scripture.
In that context, the person being brought in does not fulfill the number pertaining to the sacrificers.

As for one who dies, his agency ceases and he is unable to resume it; therefore, this partial deficiency does not constitute a fault. Regarding the scriptural injunction, "Seventeen or more should perform a Sattra sacrifice," when someone among those seventeen has died, there arises the doubt: should another be substituted in his place or not? It has been stated [in the Mīmāṃsā] that there is no substitute for the master (the sacrificer).
This being the case, [the author] says that there is a substitute. It has been stated that even a rite performed for a specific desire (kāmya), once it has begun, must necessarily be completed.
And because of this necessity, it must be performed according to one's capacity.

Therefore, although—on the basis of the statement "those who are the sacrificers (yajamānāḥ), they are the officiating priests (ṛtvijaḥ)"—the word *yajamāna* denotes both the owner and the agent, and since it is possible for an injunction to be made with respect to both ownership and agency expressed by a single term, the office of the priest (*ārtvijyam*) should be performed by the owners themselves; and even if, according to the principle of the subsequent section (*uparitanādhikaraṇanyāya*), one being brought in would not be the owner, nevertheless, setting aside that [point] alone, another person must be brought in to complete the number seventeen in the ritual action.

Soma: The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: when a rite involving many participants has commenced and one sacrificer (*yajamāna*) has committed a transgression, another should be brought in; for in that case, there is no deficiency (*avaiguṇya*). Vi: "When a participant in the *satra* has died, there should be no other [sacrificer], or rather, there should be one, just as before.
There should be one even if it is the owner's own field, for the sake of completing the group of seventeen."

Bhaṭṭa: Thus, while it has been established by reasoning that even if there is the existence of another person in some cases due to the authority of custom (*ācāra*), that person serves as a substitute, an exception is now being made: when any one of the sacrificers dies during the middle of a sacrificial session (*sattra*), another must indeed be appointed as his substitute.
This is because even a rite undertaken for a specific desire (*kāmya*) must necessarily be brought to completion once begun.

Furthermore, although the primary performer is the object of the injunction regarding the performance (*prayoga-vidhi*), and thus a substitute is not [ordinarily] required, nor is it possible to effect that [performance] through one who is dead.

Nevertheless, because the sentence "seventeen at least should sit for the Sattra" prescribes the number seventeen, the inclusion of others must be performed by those remaining in order to complete that number of seventeen. Nor can it be argued that— on account of the specific number being an attribute of the qualification conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), and because the person being brought in would not exist [as a qualified agent] according to the method to be explained, while the one already present possesses the qualification for the Sattra— the [number] cannot be fulfilled.

How can there be the attainment of the fruit for one who has fallen away from the sacrificial session (*sattra*) by taking that [fruit]? Even in the absence of being an enjoyer of the fruit, the attainment of the fruit is logical on the grounds of its residing solely in the agent.

For this very reason, even in the case of the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*), by the statement "those who are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) are the priests (*ṛtvij*)," the definition of the office of the priest is accepted for the subordinate position of the priest; and since the agency of the sacrificers is enjoined with reference to that [office], the term *yajamāna*—being in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) produced by knowledge—possesses agency characterized by being the enjoyer of the fruit, even in the absence of actual enjoyment through performance according to one's capacity. Thus, because the agency exists despite the absence of enjoyment, there is no contradiction regarding the number [of agents]. Consequently, by the very logic of the fulfillment of the required number, there is here a substitution of individuals.

And since this [conclusion] is established by logic (*nyāya*), the injunction "if they have been initiated for the *sattra*, then they should sacrifice together with him" would be redundant if it were merely intended to prescribe proximity (*nediṣṭhatva*).
Therefore, this section is solely for the purpose of training the student; for even in its absence, the arrival [of the sacrificer] is established by the scriptural statement itself.
And here, even in the event of the wife's death, because of the masculine gender used in the expression "they should sacrifice together with him," [it refers to] the sacrificer alone.
6|14. At the *sattra*, the *brahmā* priest is one who meditates on the Veda.

Vi. 6|3|14. Only Brahmins have the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the *sattra*. 6|6|3|16–23. Mīmāṃsā, p. 302. Regarding the statement "Only Brahmins have the qualification for the *sattra*," the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted.
In a *sattra*, if anyone, having performed a portion of it, wishes to abandon the *sattra* and depart, he must divide his own share among the substances such as the *soma*.
(Vi. 6.5.7). In a *sattra*, if anyone, either before or after the purchase of the *soma*, wishes to abandon the *sattra* and depart, he must perform the *viśvajit* sacrifice.
(6.5.7). In a *sattra*, only the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) shall act as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and no others.
In a sacrificial session (sattra), the sacrificers themselves are the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
"The other priests should be [the same] as in the archetype.
Commentary: Here, the *sattra* sacrifice itself is the example.
It has been stated that in those [sattras], there are many performers.

Now this is being deliberated: are those very performers of the sacrificial session (*satrin*) the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), or should others be appointed? What is the prima facie view? Others should be appointed as the officiating priests. Why? Because in the Jyotiṣṭoma, which is the archetype (*prakṛti*), other agents are to be appointed.

This is the principle of respect (*saṃmānatā*). Therefore, here too, when one acts as the archetype (*prakṛti*) along with the three [auxiliaries], the elements to be adopted must be taken according to the great rule of the model sacrifice (*codaka*);
in this way, it will be established as having the nature of the archetype.
Alternatively, they may indeed be the sacrificers; because of their connection with the designation [of the priests], they should possess the status of sacrificers.
Commentary: It is not the case that the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are different [from the sacrificers].
The officiating priests should be none other than the sacrificers themselves.
Why? Because of the connection with the designation of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

For the ritual act of initiation (*dīkṣā*), which is a refinement of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), being enjoined as designated by its well-known form based on the performance of the ritual—since it is not connected with the duties of the Adhvaryu and others—indicates that those [officiating priests] belong to the sacrificers, just like the relationship between teachers and their students.
How so? If they perform those ritual acts, then they are joined with those occasional designations; not otherwise.
From this it is understood that there is a connection with those ritual items.

What is that statement? Having begun with, "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati, initiates the Brahman, then the Hotṛ, then the Udgātṛ," all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are introduced in connection with initiation.
Therefore, it is understood that only the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) should perform the priestly functions (*ārtvijya*), and no others.
If it is argued that there is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent because of the scriptural statement, as in the case of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration),
[the reply is: The Bhāṣya says— if you think that the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) should be the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*),
that is not correct.
For in the archetype (prakṛti), those other than the sacrificer are supported [as priests];
since this case is like the archetype, it must likewise be that here too there should be others than the sacrificers—thus the prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa) is restated.
Only the refutation of what was previously stated must now be provided.
It is said in reply: It will be a refinement of the agent (kartṛ-saṃskāra) because of the scriptural statement, just like the establishment of the fires (ādhāna).
How so? Only this much is heard: "Having initiated the Adhvaryu and the Gṛhapati, he initiates the Brahman."

In that case, even if there are multiple performers, since they are unable to speak using their own respective names, the consecration (*dīkṣā-saṃskāra*) is prescribed for them; thus, it does not lead to non-rebirth (*apunarbhava*).
It is like the act of establishing the sacred fires (*ādhāna*).
Just as elsewhere the consecration of the *vijas* is prescribed in the context of the fire-establishment: "He who has kindled this fire should observe this vow for this night."
From the statement, "He shall not eat meat; he shall not approach a woman," a restriction for the Adhvaryu is enjoined.
Likewise, in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, by the rule, "All the officiating priests (ṛtvij) fast," fasting is enjoined for the ṛtvijas.
Similarly, in this case as well, this will be a purificatory rite (saṃskāra) for the ṛtvijas.
Because it is logical that they [the priests] are situated in their own respective positions, as in the case of the original model (prakṛti).
The Bhāṣya states: This is not so; that there are other priests.
What then? The sacrificers themselves should be the priests.
Why? Because regarding this doubt—whether these very sacrificers are the officiating priests (ṛtvij), or whether they are others who are distinct—the former view is the logical one.
The reasoning for this has already been stated.
"Or rather, they [the sacrificers] themselves would be [the priests], because of the connection with the designation of the officiating priests.
By this principle, we see that it is indeed they [the sacrificers].
As for what was said—that there will be a consecration of the priests similar to the *ādhāna* (fire-laying)—[that is not the case].
That is untenable.

How so? Either the initiation (dīkṣā) of the priests is enjoined for a purpose not belonging to the archetype (aprākṛta), or, being a constituent part of the archetype (prakṛti), it would be mentioned as having its archetypal function while being subordinate to the sequence [of rites] due to the plurality of sacrificers.
The mere mention of what has already been obtained is simpler,

because it involves the prescription of only the sequence. If it were a consecration of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), there would be the assumption of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) and the prescription of a purpose for the qualification.
Therefore, there is a restatement by means of the *udaka* (water) of what has already been obtained, and not the prescription of something previously unobtained by name.
As for the argument that it is like the prescription of fasting for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the prescription of vows for the establisher of the fire (*ādhātṛ*),
that is not tenable in this case.
The statement "the officiating priests fast" and "he should observe the vow on that night" is explicit;
nor is there any suspicion of it being already established there due to its being an original injunction (*apūrva*).
Therefore, in that case, it is a prescription (*vidhāna*).

"If it be argued that they should have the designation 'master' (svāmin), like the householder (gṛhapati)"; the Commentary states: This is a sūtra of objection. Now, why do these [officiants], such as the Adhvaryu and others, not have the designation "master," as the householder does?
"How will it be thus? [The opponent asks: "In this way, the purposelessness resulting from what is obtained through the *codaka* (extended injunction) will not be sublated;
and the designations such as 'Adhvaryu' and so forth will be meaningful by virtue of denoting the householder-sacrificer. To this, while that position stands, the author of the Sūtra objects:
"No, because of the acceptance of what is well-known, for that which is not connected possesses its own specific property."
The Commentary states: This has not been said; these names, such as "gṛhapati" (householder), denote ownership. Why? Because they are understood in their conventional sense.

For these names are well-known among performers as being based on the action when they perform the duties of the *adhvaryu* and so forth, but not when they are performing the role of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
It is logical that [the results] will belong to the sacrificers who are connected with the ritual actions through their names.
How is the title "householder" (gṛhapati) explained? It is said:
For one who is not connected [to the ritual], the designation "householder" (*gṛhapati*) belongs to the patron (*svāmin*) alone according to the duty of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).
Moreover, even by the well-known etymology of the word, the term *gṛhapati* denotes a master; thus, it is understood as the patron-householder (*yajamāna-gṛhapati*).
It is not, however, employed for the Adhvaryu priest, nor is this term used for the patron in the sense of "one who is known as a householder."
However, in no way whatsoever can the Adhvaryus be connected with the actions of the Master (Svāmin); thus, because they are connected with other actions, they are excluded.

Furthermore, the expression "of many" (*bahunām*) would not be appropriate as a specification among equals. The Bhāṣya states: "In this manner, in the priestly offices (*ārtvijyeṣu*), the sacrificers themselves [are the performers]."

Why? Because it says this: "He who is indeed the householder among many sacrificers is the one who attains the greatest prosperity. This specific statement regarding a single householder is appropriate here; it would not be so otherwise.

If all were to perform the duties of the householder without performing any other [distinct] ritual action, then, due to the absence of distinction, the specific mention of the "householder" would be untenable.
But if the others perform both [sets of duties], while the householder performs only the duties of the sacrificer, then the specific statement becomes logical.

Therefore, from the specific statement "these are the officiating priests (ṛtvij)," it is understood that they are so designated; furthermore, the distinction between the initiated (dīkṣita) and the non-initiated would not be tenable if [the performers] were not distinct.
The Commentary states: For this reason as well, it is understood that the Satra sacrifices have themselves as their performers.
Why? Because of the designation of "initiated" and "uninitiated.
Thus it is said: "The initiated perform the Sattra; the uninitiated perform the Ahīna.
And these two [terms] are indeed fixed as the first [categories].
Those who have been initiated perform the sacrifice for their own sake, while the officiating priests, though not initiated, cause the sacrifice to be performed for others.
Since there would be no distinction between these two roles in an Ahīna or a Sattra sacrifice, the specific designation [of one as sacrificer and the other as priest] would be untenable.

But in the *sattra*, as long as the ritual action is performed, these two remain consecrated (*dīkṣita*); whereas in the *ahīna*, it is performed by those who are unconsecrated. Therefore, the designation [of the performers] is appropriate in that case, and not otherwise.
From this designation, we understand that there is self-performance (*svayaṃkartṛtva*) in the *sattra*.
And because of the absence of sacrificial fees (*adakṣiṇatva*).
The Commentary: For this reason also, the *sattra* has itself as its performer.
Why? Because of the absence of sacrificial fees.

"They say that sacrificial sessions (*satrāyaṇa*) are without sacrificial fees (*adakṣi�ṇa*), for in this case neither a cow, nor a garment, nor gold is given. This observation regarding the absence of sacrificial fees is consistent with the view that one is the performer oneself; it would not be so otherwise.
For if another were the performer, the absence of a sacrificial fee would not be logical.

For no one indeed exerts themselves for the sake of another without some self-interest; therefore, it is understood that the *satra* sacrifices have themselves as their performers. Śabara: Even regarding the *satras*, when there is a doubt as to whether there are intermediate priests or only the sacrificers themselves, [the conclusion is] by others, due to the favoring of the general rule (*codaka*).

The statement, "Those who are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*), they are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)," is an injunction regarding the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) for the purpose of consecrating those [sacrificers] by means of the status of being a sacrificer that is already established; it is not an injunction that the sacrificer is to be the officiating priest.
Therefore, the office of the officiating priest must be performed by others.

When, by the passage "Having initiated the *gṛhapati*, [he initiates] the officiating priests," initiation is enjoined for the purpose of consecrating the officiating priests, then the word "sacrificer" refers to the officiating priest himself as one who is connected with that [initiation]; thus, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
It is not so, because it would follow that the function is non-archetypal (*aprākṛta*), and because [the rule] has the purpose of stating a specific injunction.
Furthermore, the office of the officiating priest (*ātvijya*) does not constitute a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer,
because it would follow that the function is non-archetypal.

Therefore, since the office of the officiating priests (*ārtvijya*) is a natural function, the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) are prescribed as its performers; consequently, there is a sublation (*bādha*) of others who would otherwise be obtained through the general rule (*codaka*). Soma: In the preceding case, although the plurality of performers was established by an injunction, thereby sublating the singularity of performers obtained through the *codaka*, here—because there is no injunction prescribing the sacrificers as the performers of the *ārtvijya*—the plurality of other performers obtained through the *codaka* should not be sublated. Thus, the connection [between the two cases] is established. Vi: "Are the officiating priests others, or should they be those very same persons, according to the *codaka*?"
Others, or whatever they may be, [are established] by means of perception, verbal testimony, and so forth.

And in that regard, the officiating priestly duties (*ṛtvijya*) must be performed by the sacrificers themselves, according to the scriptural statement: "Those who are the sacrificers, they are the priests," which establishes the status of the subordinate priests in the *sattra* sacrifice.

Because the sacrificers are enjoined as the agents with reference to a body [of bricks] characterized by a specific number of beings (*sattva*) and so forth, the plural number is used in the phrase "by which they should sacrifice. It is the same here as well.

Consequently, the archetypal (*prākṛta*) status of the sacrificer as the agent of the sacrifice, as well as his selection (*varaṇa*), maintenance (*bharaṇa*), and so forth, would be sublated; that must be avoided.
Thus [it is said].
This section (*adhikaraṇa*) is also like the previous one.

Here, the injunction for the *ātithya* (guest-offering) is not for the purpose of purifying the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), because it performs a function not found in the archetypal sacrifice (*aprākṛtakārya*) and because of the designation as a single act.
[This is] from the *Patta*.
The *Bhāṣya* states: "This is not tenable in the *sattra*, because [a *sattra*] has a single performer. Maṇḍana says: "In this case, however, there should be no other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)."
Why? Because of the designation as one.
How so? It says thus: "This indeed is Śaṅkara—the one who knows this here and there;
even he who accepts a corpse at the sacrificial session (satra), he alone should sacrifice"—thus, by virtue of being the archetype (prakṛti), the satra is performed by one person alone.
The Bhāṣya states: "Even the *sattra* [sacrifice], while enjoining the status of a single performer for another [type of rite], leads to the understanding of multiple performers.
As it says, 'just as in the world,' and that is logical."
In the world, [the suffix] -ṇam [is used] in other cases.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: should one person perform the sattra, or many?
Since the word being uttered is a restatement of a praiseworthy matter, what is the general rule? One person.
Why? Because it is the natural state (*prakṛti*).
It is understood that [the agent] has commenced the rites of light (*jyotiḥ-kriyā*) facing the twilight (*saṃdhyā*).
Furthermore, in the *Ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, there is a single agent.
Because that is its nature, it is for the sake of favoring the *codaka* (the general rule), as in the case of the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice.
That is appropriate in the case of the *udavasānīyā*,
for there it is prescribed that "only one person should perform the *sattra*."

But surely, many [scriptural passages] are heard: "Those who, knowing thus, sit for a sacrificial session (satra)"; "Those who, knowing thus, enter upon a sacrificial session"; and "Having offered, they sit. It has already been stated that because of the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛtva*), the mere action is enjoined after having observed the differences and the non-observation of the conclusion; and that very [action] is restated here. Thus it is said.
It is said:
for those possessed of desire, a sacrificial session (sattra) is enjoined; and they [engage] through another [means]. But here, the engagement in action is preceded by words.
And as for the word, since plurality is independent of anything else, there are indeed many [words].
Just as they perform a specific application in their individual forms, they connect with the various sacrificial sessions (*satra*).

Therefore, even though the performance of the *satra* is thus limited, because many indeed perform it, when the action is undertaken on the basis of its authoritative status, plurality is intended to be expressed; hence the plural number will occur.
Just as in the world, even if they do not act separately,

one sees the plural number used for many [agents], such as "the gods and the chosen deities would perform the *saṃnivāpa*"; and it also shows the *saṃnivāpa*, saying, "if they were to come together, many Brāhmaṇas should sacrifice."

Thus says the Bhāṣya: "In this way, many indeed should sacrifice. Why? Because even in the Veda, the performance is observed; for, following the departure from the *satra* sacrifice, there is the observation of the simultaneous pouring out (*saṃnivāpa*) by means of the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* rite. It speaks of a single simultaneous pouring out for many sacrificers, stating: "They should sacrifice."

In this case as well, [the phrase] "they should sit" or "they should approach" implies that those who are about to sacrifice many animals should gather together; thus there will be a statement regarding the Sāvitra offerings:
"Those who are going to offer oblations should gather together.
If they perform the rite after having gathered, it would apply to many on account of that specific injunction.
In this way, the simultaneous performance (*saṃnivāpa*) of these [offerings] is established.

But if one were to perform them one by one—as the Bhāṣya states: "This is not so; one person should sacrifice, not many; for if there were many, the observation of simultaneous performance would not be possible"—therefore, it is understood that [the rite belongs] to many.
He asks: "Many should sacrifice. Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "It is a sattra."
This statement appears to mean "they should sit" or "they should approach.

Furthermore, the word expressing plurality (*bahutva*) and the phrase "of many" (*bahunām*) would be redundant if it referred to a single individual. Therefore, the application [of the rite] is what is being enjoined.
This is because of the explicit scriptural statement, and because the status of having a single agent is obtained through the general rule (*codaka*).
The Commentary states: "From this as well, we see that the performance is collective."

If it is argued that these are merely figurative designations (*apadeśa*), why so? It is heard in scripture: "He who is the master of house (*gṛhapati*) among many sacrificers is the performer (*pratyarthin*) of the *sattra* sacrifice; for he attains the greatest prosperity. Thus, having observed this, the use of the plural word will be as in common worldly usage, just as it has been stated.

In the case of a single householder engaged together with many sacrificers, [the text] says, "Perform the *akṛṣi*. Even in the Veda, there is a scriptural indication: the mention of specific fruits for the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice shows the performance of many [sacrificers] together. Otherwise, since the agent would be singular in this case, the relationship between general and particular could not be established, and the mention of specific fruits would be purposeless.
It exists in every sacrificial session.
But there is a statement regarding a specific result. From this also, it is understood that many indeed should sacrifice.

[In the inquiry: "Should those performing *satras* do so individually as persons desiring results, or collectively as many?"—due to the favor of the *codaka* (the rule of extension), and because the plural number can be justified as a restatement (*anuvāda*) based on the intention that in the world many desirous persons perform a *satra* even individually, they should perform it individually.
It is not so;
for here too, the number of the agent residing in the verb is intended to be expressed through its grammatical function (*prayogajñatā*), just as it is in the case of the verbal base (*prakṛti*).
Indeed, there is no reason whatsoever for that [number] not to be intended.
And that [rule] sublates what is obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer); therefore, many should perform [the rite].

Soma—[The connection is as follows: although there is no sublation in the case of modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *mānasa* [sacrifice], it is stated that in a *sattra* there is not a single performer because of the nature of the *sattra*.
Vi—Does one person perform the *sattra*, or many, as in the archetype (*prakṛti*)?
"One person should perform [the rite]; here they should sit," having said this, many people [should participate].

Bhaṭṭa: In the case of the *sattra* and the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), although the agency [of performers] is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), because the agency of performers is enjoined by direct instruction (*upadeśa*) in the statement "those desiring [the fruit] should sit for the *sattra*," it is already established that there are many performers; however, this is taught to the student because of the contingency of sublation (*bādha*).
Maṇḍana: "The *sattra* should have many performers."
Śaṅkara: "The status of being performers of the rite belongs to many.

In the *sattra*, the sacrificial vessels must be prepared for common use. See the section (adhikaraṇa) at Mīmāṃsākośa, page 305, under the entry: "The entitlement (*adhikāra*) in the *sattra* belongs only to those sacrificers who have prepared the common vessels" (Mīko. pṛ. 305). 16|6|33-34. See the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) there.
In a sacrificial session (sattra), the purificatory rites for the sacrificers are for the benefit of all the sacrificers.
"In the *sattra*, because of the connection with the householder, it is like the *hautra*.

Commentary: Now, as for those *yājamāna* rites which are for the purpose of purification (*saṃskāra*), should they also be performed by the householder alone in the *sattra*, or by all [the participants]? It is said: [they are performed by the householder alone].
The duties are to be performed by the householder.
Why? Because of the lack of connection.
Thus, there will be no lack of connection between the designation "householder" and its actual meaning.
The meaning is that it will possess purposefulness. How so? To this it is replied:
here, by this word "house" (gṛha), the ritual action is denoted, not the physical dwelling.
When the word *śālā* (house) is mentioned, the ritual action (*karman*) is also implied, for all of them are indeed masters of the house.
But surely they are all masters of the ritual action as well?
True, this is so; however, through the conventional designation (*samākhyāna*), a superior understanding [of their status] is recognized.
For example, as in the expression "Devadatta is a Brāhmaṇa in Mathurā.
And this excellence [denoted by the suffix] must arise either from an abundance of action or from an abundance of fruit.
In that regard, an abundance of action is not possible.
Because the ritual action of others is more extensive,
a greater abundance of fruit is appropriate,
owing to the predominance of the purificatory rites for the sacrificer.

Therefore, because the designation "householder" (gṛhapati) is meaningful, the householder is the performer of the rite for men. It is like the case of the *hautra*: just as the designation *hautra* is meaningful and thus the *hotṛ* priest becomes the performer of the *hautra*, so it is here as well.

And because of the scriptural statement. The Commentary states: A scriptural statement is cited regarding the abundance of results: "He who is indeed the householder among many sacrificers in a *satra* is the master of the *satra*; for he attains the greatest prosperity."
And that [performance] would occur for this very reason:
either all [the priests] should perform them, because they are for his sake.
The Commentary states: "Or rather, all the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) should perform those acts which serve the purpose of the person, not the householder alone."
Why? Because it is for that purpose.
For ritual action is indeed for all purposes, since it is heard without distinction in the text: "Those desiring prosperity should perform the twelve-day rite.
If this [subsidiary] were connected with the refinement of only some of these, then for him [the rite] would be deficient in its accessory and thus fruitless.
In that case, the scriptural statement of non-distinction would be contradicted;
furthermore, the designation "householder" (gṛhapati) is used because of its commonality.

The Commentary states: Just as the householder himself does not perform the ritual action while others become his agents, so it is for us as well—by this commonality there is a preeminence of ownership, not a preeminence of fruit, because there is an absence of preeminence in the fruit.
"In case of conflict, the latter [prevails].
Commentary: But surely, by securing their own interests, the sacrificers cause the purpose of the sacrifice to be neglected.
To this it is replied:

Where there is no conflict between what is for the sake of the sacrifice (*ṛtvartha*) and what is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), they shall perform it for its own purpose. But in case of conflict, that which is for the sake of another [is performed], namely, that which is for the sake of the sacrifice. What is the reason? Because when that which is for the sake of the sacrifice is being performed, the sacrifice itself does not come to fruition.
But when the human purpose is deficient, the person is devoid of merit;
and since there is a contradiction regarding the absence of merit, the purpose of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*) prevails because it is for that sake.
Therefore, it must be performed.
Because the *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest) is for the sake of another.
The Commentary states: As for the *hautra*, the person is for the sake of another, not the ritual action for the sake of the person.
Therefore, it must be performed by one specific individual, not by all.
In that case, the designation would be restrictive;
here, however, the designation "householder" cannot effect an exclusion,
because another [designation] is also applicable.
Even if it were not being applied, it might indeed be useless;
however, it could never be turned back,
because there is no statement capable of turning it back.
The statement is supreme.
The commentary: And as for that view taught [in the text], "He is the perceiver of the sacrifice," that is not a [valid] philosophical view.
What then? That is a mere statement, because the abundance of the fruit has not been established;

for the nominal stem (prātipadika) constitutes the primary perception. Regarding Soma—the connection [of the rule] is that the householder alone, even though acting for the sake of others, should perform the purificatory rites for the master.
The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: in a Sattra sacrifice, the householder alone should perform the purificatory rites for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

This is because of the connection [of the term] "lord of the house" (*gṛhapati*) with that very role; otherwise, the designation (*samākhyā*) would serve no purpose. Just as the *hotṛ* priest is the performer of the *hautra* rituals due to the designation "hautra," so it is here. [Objection: "Because of the ignorance of the householder..."
He was brought for the sake of fulfilling the required number; therefore, he possesses no ownership [in the primary sense].
Soma [objects]: "Even that which is a substitute should also be a partaker of the fruit.
Thus, since the previous objection concludes with the position that there is no substitute, this constitutes the connection [of the topic].
Vi—“He is indeed the agent, yet he is the master because he has taken over that position.
Since there is no fruit for one who has not begun [the rite], he is not the master; he possesses only the status of an agent.

Bhaṭṭa—By way of refuting the previous view, this is stated: for one who is brought in [as a substitute], it is not merely the status of an agent, but also the status of a master, because he has taken over that position and because of the scriptural injunction regarding the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) pertaining to the fruit, such as initiation (dīkṣā).
This being the case, the fruit of the *sattra* sacrifice does not accrue here; for its deficiency results in the non-attainment of the harvest.
This is because, first of all, it cannot belong to one who has arrived [at the sacrifice], since he lacks the status of being an agent of the rite with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*).
For this very reason, it cannot belong to one who is dead either.
Nor can it belong to those who remain, because they lack the status of being performers of the *sattras* (long sacrificial sessions) which have seventeen masters.

However, for the sake of avoiding the reproach of the learned (*śiṣṭas*), those who remain must necessarily complete the sacrifice that has been commenced; thus, by means of methods such as the *sāman*, this [required] number is brought together to fulfill the count.

For this very reason, the destruction of the sin to be accomplished through completion—which is triggered by the commencement—is also absent for those who remain, because the condition consisting of the "commencement" is lacking.
Therefore, it is established that he possesses only the status of an agent. Maṇḍana says: "But he would not be a partaker of the fruit. Śaṅkara says: "He is merely a bringer; he is not the owner."

In a *satra* sacrifice, a substitute (*pratinidhi*) possesses the characteristics of the owner (*svāmi-dharma*), just as in the case of one's own master. (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 6.3.10.26). Regarding this, the section (*adhikaraṇa*) titled "The existence of a substitute in a *satra*" (Mīko., p. 4103) should be consulted.
In *satras*, the consumption of the *iḍā*, the *camasa*, and so forth, constitutes a form of disposal (*pratipatti*).
VI. 10|2|9: "In the *satras*, they approach for the purpose of protection.

8|1|11: "In the *satras*—those rites to be accomplished over a year or a specific period—the rules ending with the ten-day rite (*daśāha*) situated within the *satra*-form twelve-day sacrifice [apply], because of that.

8|15: "In the *satras* to be accomplished over a year, the initial rules of the *Gavāmayana* apply, because of the fact of being accomplished over a year, because of being accomplished over three hundred and sixty days, and because of the *patnī-upagānas*."

When there is a gathering of multiple sacrificers (*yajamāna*) in both *satra* and *ahīna* sacrifices, acts such as the touching of the *śukra* vessel (*śukrānvārambha*) are to be performed by any one of the sacrificers.
Bhāṣya 12|4|11|32. [This concludes] the definition of *satra* and *ahīna*.
10.6.16.60–61. In the *sattra* and *ahīna* sacrifices, one of the rites beginning with the *śukrānvārambhaṇa* is to be performed by a single sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

[The rule that] one [person] performs those acts for the sake of others in a group of sacrificers. Commentary: In a group of sacrificers at a *sattra* or an *ahīna* sacrifice, those rites which are for the sake of others—such as "the sacrificer takes hold of the *śukra* cup" and "the *audumbarī* post is of a height measured by the sacrificer"—these a single sacrificer should perform, not all of them.
For what reason? Precisely because it is for the sake of another.
No benefit whatsoever is conferred upon the sacrificer by that ritual action.
If it were so, then everyone would perform [rituals] for their own benefit.
However, that rite is performed by the sacrificer; since it has been performed by one, there is no reason for a second person to engage in it. Therefore, one person alone should perform it.

It is stated that because there is an option regarding the holding of the *soma*, there is likewise no option for the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) in the case of touching the *śukra* cup and so forth; this is the connection.

Since the sacrificers are primary as the ones who obtain the fruit, and since their status as subordinate factors (*guṇabhāva*) is impossible elsewhere, there might be a doubt that the wiping of the *audumbarī* post is for the sake of purifying the sacrificers. By making it known through the words of the text that the sacrificers do not have the status of subordinate factors, and because they must necessarily perform [the rites] as subordinate factors solely for the sake of accomplishing their own fruits, only the possibility [of such performance] is established here, in order to demonstrate the lack of restriction in what follows.
[The opponent says: "In the *sattra*, does the contact with semen and so forth belong to all [participants] or to some?
Because there is no distinction, the first [view] holds; for another, this is established by the force of the context."

Bhaṭṭa: Even in sacrifices such as the *satra* and *ahīna*, where there is a gathering of multiple sacrificers (*yajamāna*), those rites which are not for the purpose of purifying the sacrificers—such as the touching of the *śukra* cup, the grasping of the *anvārambhaṇīyā*, and the measuring of the *audumbarī* post—must be performed by only one sacrificer. This is because the number [of performers] is intended as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) of the action, and since the performance of the primary act does not depend upon the subordinate quality, the result is achieved for the others through that single performance by way of *prasaṅga* (incidental benefit).
Therefore, in the *ahīna* and similar sacrifices, there is no fixed rule [regarding who performs them].
Maṇḍana: "In a group, the rite for the sake of the sacrifice belongs to one."
Śaṅkara says: "Let it be that [the acts] are for the sake of others;
one should perform them.

In a ritual such as the Sattra or Ahīna where there are multiple sacrificers, the Audumbarī post is measured by one particular sacrificer, and the touching of the Śukra vessel must be performed by another particular sacrificer."

The extension (*atideśa*) of the vital points (*marman*) of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), which possesses the nature of both a sacrificial session (*satra*) and a non-session (*ahīna*), is established for both the *satra* and the *ahīna*. (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 228; see the relevant section under "Extension: [of] the *satra* and *ahīna*, [namely] the *satra* and *ahīna*").
In the twelve-day rite consisting of a *satra*, the consumption of the sacrificial food (*sattra-madhvaśana*) must indeed be performed (at the prescribed time).
10.6.12.32–33. See the section on *mīko.* p. 2203 under the heading “In the case of the *dvādaśāha* consisting of a *sattra*.

There is an extension (*atideśa*) of the characteristics of the *dvādaśāha* consisting of a *sattra* to the *pañcadaśarātra* and the *kuṇḍapāyināmayana*. 8.2.6.30–33. See the section on *mīko.* p. 212 under the heading “Extension to the *pañcadaśarātra*.”
In a Sattra and other rites, there is only one performer, not two or many.
(In an Ahīna sacrifice as well, there are sometimes two performers.
