Each of the performers of a *satra* acts as the performer of the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* rite by means of procuring other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
(Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2610; see the section on the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīyanyāya*, sūtras 10.2.3.42–44).

*Satratva* consists in being enjoined as a session involving sitting (*āsana*) and desiring to attain (*upāyi*); whereas *ahīnatva* consists in being enjoined as a sacrifice (*yajati*) while not being accomplished through the qualities of a single day (*ahar*).

The twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) possesses the nature of a sacrificial session (*satra*) because it is connected with the term "session" through the injunction regarding the seating of the officiants, the employment of fees, and the plurality of sacrificers.
Commentary: The twelve-day sacrifice itself is the illustrative example.
And it has been stated previously that the twelve-day sacrifice is both a *satra* and an *ahīna*.
Now, the definition of these two types is being stated: a *dvādaśāha* characterized in this way is a *satra*, while one characterized in this way is an *ahīna*.

To distinguish between them, this is said: the nature of a *satra* is understood through the injunctions regarding sitting (*āsana*) and approaching (*upāyi*), as well as by the plurality of sacrificers (*yajamāna*).
For these two injunctions—namely, "they sit" (*āsate*) and "they approach" (*upayanti*)—are always observed in connection with a *satra*.
"Those who, knowing thus, perform the sacrificial session (sattra), those who, knowing thus, enter upon the sacrificial session"—

and because of the plurality of sacrificers, it is stated that "those consisting of a maximum of twenty-four and a minimum of seventeen should perform the sacrificial session. From the observation of this indicative mark (liṅga) occurring in association with that [term], the understanding arises regarding what is associated with it.

"Because it lacks the injunction for sacrifice (*yajati*) and because the number of masters (*svāmin*) is not fixed. Commentary: Now, what indeed is the defining characteristic of an *ahīna* [sacrifice]? To this it is said:

Where there is an injunction of sacrifice (*yajati-codanā*) and the number of performers is indefinite, that is understood as an *ahīna*. The prescription of *ahīna* sacrifices is by means of an injunction of sacrifice, such as "One should sacrifice with the *dvirātra*" and so forth;
for these, the number of performers is indeed indefinite.
However, the fixed measure of *satras* is that they involve many [performers].
Furthermore, regarding the definition of that which possesses such characteristics, the purpose has already been indicated by the definition itself; nothing else need be sought.
Soma says: *Satratva* (the state of being a *satra*) consists in having many sacrificers, provided that it is enjoined as something to be performed using the *āsana* (sitting) method.

Ahīna is that which, while being enjoined by an injunction to sacrifice (*yajati-codanā*), has an indefinite number of sacrificers (*yajamāna*). Alternatively, Satra is a series of days (*ahargaṇa*) characterized by having the sacrificers themselves as the performers of the rites; Ahīna is a series of days characterized by being joined with officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) distinct from the sacrificers.
Viśvarūpa states: "Is there no difference between the definitions of Ahīna and Satra, or is there?"
They say that because of the similarity of the utterance, there would be identity; however, there is a distinction between the two due to the similarity of the sacrificial offering (*ijyā*).

Bhaṭṭa: In the *trayodaśāha* and other such rites, because they possess the injunctions for sitting (*āsana*) and officiating (*upāyi*), the Vedic term *satra* is applied; since these characteristics also exist in the *dvādaśāha*, it possesses the nature of a *satra*.

In the *ahargaṇas* beginning with the *dvirātra*, although there is the injunction of sacrifice (*yajati*), because they have an indefinite number of performers, the Vedic term *ahīna* is used. Since this also exists in the *dvādaśāha*, it possesses the nature of an *ahīna* as well. This is stated incidentally for the sake of unifying common usage. Maṇḍana: "The *dvādaśāha* should be a *satra*."

Śaṅkara says: "And the very definition of a *satra* is its nature as a *satra*. That [nature] is limited precisely to that duration; specifically, for a year-long session (*āhassamvatsara*), the status of being a *satra* is caused by the conjunction of seven periods."
Vārttika 2.2.12, p. 471:
Being a *satra* is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of having the *Soma* sacrifice as its archetype.
Bālakrīḍā, p. 119. The principle of the *Satra* (the *Rātrisatra-nyāya*).
4|3|8| 17–19. See the section titled “The Principle of the Rātrisatra” (rātrisatranyāya) on page 1323 of the Mīmāṃsākośa.
[This concerns] the fruit of the Satra; after the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the Satra.

✱ Even among those who perform a *sattra* sacrifice collectively, the full fruit is obtained by each individual alone. (PMS 6.2.11–12). This topic should be examined under the section titled "The Section on Purpose" (*prayojanādhikaraṇa*) on page 2805 of the Mīmāṃsākośa.
✱ [This refers to] the status of being a qualifying attribute (*upādhi*) for the word *satra*.

The term *satra* (sacrificial session) is applied as a designation for constant performance (*satatānuṣṭhāna*), whether it is that which is prompted by the verb *ās* (to sit), as in "they should sit" (*āghīran*), or that which is prompted by the verb *upai* (to approach), as in "they should approach" (*upeyuḥ*).
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 717). Following the resolution (*saṃkalpa*) for a *satra*, the *Viśvajit* sacrifice is mentioned for the sake of its specific fruit.
The *Viśvajit* sacrifice should take place when the [intended] ritual action has not been performed.

The Commentary states: This is recorded in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): “He who pledges himself for a sacrificial session (*satra*) pledges himself to all deities and to all *pṛṣṭha* chants; he should sacrifice with the *Viśvajit* *Atirātra*.
He thereby ransoms himself from all *pṛṣṭha* chants.”
In the context of the *āguraṇa* (the formal initiation) for a *sattra* sacrifice, the *viśvajit* occurs as the occasion.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the *viśvajit* belong to one who initiates the *sattra*—that is, one who performs the *sattra*—or to one who does not perform it? What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It belongs to both him who performs it and him who does not, because there is no distinction made.
Or rather, [the phrase] "of the subsequent [act]"—why? Because it has been stated that such a type of action occurs when there is a cause;
how then could that be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) for something that is not being employed?
This being the case, we reply:
the Viśvajit should take place when [the Satra] has not commenced;
that is, the Viśvajit occurs in the absence of the performance of the Satra.
What is the reason? For it is heard thus: "He who pledges himself to a *sattra* sacrifice shall perform the *viśvajit* *atirātra*.
This means that he who pledges, thinking "I will perform a *sattra*," shall accomplish his purpose by means of the *viśvajit* sacrifice.
It is understood that for whatever purpose he desires to perform the *sattra*, it is for that very purpose [he performs the *viśvajit*].

How so? The meaning understood from the sentence is that "he who makes a vow should sacrifice with that [substance]," or rather, "he should accomplish the sacrifice by means of it," not that "he should accomplish the sacrifice.
Why? Because the sacrifice is heard as being subordinate (guṇa). How is it subordinate? Because of its designation by the instrumental case-ending.
For if [the action] were primary, the result would have to be postulated;

however, in the other case (where the action is subordinate), the attainment of the result follows from the sentence because it is directly perceived. [Dūṣaṇa—(stating the final conclusion according to one opinion): The result must be connected with the commencement [of the action], and it is with this intention—that the action also serves that purpose—that a person engages in it.
"Having resolved upon the *satra* sacrifice" means having resolved upon its fruit.

In that case, when the fruit has been resolved upon (aimed at), the *viśvajit* is enjoined as a subsidiary (*upātva*): "Having resolved upon the fruit of the *satra* (having aimed at it), one should accomplish it by means of the *viśvajit*.
And thus, if that [fruit] has been accomplished by the *viśvajit*, there is no purpose for the *satra*.
Now, since the purpose is accomplished by means of the *satra*, it is not [accomplished] by means of the *viśvajit*; therefore, because they perform the same function, there is an option (*vikalpa*).
And thus, for one who has not engaged in the *satra*, the *viśvajit* [is prescribed].

(He states an alternative view: “Thus says the *Tantraratna*; ‘he states his own opinion’—so says the Bhāṣya-commentary. Or rather, for one who forms the resolution, “I shall produce the fruit by means of a *satra*,” when there is an inability to perform the *satra*, the *viśvajit* sacrifice is enjoined with respect to that intended fruit.
The meaning of the sentence is: “Having undertaken the *satra*, one should perform the *viśvajit* [if unable to complete it].
(He refutes the first prima facie position: If the mere undertaking (*āgoraṇa*) were the occasion [for the injunction], a single sentence would have two distinct purposes.
In this regard, there may be a difference in intended meaning; [one view is that] "the Viśvajit is for the sake of the Sattra.

[He refutes the second position: In the case of the subsidiary (aṅga) view, since the formal undertaking (āgūraṇa) is already established as obligatory, the phrase "having undertaken" (āgurya) would be redundant—just as it is not stated in other contexts that "he who undertakes the Sattra," so too here it would not be stated.
Therefore, [the correct interpretation is]: "The Viśvajit is for one who, having undertaken the Sattra, becomes unable [to complete it]."
And because of the statement regarding redemption.
The Commentary states: Thus it is heard there: "Verily, he redeems himself from all the deities and from all the *pṛṣṭha* chants.
And praise by way of redemption is not appropriate for that which has already come into existence.
Therefore, it is "the Viśvajit when [the session] has commenced.
Now, why is the connection not made thus: "Having resolved to undertake a Sattra, one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit"?
For in that case, the connection between the Viśvajit and the Sattra would be understood as occurring at the time of the formal resolve (*āgaraṇa*).
It is not so;

for the *satra* is qualified by the absence of a householder (*āgāra*), whereas if there were a connection between the *satra* and the *Viśvajit*, one would have to assume an interrupted construction.
Moreover, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) connects the *Viśvajit* with the person: "A person should sacrifice with the Viśvajit."

It is not by means of the *satra*, as in the expression "of the *satra* [consisting of] the *viśvajit*"; for such a hearing would be purposeful only if there were an *āgūra*. However, if it were a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *satra*, it would be established by the sense of the matter itself and need not be stated.
Furthermore, it is not possible to enjoin "one should sacrifice after having performed the *āgūra*" within another *āgūra*.
For in that case, a meaning not expressed by the words would have to be resorted to;
for the identity of the agent occurs only after the resolution (*saṃkalpa*) regarding the sacrificial session (*satra*).
The assembly is possessed of sound;
and because it exists at a prior time, its existence must be stated as being dependent upon the object.
Therefore, the connection of the Viśvajit sacrifice is solely with the term "having made a vow" (*āgurya*).
If that is so, then for one who, having made a vow (but being unable), does not perform the Sattra, the Viśvajit is prescribed for him.
Śā—The doubt is as follows: is the Viśvajit for one who has set out after making the vow, or for one who has not set out, or for both?

"It might apply to both; why? Because no distinction is heard in the text. Or rather, one who has already commenced [the sacrifice] should perform it, for otherwise the *sattra* would not be so. However, this too is not tenable, because it would render the scriptural mention of the occasion (*nimitta*) purposeless."
And in the case of commonality, there is a disparity regarding the human purpose to be accomplished.

Therefore, this is the expiation for one who has undertaken a *sattra* sacrifice but does not perform it. As for Soma—here too, the connection [of the discussion] arises from the objection that [the sacrifice] possesses the status of an auxiliary (*aṅga*), as in the previous case.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: "The Viśvajit [should be performed] when there is non-participation, because the fruit of the Satra exists in the non-performance of the rite. [Vi]: "He who has resolved upon the Satra—'he should sacrifice with the Viśvajit'—whether he be one who has already engaged in it or one who has not yet engaged, the former [case applies]."
Since there is no distinction [in the case] of an undertaking, let it be a *sattra*; for it would be so.
One who has fallen away from the occasion should perform this expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

In the section on the *sattra* sacrifice, the *Bhāṭṭa* school cites the scriptural text: "He who undertakes a *sattra* should sacrifice with the *Viśvajit*. Thus, the *Viśvajit* is heard [as the rite to be performed].

Having performed the preliminary resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for a sacrificial session (*satra*), if one does not actually perform that session, this [rite] is prescribed for him as a means to obtain the fruit of the *satra*, but not as a substitute for knowing the *satra*; for in that case, the resolve is heard of as being the occasion (*nimitta*). Nor should it be argued that, because the performance of the *satra* would likewise enter into the category of occasions, there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, it must be stated that when the mere resolve is the occasion, this occasional rite is prescribed for the sake of a different result.
Rather than postulating another fruit, it is more parsimonious to postulate a fruit for the *sattra* sacrifice itself, which already requires a means of accomplishment;

and although that fruit cannot be conceived as the primary fruit such as heaven (*svarga*), because if that were the case, once the desire for the fruit had ceased, the performance of the occasional rite would result in a restriction of the occasion (*nimitta*)—since the occasion (the *saṃkalpa*) would still exist—nevertheless, it is prescribed in the explanation of the *vaidhātavyā* offering for the purpose of removing the defects caused by the commencement of the ritual procedure.

For this very reason, since the non-performance [of the sacrifice] is established simply by the assumption of a word denoting such a result, that [non-performance] does not enter into the category of a *nimitta* (occasioning condition).

Consequently, even when each individual member fails to perform the rite—whether other performers are engaged to complete the *satra* or whether they are not so engaged—the injunction that "the Viśvajit must be performed by this person alone" remains logically consistent.
As Maṇḍana stated: "The Viśvajit applies when there is no engagement in the *satra*."
Śaṅkara says: "And at the abandonment of the Sattra, there is the Viśvajit.
The conclusion of the Sattra is by means of the Pṛṣṭhaśamanīya [sacrifice].
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1539). The Sāman named Satraspardhin follows in sequence.

*Satdarśanyāya*, 4116, because of the statement regarding continuity (*saṃtata*).

The restrictive factor is precisely its being of the same genus (*raghvatva*), and not by some other property of a similar kind, because that [other property] lacks the specific capacity to accomplish what is required by the *vrīhi* grain.
Thus, it should be understood in this sequence: in the absence of *vrīhi*, one takes a very similar substitute; in its absence, one takes a somewhat less similar substitute, and so forth.
Maṇḍana states: "A substitute should be accepted that is as perfect as possible."
Śaṅkara says: "[The phrase] 'a substitute for the Gaura' [is used].

Regarding the statement 'because of the injunction to press the Pūtīka plants,' since the Pūtīkas are similar to the *manda* (weak/ineffective) [Soma], and because in the absence of Soma only something very similar would be obtained, one might object:

even so, when any random substitute might arise due to the injunction for the ritual act (*karmacodanā*), this specific rule is established by the principle of similarity; therefore, since this specific scriptural statement (*vacana*) applies even prior to that, the restriction is justified."

Bhāṭṭa 6.1.3: "The benefit bestowed upon the great bears fruit before long"—this is the maxim. Its meaning is as follows: whatever assistance is rendered toward those who are great, even if they are devoid of virtues, does not bear fruit after a long time or from afar; rather, it bears fruit at that very moment.
How is the assistance unreal? The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "accompanied by days, together with the harvest, [and] with the seasons.
Thus says Kālidāsa.
*Sāhasrī*, verse 975. The transformations are similar in time.
Bhāṣya 5.4.7.24: "Even at the time of the harvest, there is [the performance] of the primary rite along with its subsidiaries.

According to the aforementioned method, since the difference in time between the *ādhāna* (establishment of the sacred fires) and the commencement of other rites is established as permanent, there would be an option regarding the commencement even on the day of sacrifice (*yajanīya*).
This has been explained in the *Smṛtis* themselves.

"Because of the Kātyāyana statement: 'That day is the full-moon day (paurṇamāsī) when the conjunction [of the moon and sun] occurs before the turning of the sun's rays from the west, provided it is similar in duration for the purpose of the ritual prescription.'"

"One should observe that in the *Saṃgraha* and other works it is stated: 'The junction of the lunar phases (*parvasaṃdhi*) occurs from the time of the *āvartana* onwards; however, because of its immediate nature, the entire [rite] is performed at the very beginning.
In the *Bhāṣya*, however, this sūtra is to be explained as belonging to the section concerning the sacrifice at night (*rātrījyādhikaraṇa*).
It is not the case that the time for study is prohibited during the night."
"One should sacrifice on that very day"—this is the settled rule (*tan-nityatva*).

Bhāṣya 10.2.8.27: Regarding the phrase "he maintains a continuous stream," this is the intended meaning of the word *saṃtata*. [In the passage] "he pours out continuously," he offers with a long stream; thus, because of the length of the stream, it is called *saṃtata*. Bhāṣya 12.3.1.28: *Saṃtatam* (continuously).
"He holds it straight, he holds it continuously, he holds it with force.
There is a combination [of these qualities] in the act of holding, because their functions are distinct: continuity, straightness, and upward direction.
12.3.1.9. He offers the stream of oblations continuously.
Saṃkarṣa 1.3.5: "Because of the statement of continuity, there is a connection between the mantra and the beginning of the action.
In the context of the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), it is heard in scripture: "He offers a continuous stream of *vaśā* [cow-milk].

Since that stream is described by the term "continuous" (*saṃtata*)—that is, by the qualification of continuity—for the sake of establishing the continuity of both the mantra and the ritual act, a connection must be made between the mantra and the commencement of the action.
The conjunction here is with the beginning, not with the end;
such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
Or rather, it is a continuum of actions, because [the action] consists of various distinct acts and the other [alternative] is impossible.
The word "or" (vā) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The *vaśodhārā* is not a single ritual action; rather, it is a series of ritual actions.
This is because, due to its consisting of multiple actions, the statement "he offers twelve sets of twelve" speaks of various distinct actions.
And thus, it is the very continuum of various actions that here constitutes a single action, as it were.
By means of that [continuum], there is a conjunction of the mantra and so forth with the action.
Such indeed is the continuum of the mantra and the action in this context.

Because it is impossible to speak of a continuity (*saṃtāna*) of another, different kind of mantra and ritual action— since ritual action is momentary (*kṣaṇika*)— therefore, even in the case of the *vaśādhārā* [sacrifice], the conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is a conjunction of the beginning of the ritual with the end of the mantra. For continuity is based upon the relationship of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumad-bhāva*).
Those cognitions which, directed toward an object, are established in the state of being cause and effect, are designated by the term "continuum" (*saṃtati*).
(*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 161). It "continues" (*saṃtanoti*); *sam* signifies unification.
The term *tanoti* means "to extend.
Extension occurs only between two things; in that context, it exists as something complete.
Bhāṣya 12.3.1.26: *Saṃtardanam* (the act of joining together) is displaced from the context of the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice and applies everywhere.
Su. Pṛ. 392: *Saṃtardana* refers to the joining of two *abhiṣavaṇa-phalaka* (pressing-boards).
It is the act of joining two boards that have been made level by placing one upon the other and securing them through the piercing of holes for the fastening pegs (*saṃśleṣapa-vat*).
Pṛ. 1302: *Saṃtardana*.

Regarding the statement "for the sake of firmness" (*dhṛtyai*) as an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) in the context of the repeated piercing of the two Soma-pressing boards over a long period of time during the *dīrghasoma* sacrifice: *saṃtardana* means a firm joining. In the *dīrghasoma* sacrifices, the *saṃtardana* of the two pressing boards must be performed; it has no application in the archetype (*prakṛti*), but rather in the modified forms (*vikṛti*). Bhāṣya 2.3.1.27. *Saṃtardana* is a firm adhesion.
In the *dīrghasoma* sacrifices, the *saṃtardana* of the two pressing boards is to be done; it does not find a place in the archetype, but rather in the modifications.
VI. 2.1.16. *Saṃtardana* (piercing together) is the firm joining of one wooden plank over another by means of making a hole in the region where the two planks meet.
Bhāṭṭa 2.3.1:
Piercing together would apply to the archetype [sacrifice] because its purpose is lost, just like the act of purchasing.
Regarding the scriptural injunction, "For stability, one should join together the two pressing-boards at the *Dīrghasoma*," the question arises:
is this joining (*saṃtardana*) to be applied only to the *Agniṣṭoma*, or is it displaced elsewhere?
Furthermore, if there is displacement, is it displaced to the *Dvirātra* or the *Ahīna* sacrifices?

Regarding the inquiry as to whether [the rule] applies only to the *saṃsthās* such as the *ukthya*, or rather to both the *saṃsthās* and the *adhīnas* and so forth, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
"Joining together" (*saṃtardana*) refers to the firm attachment of one of two wooden planks used for pressing between them.

This *saṃtardana* (piercing together) should properly belong to the archetype, the Jyotiṣṭoma, because there is no loss of purpose—that is, because its purpose is not lost. This is because, when "long" (*dīrgha*) and "Soma-sacrifice" (*somasya*) are understood as a *karmadhāraya* compound (meaning "a Soma-sacrifice that is long"), both length and the status of being a Soma-sacrifice are possible in the Jyotiṣṭoma; thus, the term "long-Soma" refers to the substance [of the sacrifice] itself.

Just as in the case of purchasing [Soma], where there is an option among substances such as cows, cloth, or gold, so too in this case, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is an option between *saṃtardana* and non-*saṃtardana*.

Alternatively, because the capacity for supporting—which is understood from the supplementary statement "for the sake of support" (*adhṛtyai*)—is possible in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *saṃtardana* (joining) is not displaced.
The phrase "like the purchase" (*krayaṇavat*) is an illustration for the absence of a loss of purpose.
Therefore, there is no displacement of the *saṃtardana* from the Jyotiṣṭoma alone.
Or rather, there is an extraction [of the rule] because of the mention of a specific detail.

Regarding the rule "In a long *soma* sacrifice, one should join [the two boards] for the sake of stability," which is heard in the context of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that this joining (*saṃtardana*) is not to be extracted from the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—is reached by the Sūtra; then, setting that aside with the word "or" (*vā*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
there should be an extraction of the joining from the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
Because of the apprehension of a specific distinction;
that is, because by the word *dīrghasoma* there is the apprehension of the Soma sacrifice in its modified form (*vikṛti*).
Furthermore, length is not the cause for the application of the term *dīrghasoma* in relation to the intended [duration].
Because all these *soma* sacrifices are long in duration relative to the requirement of being performed,
and because the *jyotiṣṭoma* lacks the quality of being a "long *soma*" (*dīrghasoma*), the conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *saṃtardana* (the thickening of the joints) must be displaced from it.
Alternatively, it belongs to the *ṛtu* sacrifice, because the specific feature [of being long] is caused by that [the *ṛtu*].
The *saṃtardana* (joining together) enjoined by the rule, "In the *dīrghasoma*, for the sake of firmness," is not displaced from the *jyotiṣṭoma* alone.
Furthermore, the status of being a *dīrghasoma* will depend upon the performer;
that is, the *soma* of a tall (*dīrgha*) or eminent (*unnata*) sacrificer is a *dīrghasoma*.
Because it is caused by that; since the length of the performer is occasional, it is possible for it to serve as the cause.
Therefore, the *saṃtardana* (joining together) should not be displaced from the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Or rather, it should be [displaced] according to the season, because otherwise the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would be untenable.

Regarding the statement, "In the *dīrghasoma*, for the sake of stability through truth," the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) suggests that this quality of being a *dīrghasoma* (long Soma sacrifice) would belong to the performer, interpreting it as "the Soma of one who is long or elevated. The proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*), rejecting this doubt by means of the word "vā" (but/rather), states:
This quality of being a *dīrghasoma* must arise from the ritual itself (*ṛtu*), not from the performer.
A Soma sacrifice performed over a long duration of time is called a *dīrghasoma*.
However, if the *dīrghasoma* sacrifice were performed by the agent (*kartṛtaḥ*), the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "for stability" (*dhṛtyai*) would be untenable;

for whether the sacrificer is tall or short, his stability remains the same. But when the *soma* is pressed over a long period of time, there arises a fear that the two *soma*-pressing stones might split due to repeated striking; thus, the explanatory passage "for stability" becomes appropriate.
Therefore, there is an extraction (*utkarṣa*) of the *saṃtardana* (joining together) from the Jyotiṣṭoma.
And it occurs in the *saṃsthās* (concluding forms), just as in the case of the performer, because there is no distinction in the maintenance [of the rite].

The *saṃtardana* prescribed by the rule "In a long Soma sacrifice, one should join together for the sake of stability" will apply to the *saṃsthās* such as the Ukthya and others, in relation to the Agniṣṭoma. The Ukthya—
Section on *saṃtardana* (4118): Because of the long duration resulting from the increased number of cups (*graha*) in the [higher] forms,
therefore there should be *saṃtardana* in the *saṃsthās*.
To this doubt of the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*), the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) replies:
"And in the case of the *saṃsthās*, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating 'for the sake of stability' would not be tenable;
for, just as in the *agniṣṭoma*, the same amount of soma is used in the *ukthya* and other *saṃsthās* as well, according to the scriptural statement: 'He measures out ten handfuls.'"
And thus, even in that case of holding [the Soma], there is no distinction whatsoever.
Therefore, the *saṃtardana* (the rite of pressing) is to be transferred to the *ahīna* and *sattra* sacrifices.
This is because, just as there is no difference in the holding of the Soma for its pressing whether the sacrificer is tall or short, so it is here.
Or rather, [the term applies] to the Ukthya and other [sacrifices], because the meaning exists there as well.

The displacement of the *saṃtardana* (joining together) mentioned in the text "for the sake of length, for the sake of continuity, for the sake of support" does not occur in the *ahīna* sacrifices and others.
The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to exclude the position of such displacement.
This is because in the *ukthya* and other sacrifices, the purpose—the meaning of the word "length"—is already present.
In the Ukthya and other sacrifices following the Agniṣṭoma, there is an increase in Soma;
for the offerings indeed increase.
If the Soma to be offered were not increased, those offerings could not be increased.
And the term "cup" (graha) applies only when it is full;
therefore, it is not possible to take up vessels that are not full. Consequently, when there is an inability to hold two planks, the state of being unable to hold them [is established].
In this regard, the phrase "for the sake of firmness" (*dhṛtyai*) is a corroborative explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).
Therefore, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) stated that the practice of *saṃtardana* (joining together) is to be applied to the sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthās*).
[The opponent objects: "If there is no distinction, then the praise is purposeless."

Regarding the statement in the section on the Agniṣṭoma, “For length, for continuity, for support,” the opponent says: since the *saṃtardana* (joining together) has been prescribed for the sake of the purity of the material to be offered (*pradeya-viśuddhi*), it must be extended to the *ukthya* and other sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthā*) because it is praised as being "for support. This being stated in the Siddhānta-sūtra, the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) replies:
the praise is useless because there is no distinction; for how can that which consists of exactly ten handfuls be increased?
Furthermore, because of the restriction on the number of joints by the rule "having three joints," it is not possible to take one with many joints.
If it is argued that because of the excessive addition of water, there is purification of the substance to be offered,
yet there is no necessity for *saṃtardana* (piercing) to that extent;
and likewise, since there is no distinction in the case of Soma, the praise "for the sake of stability" (*dhṛtyai*) would be useless.
It may be so, because of impermanence.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) objects that since the *soma* juice is without distinction—that is, identical—across the sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthā*) beginning with the *ukthya* following the *agniṣṭoma*, the commendatory statement (*stuti*) “for the sake of support” (*dhṛtyai*) would be purposeless in the case of those terminuses; to this, the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) replies:
there shall be the joining together (*saṃtardana*) in the terminuses.
Because of the purification of the substance to be offered and because of the inability to hold it [otherwise], the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) “for the sake of support” is justified.

[Objection: But surely the purification of the material to be offered is not possible even if there is a rule for ten handfuls, because a specific limit has been prescribed; therefore, he says: "Because of the variability of the lunar days (*parvan*), the length-measure is not fixed.
Consequently, Soma from a distant lunar day will be taken.

Moreover, at the third pressing (*savana*), [the stalk] is crushed by the thumb; its measure is not specifically recorded, so one will take that which has a single joint, thick joints, or long joints.
Furthermore, by the injunction for piling up, "He piles them up with the words 'For the subjects, thee'," there is an increase of the darkness as much as is required.
Thus, because the quantity of Soma is unrestricted, the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is justified.
Therefore, the piling up (saṃtardana) finds its place in the sacrificial terminuses (saṃsthās).
The same applies to the *satra* and *ahīna* sacrifices;
this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). [Question: Is there an upward displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *saṃtardana* from the *Jyotiṣṭoma* to the *dīrghasoma*?
Section on *Saṃtardana*.
The *saṃtardana* (joining together) heard of in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* pertains to the *saṃsthās*, the *ahīnas*, and the *satras*, but not to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
*Saṃtardana* (joining together) would be excluded from the archetype (*prakṛti*), just like the act of purchasing, because its purpose is lost; this is the *bhāṣya*.
Regarding the *jyotiṣṭoma*, with reference to the two pressing-boards, it is heard in scripture: "In a long *soma* sacrifice, one should join them together for the sake of stability.
In that regard, there is a doubt: does *saṃtardana* apply to the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself, or rather to those *soma* sacrifices that take a long time?
It is said:
this does not apply when the purpose is already accomplished in the archetype; therefore, it belongs to the sacrifice. He says:
But is it not also heard that non-piercing is prescribed, in the words, "The two are unpierced"?
It is replied: it shall be treated as an option, like the purchase [of Soma].
Just as there is an option between "he buys with gold" and "he buys with a cow," and so forth,
so too here there will be an option:
there will be either joining together or not joining together.

Or rather—here, there is an inquiry into the conflict or non-conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*). In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, two wooden boards are prescribed as the support for the pressing of the Soma. Regarding them, it is heard in the original context: "In a long Soma sacrifice, one should join [them] together for stability" (*dīrghasome saṃtucyād dhṛtyai*). The meaning of "having joined" (*mittvā*) is "for the sake of consolidation" (i.e., having pared down the edges of the two boards so they become flush with each other by means of carving, one should place the second on top of the first and firmly fasten them together with pins and the like).

In this regard, there arises a doubt: does the term *dīrghasoma* somehow apply to the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself, such that there is no conflict with the context (*prakaraṇa*), or does it, being inapplicable because it refers to long-duration *satra* and *ahīna* sacrifices, undergo displacement (*utkarṣa*)?
These will be the positions [to be considered] here.

Is the application [of the rule] restricted to the pure Jyotiṣṭoma alone, or to the Jyotiṣṭoma when the sacrificer is long-lived, or rather to the *saṃsthās* such as the Ukthya and others, or perhaps only to the *satras* and *ahīnas*, or even only to the Agniṣṭoma and Atyagniṣṭoma? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It is that it applies to the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself, because the term "long Soma" (*dīrghasoma*) is appropriate there in relation to the *iṣṭis*, animal sacrifices, and the [ordinary] Soma sacrifices; and because the purpose of the *saṃtardana* (the pressing with a wedge), namely firmness, is possible there; and since an option is established with the injunction for *saṃtardana*—like the choice between rice and barley—it should not be displaced from its context in order to favor the *prakaraṇa*.

Thus, regarding the statement "there is an option, as in the case of the purchase" (*krayaṇavat vikalpaḥ*), which appears later [in 12.4.15–17], this should be explained as an example provided by the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) because it establishes the combination (*samuccaya*) of the items used for purchase.

Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) alone serves as an example; for any instance whatsoever may be established as a means of comprehension through illustration.
Without even introducing the statement regarding non-piercing (*asaṃtardana*), he supports the example of "non-utility" (*anarthalopa*) by means of the analogy of "purchase" (*krayaṇavat*).
In that context, the construction is as follows: "But surely, because the Soma is small in measure, piercing in the archetype would yield little fruit.
This is not a fault.
Because it has a purpose, like the act of purchasing.

Just as, because the *soma* is of little value, when its purchase is accomplished by any one of the items such as cloth, the remaining items being offered by virtue of the force of the scriptural injunction serve to further satisfy that very person who has already been satisfied; thus they are not redundant, and it is understood from two scriptural passages that the *soma*, being pleased by this satisfaction, brings about prosperity—so too here, although the two [pressing-spoons] are not joined together, even though they have the same purpose as the original pressing, it is understood from the force of the scriptural injunction that a more firmly performed pressing is conducive to welfare; therefore, there is no deficiency.
Therefore, there is no displacement.
Or rather, there is displacement, because of the mention of a specific distinction.
The Commentary states: "Or the *saṃtardana* (the joining together) is displaced."
For a distinction is indeed perceived in the statement, "One should recite [the *saṃtati* verses] at a long *soma* sacrifice.
Compared to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the *satras* are long in terms of their duration.
Alternatively, there is a displacement [of the rule] due to its connection with a "long *soma*" as established by the syntactical context (*vākya*).
Why? "Having perceived a short [object] of the same class, the cognition of 'long' arises;
therefore, the length of the *soma* [plant] would exist only in relation to another *soma*."

Indeed, it is not logical for the *soma* sacrifice to possess length in relation to the *iṣṭi*, animal, and *vihoma* sacrifices, because they are of a different genus (*vijātīya*) and thus such a comparison is untenable.
A distinction such as "long" or "short" occurs only when a counterpart (*pratiyogin*) is present in every case;
however, the *iṣṭi* and other sacrifices are not mentioned here, such that the *Jyotiṣṭoma* could be called "long" in reference to them.
[Objection: But surely even the distinction among various *soma* sacrifices is not mentioned [in the text].
[Response: Even if it is not mentioned, there still exists the commonality of genus (*tulyajātīyatva*) as a basis for expectation.

Furthermore, because of the relationship between qualifier and qualified, when "length" is predicated of that which possesses the nature of *soma*, it is understood precisely for the purpose of excluding other types of *soma*.

Furthermore, regarding those [sacrifices], one must consider what is long and from what it is long; it is not long compared to anything other than the Jyotiṣṭoma. Therefore, others are understood [to be the referents].
And because of their being the first [mentioned], that very [Jyotiṣṭoma] becomes the basis for that comparison.
Or rather, [the rule] applies to the agent, because the distinction is caused by him.
The Bhāṣya says: "Or the *saṃtardana* (piercing) should not be removed from the Jyotiṣṭoma;
in this way, the context (*prakaraṇa*) is upheld."
And the term *dīrghasoma* will be derived from the agent;
that is, the *soma* of a long [tall] sacrificer is "long.
Or rather—since the term *dīrghasoma* can be explained in some way or another, it is not proper to set aside the context (*prakaraṇa*).
And that [distinction] is established by way of the agent;
there is no specific difference residing in the accent itself,
because in both cases it is udātta at the end.

Therefore, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Or rather, it would be so because it is not possible [to apply it] to the sacrifice or to the purpose. The Bhāṣya says: "And this is not the case, that there is an insertion in the Jyotiṣṭoma."
The Soma sacrifice is performed over a long period of time;
this lengthiness pertains to the ritual itself, not to the performer.
Why? Because otherwise, the explanatory passage (arthavāda) would be inconsistent.
The explanatory passage (arthavāda) "for support" (*dhṛtyai*) serves this purpose: because of the need for stability and so forth.
Furthermore, since the Soma is pressed repeatedly over a long period of time, the explanatory passage "for support" is appropriate given the fear that the two pressing-boards might break apart.
Therefore, [the term] "utkarṣa" [is used].
Or rather—the meaning is that the lengthening occurs from the sacrifice itself; it is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*).

What is the reason? In this way, the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) will pertain to the primary sense of both [words]; otherwise, because one would function as a subordinate qualifier of the other, there would be the impossibility of an explanatory praise whose own meaning is the principal subject.

And thus, because of the frequent pressing of Soma and the firmness of the doubt, this statement will be seen [as meaningful]; otherwise, due to the weakness of the doubt, its occurrence would be untenable.
Likewise, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "for support" (*dhṛtyai*) illuminates this very meaning.
(Thus the phrase "because of the untenability of the explanatory passage" has been applied as shown.)
And because there is a fear of the two fruit-stalks splitting apart, the illustrative example is given right there.
Otherwise, "long" would be a qualification of the agent, which would be redundant;
for whether the agent is long or short, the nature of the action remains the same.
And this external qualification is [set aside] by the internal;
an internal qualification is more intimate (*antaraṅga*) than one that is external.
Therefore, there is excellence;
and because there is no distinction in the agency regarding the collection [of the Vedas].
The Commentary: This is the aphorism following the word [in the previous discussion].
Which are the words? Furthermore, for what reason is there no insertion into the *saṃhitā*?
If that were the case, the context would be maintained, as well as the length and the word *ūma*.
For it is said that the Soma is indeed long in the Ukthya and other sacrifices in comparison with the Agniṣṭoma. To this it is replied:
even if there were a slight degree of length in the Soma during the [subsequent] rites, the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) would not be tenable.
For in that case, the Soma is exactly that much, according to the scriptural statement, "He measures ten handfuls. There is no distinction whatsoever regarding its holding;
therefore, there must indeed be a displacement [of the rite].
Alternatively—this sūtra constitutes the response to the objection:

"Let it be that [the *agniṣṭoma*] is not placed within the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice; however, in the case of the *ukthya* and other sacrifices, the term *ūm* (sacrifice) is justified by its length relative to the *agniṣṭoma*, and the context will also be upheld.
Therefore, it should be placed within all three types of terminuses (*saṃsthās*)."

It is indeed logical that the non-distinction of context has not yet been refuted by the section concerning the *saṃsthās*. Now, this very [context] belongs to the *saṃsthās*; therein, those properties which have the *agniṣṭoma* as their purpose are excluded due to the contradiction between a permanent and a non-permanent connection (*nityānityasaṃyogavirodha*).
Furthermore, since the *saṃtardana* (the joining together) is not specifically mentioned as being permanent, there is no contradiction in its scope being restricted solely to that which is permanent.
Therefore, when it is argued that [the rule] applies to the *saṃsthās* (the various forms of the Soma sacrifice), it is replied:
"But even in the *saṃsthās*, because the quantity of Soma is equal, the portion for the *amiṣ* is the same."
To say that the vowels are eternal like the agent is a futile praise.

Even though the duration of the ritual action and the time here are long, only that much Soma—ten handfuls—is pressed as obtained through the extended application (*atideśa*). However, because the act of holding remains the same, there would be an inconsistency regarding the visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

(He states the intended meaning of the commentary on the sūtra "Or [it applies] to the Ukthya and others, because the purpose exists": "Because there is no distinction, the praise would be useless"—this is the intention of the commentary on that sūtra. Since the measurements of the ten handfuls and the offering are explicitly stated in the scripture, the purification of the offering must be accomplished by means of water and so forth.
Therefore, since the holding [of the vessel] is not distinguished [from other cases], there is an upward extension [of the rule].
Or rather, because the purpose exists in the Ukthya and other rites.

Commentary: This is not the case; there is no transference [of the ritual details]. Because it is favored by the context, there is no transference. Furthermore, the term *dīrghasoma* (long Soma sacrifice) is used because of its long duration.
It is performed;
even there, the Soma is greater than the Agniṣṭoma,
for the offerings indeed increase.
Those [vessels] cannot be increased when the substance to be offered is impure;
furthermore, the term "graha" (vessel) applies to the vessel itself.
Therefore, it is possible to take vessels that are smaller in size.
Therefore, in view of the apprehension regarding maintenance, maintenance itself must be desired.
In that case, it is appropriate [to say] "it should be maintained.
If it is argued that praise is useless because there is no distinction [between the two], [we reply: no.

Commentary: If you ask this, [the answer is that] even in the case of the sacrificial forms (*saṃsthā*), an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) is possible on account of the increase in the substance to be offered.
This is not so.

For the praise would indeed be exactly the same. Why? Because there is no difference in the Soma; for whatever amount of Soma there is in the Agniṣṭoma, that very same amount is present in the Ukthya and other sacrificial terminuses as well.
In the Ukthya and other sacrifices as well, only ten handfuls of Soma are to be taken. [Objection:
But surely the quantity to be offered will increase according to the requirements. [Response: That [quantity] is fixed at ten handfuls; how could it be increased?
Furthermore, because of the restrictive rule regarding the number of joints—namely, "or three"—it is not possible to take one that has many joints.
Therefore, due to this specific requirement for retention (*dhāraṇā*), the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would be untenable in the case of the *saṃsthās*.
Consequently, there must be a displacement (*utkarṣa*).
It might be so because of impermanence.
The Bhāṣya says: This is not the case, namely that there is an "exaltation" (utkarṣa).
It would apply to the sacrificial forms (saṃsthās), because of the context (prakaraṇa).
Thus, when there is a concern regarding the retention [of the Soma] due to the increase in the quantity to be offered, this explanatory statement (arthavāda) becomes appropriate.
In what manner is the quantity to be offered increased?
The Soma will be taken at a distant point in the ritual sequence.
Moreover, at the third pressing, a single stalk (aṃśu) is pressed; its measurement is not specified,
and one shall take it as having a single joint and thick joints.
By that, the purity of the object to be given will be achieved;
therefore, the explanatory praise (arthavāda) is rendered consistent.
Consequently, it is established that [the rite] applies to the completed sacrifices (saṃsthās).
Or rather—perhaps for that reason there is an inclusion among the ritual forms (saṃsthās).
And when there is an increase in the object to be given due to the purity of the gift, the explanatory praise (arthavāda) becomes appropriate.
If it is argued that [the increase] is by means of water;
Since it serves as the means for the *soma*, by means of words and so forth, there arises the insertion of two others;
therefore, the *soma* itself is what must be expressed.
Likewise, because of the possibility of its being preceded by *khaula* and *yava*, that which has long joints (*dīrghaparva*) will be taken.
This being the case, the specific measure mentioned for the purpose of purifying the gift will be rendered possible;
furthermore, both the context and the term *dīrghasoma* become appropriate.
Moreover, it is possible to use the expression *dīrghasoma* in the sense of the first [alternative].
"Because of impermanence"—this is understood to mean that the fixedness of the specific measure is not certain;
for it is possible to exceed the previous measure by means of another method.
However, this is not tenable, because it is impossible in the case of *satra* and *ahīna* sacrifices.

Therefore, the statement "one should infer the remaining portions" refers to that inference which is of indefinite measure; this is how the phrase "because it would be non-eternal" is to be explained.

Alternatively, according to the principle of the section on *saṃsthā*, for one who asserts a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), the answer is stated as its indefiniteness due to the non-inclusion of the eternal [element].
Regarding the point that "in the third pressing, the *aṃśu* is taken by some," there is a dispute.
Nevertheless, since this [quality] is derived from Soma, even here only the remote factor (viprakṛṣṭaparva) should be stated as the cause.
Therefore, its application is to the *saṃsthās* (the completed sacrifices);
however, one must not restrict it to the *saṃsthās* alone.
Why? Because the word "long" (dīrgha) is appropriate only when there is a mere difference from the Agniṣṭoma;
therefore, as in the expression "by another [way]," it refers to a different sacrificial form (saṃsthā) within the day.

"Just as the statement 'one who would sacrifice with this Agniṣṭud and so forth' does not apply only to the *saṃsthās* (the terminuses of the Soma sacrifice) [5.1.13.17], but rather to any instance exceeding the Agniṣṭoma; likewise, the mention of 'length' (*dīrghatva*)—which is possible only in cases exceeding the Agniṣṭoma—is intended to establish [the rule] within the context of the *saṃsthās* alone. Because they are complete according to the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), those [other sacrifices] do not possess their own independent context."

For this is not some previously grasped common (prākṛta) subsidiary that is enjoined again for a specific purpose, because it falls within the midst of the Jyotiṣṭoma characteristics taught at the outset.
For this reason as well, there is no context (prakaraṇa) for the terminuses (saṃsthās).
How so? Because that [context] ceases when the principle of non-connection (asaṃbaddha-nyāya) applies.
Therefore, by means of the performances characterized by the Jyotiṣṭoma, these [rites] are interrupted.

For if the *saṃtardana* were heard within an intermediate context after the *ukthya* and other [sacrifices] had been enjoined, then there would be an apprehension of that context. However, this [rule]—by the principle of the section on the *saṃsthās* (3.6.12)—is separated from the duties of the Jyotiṣṭoma by the *agra* and subsequent [elements]; therefore, it does not connect with the performance of the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*) of the *saṃsthās*.
Consequently, neither the context nor the *saṃsthāna* is the applicator for the *saṃsthās*.
What then? It is the sentence itself.

And since that [sentence] is common to both *satra* and *ahīna* sacrifices due to the non-distinction of the "long *soma*" (*dīrghasoma*) nature, it follows that this is a property of all [such sacrifices].

(The intention is that while the word *dīrghasoma* could denote a sacrifice through a *karmadhāraya* compound, by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi*—meaning "that in which there is long *soma*"—this word denotes merely those sacrifices characterized by a long duration.)
But the sūtras should be explained in this very manner; thus it will be further clarified elsewhere below.

Because of the restriction "only in the *saṃsthās*" by the subsequent sūtra (*padottara-sūtra*), and because the word "or" (*vā*) in the sūtra "or in the *ukthya* and others" (*ukthyādiṣu vā*) is taken in the sense of "also" (*apiśabdārthe*), or alternatively, by adopting the reading "and in the *ukthya* and others" (*ukthyādiṣu ca*)—whereby the word "and" (*ca*) is included—the term "ukthya" refers to the *saṃsthās* (namely the *ukthya*, *ṣoḍaśī*, and *atirātra*), while the word "others" (*ādi*) denotes the *satras* and *ahīnas*. Thus, since the meaning of the term "long soma" (*dīrghasoma*)—namely, being a soma sacrifice of long duration—is present both in the *saṃsthās* and in the *satras* and *ahīnas*, the second prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) asserts that there should be *saṃtardana* (joining together). In response, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is established that the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the rule applies only to those other than the *agniṣṭoma*, thereby refuting the displacement as limited solely to the *satras* and *ahīnas*. However, an objection is raised by the sūtra "because there is no distinction" (*aviśeṣāt*): if the quantity of soma to be offered in the *saṃsthās* is fixed at ten handfuls, then since there is no specific increase (*vṛddhi*) in that measure, the praise would become baseless; thus, the final conclusion that the rule applies only to those other than the *agniṣṭoma* is untenable. This objection is resolved in a different manner: because the remaining portion to be added (*avaśiṣṭāṃśābhyūha*)—that is, the measurement exceeding the ten handfuls resulting from the accumulation (*samāhāra*) of the portions left over from the ten handfuls separated from the purchased soma—is not fixed, there will indeed be a specific increase in the quantity of the offering even in the *saṃsthās*. This is how the text should be explained.
The commentary (*bhāṣya*) located in the *Siddhāntasūtra* and the commentary supporting the context (*prakaraṇānugrahabhāṣya*) should also be consulted (Sudhā, p. 1310).

Śā—Regarding the remaining portions, the following statement is heard in the scripture: "If there were only this much Soma—as much as he measures—it would belong to the sacrificer alone and not to the members of the assembly (*sadasyas*), because they have no share. Therefore, he pours out the remaining portions and distributes them only among the members of the assembly."
Soma: The connection [of this topic] arises because of the objection that, as before, there is no displacement here either.
[The opponent argues: "One should perform the *saṃtardana* (joining) in a *dīrghasoma* (long soma sacrifice); does that apply to the archetype (*prakṛti*) or to the ectype (*vikṛti*)?
Since it is said 'in a *dīrghasoma*', let it apply to the archetype."

Because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is stronger than the genitive case, there is an elevation (*utkarṣa*) of the configuration associated with length; otherwise, it would not exist.

16. Bhāṭṭa: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, having extracted the two pressing-boards (*adhipavaṇaphalaka*), the non-overlapping (*asaṃtardana*) is enjoined by the statement "he does not overlap them. Then, however, overlapping (*saṃtardana*) is enjoined by the statement "but indeed, in a long Soma sacrifice, he should overlap them for the sake of stability. Overlapping refers to the joining of one board upon the other by means of a wooden pin (*takṣaṇa*) at the edge of contact between the two boards.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether that very overlapping is restricted to the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself, or whether it is displaced (*utkṛṣyate*) to Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices, [the conclusion is] that there is no displacement because of the favoring of the context.
And there is no contradiction in the statement,
because even the Jyotiṣṭoma is long in comparison with this [other sacrifice]. This concludes the section concerning the pressing of the Soma substance.
Because of the performance of the *saṃtardhana* (joining together) and because of the resulting protraction of the *dīrghasoma*,
there is an option between joining and not joining, just as in the case of rice and other grains.

Regarding that which was stated in the Sūtra as "like the purchase" (*krayaṇavat*)—meaning [the option] ending with the purchase—that should be understood as having set aside the absence of a scriptural statement, because a combination (*samuccaya*) will be taught by the statement, "He purchases with twelve [cows]."

Or rather, let it be so; since "here" (iha) is not mentioned in the context of "ihādi," and because [the sacrifice] would be eternal in relation to that, the term *dīrghasoma* would become redundant. Furthermore, as it is improper to resort to an alternative interpretation (*vikalpa*) marred by eight defects, one should accept the genitive compound *dīrghasya yajamānasya somaḥ* = *dīrghasomaḥ* in accordance with the context, and thus establish the injunction for joining [the sacrificial posts] on the occasion of the sacrificer’s long stature.

However, if—by the principle of the *niṣādasthapati* section—the *karmadhāraya* compound is indeed more logical; and since the lengthening of the sacrificer would entail the splintering of the sacrificial plank (*phalaka*), and because through that [splintering] the act of joining together (*saṃtardhana*) would be impossible, rendering the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "with clarified butter" (*ghṛtaiḥ*) untenable; then the *karmadhāraya* alone must be accepted, namely: "that which is long and is Soma."

Even then, since this [rule] applies specifically to the Jyotiṣṭoma—wherein the various terminuses (saṃsthās) such as the Ukthya and others involve a multiplicity of offerings—the long duration of the Soma sacrifice (*dīrghasomatva*) is established because the cutting of this Soma is indispensable; thus, there is a conflict between the syntactical connection (*vākya*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*), leading to a restrictive application (*nideśa*). Nor can the multiplicity of offerings be accomplished by means of water and so forth, because it is illogical for a sacrifice whose substance is Soma to be performed with another substance in place of Soma without an explicit scriptural injunction. Furthermore, since the measure of Soma consists of three years’ growth and ten handfuls (*daśamuṣṭi*), that measure would be absent if one were to take Soma with thick and long joints.

For this very reason, since there is no evidence for the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the sacrifice by the word "soma," it can also be asserted that the long-jointed *soma* plant itself is the occasion (*nimitta*) for the act of joining together (*saṃtardhana*).

In reality, however, since the injunction for collecting the remnants is given after the ten-handfuls of three years' Soma have been measured—stating, "He collects the remaining portions"—and since the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) therein, "If there were only as much Soma as the sacrificer measures, it would be so for him alone; but he collects the remaining portions for the sake of the members of the assembly (*sadasya*) and for the *prājāpatya* [offering]," constitutes a deprecation of the previously mentioned measure, we understand from it that the quantity is limited only by what is required, just as in the case of the "milking of the latter" (*uttarādohana*). Furthermore, since the principle of the *kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa* (the rule regarding the three partridges) does not apply here, there is no fixed limit to the quantity; thus, an increase in the amount of the offering material is easily established.

Nor should it be argued that even so, since the *agniṣṭoma* termination lacks ownership (*asvatva*), and because the other three optional terminations are modifications (*vikṛti*) and thus lack a *prakaraṇa*, there is no conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) in the *jyotiṣṭoma*—given that in the *jyotiṣṭoma* there is a fixed state of offering (*pradāna-dhruva-bhāva*) and a fixed state of the substance to be offered (*pradeya-dhruva-bhāva*).

Because, in the case of optional *saṃsthās*, the *jyotiṣṭoma*—which serves as their substrate—is to be understood through its own specific determination; and because all three *saṃsthās* lack an inherent context (*prakaraṇa*) of their own, while the *jyotiṣṭoma* is woven throughout them all; and because a context is established for the optional number of *jyotiṣṭoma* performances by the injunction of *saṃtardhana* (joining together);

therefore, in the performance of the *jyotiṣṭoma* with the *agniṣṭoma* as its count, there is no *saṃtardhana*, due to the absence of a specific determination regarding the offering (*pradāna*), and thus there is no optionality either.

And for this very reason, there is parsimony, because the Jyotiṣṭoma with a variable number [of offerings], which possesses the quality of length and serves as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and the Jyotiṣṭoma with a fixed number, which is the constant correlate, are both obtained from the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself.

Nor should it be argued that even if the context (*prakaraṇa*) were accepted for the Jyotiṣṭoma of other numbers as well, there would be the undesirable consequence of the pronoun "this" (*etad*) in the passage—"This indeed is the first of sacrifices, namely the Jyotiṣṭoma; he who performs another sacrifice with this [Jyotiṣṭoma] when it is in the form of the Agniṣṭoma, that becomes merely a completed rite"—referring to the Jyotiṣṭoma of other numbers, which would contradict the statement to be made later that only the Jyotiṣṭoma of the Agniṣṭoma number is to be understood from the context. This is because [the context belongs only to the Agniṣṭoma].

Since the *jyotiṣṭoma* is accepted as having a context (*prakaraṇa*) by virtue of its possessing a fruit when delimited by the nature of being a *jyotiṣṭoma*, and since the *agniṣṭoma* *saṃsthā*—being itself devoid of a fruit—is incapable of delimiting the status of being a subordinate member (*aṅga*) to anything else; furthermore, although the term "this" (*etad*) refers specifically to the *jyotiṣṭoma*-ness, the word "other" (*anya*) also denotes the *saṃsthās* because they are modifications (*vikṛti*) of that very sacrifice, and thus those *saṃsthās* also possess the temporal extension of *jyotiṣṭoma*-ness. Consequently, by implication, the context belongs only to that which has the *agniṣṭoma* number. Therefore, due to the conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), the *saṃtardhana* (the act of tightening) finds its place in the context alone.
This being the position reached, the author of the Bhāṣya has established the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) right here;
he did so by means of the two types of prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*).
However, the author of the Vārttika stated that the placement [of the *ṣoḍaśin*] occurs in every modification (*vikṛti*) where the *stoma* is increased beyond the *agniṣṭoma*.
His intention is as follows:
First of all, you yourself have admitted that length is produced by the increase in the magnitude of the Soma resulting from the increase in the magnitude of the vessels.
And since the vessels of increased magnitude are finite in number according to the scriptural statement, they are not auxiliary parts of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

And therefore, since the quality of being a *dīrghasoma* (long soma sacrifice) cannot possibly exist within the *jyotiṣṭoma*, it must refer exclusively to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*). Nor can it be argued that even in the absence of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the status of being a *dīrghasoma* is possible for those aforementioned cups (*graha*) by way of their number, because in sacrifices such as the *sarvatomukha*, the *agniṣṭoma* terminuses (*saṃsthā*) exist in the eastern and other directions while the quality of being a *dīrghasoma* exists in another direction; thus, the rule of *saṃtardhana* (joining together) would undesirably apply even to the *agniṣṭoma* terminus.

Where there is a connection with the excellence of grasping the limbs (*aṅga*), or where there is simply the excellence of what is to be given as connected, because that [excellence] consists in a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the fruit which has become the means to the *apūrva*, and because such excellence is understood from the *saṃtardhana* (joining together), and because it is prompted by number rather than being prompted by the *Jyotiṣṭoma*— due to these aforementioned modifications—
the section concerning *saṃtardhana* is established as being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that [sacrifice]. This is the section on *saṃtardhana*.

Because the injunction for "joining together" (*saṃtardhana*) is otherwise untenable, the syntactical connection (*vākya*) overrides the context (*prakaraṇa*), and thus the application is restricted solely to the distribution of the *vighasa* (remnants) as previously stated; it does not apply to the *saṃsthās* (sacrificial terminuses), since they are modifications (*vikṛti*) and therefore lack an independent context. For this very reason, because the verbal root in *saṃtṛdyāt* is transitive, the understanding arises—through the connected accusative case—that the sacrificial board (*phalaka*) alone is the object to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*). Consequently, since the status of being a "long Soma sacrifice" (*dīrghasomatva*) cannot simultaneously function both as the objective (*uddeśyatva*) and as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*), it must be regarded solely as a conditional cause (*nimitta*).

For this very reason, this is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound, nor is it a *tatpuruṣa* compound with the word "soma" indicating the sacrifice through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), even though it is governed by the accent. Rather, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound that denotes the creeper itself. Furthermore, because it is a compound, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) even when [the soma] is the cause or when it is located in a specific place.
Maṇḍana: "In the case of long-lasting [rites], there is concealment. Śaṅkara: "The *utkarṣa* (transference) is held to occur in the case of concealment (*saṃtardhana*).

By the very principle of *saṃtardhana* and *pravargya*, when there is a conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), [the rite] serves the purpose of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) on the basis of syntactical connection.
Vā. 31413124, Kṛ. 314129. *Saṃtardhana* refers to persons standing in a sequence of producer and produced.

Su. p. 10. *Saṃtardhana* is continuity (*saṃtatatva*). It is the absence of any interval of silence between the preceding and succeeding utterances; Saṃkarṣa. 4|16. *Saṃtāpana* is [the heating] after cooking below.
The heating of the potsherds (*kapāla*) is performed for the purpose of baking the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) from below, that is, for cooking it while it rests beneath them.
However, since there is no baking from below in the case of the *saurya* rice-oblation (*caru*), the heating of the potsherds should not be performed.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The heating (*saṃtāpana*) of the potsherds (*kapāla*) consists of warming them with embers.
This [heating] should not be performed for the *caru* (gruel), but it should be performed for the *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake).
Bhāṣya 10.1.16.53; the heating of the potsherds is performed by placing them upon *darbha* grass.
10|1|15|53. There is a sublation of the *saṃtāpana* by the *saurya-caru*.

10|1|15|56. Regarding the statement "In the *saurya-caru*, there is a sublation of the *saṃtāpana*," this section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted. *Saṃdaṃśa*: that which is designated as an intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).

Su. P. 891. *Sandamśa* (The Tongs): The state of being situated between two sentences concerning the same subject matter. By means of this "tongs" (*sandamśa*), an intermediate context (*antaraprakaraṇa*) is established. This is the view of the Vārtika on Vi. 3.1.10.
*Saṃdaṃśa* (the "tongs") refers to being enjoined in the interval between two things that are themselves enjoined by a single injunctive statement.
For example, the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) among the *prayāja* offerings is a *saṃdaṃśa*. Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 5.2.1.

The *apūrva* produced by the archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements is first ignited; that *apūrva*, even though separated by words with different meanings, remains connected as long as its expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) has not been satisfied.
(Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.47, *Saṃdaṃśa*).

Those ritual items which are heard as being unassigned to the archetype and which present themselves when the expectancy for their function has not been satisfied, are grasped through the principle of "enclosure" (*saṃbandhayavāya*), that is, by means of the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).

4|4|2|3. *Sandamsha* (The Pincer): That which establishes a subordinate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*) as the means of application (*viniyojaka*). According to the *Mīmāṃsā-nayakaumudī*, there are seven types of *sandamsha*; these should be examined in the section on the "eight means of proof" (*śrutyādi-pramāṇāṣṭaka*) in the *Bālamanoramā* (pp. 9–12). Without a *sandamsha*, the accomplishment of the intermediate duty (*avāntara-kartavya-bhāva*) cannot be achieved.

Su. P. 1069: "One performing malevolent magic (*abhicaran*) should sacrifice with the *saṃdaṃśa*. Here, the word *saṃdaṃśa* is the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*), not an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*).

Bhāṣya 4.4.15: "'One performing malevolent magic should sacrifice with the *saṃdaṃśa*. The word *saṃdaṃśa* [is so called] because, by means of a pair of tongs (*saṃdaṃśa*), that which is difficult to grasp is eaten; through this similarity, it applies to the sacrifice. Therefore, it is the name of a ritual action. 4.4.15: 'In the case of what is named after another context, [the application occurs] by means of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth.'"

Furthermore, it is held that when, within the context of [rites] such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa, certain elements like the *prajā* (offspring) are first known through direct statement (*śruti*) and other means, and then again, by those same means of proof, another element is known, there exists an intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) by virtue of being "sandwiched" (*saṃdaṃśa*).
This does not apply everywhere; such is the meaning of the verse.

For since there is a subsequent reference (*parāmarśa*) to all the subsidiaries, such as the *prajā* and others, once they have been mentioned in their respective sections, there arises the conception of intermediate contexts (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) extending up to that point.
Vārttika 3.1.4.24:

When a strong means of proof (*pramāṇa*) sublates [the application] for the sake of the primary action (*pradhānakarma*), and the status of being a subsidiary quality (*aṅgaguṇatva*) is understood, the possibility of "enclosure" (*saṃdaṃśa*) occurs.

And since, for all these [meditations], their status as subordinate contexts (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) has been established by means of direct statement (*śruti*) and other criteria, and because there exists no subsequent non-referential mention of them after their subsidiary nature has first been declared, one should not suspect the presence of the "sandwich" (*saṃdaṃśa*) method of delimitation anywhere.
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 1070). This is the principle of the "sandwich" (*saṃdaṃśanyāya*).

Furthermore, the word "Self" (in the passage "The Self alone is his light") does not refer to the Supreme Self, because the preceding section establishes the connection of the channels with the [individual] Self, and the subsequent section—upon considering the statement, "Which is the Self? It is this one consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart"—establishes that it refers to the individual soul (jīva) by the logic of the "sandwich" (saṃdaṃśanyāya).
This is the logic of being caught between two [clamps], as found in Advaita.

Regarding doubtful cases, there is the "maxim of falling within a pair of tongs" (*saṃdaṃśapatitanyāya*). That which is known as a "pair of tongs" (*saṃdaṃśa*) refers to the grasping of an object situated between two parts, just as an object falling between the jaws of a pair of tongs is seized. Thus, this maxim applies wherever it is intended that an object standing between a preceding and a succeeding element is to be grasped by the inclusion of both.
It is thousandfold.
The nature of the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) is that of a pair of tongs (*saṃdaṃśa*).

(Bhāṭṭa 3.1.10). The maxim of the pair of tongs (*saṃdaṃśanyāya*): see *Mīmāṃsākośa*, p. 3678, under the entry "The maxim of the pair of tongs regarding qualified injunction" (*viśiṣṭavidhi-saṃdaṃśanyāya*).
That which is doubtful is determined by that which is certain.
Vārttika 3.4.1.135. That which is doubtful is sublated by that which is certain, because [the latter] has not [otherwise] been established.
3.1.7.4, p. 860. That which is doubtful is sublated by that which is certain.

Just as sugar-candy is equal to ghee. (Bālapṛ. p. 140). The maxim is: "That which is doubtful and possesses a purpose deserves investigation. The meaning is that the state of being an object of investigation belongs neither to what is unknown nor to what is certain, but rather to that which is doubtful.
The *sāhasrī* [section].

The determination of a doubtful introductory statement is made from the remainder of the sentence. (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 7). The relevant discussion (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted under the heading "The Section on the Anointed [Butter]" (*aktādhikaraṇa*).
It has not been stated that the determination of the meaning of doubtful matters arises from the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).

Bhāṣya 2.1.12, p. 370. "But when there is doubt, there should be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) due to the difference in purpose. In the Taittirīyaka, regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the *sāmidhenī* verses are mentioned in the seventh chapter, the *nivids* in the ninth, the optional *sāmidhenī* formulas in the tenth, and the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) is prescribed in the eleventh with the statement, "It is worn; thereby one makes it a mark of the gods," followed again by the qualities of the *sāmidhenīs*.

In this regard, when it is deliberated whether the *upavīta* (sacred thread) belongs to the *sāmidhenī* verses because of its intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), or whether it is an auxiliary to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) because of the primary context (*mahāprakaraṇa*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the *upavīta* is an auxiliary to the *sāmidhenīs*. To this, the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). When it is doubted whether the sentence concerning the *upavīta* forms a single syntactical unit with the sentence concerning the *sāmidhenīs*, the determination is that there is a split of the sentences (*vākyabheda*).
The word "but" (*tu*) serves to exclude the prima facie view.

It does not form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with that [injunction], because it is separated by the *nivids* and the injunctions that establish them, as well as by the lack of connection with the *sāmidhenī* verses.
Thus, the *upavīta* does not form a single syntactical unit with the *sāmidhenīs*.

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that whatever is to be performed within the entire context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) must be done while wearing the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītin*).
Some say: "But when there is no doubt, there would be a split of the sentence due to the difference in application;
this is not a prescription for a *nivid*.
It was previously established [in 1.4.13–24] that 'when there is doubt, the determination is made from the remainder of the sentence.'"
Vārttika 2.1.12, p. 525: When there is doubt regarding the initial statement (*upakrama*), the determination is made from the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).
In the case of "He places down the smeared pebbles" (*aktāḥ śarkarā upadadhāti*), there is a doubt as to the substance used for smearing in the initial statement.

Since clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is praised in the remainder of the sentence—"Clarified butter is indeed brilliance" (*tejo vai ghṛtam*)"—the determination is that the smearing is to be done with clarified butter.
VI. 1.4.19: "In case of doubt, [the rule applies] to those in doubt. On the day of the *saṃnaddha* mantra, the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing) occurs on the very day of the *saṃdhidina*.
