The girding (*saṃnahana*) of all the wives of the sacrificer occurs at the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) and other rites. See Saṃkarṣa 12.1, Section 2; Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1813, under the heading "Of all the wives of the sacrificer. The relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted there.

In the act of girding (*saṃhanana*) and so forth, the wife belongs to the sacrificer alone, not to the Adhvaryu priest. This is because the word "wife" (*patnī*) in the formula "Gird the wife; come hither" (*patnīṃ saṃnahyāyenodehi*), which is performed by the Adhvaryu, functions to bring its own referent to mind only in relation to its correlate [the sacrificer]. Furthermore, since it is traditionally taught that "this wife is indeed the lower part of one's self" (*adho vā eṣa ātmano yat patnī*), and because husband and wife act as a single agent in household duties, just as in common worldly speech one might say, "The wife alone is skillful in domestic tasks; she requires me," the girding pertains only to the wife of the sacrificer, as she is understood from the text. This is because, like the consecration of the priests (*ṛtvij-saṃskāra*), there is the possibility of her being an auxiliary factor (*upakāraka*) to the ritual.

This being the position reached, [we reply]: because of the Vedic mantra-text, "May they go together with their merit through the wife's attainment," and because the fruit is attributed specifically to the sacrificer’s wife, and because it is observed that even when the act is performed by the Adhvaryu priest, it is the sacrificer’s wife who is understood by the word "wife" (*patnī*), the refinement (*saṃskāra*) belongs to her alone.
This is also indicated by the scriptural mark (*liṅga*): "On whose day of observance the wife becomes menstruating, the Adhvaryu should sacrifice even for her.
Furthermore, since the relationship between the Adhvaryu and his wife is established by nature, it is impossible to enjoin it again.

The tying and carrying of the cut sacrificial grass (*barhis*) are for the sake of taking it up;

These two [mantras], however, are for the purpose of bringing what has been taken up to another place; because they serve a different purpose, they do not take on the mantra of the original action.

Just as in that very same case, when the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is being led from the location of the *gārhapatya* fire to the location of the *āhavanīya* fire for sprinkling, the mantra for "bringing" (*āharaṇa*) is not employed at that time—so it is here as well.
That very same *barhis* grass, having been tied up again after being spread in the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, is spread near the *uttaravedi*.
In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the mantra for tying is "May Pūṣan tie your knot," and likewise the mantra for carrying it away is "O Bṛhaspati, I carry you on my head."

When there is a doubt as to whether these two [mantras] are to be employed for the binding (*saṃnahana*) and the carrying away (*haraṇa*) in this [modified sacrifice], or not—the view being that because the binding and the carrying away are repeated, the two mantras should also be repeated as before—it is not so. For in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the binding and the carrying away of the cut sacrificial grass (*barhis*) are intended for the purpose of bringing it to the place of the sacrificial arena (*vihāradeśa*); whereas these [two acts] are for the purpose of bringing the grass, once it has reached the sacrificial arena, to the site of the altar (*vedideśa*).
Therefore, because the two mantras serve a different purpose and are prompted by their specific ritual function (*kāryaprayuktatva*), there is no case of incidental application (*prasaṅga*).

Thus, just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the two mantras are not employed when the *barhis* grass is being carried from the *gārhapatya* fire to the *āhavanīya* fire, so it is here as well. Vārttika 3|3|4|11:

Proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*), which is the cause of perception, is threefold: conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), and inherence in that which inheres in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*).

[The first applies] to substances by means of conjunction; to the qualities, actions, and universals residing therein, by the second; and to the universals residing in qualities and actions, by the third.

However, some say that through the proximity of inherence (*samavāya-pratyāsatti*), existence (*sattā*) residing in substance, quality, action, and generality is apprehended; and since existence is a connection with that [particular] time, its belonging to the genus (*jāti*) is not untenable. We do not disregard their position.
And since sound is a substance, the relation in that case as well is simply conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Nor should it be argued that conjunction with the auditory organ is impossible in the case of sound, because, given its omnipresence (as evidenced by its perception everywhere), it possesses conjunction with the auditory organ—which consists of space—and thus, due to its omnipresence, there exists the action that serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for conjunction.

This is not so; for action does not have the status of being a generative cause with respect to that which is delimited by the property of conjunction (*saṃyogatva*), because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the conjunction of two atoms (*paramāṇu*).

However, in the case of a conjunction with a heterogeneous entity, it is logical that conjunction possesses causality by way of being an action (*karman*), regardless of the specific heterogeneous nature of that effect.
Furthermore, there is no deviation [in the rule] because conjunction is admitted to exist even between two conjuncts.

Moreover, the conjunction of all-pervading entities (*vibhu*) is established through the following inference: "Two all-pervading entities are mutually conjoined, because they are substances without any interval between them, like a jar and space."

Where no expectancy arises regarding the "what" (the end), there must be an *adhyāhāra* (supplying) of a specific [end]. Showing the consideration of the specific nature of the end (*bhāvya*)— whether it is stated as something to be done or as a desire— it follows that when the desired activity is the end, it is accompanied by an injunction.

In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that "it must be performed," he shows that the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) is indeed desire itself. In the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice, there is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) based on the requirement for a specific object to be accomplished.

Similarly, in other sacrifices and ritual instruments as well, the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) does not state that the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is what must be accomplished; rather, it is said that "either the accomplishment of the fruit is enjoined, or [the sacrifice] is enjoined when there is a desire [for the fruit]. By stating that "the fruit is the goal" (*phalam abhyudayaḥ*), he asserts that the *apūrva* is understood only when its necessity exists.
Then, by saying "surely the fruit would be what is to be accomplished," he indicates that the postulation of the *apūrva* occurs at a later time.
Even in the Siddhānta, the word does not denote the *apūrva* as the specific object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*).
Therefore, by demonstrating the requirement for a specific object through such an understanding, it is not the operation itself that is stated to be what must be performed; of what [then] is it?

If one were to argue that the Commentator has stated that the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) serves as the object of cognition by means of the *locana* [the eye], then [the opponent] asks: "In that case, by what [means] does another [cognition] arise? In this matter, there is no such thing as follows: that the subordinate status of the sacrifice (*yaji*) with respect to the fruit—which is directly perceived by both attentive parties—is severed from the unseen potency (*apūrva*) by the injunction (*nānāṣṭi*), and then proceeds toward the fruit along with the entire procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Or rather: [this is] on page 648, in the section beginning with *saptamādau* (Pāṇini 2.3.7).
By means of a specific rule of derivation (*vyutpatti*), the locative case (*saptamī*) expresses the state of being a locus delimited by time.
Once it has been established by this seventh [rule], namely the rule of extended application (*atideśa*), that "the remaining [cases] exist," [the point is proven].
Then, in the eighth [case],
because of its being the cause of awakening:
in the sentence "Caitra cooks in the house," [the relation] is that which is self-defining—
The determination of that which belongs to whom and where it occurs is established by means of the method (naya).
In the ninth [chapter], because the meaning is predominant,
the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) has for its object the effort (kṛti) as related to Caitra by the relation of subsistence; [as in] "Caitra cooks rice in a pot."
The cognition has another form.
In the tenth [chapter], there is an increase due to the assumption of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*).
In the expression "he cooks," [the object] resides in that very [action] through the relation of being the object (*karmatva*) of the act of cooking as defined by itself.
By means of reflection.
And the measure of the application is characterized by its respective insertion (*tantrāvāpa*).

For this very reason, in all cases, the meaning of the locative case [is determined] as being either the agent or the object that defines itself. This alone [is established] incidentally, because it subsists upon the purpose of another.
The holder alone is the declarer (ākhyātṛ) because of the connection [with the action], and not one who holds other causal factors (kāraka).
Page 648.
Directly.

(Regarding the matter of sustaining other grammatical factors [kārakas], he says: When it is said, "He gives to the Brāhmaṇas in Kāśī," the agent alone is immediately [understood] because the seventh case [ending] is subject to extension based on a prior direct instruction.

Because of the perception that [the king] resides in Kāśī; whereas, in the case where it is said, "The king resides in Pāṭaliputra," he awaits the completion of the first six chapters for the purpose of studying the instructions.
Or: [the word] "kāṣyām" [is used] for the Brahmins; the seventh case ending [is applied]. 4144.
Seventh [case]: 4145.

Immediately after [the statement] "only when [the object] is obstructed (as in the case of a house, etc. is there the intention to express it as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of such usage even for a jar that is not obstructed.

Regarding what was stated about being the locus (*āśrayatva*): the word "on the ground" (*kṣitau*) is to be supplied [as the complement]. In the sentence "Caitra cooks in the house," [the action] resides in Caitra.

Because it is the counter-positive of the absence of a substance other than a jar; because the absence residing in the jar and so forth does not have its occurrence in the house [as its locus]; and because even when defining the house as the locus, the counter-positive is delimited by the delimiting factor of counter-positiveness.
The point is that [the state of] being a meditator does not exist [for him].
But [one might object]: "Is it not Caitra's? [We reply:
No, because a yogi is not established [as a distinct entity].
Therefore, because it is the locus of the absence of the currently perceived potness (*ghaṭatva*),

the meaning of the locative case following the word "caitra" cannot be denied as being a cognition of an absence residing in the ground, whose counter-positive is directly delimited by existence (*bhāva*).
It is simply not possible for that which has the earth as its substratum (ilāśraya) to have that which has the agent as its substratum (kartṛsaṃśraya) as its object of meditation (bhāvanā),
because [the agent] does not exist in the upper region; for there is no such thing as "being above."

Because that is impossible, even in that case, there can be no direct cognition of the state of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*); thus, it is not possible for this [word] to produce such an understanding. [The author] provides the resolution: "In the case of Caitra and others, however, by means of the supreme agency... (*caitrādau tu parayā kartṛ-*). [He continues: "...there is no connection with the notion of a locus residing in the ground (*bhūtalaniṣṭhādhikaraṇabhāvanānanvaya*). (Thus he resolves the objection. In the case of Caitra and others, however, by means of the supreme agency... [the understanding arises].

Since this locative sense would result in the non-inclusion of that which lacks [the action], it is sublated by the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) [of *kartṛ* and *karman*] through the medium of the agent and the object.
Therefore, it is established that [the application of the term] occurs only through the medium of either the agent or the object.
Because it would result in the violation of the rule that [the locative] denotes the locus of the action;
for if the jar were construed with [negation] through the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*),
then the construction of the meaning of the locative case would [be impossible].
Because there is an absence of agency due to the absence of being the substratum of the root-meaning, and because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is untenable; [one might object]:

"But if this is so, when the object (*karman*) is intended—as in 'he goes to the village' or 'in the village'—then upon stating the agent, such as the absence whose counter-positive is the jar residing on the ground..."

There would be no occurrence of the usage "it is gone to" (gamyate); furthermore, because the locus of the action and the agent are one and the same, the dual number in the expression "the pot is not that" (ghaṭo na saḥ) would be untenable,
since [the agent] is mediated by the object.

By implication (*lakṣaṇayā*), the status of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) resides there [in the locus]; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of using the expression "the jar does not exist" with respect to the jar itself as the counter-positive (*pratiyogi*).
If it is argued that [the meaning] is "my artha" (my purpose), then there would also be the undesirable consequence of the usage "he cooks rice" (*odane pacati*),
because the connection with the relation of non-existence (*ayogitā-sambandha*) would apply to the absence, and in that absence, the locus would be the ground (*bhūtala*).

For this very reason, the view that the connection [of the object] occurs only through the result delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) has been rejected; for otherwise, it would follow that even the boiled rice (odana) [is the object]. Specifically, [the opponent might argue] that one accepts the existence of the pot as "the pot is the counter-positive of an absence residing on the ground," and thus the connection [of the object] is established. However, this is refuted because it would lead to the same undesirable consequence for the boiled rice as well.
If this is argued,
[we reply that] when verbal cognition is admitted, [the statement] "the jar exists" applies even to what is past or what is yet to come;
for in those cases as well, the reality [of the object] is possible by way of its agent.

Because the [negation] "the jar does not exist" is untenable at a time other than the present— since [otherwise] Caitra would possess the effort conducive to the act of going to the location [where the jar is perceived]— [the negation must refer to a different time].
Furthermore, because the state of possessing the effort conducive to the act of going to that location is possible for Caitra [at another time], [there is no contradiction].

Because it would entail the consequence [of such an absurdity]. Even in the case of Caitra, who possesses an action having the attainment of the village as its result through the act of cutting, there is the substratum of the village;
by this, [the statement] "there exists a pot which is the locus of the absence of being on the ground" is also [refuted].

Because [the property of] being a locus (*bhāvitva*) is absent in the agent, the verbal cognition— namely, "the action of going, which has Pramadhi as its locus and which occurs in Caitra, is conducive to [the result]"— is refuted;
for it is not possible for the state of being the locus of the action (*kṛtitva*) to reside in Caitra.
But since the agent of cooking is the pot (odanādhikaraṇa),

such a usage does not occur because the locus (adhikaraṇa) expressed by the seventh case is [already] functioning as the instrument (karaṇa). To avoid this fault, [the author] states that the locus expressed by the seventh case...

When there is a connection with time in relation to the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) by way of the relation of "qualifier-ness" (nirūpakatā), it is precisely in that [time] that the connection with the meaning of the suffix -lyap occurs; and that [suffix-meaning] has as its locus the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyātārtha). But even so, in cases such as "he cooks over the fire" (agnau pacati) or "he stands in the sun" (ātape tiṣṭhati), there is also a connection with the meaning of -lyap, and that [suffix-meaning] has as its locus the meaning of the verbal suffix.
"A bird moves in space," "standing in space," and "within space"—

in such usages, there would be the impossibility of [expressions like] "he restrains [it]" and so forth, because [space] would not function as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) distinct from the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) through the relation of opposition (*pratiyogitā-saṃsarga*), and that [opposition] would reside in the absence (*abhāva*) denoted by the negative particle (*nañ*) which is [then] in the nominative case (*prathamā*).

In the case of an object such as a jar, [existence] resides in the ground; this is because the state of existing, which is defined by its locus residing in the ground, is mediated by either the agent or the object.
Nor is it [the case] in fire...
"The pot possesses the absence whose counter-correlate is the state of being the locus of the relation with the time of measuring"—this verbal cognition [is what arises].
Thus, the claim made by some that "the usage 'he cooks' does not exist at all" is correct.
This is the verbal understanding (*śābdabodha*).
And [it is held that] in a case where there is a co-occurrence with the negative particle (*nañ*),
such as in the statement "In whichever fire one should cook this, in that [fire] the oblation is prescribed," there is a connection with number; that view is also [addressed].
Because of the statement regarding its application;
for it is not [the case] even when [the object] is conjoined with another substratum through vision. No.
Because it would result in the meaning of the seventh case (locative) being directly construed with the meaning of the verbal root;
otherwise,
it is possible for the relation [of the object] to be the determinant of the locus-ness.

Otherwise, if the agency were not intended to be expressed, there would result the use of the impersonal (bhāva) construction "caitre pacyate" (it is cooked by Caitra). [Examples of such unintended agency include:
"A person stands in the sky," or "Caitra stands within Maitra's self."
For this very reason, when the meaning of the locative case is construed with the meaning of the verbal root, the term "paramparā" (indirect connection) is employed;
otherwise, such usages as [the following] would result.
If this is argued, then in such a case, regarding the phrase "in the Gaṅgā":
Or rather, for those who accept the authority [of the scriptures],
there is a connection of the locus of the word "that" (*tacchabda*) with either the agent or the object by way of one of these two;
nor is there a direct connection in cases where a negative particle (*nañ*) is employed.

The claim made by some that this is correct regarding the postulation of grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*)—but not in the case of Caitra—is reasonable; for even in this way, the usage "caitre na pacyate" (it is not cooked by Caitra) can be prevented. (Mīmāṃsākośa 519)

The state of being the locus of a substratum residing on the ground—the property of being the locus of an existing presence residing on the ground—is well-established precisely in the case of the atomhood (paramāṇutva) residing on the ground. This very method is to be understood from what precedes.
In this way, the connection of the meaning of the suffix *laṭ* and others with the meaning of the verbal root is not abandoned.

Furthermore, since it is accepted that [the negative particle] serves to indicate the intended meaning (tātparya), the state of being the counter-positive of an absence residing in the jar at that specific time is unimpeded within the aforementioned locus-hood.

However, if one should suspect that in this view the agency of the jar is untenable because it would be construed with the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) through a direct relation, then let the verbal suffix itself have a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) for the aforementioned meaning—namely, the absence whose counter-positive is [the jar]—by means of both relations (direct and indicated), and let the word *nañ* serve merely to indicate the intended meaning.
In that state (*tasmin bhāve*), the occurrence of the pot is possible as its agency (*kartṛtva*) precisely through the relation of being the contained (*ādheya-sambandha*).

Furthermore, since the meaning of the locative case (*saptamī-artha*) occurs [in the absence of the pot] precisely through a mediated relation (*paraṃparā-sambandha*) involving the agent, there is no need to postulate a different rule of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*).

Moreover, the absence whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the state of being a locus (*āśrayatva*) in the manner described does not exist in the pot while the pot is in the state of residing on the ground; thus, by implication, there arises the cognition of the absence of the pot having the ground as its locus (*bhūtalādhikaraṇaka-ghaṭābhāva*).

Thus, in the case of "vāyau rūpaṃ nāsti" (there is no color in air), the meaning of the locative case is the state of having the same time as the action of its own relation through connection with one of the two [relata].

And that [locative] connects with the other action through direct relation; and although the preceding action functions as a qualifier of the agent or the object, it is not untenable for it to also be a constituent of the locus of the relation denoted by the locative suffix.

And thus, where an action such as "iko yaṇaci" (Pāṇini 6.1.77) and so forth is not explicitly mentioned, it should be understood that the action in the form of existence (*sattā*), namely "being present" (*sati*), is supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).

However, where the status of being a qualifier (*lakṣakatva*) for the related term is not intended, there is the employment of two separate sentences, such as "The cows are milked" and "Caitra has gone.
For this very reason, in such cases, the cognition that the preceding action serves as a qualifier for the subsequent action occurs only mentally (*mānasa*), as in the case of poets and storytellers.

And for this very reason, since there is an absence of synonymous meaning, it is not a rule for the locative case (*saptamī-vidhi*) that expresses that [meaning]; rather, it should be understood as either an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) or, in some way, a sublater of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-bādhaka*).

As for the statement—"When the agency (*kārakatva*) of those who perform an action is intended, [the seventh case suffix is used]; when the absence of that agency in those who perform an action is intended, the seventh case suffix is used"—or alternatively, "When the absence of that agency in those who perform an action and the presence of that agency in others is intended," this *vārttika* (though in reality the *vārttika* of the grammatical system is: "And when there is agency in those who are agents, and non-agency in those who are non-agents, that too is [the basis for the usage]"), which prescribes the seventh case in examples such as: "While the good are crossing over or being honored, the bad remain or are not honored; while the bad are staying or not being honored, the good cross over or are honored; while the good are staying or not being honored, the bad cross over or are honored; while the bad are crossing over or being honored, the good remain or are not honored"—some maintain that since this is already established by the rule *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*, the *vārttika* need not have been composed.

Kaiyaṭa and others, however, have stated that [this rule] is for the purpose of prescribing the locative case (*saptamī*) when the relationship between the indicator (*lakṣya*) and the indicated (*lakṣaṇa*) is not intended to be expressed. To this we reply: since a relationship other than that between indicator and indicated is not direct (*asākṣāt*), if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the prescription of the locative case in that sense being redundant. Therefore, another grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) exists to express the meaning of the locative case as "having the same time as the action related to itself" by means of a relationship characterized either by agency or objecthood delimited by fitness (*arhatva*). For instance: [The text continues with examples.]
In this context, propriety is suggested by the first two sentences,
while impropriety is suggested by the others;
and the locative case-meaning as defined above serves as the ground for establishing that [suggestion].

Furthermore, even when the words *atiṣṭhatsu* and *āsate*, which serve as the indicators (*lakṣaṇa*) for the interruption [of the action], are present, the absence of the crossing is indicated by these two alone.

Moreover, through the expressed (*vācya*) and suggested (*vyaṅgya*) modes of the terms *sat* and *asat*, the deficiency in the action is manifested. Consequently, because this relationship between indicator and indicated—which is distinct from cases such as "he went while the cows were being milked" (*goṣu duhyamānāsu gataḥ*)—is experienced as possessing a specific quality (*vaiśiṣṭya*), it cannot be subsumed [under other categories] and thus requires a separate grammatical rule.

Thus, according to the rule *ṣaṣṭhī cānādare* (Pāṇini 2.3.38), when there is an intention to express a state characterized by disregard, both the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and seventh (*saptamī*) case endings are used optionally. For example:
*rudati rudato vā prātrājīt* ("He went forth while [the son] was weeping"), meaning he went forth disregarding the son who was weeping.

Similarly, according to the rule *svāmīśvarādhipatidāyādasākṣipratibhūprasūtaiśca* (Pāṇini 2.3.39), when these words are joined with a word ending in the seventh case, both the sixth and seventh case endings are used.
"In the expression *goṣu gavāṃ vā svāmī* (the owner of cows),
the meaning of the case ending is the state of being a qualifier (*nirūpakatva*).
And that [qualifier-state] connects with the verb *asti* (exists) by way of [the relation of] ownership."

The inclusion of the pair "samānārthaka" (having the same meaning) and "svāmin" (owner), etc., is for the purpose of excluding other synonyms; this follows from the Vārttika: "Even for words that are dissimilar [in form] but have the same meaning. However, a three-word compound such as *vakradaṇḍau* is not possible here because [the rule] refers to the specific phonetic form of the words.
Haradatta explains: "Born among cows (*gavām* or *goṣu*)" means "known in order to experience the cows."

Thus, according to the rule *āyuktakuśalābhyāṃ cāsevāyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.40), the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and locative (*saptamī*) cases are used as in the examples *goṣu gavāṃ vā āyuktaḥ kuśalo vā*. Here, *āyuktaḥ* means "employed" or "engaged.
Since the locative case would have applied by virtue of being the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*), the genitive is specifically prescribed here.
"Intense application" (*āsevā*) means being solely devoted to that [object].
In the absence of that, however, "the ox is yoked with the cart" (*āyukto goḥ śakaṭena*) means "lightly yoked.
Likewise, there is the rule: *yataśca nirdhāraṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.41).

From this sūtra: when *nirdhāraṇa* (selection/discrimination) is performed—meaning the separation of a single part from a whole by means of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), or name (*saṃjñā*)—the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and seventh (*saptamī*) case endings occur to denote that [whole].

Examples include: "Among men, among men, the Brāhmaṇa is the best"; "Among cows, among cows, the black one yields much milk"; "Among those walking, among those walking, the runner is the fastest"; "Among students, among students, Maitra is clever," and so forth.
In these cases, the meaning of the case ending is the aforementioned *nirdhāraṇa*.

In that context, the meaning of the base (prakṛti) is construed with the sense of specification (*nirūpakatā*). And that [meaning] is construed with the action through the relation of residing in the Brāhmaṇas and so forth, who have become the objects of selection. Furthermore, it should be understood that this denotation of the alternative occurs only when the delimitors of the counter-correlativity of the selection—such as "humanity" or "cowness"—which are conveyed by the word, actually exist in the Brāhmaṇas and so forth who are the objects of that selection.
But when its non-existence (*asattva*) is intended there, then, because it denotes the correlate of a selection (*nirdhāraṇapratiyogivācaka*), only the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used;

this is according to the rule *pañcamī vibhakte* (Pāṇini 2.3.42), as in the example "The people of Mathurā are more eloquent than those of Kāśī. Similarly, according to the rule *sādhunipuṇābhyām āryāyāṃ saptamy aprateḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.43), the locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the example "He is good or skillful toward his mother" (*mātari sādhunipuṇo vā*).
In the absence of *arcā* (reverence), there is the genitive case in the sense of "the king’s skillful servant" (*rājño bhṛtyaḥ*).
The mention of *pratigrahaṇa* (acceptance) is illustrative. [Examples include: "skillful or clever toward his mother" (*sādhu-nipuṇo vā mātaraṃ prati*, *pari*, or *anu*).
Furthermore, this sūtra is primarily intended for that very purpose because it is logical.

Thus, from the sūtra *prasitotsukābhyāṃ tṛtīyā ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.44), which means that when used in conjunction with these two words, either the third case (*tṛtīyā*) or the seventh case (*saptamī*) may be employed, there is an option for the seventh case in such instances as *prasita utsuko vā hariṇā harau vā*.
Here, *prasitaḥ* means "attached" (*āsaktaḥ*), but not "exceedingly white" (*prakarṣeṇa śuklaḥ*).
The meaning of the case-ending is "being an object" (*viṣayatva*).
This statement [is made] regarding the optional nature of the third case-ending.

Likewise, according to the rule *nakṣatre ca lupi* (Pāṇini 2.3.46), when the suffix *aṇ*—prescribed by the rule *nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.12)—is elided from a nominal stem denoting a lunar mansion by the rule *lubviśeṣe* (Pāṇini 4.2.44), the third and seventh case-endings occur in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) after that nominal stem which denotes the time conjoined with a lunar mansion.
Thus, from the sense [of the rule], in such passages as "one should invoke the Goddess at the root with the root-mantra," the locative case is used.
Even when referring to time, if the status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) is not intended to be expressed, the nominative case is also used, as in "today is Puṣya."

Thus, according to the rule *saptamī-pañcamyau kāraka-madhye* (Pāṇini 2.3.7)—which means that the seventh (*saptamī*) and fifth (*pañcamī*) case endings occur when time (*kāla*) or distance (*adhvan*) lies between two factors of action (*kāraka*), whether they be of the same or different types—the seventh case is used optionally in examples such as: *adya bhuktvā adya hyahe dvādaśa bhoktā* ("Having eaten today, he will eat twelve times in two days"), and *ihastho 'yaṃ krośe krośārddhā lakṣyaṃ vidhyet* ("Standing here, he might pierce a target at a distance of one *krośa* or half a *krośa*").

In this regard, although there is only one person as the agent (*kartṛ*) in both instances of eating, nevertheless, because the agency defined by the act of eating at the present time is distinct from the agency defined by the act of eating at the time of yesterday, there is a state of being "between two factors" (*kāraka-dvayamadhyatva*).

In the second example, however, "this" is the agent, "the target" (*lakṣya*) is the object (*karman*), and "here" (*iha*) is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); thus, there is a state of being "between heterogeneous [factors]" (*vijātīya-madhyatva*).
In all cases, the status of being the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakty-artha*).
This is a rule intended to provide for the occurrence of the locative case (*saptamī*) in certain instances where the status of an ablative (*apādāna*) and so forth is impossible.

Similarly, when used in conjunction with the word *adhika* ("more than" or "exceeding"), as in the example "Hari is superior to the world" (*loke lokād adhiko hariḥ*), both the ablative and the locative cases are appropriate; this is because of the specific instructions found in the two Pāṇinian sūtras: *tadasminn adhikam* (Pā. 5.2.45) and *yasmād adhikam* (Pā. 2.3.9).
The meaning of the case-ending here is the state of being related to (*nirūpitatva*).
[The word *upari*] is connected with the action through the relation of "subsisting in a locus that pervades its own connection.

Thus, based on the rule *yasmād adhikaṃ yasya ceśvaravacanaṃ tatra saptamī* (Pāṇini 2.3.9)—which means that the locative case occurs when used with a *karmapravacanīya* particle having the sense of "superiority"—the locative case is employed in examples such as *upa parādhe harerguṇāḥ*. Here, the meaning of the locative case is "counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitva*).

The subordinate word (*upapada*) is that which, by not residing in a quality that serves as the locus for an excess of its own relation, connects with the action; it is a marker of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*).
Thus, from the rule *adhir īśvare* (Pāṇini 1.4.97), the term *adhi* is designated as a *karmapravacanīya* when it signifies lordship (*aiśvarya*).

When that [relation] is conjoined with its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and its sub-correlate (*anuyogin*), as in "the earth is above Rāma" (*adhi rāme bhūḥ*) and "Rāma is above the earth" (*adhi bhuvi rāmaḥ*), the locative case is used alternatively.
Here, the meaning of the locative case is, respectively, sub-correlativity (*anuyogitva*) and counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*).

The word *adhi* serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*) in the connection between the meaning of the verbal suffix and the relation to something other than the object of one's own connection.
The resulting meaning is: "The earth is the locus of the ownership whose counter-correlate is Rāma," and "Rāma is the counter-correlate of [the absence of] existence-in-the-earth.
Thus it is established that every meaning of the locative case—whether primary (*śakya*) or secondary (*lākṣaṇika*)—is invariably connected with the action (*bhāvānvayī*).
Rahasya, pp. 143–148. Locative Case (*Maṇiśekhara*).
The meaning of the locative case (*saptamī*) is "locus" (*adhikaraṇatva*),
according to the rule *saptamyadhikaraṇe ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.36). And locus-ness (*adhikaraṇatva*) is the state of being a substratum (*ādhāratva*).
This is because of the rule (Pāṇini 1.4.45): "The locus (*ādhāra*) is the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*).
And that [locus] is the state of being a support;
and that is common to both direct and indirect [support].
Succession [is established] by way of being the locus of the agent, the object, and so forth.
By means of this, there arise such usages as "he cooks in a pot," "he dwells on the ground," and "he sleeps on a mat.
Furthermore, the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is of three kinds: contact-based (*aupaśleṣika*), objective (*vaiṣayika*), and pervasive (*abhivyāpaka*).

Therefore, according to the maxim "The locative case [is used] in cases such as 'dwelling with the teacher,' 'knowledge in the jar,' or 'oil in sesame seeds' because of their coexistence," since the Soma present in a single vessel is to be consumed by all in equal portions, it is not proper for anyone to have an excess of a share; the instruction is for the sake of enduring that [inequality].

Soma. 3.5.16. Alternatively, by the principle that "it should be equal, as there is no scriptural statement to the contrary" (*samaṃ syādaśrutitvāt*), ten [partakers] each are obtained, and they are restated through the primary mode itself. Vārttika 3.5.20, p. 1022. For if it were for the purpose of purifying the agent, then, just as with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), since a division would be obtained, the rule "it should be equal" would result in ten [shares] for each.
On page 1023:

Regarding the eleven *ṛc*s (the *sāmidhenīs*), according to the principle that "there should be equality" (*same syāt*) when there is repetition up to a certain number for the first and last [verses], each is repeated three times. In this way, [the total] is accomplished.

Bhāṭṭa 10.1.8: In the case of the eleven *anūyāja* offerings, by applying the principle that "it should be equal" (*samaṃ syāt*) and thus combining them into one, there is a relationship of original form and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*). Specifically, for the *barhis*, *nairṛta*, and *śaṅkha* offerings, there are four modifications each; however, for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, there are three.

*Sankarsha* 2.3.4: By the sentence "two [fires] are in the *āhavanīya*," the *āhavanīya* fire is prescribed as the locus even for the repetition performed at the *abhyāsa-dasa*. Here, because the other remaining repetitions are prescribed by their respective sentences to have only the *gārhapatya* and *anvāhāryapacana* fires as their loci, and according to the maxim "it should be equal, as there is no scriptural statement to the contrary" (*samaṃ syādaśrutvāt*), four repetitions are obtained for each of the two loci consisting of the *gārhapatya* and *anvāhāryapacana* fires; thus, the accomplishment of ten repetitions is established.
*Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Bhāṣya*, 2.3.5–16, p. 201.

By this same principle, even when [the offering] is being abandoned for two [deities], it is understood that "the portion belongs to half-Pūṣan" (in the case of *somāpauṣṇa* and others), according to the maxim "it should be equal, because there is no scriptural statement to the contrary" (*samaṃ syādaśrutvāt*).

Nor should it be argued that, by the maxim "it should be equal," an equal division alone would necessarily follow (as in the case of increasing eleven *sāmidhenī* verses to fifteen), rather than a division of two hundred and fifty each.

For where a single meaning is enjoined for multiple [entities] by means of a single sentence, there alone is there an equal division (*samavibhāga*). When there is one thing to be enjoined, because that [enjoined object], without division, stands in a relation to the many, it extends as far as the division; thus, since the operation of the intended meaning (*vivikṣā*) is uniform there, and the sentence is of a single form in both respects regarding the operation of the intended meaning, this is the rule of equal division.

However, where multiple [meanings] are enjoined for multiple [entities] by means of two sentences, there is no occurrence of equal division, because there is no evidence for a uniform nature between the two distinct operations.

Regarding the statement in the *Pañcaśarādīya*, "on the fifth among the last days," since the injunction of fivefoldness applies to the last day, the principle that "it should be equal, as there is no scriptural statement to the contrary" (*samaṃ syādaśrutvāt*) results in the application of three [verses] each on the remaining days.
Thus, the view that the phrase "three each day" (*trīntrīnvāhaṃ*) is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) is refuted.
Bhāṭṭa 11.1.12:

In the animal sacrifice, there are eleven *prayāja* offerings. Among these, out of the five original (*prākṛta*) ones, only the fourth and fifth are repeated; the other six have deities not belonging to the archetype (*aprākṛtadevatya*). According to the principle that "it should be equal when there is no scriptural statement to the contrary" (*samaṃ syādaśrutvāt*), they are divided equally in order; thus, it is by repeating those two [the fourth and fifth] alone. Soma 5.3.20.

Since the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings together amount to five in number, according to the principle that "it should be equal when there is no scriptural statement to the contrary" (*samaṃ syādaśrutvāt*), it would follow that for the sake of two *prayājas*, one would have to bring exactly three and a half [units]. (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 12.1.29)

Since the statement "when one offers in the Āhavanīya" (yadāhavanīye juhoti)—being an *anārabhyavāda* (general rule not dependent on a specific context)—establishes that all offerings have the Āhavanīya fire as their locus, the phrase "two [offerings] in the Āhavanīya" serves to exclude other [fires]. When there is a requirement for a locus for the remaining offerings, and a doubt arises as to whether the Gārhapatya or the Anvāhāryapacana fire should be the locus, the principle "it should be equal" (*samaṃ syāt*) would result in the four [offerings] being assigned to a single fire. However, since the locuses of the Gārhapatya and Anvāhāryapacana are already established by other sentences such as "one offers in the Gārhapatya" and "one offers in the Anvāhāryapacana," the present text merely intends to prescribe the quality of being "twofold" (*dvi*) as a subordinate attribute for each of those two fires—the Gārhavanīya group and the [other] group. Thus, there is no contingency of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Su. Pṛ. 781:

In the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (yūpaikādaśinī), the attainment of equal measurement for the ten intervals between the posts is obtained through the principle that "it should be equal" (samaṃ syāt).
Saṃkarṣa. 4.1.23.

Even though the injunctions regarding the *virāj* and *sampad* [mantras] prescribe ten repetitions of each [verse], there would arise the contingency of five repetitions of the oblations (*homābhyāsa*) in each individual case—due to the injunctions concerning the *gārhapatya* and other fires merely prescribing the locus while restating the oblation—according to the principle of "it should be equal" (*samaṃ syāt*). Consequently, the reference to the four-footed [verses] would be untenable. (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Bhāṣya, 2.3.5.16, p. 201). The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: because the time of the junction (*sandhi-kāla*) is so brief that it is incapable of encompassing the performance of the ritual action along with its constituent parts (*sāṅga-prayoga-bhāvanā*), the principle of "it should be equal" implies that the portions preceding and following that junction must be equal. Thus, the entire period up to that point is implied to be divided equally.
Saṃkarṣa 3.1.2:

But in the case of those who share the same vessel, when an equal division is required by the principle "it should be equal, because there is no scriptural statement to the contrary," and a discrepancy arises, the act [of consuming the cup] must be performed after having informed [the others].
The injunction "one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa on level ground" is a restrictive rule (niyamavidhi) regarding place; it is not a mere restatement (anuvāda).

In the expression "one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa on level ground," this locative case (saptamī) is a direct Vedic statement (śruti) that serves as an application (viniyojikā), being a case-ending (kāraka-vibhakti) denoting the locus.

*Bāla.* On page 45, under the section "Samartha," it is stated: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]. This is the *prayogavidhi* (injunction of performance) for the human goal; it is the *mahāprayogavidhi* (great injunction of performance).
Page 13:
By the statement "one should sacrifice on level ground," the connection with the location is enjoined for the Darśapūrṇamāsa ritual, not a separate ritual action. Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 2.3.126.

In the case of identical [rites] joined with ritual acts, [the following applies]: "This *iṣṭi* is a *triṣṭubh*; having made the *ekaviṃśa* the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* for that *vāyavya* [rite], one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice"; and "Having made the *vāravantīya* the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* upon these very *revatī* verses, one desiring cattle should indeed sacrifice with this"—so it is heard in the scripture.

Regarding this, there arises an inquiry: Is it that cattle are the fruit resulting from the *vāravantīya* and other qualities belonging to that very *agniṣṭut*, and "one should sacrifice with this" is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), or rather, is "one should sacrifice with this" a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*)? In response to this inquiry, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
In the case of such similar distinct sentences as "One should sacrifice with this," it is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), but rather a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*).
In the case of equal [units], there would be a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*);

that is, in the case of equal groups of words such as "For sap thee" (*iṣe tvā*) and "For strength thee" (*ūrjaṃ tvā*), which are independent of one another, there would be a split of the sentence, meaning a split of the *yajus* formula.
‘For sap, thee’ is one *yajus*; ‘For strength, thee’ is another *yajus*.

This is because [the objection] that a single sentence results from the assumption of a single purpose has been rejected in the rule: “Or, when [the purposes] are equal, there should be a division of sentences” (2.1.47).

Or [it may be so]. On page 465, Bhāṣya 2.1.15: "In the case of human wealth (in the sentence beginning with *nirmimīta*), however, the genitive case will occur, and only a relationship [between the two] is thus understood; furthermore, no separate fruit need be postulated. As it has been said: 'In the case of equals, there would be a split of the sentence' (Bhāṣya 3.4.17, page 893)."
"Disagreement would be equal" (2.3.48).
This is the *pūrvapakṣa* sūtra concerning the section on *yava* and *varāha*.
The meaning is that the disagreement between the Āryas and the Mlecchas regarding the determination of the meanings of the words *yava* and *varāha* is equal.
The *Kalpataru* [states]:
"The singing of the *ṛc*s occurs only when the days are equal" (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.11).
VI. 1.2.4: "Singing on the same [notes]" (*samāsu gānam*), as in the rule "one should sing on the same [notes]";
and because the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is known from many sources, it is stronger than the principle (*nyāya*) that "singing is on the same [notes]. Section 1.15, Part 2.
When there is a conflict between rules of equal number, the performance of the primary rule takes precedence. *Bhāṣya* 12.1.8.23–24:
In the case of a contradiction between rules of equal number, the performance of the principal rule [prevails].
Bhāṭṭa 12.1.8:
The Principle of Flowing Before One's Eyes (Samakṣapravāhanyāya).
According to the principle of flowing before one's eyes, there is no contradiction between the purpose of awakening the primary [meaning] and the discernment of the meaning of the specific [term].

Śrīkara (1.3.13): Since many words denoting objects of meditation are heard in the Śrutis through the principle of equal hearing (*samaśravaṇa*) according to the distinction of qualified aspirants, their mutual difference is established. This is the Sūtra on Concordance (*Samanvaya-sūtra*;
this is indeed the section on Concordance).

By the sūtra beginning with "Because the Veda has action as its purpose" (*āmnāyasya kriyārthatvāt*), it must be stated that the authority of the Veda lies solely in its being for the sake of action; thus, having raised the objection that those passages which do not have action as their purpose lack authority, Jaimini—by the sūtra "But [they are authoritative] because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction" (*vidhinā tvekavākyatvāt*)—established their authority by demonstrating that even those sentences appearing to have established entities as their subject matter possess the nature of being for the sake of action through their syntactic unity with an injunction. That demonstration of authority was further explained by Bādarāyaṇa in the *Samanvaya* sūtra, where he established the authority of those passages concerning Brahman precisely by showing that they are independent and have no concern whatsoever with action.
Parimala on Brahmasūtra 2.1.1, p.
50: And co-utterance occurs when there is a relationship [between the terms], as in the case of "cook" and "reaper."
"We shall infer the relationship from co-utterance" (Bhāṣya on 3.2.125).
The status of being a means (*sādhanatva*), which is to be postulated based on mere co-utterance, has been rejected in the *Audumbara* section.
The word *samabhivyāhāra* denotes proximity in utterance.
Convention (*samaya*).
When this meaning is intended to be conveyed, the word "meaning" (*artha*) should be employed; this rule of usage is convention. That which is produced by convention is *sāmayika* (conventional).
*samayādhyuṣitaḥ*—*samaya* means sunset; the sun that has approached (*adhyuṣitaḥ*) that [time] is the morning sun.
Thus, *samayādhyuṣitaḥ* refers to the sun.
VI. 5|1|18 | Capable; qualified.
Furthermore, in the case of optional rites (*kāmya-karman*), capacity (*sāmarthya*) pertains to both the auxiliary and the principal elements;

however, in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*), it pertains to the auxiliaries according to the principle: "In the case of a conjunction [of duties], one is capable only to the extent that one is able. (Jaimini Sūtra 6.3.14)
The principle of capacity (*śaktinyāya*).
Thus, in the case of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), the person qualified is one who possesses the primary status of an *āśrama* and is capable (*samartha*). (Mīmāṃsā Nyāya)
It has been stated that "one who possesses the object [of desire] is authorized [to act] when capable" (6.1.15;

Bhāṣya 10.2.22.56). Regarding the rule *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.1): a grammatical operation concerning words (*padavidhi*), such as compound formation (*samāsa*) and the like, which is prescribed with reference to words, is called *samartha* (capable/competent).

The Grammarians maintain that a word is "samartha" (capable) when it has acquired the capacity to express the meaning of a sentence through its own constituent parts (*vigraha*). *Maṇiprabhā*, p. 146.

According to the followers of Gautama (p. 148), the meaning of the Sūtra is that a compound and the like, being prescribed by means of the mention of words (*padoddeśena*), is "samartha" (capable/related) when it resides in words denoting its own respective meanings.
Only one who is *samartha* (competent/qualified) has the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform the entire ritual procedure when it is optional (*kāmya*).

Bhāṣya on Pāṇini 6.1.18–19: For a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is prescribed for words that are semantically related (*samartha*). 6.1.19: For a compound (*samāsa*) occurs between words that are semantically related.
And semantic relation exists when there is the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*).
And a qualifier is non-common [to the subject].
(Nyāyasūtra 2.1.1, p. 572). When a capable cause is present, the non-occurrence of the effect is untenable.
(Kaṇikā, p. 456). [The meaning of] "capable" is repeated familiarity.
Bhāṣya 5.1.34: The word *samavatta* denotes that which is being cut off together with something else.
Vārttika 3.5.13: The *samavattadhānī* is a specific vessel for the animal sacrifice, resembling the *iḍā* vessel.
Vi. 10.7.4: It collects together.

When the term *avadyati* is to be used for the cutting of portions from many oblations (*havirbhyaḥ*), the word *samavayati* is employed. However, when the cutting is from only one [oblation], the word *avadyati* is used.
Kaiyaṭa (Vṛtti 3.5.13): *Samavāya* is the occurrence together for a single purpose.
Or [as stated in] Vākyapadīya 3.7.14, p. 822: "And inherence (samavāya) is one.
That relation by which the superstratum produces in the substratum a cognition colored by itself—that relation is inherence.
It is not, however, a relation between things that are inseparably connected (ayutasiddha)."
Because distinctness is impossible for things that are established separately (*yutasiddha*).

Since the tree and its support possess separate mobility, there would be no relation of inherence (*samavāya*) between them. (Maṇi, pp. 22–23). "By which relation the substratum, though distinct, is perceived within the substrate..."

"One should always act in accordance with [the context]; that is proclaimed as *samavāya* (inherence/connection). (*Su.* p. 375). Here, *samavāya* is extracted as a distinct category of reality (*padārtha*) based on its specific characteristic (*pratyaya*). (*Rju.* p. 197). "For *samavāya* is defined as having a common object (*samānaviṣayatva*). (*Rju.* p. 197).
For inherence (*samavāya*) is not merely coexistence in one place;
what then? It is the identity of the object (*viṣayaikatva*).
... Inherence is characterized by the two means of valid cognition having a common object that excludes [the objects of] each other.

Likewise, where even among the remaining subsidiaries (*śeṣa*) there is a single principal (*śeṣin*) to whom they provide equal assistance, one subsidiary is understood as a means by one means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and another by another. And yet, a principal whose assistance has been accomplished by one subsidiary does not require another subsidiary; in that case too, there is "co-inherence" (*samavāya*) because they occupy the same object. And since this occurs only when there is contradiction (*virodha*), contradiction is established by the very mention of co-inherence.

Therefore, the apprehension of inherence (*samavāya*) has as its object precisely that which is contradictory [to other means of knowledge]. Vārttika 3.1.7.14, pp. 822–823. We (the Prābhākaras) do not accept an eternal inherence as the Vaiśeṣikas do. Ṛjuvimalā, p. 188. Regarding inherence, there is an injunction, because conjunction would otherwise be purposeless.

Regarding the injunctions, "Having piled the fire-altar (agniciti), one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī" and "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," there arises an inquiry: does this state a relationship of subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) between the Agnicayana and the Sautrāmaṇī, or between the Vājapeya and the Bṛhaspatisava, or is this conjunction for the purpose of indicating time (*kālārtha*)? In this deliberation, the author establishes the final position (*siddhānta*): This injunction would constitute a relationship of subsidiary parts if there were a coexistence (*samavāya*) [of the two rites].
This injunction would concern the lack of connection with subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) in rites such as the *agnicayana* and *sautrāmaṇī*.
Why? Because the connection is purposeful; that is, because the connection expressed in "having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice" (*citvā yajeta*) is fruitful.
In the absence of a connection with subsidiary elements, the stated connection would be fruitless.

Therefore, the Sautrāmaṇī is an auxiliary of the piling of the fire-altar (agnicayana), and the Bṛhaspatisava is an auxiliary of the Vājapeya. [Objection: If it is argued that in the case of a mention of time, it refers to time.

The proponent [of the Siddhānta] states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) regarding what was stated in the previous sūtra: "Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī" indicates that the Sautrāmaṇī is an auxiliary (aṅga) of the Agnicayana; and "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava" indicates that the Bṛhaspatisava is an auxiliary of the Vājapeya.
[The opponent replies: The word *ktvā* in "having piled" (*citvā*) and "having sacrificed" (*iṣṭvā*) is a scriptural mention of time (*kālaśruti*), because the suffix *ktvā* denotes priority of time.
If it is argued: "Since this is a statement regarding time, it specifies only the time for the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice; it does not establish a connection with the ritual subsidiaries.
Therefore, this conjunction is for the purpose of indicating time."
"It would not serve a purpose in the absence of a sequence.
The proponent of the established view (siddhāntin) says: "The connection would not be for the sake of time."
Because there is no connection— that is, no inherence— between the purpose and the result; [therefore],
the name applies only when there is inherence.

When there is a connection with time, one would have to state an independent fruit for the Sautrāmaṇī and the Bṛhaspatisava; however, since such a fruit is not heard [in scripture], their status as subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) must be accepted.
This is the commentary (*vṛtti*).
Alternatively, *prayojana* means "that which is employed" (*prayujyate*), derived from the root with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object (*karman*).

Because the suffix employed after the *bṛhaspatisava* sacrifice indicates that the time preceding the *bṛhaspatisava* is not to be enjoined as a subordinate element of the *vājapeya*, there is no connection [between them] in that sense.
For if it were intended merely for the sake of time, the fixed sequential order between the *vājapeya* and the *bṛhaspatisava* could not be known.
Therefore, the conjunction is for the purpose of indicating time.
Thus ends the curiosity.

Or rather, what is the purpose of the word and its meaning in relation to the *cayana* (piling) of the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice? Since there is no co-occurrence (*asamavāya*)—that is, no known connection—between the *vājapeya* and the *bṛhaspatisava*, there would be a sublation of the context (*prakaraṇabādha*).

Therefore, the connection is not for the purpose of time, but rather constitutes a relationship of subordinate and principal (aṅgāṅgibhāva). Where [is this stated]? In the section concerning the eternality of inherence (samavāya), it is merely a technical definition (paribhāṣā). Why? Because...
The relationship characterized as inherence (samavāya) is non-human in origin (apauruṣeya).

It exists between an individual and its genus, between an action and its factors (kārakas), between a whole and its parts, and between qualities and their possessors. This is what "together with" (saha) means.
Manifestation and the like belong only to that which is not established by itself (ayutasiddha).
With the exception of universals, actions, qualities, and wholes, [manifestation and the like] do not depend on anything else.
Although individuals, qualities, actions, and parts do indeed depend on other things, [the term "not dependent" here refers specifically to the former].
Nevertheless, because they do not exist separately (*apṛthag-gatimantaḥ*), they are inseparable (*ayuta-siddha*).

*Ṛju.*, p. 188. The causal relation regarding the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) is such that the production of a positive effect occurs through the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*), while the causality of the substance occurs through the relation of identity (*tādātmya-sambandha*).
*Maṇi.*, p. 17. It is logical that only that which is an inherent cause is so, for it is only where the cause exists that the effect is perceived.
*Bṛhatī*, p. 216: "The effect is perceived only where there is an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); for example, the cloth is perceived only where the threads are.
*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 216: "The inherent cause.
For that which is proximate to the inherent cause is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
Just as the conjunction of threads is the efficient cause (*nimitta*) for the production of a cloth inherent in those threads (p.
161). The status of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) as a substratum is well-known (Su. p. 660).
For indeed, an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) grasps a quality that is inherent [in its substrate].

Vārttika 3.1.6.12, p. 677: The entire *praiṣa-anuvacana* (direction and recitation) belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa; the individual *praiṣas* belong to the Adhvaryu, and the individual *anuvacanās* belong to the Hotṛ.
This is the principle of the collective fifteen-day sacrifice (*samastapañcadaśarātranyāya*).
This should be consulted under the entry "Ātinyāya" on page 992 of Mīmāṃsākośa.

Regarding the mention of the aggregate in the case of the potsherds, there is the statement: "The cake for Agni is on eight potsherds" (Bhāṣya 10.1.1.1). Regarding the mention of the aggregate in the case of the *sāmidhenī* verses, there is the statement: "He recites fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses."

*Vyutpatti* (etymological derivation) is the capacity to convey its own meaning with respect to the sense indicated by the words being compounded (*samasyamāna*). Maṇi, p. 149. Regarding the theory of compounding (*samāsāvāda*), [the text cites]: "There are sixteen *ājya* offerings" in the *Darśa* sacrifice;

*Saṃkarṣa*, 2.1.2: "One desiring cattle should take seventeen *ājya* offerings; one should take five *gṛhīta* portions for the *dhruvā* vessel, while for the other two, it is as in the archetypal form (*prakṛti*)."
2|1|13. Name (*samākhyā*) is also a separate means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because there is no cause for its invalidity, such as non-comprehensiveness or being sublated.
