VI. 11|18. Although *samākhyā* (name/designation) may be weak due to its remoteness [from the act], it must nevertheless be accepted because it leaves no other alternative.
In that case, it functions merely to establish a connection (*prāpti*) and does not exclude anything else.
Vārttika 3|5|12|14: *samākhyā* [is seen] in the case of "the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses."
Even though *samākhyā* (name/designation) might establish a mere connection with the sacrifice, it is nevertheless sublated by the more powerful *krama* (order).
[Sūtra 3.2.7.20: *Samākhyā* is weaker than *krama* (or *sthāna*).

Thus, between *krama* and *samākhyā*, in the case of *krama*, the mutual presentation of the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*aṅgin*) is based solely on their common location as conceived within the Veda.
For in every case, a connection with some specific location is conceivable.
Yet we do not perceive any commonality of place established by the Veda that is associated with the name, by which this connection might be distinguished from other connections.
But surely, since the name functions precisely by denoting a connection, it follows that it is equivalent to direct scriptural statement (śruti).
This is not so;
for the relationship postulated by the name (samākhyā) is indeed one thing,
whereas the relationship of subsidiary and principal (śeṣa-śeṣitva) which is established by direct statement (śruti) is another.

First, when the relationship between things has not yet been understood by any means, the designation (samākhyā) comes into operation; however, that designation does not at all establish the relationship of the subordinate and the principal (śeṣa-śeṣitva).
Since it is established through some kind of relationship, it does not denote even the mere relationship itself;
for it has already been stated that a relationship is not denoted by derivative (yaugika) words. This is what is meant by the term "designation" (samākhyā).

They obtain these optional rites (*kāmya-karman*) when they are located in the same place, not when they are in different places. Likewise, even when there is no restriction by specific designation (*samākhyā*) regarding particular details, there is an abundance of rites; and in the absence of such a designation, these [verses] serve as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*.

Because it arises from a question, when those [elements] are already encompassed [by other means], its status as scripture (*śruti*) is not even determined except through the impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*).

Since it depends on the observation of specific details not yet encompassed by way of being a *kalpaka* (a source of inference), the name (*samākhyā*) contained within the direct instruction (*upadeśa*) is more authoritative than a postulated extended application (*atideśa*).

The specific designation (*viśeṣasamākhyā*) is more powerful because it functions more rapidly due to its independence; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Vārttika 3.6.142, p. 1060, [on] *guṇa*.
Soma. 3|7|19: For the Southerners (*dākṣiṇātyāḥ*), when a performer (*kartṛ*) is required, the designation (*samākhyā*) becomes the regulating factor.

Regarding the designations of persons such as "Easterners" (*prācyāḥ*) and "Northerners" (*udīcyāḥ*) [in the context of] the *saṃnayarta* rites (3|8|214), it is understood that first there is the designation, and afterwards the designation of direction (*deśasamākhyā*) comes into operation.
"The relationship [is defined as] being born in that which is one's abode" (Vārttika 3.3.14, p.

829). [This is established] by the reasons for its arrival: "That is his abode; he exists there. Furthermore, by means of expressing the meaning of the constituent parts [of the compound], there is the ascertainment of the absence of any other meaning for those constituent parts.
"Born there" or "come from there"—

according to Pāṇini 4.3.74–75, since it is impossible to conceive of a collective [meaning] without [the knowledge of] a relationship, and because usage is preceded by the knowledge of such a relationship,
the name (samākhyā) is able to sublate the indicative mark (liṅga).
The Bhāṣya states: "The designation (samākhyā) is known first; afterwards, the relationship is known" (Su. Pṛ. 3.3.120).
In this regard, we hold that the designation is the restrictive factor: 1202. Among those not distinct from the archetypal (prakṛta), the designation is the allocator.

It is incorrect [to say] that where the action is primary, for whose sake men are to be purchased, or where the man is subordinate; in such cases, the restriction is determined by the designation (*samākhyā*). 3|7|231. Where the man is subordinate, there the restriction is established by the designation.
Bhāṣya 3.8.216:
In that case, the designation (samākhyā) is the regulator regarding the primary status of the persons.
In that case, the designation serves as the regulator; however, it has been stated that where there is a need for an agent, the designation is not the regulator (Bhāṣya 3.8.4).
What is that [case]? It is that for whose purpose the purchase [of services] takes place.

Or rather: in that case, we maintain that a derivative designation (*yaugikī samākhyā*) is stronger than a conventional one (*rūḍhā samākhyā*) when it establishes a relationship, provided that the scriptural mention occurs only once.
That [word], too, having been brought to mind, makes known the remaining relationship.
(Vārttika 3.8.127). And that (relationship), even if not previously perceived, is a worldly term, namely *samākhyā* (name/designation). (Vārttika 3.6.13).

He proceeded to apply the designation by its mere existence alone (*sattāmātreṇaiva*) (Vākyapadīya p. 821; Bhāṣya 3.3.124, p. 856). Even a specific designation (*viśeṣasamākhyā*), though the relationship [between the two] is not perceived, becomes a sublater because it functions more rapidly than the general Vedic text (*śruti*) itself, simply by the absence of certainty regarding non-existence.

Or rather, because it is illogical to postulate a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) when the meaning is already established through etymological derivation (*yaugika-abhidhāna*), as stated in [Tantravārttika] 3.7.214: "For in the Veda, the relationship between the action and its agent is established from the very beginning;
the designations (*samākhyās*) consisting of the status of being the performer are produced for the listener as something to be understood."
When that exists, the designation comes into operation;
we,
however, are engaged in its application.

Su. Pṛ. 1203: Those benedictory mantras (*āśīrmantra*) that are not connected with a specific ritual action are not restricted [to a particular performer] by the observation of their name (*samākhyā*), since the relationship [between the mantra and the action] is not established by any other means of knowledge.
We understand them to belong to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).
From this it is known that the designation comes first and the relationship follows; thus, they are not officiating priests (ṛtvij). Vākyapadīya 3.8.165.

When there is a maker of something, the *adhvaryu* priest approaches that [object]; for a modification is inferred to be conformable to its original form (*prakṛti*), or the original form is inferred from the modification.

Although it has been stated that "the modification is a different word" and thus both are independent of each other and possess an eternal relationship, nevertheless, because the application of words is eternal, an eternal relationship serves as the cause; thus is the etymological explanation (*anvākhyāna*) of all derivative terms (*yaugika*).
For it was said in [Vārttika] 2.3.2 that the application of the word *rājya* does not depend on the presence of a king (*rājan*).
Even though there exists a relationship between word and meaning based on the nature of the signifier (*nimitta*) and the signified (*naimittika*), their coexistence is not contradictory.
In this regard, some say:

prior to this application by way of designation (*samākhyā*), the etymological nature of the designation is understood as being like the relationship already existing between the *adhvaryu* and his specific duties.
But if, on the contrary, the relationship is established first and only subsequently does the primary [meaning] arise from that designation (*samākhyā*),
then the designation would not be the means of application (*viniyojikā*).
Therefore, the application occurs only when two conventional terms, independent of one another, present themselves due to their similarity of form.
But this is not correct;

for established words do not possess the capacity to bring about a connection with ritual properties (*dharma*) merely through similarity of form, even as in the case of "He will perform the *rathaṃtara*-dharmas on the *kaṇvarathaṃtara*" (10.4.23)— how much less so here, in the case of a relationship between an action and its agent?
Or rather, the example from the *Pāñcakāvyādāharaṇa* would be appropriate;
its lack of applicability must simply be accepted.
As for the claim that a name does not exist prior to its usage:
It is true that there is no direct perception [of the Veda];
however, it will be inferred from its very designation.
For in the Veda, the relationship between the action and its agent is established from the very beginning.
While that [relationship] exists, the designation (samākhyā) comes into operation.
We, however, not apprehending that relationship through any other means of valid cognition, do apprehend it by means of observing the designation.
Therefore, it is known that the designation comes first and the relationship follows after.
In reality, however, the relationship exists from the very beginning. And although it is not perceived [at first], it brings about the application of the name by its mere existence alone.
For if this [relationship] were to have a beginning, then, due to the force of that relationship, the name would have to belong to the speaker first.
And since that [designation] does not actually exist in that way, we cannot be held accountable for it.

When one resorts to an eternal connection, and it has been established that there must certainly be some kind of connection for the designation even if it is eternal, then the relationship of subsidiary and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*) is subsequently understood through the principle of presumptive necessity (*anyathānupapatti*). Therefore, when it is established that there must certainly be some kind of connection for the designation if it is etymological (*yaugika*), the relationship of subsidiary and principal is subsequently understood through the principle of presumptive necessity.
Therefore, it is established that when a name is etymological (*yaugika*), it serves as the basis for application (*viniyoga*).

Regarding the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices, there arises the question: must the ritual items designated by names such as *ādhvaryava* (pertaining to the Adhvaryu) and *auautra* (pertaining to the Hotṛ) be performed by the Adhvaryu and others respectively, or is there no fixed rule? Since there is no restrictive rule based on direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and so forth, and since a name—having as its object merely the ritual item itself—is not an injunction and thus lacks authoritative force, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is no fixed rule. To this, the following is said in reply:
The designation [of the *adhvaryu*] is based on its beginninglessness;
therefore, when the term *ādhvaryava* and so forth are used,
they share the same injunctions.
It is proximate.
Just as the *jyotiṣṭoma*, which is the archetype (*prakṛti*), is proximate to the *śyena*, which is its modification (*vikāra*), so it is for both [the *vājapeya* and the *ṛtvij*].

And thus, because the *śyena* is not proximate while the *jyotiṣṭoma* alone is proximate, this is not a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the characteristics of the *śyena*, but rather a restatement of the characteristics of the *jyotiṣṭoma*; such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

Alternatively, if—on account of its being a new injunction (apūrvatva)—the other [rite] were to have the same designation as the Jyotiṣṭoma injunction regarding its qualified performer, then this Soma sacrifice, which is a modification (vikāra) of the Jyotiṣṭoma performed for malevolent purposes (ābhicārika), would be the case; therein it is stated: "The rest is the same as that [Jyotiṣṭoma]."

This is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the ritual details (*dharmas*) belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma, and not of the details belonging to the Dvādaśāha; such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) reached by the Sūtra. With the phrase "yadi apivā" (if, however), the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of a collection of syllables that refutes that view. Regarding this, the *Tantraratna* states: "'Yadi' is an expression of doubt where there is no doubt; thus, 'yadi apivā' should be explained as a reversal [of the previous position] for the purpose of excluding that alternative.
Furthermore, the statement "the rest is the same" (*samānam itarat*) is an injunction (*vidhi*), not a restatement, because it conveys something not previously established and serves a novel purpose.
For an injunction (*vidhi*) is indeed one whose object has not been established by another means of knowledge.
[Objection: But since the word "the other" (*itara*) is a pronoun, and because of its proximity [to the preceding], it is understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*).
[Reply: It is said in response:
The word *itarat* means "the other.

When the question arises as to why it is other, it is stated that it is "other" (*itarat*) because it is superior to the injunction pertaining to the Jyotiṣṭoma. Since the injunction resides within the Jyotiṣṭoma, those specific duties which are superior to the duties belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma are called "additional" (*adhika*); thus, the term *itarat* is used in the sense of "that which is additional."

The phrase "the other is the same" (samānam itarat) means that the word *itara* indicates those ritual characteristics (*dharma*) which are additional to the characteristics of the Jyotiṣṭoma. That which expresses them should be "the same" (*samāna*); that is, the word *samāna* should express them.
Thus, in the expression "the other is the same," the word *samāna* also denotes the additional characteristics.

And those *daivena* (divine) elements—such as wearing a red turban, wearing red garments, being girt with the sacred thread (*nivīta*), and so forth, as well as the piercing of thorns and the like—are additional to the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma.
According to the Vārttika, however, the meaning is: "in the sense of being additional to the *daiva* [elements], that is, in the modification (*vikāra*) of the *iṣu* (sacrifice).
Thus, one should understand the connection of the words as: "that which is different from the Jyotiṣṭoma injunction is enjoined for the sake of the additional purpose."
In every respect, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that this injunction—"the rest is the same as in the case of the two [deities]"—is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
Ke.
Oṃ. Even if the deity is the same, if it is separated by another [deity], the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the offering (*pradāna*) must be performed separately.

Regarding the sacrifice prescribed as: "One should offer this *iṣṭi*: an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) to Agni, a cake on eight potsherds (*puroḍāśa-aṣṭākapāla*) to Sūrya, and an oblation of clarified butter to Agni, a cake on eight potsherds," the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the two deities, Agni and Sūrya, would occur through a single performance (*tantra*), because they share the same clarified butter as their substrate.
Since the offering (*pradāna*) also occurs with a common deity, it too could logically be performed through a single performance.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhāntin replies]: Because the difference in the nature of the time following the *saurya* [offering] is intended to be significant, if the offering were performed through a single performance, that distinctness would be lost. Therefore, the offerings must be separate.
The offering and other rites are indeed performed separately.

However, in the case of curd and milk, since there is no sublation of the Sauviṣṭakṛta offerings or of the priority and posteriority of the Āgneya and subsequent rites, the establishment of a single performance (*tantratā*) is appropriate.
Saṃkarṣa 4.4.9.

A compound with a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is stronger than a genitive determinative (*ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*). Bhāṣya 6.1.13.51. In this context, "substratum" refers specifically to having a common conceptual referent.

6|6|1 | 1–11. Regarding the *adhikāra* (qualification/eligibility) in the *sattra* sacrifice, one should consult Mīko., p. 305, under the section "The qualification in the *sattra* is only for those of the same lineage" (*samānakalpanām eva*).

[The sūtra] beginning with "Or rather, they may be of different lineages" (*api vā nānāgotrāḥ syuḥ*) is intended as a Vedic statement (*vedatvena vivakṣitatayā*) for the sake of avoiding deficiency (*avaiguṇyāya*), since it pertains to the form of the *tanūnapāt* portion. Thus, regarding the offering as a single unit (*tantreṇa pradāne*), the understanding of the truth is derived from the Veda itself through the words of the authors of the Kalpasūtras. (Sudhā, p. 242).

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the chanting (*gāna*) is performed upon three verses that possess identical meters (*samānacchandaskāḥ*). Bhāṣya 9.2.4.21–22: The *sāman* is to be sung upon three verses that have the same meter, not upon those with dissimilar meters;
for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of *saṃśara* (confusion of notes) and *vileśa* (loss of syllables).
*Saṃśaraḥ* means injury.
*Vileśaḥ* means deficiency.

In the case of a *sāman* chant belonging to a longer meter, there would arise the contingency of the destruction of a portion of the *sāman* through its connection with a subsequent [verse] of a shorter meter.
But by the principle of the subsequent [element] having a larger meter, there would be the undesirable consequence of the *sāman* being deficient.
(Vi.
9.2.4) In the case of the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*) within the same ritual system (*samānatantra*), the performance follows the common procedure (*tantra*).
A maiden who shares the same *pravara* (ancestral lineage) should not be married.
VI. 13|16, Section 2.
"They have the same sacrificial grass" (*samānavarhīṣi bhavanti*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of "having the grass of the *pavamāna* [laud]" (*pavamānavarhīṣi*).
Bhāṣya 11.4.14:
In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as shaving and so forth do not have the same application (*samānavidhāna*) for both the priests and the sacrificer.
Or [it may be]. 3|8|28 | *Samānavidhi*: 4163 The act of bringing together (*samānayana*) is not a common rule (*samānavidhi*) for obligatory and occasional rites.

The fourfold drawing (*caturgṛhīta*) would not be for the purpose of the *prayāja* offerings, but rather for the purpose of the *anuyāja* offerings (Bhāṣya 3.6.13.46). Since there is no mention of desires for subordinate qualities (*guṇakāma*) through a common injunction, then—due to the absence of *anuyāja* offerings in the *ātithyā* ceremony—the fourfold drawing from the *aupabhṛta* vessel would not exist at all along with its basis;
thus, the plural number [in the text] would be untenable.

Therefore, there is an equal injunction for the primary substance and its substitute (such as *nīvāra* grains in place of *vrīhi* grains) with respect to the *darśa* sacrifice; even so, the single fourfold portion taken from the *aupabhṛta* ladle must be for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings alone.
Bhāṣya 3.6.14.39: Regarding the commonality [of the act], there is the pouring together [of the butter] into the *juhū* ladle.
The other four-fold portion taken from the *aupabhṛta* vessel is the primary injunction; this applies even to the relationship between the original and the substitute (such as the *pūtīka* plants).
However, it may well be for the purpose of the *anuyāja* offerings,
because of this indicative mark (*liṅga*) [found] in the plural number [of the word "soma"].

The bringing together of the clarified butter from the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū* is indeed the motivator (*prayojaka*), since those terms ending in the same case-ending [denoting] the properties of the clarified butter are in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

In the phrase "liṅgadarśanāt" (on account of the observation of an indicative mark), there is a relationship of qualifier and qualified between these two: the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the observation (*darśana*).
The aggregate is the observation of an indicative mark; therefore.
Regarding that, the indicative mark is explained: sublation is prescribed only in the case of identical objects. Vārttika.
That [is the meaning]: "And the system (nyāya) is the exposition (darśana);
and that is in the Bhāṣya"—this is the sense of [the sūtra] 3.6.15.40. "But surely... [etc.]
The indicative mark (liṅga) is taught; what is the established conclusion?
It is said:
here, when there is a conflict of ritual properties among primary acts that are equal in number, [the rule applies] to the first.

Namely: there are two *prayāja* offerings to be performed; in that regard, there is a need for clarified butter (*ājya*) in the *juhū* ladle, which serves to favor the ritual properties (*dharma*) of what has been recited.
"Not in the *upabhṛt* when it is empty;

the emptying of the *upabhṛt* serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), while the pouring back of the clarified butter (*ājya*) into the *juhū* is the motivator for both the [butter] and its ritual properties (*dharma*). The setting down [of the ladles] serves only a visible purpose."
In this regard, the principle concerning the bringing together of the clarified butter (*ājya*), which consists of a visible purpose, has been stated;
it should be consulted at Mīko., p. 878.
For in the case of the verbal expression, the reason lacks probative force;
however, the bringing together [of the butter] must be primary because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, after the third *prayāja* offering, [the butter] remains in the *upabhṛt* ladle. (4|1|15|40)
For the purpose of the *mānasājya*, it must be brought into the *juhū* ladle.
That bringing [of the butter] is heard of in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) in the passage: "Having passed over this [altar], [he brings it] toward the *barhis*.
Being for the sake of the remaining *prayāja* offerings, it is the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the properties of the clarified butter (*ājyadharma*).
"One pours from the *aupabhṛta* into the *juhū*.
This occurs after the *prayāja* known by that name (*itsaṃjñaka*).

And there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the *ātithyā* [rite]: "The clarified butter is taken four times; before the *prayāja* known as *bahiḥ*, the *aupabhṛta* clarified butter is poured into the *juhū*."
In that sentence, it is stated that "one who is about to perform the *anuyāja* offerings does not [perform them]";

therein, regarding this act of bringing together (*samānayana*), the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) has stated in the preceding sūtra, "But the bringing together... that it refers to the clarified butter (*ājya*) contained in the *aupabhṛta* ladle.

Regarding the doubt as to whether the butter in the *aupabhṛta* vessel is the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the *prayāja* offerings or not—therein arises this suspicion: "But surely, because of the scriptural statement, 'The clarified butters are to be taken four times each,' it serves the purpose of the *anuyāja* offerings; why then does this not constitute the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) outside the Sūtra, [leaving the following] as the Siddhānta-sūtra?"
By this statement, three portions of four ladlings each are established.
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of excluding the previously suspected prima facie view; [the meaning is that] they must indeed be prescribed as belonging to Prajāpati.
In this regard, the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) replies:
For indeed, there are two meanings for the case endings:
[one refers to] the omenta belonging to Prajāpati, and [the other refers to] the sprinkling with the remnants of the prayāja offerings.
Because when that statement in its positive form is accepted, the [other] reasons are not the motivators (*prayojaka*), whereas the bringing together (*samānayana*) is the motivator.

Regarding the capacity of what belongs to the *aupabhṛta* [ladle]: "For here (in the *ātithyā* sacrifice), the bringing together of the *ājya* from the *upabhṛt* into the *juhū* is not the primary or principal motivator."
In the subsequent sentence, "He will be about to sacrifice," [the act] would be a preparatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*) for the *anuyāja*s of the *ātithyā* [offering],
because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *ātithyā*.

The mere existence [of a reason] would be the cause; its capacity as a means of accomplishment (*sādhakatā*) would not exist, [as in the case]: "There are four portions of clarified butter, for he will not perform the after-offerings (*anuyāja*s).
It would have to be a cause by virtue of its capacity.
For an injunction does not depend upon a reason.
Therefore, in the phrase "it becomes," the plural number in "fourfold-drawn portions" (*caturgṛhītāni*) is the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The purpose of the pouring together (*samānayana*) of the *aupabhṛta* clarified butter is for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings. [Objection:
Since there is an absence of *anuyāja* offerings in the *ātithyā* ceremony, the fourfold-drawn portion intended for the *anuyāja*s would be excluded.
Thus: one fourfold-drawn portion for the *prayāja* offerings is placed in the *juhū* ladle;

[another] from the *dāśatayī* verses is brought together as a secondary mark for the *yajñāyajñīya* chant; a second fourfold-drawn portion for the *prayāja* offerings is placed in the *upabhṛt* ladle; and one fourfold-drawn portion is taken from the *dhruvā* ladle.
*Spatisavādin*, 8.3.16.12–36. As it is recorded on page 2980 of the *Mīko.*, the use of the plural number is justified.
In that context, if [the butter] belongs to the *aupabhṛta*...
In the passage "from the *dāśatayī* verses in the *bṛhaspatisava* and so forth," the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is in the act of bringing together (*samānayana*). These are the compounds.
It should be observed:
at the time of the *samānayana* (the pouring together), half of what is in the *aupabhṛta* ladle is to be poured into the *juhū* ladle.

The completion of the *Sarvasvāra* sacrifice occurs even upon the death of the sacrificer. (10.2.13.58–59). Regarding the point that "the *Sarvasvāra* sacrifice must be completed even after the death of the sacrificer," one should consult the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*). There is no fixed rule regarding the completion of even a worldly undertaking once it has been begun.

Bhāṣya 6.2.4.16–18: "Completion is the meaning of the word"—this is the maxim. "Neither beginning nor completion is the meaning of the verbal form (ākhyāta). What then? Completion is the meaning of the word."
"Because the undertaking [of an action] has purposefulness only through its completion;
therefore, it is understood that completion is the meaning of the word. (Bhāṣya 6.2.3.13)

By the principle that "the completion [of the action] is the meaning of the word," because the previously abandoned object (karman) is concealed and the subsequently being-worshipped object is manifested, there occurs a designation—such as "he worships Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇuṃ yajati*) or "Viṣṇu is to be worshipped" (*viṣṇur yajavyaḥ*)—which, by determining the object to be one, overcomes the capacity of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). However, deityhood (*devatātva*) is not denoted therein.

Even though the agent possesses primacy by virtue of being the referent of the word, because the primacy of the object (*karman*) is perceived at the time of the expectancy for the verbal suffix (*bhāṣya*) due to its nature as a real entity (*vastu*), and because it occurs later—following the perception of the agent's primacy at the time of understanding the essential nature of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)—it is intended [as subordinate] according to the maxim: "That which is completed later is the meaning of the word. (Sphuṭasiddhi, p.

1407). Furthermore, the fact that the entire Veda (*samāmnāya*) subserves this purpose has been established in the section on Arthavādas (*arthavādādhikaraṇa*) on the grounds that it is governed by the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*).
The term "samāmnāya" (recitation/canon) does not occur in the Smṛtis.
Ṛju. p. 8.
Superimposition (*samāropa*):

At the boundary of the village (*sīmanta*), there is no worldly character for the *śālāmukhīya* fire and others, because they have already been attained; rather, the superimposition applies only to that which has been specifically enjoined.
Saṃkarṣa 3.2.9.
However, the enkindling (samāropa) of the *śālāmukhīya* and other fires takes place at the *ajasrapada*.
The same applies to those whose prosperity has departed.
According to the rule for the hall (*śālā*), the same procedure applies even when fetching the perpetual *āhavanīya* fire from the kindling woods (*araṇi*).
"One should perform the re-installation (samāropa) of the fire and lead it to the boundary.
(Saṃkarṣa 3.2.34).
Following the re-installation, even though the fire is being carried around, it attains the status of a common (laukika) fire.
*Saṃkarṣa*. 3.2.9:
"The [eleven] sets of eleven should be performed on the *Prāyaṇīya* and *Udayanīya* days, because they have that as their archetype.
It is heard in scripture: "They should take the eleven sets of eleven from the *Prāyaṇīya* and *Udayanīya* Atirātras."
To this it is replied: the word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of removing doubt.
In the case of the eleven [animals] belonging to the Ekādaśinī, there would be a combination, that is, proximity.

All [the animals] should be present at the *prāyaṇīya* sacrifice, and all again at the *udayanīya* sacrifice. Because that is the archetype— since the *jyotiṣṭoma* is the archetype— for that reason, due to the *jyotiṣṭoma* being the archetype, and because in the *jyotiṣṭoma* the entire set of eleven animals designated by a single name is sacrificed on one and the same day, it follows by extension (*codaka*) that the same applies to the *prāyaṇīya* and the *udayanīya*.
Therefore, the established conclusion is that it is a compound.
Furthermore, because of the prohibition of transposition (*vihāra*);
for by the rule, "The animals of the set of eleven should be used at the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* [sacrifices] of the *atirātra*," the transposition is prohibited.
"Vihāra" means separation.
Since it was established that there should be a separation of the eleven sacrificial animals according to the rule "one should sacrifice them one by one," a prohibition of that has been made here.
Therefore, all [the animals] should be used at the Prāyaṇīya sacrifice, and all at the Udayanīya sacrifice.
Thus is the prima facie view. Alternatively, on the basis of the Vedic text, there should be a division as in common worldly practice:
all the eleven animals are to be sacrificed at each of the Prāyaṇīya and Udayanīya rites respectively.
With the word "or" (vā), he sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
There should be no combination (*samāsa*) of the eleven [animals] belonging to the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* sacrifices; rather, there should be a distribution (*vibhāga*).

This is because of the scriptural statement (*śruti*): "of the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya*"—the dual number in the scripture must be accepted as denoting duality, not through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, there is a distribution.

It is like the case in the world: when it is said in common worldly usage, "Let a hundred be given to Devadatta and Yajñadatta," the hundred is not given to each one individually, but rather it is divided;
such is the established conclusion.
And because of the nature of the distribution (*vihāra*).
Regarding the performance of the eleven animals (*ekādaśina*) at the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* sacrifices through distribution rather than collectively, he states another reason:
"Distribution" is the distribution of the eleven animals at the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya*, which constitutes the model (*prakṛti*) for that [distribution].

Regarding the "set of eleven" (*aikādaśinām*), the distribution (*vihāra*) prescribed by the rule "I shall offer them one by one on each day" is the archetype (*prakṛta*). Its modification (*vikāra*) consists of either a division (*vibhāga*) or a combination (*samāsa*); in that case, as far as possible, the distribution should be maintained.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is a division.
[The others are] combinations.
Regarding the summary:
it concerns the object and its proximity.
It has been stated that for the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* sacrifices, the eleven animals are to be performed by means of distribution.

Regarding the doubt as to how many [animals] are for the *prāyaṇīya* and how many for the *udayanīya*—since there is a dual number in the phrase "of the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya*" and thus the eleven must be divided into two groups, and since a division into equal parts is possible in every respect—the determination that five are for the *prāyaṇīya* and six for the *udayanīya* follows from the proximity (*āsatti*), that is, the closeness or presence of an equal division.
If it is argued that "three are likewise," [the response is: no.

If someone were to argue: "When the eleven animals of the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* sacrifices are to be divided in two ways, the division must be made such that there are three at the *prāyaṇīya* and the remaining eight at the *udayanīya*; for among the numbers in grammatical apposition with 'many,' the number three comes first, and there is no reason to abandon what stands first. [Response: [This is not so. Because [the rule] applies to the case where the number is not already established. Since the number three is already established by the word "eleven" (*aikādaśinānām*), it cannot be applied again. Furthermore, because the term "many" (*bahu*) denotes a plurality exceeding three, it is impossible for the number three to be the primary referent here. Therefore, the division should be made such that four animals go to each sacrifice. This is because the term "many" refers to a quantity greater than three, and since the number four is the next higher integer after three, it is the appropriate number to be assigned to each. Thus, the division is four at the *prāyaṇīya* and four at the *udayanīya*, with one animal remaining to be used as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). This is the correct interpretation.
"Not so, because of equality, as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings.

Regarding the division of the eleven animals between the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* sacrifices, there might be a doubt that the division should be three and eight, since among many numbers, the number three comes first; [the author] refutes this objection and states the established conclusion:
"This is not so."
However, the division must be made as "five" or "six," because of their equality or near-equality. And equality is stronger due to its priority.
It is like the *prayāja*s. Just as in the animal sacrifice there are six additional *prayāja*s belonging to the *dāśika* [set],
which are modifications of the first and last [of the original five].
They are divided equally; even so, having divided as equally as possible, one additional portion is taken at the *udayanīya* [offering].
Therefore, the conclusion is that the division is five and six. Who?

Compound: In the case of *devadattasya gurukulam*, a compound is formed because there is a constant requirement for a correlative (*nityasāpekṣatva*). (The meaning is: the family or house of that person who is Devadatta’s teacher.)

Because the word *guru* is a relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*), it cannot convey its own meaning without the form of its correlative, the *śiṣya* (student); for its expression of its own meaning culminates only by way of that [correlative]. Since the expression of its own meaning would otherwise remain incomplete, it enters into a connection with another word; thus, at the very moment of expressing its own meaning, it acquires the status of a dependent relation (*saṃbandhavyantara*). Because a universal devoid of particulars is impossible, even when there is a requirement for those particulars, the compound is appropriate—since there is no further operation for the word whose function of expressing its own meaning has already culminated, once the establishment of the other related entity is achieved, there is no obstruction to the completion of the sense.
Su. pṛ. 262 | Compound:
According to the statement of the learned authorities, there is no compound for words ending in the dual or plural numbers.

Bhāṣya 6.1.133: "In all compound formations, the statement of the learned (abhiyukta) is the authority," so say the venerable authors of the Vārttikas. This statement of the learned concerns the domain of numeral words (*saṃkhyāśabda*).
In brief, regarding the term *samāsavāda*:

once the state of being a compound (*samāsa*) is understood—as in "citraguḥ" (one who has brindled cows), where the relationship with the brindled cows is understood; as in "pañcamūlī" (the collection of five roots), following the relationship of a collective aggregate; and as in "upakumbham" (near the jar), following the relationship of proximity—then for one who prescribes by means of a compound, it is not difficult to enjoin multiple qualities. (Durgasiṃha on Pāṇini 2.1.51–52, p. 1273).
Bhāṣya 3.1.41–38; Durgasiṃha 7.3.13: A compound constitutes a single word (ekapada).
Sūtra, page 784: A compound functions with expectancy (sāpekṣatva) just like a secondary derivative (taddhita).

The Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas) maintain that a primary denotative power (*śakti*) must be admitted in compounds (*samāsa*), whereas the Logicians (Naiyāyikas) maintain that it is a secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*). (Maṇi, pp. 146–147). Bhāṣya 2.1.17.41.
There is neither direct denotation (*śakti*) nor indication (*lakṣaṇā*);
rather, comprehension arises precisely from the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) presented by the compound, according to the author of the *Bhāṭṭacintāmaṇi*.
This may be seen in the *Bindu* under the section "The Doctrine of Compounds" (*Samāsavāda*).

Of the two [words] contained within a compound, one cannot possibly be the *uddeśya* (the subject) and the other the *vidheya* (the predicate)—(this is because it would entail a violation of *ekaprasaratā*, so the ellipsis is to be supplied).

*Dūṣaṇa* 4|1|47. Furthermore, the action and the relation arise subsequent to the formation of the compound. *Dūṣaṇa* 6|1|6|24, p. 1273. When there is an injunction regarding a qualified meaning conveyed by a compound, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
*Bālapriyā*, p. 101: A syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by the recurrence of a compound and a nominal stem [is not permissible].
*Bālapriyā*, p. 181: It is logical that a compound sentence generates understanding through the presentation of its corresponding analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*).
For this very reason, it is also appropriate that a doubt regarding understanding arises when there is a doubt regarding the analysis.
Maṇi, p. 150. The Theory of Compounds (samāsavāda). A compound (samāsa) is of four kinds, distinguished as *avyayībhāva*, *tatpuruṣa*, *dvandva*, and *bahuvrīhi*.
Among these, the *avyayībhāva* is that in which the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapada*) is predominant.
Just as the *avyayībhāva* compound has the meaning of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) as its primary sense,
there is therefore no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the rule *sup-prati-avyayībhāve*.
The *tatpuruṣa* compound has the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) as its primary sense.
The *dvandva* compound has both members as its primary referents;
the *bahuvrīhi* compound has a referent external to its members as its primary referent—
these are the definitions.
Examples include *upakumbham*, *rājapuruṣaḥ*, *dhavasakhadirau*, and *citraguḥ*.
*Nīlotpalam* is an example of a *karmadhāraya*, and *pañcamūlī* is an example of a *dvigu*; these are varieties of the *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Now, one might object that the definition [of *tatpuruṣa*] does not apply to *unmattagaṅgam* as an *avyayībhāva*, and that the definition of *bahuvrīhi* over-extends to it.

Similarly, in compounds such as *supprati* and others, which are formed by the rule *avyayībhāve ’sup pratinā mātrārthe* (Pāṇini 2.1.9), the feminine suffix *āti* is applied despite the presence of the characteristics of a *tatpuruṣa*,
because the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is predominant.

Likewise, in *tatpuruṣa* compounds such as *ardhapippalī* and *pūrvakāyaḥ*, which are formed by rules such as *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.1.2), the feminine suffix *āti* is applied despite the presence of the characteristics of an *avyayībhāva*.
Thus, in the case of *dvibāhuḥ* (two-armed), there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of the *bahuvrīhi*,
and over-extension of the definition of the *dvandva*.

Likewise, in the case of *śaśakuśapalāśam* (hare, kuśa-grass, and palāśa-tree) as a collective *dvandva* (*samāhāra-dvandva*), because the collective is predominant, there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the definition of the *dvandva* and over-extension of the definition of the *bahuvrīhi*.
If it is argued thus, we say no;
for since those [suffixes] function as indicators (*prāpaka*), they lack the character of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
Grammarians maintain that the very fact of falling under a specific governing rule (*tattad-adhikāra-patitatvam*) is the defining characteristic of them.

In reality, the nature of an *avyayībhāva* consists in having as its primary meaning the sense of an indeclinable (*avyaya*), having as its meaning a non-existent subordinate member (*avidyamānāvayavārtha*), or having as its primary meaning a distinct external referent (*viśiṣṭānyapadārtha*).

By this definition, there is no lack of extension (*avyāpti*) in *avyayībhāva* compounds such as *unmattagaṅgam* or *supprati*, nor is there an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the definition of a *tatpuruṣa*.

On the other hand, the nature of a *tatpuruṣa* consists in being a compound whose primary meaning is that of either the first or the last member, provided it lacks the elision of a case-ending (*sup-lopa*) at the end of the word.
Therefore, in a *tatpuruṣa* compound such as *ardhapippalī*, there is no over-extension of the definition; nor is there an over-application of the definition to an *avyayībhāva*.
Likewise, the state of being a *bahuvrīhi* consists in the predominance of a meaning external to the constituent members (*anyapadārtha*).

Even in the case of *dvibhāḥ*, although it is a *dvandva* due to the predominance of the number of the combined measured objects, it is a *bahuvrīhi* due to the predominance of the number of the object to be measured that lies outside the compound.
And here, the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the "other referent" (*anyapadārtha*) is "smallness" (*alpatva*).

Thus, the rule *saṃkhyāvyayā0* (Pāṇini 2.1.25), which prescribes a *bahuvrīhi* compound for words denoting numbers, indeclinables, and so forth, is consistent as an indicator that the number to be counted (*saṃkhyeya*) is the predominant factor.

Similarly, rules such as *diṅmānādyantarāle* (Pāṇini 2.1.26) prescribe a *bahuvrīhi* by making the "other referent" the predominant factor, as in *uttarapūrvā*, *keśākeśi*, *bhujābhuji*, and *saputraḥ*.

In this context, the state of having a common relation (*tulyasaṃbandhitva*) serves as the delimiter of the meaning of the other word (*anyapadārtha*). For this very reason, it is said: "O Ketaka flower, even those who are intoxicated by the honey-drops from the chariots of Indra and the twin gods (the Aśvins) do not truly exist for you."

Thus, in such cases, there is the cognition of a limited number of individual instances. Similarly, in the expression "upadaśāḥ" (approximately ten), there is the cognition of several individual instances that constitute the meaning of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*).
Therefore, here too, the predominance of the external referent must be maintained.

Thus, in the *bahuvrīhi* compound "saputraḥ" (having a son), which is prescribed by the rule *tena saheti tulyayoge* (Pāṇini 2.1.28), the father—who is connected to the same action—is the referent of the external member (*anyapadārtha*). Therefore, the definition of *bahuvrīhi* is well-established. Furthermore, in the case of a collective *dvandva*, since the action is connected only to those things being collected, the collection itself is not primary; thus, there is no lack of application (*avyāpti*) regarding the definition of *dvandva*, nor is there an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of *bahuvrīhi*. This is correct.
Others, however, maintain that in examples such as *unmattagaṅgam*, the status is that of a *bahuvrīhi*, whereas in cases like *dvibhā*, it is indeed that of a *dvandva* and so forth.

The inclusion [of these] within the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for *avyayībhāva* and *bahuvrīhi* compounds is for the purpose of obtaining their specific properties, such as neuter gender and accentuation;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the governing rules (*adhikārasūtra*).

Nor does a contradiction with the context arise even in that case, because it is logical for the status of the context to conform to the governing sūtra (*adhikārasūtra*). This is because the *avyayībhāva* compound [formed] by the rule "in the sense of another word, when it is a name" (Pāṇini 2.1.21) possesses a literal meaning (*anvarthatā*) regarding a specific type of sacrificial offering (*sammindhyāhaviśeṣa*), and because of its being the context itself.
Therefore, they say that the definitions are exactly as stated.

(Now, the investigation of compounds: Here, the grammarians [hold that] in Tatpuruṣa compounds such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), there is a denotative power (*śakti*) residing in the whole compound to convey a person qualified by the king;
however, the cognition of the king and so forth does not arise through the denotative power of the constituent word "king" (*rājan*) within the compound.

By virtue of the great governing rule (*mahādhikāra*), "A grammatical operation concerning words [is conditioned by] semantic competency" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*, Pāṇini 2.1.1), all derivative formations such as compounds (*samāsa*) and the like are prescribed on the basis of semantic competency characterized by *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning).

The meaning of the sūtra is that a compound or similar formation, being prescribed with reference to words, is "competent," meaning it has acquired the capacity to denote the meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*).
Furthermore, *ekārthībhāva* is the state in which two words joined in a compound abandon their individual meanings and convey a single unified meaning.
And that meaning consists of both a form of difference—namely, "this is distinct from what is not related to a king"—and a form of relation—namely, "this is connected to a king.
Nor should it be argued: "Since such a presentation is possible through the established word-potencies (*śakti*) of 'king' and so forth, what is the point of postulating a potency for the compound?

For that potency is postulated to account for the aforementioned type of presentation in words such as *rājapuruṣa* (the king's man), and for the presentation [of the owner] by way of ownership in words such as *citragu* (the one with brindled cows).

Otherwise, even in the case of words such as *paṅkaja* (lotus), one would not have to postulate an additional power (*śakti*) for the sake of its presentation as a word. Furthermore, since the word *rāja-* occurring in a compound presents itself independently by its own nature, the qualification [of the king] would apply exactly as it does in the phrase *rājā puruṣaḥ* (the king's man). Nor can it be argued that this consequence is avoided by the prohibition: "There is no composition (*vṛtti*) of words accompanied by qualifiers, nor is there composition of a word already in composition with a qualifier," because that prohibition applies only to cases where the non-connection arises from the qualifier being a separate word-meaning (*padārtha*).

Moreover, since the sentence and the compound would thus have identical meanings, one would have to assume that the statement of the option (*vibhāṣā*) is intended to prevent the restriction imposed by the rule for compounds; this results in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Furthermore, in Bahuvrīhi compounds such as *kṛtavibhaktaḥ* ("one who has divided the inheritance"), *prāptodakaḥ* ("one who has reached the water"), and *uddhṛtaudanaḥ* ("one for whom rice has been served"), it is impossible for the words *kṛta*, *prāpta*, and *uddhṛta* to possess a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the senses of "the act of dividing performed by Viśvajana," "the reaching performed by water," or "the limit of the serving of rice. Moreover, in a compound like *citragu* ("possessing brindled cows"), since there is no decisive factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) to determine whether the secondary signification resides in the word *citra* or in the word *go*, it would follow that both words would have to possess a secondary signification, which would result in a redundancy of the object to be understood (*bodhyāvṛtti*). Nor can it be argued that the secondary signification must reside in the final member of the compound in order to conform to the syntactic connection with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*).
For if multiple words did not convey the meaning of another word (the *anyapadārtha*), the status of the compound as a *bahuvrīhi* would be undermined.

Nor can it be argued that other words convey that meaning merely by indicating the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*), because in the case of words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), the initial phoneme would then have to be capable of conveying the meaning [of the whole] by virtue of indicating the intention.

Furthermore, in the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one whose name is Śiva is the singer" (*śivanāmagāyakaḥ*), the understanding that "he possesses a name which is the object of singing performed by Śiva" would be utterly inexplicable without postulating a primary denotative power (*śakti*).

Therefore, a distinct power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) is postulated for compounds. Furthermore, if such a power were not admitted there, the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) would not apply due to the absence of "possessing meaning" (*arthavattva*).

Nor can it be argued that in expressions such as *citragumānaya* ("bring the one with brindled cows"), the case-endings following the compound convey meanings such as objecthood (*karmatva*), or that they convey their own meanings as residing in the referent of the entire compound or the subsequent word.
Because of the deviation [of the rule] in cases such as *ardhapippalī*, because of the necessity of postulating something else, and because of the resulting collapse of established principles;

furthermore, since a compound (*samāsa*) is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), its constituent parts—such as the word *puruṣa*—would lack the status of being nominal stems, and thus there would be no cognition of their case-role (*kāraka*).

Moreover, there would be no mutual coreferential connection (*parasparānvaya*) between the meanings of the two members of the compound, because in the absence of the presentation [of meaning] by anything other than an inflectional ending (*vibhakti*), the cognition of the case-role of the word-meaning "king" (in *rājapuruṣaḥ*) would be impossible; for a cognition in which the meaning of a nominal stem is the qualificand (*prakāra*) cannot arise without the presentation generated by an inflectional ending, unless that relation is identity (*abheda*).
Furthermore, there would have to be a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) either in the word *rājan* itself or in its relation.

It cannot be the first case, because the sentence "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) functions as the analytical explanation (*vivaraṇa*) for the meaning expressed by the compound, and thus it would contradict that. Nor can it be the second case, because according to the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that two nominal stems lacking incompatible case-endings are construed as non-different (*abheda*), this would result in the cognition: "a man whose nature is the relation to the king."
Therefore, they say that a primary denotative power (*śakti*) must be admitted for compounds. Regarding this, the followers of Gautama (*Gautamīyas*) maintain:

since in compounds the understanding "a man who is a subordinate of the king" can arise through the proximity of the already established word "king" (*rāja*) and so forth, which functions by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is not proper to postulate a separate denotative power.

Even for a compound with a primary governing element (*mahādhikāra*), its validity is established through the application of rules such as compounds (*samāsa*) based on the capacity [of the words] characterized by not abandoning their own meanings (*ajahatsvārthalakṣaṇā*).

The meaning of the sūtra is that a compound or similar formation, being prescribed with reference to a word as the locus (*uddeśya*), is "capable" (*samartha*) insofar as it resides in the words denoting their own respective meanings.

By this, the following objections are refuted: (1) the contingency of adjectives such as *śobhana* (beautiful) entering into a relation with the referent of the word *rāja* (king), and (2) the contingency of having to postulate additional words such as *kānta* (lovely) or *ukta* (spoken) in cases like *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (one who has departed from Kauśāmbī) or *gorathaḥ* (an ox-cart).

Because the word *rāja-* (king) is a part of the referent (*padārthaikadeśa*) [of the compound], there is the possibility of its connection with qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) therein; because the presentation of "one who has traversed" (*krānta*) and so forth is possible through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and because the rule for the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) of compounds and their analytical expansions (*vigraha*) is justified by the desire for cognition arising from both primary denotation (*śakti*) and secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, while there is no cognition in cases such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* or *citraguḥ* if one were to assume a primary denotative power (*śakti*) [in the same way] as in the word *rājā* itself, it is necessary to grasp that power [therein]. However, since cognition arises even when the power of the individual components is not grasped in words like *paṅkaja* ("lotus"), it is not necessary to grasp a power there; thus, the presence of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in words such as *paṅkaja* is clear.
Regarding the doctrine of compounding (*samāsavāda*): when both [words] are motivators of the action, it is a conjunction (*samuccaya*);
when one of them is not a motivator, it is a secondary mention (*anvācaya*).
The compound of those two occurs only when they are co-uttered with the particle *ca*,
because the rule "A *dvandva* [compound] is used in the sense of *ca*" prescribes a *dvandva* for those things indicated by the particle *ca* alone; whereas for the other two senses— namely,

mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) and collective aggregate (*samāhāra*)— the compound occurs in that very context because they are denoted by the meaning of *ca* alone, even without the word *api*.
For example: "The *dhava* and *khadira* trees have been cut; bring the *kuśa* and *palāśa* grasses.

Here, there is no primary denotation (*śakti*) or secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for either the cutting action or the connection with duality regarding the *dhava* and *khadira* trees presented as a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga-dvandva*).
[Likewise in] "pots, pots."
Even in the case of a *svarūpa-ekaśeṣa* (single remainder of the same form), such as *ityādi*, there is no secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).

This is because, through the word *ghaṭa* alone, both [the individual pot and the universal] are presented simultaneously by primary denotation (*śakti*), and thus the connection with duality or plurality is possible.

However, in cases of *virūpa-ekaśeṣa* (single remainder of different forms), such as *pitarau* (parents), the word *pitṛ* indicates the couple consisting of the progenitor and the consort through secondary signification, and it is in this [indicated sense] that the connection with duality occurs.

Regarding compounds such as *pāṇipādam* (hands and feet), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that even in a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), a single number is applied without contradiction; thus, the "collection" (*samāhāra*)—which consists of the state of being the object of a single cognition subsisting in all those constituent referents—is presented through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

On this point, some maintain that in a copulative compound denoting mutual conjunction (*itaretara-yoga*), the number two or more, which is presented by the case-ending (*vibhakti*), is construed with both members, such as the *dhava* tree and the *khadira* tree.

And in that case, there is no delimitation of the delimitor by *dhavatva* (the property of being a *dhava* tree), because it is delimited by the construction of the dual case-ending; for there is a rule that a case-ending expresses a number that is pervaded by the delimitor of the meaning of the stem. Therefore, the word *dhava* presents both the *dhava* and the *khadira* through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as the substratum of their conjunction (*sāhitya*). Thus, the duality is construed with the delimitation of that conjunction. Nor is the word *khadira* redundant, because its purpose is to provide the specific substratum for that conjunction.
Because the occurrence of two simultaneous functions (vṛtti) would result in a contradiction, even in the case of the word *dhava*, there must be indication (lakṣaṇā).
Therefore, an indication based on a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga-dvandva*) is necessary.
In this way, the analytical sentence (*vigraha-vākya*) "of two Mitrās and of two Varuṇas" for the term *mitrāvaruṇa* becomes logical; otherwise, the dual number would be untenable.

Thus, even in a *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective copulative compound), a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the collection (*sāhitya*) is necessary for the purpose of conveying oneness. However, in an *itaretara-yoga-dvandva* (mutually connected copulative compound), there is a secondary signification regarding the substratum (*āśraya*) of the collection.
And in this way, the grammatical rule that a case-ending conveys its own meaning as residing in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti-artha*) remains unviolated.

Thus, they say that even in the case of *sarūpaikaśeṣa* (the retention of one of two identical forms), there must be *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) for the purpose of connecting duality with the meaning presented as a collective whole.
This is not correct;

for when two meanings are presented by two distinct words through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the connection with duality is possible. Furthermore, there is no evidence that a cognition possessing the qualifier of "fitness" (*yogyatāvacchedaka*) is a necessary cause for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). Moreover, a case-ending denotes a number that resides in the same substratum as the property that serves as the delimitor of the word-meaning (*padārthatāvacchedaka-dharma*).

For this very reason, in the sentence "he fetches water with a jar" (*ghaṭena jalamāharati*), the jar is not presented as being characterized by having holes, but rather simply as a jar; and thus there is the application of duality in the expression "the jar and the cloth exist" (*ghaṭaśca paṭaśca staḥ*). By this, [the following] is also explained: because of the rule of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) defined as the denotation of a single number, it is impossible for duality to apply to that which is presented as a singularity. Therefore, in cases such as "Caitra and Maitra go" (*caitro maitraśca gacchataḥ*), the understanding arises either through the application of duality to the conjunction (*sāhitya*) conveyed by the word *ca*, or through the application of duality to the action itself.
Otherwise, if [the two] were presented as one, then in the case of the connection with duality, there would be the cognition "one is two. Thus, [this objection] is refuted.

In reality, wherever the number presented by a *sub*-suffix and the number presented by a *tiṅ*-suffix are contradictory, there the possibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) arises.

Since there is no contradiction between the singularity denoted by the secondary suffix (*sub*) and the duality denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the usage "the jar and the cloth exist" (*ghaṭaśca paṭaśca staḥ*) is appropriate; however, "one [is] two" (*ekau dvau*) is not, because in that case, singularity is contradictory.
Nor should it be argued that if there were a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), there would be no connection of the action with the hands and so forth;
for we accept the connection of the action with the hands and so forth through a mediated succession (*paraṃparayā*).

However, some maintain that even in a negative *tatpuruṣa* compound such as "a non-pot cloth" (*aghaṭaḥ paṭaḥ*), there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the negative particle (*nañ*) for mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) having the pot as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). This is because the property of having a counter-positive delimited by the delimitor of the correlate (*anvayitāvacchedaka*) is obtained through linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*); thus, the indication applies to mutual absence in general. Consequently, the cognition is: "the cloth possesses a mutual absence whose counter-positive is the pot.

Similarly, in the sentence "not a pot," there is also indication, since the negative particle is directly expressive (*śakta*) of relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*). This is the general direction [of the argument].

Regarding the deities in the *vanaspati* and other offerings, as well as those in the *samidh* and *vanaspati* offerings, they are indeed present in the *upāṃśu* [sacrifice] itself.

Furthermore, there is no evidence for postulating a meaning other than the well-known conventional one.

This being the case, the status of a deity cannot be established as directly perceptible merely by the identity of names; for [deities such as] Samidh, Tanūnapāt, and others, whose existence is based on non-worldly means of knowledge, must necessarily be *apūrva* (unprecedented) and non-worldly (*alaukika*).
