For a conjunction of things that serve the same purpose is never observed. However, there may be a conjunction of properties such as *staudha* and *śmalā* in a modified ritual (*vikṛti*) according to what is possible;
see Saṃkarṣa 4.3.12. Indeed, in a conjunction, there is a sequence of priority and posteriority.
Bhāṣya 12.3.15.132: Furthermore, when combination is possible, an option is not logical; there would be a contradiction in one alternative case.
[This concludes] the section on combination:
there is a combination of expiations intended for the removal of various defects.
But there is a combination [of rites] regarding those whose purpose is the removal of defects.
The Commentary states: "However, as for those whose purpose is the destruction of defects, in those cases there is a combination.
Which, then, are they? They are said to be those [rites] which prevent the son from performing [actions] or which involve the practice of what is prohibited."

For example: "If the sun should rise upon one whose *agnihotra* has not yet been offered, he should offer a *caru* oblation to Mitra and a cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) to Sūrya"; and: "If the sun should rise upon one whose *agnihotra* has not yet been offered, having established the fire, the husband and wife should approach it with all due care and effort."
In that case, no fault is perceived;
because of the absence of a fault, there is no lack of purpose. Rather, the ritual action is prescribed solely with prosperity as its occasion.
And this [injunction] is understood to be an auxiliary part of the ritual action because it arises within the context of that action;
furthermore, as many [auxiliaries] as are mentioned, all of them are included in the statement of performance (prayoga-vacana),
and there is a conjunction of them.

Śabara: Furthermore, as for those [injunctions] which do not aim at the removal of defects, such as the ritual injunctions regarding specific occasions like "He offers when [the vessel] is broken," there is a combination (samuccaya) of them because they are prescribed as non-alternatives, just like the Prayāja offerings.
This is merely a counter-example.

Soma: Even though many [remedies] are heard in connection with each individual cause (*nimitta*), there is no option (*vikalpa*) because—unlike the previous case—there is no hearing of a defect in the respective injunctions or their supplementary portions (*vākyaśeṣa*) that would preclude their being enjoined independently by the sentence as means for removing that defect. Rather, since these are enjoined in relation to the cause as subsidiary elements of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*), just like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, they are grasped simultaneously within the context (*prakaraṇa*) through non-exclusive application; therefore, there is conjunction (*samuccaya*). Viśvarūpa: "Is there an option or a conjunction regarding the oblations for a broken vessel, a star, and so forth? Option, as before; no, because they are prescribed for a specific defect."

Bhaṭṭa: Those [rules] which, due to the absence of any means of cognition that would apprehend a defect, are not intended for the removal of defects, but rather serve as occasional (*naimittika*) requirements based solely on an occasion (*nimitta*), in such cases where there is an occasional requirement triggered by a single occasion, there is indeed a conjunction (*samuccaya*), just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.

For example, after the *anvādhāna* rite, even before the consumption of the *iḍā* portion during an eclipse of the moon or sun, there is the injunction for a specific sacrifice accompanied by the recitation of the mantras "udayantam," "udyantam," and "citraṃ.
Indeed, no defect exists there, because even though it is enjoined by the Veda and other authorities, it does not apply prior to the consumption of the *iḍā*.

In such a context, the designation "prāyaścitta" (expiation) is merely figurative, based solely on the occurrence of a portion of expiation—just as the designation "audgātra" (pertaining to the Udgātṛ priest) applies to Vedic ritual acts performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). It does not function as a purifier of sin, because sin itself is not established [as a real entity] here. As for the two types of expiations cited by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) regarding the failure to perform the *agnihotra* oblation before sunrise, they are as follows: "The form, the time, the pouring back [of the milk], the deity, and likewise the cooking."
The first two [groups] are known as the Viddhā-pakṣas at all times.

Thus, according to the *Chandoga-pariśiṣṭa*, since it is logical that [this rite] serves to remove the fault caused by the lapse of time for those who offer the oblation before sunrise, otherwise— given that for those who offer the oblation after sunrise there would always be various distinctions in the performance of penance due to the difference in combinations— it has been disregarded.

As for what was cited by Pārthasārathi, such as "he offers in the case of the *minn* [crack]," that too has been set aside because it is reasonable to interpret it as being for the purpose of pacifying the deficiency caused by the cracking of the sacrificial vessel (*kapāla*) and so forth, and because it is mentioned in the section on secondary expiations (*prāyaścitta*).
Maṇḍana says: "If it is occasional (*naimitta*), then there is indeed a combination (*samuccaya*). Śaṅkara says: "There is a combination when there is no fault."

When a conjunction (*samuccaya*) is possible, there are the options of either sublation (*bādha*) or alternative (*vikalpa*); however, a conjunction is not possible here. The varieties of conjunction are now examined.

Although grammarians have specifically defined it as "conjunction is the connection of each [word] with a single action," nevertheless, the usage of the Mīmāṃsakas is seen to apply to the general sense of association (*sāhitya*).

For in the rule *pareṇāvedanāt* (Pāṇini 5.1.129), it is stated that even the absence of evidence for conjunction (*samuccaya*) is a cause for option (*vikalpa*), just like having a single purpose (*aikārthya*). And it has been said that "the evidence for conjunction is a single injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*).

Furthermore, in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, there is no other [single injunction] for each one of them belonging to the single performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

For in the section on the singularity of the cup (3.1.13–16), the author of the Vārttika has stated the distinction between the scopes of the two maxims—the maxim of the completion of each individual sentence and the maxim of the completion of the collective sentence—as follows: "The former applies when [the factor] is primary; the latter, however, applies when it is subordinate. This is illustrated by such examples as "I wipe" (*ahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*) and "one purchases with a one-year-old reddish-brown cow" (*aruṇayā ekahāyinyā krīṇāti*).

Furthermore, in the context of the rules for performance (*prayoga-vidhi*), since the *prayāja* offerings and the like function as subordinate elements (*guṇatva*), there is no single action distinct from each individual one; yet, there is the conventional usage of the term "conjunction" (*samuccaya*). Thus, it is established that the Mīmāṃsakas employ the term "conjunction" only in the sense of a general association (*sāhitya-sāmānya*). This very conjunction, like an option (*vikalpa*), is first of all threefold: based on logic (*nyāyagamya*), scriptural (*vācanika*), and optional (*aicchika*). Among these, conjunction based on logic is not eightfold, as in the case of an option, because conjunction is impossible for substances and the like, as well as for their absences.

Nor is this [collective] (*samuccaya*) merely fourfold—consisting of two genera, two substances, two qualities, and two actions; rather, it is fifteenfold by virtue of having objects that are either of the same class (*sajātīya*) or of different classes (*vijātīya*), and by virtue of having objects consisting of pairs, triads, and tetrads.

Among these, there are three types of collective having only objects of the same class: two substances, genus and quality, and genus and action; substance and quality, substance and action, and quality and action.
That which has objects of different classes is fourfold; however, that which has objects consisting of all four categories is one.
Thus, the examples of the fifteen types of logical conjunction (*samuccaya*) are stated in sequence.

Among them, (1) the logical conjunction of two classes (*jāti*) is as follows: "In the twelfth [book], in the section [12.1.4.13] titled *'krayaṇeṣu tu vikalpaḥ syādekārthatvāt'* (But there should be an option regarding the purchases, because they serve a single purpose), it is established by logic that cows, goats, and so forth are logically conjoined for that very same act of purchase, since they perform a single function."

(2) The combination of two substances is to be understood through reasoning (*nyāya*), as for example: in the injunction "he collects the *saṃbhāras* at the *āghāna*," the word *saṃbhāra* is etymological (*yaugika*), meaning "those things which are collected" (*saṃbhriyante*); and in the injunction "he lays down the *paridhis*," the word *paridhi* is etymological, meaning either "those by which the fire is enclosed" or "those which are laid down all around" (*pari samantād dhīyante*). Since these words denote substances, there is a combination [of the two types of *paridhis*], according to the twelfth section [of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra*] (12.1.4–14). Specifically, this follows from the rule: "But in cases where they are associated with a number, there is a combination" (12.1.4.30).

Regarding the statement, "They kindle it with four [verses]," since a collection of mantras has been mentioned, there is a combination of the *pariṣeṣaṇa* (sprinkling) in both the *āghāna* (fire-installation) and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

(3) The combination of two qualities is to be understood through reasoning, as in the case of "with a red, one-year-old [cow]," where, according to the principle of the *aruṇā*-section (PMS 3.1.12), by the rule "there would be no restriction for each individually," there is a mutual restriction and thus a combination of the redness and the number "one-year-old."

(4) The logical conclusion regarding the combination (*samuccaya*) of two actions is as follows: In the twelfth sūtra of the second section (*adhikaraṇa*), beginning with "But because of the difference in words, [there is no option] among the subsidiaries" (*aṅgānāṃ tu śabdabhedāt*), according to the *Vārtika* (wherein, by its view, the section consists of fifteen sūtras;

11.1.215–19), two prima facie positions (*pūrvapakṣa*) are refuted—the first being that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings and so forth, and the second being that they constitute the very nature of the subsidiary (*aṅgatva*). Thereafter, it is stated that because they are to be understood through a single injunction of performance (*ekaprayogavidhi*), there is a combination (*samuccaya*).

Likewise, in the twelfth [book], under the section "But in the case of purchases" (12.1.14), the combination of those things that are directly contributive (*saṃnipātika*) is stated as being established by reasoning.

Similarly, in the twelfth [book], under the section "In the case of those for the purpose of removing one's own defects through combination" (12.1.16), the combination of occasional rites that are auxiliary to the sacrifice (*naimittika-kratvaṅga-kriyā*) is stated as being established by reasoning.

(5) The combination of genus (*jāti*) and substance (*dravya*) is to be understood through reasoning, as in the case of the statement: "He purchases Soma with a ruddy, one-year-old, tawny-eyed cow. Regarding this, it was stated by the author of the *Vārttika* in his commentary on the sūtra "Because of the mention of something not seen" (*adṛṣṭavadatvāt*, 12.1.31) in the section concerning the *go* word: "In that context, since the substance denoted by the two derivative words *ekahāyinī* and *piṅgākṣī* is already expressed by the word *go*, there is a combination [of all three] according to the principle of the *aruṇā* section."
(6) There is also a combination of both genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*), as in: "They cook with a ladle that has no handle.

For it is not the case that, in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* (3.1.12), the explicit mention by its own word of that which is being restricted is part of the essential structure of the rule; rather, it requires mention in some way or another.
And here, there is the mention of the genus (*abhijāti*) through implication (*ākṣepataḥ*) by means of the act of cooking.

Therefore, by the very principle of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the act of churning—performed by means of the word *nirmanthya*—and the act of cooking, which is indicated [by the same word], because they constitute a single action.

(8) The logical comprehension of the conjunction of substance and quality is as follows: the conjunction of the substance denoted by the words "one-year-old" (*ekahāyinī*) and "tawny-eyed" (*piṅgākṣī*), and the quality of ruddiness (*āruṇya*).

(9) The logical comprehension of the conjunction of substance and action is as follows: since the word *nirmanya* is derived etymologically (*yaugika*) and thus denotes a substance, there is a conjunction of that substance with the action of churning by way of mutual restriction, according to the principle of the *aruṇā* (the red cow).
(10) The logical comprehension of the conjunction of quality and action is as follows: "The priests, wearing red turbans and red garments, perform the ritual.

For here, the word *vasana* is etymological—meaning that which is worn or put on—and like the word *nirmanthya*, it does not denote the genus "cloth. If that were not the case, since a turban is also a type of cloth, the term "red-turbaned" would be redundant once [the color] was already established by the phrase "red-garmented. Thus, it is a conjunction of quality and action.

And therefore, since the act of wearing is expressed by the word *vasana* just as it is by the word *nirmanya*, and because the quality of redness and the act [of wearing] are both understood from the verbal suffix (*pracaranti*), there is a conjunction [of the two] according to the principle of the *aruṇā* (red cow) passage.
Thus, the ten examples of the combinations of pairs that are accessible through reasoning have been stated.

In this manner, examples of the five types of logical combinations (*samuccaya*)—four involving triplets and one involving a quartet—must be stated for genus (*jāti*), substance (*dravya*), and quality (*guṇa*). These are: the triplet of genus, substance, and quality; genus, substance, and action (*kriyā*); genus, quality, and action; and substance, quality, and action. For example, in the *aruṇā-vākya*, there is the combination of the genus "cow-ness," the substance "one-year-old cow" (*ekahāyinī*), and the quality "red" (*aruṇā*), and so forth.
These fifteen varieties of logical combinations, observed in injunctions regarding genus and the rest for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), are as follows: [list follows].
In this way, fifteen types of combination (*samuccaya*) accessible through reasoning are also stated regarding the human goals (*puruṣārtha*), the castes (*jāti*), and so forth.

(1) Among these, an example of a combination of two human goals accessible through reasoning is as follows—Manu: "With sesame, barley, beans, roots, fruits, or potherbs, the ancestors of men are satisfied for a month according to the prescribed rule."
Thus [it is said].

For here, having considered the two classes of things mentioned in the *dvandva* compound "rice and barley" (*hrīyavaiḥ*), these two types of substances are enjoined as being for the fruit of the śrāddha and other rites under discussion.
The same applies to the expression "roots and fruits" (*mūlaphalena*).

(In reality, however, it appears that two pairs were accepted so that there might not be a violation of the meter; thus, it is understood that there is no injunction for a collective combination here.
Who?

(2) The logical combination (*samuccaya*) of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) and substance (*dravya*) is understood through reasoning, as stated by Mārkaṇḍeya: "The ancestors of men are satisfied at *śrāddha* ceremonies when meat is offered along with *bhakṣya*, *bhojya*, and *rasalāṇḍava-coṣya* foods.
Regarding this, Hemādri has explained: that which is eaten after being broken into pieces with the teeth is *bhakṣya*;
whereas that which is chewed and swallowed without requiring excessive effort because it is not very hard is *bhojya*.
That which is sucked by means of the lips, the tongue, and so forth, being pressed with respect and its juice drunk from the mouth, is the *coṣya* (the suckable).
For example: sugarcane stalks and the like.
The juices of *mudrā*, *lakuca*, and so forth; those boiled with sugar and other ingredients are *rāgas*;
and those mixed with sour substances and the like are *khāṇḍavas*.
In this regard, none of these terms denote genus (*jāti*);
rather, they denote substance (*dravya*).

Among them, the words *bhakṣya*, *bhojya*, and *coṣya* denote substance because their etymological derivation (*yaugikatva*) is established through primary suffixes (*kṛt-pratyaya*) applied to verbal roots that express specific meanings corresponding to those [actions].

However, since the words *rāga* and *lāṇḍava*—like the word *kulāla* and others—are subjects of the *ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, they denote substances qualified by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) precisely through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Therefore, because these are read as a *dvandva* compound here, it follows by logical necessity that there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the very substances intended for the *śrāddha* under discussion. (In this regard, we consider it appropriate to understand the word *kulāla* as denoting a substance based on its etymological derivation: "one who fashions (*lalayati*) the clay (*kuṃ-bhūmitaṃ mṛttikām*) with refinements (*saṃskāraiḥ*)," thus excluding what is to be prohibited.)

(3) Regarding the conjunction (*samuccaya*) of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), utility (*yoga*), and quality (*guṇa*): the conjunction is established through logical reasoning (*nyāyagamya*), as in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*: "He who gives what is unctuous and hot shall obtain the fruit of the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*). One should not assume that this conjunction is based solely on verbal expression (*vācanika*), because there is no identity of purpose (*aikārthya*). Furthermore, since the conjunction is established simply by the inclusion within a single sentence, the word "and" (*ca*) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Nor do the words "unctuous" (*snigdha*) and "hot" (*uṣṇa*) denote a substance, for—as in the case of "one with a red turban" (*lohitoṣṇīṣādi*)—they enjoin a quality that was previously unestablished.
However, in the case of a substance, since it is merely restated as something already obtained through the *śrāddha* injunction, [there is no such restriction].
(4) The conjunction of actions for the sake of a human goal is understood through logic, as in: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

For here, because they are mentioned by a single word—the root *yaj*—the concomitance (*sāhitya*) of the *āgneya* and other offerings in relation to the fruit is intended; this was established in the eleventh chapter.

(5) Regarding the combination of two things intended for human purpose, such as a genus (*jāti*) and a substance (*dravya*): their conjunction is established by logical necessity (*nyāya*), as in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "For a year, [one should consume] cow's milk and likewise milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Here too, the word "and" (*ca*) is merely reiterative (*anuvāda*), since the conjunction is established by logical necessity alone through their inclusion within a single sentence.

Furthermore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the injunction of *payas* (milk) and *pāyasa* (milk-rice), which are distinct word-forms and meanings; for in the section concerning the desire for sense-faculties (*indriyakāmādhikaraṇa*, 2.1.11), when an injunction for the connection between a quality and a fruit is accepted as an injunction for a distinct productive operation (*bhāvanā*), there is no syntactical split because it is an injunction for a productive operation toward a fruit qualified by both [the quality and the action].

(6) Regarding the two human goals (*puruṣārtha*), namely genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*): the combination (*samuccaya*) is established through logical reasoning (*nyāya-gamya*), as in the case of "One desiring vigor should make a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of *khadira* wood.

For here too, a single efficient-force (*karaṇa-kāraka*)—which is qualified by the genus conveyed by the nominal stem (*khadira*) and by the number one conveyed by the singular suffix—and which is indicated by the accusative case, is enjoined as a single production of the result (*phala-bhāvanā*).

In that context, because the *khadira* genus and the number one are mentioned within a single word, there is a combination (*samuccaya*), just as in the case of "One should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*).

(7) Regarding the combination (*samuccaya*) of genus (*jāti*) and substance (*dravya*), both of which serve human ends (*puruṣārtha*): as for example—(8) regarding the combination of substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*), both of which serve human ends, the combination is established through logical necessity (*nyāyagamya*), as in: "One desiring cattle should fetch [water] with a *godohana* vessel. For here too, just like the word *lādi*, a single instrumental factor (*karaṇakāraka*) qualified by the substance denoted by the derivative stem *udadohana* and by the number one conveyed by the singular ending is enjoined toward the result. Between those two, the connection with the substance...
The varieties of *samuccaya* (conjunction):
when a primary conjunction is already established by a word having the same meaning as the particle *ca*, a further conjunction is enjoined.

(7) A conjunction of actions other than those implied by the sense of the verbal suffix (*kṛtya*) is scriptural (*vācanika*), as for example: "One should give abundant and desired food—consisting of vegetables, roots, fruits, and stalks; of these various vegetables, cakes, *kṛśara*, milk-rice, and flour-cakes; and of drinks—with honey, ghee, and milk, along with alms that are easily obtained."

In this context, since the word *nirmanthya* (to be produced by churning) implies milk, and the word *pāyasa* (rice cooked in milk) implies the act of cooking as well as the substance milk—both being established by their literal meanings and the second case ending—the particle *ca* (and) enjoins a combination (*samuccaya*) in the first instance.

(8) An explicit scriptural injunction (*vācanika*) regarding the combination of a verbal derivative (*kṛtyārtha*), a substance, and a quality is found in the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "O twice-born ones, one should offer *pūrikā*, *rasāla*, and cow's milk, as well as whatever other foods there may be that are sweet and unctuous."
"Hot and pungent substances should be given in the rite of pacification (śāntika).
Here, although the word *rasālā* is a conventional term (*rūḍha*) like the word *kulāla* (potter), it does not denote a genus (*jāti*).
However, in the statement, "From the sugar comes the fourfold [sweets], this *rasālā*— the surface of which is curd—
is flavorful," the word refers to a substance (*dravya*) by way of specifying its limiting attributes (*upādhi*).
This is indicated by the word "and" (*ca*).
In the world, a combination that is well-established and favorable is what is desired;
yet, if such a combination is accomplished by means of a single instrument, another [instrument] would be purposeless.

Just as in the case of the *Saubhara* chant, where there is a connection with specific desires regarding the *puruṣa-śruti-nidhana*, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that—based on the text "One desiring rain should employ the *hīṣ* as the *nidhana*; one desiring other [benefits] should employ *ūrdhvam*; one desiring heaven should employ *ū*"—the *hīṣ* and other *nidhanas* are distinct from the fruits of the *Saubhara* such as rain and so forth. Consequently, when the performance of the *Saubhara* is for the sake of rain, the employment of the *hīṣ-nidhana* for the sake of some other rain would be purposeless.
However, no such desire for all cattle, differentiated by distinctions such as those pertaining to this world (*aihika*), is established through common worldly experience.
By this, the combination of both animals is stated;
otherwise, there would be no repeated performance even for the *citreṣṭi* sacrifice and others, and likewise for those rites intended for the sake of heaven.

(6) The optional combination (*aicchika-samuccaya*) of human goals, classes, and qualities is as follows: "One desiring vigor should make the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of *khadira* wood. This refers to the combination of both the *khadira* wood prescribed for the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice—which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*—and the low height prescribed for the purpose of the *dhṛṣṭi* rite, namely, "If one should desire that Parjanya be rainy, he should measure out the *sadas* hall low," when there is a desire for both results.

(7) The optional combination (*aicchika-samuccaya*) of human purpose, genus, and action is as follows: in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, there is the genus of "bringing earth" (*āhāryapurīṣa*) for one desiring cattle, as in the injunction, "One desiring cattle should make the altar with brought earth," and there is the action from another supplementary injunction, "Twenty-one [recitations] for one desiring stability. When there is a desire for both results, the combination is optional.

(8) Optional combination (*aicchika-samuccaya*) of substances, qualities, and human purposes, as for example: "One desiring cattle should perform the *praṇayana* with a *godohana* vessel. Here, regarding the substance *godohana*, the quality consisting of the shape of a calf's knee—as in "one desiring cattle should make the altar in the shape of a calf's knee"—or its dimension resulting from that constituent connection, which are prescribed for the sake of the fruit of cattle, there is an optional combination when there is a desire for both fruits.

(9) Voluntary combination of human purpose, substance, and action: for example, when there is a desire for both results from milking a cow and reciting twenty-one verses, there is a voluntary combination.

(10) Optional combination (*aicchika-samuccaya*) of human goals, qualities, and actions—as for example, the optional combination of the calf-knee-shaped vessel and the recitation twenty-one times when there is a desire for both results.

(11) Optional combination (*aicchika-samuccaya*) regarding person, purpose, genus, substance, quality, and action is as follows: in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, when there is a desire for cattle, there is an optional combination of the three—namely, the additional earth (*āhāryapurīṣa*), the milking vessel (*godohana*), and the form of the calf’s knee (*vatsajānvākāra*).

(12) Regarding the triad of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), genus (*jāti*), substance (*dravya*), and action (*kriyā*), there is optional combination (*aicchika-samuccaya*). For example, in the desire for the substance of cattle (*paśudravya*) and the attainment of stability (*pratiṣṭhākāmanā*), there is an optional combination of the *āhāryapurīṣa* [altar], the *godohana* [vessel], and the twenty-one recitations (*ekaviṃśaty-anuvacana*).

(13) The optional combination (*aicchika-samuccaya*) of the triad of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*) is as follows: for instance, when there is a desire for the stability of the sacrificial animal substance, there is an optional combination of the "artificial excrement" (*āhāryapurīṣa*), the "knee of a calf" (*vatsajānu*), and the "twenty-one recitations" (*ekaviṃśaty-anuvacana*).

(14) Optional combination (*aicchika-samuccaya*) of the triad of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*): for example, regarding the desire for the substance of cattle and the attainment of stability, there is an optional combination of the cow-milking vessel (*godohana*), the calf, the knee, and the twenty-one recitations (*anuvacana*).

(15) The combination of the four human goals (*puruṣārtha*) is as follows: when there is a desire for the fourfold results—namely, the acquisition of cattle, the establishment of the sacrificial fire, the form of the rite, and the fruit—regarding the four [elements] consisting of the *āhāryapuroḍāśa*, the *godohana* vessel, the calf, and the twenty-one recitations, their combination is optional (*aicchika*).
Thus, thirty varieties of optional combinations have been described.

Therefore, there are ninety varieties of combination stated: thirty established by logic (*nyāyagamya*), thirty based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*), and thirty based on optionality (*aicchika*).
Furthermore, it has been stated that these refer specifically to the absence of the combination of birth (*jāti*) and so forth.

Furthermore, these [injunctions] are fivefold: some have as their object items taught in the *prakṛti* (archetype); some have as their object items taught in the *vikṛti* (ectype); some have as their object items taught in both the *prakṛti* and the *vikṛti*; some have as their object items extended (*atidiṣṭa*) to the *vikṛti*; and some have as their object items both taught and extended in the *vikṛti*. Among these, the first example is as follows: in the Jyotiṣṭoma and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there are expiations for the purpose of removing defects regarding the purchase of cows, wild animals, and so forth, as well as the articles used in the purchase.
In that regard, twelve additional substances have been stated (12.3.16–17);
likewise, the combination of twelve *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses has been stated (12.4.12–14).

The second example is as follows: in the Daśapeya sacrifice, there is a combination of the Brahmin caste prescribed by the injunction "One hundred Brāhmaṇas consume the Soma," and the number one hundred prescribed by the injunction "Ten [Brāhmaṇas] approach each cup."

The third example is as follows: the combination (*samuccaya*) of the *pavamāneṣṭi* offerings at the *āghāna* (fire-consecration). In that regard, according to the view of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, their combination at the *āghāna* is based on a direct scriptural injunction (*vācanika*), namely: "One should offer them after a year, or after twelve nights, or immediately. According to the view of the author of the *Vārttika* as well, because they are subsidiary elements (*aṅga*), the combination of those very three is contextual (*prākaraṇika*), [namely]: "To Agni Pavamāna, to Agni Pāvaka..."
The division of the compound is:
"to Agni, the pure one."
The fourth example is as follows: "In the Saṃsava one should perform both; in the Gosava one should perform both; even in the Apaciti Ekāha, one should perform both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara."

The fifth example is as follows: in the section on *saṃsthā* (3.6.16), regarding the two *saṃsthās*, it is stated that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the *aindrāgna* offering—which is taught as being performed for the *uktha* sacrifice with the words "the second [offering] is for Indra and Agni at the *uktha*"—and the *savanīya* offering which is extended by analogy (*atideśa*).

Similarly, in the tenth book, in the section beginning "And in the case of a defect, there should be a removal of the sacrificial fee because it is not for food" (10.2.16–46), the combination of the original (*prākṛta*) and modified (*vaikṛta*) sacrificial fees is stated.

Likewise, in the section (10.2.30–70) beginning with "But in the case of the non-contingent [rite], because it is a product, there would be a combination in the archetype due to the occurrence [of both]," it is stated that there is a combination of the white quality prescribed for the Vāyavya and other animal sacrifices with the archetypal genus of goats and so forth.

Likewise, in the section concerning "that which is prescribed externally" (10.3.14.23–29), it is stated that regarding the initiation oblations (*dīkṣā-huti*), the six mantras taught for the initiation—beginning with "The fire is the form" (*ākṛtim agnim*)—are to be combined (*samuccīyante*) with the six mantras prescribed by extension (*atidiṣṭa*) for the initiation, namely "For the form, for the impulse, for the impulsion" (*ākṛtyai prayuje 'maye*), because of the injunction, "He offers twelve. Thus it is said.

Likewise, in the section on "Yajuryukta" (10.3.12–174), regarding the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is stated that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the portion for the Adhvaryu prescribed by the *yajuryukta* [text] with the portion for the Adhvaryu extended by analogy (*atideśa*).

Similarly, in the subsequent section (10.4.1) concerning the Nakṣatreṣṭi, it is stated that there is a combination of the secondary offerings (*upahoma*) prescribed by the text "He offers food" (*so 'nnam juhoti*) with the Nāriṣṭa-homas extended by analogy.

Likewise, in the subsequent section concerning the Bṛhaspatisava and similar rites, it is stated that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the other cup (*graha*) enjoined by the text—namely, "he takes the Bārhaspatya cup"—with the cups extended from elsewhere by analogy (*atideśa*).

Similarly, in the following section concerning the Vājapeya, it is stated that there is a combination of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati (*prājāpatyapaśu*) enjoined by the text with the sacrificial sessions (*saṃsthāpana*) extended by analogy.

Likewise, in the subsequent section concerning the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice, it is stated that there is a combination of the three *āmana*-offerings enjoined by the text with the three others extended by analogy.

Likewise, in the section on "accessories" (10.4.18–19), concerning the Mahāvrata rite within the Gavām ayana sacrifice, after introducing the statement, "In the quarters the drums resound," it is taught that "the wives sing along"; herein, a combination (*samuccaya*) of the wives with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), who are the extended (*atidiṣṭa*) singers, is stated.

Likewise, in the section on "And in the case of the non-saṃskāra" (10.4.16.10–12), it is stated that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the prescribed ointment of *guggulu*—as in the instruction "at the morning pressing, he anoints himself with *guggulu*"—with the extended (*atidiṣṭa*) ointment of fresh butter (*navanīta*).

Likewise, in the subsequent section (10.4.13–15), the combination of the *tābya* garment prescribed for the Mahāvrata rite—according to the instruction "the sacrificer puts on the *tābya"—and the *ahata* (unwashed) garment extended by analogy is stated.

Likewise, in the subsequent section (10.4.16–17), it is stated that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of both the *ślokas* and other *sāmans* taught specifically in the *Mahāvrata*, as well as those extended (*atidiṣṭa*) from elsewhere, such as the *gāyatra* and others.

Likewise, in the section on "the increase of the Stoma" (10.4.19–20), it is stated that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the *rājasāman*s taught in such injunctions as "the *pavamāna* [laud] consists of thirty-two [verses]" and those extended by analogy (*atideśa*).
Likewise, in the twelfth [book] (12.1.4.18), because of the injunction "he approaches with the anus," the combination of many anuses is stated in the case of a group of animals.

In this regard, whatever other varieties of conjunction (*samuccaya*) are observed—for example, the twelvefold [sacrifice] (*dvādaśāha*), or the conjunction of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses (as seen in the second variant of the commentary on 12.1.2.3–4)—[they are all subsumed here].

Or, for example, as in the case of the twelve-fold [rite] (*dvādaśāha*), there is a conjunction of mantras, such as in the passage: "He takes it up with four" (*tāṃ caturbhir abhimādatte*), and so forth.
Or, for example, in the Agnihotra sacrifice, there is a combination of the deities Agni, Sūrya, and Prajāpati.

Or, just as in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, due to the combination (*samuccaya*) of the *graha* vessels mentioned in the context, the combination of deities such as Indra—even though they are not constituent parts (*aṅga*)—is established by implication for the sacrifice; so it is stated in the *Vārttika* on the section concerning the Animal and Soma sacrifices (12.1.16–20): "Because the deities are connected with other [factors] and because they do not have the nature of an action, their being for the sake of the sacrifice is not understood through the context" (*Vārttika*, p. 519). Thus, it was stated at the outset that they "attain a connection as constituent parts of the sacrifice" only in the sense of providing assistance by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*).
Even in the concluding summary, it is summarized as: "By that [statement], the combination of the deities is also established" (Vārttika, p. 519); thus, subordination (*aṅgatva*) is not mentioned.
Such appears to be the meaning of the text.
However, Someśvara has explained the Upasaṃhāra-vārttika as being intended to establish subordination.

Or, for example, in the case of a sacrificial session (*sattra*), there is a conjunction of performers (*kartṛ-samuccaya*) as expressed in the rule: "At most twenty-four persons, seventeen at a time, should perform the sacrificial session."

Or, for example, in the *Ādhvaryava* and *Yājamāna* sections of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, regarding the mantras beginning with "By the impulse of strength" (*vājasya mā prasavena*) which are recited there, there is a combination of the two agents based on their respective designations (*sāmākhyānika*).
This was stated in the third [book] at [Sūtra 3.8.17]: "In the case of what is recited twice, both [agents perform it], because the dual recitation must have purpose."

Or, as in the case of the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice, because it is occasional (*naimittika*), there is no possibility of its [primary] fruit—which consists in the removal of the contingency—coexisting with other fruits such as the state of being purified by wealth and so forth, which consist in the removal of impurity; nor is there a mutual combination of those [secondary fruits], namely, the state of having sons, the possession of sensory power, and the possession of cattle.

Or, as when the *agnihotra* and other rites are performed for various purposes such as heaven and the like, there occurs a combination of fruits through incidental accomplishment of the results of the obligatory (*nitya*) performance.

Or, for example, as stated in the twelfth [book], in the sūtra "Because the qualities are taught in relation to a single action, they should apply to all actions" (12.3.16), there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the four qualities—straightness, upwardness, length, and continuity—as prescribed in the injunctions: "He holds [the fuel] straight," "He holds it upward," "He holds it long," and "He holds it continuously.

Or, for example, [in the case of the following injunctions]: "One should sacrifice a goat to Sviṣṭakṛt and Pārinīvata"; "In the morning, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Anīkavat"; "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Dātṛ"; and "To Viṣṇu, Śipiviṣṭa... [and so forth].

Section on the Restatement of the Aggregate (Samudāyānuvādādhikaraṇa): The correspondence with the aggregate and the postulation of affection for the aggregate have as their cause the status of being a supplement to the ritual application statement (*prayogavākya*);
thus the sense is finalized.
The second and subsequent [offerings] are likewise commenced only through a fresh effort (punaḥ-prayatna).
Therefore, due to the difference in effort, there is a distinct pouring out (nirvāpa). This concludes the section concerning the restatement of the aggregate (samudāyānuvādādhikaraṇa).

2|2|12–8. The instrument (*karaṇa*) is already established by implication and is therefore not explicitly enjoined. For, as stated under the "Paurṇamāsī-nyāya" (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2627), the sacrifice does not proceed unless [the materials] have been separated. Therefore, the suffix (*pratyaya*) that occurs in the act of offering (*nirvāpa*) should be understood as denoting the instrument.
Having specified the number, he ordains the non-dual [neuter gender].

An exception to the collective [compound] is made by three sections (2.1.51–53), wherein a connection characterized by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) is established.
Or [it may be otherwise]. 2.2.4.9. "But all [the acts] are to be performed together because they have a single purpose and possess that quality;
there is a collective performance (samudāyānusamaya).
[The Bhāṣya states: 'He offers four handfuls.'—In this case, having completed all [the individual acts], they are to be performed [as a whole]; here, the four handfuls constitute a single aggregate."

In the case of the *sāṃnāyya* offering on many days, because the spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*) are performed once for all (*tantra*), one should take two portions of curd and then take [the portion] of milk.

However, in the *Kalpasūtras*, it is stated that one should take two portions of milk first and then [the portion] of curd; this is because such a sequence is explicitly prescribed in the *Taittirīya Śruti*.
The *homa* is performed with the *tantra* method because it has a deity already established [by the *tantra*].

Likewise, regarding the anointing (*añjana*), washing (*avanejana*), and drinking (*pāna*), since there is a specific injunction for each, there is a sequential performance (*anusamaya*) by means of a single eye or a single bodily part.

However, in a multi-sacrificer *ahīna* sacrifice, having performed the anointing on both eyes of one sacrificer, that same action must be performed for another sacrificer; thus, there is a sequential performance for each individual, including the anointing and other rites performed with all the parts.

In the case of a *sattra* sacrifice, however, because the sequence of performance for each individual part (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) is prescribed by such injunctions as "Having initiated the Adhvaryu and the Gṛhapati," which mandate that the initiations (*dīkṣā*) consisting of those respective purificatory rites must follow one another, there is indeed *kāṇḍānusamaya*.
Maṇḍana [states]: "The primary [priests] and others [proceed] in groups, in sequence.
Śaṅkara [states]: "And that [sequence] has been described regarding the primary [priest] and the rest."
That is the performance according to the sequence of sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*).

The intermediate distinctions among the *apūrvas* (unprecedented potencies) are as follows: the *apūrva* of the aggregate, the *apūrva* of the antecedent [of the aggregate], the *apūrva* of the subsidiary, the *apūrva* of the principal, and the supreme *apūrva*. [Vi.
2112] The *apūrva* of the aggregate.

In the case of the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, which occur at different times, two distinct *apūrva*s (transcendental potencies) are postulated as produced by the two groups [of rites]; and these two produce the *phalāpūrva* (the transcendental potency that brings about the fruit).
For indeed, when many things are denoted by a word ending in the singular number, it refers to the group [as a whole], as in the cases of "you," "we," "family," or "assembly."
Likewise, the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* reside in the statements of the learned;
[the *pārvaṇa-homa*] is a sacrifice performed on the aggregate [of materials], not a sacrifice performed at a [specific] time. (Bhāṣya 2.2.3)

Bhāṣya 9.2.8.51–56: The formation of a collective whole occurs either through the application of a single term to the group, as in the form of a restatement of the collective, such as "He who, knowing thus, performs the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice";
or through connection with a result and so forth, as in "One desiring sovereignty [should perform] the Rājasūya.

Vārttika 2.2.12, p. 463: That which is prompted by the collective—the name-dharma of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices—is not prompted by the collective of the Paurṇamāsī and Amāvāsyā sacrifices, but rather by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result).

The principle of substance, number, cause, and aggregate (dravya-saṃkhyā-hetu-samudāya-nyāya). 1.9.1.5.19–19. Mīko., p. 2902. It is well established that the conventional meaning of an aggregate (samudāya-prasiddhi) necessarily overrides the conventional meaning of its constituent parts (avayava-prasiddhi).
The established usage of a whole (*samudāyaprasiddhi*) occurs where the meaning of the individual parts is obscured and the whole alone is perceived as distinct from them.
Vārttika 3.2.1.1, p. 747. It has already been stated that the established usage of a whole is not sublated by the established usage of its parts.
Bhāṣya 6.8.0.42, 43. Once the established usage of a whole has attained its own nature, it sublates the established usage of the parts.

Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for postulating a new, unprecedented power (*apūrvaśakti*) in the aggregate (*samudāya*). This is because the established meaning of the parts (*avayavasiddhi*) precludes the established meaning of the whole (*samudāyaprasiddhi*). The word *ahīna* denotes a group of sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*), and does not refer to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* based on the etymological derivation "that which is not deficient" (*na hīnaḥ ahīnaḥ*). Vārttika 2.2.1.17, p. 421. The established meaning of the parts precludes the established meaning of the whole. The term *ahīna* signifies a collection of sacrificial days (*ahargaṇa*), rather than denoting the *Jyotiṣṭoma* through the etymology "not deficient" (*na hīnaḥ ahīnaḥ*).
Conventional meaning (rūḍhi) sets aside etymological derivation (yoga). Conventional meaning is stronger than etymological derivation.
(Pāṇini 3.3.16): the well-known meaning of a whole [word] overrides the meaning derived from its individual parts.

6|1|6|23, p. 1369: The conventional meaning of a whole (*samudāyaprasiddhi*) is stronger than the conventional meaning of its constituent parts (*avayavārthaprasiddhi*). Just as the meaning of a sentence [prevails over its parts], the conventional meaning of the whole, which is obtained through the immediate presentation of the mere heard word (*śrutimātropanipāta*), prevails over the conventional meaning of the parts, which must first combine the meanings of the parts and then postulate a connection between them. 2|2|1|23, p. 537: The conventional meaning of a whole is stronger than the conventional meaning of its constituent parts.

In the case of words whose meaning is established by conventional usage as a whole, they are understood through their constituent syllables; however, in other cases, this understanding is remote due to the synthesis of partial meanings.
When a word denoting a non-substantial (abstract) object is employed elsewhere for a different [concrete] object, [it functions through metaphorical transfer].
In that case, the collective whole (samudāya) is established by virtue of having no other possible recourse.
For once the establishment of the collective whole has acquired its own nature, it sublates the establishment of the individual parts.

Its very essence is such that where the application of a word is observed through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) toward an object devoid of the meanings of the previously experienced parts—as, for example, the word "aśvakarṇa" applied to a tree that lacks both the nature of a horse (*aśvatva*) and the nature of an ear (*karṇatva*).

1|4|8|11, p. 344: It will be stated in the *Rathakārādhikaraṇa* (6|1|12|44–50) that the conventional meaning of a whole (*samudāyaprasiddhi*) is stronger than the conventional meaning of its parts (*avayavaprasiddhi*). Su., p. 466: When the conventional meaning of a whole is available, it is not proper for the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) to rely on the conventional meaning of its parts, as in the case of *udgātr̥bhyām*. Vā., 3|5|8|26: The principle of the completion of a sentence within a whole (*samudāyavākyaparisamāptinyāya*) pertains to matters concerning subordinate qualities (*guṇatva*).
As in the case of "He purchases [the Soma] with a ruddy, one-year-old cow" (Bāl. p. 165). Furthermore, a word denoting a whole cannot apply to its parts.
(Bhāṣya 11.4.2.3–1, p. 356). For words denoting a whole, there is no possibility of figurative application (*gauṇatva*) to their constituent parts.
Or [it is so] because words denoting a whole are perceived even when applied to its parts, as in the expression, "The village has arrived. (Vārttika 1.4.12.23–1, p. 357).
And likewise, those who study [the Veda] apply themselves to that very [text] with even greater intensity, saying, "We are studying the Veda," or "The Veda is proceeding.
But those studying the Brāhmaṇas do not speak in such a manner. (Vārttika)
By virtue of being a collective term (*samudāyaśabda*), it will be understood that the singular ending expresses many [individuals].

Bhāṣya 2.2.13, p. 479. There is no distinction between the aggregate and its constituents (*samudāyasamudāyin*). Vārttika 2.2.3.2, p. 477. There is an absolute absence of difference between the aggregate and its constituents.
Su. p. 729, 1161: Because they have a single result, there is the accomplishment of a collective whole. Su. p. 779:
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the manifestation or production of the fires for each ritual act is from the two kindling sticks (*araṇī*);
the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is from the Gārhapatya fire alone.
Saṃkarṣa 3.2.7: The maxim is "Just as waters enter the ocean.
For example, just as waters from various mouths of great rivers—such as the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Kṛṣṇā, Kāverī, Sindhu, and so forth—converge into the ocean.

The rivers—possessing various colors, tastes, smells, and fruits—abandon their own specific colors such as dark blue or yellow, their specific tastes such as sweetness, their specific smells such as fragrance or putridity, their specific qualities such as lightness or heaviness, their specific distinctions of merit equal to one, two, three, four, five, six, ten, a hundred, or a thousand *kṛcchra* penances, and their respective individual names; they proceed toward the state of the ocean alone. Having reached the ocean, by virtue of its connection, they are no longer distinguished from the ocean by their specific names, forms, or qualities; this is the meaning.
The same applies to the case at hand. [This is] the principle of the ocean waves and so forth (526).

Even though there is no difference from the ocean, which consists of water, a mutual distinction among its constituent parts—such as foam, ripples, waves, and bubbles—is observed, as is their empirical usage characterized by mutual contact and so on.

Furthermore, although they are non-different from the ocean which consists of water, there is no mutual transformation among its constituents such as foam and waves; nor, even though they do not undergo mutual transformation, do they become something other than the ocean. By this principle, although the enjoyer and the enjoyed are non-different from Brahman, there is no mutual transformation between them, nor will they become something other than the supreme Brahman.
(Śāṃbhā. 2.1.5.13; Basu:
The Ocean-Wave Principle).

The state of both difference and non-difference between Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) is established through the analogy of the ocean and its waves. [Śrīkara-bhāṣya 3.1.7] Like the meditation on the mind as the ocean and so forth;

just as the meditation on the mind as being the ocean serves a specific purpose, so too, if the desire for heaven were enjoined merely as a subordinate quality (guṇa), it would result in an unseen merit (adṛṣṭa).
This is on the front page:
Soma.
The maxim of the increase of the ocean.
This principle is intended to prevent error;
the sense is that its application occurs precisely where an action would otherwise be fruitless.
[Sāhasī 296] Inviting [others] before consuming is the characteristic property of Soma.

Having asked, "Upahvayasva" (Invite [me]), when it is replied, "Upahūtaḥ" (I am invited), the consumption [of the substance] is the rule for Soma; this applies to the *vājina* and the *surā* as well. Bhāṣya 8.2.1.12. The twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is a composite rite.
"The *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* days have the cups for Indra and Vāyu first, as does the tenth day."
Now, regarding these nine days: the first day has the Aindravāyava cup at its beginning, then the Śukra cup at its beginning, then the Āgrayaṇa cup at its beginning;
then the Aindravāyava cup at its beginning, then the Śukra cup at its beginning, then the Āgrayaṇa cup at its beginning.
Thus it is said.
Bhāṣya 10.1.2.4.7. *Samūḍha*:

That twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is called *samūḍha* where there is no violation of the sequence due to the collection of the three recurring cycles consisting of the precedence of the Aindravāyava cup, the precedence of the Śukra cup, and the precedence of the Āgrayaṇa cup.
However, where there is a reversal of these aforementioned precedences, it is called *vyūha*.

Ku. 10|1|2|4|79: "Accordingly, as is the established conclusion (siddhānta), where there is both a scriptural statement and an indicative mark (liṅga), there the *vyūha* (rearrangement) operates; elsewhere, it remains unmodified (*samūḍha*) without distinction. Bhā. 10|1|2|4|82: "The *vyūha* is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *samūḍha*. 10|1|2|4|80: Regarding the statement, "The *dvādaśāha* is a *vyūha* of the *samūḍha*; the *dvādaśāha* is a *vyūha*, [meaning] a modification of the *samūḍha*," the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted.
The Principle of Collective Reference (samūhālambananyāya):

Where there is no possibility of a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) among the objects presented [in the mind], there the cognition occurs as a collective reference (*samūhālambana*) of those presented objects.
For example, in cases such as "a jar and a cloth," since both the jar and the cloth are [simultaneously] the qualificands (*viśeṣya*), the cognition is one of collective reference.
Such is the case; however, the distinction is that in a doubt (*saṃśaya*), there is only a single qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

[The term] *sāhasī* [refers to] collective application (*samūhavṛtti*), which is twofold: like a "marched-off line" (*daṇḍakalitavat*) and like the study of a recitation-section (*prapāṭhakādhyayanavat*).
The first is the repetition like a measuring rod (*daṇḍa*) when reaching a field, where there is the performance of the whole at once, then again of the whole, then again of the whole.

In the study of a *prapāṭhaka*, however, having recited one sentence (*vākya*) with the *satvara* [intonation], one repeats the second sentence with the *satvara*, and likewise the third; this repetition continues until the end of the *prapāṭhaka*. This is the second [type of recitation], known as *guṇḍikā* (in the Marathi language).
Vi. 10|5|25. Regarding collective records (*samūhalekhyanāni*):

For the very purpose of self-protection—[specifically] so that the lineages of their own fathers, grandfathers, and so forth do not become lost due to the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*)—collective records were introduced by kings and Brāhmaṇas.
And likewise, because one remembers the virtues and faults of each [action], activities of engagement and withdrawal are observed accordingly.
Vākyapadīya 2.2.15, p. 109. The *saṃpatnīya* oblation:
in the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, after having sacrificed to Agni Gṛhapati, [one recites]: "May the wife be united with her husband through good deeds."
"Thus, with the *sruva* ladle, he offers the *saṃpatnīya* oblation into the *gārhapatya* fire while the wife holds on to him.

(Satyāṣāḍha Śrautasūtra 2.5.11). When the deity is common [to both offerings], there is indeed a single performance (*tantratva*) regarding the act of giving. (Bhāṭṭadīpikā 5.2.2). And the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is a *kāraka*.
*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 10.3.12.150: Furthermore, that which is called the *saṃpradāna* (recipient) is even more desired than the object (*karman*) itself.
*Bhāṣya* 9.1.4.6: And a factor (*kāraka*) engaged in the act of receiving becomes the *saṃpradāna*.

Section 4194: On the Accusative Case of Address; [the question of] whether the *sammārga* (cleansing) pertains to the ladle (*darvī*) or to the clarified butter (*ājya*).
Vi—In the case of the injunction "He cleanses the ladle" (*saṃmārṣṭi srucaḥ*), is there the status of being a primary object (*pradhānakarman*) called for?

Or rather, is it a subsidiary action (*guṇakarman*)? Since there is no [separate] substance [to be prepared], as in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*), subsidiarity is not possible; rather, its primacy is like that of the *prayāja* offerings.
Even if its form is not perceived, it may possess the status of a quality (*guṇatva*) by virtue of the accusative case ending.

The Bhaṭṭa [responds]: In cases such as *vrīhīn prokṣati* ("he sprinkles the rice") and *srucaḥ saṃmārṣṭi* ("he cleans the ladles"), since this [benefit] is possible as a service (*upakāra*), and because the accusative case is seen to be used even for the sense of an instrument—as in *saktūn juhoti* ("he offers groats") and *makhajān śikhaṇḍakān kuru* ("make crests from the sacrificial grass")—it is indeed a primary action (*arthakarman*), just like the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the previous section. For if it were a goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the verb *karoti* would incur the fault of having two objects (*dvikarmakatva*), which is not the case here. Thus, it does not have the status of a goal to be accomplished.
Therefore, instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is also the meaning of the accusative case.
Consequently, it follows that the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) performed with rice (*vrīhi*) as the instrument is enjoined for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

This being the prima facie view, we reply: according to the grammatical rule "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) and from usages such as "he makes a pot" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), the meaning of the accusative is precisely the state of being an effect to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*), not instrumentality.
Because it would entail the undesirable consequence of postulating multiple powers (*śakti*).
Furthermore, according to the rule "the object is that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*), *karmatva* (objecthood) is not merely the state of being most desired;

rather, according to the rule "and likewise that which is connected [to the action] though not desired," it is simply the state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*), common to both the desired and the undesired.

Therefore, because the rice grains (*vrīhi*) are understood through the accusative case to be the object to be accomplished, and because they are not identical with the sacrifice, they are perceived as being "desired" (*īpsita*); thus, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is enjoined with reference to them.
Even though a visible purpose cannot be established, an invisible effect (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in the rice grains is postulated.

For this very reason, no visible utility is assumed here, nor can it be so assumed, as is the case with the flour-meal (*saktu*). In that instance, having accepted the instrumental sense indicated by the accusative, the injunction prescribes the oblation qualified by the meal for the sake of an invisible result.

Nor should it be argued that because the connection [of the flour] is possible even as an unintended object (*anīpsita-karman*), there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of its being an instrument (*karaṇa*).

For if that were the case, since even an invisible benefit (*adṛṣṭa-upakāra*) would necessarily have to connect with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) as an object, it would follow that the sacrifice has two objects; this would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to multiple intended purposes.

Therefore, although the oblation whose instrument is the flour provides a remote benefit (*ārāt-upakāraka*), acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) provide only a direct, inherent benefit (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*).
