[Sāhasrī 524] "Om. 'All colors on the bricks'—this is the discussion regarding the lines. Regarding the scriptural statement, "One should apply all colors to the bricks," the word *varṇa* refers exclusively to forms such as white and so forth.

Since it is impossible to produce elsewhere those forms which have a nature distinct from other times, the application of substances such as colored powder, ink, and so forth is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*); however, the word *varṇa* itself does not directly denote that [application], because of its connection with the word *śabda* (sound), according to the natural sense of the Sūtra.
This is because the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *varṇa* does not reside in lines in general, as there is no conventional usage (*nirūḍhi*) for it there.
Furthermore, it would result in the word being neuter, contrary to the lexicon which states: "But *varṇa* is *akṣara* (syllable)."

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhāntin replies]: because of the injunction regarding the specific location of bricks possessing various lines, ending with the words, “straight lines are drawn behind and in front, and [curved ones] in the middle,” and because the reading of the phrase “all the colors” (*sarvān varṇān*) leads to the conclusion that the word “all colors” refers to the various lines previously introduced; and since, when the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is grasped, that [literal sense] would otherwise be untenable, it is proper to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); thus the intention is that there is an application for all the particulars from among all [the bricks].

Since the *saṃskāra* (consecration) is a rule pertaining to all the original sacrificial materials (*havir*), and since the status of being a motivator (*prayojakatva*)—expressed by the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) according to the etymology "that by which something is performed or employed"—is common to all sacrificial materials, the performance of the *śeṣakāryas* (rites with the remnants) would apply to all of them. This is the purpose of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), and thus [the statement] is well-applied. Su. p. 1440: An exception is made to the over-extension (*atiprasakta*) of the rule "Or from all, because there is no difference in the cause" (3.4.15.44), by means of the sūtra beginning with "And from the clarified butter... (3.4.15.44).

Or [it may be]. Vārttika 3.4.15, p. 985. Oṃ: The performance of the remaining rites for all [mantras]. Bhāṣya 3.4.15.45, p. 985. Oṃ: "Because it serves the purpose of expressing everything" (12.1.12.15). And without an option, it is not possible to effect the convergence of all the mantras at the conclusion of the ritual action and so forth.
What is this statement?
It is not so;
it is logic, because everything has the meaning of a statement.

"Or rather, because of the connection with the sacrifice, because of the oneness [of the sacrifice], and because of the oneness of the purpose of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and the accessories, in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there should be a displacement (*atideśa*); for that [displacement] is inherent in the rituals.

Regarding the statement "a cow is the sacrificial fee" in the *bhūman* sacrifice, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that by means of the single cow, only the cows belonging to the *jyotiṣṭoma* are displaced, not the horses and other animals; however, this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The cow is the sublater of the entire ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*) prescribed by rule.

Why? Because of the phrase "the *stotriyas* of that [sacrifice] consist of the *viśvavat* [verses]," the word "that" (*tasya*) refers back to the sacrifice named Bhū; thus, through the connection with the whole sacrifice, the injunction "the cow is the fee" applies to the modified sacrifice named Bhū. Consequently, regarding the original purpose—the function consisting of the fee—the two cows obtained through direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) would, by virtue of the text, supersede the inferred general term for all ritual fees.

An objection is raised: "In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, since the connection of the priests with the ritual action is understood through their being hired for many substances, it is not proper for those who have been hired even by a single substance to have a connection with the ritual action in that context.
Anticipating this, it is stated: "For there is a union with that" (*tatsamavāyo hi*).

The meaning is that because the connection of the priests with the ritual action is determined by means of that sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it is proper for those who have been hired—even by a single substance—when that substance is heard in scripture as being the sacrificial fee, to have a union with the ritual action.

An objection might be raised: "Since substances such as cows and the like differ from one another, it is not logical that the exclusion of horses and other animals should result from a *dhenu* (milch cow) prescribed for the purpose of purchasing a cow. Anticipating this, it is stated: "Because the quality of being a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇātva*) is one. The meaning is as follows: when there is a requirement for a means to secure the priests, the word *dakṣiṇā*—derived from the root *dā* (to give) in the sense of "giving a sacrificial fee"—denotes the act of giving. Since the *dakṣiṇā* is intended to be something to be accepted (*upādeya*), its number is restricted to one; consequently, the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*) expressing that object, and thus the act of bending or pleasing (*ānamana*) itself, is also singular.

Now, one might object: "Even though the singular number is heard in the expression 'he gives the sacrificial fee' (*dakṣiṇāṃ dadāti*), since a collective sense of the sacrificial fee is perceived in sentences such as 'the cow and the horse,' it is determined that there is a difference in purpose in those cases. Anticipating this objection, it is stated: "And because of the unity of purpose among the subordinate elements" (*guṇānāṃ cārthaikatvāt*).

By the word *ca* ("and"), it is understood that cows and the other items, when mutually connected, constitute the sacrificial fee; furthermore, because of the singular number in the statement "its sacrificial fee is one hundred and twelve," it is the collectively joined items themselves that constitute the sacrificial fee.

Because cows and the other items are the objects of the injunction (*uddeśya*), their collective nature is not intended to be expressed; therefore, they are designated by the word "quality" (*guṇa*) in order to exclude the suffix *kan*. Furthermore, the term "purpose" (*artha*) is used to indicate that the status of being a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇātva*) applies to each object of the injunction individually (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 435). Regarding the statement, "In the case of all [the mantras], because of the words 'causing to reach' (*abhigamaya*) and 'according to the truth' (*yathārthatve'), there is the form ending in *-aṭ*," this refers to the taking together [of the mantras] in the passage: "To Indra the Ruler... To Indra the Overlord... To Indra the Sovereign" (Saṃkarṣa).
Oṃ. For all [sacrifices] without distinction:

in the modified *soma* sacrifices, the *sāman* is heard through words ending in the singular number, such as "the *kaustubha* is used" and "the *kāṇva* is used. However, the *sāmans* are heard through words ending in the dual number, such as "the two *janitras* of Vasiṣṭha are used," "the two *śuddhāśuddhīyas* are used," and "the two *bhargayaśasīs* are used."

However, by the word "kaunbhāni" ending in the plural number, the *sāmans* are heard [in the text]. Thus, those very *sāmans*, such as the Gāyatra and others, which are archetypal (*prākṛta*), are obtained in the modifications (*vikṛti*).
It is understood, however, that the modified (*vaikṛta*) ones are the displacers of those archetypal ones.

In this regard, a deliberation arises as to whether all [substituted] Sāmans are the displacers of all [original] Sāmans; or whether even a word ending in the singular number displaces only one original Sāman, a word ending in the dual displaces two, and a word ending in the plural displaces many original Sāmans—displacing Sāmans that correspond in number to their own respective numbers. Regarding this inquiry, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view is stated: all modified (vaikṛta) Sāmans are the displacers of all original (prākṛta) Sāmans, because there is no distinction—that is, because there is an absence of any specific qualification.
Therefore, the prima facie conclusion is that every [modified Sāman] is the displacer of every [original Sāman].
Of all [beings],
in all [places], in all [respects]

[The author] states the established conclusion (siddhānta), setting aside with the word "or" (vā) the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) obtained through the sūtra, "Because all [the fires] are without distinction," by means of the capacity of the scriptural statement regarding one [fire] and because there is no modification of the archetype (prakṛti).
The word "vā" (or) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). It is not the case that everything sets aside everything;
rather, the rule is that one archetypal (*prākṛta*) element is set aside by one modified (*vaikṛta*) element, two by two, and many by many.
By the force of the scriptural statement— that is, by the very force of the singular number and so forth being heard—

this being the case, there is no sublation (bādha) of the modification (vikāra), because there is no modification of the archetypal (prakṛti) Sāmans and those derived from the archetype (prākṛta) which are obtained through the general rule (codaka).
Thus, by Kautsa and Kāṇva, only one archetypal [Sāman] is sublated, while there is a combination (samuccaya) of the other archetypal ones with those of Kautsa and the rest.
Thus, there is a sublation of the two natural [states] by means of purity and impurity; however, for these [latter], there is a combination. This is also the case elsewhere.
Such is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
Because it is stated "of all," there is no restriction [to a specific time].
Bhāṣya 3.1.16.15, p. 1099. The praise for all the Soma-offerings is as before.
Vi. 5.13.19. The *ājya*, *śyena*, and *haviḥ-navanīta* [offerings] belong to all [the Soma-offerings], not only to those at the time of the *sutyā*.
Regarding the statement *mīko.* pṛ. 21|14, ‘*hatinavanītaṃ iyene*’, one should consult the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*).

According to the siddhānta established by [Jaimini] at *sarveśāṃ tvaika (vaika) mantraya syāt* (3|1|14|144), the ritual application (*anuṣṭhitaprayoga*) is performed in the archetype (*prakṛti*), specifically in the *agniṣṭoma* sacrificial form.
Su. Pṛ. 1142: ‘According to Aitiśāyana, there is a single mantra for all [the cups], because they are partaken of as a collective drink; for the qualification of the *savana* (pressing) applies.

However, the requirement of being made of *śamī* wood and so forth, being prescribed by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to the *luga* and other [cups] alone, does not qualify the entire *savana*. For all purposes...’
In all cases, there is attainment [of the details]. However, where there is no injunction in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is attainment by means of the extended application (*codaka*).
Therefore, the state of being made of *parṇa*-wood and so forth serves every purpose.
If it is argued that this is because of direct observation, [we reply:
since it is not established by a general injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*), the extended application (*codaka*) operates.

When the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) asserts that "since the requirement [of the model sacrifice] is satisfied by a statement not connected to a specific context (anārabhyavacana), there is no need for the expectancy of the *codaka*," the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) objects:

"If the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) were rendered free from expectancy toward the *codaka* by a non-contextual injunction, then the observation of the *prayāja*s in the passage, 'At each *prayāja* he offers a *kṛṣṇala* grain' in the Śata-kṛṣṇala sacrifice, would be inexplicable.
For it is by the *codaka* alone that the *prayāja*s are obtained in the Śata-kṛṣṇala."
Because one hundred black [animals] are seen as *prayāja* offerings, the extended application (*codaka*) to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) is established.

Therefore, the *juhū*, *upabhṛt*, and other implements, which are taught as unattached injunctions (*anārabhyādhīta*), find their place in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*) alone, while in the modified sacrifice they are supplied by the extended application.
This is because there is no purpose for a separate injunction.
This is a *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra intended to refute the objection raised by the proponent (*siddhāntin*) in the sūtra, "If it be argued that [it is so] because of being seen" (3.6.14).

Regarding what was stated by the proponent—that the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) does not operate once the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) has been rendered free of expectancy by the *anārabhyavidhi* (a general injunction not connected to a specific rite)—on what basis is that? It is because "of the unity of purpose of the injunction" (*codanaikārthyāt*). This means that the injunction—the injunction concerning the *juhū* ladle made of *pālāśa* wood taught in the *anārabhyādhīta* section—has a single purpose, as it prescribes only one thing: the quality of being made of *pālāśa* wood.
That injunction whose purpose is a single object is "single-purposed" (ekārthā).
The state of being single-purposed is "single-purposeness" (ekārthyam).
This refers to the single-purposeness of an injunction that is not introduced in the context of a specific ritual (anārabhyacodanā).

Therefore, what was stated by the proponent of the final view is not tenable. In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the *juhū* ladle is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*). In that case, the property of being made of *pālāśa* wood is enjoined solely by means of a general injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*).

And thus, having excluded that which is prescribed by an isolated injunction (*anārabhya-vidhi*), the rule of transfer (*codaka*) brings [the details] into effect. Consequently, even when an isolated injunction exists, the rule of transfer certainly operates. Therefore, the isolated injunction pertains to all purposes.

If it is argued that this is an "origination" (utpatti), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) states that an injunction not connected to a specific context (*anārabhyavidhi*) pertains to both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*). To this, the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*) replies:
first, in the archetype, the rites are originated both briefly and in detail.
"One performs five fore-sacrifices (prayāja);
one sacrifices to the Samidhs, one sacrifices to Tanūnapāt," and so forth is the detailed exposition.
Thus, in the archetype (prakṛti), the origination occurs both in brief and in detail.

Thus, there is an extensive treatment such as "the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood" and "he whose *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira*-wood," and so forth; while the summary is "he whose sacrificial ladles (*sruk*) are of such a form.

Accordingly, just as the origin of the *ājya* offerings occurs in the archetype (*prakṛti*), exactly the same origin occurs in the non-contextual statement (*anārabhyavākya*) such as "he whose [ladle] is made of *parṇa*-wood.
Therefore, this too is an origin belonging to the archetype itself, and thus it pertains to the archetype alone, not to the modification (*vikṛti*).
If it is argued that, therefore, the injunction not being introduced in a specific context applies to the archetype itself,
we say no, because of equality.

The Siddhāntin’s assertion that the origin of subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) occurs in the archetype (*prakṛti*) through both summary and detailed treatment—and therefore the origin of such features as the *juhū* ladle being made of *parṇa* wood is also archetypal—is incorrect;
for the same principle of summary and detailed treatment applies to the origin [of subsidiaries] in the ectype (*vikṛti*) as well.
Indeed, the origin of subsidiary elements in the ectype is likewise stated both summarily and in detail.

Just as in the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice, there is a concise statement: "He offers three oblations," and an elaborate statement: "O gods, you are the support, you are the support" (*āmano 'sy āmano devāḥ*; this is the word-division in the Vedic text). In the same way, the origination of both the primary and the modified forms is characterized by both brevity and elaboration.

Therefore, an injunction not specifically commenced for a particular context (anārabhyavidhi) serves the purpose of both the archetype (prakṛti) and the ectype (vikṛti). However, because of the unity of the injunctive force (codanā) and because of the contradiction with the primary [injunction], it serves the purpose of the archetype alone.
This is the final sūtra of the established conclusion (siddhānta).
Regarding what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) in the sūtra *na codanekārthatvāt* (3.6.15), here is the specific rebuttal:

whatever purpose is served by the injunction (*codanā*) or the enjoining agent (*codaka*), all of that must be carried out in its entirety within the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), and not merely in part.
Thus, the ladle (*juhū*) made of *pālāśa* wood and the *sruva* spoon made of *khadira* wood are both matters that must be brought into the modified sacrifice by means of the injunction.

The *codaka* (the rule of transfer) extends all of those [details], not merely the *juhū* ladle or the *sruva* spoon, such that it would require dependence on a non-contextual (*anārabhya*) injunction for the sake of the *pālāśa* or *khādira* wood.
The *codaka* is capable of extending everything.
Therefore, in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the purpose of obtaining the *pālāśa* wood and so forth does not require dependence on a non-contextual injunction.

Because of the contradiction with the primary [rule]: if the *anārabhyavidhi* were to prescribe the use of *pālāśa* wood and so forth again for the modification (*vikṛti*), while the primary *codaka* (transference rule) is already operative in that modification, there would be a contradiction. This would result in the aforementioned fault of "double-stating" (*dviruktatva*), according to the principle: "Or [it belongs] to the archetype (*prakṛti*), because of the fault of double-statement" (3.6.12).
Therefore, the *codaka* does not depend upon the *anārabhyavidhi*.

Thus, due to the unity of the purpose of the injunction and the resulting contingency of contradicting the primary [rule], the *anārabhyavidhi* applies only to the archetype and not to the modification as well.
In every respect, regarding this curiosity, the word *codanā* appears in the fifth sūtra: "And because there is no single purpose for the injunction" (*na codanekārthyāt*).
In the eighth *prakṛta-sūtra*, the reading is "codakārthaḥ";
however, in the Bhāṣya manuscripts, even in the eighth [sūtra], the reading is indeed "codanā".
Considering that it is appropriate for the same word to be read in both places, we too have not adopted the Kutūhala reading for this eighth sūtra.
However, by the word *codanā*, it is the *codaka* (the model sacrifice) itself that must be understood as the object;
for this very reason, the Vārttika statement, "The *codaka* brings about what has been performed," is consistent.
[As stated in Jaimini Sūtra 12.2.1: "Or rather, it serves all purposes, because its own time is fixed."
This [Prakṛti] has the nature of both original cause (prakṛti) and modification (vikṛti), because it possesses independent origination.
This very point has been described in the section beginning with "Or for all purposes" (*sarvārthe vā*) [Vākyapadīya 3.7.19].
On page 1104, that which he will state as "or for all purposes" (*sarvārthe vā*) will be explained by the phrase "but because it is for the purpose of all purposes" (*sarvārthārthatvāt tu*).
"'And because all objects [of cognition] are mentioned, they belong to another time"—this is a portion of the sūtra 1|3|4|6.
And among all those purposes, some have been assigned to different times,
as in the case of the statement: "These [days] are for the purpose of the sacrifice, beginning with the *āmantraṇa* and ending with the *anujyā*" (Bhāṣya 1.1.3.4–6).
"The maxim that 'all undertakings are indeed obscured by defects, as fire is covered by smoke' is clearly expressed in this statement from the Bhagavad Gītā. (Sāhasrī, 929)
The ritual rules pertaining to bricks (*iṣṭakā-dharma*) are not to be performed in the *agnicayana* (fire-piling) at all *sarvapeṣu* (all-grinding rites). See Saṃkarṣa 2.1.10;
Mīko, p. 31. Regarding the statement "In the *agnicayana*, the ritual rules pertaining to bricks do not apply to *caru* and *sarvapeṣu*," one should consult that specific section (*adhikaraṇa*).
There is no repetition of the striking of all the medicinal herbs at the *agniyana*.
See the section on "At the *agniyana*, there is no repetition of the striking of all the medicinal herbs" in Mīmāṃsākośa, page 53.
The establishment (*ādhāna*) is common to all rituals, and not distinct for each individual ritual.

(1.1.12). For this, see the section under *mīko.* p. 913, "The establishment is [common] to all rituals. The fact that the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices serve the purpose of all desired results is expressed by the texts: "The *darśapūrṇamāsa* [is performed] for all [desires]" and "The *jyotiṣṭoma* [is performed] for all [desires]."

4|3|1| 25–26. See the section on the "Darśapūrṇamāsa-nyāya" at Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2075. This is the principle known as *sarvato balavatī hy anyathānupapattiḥ* (Mīmāṃsākośa 526): "For presumption (*arthāpatti*) is stronger than all [other means of proof]."

Why? If it is argued that "only the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is to be abandoned," we say no; for its falsity is determined by the fact that the negation "not this, not this" (neti neti) would otherwise be inexplicable.

As [Keśava Miśra] says: "When a connection with a description is heard everywhere, even though another word is present, if the injunction has already been transferred elsewhere, there must be a restatement (anuvāda) of what is already known."
Such is the logical principle (*nyāya*).
And because of the scriptural hearing (*śravaṇa*) that "one should sacrifice with Soma," the initial understanding is that "one should perform the sacrifice by means of Soma.
For all [words], according to the principle stated in the *Vākyapadīya* (p. 128), "In every case, there is a connection with a verb," the third case ending is used in the Brāhmaṇa.
The *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra*, p. 63:
"In all cases, it functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to that which has been designated as 'cut' (*chinnasaṃjñe*).
"For in every cognition indeed it is understood as a mental formation (saṃskāra);
and because it is not apprehended therein, there is no subsequent cognition."

Or [as stated in] Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.8.27, page 288: "And in all cases where two things that have already achieved their purpose meet, it would be for the sake of time."—But in all such cases, the *mahāmnāna* chant would be additional, as in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*).
Regarding the Bṛhaspatisava, it is heard in scripture: "He takes up the cup dedicated to Bṛhaspati."
"At the Viṣuvat [day], he draws the Arka cup," it is said; "At the Mahāvrata [day], he draws the Śukra cup," it is said;
"At the Aśvamedha, he draws the two Mahiman cups with the golden and silver vessels," it is said.
In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the cups (*graha*) dedicated to Indra-Vāyu and others are prescribed;

these are extended to the Bṛhaspatisava and other such sacrifices by the rule of transfer (*codaka*). Regarding this, the question arises: do these modified cups set aside the archetypal ones obtained through the rule of transfer, because they are connected with the word "cup" (*graha*), which is a characteristic mark of the archetype? When this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been reached, the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In all cases, such as the Bṛhaspatisava and others, whatever measure of the cups (graha) is prescribed, it should be in addition to those measures obtained from the archetype through the force of the *codaka* (extended application).
The meaning is that there should be a combination (*samuccaya*) of the archetypal and the modified elements,
because both are established by authoritative means— namely, by the *codaka* and by direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śravaṇa*).

"Because it is like the archetype (*prakṛti*). Just as in the archetype, where the injunctions "he takes the *aṃśu* cup" and "he takes the *adābhya* cup"—though not belonging to the context—are combined with those that do belong to the context, so it is here.
Furthermore, because they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the additional elements.

He states another argument for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the combination of the cups dedicated to Bṛhaspati and others with the archetypal cups dedicated to Indra-Vāyu and others, as seen in the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice and similar rites.

In all cases, where there are additional *prākṛta* (archetypal) vessels that are beyond doubt, and where there are additional *surā* vessels for the *soma* vessels— because they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*)— there is indeed a conjunction (*samuccaya*). Thus, the conjunction of the *bārhaspatya* and other vessels with the *aindravāyava* and others is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
And because of the observation of an indicative mark.

Regarding the *bṛhaspatisava* sacrifice, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the modified cups (*graha*), such as those dedicated to Bṛhaspati, with the archetypal cups (*prākṛta-graha*), such as those for Indra-Vāyu. To this, he states another reason: "And because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), there is a combination.

[The text says: "This sacrificial rite of Viṣṇu is indeed one that leads away from the gods; it oversteps the *agnihotra*, it oversteps the *ukthya*, it oversteps the *ṣoḍaśin*, but it does not reach the *atirātra*."
The word *viṣṇu* means "extended," as in the expression “golden [altars],” from which it is understood that they are "extended. If there is indeed a conjunction [of altars], such is their extension.
From this, it is heard that there is a combination (*samuccaya*). [Question: Of what? [Answer: "But everywhere, there is the measure of the cups" (*sarvatra tu grahamāna*, 10.4.21–25).
Here, having taught in the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, "He draws the cup for Bṛhaspati" (*bārhaspatyaṃ gṛhṇāti*), the combination of the cups extended by analogy (*atidiṣṭa*) is stated.

*Bāla.*, p. 177: "In all cases [a word] is etymological (*yaugika*); thus the meaning of a word is expressed. According to this principle (Vārttika on Pāṇini 3.1.16, v. 2, p. 675), the term *pavamāna* is restricted by its etymological derivation (*yoga*) to the agent of the action of purifying (*pavana*). *Kau.*, 1.4.13.3; *Su.*, p. 411: "And the true nature of the deity is understood from the Veda through the name that denotes it."
For contradiction is indeed observed most frequently by way of logic.
And because it is applied everywhere, it is illustrated by this.
Moreover, because of the proximity of the scripture, the contradiction is perfectly clear.

“Or rather: [Taittirīya Saṃhitā] 1.3.6.14, p. 242–243: ‘The “allness” is contingent upon qualification. Regarding the statement of Āpastamba, ‘Having wiped all the sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi), he performs [the rite],’ since this “allness” is an unconsidered qualifier of the object to be enjoined—or even if it were considered—then by the principle of *sarvatva* (allness) and in accordance with another scriptural injunction (*puroḍāśaṃ parvaṇi karoti*), it is established that its scope is restricted to the *puroḍāśa* alone; thus, some have argued that this Śruti lacks authority even after the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*).
That is incorrect.”
Kau. 1.3.6.14, p. 96: "The 'universality' is based on the qualification.

Even setting aside the established status of the word *viśvadeva* as referring to a specific deity, by accepting that the word *viśva* is a synonym for *sarva* (all), one arrives at the scope of all things under discussion according to the maxim "the universality is based on the qualification. Furthermore, by accepting that the word *deva* refers to deities (*devatā*), it is accepted that the ground for the application [of the term] in all three sacrifices is precisely the state of having all the deities—such as those involved in the movement (*gati*) and so forth—under discussion. 1.4.19.14, p. 251: "And their universality would exist because of their qualification."

Regarding the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) consisting of one hundred *kṛṣṇala* seeds, in the context of consuming the remnants, it is revealed in scripture: "He hands over everything to the Brahman priest.

In that case, since those portions belonging to the Brahman are the intended objects by virtue of their entitlement, the totality (*sarvatva*) must be considered; the syntactical construction (*vacanavyakti*) is: "Whatever he hands over to the Brahman, all that [is meant].

However, the distinction between those two is established by the logic of the section concerning "differentiation by a different word" (*śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*).

Just as a sacrifice (*yāga*) is merely the renunciation of one's own ownership (*svatva-tyāga*) for the sake of a deity, whereas a *juhoti* is the casting of a substance over which the sacrificer’s ownership has been directed toward a deity;

And since the connection with the deity is not possible without an act of offering, there must be an offering of the entire [cake] together with its fruit.

For although the status of the *avadāna* (cut-off portion) as the direct means of the oblation is perceptible, whereas that of the *aṣṭākapāla* (the cake on eight potsherds) is inferential, nevertheless, such inference is unavoidable;

Furthermore, because the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is prescribed by its originative injunction and requires a substance for offering, it possesses greater force. Therefore, by virtue of this strength, the statement regarding the cutting off (*avadyati*) must be explained as referring to the means:
"That which he offers in its entirety, that is for the sake of the two portions."

Furthermore, since a sacrifice whose means is the entire *puroḍāśa* cannot be performed by means of a single portion (*avadāna*) without repetition, it follows by implication that it must be repeated, as in the case of the Soma sacrifice. A person must engage in action only when they possess the capacity for its complete performance.

Since the teaching is given for one who is such [capable], just as there is a teaching for the optional *agnihotra* and other rites as they truly are, so too is there a teaching for the obligatory (*nitya*) rites exactly as they are.
Just as there is engagement in the optional rite by one who performs it in its entirety, so it is with the obligatory one as well; such is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Regarding this, various interpretations have been provided in the *Duṣṭīkā* for the phrase "because of the instruction concerning such a state. That is now cited: [The subsequent answer is as follows—] it should be understood that the *Tantraratna* resides within the *Kaṃsa*, while the *Duṣṭīkā* is indicated by the *Kaṃsa*.

1. Just as a sacrifice (*kratu*)—established by such injunctions as "He offers the *agnihotra*"—is rendered complete (free from expectancy), so too the sacrifice, consisting of all its constituent parts (*sarvāṅgīṇa*), is taught both as a duty of the agent (*kartṛdharma*) and by means of the "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) injunction; this is what is meant by the statement, "because of the teaching of that which is thus constituted."

2 (He states the interpretation: Now, just as in the case of an action performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*), the status of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) as the instrument of the process (*bhāvanā*)—which consists of a sequence of prior and posterior stages—is rendered complete by all the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) [and not by only a few], so too is it in the case of the obligatory (*nitya*) action. This is because the principle expressed in *Jaiminisūtra* 1.1.16, "But because the injunction has a single form of expression," applies without distinction to both the optional and the obligatory. Therefore, it is said that "the instruction is of such a nature" (*tathābhūtopadeśāt*); that is, exactly as the optional action is, so too is the obligatory action.

3 (He states another explanation: Alternatively, the rite distinguished by its name (namely, the rite called Darśapūrṇamāsa) is rendered complete in all its requirements by all its constituent parts; as in the case of the optional (kāmya) rite, so too in the obligatory (nitya) one. Why? Because of the grossness of that name. (For if another name were employed, then the obligatory rite would be a different rite from the optional one. Consequently, just as the properties of one sacrifice do not apply to other sacrifices, the properties of the optional rite would not apply [to the obligatory one]. However, it is taught with respect to the occasion [of the new moon] precisely as having that name. Therefore, it has been stated: "Because of such an instruction."

4 (He states another explanation: Alternatively, just as the *itikartavyatā* (the procedure) is [prescribed] in proximity to the optional (*kāmya*) rite, so too is it [prescribed] for the obligatory (*nitya*) rite; since there is no difference in their proximity, it is said "because of such an instruction" (*tathābhūtopadeśāt*).
The meaning is that the proximity of the procedure is equal for both.

5 (He states another explanation: Alternatively, because the causes for the reciprocal conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) [of the factors] in the reflexive voice (*bhāvanā-manepada*) are equal—and because the case endings expressing the reciprocal conjunction found in the names and the verbal form share the same structure as the sentences expressing desires (*kāmyavākya*)—it is said that there is inherently oneness of the ritual action (*karman*).

And when there is oneness of the ritual action, it is logical that the auxiliary properties (*dharma*) should also possess a uniform character; it is not logical for there to be such diversity as having completeness in one instance and deficiency in another. Thus, it is because of the teaching of such a state.

6 (He states another explanation: Alternatively, it has been said that because the human purpose (the subject matter of the Bhāṣya) exists in both cases (the optional and the obligatory), there is instruction regarding such [a purpose].

For if, on the occasion of a specific cause (*nimitta*), one were required to perform merely the action itself without any fruit—since it is understood that the essential nature of the rite is accomplished even without its auxiliary parts (*aṅga*)—then the performance would occur even with deficient auxiliaries, as the fruit would be possible in both instances alike.

And because that [sacrifice] is established through the totality of its constituent parts exactly as they have been heard, it must be performed with all its components; for this performance is heard of as a means to achieve the result, and thus, like an optional (kāmya) rite, there is a requirement to include all auxiliary members even in the case of a mandatory (nitya) rite.
The meaning of the Sūtra is: just as an optional rite is taught for the sake of a specific fruit, so too is the mandatory rite of that very same nature.

Alternatively, it may exist even when only one part [of the auxiliary details] is present; for the purpose of the primary act is accomplished, while the other [details] are merely subordinate, since they exist for the sake of that primary.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether obligatory rites such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa must be performed with all their qualities (saguṇa) and complete, or whether they must be performed somehow according to one's capacity—even if lacking some qualities—the phrase "also" (*api ca*) serves to refute the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it must be performed with all qualities.
Even when there is a deficiency in the knowledge [of the details], the obligatory performance may still take place.
For indeed, when the primary act is performed, there occurs the fulfillment of the purpose— the accomplishment of the result in the form of the absence of transgression—
and this certainly happens in the case of obligatory (*nitya*) ritual action.
However, that which is other than the primary act, namely the collection of subsidiary parts (*aṅga*), is merely a subordinate factor (*guṇa*).
The [subsidiary] is not known [to be the primary], because its purpose is for that [primary], because its purpose is the primary, and because it nourishes the primary.
However, the primary, together with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*), is indeed superior.
If some incapacity arises in the sacrificer, even a deficient [performance] yields the fruit.

Regarding the scope of the term "one part" (*ekadeśa*) of the *sūtra*, the authors of the *Vārttika* have stated: "The word 'entirety' (*kṛtsna*) denotes [the principal act] along with its auxiliary members (*sāṅga*); the word 'one part' is used in relation to the principal act alone. The meaning of that [sūtra] is: "Even when performed with only one part, [the rite is considered] obligatory.
And since there is a fault in the non-performance of that, therefore there must be a distinction from that [other case], because of its connection with the primary [element].

Having stated the established conclusion—that even when an obligatory rite such as the *agnihotra* is performed with the omission of certain subordinate parts due to incapacity, the avoidance of transgression still occurs—the author speaks in order to dispel the following doubt: "If the subordinate parts are not the motivators [of the rite], then the primary element itself would also not be the motivator."
In that case, there would be a fault— consisting of the destruction of the fruit— in the non-performance of that primary act;
therefore, there would be a distinction for one who performs the subsidiaries other than that primary act,
because of the connection of the subsidiaries with the primary.
However, when there is the performance of both the auxiliary and the primary rites, there will certainly be a distinction even regarding the result, namely the avoidance of obstacles.
Nevertheless, in the case of a compulsory rite (*nitya*), there is no fault even if the auxiliaries are omitted due to incapacity;
the primary rite must simply be performed.
The word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) does not appear in the *Kutūhala*.

However, Jaimini [asserts] the non-difference of the ritual action (*karmābheda*), because the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) is one; thus, there would be an instruction for all [auxiliaries].

Regarding the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that in a ritual performed for a specific desire (*kāmya-karman*), there is a necessity for the concomitance of all auxiliary parts (*sarvāṅga-sāhitya-avaśyakatva*), whereas in a compulsory ritual (*nitya*), there is no fault even if some auxiliaries are omitted due to incapacity—the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) raises this objection.
The teacher Jaimini maintains that there is no difference between obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites.
The word "but" (*tu*) serves to set aside the prima facie view.
Because the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) is one—meaning that for both [types of rites] there is only a single injunction of performance.

Because of such similarity, there is a distinction between optional (*kāmya*) and obligatory (*nitya*) rites. [For instance,] the injunctions "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day" and "One should sacrifice with the Amāvāsyā on the new moon day" teach that all [rites], including their auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), are primary (*pradhāna*). Therefore, even in the case of the obligatory, the requirement of being accompanied by auxiliary parts is the same as in the optional.
Thus [it is said].

Even when only one specific purpose is employed, it would occur as in other sacrifices; and although there is a distinction between optional and obligatory rites, the view that all auxiliary parts must be complete is established by the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie argument) in the Sūtra. To this, the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*) replies:
Because the purpose— the primary rite— is distinct from its constituent parts,
due to being separated from them, there would result for even a single, isolated, and deficient primary rite, when performed as an obligatory duty, a fruit consisting in the absence of transgression,
just as it occurs in other sacrifices, both archetypal (*prakṛti*) and modified (*vikṛti*).
Just as there is no transgression when a modification (*vikṛti*) is not performed once the archetype (*prakṛti*) has been completed, so too it is in this case.

Therefore, regarding obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*), there is no rule requiring the performance of all constituent parts (*sarvāṅga*). Furthermore, because completion is observed even when there is a failure in the injunctions.
In the Siddhānta, he states another reason:
the word "ca" (and) is redundant.

Even when there is a transgression of the injunction—that is, even when the prescribed act is not performed due to incapacity or other reasons—even in the case of a transgression of the injunction consisting of the spilling of the Agnihotra substance, completion is observed. This shows that completion occurs even when there is a deficiency, as indicated by the statement: "That very [act] is to be offered, however it may be, and in whatever manner."
Therefore, there is no fault even if there is a deficiency in the obligatory rite (*nityakarman*),
because of the prescription of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
He states another reason for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
The term "vidhyaparādhe" (in the case of a transgression of an injunction) is carried over from the preceding sūtra.
The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate another reason.

Because expiations (*prāyaścitta*) are prescribed for transgressions of injunctions—such as "one offers an oblation when [the vessel] is broken" and "one offers an oblation when [the grain] has spilled"—it follows by this indicative mark (*liṅga*) that there is no fault even if there is deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) in an obligatory rite (*nitya-karman*).

If [the rite] were indeed defective and fruitless, what need would there be for its constituent parts? Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the performance of even defective obligatory rites (nitya-karma) must be carried out. This is the section concerning "all-capacity" (sarvaśakti).
Eligibility (adhikāra) for optional rites (kāmya) belongs only to one who is capable of performing all the constituent parts.
In rites performed for specific desires, all the constituent parts must be carried out in their entirety.

Otherwise, a general term would have to be restricted to a specific case without any [stated] qualification.

[The ritual act] is one and the same, as evidenced by all the recensional branches (*śākhā*).

The Discourse on Omniscience (Sarvajñatāvāda) 4216: The Meaning of the Discourse on Omniscience.
An entity (*bhāva*)—such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth—is non-existent precisely within that which is its own continuum (*saṃtama*).

For it proceeds toward an action that produces a different characteristic, namely one that has fallen away from it or is its opposite; thus, there would be the realization of opposition in the form of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthiti*).
And thus, it has been stated that there is no absolute non-existence of omniscience even when it exists;
nor is the latter [alternative] tenable.

For indeed, omniscience does not enter the path of cognition as something devoid of existence and so forth, nor do existence and so forth enter the path of cognition as something devoid of it, like the categories of being and non-being.
And it has been stated that there is no pervasion of those [beings] by omniscience.
This might be so:
in the composition of this treatise, there is a sublation of the vision of the reality of all things.

For instance: instruction is the source of conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*), and since conceptual cognition is false by virtue of having superimposed objects as its domain, the cognition of a Tathāgata cannot be of that nature.

Therefore, this instruction is the effect of a conceptual-cognition-involving-superimposition that is opposed to the cognition of reality regarding all objects to be negated; thus, by the observation of a contrary effect, the proof for the absence of omniscience in [the Buddha]—such as his intellect and so forth—is established.

Alternatively, if there were no instruction, its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be in vain; or else, if one accepts that the injunctions for such acts as bowing to a shrine (*caityavandana*) are not heard from him merely because of his proximity, there would be a lack of confidence [in his authority].
In this regard, because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is in contradiction with all [true] consciousness,
conceptual construction is indeed twofold: that which is based on error (*viparyāsa*) and that which is not previously established.
In that regard, because he is not preceded by error (*viparyāsa*), he is one who possesses all-knowledge (*sarvavedin*) and exists as such from the very beginning.

Indeed, he is neither deluded nor possessed of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); rather, having fully understood the entire expanse of the reality of all things, his mind is independent of the faults of the [defiled] moments, and he desires to teach out of compassion.

Since that [teaching] would be impossible without speech, and since speech is not possible without conceptual construction, he employs it even while knowing its lack of ultimate reality (*atāttvikatva*).

Just as one who knows the reality of selflessness (*nairātmya-tattva*) negates superimposed conceptual constructions, saying "this has no self," or just as the preeminent grammarian, though knowing that words such as *gāvī* and others are incorrect, does not become a user of corrupt speech when employing them with the intention of instructing ordinary people— so too, this assumed form is not ultimately real; thus, for one who knows the truth, there is no contradiction with the teaching.
Nor does it belong to one possessed of passion and so forth;
for indeed, compassion does not fall within the category of passion.
"May I be extinguished" and "may the suffering of others be removed"—this is precisely passion.
Not so;
for passion (*rāga*) is not mere desire, but rather it is the defilement of the mind, an obscuration to vision consisting in the delighting in unreal qualities, which arises from passion.
Indeed, no one who is overwhelmed by thirst for their own self-interest acts while possessing the vision of a permanent self.

For just as Caitra, observing Maitra who is distinct from himself and being overwhelmed by a thirst for his own pleasure, does not strive for the pleasure of Maitra; so too, one who directly observes the self as mere consciousness—distinct in each preceding and succeeding moment—engages in actions that produce benefit characterized by qualities other than those [moments] and their opposites, and engages while being overwhelmed by a thirst for his own purpose. Therefore we understand: he certainly understands "I am this," even though he is distinct [from moment to moment], through the unity of the moments of his own mind.
This innate non-perception of a self (*ātman*) is the primary cause of passion and the other afflictions.
As it is said: "May I be happy, and may I not suffer"—the very notion of "I" that arises in one who desires such [states] is the innate perception of a sentient being (*sattva*).

Furthermore, even the compassion of an omniscient one, which takes the form "I shall benefit others," is not a constituent part of the perception of a sentient being, because it proceeds toward the self through the desire for its own fruit.
The meaning of the discourse on omniscience: the meaning of the discourse on omniscience [is established] through dependence upon form and so forth.

The mind (*manas*) is not a faculty of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is not observed [to function] with respect to pleasure and so forth [i.e., because no prior cognition having those as its objects is observed].
(Thus, first of all, even though the internal [objects] are its domain, the dependence of the mind upon specific auxiliary factors has been established.)

Now, preceded by deliberation, he determines that dependence (*pāratantrya*) consists precisely in being an object of the sense-faculties: "Furthermore, let there be dependence either due to the restriction of objects or due to the requirement of specific auxiliary factors" (deliberation). Dependence is logical (for it is logical that the mind proceeds toward whatever is the object of a particular sense-faculty, being dependent upon that very faculty), because we observe it to be so in the case of recollection.

Furthermore, one who asserts that the instrument of mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) has as its object a [sensation] of the same class (*tulyajātīya*) produced by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) cannot, at the outset, claim that they are of the same class simply because they are apprehended by the same sense organ; for this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Thus he says: "And if [sensations] of the same class were admitted to be apprehended by the same sense organ, there would be the consequence of perceiving other colors [simultaneously]. For instance, a visual mental perception of yellow would also operate toward blue, even though [blue] is not in contact with the eye, since the fitness for being apprehended by that sense organ is indistinguishable in both cases."

If, however, one considers [the cognition] to depend on a different birth in another existence (*bhavāntara-jāti*), then there would follow the consequence of it belonging to a different continuum (*bhinnasaṃtānāpāta*). [That is to say:

a clear mental [cognition] would arise having as its object a blue thing produced within a single continuum, even though its object is a blue thing produced within another continuum not in contact with the sense faculty; for there is no difference in the genus (*jāti*) between those two internal continua.

(He concludes: Therefore, by one who asserts that the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyayatā*) exists at the cessation of a single continuum, it is effectively stated that [the mental cognition] grasps the objects of the eye and other senses, because there is the manifestation of the distinction between moments (*kṣaṇaviveka*).

(Now, one might object: "Granted that the difference between moments does not appear, but from what source is their non-difference known? To this he says: Because of the appearance of non-difference—for the venerable intuition, as it were, in the form "this is that same crystal," will establish the crystal as non-different. (Anticipating the objection that those who perceive only the immediate range, being ignorant, determine "this very pillar" and so forth with respect to moments characterized by a continuous succession of similar arisings—moments which, at their end, undergo differentiation—he says: Because of the rejection of momentariness.

Moreover, since there is no perception of form and so forth when the eyes and other [faculties] are absent, even when the mind is impaired, it is determined that [perception] arises from both [the mind and the senses]. [The opponent] objects:

"If it is argued that because the capacity of the sense-faculties is established in the very first moment, and because [perception] occurs in the second moment, the fact that [objects] are cognized by the mind alone (*kevala-manovedyatā*) is inferred.
[The author] refutes this: No, for in that case there is no reason for the capacity of the eyes and other faculties to have ceased.

And because that cognition is seen to be continuous. (Now, one might object: "In recollection, the mind operates independently alone, since even the blind and others are observed to have recollections of form and so forth. To this he says: In recollection, however, the dependence [of the mind] is indeed perceived, because its object is something already apprehended by another means of knowledge.

(Nor is the mind independent in inference and the like; to this he says: In inference and the like, there is dependence because there is no cognition in the absence of a mark (*liṅga*). Thus, in no case does the mind operate directly and independently with respect to an immediately preceding [object]; therefore, the internal [object] alone—such as pleasure and so forth—is the direct object.

In that very [state], one should experience the direct manifestation of reality (*itthya*) as it is conceived, not regarding external objects. (Now, if it is argued: "Granted that sensory and mental perception may not be all-encompassing, let there be a perception consisting of creative contemplation (*bhāvanāmaya*)," to this he replies: Knowledge consisting of creative contemplation is not an independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is dependent on scripture and inference—just like an inference concerning what has already occurred—since contemplation cannot arise spontaneously and because it conforms to the objectivity of a prior cognition (i.e., its being based on what has already been known). Thus, it is dependent and lacks the status of a *pramāṇa*.

(Now, someone with a scent of Prabhākara-ism objects to the established refutation: But surely there is no restriction by time regarding faith and the like [in the case of "this is silver"], because there is no perception of a silver that is not present.

For there is no perception of mother-of-pearl and the like [as silver], because a consciousness having one form cannot have another thing as its object (for if that were possible, there would be no restriction regarding what constitutes an object); and because [consciousness] would lack a basis (for if a consciousness having one form were to have another thing as its object, then since consciousness would deviate from its own object, the undesirable consequence of universal nihilism would follow; thus, no prudent person would ever act toward anything or refrain from anything; therefore, [the cognition] must indeed have silver as its object).
[Now, he objects to the claim that] "the mind is dependent on the external" [in the case of dreams]: "And the mind has attained independence in dreams."

Furthermore, dream-cognition is not memory, because it does not possess the nature of that [memory]. For the nature of memory is the non-forgetting of an experienced object; and this "non-forgetting" consists in the mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*) of the experience as something previously experienced.
Dream-cognition is not of such a kind.
Thus, it is established that the mind is independent with respect to external objects.
[The author] refutes this view of those who smell like Prabhākara (the Prābhākaras): "This is not sound;
for, the dependence on an object is useless, as the cognition of another form is equally [unaccountable]."

For embodied beings, even though memory is clear in a dream, it appears as a present object such as mother-of-pearl and the like because of the absence of the eyes and other sense organs; this is because [the cognition] depends upon them. Otherwise, if it did not depend on the mother-of-pearl and so forth, that proximity would be useless, since the perception of silver would occur even in the absence of that object.
And as for what was said [regarding] the meaning of the doctrine of omniscience:
the meaning of the doctrine of omniscience.

[The opponent claims: "Cognition has no other object [than the present]. To this, he replies: If the appearance of silver does not have the mother-of-pearl as its object, then the appearance of the present likewise would not have the present as its domain.

[He says: By virtue of a defect, even that which is not present is perceived as being present; thus, the appearance of the present for the entire universe—which actually has the non-present as its domain—occurs through defect.
This is the same for the other case as well: the appearance of silver even when the object is mother-of-pearl is exactly the same.

Having thus stated that they are similar in their initial appearance, he states the distinction of his own position: In the present mother-of-pearl shell (*śukti-śakala*), there is the manifestation of non-present silver; it is not the case that in non-present silver there is the manifestation of the present.

(This is because the cognition "this is silver" has as its object something remote from itself, and not an object that is past. This is because the proximity of the object must be fruitful! Furthermore, the negation of what was previously apprehended is logically possible in the form "this is not silver. (By pointing with a finger, people negate the very piece of mother-of-pearl as being silver, and thus contradict themselves.)
In that case, it is understood that silver was previously apprehended by a prior cognition;
however, the cognition of a mass of hair by one suffering from ophthalmia occurs with respect to light and so forth. Thus, this deviation does not depend upon the perspective of an ordinary person.

(Regarding what was stated—that the mind, having attained independence, exists externally during the state of dreaming—he reflects upon this and asserts his own position: In the case of a dream, is it the memory that possesses the appearance of being present, or is it the independence of the mind [in that state]? Upon such reflection, it is logical that the memory possesses the appearance of being present, because there is a clear memory of what was experienced on the immediately preceding day, which is complete and without addition. [Note: In place of "avikalā... smṛteḥ," the Kaṇikā commentary reads: "even though there is a clear memory of something additional to the conceptualization."]
The root text alone is indeed correct: [the mind's independence regarding external objects] is not tenable due to being overwhelmed by the defect of non-perception as if it were present.
Nor is there an excess of capacity arising from defects (by which the mind might independently produce knowledge of reality regarding external objects).

"But due to error, [it arises] from the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) alone," because that [mental formation] is the cause for removing the defect (the word "that" refers by implication to the capacity).

[Objection: But surely there are some dream-visions that are real; therefore, one must admit the independence of the mind in those cases. [To this, he says: As for the vision of a true dream, it is possible if it is a perception of something present in that manner. [Objection: It is observed that upon waking, there is a correspondence with the objects described in the dream. [He refutes this: No, because there is an absence of correspondence with the description.
The correspondence with the narrative, however, is merely a coincidence (*kākatālīya*).

How can the perception of future events as if they were present be true? (The objector says: Let it not be true; at least there is independence of the mind (since the latent impression [of the future] is impossible). (The respondent states his own view: Even that is the recollection of something previously experienced elsewhere of that same kind.

(For nothing that has been experienced in every respect is perceived in a dream; rather, there is the possibility of a delusion consisting in the non-experience of [objects] that have arisen at some time, in some way, and in mutual contradiction with one another.
Otherwise, one would have to postulate an unseen capacity (*adṛṣṭasāmarthya*) for the mind (which leads to the fallacy of over-extension).

If it is a specific merit (*dharmaviśeṣa*) [that is the cause], then [if it were the cause for the experience of pleasure in a dream, it would follow that] it is a cognition of things as they truly are (*yathārthadarśana*).

Because an unseen capacity (*adṛṣṭasāmarthya*) would have to be postulated for that specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*)—which consists in the mind’s independence—with respect to its effect [recollection], there follows the undesirable consequence of such a postulation.

And if dream-cognition is not memory, then it is not even a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because there is no external object to be grasped [if dream-cognition were not memory, it would lack validity as experience].
If this is argued, we say: no, because there is no external object to be grasped, and thus no validity.

(He provides the answer to the objection beginning with "yadi ca" [and if...]: In that case, the mind is not independent with respect to external objects; for in a dream, such [an object] is ungraspable, or if it is graspable, it is the grasping of what was previously experienced, as that is how it is observed. It is not due to a defect, nor is it a result of an excess of power from the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*); thus, in both cases (whether the external is graspable or ungraspable), the mind is not independent regarding the external.

By this same method—[in the printed version there is no *avagraha*]—which demonstrates the path of the thread [of reasoning], the view that the perception of hair and such by one suffering from ophthalmia (*timira*) is mental (*mānasa*) is refuted; for that cognition has particles of light as its objective support (*ālambana*), and it is caused by a defective eye.

[Now, he refutes the Naiyāyika position that the entire universe is the object of the yogi’s cognition: In the world, the certainty of an appearance arises from a semblance of a logical mark (*liṅgyābhāsa*). One who possesses complete knowledge [perceives] everything; there is no one at all who perceives the full when it is incomplete.

Even if it is argued that, because there is no dependence on sense organs (*akṣa*) or inferential marks (*liṅga*) in the intuition "my brother will come," the mind is seen to be independent and external; and if it is further argued that everything—whether as "all" or by means of categories such as existent and non-existent, substance and so forth, or through distinctions such as primordial matter (*prakṛti*), spirit (*puruṣa*), or the aggregates (*skandhas*)—is the object of the mind according to worldly means of valid cognition (that is, the object of supramundane perception characterized by a vivid appearance consisting of meditative cultivation)—even so, this independence of the mind with respect to external objects is unproven. To this, it is replied: [The text continues: ...In this regard, it is said: "Just as in the case of a dream, the mind appears as an object even without external things, so too in the waking state, the mind appears as an object even without external things. Furthermore, since the mind is observed to appear as various forms such as blue, yellow, long, short, male, female, and so forth, and since these forms do not exist externally, the mind itself appears in those forms. Moreover, since the mind is observed to appear as the forms of mountains, forests, and the like, and since these forms do not exist externally, the mind itself appears in those forms. Also, since the mind is observed to appear as the forms of pleasure, pain, desire, hatred, and so forth, and since these forms do not exist externally, the mind itself appears in those forms. Furthermore, since the mind is observed to appear as the forms of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and since these forms do not exist externally, the mind itself appears in those forms. And since the mind is observed to appear as the forms of the five elements (*pañcabhūta*), and since these forms do not exist externally, the mind itself appears in those forms. Thus, because the mind is observed to appear as all these various forms, and because these forms do not exist externally, the mind itself appears in those forms. Therefore, the mind is indeed independent and external. This is established by the following inference: "The mind is independent and external, because it appears as various forms, just like a dream. To this, it is replied: "That is not so. Because the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For example, just as in a dream the mind appears as an object even without external things, so too in the waking state the mind appears as an object even without external things. Furthermore, because the mind is observed to appear as various forms such as blue, yellow, long, short, male, female, and so forth, and because these forms do not exist externally, the mind itself appears in those forms. Also, because the mind is observed to appear as the forms of mountains, forests, and the like, and because these forms do not exist externally, the mind itself appears in those forms.
