First, regarding supramundane eloquence (*pratibhāna*), since it is a subject of dispute in terms of its existence, the mind does not possess independence therein; its nature must be realized through direct penetration (*pratyakṣa*).

Mundane eloquence, however, which expresses what is pleasant or unpleasant, is not characterized by independent mental clarity, because it generally arises from fallacious signs (*liṅgābhāsa*) such as the appearance of concomitance, exclusion, or affirmation. For this very reason, it is non-conclusive in nature; thus they designate it: "Such is eloquence, but it is not certainty."

Because it touches upon both alternatives, it is not of the nature of doubt—[the printed root text reads *saṃsparśitvāt tulyatvācca*; however, we have adopted the reading found in the Kaṇikā commentary]. Rather, it is merely a flash of intuition (*pratibhā*); therefore, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because its result is non-conclusive and because it lacks the certainty that depends upon a valid means of knowledge.

(He concludes: Thus, because it belongs to the same class as [fallacious] logical marks and the like (i.e., because it depends on fallacious logical marks), there too exists dependence [of the mind] (even in the case of intuition, the mind is dependent).

Otherwise, if the connection with external objects were established by the mind alone without depending on those [marks], then for everyone, everything would exist everywhere at all times (i.e., everyone would be everything).

If it is argued that there is no over-extension of the principle because the mind (*manas*) is independent with respect to external objects due to a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*), such that it perceives only for someone at a certain time, the author replies: Even if an object exists externally, the mind—dependent upon the sense organs, inferential signs, and so forth—perceives only by engaging the eye and other senses for a particular person. This is because the mind itself is conditioned by that very same specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*). Furthermore, since the mind would otherwise be capable of apprehending all forms and other objects, its existence would be redundant; for if the mind were the agent independently, the action of discerning forms and so forth would be accomplished by the specific unseen force alone, rendering the mind a non-instrumental agent. Thus, the mind's independence regarding external objects is untenable.

Furthermore, even if an object is unseen, it certainly does not accomplish its purpose without a means; for that reason, the external operation of the mind is dependent upon the senses, marks, and so forth, rather than being autonomous.

For this very reason, mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) does not occur with respect to all objects arising from yoga-born dharma (*yogaja-dharma*), because the establishment of [external] objective perception requires the means of sense-object contact (*saṃnikarṣa*). This is because you, who advocate for yoga-born dharma, do not admit the relation of "conjunction-with-the-conjoined" (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving objects obstructed by walls and the like; for [if that were so], everyone—including people such as ourselves—would perceive everything.
Furthermore, [this being the case], inference too would lapse into being perception, since inference is impossible regarding things that are unmanifest or extremely distant.

For this very reason, there is no "conjunction" (*saṃnikarṣa*)—defined as the mutual coexistence [of the sense organ and the object] directed toward the production of knowledge—between the sense organ and the object. This is because past and future objects do not exist even at that time (the moment of cognition); otherwise, it would follow that one could perceive obstructed objects, and it would result in inference and other means of knowledge being classified as perception. Furthermore, this is necessary for the purpose of including conjunction within the definition of perception.

Now, an objection is raised: since past and future objects are known through their specific locations and other attributes—as in the cognition "this king was [or will be] such-and-such on this earth"—and since that cognition (of the object) and its specific location serve as the objective support (*ālambana*), there is a possibility of sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) between the eye or the mind and those [locations and so forth]. Furthermore, because those [locations and so forth] exist and are present, the status of sensory-object contact is unimpeded for the cognition of what has not yet arisen or what has already passed.
(The underlying sense is that even if the specific character is not manifested, it still serves as the objective referent.)

Furthermore, if the definition of inference and so forth is "knowledge produced by the contact of a sense organ with its object," then inference and the like would not be [distinct] realities. [This is because] there is no capacity for formulating separate definitions for inference and so on; and in the absence of such definitions, the definition of perception would simply be "that which is produced by the contact of a sense organ with its object. [The author] refutes this: if, first of all, any object whatsoever [is perceived], and knowledge [arising] from the contact of a sense organ with that [object] is perception, then it follows that memory would also be perception.

(He raises an objection: "Now, [if] the object of cognition (*prameya*) [is] location and so forth, (he refutes it: let there be perception of the mere location and so forth due to contact with that alone, but not of the qualifier. (He raises another objection: "If it is argued that because the cognition of the qualified (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) is perceptual, the qualifier is also perceptual by implication of that [cognition]. (He refutes it: No, because there is no contact with that [qualifier], which—unlike the qualified—is not present before the senses. For when the qualifier is absent, [the cognition] does not occur even though it pertains to the qualified.

Because it would follow that everything is such [i.e., present]. (If there is no distinction between the absence of a specific property and the lack of presence, then) when the mother has passed away, why is it said, "Yajñadatta is the son of Devadatta"? (He asks this with a hidden intention to resolve the difficulty: What is the point here? (The questioner asks: How so? (The respondent says: At that time, he does not enter into linguistic usage as a qualified entity (i.e., as "the son of Devadatta"), because that which is not present is unfit for linguistic usage.
The respondent says: "If, then, that which is not present is unfit for conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), then Devadatta too would be unfit for conventional usage as a qualifier.

The objector says: "But there is conventional usage by means of the qualifier 'having previously existed' (*bhūtapūrva*). The respondent says: "By such a state of being qualified [by a past occurrence], the conventional usage is not barred, even though it has passed away.
However, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), this is not so."
This is the definition of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

As for an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), however, the distinction between these two—the qualifier and the indicator—is based solely on proximity and non-proximity: because the particular (*viśeṣa*)—which is distinct in form (the *svalakṣaṇa* possessing a specific configuration)—is not present [in the case of an indicator], since it does not possess the configuration of the intended object.
Therefore, when the qualifier is not in contact [with the senses], the qualified object is not in contact.

Furthermore, if the qualifier must also be an object of cognition (*prameya*)—just as universals (*jāti*) and other categories are objects of cognition—for the sake of establishing the qualified object as an object of cognition, then it follows that even a cognition whose object is not in contact would be perception (since there is no contact with the qualifier therein); yet such a thing is not possible.
Because it lacks the definition [of perception as stated by the Naiyāyikas] (i.e., because it lacks the definition of perception as stated by the Naiyāyikas).

[Objection: Let there be no definition; since it is produced merely from the sense-object contact with the substantive (*viśeṣya*), and perception is indeed admitted [to exist] due to its clarity (*vaiśadya*). To this, he says: "Because the sense organ depends upon the object. [Objection:

Now, let the particular place alone be the object of cognition (*prameya*) and not its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); thus, there is no lack of that definition (i.e., no lack of the definition of perception), because there is contact with that which is being sought.

(Answer: In that case, there would be no non-apprehension of place and so forth by one who meditates through ignorance, nor would there be the vision of things as unarisen and so on. [“In that case, there would be no non-apprehension of place and so forth by means of knowledge, nor would there be the vision of things as unarisen” — this is the reading of the *Kaṇikā* commentary. If it is admitted that perceptual knowledge arises—due to contact with a single part of the object of cognition—with respect to the entire universe existing in the present (insofar as it has somehow become a qualifier), then everyone would be a seer of everything, since it is possible for anything to serve as a qualifier in some way for something in contact with the senses.

Even though the definition of inference is absent, there is the undesirable consequence of [such a cognition] being perception when there is a recollection of an object currently present through perception. (That is to say: when the definition of perception is established as applying to an object not excluded by the definition of inference, then, upon seeing some similar object such as a *gavaya* in a perceptual situation, because of the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), there is the recollection of another similar existing object such as a cow; thus, there is the undesirable consequence of this being perception. (The opponent objects: "In that case, the latent impression is the cause, not the existence of the object, because [recollection occurs] even when the object is non-existent.
(The reply: "The same applies to the other case as well."
Because the dharma born of yoga (*yogajadharma*) is the cause [of yogic perception] independently of the existence of an object;

for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the employment of an object therein, since it is accepted that yogic perception arises in all cases—whether the object is present or absent, concealed or unconcealed, and whether it is occurring or not occurring.

By stating that "there is apprehension of the present place and so forth in the absence of a [specific] mark," the convergence (*saṃplava*) would be rejected. (That is, by you, the objector, the convergence of means of valid cognition—whereby the cognition of a single object of knowledge such as the Self is shown to occur through one, two, or many means of valid cognition—would be rejected; thus there would be a contradiction with the *Bhāṣya*.
Furthermore, what was proposed [as a solution] would be abandoned.)

(He raises an objection: "If it is argued that [the definition of perception] has not been abandoned because the absence of the mark (*liṅga*) and so forth is excluded by the phrase 'because of sublation by inference and the like' (since the definition of perception also functions as such a sublation), [the author] refutes this: the explanation of the word *anyathānupapatti* (found in the *Bhāṣya*) for the purpose of excluding verbal testimony would be improper. Furthermore, the acceptance of six kinds of sense-object contact and the mention of the 'grasping by the sense organ' (as found in the *Nyāyasūtra*: 'perception is the contact of the five senses with their objects') would be contradicted, since these were stated in the *Sūtra* and *Bhāṣya* for the purpose of excluding inference and the rest."
Therefore, the mind (when directed outwardly) is dependent upon the senses, inferential signs, and so forth.

Furthermore, if everything were complete [in its nature], it would fall within the scope of worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and if even one who operates with worldly means of valid cognition possessed complete knowledge, there would be no distinction between such a person and one who is considered to possess supramundane knowledge. [The opponent] objects: "If the distinction lies in the fact that supramundane knowledge has a clear manifestation (*spaṣṭāvabhāsa*)."
[He] refutes [this]: "In that case—when everything has been fully grasped—there is no utility for that [clear manifestation].

[The opponent] objects: "If [it is argued that] certainty (*niścaya*) is the specific feature arising through supramundane [cognition], and not through mundane [cognition]; [the author] refutes this: That [certainty] is equal [in function] for the other [mundane cognition] as well, insofar as it possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)."

(He raises an objection: For one who perceives through direct perception (*pratyakṣadarśana*)—that is, for one who perceives all objects directly (*sarvārthapratyakṣadarśin*)—there is a lack of expectancy regarding all objects because every form of valid cognition (*pramiti*) culminates in direct perception. This is even more so for another person (an ordinary worldly person who perceives all objects directly by means of another instrument of knowledge).

(He refutes this: Even if that [knowledge] were complete without being perceived [by another], then what measured by another instrument of knowledge would it expect? Indeed, there is no expectation of another instrument of knowledge [for such a person], because for one possessing extraordinary knowledge (*alaukikajñānavat*), every object of knowledge (*prameya*) is already established.

If it is argued that even in this case, because the object of knowledge (*prameya*) perishes very quickly, there would be a further requirement for another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish that object once again—[we reply: no, because that [object] has already been established repeatedly by the previous [knowledge born of yoga], and there is no reason to require the establishment of what is already established. If, however, the existence of other means were desired on account of the diverse dispositions of those who seek to understand, then there would only be a desire for other means; there would not be a desire for other objects of knowledge. Furthermore, if a particular pleasure were sought through another means, that [pleasure] is already established by the observation of the previous means of knowledge; thus, another means of knowledge would be useless.

Furthermore, because other means [of knowledge] exist, even that which has been seen by one's own direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) may be investigated by others [through means such as inference (*anumāna*)], for this cognizer possesses diverse intentions; [it is not the case that] all valid cognition culminates in direct perception.

If it is argued that the distinction lies in the fact that direct perception consists of the ascertainment of particulars, whereas inference and the like—which are non-ascertaining due to their fallibility—are different, then this too is refuted, because there is no fallibility in inference and the like when they are established according to their aforementioned definitions.
However, the deviation of the appearance is equally present even in the case of perception.

[The author] states the subsequent refutation of the gross [object]: "In that case, the expectancy arises precisely because [the object] is not cognized; for that which is deviant—and therefore of an uncertain nature—is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). [Objection: Perception is capable of [producing] a means of knowledge due to its proximity [to the object] (because it is present), whereas inference and the like are not [so capable], since they have as their domain objects that are remote in space and time.

[The opponent] objects: "In that case, [the senses] would require movement and so forth for the sake of contact (*saṃnikarṣa*), but not as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the [resultant] cognition (*pramā*) is already established through inference alone. [To this, he replies:
"Furthermore, in the production of a cognition, contact is the cause of the means of cognition and so forth;
and what is under discussion here is extraordinary perception (*alaukika-pratyakṣa*)."
[He] refutes [the opponent's view]: it would follow that the cognition of a universal (sāmānya) is perceptual.
If it should be thought that the manifestation in the form of experience has as its nature that which is proximate and present;

And it is not the case that the universal (*sāmānya*) is unreal, nor that it is non-proximate or non-present; for such [a universal] is perceived by yogins who have ascended to certain stages (*katipayabhūmikā*), as well as by Tathāgatas who have reached the tenth stage (*daśamabhūmikā*) regarding all objects.
[The author] refutes this: that is incorrect, because the previously mentioned fault remains unaddressed.

(Although the universal exists as something unconnected precisely because it is not ultimately real, nevertheless, since it appears in that manner, its apprehension would result in being a case of perception due to the operation of the form of experience; thus, the aforementioned defect is incurred.

(Regarding this very point, another refutation is stated prior to the eighteenth verse: Furthermore, because one perceives things as they are—even when they are present, past, or future—[the reading "because one perceives them as they are not" seems more appropriate], the cognition of the present would be nothing but false knowledge, just like the perception of those [past and future] things.

But perception does not consist of [the mere appearance of] clouds; its defining characteristic is that it is produced by the capacity of the sense-faculty and the object. Otherwise, for what reason would the vision of hair and the like caused by the impairment of cataracts and so forth not be accepted as perception? [Because it lacks clarity. (The Proponent of Representationalism [Sākāravādin] objects: All perception indeed has an unconnected appearance. The conjunction with the object occurs through a causal relationship [and not here according to a one-to-one correspondence], because there is a difference in time.

(The proponent of the critique, with a hidden intention, asks: "What is it that shines forth? (The challenger says: "It is the form of cognition (*jñānākāra*), [referring to] blue and so on located in a proximate space and time.
(The wise one reveals his intention: "For at this moment, there exists no one who perceives directly the nature of objects in all places.

(The challenger, who perceives all objects directly, objects: "Since worldly practice is observed precisely through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the experience of an object within the form of cognition, there is no loss of the perception of the object."
(He refutes this: How can there be a determination of something else in the absence of cognition (i.e., in the absence of a cognition possessing a form)?
(The opponent says: It is the determination of an external cognition.
(The challenger asks: Because it has ceased; for ignorance—characterized by the habitual attachment to grasping objects—is beginningless. (This is a genitive case.)

(He refutes [the opponent] with derision: "In that case, may there be well-being for 'omniscience,' which is but a severe delusion caused by excessive ignorance! It would be better to have merely 'partial vision'—that is, that in which ignorance is minimal.

Moreover, even according to your own technical definition, perception would occur only with respect to a single part [of the object], based on the principle that 'the state of being an object of cognition' is itself the cause capable of imparting its form to the cognition; it cannot be so with respect to everything, because that [totality] is not a cause, owing to its non-proximity either spatially or temporally."
Otherwise, [if it were a cause] even in the absence of proximity, it would follow that everyone—even those such as ourselves—would be all-knowing.

(An alternative explanation of the first half [of the verse]: Or else, is cognition merely a response to a present object, or does it also take the form of the past and the future? In the former case, because everything is not of such a nature, [cognition] would be false.
In the latter case, because it functions by conceptualizing forms such as the past and so forth, it is not perception [since perception is defined as being free from conceptual construction].

However, as for the one who thinks: "Let it be that perception has only the present as its object; nevertheless, it has all things as its object because even the past and future are present by virtue of their being past and future," in order to refute that, he states another explanation of the meaning of the eighteenth verse: "Or else, everything would be known either at the time of the cognition by assuming a different state [than it actually has], or as it exists [in its own state] (meaning: whatever is in a certain state, it is known as such). In the former case (the first position), there is falsity (because of apprehending what is in one state as being otherwise)."
In the latter case, not everything is perceptible, because other states cannot be perceived.
(He explains the second half [of the verse]: Furthermore, it is not possible to comprehend everything sequentially, due to its infinity.
For there is no finality in the arising of the knowable, which is devoid of prior and posterior limits.

Even in the case of eternal things such as atoms, which possess a fixed form, there is no determinate limit; how much more so, then, for that which has an unfixed form? Therefore, it is not [perceived] simultaneously, precisely because of infinity.
Furthermore, if the limit were undetermined, there would be no distinction between the cognition of the whole and the cognition of a single part.
[The opponent objects: "But even if the limit is undetermined, one perceives the entirety of its form simultaneously."
(He refutes this: This is not sound.

For when the exact extent [of a thing] is not determined, neither the whole nor a part is determined, because there is no exclusion of the others (that is, because there is no exclusion of the other parts when only the limited form of one part is grasped).
By this much, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is shown.
And since a superior degree of knowledge is perceived, it follows that in some cases it reaches its ultimate limit and has all things as its object.

(The answer is stated: It is said: "Even if a limit exists—granting it may be supreme—because it is impossible [for it to exist] in the case of produced substances, and because there is no exclusivity regarding qualities such as heaviness (*garima*) and so forth."

(Refutation by way of an alternative: Suppose that which beyond which there is nothing is the ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhā*); let it be so. However, in that case, the establishment of [the self] as having all things as its object (*sarvaviṣayatva*) does not follow.
Rather, it would have only a vast range of objects (*bhūyiṣṭhaviṣayatva*).
Just as a clay sphere, in relation to other clays (or in relation to mountains), occupies a much larger space of ether, yet lacks omnipresence (*sarvavyāpitā*).
(He anticipates another objection: "Now, that beyond which nothing further can be conceived is the ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhā*).
(The author refutes this: There is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of produced substances (*kāryadravya*).

For even jars and the like—[referring to *kuṭa*, *kumbha*, and *maṇika* according to the *Kaṇikā* commentary]—do not surpass one another in terms of dimension (*parimāṇa*) such that no further state is possible; for otherwise, it would follow that there is no room for anything else, since [according to your view] all space would be pervaded by a single substance.

If it is argued that the qualification "being a quality" (*guṇatve sati*) is intended to avoid fallacy, [the author] replies: It is not correct to say that the first [category] possesses the properties of a quality (*guṇadharma*). For [properties such as] heaviness (*garima*) and so forth, which belong to those things that possess them (i.e., effects or substances), such a state [of being a quality] is impossible, because—as with the case of all-pervasiveness (*sarvagantṛtva*)—there is no beginning of a single effect [from them].
Furthermore, there is a distinction in effort regarding the reaching of near or distant objects by humans, wind, deer, lions, and birds.
Yet, it is not the case that the excellence of that [effort] is impossible to surpass, because space is infinite;
otherwise, there would follow the consequence that some things which have reached the limit of excellence would fall [from it].
For effort would be unsurpassed only upon reaching all destinations that are to be reached without remainder;
since those [destinations] are infinite, how could this [effort] be unsurpassed?
Therefore, there is a deviation [from the rule] due to the quality of effort, which is common to all, or due to the quality of cognition.
That [state] is not the ultimate limit of dharma, which has sovereignty as its fruit;
rather, it is designated as such because it generates that sovereignty.

Since the sovereignty of Īśvara is the fruit of dharma (or, according to an alternative reading, "because it would follow that it is the fruit of dharma"), [it is argued that] from the perspective of ultimate reality, Īśvara is devoid of afflictions, karma, their maturation, and latent dispositions (since he is free from afflictions and the like). [To one who maintains that even the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord is produced by dharma, he says: because it would entail the consequence of there being many lords, and because the sovereignty of all [would then be] obstructed.

Furthermore, regarding what was stated—that "the attainment of the limit is perceived"—that is refuted by means of a dilemma: Moreover, if space were not limited because its ultimate state is inconceivable, then, on account of its infinity, it could not serve as a measure for its own [parts].

[If space were non-existent as an external reality, it could not be conceived of as limited; this is the logical connection. If space were limited, why could something greater than that not be conceived? This very possibility must be admitted precisely because we observe degrees of magnitude. [The opponent objects: "But its nature is infinity. [Desiring to dispel this doubt, the author asks: What is this "infinity"? [The objector replies: It is the state of being undivided. [The response: But is this not simply the absence of limitation (conceived through a different mode of expression)?
Thus, this much indeed is the measure [of knowledge] (and its opposite is its absence).
By asserting that the knowledge of the Lord has reached such a limit, one reveals [the Lord's] ignorance (since he does not fully comprehend his own very own consciousness in its entirety);
this is like the rising of a vetāla spirit during a rite for peace.
(Regarding the establishment of God's infinity, [it is argued that] God Himself possesses the characteristic of ignorance regarding reality.
(The Naiyāyika objects: "In that case, His omniscience follows precisely from His being the agent of all effects;
for potters and other such agents are indeed cognizant of the material cause, the instruments, the recipient, and the purpose."
In this context, the "appropriation" (*upādāna*) consists of the four types of atoms;
the "instrument" (*upakaraṇa*) consists of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which cause the manifestation of the entire field (*kṣetra*);
and the "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*) consists of the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*), whom the Blessed One intends through their own actions.
The purpose is the attainment of enjoyment;
as for the objects of the potter’s and other agents’ activities, such as the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth, they are already well-known.
Furthermore, since God is the agent of all effects, he is designated as the source-material of the entire range of effects, and thus he is omniscient.

(He begins to refute this doctrine established by the *Paratantra* school: Are these [potters and others] cognizant of every single instrument for their own work, or cognizant of only a few? First, they are not cognizant of every single instrument, because they lack knowledge of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).
Nor are they cognizant of the specific recipient and purpose, since those may be manifold. Even if the Lord (*īśvara*) were cognizant of only that much, his omniscience would not be established.

Furthermore, children, the insane, and others do not possess knowledge of the purpose and so forth of all actions; therefore, by observing them, even the Lord’s knowledge of those [purposes] alone is not established.
If, on the other hand, agency is something to be proven, how can it be established as inherently containing omniscience without a logical reason?
[Objection: But surely this is already established, because configurations and so forth are preceded by an intelligent agent.
[The author refutes this: This is understood.
Although all things possessing configuration and the like are indeed preceded by an intelligent agent, [it is not proven that they are created by a single, omniscient creator].
How can there be a single cause for well-known things such as [the specific] arrangement and so forth? || 22 ||

Furthermore, even if the arrangement of the earth, mountains, oceans, and so forth were like that of a house built by a carpenter out of a prior intention and faith, the proof of mere consciousness [in the creator] would still be established for others through the commonality of mere arrangement (this connects with the opponent's position). However, even if that were the case, the proof of mere consciousness would be refuted by the absence of a purpose, because there is no observation of suffering or of benefit to others in the act of differentiation. Moreover, how could that [Lord] possess unity? For jars and other such things are not preceded by a single intelligent agent.

(He raises an objection: "If it is argued that because every class of effects has God as its antecedent—that is, because they have God as their agent—likewise, there is a single agent for all; (he states the reply: that [state of having God as the antecedent] is itself yet to be proven. How then can it be adduced as something to be proven? (He raises the objection again: Since a specific arrangement is invariably concomitant with a conscious being, and since this is observed in some cases (such as jars and the like), it follows that the same must be the case elsewhere (as in the earth and so forth); thus, it is established that they have God as their antecedent and possess a single agent. If this is argued:

(He refutes this: There is an absolute lack of consistency between the example and the probandum; for while in the example, such as a jar, there is a single maker like a potter, in the probandum, such as the earth and so forth, there is Īśvara. Thus, due to this deviation (*vyabhicāra*), neither "being produced" nor "having an insentient material cause" can prove that the creator of mountains and the like is merely a conscious being, since both the example and the probandum are seen to have multiple makers.

But if everything were to be proven as having God as its antecedent cause, then, because things such as pots would be included in the subject (*pakṣa*) by virtue of having God as their antecedent cause, there would be no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*); thus he says: "If everything is the probandum (*sādhya*), there is an absence of a corroborative instance."

And if there were two agents for the jar and so forth—[that is, if it is argued that both God and the potter are the makers of the jar and so forth]—then the world and so forth would likewise have two agents; thus, because of the consequence of a "Lord of Lords," there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) [just as God presides over the potter who makes the jar, so another Lord would preside over the God who makes the world, and yet another over him, leading to an infinite regress]. (The opponent objects:
For this very reason (precisely because of the consequence of an infinite regress), the second inference is not valid.

(He refutes: "In that case, let there not even be a single inference; nevertheless, since the infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is equally applicable even in the case of a single inference—meaning that when an effect characterized as the earth and so forth arises from the conjunction of atoms and so on, this same [problem] applies equally to the inference of this very Lord (*īśvara*).

(The opponent objects: 'But surely pots and the like do not have multiple presiding agents; rather, everything has a single presiding agent. (He refutes: Thus, the establishment of omniscience does not follow."

(He raises an objection: "In this world, even those things composed of various parts, such as chariots and the like—which are constructed from diverse materials—are generally seen to stand in a relationship of mutual benefit and dependence; and thus, since it is observed that 'chariots, houses, and so forth are preceded by a single [agent],' it follows that 'the world also must be preceded by a single creator'—that is to say, whatever is established as existing through mutual benefit and dependence is seen to have a single creator, just as the parts of a chariot are seen to be preceded by a single [maker], and likewise the body, the universe, and so forth.
(He refutes this: This argument is fallacious (*vyabhicārin*), because we observe that there are also things preceded by multiple [agents].
An effect is not inferred from the absence of a cause;
for those who possess intelligence, such a view based on mere non-perception is logically untenable.

For in the absence of the accumulation of karma (*karma-śaya*), neither the connection with a body and sense organs, nor intellect, nor sovereignty is possible for that [Lord] (*īśvara*); thus, the cessation of the means of knowledge [regarding Him] would follow upon the acceptance of such [a state]. This is because an effect cannot arise in the absence of a cause.

Or, if it were to arise, His knowledge of the specific arrangement [of the universe] would have to come from another [source], namely, that accumulation of karma by which His body and other attributes are to be produced.

[The opponent] objects: Is it not precisely because of this—that is, because of the absence of the effect when there is an absence of the cause—that there is an inference of that [cause] (namely, the inference of an intelligent cause for the body, the world, and so forth)? Otherwise, if the effect were to exist even in the absence of the cause, then the refutation stated in the verse would also be untenable. Or rather, some distinction must be stated, whereby one is a refutation and the other is a proof. (For both the proponent of the refutation and the proponent of the proof are engaged in asserting that the effect is absent when the cause is absent; so why is only one of them questioned? [The author] replies by showing a distinction in his own position: It is said as follows.

For arrangements that are not preceded by perception are indeed distinct from perception; they would thus be beyond the reach of perception (*apratyakṣavedya*). But this is not so for the intellect (*buddhi*), because it is inferred from its observed characteristics. Furthermore, [if the intellect were eternal], it would be eternal, non-universal in its objects, and perceivable even in the beginning of non-existence; therefore, it must be inferred as being of two kinds [eternal and non-eternal]. And in that case, there would be a contradiction regarding its eternality and its universality of objects—this is the specific point of the refutation.

Moreover, even when [the equality of] proof and refutation is admitted, the refutation [is merely a counter-argument], whereas the proof—being one whose counter-argument has been eliminated—remains a proof for the establishment of the thesis (*sādhyasiddhi*), and not a mere counter-argument while remaining subject to opposition (*sapratipakṣa*).
This is the meaning of the doctrine of omniscience; [it concerns] words that are universal terms (*sarvanāmaśabda*).

(The author explains the meaning of the *kārikā* regarding the subject matter: "And an intelligent being is not the cause of the arrangement; rather, it is *medhā*—that is, a specific discerning intelligence (*prekṣā-buddhi-viśeṣa*) consisting of the deliberation and determination of the purpose of the arrangement.
And that [intelligence] is not possible in him (the Lord), because he lacks any orientation toward his own self-interest.
[With this much of the text, the view that there exists some omniscient being has been refuted.]
In this regard, the doctrines established by the Buddhists and the followers of Nyāya have been refuted.
Now, he refutes the view that there is some being established through yoga who, having performed that action once, is the director [of all things].
To that end, he presents the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa): "But surely, let there be no omnipresent director, yet let merit (dharma) be accepted."
It has been stated that no restriction regarding the objects of form, the eye, and so forth is established.
As for the lack of restriction by time, when something is present, its being an object of the eye and other senses—even if they possess excellence—is not contradictory.
Furthermore, it has been stated that if there were absolute non-presence, there would be absolute non-existence, like a sky-flower.

In that regard, the duty (*dharma*) of the *Kuru* people consists of six rites, because they accept sacrifice and so forth as their duty, and since no other deity is possible, [the rites are distinguished] by a qualifying attribute (*guṇa*) as the differentiator.
Among those, for some, the very sense organs (*indriya*) are the oblations (*havis*).

In other cases, however, only a single sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) the size of a chariot wheel is prescribed. When that is prepared, a deliberation arises: whether, due to the difference in ritual acts (*karman*), there is a difference in the subsidiary rites (*śeṣakārya*), or whether there is unity because of the oneness of the substance (*dravya*).

But is this not already determined in the eleventh book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*], where it is established: "The unity of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) regarding a single substance has been explained" (1.1.4.12)?
Therefore, this need not be investigated here.
It is said: This substance to be established admits of action along with its differentiation.
And Khaṇḍa is the protector because he knows the names of the principal [deities].

Although the discussion regarding the eleven [subsidiaries] follows later, nevertheless, here too, as a consequence of the remaining rites (*śeṣakārya*), the subsidiary (*śeṣa*) is also treated, since it consists of investigation.
And in that regard, because there is a single substance, its application is established as being common (*tantra*); for wherever there is a substance, that very thing benefits all the rituals.

Furthermore, no other purpose for the division of the substance is observed, nor can it be established. However, since the primary purpose of this [substance] is its utility for the principal rite, and the consecration (*saṃskāra*) serves as a means to assist that [utility], the division resulting from the distinction of the principal rites cannot be effected because of the unity of the substance.
And yet, even when one part has been presented, there occurs the presentation of what is contained within the other part.

Since the locations for the portions to be cut off (*avadāna*) are distinct, there is also a distinction between the northern and southern halves; thus, it is understood that this [act] which produces the oily consistency must be repeated.
Furthermore, because the remainder is undivided, it is not differentiated with respect to all [the deities].
The Commentary states: "We say that it should be performed only once."
Because there is no division of the remainder.
There is no division here of all the sacrificial portions of the *puroḍāśa*.
The *sviṣṭakṛt* portion is to be cut from the northern half.

From one [portion], there is the upper half; when that is being cut off, no distinction is perceived as to which part should be offered and which should not. It is the same here with the length as well.
Therefore, it should be offered only once;
that is, it is performed just once.
Why? Because this is not intended to be a consecration of the sacrificial act (*karman*) of what is being offered.
However, because it is equal to the remnants of the *huta* (offered portion), its status as a primary ritual (*tantra*) is understood.

Whether it takes the form of a refinement of the action (*karma-saṃskāra*) or has the purpose of refining that which is being offered (*hūyamāna-saṃskāra*), there would be non-difference [of the rite] due to the non-difference of that [remnant].
But this is a refinement of the remnant (*śeṣa-saṃskāra*).
And that remainder is common [to both].
Of that, the southern and northern halves are taken;
there is no injunction to consume the principal portions.
Because that [subsequent half] is not enjoined in its original context;
and consequently, it can be said that there is no perceived distinction [between the two halves].

For even if one were to take the subsequent half with reference to the *ekadhana* vessels, nevertheless, the other principal elements would still fulfill their purpose through that which was enjoined.
Therefore, it is a *tantra* (a common procedure). As for the claim that it is to be divided, it is useful for that purpose when performing the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*).
Śā—In the *Sarvapṛṣṭhyā*, six rites are prescribed by means of [the formulas] beginning with “For Indra, who is connected with the *Rathantara*,” and so forth.
In this regard, there arises the doubt: is this *sviṣṭakṛt* offering to be cut from each individual ritual act (*pratikarma*), or only once?
In that case, because of the multiplicity of acts, the conclusion is reached that it should be performed for each act;
for by means of the extended injunctions (*codaka*), the remaining rites are also prescribed for each individual act.
Therefore, it might be argued that one should cut portions for each individual action.

To this, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is stated: "The remnant is common to all; therefore, it is cut once. For by that much alone, the requirement for all would be fulfilled, as there is no distinction."
Regarding *soma*: the connection [of this section] arises from the context of the remaining rites (*śeṣakārya*).

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: even though there is no difference in the substance, because there is a difference in the ritual acts (*karmabheda*), the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other offerings are performed separately for each act.
[Objection]: "The Indra [invoked] by means of the *rathantara* and other [sāmans] is not different;
therefore, does the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and the subsequent ritual acts (*śeṣakārya*) therein differ or not? [Response]:
They do differ, because of the difference in the ritual acts (*karman*), being separately woven together by the archetypal injunctions (*codaka*)."

Since the remaining [procedures] are entirely identical [to the archetype], their performance should take place all at once. Bhaṭṭa: In the *Sarvapṛṣṭhyā* sacrifice, regarding the offering of six oblations where it is said, "He offers to Indra associated with the *Rathaṃtara*, to Indra associated with the *Bṛhat*, to Indra associated with the *Vairūpa*," and so forth—after having offered to all six and performed the threshing and grinding together, and when the division [of the flour] would normally follow according to the archetype, one performs that division; then, by virtue of a specific injunction, one makes a single sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) the size of a chariot wheel, and following the injunction, "He cuts portions from all sides," he cuts portions from all sides and performs the principal offerings.
In this context, the word "on all sides" (samantataḥ) serves as the indicator of the distinction between ritual acts;

otherwise, if there were a single act—as in the case of "the entire iron [mass] at the front"—it would follow that the portioning should be performed only once. Alternatively, the distinction between the acts arises from the difference in the *yājyā* verses.
And in that case, there is a single performance because of the unity of the principal offerings, such as the *sviṣṭakṛt*.

Nor can it be argued that there is a single performance (*tantra*) due to the unity of the substance, because of the distinction between the various portions such as the "upper half" (*uttarārdha*) based on the difference in the locations from which the cuttings (*avadāna*) are made. Furthermore, it should not be said that "the substance is one" because the upper half is common to all since it is a portion of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), given that there is no evidence for a mutual syntactic connection (*parasparānvaya*) among the sentences enjoining the preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*), and thus the upper half lacks a relationship with the specific location of the cutting; rather, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is understood to have a relationship with the oblation (*havis*). [This is refuted by: [The text continues: ...because for each respective deity, a large amount has been measured out...

The *sarvapṛṣṭheṣ� offering* (4231) follows the principle of the gift of one's entire property (*sarvasvadāna*), because the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) lacks the status of an oblation (*havis*) here; its status as an oblation has been set aside due to its being the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the oblation.

Nor should it be argued that, even so, because the oblation (*havis*) is mixed and thus common to both, at the time of the *āgama* (offering), even though there is an individual intention (*saṃkalpa*) such as "that which was offered to Indra Rāyantara is mine alone, not his," the subsequent rites of disposal (*śeṣakārya*) must be performed collectively (*tantratva*) because the specific details of the mixed *ājyabhāga* and other offerings cannot be distinguished. For even in that case, just as in the rule "he does not [eat] the *anuyāja*s here," the statement "he eats two portions of the Indra-remnant, for he utters the *vaṣaṭ* twice over it" makes it understood that the difference in the act of offering (*pradāna*) is the cause for the difference in the rites of disposal. Therefore, although the distinction [of the portions] is established by the necessity of explaining that [textual injunction] otherwise, the distinction [in the disposal] follows from that.

This being the position reached, [the following is argued]: in the case of the statement "thereby the student is made" (*tena chātraṃ kriyate*), the present tense (*laṭ*) refers to a past time characterized by the action; however, because its purpose is merely to provide a reason (*hetu-stuti-mātra-paratvāt*), it falls within the scope [of the rule regarding the reason]. Furthermore, since the mere indication [of the reason] is established by general principle (*nyāya-prāptatvāt*), there is no possibility of sublation (*bādha*); thus, the remaining grammatical operations (*śeṣa-kāryāṇi*) apply only once.

In the case of "not a student" (*na chātra*), however, the distinction is that because there is an absence of such a characteristic (*lakṣaṇābhāvāt*), it is a rule concerning the reason itself (*hetu-vidhitvam*).
In the case of the Aindrāgna [cup], on the other hand, there is a difference: the repetition of the consumption (*bhakṣāvṛtti*) occurs precisely because of a direct scriptural statement (*vacanāt*).
Maṇḍana: "In the Sarvapṛṣṭhīṣṭi, [the ritual] is performed once.

This means that in the rite of the Sarvapṛṣṭhīṣṭi, the subsequent ritual action regarding the remnants (śeṣakārya) is performed "once" (sakṛt)—that is, it occurs only a single time from the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) offered by the giver.
Śaṅkara: "That [procedure] is the common framework (tantra) for the Sarvapṛṣṭhyā."

In the Sarvapṛṣṭheṣṭi, there are six *indrāḥ*—the Rathantara, Bṛhat, Vairūpa, Vairāja, Śākvara, and Raivata—and a single cake (*puroḍāśa*) on twelve potsherds. It is heard in the scripture: "He cuts off portions from all sides."
In this case, there is a distinction among the offerings; however, the remaining ritual acts (śeṣakārya) should be performed only once, not separately six times. [Vi.
3.5.4] By the name "Sarvapṛṣṭha," there is an extension (atideśa) of the six Pṛṣṭha-stotras to the Viśvajit sacrifice known as Sarvapṛṣṭha.

*Mīmāṃsādarśana*, Vol. 7, Part 3, pp. 13–16, p. 220: “*Atideśa*: In the case of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the six-day *pṛṣṭha* [rite] applies. This point should be examined in the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*). Even one’s entire property (*sarvasva*), though it may be more than that, must be given to the priests as their own share in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice by means of the twelve-hundred-cow sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Vi. 6.7.9: In the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, only what is currently possessed is to be given as one’s entire property.

6|7|4|16. *Mīmāṃsā* p. 3689: Regarding the statement "In the Viśvajit sacrifice, there is the giving of whatever *sarvasva* (all one's possessions) exists," this section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted.

There is an option (*vikalpa*) between giving all one's possessions as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and not giving any fee at all, depending on whether the simultaneous occurrence of disconnections (*apaccheda*) takes place.
6|5|18|9–53. *Mīmāṃsā* p. 497: Regarding the statement "When there is a simultaneous occurrence of disconnections, there is no sacrificial fee," this section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted.
The gift of all one's possessions (*sarvasvadāna*) occurs even in the *viśvajit* that is part of the eight-night sacrifice (*aṣṭarātra*).

(Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 750). Regarding the statement "the gift of all one's possessions [occurs] even in the *viśvajit* of the eight-night sacrifice," one should consult the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*).
The gift of all one's possessions occurs even in the *viśvajit* that is part of a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*).

VI. 6|7|8. The gift of one's entire property (*sarvasvadāna*)—and not the [gift of] one hundred and twelve—is [the rule] when there is a subsequent interruption (*apaccheda*) of the *udgātṛ* priest during the subsequent performance caused by that [interruption]. (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 122). Regarding the phrase "when there is a subsequent interruption of the *udgātṛ*," the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted.

Furthermore, even in the case of the *viśvajit* sacrifice, although there is a gift of one's entire property, he will state later (VI. 7|3|4) that horses and such are not to be given because they are prohibited.
Vārttika 3.4.10.28, page 961: The Principle of the Gift of All One's Possessions (*sarvasvadānanyāya*).
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, when there is a gift of all one's possessions, one's father and other such relatives are not to be given away.
In the case of one's own property (*svadāna*), everything [is to be given] because there is no distinction.
The Commentary states: There is this injunction: "In the Viśvajit sacrifice, one gives away all one's property" (*sarvasvaṃ dadāti*).

Regarding this, there is a doubt: does "all" mean everything that is designated by the word *sva* (one's own), such as even one's mother and father, and thus all that must be given; or does it mean only that which is designated by the word *sva* through the connection with ownership (*prabhutva*)?
What is the conclusion? Because there is no distinction, it should be given in this way even to the mother and father.
But surely it is said that "giving" consists in the cessation of one's own ownership and the production of another's ownership;
in that case, it is impossible to cause the cessation of ownership for the father and others.
For in no way does one who is a father cease to be a father.
It is said: True; it is not that he ceases to be a father.
However, it is possible to make [the recipient] subject to another's command.
Neither the sentient being (*sattva*) nor the material object (*dravya*) is the meaning of the root *dā* (to give);
rather, from the meaning [of the root], it is the relinquishment of ownership (*svatvatyāga*).
Therefore, everything should be given;
or rather, it should be given by one who is its master, because for anyone else it would be impossible.
The Commentary: By the word "or" (*vā*), the position is reversed.

That which possesses ownership by virtue of its lordship is what must be given, not this [other thing]. Why? Because the former is possible for one who exercises authority, whereas the latter is impossible.
For it is not possible for one to renounce one's ownership over parents and the like. But was it not said that making others perform [the rite] on one's behalf is possible?
It is replied:
In this context, "one's entire possession" refers to that which is being given by the practitioner himself;
it does not mean the giving away of one's own self when not acting as a practitioner. Nor is it logical that the father and others should serve as attendants.

And he for whom even that which consists of consciousness might exist, he should indeed give it; this is the principle of the *sarvasva-ananya* [offering]. Regarding the *sarvasvāra* sacrifice, it is said here: [4232]... [he should give] everything.
But surely, when it is said, "This is for whom the word 'own' (sva) applies," it is understood that the father and others are to be given;
therefore, with respect to them, one should strive even by setting aside the traditional rule (smṛti).
To this, it is replied:

The word "own" (*sva*) here denotes each of one's property, wealth, and kinsmen individually, not the collection as a whole. In that regard, once "entirety" (*sarvatā*) has been established with respect to one's property—thereby fulfilling the purpose of the scripture—"entirety" should not be assumed for kinsmen who are incapable [of being fed], nor should the Smṛti be subverted.
Furthermore, since one's own cattle and so forth are obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), entirety must necessarily be adopted with respect to one's own property.
And once that [debt] has been taken up, the purpose of the treatise has been fulfilled; thus, there is no reason for it to apply to the distribution among kinsmen.
Therefore, fathers and others are not to be given. And for this very reason, ownership arises through the exercise of dominion; that alone is what is to be given.

Soma: In the preceding quarters (*pādas*), the determination [of the scope of application] was stated based on the lack of distinction due to the examination of individual words, because of the context of the subject matter, and because there was no interruption from other words or sentences;

however, here, since the application arises without distinction upon the examination of a word, the determination is made in a specific sense by the force of that very word. Thus, because the existence of other quarters is subtle and because of their infinity:
Ci— "In the gift of one's entire property, even in the case of parents and others, it is only in that wealth [that the rule applies]."

[Objection: Because of [the requirement of] one's own ownership and so forth, [the gift] is not possible in the case of a father and so on, precisely because there is no relinquishment [of what is already owned].
[Response of the Bhāṭṭa: In the Viśvajit sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "He gives away his entire property.
In that context, since fathers and others are also denotable by the word "property" (sva) by virtue of being relatives, they too must be given away like wealth.

Furthermore, since the kind of ownership (*svatva*) consisting in being subject to disposal at will—as in the case of one's father and others—is impossible due to the reasons for ownership stated in such texts as "One is an owner through inheritance, purchase, partition, acceptance, or finding," and since there is no sense of "belonging to oneself" apart from the relationship of being a father and so forth, it would be untenable for the status of being the object of the act of giving (*dattākarmatva*) to be constituted by such ownership.

This is because the Smṛtis also mention the giving away of daughters and sons, thereby acknowledging ownership even in those cases. Alternatively, let it be that, in accordance with those [Smṛti] passages, the meaning of the word "giving" (*dāna*) is simply the production of another's ownership.

This being the case, since the word "giving" (*dāna*) is not applied to a mere written document simply by virtue of its execution as a prohibitory act, the meaning of the term "giving" consists solely in the transfer of ownership to another preceded by the relinquishment of one's own ownership.
Furthermore, there is no evidence for ownership in the father or others, due to the absence of any grounds for ownership;
and in cases such as the "giving of a daughter," the verb *dadāti* (to give) is used in a figurative sense.

And recourse to that [interpretation] is not appropriate here, because the word "one's own" (*sva*) can be justified even by taking it to mean wealth, which serves as the substratum for ownership. Furthermore, this word "one's own" operates with respect to one's belongings, kinsmen, and oneself through distinct individual powers, as there is no single inclusive determinant for a unitary power. Consequently, in a single usage, since only one meaning can be understood at a time, only wealth is to be grasped in accordance with the context of ownership and so forth.

Maṇḍana: "In the case of one's entire property [being given away], there would be no kinsmen. The intention is that when the entirety of one's possessions is prescribed as the object to be given in the Viśvajit sacrifice, kinsmen—such as one's father and others—are not included; rather, only the forest of cattle and so forth is meant.
Śaṅkara: "In the case of one's entire property, [the giving] does not include the father and others."
"The Sarvasvāra sacrifice is for one who desires death;
indeed, he who desires death should perform this [sacrifice], he who should desire, 'May I go to the world of heaven free from disease.
And that [sacrifice] must be completed by the officiating priests after the death of the sacrificer.
The sacrifice named Sarvasvāra;
the Śunaḥkarṇa Agniṣṭoma.
Regarding the *śunaḥkarṇastoma*, Somanāthī states:
"The *śunaḥkarṇastoma*," while Kutūhala notes that "some [reciters of] the Śākhās say: 'The *śunaḥkarṇastoma*.
The injunctive statement is: "One who desires death should sacrifice with this; he who should desire, 'May I go to the world of heaven free from disease.'"

And in that context, it is said: "When the Ārbhava-pra-stāva is being chanted, having wrapped the Audumbarī post with the cloth from the Sadas, he enters after issuing the command: 'O Brāhmaṇas, complete my sacrifice!
If this were merely a directive (preṣa), it would serve the purpose of an injunction (ahīna).
Therefore, by means of the indicative mark of the command (saṃpreṣaṇa), the completion [of the sacrifice] itself is what is enjoined.
For example: "If they should carry off the Soma, one should say, 'Run and fetch it!
Now, as for what was said—that one who is alive is an agent, not one who is dead—that is not so.
The statement was spoken by one who is living:
"One should bring what has been begun to completion. Therefore, the completion occurs precisely through that [act].
To this he replies: When he applied it, at that time its completion was not yet effected by him;
when it was completed, at that time he no longer existed.
Who is the agent of completion?
To this it is said:
this is equal to [the case of] one whose doubt has been dispelled.
Since you consider the agent to be alive without any doubt, this [case] is equal to that.

Even for one who is sent away and remains alive at the time of completion, his being alive at the time of completion is of no assistance; rather, his status as an agent is established by the very previous sending.
And that previous sending is the same whether he is alive or dead.
[The opponent claims: "He performs [the action] even while living.
To this it is replied: "Agency is possible because of the existence of a living being."
This too is exactly the same:
even while living, the person (puruṣa) is the agent, not the body;
and that person exists even when the body has fallen.
Therefore, it might be argued that [the ritual] is completed at that very point;
for,
since the sacrificer is no longer present, it is necessary to perform the subsequent procedure (*tantra*) intended for one who has gone to his destiny (*diṣṭagata*).
"Therefore, that word does not cause [the application]," [one might argue]. This is not so; it will cause the application with the exception of that which pertains to the sacrificer.
Therefore, there is no fault.
Alternatively, the statement "O Brāhmaṇas, complete my sacrifice" is itself a declaration of completion;
consequently, that alone shall constitute the duty of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).
Śā—The sacrifice named *Sarvasvāra* is prescribed for one desiring heaven.
In that rite, at the time of the *Ārbhava-stotra*, the sacrificer, having given the command (*preṣa*) to the officiating priests, "Complete my sacrifice," dies.

Regarding the doubt as to whether the remaining ritual acts must be completed when he has died or not—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) being that it need not be completed because agency is impossible for one who is dead.
He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "In this way, agency (*kartṛtva*) would exist [for the sacrificer] as far as possible;
however, while still alive, he relinquishes the remaining agency through the formal dismissal (*saṃpreṣa*).

The agency of the sacrificer even during the state of being alive consists precisely in the performance of the common rites such as the choosing (*varaṇa*) and supporting (*bharaṇa*) of the priests. And that [agency] is possible even regarding the remainder of the ritual (*karmaśeṣa*) occurring after death, provided it is arranged while one is still in the state of being alive.
Moreover, the completion [of the rite] is directly perceived through the injunction "he completes," and this cannot be denied.
Furthermore, since [the rite] ceases upon the mere absence of the desire for Soma, what need is there to mention its cessation when the desirer is absent? This is the connection.

Regarding the meaning of the Sūtra: it is taught that if the sacrificer dies while the *sarvasvāra* sacrifice is in progress, its completion does not take place; for every ritual action has the living person as its qualified agent (*adhikārin*), and thus qualification is impossible for one who is dead.
As stated in the *Cintāmaṇi*: "The *sarvasvāra* should either be abandoned after death or completed.
It should be abandoned due to the absence of an owner [the sacrificer]; otherwise, it should be completed by others through the formal directions (*praiṣa*)."

Bhaṭṭa: There is a sacrifice named Sarvasvāra, enjoined for the purpose of attaining heaven by the scriptural statement: "One who desires death should indeed sacrifice with this; he who should desire, 'May I go to the world of heaven free from disease.
For here, death is the result, because it is the primary objective (*nirhatya*). Moreover, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) if multiple objectives were intended.
Therefore, the meaning is that the subject under discussion is "one who desires death.
Furthermore, because the means [of performance] are prescribed by the statement, "When the Ārbhava-prastāva is being chanted, he enters the Ārbhava," death itself is enjoined here as a duty.

Consequently, when the question arises whether or not that sacrifice must be completed after death, since the agency [required for the ritual] is possible through the "bone-sacrifice" (*asthiyajña*), and since the sacrifice ending in death alone is the means to attain heaven, it need not be completed.

This being the prima facie position, [the conclusion is as follows]: because of the scriptural injunction, "When the Ārbhava-praṣṭhāva is being chanted, having wrapped the Audumbarī post with a cloth from the Sadas, he enters after giving the command: 'O Brāhmaṇas, complete my sacrifice!'"—and because that injunction for completion serves to demonstrate the existence of a scriptural rule for completion (which otherwise would be inferred), and because it is possible for even a deceased person to act as an instigator of the priests by virtue of being a constituent part of that rite, the sacrifice must indeed be completed.

As for the claim made by some that this very *praiṣa* (directive) serves as an injunction for completion—just like the rule "one's own Veda is to be studied"—that is required [only] because the power of the injunction is obstructed by the vocative address "O Brāhmaṇas," and because its application at the time of the ritual performance would otherwise be untenable. In reality, however, even in the absence of a specific directive for completion, [the conclusion follows].
(Mīmāṃsākośa 530)

Since both the selection (*varaṇa*) and the death (*maraṇa*) of the officiants are performed for the sake of the sacrifice itself—just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*)—and because of that, the agency of the officiants is established both during their lifetime and upon their death;
therefore, by this very principle, the completion of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites by the officiants even when death occurs midway must be understood in the same manner.

And thus, although the instruction (*preṣya*) serves as the basis for inferring a rule (*vidhikalpaka*), it should be noted that its purpose is seen (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) precisely in its role as the means for completing the rite.
22. Maṇḍana: "The Sarvasvāra sacrifice is concluded. 24. Śaṅkara: "The Sarvasvāra sacrifice is concluded.
Just as [the rites] following the Sarvasvāra are performed.

(Regarding the portion of Sūtra 5.1.2.136: *yathā pareṣu sarvasvārāt*): Regarding those rites prescribed for study that follow the *sarvasvāra* mantra after the sacrifice, their recitation in the first half [of the month] would have to be accepted as serving only an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
But that is incorrect. (Bhāṣya on 5.1.2.136):
There is no completion of the *sarvasvāra* at the time of death, because the rite is connected with the living.
"The Sarvasvāra sacrifice is the Śunaḥkarṇa Agniṣṭoma; one who desires death [performs it] at the three pressings on the day of the Savanīya offerings, and at the third pressing of the horse."
Dvaidhaprśna 12.2–12.32: The cups (grahas) are intended for the purpose of the three pressings (savanatraya). Mīmāṃsākośa, p.
1628; see the section titled "The Section on the Cup" (grahaṇamadhikaraṇam) there. In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there are ten chamasas (cups).

In that regard, there are four *camasa*s for the officiants who perform the duties from the middle [of the sacrificial ground]—namely, the *hotṛ*, *brahman*, *udgātṛ*, and *yajamāna*—and six for the *hotrā* priests, namely the *maitrāvaruṇa*, *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, *potṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, *acchāvāka*, and *agrī*.

Among these, at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), during the distribution of the *śukra* and *manthin* cups, nine *camasa*s—the principal ones of the pressing—are first offered to Indra, with the exception of the *acchāvāka*’s cup.
(See *Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa* 3.2.12.4; cf. *Mahābhāṣya* on *Pāṇini* 5.1.17.30).

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: just as the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), being postponed due to divine or human obstacles, causes the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) to be postponed, so too the *Sāṃtapanīyā* offering, when postponed, would cause the morning *Agnihotra* to be postponed. (Bhāṣya 5.1.17.30). [See also] *savanīya*; *savanīyānubandhyāḥ* 4238; the principle of the *savanīya* and others (*savanīyādinyāyaḥ*).
The Principle of the Savanīya and Others (Savanīyādinyāya) [4239]:
The Savanīya and others—the Agnīṣomīya, Savanīya, and Anūbandhya animals—[are related] to the Jyotiṣṭoma;
[this concerns] the cake (puroḍāśa) [offered] when the animal sacrifice has commenced, by which [the procedure] is heard [to apply] within the framework (tantra).
In the Ṣoḍaśī-stoma,
their sacrificial posts (yūpa) follow a common ritual procedure (tantra). This is the section on the sacrificial posts (yūpādhyāya).
Bhāṣya 11.3: From the [preceding] rule, the animal ritual procedure would apply to the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa),
even though it is absent there.
In the case of the *śravaṇa* [sacrifice], because it falls within that [interval], there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it being subordinate (*niśrīdhitva*).
Just as in the case of the *savanīya* and other offerings, as well as the *stotra*s and other elements included within the *savana*, [the same applies].
Therefore, he says: "The principle of the midnight hour (*niśīthinyāya*) also applies here" (12.2.5).
*Savana* means *svara*. (Su. Pṛ.
1180) [It occurs] in the *savanīya* offerings and so forth.
It does not exist;
for in that case, when ten [elements] have proceeded by means of several constituent parts,
the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice applies to the animals due to the injunction of the *ālabhati* (the act of immolation).
When that [cause] has been performed, then, because of that cause, there is the effect.
By way of generality, there is a distinction based on the commonality of the injunction, as in the case of sacrificial animals.
It is said: the *paśu* alone is the string (*tantrī*).
For it is there, from the very beginning, that the consequence is clearly established.

Regarding the formulas for the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana), such as "This sacrificer has chosen Agni as the Hotṛ," and so forth—even though the commencement occurs simultaneously with the animal sacrifice—it is not possible, by considering that fact, to determine which sentence's injunction is the primary one (tantrita) performed by the Maitrāvaruṇa priest for the Āgnīṣomīya animal, and which is merely incidental (prasaṅgita).

Nevertheless, it is further stated: "The sacrificer has chosen Agni as the Hotṛ; this [offering] is well-pressed," and so forth, because the animal sacrifice is concluded at the third pressing (*savana*). Thus, since the *saṃvanīya* animal sacrifice falls within the framework of the ritual procedure (*tantra*), the status of being the principal (*tantritva*) belongs exclusively to the animal sacrifice. This very point is recited: if the *puroḍāśas* were the principals, then the act of bringing forward (*pākaraṇa*) the *saṃvanīya* animal would not apply to the *saṃvanīya* *puroḍāśas*.

When there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) as that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*), although the masculinity (*puṃstva*)—which is the substantive (*viśeṣya*)—is also [part of] that which is to be brought about, the status of heaven as that which is to be brought about is established by the maxim "for when [the object] has a qualification... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.12). When it is said that the axe is the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the exertion and so forth that are conducive to the action of splitting (*dvaidhībhāva*), by the maxim "for when [the object] has a qualification...", it results in the conclusion that the axe is the instrument in the accomplishment of the splitting.

Similarly, in the case of "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), the status of the sacrifice as a means—characterized by both visible and invisible auxiliaries, consisting of the performance of acts such as threshing and the *prayāja* offerings, and taking the form of an activity conducive to heaven—is ultimately established as leading to the production of heaven, according to the maxim "for when there is a qualification... (*saviśeṣaṇe hi*). It is precisely on this basis that the popular doctrine holds that the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) consists in being the producer of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*). *Bāla.*, p. 52: That which assists what is directly enjoined for the purpose of purifying it—namely, a Vedic ritual action consisting of an activity directed toward the *kratvartha* (that which serves the sacrifice), such as the offering made when establishing the *khalevālī* (the threshing-post)—is a *saṃnipatyopakāraka* (directly contributing auxiliary) that has an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose and is intended for the purification of the material used.
(However, this is an improper example.)

*Bāla*, p. 83: A Vedic action that is of the nature of an activity for the sake of the *kratvartha* (ritual purpose) as a directly contributing subsidiary (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), involving the refinement of a substance (*dravyasaṃskāra*) intended for a visible purpose or an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), is as follows: "The oblation is to be placed on the *ulaparājī* [grass-bundle]. This [oblation] should not be performed, because it is merely the bringing of two portions for the sake of the *taras* (flesh), since its purpose is the refinement of the sacrificial post (*yūpasaṃskāra*)—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the tenth [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra].

*Bāla.*, p. 83: A Vedic action that is directly enjoined as an auxiliary (*upakāraka*), which serves the purpose of preparing a substance (*dravyasaṃskāra*) for use, and which has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), is a "directly contributing auxiliary" (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) belonging to the ritual purpose (*kratvartha*). An example is: "One should touch the calf" (*vatsamālabheta*). Here, Bhavadeva states in the *Paśusomādhikaraṇa* (p. 82) that because the calf is an auxiliary to the substance used in the enjoined milking, the act of touching is for the purpose of preparing that substance. *Bāla.*, p. 82: An injunction regarding the comprehension of an object established through the connection with the material cause (*upādāna*) of what is directly enjoined is an "injunction of comprehension" (*pratipattividhi*). An example is: "He sprinkles [it] with water" (*śakṛt praviyati*).
