"The Puruṣa is neither a modification (*vikāra*), nor the primal nature (*prakṛti*), nor a further modification (*vikṛti*). Thus [it is said]. Those [reasons] that have been established are not sublated.

*Sāṃkhyādhikaraṇa* (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.1–10). On page 163 of *Saṃkarṣa*, [it is stated]: "For the Sāṃkhyas, the entire world is indeed eternal. The Sāṃkhyas maintain that bondage is caused by karma, but karma itself has ignorance (*ajñāna*) as its cause. Regarding the establishment of the absolute eternity [of the soul], [the Sūtrakāra] says: "But because there is no production [of bondage] through the knowledge of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, there is no arising of karma; and since there is no bondage, liberation is established" (*Sūtra*, p. 131).

But surely, in the section concerning Sāṃkhya (Sūtra 2.2.1), it was established through inference that the Sāṃkhyas do not produce effects without the superintendence of a conscious being—thus proving the existence of God—and here [in the present discussion], the validity and invalidity of knowledge are determined as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*). How, then, can that [previous conclusion] be set aside? This is not a fault; for there [at 2.1.1], the Sāṃkhyas (as cited by Vaidyanātha on page 14 of 1.1.12) hold the following view: [they maintain that the world arises from primordial matter (*prakṛti*) alone].

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), relying on the rule observed in clay and other materials—that the cause conforms to its effect—the atheistic Sāṃkhyas maintain that primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is insentient and consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Having thus easily grasped this, the Sāṃkhya infers from the example of clay and the like that the cause of the world—which is non-delusive in nature—is a principle consisting of the specific evolutes beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), existing for the sake of the experience of sentient beings; and they assert that [this cause] transforms itself into the form of the manifest universe. And that [is as follows]: [The Sāṃkhya says: "Just as clay, which is insentient, transforms into the form of a jar for the sake of human enjoyment, so too does primordial matter (*pradhāna*), which is insentient, transform into the form of the manifest universe for the sake of the enjoyment of sentient beings. [The Siddhāntin replies: This is not so. Just as clay transforms into the form of a jar through the agency of a potter who possesses intelligence, so too must primordial matter transform into the form of the manifest universe through the agency of one who possesses intelligence. For it is observed that insentient things do not act without being directed by a sentient agent. Therefore, the Lord alone is the cause of the world. Furthermore, it is stated: "As a spider creates its web, as plants grow from seeds, and as hair grows from a living body, so does the world emerge from the Imperishable. Thus, the Lord alone is the cause of the world. Moreover, the scripture states: "He who, dwelling within the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, and who controls the earth from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3). Since the existence of the inner controller is established by such scriptural passages, the Lord alone is the cause of the world. Therefore, the doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas is refuted. Thus ends the section concerning the Sāṃkhya. Now begins the section concerning the Vaiśeṣika. The Vaiśeṣikas hold that the world arises from atoms. They say: "Just as a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) arises from two atoms, and a triad (*tryaṇuka*) arises from three dyads, so too does the entire world arise from atoms. But this is not so. If atoms were to combine without a conscious agent, they would never cease combining, and thus there would be no dissolution of the world. Furthermore, since atoms are eternal and partless, they cannot possess the property of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which requires parts. Therefore, their doctrine is untenable. Consequently, the Lord alone is the cause of the world. Thus ends the section concerning the Vaiśeṣika. Now begins the section concerning the Jaina. The Jainas hold that the world arises from the six substances (*ṣaḍdravya*). They say: "The six substances are: soul (*jīva*), non-soul (*ajīva*), merit (*puṇya*), demerit (*pāpa*), influx (*āsrava*), and bondage (*bandha*); and liberation (*mokṣa*) is the cessation of these. But this is not so. Since the soul and non-soul are distinct, there can be no liberation, for liberation would imply the destruction of the soul. Furthermore, since merit and demerit are imperceptible, their existence cannot be proven. Therefore, their doctrine is untenable. Consequently, the Lord alone is the cause of the world. Thus ends the section concerning the Jaina. Now begins the section concerning the Buddhist. The Buddhists hold that the world arises from momentary consciousness. They say: "All things are momentary; there is no permanent substance. Consciousness alone exists, and it arises in a continuous stream like a river. But this is not so. If everything were momentary, there could be no recognition of objects, nor could there be any moral responsibility for actions. Furthermore, since consciousness is insentient by nature, it cannot perceive objects. Therefore, their doctrine is untenable. Consequently, the Lord alone is the cause of the world. Thus ends the section concerning the Buddhist. Now begins the section concerning the Mīmāṃsaka. The Mīmāṃsakas hold that the world is eternal and uncreated. They say: "The Veda is eternal and self-existent; it is not the work of any person. Since the Veda is the source of all knowledge, the world is eternal and has no creator. But this is not so. If the Veda were eternal, it would be impossible to explain how it was revealed to sages like Manu. Furthermore, since the Veda contains injunctions regarding rituals, it must have been composed by someone. Therefore, their doctrine is untenable. Consequently, the Lord alone is the cause of the world. Thus ends the section concerning the Mīmāṃsaka. Now begins the section concerning the Cārvāka. The Cārvākas hold that the world arises from the four elements. They say: "There is no soul other than the body. Consciousness arises from the combination of the elements, just as the power of intoxication arises from fermented grains. When the body perishes, consciousness perishes; therefore, there is no afterlife, no heaven, and no hell. But this is not so. If consciousness were merely a product of the elements, then a corpse should also possess consciousness. Furthermore, since the elements are insentient, they cannot produce consciousness. Therefore, their doctrine is untenable. Consequently, the Lord alone is the cause of the world. Thus ends the section concerning the Cārvāka. Now begins the section concerning the Materialist (*Lokāyata*). The Materialists hold that the world is a mere illusion. They say: "The world is like a dream or a magical illusion. There is no reality behind appearances; everything is empty and void. But this is not so. If the world were an illusion, then liberation would be unnecessary, as there would be nothing to be liberated from. Furthermore, since the perception of diversity is universal, it cannot be dismissed as a mere illusion. Therefore, their doctrine is untenable. Consequently, the Lord alone is the cause of the world. Thus ends the section concerning the Materialist. Now begins the section concerning the Yoga. The Yogas hold that the world arises from the union of the individual soul and primordial matter. They say: "The individual soul is pure consciousness, while primordial matter is the source of the material world. Through the union of these two, the world is produced. But this is not so. If the soul and matter were eternally distinct, there could be no liberation, for liberation would require the destruction of the soul. Furthermore, since matter is insentient, it cannot act without being directed by a sentient agent. Therefore, their doctrine is untenable. Consequently, the Lord alone is the cause of the world. Thus ends the section concerning the Yoga. Now begins the section concerning the Pāśupata. The Pāśupatas hold that the world arises from the grace of Śiva. They say: "Śiva is the supreme lord; he is both the efficient and the material cause of the world. By his grace, souls attain liberation. But this is not so. If Śiva were the sole cause, then all souls would attain liberation simultaneously, which is contrary to observation. Furthermore, since Śiva is eternal and unchanging, his grace cannot be the occasional cause of liberation. Therefore, their doctrine is untenable. Consequently, the Lord alone is the cause of the world. Thus ends the section concerning the Pāśupata. Now begins the section concerning the Śaiva. The Śaivas hold that the world arises from the five principles (*pañcatattva*). They say: "The five principles are: Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā. From these, the entire universe evolves. But this is not so. If these principles were eternal and unchanging, there could be no creation or dissolution. Furthermore, since these principles are insentient, they cannot act without a conscious agent. Therefore, their doctrine is untenable. Consequently, the Lord alone is the cause of the world. Thus ends the section concerning the Śaiva. Now begins the section concerning the Vaiṣṇava. The Vaiṣṇavas hold that the world arises from Viṣṇu. They say: "Viṣṇu is the supreme lord; he is the creator, preserver, and destroyer of the world. He is the soul of all beings. But this is not so. If Viṣṇu were the sole cause, then he would be subject to change and transformation, which contradicts his nature as the immutable. Furthermore, since Viṣṇu is omnipresent, there would be no distinction between the liberated and the bound. Therefore, their doctrine is untenable. Consequently, the Lord alone is the cause of the world. Thus ends

It should be understood here that even for an insentient cause of the world, the superintendence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by a sentient being would have to be established; this is the point. (Maṇi., pp. 51–53). As for the Sāṅkhyas: the view of the atheistic Sāṅkhya—that the independent *pradhāna* is the cause of the world—is that there is no Puruṣa who is an agent, but only an enjoyer.

However, it was stated merely that [the qualities] would have to be established; it was not intended to mean that the independent Lord (*īśvara*), consisting of the *guṇas*—*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—is conceived as the unmanifest *pradhāna*, *prakṛti*, and so forth, in the form of the *mahat* and the rest.
Parimala (on BS 2.1.7.41) states that [the Sāṅkhyas] say that the evolved great elements (*mahābhūta*) initiate the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

Ratnākara, in the refutation of the objections regarding the lack of connection raised by the Buddhists and others against the negation of the *pradhāna* and other principles imagined by the Sāṅkhyas and others, states in verse 87: "If it is argued that there is a confusion of application due to the superimposition of pleasure, pain, and delusion [upon the self], we say: no."

Or rather, the Sāṅkhyas consider *pradhāna*—which consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* and is characterized by delusion—to be the cause of the world. (Sāṅkhya Kārikā 1.4.12–13, p.
359; Su., p. 131). As for the followers of the Sāṅkhya with God (*seśvara-sāṅkhya*), [the text] refutes their non-dualist position that *prakṛti* alone is the creator.

If [it is argued that] the followers of the Upaniṣads are subverters [of truth], because they maintain that the ripening [of karma] is inexhaustible due to the persistence of attachment, aversion, and clinging—characterized by ignorance regarding the unity of the Self—then how is this so? We reply: it is not through such characteristics that we speak. Rather, we speak by taking as our basis the Lord (Īśvara), who is all-pervasive, denoted by the word "Puruṣa," and free from such distinctions.
For in common usage, the term "distinction" (vailakṣaṇya) is well-known to refer to difference and the like.
They say that He creates the world through the sequence beginning with Mahat and Ahaṃkāra.
For instance, speakers say of things that are very similar, "There is no difference whatsoever between this and that," yet even that is not the case. (Maṇi, pp.

51–53). Likewise, this same process applies to selves—whether they be humans, animals, or gods—who exist within distinct bodies as manifestations of the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth; having set aside their connection with the body, primordial nature (prakṛti) transforms solely in its own essential form.

For instance, when Nature (prakṛti) is examined through the intellect (buddhi)—which is denoted by the term "the Great" (mahat)—it does not transform into any form whatsoever, even as subtle as the duality of two atoms.

Furthermore, there is a distinct difference between the Great Principle and the ego (ahaṃkāra); it is with this intention that the doctrines of unity and the doctrines denying plurality [are established].
Likewise, from the ego arise the five subtle elements (tanmātras), and thus there are doctrines denying [the existence of] smell, taste, form, touch, and sound.

It is precisely with this intention that the following statement of the Blessed One was made: "The wise look with an equal eye upon a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and even an outcaste. Thus, there are eleven sense-faculties (*indriya*): five faculties of cognition consisting of sight, touch, taste, hearing, and smell; and [six] faculties of action... [the text continues].
Thus [it is said].

And the organs are the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech, which perform the functions of excretion, procreation, grasping, locomotion, and speaking; likewise, the mind is common to all. Furthermore, as it is said: "By means of his powers of illusion (māyā), the Person (puruṣa) assumes various forms.
And the mind is common [to all].

The subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the gross elements (*bhūta*), such as earth and the rest, are themselves devoid of distinct characteristics; yet, through the power of their conjunction with the five [subtle elements] in due order, the Self—though itself undifferentiated—is perceived by delusion as having various distinct forms, such as the bodies of humans, animals, and so forth. This means that [the Self appears as] earth from the conjunction of all five, water from four, fire from three, air from two, and [space] from one.

And those who claim that liberated *kṣetrajñas* (knowers of the field) go to the sky together with *Miśra*— as well as those who maintain doctrines of unity such as "Prakṛti consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion"— they too [are incorrect], because there is an absolute state of difference [between them and the liberated] due to transformation.

The Puruṣa is distinct from those. Thus they say: "The root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) and the seven principles beginning with Mahat are both natures and modifications (prakṛtivikṛtayaḥ); the group of sixteen is modification only; and the Puruṣa is the agent, the Lord, the source of Brahman. And so another Śruti says: "When the seer beholds the golden-hued one, the maker of light, the immortal, the lord, the Puruṣa who is the source of Brahman."
Then the wise one, having shaken off both merit and sin through the realization of Sāṃkhya, and being stainless, attains the supreme state of equality.
Thus, this demonstrates that the liberated one attains indeed the state of identity with the Lord.
Likewise, it was said by the Blessed Vāsudeva: "Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature;
even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer."
As for the statement of the Blessed One, "In the world of living beings, a portion of My very self becomes the eternal individual soul," that refers to His status as the Lord.

Just as ministers are designated as portions of the king, so too the individual soul (jīva) is said to be a portion of the Lord (īśvara). Because this [soul] perishes through the destruction of its state as a soul, its eternity is untenable. As for those [scriptural passages] such as: "When ignorance, which produces differentiation, has gone to absolute destruction..."
Who will create this non-existent distinction between the self and Brahman?
The meaning of such Purāṇic statements is precisely this:
the difference between the individual soul (*āraman*) and Brahman—which is entirely non-existent—is caused by ignorance; when ignorance is destroyed, that difference dissolves of its own accord.

Indeed, the distinction between the higher and lower persons (*puruṣa*) is clearly demonstrated in the *Gītā* and other texts: "But the Supreme Person is another, declared as the Supreme Self" (*uttamaḥ puruṣastvanyaḥ paramātmetyudāhṛtaḥ*); and "The witness, the permitter, the agent (the sustainer), the enjoyer, the Great Lord."
And he is also called the Supreme Self (paramātman), the supreme person within this body.
Thus it is said.
Enough of going too far.
(Because this has not been refuted, this critique of the Advaita view composed by the Sāṃkhya would indeed be in agreement with Pārthasārathi.)

The Sāṃkhya doctrine and the refutation of its principles: The Sāṃkhyas maintain that there is a plurality of selves (*ātman*) and that the world is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Sāṃkhya is twofold: that which is without a Lord (nirīśvara) and that which is with a Lord (seśvara).

Those who maintain the doctrine of no Lord say this: "Prakṛti is insentient, composed of the three guṇas, and designated by the term 'pradhāna'; it transforms into the form of the manifold world, from the mahat down to the specific elements, for the sake of the experience of sentient beings.
Those who maintain the doctrine of a Lord also say this.

However, there is this much distinction: the Puruṣa, as the subject of cognition, relies upon the Lord—who is untouched by afflictions, karma, its fruition, or latent dispositions—and thus Nature creates the world.

For just as a seed, presiding over a cultivated field, initiates a great tree through the sequence of sprouts and so forth by virtue of its contact with that field, so too Nature, which is all-pervasive, presides over the all-pervasive Lord and, by virtue of its contact with Him, undergoes transformation through the sequence of the Great Principle (mahat), ego (ahaṃkāra), the elements, and so on, initiating the manifold universe up to the level of specific objects.
This very view is generally held even in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas:
this creation has primordial nature (prakṛti) as its material cause (upādāna), while the Lord (īśvara) is merely the efficient cause (nimitta-mātra);
the individual souls (kṣetrajñas) are the enjoyers.
Prakṛti alone is the object of action for all effects; thus, she is the object of enjoyment.
And she is one and the same for all.
Yet, because of the difference among the enjoyers, the distinction between the bound and the liberated is logically established.

And likewise: "The one unborn [Self], red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form—another unborn [Self] lies beside her, enjoying her; yet another unborn [Self] leaves her once she has been enjoyed."

Thus, it has been clearly shown that there is oneness of *prakṛti*—the object of experience—which consists of the forms of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*; and that the distinction between the bound and the liberated is established due to the diversity of the experiencers (*bhoktṛ*).
Therefore, since this creation of the manifold world has *prakṛti* as its material cause (*upādāna*), there is no perception of a [creation] occurring without a material cause.
(Now, the refutation: To this, it is replied:
How indeed does a single, uniform primordial nature (*prakṛti*) give rise to the manifold world (*prapañca*), which is divided into the distinctions of humans, animals, and beasts?
For an effect that is non-distinct [in its cause] cannot produce an effect that is distinct.

If it is argued that this diversity arises through the coexistence of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) residing in the individual knower (*kṣetrajña*), we say no; for merit and demerit are functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Furthermore, since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is included within the category of effects, and because all effects beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) dissolve into primordial nature (*prakṛti*) during the reabsorption into nature (the dissolution of all things into *prakṛti*), merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) are likewise non-existent in that state; thus, variety cannot arise through their power.

And what is the cause of this [nature] producing transformations such as the Great Principle? If you say it is its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), then there would be the consequence of production occurring at all times; consequently, dissolution would be impossible.

If it is argued that [the order of creation] is modified by the will of Īśvara, we say no; for in Īśvara, who is free from all afflictions (*kleśa*) and has cast aside all desires, the existence of will is impossible.
Furthermore, since will is a property of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it cannot exist at that time [of dissolution].

Moreover, during the elemental dissolution (*prākṛta-pralaya*), only primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the pure Self (*ātman*) remain, and all selves (*ātman*) are without distinction, because they consist solely of the nature of pure consciousness (*caitanya*).

Furthermore, no differentiation among selves caused by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) is possible, because those two are not attributes of the self, since they reside in the functioning of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and that [organ] is absent at that time.

Thus, if it is argued that at the time of creation, *prakṛti* binds the selves to the commencement of a body while they remain undifferentiated and devoid of merit and demerit, then she would bind all of them—both those who were liberated in a previous creation and those who were not—since there is no distinction between them.

Likewise, for all those who, having performed the Aśvamedha and experienced its fruit, remained in a previous creation, as well as for those who committed the killing of a Brahmin (brahmahatyā), their status would be of one and the same kind, due to the distinction between the merit and demerit previously performed. Now, [the opponent objects: "Destruction does not mean absolute non-existence, but rather the mere concealment of effects within their cause—this is the doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas; likewise, origination is also merely the manifestation of things already existing. (Sāṃkhya-kārikā 9). 4257 [This is the view of] the Sāṃkhyas.
In the cause, there is merely the manifestation of effects;

for the production of that which is absolutely non-existent is impossible, because it would follow that even a rabbit’s horn could be produced. Furthermore, if the non-existent were seen [as the cause], everything would exist everywhere and there would be no restriction, such as "cloth from threads" or "a jar from clay. As they have said: "Because of the non-production of the non-existent, because of the selection of a material cause, because of the absence of the possibility of everything [arising] from everything..."
Because that which is capable produces only that which it is capable of producing, and because of this causal principle, the effect exists [in the cause].
Thus it is said;
likewise, there is the statement of the Blessed Lord: "The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being."
Therefore, since dharma and the other factors exist in a potential state during the dissolution, the diversity of creation is logically consistent with their perception.
This is not so;
for potness does not exist in the state of a lump of clay or in the state of potsherds, as this contradicts what is observed.
As for the statement, "The being of the non-existent is not found," that refers to the Self (ātman).
For it was stated previously: "Never indeed was I not, nor you, nor these lords of men;
and yet we shall all certainly not cease to be hereafter."
By this, that which was already begun to demonstrate the impermanence of "it" (the effect) is stated:

there is no arising of a non-existent self, nor is there destruction of an existent one; all selves indeed possess the nature of being neither produced nor destroyed, and are eternal. However, it has been said that this does not mean that the entire class of effects is merely eternally manifest, because [such a view] would entail a lack of omnipresence and contradict the fact of non-perception. At most, if one relies on the non-difference between the material cause and the effect, it might be said that the jar existed at the outset in the form of the clay; yet even by that much, the production of an effect is not established.
For water cannot be carried by a jar made of clay that is soft;

likewise, even though merit and demerit exist in their own nature and abide as the essence of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), they are not sufficient for their own manifestation, and thus the possibility of diversity does not arise from them.

Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the transformation of primordial matter into the Great One (*mahat*) and the rest, because the words of the Puruṣa do not fall within the scope of other means of valid cognition, and there is an absence of such other means of valid cognition.
The Vedas also lack authority because they are the product of human agency, like the speech of any other person.

However, if one accepts the succession of creation and dissolution as beginningless, then at every creation [it is held that]: "In the beginning, he fashioned for all beings their respective names, actions, and distinct conditions from the words of the Veda alone."

Although the authority [of the Vedas] is accepted by relying on their eternity—based on such statements as "and so forth," which establish the reality of the usage of names and powers through the logic of the conch and its mark (śaṅkhaliṅga-nyāya), whereby words and the Vedas possess an eternal relationship with their meanings—nevertheless, if a single Prajāpati were the originator of the tradition, the suspicion that they are artificial (kṛtaka) would certainly arise.

Furthermore, if one were to dispel the suspicion that [the Veda] is a product by establishing its eternity—relying on the fact that many great seers (*maharṣi*) who, in accordance with such statements as "eighty-eight thousand transmitters of the tradition," possessed the Veda studied in a previous creation and acted as transmitters of the tradition according to the maxim of "waking from sleep"—nevertheless, it remains impossible to accept the creation of the world without a material cause (*upādāna*).

Bhaṭṭa: When there is a deliberation as to whether the Agnihotra should be performed at its own time upon the postponement of the Sāṃtapanīyā—which is being performed at midday—due to an obstacle arising from either divine or human causes, [the conclusion is] that it should not be postponed. Because if it were performed at its own time, there would be the possibility of re-consecrating the fire (agni) that was previously brought forward for the sake of the Sāṃtapanīyā; thus, a deficiency (vaiguṇya) would arise through the omission of the consecration accompanied by mantras. Furthermore, since the time is subordinate to the ritual act (padārtha-guṇa) and serves as a qualification for the injunction of performance, and because it is understood as occurring subsequent [to the primary act], there is no deficiency even if it is omitted; therefore, there should be a postponement.

This being the case, since time is not something to be adopted [as a primary factor], and because in the case of a compulsory (*nitya*) rite, the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) must be adopted according to one's capacity—as will be explained in the sixth book (6.1.1)—it is more logical that the time should be accommodated even by omitting the *praṇayana* (the carrying forward of the fire). Furthermore, the evening and morning times are even more worthy of accommodation, as they function as specific qualifications for the occasion (*nimitta*), namely, the state of being alive.

In reality, however, since it is established in the context of the *darśa* and other rites that the *agnihotra* does not incur a defect (*vaiguṇya*) even when its dependence on the assistance generated by the *praṇayana* from another source is absent, there is no deficiency even if the *praṇayana* is omitted.
Therefore, having performed the Agnihotra at its own proper time, the Sāṃtapanīyā must be performed; thus, no regard need be paid to the sequence of the Sāṃtapanīyā injunctions.
And here, "Sāṃtapanīyā" is an elliptical expression for any rite that has been commenced, while "Agnihotra" is likewise an elliptical expression for whatever is obligatory.

This is because there is a prohibition regarding the non-consecutive performance of rites: "That which is performed when the ritual framework (*tantra*) of one [rite] has been extended while the framework of another is already spread out is indeed cut off from the sacrifice.

Nor does it follow that, even if the *anīkavat* sacrifice is postponed, the *sāṃtapanīyā* would consequently fall on the midday; for if that were the case, since the *sāṃtapanīyā* must occur immediately after the *anīkavat*, the postponement of the carrying forward of the fire (*praṇayana*) would necessarily interrupt the performance. Therefore, it is better to suspend only the single factor of the midday time.

The Sāmans: *anuṣṭup*, *abhīvarta*, *ānvīgava*, *āmahīyava*, *auśana*, *kārpaṇa*, *kāleya*, *kāva*, *kautsa*, the *krauñca*s, *gāyatra*, *naudhasa*, *pauṣpala*, *yajñayajñīya*, *yaudhājaya*, *rathaṃtara*, *raurava*, *vāmadevya*, the body of the *janitra* of Vasiṣṭha—these are the *āvaśya*s; as well as the *śloka*, the *saṃhita*, and the *sapka*. (Vi. 9.2.6, varṇaka 2–4; 10.4.6, 9, 10, 11). A Sāman should be sung upon a single sentence that is complete in its meaning.
Regarding this, the Śabara-ācāryas say: "The chanting should be performed verse by verse.
Even in cases where the chanting is applied to half-verses (*ardharca*), the chanting must be performed upon the verse itself. An incomplete sentence constitutes an 'half-verse'."
"But in the case of the *ṛc*, it is completed [in the verse-quarter].
This means that in the case of those [hymns] sung by quarter-verses, the singing must be performed on the quarter-verse itself;
for it is on the quarter-verse alone that that sentence is complete.

Just as in the case of "Goṣṭha" and "Vāsiṣṭha," which are two *sāmans* [named after sages], so too should a *sāman* be brought to completion over as much [of the verse] as constitutes a complete sentence. In some cases, a complete sentence occurs within a quarter-verse (*pāda*), and in others, even within a whole verse (*ṛc*). In some instances, it occurs below [the verse].
Regarding the Sāmans (4276): "The Sāmans [are] from the Sāman; some say the Sāmans are the Mantras, because of tradition and instruction.

Is the Sāman the chanted mantra-text, or is the Sāman merely the melody? In this discussion—which serves as a preliminary reminder for the sake of establishing the subsequent deliberation—the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Some consider that the *mantras* which are chanted are the *sāmans*,
based on both traditional recollection (*smṛti*) and instruction (*upadeśa*).
For the students of the Vedas (*chāndasa*) indeed record in their tradition that "a *sāman* is a *mantra*-sentence that has been chanted."
"O Aghnyā, protect for me the mantra which the seers know as the Knower;
[it consists of] the Ṛcs, the Sāmans, and the Yajus"—such is the nature of the mantra, and there is also the instruction that "the Sāmans [are so called].
Therefore, based on both this traditional authority (smṛti) and the scriptural instruction, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that the chanted mantras are the Sāmans.

Alternatively, in the inquiry as to whether the *ūha-sāmans* are eternal and authorless (*apauruṣeya*) or non-eternal and authored by humans, some maintain that they are authorless, consisting of mantras, eternal, and revealed by seers (*ārṣa*).

This is because of both traditional recollection (*smṛti*) and instruction (*upadeśa*): from the traditional recollection that "these are mantras; these are revealed by seers and are eternal," and from the instruction in the Brāhmaṇa texts stating, "the *ūha* is intended to be performed."
And "that which is intended to be done" (cikīrṣita) here means "this [world].
Furthermore, if this were of human origin, it would not be a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Therefore, the prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa) is that it must be inferred as eternal.
That is the refutation of that [objection]. That which was stated by the proponent—that "the Ṛks are the Sāmans"—is the refutation of that; the fault regarding that is "that refutation of that."

If the *ṛc* were the *sāman*, the injunction regarding the *ṛc*—namely, "He sings the *rathaṃtara* in the *akavatī* verses"—would be untenable; it would result in either a designation of location (*deśalakṣaṇā*) or a designation of property (*dharmalakṣaṇā*). This has been stated [at 7.2.1.13]. Therefore, the *sāmans* are melodies (*gītayaḥ*), not the already-chanted mantra-texts.
This is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Alternatively, as for what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*)—that the modification (*ūha*) is eternal and so forth—that statement of yours actually points out its own defect; the defect of that position is stated by your very words.
Your statement is that "the modification (ūha) is what is intended to be performed. For the suffix *san* is prescribed when there is a desire;
if something is desired to be done, then it is performed.
Therefore, Āditya’s rebuttal is as follows:
As for what was stated— that Smṛti is eternal— that Smṛti is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
for its basis is indeed perceived.

For there is indeed the statement, "He sings the Rathantara on the Kavatī verses. From this scriptural statement of extended application (atideśa), there first arises a cognition based on scripture that it must be sung in this manner according to the logical principle.
From that, this [subsequent] recollection arises.
Therefore, modification (ūha) is artificial.
It is invalid. Therefore, when there is a contradiction with logic, it lacks authority;
this is the established conclusion (siddhānta).

The *sāmans* are: Rathantara, Bṛhat, Vairūpa, Vairāja, Śākvara, Raivata, Naiśoka, Gāyatra, Āmahīyava, Raurava, Yaudhājaya, Auśana, Vāmadevya, Naudhasa, Kāliya, Saṃhita, Dyāvāśama, Āndhīgava, Sapha, Pauṣkala, Kāya, Yaśāyaśīya, Simā, Santani, Yataya, Evāgapatya, and Śākaravarṇa.
Sāmans).
The *rathaṃtara*, *bṛhat*, *vairūpa*, *vairāja*, *śākvara*, and *raivata*—these *sāmans* are sung in sequence on the six days of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* occurring within the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice (Vi.
10.6.13). In the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the *pṛṣṭha* stotra is accomplished by means of a single *sāman*.
In the modified form (the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* of the Gavamayana), it should also be accomplished by means of one [day] alone, in order to favor the extended injunction (*codaka*).
It should be praised with equality alone. (Bhāṣya 10.6.13)
Only a verse that has been chanted (pragītā) possesses the status of being a means for the new transcendental result (apūrva) of the modified sacrifice.
Now, there might be this argument: "It would be a ritual procedure (kalpa), because the two [Vedas] have that as their purpose.

The Commentary states: In a certain specific rite it is heard: "They praise with the Ṛk," "They praise with the Sāman," "When they praise with the Ṛk, the Asuras followed after that; when they praise with the Sāman, the Asuras did not follow after that.
One who knows thus should praise with the Sāman."
In this matter, the meaning is subject to doubt. What, then, is the prima facie position? It is that there is an option: either with a *ṛc* or with a *sāman*.
This appears to be a distinct sentence: "When they praise with a *ṛc*, the Asuras followed after it."
When the praise is being performed with a *ṛc*, the Asuras followed along;
we see that the sentence is complete at this point. This is mentioned for this purpose: namely, so that it may be understood that one should praise with a *ṛc*.

For what purpose? So that it may apply to that specific ritual action in which it is heard. Because of its functional capacity, it is understood from the statement of performance. But is it not a censure because of the mention of "Asuras"? No, he says.
We do not know whether the Asuras are those who censure or those who do not censure;
this is because their duty [to praise] is established through the mention [of the act].
Thus, "They praise with the Sāman" is a separate sentence.
Therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*).
Since both the *ṛc* and the *sāman* serve the purpose of praise, each has the same function.
For since praise is accomplished, it is achieved by either one; thus, there is an option.
It should be praised with either a *ṛc* verse or a *sāman* chant.
Why? Because it occurs in both cases.
If an injunction for the *sāman* were heard, then, by postulating some form of censure [of the *ṛc*], there would be syntactic unity with the praise of the *sāmans*.
But no injunctive [word] is heard.
Therefore, it must be assumed that the injunctive element exists in both cases through the praise alone.
[Objection: But surely a censure is heard in the *ṛc*.
It is said:
Why is this the opposite?
It is because the *ṛc* is thus beautiful that even the Asuras, though they had never been there before, come there.
The application [of the Sāman] would be by virtue of the scriptural statement.
The Commentary says: This is not so; it is not a case of option (vikalpa).
The application of the Sāman would indeed be [determined] by the statement.

Why? Because there is a statement that enjoins it: "When they praise with the *ṛk*, the Asuras followed after; when they praise with the *sāman*, the Asuras did not follow after. He who, knowing thus, praises with the *sāman*... Thus, praise by means of the *sāman* is extolled by an explicit statement of praise. The other [interpretation] would be a mere assumption (*kalpā*): "The Asuras followed when praising with the *ṛk*; therefore, one should praise with the *ṛk*."

If, on the other hand, the *sāman* is praised for its own sake, then the statement, "When they praise with the *ṛc*, the Asuras followed after that," would be a censure of the other [the *ṛc*], and nothing [further] would need to be imagined.
How is it understood that this is a statement of censure? From the fact that it is a statement praising the other.
Therefore, one should praise by means of the *sāman* alone.

Regarding the injunction for praise with the *Sāman*—namely, "They praise with the *Sāman*"—this forms a single syntactical unit with the censure of the Asuras' failure to arrive, expressed by the phrase "When they praise with the *Ṛk*. By means of the censure of the Asuras' arrival, this [injunction] attains syntactic unity with the *Sāman*. Otherwise, the other [phrase] would be a censure; thus, one would have to construct two separate sentences by assuming that the censure [of the *Ṛk*] is intended as a praise for what is being censured.
Furthermore, two unseen results (adṛṣṭa) must be postulated because there are two distinct sentences;
nor can the meaning of the sentences be reversed, since they are heard in connection with the Sāmans in the concluding passage: "He who, knowing thus, praises with the Sāman."

In certain specific modifications (*vikṛti*), some non-archetypal (*aprākṛta*) hymns (*stotra*) are prescribed. For these, some means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*).

This is because the archetypal *Sāmans*—such as the *Gāyatra* and *Rathantara*, which are fixed to the archetypal *Bahiṣpavamāna* and other praises—are to be applied to those non-archetypal [hymns]; therefore, those [non-archetypal hymns] directly require them.

Regarding this, it is heard in scripture: "When they praise with the *ṛc*, the Asuras follow after that; when they praise with the *sāman*, the Asuras do not follow after that; therefore, one who knows thus should praise with the *sāman*.
In this context, the mention of the *ṛc* refers to the *ṛc* that is not chanted (*apragīta*), because the *ṛc* that is already chanted is established by the very instruction regarding the *sāman*.
For praise is performed by means of the manifestation of the syllables through the *sāman*, not directly.
Therefore, the injunction "one should praise with the *sāman*" means that one should praise by means of the syllables of the *ṛc* through the manifestation of the *sāman*.
If this is so, then the mention of the *ṛc* refers to it in its non-chanted form.

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the hymn be chanted with either the *ṛc* or the *sāman*, or with the *sāman* alone? Since both are mentioned, an option (*vikalpa*) might be presumed; however, it is said in reply:

because the *sāman* is understood to be the enjoined element through its explicit praise in the concluding portion, the mention of the *ṛc*—which is censured by the arrival of the Asuras—is for the purpose of praising the *sāman*.
Therefore, one should praise with the *sāman* alone. [Objection: As before, it is argued that here too there is an option (*vikalpa*). [Response: The connection is as follows:
Is the praise performed by means of both the *ṛc* and the *sāman* optionally, or by the *sāman* alone? This is the point of doubt.
Not so, for this is not the case, since the purpose [of the passage] is to express the lack of praise for the disparagement of clay.

Bhaṭṭa: In the Sāmaveda, various modalities of a single *sāman*—which consists of a collection of musical notes—are traditionally taught according to differences in branches (*śākhā*), such as ascending and descending scales; this is like the different modes of a single melody according to regional variations.

Since these modalities serve the same purpose of singing, their optionality (*vikalpa*) is established by the very nature of the injunction, just as in the case of rice and barley. Or rather, in certain specific modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), some non-original (*aprākṛta*) hymns (*stotra*) are prescribed.

Furthermore, in those [sacrifices], there is no application of the ordinary *ṛks* of the *rathantara* and other *sāmans* for the purpose of spreading the sacrificial posts (*yūpa-vātāstarana*), because they are restricted specifically to the original (*prākṛta*) stotras.

Regarding their performance, this is heard in scripture: "When they praise with an *ṛk*, the Asuras follow after; when they praise with a *sāman*, the Asuras do not follow after. Therefore, one who knows thus should praise with a *sāman*.
In that context, the word *ṛk* refers to an *ṛk* that is not chanted (*apragīta*).
Because that which has already been chanted is obtained solely through the injunction for the *sāman*,

and it is not possible for a *sāman* to serve as a basis for a hymn (*stotra*) and so forth without being supported by an *ṛc*. Since the hymns are devoid of meaning, it is impossible for the *nūka-sāmans* supported by them to function as the basis for a hymn in the form of an injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*).

Therefore, regarding the deliberation as to whether the means [of accomplishment] consists of a choice between chanted and non-chanted *ṛc*s, or only of the chanted one, [the conclusion is reached]: because the final *sākalya* (completeness) and the word *yat* are appropriate, and because it is an injunction of the *sāman*,

and because the *leṭ* (subjunctive) is determined by the fact that the initial [use] of the *sāman* alone has not been previously established, there is an injunction for both the *ṛk* and the *sāman*.
In effect, this is an alternative view establishing that they have an identical purpose.

Nor can it be argued that there is no injunction for them because the *ṛks* are censured by the arrival of the four [other classes], for without being part of a single syntactical unit with a prohibition, the status of "censure" itself would not even be established.

Therefore, since even the *ṛks*, which are extremely difficult to propitiate, are brought under control, this constitutes a praise of the [mantra] precisely because it is a sentence prescribing [their use].

This being the position reached, in order to avoid defects such as syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), unequal injunction (*viṣamaśiṣṭa*), and option (*vikalpa*), it follows that even the optative suffix (*liṅ*) associated with the word *yat* is the enjoiner of the *sāman*, and not the two [suffixes] which are ambiguous due to their being in the *leṭ* mood.
Thus, this praise pertains to the *sāman* alone.

Even the censure of the *ṛc* is, according to the maxim "no censure without praise" (*na hi nindā*), intended solely for the purpose of praising the enjoined *sāman*; therefore, the means of accomplishment is the *sāman* itself when it is chanted (*pragīta*).
Furthermore, regarding this legal topic (*adhikaraṇa*), where a *sāman* is to be applied to a different hymn (*stotra*), its source-verse (*yoni*) is not recited in that very place;
for otherwise, since the status of the *sāman* and the verses as subsidiaries would be established through context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, the injunction of the *sāman* would be redundant.
Therefore, in the present example, because the singular number is employed in the phrase "with the *sāman*" (*sāmnā*), it follows that there is only one *sāman*, such as from the Sāmaveda.
And in that context, the *ṛc* is indeed the source.

According to the principle of the rule for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and *āvāhana* offerings—namely, "one *sāman* is made upon a single [verse]," "that which he sings on a different verse," and so forth—the [application] belongs only to the original (*prākṛta*) [verse], because there is no mention of the non-original (*aprākṛta*) [verse] as the object of reference.

Due to the requirement of the qualities such as the fourfold *stoma* of the original, there is the commencement of that many [repetitions] of that very same single *ṛc* which has been chanted (*pragītā*).

But surely, in such cases where a *yoni* verse and its subsequent verses (*uttarā*) are recited within the context of another non-archetypal (*aprākṛta*) stotra, there would be no authority for applying the *sāman* to those subsequent verses. Furthermore, where another stotra is introduced by means of a name (*saṃjñā*) and so forth, and neither the verses are recited in that context nor is there an injunction for the *sāman* as in the present example, then since it is impossible for that passage to be an injunction for a stotra, there would likewise be no authority for bringing in the *sāman*, even if the verses were brought in.

If it is argued that, because a *stotra* consists precisely in the designation of the qualities of a mantra recited with singing, the injunction for a *stotra* would otherwise be untenable and thus implies the *Sāman*, and consequently, since that same *Sāman* is obtained here as well, the injunction "one should praise with a *Sāman*" (*sāmnā stuvīta*) is redundant; [we reply: this is not so, because the injunction "one should praise with a *Sāman*" is studied independently (*anāramyādhīta*). Since it cannot be applied to the archetype (*prakṛti*) due to its lack of purpose there, it is logical that it serves as an injunction for the *Sāman* in all *vikṛti* (modified) sacrifices where the *stotra* is non-archetypal (*aprākṛta*).

According to the writings of the Bhāṣyakāra and others, because this [term] is read within a specific section concerning modifications (*vikṛti*), it should be understood that this is not actually an injunction for the *Sāman* itself; rather, it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to support the technical usage (*yājñika-prasiddhi*) which determines the meaning of the word "stotra," or it serves the purpose of enjoining a non-original (*aprākṛta*) stotra, or for the purpose of enjoining the singular number.
Maṇḍana states: "The stotra is performed by means of the *Sāman* alone. Śaṃkara states: "That which begins with 'śaṃ' is the praise (*stuti*)."
13. *Sāmabhiḥ*: By means of the *sāmans*, there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) *sāmans* through the use of unqualified mantra-texts.
Bhāṣya 10.4.10.20: "At the Vājapeya sacrifice, one gives a chariot equipped with *sāmans* to the Udgātṛ priest, and neither another [gift] nor to anyone else.
10.3.12.75: Regarding *sāmabhiḥ*: by those *sāmans* prescribed for the Viṣṭut-stomas in the ritual, there is the absence of the archetypal *sāmans*.
The application of the term *sāman* by way of a denotative word follows its own traditional usage.

It is now considered what exactly is expressed by the word *rathaṃtara* in such injunctions as "He sings the *rathaṃtara* on the [first] two [verses]" (*rathaṃtaram uttarayor gāyati*) and "He sings the *rathaṃtara* on the *kavatī* verses" (*kavatīṣu rathaṃtaraṃ gāyati*).

Although it was established in the rule "The designation *sāman* applies to the melodies" (*gītiṣu sāmākhyā*) that words such as *rathaṃtara* denote the melody (*gīti*), nevertheless, this is investigated once again for the sake of clarity, according to the maxim of "driving a wedge into a post" (*sthūṇānikhanananyāya*).
In that regard, the first prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), which is independent of the sūtra, holds that the term *rathaṃtara* and others denote the individual *ṛc* verses alone.
Considering this position to be untenable, the sūtra states the second prima facie view.

The term *sāman* is applied by its designating words—such as *rathantara*, *bṛhat*, and so forth—in accordance with how it was handed down; that is, without deviating from how it was taught to disciples, the application of words like *rathantara* occurs according to that traditional transmission.

The word *sāman* is employed by experts to denote a *ṛc* (verse) that possesses specific *stoma*, accent (*svara*), time (*kāla*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), and modifications (*vikāra*), and which includes the *haṃkāra*, *praṇava*, *prastāva*, *udgītha*, *pratihāra*, *upadrava*, and *nidhana*.
Therefore, it is precisely that [the verse] which is called *sāman*.
"Because it is a designation based on either the word itself or its meaning, there would be no application [of the term] to anything else, since the connection belongs specifically to the action.
This refutes the position stated in the preceding sūtra—that the word *rathantara* and others apply to a *ṛc* (verse) qualified by its specific *stoma* (hymn-form) and so forth.
The word "but" (*tu*) indicates precisely this rejection of that position.
The meaning is "by means of words [expressing] words.
The instrumental case used for the sense of the genitive is a Vedic (sautrī) usage.

Because the meanings of words are manifold, because they are intent upon the various forms of meaning, and because they are intent upon the expression of meaning, the word *rathantara* denotes the *ṛk* verse known as the *abhivatī*, namely "abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ."
Furthermore, because of the injunction, "One sings the Rathantara on the *kavatī* verses," it must be sung upon the verse beginning with "kayā naś citra ābhuvat";
however, this particular verse expresses a different meaning.
And [the word] "abhivatī" expresses something else;
therefore, there would be no application to another meaning, because it is impossible to say that it expresses the object through its fruit.
It would instead apply to another meaning.
Because of their distinctness and because of the difference in meaning between the *kavatī* verses and the *abhivatī* verses,
an extension (*atideśa*) of the *kavatī* verses to the function of the *abhivatī* verses is not tenable.
Therefore, this statement, "He sings the *rathaṃtara* on the *kavatī* verses," is not an extension of a function.
Nor can it be said that the *abhivatī* possesses the quality of being a *kavatī*, because they are distinct entities.
For a word does not inhere in another word; rather, each remains separate.

Therefore, in the injunction "he sings the *rathantara* on the *kavatīs*," since the action—the act of singing—is connected with the word *rathantara*, the sense is that "whatever giving [of praise] occurs in the *abhivatī*, that should be performed on the *kavatīs*. Consequently, words such as *rathantara* do not apply to the *ṛc* (verse) itself.
The word *rathantara* and others do not denote the *ṛc* (verse).
However, if the reading is "in the action" (*kriyāyām*), the meaning is that the words *rathantara* and so forth are connected to the action—that is, the act of singing.
Alternatively, they may be used in their own primary sense; for there would be a purpose for the action [of singing] insofar as they are taught as being subordinate members (*aṅga*) of it.
By the word "or" (vā), an alternative view is proposed:

in the case of the statement, "One sings the Rathantara on the *kavatī* verses," the *abhivatī* verses might be taught as being subordinate to the *kavatī* verses—that is, as their constituent parts—while they are currently present [in the ritual].
In that case, the purpose would be an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) merit.
This means "because of being an action" (*kriyātva*). For an action indeed has a purpose;
and the recitation of the *ṛc* is an action.
Since an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭa*) would have to be postulated, this position is also not tenable.
If it is argued that it is "mere sound" (*śabdamātra*), [we reply]:

in the case of the statement, "He sings the *rathaṃtara* on the *kavatī* verses," if the word *rathaṃtara* does not denote the mere *ṛc* verse, nor denote the *ṛc* verse as qualified by its specific melody and so forth, nor even denote the absence of the *abhivatīs* and the presence of the *kavatis*, then it would indeed be mere sound.

If it is argued that the meaning of the sentence would be that the word "Rathantara" should be employed in the *kavati* verses beginning with "kayā naś citra ābhuvat," and thus only the word itself is being enjoined; [we reply:]...
Because [the relationship] is innate.

As for the statement that the word *rathantara* should be applied to the *kavatī* verses—beginning with "kayā naścitra ābhuvat"—in accordance with the injunction "he sings the *rathantara* upon the *kavatīs*," that is not correct;
because the relationship between a name (*saṃjñā*) and its bearer (*saṃjñin*) is innate, established by origin, and beginningless.
Furthermore, the word *rathaṃtara* cannot be applied to the *kavatī* verses, because there is no connection between the two;
otherwise, the scripture would be rendered meaningless.
The position stated in the sūtra, "If it be argued that it is merely a word" (7.2.1.4), has been refuted by the sūtra, "Because it is not innate" (7.2.1.5).
For that very purpose, this sūtra is also [stated].

Likewise, under the view that "there is the employment of the mere word," the scripture would be useless; the extended application (atideśa) scripture stating "one sings the Rathantara on the kavatī verses" would be rendered meaningless because it would be impossible to carry out.
However, the commentator Upavarṣa held that "the scripture regarding singing would be purposeless in its literal sense."
The intention of this [Bhāṣya] is as follows: "When a [viable] course exists, it is not reasonable for the learned to accept such a great effort as being fruitless.

The author of the Sūtras uses the word *ca* (and) in order to add another reason for the refutation of the position that [the accentuation] is merely verbal (*śabdamātra*). [An objection is raised: "But what about the tone (*svara*)?"

Regarding the statement, "One sings the Rathantara on the *kavatī* verses," what is the meaning of the word *rathantara*? The fifth position (*pakṣa*) is stated here: that the meaning of the sentence is the *ṛk* (verse).
In this sentence, the transfer (*atideśa*) of the musical tone (*svara*) is being expressed.
In common usage, the word *sāman* denotes the musical tone, as in the expression "Devadatta has a beautiful *sāman*," which means Devadatta has a pleasant voice.
"Pitch" (*svara*) and "sound" (*nāda*) are synonymous terms. The *Rathantara* is a *Sāman*.
Therefore, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the *Rathantara* pitch to the *Kavatī* verses beginning with "kayā naścitra ābhuvat."
If this is argued, it is not so; for there is no lack of connection because of the absence of meaning.

In the sentence "He sings the Rathantara on the Kavatis," there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the name of the *rathantara* melody to the *kavati* verses—namely, the verse beginning "kayā naścitra ābhuvat"—and thus there is an extension of the *rathantara* melody to those *kavati* verses.
Because of the absence of the meaning; for the meaning of the *abhivatī* verse, "We praise thee, O Hero," and its specific accent do not exist within the *kavatī* verses,
nor can they be brought about in that manner.
For it is not possible to produce the *abhivat* melody within the *kavatī* verses, nor can the *nāda* be produced within them.

Thus, because the literal meaning of the scriptural reading "he sings the *rathaṃtara* on the *kavatī* verses" would be impossible, there could be no mutual connection between the texts regarding the transfer of musical notes (*svara*).
Consequently, the syntactical unity (*vākya*) would be sublated.
Therefore, there is an extension of the accent;
because in the production of accents, the place of articulation, duration, and phoneme are inseparable.
The word "but" (tu) is used to adopt an alternative position.

If the instruction "he sings the *rathantara* on the *kavatī* verses"—namely, "with the verse beginning 'abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ'" for the *svarasāman* that begins with "abhi," and "with the *kavatī* verses" for [the *sāman*] beginning with "kayā naścitra ābhuvat"—were not to be understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*), then it would be acceptable.
The formulation of the statement would be: "He sings that *rathantara* which is [to be sung] on the *kavatī* verses. It is thus.
The *svara* is the *abhivatīsvara*.
In the productions and utterances of the *kavatī* verses, as well as in the *abhivatī* verses, many measures (*mātrā*) and phonemes (*varṇa*) exist that are undivided and identical.
This very *abhivatīsvara* exists within the *kavatī* verses as inherent in the common phonemes.
This statement, "He sings the Rathantara on the kavatī verses," is a restatement of that very accent;
therefore, it is a restatement of the accent. This is also because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).

Having recited the verses beginning with "abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ," one should then recite the *kavatī* verses beginning with "kayā naścitra ābhuvat. Because there is a similarity in the number of syllables and phonemes, this is a restatement of the *abhivatī* accent found within the *kavatī* verses: "Sing the Rathantara Sāman upon the *kavatī* verses; [it is] among the Sāmans, of the Sāmans."
The two subsequent *ṛc*s are recited in the *Uttarārcika*, the latter book of the Saṃhitā:
"One who has not been taught knows how to cook rice or molasses.

Therefore, a certain *sāman*—even if it is sung upon an *ṛc* that is not its proper source (*ayoni*), i.e., one different from its source—is studied during the time when ritual action is not being performed, because there is no difference in its substratum (*āśraya*).
And thus the Śruti states: "The Bṛhat is performed upon Gāyatrī verses," which is appropriate.
Therefore, according to the view that it is a purificatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*), its performance occurs at a time other than [the primary] ritual action.
Likewise, the Sāman is generally sung upon a triplet (*tṛca*) consisting of verses in the same metre.
It is not meaningless;
such a *sāman* is called "according to the source" (*tathāyoni*).
Furthermore, when a certain *yoni*-verse is sung even though the meter differs from that of the *sāman*, such a *sāman* is called "not according to the source" (*atathāyoni*).

And thus says the Śruti: "He who indeed composes a Sāman in a non-metrical [verse]. This being the case, some [Sāmans] might be without a source (ayonīka); and because some are without a source, the word "Sāman" cannot necessarily be denotative of the Ṛk verse.
Therefore, it is denotative of the song alone.
If it is argued that there is no inconsistency when there is a single purpose,
the proponent objects to what was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the sūtra "And for the sake of grasping the action" (7.2.1.5):
namely, that the singing of the *rathantara* is of one and the same form everywhere.

Furthermore, since the repetition in the verse "abhi tvā śūra" (which belongs to its own source) serves as a forceful reinforcement, and since the two subsequent verses can be employed at the time of performance because they are capable of being chanted, reciting them outside that context is useless.

As it has been said: when the chanting of the *rathantara* is of a single purpose and uniform character, there is no diversity or difference in the chanting of the subsequent [verses]; thus, there is no need to take account of the action intended for the purpose of grasping [the Soma].
Therefore, if it were a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*), its performance at a time other than the ritual action would be entirely meaningless.
If this is argued, [the reply is: there would be the undesirable consequence regarding other matters; thus, it follows by implication that [the practice] pertains to cooking.

Regarding the doubt that because the singing of the *rathantara* is of a single form, once the singing of the *yoni* has been practiced, the performance of the singing of the *uttara* verses at a time other than the ritual action would be useless—the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) states the answer.
There may be a difference in form (*vairūpya*) because the *rathantara* chant is performed on one *ṛc*, yet it is also performed on another;

for even when there is repetition (*abhyāsa*) on a single *ṛc*, if the *rathantara* chant repeated across different verses (*ṛgantara*) were not intended to convey distinct meanings, then its repeated performance across those other verses would be purposeless.
Even though the *rathantara* chant remains uniform in its own nature, if the action varies due to the difference in its substrates (*āśrayabheda*), then the repetition certainly becomes meaningful.
For that purpose, separate practice is necessary,
just as in the case of cooking;
for "cooking" is indeed a single thing.
However, the cooking of the rice has one characteristic, that of the soup another, and that of the molasses yet another;
since the cooking of the rice is thus apprehended, there is no syntactic coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) among these words.
Regarding what was stated [by the opponent], "And there is an inconsistency of the words" (7.2.1.7), the proponent offers this reply:
In this way, if both the *sāman* and the words such as *rathantara* denote the melody (*gīti*), then consistency is achieved for the words *sāman* and the words *ṛc*.

Thus, in the injunction "He sings the *rathantara* upon the *kavatī* verses," the word *kavatī* will refer to the verses beginning with "kayā naścitra ābhuvat," and the word *rathantara* will refer to the *sāman*.
And thus there is no contradiction; therefore, it is established as the conclusion that the word *sāman* refers to what has been sung.
Regarding the *sāman*, the first verse in the *ṛc* which serves as its basis is called the "source" (*yoni*), and that is prescribed in the "Source-Section" (*Yonigrantha*) of the *Pūrvārcika*.
The two subsequent *ṛc*s are called "Uttare" (the latter ones), and they are prescribed in the *Uttaragrantha*, specifically in the *Uttarārcika*. (Vi.
10.4.24). Regarding the Sāman, the statement "ghoḍayuyusare" is a restatement of the *prāya* [chanting] at the *Aṅgirasāṃ dvirātra* sacrifice.
(10.1.13.5–54, Varṇaka 2). See the section on "Aṅgirasāṃ dvirātra" on page 189 of the Mīmāṃsākośa.
Regarding the two Sāmans, Saubhara and [the one with] the *hīṣ* finale and so forth, there is a statement of their results, such as "the *Bṛhat*[-sāman]," and so on.
Here, there is an injunction for the removal of specific *nidhana*s. Vi. 2.2.13.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, when the singing of the two Sāmans, Geya and Aujigīya, has been accomplished by means of the first [verse], in the triplet (*tūca*) belonging to the *Bṛhatī* meter, just as in the case of the *Vihāra* of the *Bṛhatī* and the *Paṅkti*.

The purpose of the *sāmans* is the manifestation of the syllables. Maṇi, p. 5. By means of the addition (*āgama*) of non-original *sāmans*, the full completion of the desired additional ritual form (*saṃsthā*), such as the twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*), must be performed in the *atirātra*.

Regarding the *avabhṛtha-sāman* and others, [the rule] "loudly" (*uccais*) applies;

because there is no mention of the *savana*, it will serve for the fruit of the primary rite (*pradhāna-karman*) accordingly. In that case, since the fruit of the action is not contradicted, the accent belongs to the Veda itself.
Or [it may be]. 3|2|12|9 p. 813. *Sāman* means knowledge.

Furthermore, it is said: "Having commenced the vows on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, one should study the Veda for seven and a half months during the Gāyatra and other [metres] of the Mādhyandina and Ārbhava Pavamāna [stotras], which are adventitious.
Such is their application.
But in the case of the *vahiṣpavamāna*, it will serve for the sake of a fruit;
the others, being prescribed for men, have the *paryāsa* as their final [verse] among the *stomas*.
5|3|4|11-12. It would be determined by the ritual action of the *sāmans*;
therefore, it is also a primary action (*pradhānakarman*).

*Bāla*, p. 140: Regarding the *sāmans*—specifically the *ādhāna-sāmans*—the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is a property of the primary rite (*pradhāna-dharma*), because it is caused by contact with the primary rite. *Vārttika* 3.2.12, p. 811; p. 813: Because the *sāmans*—namely the *ādhāna-sāmans*—are enjoined by the injunctions of the primary rite belonging to the Yajurveda, they are to be performed in a whisper.
