See the discussion under Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 3668, regarding "the *mādhyandina-pavamāna* and *ārbhava-pavamāna* in sacrifices with increased or non-increased *stomas*.
The *sāman* is subordinate (*guṇatva*) to the *ṛc* (verse).
The *sāman* lacks primacy because it is subordinate to the preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*) of the *ṛc*;
or rather, the ritual act is characterized by its injunction (*vidhilakṣaṇa*).
Commentary: These very [verses] are the examples.
The meaning for them is that the *samādhi* is attained; thus, *gīti* (chanting) is expressed by the word *sāman*.
Consequently, this is now doubted: is the chanting (*gīti*) primary with respect to the *ṛk* (verse), or is it secondary?

Now, it has already been established that the word *sāman* denotes a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*); however, it might rather be a refinement of the *ṛk* for the purpose of making it intelligible, because it adopts what is already well-known.
It is said: True, it proceeds by way of objection;
that itself will be the final determination.
What is established? That the word *sāman* denotes a primary action (*pradhānakarman*).
What is the reason? Because here there is the characteristic of a primary injunction, namely the accusative case-ending—as in "he sings the *Rathantara*," "he sings the *Bṛhat*.
Therefore, it is a primary action.
Furthermore, the singing occurs at a time when there is no ritual action.
If it were for the purpose of preparing the substance, then the substance would have been prepared by means of an invisible refinement; it cannot be refined again at the time of the ritual action.
For it is not possible to perform the act of lubricating that which is already lubricated, nor the act of grinding that which is already ground.
This very point has been accepted by those who hold the view [of the Sāman]: that it is a purificatory act (*saṃskāra*) performed at a time other than the time for the ritual action itself.
However, against the position that it is not [a purificatory act], the following objection is raised:
"But surely, in the seventh [book], it was determined that the Sāman is a purificatory act."
It is said:

even if it were a primary action (*pradhānakarma*), its accomplishment would still be established in every respect. In this case, the status of being subordinate (*guṇatā*) or primary (*pradhānatā*) must necessarily be investigated.
If the primary element is the melody, then the *sāman* follows the requirements of the singing;
if, however, it is subordinate, then the opposite is the case.
That substance [is determined] by the scriptural statement, as in the case of the *pākayajña*.
The Commentary says: It is called a primary object (*pradhānakarman*);
yet this is not a primary object.
For this [act] does not itself bestow the fruit;
and if one were to postulate a fruit for it, something not mentioned in the scripture would have to be assumed.
Therefore, it is subordinate to the sacrifice.

If it is not subordinate (guṇabhūta), what is its substance (dravya) in relation to which this [mantra] is primary? To this it is said: the *ṛc* is the substance; the *ṛcs* stand in the place of a substance for it.
Just as the material substance is the means for accomplishing another ritual act, so too is the *ṛc* the means for accomplishing this one.
Therefore, this [material] is subordinate with respect to the *ṛc*.
For it is the established fact that the two are taught as being in the middle.
But how is this a substance? Because of a scriptural statement.
This scriptural statement is: "He sings the Sāman on the Ṛc.
Just as, in the case of the Pākayajñas, there are specific substances prescribed by scripture, such as parched grains (lāja), fried grains (dhānā), rice grains (taṇḍula), and clarified butter (ājya).
In the same way here as well, the *ṛc* is the substance, because it is so stated.
In that case, there is no contradiction regarding its distinction from other substances and its application.
The Commentary says: "He says."

That which is expressed by the words of this *ṛc* becomes this very substance (*dravya*). How can there be an injunction regarding another substance when there is already a distinct substance? And how is it that this is called *sāman*?
To this, it is replied:
This is not contradictory;
for the Sāman is merely a melody,
while its material substratum is established by direct scriptural injunction.
That which is prescribed as a general rule is set aside by that which is prescribed as a specific rule regarding another substance.
In this case, since there is only the melody apart from the substance, it does not matter whether it is the *Bṛhat* or the *Rathantara*;
therefore, the *Sāman* is a primary action.
Because it is the meaning of the word, it cannot be so.
The Commentary: The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position. This cannot be the case; namely, that the *sāman* is the primary object (*pradhānakarman*).
It would be a subordinate action (guṇakarma). Why? Because it is the meaning of the word;
the *sāman* is directly perceived as that which assists the word.
It is perceived:
when the *sāman* is being performed, the syllables of the *ṛc* are uttered;
since that is so, one need not postulate an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
"And because words have another purpose.
Commentary: Words have another purpose; they are for the sake of praise.
For praise has been enjoined, as in: "They praise with the *ājya* hymns," "They praise with the *pṛṣṭha* hymns."

That [deity] is perceived directly through the syllables of the *ṛc* being recited; therefore, while the *ṛcs* are true in their purpose of praise, the existence of the deity is merely postulated. And there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a postulation.

Therefore, for this reason also, the *sāman* is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the word "loudly" (*uccaiḥ*). Furthermore, there is no connection with the ritual action (*karman*), because the two words have distinct meanings.
Commentary: For this reason as well, the *sāman* is subordinate.
Why? Because there would be no connection between the *sāman* and the *stotra*.
If the praise were taught by means of the *sāman* through its being subordinate to that [the *stotra*], then the *sāman* would not belong to the praise;
in that case, the scriptural injunction—"The *Bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant," "The *Rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant"—would be contradicted.
It is taught that "the *pṛṣṭha* has the *rathantara* as its quality" and "the *pṛṣṭha* has the *bṛhat* as its quality. For that purpose, the similarity [of the two] must be stated;
for then it directly performs the function of assisting the *pṛṣṭha*.

That which makes manifest the word expressive of this [Sāman]—namely, the word *antara*—can be understood to have the same meaning as the word *pṛṣṭha* because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
If they had different meanings, however, there would be no connection.
Therefore, by that [word *antara*], the Sāman is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*).
Even in the section concerning *saṃskāra* (consecration), it would be distinct because it is employed [for a specific purpose].

The Bhāṣya states: "Now, as for what was said—that singing at a time other than during the ritual act should be considered a consecration, like the laying of the fires—this is because it is employed [for that purpose]."
That must be refuted.
Furthermore, the application of words is understood to be purposeless.
The Bhāṣya states: For if the singing were performed at a time when there is no ritual action and were to persist until the time of the ritual action without perishing, [it would be useless].
Consequently, non-performance is understood. Or, if it were impossible to perform them at the time of the ritual action, even then there would be non-performance;
however, chanted words can indeed be performed again.
Therefore, since those [mantras] employed at the time of the ritual (dharma) are not effective, they should be employed at the time of the action (karman).
Thus, there will be no fault,
because [the mantra] is dependent [on the proper timing].

The Commentary states: Furthermore, it shows that the singing is dependent upon the time of the ritual action, as in the injunction: "Having touched the Audumbarī pillar, the Udgātṛ priest should sing without leaning on it.
The Audumbarī is the central pillar of the Sadas.
By saying "having touched it," [the text] shows that the singing takes place within the Sadas.
Therefore, it should be understood that singing at the time of the *abhyudaya* [eclipse] is to be performed just like the *agnyādheya* [establishment of the sacred fires].
If it is argued that it is "employed" (*prayujyate*), the Commentary states: "Now, as for what was said—that the study of the Veda, which possesses meaning, is employed so that it may bear fruit."
That must be refuted. [Objection:
It might be employed for the purpose of apprehension.
[Bhāṣya: For it cannot serve as a means to a result.
For in that case, something unseen would have to be postulated. Here, however, a visible purpose is observed:
when one who is not his teacher studies in the presence of a pupil, it is for the sake of the pupil's acquisition.
Whatever [is mentioned] is for the sake of that group.
For the purpose of grasping and for the purpose of application, the ground is superior, having been purified.
For example:
Just as one who practices on the ground by drawing a chariot on the earth trains for swiftness in battle,
and just as a student practices with dry wood thinking, "I shall become swift in practical application," so too should this be understood.
Therefore, when something is directly perceived, there is no assumption of the unseen. Consequently, it follows that this [singing] is for the purpose of consecration (*saṃskāra*).
Śabara: The inquiry is whether the *sāman*s are primary with respect to the *ṛc* verses, or whether they are subordinate, being for the purpose of consecrating them.

In this regard, since it is employed even at a time when there is no ritual action (*akarmakāla*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) suggests that it possesses primacy, as follows: "The manifestation of syllables is the perceived purpose of the *sāmans*;
the praise [of the *sāman*] is for the sake of manifesting the syllable; and it is enjoined by the ritual injunction."

Thus, when a visible result has been obtained, there is no postulation of an invisible result. But surely, because the syllables of the *ṛc* are not enjoined [for that purpose], there can be no preparation, just as in the case of the flour-meal (*saktu*) with the oblation; [we reply: it is not so, because [in our case] a visible result exists.
No purpose for the groats (saktu) is seen, nor even heard;
therefore, the established conclusion is that the *sāmans* are purificatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*).
As for the fact that singing is prescribed at times other than during a ritual action, that must be for the sake of training, just as in the case of [the practice of] *yoga*.

Soma: "That for the sake of which it was deliberated whether [the *gāna*] is the *sāman*, that is now being deliberated. This is the connection (*saṃgati*) characterized by the [present] occasion. As for the meaning of the Sūtra: "The *sāman* is a primary act (*pradhānakarma*), because in the case of the *rathantara* and others, the accusative case is heard as distinct from the primary [act]. Viśvarūpa: "Is the *sāman* primary, or is it subordinate (*guṇa*) because of its external recitation? Recitation is for the purpose of practicing the primary; the subordinate element is the syllable of the song for the sake of the praise (*stuti*)."

Bhaṭṭa: When there is a doubt as to whether the *sāmans* hold primacy or subordination with respect to the *ṛcs*, since the *ṛcs* are enjoined as subordinate members of the *stotra* by means of sequence and direct injunction (*krama* and *karana*), the *sāmans* also attain the status of being subordinate members of the *stotra* for that very reason; thus, there is no mutual relationship of primacy and subordination between them.

However, if the indicative power (*liṅga*) consisting of functional capacity (*yogyatā*) is prioritized, then even the syllables of the *ṛcs* would be subordinate members of the *sāman*, because they possess the capacity to delimit the duration of the singing.

Nor can the Sāmans be considered ignorant of the Ṛks merely on the ground that they manifest the syllables of the Ṛks; for when both possibilities exist, the status of the Ṛks as subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the Sāmans is established by the locative scriptural statement (*saptamī-śruti*), such as: "He sings the Sāman superposed upon the Ṛk," "That which he sings with the *ṛc* [is the same] as he sings with the *uttara* [verses]," and "He sings the *Rathantara* upon the *Kavati* verses.

Furthermore, since only a Ṛk whose syllables are joined together serves as the generator of the praise consisting of the expression of qualities (*guṇābhidhāna-rūpa-stotra*), it is logically impossible for the Sāman—which manifests those specific syllables—to be the manifester [of the Ṛk], as their purposes would be contradictory.

For this very reason, the view that the *samasyā* (the combination of verses) possesses the characteristic of being primary—based on the logic of the *prayāja-śeṣa* (the remnants of the fore-offerings)—is also refuted.
This is because the logic of the *prayāja-śeṣa*, as previously stated, has been superseded by the logic of the *niṣṭhā* (the concluding rites) regarding the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*).
Thus, having first performed the separate recitation of the *ṛc*s as subordinate elements of the *stotra*, they must then be employed again as the substrata for the *sāman*.

Furthermore, if this were the case, the application of the *sāmans*—which, by their own indicative mark (*liṅga*), would apply to the performance of the hymn (*stotra*) through the medium of manifesting the syllables of the *ṛc* verses according to the sequence and context of the [original] injunctions—would be rendered useless in such injunctions as "one should praise with the *yajñāyajñīya*," "the *pṛṣṭha* is the *bṛhat*," and "the *pṛṣṭha* is the *rathantara*.
Therefore, in order to avoid such futility, the *sāmans* must be subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the hymn by way of providing indirect assistance (*ārādupakāraka*).

Nor does this entail an inconsistency in the designation of them as instruments (*karaṇa*); for even that which provides indirect assistance can be established as an instrument toward the mode of the hymn by means of the transcendental result (*apūrva*) produced by the essence of Bṛhaspati.

Furthermore, it can also be easily stated that even for those *ṛc*s which have become subordinate members (*aṅga*) of a *sāman*, there is an incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*) benefit to the *stotra*, despite the absence of their separate recitation.

This being the position reached, [we reply]: because the word *stotra* (hymn) is used by ritualists (*yājñika*) to denote the expression of qualities through chanted mantras and the like, and because a distinction between the hymn and the *ṛk* verses would otherwise be untenable; and because the status of a *stotra* arises from the expression of qualities produced by the knowledge of the connection with *ṛk* verses qualified by chanting; and because such a *stotra* cannot be accomplished without chanting since it is to be realized through chanting that manifests [the qualities]; it is indeed proper that the *sāman* serves as a means for the *stotra* by way of manifesting the syllables of the *ṛk*. Thus, by the indicative power (*liṅga*) itself, assisted by the context of sequence (*krama*) and the section (*prakaraṇa*), the *ṛk* verses are subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the *stotra*, and likewise the *sāmans* are for the purpose of manifesting the syllables of the *ṛk*.

For this very reason, since the Sāman—which exists for the purpose of manifesting the syllables of the Ṛk—is also incidentally established as having the Ṛk as its substratum, the statement “he sings the Sāman as mounted upon the Ṛk” (*ṛcyadhyūḍhaṃ sāma gāyati*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Moreover, being a restatement is necessary because even for one who maintains that the Ṛk is a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of the Sāman, the fact that those Sāmans have the Ṛk as their common substratum is already established by the very recitation and so forth.
However, in passages such as “as he sings on one [verse], he sings on the next two,” the locative case denotes predominance (*prādhānya*), otherwise the substitution (*ādeśa*) would be inexplicable.
For it is not possible for the injunction of being the substratum to apply to only one of the two [the *ṛk* and the *sāman*],
according to the principle that the primary must be performed in accordance with the subordinate.

Furthermore, since the status of the *tṛca* (three-verse set) as the substratum is enjoined by the rule "one *sāman* is performed upon a *tṛca*" in your own view, it is untenable for the three verses to be treated as optional alternatives.

Since the fact that [the *sāman*] rests upon a *ṛc* triplet is established by the phrase "one *sāman*," and since the intended *ṛc*s can be obtained through recitation and so forth, the phrase "as the other" would otherwise be rendered redundant.
Therefore, neither of the two [the *ṛc* and the *sāman*] is enjoined here; rather, for the sake of establishing their primary status, metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is necessary.

By this [argument], the following view is refuted: that although the *ṛks* are subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of the *sāmans*, since the manifestation of syllables (*akṣarābhivyakti*) occurs as a necessary consequence (*ānuṣaṅgika*), the performance of the ritual act of *stotra* is accomplished by taking up the *sāman* alone; therefore, the *sāmans* are not subsidiary parts of the *ṛks*.

For if the syllables of the *ṛk* were absent, it would be impossible to extend (*atideśa*) the *sāman* to another *ṛk*. Thus, because the *ṛks* are primary, and because the *sāman* undergoes a transformation (*anyathābhāva*) through the subsequent phonemes, the sequence (*krama*)—even when described as "upward" (*ūrdhva*)—is not untenable.
Maṇḍana: “The Sāman is that which consecrates the Ṛc. Śaṅkara: “And the Sāman is also that which is consecrated.
Regarding the Sāmans—specifically the Pravargya-sāmans—it should be stated: ‘One performs the Pravargya loudly.’”

Or, [as stated] on page 813 (3|12|9): "The sublation of the original *sāmans*—specifically those such as the *Kautsa* and others—is restricted to those very *sāmans* mentioned in the context of particular modified rites (*vikṛti*), and does not apply to all of them.
"There is a sublation of the original *sāmans* when they are superseded by the *Kautsa* and other *sāmans* heard in the context of a specific modified rite."

10.4.1.17 (Section 2): There is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the original (*prākṛta*) *sāmans* with the *sāmans* belonging to the verses and so forth used as means for the *gastottarā* in the Mahāvrata.

For among the *sāmans*—that is, all the *stotras*—only *ṛc*-triplets (*tṛca*) are employed. Vārttika 3.5.10.13: "Among the *sāmans*, at the times of the *suyajña* [and other such rites], within the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, such as the *anukathya* and others."

Regarding the *sāman*s [in Sūtra 4286], the principle of the *sāman*-sublation applies: for those *sāman*s beginning with the *anubandha* and ending with the *parisāman*, which are distinct from those occurring at the *avabhṛtha* bath,
because they are prescribed as being separated by equal intervals (*aharhyatayā*), the accentuation obtained by their own nature is appropriate according to the specific Veda alone.

There is the cessation of the original *sāmans*. Now, when the effect characterized as praise (*stuti*) is heard—as on page 1183 of the *Sūtraprakāśa*—in cases such as the *Kautsa* and others, one might perceive a modification of the original *gāyatra* and other *sāmans* because of the hearing of a different capacity; however, due to the hearing of another capacity, it is understood that there is no modification.

There would be a sublation [of the original rule], because it is a subsidiary element, like the Gāyatra and other Sāmans of the archetypal rite; thus [it is concluded] that the Kautsa [Sāman] applies. 10.4.8.16.
"Because these [verses] also serve the purpose of praise.
Thus, O Mahāmati, they praise the assembly beforehand with a verse. Anu-...
Following the verse "Because of the hearing of another capacity" (10.4.8.16), there is the statement: "And looking at the *cāravāla* with the *kaughna* [chant].
In this context, O Great-minded One, the *sāmans* such as the *Śloka* and others, which were taught and subsequently extended, are heard;
the archetypal (*prākṛta*) *sāmans* are not obtained by what has been stated.

What is the conclusion? That it follows the phonemes of the *yoni*.

Why? Because in the original [archetype], when the vowel *a* is combined with the vowel *ī*, the sound *ī* is pronounced; subsequently, even in the other [subsequent] cases, there is the cognition of the vowel *a* within that combined form.

Because it is impossible to carry out an injunction whose object is unattainable, there would result a contradiction of its capacity to incite action; since every injunction necessarily requires efficacy (*sāmarthya*), even though that efficacy is cognizable through other means of knowledge, the Veda’s independence remains unimpaired because the specific subject matter is not known from any other source. "And the generality of substances, qualities, and actions possesses the division of higher and lower. Vārttika: "And the generality of substances and so forth..."
Existence (*vastutva*) is the first [universal] therein; likewise, the second is substantiality (*dravyatva*).
Furthermore, these are distinct from pervasiveness (*vyāptatva*), fire-ness (*tejastva*), earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*), selfhood (*ātmatva*), and so forth.
From earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) arises pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*), which is fully instantiated in its individual instances.
In this way, from "treeness" one understands "śiṃśapā-ness" and so forth as distinct;
from "bodiness," "cowness" and the like are understood;
and from "horseness," "horseship" and other qualities are considered to be cognized.
From the state of being an elephant, there arise the various species such as the Bhadra, Subhadra, and other lineages of elephants;
from the state of being male, there is attained the status of being a Brāhmaṇa, a Govindaka, and so forth.
Likewise, there are qualities such as "quality-ness," "action-ness," "form-ness," "birth-ness," and the like.
Therefore, the cognition of a universal among the qualities that manifest it— beginning with purity—
is the definition of a universal.
A general cognition is sublated by a specific one.

The *vedi* (altar), which is prescribed after the sprinkling of the oblation (*havir-abhivāsana*), is drawn forward to the preceding day on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) due to a specific statement. The eleven types of injunctions beginning with the general [injunction] are fourfold, according to possibility, based on the objects being genus (*jāti*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*kriyā*).

The state of having genus (*jāti*) and so forth as its object is also threefold—pertaining to the subject portion (*uddeśyāṃśa*), the predicate portion (*vidheyāṃśa*), and both portions—and thus there are one hundred and thirty-two varieties (114 + 4443 = 132). *Bālapriyā*, p. 21. Inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭam anumānam*) is twofold: for oneself (*svārtha*) and for others (*parārtha*). *Bālapriyā*, p. 8. An example of inference based on general observation is as follows: having perceived that Devadatta’s arrival at another location is preceded by movement, one recollects the movement of the sun.

Thus [says Manu].
Here, the purpose is the state of having a minor fault (*alpadoṣatva*).

Bāla. pṛ. 16. Regarding the general form, there are the objects of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the objects of restriction (*vyāvṛtti*), and the rule of permission (*abhyanujñāvidhi*). The means of proximity known as the universal-characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā pratyāsatti*) consists of either the cognition of the universal or the universal itself as it is being cognized. Through that relation, by means of sense-object contact, there arises the perception of the individuals belonging to that universal.
And this [theory] is necessary;

otherwise, if the apprehension of the word-potency (*śakti*) occurred only with respect to a jar within the sphere of linguistic usage, then because all individual jars would be imperceptible, there could be no error regarding potency with respect to all of them.

Gaṅgeśa, however, [argues that] when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is perceived in the smoke of a kitchen, since the cognition of all smoke is established through the universal-characterized mediation (*sāmānyalakṣaṇapratyāsatti*), the doubt "Is smoke pervaded by fire or not? would not arise.

Because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is ascertained through perception in the case of well-known smoke, and because there is no knowledge of any other [smoke], doubt is untenable. Furthermore, there would be no engagement in the act of producing smoke, since there is an absence of desire for that which is already established.
Furthermore, because that which is unestablished cannot be known,
there would likewise be no desire for pleasure and so forth. Moreover, the perception of the prior non-existence of a jar in its shards would not occur.

Because it is impossible for ancient jars to function as counter-correlatives (pratiyogin), there would be no knowledge of the jar that serves as the counter-correlative for the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) acting as a qualifier.
Consequently, even the verbal cognition—"the jar is the counter-correlative of a present prior non-existence residing in the potsherds"—would not occur.
Therefore, one must accept the presence of "universal-characterized" perception (sāmānyalakṣaṇā).
On this point, Śiromaṇi [states]:

Even though there is a certainty regarding the pervasion of that smoke by its nature as smoke when it is a well-known smoke, because there is no certainty regarding it by way of its nature as "smoke" (dhūmatva), the aforementioned doubt is not untenable;
for only a certainty possessing the same mode (samānaprakāra) is the antagonist to doubt and the like.
For when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is ascertained through the nature of smoke, the absence of doubt is accepted [as a necessary condition].
Likewise, since desire and purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) are also caused by an ascertainment that possesses that specific mode (*tatprakāraka-niścaya*), there is no inconsistency.

Furthermore, by accepting that the knowledge of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) is a cause for the knowledge of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), and by accepting that an ascertainment possessing the mode of the delimiting property of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedakaprakāraka-niścaya*) is a cause for the cognition of the relation of a qualifier (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyabodha*), the perception of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is not untenable.

Furthermore, even regarding prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), in the cognition "a jar will be here," there is no apprehension of the prior non-existence of the jar itself, but rather of the prior non-existence of its production.

And since that [production], being of the nature of a relation with time, is not perceptible, the prior non-existence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is that [production] is all the more imperceptible; therefore, for the sake of perceiving the object that is its counter-correlate, the "universal-characterized" [perception] (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*) is required.
For instance, in such cases as "it will be" (*bhaviṣyati*) or "it will come to be" (*bhavitā*), it is "production" (*utpatti*) that is the expressed meaning.
The meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) is the operation conducive to that [action].
By this, there is the application of the maxim of the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*) regarding the general characteristic existing at a time subsequent to the present time.

The understanding is that "the jar possesses an activity conducive to origination based on [its material cause] the potsherd," or "the jar possesses an activity conducive to origination which is the counter-positive of its present non-existence"; or alternatively, it is "that which is the substratum of the meaning of 'origination'.

Similarly, in the case of the negative particle (*nañ*), destruction (*nāśa*) is the meaning of the verbal root (*ghātyartha*). Future-ness (*bhaviṣyatva*), which consists in being an origination that is the counter-positive of its present non-existence, connects with the meaning of the verbal root through the relation of being a counter-positive (*pratiyogitā*).

The resulting cognition is: "The jar is that which has as its counter-positive a destruction residing in the potsherds, where that destruction has as its counter-positive an origination that is the counter-positive of a present prior absence.
Furthermore, in this case, the property of being subsequent to the present time does not connect with the prior absence, nor with its counter-positive (the jar), nor with the past [absence].
Otherwise, there would result the undesirable application of such expressions as "it will exist after a year," "it will perish after a year," "it will exist tomorrow," and "it will perish tomorrow."

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage "Devadatta will go out from the house tomorrow" being interpreted as "going out from the house will exist [now]," because Devadatta has already arrived at the house today.

Therefore, the relation of being subsequent to the present time must apply only to the act of arising (*utpatti*); thus, there is no need for a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*) for that purpose.
In reality, however, since there is no proof for antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), all of this is like a miscarriage.

In reality, since there is no inclination toward objects already established as desirable, it is logical that *sāmānyalakṣaṇā* (generic cognition) is necessary for the sake of knowing what is not yet established as desirable, for the sake of grasping the status of a word as a cause for generating inclination toward a specific object such as a staff, and for the sake of grasping the denotative power (*śakti*) [of words].
(Maṇi, pp. 27–29). A word denoting a general category is not restricted to a particular instance.

(Pāṇini Bhāṣya 4.1.120). Specification by means of a word denoting a general category is indirect (*parokṣa*), whereas specification by means of a word denoting a particular instance is direct (*pratyakṣa*).
Direct perception is more authoritative than indirect inference. A specific statement is more authoritative than a general statement.

1|1|5|11, p. 672. The maxim is that a general statement finds its final application in a particular case by conforming to a specific statement; as for example, "He divides the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) into four parts" and "He divides the cake dedicated to Agni into four parts.

General scriptural statement (*sāmānyaśruti*): In this context, a general statement is restricted to a specific case when it would otherwise have a meaning exceeding that of a specific injunction (*viśeṣaśāstra*).

For example, the general statement "He divides the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) into four parts" is restricted to the cake dedicated to Agni by the specific rule "He divides the cake for Agni into four parts. In that regard, if only "He divides [the cake] into four parts" were heard and not "He divides the cake for Agni into four parts," then the division would apply even to cakes not dedicated to Agni; thus, both statements serve a purpose.

The designation of commonality (*sāmānyasamākhyā*) and the designation of particularity (*viśeṣasamākhyā*) constitute the two types of designation. Bāla. p. 12. (Regarding the designations: The designation of particularity is stronger than the designation of commonality.
The general designation of a performer is set aside by a specific designation.
(Bhāṣya 3.7.2.41–42, p. 1106; Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1251). Regarding this, one should consult the section [adhikaraṇa] on the statement: "The priests have no fixed status regarding the ritual acts."

Regarding the premature termination [of a Sattra], the Viśvajit sacrifice is to be performed after the Soma has been purchased, because of its connection with the distribution [of the sacrificial fee]. As it is stated: "If one should prematurely terminate while consecrated for a Sattra, having purchased the Soma, he should sacrifice with the Viśvajit Atirātra," and regarding premature termination: "They should sacrifice with the Adhiveda-dakṣiṇā. Thus, the Viśvajit sacrifice which is enjoined as something to be performed when the abandonment of the Sattra has been made by someone due to premature termination, that should take place once the King (Soma) has been purchased;
it is to be performed after the purchase of the Soma.

Because of the connection with partition, as in the injunction, "Having partitioned the Soma, they should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," there would be a deficiency [of the ritual] prior to the purchase of the Soma,
since the partitioning of the Soma is impossible before that point.

Therefore, if any sacrificer, having commenced the Sattra, desires to abandon it for some reason, he should— after the purchase of the Soma— partition his share of the Soma, take possession of it, and perform the Viśvajit sacrifice with that portion.
And therefore, those who have purchased the King [Soma] should perform the Viśvajit when rising [from the sacrifice].
This is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa).
Or rather, [the Viśvajit occurs] because it is occasioned by the commencement [of the rite].

The author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), setting aside with the word "or" (*vā*) the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) established by the sūtra that the Viśvajit sacrifice—enjoined by the rule, "If one should rise prematurely while consecrated for a *satra*, he should purchase the Soma and sacrifice with a Viśvajit Atirātra"—is to be performed only upon rising after the purchase of the Soma.
[He argues that] it should be performed even upon rising after the commencement of the *satra* (i.e., the mere beginning of the procedure) and prior to the purchase of the Soma;
because the occasion (*nimitta*) for the Viśvajit—the premature rising—is applicable even before the purchase of the Soma.
The cause for the Viśvajit sacrifice is the simultaneous rising (sāmyutthāna), which is the rising from half [of the ritual], but not the purchase of the Soma.

Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that when there is a simultaneous rising—whether before or after the purchase of the Soma—occurring during the performance [of the ritual], then the Viśvajit takes place.
Some read the word "pravṛttau" [in the text].
But the meaning is not so;
for in the context of the *sāmidhenī* verses,
the scriptural statement is intended for the purpose of instruction regarding the others.

Regarding the injunction, "If one who has been consecrated for a sacrificial session (*satra*) should depart prematurely, he should purchase the *soma* and perform the *viśvajit* sacrifice with an *atirātra* [ritual]," the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) asserts that this *viśvajit* must be performed even before the purchase of the *soma*, triggered by the occasion of premature departure. Against this, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) raises the objection: "If one departs while the King (*soma*) has not yet been purchased, they would perform a defective rite due to the absence of the distribution of the *soma*. To this, the proponent of the final view replies:
"The other scriptural passage is intended as an instruction (*ādeśārthā*)."
The term "instruction" (ādeśa) is merely an illustration.

In the case of the statement, "Having drunk the Soma, one should rise," the scriptural injunction "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit" serves as an alternative; thus, even though this scriptural text is recited in the midst of that [Soma-drinking], the "instruction" regarding the Soma and other substances is intended to indicate all materials.
For whoever would rise from [the Soma] by implication, he should rise having separated his own portion from the entire mixed substance.
In that case, even the Soma might be divided;
however, the sole cause for the performance of the Viśvajit sacrifice is the rising together [of the priests], not the purchase of the Soma nor the division of the Soma.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the Viśvajit is to be performed as soon as the rising together has occurred.

Regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses, the injunction "One desiring stability should recite twenty-one" applies specifically to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
In that case, the addition (*āgama*) of six verses must be performed.
And their insertion occurs at the end of those [mantras] that are adventitious.
(Those who know the tradition, however, explain it otherwise; this should be seen in the commentary on *Saṃhitā* 2.5.10).

In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is heard in scripture: "And that at which they press [the Soma], there he recites the *Sāmidhenī* verses. Regarding the statement, "He recites that Sāmidhenī [verse]," the word *tat* (that) functions with the sense of the locative case; because it refers to the southern *havirdhāna* cart situated between the study area and the *havirdhāna*, it is prescribed as an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the Sāmidhenīs.
The meaning is that the recitation of the Sāmidhenī verses must be performed there.

Regarding this, the *Sudhā* commentary states: "By the word *yat* ending in the locative case in the phrase 'yat sunvanti' (where they press), the *havirdhāna*, which is the locus of the pressing, is indicated; [therefore] 'he recites that'."

Because of the reference by means of the word *ayayac* ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*), the meaning of the Vedic text is understood as: "Between the two *havirdhāna* carts, in whichever *havirdhāna* they press the Soma, in that one they recite the *sāmidhenī* verses.

From the statement "He recites those *sāmidhenīs*," the meaning of the Sūtra is that, between the two *havirdhānas*, the *havirdhāna* which serves as the support for the pressing is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *sāmidhenīs*.
Or rather, it is merely a location directly perceived, serving the purpose of the Soma ritual.

In the context of the *sāmidhenī* verses, with reference to the repetition already established, there is an injunction for "breath-holding" (*nirucchvāsatva*) by means of the portion [of the text] designated as "without a break" (*niranvaya*).
The meaning is that one should recite from the beginning up to the end of the third repetition with a single breath, and may breathe in the middle.

If the injunction for non-pause (*anavāna*) were intended merely with reference to the *ṛk*-meter, then it would follow that a breath (*niḥśvāsa*) would occur within every repetition of the mantra; yet, in the absence of a breath, [the rule] would not apply.
Consequently, there would be an implied necessity for the injunction "three times" (*tris*), since the mere repetition could be obtained through another injunction.

Thus, because the meaning of "O venerable one, come" (*ama āyāhi*) is already established by the very recitation [of the preceding verse], the repetition of either one would result in redundancy; therefore, in the passage "The first day has the *aindravāyava* draught," only the fact that it follows immediately after the preceding [verse] is intended to be expressed.

The mention of the *ṛc* (verse), however, is a mere reiteration, just like the word "day" (*ahar*), since it is only that specific verse which follows immediately after the third recitation (*anuvacana*).

And thus, since the first, second, and third recitations (anuvacana) are intended for the purpose of the *prabhava* and *vājīya* [hymns] associated with the second and third recitations respectively, the continuity (*sāṃtatyam*) is established. In reality, because the [verse] "O Agni, come hither" (*ama āyāhi*) is present through proximity, it is this very [verse] that is intended; therefore, it is only in the third recitation that the praise of the *praṇava* as the cause of continuity and posteriority is logically consistent.

"Having uttered the *ṛc*, one should utter the *praṇava*," and so forth; because there is no relationship of substratum and superstratum [between the *ṛc* and the *praṇava*], there is a modification of another syllable.
*Saṃkarṣa.* 4.1.12.
The injunction regarding the *praṇava* in the *sāmidhenī* verses applies precisely in the place of the syllables of the *ṛc*.

In that very context, following the injunction "one places the *praṇava* in the *ṛc*," it is stated that the *praṇava* should be employed. Although it may be conceived in two ways—either as being mixed with the syllables of the *ṛc* like a jujube fruit in a bowl, or as being blended with it like sugar in curd—nevertheless, it is proper that it be merely subsequent to it, like the *ājya* and *puronuvākyā* mantras following the main sacrifice, rather than being identical to the bowl or the curd. This is because not even a single one of the syllables of the *ṛc* as traditionally handed down can undergo modification.

"Whatever is the *praṇava* of the *sāmidhenī* verses, that is the ninth syllable of the *gāyatrī*"—by this other scriptural statement (*śruti*), it is established that [the *praṇava*] follows the syllables.

This being the case, since the relationship between two words to be uttered in sequence lacks the inherent logical force of a relationship like that between two fingers, and since the locative case in the word "in the *ṛc*" (*ṛci*) denotes a container-and-contained relationship (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) which is merely a matter of explicit textual injunction (*vācanika*), there is no fault in the modification of the syllable; thus, by the force of the injunction "the *praṇava*," it is inserted precisely while modifying the syllable.
However, due to the difference in properties such as being whispered (*upāṃśu*) or loud (*uccaiḥ*), the syllable of the *upāṃśuyāja* and so forth is not [the same as] that [of the *navasvara*].

Even though the syllable of the *akṣarākṣara* is redundant in the middle of the sacrifice (*kratu*), it is stated to be the "ninth syllable" because it is recited by that [person] who is qualified for it during the *brahmayajña* and other rites, according to his intention. This is seen from the statement, "He holds two *saṃyuj* [verses]," even though they are being performed at different times.
(Saṃkarṣa. 4.1.11)
In the case of the *sāmidhenī* verses, it is the syllable *oṃ*—the referent of the word "praṇava"—that is prescribed, and not the word "praṇava" itself.
Because of the injunction, "One places the *praṇava* in the *ṛc*," the word *praṇava*—which is merely a syllable—is to be inserted.
This is because it is logical that the sound heard in the *ṛc* should be the object of insertion, as seen in such [Vedic] passages as "The *airaṃ* [should be placed] in the *kuṣitaka*.
This being the position reached, the *oṃ* alone is to be inserted at the end.

Because the referents of words, such as the earth and so forth, lack any manifestation prior to the word, even when defining the nature of sound (*śabdasvarūpa*), there is no evidence for a secondary application (*lakṣaṇā*) to the syllable *praṇava* as a specific sound that possesses the power of denotation; for if one were to apply secondary application to the denotative word itself, there would be no justification.

Furthermore, while it might be reasonable to restrict the mental application of synonyms that denote deities such as Agni when they are subject to the contingency of being unrestricted, it is unreasonable to apply such restriction to what is denoted by the word "Veda" itself.
Indeed, when it is said, "One should study the Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas," the meaning understood is not "one should study the words 'Veda' and so forth."

Therefore, having considered the sūtra, "Om [is used] in the *sāmidhenī* verses by connection with the *sāmidhenī* itself" (1.2.34), it follows that those [mantras] should be employed in exactly those [contexts].
This being the case, since only the *gāyatrī*, *triṣṭubh*, and *jagatī* meters are under discussion here, the term "all" (*sarva*) refers specifically to these three.

For this very reason, even in the context of the *naidhātavīyā* sacrifice, after stating, "These three alone are all the meters; they are the fuel-sticks for this [fire]," the subsequent praise—"The vigor of the *triṣṭubh* indeed... and so forth—is appropriate as a means of establishing that the other four meters are essentially identical to these three.
(Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa 4.1.2)
The recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses takes place at the location for the offering of the southern oblation in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the location for the offering of the oblation is indicated by the sentence "uta yat suvanti" for the purpose of the *sāmidhenī* recitation (*Mīmāṃsākośa*, p.
1607). Regarding this, one should consult the section [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] beginning with "In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, by what is heard such as 'uta yat suvanti'... (3.7.7.16–17).

Since the *sāmidhenī* recitations and so forth are prescribed in the *Ṛgveda*, while the *anvādhāna* mantras and so forth are prescribed in the *Yajurveda*, there arises—by the logic of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—the possibility of obtaining [these rites] from various Vedas. However, by the logic of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), these are set aside. When there is a general injunction regarding the primary acts, the specific mention of mantras and so forth serves as a sublation; because the former applies to the primary acts, it is subsequently sublated in the case of the subsidiary acts (*aṅga*). (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1184). The section on similarity concerns similarity (*sārūpya*).

In the cases "the sacrificer is the sacrificial post" (*yajamāno yūpaḥ*) and "the sun is the sacrificial post" (*ādityo yūpaḥ*), there is a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) of the sacrificial post's identity with the sacrificer and the sun respectively.

therefore, similarity (*sārūpya*) is the cause for the figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) here.

In passages such as "The sacrificer is the sacrificial post" (*yajamāno yūpaḥ*), the word "sacrificer" is used figuratively based on the ground of similarity, whereas the sacrificial post is the primary referent.
Similarity.

But surely, in every case, figurative usage (*gauṇatva*) is based on similarity?
True, this is so.
Here, however, there is a separate mention of the eye and the Brahmin.
For the verticality of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is visual, and its luminosity is caused by the act of anointing.
By means of that [animal], it is touched upon by the two words "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) and "sun" (*āditya*).
For there is a contradiction in explaining the meaning of its own word for the sacrificer, who is already enjoined as being connected to the animal and is thus fixed;

And if someone were to take up some substitute for burning, even that would result in the establishment of a figurative application; therefore, it is better to resort to praise alone, whereby there would be the status of an injunction.

Soma: But surely, even if the injunction for the sacrificer’s function—such as the tying [of the animal] to the sacrificial post—is possible, how can there be the possibility of an injunction regarding a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) in that sentence (*ādityo yūpaḥ*), since it is impossible to enjoin the sun (*āditya*) therein? Nor is it tenable to argue that the word *āditya* figuratively denotes the *bilva* tree itself on the basis of its partial birth—namely, "from where that Āditya was born, from there the *bilva* arose"—and that this very [tree] is enjoined to perform the function of the sacrificial post, like the *khalevālī* (the threshing-post used as a boundary marker).

If that were the case, it would follow that the word "Āditya," which conveys the object to be enjoined, would have to be taken in its secondary (metaphorical) sense; therefore, it is more appropriate that it be considered merely an explanatory passage (arthavāda), as it depends upon that [enjoined action].

By this [argument], one might hold that: (1) accepting that the word *aditi*—the base of the word *āditya*—denotes the earth, a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) made of clay should be used; or (2) accepting that the word *āditya* denotes the *arka* tree, a sacrificial post made of the *arka* tree should be used; or (3) relying on the fact that the *nimba* tree is the dwelling place of the Sun (*āditya*), a sacrificial post made of the *nimba* tree should be used; or (4) having produced a reflection of the Sun upon the sacrificial post, the animal should be tied there; or (5) the tying should be performed upon an image of the Sun, according to the rule *ive pratikṛtau* (Pāṇini 5.3.96), which prescribes the suffix *ka* for images, including those intended for worship such as paintings.

The methods for establishing [the view] as a prescription of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*)—namely, that one should perform the tying (*niyojana*) after fashioning a representation of the sun (*āditya*) on the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), or making it resemble the form of the sun, based on the traditional rule: "In the case of a substitute, there is elision; [the suffix] *kan* occurs in cases such as *devapatha* and others"—are refuted. This is because those views are flawed by the assumption of meanings not supported by the well-known sense of the word *āditya*. If it is argued that [the sun] is indeed an accessory, since the sun can serve as a means for various functions of the sacrificial post—such as in the injunction: "He stands between the sacrificial post and the Āhavanīya fire with the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*)"—and so forth, whereby the sun may be prescribed for some of the post's functions; [we reply: no. Because the sun cannot possibly accomplish the primary functions of the sacrificial post. Furthermore, even if the sun were prescribed for a few of the post's functions, such as standing between the post and the Āhavanīya fire, this would still not establish the sun as the primary object of the injunction. Thus, the status of the sun as the principal element (*pradhāna*) remains unrefuted. Therefore, the sentence must be understood as a distinct injunction (*vidhi*) for the sacrificial post. Consequently, the view that the sentence is a mere descriptive restatement (*anuvāda*) is rejected. Hence, the sentence is a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). This being established, the conclusion is reached that the sentence is a mandatory injunction for the sacrificial post. This concludes the section on the discussion of the sacrificial post. It should be understood that the author of the *Śāstradīpikā*, with the intention that the application of the word [to the sacrificial post] is immediately perceived as being caused by that [similarity] due to the manifest association of the "Eye" (*cakṣus*) with the "Brāhmaṇa," has employed the ablative case in the phrase "on account of non-similarity" (*asārūpyāt*) within the Sūtra—even though the word "similarity" (*sārūpya*) occurs at the end of a compound—to indicate the purpose of excluding the sense organ, the eye.
However, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* maintains that in cases such as "The sacrificial post is the sun" (*ādityo yūpaḥ*), similarity is an object of verbal cognition because it is perceptible.
However, they say that in cases such as "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), substantial similarity (*sattvāsārūpya*) is required;
whereas verbal cognition is based on being the cause of similarity through the performance of functions and so forth—this is the distinction.
But that is not correct.

In this context, the perceptual establishment of similarity must indeed be stated as its [the figurative usage's] cause, because its causal factors—such as luminosity (*tejas*) and verticality (*ūrdhvatva*)—are themselves perceptible.

Likewise, here too, since the causal factors of similarity, such as luminosity and so forth, are present at the very first moment of apprehension, there is the possibility of the object being the content of verbal cognition.
Therefore, because similarity exists, in cases such as "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), it serves as the restrictive factor.

Section on Similarity (Sārūpyādhikaraṇa): If the principle of "desiring everything" (sārvakāmya) were to apply here as well, then it would also apply in this case; for if one accepts that similarity consists in being an object of verbal cognition, then [the same logic] would apply even to such statements as "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ), and thus this [objection] is trivial.

Regarding the term *sudhāmbastha*: because we observe the nominative plural in the compound *liṅgasamavāyāḥ*, its formation is established by the fact that it is always analyzed with the nominative case in every instance—as in "jātiśca jātiśca," "sārūpyaṃ ca," "praśaṃsā ca," "bhūmā ca," and "liṅgasamavāyaśca. Furthermore, although similarity (*sādṛśya*)—such as the similarity between the introductory section (*prastāva*) and the *rūpya* measure—is possible on the basis of a commonality of properties such as performing the same function, it is not the ground for the application of a word. This is because such similarity terminates merely in the performance of that function and thus lacks the status of being an object of verbal cognition; and since that which is not an object of cognition cannot serve as the ground for the application of a word, which consists in the communication [of meaning], it is not the ground for the application of the word.

However, the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) has been supplied [in the original text] to demonstrate the difference [between the post and the sun], namely that the similarity between the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the sun—the sacrificer—is the ground for the application of the word (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*), because it is an object of verbal cognition.

For, since there can be no figurative usage (*gauṇatva*) without similarity, even if that similarity were the cause of figurativeness, there would be no word other than "jar" (*ghaṭa*) to denote [the jar]; and since a cognition without an object is impossible, that which is the object of verbal cognition itself must be stated as the ground for the application of the word.
Furthermore, it is not logical for something to be the object of a verbal cognition without the determination of the word’s intended meaning (*tātparya*).

Moreover, since similarity (*sārūpya*) is based on its being the cause of that [cognition] and so forth, it is impossible for a word whose application is restricted solely to that [similarity] to have its intended meaning determined.
In this case, however, it is appropriate that perceptibility itself be the ground for the application of the word.
"Thus [it is said]:

because the eye is the primary subject in the *Brāhmaṇa* passage, and because it is possible to establish its identity through similarity, this [similarity of form] is mentioned here separately and uniquely—by means of the ablative case—as being for the purpose of prescribing a specific ground for the application of the word (i.e., its denotative function) in the form of being the object of verbal cognition; whereas other grounds for secondary usage (*gauṇatva*), such as performing its functions and so forth, are merely instances of similarity.
Thus [it is said].
Vi—In the case of "The sacrificial post is the sun," praise arises from the word "sun";
and in the case of the door, there is a similarity to the eye, as well as that [similarity] for the clarified butter and the fuel, because of their brilliance.

Thus, in the case of "The sacrificer is the sacrificial post" (*yajamāno yūpaḥ*), the sacrificial post is praised by means of the word "sacrificer" because of the commonality of the verticality that is perceptible to the eye. The Bhaṭṭas [hold] that in cases such as "The sun is the sacrificial post," similarity (*sārūpya*) is the basis for the secondary metaphorical usage (*gauṇī*). But is that the only basis in all cases? What is the distinction here? The ancients maintain that the basis here is the quality of being fiery light (*tejastva*), which is perceptible to the eye.

In reality, however, in other cases it is only a quality that serves as the cause for the verbal designation which functions as the qualifier (*prakāra*) through its relation as a quality of the same class as itself, but not similarity (*sārūpya*), because the latter functions as the relation (*saṃsarga*).

Here, by contrast, since it is precisely similarity—in the form of possessing a quality belonging to the same class as the quality residing in the object denoted by the primary sense—which functions as the qualifier through relations such as inherence (*samavāya*), that alone is the cause; this is the distinction.
Maṇḍana [states]: "The statement 'the sun is on the sacrificial post' is a praise (*stuti*)."
14. Śaṃkara: "And because of similarity of form, it is considered [to be] metaphorical in some cases. This is the section on similarity (*sārūpyādhikaraṇa*). It is held to be figurative (*gauṇī*).

If explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) were not intended to convey the meaning of their constituent parts, there would be a contradiction with the section on "similarity" (*sārūpyādhikaraṇa*). In that context, the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is established as referring to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) through a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*), based on its connection with the quality of verticality.
[The principle of] "desiring everything" (*sārvakāmyam*) [is established] by those desiring specific subsidiary results from the context.

"Or rather, other [sacrifices] are performed here for the sake of a single desire, while the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa) are for the sake of all [desires]"; and likewise, "Or rather, other seasonal sacrifices (ṛtu) are performed for the sake of a single desire, while the Jyotiṣṭoma is for the sake of all [desires].

And in this context, that which is stated regarding the universal desirability (sārvakāmyatva) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices and so forth, includes both the desires for the subsidiaries (aṅgakāma) and the fruits of the subsidiaries (aṅgaphala). Universal desirability is understood as including both the desires for the subsidiaries and the desires for the subsidiaries themselves.

Because of the context— namely, because of the employment of terms such as "Darśapūrṇamāsa" and so forth— and because the injunctions for those desiring specific results are prescribed within that context, the previous position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the aforementioned sentence is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of all the results, not an original injunction (*vidhi*). Alternatively, it is an instruction regarding the result (*phalopadeśa*), because of its connection with the word denoting the primary act.

Regarding the statements "The Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices] are for all [desires]" and "The Jyotiṣṭoma is for all [desires]," the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view—reached by the Sūtra—is that what is stated concerning the universal desirability (*sārvakāmya*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites is a restatement (*anuvāda*), not an injunction (*vidhi*). To this, the author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): the word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the prima facie view;
this is not a restatement of universal desirability, but rather it is an instruction regarding the fruit (*phalopadeśa*), an injunction of the fruit (*phalavidhi*).
Why? Because of the connection with the words denoting the primary rites.
Through words expressing the primary rites—namely "the Darśapūrṇamāsa" and "the Jyotiṣṭoma"—the connection with all fruits is prescribed.
Therefore, this is not a mere restatement (anuvāda).
However, it will be stated in the subsequent section that there is a separate performance for the sake of the specific reward.

Regarding the desire for all fruits (*sārvakāmya*) in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, this is an injunction of results; it is not a restatement (*anuvāda*) together with those who desire the subsidiaries. Bhāṣya 4.3.1.25–26. Furthermore, this desire for all fruits occurs successively, not simultaneously.

That which has scope is [superseded] by that which has no scope.
The subsidiary by the principal;
the property of the subsidiary by the property of the principal;
that which is to be adopted by that which is not to be adopted.
(The word "is sublated" is to be supplied). Bāla., p. 132. That which has scope is sublated by that which lacks scope. [This refers to] the sixteen previously mentioned.

Vārttika 3.1.14, p. 860: That which has room for application (*sāvakāśa*) is set aside by that which has no room for application (*niravakāśa*). For example, the *upāṃśutva* (whispering tone) prescribed by the word *kiṃcit*—which signifies "whatever" in the rule "whatever is prior [to the Agniṣomīya]"—has scope elsewhere than the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, specifically regarding the particular side preceding the Agniṣomīya; however, this *upāṃśutva* is set aside by the accent prescribed for the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and its subsequent rites alone, as that latter accent has no other scope. Bāla, p. 132: Between that which has room for application and that which has no room for application, the one without scope is stronger. Vi. 3.6.3: This is the principle that between that which has room for application and that which has no room for application, the one without scope is more powerful.
That which has another possible object is "with scope" (sāvakāśa); that which is not so is "without scope" (niravakāśa). By that which is without scope, an injunction with scope is sublated.

For example, the prohibitive statement "One should not harm any living beings" is sublated by the statement "One should sacrifice a white animal," which is without scope; for the former has scope there [in the case of the sacrifice] through its connection to objects other than the specific instance of harming.
Because there is no other object for the seizing of another's property, its scope is restricted;
the same applies elsewhere in the world as well. Thus says Sāhasī.
The principle of the "possessing scope" versus the "lacking scope" (*sāvakāśa-niravakāśa-nyāya*):

In a case concerning something other than one desiring cattle, the *camasa* cup has scope (*sāvakāśa*), whereas the *godohana* vessel lacks scope (*niravakāśa*). According to the *sāvakāśa-nyāya*, the *godohana* is more powerful.

Bhāṣya 8.1.5.20: The *sāvitra* oblation, followed by the preparation of the fire-pot (*ukhā-saṃbharaṇa*), and then the initiation rite (*dīkṣaṇīyā*) and so forth, must be performed exactly according to the order of the text; for the direct order of the recited text (*pratyakṣa-pāṭha-krama*) has greater force than the extended application (*codaka*).
VI. 5.1.99. Regarding the Sāvitra oblations in the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), [it is stated]: "He offers the Sāvitra oblations.
This is the principle of the Sāvitra oblations.
In the piling of the fire-altar, the Sāvitra oblations are to be performed prior to the initiation sacrifice (*dīkṣaṇīyā*).

The Bhāṣya states: Regarding the injunction, "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar," it is traditionally taught that there are first the Sāvitra oblations, then the preparation of the fire-pan (ukhā), the bricks, and the animal sacrifice.
Should those very rites be performed first, or the Dīkṣaṇīyā?
What is the prima facie view? That the modified rites (vaikṛta) are to be performed at the end, according to the principle "But at the end, Bādarāyaṇa [says].
This being the position, we reply:
first come the Sāvitra oblations, the bricks, the animal sacrifice, and the preparation of the fire-pan (ukhā).
Why? Because of the direct textual statement (*pratyakṣapāṭha*).
Furthermore, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is prescribed there;
and prior to it, the *sāvitra-homas*, the bricks, the animal sacrifice, and the preparation of the fire-pan (*ukhā-saṃbharaṇa*) are mentioned.
Therefore, their performance must come first.

[The *Ṭupṭīkā* states: Having prescribed the *sāvitra-homas*, the preparation of the fire-pan (*ukhā-saṃbharaṇa*), and so forth, the subsequent sentences describing the qualities of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice indicate that very locus as possessing those qualities.
Thus, because this textual sequence is directly perceived, the *sāvitra-homas* come first, followed by the *dīkṣaṇīyā*.

Śabara: Having performed the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, there arises a doubt as to whether the *sāvitra* offering should come first or the reverse. In this regard: "Because of the prior cognition of the archetype (*prakṛti*), the archetypal rites are to be performed first; the modified (*vaikṛta*) rites should follow, according to the view of Bādarāyaṇa."
It is said: "Even for those [words] heard for the sake of a quality (*guṇa*), the principle of the *sāvitra-homa* applies; the lion [is established] by direct recitation."
Since they are understood later, their performance is appropriately subsequent.

The connection [of this section] is for the purpose of rebutting the objection that "in this case, even though the *soma* is perceptible, the order of recitation (*pāṭha*) is not a restrictive factor.
It is explained: just as previously [in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others], the *Sāvitra* and other rites [are performed according to the sequence of the text].
Because it is archaic (Prākṛta), the original text here might have been different; this is another direct reading.
The *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

The *Cayana* (fire-piling), however, is taught outside of any specific introductory context (*anārambhādhīta*) as an optional subsidiary (*vaikalpika*) of the Soma sacrifice. When that [Cayana] is performed, the duties such as the *Sāvitra-homa* and the *Ukhā-saṃbharaṇa* are heard in scripture as being constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the Cayana.
Furthermore, certain subsidiary elements (*guṇas*) are heard in the application of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, which is a constituent part of the *savanajyotiṣṭoma*.

In this case, because the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is understood to have a fixed sequence (*baddhakrama*) through its recitation together with the preceding items of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* generally prescribed within the *soma* context, and because there is no such recitation for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* in the *cayana* (fire-altar construction) context—where only the subsidiary elements of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* are heard—the placement of the adventitious elements such as the *sāvitra* offerings occurs at the end of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and subsequent rites.

This being the prima facie view, [we reply]: because there is an introduction by means of a quality (*guṇa*), and because in that sentence the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) is mentioned as the subject (*uddeśya*), there is a co-location (*ekasthāna-svāgati*) of the quality and the possessor of the quality; furthermore, since the explicit reading (*pāṭha*) as a specific [rule] sets aside the reading in its general form, it is established that the *sāvitra* and other rites come first, and the *īkṣaṇīyā* comes later.
Maṇḍana says: "And from the bringing together of the animal's tethering-post (*paśu-trākhā-saṃbharaṇa*), the initiation (*dīkṣā*) [follows].
Śaṅkara says: "The initiation is subsequent to the *sāvitra*."

An injunction may be inferred from a statement of an established fact, a narrative (*arthavāda*), or a descriptive passage (*kalpa*), as for example: "There are indeed three bellies of the sacrifice: the *gāyatrī*, the *bṛhatī*, and the *anuṣṭubh*.

3|2|16–19. The *sūktavāka*.

The *sūktavāka* is a sentence that, while containing deity-words situated in the middle of the ritual application (*prayoga*), is endowed with the deity-words heard at the end, and serves to manifest the desired deity.

Consequently, whether there is one deity-word or many, and whether they are archetypal (*prākṛta*) or modified (*vaikṛta*), as long as they stand within the framework of the ritual procedure (*tantra*), the entire *sūktavāka* remains a single unit.
Therefore, the *sūktavāka* should be understood as established in exactly three ways.
Regarding the time of private recitation (*svādhyāya*) and the time of ritual performance—whether in the archetype (*prakṛti*) or the ectype (*vikṛti*):
in the case of private recitation, it is intended that [the mantra] has all the archetypal deities as its object;
whereas in the case of the two groups in the archetype, it has inferior deities in its midst.

The *sūktavāka* is understood to be modified in the middle of the words beginning with "Sūrya" and so forth; for it is taught that the *sūktavāka* is to be used exactly as it has been defined in that very context. (Vārttika 3.6.19, p. 770). The *sūktavāka* is prescribed as a mantra for the throwing of the grass-bundle (*prastara-praharaṇa*), and its connection with the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is not for the purpose of indicating time.
Bhāṣya 3.2.15.19–15: The *sūktavāka* is for the throwing of the *prastara* grass-bundle.
And the *prastara* is incidentally [connected] with the deities of the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes (though it is actually for the sake of the animal sacrifice).

Regarding the Sūtra (Saṃkarṣa 2.4.3): "The *sūktavāka* is the *yājyā*; the *prastara* is the oblation; the *idhmah* is offered as the first of the oblations"—this has been explained by that [sūtra]. Having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the throwing of the *prastara* and the placing of the *idhma* are of the nature of a *homa* (oblation), because the statement "The *sūktavāka* is the *yājyā*, the *prastara* is the oblation" and the supplementary passage "The *idhmah* is offered as the first of the oblations" indicate they are *homas*, and because the deities are specifically obtained from the wording of the mantras; the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached by the sūtra: "Or rather, it is praise or a consecratory act (*saṃskāra*) of the *prastara*, because of its proximity; the *idhmah* is for the purpose of kindling. This is merely praise by way of treating them as oblations, because the throwing of the *prastara* is a disposal (*pratipatti*), since the *prastara* is presented with an accusative ending as something already utilized for the maintenance of the sacrifice, and because the placing of the *idhma* serves a visible purpose, namely for the sake of the fire.
Jaimini Sūtra 3.2.152: The *sūktavāka* is the *yājyā* (offering verse); the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is the substance; having designated the deities [therein], the sacrifice is performed.
In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, this is also a disposal (*pratipatti*).
Bhāṣya 3.2.15.19–15: Thus indeed is the *sūktavāka*.
But for the *savanīya* offerings, [the requirement] is established by incidental application (*prasaṅga*).

(1.3.16.54) By the statement, "He throws the grass-bundle (*prastara*) with the *sūktavāka*," the *sūktavāka* mantra is enjoined for the act of throwing through the force of the instrumental case-ending; thus, the mantra serves the purpose of the throwing.
This is because the mantra and the act of throwing have two distinct deities.

However, as for the portion consisting of the relinquishment of the substance (*dravyatyāga*), it serves a purely transcendental purpose (*kevalārtha*). Such an act, which is both visible and transcendental, is a purifier of the substance (*dravyasaṃskāraka*) that provides assistance through its presence (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*).
The *sūktavākya* is a Vedic ritual act consisting of the performance for the sake of the sacrifice (*ṛtvartha*).
