In the *sūktavāka*, the portion beginning with "He prays for long life" (*āyurāśāste*) and so forth, which pertains to the sacrificer, must indeed be recited in the *sarvasvāra* sacrifice.

This is because, from the conclusion of the *sūktavāka* until the end of the *ārambhaṇīyā* [offering], the attainment of those respective fruits may occur either in this life or in another birth. (Ci.
Regarding the *sūktavāka*, there is an injunction concerning time, because it serves another purpose.
It is heard in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices: "He throws the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*.

In this regard, a discussion arises as to whether the *sūktavāka* is enjoined for the purpose of the throwing of the *prastara*, or whether this is merely an indication of time. To this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) speaks.
In the *sūktavāka*, that is, in the *sūktavāk* formula, there would be an injunction regarding time, similar to the non-release [of the *prastara*].
That is to say: "When the *sūktavāka* occurs, then the throwing of the *prastara* [should take place]"; however, the *prastara*-throwing is not the *sūktavāka*.
This is because both are subservient to another purpose: the *sūktavākya* is intent upon the praise of the deities, and the *prastara* is for the purpose of supporting [the oblation].
Therefore, it is a rule regarding time; the *sūktavāka* is for the purpose of proclaiming the deities intended for the sacrifice.

(Mīmāṃsākośa 541) The word "or" (*vā*) in the sūtra sets aside the prima facie view—that in the sentence "He throws the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*," the *sūktavāka* is a rule regarding time, meaning it is to be recited at the time of throwing the *prastara*—and states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). This is because the word "offering verse" (*yājyā*) does not apply to it in this context.
Instruction: The *sūktavāka* mantra should pertain to the throwing of the *prastara* grass-bundle.
In the throwing of the *prastara*, the *sūktavāka* is the instrumental mantra.

This being the case, the word "offering verse" (*yājyā*) in the supplementary statement—"The *sūktavāka* itself is the offering verse; the *prastara* is the oblation"—would not occur without cause. Thus, it would be inexplicable without a reason.
The term *yājyā* would not be inappropriate;
otherwise, it would indeed be inappropriate.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *sūktavāka* is taught as being a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the act of throwing [the offering].
That [mantra] has the deities as its purpose because of its connection with them.

Regarding the statement, "He casts the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*," the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated that the *sūktavāka* is enjoined as a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) to the casting of the *prastara*.
Now, if it is objected that the *sūktavāka* is capable of proclaiming the deities, but not of performing the casting of the *prastara*, the author replies to that.
That *sūktavāka* has the deities as its purpose; in a sacrifice where the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is the offering, it serves to designate the deity.
And since it has the deities as its purpose, by virtue of its connection with them—and because of its connection with the act of throwing (*praharaṇa*)—it is also an auxiliary to that throwing.
Its status as an auxiliary to the throwing follows from the connection with the instrumental case-ending in the scriptural statement, "with the *sūktavāka*" (*sūktavākena*).

If it is argued that this is a *pratipatti* (concluding disposal), [the opponent] might say: "But surely the throwing of the *prastara* is a *pratipatti*; and if that were so, the status of the *sūktavāka* as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that act would not be established. Therefore, let the connection be for the sake of time alone. To this, the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) replies: "It must be a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the substance intended for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering."

If it is argued that because one "casts the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*," the casting of the *prastara* is a *pratipatti* (disposal), and therefore the *sūktavāka* is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to it—[we reply:
the casting would be a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for both.
It serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) in its aspect as a sacrifice, while in its aspect as the act of throwing, it is a *pratipatti*.
By the term "dual consecration" (*ubhayasaṃskāra*), it is intended that there is a dual nature.

Alternatively, it should be understood as a dual consecration in that the consecration of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) occurs through the act of casting [into the fire], while the consecration of the deity already employed occurs through the portion of the dedication (*uddeśa*).

Regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt*: the substance is the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice; through the act of casting, it is the consecration of the oblation already employed, and by means of the word of the mantra, it is likewise the consecration of the deity who was the object of worship.
Therefore, the *sūktavāka* is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the throwing of the grass-bundle (*prastarapraharaṇa*).
Alternatively, just as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is for the purpose of consecrating the sacrificial material, so too is the principle of the *sūktavāka* [to be applied] in the *sūktavāka* section.
Because the fire has been prepared by the *siddhaka* [preparation] and thus its purpose is fulfilled, it constitutes a subordinate element (*śeṣa*);
nevertheless, it does not forfeit its status as a sacrifice (*yāga*).
Thus, there is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of both, each of which has its own fulfilled purpose.
The sacrifice will be one that accomplishes an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) while also serving the purpose of another.
Regarding the term *ubhaya-saṃskāraḥ*, in the latter sense it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "a refinement (*saṃskāra*) that has both forms.
In the former sense, it is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the refinement of both [namely], the substance and the deity."
In the *sūktavāka* belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the word "yajamāna" (sacrificer) must be modified (*ūhitavya*) when the rite is performed by multiple agents.
In the *sūktavāka*, when the name of the sacrificer is to be specified, two names are to be mentioned; however, for one who has performed the Soma sacrifice, a third name may also be included.

The Śruti states, "one should take up names" and "one should take up a name. Since this is for the purpose of making the sacrificer known by a specific name, even one who possesses many names should take up any single one; therefore, multiplicity is not intended in the injunction. This being the prima facie view, it is replied: having prescribed that "one should make names of two or four syllables," the subsequent injunction, "one who has performed the Soma sacrifice should make a third name," indicates that the rule regarding multiple names is intended for the performer of the Soma sacrifice. Thus, [the rule] is restricted.

The principle of the *sūktavāka* (the explanatory recitation) serves as the introductory topic (*prakṛta-viṣaya*) for this section by way of providing a distinction; it also serves as the intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*) by way of being an exception (*apavāda*).
As stated in the *Śāstra*: "In that case, because both have fulfilled their purpose, the relationship between the signifier (*jñāpaka*) and the signified (*jñāpya*) is established."
"Therefore, their connection is for the purpose of time, just as in the case of the *daśāpavitra* and so forth.
This being the position reached, we reply: "By direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), the *sūktavāka* is understood to be subordinate to the offering (*praharaṇa*);
therefore, the oblation shall take place precisely through its connection with those deities [mentioned therein]."
Therefore, it is appropriate that the *sūktavāka* itself possesses the character of an offering (*praharaṇa*) precisely while the chosen deity is being invoked.
As for Soma—here too, the connection is established as being solely for the purpose of time; this constitutes the connection because of the counter-argument.

The practical application (*prayojana*) is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the offering lacks the nature of a *homa*, there is no status as a thing to be aimed at (*uddeśyatva*); whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), that status exists.
Vi— "One should cast the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*": this is the cognition of time.
Whether it is ignorance or knowledge, time would be ignorant because of its otherwise nature;
for the act of casting (*praharati*) involves a connection with that [time], as it is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the sake of the deity.
The status of being an *ājñā* (injunction) is established through the third [type of] scriptural statement (*śruti*) by means of the deity.
In the Bhaṭṭa school, regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "He throws the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*.

In that context, since the mantra denoted by the term *sūktavāka* has fulfilled its purpose by proclaiming the deities who have been sacrificed to, and since the throwing of the *prastara* has fulfilled its purpose as the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *prastara* already employed, the relationship between them is for the sake of time (*kālārtha*), just as in the case of the statement: "Having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice with Soma."

And the third [instrumental case], being used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*), indicates the connection of the *sūktavāka* with the throwing by way of a temporal relationship; thus, its application is not improper.
Nor is this a case of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because even that is possible since it is sanctioned by grammatical rule.

Therefore, following the utterance of permission, the throwing itself—qualified by that specific time—is enjoined with reference to the grass-bundle (*prastara*), but the status of the *sūktavāka* as an indicator (*añjana*) of the throwing is not [enjoined].

This being the position reached, because of its frequent usage and for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the third case-ending lies in instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) alone, and not in the sense of "characteristic of such a state" (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*). For although the latter is sanctioned by grammatical rule (*ānuśāsanika*), it is justified as being merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*). Consequently, since the status of the *praharaṇa* (the striking) as an act of offering is understood through direct statement (*śruti*), there is no contradiction in the root *praharati* indicating a *homa* (oblation) in the form of an *āśrava-karma*, by means of the deity inferred from the wording of the mantra.
For this very reason, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of a sacrifice—namely, the statement "the *sūktavāka* itself is the *yājyā*"—is also consistent.

And although its primary status as a *yājyā* (offering verse) is not possible—unlike [the status of] a *mantra* and so forth—because it is not an object of conventional usage among experts, since this indicative mark (*liṅga*) is accompanied by the particle "eva" and thus cannot establish its status as a *yājyā*; nevertheless, because it is designated as a *yājyā* merely by virtue of being an instrument of sacrifice, it possesses the character of a sacrificial indicative (*yāgaliṅga*).

Consequently, even though by direct statement (*śruti*) the mantra is known to be an auxiliary to the *praharaṇa* (the throwing), there is no sublation here of its primary status, for that [status] is also compatible with the *praharaṇa*.
Maṇḍana [says]: "There would be a sacrifice with the *sūktavāka*, [and] the *prahāra*."
Śaṅkara: "In the *sūktavāka*, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is intended.

By the principle of the *sūktavāka*, there will arise the cognition that the mantra 'pūṣā'si', which is enjoined by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) as an instrument, effects the sacrifice through its capacity to bring about the deity.
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 132). The *sūktavāka-praiṣa* ('agnim adha') is a specific characteristic (*vaiśeṣika-dharma*) of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*).
Because of the incapacity of the Āgnīdhra,
the *niyoktṛ* (the one who gives the command) must be the Maitrāvaruṇa.
However, there is no animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for the Maitrāvaruṇa.
Regarding the *sūktavāka* injunction in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), [the formula] is "The divine Hotṛ-priests have been chosen for the sacrifice" (*iṣṭitā daivayā hotāraḥ*).
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni-Soma (*agnīṣomīya paśu*), this is modified as "He chose Agni as the Hotṛ" (*agnim adha hotāram avṛṇīta*).
Furthermore, it is modified in the Savanīya animal sacrifice [with the words]: "The sacrificer has chosen Agni as the Hotṛ, O Suta-suvī.

(Drahyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra 12.1.2.13). And the Sūktavāka mantra, in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, is to be applied by dividing it according to the force of its indicative marks (liṅga) and the force of the syntactical connection (vākya).
VI. 3|2|6, 3|15: The throwing of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) onto the fire is performed with the *sūktavāka* mantra.

At 3|15, in the *sūktavāka* mantra, where [the singular form] "this sacrificer (*ayaṃ yajamānaḥ*) desires long life (*āyurāśāste*)" and so forth occurs, it must be modified here to "these sacrificers (*ime yajamānāḥ*) desire long life" and so forth; this is because there is a plurality of fruit-receivers (*phalin*) and because the mantra reveals the fruit.
In the *sūktavāka* mantra, where it says "the sacrificer desires long life," the modification (*ūha*) in a *sattra* sacrifice is "the sacrificers desire long life."

The application of the *sūktavāka*: 4327. The principle of the division of the *sūktavāka*; the application of the *sūktavāka* is according to the sense [of the words]. Vi. 3.2.6. The principle of the division of the *sūktavāka*.
The application of the *sūktavāka* in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is by way of division.
Because it is taught in its entirety, the whole formula is to be used in both [sacrifices].
The Commentary states: Regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "With the *sūktavāka*, he throws the grass-bundle (*prastara*) into the fire."

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the entire *sūktavāka* be recited at the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), and the entire one at the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*), or should it be applied according to its respective capacity by extracting [the relevant portions] as appropriate? To this it is replied:
in both cases, the word "entire" applies.
Why? Because the entire mantra is called the *sūktavāka*.
Without even a single word, it would not be the *sūktavāka*;
in that case, the offering would not have been performed with the *sūktavāka*.

Therefore, the entire *sūktavāka* should be recited in both cases. [The author] now examines the application of the governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*): Should the complete *sūktavāka* be employed in both the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices, or should there be an extraction [of specific parts] according to the deities intended for each sacrifice? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That it should be complete in each individual case.
Why? "Just as the *sūktavāka* mantra is recited within the *sāman*, if it were extracted from that [context], it would no longer possess the character of a *sūktavāka*.
Consequently, the offering would be performed with what is not a *sūktavāka*."

Or rather, it is according to the actual meaning, due to the refinement of the remaining elements. The Commentary states: Those words which denote the deities of the Full Moon sacrifice are to be employed at the Full Moon sacrifice, not at the New Moon sacrifice.

Those [mantras] which denote the deities of the new moon sacrifice are to be used at the new moon sacrifice, not at the full moon sacrifice. It has been stated that mantras assist the deities who constitute the remnants [of the offering] when they have been consecrated, and not otherwise. Therefore, those mantras which assist in a particular context should be employed there; thus, the entire set is not used at the full moon sacrifice, nor is the entire set used at the new moon sacrifice.
Or rather—it has been stated in the *Sutaśākhādhikaraṇa* (2.1.5) that there is an omission of these and similar elements, and it was also stated in the *Pūṣādyanumantraṇa* section (3.1.12).
For if these were distinct deities known only from the [specific] offering-formulas (*praharaṇa*), then the entire formula would be employed in both cases.
However, since those very same deities, such as Agni and the rest, are recognized here as well, there is no reason for such a distinction.

And for this reason, because the *sūktavāka* depends upon the manifestation of the intended deity, the striking [of the sacrificial post] is not the motive; rather, it is understood that the *sūktavāka* is dependent on the deities invoked by the primary rites, since it rests upon them as its basis.
And those primary rites are performed according to their respective deities, not without distinction.
Therefore, there must be a displacement [of the formula].
If it is argued that this is because of a scriptural statement (vacana),
the Bhāṣya says: Now, as for what was said— that there will be this scriptural statement, "He offers with the Sūktavāka"— in that case,
even by means of this single word, the offering would not have been performed with the Sūktavāka.
"For there is an instruction for the entire *sūktavāka*.

Or—if it is asked how the word *sūktavāka* [is applied]—he says: [In the *Sudhā*, this *vārttika* is introduced by the passage: "Because the word *sūktavāka* is well-known for the collection of words beginning with 'idaṃ dyāvāpṛthivī' and ending with 'devatebhyaḥ', which serves to manifest the deities of the Full Moon sacrifice; and because, since the deities of the New Moon sacrifice are mentioned at the Full Moon sacrifice, or the deities of the Full Moon sacrifice are mentioned at the New Moon sacrifice, it applies to the meaning of its constituent parts; thus he explains it with the intention that it is a conventional term (*rūḍhi*)."

Commentary: This is stated:
the word "entire" refers to both the Full Moon and the New Moon sacrifices, because both constitute the context.
The whole is said to belong to both; [it is like saying] "a part [belongs] to a part.
(Now the author of the Bhāṣya refutes the Sūtra: This is not so;
for the relationship with the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) does not consist in mutual dependence.
For the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is not heard as being qualified by these [actions];
rather, these [actions] are understood as being qualified by the procedure.
Why? Because actions are not enjoined with respect to the procedure; their injunction is with respect to the result.
The manner of performance (itikartavyatā), however, is enjoined by means of the action.
In that case, because there is no distinction due to proximity, it is not understood which [action] is enjoined with which [manner of performance] and which is not;
for all [actions] are indicated as being instrumental means, and because the manner of performance is in proximity yet remains unexpressed [as belonging to any one specifically].

Because this indicative mark of the context (*prakaraṇa-liṅga*) is without distinction, the entire context is required for each individual [deity] when it is complete in itself and has no further expectancy, not for that which is seeking assistance.

There are many such formulas in which words denoting the principal deities are placed in the middle, while common words are uttered before them as well as after them.
For example: "May Agni accept this oblation; he has grown great and performed a more glorious deed," and "May Agni and Soma accept this oblation; they have grown great," and so forth.

As for the claim that silver is accepted [as real] in order to establish the causality of the object and the ordinary sense-contact in the case of the worldly perception "I see silver"— which is asserted as having both creation and dissolution— that too is refuted by accepting that the silverness residing in the object before one is worldly (laukika) in its aspect as a substrate, yet non-worldly (alaukika) in its aspect as silverness, because it is produced by a defect (*doṣa*). Furthermore, as for the argument that there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in taking silverness as the delimiting condition of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) rather than the cognition of silver, that too is indeed more parsimonious than the postulation of ignorance (*ajñāna*) as the cause.

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of [the world] being non-perceived even when there is knowledge of its substrate, because the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of its worldly existence acts as an obstacle to that knowledge.

Furthermore, passages from scripture such as “One should know Māyā to be Prakṛti” can be explained as referring to the intellect in a dream state (*svāpnabuddhi*), or by taking the word *māyā* to mean a defect (*doṣa*). This is the summary.
Some, however, hold that the Supreme Self alone, by His own will, produces the ether and so forth as ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) itself.

The Śrutis—such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone; it desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" "From that very Self, space was produced," and "This is indeed the Person; there is no diversity here whatsoever"—proclaim this very same meaning.
For here, by the first two Śrutis, the causality of the Self—which existed previously in its own nature like a seed—is stated, as well as its being the effect, like a sprout.
By the other two Śrutis, the absence of any difference in the substrate (the underlying reality) is stated.
The various scriptures are to be understood as being situated upon the tree [of reality], like branches of a single trunk.

As for those passages that establish the doctrines of falsity, such as "The Self alone is this truth," or the doctrines of reality, such as "Indra moves through his powers of illusion (māyā)," or those that explain *māyā* itself, they all demonstrate its very impermanence.
Or, it is like the expression "others are inferior to the cattle and horses."

Even for these [illusory appearances], the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-satyatva*) is [taught] either for the purpose of generating enthusiasm or for the purpose of generating detachment, or else for the purpose of establishing that it is not the ultimate reality, because they are equal to a dream.
This is clearly stated in the Śruti: "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'mukti' alone is the truth. The meaning is this:

by knowing the clay-lump, there is knowledge delimited by all its modifications; by the knowledge of the "commencement" (*ārambha*), there is knowledge of the entire phenomenal world consisting of that [clay].
Although there is no knowledge [of the world] as being the expansion (*vyāsa*), it is nonetheless established that there is knowledge of it in its contracted form (*samāsa*).
And this is possible only if the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is real;
for there can be no knowledge of what is unreal within a cognition whose nature is real, as that would entail the absurd consequence of knowing things such as a rabbit's horn.
Therefore, they assert that it is logical for the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) to be real.

However, the atheistic Sāṃkhya school asserts that *prakṛti*—which consists of the qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* and is denoted by the term *pradhāna*—is non-conscious, yet undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*) into the form of the specific phenomenal world beginning with the *mahat* for the sake of the experience of conscious selves.

However, the *Sāṃkhya* with God (*seśvara-sāṃkhya*) maintains that primordial matter (*prakṛti*), presided over by the Lord—who is designated by the term "Puruṣa," who is all-pervasive, and who is untouched by ignorance, latent dispositions, attachment, aversion, clinging, karma, its fruition, and so forth—creates the world through the sequence of the Great Principle (*mahat*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and so on; just as a field, when prepared, creates trees and the like through the sequence of sprouts and so forth once it has been presided over by a seed. Therefore, creation has primordial matter as its material cause (*upādāna*), and it is enjoyed by the immutable individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) who are distinct from the Lord.
Furthermore, the diversity of the phenomenal world is established by the very fact that there is a plurality of enjoyers (*bhoktṛ*) within primordial matter itself.
The Upaniṣadic [teaching], however, explains the very identity of the Self as being based on similarity;
likewise, it negates all plurality.
It is with this very intention that [it is said]: "In a Brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and humility, in a cow, in an elephant..."
The wise perceive equality in both a dog and an outcaste.

Thus it should be understood from the passages, "Indra moves through his powers of illusion (māyā) as a person," and so forth. Even those doctrines which assert the identity of the liberated self with the Lord must be explained either by way of extreme similarity or by the absence of any distinction [other than that].
"When the seer sees the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person whose source is Brahman, then the knower,
having shaken off both merit and evil, becomes stainless and attains supreme equality."
Because the state of supreme equality is declared by the Śruti:
"Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature;
even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer. (Gītā 14.2)
This is because equality is also stated by the words of the Blessed One:

"And by the words of the Blessed One, 'In the world of living beings, that which has become a living soul is an eternal portion of Me myself,' [it is clear]. Furthermore, [the following objection] does not hold: 'When the knowledge that produces the sense of difference has undergone absolute destruction, who will ever again create an absolute difference between the Self and Brahman?'"
Furthermore, there would be an inconsistency with the statement in the Purāṇa, for that passage is consistent as it makes known the relationship between master and servant between those two.

And thus: "But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self" (Gītā 15.17); "The witness, the permitter, the agent, the enjoyer, the Great Lord—He is called the Supreme Self, the highest person in this body. (Gītā 13.22)
Thus, the perception of difference is established.
Therefore, they say that this phenomenal world has *prakṛti* as its material cause (*upādāna*).

But that too is not correct, because since *prakṛti* is of a uniform nature, it would be impossible for there to be a diversity in its effects, such as humans, animals, and so forth, based on its character as a cause.

Regarding the creation and dissolution resulting from the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), even the claim that there is a distinction between the objects of creation and dissolution cannot be maintained; for since the unseen merit and demerit are included within the effects themselves, they dissolve into primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and thus cannot serve as the cause.

Or from what cause does the commencement of transformations such as the *mahat* and so forth arise by their own nature (*prakṛti*)? If you say it is "by the will of God" (*īśvarecchā*), that is not so, because He has cast off all desires.

Furthermore, since at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) only primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the selves (*ātman*) remain in an undifferentiated state, and since merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) consist of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and thus do not exist then, there would be no distinction between those who have performed meritorious deeds and those who have committed evil in their previous lives.

Nor should it be argued that, because the production and destruction of things such as a hare’s horn are never observed, and because the production of existent things is seen to be necessarily determined, the diversity [of the world] is established through the power of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—which remain in a state capable of being acted upon—by way of the manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) and concealment (*tirobhāva*) of production and destruction;
for this is contradicted by the non-perception of the existence of a jar during its states as a lump of clay or as potsherds.

However, the statement "there is no existence of the non-existent" (*nāsato vidyate bhāvaḥ*)—since it begins with the demonstration of permanence in the passage "I was never not-existent" (*na tvevāhaṃ jātu nāsam*)—establishes that mere commencement possesses the properties of non-arising and non-destruction, but it does not apply to the entire range of effects. Or, even if we grant that [the effect] persists in the form of its cause, nevertheless, just as water cannot be carried by a lump of clay because it remains in the state of clay, there can be no production of diversity from merit and demerit while they remain in the state of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

If, however, the succession of creation and dissolution is beginningless, then the eternity of the Vedas—which consist of words whose meanings are likewise beginningless—is established by the following [scriptural] statement: "In the beginning, he fashioned the names and the distinct functions of all beings, as well as their various objects, from the very words of the Veda."

In accordance with the statement, "Thus," it is accepted that there is praise for the practice of having a single author and a common name; or, in accordance with the statement, "Eighty-eight thousand [sages] are the propagators of the tradition," it is accepted that its creation was by multiple authors.

Even in that case, because [the scripture] has primordial matter (*prakṛti*) as its material cause (*upādāna*), and because it is impossible to produce something without a material cause, the fact that it possesses a material cause is established.
This is the summary.
Maṇi, pp. 45–53.
Just as creation and dissolution occur in the present, so too have they occurred from beginningless time.
However, it is not possible for there to be a creation and dissolution of the entire universe; thus, according to Mīko, p. 1733, "the world is beginningless."
"And there is no creator for that," as should be seen in the *Ślokavārttika* on the *Bindu*.

The stream of creation and dissolution is beginningless—the Vaiśeṣikas say so; "beginninglessness" refers to the stream of creation and dissolution. At the end of a hundred years of Brahmā’s life... [Mīmāṃsākośa 543].
When the Blessed Maheśvara develops the desire to dissolve the entire world, from the conjunction of the Lord with a self possessing that desire, actions of disjunction arise in the atoms.

Consequently, when all things have been mutually disjoined down to the level of the dyad (dvyaṇuka), due to the destruction of all constituent parts, only the atoms remain—those of earth, water, fire, and air—as well as ether, time, space, self, and mind; and merit and demerit, obstructed by the will of the Lord for that duration and not yielding their fruits, remain within those respective [substances] awaiting a new commencement.
Furthermore, O Sātvatī, when time has passed, that very Blessed One, seeing that the self is devoid of the experience of karma and being overcome by compassion, develops a desire to create.

Then, from the conjunction of the Lord and the self accompanied by that desire to create, action arises in the atoms; through that [action], they mutually conjoin, and by means of the sequence of dyads (dvyaṇuka), earth and the other elements are initiated.

Thereafter, by virtue of His will alone, various elemental species are initiated through diverse actions whose obstructions have been removed and whose potencies are manifested, resulting in a manifold variety of subsequent forms.
Then that very Maheśvara creates the Vedas for the purpose of establishing dharma and adharma;
thus, in each successive creation, the Vedas are different ones.
However, the stream of the Vedas, as well as the process of creation and dissolution, are beginningless.
And the creator is Maheśvara, who is indeed beginningless.
Furthermore, since atoms are the material cause here, there is no lack of a material cause for creation.
Thus it is said.
Ratnākara, pp. 616–617:
Regarding the doctrine of creation and dissolution—the statement concerning the creation and dissolution of the entire world is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise).
Furthermore, it must necessarily be asserted that the Upaniṣadic portion, which is enjoined by the rule of Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*), has as its primary purpose a meaningful goal.

Therefore, this doctrine of creation and dissolution is intended to explain the power of destiny (*daiva*). Even in the absence of all human effort (*puruṣakāra*), everything proceeds by the force of destiny at the time of creation; and at the time of dissolution, even though human effort exists, it ceases precisely because destiny has come to rest. Consequently, one should strive solely for the performance of dharma—this is the primary purpose of the discourse on creation and dissolution.
(Ratnākara, *Saṃbandhakṣepaparihāra*, 112).

The utility of reasoning concerning creation and dissolution for the sake of *dharma* is as follows: whether human effort (*puruṣakāra*) exists or not, an effect proceeds by the power of destiny (*daiva*) and ceases when destiny subsides. Furthermore, at the beginning of creation, the world arises from destiny alone even in the absence of human effort; and at the time of dissolution, the world ceases when destiny subsides even though human effort exists. Therefore, realizing that destiny possesses greater power than human effort, one should strive in the performance of rites prescribed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis—this is what is understood [from this]. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 131)

These [points] are here collected according to the sequence of the words in the first sūtra: Regarding the statement that for some, Soma comes before the Agnyādheya (the establishment of the sacred fires), because of the injunction regarding the passing over of the season and the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*); for if it were otherwise, that [injunction] would be rendered meaningless. Even though—on account of the scriptural injunction—the Agnyādheya must indeed be preceded by the *Iṣṭi* (sacrifice), such that after performing the Agnyādheya one must then perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and thereafter the Soma sacrifice at the proper time; nevertheless, for certain followers of particular recensions (*śākhins*), Soma may occur even before the *Iṣṭi* following the Agnyādheya. That is to say, for them, Soma comes first after the Agnyādheya, and the *Iṣṭi* follows after that.
The word "ca" (and) is intended to include the [rule] regarding the single [instance].

Why? Because the *ādhāna* (the act of laying the fires) must be preceded by the *soma*; having grasped the immediate sequence of the *soma* following the *ādhāna* on the grounds that the latter ends with the former (*tadanta*), the meaning is as follows:

"Because of the statement regarding the transgression of seasons and constellations"—that is, the transgression of the season such as spring which is the time for the *soma*, and the constellation such as Kṛttikā, is stated in the scriptural injunction: "He who, intending to sacrifice with the *soma*, lays the fires, shall not wait for the season nor for the constellation."

If there were no interval between the Soma sacrifice and the installation [of the fires], the statement regarding the transgression of the seasons and the lunar mansions would be entirely meaningless.
Here, the word "hi" has the sense of "eva" (indeed). Therefore, the Soma sacrifice must precede.

Regarding the phrase "tadantena"—if the reading were *tadarthena*, the meaning would be that a statement which sets aside the [specific] time (*kālabādhaka*) when joined with *tadarthena*—that is, with the purpose of establishing the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣasiddhyarthena*)—would be entirely redundant. (In the Vṛtti:
A statement joined with the present tense (*laṭ*) in *yakṣyamāṇa*, which denotes the time immediately following that [purpose], would be redundant.
Alternatively, the meaning is that a statement joined with the *luṭ* suffix—which denotes the present or future time—would be purposeless and redundant.
(In the *Kutūhala*:
Therefore, there is immediate succession between the *ādhāna* and the *soma*.
And because of the statement regarding that purpose; it is not so because there is no distinction as to its being for that purpose.

[The author] states another reason for the conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) must precede the *soma*, namely: "After the *ādhāna*, first comes the *soma*, and then the *darśapūrṇamāsa*s.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of conjunction.
The statement, "He who, intending to sacrifice with Soma, should establish the sacred fires," refers specifically to the purpose of the Soma sacrifice.
For otherwise, even one intending to sacrifice after a year might establish the fires for the sake of the Agnihotra and other rites along with the Soma;

since there would be no distinction between that which is for the purpose of the Soma and that which is for the purpose of the Agnihotra and so forth, the specific status of being for the purpose of the Soma would not exist.
And there is a statement regarding the Soma; therefore, this statement declares that the Soma is for the purpose of the Soma, namely,
that the Soma [is for the purpose] of the fire-consecration (ādhāna).
Therefore, this statement is for the purpose of establishing the immediate succession between the Soma sacrifice and the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya).

Thus ends the priority of the Soma sacrifice. Furthermore, because the time for the Pavamāna oblations of the one about to perform the Soma sacrifice is specified immediately after the giving [of the dakṣiṇās], there would be a distinction [between the two cases].

The sūtra is intended to demonstrate another argument for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) may be preceded either by an *iṣṭi* sacrifice or by the *soma* sacrifice as alternatives.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of conjunction.

Because of the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), for one who is about to sacrifice with Soma immediately after the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), there is no room for doubt or suspicion regarding the absence of the *soma-pūrvatva* (the state of having Soma first) on account of the specific time of the *pavamāna-havis* offerings (the *pavamāneṣṭis*). This is because, having heard the scriptural injunction: "He who, being about to sacrifice with Soma, establishes the fires, should not offer oblations before a year [has passed]," the specific time for the *pavamāna-havis* is thereby indicated.
Thus, the word *viśva-* here is devoid of the negative sense (*nañ-artha*).

The meaning is that, according to the Śruti, by the word "yakṣyamāṇa" (one who intends to sacrifice), it is stated that this applies immediately after the *ādhāna* for one who will not sacrifice with Soma.
Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is an option between having the *iṣṭi* first and having the Soma sacrifice first:
for one intending to perform the *iṣṭi*, the Soma sacrifice comes first for the sake of that [Soma].
This sūtra is intended to state the purpose of the topic (adhikaraṇa) established by the sūtras from the fifth to the eighth.

Thus, for one who will not sacrifice with Soma at this time—contrary to one who is about to sacrifice with Soma—the Darśapūrṇamāsa iṣṭi is to be commenced after the establishment of the fires (ādhāna). If the establishment of the fires were for that specific purpose alone, namely for the sake of Soma, then the sequence must indeed be preceded by Soma.

For one who intends to sacrifice with Soma for the first time, the Soma sacrifice must be performed immediately after the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), even before the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*); the *darśapūrṇamāsa* offerings will follow afterwards.

Bhaṭṭa 1.1.3.14: The Jyotiṣṭoma is the original archetype (mūlaprakṛti) of the Soma sacrifices. Vi. 8.1.3, Section 2: In the Soma sacrifice, the carrying forward of the fire (agnipraṇayana) possesses its specific ritual characteristics (dharmavat).
Bhāṣya 7.3.8.19:

In the Soma sacrifice performed by one who has built the fire-altar (agnicit), there is a combination of both the northern altar (uttaravedi) and the two ancient fires (purāṇāgnidvaya), as well as the twenty-one strides (ekaviṃśati-lokaṃpraṇā).

Since the *iṣṭis*, *pṛṣṭhas*, and *stomas* are specifically mentioned as occurring after the *cayanam* (the piling of the altar), it follows that all [of these] have "ancient" (*purāṇa*) material. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: because of another scriptural statement—"Now, those who perform this [rite], those who undertake this [rite], should sacrifice with Soma at the very place where they previously sacrificed; there, on the *uttaravedi*, they should also sacrifice with twenty-one *lokaṃpraṇās*"—this other injunction prescribes a different material for the Soma sacrifice. Consequently, by means of the general statement, the injunction regarding the "ancient" material applies here specifically to the *iṣṭis* and *pṛṣṭhas*.

In reality, even in the sentence "yadīṣṭyā" (if by an iṣṭi), because the mention of Soma as the qualificand would otherwise be inexplicable, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the twenty-one *lokampṛṇā* bricks—which have the *uttaravedi*, *yūpa*, and fire-altar (*agni*) as their substance—with the *agni-citi* in the Soma sacrifice. However, for the *iṣṭis* and *pṛṣṭhas* included within the Soma sacrifice, there is an absence of the twenty-one *lokampṛṇās*. (Saṃkarṣa 1.3.12). In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice of the Soma ritual, the eleven *prayājas* prescribed do not exclude the other archetypal (*prakṛta*) *ājyas*. Because of the specific statement regarding the Soma, no consumption (*bhakṣa*) [of the *ājya*] occurs.

When the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice is underway and the *soma* has been offered, there arises a doubt as to whether or not there is a consumption of the remnant. This is the sūtra of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position:
"In the case of *soma*, there is no consumption, because there is no scriptural injunction; for there is no statement such as 'Soma is the substance to be consumed.
[The Siddhāntin replies: "Or rather, it should exist, because of the observation of another purpose."

The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to refute the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that there is no consumption (*bhakṣa*) of the Soma remnants in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. There must indeed be such consumption, because of the observation of other purposes (*anyārthadarśana*), as seen in the statements: "He shall consume [the Soma] while moving around from all sides," and "They set down the portion that has been consumed and replenished, supporting it from the southern seat. When a statement, though having another purpose, indicates consumption, it is called an "observation of other purposes."

The intention of the commentary regarding the first sentence is that the vessel for the Āśvina cup is to be carried around—that is, it must be moved completely and on all sides—around the head before the consumption of that cup. As for the second sentence, however, its purpose is to prescribe that after the consumption, one should cause the *camasas* (cups) to swell—that is, increase them—with the remaining Soma juice, and then place them below, between the two poles (*īṣā*) of the cart (*anaḥ*, literally "cart") situated in the southern region.
"But the verbal injunctions, because they are unprecedented, should be according to the instruction; this is the sūtra of the final conclusion (siddhānta).
In the previous sūtra, a scriptural observation supporting the final conclusion was stated."
However, this [sūtra] is subtle for the purpose of demonstrating an injunction;
the word "tu" (however) serves to show a distinction from what preceded.

Those "observations of other purposes" mentioned in the previous sūtra are, in reality, statements that enjoin consumption, as in the passage beginning with "He shall consume [the soma] while moving around on all sides."
There exists a consumption [of the offering] based on that [text], which is distinguished by its radiance all around one's own head;
for this consumption is unprecedented, as it has not been obtained through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, because of the existence of the statement regarding consumption, according to the injunction, by whichever officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) [it is performed] and for whichever deity it is intended—
Just as it is said that certain vessels are to be consumed by means of specific words, so too shall there be various modes of consumption.
In every respect, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is indeed a consumption of Soma.

Having conducted a general inquiry regarding consumption based on the rule "there is no consumption because of the word *someḍ*" (3.5.6.19), this specific inquiry ("But in the case of the offering to Indra-Agni," 3.5.18.8) ought to have been undertaken.

Or [it is as follows]: On page 997, sūtra 3.5.188, we shall explain in the section beginning with "Because of the statement regarding Soma" (3.5.188, p. 992) that just as when the mere preparation of the oblation (*havis*) has been performed for the *graha* cups, there is no complete offering (*sarvahoma*), so it is here as well.
On page 992, sūtra 3.5.188.
In certain cases, when Soma is unavailable, a substance similar to it is obtained.
When such a substance has been obtained, one that is slightly similar is prescribed by the rule: "If one should not find Soma, one should press Pūtīka plants" (Bhāṣya 3.6.15).

The *āgnimāruta* recitation (*śastra*) should not be performed at the *savanīya* offering, which is a modification of the *soma* sacrifice and not an integral part of it. (Bhāṣya 4.1.12). In the *soma* sacrifice, the prohibition of the *ājyabhāga* offerings is a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*); in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the prohibition of the *ājyabhāga* offerings is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
See the section on the "Principle of the Animal-Sacrifice Ājyabhāgas. Regarding the *barhis* grass being trimmed at the commencement of the *ātithya* rite in the *soma* sacrifice.

The procedure for the three—namely the *ātithyā*, the *upasad*, and the *agniṣṭomīya*—is common to all three; there is a single injunction applying to each of them individually. Furthermore, the ritual duties (*dharma*) performed therein are common to all, with the exception of the final disposal (*pratipatti*), such as cremation.

But it is not merely the taking of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the sake of hospitality that is employed; other ritual properties, such as those for spreading [the grass], and this *upasad* [rite] are also employed for the *agniṣṭomīya* [animal sacrifice].

Regarding the statement that "the word *ṛtvij* does not apply to all ritual acts of a sacrifice, but rather to the state of being seventeen," one should consult the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*). In the *Soma* sacrifice, when there is a commonality regarding a single vessel, an equal division is obtained by the principle that "it should be equal, as there is no scriptural injunction to the contrary" (10|1|53).
In that case, if one were to drink without having divided [the portion], it might happen that while another is to drink, someone else drinks instead;
in such a situation, it is possible to request permission, saying:
"O Noble One, this must be drunk by me."

(Saṃkarṣa 3.2.13). Regarding the Soma sacrifice, there is the consumption from the cups (*camasabhakṣa*); in the *iṣṭi*, however, since [the cup-consumption] is not established here, the first consumption consists of all [the portions] for the purpose of hiring the priests—this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The established conclusion is that the ritual performances constitute the consumption.
This is because, according to the rule, "The five, including the sacrificer, together consume the *iḍā*," the sacrificer also possesses the status of a consumer;
mere consumption does not arise through the act of hiring.
Even in the *satra* sacrifices, there are indeed the consumption of the *iḍā*, the cups (*camasa*), and so forth, because they consist of ritual performance.
Regarding the Soma sacrifice, it is said: "It has one hundred and one *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings."
Bhāṣya 8.1.34: This is a statement regarding the combination of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings belonging specifically to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites that constitute the Soma sacrifice.
Furthermore, it is possible to say "of that" (*tasya*) even with respect to a subordinate part of a rite, just as one says "the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of the Vājapeya."
Regarding the selection of the Brahman priest (*brahmavaraṇa*) in the Soma sacrifice:

In the Soma sacrifice, regarding the ritual acts pertaining to the *iṣṭi*—such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others—the selection of the Brahman priest obtained through the force of the general rule (*codaka*) need not be performed for each individual rite (*prati-tantra*). This would be purposeless; since the requirement is already fulfilled by the selection of the Brahman performed in connection with the Soma rites, therefore the selection of the Brahman need not be performed [again].
The selection of the Brahman priest has a visible purpose.
Bhāṣya 12.1.8.136–41: In certain iṣṭi-type rites such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā, the selection of the Hotṛ priest is obtained through the rule of extension (codaka).
Since that selection pertains to one who is already engaged [in the rite], the selection of the Hotṛ must be performed for each individual performance (tantra).
In that case, regarding the unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), there is no multiplicity [of fires].

(Jaimini Sūtra 12.1.8.136–41). In certain rites such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others belonging to the *soma* sacrifice, the state of maintaining the sacrificial fire (*agni*) established for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśika*) persists.
In the *soma* sacrifice, after the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, the fire does not become worldly (*laukika*); rather, it becomes worldly only when the *soma* sacrifice is completed.

Regarding the Soma sacrifice, in the injunction "He gives the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa," when there is a requirement for the purpose of the gift qualified by the staff, it is applied as being for the sake of the recitation of the *praiṣas* (directions), according to the rule "The one with the staff recites the *praiṣas*. Bhāṣya 11.3.1.8:

When the Soma sacrifice is completed, the carrying forward of the fire (agnipraṇayana) is for the sake of the entire Āhavanīya fire; this is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa). It is not for the sake of the whole, but rather for a single part; this is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
Saṃkarṣa 3.2.11: Regarding the Soma sacrifice, the *sutyā* (the day of pressing) must indeed occur on the very day of the conjunction (*parva-saṃdhi*).

Although there is a scriptural injunction regarding the various times for the stages beginning with initiation (*dīkṣā*) and ending with the departure from the sacrificial ground, and thus a doubt arises as to whether the *sutyā*—which constitutes the essence of the Soma sacrifice—may optionally be performed either on the day of the conjunction or on another day, [the conclusion is that] the entire *sutyā* must take place precisely on the day of the conjunction.
Even though the time of the junction (*saṃdhi*) itself is not [the primary object], the connection of the ritual action with the preceding and succeeding times implied by it is unavoidable;

furthermore, there is no perceptible statement that sublates this. Thus he says: "Because of the conjunction of the strides (*vikrama*), there is indeed another perception resulting from that connection.

On the contrary, the Kauṣītaki statement is indeed perceptible, as stated in the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana* regarding the section on the *parvan*: "In the Soma-field, when the *parvan* is mixed with the first day (*pratipad*)."
"The Kauṣītaki Śruti states that the Soma-pressing ceremony (somasutyā) should be performed."

The Commentator (Bhāṣyakṛt), however, being well-acquainted with the two-fold division of time, presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the time for the sacrifice is indeed twofold, based on such scriptural statements as: "That which is seen every day before and after [the moon], one should sacrifice having approached it on the day when it has risen; that which is the earlier full moon is Anumati, and the later is Rākā. By means of this Sūtra, he establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that there is only one single time, because those [statements] lack the power to directly indicate a duality of time, and because of indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as "There are twelve full moons in a year" (Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa 3.2.16).
In the case of the *saumyacaru*, the oblation (*homa*) is performed using only the vessels belonging to the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, not those belonging to the *soma* sacrifice.

Regarding the *soma* sacrifice, because of the explicit statement "as long as [the vessel] exists," there is the cleaning and holding [of the vessel], but there is no disposal (*pratipatti*) upon the knowledge that the *agnīṣomīya* animal has been offered.

Among *Soma* sacrifices, the following are the indicative marks (*prakṛtiliṅga*) that effect extension (*atideśa*): being enjoined by an unmanifest injunction (*avyaktacoditatva*), being a multi-day session (*ahargaṇatva*), being an *Ahīna* sacrifice (*ahīnatva*), being a *Satra* sacrifice (*satratva*), being a *Saṃvatsara-Satra* (*saṃvatsarasatratva*), and being one from which fees have been distributed (*niṣkayitva*), and so forth.

Bhāṣya 1|13|5.
Just as in the case of the Śālāmūlīya [sacrifice], for one whose prosperity has departed at the end of the Soma sacrifice, there is likewise the formal consigning (*samāropa*) of the Āhavanīya fire.

By this same principle, although the absence of re-installation (*samāropaṇa*) would apply even to the *śālāmūlīya* fire—which is not small—since its door is also permanently established for the sake of all ritual actions, it too must be re-installed. This same principle applies to those belonging to the *śālā* (the sacrificial hall) as well, regarding the rule that the *āhavanīya* fire is to be maintained perpetually in the *śālā*. Saṃkarṣa. 3.2.30. 卐 At the Soma sacrifice, the re-installation belongs only to the *śālāmūlīya* fire.

Since the maintenance of the fires such as the *śālāmukhīya* is mandatory, and since expiation for those fires that have gone out is prescribed in the scriptures by such passages as, "If the *āhavanīya* should go out, one should take it from the *gārhapatya*," all of them must be consigned (*samāropaṇīya*) at the conclusion of the Soma sacrifice and the *parvan* festivals.
This being the prima facie view, the correct conclusion is that only the *prājahita* fire is to be consigned,
because the maintenance of that fire alone serves the purpose of all [the others].
Because maintaining the fire otherwise would constitute a violation of the Soma festival; and because the expiation has already been performed;
therefore, for others, since the non-performance of the ritual constitutes a worldly act, there is the formal relinquishment (*samāropa*).
Saṃkarṣa 3.2.29: Oṃ. In the case of stealing Soma, only one cow should be given as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), not one hundred and twelve;
however, items such as "a horse, a mule, and a donkey" must indeed be given as the fee.

Vi. 10.3.15: In cases such as the theft of Soma, the number one hundred and twelve belonging to the obligatory rite is set aside by the sacrificial fee of one cow and so forth, but this does not apply to the horse and other items.
"One [cow] and five [cows], like a milch-cow.
The Commentary states: "If they should take away the Soma-drinker's [portion], one should give a cow as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); in the case of the Abhimantha sacrifice, five cows.
Here there is a doubt: do the one and five cows mentioned in the scripture set aside the entire sacrificial fee of the rite, or only the cows?
What is established? That "one" and "five" [are substitutes] like a cow.
Just as a cow is a substitute for the entire [gift], so too would "one" and "five" be.
For their connection with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is heard directly in the scripture.

Therefore, they bring about the effect of the primary elements (*prākṛtī*); and the primary elements, being inferential, cease. In that case, the principle of the "intermediate pregnant woman" applies, and thus the Sūtra is explained otherwise.
Furthermore, one and five [cows] exclude the entire sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of the seasons, as do the three *vastra*s.
And there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) to this effect.
Thus, even though they stand upon an identical scriptural statement (*samāna-śruti*), it follows that they exclude everything.
This view is thus established:
for their rivalry has indeed ceased.
However, some [hold that] because it is based on the Vedic text, one should [select] a cow by means of number and a specific gender.
Commentary:
This is the reply to what was previously stated—that one or five [cows] exclude the entire sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of the *ṛtu* sacrifice.
This is so.
However, some objects are excluded, some cows are excluded, while horses and the like are not excluded.
Regarding this rule—"one is to be given, five are to be given"—it pertains specifically to cows.
Why? Because of the connection with a number qualified by "cow."
Regarding this statement, "One should give one; one should give five," the connection is not made in this way: "He gives one sacrificial fee.
How then? It is "one cow. For the connection with the cow is stronger because it is the primary element.
Moreover, the connection of the number with the word "cow" (go) is direct;
its connection with the word "sacrificial fee" (dakṣiṇā) is indirect, being mediated by the word "cow.
And in this way, the word "cow" retains its primary meaning.

Otherwise, there would be figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of "one cow" or "horse, etc. Therefore, by means of the specific gender, the number is applied to the cows. And thus, when all the *sāmans* are transferred, there will be favor toward the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) regarding the preservation of the original state (*yathāprakṛtibhāva*) for the *aśvādis*.
"Therefore, one [cow] and five [cows] are the substitutes for the cows.
Śā—It is heard in scripture: "If they should carry away the Soma, one should give a cow as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for that; if the Soma is crushed, one should give five cows.
In this regard, there is a doubt: do one and five cows replace the cows, or do they replace the entire sacrificial fee?

For that purpose, this is investigated: is the connection "he should give one cow" (*gām ekāṃ dadyāt*), or "one [cow] among the cows" (*ekāṃ gām*)? In this regard: "By the force of the direct hearing of the accusative case-ending, there is a syntactic connection with the action of giving (*dadāti*). By means of the word 'one' (*ekayā*), all that is to be given along with the five is set aside."
It is said: "If [the word 'cow'] is used in conjunction [with the verb], there would be an indication (lakṣaṇā) regarding the word 'cow';
or else, it would be a partial restatement (anuvāda), for the sentence would be split if it were a prescription (vidhi)."

In the case of the theft of Soma and similar instances (soma-apahārādau), regarding the alternative of performing the Soma-sacrifice with a substitute (somādhāna-pakṣe), the connection [of this topic] is established because it is stated here as well that there is a cessation of the entire sacrificial fee (*kṛtsna-dakṣiṇā-nivṛtti*). Even in the cases of "one" or "five," the meaning of the sūtra is that there is a cessation of the entire sacrificial fee, just as in the case of the *dhenu*.
Should one [cow], five, or the entire number of cows be excluded?
It might be the first [option] because of its connection with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); but it is not so, because of the intervention [of other factors].

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the gift of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard in scripture: "If they should steal the Soma, one should give a cow as the fee for that [occasion]; at the Abhimantha [rite], five cows. Even though this is an occasional (*naimittika*) rule, by means of the third mode of injunction (*vidhi*), through the desire for gain (*lipsā*), there is an injunction of a cause characterized by oneness and cowness (*gotva*) by way of the giving of the fee. Consequently, just as in the case of the *anu* [cow], the twelve-hundred [cows] are set aside by the substance of the cow and by the number.

This being the case, since the intended meaning is fully conveyed by the mere statement "one should give a cow," the mention of the number "one" would be redundant if it were intended to apply to the acquisition [of the cow] and so forth. Furthermore, in the second sentence, if the number five were also enjoined as a qualification of this very [cow], a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) would result. Therefore, accepting another type of injunction (the fourth), there is an injunction of the number alone with reference to the cow. And since the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is established through the intermediate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*), the number does not apply to the cows used for milking and other purposes. Consequently, although the number [five] sets aside the "one thousand twelve hundred" [cows] in that context, it does not set aside the horses and other animals.
Maṇḍana: "The phrase 'one and five' is a restriction regarding cows.
Śaṅkara: "'One and five' refers to [the number] like that of a milch cow.

In the section concerning the *aupavākyas*, it is recited within the context just as the *aṃśu* and *adābhya* [are prescribed];
however, those two mantras are recorded in the *tantra* before the *tūṣṇīṃśaṃsa* and other elements.

There, although there is a specific presence of all sacrifices, for the sake of avoiding defects such as redundancy (*dvirukta*) and so forth, and because of the requirement to perform them in a manner consistent with their proper placement, the power of the contextual statement (*prakaraṇika-vākya*) prevails; therefore, the *aṃśu* and *adābhya* belong to that very [context].
By way of this corroboration, the subordinate injunctions (*guṇavidhi*) are found in the *Aupavākyakāṇḍa*;
for it is possible that they apply to the archetype (*prakṛti*) precisely by virtue of being within the scope of the primary injunctions (*pradhānavidhi*).
Therefore, immediately after the Adhvaryu, the performance of those two [mantras] occurs according to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).

This being the case, according to the principle "because it is repeated, there is a scriptural mention of both," since [the two mantras] are excluded from being injunctions of subordinate qualities (*guṇavidhi*) even in the *upavāka*, they cannot be injunctions of the principal action (*pradhānavidhi*) either.

Furthermore, because there is no sequential order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) for those two together with the other archetypal (*prākṛta*) mantras, their performance occurs at the very time of the manner of taking up the other vessels.

In reality, even if the injunction is accepted as being in the *aupavākyam* section, since its placement must occur only after [the main rite]—in accordance with the principle that "Bādarāyaṇa says it should be at the end of the archetype" (*prakṛtau*)—and since it is appropriate to accept its purpose as being for the sake of sequence and so forth in order to avoid the redundancy of its repeated recitation within the context, there is no difference in the result between the prima facie and final positions.

If it is argued that the recitation of the mantra is more powerful than the recitation of the Brāhmaṇa because its practice occurred even earlier than the *upāṃśuyāja* and other rites, then for that very reason, its performance would be established even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In reality, this is already established by the sequence of the Śruti itself, as in the statement: "Having performed with the *avyavaniyāpoddhigraha*, one performs with the *aśvadagdhī*.

Commentary: The substances for the purchase of Soma are enumerated: "He purchases with a goat; he purchases with gold," and so forth—this is the *somakrayanyāya* (the rule concerning the purchase of Soma), beginning with the female goat used for the purchase of Soma (*somakrayanī*).
Regarding those means of purchase, there would be an option,
for all of them are prescribed as independent means for the act of purchasing,
just as rice and barley are prescribed for sacrifices.
Likewise, there are [the injunctions]: "He buys with a goat," "He buys with gold," and "He buys with cloth.
These serve the same purpose;
therefore, there is an option among them.
Or rather, there is a combination (samuccaya), because of the inherence of the substance in the performance [of the action].
The Commentary states: The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position. And this is not the case, namely, that there is an option (vikalpa).
But rather, there is a combination.
Why? Because of the coexistence of substances in the performance.
In the performance of the purchase, the coexistence of even an additional substance is possible.
In that case, the inducement of the seller is accomplished by means of the price;
thus, the ground [for the transaction] becomes much easier to secure.
Consequently, even though that substance is traditionally prescribed [as the offering], it is of no consequence.

Furthermore, all [the items] are included by the statement of the performance (*prayoga-vacana*) because they are all projected [simultaneously]. Moreover, these items are unequal—such as "he buys with a horse-hoof" and "he buys with a pair of cattle"—and thus they are capable of effecting the completion [of the purchase] through conjunction (*samuccaya*), not through option (*vikalpa*).
If they were treated as optional alternatives, they would result in meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*).
Therefore, there is a combination.
And it demonstrates this combination.
The Commentary states: "One purchases him with ten; the Virāj consists of ten syllables; thus one attains the Virāj. This is a restatement (anuvāda) regarding the act of purchasing.

Nor can there be a combination (samuccaya) or a possible combination based on the requirements of the non-excessive form of the act by the seller, because that single substance must be procured in accordance with its being an independent means for the seller. This being the position reached, [the conclusion is: since the statement "He buys it indeed with ten" is a restatement (*anuvāda*), there is a combination.
For this [text], because it has attained the status of being syntactically connected with another injunction and because it is of the nature of a restatement (anuvāda), is indeed a restatement.

Consequently, in accordance with those factors that apprehend the meaning of these words, there is a combination (samuccaya) of as many [elements] as are necessary to bring about the satisfaction of the seller. It is precisely with this intention that the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) stated: "Just as in the case of purchase, there is a combination of possibilities for various purposeful rites.
