Therefore, they do not share the same injunction.
Or rather—by means of these two sections, it has been stated that the ritual properties (*dharma*) are common because they are prompted by the purpose (*kārya*).
Furthermore, the *phalacamasa* (the fruit-cup) also functions in the role of Soma because it is a modification (*vikāra*) of what is desired.

Therefore, the injunction of Soma-properties applies to it as well, just as in the case of the common [application] of properties such as "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) to the barley-grains.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
It is appropriate that the properties of the *vrīhi* rice are applied to the *yava* barley,
because both, being optional, are of an equal nature as non-obligatory elements.
Furthermore, the *soma* substances, being grasped by the *apūrva* of the obligatory Jyotiṣṭoma like the obligatory [elements] themselves,
deserve to resort to that very door [of the sacrifice] eternally;
thus, for the *soma*, there is no fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) as a substitute.
Because there is no injunction for the *brāhmaṇa* position [in that context].

If the *phalacamas* were to exist by the crushing of all the *soma*, then, due to the absence of the *rājanya* and *vaiśya* alternatives, the *soma* would also be non-obligatory (*anitya*), and thus they would be equal. However, although it is excluded from the *yajamāna-camasa* alone, it is obligatory (*nitya*) because it is possible in other cups.
Therefore, the ritual properties do not deviate from that [Soma].
Since they are connected to it, one might ask: "How will they apply to the fruit-cup (phalacamasa) now?
We reply: they apply by virtue of the function.
He asked:

Is the occurrence of the function (*kāryāpatti*) something other than direct instruction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*), or is it included within these two? Some consider it to be distinct;
however, if that were the case, there would be no knowledge of the destruction of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, it must be stated that [the rule] is included within the *atideśa* (extended application).

If it is asked, "But how can an *atideśa* be postulated for the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself?"— it is true that it cannot be so postulated in cases where there is an *atideśa* of the properties of the ritual action (*karmadharma*).
Indeed, for what action does the relationship between material cause and modification (prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva) arise by itself?
This is rather an extension of the properties of the substance;
for even when the action is identical, a difference in the substances is directly perceived.
Just as an action that requires supplementation takes up other properties from another action, so too does a substance.

Therefore, one should effect the sacrifice by means of the *phalacamas* (the fruit-cup). How? Because it is understood through immediate proximity (*anantara-viparivṛtti*) and through similarity of substance (*dravya-sārūpya*) that it is like the *soma*; thus, the extended application (*atideśa*) is established.
What is the purpose when the properties of the *soma* are performed in both cases?

Even though the instrumentality [of the sacrifice] exists in both cases, just as elsewhere there is a purpose consisting in the engagement or non-engagement of one desiring a specific result regarding the original (aupadeśika) and the extended (ātideśika) rites, so too should it be understood here. For it can also be said that this is due to the cessation [of the original form] and the difference in substance; for those [elements] which depend on the *soma* in rites such as the *abhiṣava* (pressing) are understood as the means for achieving the fruit.
How then will they [the other cups] accomplish the fruit of the *phalacamasa*?

Since the *phalacamasa*, functioning as a means for the sacrifice (*kratu*), can only include those elements that fall within its constituent parts and are performed for the sake of the sacrifice, it cannot include those intended for the sake of the fruit.
Therefore, the exclusion of those [other cups] is established.
By this very [principle], it is stated that modification (*ūha*) must also be performed.

For even though the context of the ritual action (*karmaprakaraṇa*) is the same, since there is no common injunction regarding the substance (*dravyasāmānavidhya*), when the word *soma*—which would otherwise apply by the principle of functional substitution (*kāryāpatti*)—is found to be incapable [of performing the function], its transformation (*vikriyā*) is understood. As the Śāstra says: "Since the injunctions for consecrations (*saṃskāra*) pertain to being a means to the *apūrva*."

Therefore, they should also exist in the occasional (naimittika) rite, since there is no difference in their status as means of accomplishment. Just as rice and barley are both obligatory (nitya) and subject to the same injunction, so too are the substances in the obligatory and occasional rites subject to the same injunction.
It is said that the connection with the eternal refinement belongs to the means itself;
it is not connected by way of its own form, but is joined by way of what is not its own form.

Soma—just as there is a common injunction for those [rites] studied outside of a specific context because there is no difference in their being means to the *apūrva*, so too is it for the *phalacamas* (the fruit-cup); thus, the connection is established through direct perception.

The purpose [of this discussion] is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there would be the application of desires for qualities (*guṇakāma*) in the case of the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*), as well as the fulfillment of the mantra "I buy the *vrīhi* grains for you" just as there is the fulfillment of "I buy *soma* for you," and so forth. However, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is no application of desires for qualities; thus, in the drinking of *soma*, the mantras such as "I buy *soma* for you" and the like do not apply, as they are restricted to the specific properties of *soma*.

Furthermore, the status of *soma* itself is not intended here; for even by the principle of "substitution of place" (*sthānāpatti*), there would result the necessity of performing the *abhiṣava* (pressing) and other rites [which are specific to *soma*].
Nor is it untenable for the occasional *phalacamasa* to serve as the means (*dvāra*) when the constant *abhiṣava* and other rites are connected with the constant [ritual context];

because even in the case of constant rites, the constant status of *soma* or the status of being the objective (*uddeśyatva*) of the occasional *phalacamasa* serves as the subverting factor (*bādhaka*).

For it is indeed accepted that for obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) acts such as *homa* offerings, there is an injunction regarding qualities like being performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), as in the rule "one should perform with a low voice using the *yajus* formula," and so forth. Nor is there an inequality [between the occasional and the obligatory] on the grounds that the occasional act has a delayed cognition because its application (*viniyoga*) and origin (*utpatti*) depend on the existence of the obligatory; for there is no evidence for such a state of affairs. Furthermore, even if such dependence were to exist in some cases, there is no evidence that it is overridden by the subsequent injunction of a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra-vidhi*), and thus there is no inequality. Or, let that be granted; nevertheless, the fact that the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the objective of the preparatory injunction remains intact in the case of the *phalacamasa* (the fruit-cup) cannot be denied.

Nor should it be argued that the *phalacamas* (the fruit-cup) is not included because, in the case of a purificatory injunction (*saṃskāravidhi*), one accepts that the object to be understood is a specific *soma* characterized by the general property of being a means to the *apūrva*.

Even so, since this would preclude the purificatory injunction from having *soma* as its intended referent, it would follow that even in the modified *phalacamas*, there would be the contingency of it being the qualificand of something non-original (*aprākṛta*), which would lead to the application of [ritual acts] such as pressing (*abhiṣava*).

Therefore, in every purificatory injunction, the cognition must have as its qualificand a specific thing that is not a means to the original [sacrifice], while the mode of that cognition is the status of being a means to the *apūrva* as determined by the context.

Thus, having established that, he demonstrates by way of extension (*atideśa*) that even in the case of a modified (*vikṛta*) means of accomplishment, there is an acquisition of properties (*dharma*), just as there is [an acquisition] despite the absence of identical injunctions (*samānavidhāna*).

In the present case, however, because the *phalacamasa* (the fruit-cup) is indeed a means for the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the archetype (*prakṛti*), it falls within the scope of direct instruction (*upadeśa*), just like the [Soma] and so forth.

This being the position reached, [the author replies]: True; in every injunction regarding a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), [the cognition] has as its qualificandum the connection with the transcendental result of the archetype, and as its qualifier, the state of being connected with the transcendental result of the archetype.

Thus, *pārśvantaka* is the understanding of the subject (*uddeśa*). Nevertheless, that relationship [of the subject] is such that it is first cognized as being delimited by a certain property (*dharma*) through the verbal cognition produced by the injunction prescribing the ritual preparation (*saṃskāra-vidhi*); subsequently, there is the conventional usage of that which is so delimited as the object of the instruction for the ritual preparation, and not of anything else. For that which is not perceived as such—like a jar or other objects—is unfit to be the subject (*uddeśyatva*), since it lacks that specific character.

And here, although in the statement "one pours curd into the milk" (*tate payasi dadhyānayati*) and so forth, the pouring of curd is enjoined initially with reference to that which is delimited by the nature of milk (*payastvāvacchinna*), nevertheless—because the status of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) delimited by the capacity to be a means to the transcendental result (*apūrvasādhanatva*) occurs only after the understanding of the milk as a means to the transcendental result has arisen—the milk alone is the subject matter of the injunctive teaching (*upadeśavidhi*). This is because of the inclusion of the term "ultimate" (*paryantika*) [in the definition], which precludes any contradiction.

In the present case, the status of being a means to the *apūrva* (transcendental result) is already established prior to the injunctions for pressing (*abhiṣava*) and so forth, specifically with respect to the qualification of being a *phalacamasa*. This is because, were that not the case, the subsequent restatement—“If he should desire to consume Soma, one should give him the portion to consume, but not Soma”—would be untenable.

Therefore, in accordance with the supporting evidence of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), even though the *phalacamasa* is delimited by the same qualifier as the objective (*uddeśyatā’vacchedaka*), it is not the object of the original injunction; thus, there is no injunction of equal status (*asammānavidhāna*).

Consequently, even though the ritual action (*karman*) remains the same, when there is a desire for its specific properties (*dharma*), the Soma-ritual properties such as purchase (*kraya*) and pressing (*abhiṣava*) are obtained through a figurative extension (*atideśa*) known as "assumption of status" (*sthānāpatti*).
For this very reason, because its scope is distinct from that of the original direct injunction (*prakṛti-upadeśa*), it is described as being merely a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*).

In reality, however, just as in the case of [injunctions] involving optional qualities (*guṇakāma*), a distinct productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is enjoined here due to the adoption of multiple qualities.
And for this reason, it is also possible to speak of the conceptualization of an extended application (*atideśa*) precisely because of that very expectancy regarding the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

For this very reason, some maintain that in the case of the injunction "having struck [the fruit] with *nyagrodha*-stumps," since the act of striking is directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*), there is no purchase (*kraya*).

The practical purpose [of this discussion] is the engagement or non-engagement of those desiring specific qualities (*guṇakāma*), as well as the omission or modification of the mantra containing the word "Soma."

In the context of the Soma sacrifice, regarding the statement, "Having performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa), one should sacrifice with Soma," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this prescribes a distinct ritual action—specifically the particular time of the *parvan*—as subordinate to the fruit-bearing Soma sacrifice, while retaining the characteristics of the Darśapūrṇamāsa itself. This rebuttal here is fallacious.
Some say: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma"—thus a sacrifice connected with a fruit is enjoined, like the Udbhid and others.
Having referred to that [sacrifice] which desires a substance (as in "one should sacrifice with Soma"), Soma (the substance) is enjoined.

When there arises the expectancy for its manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāva*), both the drawing of the cups (*grahaṇa*) and the hymn (*stotra*) are subsidiaries [of the sacrifice], the former by direct statement and the latter by context (*prakaraṇa*).

Regarding the statement, "having taken up a *graha* or having poured out a *camasa*," even though time and other factors are possible, the name [Jyotiṣṭoma] has been applied by accepting the possessive sense—that this [sacrifice] possesses the *jyotis*, which are the *soma* offerings—based on the context alone of the Soma sacrifice (namely, that the *stotras* belong to it), after the connection with the fruit has occurred.
(He states his own view: Alternatively, this [sentence, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma"] is not an originative injunction (*utpattivākya*).
Nevertheless, there is no injunction for all [the constituent parts] regarding the fruit.
How so? Regarding this name "Jyotiṣṭoma," does it denote the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites as well, or not? (Having thus deliberated, he adopts the final position: We say it does not.
(Why? Because the Jyotiṣṭoma is that sacrifice whose stoma-chants consist of the "lights" (jyotīṃṣi).
Furthermore, the *jyotis* chants have not been understood as the *stomas* of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites in any manner whatsoever.
Moreover, even though there is no relationship [of identity] based on time and so forth, there exists a relationship by way of the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
With this in view, the word *jyotiṣṭoma* is applied to the Soma sacrifice.
Therefore, that which is denoted by the word *jyotiṣṭoma*—namely, the sacrifice known as Soma—is enjoined with respect to the fruit [of heaven].

However, because the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are not auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the cup-offering (*graha*), there is no direct connection [between them and the fruit], nor is there a connection by way of being the indicated and the indicator (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇatayā*).
Consequently, the fruit does not result from those [subsidiary rites].

(He states another alternative view, which is merely a conceptual construction: Alternatively, even without the relationship of the characterized and the characteristic, there exists an indirect connection.

(How so? [It is as follows:]—) The act of drawing the cup (*grahaṇa*) is a subsidiary element of the sacrifice; and for that [act of drawing], which possesses its own fruit, the [recitation] is a subsidiary means (*upakaraṇa*).
There is no direct relationship of principal and subsidiary between the means and the hymn of praise (*stotra*).

But there is another connection [by way of immediate sequence]; through this indirect channel, there is a connection between the *stotra* and the *soma*-sacrifice. And likewise, there is the observation of other purposes. The Commentary states: "The *dīkṣaṇīyā* is indeed the head of this sacrifice," and such indicative marks (*liṅga*) are observed.

Furthermore, the subsidiary elements (*guṇa*) such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* are seen in the modifications (*vikāra*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, as in: "One should give gold weighing twenty-four *mānas* at the *dīkṣaṇīyā*."
"In the *prāyaṇīyā* and the two *caturviṃśatimāna*s," it is said;
thus the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites will proceed as being equal [in status].
Therefore, for this reason also, the Soma sacrifice is the principal (*pradhāna*).
Śa: "In that case, since there is no distinction in the verbal suffix (ākhyāta), is the Dīkṣaṇīyā not the primary [act] among all sacrifices? Or rather, it would be the primary one. Vi:
"The name, having a well-known meaning, qualifies the verbal suffix; for its ownership is [that of] Soma, as it is said:
'The lights are its Stomas'."
The hymns (stomas) are not indeed well-known as being called "lights" (jyotis), since they have the Soma as their sole object. Thus, primacy belongs only to the Soma sacrifice,
and not to any other sacrifice.

According to the Bhaṭṭa school, where the application [of a term] occurs part by part, it is understood from the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" that the connection with the fruit of heaven is not for the Soma-sacrifice alone, but rather for the entire sequence beginning with the Prāyaṇīya and so forth. However, the word *jyotis* does not denote the *stomas* (liturgical chants) such as the Trivṛt and others exclusively; rather, since there is no distinction among all the sacrifices included therein, the term applies to all of them by virtue of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).

Or, let it be that the *trivṛt* and other elements are designated by the term "Jyotiṣṭoma" because they are enjoined with a view toward a specific result; nevertheless, since all these sacrifices are equally characterized as Jyotiṣṭomas, and because of their connection to that [result] and their status as primary acts,
there is no contradiction regarding the name "Jyotiṣṭoma" for that which is enjoined within its own sentence.

Regarding the modifications of Soma (somavikārāṇām), there is the section concerning the knowledge and progeny of Soma (somavidyāprājādhikaraṇam): "Having performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma.
By the force of the injunction itself (codaka), the ritual details (dharma) apply here just as they do in the case of the cow and other such [archetypes].
Therefore, those [rites] must also be performed after the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. [Duh]:
When the time for the Soma sacrifice is enjoined as following the time of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the sequence of being subsequent to that [Darśapūrṇamāsa] applies to the *vikṛti* sacrifices as well.
Therefore, since this is already established by the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*), it should have been commenced in that very same manner.
The introduction is made by the statement, "Soma is also heard of even prior to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Here, the deliberation concerns whether cows and other items come after or before [the Soma sacrifice]. Since there would otherwise be no fixed rule, it is stated:
For there is no scriptural statement regarding the time for the Soma sacrifice or for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
From what, then, [is it known]? It is obtained through the force of the context (arthaprāpta).
And this injunction does not bring about what has already been obtained.
If it were argued that the time for the Soma sacrifice follows immediately after the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) because of a scriptural statement,
that is not possible.

For it is not possible for [a requirement] to be already included by the archetype (*prakṛti*). For when it is included by the archetype, it is not yet included by the modification (*vikṛti*); and when it is included by the modification, it does not exist prior to the occurrence of the archetype.
Therefore, if it is already included by the archetype, it cannot belong to the modification.
If it is already included by its very nature (*prakṛti*), then by implication there is no [need for] these [other rules].
Therefore, it is established that this [procedure] follows immediately after the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
Śā—Both the state of being preceded by an *iṣṭi* sacrifice and the state of being preceded by the Soma sacrifice have been transcended.

Therefore, one might think that, as with the archetype (prakṛti), the modifications of the Soma sacrifice (somavikāra) are also possible both before and after the Iṣṭi. But this is not so: "It is not enjoined here that the performance [of the Soma] occurs prior to the Iṣṭi, nor that it is assisted by the Soma. However, because it is stated immediately after the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna), its priority is established by implication."
Furthermore, the status of the modifications (*vikṛti*) as being subsequent to the *āghāna* sacrifice is not established,
because they occur after the Jyotiṣṭoma, and that [status] is impossible for those two.
Therefore, the performance of the Soma-modifications occurs after the Darśa and other sacrifices.
Thus has the sequential arrangement of the six means of valid cognition been correctly described.
Soma: Through the recognition of prior dissimilarity, the connection is established.
Dhi: "The restriction regarding the one-day sacrifices is either immediately after the New Moon sacrifice or later."
One who considers the Soma sacrifice to be distinct from this [Agniṣṭoma] should not think so; for it would be merely a vertical extension (ūrdhvatā) of that same rite.

The Bhaṭṭa [responds]: In the case of the Soma sacrifice, its status as a modification of the *iṣṭi* is due to the absence of causes such as the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), and its nature is optional (*vaikalpika*) and distinct.

Therefore, in these [sacrifices], even though the sequence beginning with that [Agnihotra] is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) in the same manner, it is only the sequence following the *iṣṭi* that applies. This is because it is impossible to establish for them a sequence following the first day of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) and so forth, since they follow the *Jyotiṣṭoma* as prescribed by the statement, "This indeed is the first. Consequently, since the immediate succession to the fire-installation is already occupied by the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is not extended; thus, it is established that the sequence following the *iṣṭi* is what is extended to them. In this way, the sixfold basis of sequence is proven.
Maṇḍana: "After the *iṣṭi*, the modification characterized by Soma [is to be performed].
The meaning is that the modification characterized by Soma—that is, the sacrifice involving cows and other materials—is to be performed only after the *iṣṭi*.
Śaṅkara: "The Soma modification follows the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*)."
The time for the Soma modification (somavikārakāla) is the completion of the Yajñāyajñīya Sāman.

This is the rule that the terminuses (saṃsthās) of the Soma modifications themselves, as well as the one-day sacrifices (ekāhas) and so forth, are not to be performed prior to the performance of the Agniṣṭoma.
VI.5|3|14: In the Soma modification (vikṛti), the status of being subsequent to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices applies.
VI.6|6|9: In the Soma modification, the rule "if [the sacrifice] has the Jagat-sāman, one should draw the cups beginning with the Āgrayaṇa" is inserted;
and this applies likewise to the Viṣuvat day in the Cāmakīya Soma modification which possesses the Jagat-sāman.
10|1|26 Section 2: The performance of all Soma sacrifices occurs subsequent to the Agniṣṭoma.

Bhāṭṭa 5|3|15. The Soma-seller is distinct from the officiating priests (ṛtvij). 3|7|15|1. See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1835; the relevant section concerning "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Soma-seller is distinct from the officiating priests" should be consulted there.
In the section [sūtra] 6.2.11, "Because of the connection with Soma, knowledge, and offspring," it is stated that occasional rites (*naimittika-karma*) have no fixed cause.
Bāla. p. 85. The necessity of Soma, knowledge, and offspring depends upon the authority of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
Su. p. 66. This is the section on Soma, knowledge, and offspring (*somavidyāprajādhikaraṇa*).
The knowledge of Soma, progeny, and [the study of] the Veda are obligatory for the Brāhmaṇa, as well as for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya.
However, for the Brāhmaṇa alone, these three—Soma, Vedic knowledge, and progeny—are required because of their connection with specific scriptural injunctions.
Commentary: This is heard in scripture: "One should sacrifice with Soma," "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception," and "One should procreate offspring."
In this regard, there is a doubt: are these [rites] eternal or non-eternal? What is the prima facie view? Because they are connected with desire (*kāma*), they are non-eternal.
This being the position, it is said in reply:
The Soma sacrifice and other rites are obligatory for Brāhmaṇas and others.

Why? Because there is a connection with the statement regarding debts: "A Brāhmaṇa, indeed, when being born, is born burdened with three debts—to the sages by means of studentship, to the gods by means of sacrifice, and to the ancestors by means of progeny; he is indeed free from debt when he has sacrificed, lived as a student, and had offspring."
The mention of debt establishes that it must necessarily be performed;
therefore, these [rites] are obligatory (nitya).
Now, while the indicative mark (liṅga) is the means of proof, let the underlying reasoning (nyāya) be stated, which serves as its illuminator.
It is said:
there are indeed separate sentences connected with independent desires,
such as "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring," "One performs the Agnihotra as long as one lives," and "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa as long as one lives."
Likewise, "one should study the Veda," and likewise,
"offspring must be procreated.
Thus, this serves as an indicative mark (liṅga) for the established necessity [of these acts].
Alternatively—this is another meaning:
"But for the Brāhmaṇa, because of the connection with the scriptural injunction regarding Soma, Vedic study, and progeny.
Are Soma and the others restricted to the Brāhmaṇa, while they are unrestricted for the Rājanya and Vaiśya, or are they restricted for all?
Thus [the question arises]. What is the prima facie view? That the rule is obligatory for the Brāhmaṇa, but not for the other two.
Why? Because it is heard in scripture thus: "A Brāhmaṇa, indeed, when being born... In this way, a restrictive rule is observed for the Brāhmaṇa, but not for the other two.
Because of the mention of the Brāhmaṇas.
This being the position reached, we reply:
there is a restrictive rule for all.
Why? Because the injunction of a restrictive rule (niyamavidhi) that is made without distinction is a restrictive rule for any statement not connected with a specific desire;
that [rule] is common to all.
Therefore, the restriction applies to everyone.
But is it not the case that the term "brāhmaṇa" is mentioned in the passage, "Now, a brāhmaṇa, being born..."? It is replied:
the mention of the brāhmaṇa in that statement refers to one who abides in [the state of] being (bhavatsaṃstha).

For this statement is not an injunction of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Rather, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a restriction already prescribed by texts connected with that specific desire, intended for the purpose of praising non-giving. Therefore, by the mention of the Brāhmaṇa here, it is understood that there is no such restriction for the Rājanya or the Vaiśya.
The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa," however, is for the sake of illustration;
it refers to the Brāhmaṇa, the Rājanya, and the Vaiśya. Likewise, it refers to one who is being born and one who has already been born.
Śabara: When it is argued that these [sentences] have as their purport the qualification of one who desires results (*phalakāmādhikāra*), we reply: they are obligatory (*nitya*).
Why? Because the spring, expressed with repetition (*vīpsā*), is understood as the occasion (*nimitta*);
therefore, the rule regarding Soma is established for as long as the spring lasts.

As long as the spring [season] is enjoined as the very occasion for the repetition of the sacrifice, one attains this repetition through the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice). Therefore, because it is prescribed with spring as the occasion, Soma must necessarily be performed whenever spring arrives; thus, it is obligatory (*nitya*).

Vedic study (*adhyayana*) is also obligatory because, although its fruit is not explicitly heard [in the texts], it results in the knowledge of *dharma* and *adharma* through the sequence of grasping the syllables and so forth, and that [knowledge] is necessary.

Procreation (*prajā-utpādana*) is also obligatory because its fruit is heard to be unproduced [otherwise], based on the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) and the conviction [expressed in the verse]: "He who departs without having procreated sons...
Therefore, *soma*, Vedic knowledge (*vidyā*), and progeny (*praja*) are indeed obligatory (*nitya*).
Nor does the necessity there pertain exclusively to the Brāhmaṇa because of the mention of him, since no such distinction is heard in the injunctive statements;
for the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended as an illustration. Therefore, the Soma sacrifice and the others are necessary for all three castes.

The connection [of this section] is established by way of a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), based on the misconception that while following the teacher and other such duties are obligatory (*nitya*), the *Soma* sacrifice and the like are not.

In the second interpretation (*dvitīyavarṇaka*), it is thought that because of the statement regarding debts (*ṛṇavākya*), the *Soma* sacrifice, Vedic knowledge, and progeny are indeed mandatory for the Brāhmaṇa alone due to their specific association.
The meaning of the Sūtra is that this is not correct, because no such distinction is heard in the injunctive statements (*vidhivākya*).
Vi— "The Soma sacrifice is performed for the sake of a desired result, or it is obligatory; [one should perform] Agni according to one's desire.
Because of the injunction involving repetition (*vīpsā*), it is accepted as being of the same class [as other obligatory rites].
Bhāṭṭa—The obligatory nature of the Soma sacrifice follows precisely from the scriptural statement: "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring."

Nor is this an injunction regarding time, because that is already enjoined by the very sentence containing the repetition: "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma in the spring. Nor is there a lack of a determining factor [for choosing between the two].

The injunction of repetition (*vīpsā*) and pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established in accordance with the subordinate factor of time, through the extension of the primary duty to be performed; this is because, due to the division of sentences (*vākya-bheda*), there would otherwise be a purposeless restatement of repetition and pervasion already implied by the principle that for every occasioning cause (*nimitta*), the occasional rite (*naimittika*) must be performed. Therefore, it is determined that the repetition found in that very sentence is intended solely to refer to the occasioning cause.
However, the obligatory nature (*nityatva*) of the *agnihotra* and other such rites remains firmly established;
the same applies to sacred knowledge (*vidyā*) when accompanied by study.

The status of [the Vedic study] as a compulsory duty (*nitya*) arises from the fear of the sin incurred by its non-performance, as stated by Baudhāyana: "He who has studied the Veda but does not understand its meaning is a mere bearer of a burden like a pillar," and "Those who do not study become outcasts.
Likewise, the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is also compulsory because no sin is heard of in the scriptures for performing it after the sixteenth year or other such limits.

As for the mention of results in the sixth [book], such as "one desiring food should initiate [the student]," that is better understood as being optional (*pākṣika*), because initiation and so forth are mandatory. In those cases where [initiation] is mandatory, since the knowledge required for the rites (*ṛtu*) and other factors are also mandatory, it is effectively stated to be obligatory; however, because the necessity of knowledge as a prerequisite for the rites has been refuted, there is no fault in its non-performance. Furthermore, since one lacks the qualification for the rites if knowledge and so forth are not performed, there is no requirement for them [as prerequisites for the rites].

Likewise, the procreation of offspring is also eternal, because for one who does not cease from this duty, no contrary injunction is heard—such as, "Desiring liberation through delusion without having procreated a son, he falls downward.
Regarding the section on Soma and Vidyā (Sūtra 6.2.18):

for this very reason, the scriptural passage, "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born with three debts: to the seers by means of studentship, to the gods by means of sacrifice, and to the ancestors by means of progeny," is also consistent [with this view].

Nor can it be argued that because the word "Brāhmaṇa" is heard here, these [rites] are obligatory for him alone, while for the other two [castes] they are not necessary; for, since this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) subordinate to the injunction regarding the cutting of the portions (*avadāna*), it lacks injunctive force, and thus the word "Brāhmaṇa" functions as an inclusive indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Maṇḍana states: "Sacrifice, progeny, and study are obligatory."
"In these three castes, these three [acts] should be performed constantly.
Śaṅkara says: "And also because of the constant [performance] of the Soma sacrifice and so forth. This rule regarding the Soma sacrifice is to be understood as a general rule.
*Bāla*, p. 21: The word *soma* denotes the generic form (*ākṛti*), not the individual instance (*vyakti*).
*Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā* 2.1.6–7: The word *soma* is well-known to refer to the plant (the creeper), not to the juice.
2.1.6–7: The word *soma* is not a name for a ritual action; therefore, it does not effect the extension of ritual properties (*dharmātideśaka*).
Vi. 4|1|146. The state of having *soma* as its sacrificial oblation (*somahaviṣkatva*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*) for the word *soma*.
Su. 1. 7|7. [This concerns] those who are entitled to consume the remnants of the *soma* (*somaśeṣabhakṣaṇādhikārin*).
3|5|122. See the section at Mīko., p. 1699, regarding "the consumption of the *soma* remnant by the *camasins* in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*."
The combined [act of] offering (homa) and eating (amiṣva) is the cause for the consumption of the remnant of Soma.
(3|5|132). See the section in Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1833, under the heading "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the offering and eating are combined as the cause for the consumption of Soma.
The consumption of the Soma remnant by the officiating priests and the sacrificer is established by the designation (samākhyā) "Camasa" [cup].

VI. 3.5.7. The injunctions regarding the preparation of Soma, such as "he buys" and "he presses," apply specifically to the Soma sacrifice; however, in the case of the *phalacamasa* (the fruit-cup), the preparatory rites are accomplished through extended application (*atideśa*).
VI. 3.6.123. Consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) serves as a preparatory rite for the Soma.
Vārttika 3.5.121.32. The various forms of the Soma sacrifice (*somasaṃsthā*) do not share the same set of injunctions (*samānavidhāna*).
3|6|16| 41–47. See the section titled "Saṃsthādhikaraṇam" on page 4051 of the Mīmāṃsākośa.
Among the Soma-saṃsthās, the Agniṣṭoma has primacy due to both the context (prakaraṇa) and indicative marks (liṅga).
5|1|3|137–38. See the section titled "Agniṣṭomasya yajñeṣu prāthamyam" on page 71 of the Mīmāṃsākośa.
"Soma is the oblation.
"The pure Soma-oblation is not placed [on the altar].

Bhāṣya 8.1.136. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that words such as *soma* and *hiraṇya* denote substances (*dravya-śabda*); words such as *suvarṇa* denote qualities (*guṇa-śabda*); and words such as *citrayā* and *aindrī* denote actions (*karma-śabda*), all of which have the transcendental result (*apūrva*) as their primary meaning.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is understood through the verb; it is grasped from the word denoting the action (*bhāvārtha-pada*) which ends in a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-pratyaya*). (Vi.
2.1.1, Section 2). The first triad consists of "A cake on eleven potsherds for Soma and Pūṣan" and so forth, where "a dark-colored animal is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
The second triad consists of "A cake on eleven potsherds for Agni" and so forth, where "a dwarf (*vāmana*) is the sacrificial fee."
All of this pertains to the Rājasūya.
In that context, regarding the pair of triads, this [distinction] arises from the difference in performers due to the difference in sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
(Vi. 1.1.41) The offering to Soma and Pūṣan on eleven potsherds is the first oblation in the second triad-conjunction of the Rājasūya.

Bhāṣya 11.1.412: In the case of an animal sacrifice dedicated to Soma and Pūṣan (somāpauṣṇa), the Audumbara post prescribed therein supersedes the original Khadira post intended for the sacrificial stake (yūpa). Mīmāṃsākośa (Mīko.), p. 1539: The relevant section should be consulted under the heading "Of the original Khadira post in the animal sacrifice to Soma and Pūṣan.
In sacrifices dedicated to two deities such as Soma and Pūṣan, there is no grinding of the offering for Pūṣan; for that [grinding] applies only when there is a single deity.

VI. 3.1.20: "One who desires offspring should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra made of black rice; [he should use] sacrificial grass (*barhis*) made of *śara* reeds. By this, the original *kuśa* grass is set aside by the *śara* grass. Bhāṣya 10.1.411–2, Section 2: In the *caru* oblation for Soma and Rudra, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is to be done with clarified butter (*ājya*) alone.

In that context, regarding the preparatory command (*praipa-mantra*) "having placed the *prokṣaṇī* waters," the word *prokṣaṇī* denotes a consecrated substance; thus, there is an application of the term to the clarified butter.

In the second view, that [the word *jāti*] denotes the genus (*jāti*), the modification (*ūha*) is "having placed the clarified butter" (*ājyam āsādya*). However, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that it is etymological (*yaugika*), the usage is according to the gender and number of the word, namely "having placed the sprinkling-water" (*prokṣaṇīm āsādya*). (Soma. 1.4.9). In the sacrifice to Soma and Rudra, there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the *kuśa* grasses by the *śara* reeds that have been prescribed.
10|1|411-2 Section 2. See the *adhikaraṇa* under the entry "Śara-nyāya" on page 3884 of the Mīmāṃsākośa.

In sacrifices such as the Soma-Raudra, the barley prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) is set aside by the rice (*vrīhi*) qualified by attributes such as purity (*śuddha*) mentioned in the scriptural injunction.

However, in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there would be no fixed rule, because—as in the case of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*)—the taking [of the material] is for the sake of the attribute, and since both are prescribed, the rule regarding the attribute (*guṇa-śāstra*) would apply.

The Bhāṣya states: "One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer a caru-oblation to Soma and Rudra made of pure rice; one should offer a caru-oblation to Soma and Rudra made of black rice; one should offer that same caru-oblation to Netra made of black rice; one should offer a caru-oblation to Surya made of black rice. In this regard, there is a doubt: should one sacrifice with rice alone, or [is there no restriction]? What is the prima facie view? Since the contradictory elements are being adopted in the modified rite (vikṛti), there would be no fixed rule; [the view is] that one should sacrifice with rice alone.
Why? Because the act of taking up [the substance] is for the sake of a subordinate element (guṇa);
[it applies] to the sacrifice to Soma and Rudra, or to another sacrifice, because that is the logical principle due to the distinction between ritual acts.

Commentary: Or rather, that observation will apply to another sacrifice, just as it does in the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Even though the sacrificer is prescribed [to offer] four portions (*caturavatta*) in the New and Full Moon sacrifices, nevertheless, later on, he becomes one who offers five portions (*pañcāvatta*). In other rites, however, there is the fourfold portioning.
In another case, there is a fivefold division (*pañcāvatta*).
Even though there is a restrictive rule regarding such cases, nevertheless, the observation of a fourfold division (*caturavatta*) is still applicable.
As stated in the Śāstra: "One should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra made of white rice; one should offer a *caru* oblation to Nirṛti made of black rice."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is there an option (*vikalpa*) between rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*), and is the injunction regarding white, black, and so forth applicable only to rice such that rice alone is always used?

In that case, since the mention of rice is for the purpose of connecting it with qualities such as whiteness and is not itself an injunction [of rice], there is no sublation (*bādha*) of barley. Therefore, there is an option.
It is not so;

for it is not possible for a single sentence to enjoin both the sacrifice—as obtained through a general injunction (*codaka*)—as the locus, and the quality as the object of injunction. Therefore, the action qualified by substance and quality is the subject matter of the Mīmāṃsā-dvaidha [section], namely, the *Somendra-śvara*.
If there were another means of valid cognition [to determine the number], then in other cases as well, the principle of the *kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa* would apply.

For example, in the case of "He places bricks with the *Āgneyī-sūkta*," one takes as many *Āgneyī-sūktas* as there are [verses] therein; however, the principle of the *kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa* does not operate there.
Maṇḍana [states]: "The purchase of the man [is made] according to the meaning."

Regarding the purchase of *manu* (verses): those which are prescribed in a modified ritual (*vikṛti*) should be employed according to the purpose—that is, according to the requirement—as many as are necessary for the purpose consisting of the kindling to be accomplished; it is not the case that all [verses] must be used, such is the remainder [of the argument]. Śaṅkara says: "as many as all the purchases of *manu*.
Somendra says: "[This applies] in the event of an accident involving the sacrificer's drinking of *soma*."

Because there is no distinction in all cases. The Commentary states: "In the event of an accident involving the drinking of Soma, this ritual dedicated to Soma and Indra (somendra-karman) should take place in all instances of vomiting—whether performed by the officiating priest (ārtvijya) or by the sacrificer (yājamāna). Why? Because it is not restricted [to a specific case]."
No specific distinction is established regarding this vomiting—namely, that it "should exist" or "does not exist.
Therefore, it should apply in all cases.

Or rather (*vā*): even though it is established that the master is the agent because he knows the ritual (*karmajña*) when no prohibition is heard, it is now deliberated whether his own vomiting is the cause, or whether the officiating priest's (*ārtvijya*) is also a cause.
What is established? Since no specific distinction was previously mentioned, it should apply to both cases.

Just as there is the destruction of the ritual performance through vomiting due to being a sacrificer (*svāmin*), so too is there destruction through vomiting due to being a priest (*ṛtvij*), because both consist of the refinement of the substance.
Therefore, whether this rite is for the purpose of removing a fault or for the purpose of providing a transcendental benefit (*apūrva*), it must be performed in both instances of vomiting.
Or rather, it belongs to the master, because it is for his sake.
Commentary: Or it may belong to the master (svāmin) in the case of vomiting.
Why? Because it is for his sake.
Indeed, it is for his sake—that is, for the sake of the sacrificer—at which point the Soma is vomited.
Whatever ritual action dedicated to Soma and Indra is performed here, that too is for his sake alone;
for this is heard as being for the benefit of the owner of the Soma,
and it is able to benefit the sacrificer who owns the Soma, not the officiating priests.

For that ritual act in which Soma is vomited does not have the officiating priests as its purpose. It might be argued: "The officiating priests belonging to the Adhvaryu or the Hotṛ who has vomited the Soma will perform their duties for him during those [subsequent] extractions. If that were the case, then in the event of the failure of the ritual act due to the vomited Soma—whether it be the Adhvaryu’s or the Hotṛ’s—the Adhvaryu and others, being entirely subordinate agents, would fail to obtain the fruit by having the rite performed by their own officiating priests.
And for that reason, since the ritual actions do not function for the benefit of the sacrificer, they are not performed when the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) vomit.
Or rather—even if they were indeed *ārādupakāraka* (indirectly beneficial) acts—they must nonetheless take place in the case of the master’s vomiting.
Why? Because the status of being the cause for the connection with the word "prior" (*pūrva*) does not arise [in the case of the priests].
Thereafter, through that connection, it is understood by the agents.
"Whoever vomits Soma, he shall offer [the oblation]"—due to the connection between the words "whoever" (yaḥ) and "he" (saḥ), it is understood that the sacrifice and the vomiting have a single agent.
In that regard, the occasional rite (naimittika) is beyond doubt in having the owner as its agent;
by means of that which is certain, the doubtful act of vomiting is determined.
Even that [act], being performed by the agent himself, serves as the occasion;
nor is the occasion something entirely independent, for a pure verbal suffix does not convey the notion of an occasion.
It is that which is connected with the word *yat* that expresses the occasion.
If there is a connection with that [act], then first there is the commonality of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*), and subsequently the cognition of its being a cause (*nimittatva*).
Now, the priests (*ṛtvij*) relinquish wealth for the sake of the deity and for the sake of their own purchase (*parikraya*);
therefore, because it is contradictory for them to purchase themselves, they must necessarily choose other priests, such as the *adhvaryu* and others.

However, because the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) used in the context of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) indicates that the fires have no connection with any person other than the one performing the consecration, the sacrifice must be performed using those fires for the sake of their own master.

Consequently, if they perform it with the intention of benefiting the performer who vomited the *soma*, then—due to the difference in place, time, and performer—the rite becomes defective; it is not accepted by that primary act.
Furthermore, no difference in place and so forth is prescribed regarding the oblation itself, such that one might assume non-defectiveness even when there is a change in those factors.

Furthermore, since the purpose is already accomplished by the vomiting of the master (*svāmin*), permission for [the performance] in another location and so forth is not granted by this very scripture alone.

Or how could a single scripture rely on the identity of place and other factors in the case of the master’s vomiting, while relying on their difference in the case of the priests’ (*ṛtvij*) vomiting? Moreover, if they were to perform it solely with the intention that it is for their own sake, even then, because that which was undertaken for the sake of the sacrifice lacks the status of being for the person's sake once again, there would be a unity of the action performed for that purpose.

But if, for the sake of establishing this [result], the scripture were to establish that it is indeed a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), then, because of the abandonment of the [already] present [result], even the postulation of heaven and so forth—which are not immediately present—would constitute a remoteness (*viprakarṣa*) here.
This same [criticism] applies equally to the case of vomiting in the worldly context; thus, it would not apply to the sacrifice.
And that has already been refuted previously.
Therefore, it should be the vomiting of the master.

But if, even in the case of the vomiting of the *adhvaryu* and others, the master alone were to consume the substance, then that same state of having different agents would result. Or, if one were to justify that [state]:
There would be the assumption of an unmentioned genitive sense and a contradiction of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Furthermore, if such an assumption were made, it would follow that vomiting by the master (*svāmin*) would not be the cause [for the rite].

Or, if both [the master and the priest] were relied upon, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) caused by heterogeneity (*vairūpya*), based on the distinction between "he who vomits the Soma" and "he whose Soma the priest vomits."
However, if one of the two [options] must be accepted, it is logical to adopt the "vomiting by the owner" (*svāmivamana*), because it accords with the literal sense of the word.
This applies first of all to the case where [the vomiting] is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*).

But when it is postulated that the [offering] is performed as a remedial rite (*pratisamādhāneṣṭi*) to counteract the impossibility of obtaining the fruit—which arises from a failure in the rule for the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the sacrificial remnant brought forward by the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*)—then, since the fruit belongs to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), it would be entirely unseen (*atyantādṛṣṭa*); thus, the doubt regarding that [impossibility of obtaining the fruit] would be settled by that very [remedy], making it improper to say that the remedial rite must be performed.

Since the fruit of the priests consisting of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is seen to be obtainable whether vomiting occurs or not, the *iṣṭi* does not take up that [fruit], because it lacks a basis and its counter-measure is not required.

Even if it is assumed that eating is for the purpose of purifying the eater—based on the restriction regarding the agent of the action at hand—and that consequently a deficiency arises in the agent due to aversion, because the purification of the substance consists in its being made fit for use; even then, since that [purification] would result in an unintended consequence for the fruit being abandoned (which is not heard in the text), and because it is dependent upon that [agent], and because of the designation by the pronouns *yat* and *tat*, it must apply only to the vomiting of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
By this, the view that it is for the purpose of a transcendental purification (*apūrva-saṃskāra*) is also explained away.

For even when one considers that by vomiting the Soma, neither the performance of a prescribed act nor the indulgence in a prohibited one occurs—and thus, without relying on the view that the *iṣṭi* is for the purpose of removing a fault, [the *iṣṭi*] is understood as an occasional (*naimittika*) rite—nevertheless, because the person is mentioned by the word "yat" (when), it is determined, according to the principle of the moving [person] (3.4.15–16), that it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person situated within the context; and even then, its necessity for performance is established by the rule "But [these acts] belong to the sacrificer" (3.8.2.4). Furthermore, since it pertains to the same subject matter as vomiting, the occasion for the rite is specifically the vomiting of the sacrificer.

As for the claim that even in the case of vomiting by the Adhvaryu and others, there is a failure in the disposal of the substance (*dravyapratipatti*) or a destruction due to the loss of the agent’s refinement (*kartṛsaṃskāra*), and thus it requires a remedial rite (*samādhi*): although it may indeed require one, nevertheless, because it is not prescribed, it is not adopted. And it has been stated that in all matters pertaining to the person of the Adhvaryu, there is no prescription regarding the vomiting of a priest. Therefore, if that vomiting is not defective, he should simply remain seated as he was.
Now, that which is defective must be remedied by performing some general injunction.
(The *Sudhā* commentary states: "It should be offered with the mantra 'sucaḥ svāhā' according to the *Mīmāṃsā* tradition.

Furthermore, since there is no purpose in determining one specific alternative over another here—given that they all serve the ritual (*kratvartha*)—one need not strive excessively for such a determination.

Moreover, if the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is the purpose, then the position that [the sacrifice] is in the process of being performed (*jaṅgamyamānapakṣaḥ*) must be accepted—that is, the position that the human goal resides in the act as it proceeds (*ṛtagatapuruṣārthatvapakṣaḥ*) must be adopted.
And thus the author of the Sūtras says: "Or rather, [it belongs] to the master [of the sacrifice], because it is for his sake" (3.4.13–15).
And because of the observation of an indicative mark.
The commentary states: And there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) regarding the sacrificer who has vomited the *soma*.
How so? "He who vomits the *soma* is indeed deprived of his *soma*-drinking.
When the *soma*-purification is ruined, the sacrificer’s rite becomes defective; thus he is deprived, but in no way is there any deprivation for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
The connection would be with vomiting as in "the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) of whom vomit the Soma," and not as "he who vomits the Soma.
Therefore, for this reason also, when the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) vomits, [the offering is] to Soma and Indra.
Or rather—it must be stated that he is excluded from whom prosperity is sought through the drinking of Soma.
And because of its qualities, a doubt arises regarding the [result].
Since both of these belong to the master, it is his alone that is desired.
Śā—In this regard, since there is no distinction, it would apply to all vomiting; therefore, it is said:
"He who vomits Soma should offer a caru-oblation to Saumendra," so it is said.
From the word "yat," that which is qualified [by the relative pronoun] alone is understood when there is a common agent.
And in the case of a sacrifice, because it is subsidiary to the ritual season, only the owner himself is enjoined.
By virtue of being the agent, even the act of vomiting is performed by that [person]; therefore, it is established that vomiting is not the cause for death, but rather the cause for the rite itself.
The connection is incidental to the Soma [libation].
Furthermore, the connection should be understood as arising from the reliance upon the reason established in the conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*).
As stated in the Vivaraṇa: "Even in the case of vomiting by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), this [penance] belongs to the agent alone, because of the exclusion [of the priests]."
The particularity is dependent [on the universal]; do not say so, for it is determined by the agent alone.

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the inquiry whether this [expiatory] rite should occur only upon the vomiting of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) or also upon that of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), it is argued that since a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) necessarily arises even from the omission of the disposal (*prati-patti*) when a priest vomits, the sacrifice must indeed be performed as an expiation for its sake.

This being the prima facie view, the reply is: this sacrifice should be performed by the sacrificer because he is the one who possesses the status of the patron (*yajamāna*); for the priests are unable to relinquish the substance belonging to the sacrificer. Furthermore, if they were to perform it with their own substance for their own masters, it would no longer be possible for the act to serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).

Furthermore, the vomiting by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) cannot be the occasion for the rite performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), because by the force of the word "who" (*yaḥ*) in the phrase "he who vomits Soma," it follows that the sacrifice must have the same agent as the vomiting; and since that [agent] is intended as a qualifying attribute of the thing to be enjoined (*upādeya-viśeṣaṇa*).

And therefore, by virtue of the requirement that there be a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*), whether this *iṣṭi* is occasional (*naimittikī*) and auxiliary to the sacrifice, or non-occasional and thus an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakārikā*) for the sake of remedying a deficiency in the rite due to the force of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), or whether one accepts that vomiting and yawning are the implied conditions (*nimitta*) and this *iṣṭi* is likewise a purificatory rite for the person connected to the sacrifice as indicated by the genitive case—under all circumstances, it would apply only when the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) vomits. However, in the case of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) vomiting, the general expiation (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed by the rule "that which is performed with a *yajus*" should be performed.

Maṇḍana: "The sacrifice should belong to the master [of the ritual] in the case of vomiting. Śaṅkara: "If that [sacrifice] is to be performed when there is no vomiting. 19. The Buddhists do not acknowledge caste.
That opinion and its refutation are to be found in the *Mīmāṃsākośa*, page 884, under the entry "Ākṛtivāda," as well as in the *Śāstradīpikā* and other works.
In the *Saugandhika* sacrifice, one is anointed during the third pressing; this is known as the *Añjanābhyañjana* sattra. (Bhāṣya 10.4.6.10).

*Saumyamahaḥ* is a word ending in the plural number. Bhāṣya 9.1.6.21 states that because it is a *sutyā*, they call the animal to be offered at the *savana* the *sautya*. Thus, the *sautya* is the *savanīya* animal among animals.
The *makha* at the *sutyā* is the *sautya*. (Vi. 8|117) The *sautya* is the place for the sixth half-month on account of the eleven animals (*ekādaśinaḥ paśavaḥ*).
Regarding "atideśa: ekādaśineṣu paśuṣu" (extension by analogy: in the case of the eleven sacrificial animals), the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted at Mīmāṃsākośa, page 200.
On the day of the Soma pressing (*sautya-ahar*), there is the measuring of the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) that are to be consecrated with fire. Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa 4.4.17.
Regarding the statement "the measurement of the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) fixed with fire is on the *sautya* day," one should consult the relevant section in Mīmāṃsākośa, page 3259.

The Sautrāntikas, for the sake of establishing the diversity of cognition, postulate that the object (*artha*) itself possesses various forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth, rather than being formless. Since the very fact of the object's providing a form constitutes its causality, they claim that this is the "cognition" (*āhaṃ*) of the object; thus, there is no application of the definition of a wise person [who would otherwise require a separate act of perception].

As it has been said: "If it is asked how that which exists at a different time can be an object of cognition, the wise declare that its very nature as a cause is what constitutes its objectivity; this is stated to be sufficient for the production of the form of the cognition."

[Objection: But if this is so, since the object that produces the cognition is past, how can it have a present existence? [Reply: It is the form of the cognition (*jñānākāra*) that is known as being present; however, the object is merely postulated as being past because it is what supplied that form. Therefore, there is no fault.

Furthermore, how is it that the manifestation [of the object] is perceptible by means of perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣajñāna*)? This alone is the perceptibility of the object: namely, its direct production of a cognition possessing a form.
That which produces a cognition with a form only through a mediated succession is inferable.
Just as the characteristic of fire and the characteristic of smoke, through the observation of the former and the conceptualization of the latter, produce a cognition of the object to be inferred;
for this very reason, there are only two means of valid cognition: perception and inference.

This is because that which is directly perceived is perception, while that which produces [cognition] through a causal chain is the object of inference, and that which does not produce [cognition] cannot be apprehended; therefore, nothing other than these two is possible.
Ratnākara: (In the *Dṛśyavāda*, pp. 283–284) | Sautrāmaṇi:

Regarding the injunction, "Having piled the fire-altar (agnicit), one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī," this prescribes a distinct ritual act— characterized by its temporal priority to the piling of the fire-altar— for that specific purpose; furthermore,
it is an auxiliary (aṅga) to the fire-altar and is prompted by the fire-altar itself.
Bhāṭṭa 4.3.10:
Here, the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice is enjoined as a subsidiary to the Agnicayana, and not for the purpose of indicating a time.

The Sautrāmaṇī, although it is a subsidiary of the *abhicayana* (the piling of the fire-altar), must be performed on a *parvan* day because it has the *iṣṭi* as its archetype; it is not to be performed at the very time of the piling itself.
(Vi. 4.3.20). Regarding the Sautrāmaṇī as a subsidiary of the piling: "Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī.
Thus, the Sautrāmaṇī’s status as a subsidiary of the piling means it is to be performed on a *parvan* day occurring after the performance of the sacrifice, and not immediately following the piling.
And likewise, the Sautrāmaṇī is prompted by time:
Bhaṭṭa 4.3.15.
The Sautrāmaṇī, enjoined by the rule "having piled the fire-altar," is an auxiliary of the sacrifice (*ṛtu*), not an auxiliary of the piling (*citi*).
Saṃkarṣa 1.1.6; Mīko, p. 97: "Having piled the fire-altar" (*agniṃ citvā*) [in the context of] the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice—here the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) is to be consulted.

The Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice: because of the statement, "Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī," the Sautrāmaṇī is a subsidiary part of the ritual (ṛtvaṅga) due to its being connected to the act of piling; and because of the risk of deficiency in the ritual, it must be performed immediately after [the piling].
Saṃkarṣa. 1.1.6.
The Sautrāmaṇī is a subsequent subsidiary of the Abhicayana sacrifice, according to the rule: "Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī" (Vi.
10.2.12). Furthermore, the Sautrāmaṇī is also a subsidiary of the piling of the altar.
Regarding this, one should consult the section titled "The Principle of the Bṛhaspatisavana" on page 2984 of Mīmāṃsākośa. The Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice involves three animals;
in those animals, the ritual details of the Ekādaśinī (the set of eleven victims) are found to apply.
Soma. 8|1|8 | The Sautrāmaṇī is twofold: as a subsidiary (aṅga) and as a primary rite (aṅgin).
Among these, that which is a subsidiary to the Abhicayana is indeed a distinct ritual act from the well-known Sautrāmaṇī.

In that case, there is an extension of the well-known *sautrāmaṇī* ritual characteristics to its constituent parts (*aṅga*), because the word *sautrāmaṇī* is applied to them, as in the case of the *māsāgnihotra* (Vi.

4.3.12). Although the subsidiary fires of the *sautrāmaṇī* are involved, the performance does not take place at the time of the principal rite (*aṅgin*), but rather at its own proper time, the *parvan* day.
Even though the Sautrāmaṇī is an auxiliary to the *cayana* (fire-altar construction), it must be performed at its own time [i.e., at the time of the New and Full Moon sacrifices].
See the section in Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 27, under "The Sautrāmaṇī and others which are auxiliaries to the fire-altar construction.
Because the injunction for the Sautrāmaṇī is similar [to that of the Darśapūrṇamāsa], its time is that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Bhāṣya 4.3.16.41: In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, there are animal-cakes (paśu-puroḍāśa) dedicated to different deities, and the animals themselves are dedicated to different deities.
10.1.9.24: In the Sautrāmaṇī, the goat for the Aśvins, the ram for Sarasvatī, and the bull for Indra—such are the various animals of distinct types.

11 | 4.10.37-38: In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, there are three vessels for liquor (surāgraha): one for the Aśvins, one for Sarasvatī, and one for Indra. Then follows the reduction of the ritual performance.

Likewise, they offer the oblations for the performance on the northern fire-altar, and the vessels of liquor on the southern fire-altar.
He purchases some Brāhmaṇa to consume the remainder of the *graha* offerings;
or he pours it out into the omentum of a *vahlīka* goat.
Of that very same remnant, they distribute a certain portion into a jar with a hundred holes (*śatacchidrā*).

3|5|3|4–15. In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the Surā-grahas (liquor-cups) are prescribed by the injunctions beginning with "He takes the Āśvina cup," and so forth. In that context, because of the similarity to the sacrificial oblations of the Iṣṭi, the procedure of the Iṣṭi applies, but not the procedure of the Soma sacrifice. Vi. 8|2|1.

In the Sautrāmaṇī, regarding the animal sacrifices dedicated to the deities Aśvin, Sarasvatī, and Sutrāman, the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) for Indra-Vāruṇa and Indra are prescribed; they are supplied from the context of the animal sacrifice itself.
They should be extracted from the *saṃskārapaka* [section].
And regarding the purpose of closing the gaps, an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) has been stated: Bhāṣya 10.1.9.22.
In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, when there is a displacement of the deities of the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa), the statement regarding displacement is appropriate only as a refinement of the deity:
"If, in this Sautrāmaṇī, there is a displacement, it is because its cakes for the animals have different deities and the animals themselves have different deities.
If this is the case, then the statement regarding displacement is consistent with the view that it is a refinement of the animal.
That is not so;
for even on the view that [the word] denotes a *saṃskāra* (a mental impression), the mention of "removal" (*vyuda*) is not tenable,
because there is nothing removed therein.
The sacrificial rite becomes successfully accomplished only by means of sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) dedicated to the deities of the *viprīt* [ritual].
For thus it is said: "In that there are sacrificial cakes for different deities and animals for different deities, thereby it becomes successful for him."
The defect that exists in both positions does not belong to either one alone.

For just as in the position of [the injunction being] a preparatory act (*saṃskāra*), the statement regarding the removal (*vyudavacana*) is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), so too in the other position it will be an explanatory praise.
This is not so.
In your position, nothing at all is omitted.
When the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) is being performed for another deity, nothing is omitted from the animal-deity;
in that case, there is merely a displacement (*vyudava*) of the invocation.
In my view, however, the manifestation of the deity—which is a subordinate element—is lost.
It is said that something else occurs when the word *vyudam* is uttered;
for when the word *vyuda* is pronounced, the meaning of the word is not grasped.
In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, regarding the cups (grahas) dedicated to deities who are already established [in other rites], there is a statement concerning sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa):
"There are no sacrificial cakes for these animals; these animals have the cups as their sacrificial cakes.
It is not, however, that they do not exist at all.
This is said with reference to the absence of consecratory refinement (*saṃskāra*) in those [offerings] for which the deities have already been satisfied.
"The *puroḍāśas* are their *grahas*; for these are indeed *graha-puroḍāśas*.
What is common to them as their *puroḍāśas*? If they are for the purpose of refining the deities.

If the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are also for the purpose of consecrating the deities, then this [interpretation] becomes plausible. Therefore, the view that they are consecratory acts (*saṃskāra*) is indeed superior. Thus it is said: "They do not take a draught for this animal; this animal consists of the sacrificial cake."

By stating that the absence of a cup-offering (*graha*) is caused by the mention of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), [the text] demonstrates the identity of purpose between the cup-offering and the cake-offering.
In that context, it is understood that the cup-offering serves to consecrate the deity;
if the cake-offering also serves to consecrate the deity, then this [identity of purpose] becomes logically consistent.
Now, as for what was said— that there would be a displacement of the *puroḍāśa* cakes dedicated to Indra, Varuṇa, and Viṣṇu from the context of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice—
this is the response:
for that sacrifice is indeed for the purpose of consecrating the deities and for the purpose of closing the gaps [in the ritual].

And this [statement] was spoken with the intention of the author of the Sūtra and Bhāṣya, based on his view that even from another source there is a scriptural statement [to the effect]: "One purchases a Brāhmaṇa."

But when, according to the method stated in the Vārttika, another sacrifice with *surā* as its substance is enjoined for the purpose of purifying the deity— on the grounds that there is "no one to drink the remnant" (*uccheṣaṇasya pātāraḥ*)— then even in that case, the application is based on the explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*), namely: "They cause the hundred blades of grass to be scattered."
[This refers to] the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), by virtue of its consisting of substances other than ghee and milk.
