Thus, a connection with three distinct fruits is made for that which is already obligatory.
Furthermore, there is the well-known tradition:
"The name of this [person] is Saudhanvana;

one should employ the *nidhana* 'hīṣ' for one desiring rain, and 'ūrj' for one desiring food. Even though the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*) is of mixed caste (*saṃkara*), he has the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the *āghāna* (establishment of the sacred fires).
It is heard in the scripture: "‘Ūm’ for one desiring heaven.

In this regard, as for whether the specific *nidhana*s such as *hīṣ* and others produce a different result from the result of the *soma* sacrifice, the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted. (See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 3285, under the *Rathakārādhikaraṇa*).

Are they prescribed? And thus, when the *saumara* sacrifice is commenced by one desiring rain, the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*)—who is another name for the *saudhanvana* and belongs to a different caste (*jātyantara*) being slightly inferior to the other three castes (*traivarṇika*)—is entitled to perform it; at that time, he is also entitled to the two *nidhana*s, "ūrk" and "ū," which yield their respective fruits. Bhāṣya 6.1.2.50.

The application [of the *hiṣ* and *nidhana*] is by way of desire, and there is the cessation of the *hiṣ* and *nidhana*: "One desiring rain [should think], 'In the knowledge of the means of the Sauparṇa [hymn], Vinatā [sent] Garuḍa for the sake of the nectar';
I shall praise with the Sāmarasa-sāman. And "One desiring food is sent forth with the word 'ūrj'.
(Vārttika 2.1.732).

"I shall perform the *nidhana* in the *saubhara* melody"— this refers to a specific *sāman* called the *phala-saubhara*, which is obligatory in the *ṣoḍaśī* sacrifice. Furthermore, that very *saubhara*, while accomplishing its own inherent fruit, is also performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*), and it is also performed as a contingent rite (*naimittika*) in the *atirātra* sacrifice.
VI. 2.1.23: The *nidhana* is prescribed as being separated by the hall (*śālāntarita*). And thus, for one desiring rain, the *saubhara* [is performed] with the syllables *hīṣ*, *ūrk*, *ū*.
"He who desires rain..."
The *nidhana* should be performed as "hīṣ" in the *saumara* [chant]; rain alone is to be prayed for. Thus, he who desires food and he who desires heaven should praise with the *saumara*.
The same should be understood regarding the connection between the desire for food and the desire [for heaven] in this context.

This constitutes one statement. Regarding the deliberation, "The *nidhana* for one desiring rain is *hīṣ*; [the *nidhana*] for one desiring food is *ūrj*; [the *nidhana*] for one desiring heaven is *ū*," he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). One should perform [these] because they are heard in scripture as having results such as rain and so forth.
In the case of the *saumara* *sāman*, there is a connection with specific desires (*kāma-saṃyoga*) regarding the *hīṣ* and other *nidhana* endings; this constitutes a separate sentence.
In these two sentences, whatever fruit such as the release of rain and so forth may exist [belongs to them].

Because of the scriptural mention of the person (*puruṣaśruteḥ*), one who desires the specific result [of the *saumara*] through words such as "one desiring rain" should adopt that [result] separately; and when both are combined, there is an abundance of results.
This is because the person is heard of separately in relation to both the *saumara* and the *nidhana*.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it should be so.
The abundance of fruits such as rain and so forth belonging to the Saubhara is for the sake of other results;
thus, there is an injunction regarding the *nidhana* [concluding chant] within the Saubhara.
For in this way, [the elements] such as *hīṣ* are restated in the sentences, and there is no separate independence between the two sentences.

Since everything has already been stated, the scriptural mention of *kāma* (desire) in that context serves merely as a restriction for the *hīṣ* and other *nidhanas*; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). There would, however, be a further scriptural mention of the *nidhanas* in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, where the Saubhara is the *brahmasāman* of the *ukthya* chants.
The *saumara-sāman* and its *hīṣ* etc. *nidhana* are prescribed. Or [it is] the eternally qualified *ṣoḍaśī*. 2|1|3|28. *nityaviśiṣṭu ṣoḍaśī-* [is the rule].

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that the results, such as rain and so forth, are distinct; by the word "or" (*vā*), this is set aside, and he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "The injunctions regarding the *saṃsthās* [are for the sake of] the *saubhara*, which consists of a single syllable... (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 873).

There is no separate fruit, because it is impossible for everything to be the substratum when it is to be accomplished as a whole, and because [the fruit] must be a substratum suitable for that. Furthermore, regarding the Saubhara ritual, which is a constituent part [of the Jyotiṣṭoma], there are other scriptural statements such as "he who desires rain," etc. (Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya, p. 486).
Saubhara 4370; Saubharādhikaraṇa 4371; The Section on Saubhara; The Section on Saubhara.

The Section on the Saubhara. Because it has been stated—that is, because it has been stated that [the Saubhara] has results such as rain as its fruit—the scriptural injunction regarding desire (*kāmaśruti*) in the passage "for one desiring rain" and so forth, within that very fruit of the Saubhara, serves as a means of recognition for the fruit of rain and the like already mentioned in the sentence concerning the Saubhara; specifically, the words "one desiring rain" and the rest, which denote the fruits of rain and so forth, would be the indicators of the fruit already expressed in the Saubhara sentence itself.

If it is objected: "If there is only one and the same fruit in both the Saubhara sentence and the *nidhana* sentences, then the repeated mention in the *nidhana* sentences of 'for one desiring rain' and so forth would be redundant," the author replies to this:
The repetition of the scriptural statement is for the purpose of the *nidhana*, specifically for the purpose of prescribing the regulation of the *nidhana*:
when the *saubhara* chant is intended for one desiring rain, "hīṣ" alone is the *nidhana*; when it is intended for one desiring food, "ūr" alone is the *nidhana*.

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the fruit belongs to the *saubhara* itself as qualified by each respective *nidhana*, and not that some fruit arises from the *nidhana* alone.
[Ke:
The performance [of the rite] is undertaken through the intense desire for its own specific fruit.
Furthermore, even between two prayers for rain, a distinction must be made if there is another result [besides rain].

But if, on the other hand, there is a restriction regarding the *nidhana*, then only *hīṣ* is prescribed; thus, when the rain is prayed for, there is no room for an alternative interpretation. This is stated: "First of all, a doubt is not tenable, because of the distinction between the words of the injunction."
For a connection between the *hīṣ* and the *nidhana* is not desired because of the intervention [of other elements].
"‘Hīṣ’ is the *nidhana*": this would result in an undesirable hearing (*aniṣṭa-saṃśrava*) due to the fault of postulating a disconnected relationship.
Likewise, in the latter view as well: "If the placement of ‘hīṣ’ were in the *nidhana*, it would be qualified by the desire for rain;
because it would then be a restatement of a qualified object, a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) would clearly occur."
If *hīṣ* were prescribed by way of restating the *nidhana*, the word expressing the result would be meaningless, and there would be the redundancy of a repeated scriptural injunction (*punaḥśruti*).
For the *nidhana* alone is already obtained through the mention of the *saubhara* itself; thus, this [mention of *hīṣ*] would be a mere restatement of that which is already established.

In that case, if one were to apply *hīṣ* to that specific final *nidhana* of the *saubhara* intended for one desiring rain—understood as "that which is the *nidhana* of the *saubhara* for one desiring rain"—then it would differ from the teacher's position because it would involve a performance characterized by multiple names.

Although the *saubhara* chant for one desiring rain and its *nidhana*s have been established there, since even multiple [elements] are present therein, an effort must necessarily be made for the sake of exclusion. Consequently, the conclusion that it has multiple purposes is weak.

Furthermore, the refutation of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not properly executed, because the *nidhana*s such as *hīṣ* and others are already established by the very recensional tradition (*samāmnāya*).

Therefore, it should be described in this way. (Having stated the objection, he begins to explain the Bhāṣya according to his own view: "When there is a connection with the very word 'desiring rain,' a doubt arises;
for the capacity of the sentence is observed [to indicate] that [the sacrifice] is a means to the fruit."

In this context, while the rule "the syllable *hīṣ* for one desiring rain" remains thus established, a doubt arises: is the connection of *hīṣ* with the fruit direct, or is it a qualification of the means indicated by that fruit?
In that case, the author of the Bhāṣya has shown, as it were, a verbal construction such as: "The *nidhana* is *hīṣ*; this [syllable] becomes the fruit.

As for the statement "for one desiring rain," this is a qualification of the *saubhara*, because in the sentence concerning the *nidhana*, the *saubhara* itself is not mentioned by its own name; therefore, its status as a qualification occurs only through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

The phrase "na hīṣā saṃśravaḥ" is intended to establish a connection with the nature of the result. In that regard, one interpretation is that the repeated mention of the injunction (*vidhi*) is required for that very purpose; otherwise, it would be established simply by the force of the performance-injunction (*prayoga-vacana*). For if the *nidhana* alone were restricted while the *saubhara* itself remained operative in its own right, then since the *iṣ* and other elements would already be brought forward by that performance-injunction, the injunction regarding the *nidhana* would become redundant.

However, in the view that there is a connection with the fruit, the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) is not capable [of establishing the relationship], and thus there is purposefulness. Furthermore: "In this context, by the word *vṛṣṭikāma* (desiring rain), the person is denoted by direct audition (*śruti*) itself; for when the *saubhara* chant functions as the means, there is a syntactical connection (*pada-saṃgati*) between the *hīṣ* and other syllables."
Otherwise, by this [rule], the *saubhara*—though situated within its own context—would be indicated as being endowed with the capacity to produce rain.
And there is no purpose whatsoever in resorting to that [indication].

Thus, it is understood that this very interpretation is intended even by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) when he says, "In a case of conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*)."

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows: "That very desire which was previously mentioned for the entire Saubhara [chant], that same one is now restated in order to restrict its concluding cadence (nidhana)."
"This connection with the desired result for the entire *saubhara* is merely being restated as something already previously mentioned and recognized; thus, there is no attainment of a new result.
But for what purpose is there this repeated mention of that which has already been established? He says: 'The repeated mention is for the sake of the *nidhana*.
Why, then, are *hīṣ* and the others not connected with the result obtained through the repeated mention?"

To this it is replied: "Just as the Vāravantīya is not intended to obtain a substrate [other than the Sāman], so too the *hīṣ* and other such elements are not intended to obtain a substrate for their substrate [the Sāman]."
For if it were understood that "one should accomplish rain by means of *hīṣ*," there would necessarily arise the requirement: "What is it dependent upon?
In that regard, the *saubhara* which is the subject under discussion cannot be accepted as the substratum;
for the word *saubhara* denotes the *sāman* in its entirety.
And that *hīṣ* cannot be established [as a means] in that way, as is the case with curd for the oblation (*homa*). For curd is able to pervade the entire oblation,
whereas *hīṣ* does not pervade the *saubhara*.
Because it is accomplished through many [factors], and a relationship between a substratum and its own substratum is not possible based on that [substratum].

Furthermore, since the *nidhana* can be established by it as being pervaded [by it], there is no context (*prakaraṇa*) for it; thus, it does not attain the status of a substratum through syntactical connection (*vākya*) and the like.
In that case, if the attainment of the substratum occurs only through the syntactical connection with the result, then the sentence is split.

Likewise, when *hīṣ* and so forth are connected by restating the *nidhana* alone, the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside; this would lead to the undesirable consequence of applying them to all *sāmans*. Furthermore, the phrase "of the *saubhara*" would have to be qualified in some way by the word "that which" (*yat*), and even there, the mind must again be strained. Moreover: "Even if it were a means to the *saubhara* by way of its constituent parts..."
Nevertheless, because devotion is manifold, it is not understood as being uniform.
First, the *nidhana* established by the statement regarding the *saubhara* does not thereby establish that the *prakaraṇa* (context) is non-*saubhara*,
because the constituent part is not perceived as being the *saubhara* itself.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that there is no such assumption as "it should resort to whatever capacity [is available]."

Even if they were to become subordinate (*āśrayatva*) to the *prastāva* and so forth—since there are many such divisions within the *saubhara* chant—it is not at all known which specific division the *hīṣ* and other syllables should be employed in.

According to the principle "Or rather, it belongs to the primary [part], because of the prior injunction, as in the case of the world" (*mukhyaṃ vā pūrvacodanāllokavat*, 12.1.10.15), they would apply to the *prastāva*.
In that case, however, it is not appropriate for them to be mentioned in the restatement (*anuvāda*) as "the *nidhana*."

Now, it might be argued that just as the *ukthya* and other elements, though enjoined for a specific result and belonging to the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma, are not combined [with the whole sacrifice] yet find their place at the end [of the sacrifice] by virtue of another scriptural statement— even though they consist of multiple parts— so too here, although the *hīṣ* and other syllables are prescribed for a result and approach the *saubhara* as its substratum, their status as *nidhana*s (concluding sections) is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) on the strength of the traditional recitation (*samāmnāya*).
That is correct.

Why? Because its application is established in the Ukthya and other rites by virtue of having no other object; however, since *hīṣ* and the others have many possible locations, it is not understood which one should be used.
It is logical that the *yukta*, *mukthya*, and other such rites—being seen in other locations and being non-worldly (*alaukika*)—are like specific types of other sacrifices;
for their location has never been seen before.
Furthermore, for those whose specific location is unknown, there can be neither the assumption of a form nor a connection with a fruit.
Furthermore, the possibility of [the *hīṣ* etc. being located in specific places such as the *ukthya* is not prompted by their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).

Even that acquisition of a specific location through another scriptural statement is understood to have that very purpose—namely, the injunction of the result—because it is grasped precisely through the cognition of their distinctness; thus, it is known to serve that end alone.

As for the *hīṣ* and so forth, however, the mention of a specific location obtained from the traditional recension (*samāmnāya*) has already been utilized by the injunction of the *saubhara*, both as a subordinate element of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and as a fruit of the *saubhara*.

Now, however, because the *hiṣ* sound is prescribed as an independent result (*phala*), its specific location—whether it resides in the world (*loka*) or elsewhere—is not known, since it does not function according to the established usage (*bhakti*).
If it were understood to be prescribed only in the context of the archetype (*prakṛta*), then, because its location would already be known, no doubt would arise.

But surely, since the word is one and the same, whatever meaning it has in the archetype must be the same in the world and so forth; therefore, even when it is grasped there, that very same location will serve as its specific place.
This is not so.
Why? Because even though the word is one, there is a distinction in its capacities according to the purpose;
thus, its application to one effect would not preclude its application to other effects as well.
One cannot assert that because a certain function is observed to have efficacy in one location due to the identity of the word, it must be the same in another location as well.
For it is not understood that whatever place is known to belong to Devadatta while he is walking is the same as that which belongs to him while he is eating;
for specific locations and so forth are determined by the function, not by the essential nature [of the agent].
Because its own nature remains undivided even when in another position,
therefore, due to being the final element of the ritual action (*kārya*), even a single [syllable] attains different positions.
Furthermore, it is not possible to determine that the very position occupied by *hīṣ* when prescribed for the *saubhara* chant is the same as that for the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

If it is argued that this is because they serve as the means for the *saubhara* by way of being incidental (*prāsaṅgika*), we say no; for that very [status] is not established, since it consists merely in the attainment of a specific position.

Indeed, there would be a circularity (*itaretarāśraya*): the existence of the specific position depends on its being a means for the *saubhara*, and its being a means depends on the existence of the specific position.

But surely, just as in the *āmyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice, even though the middle and other portions of rice are to be taken up, those belonging to the archetype (*prakṛta*) are what are grasped, so too in this case, the *hīṣ* and other [syllables] will be grasped.

In that case, it is appropriate because the sentences requiring the connection with deities—which are the subject under discussion—are divided by their inherent [syntactic] requirements; thus, even the word [‘iṣ’] possesses the nature of being divided from ‘madhya’ and so on, and there is no inclusion of others apart from the effort directed toward the subject at hand.
But here, since ‘hiṣ’ and the others do not possess such a character, ordinary usage is not excluded.
Therefore, since this sentence-meaning is not possible, another alternative is adopted.

When, despite being sought in every possible way, no connection with a fruit is found through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), then the *śruti*—lest it be rendered sublated—is understood through an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the means under discussion.
In that case, the meaning is as follows:
"The word *hīṣ* is indeed an instrument for the rain that is under discussion."
Furthermore, the word "rain" (vṛṣṭi), which refers to the subject at hand, indicates only the Saubhara chant which serves as its locus, and not anything else;
nor is there any cognition of something else serving as the means.
For even though the *hīṣ* and other syllables are already established, it has been stated that the sentence exists for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārthatvāt*).

And since those elements such as *hīṣ* and the rest are adopted by the *saubhara* chant exactly as they exist in reality, they are restricted precisely in that form; thus, even without a connection to the *nidhana*, the status of being a *nidhana* is established and subsequently reiterated.
This is shown in the passage beginning, "For one desiring rain, [the *hīṣ* is used] in the *saubhara*," and so forth.

Furthermore, this section serves as an exception (*apavāda*) even to the two intermediate sections which are devoted to establishing that the fruit of a subsidiary action (*guṇakriyā*) belongs to the ritual act itself.
This result is established by the very words "rain" and so forth through an indication of the means (*sādhanalakṣaṇā*); for it is these that are being taught.

As for the objection regarding a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) that was raised, that would occur if there were a connection with the *nidhana* or if the *saubhara* were taken as a qualifier by direct statement (*śruti*). But neither of those two cases applies here.
Because it is connected with the word *hīṣakāma* itself, and because its status as a qualifier of the *saubhara* is obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*),
and a sentence does not constitute a syntactical connection (*vākya*) for qualifiers that are already obtained through context;
therefore, there is no fault.
This indicative mark (liṅga) must be examined:

whether the *hīṣ* and other syllables, which serve as means for rain and so forth, are restricted to the *saubhara* chant studied in any particular school (*śālā*), or whether they should be employed in rites such as those desiring rain only when they are recited with the *hīṣ*-finale within that specific school.
A similar investigation applies to the *ūṣ*-finale and the *ūn*-finale.

In this regard, it might be argued that since the application of the *saubhara* chant brought from the *sahasra-stoma* sacrifice is unrestricted, and since *hīṣ* and other such syllables are restricted to specific occasions such as the desire for rain (*vṛṣṭikāma*), [the rule] is established as follows: Wherever that *nidhana* (concluding phrase) is recited, the entire singing—including the *gīti*, the *stobha*, and the *pāda*—pertains only to that specific *śākhā* (recensional branch).
Why? Because one does not enter into the connection with a different *gīti* out of fear of destroying the established form.
Therefore, this [sacrifice], being conceptualized as a whole, must be regulated according to its traditional sequence.
For its form is understood from the sacred tradition (samāmnāya), and that [form] becomes non-existent even through a slight deviation from it, because it is not recognized.

In that case, if a melody belonging to another scripture (*śāstra*) were applied to a finale (*nidhana*) belonging to another scripture, there would be a change in form (*rūpānyatva*). Furthermore, this does not occur even in the absence of an explicit statement, as in the case of "airaṃ kūcodreyaṃ" (derived from *airat*—"one should not say *girābhiḥ*; [therefore] *airaṃ kūcodreyaṃ*"). By the force of this scriptural statement, even though the word *irā* replaces the word *girā* in the *yajñāyajñīya* sāman, it does not do so in the original context; thus, this serves as a counter-example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*).
This is because the application is established without distinction by adopting the melody as it has come down in that specific scripture.
Because it is impossible [to be] everywhere, it has space as its locus;
and there is movement here.
And this rule applies when an alternative is reached.
Furthermore, since the entire *sāman* constitutes the meaning of the word, even the possibility of an option is not perceived;
therefore, there is no injunction for a *nidhana* belonging to another [sāman].
Consequently, according to the principle of Kāṭhyabhojin, what was initially a restriction to a single part results in a restriction to the whole.
This sentence-meaning is also possible here:
when both [the Saubhara and the *hīṣ*] are already established, only their connection is enjoined;
namely, that for one desiring prosperity, the *hīṣ* should be employed as the *nidhana* of the Saubhara in a single instance.

Therefore, it is established that there is a rule for the entire *gīti* (melodic chant). Regarding this, the *Śāṅkhāyana-śrautasūtra* states: "He who desires rain, he who desires other [benefits], and he who desires heaven—let him praise with the *saubhara*. Having introduced the *stotra* of the *brahmasāman*, the *saubhara* is prescribed as its means for achieving three results. With reference to the *saubhara* which serves as the means for these three results, they recite: "One should employ the *nidhana* (concluding syllable) as *hīṣ* for one desiring rain; as *ūrj* for one desiring food (*anna*); as *ū* for one desiring heaven."

In this regard, there is a doubt: are the specific *nidhanas* such as *hīṣ* and others enjoined for a different result because they belong to the *saubhara*, or are they restricted—while accomplishing that same result of the *saubhara* itself—that which was obtained through non-mandatory recitation?
Since the person is the primary factor (*śrotṛtva*), it is understood from the fourth [chapter] that the *hīṣ* and others are for his sake alone.
And their status as subsidiary to him is by virtue of being the means to a result conjoined with that [person]. Thus, these are indeed for the purpose of the result.

In the context of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), however, *saubhara* is indicated by words such as "one desiring rain" (*vṛṣṭikāma*). And when direct denotation (*śruti*) is possible, indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not possible.
Therefore, *hīṣ* and the other [syllables] are qualities that lead to distinct results.
This being the case, we reply:
since the previously mentioned results such as rain are recognized here in their reverse order, there is no attainment of a different result.
Therefore, the *hīṣ* and other qualities do not lead to a different result.
In the *saubhara* chant, however, [the notes] are enjoined and regulated according to what has already been established.

As for the connection with Soma, it should be understood from the counter-argument that even though there is a conflict regarding the relationship between a quality and a fruit in the sentence concerning the *revatī* verses, such a possibility exists here as well.

The meaning of the sūtra is this: because of the connection with a person in expressions such as "one desiring increase," there is a connection with a fruit in the case of *hīṣ* and so forth, which are established within the *saubhara*.
Thus:
"The Saubhara hymn is prescribed for those desiring rain, food, and heaven;
and the *nidhanas*—namely *hīṣ*, *ūrg*, and *ga*—are likewise for those desiring rain and the other benefits."

Is another result—such as rain and so forth—the fruit of *hīṣ* and the other syllables, or is it that when the *saubhara* chant has been mentioned, a specific *nidhana* is enjoined for a distinct result? Another result is stated in four ways: "For one desiring rain, [the *nidhana*] is *hīṣ*."
Having stated, "Desire rain as the fruit of the Saubhara," [the rains] increase;
this very [injunction] is recognized for those who desire high rainfall.
Even in the case of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), it is appropriate because of the sense of purpose expressed by the dative case.

Bhaṭṭa: With reference to the hymn named *brahmasāman*, the *saubhara* Sāman—which is based on the hymn mentioned in the scriptural passage, "He who desires increase, he who desires another [desire], or he who desires heaven, should praise with the *saubhara*"—is enjoined for the sake of three distinct results.
This is because, due to the multiplicity of the objects to be specified, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is recognized through the ellipsis (*anupaṅga*) of the verb "should praise" (*stuvīta*).

In the Saubhara chant, according to the division of Vedic recensions (*śākhā-bheda*), the final limit of the *nidhana* (concluding phrase) is reached at various points; thus, "hīṣ," "ū," "ūrj," and so forth, are recited as the final syllables. At that very point, with reference to the Saubhara, it is heard in scripture: "One should employ 'hīṣ' as the *nidhana* for one desiring rain, 'ū' for one desiring heaven, and 'ūrj' for one desiring other [benefits].
In this context, since the words "one desiring rain" and so forth denote the results (*phala*), the qualities such as "hīṣ" are enjoined specifically for the sake of those results.

Furthermore, because the *saubhara* chant—by virtue of being the substratum for the *upādi* (the beginning) and the *nidhana* (the conclusion)—serves as the regulator for the recitation of *hīṣ* and other syllables, it cannot be claimed that parts of the chant other than the *nidhana* become the substratum; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting other syllables such as *stobha* in other sections.

Nor can it be argued that, on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), these syllables like *hīṣ* merely serve to establish a restriction for those *hīṣ* etc. which were already obtained without restriction in the *saubhara*-conclusion (*nidhana*) as a means to rain;

for if that were the case, there would be the necessity of resorting to *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication) by the words "one desiring rain" (*vṛṣṭikāma*) and so forth to indicate the *saubhara* as the specific means to that end.
And since that [syllable *hīṣ*] functions as a qualifier of the specific [melodic] death (*nidhana*), it is dependent upon a specific location.

Therefore, *hīṣ* and the others are distinct results from the result of the *saubhara*. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: by following the force of the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) and in accordance with the terms "one desiring rain" and so forth, even while accepting the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the *saubhara*—the means for rain—the restrictive injunction regarding *hīṣ* and the others is indeed adopted. Furthermore, since the possibility of the alternative (*pakṣaprāpti*) arises precisely from the order of recitation and other factors, the restriction also attains the status of occupying that very position.

In reality, however, in accordance with the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) regarding restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*), it is accepted that *hīṣ* and the other syllables serve the purpose of rain and so forth precisely through their relationship as being means for the *saubhara* chant; thus, there is not even a case of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, the *saubhara* that constitutes the link in this relationship is not the *saubhara* in general (*saubharatva-avacchinna*), but rather a specific instance of the *saubhara*.
For, according to different Vedic branches (*śākhā*), various distinct types of *saubhara* chants are recited in some places, accompanied by different concluding phrases (*nidhana*).
In that case, since *hīṣ* is not established even as an option for the *saubhara*, it cannot serve as a factor constituting a relationship with that *saubhara*.
Rather, it belongs only to that class of *saubhara* in which *hīṣ* and other syllables are recited without restriction.

Consequently, because the rule "hīṣ" is established through the aforementioned relationship for the sake of *hīṣ*, just as there is an exclusion of other *nidhanas* within the *saubhara* that constitutes that relationship, there is also established the exclusion of other types of *saubhara* from having rain and so forth as their purpose.

Therefore, the distinction is that this [injunction] pertains exclusively to the context of its constant application (*nityaprayoga*). Maṇḍana states: "The *hīṣ* and other [syllables] are taught as restrictive rules for the fruit of the *saubhara*. *Saubhara* is a specific *sāman*, and *nidhana* is the final section of a *sāman*.

That which has the fruit of the *Saubhara* as its very fruit is the specific *nidhana* such as *hīṣ* and so on. For the sake of restriction—that is, with regard to the expectation of a specific fruit—it is "taught" (*śiṣṭa*), meaning it is prescribed, to restrict the employment of the *nidhana* to *hīṣ* alone, thereby precluding other *nidhanas*. Śaṅkara states: "The *hīṣ* and so on do not have fruit as their purpose;
rather, there is a fixed rule regarding the *nidhanas*."

"Oṃ. One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation of white rice to Soma and Rudra in clarified butter. In this case, the mention of the white color is an injunction (*vidhi*), not a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Bhāṣya 4.2.12.

Oṃ. When the sacrifice to Soma and Rudra and others is heard [in the scripture], there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the original barley by means of rice grains qualified by attributes such as whiteness.

10.7.19. 64–71. See the section under *mīko.* p. 4359, ‘In the case of the sacrifice to Soma-Rudra and others as heard in the scripture...’. Oṃ. But the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) belonging to the Soma sacrifice is not to be mentioned, for the other is [already] stated. The carrying forward belongs to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dāśapaurṇamāsika*).
It is not to be enjoined as something unexpressed, because it is already established by the *codaka* (the general rule).
The word "but" (*tu*) serves to exclude the alternative view.

In the *Vārttika*, however, this is refuted by the statement: "Having adopted the view that the [fire] is to be carried forth according to the *darśa* ritual, the carrying forth according to the *soma* ritual is set aside."
Thus, it was stated that the word "tu" (but) is meaningful in the phrase "praṇayanaṃ tu" (but the carrying forward).
However, in the *Kutūhala*, it is stated that this Soma-related carrying forward belongs to the Siddhānta (conclusive) position alone;
whereas in the *Subodhinī* and the *Bhāṣya*, the Soma-related carrying forward belongs to the Pūrvapakṣa (prima facie) position alone.
In this regard, the ritualists (yājñikas) accept the position of curiosity;
and the prohibition of the *uttaravedi* is likewise.

Regarding the statement that "in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the carrying forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) at two of the seasonal festivals is like that of the Soma sacrifice," the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) states another reason.
The particle *ca* serves to conjoin two reasons.
Since it has been stated that "one does not prepare the *uttaravedi* in the *vaiśvadeva*, nor in the *śunāsīrīya*," there is a prohibition of the *uttaravedi* for the first and fourth parvans.

And because a prohibition presupposes a prior application (*prāpti*), and since the *uttaravedi* is present in the Soma-related (*saumika*) carrying forward of the fire (*praṇayana*), it is precisely this Soma-related *praṇayana* that is extended by analogy (*atideśa*).

In the same way, just as the fact that the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) of the *prākṛta* [sacrifice] is not explicitly stated leads one to infer the *saumika* [rite], so too the prohibition of the *uttaravedi* in certain cases leads one to infer the *saumika* carrying forward characterized by the *uttaravedi* elsewhere; such is the meaning.

According to the *Vārttika*, this sūtra is for the purpose of refuting the position of the *dārśika-praṇayana*; according to the *Kutūhala*, it consists of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the *saumika-praṇayana*; and according to the *Subodhinī* and the *Bhāṣya*, it is for the purpose of establishing the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) for the *saumika-praṇayana*. However, there is no difference in the literal sense of the words.
"Or rather, it is archetypal (*prākṛta*), because it lacks a specific name.

By using the word "or" (*vā*), [the author] sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—established by two preceding sūtras—that in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the carrying forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) in the two festivals is that belonging to the Soma sacrifice—and states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
This carrying forward of the fire is archetypal, belonging to the Full and New Moon sacrifices (*dāśapaurṇamāsika*).
Why? Because the *praṇayana* (carrying forward) belonging to the Soma sacrifice is not named [by that term].
The meaning is that this word is not its designator;
even the word *praṇayana* is a designator of the original (*prākṛta*) [rite] alone.
On this point, the Vārttika states: "A different carrying forward of the fire (praṇayana) is prescribed for the Varuṇapraghāsas and the Sākamedhas.
After the initial carrying forward of the fire, it is heard in scripture: 'They carry forward two fires from the Āhavanīya.
Therefore, the word 'Āhavanīya' here does not serve to indicate a location."
Thus, immediately after its introduction, it is prescribed.
"Or the original" means "by nature.
This is precisely the explanation of the Bhāṣya's statement, "because it is not named."
Thus [ends the section].
Herein is the Saubharādhikaraṇa (Section on Saubhara), number 4375, concerning the Sausika.
Regarding the rites for Soma:

in another treatise concerning those rites for Soma, it is heard in the scripture that after the carrying forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*), the two priests— the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ— carry forward two fires from the Āhavanīya.
In accordance with that same syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*), the phrase "they lead forth from the two" (*dvayoḥ praṇayanti*) also prescribes the leading forth from the Āhavanīya fire.

Consequently, this leading forth—which is distinct from that which is obtained through the *codaka* rule (the archetype) as being from the Gārhapatya—is for the sake of a different purpose (*adārthika*) and is non-sacrificial (*asaumika*).
However, in the *Kutūhala*, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the leading forth follows the procedure of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dāśapaurṇamāsika*).
Thus it is stated in the *Subodhinī* and the *Bhāṣya*.
The scriptural mention is for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), for the purpose of a secondary quality (*guṇa*), or as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
It has been said that in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, the *Agnipraṇayana* is performed like that of the *Dāśika*.
In this case, however, the proponent (siddhāntin) supplies the predicate for the statement "they lead [the fire] for two.
The hearing of the phrase "they lead for two" is for the purpose of exclusion (parisaṃkhyā), meaning they lead for two and not for four;
or it is for the purpose of a subordinate quality (guṇārtha), namely the quality of leading to the eastern region; or its purpose is as an explanatory praise (arthavāda).

"Therefore, they proceed with two" is [an] explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). The meaning is that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) for the purpose of praise (*stuti*).
Regarding this, the Vārttika states: "It serves to establish the purpose of the first [position], namely the *dāśika* method of carrying forward."
"In these cases, the repetition should be applied according to what is possible.
This method of carrying [the fire] is like the Soma-sacrifice's carrying—this is the view of Kutūhala following the ritualists' (Yājñika) position;
it is like the Dāśika sacrifice's carrying—this is the view of the Subodhinī and the Bhāṣya; and it is neither the Soma-sacrifice's nor the Dāśika's—this is the view of the Vārttika.

It is not the case that the selection (*varaṇa*) of the *hotṛ* priest pertaining to the Soma sacrifice will accomplish the purpose of the New and Full Moon sacrifices by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*).

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is no *prasaṅga* (extension of application) of the *dāśika-jāgaraṇa* (the watch at the time of the animal sacrifice) by the *saumika-jāgaraṇa* (the watch at the time of initiation).
See the section on the "Jāgaraṇa-nyāya" at Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1753.
Regarding the *saumya-darvihomas*, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that Soma is the substance.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that clarified butter (*ājya*) alone is the substance [for the oblation]. *Saṃkarṣa* 3.2.10.

Furthermore, in the fire-laying (*agnipraṇayana*) belonging to the Soma sacrifice, there is the northern altar (*uttaravedi*), but not in that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dāśapaurṇamāsika*).
Bhāṣya 7.3.8.20: *Oṃ saumike ca kṛtārthatvāt*.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding the Avabhṛtha bath, it is heard in scripture: "Whatever substance has the character of Soma, with that they go to the Avabhṛtha."

In this regard, when considering whether the carrying of substances such as the *ṛjīṣa* (soma-residue), the *āvyā* (clarified butter), the *bhakṣaṇaphalaka* (eating-spoon), and so forth—which have been in contact with Soma—to the *avabhṛtha* (final purificatory bath) constitutes a *pratipatti* (disposal) or an *arthakarma* (a primary ritual act), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated by this sūtra.
From the preceding sūtra, the word "disposal" (*pratipatti*) is carried over.
By means of the word "not" (*na*), the proposition that the carrying of the Soma-contacted *ṛjīṣa* and other items to the *avabhṛtha* is a disposal is indicated.
In this regard, the reason is: "Because they have fulfilled their purpose in the *saumika* [rite].

Since the *śrāva* and other elements have already fulfilled their purpose—that is, completed their function—within the *saumika* rites involving the proximity of the *soma* and actions such as its pressing, it is logical that when there is a transition to another purpose in the form of going to the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), they should serve merely as a disposal (*pratipatti*).
Or rather, they constitute a primary act (*arthakarma*), because of their connection with a specific designation.

This is the sūtra of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the carrying away of substances stained by Soma during the Avabhṛtha rite is not a disposal (pratipatti), but rather a primary act (arthakarma). Because of the connection with the principal Avabhṛtha—expressed in the injunction "with that they go to the Avabhṛtha"—and because of the predominance of that connection, it is understood to be a subordinate element (guṇabhūta).
Therefore, it is a ritual act for a purpose (*arthakarma*).
The word "or" (*vā*) serves to exclude the alternative view stated in the preceding sūtra.
Or rather, it is a disposal (*pratipatti*); because it follows that principle, the scriptural mention of the *avabhṛtha* bath is for the sake of the location.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding the carrying away of the Soma-pressing stones, the pressing boards, and other implements used in the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this movement constitutes a primary ritual act (*arthakarma*). To this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated: the word "but" (*vā*) sets aside the prima facie view.
The carrying away of the pressing stones and other items to the *avabhṛtha* is not a primary ritual act, but rather a disposal (*pratipatti*).
Because it follows that principle which establishes the understanding [of the term] through its application, namely: "that which has fulfilled its purpose in one place is conveyed elsewhere.

Now, as for what was said—that the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is primary because of the second-case (accusative) Vedic hearing (*śruti*) stating "they go to the *avabhṛtha*"—to that it is replied: the *avabhṛtha*-hearing has location as its meaning.
The word *avabhṛtha* indicates a location.
"They go to that place where the *avabhṛtha* [concluding bath] takes place.
However, according to the principle of disposal (*pratipatti*), the departure of those defiled by the *soma* is established as being merely a disposal (*pratipatti*). (Phe.)
In the ritual procedure (*tantra*) pertaining to Soma, the *vaṣaṭ*-call is prescribed (Bhāṣya 8.4.14).
In the Soma-related Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the placing of the whey (*vājina*) on the northern [altar] is an injunction regarding a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).
The accomplishment of that oblation is the cause and purpose.
We shall make it broad, long, and easy to handle.
And in the Soma-related Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the archetypal [details apply].
Regarding the rites pertaining to Soma:

the chapter on the sacrificial fees for the Soma rites prescribes the *utkara* and the *paridhi* by way of restating the *sādana* (placing) and *niyojana* (binding); these constitute an annulment (*bādha*) of the original *veda* and *paridhi*.

Regarding this, one should consult the section at Mīmāṃsākośa, page 1694, under the heading: "In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices belonging to Soma, the placing and tethering are those prescribed for the archetype.
The altar used in the Soma sacrifice is intended for the performance of the ritual proceedings.
The altar pertaining to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dāśapaurṇamāsikī*) serves the purpose of placing the oblations (*havis*). Bhāṣya 12.1.3.18.
The Soma-altar (*saumikī vedī*) benefits both the primary and the subsidiary rites; thus, it serves both purposes.
VI. 3.7.3: The *saumikī vedi* (the sacrificial altar for the Soma sacrifice) is a plot of ground sufficient for the *sadas*, the *havirdhāna*, and other structures.
This plot of ground includes the *dāśikī vedi* (the altar for the animal sacrifice), as well as the pavilion known as the *prācīnavaṃśa*, which lies to the east of it.
A separate *aiṣṭikī vedi* (altar for the *iṣṭi* sacrifices) need not be constructed apart from the great *saumikī mahāvedi*.
There is no extension (atideśa) of the ritual details pertaining to the *āmiṣeṇa* offering at the Soma sacrifice to the *āmiṣeṇa* offering at the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
See the section titled "The Section on Carrying Forward" (*praṇayādhikaraṇa*) on page 2703 of the Mīmāṃsākośa.
The ritual characteristics (*dharma*) of the *saumika-avabhṛtha* are extended by way of the name "avabhṛtha" to the *avabhṛtha* of the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice.
See the section titled "Extension (*atideśa*) to the Varuṇapraghāsa-avabhṛtha" on page 216 of the Mīmāṃsākośa.

The word *vaiṣṇava* occurring in the *Atithyeṣṭi* belonging to the Soma-sacrifice does not extend the ritual details (*dharma*) to the *vaiṣṇava* and other vessels belonging to the preceding triad in the *Rājasūya*.
See the section titled "The Vaiṣṇava-nyāya" on page 3059 of the Mīmāṃsākośa.

In the Soma-sacrificial *iṣṭis*, the purpose of the *patnīsaṃyāja* (offering to the wives) performed in the Daśapeya sacrifice is accomplished through *prasaṅga* (incidental application) by means of the *patnīsaṃyāja* performed in the Soma-sacrifice itself.
Regarding the statement "The accomplishment by way of *prasaṅga* [occurs] through the *patnīsaṃyāja* of the Soma sacrifice" (Mīmāṃsākośa, p.
2831), one should consult that section (*adhikaraṇa*).
The sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) of the Soma sacrifice do not accomplish by way of *prasaṅga* the consumption of the remnants in the *Soma-Agni* sacrifices.

See the section on *mīko.* pṛ. 2829: "The contingency does not apply to the consumption of remnants belonging to the *somāgneyī* sacrifice regarding the *saumika* sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). *Oṃ*, this is the chapter on the *saumika* sacrificial fee. The *anvāhārya* fee, which is archetypal (*prākṛtī*), should not be given in place of the *saumika* sacrificial fees and the like.
"And because they have already received their wages, there is no hiring.

The Commentary states: Regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the hiring of priests for the purpose of the *anvāhārya* (subsistence fee) is prescribed; however, when this [requirement] is extended here by the *codaka* (general rule of transfer), it should not be performed.
Why? Because they have already received their wages (*bhṛtatvāt*).
Those officiating priests (ṛtvij) have died for the sake of the Soma, having been hired with the fee [stipulated] by the rule, "Its sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is one hundred and twelve.
Furthermore, the status of being the performer (kartṛtva) applies to the subsidiaries and the primary rite in terms of place, time, and agent.
Therefore, the performances belong to those who possess knowledge of the ritual.
Therefore, there is no separate purchase of waters. Consequently, the *anvāhārya* fee is excluded.

Śā—In the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, when there is a doubt as to whether the *anvāhārya* fee obtained through the rule of extension (*codaka*) should be given or not, it was stated in [Sūtra] 3.7.5 that because of the injunction "The Soma sacrifice has no fee," the twelve-hundred-fold fee is intended solely for the primary sacrifice.
Therefore, the dakṣiṇā for its own sake must indeed be given in the subsidiaries.

(He states the established conclusion: It need not be given because it is accomplished through incidental application (prasaṅga), for this [dakṣiṇā] exists solely for the sake of the primary sacrifice.

From the commencement until the conclusion, the [main sacrifice] proceeds without interruption; thus, the injunctions for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites—which depend precisely upon that [main sacrifice]—are not logically consistent even with their own purposes, let alone with those obtained through the *codaka* (transfer rule).

Furthermore, because the satisfaction of the priests (*ānati*) differs when there is a separate sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it would follow that there is a difference in agents (*kartṛbheda*) for the subsidiaries and the principal rite, though this is not scripturally stated.

And since a difference in agents necessitates a difference in performance (*prayogabheda*), it is illogical given that the performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*) understands only a single performance.
In some cases, because a difference in sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) is heard in the scripture, a difference in performers (*kartṛbheda*) is not a defect.
And in the case of the Vājapeya and Bṛhaspatisava, because it is heard in the scripture, even a difference in performance (*prayogabheda*) is not a defect.
Furthermore, one follows the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) at that very time when the primary rite is to be performed.

The learned twice-born ones did not perform [the subsidiary acts]. Once it is determined that the scriptural meaning is that the primary act alone can be accomplished, then for those who are ignorant, even the subsidiaries must necessarily be performed because they are established by the context (*prasaṅga*). Therefore, no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) can be assigned to the subsidiaries. [Objection:

Since the fee is intended solely for the primary act, only the primary acts themselves should be performed; thus, because the purpose is already served even regarding the subsidiaries, the giving of the fee must be performed, just like the eating of the remnants (*śeṣabhakṣaṇa*). This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). [Conclusion: This is the connection (*saṃgati*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: since [the sacrificer] has already been hired by the very sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of Soma, there is no separate purchase (*parikraya*) by means of the *Anvāhārya* rice-offering. Vi— "In this case (of the Soma-related sacrifices), should the *Anvāhārya* be given or not? It belongs to the Soma sacrifice alone; because the sacrificial fees such as cows and so forth are excluded from the ritual procedure (*tantra*) that follows the injunction."

Bhaṭṭa: In the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and subsequent rites, the *anvāhārya* dakṣiṇā obtained through the *codaka* (extended injunction) need not be given, because the giving is accomplished by way of *prasaṅga* (incidental benefit) from the dakṣiṇā intended for the Soma sacrifice. Nor does the principle of the Soma-dakṣiṇā apply here on the grounds that the statement "the dakṣiṇā belongs to the Soma" serves to exclude [other] commonality; this is like the principle regarding the Soma-altar (*saumika-vedī*).
It is also possible to avoid this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*).

For if that were the case, a difference in the agent would result due to the difference in the act of hiring (*ānati*), leading to the recognition of a distinction between the performance of the subsidiaries and the principal rite as separate acts.

Therefore, since the hiring is accomplished by the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) alone for the Soma sacrifice, and because the status of being a single performance (*tantrya*) is not lost even for those rites that depend on that hiring—just as in the case of the animal sacrifice, the *prayāja* offerings, and so forth.
The *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other such rites do not have separate applications for the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Nor is there an absence of purpose in avoiding the commonality of the subsidiaries;
for in the case of the *nirūḍhapaśu* and others, the [fees] consisting of one hundred and twelve [cows] serve the desired purpose.

Therefore, in that context, there is an extensive discussion regarding the substance [of the fee]—whether it be the primary one or another brought in—that serves as the means for the direction of the implied meaning, such as "the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is the substance. Maṇḍana says: "It may be that the sacrificial fee is not mentioned here; however, it is prescribed in the Darśa sacrifice and in the Soma and Agni sacrifices. Here, "here" refers to the Soma and Agni sacrifices.
Śaṅkara says: "There is no sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for Soma-Agni.
This is the principle regarding the sacrificial fees of the Soma sacrifice.

Based on the statement, "The sacrificial fees belong to the Soma," even though the fee is intended solely for the primary rite, it serves to exclude those [fees] that would otherwise be obtained through extended application (atideśa).

Even if there were some reason for a connection with the *pradhāna* alone (such as the sweeping of the ladles), nevertheless, because the requirement is fulfilled through *prasaṅga* according to the principle of the Soma-altar and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it is not appropriate to include the original [sweeping] within the *sāṃtapanīya*.

By means of the *saumika-dīkṣā-hatimantras*. There is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the *dīkṣā-hatimantras* heard in the section on the *agnicayana*. See Mīko., p. 49, regarding the *dīkṣā-hatimantras* heard in the *agnicayana*.
In this context, the *adhikaraṇa* (section) is to be examined.
The extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual details (*dharmas*) pertaining to the Soma sacrifice applies to the indistinct sacrifices (*avyaktayāga*), such as the *udvitsava* and others.
Regarding the statement "mīko. pṛ. 199: 'Atideśaḥ udvaidādiṣu'," one should consult that section (adhikaraṇa).
[This refers to] from the ritual elements of the Soma sacrifice.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, during the Sutyā [pressing day], the preparatory rites such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) belonging to the Pauroḍāśika section occur prior [to the main offerings].
These are performed using the Soma-vessels, specifically the Ṛtu-camasa cups.
In the case of the Savanīya-puroḍāśas and other offerings within the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is no extension (prasaṅga-siddhi) of the Darśika vessels, such as the Juhū and others.
See the section on Mīmāṃsākośa, page 2828, regarding the topic: "The *prasaṅga* does not apply to the *savanīya* in the Jyotiṣṭoma.
✹ [This applies] to those intended for the spreading of the Soma-offerings.
"Spread the fires; strew the sacrificial grass," and so forth, is the *preṣa* (directive).
Saṃkarṣa. 1.3.15;
Mīko., p. 2910. The directive "strew the sacrificial grass" (*barhiḥ stṛṇīhi*) pertains to the Soma sacrifice.
In this context, the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is to be understood as referring to the Soma-altar (*saumikavedi*). Its purpose is for both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary rites (*pradhāna*).
Regarding the *mīko.* page 1700, the section titled "The Principle of the Desire to Act" (*cikīrṣānyāyaḥ*) should be consulted.

✷ The Principle of the Soma Altar (*saumikavedinyāyaḥ*): In the Soma sacrifices, such as the *Iṣṭis* dedicated to Agni-Soma, the altar used for the Soma sacrifice (*saumikavedi*) serves the purpose of the New Moon altar (*dārśikavedi*) by way of incidental fulfillment (*prasaṅga*).

Because they serve different purposes, the rite of the altar (*vedi*) should be performed separately for those rites based on the *darśapūrṇamāsa* that occur during the *soma* sacrifice. Commentary: Regarding those rites based on the *darśapūrṇamāsa* which take place upon the great altar (*mahāvedi*) during the *soma* sacrifice, there is a deliberation as to whether their altar should be constructed separately or not. What is the prima facie view? It should be constructed separately.
What is the reason? It causes the *codaka* (the rule of extension) to apply.
In this way, there is favor toward the *codaka*.
But is it not the case that the purpose is accomplished through the incidental application (*prasaṅga*) of the Soma-altar?
To this it is replied:
it is not established.
Why? Because of the multiplicity of meanings.
These two altars serve different purposes:
the altar of the Darśapūrṇamāsa is for the purpose of placing the oblations and so forth, while the altar of the Soma sacrifice is for the purpose of the ritual performance.
Therefore, the principle of *prasaṅga* (extended application) is not applicable here.
When a subsidiary belonging to one ritual procedure is performed by someone ignorant [of its specific application], it results in a connection with unintended purposes,
as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings belonging to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*) when they are performed in relation to the cake-offerings (*pauroḍāśika*).
But it is not so here;
therefore, an altar (vedi) must be constructed.
Otherwise, it would be a non-performance, as it would be defective due to the previously performed [preparation].
Commentary: Or rather, the altar for the Darśa sacrifice need not be constructed. Why? Because it would be a defilement.
If it were constructed, it would merely cause defilement to the already prepared altar of the Soma sacrifice.
It accomplishes nothing for its own purpose.
But surely the placing of the oblation (*havis*) will be performed there? However, that can also be done on the great altar (*mahāvedi*).
But surely, the setting up of the altar (setu) is for another purpose;
even though it serves that other purpose, it is capable of serving as the substratum for the placing of the oblation (havis).
For the placing of the oblation on the altar is what is prescribed by scripture.
And this [same] altar [is used here as well].
There, no distinction is heard in the scripture such as "it is for that purpose" or "it is not for my purpose.
Therefore, the altar belonging to the Darśa sacrifice must also be prepared.

Śā—In the Jyotiṣṭoma, when the great altar (mahāvedi) has been prepared, there arises a doubt as to whether or not a natural (prākṛtī) altar should be constructed separately for those rites that have the Darśapūrṇamāsa as their archetype. Even though the great altar serves the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the principal rite, nevertheless, because of the practical requirement of placing the oblations (havis), the natural altar must be constructed for that specific purpose to accomplish the task. This is the principle of the Saumika-vedi. [Section 4379] Regarding the Saumika altars...
It is not so;
for even though it serves the purpose of spreading [the grass], it is also capable of accomplishing the placing of the oblation by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*).
For the placing of the oblation performed upon that [grass] does not become defective.
For in the archetype sacrifice, the placing of the oblation on the altar is prescribed, not for its own sake alone.
Therefore, by way of extension, the placing is for the purpose of the ritual performance;
thus, through the consumption of the *saumika* and other portions, there is [the consumption] of the *saumya*, *tvaṣṭra*, and *vaiṣṇava* offerings.
On page 1818, regarding the statement "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, at the Prāyaṇīya and other rites, there is the Dākṣika vow," one should consult that section.

The consumption of the Soma-cups and other offerings belonging to the Soma-sacrifice does not result in the fulfillment of the requirements for the consumption of the remnants of the Iṣṭi-sacrifice by way of *prasaṅga* (extended application).
12.12.15.131–32. See the section in Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2831, under *prasaṅgasiddhi*, regarding the consumption of the *saumika-vrata* as a supplement to the *aiṣṭika-śeṣa-bhakṣaṇa*.
However, in the case of the injunction "one should offer a *caru* to Soma-Indra," the procedure is indeed like that of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice due to its connection with Soma.
Bālakrīḍā, p. 120: The *saumendra-caru* is for the sacrificer alone in the event of vomiting Soma, and not for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) either.

VI. 3.14.137. The *saumendra-caru* (the sacrificial pap for Soma-Indra) is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the drinking [of Soma] by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and others. 3.4.13.34–36. See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 4362, under the heading "The *saumendra-caru*: [expiation for] the drinking by the sacrificer and others.

In the injunction, "One should offer the *saumya-caru*" (*saumyaṃ carum ālabheta*), there is an injunction for a sacrifice (*yāga-codanā*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because the act of offering (*ālabhana*) is... [incomplete].
1147–51. In the statement "In the *saurya* [offering], there is a *caru* cooked in milk," the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is to be understood.
The *saurya caru* is an optional rite (*kāmya-karma*). Vi. 6.3.2: Is the *saurya caru* a collective heading (*samudāyādhikāra*)? It is not a collective heading.

Bhāṣya 8.1.12–24: Regarding such injunctions as "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya," there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual properties belonging to the *āghāra* and other primary rites based on inference.
The inference is as follows: "The sacrifice requires auxiliary implements (*upakaraṇa*), because it is an instrument (*karaṇatva*), like eating, or like the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
Vi. 7.4.1: "One desiring spiritual luster should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya."

In that regard, when there is an expectancy for the specific ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*), the procedure belonging to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* is applied by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the word "offers" (*nirvapati*), due to its connection with the procedure of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*.
Even there, the procedure of the *Āgneya* sacrifice is restricted by the indicative mark of being a single deity or the commonality of the vegetable offering (*oṣadhi*).
Bhāṣya 8.1.12: "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* to Sūrya."
In that context, for the purpose of [the ritual acts] such as *ayāṭ* and *ujjiti*, the word "sūrya" itself must be used in these [formulas]:
*saurye* (4384), *sauryādīnām* (4385),
and *sauryacaroh*.
In the case of the *saurya* oblation of cooked rice, there is a sublation of the act of drawing out [the portions].
The removal and the placing [of the potsherds] are not prescribed in the archetype (prakṛti).
The commentary states: In the archetype it is heard, "He places the oblations within the altar.
Therefore, in the archetype, the placing is performed after removing [the oblation] from the potsherds.

Regarding the *saurya* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*), there is a doubt: should the rice be drawn out from the cooking vessel and placed separately for the sake of the offering to the Sun, or should no such drawing out be performed?
Since it was performed in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it follows that it should be performed here as well;
however, the act of drawing it out and placing it [elsewhere] was not explicitly prescribed in the archetype.

It is not heard in the original injunction (*prakṛti*) that the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is to be set down after having been separated from the potsherds (*kapāla*). It is separated for the sake of the purpose; as it is done for the sake of the purpose, it is not the meaning of the injunction itself.
Therefore, the removal [of the charu] should not be performed.
Moreover, if the removal were performed, it would be removed as a remnant, like the *kapittha* fruit;
in that case, there would be a breaking of the vessel.
Therefore, the setting down (*āsādana*) after having scooped out (*vyuddhṛtya*) [the portion] should not be performed for the *caru*.

Soma—Regarding the setting down after scooping out: as for the setting down outside [the altar] of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) that has been cooked on the potsherds, after having scooped it out from them—that should not be performed, because it is not mentioned in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Although it appears from the Sūtra that neither the scooping out nor the setting down should be performed, nevertheless, upon considering the reason "because it is not mentioned," only the scooping out should not be performed; for while the setting down is implied by the purpose, it is not explicitly mentioned in the archetype.
However, it should be understood that the placing [of the oblation] must indeed be performed because it is heard in the scripture: "He places it within the altar.
In the case of the *saurya* oblation of parched grain, only that which is explicitly heard as the fruit [is to be aimed for];
nothing else is to be performed.
4|1|120–24. Regarding the statement, "For those actions whose fruits are heard within their own scriptural injunctions, heaven is not the fruit," this section (adhikaraṇa) should be consulted.
In the case of the *saurya* oblation of parched grain (*caru*), there is a sublation of the act of pouring out [the grains].
And because it serves the purpose of a single mass, there is a mixing together.
The Commentary states: the *caru* and the *veda* are the examples.
In the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is heard in the scripture: "He mixes the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) with the *praṇītā* waters."
Therefore, in this case, should the pouring together (*saṃvapana*) be performed for the *caru*, or not?
It should be performed;
for it is possible to perform it.
This being the case, we reply:
even though it is possible, it is not performed;
for that is for the sake of the *piṇḍa*.

The purpose of the *piṇḍa* (ball of rice) is for the sake of the cake (*apūpa*), not for the cooked grain (*caru*). Soma says: "One mixes with the *praṇītā* waters"—thus, the pouring together (*saṃvapana*) or mixing with the *praṇītā* waters should not be performed, because the *piṇḍa* is intended for the production of the cake, and cakes are used only for the cake, not for the cooked grain.
*Vi-* refers to the mixing of flour with water;
in the *saurya* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*), this act of mixing is set aside.
"And the pouring together [of the grains] is for that purpose.
The Commentary states: Because of the mention of the *caru* (rice-oblation) in the case of the *saurya* sacrifice alone.
It is heard in the archetype (*prakṛti*): "Impelled by Savitṛ, he pours together [the grains] with these deities."

In this case, regarding the *caru* (cooked rice offering), there is a doubt: should the pouring together (*saṃvapana*) be performed, or not? What is the prima facie view? It should be performed because it is possible and because it is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*).
This being the position, we reply:

For that [pouring] is performed upon the original substance (*prakṛti*), not for the sake of the pouring of the cooked rice-offering (*caru*). Soma says: "One pours the flour into the vessel containing the filter (*pavitra*). That pouring into the vessel is also not to be performed, because the purpose of pouring is for the sake of further pouring, and that [subsequent pouring] is absent.
*Vi-vāpa* is the throwing of the flour into the vessel for the purpose of mixing it with water.
In the case of the *saurya* oblation of cooked rice, there is a sublation of the *saṃtāpana* rite.
Heating is due to baking [the potsherds] below.
The Commentary states: There is doubt regarding the *caru* itself.

In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the heating of the potsherds is performed with the mantra: "O you who belong to the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Bhṛgus, and the Aṅgirases, be heated by the austerity of Dharma."
There arises a doubt: should the heating be performed for the flour, or not?
Based on the principle that it should be done as in the archetype (prakṛti), it is initially concluded that it should be performed;
for that [heating] is intended for the purpose of cooking [the grain] over a fire.

Therefore, the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) does not extend [the requirement] to the *caru*. Soma says: "By this mantra, 'O Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases, heat yourselves with austerity,' the heating of the potsherds (*kapāla*) with embers should also not be performed; for that [heating] is intended for cooking from below (*adhaḥśrapaṇa*), and its utility lies only in the case of a *puroḍāśa*, since there is no cooking from below in the case of boiled rice (*odana*). Vi [says]: "Heating (*tāpa*) is the warming of the potsherds with embers."
In the *saurya* oblation, because the modification "to Sūrya, the acceptable" (*sūryāya juṣṭam*) is not praised, it does not possess the status of a mantra.

The *saurya* and other such rites are distinct sacrifices (*kratvantara*).
Since the *ārambhaṇīyā* is for the purpose of the sacrifice,

The Saurya and other such rites proceed within the Vaitanika fire. (Śābarabhāṣya 7.4.2) vi. 12|1|6.
The Saurya and other such sacrifices are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the Āgneya sacrifice, but not of the Āgneya and others that are subject to doubt.
(Vi. 9.1.18) In the performance of the optional (*kāmya*) Saurya and other sacrifices, the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is not a restrictive factor.
Performance according to one's desire.
If [the subsidiaries] that provide remote assistance were performed separately, there would be a division of the *tantra* (common procedure), as in the case of the *saurya* and other sacrifices.
In the *saurya* and similar rites, the *itikartavyatā* (procedure) is extended by *atideśa* (transference).

Regarding the statement, "The extension (*atideśa*) of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) applies to the *saurya* sacrifice and others," one should consult the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*). In rituals such as the *saurya*, there is an extension of the properties (*dharma*) from a specific, fixed ritual;
there is no lack of restriction [as to] from which particular [ritual] they are extended.

In the case of the *saurya* sacrifice and others, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of these five factors—the fruit such as heaven, the rule regarding lifelong performance, the agent desiring heaven, the collection [of materials], and the conjunction of the *āgneya* and other offerings—because extension applies only to the primary element.

In the case of the *saurya* sacrifice and others, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the *āmikṣā* belonging to the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, because [the *saurya*] has a single deity and its substance is an herb (*auṣadha*). However, this does not apply to the *āmikṣā* of the *aindrāgna*.

Furthermore, in the *saurya* and other such sacrifices, there is no extension of items such as the *godohana* vessel used for the sake of the person and so forth, which belong to the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.
However, it is precisely the *ṛtvij* (sacrificial priest) who is extended by analogy (*atideśa*).
In rites such as the *saurya*, there is no extension of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*’s threshing (*avaghāta*) or the oblation (*homa*).
This is because the two *pārvaṇa* sacrifices possess ten components, whereas the *saurya* and others lack the status of being modifications of a group (*saṃghavikāra*).

In the Saurya and other such sacrifices, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the fruit, the restrictive rule, the agent, or the collective [of subsidiaries] belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Dārśapūrṇamāsika).
(Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 250; see the section under *atideśo na phala-niyamaḥ*).
Since there is no instruction regarding the ritual details (*dharma*) in the Saurya and others, the acquisition of those details occurs through extension.
There is no extension (*atideśa*) of the Vedic injunction (*vidhi*) to the Saurya and other such rites.

In the case of the Saurya and other such rites, which are enjoined with their own specific procedures (*itikartavyatā*), there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the procedure belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

In rites such as the Saurya sacrifice, where there is a conflict of deities, the original deity-words (*devatāpada*) are excluded from the final *prayāja* offering according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
