The *vikṛti* sacrifices such as the Saurya are to be performed at their own specific times.

In a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) such as the *saurya*, the modification (*ūha*) consists of the instruction of words denoting the modified materials and so forth within the mantra that has been extended by analogy (*atideśa*). See the section titled "The Principle of Mantra Modification" (*mantrōhanīya-nyāya*) at Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 3118, under Sūtras 9.1.12–2, 4–8.
In modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the *saurya*, the deities are to be manifested in the invocations (*āvāhana*) and other formulas by means of the very words prescribed in the injunction.
Regarding this, one should consult the section on "Deities [are to be manifested] by the very words found in the injunction" (Mīmāṃsākośa, p.

229). In the mantras of the final *prayāja* in modified sacrifices such as the *saurya*, one must effect the substitution of the modified deity by omitting the word *agni* and other terms denoting the primary deity.

In the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the *Saurya*, in the mantra for the pouring out (*nirvāpa*), the phrase "pleasing to Agni" (*agnaye juṣṭam*) must be changed to "pleasing to Sūrya" (*sūryāya juṣṭam*), "pleasing to Indra and Agni" (*indrāgnibhyām juṣṭam*), and so forth, because it denotes a deity who is connected with the specific ritual action. If it is argued that in the *Saurya* and other modified sacrifices, while the word "Sūrya" and others are employed in the sacrifice itself, in the *nigama* mantras (recitations) one must denote the deity by some other synonym, we say: no.
Even in the case of nigamas obtained through extension (*codaka*), the deity must be designated by using the specific term "Sūrya" and so forth, and not by a synonym.

Since the quality of being a plant-offering (*auṣadha*) is common to both, the specific indicative mark (*viśeṣaliṅga*) of the deity’s singularity determines that in the *saurya* rite, the ritual details (*vidhyanta*) of the *āgneya* sacrifice apply, and not those of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice.
The cooking of the oblation for Sūrya takes place in a pot alone.
That [cooking] should apply to the *kapāla* (potsherd), because no other [vessel] is mentioned in the text.
The Commentary states: There is a *caru* offering: "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* to Sūrya.
In this case, the meaning is that the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is prepared with cooked rice (*odana*).
Now, a doubt arises as to where this rice is to be cooked. What, then, is the prima facie position? There should be no restriction that it must be cooked in a pan alone.
When something is obtained through the purpose (*artha*), one might cook the substance upon it.
For if the *kapāla* (potsherd) were obtained by the extended application (*codaka*), then the number [of potsherds] would also be obtained by that extended application.
Indeed, there is no such injunction in the archetype (*prakṛti*) as "one must cook upon potsherds."
What then? It is that "it exists on eight potsherds.
When a number is to be obtained, its state of having eight potsherds (aṣṭakapālatā) is enjoined, and not otherwise;
yet in this way, the number is not obtained.

For rice cannot be cooked upon many potsherds in the manner of a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). And if only a single potsherd were obtained, that which is enjoined as "eight-potsherd" would not be attained at all.
Therefore, the caru is to be cooked in whatever vessel is suitable for cooking a substance.
This being the case, we reply:
"That [grain-offering] should be on a potsherd by virtue of its original form, and another would result from the absence of scriptural injunction.
This very *cara* (grain-offering) should indeed be on a potsherd; in this way, the word expressing the original form (*prakṛti*) is maintained.
And no other substance whatsoever is taught [in the scripture];
therefore, it is manifold.
Furthermore, number is also [a quality], like the potsherds.
Commentary: That which has been stated must be refuted.

Or, because of contradiction, [the offering] should be cooked in one [vessel]. Commentary: If it is not possible to cook the sacrificial oblation (*cara*) in many potsherds, then, due to the contradiction, it should be cooked in one.
Regarding what is stated, "It is on eight potsherds," this means it is to be cooked upon eight potsherds.
And whatever [vessel] is obtained as a specific requirement, that would be obtained because of the restriction to potsherds.

Alternatively, because of its connection with another purpose, the vessel used for cooking the cake serves the purpose of holding it in the case of the *caru*; in that case, there would be the acquisition of eight vessels, as there is no restrictive rule due to the absence of specification.
Commentary: Or rather, it should not be cooked in potsherds. Why? Because of its connection with a different purpose.
When a potsherd is employed for the baking of a cake (*apūpa*), it is so that the cooking which produces the cake may occur through the heat provided by that [potsherd].
In that case, the potsherd being taken up for the purpose of holding water serves [a different function];
the cooking of rice which is accomplished by heat transmitted through the water is not accomplished by the heat residing in the potsherd.
Therefore, the potsherd being taken up for the purpose of holding water would not serve its original function, and thus the *codaka* (the rule of extension) is not upheld at all.
Therefore, there would be the acquisition of a different meaning. And because of the lack of distinction [between them], it would be restricted; but what is that?
Or rather, it applies to the *caru* (porridge), because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Commentary: Or, the cooking may be performed in a pot;
for there is an indicative mark [to this effect].
"In whichever vessels there are Soma juices, those should be the *caru* offerings.
This indicates that the *caru* is to be cooked specifically in the Soma-vessels (*somasthālī*), thereby demonstrating the particular vessels required for preparing the *caru*.
An objection is raised: "This is merely a scriptural indication (*darśana*); it does not constitute a rule of application (*prāpti*)."
To this it is replied: that cooking known as *cara* is accomplished in a pot (*sthālī*), not in a frying pan (*kaṭāha*) or on a potsherd (*kapāla*).
Therefore, the *cara* is to be cooked in a pot.

What is the purpose [of this inquiry]? If it is a modification of the potsherds, and if the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is modified by means of the boiled rice (*odana*), then: if it is a modification of the potsherds, the grinding (*peṣaṇa*) must be performed because its purpose is lost [in that case]; but if the sacrificial oblation is modified by means of the boiled rice, there is no performance of grinding, because [the rice] is the cause for the cake (*apūpa*). Furthermore, kneading (*saṃyavana*) must be performed in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) because it is for the sake of forming a lump, but not in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The kneading is likewise;
and the heating as well as the cooking must be performed during the first fortnight, not in the second.
The placing [of the bricks] is exactly the same.
And while the *pṛṣṭha-kṣaṇa* (the act of sprinkling) is to be performed according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is not so according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Likewise, the igniting of the coals by blowing upon them is exactly the same.
The placing [of the vessel] after having pushed the coals aside (*vyudūhya*) is, by implication, to be performed according to the prima facie view.

It is not established in the final doctrine that the object does not exist; for the placing [of the offering] is performed according to the purpose, not as obtained through the verbal text. And what is performed for the sake of the purpose is not brought forward by the extended injunction (*codaka*).
Śabara: There arises this doubt: is this sacrificial pap (*cara*) to be cooked on a potsherd (*kapāla*), or anywhere at all, or in a cooking-pot (*sthālī*)?
It would be on a potsherd due to the application of the archetypal rule (*codaka*).
But surely, the potsherd is restricted to being eightfold by that same archetypal rule?
Furthermore, the *cara* cannot be cooked in eight potsherds (*kapāla*).
It is true that the number eight is obtained, but that [number] is set aside due to impossibility; however, by its removal, the potsherd itself ought not to be removed.
Therefore, it should be performed on a potsherd.
It is not so, because it serves a non-original purpose.

For in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the cooking of the oblation is accomplished by the heat of the potsherds; however, the *caru* is to be cooked by the heat of water. In that case, a potsherd being employed for the purpose of holding water would serve a non-original purpose, and thus there is no extension of the archetypal rule (*codakānugraha*).
Therefore, when it is argued that "it may be cooked anywhere," we reply:
it must be in the pot alone; for it is in the pot that the cooking, which has the movement [of the food] as its cause, is accomplished, and not elsewhere. Therefore, it should be in the pot.

If, even when the word *caru* denotes boiled rice (*odana*), the cooking takes place in the pot itself, then what difference would there be in practice between the two positions of the previous section—namely, that the *caru* is a modification of the potsherds (*kapāla*) and that the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is modified by the boiled rice? For in both cases, the oblation is cooked in the pot; having raised this doubt, [it is said that] the purpose [of the present discussion] is stated in the section concerning the fire-holder (*agnidhara*). Soma [concludes]: Since no other [vessel] is prescribed, the function of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is performed by the *caru*, and the function of the potsherds is not fulfilled [by anything else]; thus, the connection with the guest-offering (*atithi*) is established.
The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: "That cooking would occur on the potsherd itself by virtue of the attainment of the original state. [Vivaraṇa:
"The sacrificial oblation (cara) is to be cooked either on the potsherd, or on some other suitable [vessel];
for it is not logical that it should be on the potsherd alone, since that [location] is obtained through the force of the general rule (codaka)."
Because it lacks the capacity for movement, [the rice] does not move in the pot; there is no fitness for it in the cauldron.
Here, the result of the thought [of the injunction] is the cessation of actions such as grinding.
Grinding, crushing, sowing, heating, placing on the fire, and spreading [the ashes].
"Cleaning, shifting, kindling, as well as removing and placing—these are to be performed by one of dull intellect; such is the delusion.
That these are suitable only for a cake is established by the Sūtras."

The injunctive character of that which is connected with [the mention of] Brahmins and others by means of a laudatory statement is not precluded, because it is consistent with that [injunction]. Vārttika 2.1.3.4, p. 8593. *Stibhinī* refers to the fruits of the *nyagrodha* (banyan) tree; [some say] "the tips of the roots" (*jaṭāgrāṇi*), but this is the opinion of Valānda.
But the *stotra* and *śastra* are purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), like the *yājyā*, because they denote the deity.
For both praising (*stavana*) and reciting (*śaṃsana*) are heard in the texts: "He recites the *prauga*," and "They praise the *āghāra*."
In the inquiry as to whether [the stotra and śastra] are subordinate to the deity or primary with respect to it, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The word "but" (*tu*) indicates the difference from the previously mentioned acts such as the cleansing (*saṃmārga*).
The fruit of the praise (*stuti*) and recitation (*śastra*) is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the deities.
Therefore, it is not a mantra recited in song,
because it designates a deity and is intent upon praising the qualities of the deity;
it is like a *yājyā*, for just as *yājyā* mantras are intent upon manifesting qualities by way of illuminating those qualities, so too is this.

Therefore, the *stotra* and *śastra* are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) with respect to the deity. However, the deity is set aside by the purpose, because the injunction regarding the deity is subordinate to the purpose. Having stated that "the *stotra* and *śastra* are subordinate with respect to the deity," he states the refutation of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The word "tu" (but) indicates that the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not accepted.

If the *stotra* and *śastra* were acts intended for the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the deity, then, because the *stotra* and *śastra* would be subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) and auxiliary (*śeṣa*) with respect to the purpose—the form of the deity such as Indra—the injunction regarding the name of the deity would be displaced by that purpose.
The "name of the deities" refers to words such as "Indra" and so forth.
*Codanā* means injunction (*vidhāna*).

Regarding the injunctions for those [ritual acts] called *stotra* (hymns) and *śastra* (recitations), which consist of mantras not containing the names of deities: where the primary factor is determined by the purpose, namely the objective of manifesting Indra and other deities, that is the section concerning *stotra* and *śastra*.
"In the Vācastoma, all Ṛks, all Yajus, and all Sāmans [are used]; in the Vācastoma, he recites the Pāriplava.
Likewise: "If the sun should not rise while the Āśvina-śastra is being recited, one should recite all the verses of the ten Maṇḍalas (Dāśatayīs).
Therefore, there is purposefulness for those [mantras] that have been displaced [from their original context].
Therefore, the prima facie view is that the *stotra* and *śastra* are actions belonging to the category of *saṃskāra* (consecratory acts).

Alternatively, because of their connection with direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the terms "he praises" (*stauti*) and "he recites" (*śaṃsati*) within the context (*prakaraṇa*) should enjoin the origination of these two actions.
The meaning of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that the hymn (stotra) and the recitation (śastra) are subordinate to the deity.

[This is refuted by] the word "adhipāśadaḥ". Because of the connection with the verbal roots heard in the texts—"they praise with the Ājya hymns" (ājyaiḥ stuvate) and "he recites the Prauga" (praugaṃ śaṃsati)—which mean "they praise" and "he recites," these two [acts] should be understood as enjoining the production of an action within the context under discussion, such as the sacrifice to Mahendra, and the production of the transcendental result (apūrva) arising from that action.

Regarding the phrase "due to connection with a direct Vedic statement" (*śrutisaṃyogāt*): in the case of "they praise with the *kavatī* verses," there is a connection with the act of praising (*stuti*) that is not [otherwise] considered;
in "he recites the *prauga*," there is a connection with the act of reciting (*śaṃsati*) by virtue of the accusative case-ending;
and in "I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra," there is a connection between the deity and its attributes by virtue of the genitive case-ending.
"‘Indra is the king of what has gone and what stands’—thus, first of all, there is a connection with the qualities of the deity.
In this way, the fourth [type of] connection through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is explained in the *Bhāṣya*.

Regarding the term "context" (*prakaraṇa*), the *Sudhā* states that it is understood as follows: having accepted the word *prakaraṇa* in its passive sense (i.e., "that which is performed"), because of the proximity (*saṃnidhi*) consisting in the presence of the injunction for the *rathaṃtara* in the *prauga* stotra—which is the subject at hand and a constituent part of the *māhendra* sacrifice—there is a connection of the *aindra* *pragātha* as a constituent element (*akṣa*) by means of a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) established through that [proximity].

Furthermore, as for the statement that this is a *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra, [it is not so], because by eliding the vowel 'a' in the phrase "api śrutisaṃyogāt" (due to connection with scripture), the fault of a non-connection with scripture (*aśrutisaṃyoga*) would result;
thus a portion of the sūtra has been interpreted by the author of the Vārttika.
This is stated in the *Sudhā*.
This is a siddhānta-sūtra (concluding aphorism), and as such, it is universally accepted.

Furthermore, this has been stated in the *Sudhā* commentary regarding the passage beginning with "because of the connection with the Vedic text (*śruti*)—since the verbal roots *stu* and *śaṃs* denote praise by direct audition.
In every respect, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *stotra* and *śastra* are primary ritual acts (*pradhāna-karman*).
And because of the distinctness of sound.
In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the *stotra* (hymn) and *śastra* (recitation) are primary acts (*pradhānakarma*), he states another reason:

"Because of the distinctness of the word [‘twelve’], the *Jyotiṣṭoma* consists of twelve *stotras* and *śastras*. By the word ‘twelve,’ the distinctness of the *stotras* and *śastras* is known. And that [distinctness] is appropriate if they are primary; otherwise, since recitation and praise would each be a single unit, the number twelve would not be possible.
Therefore, the *stotra* and *śastra* are principal acts;
otherwise, that statement would be purposeless.

If the *stotra* and *śastra* were not primary acts (*pradhānakarma*) because they function as remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*), then the mention of them [in the injunctions] would be purposeless. Furthermore, in the *Abhiṣṭut* sacrifice, when the connection with Agni is enjoined by restating the archetypal cups (*graha*)—as in "The cups belong to Agni" (*āgneyā grahā bhavanti*)—the subsequent injunction "They praise with verses addressed to Agni" (*āgneyīṣu stuvate*) would be redundant, since the verses addressed to Agni already serve to manifest Agni.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *stotra* and *śastra* are primary acts that provide remote assistance, and not subordinate acts (*guṇakarma*).
Elsewhere, the meaning is understood.
From the statement "he recites following the *stuti*," a meaning distinct from that of the word *stotra* is understood for the word *śastra*.

If both were intended solely for the purpose of praise (*stuti*), there would be a contradiction of the scriptural injunction; furthermore, because of the statement regarding the relationship of priority and posteriority between the *stuta* and the *śastra*, a meaning other than the perceived one is understood.

If their purpose were the perceived one consisting of illumination, then since that [illumination] is a single thing and thus has a single purpose, it would result in an option (between the two), which would render the relationship of priority and posteriority untenable.
Therefore, the *stotra* and *śastra* are principal acts that provide assistance from a distance (*ārādupakāraka*),
and they are designated as such because of their status as objects (*karmatva*).

In the injunctions "He offers the *samidhs*" and "He offers to *tanūnapāt*," as with primary acts, we observe the use of the accusative case in "He recites the *prauga*" and "They perform the *pṛṣṭhas*," which expresses the nature of these as sacrifices (*iṣṭi*).
Therefore, the hymns (*stotra*) and recitations (*śastra*) are primary acts,
and they bring about a result.

The accomplishment or production of the fruit—expressed in such passages as "Thou art the praise of the praised" and "May we, accompanied by Indra, win; may we be joined with offspring and food; may that [prayer] of mine regarding the possession of horses become true"—is seen to result from the *stotra* (hymn of praise), not from the deity.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *stotra* and *śastra* are primary ritual acts (*pradhānakarman*), and not subordinate elements directed toward a deity.
Section on the Hymns and Recitations (Stotra-Śastra).
The hymn and the recitation are principal acts.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the hymn and the recitation are principal acts; they are not preparatory rites for the deities.
The section concerning Mahendra;
the section concerning Indra and Mahendra.
Topic on the Stotra and Śastra: But the Stotra and Śastra are purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*), like the *Yājyā*, because they denote the deity. 2.1.5.13.

The Commentary states: "He recites the *prauga*," "He recites the *niṣkevalya*," "They praise with the *ājya* hymns," and "They praise with the *pṛṣṭha* hymns"—thus, both praising (*stavana*) and reciting (*śaṃsana*) are expressions of qualities, as in the passage:
"I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra.
Regarding this which is heard as an expression of qualities, is it subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) toward the deity, or is it the primary element (*pradhāna*)?
To this it is replied: "The stotra and śastra are preparatory acts (saṃskārakarma). Why? Because they consist in the naming of the deity."
When a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) is being brought into effect, the possessor of that quality—the deity—is invoked; otherwise, it would not be a word expressing that quality.

In that case, the direct naming of the deity is understood, and the direct manifestation of the deity is a visible benefit, namely the accomplishment of the sacrifice. Therefore, these are preparatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*).
It is like the *yājyā*.
Just as the statements "he recites the *yājyā*" and "he recites the *puro'nuvākyā*" are expressions of praise that serve the purpose of manifesting the deity, so too is this [the *stotra*].

Or rather—the presentation of the *stotra* and *śastra* serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "by those [acts] through which a substance is intended to be prepared" (*yaistu dravyaṃ cikīrṣate*).
Praise itself is the *stotra*; the *śastra* is also that very same thing, accomplished by means of mantras not set to chant.
Furthermore, praise is prescribed as the proclamation of the relationship between a quality (*guṇa*) and its possessor (*guṇin*).
And that [praise] is first brought about by means of both the quality and the possessor of the quality.

In the absence of that [the object of praise], since mere utterance of sound pervades the place of praise, the qualities [of the subject] are not themselves the primary objects of action because they lack purpose; rather, they serve exclusively for the sake of praise. Regarding that praise which is thus brought about, does it become a subordinate element (*śeṣin*) by way of reminding the object of praise, or does it exist for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) through its own primacy?

What is established? Since they establish the Smṛti for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice through what is seen, therefore the Stotras and Śastras must be purificatory rites (saṃskāra) directed toward the deities.
It is designated by its purpose; there is no injunction regarding the names of deities, because the deity is subordinate to the purpose.

Commentary: If the *stotra* and *śastra* were merely acts of consecration (*saṃskārakarma*), then the deity would be displaced by the purpose, because the purpose [of the act] is subordinate to the meaning of the name of the deity. Since the mantra is subordinate to the purpose of the deity, when that [purpose] is not primary, it should be led to where the primary element is. In that case, the sequence and proximity would be set aside.
Therefore, this faulty position must be rejected.

What, then, is that mantra? It is the *aindra* *pragātha* beginning with "Ami tvā śūra," which is recited in proximity to the *māhendra* cup-offering; it would have to be displaced wherever Indra is present.
Or rather—first, the refutation is stated on the grounds of contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For it is said: "If a mantra whose meaning is non-existent here is employed for the purpose of praise, then because its meaning is displaced, the sublation of the *prāpa* (the rule of application) would result."

That which is a praise connected with this name—meaning a praise by way of an injunction, because it is being enjoined—is, due to its being intent upon that [other] meaning, does not function for its own [literal] meaning when that [other purpose] exists. Consequently, the praise addressed to Indra (*aindrī-stuti*) would bypass the proximity of the sacrifice for the cup dedicated to Mahendra (*māhendra-graha-yaji-saṃnidhi*) and go wherever Indra is present. And thus, there would be a sublation of both order (*krama*) and proximity (*saṃnidhi*). Here, "order" refers to the sequential reading of the subsequent verses according to their numerical sequence.
Proximity, however, consists either in the presence of the injunction for the *rathantara* [sāman] or in the reference to the context;
it would serve the purpose of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), like the case of the heifer (*vaśā*).

Commentary: This position should not be rejected; the *stotra* and *śastra* are indeed acts of consecration (*saṃskārakarma*), precisely because they denote a deity. As for what was said—that there is a displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *pragātha*—that is not so.
By the word "Indra," Mahendra will be denoted; that very Indra is called "Mahendra" by virtue of the quality of greatness.
For we directly perceive the word *indra* as denoting a deity, and the word *mahat* as denoting greatness.
This is just like [the terms] "king" and "great king," or "brahmin" and "great brahmin," as in the case of a cow (*vaśā*).

Just as when a ritual is enjoined by the words "unborn cow" (*ajā vaśā*) in the passage, "This very one is dedicated to all deities; one should sacrifice a cow to Vāyu," the ritual recitations (*nigama*) employ the word "goat" (*chāga*), so it is here.
When that which possesses qualities is enjoined, there will be a designation by means of that which is devoid of qualities;
therefore, there will be no displacement [of the ritual].
Or rather—there is no fault in the meaning.
What is the reason? "In that case, the mantra would be drawn away from where it belongs if it were to apply to a different meaning;
for the expressive power [of the word] is meaningful, being the same for both Indra and Mahendra."

For that very Indra who is praised by the *abhivyañjanī* verses is the one worshipped in the *māhendra* cup-offering. In that case, there would be no displacement of the deity, because [the praise] is inherently connected with the scriptural text (*śruti*).
Commentary: This is not so.
That Indra is the deity of this cup is understood through its connection with a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).
Furthermore, for this [cup] which requires greatness, a connection with a secondary derivative suffix is not possible.

Alternatively, the assumption of a compound (*samāsa*) occurs because of the connection with "greatness" (*mahattva*), which depends upon the connection with a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). However, there is no connection with "greatness" for that which has already functioned [to denote] the meaning of a secondary derivative; nor is there a connection with a secondary derivative for that which has already functioned [to denote] the meaning of a compound.
These two—functioning for the meaning of a compound and functioning for the meaning of a secondary derivative—do not occur within this very same single usage.

Furthermore, this word "Indra" does not connect with its own meaning through a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) as if it were unformed; rather, like that which is formed, it connects with another meaning through the quality of greatness. It is clearly understood that "Mahendra" means "the Great Indra";
that is, he is the Great Indra, thus "Mahendra."
Furthermore, if Indra were the deity of the oblation, both [the name and the quality] could not be expressed in a single utterance.

Therefore, Indra qualified by greatness is the deity (this will be explained in two ways in the Vārttika: by means of the elision of a syllable and by the absence of such elision). The secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is produced from the word *Mahendra*.

Therefore, it is understood that this is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); it is not possible to postulate anything else [between them]. (This concludes the refutation of the interpretation of others.)

Furthermore, since Indra and greatness (*mahattva*) are qualities that reside in the substance [as their substratum], they do not establish a mutual restriction between themselves—just as in the case of "one-year-old" (*kahāyanī*) and "red" (*aruṇa*).
Therefore, Mahendra is none other than Indra himself as qualified by greatness; no other [deity] is meant. Thus, a mutual restriction is obtained.
For it is not [possible] in the absence of an action;
thus it is established.
Nor [is it possible] when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is formed after first creating a compound.
There is no simultaneous occurrence, nor is there the capacity to bring about the subordination of a qualifier;
for something lacks such capacity both at the time of compounding and at the time of secondary derivation. Furthermore, even when a dual deity exists, there is the occurrence of a *dvandva* compound.
And because no other significant meaning is conveyed by the two unformed compounds,
nor is there a purpose for their double utterance.

Because the two words [indra and śakra] would have the same referent (*ekārthatva*), there would follow the contingency of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) caused by the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) being intended to convey their respective relations; furthermore, there would arise the contingency that the multiple meanings conveyed by a single uttered word could not be connected through secondary suffixes (*taddhita*).
Furthermore: "If these two [cups] are indeed *suvant* (libation vessels), then no;
for the *māhendragraha* consists of the nature of the *vṛtti*."
And each one [is a separate act].
These are the topics concerning the Stotra and Śastra hymns.
"Teacher" and "maternal uncle"—though these are [merely] designations of substance, they are seen [to be used]; they are spoken for the sake of praise.
And yet, Indra does not become greater, because worldly usage occurs as distinct through the difference in the causes of dependence upon qualities.
"Even if it were prescribed after being perceived [as a defect],
therefore it is stated that the rule regarding the internal [quality] is indeed one already established,
occurring subsequent to Indra's slaying of Śatru."

Previously, for one who has everywhere already attained the status of a deity through their pure self, this quality subsequently serves only for the purpose of praise in the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses; it is not considered to be included within the very nature of the deity itself. As for the latter part of this [passage], its meaning has already been explained.

Commentary: This being so, the perception of a distinction between the *yājyā* and the *puronuvākyā* becomes logically consistent. When the *yājyā* for Indra—beginning with "aindraṃ sānasiṃ rathimam"—is established, there is the manifestation of the deity in his pure form; whereas the *puronuvākyā*, beginning with "mahaṃ indro ya ojasā," manifests him either as distinct and pure, or as qualified [by attributes]. Even when the deity is qualified, it shows the pure [form] of Mahendra. If they were one and the same, this would have to be treated as an option (*vikalpa*).
In that case, [the view] that deityhood belongs to the *pakṣa* (the side/verse), or that deityhood belongs to the *caraṇa* (the foot) as qualified by the pure word,
is improper because it is possible to establish a seen purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) through some form of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
As for what was stated— that [deityhood] belongs only to those possessing the quality of being a *ṛk*— [that too is incorrect].
That is incorrect.
Why?
Because "the state of being subordinate to the subject matter [is established] by direct statement (śruti) and by the assumption based on proximity (saṃnidhi)."
And without a general connection, an indicative mark (liṅga) is not a means of application.

For if it were determined with absolute certainty that the purpose is exclusively visible (*dṛṣṭārtha*), then the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*)—which is inferred through the proximity of sequence (*krama-saṃnidhi*)—would be sublated.

However, since the postulation of a purpose follows from the application (*viniyoga*), the application itself is not for the sake of that purpose; therefore, when an application is established by sequence and proximity, there is no contradiction in postulating either a visible or an invisible purpose.
Furthermore, there is no reason for the aforementioned *pragātha* to be applied elsewhere.

For *liṅga* (indicative power), by virtue of its capacity to reveal the deity, enjoins that mantra for its own form; and thus there arises the contingency of its being something else [than a means to an action]. However, in relation to an action (*karman*), no visible function is observed.

Therefore, if this *liṅga* establishes a general connection with some action, then when it is required how it may be of assistance, it enacts the injunction—by resorting to the principle "as it is capable"—through the medium of revealing the deity.
Furthermore, we do not perceive any cause for a general connection here.
Therefore, since the [mantras] would otherwise be rendered useless when applied to superior [rites], it is logical that they serve a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*).
Moreover: "In this way, the locative, genitive, accusative, and the praise [are established]."
In that view, they will exist as having the nature of scripture, and there will also be the state of being for another purpose.
Since the qualities, the qualified object, and the act of naming are non-distinct from the syllables, the connection with the locative case (*saptamī*) is appropriate.
As for the act of illumination, since it functions as a cause or an instrument, the *kavati* verses and so forth would be heard [as being expressed by the instrumental].
But surely, even in the case of praise, since the *kavati* verses function as an instrument, the third case ending alone should apply?

This is not a fault; for these [factors] possess both the status of being a locus (*ādhāra*) and the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*). Therefore, their designation as either is appropriate according to one's intention.
Furthermore, manifestation (*prakāśana*) has the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) as its substratum (*ādhāra*) when considered as the agent;
and because it is that which is pervaded (*vyāpyatva*), it has the deity as its substratum following the realization of its status as the object (*karman*).
In this regard, there is a disparity, since the *kavatī* verses possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*) in only a single instance.
Furthermore, [in the injunctions] "he praises" (*stauti*) and "he recites" (*śaṃsati*), the production of praise is heard as the primary purpose.

In that [production], the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the remaining factors of action (*kārakas*) are invariably produced and connected within the meaning of the verbal root.

In that case, if the mantras serve the purpose of accomplishing the praise, then—by performing the required function—they accomplish a purpose seen in the scripture (*śāstra-dṛṣṭa-artha*) and thus possess a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).

But if they were to perform the act of making known [the deity], they would be performing an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) for which no means of accomplishment (*karaṇa*) has been enjoined. Therefore, it is better that the praise itself serves an unseen purpose.
Furthermore, "The genitive case-ending itself declares to us the subordination of the deities."
The primary is not superior to the qualities; therefore, the primary status belongs to the praise.

For if the deity were the primary referent, then because it would be the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the word "Agni" in the phrase "Agni is the head" (*agnirmūrdhā*) would be heard with only the nominative case-ending, since its meaning would not be distinct [from the stem].
Even if some other case-ending were heard, that too would serve solely to connect a quality (*guṇa*), by virtue of suitability, deficiency, or singularity—just as in the expression:
"Indra is the king of all that moves and all that is stationary."
Nor is there any utility for the subordinate elements (*guṇas*); therefore, it is logical that they are based on the principal element solely for the purpose of praise (*stuti*).

The word "satyam" marks the end of the section (or the conclusion of the sentence). Therein, by the principle of the first [case], since the meaning of the subordinate element follows from the meaning of the principal element, even though it was possible for the primary status to be established previously, it is more appropriate that the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) serves the purpose of praise alone.
Nor will the roots *stu* (to praise) and *śaṃs* (to recite) have the meaning of "manifesting" [the deity] in this way; rather, praise itself is the primary element.
And because of the distinctness of the words.
The Commentary states: "By the word itself, distinctness is indeed understood."
The Agniṣṭoma consists of twelve stotras and śastras;
otherwise, there would not be a twelfth [total] of stotras and śastras.
There is only one recitation (śaṃsana) and one pressing (sāvana).
Now, if a distinction is resorted to, then the number twelve does not remain established.

Or rather—the numbers two and twelve, which reside separately [in distinct units], are not expressed by the word when there is no difference in the manifestation [of the parts]. Or, if there is a focus on the general [whole], because that [number] ceases to apply to each individual verse (*ṛc*) or each individual line (*pada*), it does not remain established as twelve.
But surely this is the same even in the case of praise.
For it has been said: "The general praise is one and the same, yet the specific praise resides in each verse;
nor is there any other intention [of the speaker] by which the number twelve would be established."

Now, if the hymns (*stuti*) accomplished by a collection of verses (*ṛksamudāya*) numbering one hundred *stomas* are being counted, then illumination (*prakāśana*) would likewise be a distinct [action]. It is said: "Actions always consist of a group of those that terminate with the attainment of their fruit;
and because of the twelvefold nature of the *apūrva*, the state of being twelve is determined."

For if it were by way of manifestation, since that [manifestation] is seen to cease with each *ṛc* and each *pāda*, there would be no basis for a single action through which the number twelve could be delimited. However, if they serve a transcendental purpose (*apūrva*), then because they are known through scripture, and because there is no evidence for their completion prior to the attainment of the prescribed *stoma*, they must recur as a collection of *ṛcs*. Thus, by means of that [collection], due to the equality of the action, they serve as a defining characteristic; consequently, the twelve-fold nature of the praise is established through the twelve-fold nature of the transcendental results.
For there is no authority whatsoever for such a construction [of the mantra] with respect to each verse or for all the *stomas* combined, as there is for the observation regarding its manifestation.
Moreover, that statement would be purposeless.
The Commentary states: In the *Agniṣṭut* sacrifice, it is heard: "The cups (*grahas*) are dedicated to Agni."

Furthermore, it is stated there: "They praise with verses addressed to Agni" and "They recite with verses addressed to Agni. In that case, these must indeed be injunctions if they are preparatory acts (*saṃskārakarman*).
Therefore, for this reason as well, they are principal acts (*pradhānakarman*).

Or rather—since the *ṛc*s are already established by the injunction for the *āgneya* cup, the praise and recitation of those verses addressed to Agni are accomplished by that very injunction; therefore, the statement "they praise with verses addressed to Agni" (*āgneyīṣu stuvate*) would be redundant.
Another meaning is perceived [from the text].
The Bhāṣya says: "The *stotra* and *śastra* are indeed the *saṃpradāna* (the recipient)."
If the stotra were one thing and the śastra another, then there would be a connection between the two;
or, if they were expressed as something unprecedented, then the stotra would be one thing and the śastra another.
Otherwise, that which is the stotra would be the very same as the śastra.
Or rather—the distinction between the *stotra* and the *śastra* follows from the mention of their relationship, since a relationship is based on difference.
And that [distinction] would result from their being manifesters of a single [deity].

But is this not equally applicable to the other [the *śastra*] because it is also an object of praise? Or if the distinction is based on the connection with mantras that are either chanted (*pragīta*) or not chanted (*apragīta*), or by way of their being "without holes" (*acchidra*), then that [distinction] is no different even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In this regard, the answer is that it is like the number twelve.

For, due to absolute difference, one speaks of a relationship by metaphorically attributing a distinction in action through the intermediacy of the *stotra*, the *śastra*, and the *apūrva*; however, the manifestation itself does not differ either intrinsically or in terms of its result.
And the designation is like the object.

The Commentary states: "In the case of 'of the primary object' (*pradhānakarmaṇaḥ*), there occurs a designation by means of connection with the accusative case, as in 'he recites the *prauga*,' 'he recites the *niṣkevalya*.'"

Or rather—this designation for the sake of the action presented as second [in order] is another reason for its primacy. For a primary action is required by someone, as in "he performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice" or "he pours the *āghāra* libation," whereas a preparatory (*saṃskāra*) action is not, because it is entirely subordinate. Alternatively, it is for the purpose of making known the primacy therein through the designation of the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns.
Otherwise, there would be the designation "illumination" alone; here, due to the difference between "I" and "the other," there would be neither [illumination] nor the accomplishment of the fruit.
The Commentary states: Furthermore, the observation of the accomplishment of a fruit occurs.

In passages such as "Thou art the praised of the praised," and so forth, up to "We, possessing Indra, win and obtain; may this progeny of mine be the true fulfillment of the sacrifice's blessing"—the fruit of the praise is restated, not that of the deity.
Therefore, the *stotra* and *śastra* are principal acts (*pradhānakarman*).
Elsewhere, this is the purpose of the Sūtra:
In the tenth chapter, [it is stated]—"There would be an inquiry [regarding] the Stotra and Śastra as being primary acts, because the cups have deities as their objects" (10.4.24).
Or rather: these blessings for results found in the mantra are consistent with the primacy of the Stotra, because prayers everywhere have the primary act as their object.
But in reality, since the deity alone is the primary factor, it is the deity that should be petitioned for the fruit, just as in the case of a ritual act;
for while the master is present, no servant would petition for the fruit.
*Śāstra*: Praise (*stotra*) is the designation of a connection between a quality and its possessor through the excellence of a chanted mantra (*pragīta-mantra*).
*Śastra* is likewise praise itself, but it is accomplished by means of unchanted mantras (*apragīta-mantra*).

There is an inquiry as to whether [acts such as] "they praise with the *ājya* hymns" (*ājyaiḥ stuvate*) and "he recites the *pra-uga*" (*pra-ugaṃ śaṃsati*) are subordinate acts (*guṇa-karma*) or principal acts (*pradhāna-karma*).

And for that purpose, are these [mantras] subordinate with respect to the deity for the sake of manifesting it, or are they primary with respect to the deity for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*)?

In this regard: "The recollection of the deity is a visible purpose; it is not reasonable to assume an unseen result. Therefore, because they are for that purpose, the *stotra* and other such acts are subordinate actions (*guṇakarma*)."
It is said:
"It is true that having a visible purpose is logical if it does not contradict the Vedic revelation;
however, if it were for the purpose of remembering the deity, the form [of the mantra] as revealed in scripture would be subverted."

Therefore, the *stotra* and *śastra* are principal acts (*pradhānakarman*). Since it was previously established that [acts like] the *soma* are subordinate acts (*guṇakarman*), there is a connection here by virtue of the presence of that same cognition. Furthermore, because they possess the character of principal acts as stated in the section on the two-fold division (2.1.3), there is a connection with that [section] through syntactical unity (*vākyaikatva*).

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding [the injunctions] "They praise with the Ājya-stotras" and "He recites the Prauga-śastra," since the stotras and śastras reveal the deities of the sacrifice, they possess a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) just like the *yājyā* mantras; therefore, like the act of threshing (*avaghāta*), they constitute a direct auxiliary (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*).

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhāntin replies]: In common usage, it is well known that only the expression whose purport is the quality as qualified by another quality is denoted by the term "praise" (*stuti*). Furthermore, since the terms *stotra* (hymn) and *śastra* (recitation) denote precisely those expressions—whether accomplished by chanted (*pragīta*) or non-chanted (*apragīta*) mantras—whose purport is the quality as qualified by another quality, these mantras cannot possibly have the manifestation of a quality as their purport. Therefore, these mantras do not serve the purpose of manifesting a quality; rather, because the hymns and recitations—which consist in the manifestation of qualities—are remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) by virtue of having an unseen spiritual result (*adṛṣṭa*) as their purpose, such as their commencement and conclusion, the mantras themselves have that [hymn or recitation] as their sole purpose.

Nor can it be argued that, following the logic of the *prayāja* remnant sprinkling (*abhicāraṇa*), the mantra’s nature consists in the manifestation of a quality (*guṇaprakāśana*) through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in order to conform to its visible purpose; for since such a result is already established by the indicative power (*liṅga*) itself, the injunction would be redundant.

Thus, in proximity to the sacrifice to Mahendra, the *aindrī* [mantra] serves as a praise. Otherwise, since the deity inherent in the word must be expressed in the ritual formulas (*nigama*) by the very word used in the injunction, it could not be manifested by using the terms "Mahendra" or "Indra."

Therefore, where Indra alone is the deity, there the aforementioned contingency arises; or, due to the absence of any means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a general connection, there is the contingency of the manifestation of the state of being Indra or Mahendra through the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the mind’s capacity for speech.
Consequently, the *stotra* and *śastra* are subordinate acts (*guṇakarma*).

There would be an exclusion of the *stobhas*, and there would be no extended application (*atideśa*),
because of the disappearance of the purpose (*arthalopa*).

In the Agniṣṭoma, the Avabhṛtha-sāman is sung upon a verse addressed to Agni, beginning with "I consider Agni the Hotṛ, the giver" (*agniṃ hotāraṃ manye dāsyantam*). In that [verse], there are musical interjections (*stobha*) such as "Agni, O Lord of the House, burn against [the enemy]" (*agnighpati pratidahati*).
Furthermore, it is heard in certain modified Soma sacrifices (*vikṛtisoma*) that "one sings the Abhyasāman on a verse addressed to Indra" (*aindyām abhyasāma gāyati*).
And Indra’s sequence of cold is understood as being like the remainder of a sentence;
therefore, since the purpose of the previously mentioned *stobhas*—such as heating, burning, and so forth—is absent there, their cessation alone must be accepted.
And by virtue of that similarity, there would likewise be no extension (*atideśa*) of the *stobhas* elsewhere as well.
Regarding the *stobha*:
the section on *stobha* [states] that the connection [of the *stobha*] would be an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).
The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position, which was reached by the rule "or cessation" (*nivṛttir vā*), is refuted by this [sūtra]. The word "or" (*vā*) serves to set aside the prima facie view.

Stobhas of this kind, such as "abhiṣarpata," would have their application in the *aindrī* verse; furthermore, there would be an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in the supplementary portions concerning Indra's act of approaching the Sītā.

In every respect, since praise is possible, there is no contradiction with the supplementary portion of the text (*vākyaśeṣa*). Therefore, even when the *aindrī* verses are not sung during the *avabhṛtha* rite, the non-specification of the *stobhas* such as "abhiṣarpati" and so forth is not contradictory.
Thus, it is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that there is a non-specification of *stobhas* everywhere.
The extension (*atideśa*) of the *stobhas* must also be performed.
Thus, there is an extension of the *stobha* "o ho ho hāī" from the source verse (*yoni*) of the Vāmadevya Sāman to its two subsequent verses as well.

The purpose of the *stobhas* is the completion of the duration of the *sāman*. Maṇi., p. 5: According to the view of the *Stobhabhāṣya* composed by Kātyāyana and others, the *stobhas*—such as *huṃ*, *phaṭ*, and so forth—serve the purpose of expressing meaning.

The naming [of these syllables], however, serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), like the word *stotra* and so forth. Although it will be stated in the ninth book (9.2.1.138) that the *stobha* syllables possess a meaning, there is no fault, because that statement intends to show that they lack syntactic unity with the *ṛc* which is the source of the melody (*sāma*). (Ku. 1.4.143, p. 46). The *stobha* syllables are inserted in some cases for the purpose of delimiting the duration of the singing.
Bhāṣya 9.2.10.35. Section on the Stobhas. Extension by Analogy (Atideśa).
Of the *stomas* established in the womb, [the application is] in the two subsequent verses.
Some maintain that there is a substitution of one substance for another in the *stobha*.

The Bhāṣya states: “He sings the *Rathantara* on the *Kavati* verses,” “He sings the *Rathantara* on the subsequent [verses],” and “Whatever is on the *Yoni*, that he sings on the subsequent [verses]. In this regard, it has been established (9.2.9) that it should be sung by means of the subsequent syllables.

Now this is being deliberated: are the *stobhas* extended [to other chants], or not? What is the prima facie view? That they are not extended. Why? Because the *sāman* is the melody (*gīti*), not the *stobhas*.

That which is the *gīti* (the act of singing) is what is indicated by the rule, "What is [sung] on the *yoni*, that one sings on the two *uttara*s," because of its connection with the word *gāyati*. Furthermore, the *stobha* (interjectional filler), not being connected with the meanings of the words of the *ṛc*, would be purposeless.
Therefore, for this reason as well, it is not indicated.
Furthermore, there occurs a statement: "He sings while practicing on the verse addressed to Indra. In that case, an inconsistency would arise;
for in the supplementary portion of the passage, Indra is understood to have the quality of coolness (*śītakarman*).
There would be no connection for that [word] with the term "it shines" (*tapati*).
Therefore, there is an exclusion of the *stobha* in another *ṛc*;
just as there is an exclusion of the syllables of the *ṛc* because they are not sung, so too is there an exclusion of the syllables of the *stobha*.
But there would be a modification involving the extension of everything, like light in general.
The Bhāṣya says: "It is not the case that there is an exclusion of the stobhas";
rather, there is an extension of everything.

The word *sāman* denotes a song characterized by specific *ṛk*-verses, *stomas*, musical notes (*svara*), durations (*kāla*), and repetitions (*abhyāsa*). How is this understood? From its usage therein.
If the *stobha* syllables were excluded, the particularity produced by them would not be included.
In that case, the word [of the Vedic text] would be contradicted;
therefore, the *stobhas* should be prescribed.
As for what was stated—that the *stobhas*, being unconnected with the words and meanings of the *ṛc*, would be purposeless—[that is not so].
To this we reply: they will not be meaningless, as is the case in the world.
Just as in the world, when singers insert certain "limb-substances" (aṅgavastuka), those are uttered for the purpose of counting the songs, not for the sake of a connection with meaning.
For the duration of a song is indeed measured by syllables;

therefore, even here, the *stobha* syllables should follow for the purpose of measuring time. [Objection: This statement in the *Bhāṣya*—"the word *sāman* denotes a song characterized by its ṛk, *stoma*, accent (*svara*), and duration (*kāla*)"—is incorrect.
Because it has been stated [in Pāṇini 2.1.136] that "the designation *sāman* applies to the songs (*gītiṣu*)," it is therefore explained otherwise:
although the *stobhas* are not denotable by the word *sāman*, they are nevertheless extended [to them] by analogy.
How so? The *sāman* is an auxiliary to the syllables of the *ṛc*.
While it assists them, the *stobhas* assist that which is assisting by providing visible support.
Furthermore, if the *stobhas* were not to follow upon its extension (*atideśa*), the assistance rendered by them would also be lost.
Therefore, they are extended [to other cases]. And he also demonstrates their positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

The Commentary states: "He demonstrates the positive concomitance here as well by means of the *stobhas*: 'Wherever the words of the Rigveda verses cease, the *stobhas* follow along with the *gehamābhyas*.'"
The *stobhas* are indeed the hymns (*stomas*);
the *gehamas* are the musical tones (*svaras*).
Therefore, the *stobhas* are also prescribed.
The Section on Stobhas:
The Section on Stobhas; or rather, there is cessation because of the loss of purpose.
Commentary: By the word "or" (vā), the position is reversed.
There is the cessation of stobhas of that kind, such as "abhiṣarpati.
Indra, whose function is cold, is perceived in the remainder of the passage.
Therefore, praises of this kind should not be connected with it;
or rather, they may be a corroborative explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).
Commentary: That which was stated—that [praises] are connected with something else as in common worldly usage—must now be refuted.
It is said: Stobhas of this kind are indeed to be connected [with the deity].
For we do not perceive the form of Indra through direct perception.
And as for the statement in the supplementary portion of the text, that is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

Śā—Regarding the extension (*atideśa*) of the *sāman*, when there is a doubt as to whether there is an extension of the *stomas* or not, [the prima facie view is]: because the *stomas* are subordinate to the *sāmans*, they are not extended, just like the syllables of the *ṛc*.
Even though they are distinct, since they constitute parts of the *sāman* by delimiting the time of the singing, their extension follows from the extension of the *sāman* itself.
For the *sāmans* in the original source (*yoni*), by that very portion through which they manifest the syllables, perform a visible service to the praise (*stuti*).
However, by means of the portion consisting in the manifestation and accomplishment of the *stobha* syllables, they perform the praise as something conditioned (*upadhika*).

Therefore, if the *stobhas* were not extended [to the new context], there would be a deficiency due to the loss of the assistance provided by them, resulting from the omission of that portion of the melody (*gīti*) which is accomplished by them; thus, they must be extended.
But because the *ṛc* syllables are primary, they are not extended on account of the *sāman*.

Soma: If the extension (*atideśa*) of the *sāman* is by way of the assistance consisting in the manifestation of the syllables of the *ṛc*, then since the *stobhas* are not useful for the manifestation of the syllables of the *ṛc*, the question arises as to whether they too are extended; this constitutes the connection (*saṃgati*).

The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that although there is no extension [of the *stobhas*] because they are distinct and lack the status of being denoted by the words "Rathantara" and so forth, nevertheless, through the extension of the primary element—the chant (*gīti*)—which is known by the words "Rathantara" and so forth, there is an extension of those [stobhas] as well.

Although the portion of the *sāman* produced by *stobhas* does not assist the praise (*stuti*) through a visible means—namely, by manifesting the syllables of the *ṛc*—it was established in the *yoni* verse as assisting the praise through an invisible means (*adṛṣṭa*). If the portions of the *sāman* produced by *stobhas* were not extended to the two subsequent verses, the praise would suffer a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) due to lacking that invisible result to be accomplished by them. Therefore, since it is established that the *stobha*-related assistance to the praise exists in the form of an invisible effect for the purpose of manifesting the syllables of the *ṛc*, the extension of the *stobhas* themselves is also necessary, as they are the very instruments that bring about that [assistance].

The meaning of the Sūtra: Some teachers state that there is an exclusion of *stobhas* within the *ṛc* verses. [The commentary] says: "Stobhas are not indicated [as part of the text], because they are not sung like the syllables;
rather, they are indicated like the musical notes (*svara*) and so forth, because they are useful for the duration of the singing."
Bhāṭṭa: A certain portion of the *sāman* is based on the syllables of the *ṛk*, and another portion is based on the syllables of the *stobhas*.
In cases such as the two *prajāpati*s, it is based solely on the syllables of the *stobhas*.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether, when there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the *sāman*, there would also be an extension of the *stobhas*: since the purpose of manifesting the syllables of the *stobhas* is equal to the purpose of manifesting the syllables of the *ṛk*—just as the *sāman* manifests the syllables of the *ṛk*—there is no extension of the *stobhas* either, just as there is none for the *ṛcs* which are the primary elements, because they must conform to their subordinate qualities (*guṇa*).

Nor should it be argued that because *stobhas* are generally meaningless, they cannot be considered primary since they lack purpose in their connection as components of a *stotra*; for, by delimiting the duration of the melody (*gīti*), they constitute an integral part of the song (*gīta*), and thus when that [song] is extended [to another rite], the extension of the *stobhas* is logically established.

This is because, even though the syllables of the *stobhas* mentioned by the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) in passages such as "he approaches" (*abhiṣarpati*) are determined to form a single syntactical unit with the *ṛc*, they can independently function as the means of performing a *stotra* by way of praising the qualities [of the deity]; therefore, the primacy of the *ṛgveda* is established.

Even in the case of those *stobha* syllables such as *huṃ*, *phaṭ*, and so forth, which are devoid of meaning, their status as primary *ṛk*-syllables would arise from the doctrine of performance (*anuṣṭhānavāda*) through the medium of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), or else they would simply constitute the *stotra* by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors; thus, there is no occasion for postulating that they are auxiliary to the *sāman*.
Furthermore, there is no determining factor to decide whether the *sāman* itself has an unseen purpose or whether the *stobhas* do.

This is because the very presence of such a discrepancy—that one part of the *sāman* serves a visible purpose while another part serves an unseen purpose—serves as the determining factor [against such a postulation].

This being the case, in instances such as "one should praise with the *yajñāyajñiya*," the application (*viniyoga*) of the *sāmans*—both generally and specifically—is the sole regulator; thus, regarding that portion [of the *yajñāyajñiya*], the utterance of the *sāman* has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*). However, the *stobhas*, being devoid of semantic meaning, have only a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) insofar as they serve to delimit the duration of the singing. Otherwise, since the intended meaning of the entire *sāman* would be obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*) and other means, the injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) would result in futility.

Therefore, since the purpose is attained immediately through the force of the application (*viniyoga*), the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) which serves as the means is also postulated immediately in that very context, and not in the *stobhas*, because [in their case] there is a requirement for postulating a connection for the sake of completing the hymns (*stotra*) and so forth.

Consequently, since the *stobhas* and the like serve as the rhythmical basis (*kāla*) for the singing, when that [singing] is extended by analogy (*atideśa*), the extension is logically justified; thus, there is no occasion for the omission of that part.
Otherwise, it would be a different matter.

However, in the case of *stobhas* that possess meaning, since they serve as an adjunct to the hymn (*stotra*) and so forth by means of the very syllables of the *ṛc*, it appears that the melody alone constitutes their status as a constituent part.

For this very reason, in the case of meaningless *stobhas*, if an *ṛc* is present, the *sāman* has a substratum; in its absence, it serves solely for the sake of an invisible transcendental result (*adṛṣṭa*).
This concludes the section on *stobhas*.
Maṇḍana: "There is an extension (*atideśa*) of the *stoma*. Śaṅkara: "In that case, there is an extension of the *stobha*s.
In this regard, however, let the subsequent [verses] follow.
17. The Characteristics of Pride (stolalakṣaṇam)
"Furthermore, [the *sāman*] is more numerous and discolored, according to Jaimini, because of the word 'stoma'.
The Commentary says: Now, what is called a "stoma"? Its definition must be stated. It is said:
That which exceeds the syllables of the *ṛc* and is not of the same phonetic quality as them is called a *stoma*.
For it is in such cases that people in common usage apply the word *stoma*;
for example, when it is said, "Devadatta, while prattling excessively in the assembly, spoke with much *stoma*."
Having observed that which is more than what is stated in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and which is of a different color, they thus become blind.
Indeed, the purpose of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇakarma*) need not be stated;
for the very purpose of a defining characteristic is simply that the thing being defined shall come to be so defined.
For what purpose has both been stated in the Sūtra?
Is it not the case that one [of them] is already implied by the other, whether as "excessive" (*adhika*) or as "discolored" (*vivarṇa*)?
No, he says.
For there is indeed some increase, not a change of color;
as, for example, repetition [is required] when there is an increase in the *stoma*.
Or rather, [the increase] is by means of *āgama* (addition), because there is no scriptural statement regarding repetition (*abhyāsa*).

In the case of rituals characterized by increased *stomas*, such as the twenty-one-fold and nine-fold *atirātra*s, the filling of the higher number must be accomplished through the addition of *sāmans*, and not by the repetition of the original *sāmans*. This is because, from the perspective of the principles of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is no scriptural statement for repetition; that is, because there is an absence of an injunction, and thus no scriptural authority exists for it.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Furthermore, because number resides in distinct entities,

he states another reason for the conclusion that in rituals where the *stoma* is increased— such as the twenty-one-fold and nine-fold *atirātra*s— the filling of the higher number is achieved through the introduction (*āgama*) of non-archetypal (*aprākṛta*) *sāmans*.
Because numbers such as twenty-one and so forth are established through the inclusion of distinctness— that is, they are established by their very nature in distinct entities—
as seen in cases such as "eight jars," where the number is observed to reside in distinct things;
however, in the case of repetition, there would be no inclusion of distinctness.
Therefore, the completion of the number is by means of *āgama* (addition).
Because of the word "parāñc" (furthermore),

he states another reason for the final position (*siddhānta*) that in the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtu*) characterized by increased *stomas*, such as the *ekaviṃśa*, *navadaśa*, and *atirātra*, the completion of the additional number is by means of the addition of non-archetypal (*aprākṛta*) *sāmans*.
From the word *parāk*, as in the passage "They chant the Bahiṣpavamāna facing away (*parāk*)," the word *parāk* denotes that which is not repeated.
Just as in the case of "He recites the Sāmidhenī verses facing away," it is understood that they are not repeated;
therefore, the number is not completed by repetition.
And because there is no modification of the *utthāna*s.

Regarding the completion of the number in the *ekaviṃśati* and *navāyātayāma* sacrifices which have increased *stoma*s, the author states another reason for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that it is by means of the addition (*āgama*) of *sāman*s:
"Because there is no modification of the *utthāna*s" (*utthāvikārāt*), meaning because there is no alteration of the *utthāna*s, no repetition, and no recitation over again.
For it has been stated that repetition entails the fault of redundancy:
"Indeed, a redundancy is created in the sacrifice when one and the same thing is performed again.
Therefore, there should be no repetition.

"If it is argued that this is because there is no scriptural injunction [for repetition],"—this is the objection raised by the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) when the established view (*siddhāntin*) has stated: "In the case of those sacrifices where the *stoma* is increased, such as the twenty-one-fold and nine-fold *atirātra*s, the completion of the number is achieved through the introduction (*āgama*) of additional *sāman*s, because there is no scriptural injunction for repetition" (10.5.16).
The proponent then objects: "Since there is likewise no scriptural injunction for introduction, the completion of the number cannot be achieved through introduction."
If this is argued, [the response is:
"There would be a rule regarding the measure of those things enjoined by the purpose.
To this, he states the answer to the sūtra: "(10.5.16.20) 'Because there is no scriptural statement.'"

The *parimāṇaśāstra*—the injunction regarding the measurement of the *stoma* by means of the "twenty-onefold" and "twenty-sevenfold"—would serve as the provider for those [verses] whose number is enjoined by the purpose, which are obtained through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) based on the nature of the numerical injunction.
For the number stated in connection with the *sāmans* does not exist in its own form without that many [verses].
Therefore, the completion of the number occurs only through external addition (*āgama*).

Furthermore, the statement regarding "insertion" (āvāpa) is not tenable in the case of repetition. The proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) refutes the position of repetition on the grounds that it is untenable, asserting that in sacrifices where the *stoma* is increased—such as the twenty-one-fold and nine-fold *atirātra*s—the required number must be completed through the addition of new verses. He states: "There are indeed three [metres] for the sacrificial *stomas*: the *gāyatrī*, the *bṛhatī*, and the *anuṣṭubh*; for it is here that they insert [verses]. This statement concerning insertion would be inconsistent if repetition were accepted.
For in the case of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), there is no insertion at all;
therefore, it must be based on scriptural tradition (*āgama*).
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate another reason.
And because of the inherent capacity for the origination of *sāmans*.

Regarding the completion of the number in the *ekaviṃśati* and *navāyātayāma* sacrifices where the *stomas* are increased, the author states another reason for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the completion of the number is by means of the introduction (*āgama*) of *sāmans*, not by repetition (*abhyāsa*).

This is because, according to the *Sāma-śāstra*, the capacity for the origination of *sāmans* exists; therefore, the completion of the number is achieved solely through introduction and not through repetition.
And it is said: "Ten thousand and fourteen hundred Sāmans—those thousands of Sāmans which the chanters of the Sāman sing;
this [collection] consists of one hundred and eighty Pāvamānas and four hundred [others]."
"Those which the Sāma-singers sing as the twenty-seven [Sāmans] dedicated to Indra"—
if the completion of this number were achieved through repetition, the originative injunction (*utpatti*) of these Sāmans would be rendered purposeless.
Therefore, the completion is by means of [additional] arrivals.
If it is argued that this applies even to the *dhurya* [stotras]:
if there were no repetition of the *sāmans* in the sacrifices (*ṛtus*) characterized by increased *stomas*, then there would likewise be no repetition of the *sāmans* in the *dhurya* stotras as well.
If that were the case, it would contradict the previously stated rule regarding the repetition of the *dhuryas* (10.5.13.11).
If the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) should say:
"No, because it is a property of repetition;

for if there were no repetition of the Sāmans in the twenty-one-night sacrifices where the Stomas are increased, it would not exist even in the *dhurya* [verses]," the proponent's doubt is answered by the established conclusion (siddhāntin).
There is no contradiction among them regarding the *dhuri* verses; however, in the matter of the *stoma*, there is a distinction in the *stoma* distribution.
Because of the statement, "They chant the *dhurs* repeatedly; he worships the *dhurs* repeatedly," repetition is their inherent property.
Therefore, by virtue of that statement, they are repeated.
However, in the case of sacrifices characterized by increased *stomas*, there is no such statement regarding repetition.

Therefore, the established conclusion is that the completion of the number is achieved through scripture alone, not through repetition. Regarding the increase of the *stoma* in the *bahiṣpavamāna*, additional verses should be inserted before the *paryāsa*; for this is seen in the case of the *dvādaśāha*.
In the *agniṣṭoma*, the *bahiṣpavamāna* consists of the *trivṛt* *stoma*, which is composed of nine verses.

"One should sacrifice for one desiring offspring with the twenty-one-fold *atirātra*; for one desiring vigor with the twenty-seven-fold; for one desiring stability with the thirty-three-fold"—thus are the sacrifices with increased *stomas* recited.

And it will be stated later (10.5.12–16) that the fulfillment of the increased number is by means of the arrival of additional *ṛks*. In this regard, there arises the inquiry: should those arrived *ṛks* be inserted at the end, or should they be inserted before the *paryāsa*? Regarding this, he states the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) view.
When there is an increase in the *stomas* among the twenty-one-fold chants, the additional *ṛc*-verses in the *bahiṣpavamāna* stotra should be placed before the *paryāsa*,
not at the end; for it is indeed observed thus in the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice.
For it is stated therein: "There are two triplets (ṛcas) consisting of the *stotriya* and the *anurūpa*; there are triplets containing the word *vṛṣan*; the final triplet is the *paryāsa*.

On the second day of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), after reciting the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* triplets belonging to the daily portion (*bāḍahika*), new triplets containing the word *vṛṣan* are recited;
then the final *paryāsa* is recited.
Since their placement before the *paryāsa* is observed in the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), it ought to be the same in the archetype (*prakṛti*) as well.
Furthermore, *paryāsa* is a term for the end.
In the preceding sūtra, it was stated "before the *paryāsa*"; regarding what this *paryāsa* is, it is explained by the word *paryāsa* itself through the following sūtra.
In common usage, the term *paryāsa* is a designation for that which is at the end or the limit,
as in "the edge of a field" (*kṣetraparyāsa*) or "the edge of a river" (*nadīparyāsa*).
Or rather, it is said to be at the end.

Regarding the passage: "One desiring offspring should sacrifice with the twenty-one-fold *atirātra*; one desiring vigor with the twenty-seven-fold; one desiring stability with the thirty-three-fold," when there is an increase in the *stomas* and the number is completed through the addition of [hymns], the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—established by the rule that the newly introduced *tṛcas* are to be inserted before the *paryāsa*—is set aside.
By the word "or" (*vā*), the prima facie view is excluded. The insertion of the newly introduced [hymns] is not before the *paryāsa*, but rather at the end.
Their placement is precisely in the locus of perversion.
That has been stated there;
the reasoning that establishes it was previously mentioned as "But at the end, Bādarāyaṇa" (Sūtra 5.1.19).
Therefore, the insertion of the guest-hymns occurs at the end.
However, according to the scriptural statement, this takes place on the twelfth day.

In the case of the formulas "the twenty-first Atirātra," "the twenty-nine-fold Atirātra," and "the thirty-three-fold Atirātra," when there is an increase in the Stomas, the completion of the number in the Bahiṣpavamāna will occur through the addition of three-verse hymns (tṛcas).

Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the guest *ṛc*-verses should be inserted before the *paryāsa* triplet, the example of the *vṛṣaṇvat* triplets in the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) was cited in the sūtra:
"In the case of the *stomabhṛt* [verses]. Thereupon, the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) refutes that example by pointing out its dissimilarity.
It is true that, in the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), on the second day of the daily rites (*bāḍahika*), the insertion of the *vṛṣaṇvat* triplets occurs before the *paryāsa*;
however, this is due to the scriptural statement, "The *vṛṣaṇvat* triplets [are used]; the final triplet is the *paryāsa*," and not by logical necessity (*nyāya*).

However, regarding the *ekaviṃśaty-atirātra* sacrifice, since there is no explicit scriptural statement (*vacana*) regarding its nature, the determination must be made through logical reasoning (*nyāya*).
And the principle is that "accessory elements (*āgantūnām*) are placed at the end," as stated in the sūtra: "Or rather, they are at the end, for so it is said.
Furthermore, this [sacrifice] is not a modification (*vikāra*) of that [standard *atirātra*].
This is a sūtra representing the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Although in the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) the triplets beginning with *vṛṣaṇvat* occur before the *paryāsa*, the twenty-one-night sacrifice and others are not modifications of that [twelve-day sacrifice], nor are they modifications of the twelve-day sacrifice itself. Therefore, the triplets brought in for the purpose of completing the number should occur only at the end.
"Paryāsa" is the designation for the final triplet (tṛca).
Even when it is modified, because it is an original (apūrva) element,
even in that modification, the insertion of the *vṛṣaṇvat* verses and the additional (*atirikta*) verses occurs only at the end of the *ahīna* and *satra* sacrifices, not before the *paryāsa*.

Because it is unprecedented (*apūrva*), its position has not been established; for those [verses] containing the word *vṛṣan*, their position prior to the *paryāsa* has been determined by the order of recitation. However, since there is no established position for those [verses] containing the word *vṛṣan* that are designated as *vihāna*, it is logical that they should be inserted at the very end.

Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that when there is an increase in the *stoma* during the *bahiṣpavamāna*, the additional (*āgantūnām*) triplets (*tṛca*) must be inserted at the very end.

This is because the word "triple" (*trivṛt*) is seen elsewhere in the context of the *stoma*, as in the expression "the *bahiṣpavamāna* is triple" (*trivṛd bahiṣpavamānaḥ*), where its application to the *stoma* is evident. [Mīmāṃsākośa 552; Mīmāṃsākośa 4410:
regarding women in the context of the *stoma*].
[The word *stoma*] is thus delimited.

Likewise, in the case of "the *iṣṭi* sacrifice is performed with *triṣṭubh* [verses]," that same word, when uttered, would cause that very [number] to be brought to mind through inference by virtue of its connection.

Bhāṣya 10.6.7.23. The two words *stoma*—as in "one should cause one desiring progeny to sacrifice with the twenty-one-fold *atirātra*" and so forth—will be explained in the tenth [book] as the completion of a number according to scripture (*āgama*).

Su. p. 809: Because the word *stoma* transcends its common worldly usage as a mere collection and denotes a collection of *stotrīyā* verses due to its established usage in the Vedas, the Vedic grammarians (*vedayāśika*), and grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).
Su. p. 217: *stauti* and *śaṃsati*.
