Here, although these two words, *stauti* and *śaṃsati*, have the same meaning of "praising," their respective objects are fixed.

The term *stauti* (he praises) is used for mantra-passages that are sung, while the term *śaṃsati* (he recites) is used for those that are not sung. For example: "He recites the *prauga*," "He recites the *niṣkevalya*";
and "They praise with the *ājya* [stotras]," "They praise with the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]."
Bhāṣya 7.2.1:
"Woman" (strī) is a particular individual.
Bhāṣya 9.1.9.13: These—woman, man, and neuter—are indeed specific types of substances (dravyaviśeṣa).
3|1| 6|12: A woman is not equal to a man.
The sacrificer is a learned man; the wife is a woman who is both ignorant and unlearned. 6|12|14: [Regarding] women.
For women are connected with buying and selling;

they are sold by the father and purchased by the husband. Because they have been sold, [the claim that] there is no property belonging to the father does not hold true for a woman who is without wealth.
For she possesses property; women are wise regarding wealth; and because, according to the prima facie view, the husband's riches belong to her by virtue of being his wife.
And this is not the case that a woman is destitute of wealth; for she possesses property, and through that property,
she attains a state of ownership.
Thus, at the time of giving her away, an agreement is made: "She must not transgress in matters of dharma, artha, or kāma.

Furthermore, they do not approve of a sale that contradicts the Śruti, as recorded in the Smṛti: "The wife has no power over the property acquired through marriage" (this being the established conclusion).
It is established that both husband and wife are "possessors" (svavantau).

6.1.4.17: Because a woman lacks the capacity for Vedic study, she is unable to perform sacrificial acts such as the *upasthāna* (prayer) and *anumantraṇa* (recitation); these must be performed by the man alone. However, the wife must perform whatever is specifically prescribed for her, such as "the wife gazes at the clarified butter (*ājya*)" and "you have been [established] in celibacy (*brahmacarya*)," and so forth.

Vi., Bhā. 6|1|6|24: This prohibition of women’s study pertains to a subject already established by a mandatory injunction; it is a prohibition intended for human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), and such a human purpose must be inferred. Bāla., p. 31–32: Women also possess the entitlement to perform ritual acts, because in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," the masculine gender—being a property of the subject (*uddeśya*)—is not intended to be significant, just as the singular number is not.

VI. 6.1.3. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is the opinion of Bādarāyaṇa that women also have the right (*adhikāra*) to perform sacrifices during their fertile seasons (*ṛtu*). The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is the opinion of Aitiśāyana that they have no such right.
Bhāṣya 6.1.16–16, 19–21: Women also have the right to perform sacrifices during their fertile seasons.
6|1|16–16, 19–21. Regarding this, the section (adhikāra) found at Mīko., p. 288, under the heading "Also for a woman in the seasonal rites" (ṛtuṣu striyā api), should be consulted.
Although a woman has the right to perform ritual acts, she does not have independent authority;
for the husband and wife possess joint authority.

By virtue of their joint entitlement (*sahādhikāratva*), the very knowledge possessed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) effects the accomplishment of the rite for the wife as well. Regarding the inquiry as to whether or not a woman possesses property (*dravyavattā*), this should be consulted in the *Mīmāṃsā-kośa*, page 288, under the section on entitlement (*adhikāra*) titled "The woman also has entitlement to the seasonal sacrifices" (*ṛtuṣu striyā api*). Whatever property a woman has acquired—whether through receiving food and service or through spinning and other such means—that too belongs to him to whom she herself belongs.
The Sthapati-isti does not effect the consecration of the sacrificial post (sthāṇu).
Because there is no specific statement regarding its being established [in that manner].
Thus (6.8.3.20–21). Parimala 3.4.1.14–42 (Brahma Sūtra).

Oṃ. Regarding the Sthapati-iṣṭi: the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) should be employed as it is in the case of the Prayāja offerings; furthermore, it may be dispensed with because of its specific purpose.
Having prescribed the Raudrī sacrifice, it is enjoined: "One should cause the Niṣāda-Sthapati to sacrifice with this.
This Sthapati-iṣṭi—the sacrifice of the Niṣāda-Sthapati—should employ the establishment of the sacred fires.

Having performed the *ādhāna* (establishment of the sacred fires) for the purpose of becoming a *sthapati* (architect or chief), one should perform the *iṣṭi* (sacrificial offering) in the fires consecrated by that *ādhāna*.
For without the *ādhāna*, the acquisition of consecrated fires is not possible.
Just as one employs the *prayāja* offerings through the force of the injunction (*codaka*), so too should one employ the *ādhāna*.

And because the *agnyādheya* (the laying of the fires) is for that purpose—since it is employed solely for the sake of the *iṣṭi*—then upon the completion of the *iṣṭi*, the *ādhāna* (the act of laying) would also be completed and concluded. The meaning is that after having laid the fires and performed the *iṣṭi*, the fires are to be relinquished by the *sthapati*. Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the *sthapatīṣṭi* takes place when the fires have been consecrated.
Alternatively, it may take place in the worldly fire (*laukika-agni*), because the act of laying the fires (*ādhāna*) is not subsidiary to all [rituals].

Regarding the *Niṣādasthapatīṣṭi*: the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—established by the sūtra—is that it should take place in fires consecrated by the *ādhāna*. Rejecting this with the word "fire" (*agni*), the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*):
the *Sthapatīṣṭi* should take place in the worldly fire, not in one that has been consecrated.

Because the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is not a universal requirement for all, and because there is an absence of knowledge regarding sacrifices performed by every type of person— since the scriptural injunctions on the origin of the *ādhāna* state that it is to be performed by those of the three higher castes (*traivaṇika*), thereby implying they alone possess the requisite knowledge of sacrifice— and because the *niṣādasthapati* (the chief of the Niṣādas) does not belong to these three castes and thus lacks the entitlement to perform the *ādhāna*, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *sthapati-iṣṭi* is to be performed using only ordinary, worldly fires (*laukika-agni*). Ke.

Regarding the *Sthapati-iṣṭi*: its performance is to be carried out in worldly fires and so forth. (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2389). One should consult the section titled "The *Niṣādasthapati-iṣṭi* in worldly fires" (*mīko pṛ. 2389 'niṣādasthapatīṣṭiḥ laukike'gniṣu'*). The maxim of the heavy stick for an old man (*sthaviralagudhanyāya*): Just as a very heavy stick held by an old man does not fall from its place, this maxim applies where there is no falling away from the intended mark. (*Sāhasī*, 502).
"Oṃ. But in the case of the *sthāṇu*, because it is merely a location, non-cessation [of the ritual] is understood.
[The text] 'He offers the *sthāṇvāhuti* on the *sthāṇu*' is heard in the context of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
*Sthāṇu* refers to the remaining portion of the tree once the sacrificial post has been cut."
In that context, there is the *ājyāhuti* (clarified butter offering), which is the *sthāṇvāhuti*.
"Sthāṇu" is stated merely as the location, serving simply as the locus for the oblation.
And thus, because it is merely a location, it is understood that the completion of the offering does not occur within the sacrificial post itself.
There is no cessation [of the rite]. Rather, when there is a *khalevālī* post in the *Sādyaska* sacrifice, the *sthāṇvāhuti* (offering to the stump) must be performed upon any stump whatsoever.
This ritual act is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*).
Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
However, because it is subsidiary (*śeṣa*), it is understood as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of that [sacrificial post].

Regarding the question—whether the *sthāṇv-āhuti* (the oblation at the stump) should be performed for the sacrificial post in the *Sādyaska* sacrifice, and whether that oblation is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakārikā*) or a consecration of the post—the prima facie view is that the *sthāṇv-āhuti* is a remote auxiliary and, like in the case of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, it should be performed in the *Sādyaska* as well. The word "however" (*api vā*) is used to refute this prima facie view.

Regarding the *sthāṇvāhuti* (offering at the stump): in the case of the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-paśu*), it is understood as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of that [stump]; specifically, it is perceived as a consecration of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), because the stump is a subordinate part (*śeṣa*) and is thus a subordinate part of the sacrificial post.
Since the stump serves as the substratum for the offering, it functions as a consecration of the sacrificial post. Therefore, the *sthāṇvāhuti* is a consecratory act.

And because that entire [sacrifice] is absent in the *sādyaska*, there is no *sthāṇvāhuti* either; such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). And the designation (*samākhyāna*) is likewise. Just as in the case of the intermediate context of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the designation of the oblation as "the *sthāṇvāhuti*" indicates that the oblation serves the purpose of consecrating the sacrificial post.
And consequently, there is the *sthāṇvāhuti* (the offering to the stump): it is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) by means of the stump.

And since, in the *sādyaska* sacrifice, the possibility of the *khalevālī* (the threshing-block) being treated as a sacrificial post has been stated, the *sthāṇvāhuti* applies there as well; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
And the wording of the mantra is likewise [indicative].

"Therefore, O divine Lord of the Forest, grow forth with a hundred branches"—this mantra, addressed to the sacrificial post (*sthāṇu*) as if it were the post itself, indicates that "you, who have been cut by me, grow forth in many ways from this place of felling.
Just like the name [of the rite], this wording of the mantra makes it known that the *sthāṇv-āhuti* (the offering to the stump) is a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that this [offering] should not be performed for the *khalevālī* used as a sacrificial post in the *Sādyaska* sacrifice.
In the sūtra "But [the offering] on the stump, because it is merely a place" (10.1.16.10–13), the offering on the stump (*sthāṇvāhuti*) is to be performed upon the threshing-post (*khalevālī*);
this is the principle of the offering on the stump (*sthāṇvāhutinyāya*).

Having raised the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that [the *sthāṇvāhuti*] is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakārin*) because it consists in the felling of a post already employed for its purpose, or rather, the felling of a stump not so employed, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached: "This stump from which the post was cut must not be treated [as waste], for it serves the purpose of consecrating the post by means of that very consecration.
(Bāla, p. 83).
This is the *sthāṇvāhuti* in the context of the *abhīṣomīya* animal sacrifice.

Bhāṣya 10.1.6.10: *Sthāṇvāhuti* (the oblation for the stump). When the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) has been cut, the remaining tree-root is the "stump" (*sthāṇu*); the oblation offered there is the *sthāṇvāhuti*. [The rule states:
"He offers the oblation on the cutting-block (*āvraścana*) with the mantra: 'O Lord of the Forest, grow forth with a hundred branches!'"
VI. 10.1.16, the principle of the oblation to the tree-stump (sthāṇvāhutinyāya): in the Sādyaska sacrifice, the oblation to the tree-stump is not to be performed.
Regarding the *sthāṇu* (the wooden post), however, because it is merely a location, its non-performance [of the offering] is understood.
The Bhāṣya states: In that very *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "He offers the *sthāṇvāhuti* (offering at the post) upon the post.
Consequently, in the *sādyaska* sacrifice, this same point arises: does the *sthāṇvāhuti* become applicable, or should it be performed in the *sādyaska*, or not?

In this regard, first of all, this must be examined: Is the *sthāṇvāhuti* (the offering at the stump) an act that provides indirect assistance (*ārādupakāraka*), or is it a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)?

If it is an act providing indirect assistance, then it should be performed; but if it is a refinement of the post, it should be omitted. How would it be an act providing indirect assistance, and how would it be a refinement of the post? If the connection is made such that "the *sthāṇvāhuti* is to be performed for the purpose of cutting the post," then it is a refinement of the post.

Now, if the injunction "one should cut the sacrificial post" is not connected with the primary context, then it is a remotely contributory act (*ārādupakāraka-karman*). What, then, is the prima facie view? It is that it is a remotely contributory act;
for this is understood to be the purpose of the ritual action.
For indeed, that which has ceased to exist is no longer a functional object.

Moreover, an oblation connected to a post-stump whose purpose has already been fulfilled—how could it benefit the sacrificial post? For an action performed upon something connected [to an object] would benefit that very object;
however, the stump is distinct from the post.

Moreover, that *yūpāhuti* (post-offering) of mine will take place at the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice, provided it were an act of direct assistance (*ārādupakāraka-karma*). For in that case, no repetition would be required, as it would not be heard [elsewhere].
Furthermore, by an unqualified statement, the *sthāṇvāhuti* (offering on the stump) is heard;
and that would have to be restricted by the context (*prakaraṇa*) to the specific stump from which the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) was cut.
Therefore, the *sthāṇvāhuti* is an auxiliary act (*upakāraka-karma*); it should be performed in the *sādyaska* sacrifice as well, for the sake of favoring the extended injunction (*codaka*).
Alternatively, because it is a residual element (*śeṣabhūta*), it is understood as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of that [residue].
Bhāṣya: This being the position reached, we reply as follows.
The word "api vā" (or rather) serves to exclude the alternative view.
It is understood that this is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Why? Because of the specific context (*prakaraṇa-viśeṣāt*); it is understood that the *sthāṇvāhuti* (oblation at the stump) is prescribed for one who has cut down the sacrificial post.
For he who thinks that by an unqualified statement it is enjoined merely for the location of the sacrificial post (*sthāṇu*) must assume a result [for that act].

He who also thinks that, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it becomes a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) to the *Āgneyī* offering—even so, the general context is sublated by the specific context.

Furthermore, the sacrificial post is a subsidiary part of the ritual because it serves a purpose; therefore, if the *Aṣṭakā* and other rites were connected with it as remote auxiliaries, they would be rendered as having no assumed purpose.

Therefore, it is set aside by the principle of what is well-known (*prasiddhi-nyāya*), as in the case of "one with tears on his ears. Furthermore, even when the post has served its purpose and the stump has ceased to be a post, because one considers it "this is the post-related [stump]," the *sthāṇv-āhuti* (stump-oblation) performed there becomes connected to the post; thus, it is performed at the time of the felling.

Just as for a garland that was worn on the head, once it has been removed from the head, a consecration such as placing it in a pure location must be performed, considering it to be "belonging to Devadatta";
so too is the case with the *sthāṇv-āhuti*.
And in the context of the *ekādaśinī*, since the immediate proximity is not intended to be significant when the oblations are to be enjoined along with the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*).
Therefore, the position that it is a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is indeed superior.
And the designation is likewise [in favor of this].
The Commentary states: "The designation 'Sthāṇvāhuti' (the Oblation for the Post) applies to an oblation that has the sacrificial post (*sthāṇu*) as its primary element."
How so? This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The genitive case is used for the object (*karman*), and the object is that which is most desired to be reached (*īpsitatama*).

The seventh-case compound (*saptamī-samāsa*) is not to be accepted here on the grounds that it would be a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-pakṣa*). Rather, in the case of *duḥ-sthāṇvāhutiḥ*, this is a sixth-case compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), because a seventh-case compound is impossible.
Why? Because a word ending in the seventh case forms a compound with words such as *śauṇḍa* and others (according to Pāṇini 2.1.40: *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ*).
Objection: But surely the compound will be formed by Pāṇini 2.1.44, "saṃjñāyām. Response: It is said: in that case, the suffix *aluk* would apply, as for example in the word *aravītilakāḥ*.
This is not so; that [suffix] is prescribed after a word ending in a consonant or a vowel. And this [word] ends in the vowel *u*.
Therefore, it is simply *lup*.
If that is so, then the restriction is otherwise:
for a compound is indeed connected with its meaning.
In a locative compound (saptamī-samāsa), the indication has the locus as its primary meaning;
therein, the oblation is an indirect auxiliary (ārādupakārikā).
In a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa), the relationship is the primary meaning.
In that context, the oblation (*āhuti*) is a consecration (*saṃskāra*).

There is a certain application of a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) that has been separated from its [original] stump (*sthāṇu*), by which it attains the status of being something to be consecrated (*saṃskāryatva*).
Furthermore, among the two types of auxiliaries—those that assist indirectly (*ārādupakāraka*) and those that are integral to the substance (*sāmavāyika*)—the latter is more significant.
[Objection: But surely [it] would be understood.
Precisely for this reason, since it would be of unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha) regardless of which particular post (*sthāṇu*) it refers to, what here is the greater weight? It is said in reply:

Since it is already established as an instrument (*karaṇa*), even the *sthāṇvāhuti*—occurring in the seventh month—is indeed for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*); however, its connection as an inherent relation (*samavāya-sambandha*) is already established. It is certainly not a name (*nāmadheya*).
Furthermore, the relationship of the word *āhuti* with the *śauṇḍādi* group cannot be assumed as being formed by the suffix *ka*.

In that case, since there is no single recitation (*ekapāṭha*) within the context (*prakaraṇa*), the application of the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) would be untenable; even if it were so, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyatā*) regarding the technical name (*saṃjñā*).
For that [result] is possible even by means of the injunction for the seventh month;
nor does the wording of the mantra at that time imply the same.

There is no risk of an *aluk* compound here—as in the case of *aravindatilakāḥ*—because the Bhāṣya states that it occurs only when preceded by a consonant (*hal*) or the word *adanta*. From this also we see that it is a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*), since...
Because there is no possibility of that [suffix] occurring at the end of a word ending in *u* by means of this *taddhita* suffix, it is the "place" (*sthāna*).
It is the place.
Regarding the beginning of the *mantra* and so forth:

since even proximity (*saṃnidhi*)—such as that of the sacrifice involving rice or barley arising from a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*)—would result in [being considered] sequence (*krama*), it is proper [to specify] the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).

The first qualification is for the purpose of excluding the possibility of "position" (*sthāna*) being established between the subordinate sentence-meaning (*pradhānavākyārtha*) and the sentence-meaning of the *prajāyājña*.

They say that because the proximity of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha-saṃnidhi*) has already been stated, there is no inclusion of [the injunction] as it exists at the stage of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-daśā*). (Bhāṭṭa 3.1.6)

In this context, because the meaning of the *upahoma* sentence consists of an activity (*vyāpāra*), it is fit for connection as a procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Otherwise, even the expectancy for a procedure to be produced would not result in such a connection, as that would lead to an infinite regress. Furthermore, "proximity" (*saṃnidhi*) cannot be defined merely as proximity in the text or proximity according to the order of recitation; for even though there exists proximity between the rice-offering (*vrīhi-yāga*) and others, or proximity between the principal sentence-meaning and sentences concerning offspring (*prajādi*), the relationship of subsidiary and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) can still be sublated by the maxim "principal [matters] prevail over designations" (*pradhānaṃ vyapadeśā bhavanti*). Moreover, since that would render the two qualifying terms ["removing that" (*tadāraka*)] redundant, this [definition of proximity] is rejected.
Some, however, say that "identity of place" (*deśasāmānya*) means the occurrence in a place characterized by the transposition of the primary [rite].

Therefore, they argue that there is no room for the following objection: "If one intends to express concomitance with the *prāyaṇīya* and other rites by the word 'sāmānya,' then cases of non-different location are included; if one intends to express non-difference, then inclusion occurs because of similarity of location.

This is incorrect, because the qualification of the transposition of the primary rite is not intended in the case of the location; for even in the location of the *upahoma*s, there is a transposition of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* rites, as established by Smṛti and other authorities.
In some cases, because the subordinate offerings (*upahoma*) exist, there is a dependence upon their being constituent parts (*aṅga*) of that [main rite].

Nor is "being scriptural" (*śāstrīyatva*) a qualification for the mental recollection (*viparivṛtti*); therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply, since they are produced by the recollection of the scriptural injunctions for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
This is because even the mental recollection of the scripturally enjoined New and Full Moon sacrifices is possible therein.

Nor can it be argued that there is no fault because the occurrence in a specific location characterized by the transposition of the principal (*pradhāna*) does not serve as its own regulator, since the Upahoma offerings lack the status of being the principal in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. For if one were to include "not being the principal"— defined as not being the specifier of subsidiarity— within the very structure of the sequence (*krama*) that generates the knowledge of subsidiarity, it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Therefore, even when incomplete, the application based on proximity (*sādeśya*) is more powerful.
Furthermore, this twofold sequence (*krama*) is an applicator (*viniyojaka*) both through mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*) and through one-sided expectancy (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*); thus, it is manifold.

Among these, when the primary rite is a modification (*vikṛti*), application by proximity of performance (*anuṣṭhānasādeśya*) occurs through one-sided expectancy, as in the case of the proximity of performance of the *dharmedhya* and *līyā* rites for the animal sacrifice; for since the primary rite has its requirements already satisfied (*anirākāṅkṣatayā*) by the established auxiliaries (*klṛptopakāraka*), it lacks expectancy.

However, when the primary act takes the form of a *davihoma* (offering with a ladle) or similar rites, which do not determine their own *prakṛti*, then the application of the rule of proximity in performance (*anuṣṭhānasādeśya*) occurs through the mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*) of both elements. Likewise, for mantras recited in the order of the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the *aindrāgna*, their status as its subsidiaries arises from their position in the sequence, assisted by the expectancy of one of the two factors.

Although, in the case of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras, the sequential reading serves only to indicate their status as means for accomplishing a specific *apūrva*—since they are applied by virtue of their indicative power (*liṅga*) and not by the sequential reading itself—nevertheless, in the case of mantras such as those used for *japa* which are applied by *liṅga* and are read in sequence within a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it must be sought that the sequential reading itself acts as the applicator (*viniyojaka*) in conjunction with one of the two mutual requirements (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*).

For this very reason, the sequential reading of mantras for *japa* and so forth that constitute parts of the *davihoma* and other rites is cited as an example where the sequential reading acts as the applicator through the requirement of both [the mantra and the rite].

Thus, the recitation in proximity (*saṃnidhi-pāṭha*) within the *Upahomīya* section, when assisted by the expectancy of one of the two, serves as an example of that. Regarding the *śundhana-mantra*, its application (*viniyoga*) in the cleansing of the *sāṃnāyya* vessels occurs through indicative power (*liṅga*) alone; therefore, although its recitation in proximity to the *sāṃnāyya* is not the direct means of application, it functions as a prompter for the application because it indicates its status as a means for a specific *apūrva*. This is thus an example of proximity assisted by the mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*) of both.
Indeed, no other example is possible.

This is because the *dārśapaurṇamāsika* auxiliary (*dārupakāra*), which is recited in proximity to the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*) that does not itself possess a *prakṛti*, is subject to application by way of *prakaraṇa* (context).

Here, it is clear that mere *krama* (sequence), even when assisted by one-sided expectancy (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*), is weaker than *prakaraṇa*, since it only suggests the requirement for a procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

Furthermore, both *sthāna* (position) and *samākhyā* (name), even when assisted by mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*) and recitation according to sequence, are weaker than *prakaraṇa*, which is constituted by the proximity of the injunction (*vidhi-saṃnidhi*).
Thus, because proximity (*saṃnidhi*)—even when assisted by the context (*prakaraṇa*) that provides the application—is inherently incapable of effecting application, it is weak.

Furthermore, because *krama* (order) is weaker than *prakaraṇa*, it has been stated in the section on the relative strength of authorities (*balābalādhikāra*) that, although acts such as gambling (*videvana*) are recited in proximity to the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice—which is part of the *rājasūya* complex of *iṣṭi*, *paśu*, and *soma* sacrifices—their application is not restricted to the *abhiṣecanīya* alone; rather, due to the context of the *rājasūya* as a whole, they apply to the entire *rājasūya*. This is because their recitation in proximity is assisted by the mutual requirement (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*) between the two.

Furthermore, even in the case of the *rājasūya*, since it consists of a collection of modified (*vikṛti*) rites and is thus satisfied by the archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries alone, there would be no possibility of a context (*prakaraṇa*). This is because, although the individual ultimate transcendental results (*paramāpūrva*) produced by each [sacrifice] are satisfied by the archetypal subsidiaries, the ultimate result of all the sacrifices taken together remains expectant; and since the context is established through the fulfillment of that expectation by generating the applicability of the archetypal subsidiaries toward each of those individual ultimate results conducive to it, the presence of context is logically justified. Nor is there a lack of evidence for an ultimate result produced by all the sacrifices collectively, for the scriptural hearing of the combined means in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* finds its place in a collective transcendental result.

This is because, in that context, the authority for [the performance] rests solely on the scriptural statement regarding the means (sādhanatā) delimited by the nature of the *rājasūya*—which consists of the entire collection of sacrifices—just as [the authority for subsidiary acts] rests on specific locations and so forth.

Even if that [direct statement] were not accepted, the context (*prakaraṇa*) is established through the following: from the *pavitra* sacrifice up to the *kṣatrasya dhṛti*, among the injunctions for the subsidiaries, there is an introduction with "He purifies these for the sake of the *rājasūya*" and a conclusion with "By the *rājasūya*, he attains a full lifespan. Thus, by the declaration of the verbal requirement (*vācanikākāṅkṣāsaṃdeśa*), the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for all [subsidiaries] is stimulated in the form of the *rājasūya*, and therefore the context is logically consistent.
In this manner, the wise should infer, as far as possible, examples of the relative strength and weakness of other types of sequence as well.
Thus concludes the determination of position (*sthāna*).
Murāri, pp. 1184–1188.
Position (*sthāna*) is more powerful than name (*samākhyā*).

The mantra for purification (*śundhana-mantra*) belongs to the vessels of the *sāṃnāyya* offering because of its proximity in the text, and not to the vessels of the *puroḍāśa* cake because of the name "Pauroḍāśika. According to the Mīmāṃsā, the preparation of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice comes first by virtue of position; after that follows that of the *dakṣa*, and after that that of the *anubandhya*. This is because, in the absence of any other restrictive factor, the natural order of sequence established in the archetype (*prakṛti*) is accepted as the regulating principle.
Bhāṭṭa 5.1.6:
"On account of connection with place and origin.

5.1.6.13: In the sacrifice named Sādhama, it is heard in the scriptural text, "One sacrifices the animals together," that there is a simultaneous performance of the three at the time of the Savanīya animal.

Nevertheless, regarding the inquiry as to whether the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice should be performed first or the *savanīya*, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) maintains that the *agnīṣomīya* alone should be performed first because it is so established in the archetype (*prakṛti*). To this, the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*):

the *savanīya* animal sacrifice alone deserves to be performed first, because of its position [in the ritual sequence]; for, by virtue of the departure following the drawing of the *āśvina* cup, it is that very sacrifice which presents itself first.

"Having drawn the Āśvina cup and having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-twisted rope, one dedicates the Savanīya animal to Agni"—since this is the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), the Savanīya is connected with that specific time.
Therefore, the sequence is: first the Agniṣomīya, then the Anubandhya;
this is the sequence of position (*sthānakrama*).
From this position, the Savanīya animal itself must be sacrificed first.

In the Sāmakrama [text], it says, "He sacrifices the animals together"; thus, when the sacrifice of the animals is to be performed at the place of the Savanīya, the sequence is that the Savanīya, the Agnīṣomīya, and the Anūbandhya [are to follow].

Bhāṣya 5.1.6.13, Section 2: Although *prakaraṇa* (context) is stronger than *sthāna* (position), nevertheless, according to the principle of the *upāṃśuyāja-anumantraṇa*, it is understood that here *krama* (order) supported by *liṅga* (indicative power) is indeed more powerful. Vārttika 3.6.125: Furthermore, this is the definition of *sthāna*: namely, the connection of ritual details (*dharmas*) with the primary act (*pradhāna*), which has arisen through its own expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*), regarding the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāva*). (Mīmāṃsākośa 553).
3|6|125. Section on the Examination of Conflict and Non-conflict of Position with Preceding Elements.

Bhāṣya 3|6|17 to 3|7|7. The property of the first position and of that which arises [therein] is the threefold effort in the *sāmidhenī* verses. This is the section concerning the order of position (*sthānakrama*).
In the Atirātra sacrifice, for those [somas] characterized by the Triṇava and other Stomas, the Ṛks are to be employed strictly according to the order of the Kāṇḍas.
On account of place, arising, and connection.

(5.1.6.13) The commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the section reads: "One desiring offspring should sacrifice with an Atirātra consisting of twenty-one [stotras]; one desiring vigor with those of twenty-seven; one desiring stability with those of thirty-three," and so forth. This is what is heard in the scripture.
In that regard, it will be stated that "the completion of the number is by means of insertion" (10.5.8.27).

When such an insertion is being performed, should all the verses be inserted without a fixed order, or according to the sequence of the *kāṇḍas*? What is the prima facie view? That there is no fixed order.

Why? Because in the Atirātra sacrifice, when the Triṇava and other stomas are increased, these [verses] are obtained. In that case, there is no sequential order of recitation for those verses as they are being obtained.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
Since there is a specific place for their inclusion, they are restricted here to that very spot.
Those which were previously recited must be employed first;
for this is the observed purpose of sequential order.

Since that which is the subsequent expansion is also indeed intended to be performed, there arises the view that this constitutes a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*): because these [mantras] are obtained through the method of conjunction (*yogapathena*) with the *atirātra* sacrifice by means of words such as "triṇava" and so forth, the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is not intended to be significant.

[Dvaidhasūtra-bhāṣya: Even though there is no fixed rule regarding the selection of the first mantra, nevertheless, the preceding mantra, by the very fact of its recitation, excludes the subsequent one.
Just as [the meaning] is understood from the traditional recitation of the mantras, so too is that which is qualified by sequence understood.
The only distinction is that the ritual acts (padārthas) are enjoined through the recitation of the Brāhmaṇa;
however, the comprehension of the sequence is equal for both, since it is understood from their respective study (svādhyāya).
Therefore, it is equal according to the order of recitation.

The property of position regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses applies to the triple recitation of the first and last verses, and not solely to those beginning with "pra vo vājā" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.7.1).
Bhāṣya 9.1.1.
The specific locations and so forth are prompted by the ritual purpose (*kārya*), not by the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) [of the elements].
"Substitution" (*sthānāpatti*) is the means of proof for modification (*ūha*).
*Maṇi*, p. 13: "The extension by way of taking the place (*sthānāpatty-atideśa*) is a sub-division of the extension by means of inferential statements (*ānumānika-vacana-atideśa*).

*Bālakrīḍā*, pp. 117–119: Bhaṭṭa Someśvara states in the ninth [chapter] that there are five grounds for the principle of taking the place (*sthānāpatti-pramāṇa-pañcaka*): "Due to the absence of a direct [injunction], due to the prescription of a modification (*vikāra*), due to its own word (*svaśabda*), and due to the restatement of a prohibition; thus there is the performance of that function."
Thus [it is said].
Bāla. pṛ. 126.
Substitution (pratinidhi) is a modification (ūha) based on the authority of "application by position" (sthānāpatti).
Because the *dharma* is produced by the purpose, when there is a prohibition against the modification of substances and qualities, the injunction remains connected due to its inherent association.
Commentary: In the *Vājapeya* sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "He offers a sacrificial pap (*caru*) for Bṛhaspati, made of wild rice (*naivāra*), in seventeen potsherds.
And in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the *vrīhi* rice.

Regarding that, there arises a doubt as to whether [the rule] applies to wild rice (*nīvāra*) or not. Similarly, there is a doubt concerning the eating of parched grain (*mañca-aśana*) and the duties of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha-dharma*), based on the text: "Indeed, at this time speech becomes exhausted; if the six-day period concludes, one should not speak much, should not question another, and should not speak to another.
When the six-day period has concluded, one should eat parched grain or ghee. Here, the question is whether the duties of the six-day period apply to the eating of parched grain or not.
Likewise, it is heard in the context of the Rājasūya sacrifice: "He places a *caru* offering for Nirṛti in the house of those suffering from nail-disease.
In the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the mortar and pestle, as expressed in the text:
"By means of the sprinkled mortar and pestle [the grains are ground]."
In that regard, there arises the doubt as to whether it exists or does not exist.
Likewise, in the context of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "One should bind the animal to the *paridhi*.
Therein arises the doubt as to whether the duties pertaining to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) should be performed on the *paridhi* or not.

Likewise, regarding the passage: "One should not say 'girā girā'; if one were to say 'girā girā', he would burst his own self asunder; therefore, having substituted 'irā', one should utter it. There arises a doubt: do the properties (dharmas) belonging to the word *girā* apply to the word *irā*, or do they not? What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? The properties prescribed for rice (*vrīhi*) and so forth do not apply to wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like.
Therefore, they would not exist in those [substitutes].
This being the position reached, we reply:
there should be a connection with the injunction regarding wild rice and the like.
For that *prakṛti* (archetype) inheres in those [procedures];
the *dharma* (ritual duty) belongs to that which is conjoined with the *apūrva* (transcendental result), not to the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) and so forth.
By this, it is established that this specific means (*sādhana-viśeṣa*) is a *dharma* in respect to the *apūrva*, and not in respect to the rice-grains and so forth.

And it is understood that wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like perform the function of cultivated rice (*vrīhi*) and the like. Regarding wild rice, there is indeed an injunction: "An oblation (*caru*) of wild rice must be prepared. And that wild rice does not assist the sacrifice in any other way than by producing rice grains.
It is understood through direct perception that it functions as the effect of rice;
therefore, the properties of rice should apply to wild rice (*nīvāra*).
Similarly, when there is an injunction stating "one should worship with a *ṣaḍaha*," the meaning is that when the *ṣaḍaha* is completed, one does not worship with the *ṣaḍaha*.

It is understood that one should perform the service by means of eating honey and ghee; for when the absence of one thing results in the presence of another, it is understood that the latter takes the place of the former. Thus, by prescribing the eating of meat at the conclusion of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), it is understood that he is enjoining the function of the six-day rite itself.
Therefore, the duties of the six-day period—whether they be vows (*vrata*) or restrictive observances (*niyama*)—apply to the eating of *māṃsa*.
Because there is no sacrifice (*yāga*), the cups (*graha*) occasioned by it do not proceed.
Since one "initiates the chant (*stotra*) after having taken a cup or having drawn a bowl (*camasa*)," in the absence of cups and bowls, there is an absence of chants.
Because of the absence of the *savana* [pressing], the *savanīya* [offerings] do not proceed; thus, these and other such [rites] do not proceed. However, those [other] rules (*niyama*) do proceed.
If [a requirement] is obtained through another means, it does not apply to those [items] that have fallen into one's own possession.
Otherwise, they would not become purified by the *svāhā* [utterance].
If those husks were not being winnowed by them, then it would be understood that "new" [grain] is prescribed for the release from the fast;
therefore, it follows that they are connected with the properties of the mortar and pestle.
Likewise, the statement "the *paridhi* functions for the purpose of the sacrificial post" is quite explicit; thus, there is the injunction: "One should tie the animal to the *paridhi*.
Therefore, the ritual properties (*dharmas*) should belong to the *paridhi*.
Similarly, regarding the passage "One should not say *girā girā*; having uttered *aira*, one should sing," it is not the case that both of these are injunctions—the prohibition and the *irā* word.
For in that case, the sentence would be split; moreover, no such statement is heard from the authoritative source,
whereas in the case of a prohibition, it is possible for it to be a restatement (anuvāda).
When there is the word *irā*, then clearly there is not the word *girā*;
thus it is understood as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*).
Since this defect belongs to the word *irā*, therefore the word *irā* is excluded.
If, however, a distinct syntactical form were resorted to, there would be the assumption of a greater number of unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*).
For in the phrase "one should not swallow oneself," a fault (*doṣa*) is enjoined; yet it is impossible to swallow one's own body.
There is no fault in [interpreting it as] the Supreme Self;
however, the split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) remains exactly as it was.

Therefore, the utterance of the word *irā* is for the purpose of demonstrating the substitution of that word for its effect, as expressed in the rule: "One should not chant with the words *girā gireti*; rather, one should chant with *udgītha*."
Therefore, the properties of the *irāpada* should apply to the *irāpada*.
Everything is concluded.
Now, another discussion must proceed.

Objection: Although it has been established that ritual duties (*dharma*) are prompted by the *apūrva*, nevertheless, since there is no proof of the transfer of duties (*kāryāpatti*) through the principle of functional equivalence (*kāryāpatti*), this present section establishes such a transfer.
And that [transfer] is fivefold.
As for the actual [transfer], it is of two kinds: based on perception and inference.
From verbal testimony, [the inference] is threefold:
from the word itself; the inference of the word itself through negation; and the inference of negation through configuration, and from that negation, the word [is inferred].
Among these, first, from direct perception: "The sacrificial pap for Bṛhaspati is made of Nīvāra rice."
But surely, by their own words alone, the *nīvāra* grains are enjoined for the function of rice?

It is replied: the word *nīvāra* denotes the *nīvāra* grains themselves; the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) denotes the modification; the word *bārhaspatya* denotes the deity; and the word *caru* denotes the substance.
Which one is the case of *kāryāpatti* (transference of function)? Therefore, in this instance, it is *kāryāpatti* established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Rice grains (*vrīhayaḥ*) serve the purpose of the sacrifice by means of producing the sacrificial offering (*havis*) called the *puroḍāśa*.
Similarly, wild rice (*nīvārāḥ*) are also directly perceived as serving the purpose of accomplishing the sacrifice by means of producing that same offering.

Therefore, just as one employs the ritual factors (*dharmas*) for rice grains because they serve a transcendental purpose (*apūrva*), so too does one employ them for wild rice (*nīvāra*). However, from the statement "there is no *caru* offering of husked [grains]," one observes through inference that the fruit of threshing is the removal of the husk; it does not mean that the functions of the mortar and pestle persist even when the husks have been removed.
Similarly, in the injunction "one should tie the animal to the *paridhi*," the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is performed by the *paridhi* itself by virtue of its own designation.
Regarding the statement, "One should not say 'girā, girā'," the prohibition of the word *girā* indicates its function;
therein, the injunction for the word *irā* is indicated. In that case, it is impossible to enjoin [the word *irā*] through the word itself.
Therefore it is said: "From the prohibition, there is an inference of its own word.

Here, the term "its own word" (*svaśabda*) refers to *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication). In the passage, "Speech indeed becomes exhausted at this point, if the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*) is completed," there is a prohibition of the number [six].
Therefore, that is its function.
In those instances of the injunctions regarding couches and food,
the word "self" (sva) is used here by means of indication (lakṣitalakṣaṇā).
This is not tenable.
How so? If the injunctions for the cart and the food were to function as the work of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), they would thus be means for accomplishing the result;
in that case, the scriptural statement, "One desiring offspring should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*)," would be contradicted.
For by this [text], sacrifices are enjoined with respect to the fruit;
and they are qualified by the number twelve. It is not the case that there is a sacrifice in the injunction for eating the sacrificial post (mañca).
If it is argued that, like the Rājasūya sacrifice, there is a duality of results for those two [sacrifices] numbering fourteen, we reply:
not so.
Otherwise, indicative marks such as "This twelve-day sacrifice is indeed a body of thirty-six parts" would be contradicted.
Furthermore, if another [sacrifice] were to take over its function, then the six-day period would be excluded;
consequently, the originative injunction of that [twelve-day sacrifice] would be rendered purposeless.
This remains true even in cases where there is a conflict of grammatical gender.
How can it be accepted that [an action] which is understood to be a refinement of the agent (*kartṛsaṃskāraka*) is also a means of accomplishing a fruit?
And all of this is improper.
Regarding this, they explain:
here there are two [aspects], namely, being the means of attaining the fruit and being the means [itself].
Among these, it is not the firmness of being the means of attaining the fruit [that is meant].

But because they are means [to an end], that is appropriate. Just as these two perform the function of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), so too should they assume its characteristics, just like wild rice (*nīvāra*).
And it has already been stated that these [six days] do not function as the work of the *ṣaḍaha*.
Therefore, because of that ignorance, the attainment of the *dardara* does not occur.
What then? It occurs through the transference of function (*kāryāpatti*).

Therefore, another example is cited: "when [the agent] exerts effort from his position," which means that action is destroyed due to the destruction of the substance. By this, the negation of the destruction of action is indicated;
and because of this negation, there is the word for itself (*svaśabda*).
This also is certainly not the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in this section.
Therefore, an example for this must be sought from among our own [texts].
Śā—In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) and other such acts enjoined regarding rice and other materials are not prompted by the mere nature of those substances.

However, those [cognitions] which determine their objects as mere [sensory] elements (tanmātra) pertain to the unique causal efficiency (apūrva-bhāvanā) characterized by specific means enjoined in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*).
For instance, by the rule "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ*), a sacrifice having the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) as its substance and Agni as its deity is enjoined.
By way of producing that [sacrifice], the rice grains are enjoined.
They attain the status of being the material cause for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). This is the meaning: having prepared the sacrificial cake with rice grains, one should sacrifice with it;
thereafter, one sprinkles those very same rice grains and threshes them right here.

And thus, when all [the words] are combined, this meaning is established: "Having prepared a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with rice grains that have been consecrated by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and purified by threshing (*avaghāta*), one should sacrifice with it.
This alone is the ultimate sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*);
the sentence-meanings such as "rice" and so forth are merely the constituent word-meanings (*padārtha*) that serve as its means.

If, in this way, the state of being for the purpose of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth is subordinate to the meditation on the "Immeasurable" (*āmeyādi*) and other such [deities], then its application (*adhikāra*) is extended by analogy (*atideśa*).

In that case, because the oblation-pot (*caru*) takes the place of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) in the *naivāra* (wild rice) offering, and wild rice (*nīvāra*) takes the place of *vrīhi* rice, everything else remains as established by the analogy. Thus, regarding the injunction for the *naivāra* oblation—"He offers the *naivāra* oblation like the *āgneya*"—which is produced from the place [of the model] as both heard and inferred, the meaning is this: having performed the *naivāra* oblation according to the rule with [the materials] sprinkled, spread, and purified, one should sacrifice with that.
By this, modification (*ūha*) is established in the case of *nīvāra* and other grains that take the place of *vrīhi* and so forth;
it is like the "sample from the cooking pot" (*sthālīpulāka*).

Just as with the "sample from the cooking pot," the application of the rules for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is established even in those sacrifices where no [grains] are visible.
Bhāṣya 8.1.4.11: The *sthālīpāka* and the *darvihoma* are worldly (*laukika*).
Vi. 8.1.2: The term *darvihoma* is the name for the *smārta* rites beginning with the *sthālīpāka*, as well as for the Vedic *vāstuhoma*.
Bhāṣya 8.4.2.2–3: Mīko., p. 2018: "The term *darvihoma* [applies] to the *smārta* [rites]."
In this context, the *adhikaraṇa* (section) should be examined;
it follows the logic concerning the realm of the stationary and the moving.

Just as in the case of the cognition of silver and the subsequent sublation-cognition thereof—where the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is well-known regarding both the moving (such as the illusion of silver) and the stationary (such as the absence of all one's property)—so too is it in the present case.
*Sāhasī* (the bold/impetuous one) is the name for the *prakriyā* (methodological exposition) of the Sāṃkhya, which is a synonym for *sthitisiddhānta* (the established tenet of persistence). Su. p.
131. [The maxim of] the firming of a pillar by repeated hammering.
According to Amarasimha, "sthūṇā" refers to the pillar of a house;
by the use of the word "api" (also), it also includes a metal image.
Just as a pillar becomes firm when it is repeatedly pulled and then driven back into the ground, so too [is the meaning established] by the subsequent text from the preceding...
The doctrine of Sphoṭa; now, the following view is held.

It is true that the manifestation of the sphoṭa does not occur through the causes of memory; however, those impressions (*saṃskāras*) produced by sound, residing in the auditory organ, which are the causes for the perception of the phonemes (*varṇas*), will effect the manifestation of the sphoṭa just as they do for the phonemes. Why then should one postulate further impressions?
That is incorrect.
Because they are momentary.
For the impression (*saṃskāra*) which is the cause for the perception of the first letter does not persist at the time of hearing the other letters.
If it were to persist, then even at the time of hearing the *visarjanīya*, the hearing of the letter *ga* would continue.
Therefore, they are subject to momentary destruction;
consequently, they cannot collectively manifest the *sphoṭa*.
Furthermore, it has been stated that in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), each subsequent [moment] would be purposeless.
Alternatively, the refinement of the auditory organ (*śrotra-saṃskāra*) is nothing other than the conjunction with the sound-vibrations (*dhvani*);
and since those vibrations are by their very nature transitory and perishable,
there must therefore be other enduring refinements that serve as the causes of the result.

Thus, the hypothesis that there is a word-entity (*śabda*) distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*) results in many things lacking scriptural authority. In my view, however, since it is the phonemes existing within a firm memory that possess the expressive power (*vācakatva*), nothing is deficient.
[Objection: But if the expressive power belongs to those phonemes being remembered simultaneously, then even phonemes uttered out of order would be expressive.
No;
for even that sequence is a subordinate factor (aṅga).

But what is this sequence? It is not something distinct [from the letters], for there can be no sequence in the letters themselves by virtue of their own nature, since they are all-pervading and eternal.
There is no sequence of cognition, because that [cognition] consists of a single unit in the form of memory.
If this is so, then there is no fault, for the sequence of sounds (*dhvani*) which is superimposed upon the phonemes (*varṇa*) and appears [therein] is the cause.
Therefore, the phonemes, being remembered as they are manifested by the sequential arrangement of the manifesting sounds, are the denoters.
It is established that there is no other sound [than the sphoṭa].
Thus ends the doctrine of the sphoṭa (pp. 92–97).
The Theory of Sphoṭa (Sphoṭavāda).
[From the *Bṛhatī*: "Now, in the word ‘cow’ (*gauh*), what is the word?
What kind of question is this? This is a question [asked] if the word, without undergoing transformation, [denotes] the object.
It establishes that the cause is merely the causal factor, and not specifically the continuity of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
This is perceived because a specific distinction is observed in cases such as the seed and the sprout;
however, in this case, since the formative force is inferential, the perception of a specific distinction is not possible.
Therefore, we consider that only *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) is logically tenable.
For this very reason, the following [objection] is also improper.
What was said? "And that [transformation] and the conceptualization of words" (*Bhāṣya*).

How is this incorrect? For in the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), what indeed is this conceptualization of "word" (*śabda*)? Since it has been stated that the single reality, upon which limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are superimposed, is cognizable through all means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, this claim that there is an innate relationship (*autpattika-sambandha*) between word and meaning despite their being distinct is simply a lack of understanding of words.
But surely, even for one who maintains their identity, this distinction cannot be understood—namely, "this is the Jyotiṣṭoma," or "these two are the Darśapūrṇamāsa"?
For if there were unity, the very nature of being a sentence would not be established;
for all sentences would attain oneness, just as there is oneness perceived among the phonemes within a word and among words within a sentence, simply because of the cognition of unity.
Indeed, in all sentences, there arises the single cognition: "sound, sound."
And since the meaning of a sentence resides in every sentence,
this entire collection of rituals, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, would consequently become undifferentiated.
Furthermore, we observe distinctions in qualification that are both contradictory and non-contradictory.
"Contradictory" means having contradictory results;
"non-contradictory" means having non-contradictory results.
Among these, the "contradictory" are the *kṛṣṇala-caru* and the *varṣārādāya*; the "non-contradictory" are the *agnihotra* and so forth.
And this [oneness] is not tenable in the case of identity.
True, it is not tenable in the case of identity; these sentences have distinct meanings, and oneness exists for the sake of apprehending a single meaning.
Yet, in this case, a single meaning is not determined.
Therefore, while the denial of words and phonemes within a single sentence is logical,
what grounds could there be for denying an entirely different sentence?
Consequently, this injunction regarding the contradictory and the non-contradictory is established as valid.

For those who maintain that verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition (*śabdaprāmāṇyavādin*), a word connected with its meaning is what is intended by the term "word," and not even the cawing of a crow, which is not perceived by the auditory organ and so forth.
But was it not stated by you, while describing the distinctions of the auditory organ and so forth, that all this collection [of phenomena] is merely ignorance (*avidyājāta*)?
Why then do you now propose this "half-old-woman" argument (*ardhajaratīya*), asserting that there is a distinction between the sentence and the sentence-meaning?
It is not the intention of the gods that [the Self] is dear [to them].
That Brahman has been declared to be non-different;

by what means could difference be predicated of it in its true nature? And once the meaning of the scripture is understood, by whom can difference be sublated, as in the case of the auditory organs and so forth? It is true that it cannot be sublated.
But ignorance (avidyā) would follow [as the cause];
yet knowledge (vidyā) is intended as the Vedic goal.
How, then, can it be said that prosperity (abhyudaya) arises from ignorance?
Ignorance is indeed the causal condition for this;
it is true as you have said.
However, conditions are relative.
For all [actions] lead only to the cause of destruction; however,
the difference is that in one case (such as the killing of a Brahmin), there is only an obstacle (*pratyavāya*),
whereas in the other (Vedic purpose), there is also a means (*upāya*).

Therefore, nothing here is contradicted by what follows [namely, the statement of non-difference, which is intended from the perspective of ultimate reality, by the subsequent statement of difference based on ignorance]. But surely, even if there is a distinction between the sentence and the meaning of the sentence, how can it be said that those expressing qualities are identical in meaning through the accumulation of ritual acts? It has been stated that even though they are distinct, their performance is established as one, just as in the case of the obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) applications.
Therefore, everything is logically consistent.
(He begins the established conclusion: This would indeed be so if there were a single cognition; however, there is no single cognition here.
But surely, in all words, there exists a single cognition, namely, "this is a word, this is a word.
And if such a single cognition did not exist, even the status of being denotable by the word "word" would not belong to all words.
For being denotable by a single word is due to a single cause, and not because of numerical oneness.
(Ṛju—There is no cognition that has the single form of a phoneme.
This is because the application of a single word cannot occur without a single basis (*nimitta*).
And that basis is either a genus (*jāti*), an action (*kriyā*), a quality (*guṇa*), or a substance (*dravya*), as in the examples: "cow," "goer," "white," and "horned."
In some cases, there is identity with the object itself, as when the word "space" is applied again and again to that very same object. However, identity is not its sole cause.
Therefore, because the application of a single word is inconclusive, a single cognition is not established.
And here there is one reason: the term "word" (*śabda*) is well-known in the world as that which is grasped by the auditory organ (*śrotra*).
But what is the reason that it is grasped only when summoned by the auditory organ, and not rather like "cowness" (*gotva*), where the property of being a word (*śabdatva*) is relied upon?
(The answer: It is precisely the cognition whose object is a universal-particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) that is at fault for one who objects in this manner.

(He asks: What, then, is the cognition whose object is both the universal and the particular? (The answer: This is the cognition which, when an entity is apprehended, serves as the locus for recollection of the properties associated with previous perceptions. See the discussion on the "locus of substance" (*dravyādhikaraṇa*) at Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2157.

The establishment of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices follows the conjunction of *smṛti* (tradition) and other sources; Vi. 3.1.5. However, there is a *yajus* mantra based on *smṛti*: "vasiṣṭhābhyāsama" (Śrāddhamayūkha, p.
51, edited by Dhārapura). Tradition (*smaraṇa*) is beginningless and cannot be subjected to questioning.
*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 10.4.12.23: *Smaraṇa* (Recollection).
For recollection is considered to be precisely the reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of that which is not present to the senses.
*Bṛhatī*, p. 80: "And recollection is stated to be more authoritative than [mere] practice (*ācāra*)."
"Or [it is] so. (Vārttika 1.3.8.27, p. 280). "Recollection (*smaraṇa*) is the grasping of what has already been grasped" (Nyāyaratna, p.
52). "Recollection is a cognition that depends upon a previous experience" (p.
80). "And recollection is accepted because it is [the result of] a latent impression (*pramuptatva*)."
Maṇi, p. 26: Mantras are reminders; and their fixed recitation is for the sake of restriction. Mīmāṃsāsūtra 1.2.4.31–4.
By Smṛti, p. 169. By Smṛti whose purpose is unseen (adṛṣṭārtha), that whose purpose is seen (dṛṣṭārtha) is sublated, because the latter has not attained its object; [Śābarabhāṣya] 3.3.7.4, p. 860.
By an uncontradicted Smṛti, a contradicted Smṛti is sublated, as for example: "One should not be a thief," and likewise, "When all the food has been consumed, six portions of food remain uneaten."
One may take from a person of inferior conduct according to the rule of not providing for the morrow.

Thus it is also stated in the *Āsasamṛti*. However, in this context, the Smṛti is sublated [by the Śruti] because its purport is merely the absence of punishment or because it refers to cases of minor fault (*bāla.*, p. 139). Custom (*ācāra*) is sublated by Smṛti, as for example: "Having married the daughter of a maternal uncle, and likewise one who bears the same lineage as one's mother..."
And having married a woman of the same pravara, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
"By this Smṛti [text], the custom of marrying the daughter of a maternal uncle (mātulakanyāpariṇayana) belongs to the Southerners (dākṣiṇātyānām).

Bāla. pṛ. 138. By a Smṛti—by an uncontradicted Smṛti—an uncontradicted Smṛti is sublated, because it has not attained its scope [elsewhere]. Vārttika 3.3.7.4, p. 860. By a Smṛti—by an Āsma-smṛti—an Anāsa-smṛti is sublated."

For example, the Smṛti of Pañcaśikha and others stating "one should cast off the body in Kedāra" is sublated by the Smṛti of Manu and others stating "one should not kill oneself," because the latter is based on Śruti, while the former is based on indicative marks (liṅga) or explanatory passages (arthavāda), and thus lacks independent authority.
(Bālakrīḍā, p. 139). Smṛti originating from Śruti sublates Smṛti originating from liṅga or arthavāda, as it possesses greater force.

Vārttika 3.3.7.4, p. 860. A Smṛti originating from Śruti (direct Vedic revelation) sublates a Smṛti originating from a *liṅga* (inferential mark). For example, a Smṛti originating from Śruti such as "Having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* in the middle of the house, one should exclude the son... sublates a Smṛti originating from the *liṅga* of the prohibition of the adopted son (*dattaka-putra*), such as "There is no other-born [son] before him," which originates from the passage: "Those born of whose seed they are, belong to him and not to the other. Bālakrīḍā, pp. 139–140. The basis of Smṛti in another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*).
*Bṛhatī*, p. 120: Since Smṛti is stronger on account of its object of cognition (*prameya*), it possesses only the status of being non-contradictory to Śruti, but not the power to sublate Śruti.
*Sūtra-bhāṣya*, p. 180: Smṛti has its root in Mantras and Arthavādas.
It is perceived directly that the source of Smṛti is the knowledge derived from both the Mantras and the Arthavādas.
For those who perceive the meaning of the mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas) through mere superficial observation, that [Smṛti] has its root in memory.
However, for those who examine them with precision, it is sublated; yet even so, it may still serve as the basis for someone's memory.
And from that very fact, it is Smṛti.

Bhāṣya 9.1.4.9, p. 1653: "The source of the Smṛti is not perceived—'Because the Śākhās are scattered, because of human negligence, and because of the decay of various [transmission] methods, the source of the Smṛti is not perceived.'"
Vārttika 1.3.1.2, p. 164: Smṛti whose basis has been sublated is invalid.
Vivaraṇa 1.3.1.4: Vedic indicative mark (liṅga) is stronger than Smṛti.
Vārttika 3.3.7.4, p. 841: Smṛti that contradicts Śruti is invalid.
Bhāṣya 1.3.2–4: "When the root [of a Smṛti] is determined to be the Veda itself—since it has no other root—even if there is a contradiction, the authority of the Smṛti is not precluded by the Śruti."

"From the perception of a similar object, there arises the recollection of another similar object. (*Bṛhatī*, p. 54). "The validity of recollection as an independent means of knowledge is indeed accepted. (*Vākyapadīya* 1.3.12, p. 172). "In the case of recollections, disagreement is not at all a cause for their invalidity. (*Vākyapadīya* 1.3.17, p. 198).
For indeed, even among the Vedas, a great deal of mutual contradiction is observed.
If those [scriptures] which have their basis in censured statements were themselves uncensured,
then they would lack authority because of the contradiction with their basis.

1.3.8.27, p. 286: In some Smṛtis, whose content contradicts the statements found within their own Vedic schools, a contradiction with the studied Vedic texts is observed; yet, on that account alone, it is not appropriate to reject the Śruti (the Vedic text serving as the basis for the Smṛti) established by a more firmly rooted tradition. For the retention of the Smṛti is practiced just as much as the study [of the Veda]. 1.3.13, p. 170: The authority of Smṛtis concerning matters such as Dharma is established because they have the Veda as their sole refuge.

Su. Pṛ. 41: The opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra is that when Smṛtis conflict with direct Vedic revelation (pratyakṣaśruti), they lack authority by their very nature (svarūpeṇa). In this regard, the opinion of the Vārtikakāra is that while there is non-authority characterized by non-performance, there is no lack of authority in their essential form (na svarūpataḥ). Ku. 1.3.4–5, p. 56: Because Smṛtis are rooted in the Veda, they possess equality with the Veda.
Vārttika 6.2.22: The lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the Smṛtis of the Śākyas and others.
Bhāṣya 1.3.15, Section 3: The authority, characterized by practice (*anuṣṭhāna*), of those Smṛtis that contradict the Śruti.
Bhāṣya 1.3.12.4, Section 2: The universal applicability (*sarvadharmatva*) of the Smṛtis in the absence of a specific [contradiction].

1|3|17|25–26. The authority of the *smṛtis* (such as those of Manu and others) consists in their being "grasping what has not yet been grasped" (*agṛhītagrāhitva*), by virtue of having as their object a state of affairs that was not the object of a cognition formed in the immediately preceding moment by a sentence co-referential with themselves.
Maṇi, p. 13. "Therefore, those *smṛtis* which are contrary to the Veda lack authority.
[This concludes] the section on *Smṛti* (4833). *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa*.
For since those [scriptures] have their roots cut off, as their authority in hearing and inference has been obstructed.

Or [as stated in] Vārttika 1.3.2.3, page 104: "Therefore, the authority of those Smṛtis which contradict the Vedas and whose purposes are perceived through worldly means must not be undermined even in the slightest degree by [such] arguments."
Page 172, 1|3|13: "For it is not possible for Smṛtis to possess direct authority [as independent means of knowledge].
For the direct perception of the subject matter of those [Smṛti] meanings is simply not found in the case of Vedic sentences."
"But when [the Vedic word] is being heard directly, there is no inference based on behavior;
for even when an elephant is seen, one does not seek to infer it by means of its footprint."
Meanings flash forth before one, independent of inference,
for only so long as their root is not uprooted by the science of direct perception.
1|3|13, p. 172: In the *Smṛti*, knowledge functions as a cause by way of being an experience (*anubhava*).
*Maṇi*, p. 30: In the *Smṛtis*, there is an absence of the term *samāmnāya*.
*Ṛju*, p. 8.
The section on Smṛti. Smṛti is an authoritative means of knowledge regarding Dharma.
"Because Dharma has its root in the Word (śabda), [the Smṛti] would be independent of the Word.
Commentary: Thus far, the authority of the established Veda has been stated.

Now, however, regarding those cases where this [Smṛti] does not have a Vedic word as its root, yet people remember that "this matter must be performed in this way for this purpose," [the question arises].
Would it be exactly so?

For example: "The Aṣṭakā rites must be performed," "The teacher must be approached," "A pond must be dug," "Offspring must be produced," "The duty of maintaining [the world] must be carried out"—such are the cases.
To this it is replied: "Since Dharma has its root in the Word (śabda), it would be independent of the Word."
It has been stated that Dharma is characterized by verbal testimony, namely:
"Dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by Vedic injunction.
Therefore, because [the opponent's position] lacks a foundation, it must be disregarded.
Now, one might object: "How could those who know that these two matters must be performed as such say that they are not to be performed at all? [The answer is:
Because of the impossibility of their being remembered.

For that which has never been experienced or heard is not remembered; nor is the memory of this [Smṛti]—which is neither Vedic nor worldly—possible, because there is no cause for a prior cognition [of it].

For if a barren woman were to remember, "This was done by my grandson," one would never accept her cognition as valid, since she has no daughter. Even so, just as their Smṛti is authoritative because it is "this Veda" through an unbroken tradition, so too this [Smṛti] will be authoritative.
This is not so.
Because it is perceived through direct observation, there is no lack of a prior cognition in other cases.
However, in rites such as the *aṣṭakā*, which have unperceived purposes (mī.
ko. 555), since there is an absence of a cause for a prior cognition, it is understood that these are merely memories based on delusion (*vyāmoha*).

For example, suppose a person blind from birth were to say, "I remember a particular form. If questioned, "How do you have prior cognition of this? he would point to another person who is also blind from birth. [If asked], "How did that one [acquire it]? [he would reply], "From another previous life."
Thus, even if there were a succession of those blind from birth, those who perceive it would never recognize, "This is right vision.
Therefore, a work of this kind, whose purpose is not perceived, cannot be independent [of other means of knowledge].

Alternatively: Thus far, the utility of the Veda with respect to *dharma* has been established on the basis of its injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), mantras, and names (*nāmadheya*). Now, the consideration concerns the *smṛtis* composed by Manu and others, as well as the *āgamas*, regarding all matters that have human origins.

In this regard, having extracted certain points, an investigation must be conducted; thus, the recollections of Manu and others, such as the *ekādi-smaraṇas*, which have been established by them, are cited here as subjects for the investigation into what constitutes valid and invalid authority (*pramāṇa* and *apramāṇa*).
Furthermore, the cause of doubt is also stated:
"Because they are dependent on others, there is no definitive determination of their validity."
However, the doubt regarding their lack of authority is dispelled by their very firmness.

Since the words of Manu and others fall under the category of *smṛti* (tradition), and *smṛti* must depend upon an underlying source of authority (*mūla-pramāṇa*), the certainty of their authority—unlike that of the Veda—is not established for even a single one of them.

Nevertheless, because they have been accepted through an uninterrupted lineage without distinction from the Veda itself, there is no room for the suspicion of invalidity; thus, it is logical that [the Smṛtis] are considered authoritative.

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) says: "The validity of these [subsequent cognitions] need not even be considered. Why? Because a cognition whose object is the same as that of a prior cognition is called memory;
without a prior cognition, its validity cannot be determined."
"For all recollections (smaraṇa), arising in accordance with an object already apprehended through direct perception (pratyakṣa), establish that object as it truly is.
Thus, it has been established here that the fact that the Aṣṭakā and other rites are means for attaining heaven and so forth cannot be grasped through direct perception and the like.
Furthermore, while the Vedic meters (chandas) are perceived directly in the case of the Agnihotra and other such rituals, the mantras are not perceived in this same way."
"And when there is neither perception nor non-perception of a word, the postulation of its existence [is made];
however, a property (dharma) would indeed be even more remote from being established by such a means of knowledge."

"In the case of sound (*śabda*), there is only one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely perception (*pratyakṣa*). Even if it is said that [the Veda] exists though it is not apprehended by consciousness, it would be better to accept that the nature of *dharma* remains simply without any means of valid cognition. Or rather, let there be no means of valid cognition at all for this [Veda] when one imagines its mantras and so forth to be true to their literal meaning."
For such an interpretation is not seen in the Smṛti; otherwise, there would be no basis for inference.

"Just as something proceeds from the perception of a correspondence with the nature of things (*dharma*), so too does [the cognition] of *akāra* and the rest. Or rather, there is no apprehension of that [object] through a means of knowledge (*āgama*), whether it be eternal or produced."
There is no confidence in that which is artificial, nor can it ever be established as eternal.
Even though it is possible for the Vedas and other scriptures to be understood through human-authored traditions— such as those concerning the existence of sense organs and so forth—
nevertheless, because they abound in deception, one must conclude that their words are untrustworthy.
For some are seen to speak even of things that are not scriptural by superimposing upon them the status of being scriptural;

consequently, those whose minds are agitated by wicked persons may harbor doubts as to whether Manu and others, when composing their own works, spoke of a Veda they had actually perceived today, or whether their words are to be accepted merely because they were not perceived [as such]. And by that much, the authority [of the texts] is undermined.

An eternal word has no function whatsoever in establishing that which possesses a beginning, such as greed; nor do the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of mantras themselves establish their own status as a source (*mūla*),
because they are dependent upon reflection.
Nor do they indicate any other source that is consistent with reason, because those [other sources] have a different purpose. Furthermore, there is no scripture for all the authors of the Smṛtis.

By which [means] there could be the status of having a previously heard Vedic source established through the force of human effort? Furthermore, it is not known what kind of sentence was determined by them;
for we see many people exhausting themselves with [texts] consisting of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like.
If it were understood through reason alone that the sentences were indeed perceived by Manu and others exactly according to the prescribed rule,
then some such assumption might be possible; for even today, people are seen to exert themselves in learning other branches of knowledge from the original utterances.
Consequently, there arises a suspicion regarding those [scriptures] as well.

Just like a legal proceeding based on the testimony of the deceased, whatever is asserted by someone on the basis of the characteristic of having its root in a vanished school, that person should treat it with caution.
Therefore, even through scripture, the discovery of the root [of tradition] is possible.

"Analogical inference (*upamāna*) is not accepted as a means of establishing a root scripture when the object is unseen and its similarity has not been determined; therefore, by that [means] as well, a root [scripture] is not established.
