Even by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), it is understood that there is some root [text]."
And even in the case of [the Smṛti] being non-authoritative, error and so forth are not contradicted.
For if the Smṛti were not possible without the postulation of a Vedic revelation (śruti), then it would have a Vedic basis;
however, since it is possible for it to be based on its own [human] cognition, there is no contradiction with other [authorities], as its meaning is established through consistency.
Or because of the application of the *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* (inference from general observation) [reasoning].

Therefore, even though there is scriptural knowledge (*śruti*) whose object is non-perception, there arises the conceit that it has a basis, due to the absence of another root [i.e., perception] which would establish the existence of its own root.
[Objection: "But surely those who know [this] understand that a ritual act prescribed by scripture—possessing such a procedure and such a result—is to be performed."

Alternatively, those who know that "this must be done" in this manner— being thus cognizant— how could such persons, when advising others, fail to say "this must not be done" in order to deceive them?
But surely some say one thing, while others say "it must be done," and still others say "it must not be done."
How is there positive concomitance (*anvaya*)? When it is asked, "How is it that for them [the ancients] this would also have been so?", how can such a realization arise?
Alternatively, how could Manu and others—who knew that "this matter must be performed"—have spoken without fault in order to deceive the world by saying, "This must indeed be done"?
This is because "recollection would be impossible" (*smaraṇānupapatti*).
First, as for those persons who lived before Manu and others, their [knowledge of] sacrifices is indeed *smṛti* (recollection), because its object was previously unknown to them.
Even for Manu and others, recollection could only occur if some prior means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were first possible; otherwise, it would not.
But why, then, was the example of a barren woman giving birth given, rather than one of a son or a daughter?
Because it is based on a prior cognition.

For the prior cognition of Manu and others regarding their sons and so forth is the very memory that serves as the basis for [the knowledge of] their grandsons. Just as one considers the memory of a grandson to be an error when reflecting upon the state of being a daughter, so too, by reflecting on the impossibility of direct perception, the memory of Manu and others regarding the *Ṛgveda* and other texts must be understood as false.
This was stated with the intention of inferring the Vedic text from the statement: "Just as this Veda has been handed down through an uninterrupted tradition."

Thinking that the non-interruption of the meaning for others constitutes "recollection" (*smaraṇa*), he stated "he said"; yet, considering that [the source] is once again rootless, he further explains: the Veda, moreover, is distinct and accessible through direct perception; in that regard, people remember the source of another person just as they do with a jar or similar objects.
By them, too, having perceived what was remembered, others remember it, and those others likewise hand it down, and so forth.
Furthermore, since the apprehension of every sound is possible through its filling [of the auditory cavity] and its recollection, there is no lack of a basis [for linguistic usage].
Moreover, in this context, the mere acquisition of the relationship between a word and its meaning depends solely upon the linguistic practice of elders.

For even prior [to such practice], one may perceive entities possessing Vedic words—whether distinct from other Vedas or otherwise—as having forms such as the Ṛgveda and so forth, and as being distinct from others in the case of the mantras and their forms.

Furthermore, the postulation of a capacity in him that is contrary to the nature of all contemporary human beings has already been refuted in the discussion regarding the omniscience of Manu and others; moreover,
the view that he is merely a human being whose words are authoritative has also been refuted through the succession of other arguments.
For indeed, no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is ever seen that is without a basis or unestablished;
likewise, even in the case of deception, such a [basis] is postulated.

The motive for the world's desire to deceive is the persistence of that delusion for an extremely long time, which must be considered as being due to factors such as the intellect (citi) and so forth.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with what is observed, because the validity of the perceived means of knowledge would be negated by something that has not yet arisen.
Therefore, the ritual procedure consisting solely of cooked rice (*odana*) is superior;

But all the remaining factors, such as acceptance by the great multitude (*mahājana-parigraha*) and so forth, are followed accordingly.
And it is possible that for Manu and others, the cause of their prior knowledge was the Vedic injunction (*codanā*).

However, when the Veda is assumed as the source, and other causes have been ruled out, then, due to the absence of any other root, the specific possibility remains that the Veda is the source. As for the question, "Why is the Veda not perceived?"— *Note: The term *codanā* here refers to the Vedic injunction or revelation.*
Regarding this, some say:
those [phonemes] are always inferable and are never articulated,
just like the grammatical markers (liṅga) and so forth that have been mentioned.
If it is asked, "How can there be the establishment of the root [of the Veda] for those who have followed it in succession?"—
this is not a fault;
for its establishment is achieved through memory by means of an uninterrupted tradition of recitation.

For just as a text that exists with its tradition unbroken possesses existence, so too, by means of the proposition, is the non-interruption of the tradition of the eternally inferred *śruti* established. That is incorrect;

for the existence of a Vedic injunction (*codanā*) that is never uttered through any other lineage is even more difficult to establish, since it lacks the scope of perception and other means of knowledge for all persons.
And thus, for Smṛti as well, that very same status of being a cause for the understanding of [dharma]—such as in the case of the barren woman and so forth—is established.

However, because the inferential marks (liṅga) and other such means are eternal, it is not contradictory for them to serve as the cause for inferring a Śruti that has not been traditionally transmitted.
Therefore, it is better to simply infer a lost Śruti.
Nor is its destruction impossible;
for it is observed that through negligence, laziness, and so forth, there is a state of not being pervaded by human effort.

This is because the inference of a Vedic revelation (śruti) is obtainable through the otherwise inexplicable nature of the recollections in the hearts of cultured *trai-varṇika* people;

Because the Smṛti consists of various sections, its source is not perceived.
As for the question, "Why were the Vedic sentences themselves not collected [into the Smṛti]?"—

For it is heard in scripture that even the private recitation (*svādhyāya*) must be performed established in a specific sequence;

Moreover, by this explanation—or rather, by way of illustration—others might study merely the ritual injunctions or merely those conditioned by specific rites;

Furthermore, Manu and others were not necessarily students of all the Vedic branches (*sarvaśākhādhyāyin*).
For they, having heard [the texts] with great effort from students of other recensions (*śākhā*), would explain them in their own words according to the principles of brevity;
yet no specific wording (*vākya-viśeṣa*) would be known.
Just as there is no lack of authority for a Smṛti because it has a basis in [Vedic] recollection, so too there is no lack of authority for one based on an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
For they are indeed capable of distinguishing between an injunction (*vidhi*) and an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

In that regard, since the *smṛti* possesses the nature of an injunction, its status as being preceded by an *arthavāda*—which would have to rely on the performance of the act as it is traditionally handed down—is without any basis of proof. Furthermore, since the *smṛtis* themselves have established and entrusted their own authority by stating, "The entire Veda is the root of Dharma" and "All of that is declared in the Veda," and since their application at the time of their composition was observed by their authors through the medium of the Veda, it is established that their validity is mediated by the Veda.

However, for one who seeks to establish either *svataḥ-prāmāṇya* (intrinsic validity) or *vedamūlatva* (being rooted in the Veda) through inference based on the identity of the author, there is no certainty because of the practices of those whose hearts follow the meaning [of the texts]. Furthermore, there is a contradiction because it would result in validity being dependent upon the currently heard revelation (*śruti*). Therefore, it is *arthāpatti* (presumption) alone that is described here as "inference" by way of metaphorical usage, due to its non-deviation from the fact; as it is said:
"This very [presumption] is the basis for the Smṛti."
Alternatively, there is an inference of the cause based on what has been observed, or rather, based on the fact of being observed.

For it is said: "Indeed, humans [do not remain] right here," because death—which cuts off all residual impressions (*saṃskāra*)—intervenes, making it impossible to connect with the fruition of the results.
"Because of the commonality of the authors of the Smṛtis and the Vedic subjects, the connection with the Veda is established for those belonging to the [three] castes.
This is due to both the possibility of the Smṛtis being rooted in Vedic injunctions (codanā) and the attainment of the status of authoritative words.
Furthermore, "even forgetfulness is possible."
For even today, the loss of meaning and the disappearance of textual compositions are observed;
and even when those scriptural passages still exist in other recensions, there is likewise a forgetting of which specific passages are recited in which particular recension.
They, however, preserve the mere quality of being Vedic for the sake of establishing its authority;
for that knowledge of the remainder, being non-eternal, is certainly not to be performed.
Thus it is said: "Likewise, of those rules presented [only] on specific occasions."
"Those [acts] which are enjoined with respect to a sign that has arrived— such as the attendance upon elders and so forth—
their authority arises precisely from their having a visible purpose. This is incorrect.

Why? Because this is the section concerning the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*).

Furthermore, if following the teacher and so forth had only a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), then, like agriculture and the like, they would lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*) with respect to Dharma and should not have been introduced here.

No;
for if that were the case, the sūtra "And because of the observation of a cause" (hetudarśanācca) would have to be cited [as a counter-example].
Therefore, the observation regarding "the better" (śreyāṃsam) is fruitless.
Furthermore, attainment does not necessarily depend on the branch [of Vedic study];
for it is possible to cause the teacher to perform the teaching and other duties by other means, such as conciliation or bribery.
In that case, there would be an absence of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*).

Furthermore, in every case, it is possible to state that there is a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*), such as the assistance in worldly activity, the acquisition [of materials], protection, or the production of pleasure, as described by the author of the Bhāṣya.
However, one cannot claim that the Veda is the source of authority merely because acts like *avaghāta* (threshing) or rites for those desiring rain have a visible purpose.

Therefore, even when a visible purpose is possible, the Veda may still be the source of authority, because the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule (*niyama*) is established through a means of knowledge other [than perception].

And for this reason, since following the teacher and so forth are contingent upon specific causes, there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) from their non-performance, nor does [the result] arise from their performance.

Furthermore, the desired outcome—such as "the pleased teacher will teach me"—is accomplished; and through the observance of the rule (*niyama*), even if [the teacher] is not personally gratified, the accomplishment of the unseen merit (*apūrva*) results.
And thus, in the case of [the rule] "when [the agent] is not being censured on account of conduct" (Pāṇini 6.1.10–31),
a deliberation as to whether the performance is once or repeatedly is appropriate.
Otherwise, however, there would necessarily be a restriction— just as in the case of comparison and so forth— based solely on its having a visible purpose.

As for the statement made by the author of the Bhāṣya that their authority arises precisely from having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), that is intended to emphasize the strength of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

What is meant is this: while those Smṛtis whose purposes are invisible might somehow establish religious duties (*dharma*), how could these others—concerned with matters such as following one's teacher—possibly lack authority?

Although no specific Vedic revelation (*viśeṣaśruti*) can be inferred for the rules regarding assemblies and the like, nevertheless, because they are all included under the general injunction for "benefiting others" (*paropakāra*), they possess authority.
Therefore, he shows that this [act] is consistent with the collection of means for achieving what is desired, even when it is established through other Smṛtis and by following the ass.

Just as water-stations established in waterless places benefit others, so too—in a sentence primarily intended to praise the deity—is seen the fact that [the act], being already established, exists for the sake of another through its grace.
Even in the case of carving a clan-mark on a stone, there is a restriction of practice; and since its purpose is unseen (adṛṣṭa), its utility is limited to that alone.
For it is possible that the *gotra* was remembered by means of another method; therefore, this is indeed a different intention.

First, for the sake of establishing the division into four classes (*cāturvarṇya*), six castes (*ṣaḍjāti*), and so forth, the *gotra* must necessarily be independent, being the basis for such actions.
Consequently, let the authority of the *Śilākalpa-smṛti* be accepted even for the purpose of identifying its characteristics.
Therefore, because it is not seen otherwise and has no other possible source, its status as a human goal will be established.
By this, the validity of all Smṛtis is proven to be purposeful.
Among them, whatever pertains to Dharma and Mokṣa originates from that [Veda].

However, it must be discerned that those [statements] whose objects are easily understood are preceded by worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*). In this same way, the status of the sentences concerning sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) in the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* is to be explained.
As for the means [of persuasion], they have been explained among the *arthavādas*.

As for the description of the divisions of the earth, it is based partly on direct observation and partly on the Veda, intended to distinguish the locations for the performance of merit and demerit and for the enjoyment of their fruits. The genealogical succession is also based on observation and tradition, intended for the knowledge of the lineages, castes, and clans of the Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas.
The measurement of space and time is likewise based on observation, calculation, and traditional inference, intended for the successful practice of worldly affairs and the science of astronomy.

Even the description of future events is rooted in the Veda by way of its focus on the fruits of the performance of dharma and adharma according to the nature of the *yugas* as they have proceeded from beginningless time.
Furthermore, it should be discerned that even the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgavidyā*) teach the goals of human action (*puruṣārtha*) by being preceded by worldly experience and the Veda.

Among these, first, in the science of phonetics (*śikṣā*), the exposition of the distinctions between letters, articulations, accents, durations, and so forth, is preceded by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
As for the fact that a specific result arises from the correct application of such knowledge—

namely, the recollection [of the mantra] as expressed in the traditional teaching, "A mantra deficient in accent or phoneme [is ineffective]"— that is rooted in the Veda. Likewise, in the Kalpasūtras, the compilers have accepted as authoritative the characteristic of synthesis (upasaṃhāra), which is obtained through reasoning from various other branches of scripture scattered throughout.
Furthermore, certain linguistic usages that involve contradiction are based upon worldly convention and are adopted as means for the sake of pleasure.

Even in grammar, the knowledge of the distinction between "word" (*śabda*) and "phoneme" (*varṇa*) has as its direct cause the distinction between [objects] such as trees, even though that [distinction] is not perceptible.

The Vedic tradition holds that the attainment of results comes from the use of correct words (*sādhuśabda*), whereas the use of corrupt words (*apaśabda*) leads to a deficiency in those results. Furthermore, the rules for the *gāyatrī* and other meters as established in *Chandoviciti* are directly perceived in both the world and the Vedas, just as before;
and it is taught in the Śruti that the result arises from employing [the meters] with prior knowledge of them.

And likewise, it is heard constantly [in the scriptures]: "He who, indeed, performs a sacrifice or officiates at a sacrifice with a mantra whose seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), deity (*daivata*), and explanatory portion (*brāhmaṇa*) are unknown," and so forth.

In the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*) as well, the calculation of the duration and movement of the *yugas*, the knowledge of lunar days (*tithi*) and constellations (*nakṣatra*) through the division of the motions of the moon, sun, and other bodies, and the inference based on mathematical computation rooted in an unbroken tradition—all of which indicate the ripening of the fruits of previously performed good and evil deeds and the unfavorable conditions of eclipses—is likewise rooted in the Veda by way of prescribing rites for pacification (*śānti*) and other such measures.
By this, the sciences of physiognomy (*sāmudra*) and architecture (*vāstuvidyā*) are also explained.
Or rather, such objects are to be inferred everywhere:
that when there is such an arrangement of houses, temples, and so forth, this particular deity is to be understood [as being present].
Mīmāṃsā, however, proceeds in the world through perception, inference, and so on, as well as through the scholarly practices of an uninterrupted tradition.
For no one at all is capable of compiling such a collection of arguments from the very beginning;
by this [work], one may explain the expansion of the Nyāya system.
"The subject matter of the Vedic sentences is established through the meanings of the words."
And these [objects], mixed together on the path of the world through distinctions such as genus and so forth,
can be distinguished directly by means of those very instruments— perception and the rest— which are both subtle and distinct,
when sought for the purpose of investigation; but not by themselves.

Even the Veda, though its nature is scattered, accomplishes its own purpose only when determined by perception and the other means of knowledge; thus they should be understood from the expansion of Nyāya.
And likewise it has been stated in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "Perception, inference, and verbal testimony consisting of various traditions..."
One who desires the purification of Dharma must thoroughly understand three things.
Likewise, by such statements as, "He who investigates with reasoning knows Dharma, and no other," the purification through reasoning (tarka-viśuddhi) is adopted.
Generally, because humans are so highly esteemed, their intuitive flashes (*pratibhā*), being bound to their own limited knowledge, operate toward those wrong paths.

In this regard, the *Lokārthavāda* [section] demonstrates all the various points of misconception arising from the *Upaniṣads*; the *Tarkaśāstra* [sections] explain the logical justifications for them and the means of reaching certainty preceded by those powerful arguments.
Otherwise, however: "Indeed, novel arguments that appear of their own accord to men, though highly esteemed, are errors; they are made to appear true by the awakening of knowledge.
And all [these arguments] are distinguished by their independence once they have been presented.
Some of those born from that [tradition] will accept it as authoritative.

Furthermore, even the one-sided demonstration of such categories as eternal and non-eternal, distinctness and unity, universals and particulars, and exclusion (vyatireka), is impossible without partiality, because one is incapable of defining either side [exclusively].

Moreover, since it is impossible to grasp a thing that consists of all [attributes] simultaneously, one must diligently define each individual attribute by distinguishing its specific object from others, like the act of covering the moon with one's hand.

Otherwise, those logical grounds for the existence of universals, particulars, and so forth—such as the extraction of a specific portion of the world from the whole by means of a word denoting a foot [of a verse] placed in the hand of a person—would not be established at all. Furthermore, the praises and censures found in mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), which function as injunctions and prohibitions in their respective contexts by depending on qualities such as truth, falsehood, permanence, impermanence, unity, and diversity, would be without support, like a mountain of dharma established through mere partiality.

Furthermore, all these theories—such as those concerning Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Īśvara, and atoms—which are perceived in the form of creation, dissolution, and so forth, are to be understood through the Mantras, Arthavādas, and injunctions, as well as by observing the investigation into the nature of subtle and gross substances as they appear.
And the purpose [of this] is the knowledge of the distinction between the means for attaining heaven, performing sacrifices, and so on.
Even the description of creation and dissolution is for the sake of demonstrating the distinction between the power of destiny (daiva) and human effort (puruṣakāra).

For everywhere it proceeds by its own power, [asserting] "it is like that, it is like that. And in all cases where direct experience is impossible—such as when a result occurs at a later time—it is the Śruti that serves as the authority.

Regarding the fruit of the *sāṃhitika* [Vedic] tradition, however, in cases such as augury and magic (*vidyā*), authority is established simply by observing their practical application among other people; thus, the distinction is proven.

Śā— "Because they are remembered by those versed in the Veda, because of the firmness of their acceptance, and because it is possible that the Smṛtis are rooted in the Veda, the Smṛtis have their basis in the Veda."

Soma [the author] states: Since the *codanā* (Vedic injunction) directly and independently generates knowledge of dharma, its authority was examined first; immediately thereafter, that of the *arthavādas* and other elements which form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with it. Thus, after examining the authority of the entire Veda, the authority of the *smṛtis* is now investigated because they derive their validity from being rooted in that [Veda]. This is the meaning of "immediate succession" (*ānantarya*).

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: Since injunction (*codanā*) alone is the authority for *dharma*, and since *dharma* has the Veda as its sole root, the Smṛtis and other texts—which are not rooted in the Veda—are not to be relied upon as authorities for *dharma*. As it is said: "Because they arise from egoism and the like, the Smṛtis have no authority regarding *dharma*; nor do they possess authority because they lack a [Vedic] source. That which is without a source is not authoritative; that which is based on the Veda and so forth is meaningful."
The Section on Smṛti (Smṛtyadhikaraṇa):

Since they are remembered by those learned in the Vedas, it is possible that the Smṛtis have their root in the Veda. Because they condense scattered matters and include explanatory passages (arthavādas), they possess authority.

The Mīmāṃsaka says: "People do not consider those Smṛtis to be authoritative, because the root Veda from which they are inferred is impossible. The Bhāṭṭa replies: There is a doubt as to whether the Smṛtis composed by Manu and others—which are accepted by cultured people (śiṣṭas) and merchants—possess authority regarding dharma and adharma or not; [the opponent claims] there is no authority because there is no certainty regarding their having a valid root.
For in this case, perception and the other means of knowledge do not serve as a basis, because they do not operate with respect to dharma and adharma;
nor is there the perception of a Veda recited [therein],
for if it were perceived, the composition of the Smṛti would be rendered useless.

Furthermore, it is impossible to postulate that the Veda, which is directly recited and whose destruction has just occurred, could have been preserved by the Vaidikas through the preservation of even a fraction of its branches while omitting other portions.

This being the position reached, we reply: because cultured people (*śiṣṭas*) have accepted the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other rites here as *dharma*, and the eating of garlic and the like as *adharma*, through a continuous tradition of what has been studied; and because Manu and others, being members of the three higher castes, could have perceived the Veda; it is therefore proper that these [Smṛtis] are indeed rooted in the Veda, and not rooted in error and the like.
Furthermore, there would be the burden of postulating both that cause and the word *adhyāya*;
moreover, the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) itself, as directly recited, is the root authority.
Nor is the composition of the Smṛti text purposeless.

Because the composition of the Smṛtis is purposeful through the synthesis of different Vedic branches, the extraction of the meaning from explanatory passages (arthavādas), and the statement of matters established by logic;
therefore, it is established that the Smṛtis serve as the motivators for dharma and adharma precisely by bringing to mind their foundational Vedic texts (mūla-śruti).

[The *nibandhana*] is the statement of the necessity of performing those rituals whose details are scattered here and there, found in other contexts, mentioned as if already established, or are yet to be told, and which cannot tolerate the presence of [unrelated] qualities within the injunctions;
for the authors of the *Smṛtis*, such as Manu and others, are indeed more reliable authorities.
That tradition is endowed with merit because it was composed by a virtuous author and because it differs from the conduct of ordinary people;
thus this is evident.

Furthermore, since the practices of those who perform them are scattered throughout various other contexts and lack intrinsic merit, one must necessarily accept that these were understood and then established for practice by the great sages (*maharṣis*) themselves after they had realized their efficacy.

Therefore, since conduct (*ācāra*) is a source of knowledge only through the postulation of a Smṛti—which itself is a postulation of something that has already occurred—it is difficult to establish its authority according to the principles of the *Chāndogyopaniṣad*.

Furthermore, by means of conduct, only the mere form of the action (*karmasvarūpa*) is perceived directly; however, its status as something to be performed (*kartavyatā*) must be inferred through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), after first investigating other possible causes such as the meaning of the words or direct Vedic revelation.
And having inferred that [status], one subsequently infers the existence of its source (the Veda); thus, there is a great remoteness (*viprakarṣa*).

Furthermore, in the Smṛtis, the duty to act is understood immediately from other sources, whereas only the root [the Veda] remains to be inferred; thus, there is proximity [of the Smṛti to the Veda]. Moreover, in all cases where conduct contradicts the Smṛtis—such as matters concerning marriage with the daughter of a maternal uncle—an alternative cause such as desire is clearly observed; therefore, it is not possible to even conceive of a basis in Śruti for these practices in any way whatsoever.
Furthermore, since an option (vikalpa) is impossible here, validity cannot belong to both [Smṛti and Śruti], because an option is only possible regarding a factual matter (vastu).

For it is not possible that there be confidence in the marriage of a maternal uncle’s daughter, nor can its long-term non-arising be established; thus, one must resort to the invalidity of one or the other.
In this case, it is established that the practice whose cause is being perceived is invalid; therefore, it is proven that such types of practices constitute bad conduct.

Bhāṭṭa: Where there is a conflict between Smṛti and Ācāra, as in the case of marrying the daughter of one's maternal uncle and so forth, both have the capacity to imply a Śruti and are of equal strength.

This being the prima facie view, [the Siddhāntin replies]: because the Smṛtis were composed by persons of reliable authority and because in the Smṛtis one hears an injunctive suffix expressing that something "must be done," the Smṛtis possess greater force.

Regarding *ācāras* (customary practices), however, there is weakness [in their authority] because they depend upon those who practice them, because there is an absence of trustworthiness, because they are understood as having come down through a tradition scattered here and there, and because the injunctive suffix (*vidhi-pratyaya*) expressing the necessity of performance must be inferred from the mere observation of another's conduct.

For this very reason, when one observes contemporary custom, one infers a *smṛti* or an instruction based on that [custom] by assuming a seer of the *śruti*, and thus speaks of its status as *smṛti*; whereas for the [ancient] *smṛtis*, the distinction is that they are [based on *śruti*] directly.
Therefore, in the event of a conflict with *smṛti*, there is no authorization for conduct (*ācāra*) until a corresponding *śruti* or *smṛti* is observed.
According to the views of Maṇḍana and Kumārila, the relative degree of authority between *smṛti* and established conduct is examined in this section.

While the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that both possess equal authority because both are rooted in the Veda, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that *smṛti* alone possesses the stronger authority; for *smṛti* is directly rooted in the Veda, whereas it is only possible to assume that established conduct is rooted in the Veda through its dependence on *smṛti*.

Even following this logic, one should not accept either that [prior] truth or its subsequent [contradiction].
For there is no contradiction in the moonlight appearing at its own proper time. (Satyāṣāḍha Śrautasūtra 8.8.27) *Jyotsnā* commentary.
This is the sūtra of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position regarding the subject matter of the form of a woman pregnant with a fetus:

"He who, intending to sacrifice with Soma, establishes the sacred fires (agnyādheya), shall not wait for the season nor for the lunar mansion. This raises the question: is this a prohibition of certain times for the establishment of the fires, or is it a prohibition of the time for the Soma sacrifice? In considering this, the author states the prima facie view.
From the sūtra, "The Soma sacrifice should belong to the Brāhmaṇa in cases of advancement" (5.4.14.0), the word *soma* is carried over [from the previous context].
The Soma sacrifice should take place at its own [prescribed] time;

however, there would be a sublation of the time for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), because there is no contradiction, as there is no conflict between the time of the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the primary (*adhika*).

But if there were a sublation of the primary time, there would be a conflict; or rather, there is a removal [of the restriction], because the *iṣṭi* sacrifice may take place at all times. This is the sūtra of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In the case of the view that the *ādhāna* (fire-laying) is preceded by the *soma* sacrifice, there would be an exclusion (*apanaya*) or sublation of the time of the *soma* sacrifice itself by the rule: "One should not wait for the season, nor for the lunar mansion.

Since the time for the *ādhāna* is unrestricted—as it is stated, "On whatever day faith comes upon him, on that very day he should perform the *ādhāna*"—the prohibition [of waiting for a specific time] need not be made;
the *ādhāna* should be performed at all times.
The word "or" (vā) is for the purpose of refuting the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
Therefore, there is only a sublation of the time of the Soma sacrifice.
Who [says this]?

In the *Tantraratna* commentary on the section [Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 5.4.15], "Because there would be no contradiction at its own time," the statement from the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, "Whensoever he might come, he should study; then he should sacrifice," is treated as the subject for the injunction of another season within the Jyotiṣṭoma.
It is stated by implication that the remainder of that passage, "The seasons are indeed free from evil," has the character of an injunction regarding time.
The maxim is that one's own species returns more quickly;
there is a verse on this point as follows:

On the bank of the Gaṅgā, a female mouse fell from the sky after being dislodged from the root of a tree belonging to a certain sage. Seeing her, the sage, his heart moistened with compassion, transformed her into a human girl by the power of his ascetic yoga and gave her to a childless woman of his own caste.
Having been raised in that manner, she became a young sow.

Then, after the Sun, Parjanya, and the Mountain had arrived to seek her hand in marriage, the sage said to his daughter: "My daughter, choose whichever one you prefer among these. Having observed them—the Sun and the others—who were named Deha, Kṛṣṇavarṇa, Vajraḍāmaraka, Aticapalātman, and Kaṭhinastabdhagātra, she chose the latter.
Then that sage, having announced the mouse by name, said to the girl: "Daughter, choose him.
Then, upon seeing the mouse, she became delighted and said to the sage: "May he be like my own kind."
She said, "Venerable sir, having turned me back into a mouse as before, give me to the rat.
The sage did exactly so, and said:
"The sun, the husband, the eldest brother, the rain-cloud, the wind, and the mountain..."
"The mouse has attained its own kind; its own kind is swift in its course.
Thus ends the *Sāhasī*, verse 808.
"The very nature of the good is to be for the sake of others, just as the validity of perceptions is inherent in them"—this is the maxim expressed by Śrī Harṣa. Its meaning is as follows:

"hi" means because; since the quality of being for the sake of others—that is, the inclination toward helping others—arises from the very selves of the good, that is, from their own innate nature (*svabhāva*). This is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Just as cognitions—that is, acts of apprehension—are intrinsically true, so too is their validity (*prāmāṇya*).
The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the validity of cognitions is intrinsic and not extrinsic (*parataḥ*).
This is because when objects are grasped, they are known [by the cognition itself].

The term "by these" (*ebhiḥ*) refers to the organs of perception (*grahaṇāni*), that is, the sense faculties (*indriyāṇi*). Their "conformity to the object" (*yathārthatā*) means their functioning without overstepping the objects; the meaning is that they grasp each their own respective object.

Just as the sense faculties, such as hearing and the rest, perceive proximate objects like sound and so forth independently of anything else, so too do the virtuous (*sādhavaḥ*) benefit others without depending on the instigation of another—this is the intended meaning. (Sāhasī 973)

The intrinsic nature (*svatastva*) of validity consists in its not being dependent upon the excellence of the causes, corroboration by another cognition, or the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
This refers to the intrinsic nature of validity as constituted by correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*).
Intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇyam*) means not being dependent upon the excellence of the causes, corroboration, or the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*).
Bāla. pṛ. 5–6. The intrinsic validity of an injunction (*vidhi*) is due to the absence of the two causes of invalidity: non-accomplishment and dependence [on external factors].
Vi. 1.1.5; the validity of the injunction is intrinsic.
Because the intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of injunctions is accepted, there is no requirement for corroboration through results or other means in certain cases. (Vi. 1.1.5).
In the view of those who maintain that validity is intrinsic, a means of knowledge does not possess dependence on external factors.
Ownership.
And ownership by the deity does not arise merely through the act of relinquishment.
For in the act of appropriation, a relationship between owner and owned arises.
Bhāṣya 3.1.144. Ownership is characterized by the capacity for disposal according to one's will.
Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1534.
The means of ownership (*svatvopāya*): as in the case of grass and other items not previously appropriated by another, there must be an act of appropriation (*parigraha*). (Su. p.
1628). Even in the case of sale, there exists the relinquishment of one's own ownership and the transfer of ownership to another.

Or [it may be so]. PMS 3.4.1028, p. 961: "In the giving of one's own property, everything [is included] because there is no qualification. In the Viśvajit sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "He gives away his entire property (*sarvasva*)."
Therefore, when one must perform the gift of one's own property, then wealth, mother, father, land, and so forth—whatever is one's own—all that must be given.
This is because there is no distinction; since there is an absence of a specific statement such as "this is to be given" and "this is not to be given," [all is included].
Such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
Alternatively, it belongs to one who is its master, because for anyone else it is impossible [to give].

In the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, regarding the gift of all one's possessions (*sarvasva-dāna*), since even one’s father and others are one’s own property, they should be given; this is what was established by the *sūtra* of the prima facie view. By using the word "or" (*vā*), [the author] sets aside that position and states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

It should not be given by the father and others; rather, only that which the sacrificer is the master of may be given. Since it is impossible to give that over which one has no mastery, such a thing is not subject to being given.
Nor is a son the master of his father;
therefore, [wealth] such as that belonging to a father should not be given away.
In this regard, the reading from the *Kutūhala*, "for whomsoever there is mastery, because it is impossible for the other," is also more appropriate.
For the intellect that possesses thorough knowledge of itself leads to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
*Bṛhatī*, p. 167.

The principle of self-luminosity and non-dependence: just as light does not depend on another source for its own manifestation, so too, for actions whose fruits are heard in their own scriptural injunctions, heaven is not the fruit.

In the case of an optional rite (*kāmya-karman*), heaven is constant, just as the ritual purpose (*kratvartha*) is constant in a subsidiary part of a sacrifice. Commentary: Optional rites are the examples, such as “One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya,” and so forth.
In this regard, there is a doubt: is heaven the fruit of these optional rites, or is it only the specific desire [stated in the injunction]?
What is established? That in the case of optional (kāmya) action, heaven is the constant result.
How so? A word expressing a general human goal does not become restricted to a specific [result];
for it can indeed be connected with this term "desirous of heaven" (svargakāma), even though that term is difficult to apply [in the context of obligatory rites].
He said: "But surely a qualifying word is heard, namely 'desiring spiritual luster' (brahmavarcasakāmaḥ). [The opponent replies:
"This is not a qualifier."
This is an instance of a secondary condition (*upādhi*).
For example, when someone has set out to fetch firewood, one says, "You must also fetch some vegetables.
Here, the fetching of vegetables is made a secondary condition for the fetching of firewood.
Why is this "accessory" (upādhi) employed?
A second object is placed near the agent of the act of fetching wood,
with the sense that "when the fetching of wood has taken place, this other thing must also be done."
In the same way here as well, another result is added to the result that is heaven: "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should bring about heaven by means of sacrifice.
For the statement regarding the result of spiritual luster there does not constitute a prohibition of the result of heaven;
it is just as [the injunction] regarding a subsidiary of the sacrifice for the sake of the ritual: "One desiring cattle should fetch water with a milking vessel."
"One who desires cattle should accomplish the carrying forward [of the fire] by means of the milking of cows. [Śabara says:
"The injunction 'one should offer' impels every person.
In that case, if heaven is desired as the fruit, there is no contradiction of the expression denoting human effort."
For everyone desires nothing but pleasure;
therefore, heaven is the fruit [of action].
And because when the cause has ceased, [the result] necessarily follows.
Commentary: When the cause has ceased, when the desire for the fruit has vanished, or when the fruit has been obtained, a rule of completion is observed.
For example, regarding the desire for rain: "If it rains, one should offer the oblation at that very time;
if it does not rain, one should offer it on the following day."
If heaven were not [the result], for what purpose would there be a rule regarding completion?
Therefore, heaven is eternal.
Or rather, desire is enjoined through its connection with that.
Commentary: Or rather, the result may be desire itself, not heaven.
Its injunction occurs through connection with that [desire], not through connection with "one who desires heaven.
Its status as being part of the same sentence with "one who desires heaven" is merely inferential.
But it is directly perceived in the case of the statement regarding desire; and direct perception is more authoritative than inference. Therefore, desire alone is the fruit.

Because it is a subordinate element (*guṇa*) in a subsidiary part (*aṅga*). Commentary: Now, as for what was stated, “just as in the case of a subsidiary part of a sacrifice,” that is correct, because it is a subordinate element in a subsidiary part.

In that case, the connection with the season (*ṛtu*) and with desire (*kāma*) is directly perceived [in scripture], as in: "He who desires cattle should accomplish the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) by means of the milking of cows.
But here there is no direct scriptural statement such as: "He who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should accomplish heaven by means of the sacrifice.
How then [is it understood] that "he who desires spiritual luster should accomplish it by means of that sacrifice"?
Therefore, it is appropriate [to conclude] that it is like the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).
And the restriction regarding the *vīta* [rite] is for that purpose.

The Commentary states: Now, as for what was said—"Whether the desire for the fruit has ceased or not, a restriction regarding the completion [of the rite] is observed when the fruit is absent"—[this is the point].
To this we reply:
"The restriction applies when [the substance] has been used, for that purpose.
The restriction occurs when it has been used, for that specific purpose.

For what purpose? To avoid being censured by enemies. For if one were to begin a work and fail to complete it, the learned would immediately criticize him, saying, "This man is a coward who merely started something."
For those who, having intended an oblation for the gods, do not bring the sacrifice to completion, the learned (śiṣṭas) censure them.
Therefore, it must necessarily be completed.
Consequently, that scriptural observation will be consistent: "If it rains, one should offer only so much."
Therefore, for optional rites (*kāmya*), desire itself is the fruit.

Śa [objection]: In cases where a fruit is heard in scripture, such as "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya," is that [rite] for the sake of heaven and for the sake of the heard fruit, or only for the sake of the heard fruit? This is the doubt.
In this regard: "The injunction (*vidhi*), in its general form, is indeed the motivator for all [rites]."
And heaven is sought by all; thus, there is the determination that [the action] has that as its purpose.
Now it is said: "That [cognition] which arises from a word alone as a non-specific perception is established as such only when there is syntactic unity with other words and so forth."
If this injunction were intended for those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) and so forth,
there would likewise be a mutual dependence (*anyonyasaṃśraya*).

Therefore, *brahmavarcasa* (spiritual luster) alone is the fruit. Soma [says]: "In the case of optional rites (*kāmya-karma*), heaven is the fruit; however, in rites with obligatory fruits, *brahmavarcasa* and so forth are the *anvācya* (incidental) fruits. This is just as in the case of ritual subsidiaries such as the throwing of the *prastara* grass-bundle: while the assistance to the sacrifice (*ṛtūpakāra*) is obligatory, the manifestation of the *sūktavāka* hymn and so forth is the incidental fruit; it is the same here."

In the Bhāṣya, however, based on the usage of the Sūtrakāra in such passages as "one should desire a ritual act for the sake of the sacrifice" (*kratau kratukāmaṃ kāmayeta*) or "a subsidiary of the sacrifice [fulfills] the desire for the sacrifice" (*yajñāṅgaṃ vā yajñāṅgakāmam*), the term *yajñāṅga* (subsidiary of the sacrifice) is intended to include things like the *godohana* vessel and so forth. Vi: "Whether the result is mentioned in the scripture or not, one [result] is indeed heard; the *saurya* sacrifice is said to have all [results]. Ādyo: "Not so; because the expectation for a result is satisfied by what is explicitly stated in the scripture alone."

The Sūtra has been composed for the benefit of students to dispel the doubt of those of dull intellect who might think: "If even in cases where the fruits are explicitly stated—such as Vedic learning (*śruta*), Brahmanic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*), and so forth—the assumption of heaven (*svarga*) is made for the sake of securing a 'great scope' (*mahāviṣayatva*) for the scripture, while Brahmanic splendor and the like are merely incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*), like long life and other such benefits, then what need be said regarding the Rātrisatra?

[The answer is: When there is a desire for a fruit, the fruit that is actually heard in the text (*śrutaphala*) itself satisfies that requirement; furthermore, because it would lead to the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the introduction of multiple [fruits], there is no assumption of heaven.
Moreover, the absence of a "great scope" is not a defect when there is a specific statement [of a particular fruit].

Although longevity and so forth are mentioned as two types of results [in other contexts], they are not applicable here because they are merely incidental. Maṇḍana: "In the case of rites performed for specific desires, each respective result is heard [in scripture].
Śaṅkara: "But heaven is not the result when another result is heard [in scripture]."

"According to the principle that 'a person is enjoined by an injunction to his own activity,' the injunction implies a productive urge (*bhāvanā*) consisting of human activity. (Kauṇḍinya Bhāṣya 2.4.13, p. 109).
This word "svarga" (heaven) denotes each individual [person] as one who destroys their own wealth, not the collective group. Bhāṣya 6.7.12.
The word "sva" (one's own) is indeed a means of proof based on the attainment of a specific function.
Bāla, p. 8:
From its own word, there is the assumption of the function [of another].
By the very word "paricarya," it is employed in the function of the sacrificial post (yūpa) in the injunction, "One should bind the animal to the paricarya."
Ḍuṇḍubha 9|2|12|40:
That which is prescribed in another branch of the Veda is set aside by that which is prescribed in one's own branch, because [the latter] has not [otherwise] been established.
Vārttika 13|7|14, p. 860.
That which is prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (śākhā) supersedes that which is prescribed in another Vedic branch;
for example, the offering after sunrise and so forth is superseded by the offering before sunrise and so forth.
Bālakrīḍā, p. 141.

Since the knowledge prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*), which arises from the study of one's own recitation (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*), is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the ritual action, when that [knowledge] is available, there is no requirement for another.
Bāla. pṛ. 99.
However, for those such as Brāhmaṇas who act according to their own capacity, the status of being an auxiliary is intended to be independent of what is possible or impossible [for them].
Or [it may be] so. (Vārttika 13|7|14, p.
825). Because they have been performed in their proper sequence by increasing them from their original position, there are three *upasads* in the *agniṣṭoma*.

In the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, there are six *upasad* rites. Regarding this, is there a repetition like that of a "staff-beating" (*daṇḍakalitavat*), where one performs three in sequence at once, and then those same three again in sequence? Or is it a purification in its own place (*svasthānaviśuddhi*), where the first is performed twice, the middle one twice, and the third twice? While the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that the repetition is like a staff-beating—is reached as a conclusion contrary to the established rule (*utsūtra*), the author states the final settled position (*siddhānta*).
The word *tu* (but) indicates that there is a fivefold repetition.
The *upasads* ought to increase from their own respective places;

because their sequence was established in the archetype (*prakṛti*), they possess a fixed order, and thus even in the fire-altar construction (*cayana*), it is possible to follow them by performing them according to their own specific places.
If, however, there were a repetition like that of a felled stick (*daṇḍakalitavat*), the established sequence would be sublated, because the first [vowel] would follow immediately after the third;
this would result in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the *kar* [suffix]. Why?
Purity of one's own position is like the study of a recitation chapter:
one should repeat a single section many times, the second section should be repeated many times, and likewise the third section.
Thus [it is stated in] Vi. 5.3.1 and 10.5.25.

Through purification in its own place (*svasthāna-viśuddhi*), there is repetition in the *Gavāmayana* sacrifice regarding the *nyūnīkā*. (See *Mīmāṃsā-mīmāṃsā-kośa*, p. 1979, under the section ‘*nyūnīkā-adhikaraṇa*’).
Through purification in its own place, the number of *upasads* is attained, but not in the manner of a "repeated staff" (*daṇḍakalita*).
Bhāṣya 5.3.12:
"The performance [of the ritual] by those who have undergone initiation for twelve days is through the purification of their own respective positions.
This is the maxim: "He asked for a sweet stick even while kissing his own child.
From such urine comes the attainment of a sweet stick;
the meaning is the acquisition of what was longed for by one's master.
The assignment (*nyāsa*). In the *Svatantrottara* and the *Mahāvrata*, there is a combination [of rites] such as heating (*tāpya*) and so forth for the dwelling in non-violence (*ahatāvāsa*).
See Mīko, p. 3132; regarding the phrase "in the *Mahāvrata* by means of heating and so forth," the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted.

A prohibition based on an independent explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is of two kinds: that which is based on an explanatory passage concerning a defect (*doṣa*), and that which is based on an explanatory passage concerning an established duty (*siddhakartavyatā*). Bāla. p. 30. An injunction (*vidhi*) [as a means of knowledge] based on an independent explanatory passage is of three kinds: that which is based on an explanatory passage concerning a result (*phala*), that which is based on an explanatory passage concerning an established duty, and that which is based on an explanatory passage concerning a narrative (*upākhyāna*).

Only when there is an independent desire [for milk] should the *godohana* vessel, which is prescribed for the purpose of the animal sacrifice and is to be employed with the animal, be used.
*Bhāṭṭadīpikā* 4.1.2, Section 1.

Exclusion of sleep (svapnaparyyudāsa): An injunction for the exclusion of sleep based on a cognition of dreaming is, for example: "One should not look at the rising sun" (Bālambhaṭṭī, p. 20). A svadhiti is a weapon used as an instrument of cutting (a small knife).
Ci. 914|2. The axe (svadhiti) is that which possesses the property of being well-cut. Bhāṣya 6|3|126: "He cuts with the axe.
According to its capacity, the axe is employed for the taking of meat.
"Or he anoints the animal with the blade of the *svadhiti*.
(Bhāṣya 9.13.188). Dream is an object of apprehension.

For instance, in a dream, objects such as the severing of one's head—which belong to places and times experienced during the day—appear as if they were occurring within the self due to sleep, while being remembered through the force of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), under the influence of the defect consisting of sleep.
Thus, there is the appearance of things understood as being related to one [object] as being related to another, like the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
Nor should it be asked how there can be such an appearance regarding external objects since the mind is not then connected to them;
for there is no fault, because we accept the "cognition-characterized" (jñānalakṣaṇā) proximity, or because of the presentation of that which has its "that-ness" (tattā) obscured.

Therefore, it is established that dream-cognitions have external objects as their content. *Maṇiprabhā*, p. 96. *Oṃ*—The maxim "In a dream, one is a king": this refers to the passage, "Just as in a dream, having become a king, one enjoys desired pleasures..."
Having conquered his enemies on the field of battle and emerged victorious over other kings, he entered the forest and practiced austerities; there,
he considered even a mere moment to be the duration of a kalpa.
"In the very same way, even while awake, he forms such desires;
yet, due to the force of time, he does not perceive that his lifespan has been exhausted.
Thus it is said.
[The case of] the impulsive [act]. 907. The mantra "O Agni, you are heat" is for the purpose of [inducing] sleep.
One employs this mantra with reference to the entire night.
When, having awakened, one sleeps again, there is a repetition of the mantra, as in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Bhāṣya 9.14.1750: For even in dreams and the like, there is the occurrence of thought, vision, and so forth;
indeed, even in a dream, one experiences the suffering of sleep.
[This is] because the unseen [force] (adṛṣṭa) is the cause of pleasure and pain.

Therefore, it is established that dream-cognition and the like have the unseen (adṛṣṭa) as their cause, while some [cognitions] have reflection and the like as their cause; thus, it is logical that dream-cognition is equal to the cognition of mother-of-pearl and similar objects.
(*Bṛhatī*, p. 55). Dream-cognition and the like are first established as false.
If that [dream-cognition] were indeed based on an external object, then its falsity would not be possible.
It is like the cognition of one who is awake, which possesses correct conviction.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to postulate another cause for falsity even when an object exists;
therefore, the Buddhists maintain that falsity consists precisely in the absence of an object.

*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 54: Because it produces cognitions such as dreams, another [factor] generates pleasure and pain that are not seen by others; thus, the dream-eater [is the cause]. *Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 55: From the commencement of the dream until its conclusion, the mind (*manas*) which exists in a state of sleep (*sannidra*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the cognitions arising [during that time]; therefore, sleep (*nidrā*), being a defect of the instrument, is the cause of falsity (*mithyātva*).
Vaidyanātha, p. 30: The cause of dreams.
Furthermore, it is not only the thought occurring at that very moment which is the cause of a dream, but rather even one produced at some other time by way of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, even a thought existing during the waking state is a cause of a dream, as is the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).

(Ṛjuvimalā, p. 55). Even though the knowledge of an elephant and so forth produced in a dream is false, it possesses the nature of Dharma because it serves as a means to attain the highest good (*śreyas*).

*Maṇi*, p. 9: Dream-cognition, first of all, because it lacks present causal instruments (*karaṇa*), and because that which was experienced on the immediately preceding day appears in the dream as if it were occurring now, is merely a memory born of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Consequently, even if something not experienced in this life is experienced in a dream, its existence is established by the necessity of explaining it otherwise (i.e., through experience in another life). *Ratnākara*, p. 327: "Oṃ; likewise in the case of the *svapnan-daryatābhivarṣaṇa* [mantra], the *amedhya-pratimantra*, and so forth."
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, for the ritual recitation upon dreaming or sleeping, the mantra is: "O Agni, you are the burner.
For crossing a river, it is: "O divine waters... For being rained upon, it is: "Wetting, they bestow vigor. And for seeing something impure, it is: "This eye has seen blood."

When, however, one who has awakened during a single night sleeps again; when one crosses a river with many currents; when one grows in continuity; or when one sees various impurities for the duration of a kalpa—at that time, regarding the deliberation that there should be a repetition of the mantra for each instance and its initial application once, he states the established conclusion: in the case of dreaming, crossing a river, raining, and impurity, the mantra is applied only once, just as in the case of [the aforementioned] throat-related [acts]. What is the basis for this conviction regarding the dream?
On the other hand, the falsity of dream-cognition is understood from its opposite [waking cognition];
for the dream-cognition of one who is asleep arises due to the weakness of the mind. 4851. It is a vision of heaven.

Sleep is the cause of the state of non-apprehension (*mithyābhāva*) in dreams and the like; and at the end of a dream, there is indeed the absence of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Upon waking, one says, "My mind was exhausted by sleep.
Even during a dream, the intellect (*buddhi*) was dependent upon deep sleep.

Prior to awakening, due to the perception of error within the void (of the mind), as stated in the *Bhāva-vṛtti* commentary on verse 1.15.5, pages 29–30: "The logic of the analogy of a dream. For example: a tiger seen in a dream, having been dissolved in that dream by one who remains there, dissolves along with itself in its form as an object of negation; so it is in the present case as well.

VI. 3.3.1: The accent of the Veda that enjoins [the rite] (viniyojaka-veda-svara) is stronger than the accent of the Veda that produces it (utpādaka-veda-svara).

In optional sacrifices (kāmyeṣṭi), the low-voiced quality (upāṃśutva) applies only to the principal act; however, for the subsidiary acts (aṅga), the sound follows the Vedic accent of those specific subsidiaries.
Even the *ṛc* verses contained within the *Yajurveda* are to be recited in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). [Discussion on accents:

But surely, by this same principle, even the *stotras*, *śastras*, and so forth belonging to the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice prescribed in the Yajurveda would also attain the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*).
True, it would follow; however, due to specific scriptural injunctions (*vacana*), other accents are obtained in all such cases.

How so? First, regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, when various Vedic accents would apply to the subsidiary parts (aṅga) prescribed in different Vedas, the rule concerning the conflict between the subordinate and the principal (guṇamukhyavyatikrama-nyāya) establishes that the property of the principal—namely, the Yajurvedic quality of whispering (upāṃśutva)—would prevail. Subsequently, however, there occurs a scriptural (vācanika) accentuation: "with a low tone until the end of the Ājyabhāgas," "with a medium tone thereafter," and "with the highest tone from the Anuvākyās onwards."

Likewise, when the three accents of the archetype (*prakṛti*) would apply to the modified rites (*vikṛti*) such as the *iṣṭi* and *putra* sacrifices, and the accent of the primary Veda (*pradhāna-veda*) would consequently be applicable through direct instruction, the accent brought by the extended application (*codaka*) is indeed preferred. This is because, according to the principle "or, by taking that [the archetype], it should have its own property," the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*) is weaker due to its dependence on the extended application. Thus, the acceptance of the accent introduced by the extended application is desired.

Thus, even in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma and its subsidiaries such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā, when the archetypal (prākṛta) accent would apply but is set aside by direct instruction (pratyakṣopadeśa), it is reinstated by the superior force of the extended application (codaka). However, since the Jyotiṣṭoma belongs to the Yajurveda and does not adopt the archetypal qualities whose utility is already established elsewhere, when there arises an occasion for applying those subsidiary qualities according to the principle of the transposition of the subordinate and the principal (guṇamukhyavyatikrama-nyāya), these accents—namely, "one should recite the Dīkṣaṇīyā with as much voice as one desires"—belong to the entire ritual, including its subsidiaries, by that very principle of the transposition of the subordinate and the principal.

Therefore, because the scripturally prescribed division of accents for the Jyotiṣṭoma—consisting of the determination of low (*mandra*), middle (*madhya*), and high (*uccaiḥ*) intonation—is established, all those who know it acquire the original accentuation of low, middle, and high intonation through the primary rite itself.

Consequently, regarding the rule "Whatever is prior to the Abhiṣomīya, they perform that in a low voice" (*upāṃśu*), which establishes low-voiced performance for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites along with their subsidiaries, these specific tones—prescribed by the words *dīkṣaṇīyā* and so forth for the primary rites alone—are applied only to the primary rites themselves, according to the injunctions: "One should recite the *dīkṣaṇīyā* with as much voice as one desires; [one should recite] softly at the *prāyaṇīyā*; [and] with a soft tone during the *upasads*."

In that context, since the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is already established by the preceding all-pervasive injunction for whispering, the mention of the conclusion regarding the pitch of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites is merely a restatement (*niṣṭhānuvāda*). However, in the case of the *agnīṣomīya*, there is a reinstatement of the original (*prākṛta*) pitches—such as "the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are in a low tone" (*mandrā ājyabhāgau*)—by means of the pitch according to the division of the *savana*. Alternatively, the division of the *savana* should be performed by dividing the entire ritual performance, including its subsidiaries, into three parts and accomplishing the utterance in low, middle, and high tones respectively.
By this, the specific modes of pronunciation for the *anūbandhyā*, *abhyudayanīyā*, and *udavasānīyā* sacrifices are also explained.

Although the same accent would thus apply to the *savanīya* offerings and others belonging to the time of the *soma* extraction (*sutyā*), their accents are determined according to the respective *savana* (pressing) because they occur within the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).

If it is argued that—since the word *savana* denotes parts of the *soma* sacrifice—the *savanīya* offerings should lack their own specific accents just as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* does, we say no; for by the use of the locative case, one relies merely on the fact that they are performed at those specific times.

If the genitive case were used where it follows the word *savanebhyaḥ*, then there would be a twofold [application] of the low pitch (*mandra*) only in the mantras that are its subordinate parts (*aṅga*). However,
when the locative case is used, the entire mantra which is employed as the substratum (*ādhāra*) for that [pitch] is affected.
The application of the *mandra* (low) pitch has been traditionally taught for all of that [the *savana*s].

Some say: "In this context, when [the *savana*s] serve merely as a substratum (*ādhāra*), then for them [the *savana*s] there would be no *mandra* pitch and so forth, because they are heard in scripture as not being things to be supported (*anādheyatā*)."
That which is heard as being subordinate (*ādheya*) to the base (*ādhāra*),

namely the *savanīya* sacrifice and so forth, should have its recitation performed in a low tone (*mandra*). However, whatever remains of the *savana*— such as the *stotra*, *śastra*, and *anuvākyā*— [is to be recited in a loud tone].
And because there is no genitive case [expressing possession], these notes such as *mandra* and so forth are logically connected to that [Svara];
when this is said, there is no fault, because even without the genitive,
this meaning of the genitive— conceived as its being the substratum— is indeed possible.

For just as a bird is perceived on a tree, or a foot on an animal, so too is that object which possesses the property of being located [in it] perceived there; both of these are indeed enjoined. Or rather, for us, the stotra, śastra, and so forth, constitute the very command for the soma-pressing.
The substratum for that [chanting] is likewise [the same] as in the case of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice.

Therefore, the various Vedic accents obtained at the outset for the *stotra* and other elements are subsequently set aside by the quality of being "unmanly" (*apuṃśu*), due to their lack of authority over the primary act.
Then, by means of the scriptural injunction itself,
we employ all the cognitions pertaining to the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*), characterized by the [three] pressings and beginning with the *mandra* [pitch].
By this, all modifications of the Jyotiṣṭoma— the *ekāhas*, *ahīnas*, and *satras*— are explained.
Regarding the discussion on musical notes (svaracarcā) [in sections] 44–55: if there is only one *svara-sāman*, how then will there be space for the various Vedic accents? It is replied:

it should be understood through postulation (*kalpanīya*), just as in the case of the rule: "Or, because of the mention of that, it shall have its own property, due to the force of the governing context, being manifest in the remainder."
As for the claim that when a modification (*vikṛti*) is endowed with the accents of the original form (*prakṛti*), an unprecedented subsidiary (*apūrva-aṅga*) belonging to another Veda is enjoined;

[the opponent objects: "But even there, by the principle of the conflict between the subordinate and the principal (*guṇa-mukhya-vyatikrama-nyāya*), it is simply the status of the principal's property [that applies].

[The proponent offers an alternative view: "In that case, the subject matter is as follows: when a modification occurs in a particular Veda, regarding its remaining subsidiaries which have attained their status according to the original form, that which is enjoined in that very same Veda as an intermediate unprecedented element (*antarapūrva*) is the scope [of this rule]."
(Objection: That [accession] also is obtained only by way of the primary sacrifice.
(Another alternative objection: In that case, the primary sacrifice itself is the object [of the injunction], no; for even that is already encompassed by the original [archetypal] form. (Response:
Therefore, there is no acquisition of a new subsidiary by way of the primary sacrifice; thus, that [new subsidiary] alone is the object.
Even so, this is not the case, because that which is the characteristic of the primary [element] exists there as well.

Furthermore, when the sacrificial portion (*yajñabhāga*) and the sin (*agha*) have been divided into three parts and established in the accent (*svara*), even that which is unprecedented (*apūrva*) is included therein; thus, it does not possess the same status as the accent of the sacrificial post-hole (*yūpāvaṭasvara*) or the *barhis* grass. Therefore, it must necessarily be governed by the archetypal (*prākṛta*) rule. For this reason also, there is no scope [for the objection].
Furthermore, the recitation [of the rules] according to their respective contexts would be utterly meaningless.
(He resolves both doubts: Here is the solution: first of all, the rule "one should recite the Yajus in a low voice" is purposeful with respect to all types of Yajus-mantras.

The Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda also possess purposefulness regarding their auxiliary elements (aṅga) that are performed for specific desires (kāmya) or on specific occasions (naimittika). For instance, the rule "the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana) is to be chanted softly" (mandram), because it is permanent (nitya), cannot be superseded by the non-permanent (anitya) rites performed for desire or occasion; thus, it remains applicable specifically to the permanent rites.
Consequently, whatever is enjoined as either a desired or occasional rite by means of the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda must all be performed loudly (uccaiḥ).
Likewise, [the text says]: "One should touch that which is broken, thinking 'this is mixed with this,'" and so forth.
In this manner, the *upāṃśutva* (whispered tone) prescribed in the Yajurveda should also be cited as an example.

Similarly, regarding those auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) that take place after the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing), since there is no mention of the *savana* (pressing-period) in them, the accentuation follows the specific Veda itself; thus, the loudness (*uccaiḥ-svara*) of the *avabhṛtha-sāman* and other such elements is established.
Otherwise, the application [of the rules] would be arbitrary.
However, in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, there is low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) by virtue of the rule "prior to the *agnīṣomīya*";
whereas for the *pravargya-sāmans*, there is loud recitation (*uccaiḥ*) by the rule "the *pravargya* is with a loud voice."
However, regarding the *ādhāna-sāmans*, the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) applies to that Veda which is prescribed by the rules of the Yajurveda;
for the statements such as "He who, knowing thus, sings the Vāmadevya [sāman]" are indeed sentences of the Yajurveda.
(Vārttika 3.2.19, p. [number]).
Regarding the rule on pitch: "With whatever degree of voice one desires, with that same degree of voice [one should perform] the *dīkṣaṇīyā*.
This is not for the sake of the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, but rather only for the sake of the *apūrva* of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*.
Bāla. pṛ. 142.
Through specific accents, such as the acute (*udātta*) and others, one is able to understand the specific meaning in the determination of compound types such as the *bahuvrīhi* and *tatpuruṣa*. [Vi.
9|2|8, Description 3].

Since the word *svara* is seen in such passages as "The wind moving within the chest produces the deep tone (*mandra*) called *svara*" (Pāṇinian Śikṣā, verse 7), it is understood to refer to that which is produced by the conjunction and disjunction of air—namely, the sound (*nāda*), also known by the synonym *dhvani*, which is another name for the *mārutaka* sound.
Accent and grammatical refinement are capable of being endowed with a local quality (*prādeśika-guṇa*). (The root text of Yāska reads *syātām*.
Bhāṣya 10.4.

The first [day] has the Svarasāman as its leading element, the second has the Aindravāyava as its leading element, and the third has the Śukra as its leading element. (Tup. 10.5.25.85). In the Gavāmayana, there are three Svarasāmans surrounding the Divākīrtya; in the Aṣṭarātra, there is the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha and two Svarasāmans.
And two of those three elements are the *āhāva* (the call for response).
Bhāṣya 7.3.1.26:
"The *svarasāman*, the one-pot offering (*ekapāla*), and the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) [are to be understood as such] because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*)."
"They transpose the position for the sake of the subsequent *stomas* and for the sequential order of the three *saptadaśa*s"—so it is heard in the Śruti.

The meaning of this is explained in the *Kutūhala*: in the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), there are six days with the *stomas* of *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa*, *saptadaśa*, *ekaviṃśa*, *triṇava*, and *trayastriṃśat* respectively.
Here, the third day, which is the *saptadaśa* day, must be moved forward to the position of the *trayastriṃśat* day.
That being the case, there would be a continuity of three stomas—namely the *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa*, and *ekaviṃśa*—each exceeding the number sixty;

likewise, following the *trayastrimśat*, there would be an elevation of the *saptadaśa*, such that this one *saptadaśa* and the two *svarasāmans*, which are themselves *saptadaśa*, would constitute a continuous sequence of three *saptadaśas*. Thus, this term *svarasāman* occurring in the context of the *ahīna* sacrifice would be both a transmitter (*grāhaka*) and an extender (*atideśaka*) of the characteristics of the *svarasāmans* belonging to the *gavāmayana*.
Because the indicative mark (liṅga) is seen in the remainder of the statement:
only when the two Svarasāmans occurring in the Aghara and Rātra are seventeenfold does the continuity of three seventeenfold units occur, and not otherwise.
From this observation of the indicative mark, the term "Svarasāman" is a grasper of the property (dharma).

Likewise, in the Vaiśvadeva-parvan, it is heard in scripture: "There is a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth. Its specific ritual details (*dharmas*) are: "He offers it entirely" (*sarvahutam juhoti*), and "He offers it without turning [the ladle back]" (*aparyāvartayan juhoti*). In the Āmayana sacrifice, after prescribing the cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth, a sentence intended to enjoin clarified butter (*ājya*) states: "That he makes an entire offering is one fault (*paricakṣā*); that the offered oblation turns back is the second; therefore, one should sacrifice to Heaven and Earth with clarified butter alone. This shows that the two ritual details belonging to the Vaiśvadeva—namely, the complete offering and the non-turning—are understood as applicable here.

From this observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), the term *ekakapāla* occurring in the context of the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice is the indicator of the ritual properties belonging to the *ekakapāla* offerings within the *Vaiśvadeva* section.
Likewise, in the *Vaiśvadeva* section, there is the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) for the Viśvedevas;
therein, the distribution of the whey (*vājina*) takes place.
And there is the *āmikṣā* for Mitra and Varuṇa;
in that context, the performance with the *vājina* is prohibited by the statement, "They do not proceed with the *vājina*.
From this observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is understood that the *āmikṣā* for Mitra and Varuṇa adopts the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the *āmikṣā* for Viśve Devās.
Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the words *svarasāman*, *ekapāla*, and *āmīkṣā* are appropriators of ritual properties (*dharmagrāhaka*).
[The Sūtra states: "Or, because of the commonality of the injunction (*codanāsāmānyāt*).
And the indicative mark (*liṅga*) mentioned has been grasped on account of the commonality of the injunction.

And because of the commonality of the injunction (*codanā-sāmānyāt*), there is a commonality in the form of being *svarasāman*, a commonality in the form of being a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*), and a commonality in the form of being *āmīkṣā*.
[This refers to] the section concerning *svarasāman*, *ekakapāla*, and *āmīkṣā*.

There is an extended application (*atideśa*) of the characteristics of the *svarasāman* one-pot-sherd offerings and the curd offerings belonging to the Gavāmayana sacrifice to the *svarasāman* one-pot-sherd offerings and the curd offerings belonging to other ritual actions.
The *Svarasāman* [stotra], the *ekakapāla* [cake], and the *āmikṣā* [curd-mixture] [are to be taken from the *gavāmayana* sacrifice], because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
Commentary: In the *Gavāmayana*, it is heard: "On both sides of the *divākīrtya* day, there are three *svarasāman* days.
Their specific properties are prescribed, such as: "They consist of seventeen [verses]; the *atigrāhya* cups are drawn continuously," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is heard elsewhere: "The *ṣaḍaha* sacrifice consists of six days and two *svarasāman*s.
Likewise, in the *vaiśvadeva* [parvan], it is heard: "There is a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*).
