In that context, specific ritual details are prescribed: "He offers the entire oblation; he offers without turning [the ladle] back."
Furthermore, elsewhere it is said, "The sacrificial cake is for a single deity.
Likewise, in that very same context, it is heard: "The curdled milk is for the Viśvedevas.
There too, certain specific ritual details have been prescribed.
Furthermore, elsewhere it says, "The curd-offering belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa.

In that regard, there is a doubt: does the term *svarasāman*, when heard in another context, take over the ritual details (*dharmas*) from the *svarasāmans* belonging to the Gavāmayana sacrifice, or not? The same applies to the terms *ekakapāla* and *āmikṣā*.
In this regard, since it was established that "one should not take [the details] in the case of subsidiary injunctions of qualities because of their equality" (7.3.6.17), this is now stated:
the *svarasāman*, the *ekakapāla*, and the *āmikṣā* are the appropriators (*grāhaka*) of the ritual details.
What is the reason? Because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
An indicative mark (*liṅga*) is seen there by which it is known that all these are recipients of the ritual details (*dharma*) of the *gavāmayana*.

Regarding the *svarasāmans*, after stating, "The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period consists of two *svarasāmans*," it says: "In that regard, they transpose the seventeenth day, which is the third, to the position of the thirty-third [day], for the purpose of avoiding the subsequent *stomas* and for the sake of the sequential order of the three seventeen-fold [days].
If these two *svarasāmans* were recipients of the *gavāmayana* ritual details, then those two would also be seventeen-fold days.
Likewise, in this case, there are three sets of seventeen [stotras] arranged consecutively;
in that context, this statement is appropriate: "for the sake of the consecutive arrangement of the three sets of seventeen.
Likewise, in the Āgrayaṇa...

Having prescribed a cake on one potsherd for Earth, the text says: "That he performs a complete oblation (sarvahuta) is the first reproach; that the offered oblation turns back unoffered is the second; therefore, one should sacrifice to Heaven and Earth with clarified butter alone. This statement, which is intent upon prescribing clarified butter, shows that the two characteristics of the Vaiśvadeva—the complete oblation and the non-returning of the offering—are applicable here. Similarly, regarding the curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa, the text says, "They do not proceed with the whey (vājina)," and by thus prohibiting the whey, it indicates the applicability of the Vaiśvadeva characteristics to that rite.

From these signs it is known that they are the perceivers of the factors (dharmas) as they truly are. This was said considering the ritual action for the sake of attainment to be a matter of one's own will.
He says:
The indicative mark has been extended by analogy. Why?
Because there is a contradiction.
It is said in reply:
Acquisition is by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*); the adoption of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is by means of indication.
(Or, because of the commonality of the injunction. [Note:
In the Vṛtti manuscripts, the sūtra "codanāsāmānyādvā" does not appear after the sūtra "svarasāmaika0".]
Thus, this is indeed found everywhere.
Even in the Ānandāśrama edition of the *Māṣya*, that sūtra has been printed as its commentary (*bhāṣya*), albeit with some lacunae;
the same is the case in the Ma and Sā manuscripts as well.

However, the text printed as the commentary (*bhāṣya*) by this [same] Sūri does not accord with the meaning of the Sūtras in any way whatsoever. A single passage beginning with "From the indicative mark (*liṅga*), there is the acceptance of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), because of the commonality of the *svarasāman* quality" has been excised precisely from the section concerning the *saṃśardhaka* rite. We consider all of this to be rooted in negligence.

And there is the claim that "this Sūtra has not been explained by the Bhāṣya," and that two incomparable commentaries (*vṛtti*) exist on this point. Nevertheless, a doubt may arise that the Sūtra "codanāsāmānyādvā" (or [it is so] because of the commonality of the injunction) was indicated as a *jñāpaka* (indirect indicator) by the author of the *Tantraratna*. This is because, while commenting on the Svarasāman-sūtra (*yasya liṅgamarthasaṃyogāt*, 8.1.2.12), he introduces the *Vārttika* with a detailed passage stating, "by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) which makes one infer the injunctive sentence (*codakavākya*)," and with the words, "But what is the connection of the introduction of the name *āmīkṣā* with the extension (*atideśa*) caused by the indicative mark (*liṅga*), which is the injunction (*codanā*)? Thus, through these indications, the possibility of such a doubt exists.
Therefore, it must be accepted that this line of commentary would be as follows:
[Ke.
on account of the commonality of having the *svarasāman* chant, the commonality of having a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*), and the commonality of the *āmikṣā* curd-mixture.
The objection is raised by the rule "yasya liṅgamarthasaṃyogāt" (8.1.2.12). [The author] replies: This is commenced as a counter-exception to a previous exception;
it is an extension (*atideśa*) by means of a name.

The phrase "the *svarasāmans* belong to this" is a prescription of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*), just as in the case of the *Gavāmayana*, so too elsewhere in the statement: "The *ṣaḍaha* consists of the *pṛṣṭhya* [stomas], and there are two *svarasāmans*.
Furthermore, the mention of the *āmikṣā* and the *kapāla* are also prescriptions of accessories, because they prescribe specific substances.

Thus, since this is an injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*), when the absence of extension (*atideśa*) would otherwise result, extension is obtained by the rule "that which has a mark [of similarity] through connection with the meaning" (8.1.2.12). Śā—Because of these marks that have no other recourse, and which are reinforced by the words of the injunction such as *svarasāman* and so forth, there is the status of being its subject matter (*tadadhikāratva*). Soma—The connection here is due to the incidental occurrence of the fact that even the *ābhīka*, which is a specific extension based on the mark of the injunction (*codanāliṅga*), is a name (*nāmadheya*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because it is an injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*), even though there is no extension (*atideśa*) from the *Svarasāman* and other [archetypes] to the [Sāmans] in question, one may nevertheless assume an extension on the basis of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the injunction; thus, it is logical that they constitute modifications (*vikāra*) of the *Gavāmayana* and so forth.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Mādhavīya-vistara* that the rule "they carry around the position of the thirty-three" is an injunction of procedure (*vyākhyāvidhi*).
Nevertheless, it should be understood that the intended meaning of the seventeenth [section] is precisely as described above, and not a restrictive application (*viniyama*).

Regarding this, some say: "Since this *vājina* (curdled milk) is the primary substance and lacks the status of a subordinate (*aṅga*), it is not extended [to other rites]; therefore, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the observation of the non-prohibition of the *vājina* has been stated. This is incorrect.

Because the purpose of the substance in the *vājina*-vessel remains intact, and because this impermanent [substance] cannot be the object of an injunction of entitlement together with the permanent *īkṣā*-sacrifice and others, the prohibition of the *vājina* is appropriate, as its occasional status as a subordinate is likewise logical.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: because of the observation of the previously mentioned indicative marks (*liṅga*), the *svarasāman*, the *ekakapāla*, and the *āmikṣā* do not adopt the ritual details (*dharma*) of the Vaiśvadeva [parvan] within the Gavāmayana sacrifice.

Vi— "Are the *svarasāman* and so forth modifications (*vikāra*) or non-modifications? They are not, for they are not like the Vaiśvānara [sacrifice]. Do not say so; it is otherwise, due to the force of the indicative marks."

Bhaṭṭa: Previously, when the extension (*atideśa*) of the Soma-consecration ritual was refuted by the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the prohibition of the *uttaravedi*, the present section introduces an exception to that refutation by showing that there is indeed an extension even from such a mark.
In the *Gavāmayana* sacrifice, seventeen sacrifices characterized by the *saptadaśastoma* and other properties are enjoined under the statement: "There are three *svarasāman*s."
Elsewhere also, it is said: "There are two *svarasāman* [chants].

Likewise, in the Vaiśvadeva section, there are two sacrifices possessing the same characteristics (*sadharmaka*), namely: "The curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) for the Viśvedevas, and the cake on one potsherd (*ekapāla*) for Heaven and Earth.

Elsewhere as well, sacrifices having curd-mixture and a cake on one potsherd as their materials are heard in the scriptures, such as: "The curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa, and the cake on one potsherd for Ka," and so forth.

In considering whether the Svarasāman sacrifices—such as the Gavamaya—are of the same nature as the Vaiśvadeva Svarasāman, or whether other Āmikṣā sacrifices are of the nature of the Vaiśvadeva Āmikṣā sacrifice, and whether other Ekakapāla offerings are of the nature of the Vaiśvadeva Ekakapāla, the conclusion is that they are not. This is because the requirement for a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is satisfied by an extended application (*atideśa*) based on a figurative description (*guṇavāda*), and since terms such as "Svarasāman" function merely as injunctions of qualities—namely, the *sāman* called "Svara"—they do not effect an extended application; thus, these sacrifices do not have the Vaiśvadeva as their archetype (*prakṛti*).

This being the case, because the assumption of an extended application (atideśa) based on the indicative mark (liṅga)—which is supported by specific features such as having naturally occurring *sāman* chants and which takes into account the association with qualities like [the *guṇa*]—is more appropriate than [relying on] the indicative mark of the injunction (*codanāliṅga*), it follows that [the sacrifice] has that [original sacrifice] as its archetype (*tatprakṛtika*).

And regarding the *liṅga* (indicative mark) in the context of the *svarasāman*s, after stating, "The six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) consists of the *pṛṣṭhya* and two *svarasāman*s," it says: "In that regard, they transpose the seventeenth day, which is the third, to the position of the thirty-three-fold hymn-form (*trayastriṃśat-stoma*); this is for the sake of the non-interruption of the subsequent hymn-forms and for the sequential order of the three seventeen-fold hymn-forms. This shows that the two *svarasāman*s consist of the seventeen-fold hymn-form. Furthermore, in the *Maitrāvaruṇa-iṣṭi*, [it says]: "Or rather, the *svaru*..."
The *svaru* is mentioned;
however, in your view, there is an even greater contradiction with the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
The meaning is the locus (dharmin) of the word;
the word, too, is the locus of the sequence. When one desires to favor the property of the word, its locus is sublated.
This is the sublation of the primary by the subsidiary.

Therefore, because the word "sacrificial post" (yūpa) functions as a secondary indicator (lakṣaṇā), the other mode of expression is that "that which one makes into a svaru, that belongs to the sacrificial post. With this intention, he says: "Even the direct Vedic statement (śruti) is set aside, as is the syntactical connection (vākya)," and also because of the mention of the splinter (śakala).
Commentary: For this reason as well, there is the taking of that which is produced as a by-product of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Why? Because of the scriptural mention of a "chip" (*śakala*).
There is a scriptural mention of a chip in the form of the *svaru*.
"That first splinter which falls away should be made into the *svaru*"; here, "splinter" (*śakala*) refers to a single part; it is that which necessitates a single part.
Because it is a relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*),
it refers to the whole by way of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

In that context, through the force of the subject matter (*prakaraṇa*), this [term] forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the previously mentioned act of selecting (*joṣaṇa*) and so forth— which is for the purpose of the sacrifice— by means of the *khadira* wood and other materials intended for another purpose.
One selects, cuts, and fashions the *khadira* wood and other materials for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

In that context, it is said: "The first chip that falls away, one should make that into a *svaru* for the purpose of anointing. In this case, the word *svaru* is used merely as a figurative reference (*anuvāda*) to that [first chip].
Therefore, it is not the case that the *svaru* is produced separately, such that it could be [obtained] from another tree as well.

Consequently, its being denoted by a different class [of wood] is a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*), and the term "chip of the sacrificial post" (*yūpaśakala*) serves the same purpose. Furthermore, this is because we observe [the practice] for every sacrificial post (*pratiyūpam*).
Commentary: For this reason as well, the *svaru* is produced separately.

Why? Because it is observed in connection with each sacrificial post (*yūpa*) in the context of the set of eleven posts (*ekādaśinī*). The text, "Having anointed the animals with the *svarus* in their respective order, he takes hold of his own respective post-shavings on the middle loop of the cord," demonstrates the plurality of *svarus*.
If the *svaru* were produced independently, then a single one would suffice to accomplish the purpose through a common procedure (*tantra*) in the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice.

However, since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the washing of the *svaru* was performed as a by-product of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the extended injunction (*codaka*) likewise applies to the *ekādaśinī*.
Thus, it brings about the very shavings of one's own post, and so the plurality [of *svarus*] becomes logically established.
And the non-mention of its own sacrificial post-shard (*svayūpaśakala*) is inferred from the mention of the ordinary one;
for that which is the ordinary one must be taken as it is, not as something distinguished.
Therefore, the *svaru* is not the motivator (*prayojaka*) of its production.
The word "karoti" (he does) is used in the sense of taking up.
Commentary: Now, as for what was said—that its production is expressed by the word, such that "he makes the *svaru*," and thus the word "makes" (*karoti*) will be appropriate—it is replied:
the word "makes" will apply to the act of taking up [the wood].
"He makes the *svaru*—he takes up the *svaru*.
Just as the word "makes" (*karoti*) is used in the sense of taking up, as in "he makes [fuel] from wood" or "he makes [fuel] from cow-dung," so too should it be understood here.
(In the Ānandāśrama edition of the Bhāṣya, the reading is *svarustu*).
The commentary on these six sūtras by the author of the Bhāṣya, arranged as separate sentences, has been printed;
however, we do not include it here.
Regarding this, it is stated in the marginal note (ṭippaṇī): "The Bhāṣya is found in one manuscript, but not in another."
Śālikanātha:
"The root *kṛ* (to do) expresses *bhāvanā*, and that [bhāvanā] is enjoined by direct statement (*śruti*).
Otherwise, there would be an injunction of a sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) or a recourse to indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*)."
"Thus, the *svaru* would be the instigator [of the act].
This is not so;
for in this way, there would be an injunction of many things, and it would involve the secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the primary term.
From this [source], there is an injunction for a minor purpose, and the indication of that which is inferior.
Since it is produced as a by-product (*anuniṣpanna*) from the wood-chips (*śakala*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the *svaru* is not an independent motivator (*aprayojaka*).
Regarding the Soma sacrifice: is this *svaru* a motivator for the cutting and other operations of the *khadira* and other woods, or is it not?
For that purpose, one must determine whether the *svaru* is to be taken as something produced separately from the post, or as a by-product (*anuniṣpanna*) of the post itself.

Regarding this, there arises a doubt: does the injunction "he makes the *svaru*" enjoin the production (*bhāvanā*) of the *svaru*, or does it enjoin the material source for the procurement of the *svaru*? [The conclusion is:
if the *svaru* is destroyed, the offering must be performed with any fragment whatsoever, and one should not again employ a carpenter or others for the sake of the *svaru*.
For it is said: "In the statement 'he makes the *svaru*,' the cutting is distinct from the *svaru* itself."
Or let it be by means of that which is to be employed; for it belongs to the qualified [agent] because of the injunction.
Since the first sacrificial post-section is enjoined with the specific qualification of being a *svaru*, there is parsimony [in this view]; therefore, it is indeed a by-product (*anuniṣpanna*).

In the *Bhāṭṭa* school’s interpretation of the animal sacrifice (*daikṣa-paśu*), it is heard in scripture: "He makes a *svaru* from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); he anoints the animal with the *svaru*.

Since the word *svaru* is not well-known [in common usage], the first sentence ("He makes a *svaru* from the sacrificial post") enjoins a productive operation (*bhāvanā*) having the *svaru* as its object.

In that context, when there is a requirement for a substance to serve as the instrument, the statement "The first splinter (*śakala*) that falls off shall be the *svaru*" establishes that the splinter is the instrumental means.

Because the word *svaru* [is used] repeatedly, when there is a requirement for the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*), the acts such as anointing and sprinkling are enjoined by means of the term *yūpa* through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of its properties.
Alternatively, just as in the final position (siddhānta) the meaning of the genitive case is the state of being made into a sacrificial post (yūpa),
so too the relationship consisting in the possession of the characteristics of a sacrificial post is the meaning of the genitive;
thus, there is not even a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
And for that which has been thus produced, there is an application (*viniyoga*) by means of the second sentence (*"svaruṇā paśumanakti"*).

Or rather, let it be that, based on the second sentence, there is an injunction of only the properties of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) whose object is already established; even so, it is not a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).

Nor is this the case, because the status of belonging to the sacrificial post (*yūpīyatva*) is established for the splinter (*śakala*) precisely from its being a correlative (*saṃbandhika*), as in the case of the "upper part" (*uttarārdha*) and so forth.
There is the consequence of [the argument] being non-conclusive (*aprayojakatva*).

For even if the wood is not the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the *svaru* itself, it is still possible for it to be the motivator of the properties such as cutting and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) residing in the *svaru*.

Precisely for this reason, when there is a suspicion that it might motivate other pieces of wood by virtue of being the motivator of those properties, the censure—"If one were to make the *svaru* from another tree, others would not ascend to his world"—is also consistent as a means of removing that suspicion.

Moreover, even if [the *svaru*] is a subordinate element (*prayojaka*) of the ritual action, it is not inconsistent to observe a distinction between the *svarus* based on the distinction between the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) in the case of the "eleven posts" (*yūpaikādaśinī*), as stated in the rule: "Having anointed the animals with the *svarus* according to their respective order.
Nor does this [distinction] fail to hold even if [the relationship] is explained through the connection of being a part of the post;
for there is no restrictive rule [to the contrary] provided that the intended relationship is precisely that of possessing the properties of the post.

Since the status of being "belonging to the sacrificial post" (*yūpīyatva*) is established by the very fact that it is produced from a chip (*śakala*), the first sentence would otherwise be rendered purposeless; therefore, it must serve as the restrictive rule.
This being the position reached, we reply: the meaning of the genitive case is not a relationship of possessing the characteristics of the sacrificial post (*yūpadharmakatva*).
For its meaning is justified as a relationship of being a part of the sacrificial post, in accordance with grammatical instruction (*ānuśāsanika*).

Nor is the injunction for that [the *svaru*] redundant because it is already obtained through the mention of the wood-shavings (*śakala*) alone; for if this specific injunction did not exist, then—just as the acts of going to the forest, taking up the axe, felling the tree, and offering the oblation to the stump would have the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) as their purpose even when performed with wood other than that for the post—it would likewise be possible for them to have the *svaru* as their purpose. Consequently, the scriptural mention of the wood-shavings would be logically consistent only if they were related to the tree itself.

For this very reason, even in cases such as a performance according to one's capacity where no sacrificial post exists, the accomplishment of going to the forest and so forth is for the sake of the *svaru* alone.

The cutting of the second sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and so forth, enjoined by the sentence "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*), is for the purpose of establishing the measurement of five *aratnis*. Let that [cutting] cease when the sacrificial post is lost; however, even going to the forest and so forth should not cease. Therefore, the injunction regarding the sacrificial post's dimensions is indeed meaningful for the purpose of accomplishing what is produced as a secondary result (*anuniṣpanna*) of the sacrificial post which possesses that threefold fruit. For this very reason, if the first cutting produced as a secondary result of the sacrificial post is destroyed, the animal is bound with any other wood.
Since there is no evidence that sprinkling and the other rites are for the sake of the *svaru* itself, the *svaru* is not the motivator (*prayojaka*) of those rites.
Furthermore, the Sūtras are explained by the wise in this very sense, and not according to what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya.
Maṇḍana [states]: "A portion of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is the motivator of the *svaru*."
Regarding the *śamkara-svaru*, [it is argued that] *khadira* wood and the like are not used for its purpose.
This is because it is a part of the *svaru* itself.
In the context of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*āmīṣomīya-paśu*), it is heard in the scripture: "He anoints the animal with the *svaru* which has been sharpened."
In the inquiry as to whether this *svaru* is a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) or a subsidiary part of the animal victim, this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
By the word "also" (*api*), the author provides as an illustration the fact that the girdle (*raśanā*) was established in the preceding section as being a subsidiary part of the sacrificial post.
Just as the girdle is a subsidiary part of the sacrificial post, so too the *svaru* should be a subsidiary part of the sacrificial post.
Because the *svaru* is a part of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
At the time of cutting the post, the first chip that falls is called the *svaru*.
Therefore, the *svaru* is an accessory (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post.
And the ransom is likewise connected to that.

The sūtra provides another reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the *svaru* is an accessory (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). The explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) demonstrates this by stating: "The *svaru* is an accessory of the post; it is the ransom-price of the post. [The passage continues:
"In ancient times, those seers who brought forward the post used to remove it after splitting the *sruk* ladle; they thought, 'This act would surely lead to the ruin of the sacrifice.'"
They saw the *prastara* as the ransom for the *kṛcchra*, and the *svaru* of the sacrificial post as the ransom for the *ayaśas*.
Some, moreover, used to throw the sacrificial post into the fire at the end of the sacrifice;
and having broken and split the *luca*, they threw it into the fire.
Regarding this, some other sages considered that for certain verses, the ritual act serves only to cause the "desecration" (*veśa*) of the sacrifice—that is, its destruction.
How, then, should it be performed? The *prastara* (grass-bundle) is the substitute for the *sruva*-ladles, and the *svaru* (wooden chip) is the substitute for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
This being so, in place of the *sruvas*, the *prastara* alone is to be thrown into the fire, and in place of the *yūpa*, the *svaru* is to be thrown.

Therefore, the meaning is that there should indeed be the casting into the fire, and yet there should be no destruction of the sacrifice. Consequently, the *svaru* is an accessory (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), not an accessory of the animal (*paśu*).
Or rather, it is an accessory of the animal, because [otherwise] it would lack its own specific ritual purpose (*adharmakatvāt*).

Regarding the statement, "He anoints the animal with the *svaru*," the opponent maintains in the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) view—supported by two sūtras—that the *svaru* mentioned in the context of the *āmīṣomīya* sacrifice is an accessory of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). The author refutes that position with the word "but" (*vā*) and establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*):
the *svaru* is not an accessory of the post, but rather an accessory of the animal, because its function is for the sake of the animal.

The purpose is the motive. The anointing of the sacrificial post with clarified butter is the purpose, the action, and the essence of the *svaru* (wooden chip) for the sake of the animal victim; thus, the *svaru* is the reality of the animal’s anointing.
It serves as the means;

and thus, because the *svaru* is an instrument for the limbs of the animal sacrifice, it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the animal sacrifice. And the visible purpose is that which constitutes an auxiliary to the animal sacrifice.
If, however, it were a subsidiary part of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) would have to be postulated.
Therefore, the *svaru* is a subsidiary part of the animal sacrifice. The statement regarding its "purchase" is merely figurative.
Regarding the statement, “He anoints the animal with the *svaru*,” which is heard in the context of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*āgneyīya-paśu*), the *svaru* is [the subject].

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is argued that the *svaru* is an accessory (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and the scriptural reference to the "ransoming" (*niṣkraya*) of the post by means of the *svaru* is stated as the reason for this.
The refutation of that position is carried out by the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) through this sūtra.
This statement regarding a "ransom" (niṣkraya) that has been mentioned is figurative; it would be equal to a quality.
When the *svaru* is thrown into the fire, the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) itself remains—as if the post had been ransomed by means of the *svaru*. That is the scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *svaru* is indeed a limb of the animal sacrifice.

Ke. ❀ Regarding the doubt as to whether the *svah* [formula] is the motivator for acts such as cutting the wood of the *khadira* tree or not—the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is not; this [formula] is a secondary consequence (*anuniṣpanna*) resulting from the cutting performed for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
The *svah* is the ritual procedure (*tantra*) intended for the purpose of maintaining the animal sacrifice.

The *agni-svara*: 4464. The section on the *svaru* (wooden chip), 10.27. The *svaru* is a ritual by-product (*pratipatti*); it is thrown into the fire at the conclusion of the Soma sacrifice, according to the rule: "It is cast into the fire when the sacrifice has been concluded."
This is the essential point: "With this [verse], he throws the prastara-bundle or utters the svaru.
"Praise through devotion" (bhaktyā stutiḥ).

What is the purpose? It is that on a single sacrificial post (ekayūpa), the maintenance of as many Anubandhya animals as required must be performed; however, when eleven animals are bound, then the ritual disposal (pratipatti) belongs to only one animal, namely the Agniṣomīya animal.
In the *samaja* sacrifice, this applies to the former position (*pakṣa*);
for all [other sacrifices], it applies to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

And there is a verse regarding the animals produced from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*): "If it is argued that the destruction of the animals produced from the post occurs by means of any [wood] whatsoever, then the anointing of the animal with the wood of the post itself should not be performed. Thus, the anointing of the animal is not to be done with the wood of the post.
Bhāṣya 4.2.1:
*nam*.
[This is the section] concerning the equal distribution among all when many [animals] are tied to a single sacrificial post (*yūpa*). All [animals] share the same substratum.
Svara: the limb of the animal.
Nam.
Thus,
in the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, the accent serves the purpose of the animal.
Because it is a part of its own nature.

The Bhāṣya states: "In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma which is subordinate to the Soma; 'When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma,' it is so stated.
In that context, it is heard: 'He anoints the animal with the *svaru* or with the axe.'"

In this regard, there is a doubt: is the half-svara [of the post] a part of the sacrificial post (yūpa), or is it a subsidiary element of the animal sacrifice (paśu)? What is the prima facie view? We say it is a part of the sacrificial post.
Why? Because it is a constituent part of it.

A single part [is mentioned] as the essential form (*svarūpa*); it is heard in the text: "He makes the *svara* with the *svaru*. The meaning is that one should make the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) ending with the *svaru*.
In this way, it becomes a sacrificial post.
As in the case of the *capāla* [wooden ring];
and the extraction (*niṣkarṣa*) is like that of one who knows it.
The Commentary states: "The doctrine of extraction shows the accent to be like half of a sacrificial post (*yūpa*)."

"Indeed, in former times, the seers who brought forward the sacrificial post (yūpa) did not see [the cutting of] the prastara-bunch from the sacrificial ladle (sruk); they considered this act to be a slaughter of the sacrifice. They saw the prastara as being separate from the ladle, for the sake of avoiding the slaughter of the splendor and glory of the post. From this explicit scriptural statement, their ignorance is understood. Therefore, it is half of the post.
Or rather, it is a part of the animal-offering, because it serves a specific purpose.
Commentary: Or rather, it is a part of the animal, for there is a need for the *svaru* for the purpose of anointing it.
For thus it is heard in scripture: "He anoints the animal with the *svaru*. That [act of] anointing necessitates the production of the *svaru* from the animal.
If the *svaru* is for that very purpose [of cutting], then its purpose is visible (*dṛṣṭa*).
But if it is for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), then its purpose is invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) and must be inferred. Therefore, it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the animal sacrifice.

Through figurative application (*bhakti*), there would be a statement of essential extraction (*niṣkarṣavāda*). The Commentary says: By what kind of figurative application? It speaks thus: "This sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is indeed praised;
for it is the *svaru* that is thrown [into the fire]."

Therefore, the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is subordinate—just as in the statement "the animal [is tied] with the *svaru*"; such is the relationship between the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*).
The *svaru* is a subsidiary part of the animal, while the animal itself holds the status of the primary object.
Thus, the *yūpa* (sacrificial post) exists for the sake of the animal (*paśu*).
The connection [of this case] with the example is based on the conclusion that the *svaru*—which possesses a rope like the *soma*—is indeed half of the *yūpa*.

As for the meaning of the *sūtra*: the *svaru* should also be half of the *yūpa*, because the force of the genitive case in the statement “he makes the *svaru* of the *yūpa*” results in the sense “he makes the *yūpa* possessed of a *svaru*,” and thus, as a single part of the *yūpa*, it is appropriate for it to be a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to it.
Vi— "Whether it be the *svaru* or the animal, it is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," so says the subsequent statement.
Since the *svaru* is associated with mantras for the animal and the like, its status as a subordinate part of the animal is clear.

Bhaṭṭa: From the statement, "He makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," it is understood that the *svaru* is for the sake of the post; therefore, the act of anointing the animal with the *svaru*—as in the text, "He anoints the animal with the *svaru*"—is a disposal (*pratipatti*), just as in the case of the text, "Whatever has been touched by Soma, with that they proceed. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the reply is: since the *svaru* would serve no visible purpose if it were merely for the sake of the post, and since its status as a limb of the animal is justified even on the grounds of being a distinct part [of the post], and because the instrumental case in "with the *svaru*" (*svarūṇā*) expresses instrumentality, it is for the sake of the animal-limb itself.

As for the *somalipta* (soma-smeared) [wood], it has already been stated (4.2.8) that its acceptance as a secondary (*gauṇa*) term in the context of the *avabhṛtha* rite is due to its mention at one time.

The purpose [of the discussion] is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), in the case of a single sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the anointing with the *svaru* would apply to only one animal; however, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it applies to all of them.

Furthermore, according to the opinion of Pārthasārathi, since the restriction regarding the *āghāra* offering would result in being for the purpose of purifying the animals—following the logic of the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings—the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of anointing all [the posts] would follow even in the *pūrvapakṣa*, and thus the stated purpose would be untenable; this also constitutes a contradiction with the *bhāṣya*.
Maṇḍana: "The *svaru* is mentioned as a quality of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); it is not a genitive [relationship].
Śaṅkara: "The *svaru* should be a part of the animal (*paśvaṅga*). [This concerns] the justification for the difference in nature between the function of the *svaru* and the *svaru* itself.
The function of the *svaru* is known through the ignorance of the animal [sacrificer].
Bhāṣya 1.1.13:
The derivation of the word *svaru* and its meaning occurs through its association with well-known words, even though it is not established in common worldly usage but only in the Veda.
Essential nature (*svarūpa*). The form characterized by its defining mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is the essential nature.

VI. 1.12: Even though [the self] cannot be an object of injunction in its essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is possible for it to be an object of injunction in its qualified form (*viśiṣṭarūpa*). (Su. p. 864).
"The non-specification of things in their essential nature" is the principle of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) at the beginning of the tenth book.
Soma.

Regarding the proof of the essential nature (*svarūpa*): it should be understood that there is a *visarga* (the mark :), as in the term *hetvābhāsāḥ*. Maṇi, p. 41. By the force of the essential nature, the invalidation of the status of being a locus (*āśrayatva*) will be explained in the section concerning the *pikanema* [dispute].
Su. Pṛ. 107. Establishing the Difference of Essential Nature (*svarūpabheda*).
Now, the difference of essential nature is established.

There is no property called "difference" existing apart from this specific form (*rūpa*) common to substances, qualities, and so forth; for the linguistic usage of "different" is accounted for by the essential nature alone.

Now, if difference were merely the essential nature (svarūpa) itself, then the conventional usage of "difference" would occur as soon as the essential nature alone is perceived; yet it is not observed to be so. True; at the very moment the essential nature is present, there is no conventional usage of "difference. Nevertheless, difference does not exist apart from the essential nature; rather, the conventional usage of "difference" is dependent upon a counter-correlate (pratiyogin). Therefore, since that [counter-correlate] is absent when only the essential nature is perceived, there is no contingency of the conventional usage of "difference" [arising at that time].

[Objection: In that case, difference (*bheda*) depends upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), whereas the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is independent of a counter-correlate; how, then, can these two be one? [Reply: It is not so. Difference itself does not depend upon a counter-correlate; rather, it is the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding difference that does. For this very reason, in indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), because there is an absence of the cognition of a counter-correlate, there is an absence of the linguistic usage of difference. [Question: Then what is the object of the linguistic usage regarding difference? [Reply: It has been stated that it is the mere essential nature (*svarūpamātra*) alone.

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of treating the mere perception of essential nature (*svarūpa*) as the conventional usage of difference; for difference is indeed difference from the perspective of essential nature, yet essential nature alone is not difference.
Just as Devadatta is a son only in relation to [another], but Devadatta alone is not a son, and yet he is not a son even when distinct from Devadatta.
Now, what is the use of this laborious conceptualization? Difference is indeed perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the form: "This is different from that."
It is true that there is a cognition [of it] (Mīmāṃsākośa 559).

Furthermore, its status as a property of substance is not tenable while it remains unmanifest in its own nature, because it would be included among substances, qualities, and so forth, and because it is absent from qualities and the rest.

Nor is it appropriate to postulate that these are distinct entities, because the cognition of difference and its conventional usage are accounted for by having the individual forms themselves as their sole objective basis.

[Objection: In that case, since individual forms occupy different locations from one another, they would not constitute a single unity. [Reply: This is not so; for this [unity] is established by treating the form as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) precisely insofar as it is dependent upon its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

Now, it was stated that difference is a nature dependent upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*). What, then, is this so-called dependence on a counter-correlate? If it is merely the nature itself, then the aforementioned fault remains. If, however, dependence on a counter-correlate is a distinct attribute (*dharmāntara*), then that [attribute] alone is the difference; thus, a difference extrinsic to the nature has been admitted.

It is not so; for one must admit that the property called "dependence upon a counter-correlative" (*pratiyogy-apekṣatva*)—which belongs to false differences and the like—is indeed distinct from difference itself, such as the difference between properties and so forth. Otherwise, since the non-difference of a thing would be perceived by its mere nature as a jar, there would follow the absurd consequence that the linguistic usage of "difference" would be established by that alone. If it is argued that the cognition of difference occurs only through the mediation of [the cognition of] relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), this is not so; for the linguistic usage of difference is expressed as "the cloth is different from the jar," and not as "conjunction and so forth. In that case, there is never any cognition such as "this is the conjunction of these two."

Thus, for one who has already apprehended the difference through the cognition of the two relata (*saṃpratigotvena*), the subsequent statement that "the difference between these two is merely conventional" implies that dependence upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogyapekṣatvam*)—which is accepted [by all] as being inherent in every kind of difference—is simply the nature of the difference itself; let this very nature, which requires a counter-correlate, be the cause for the linguistic usage of "different. What is the use of postulating an internal "property of difference" (*bhedadharma*)? Surely, it is appropriate for the proponent of properties (*dharmavādin*) to accept that the property itself depends on a counter-correlate, since such dependence is observed in all cases.

"But its own nature (*svarūpa*) is not [the object of cognition], because the own nature is never known independently of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); therefore, there is no establishment of a parallel case. This is not so; for here too, dependence upon a counter-correlate is not the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of the own nature itself, but rather of the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of difference. Now, it may be argued that a distinct usage is sometimes seen to be based on something other than a distinct object of usage, as in the usage: "Difference is different from the pot which possesses difference"—here a distinct usage exists, yet there is no actual distinctness [in the object]; therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
If one accepts the statement "the denoter is different from the denoted," then by another name, the doctrine of the difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*) would simply have been adopted.
Now, [it may be argued that] therein the difference in essential nature is being established.

If there is no such thing as a conventional usage characterized by identity and so forth for the sake of establishing a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa*), then in the case of the expression "the pot is distinct," there could not even be a conventional usage characterized by a distinction from that which is not accepted as identical. Therefore, it is not logical to admit a difference apart from the essential nature itself.

Now, one must state the dependence of the essential nature upon a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*); in this regard, a dilemma must be considered: is the counter-correlative different from the essential nature, or is it non-different?
It cannot first be non-different [from itself], because that would entail the absurdity of something being its own counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).

Nor can it be different; for if difference exists, the status of being a counter-correlative is established, and if the status of being a counter-correlative is established, difference is established—thus there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
If, on the other hand, the counter-correlative is different by means of another difference, then there follows the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

It is not so; for even for one who maintains that difference is a distinct entity (*dharmabhedavādin*), there is indeed a dependence upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). In that case as well, the same dilemma and the same fault apply, and whatever solution is offered there applies here too.

Objection: But the theory that difference is the essential nature (*svarūpabheda*) contradicts experience. To explain: in the cognition "the jar is different from the cloth," difference is perceived as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). According to you, however, since there is no difference apart from the essential nature itself, such a qualifying entity simply does not exist; consequently, the conventional usage would have to be "difference is the jar" (*bhedo ghaṭaḥ*).
Heaven:
[The terms] heaven and so forth refer, for their part, exclusively to the world beyond.
However, in the case of cattle, sons, and so forth, there is both a present-worldly (*aihika*) and a post-mortem (*kāmuṣmika*) nature, but not an exclusively post-mortem one.
In their absence, however, there is only a present-worldly nature.
But where the desire is directed toward the visible and so forth, which are strictly present-worldly, there is an exclusively present-worldly nature.

Even in the case of visible results (*dṛṣṭa*) and so forth, there is a desire for results pertaining to the next world (*pāratrika*) when such a possibility exists; however, when only this-worldly results are possible—as in the case of obtaining sons, cattle, and the like—there is only a desire for the present life. (Bhāṭṭa 4.3.12–28, Section 2). As for heaven (*svarga*), it occurs only in another birth.
For that unsurpassed bliss, being conformable to desire, cannot be experienced in this birth;
since in this world, people experience [only] moments of suffering.
Therefore, another place—distinct from the realm of action—is postulated on the grounds that it is otherwise impossible for such unsurpassed bliss to be experienced.

And that [immortality] is not possible for a flower; therefore, heaven exists only in another birth. (Tup. 4.3.11.28, Section 2). Heaven is desired by all persons because it is unmixed with suffering and because it is unsurpassed bliss.
"That which is not mingled with suffering, nor seized by it..."
"Heaven is by way of its qualities; action is by way of its predominance.
Regarding this, they describe it as follows:
"Heaven is a substance (dravya)."
How is this understood? For all words, worldly usage regarding the knowledge of their meaning is not a valid means [of determining their primary sense].
And in that worldly usage, the word *svarga* is found to denote a substance:
"Silken garments are *svarga*, sandalwood is *svarga*, women who rain down wealth are *svarga*"—whatever substance is pleasurable is designated by the word *svarga*.
Therefore, because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*), we consider that heaven is a substance possessed of pleasure.

If it is argued that the application of the word [“heaven”] is based on analogy (*upamāna*), we reply: no, for there is nothing well-known in the world that has not been previously experienced, which could serve as the basis for this analogy. Thus, this is not an analogy.
Therefore, [some say] heaven is a substance. No, he says;
heaven is pleasure.
It is not a substance,
because of the deviation;
for that very same substance, in a certain state, is not denoted by the word "heaven."
But he does not designate pleasure as being denoted by [the word] in any state whatsoever.
Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), it is understood that the word "heaven" (svarga) applies to that which is pleasurable.
It is not the case that the word "heaven" is a direct designator of pleasure itself.
Why? Because pleasure (*prīti*) is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
That which is a qualifier is not denoted by the word itself;
for example, the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) is a term for a person based on the staff.
The staff is its cause, not its denotation;
likewise, it is not a word for pleasure itself,
but this word "svarga" (heaven) denotes the means of attaining pleasure.

But is it not the case that the word "heaven" (svarga) is well-known in the world as a particular region where there is neither heat nor cold, neither hunger nor thirst, neither discontent nor exhaustion;
and only those who have performed meritorious deeds go there after death, and no others?
To this it is replied:
if some immortals do not go there, or if they return from there without being born [again], then that perceptible place would not be of such a nature;
nor can it be known through inference.
Not by anyone else.

But surely others have seen [the truth] and they have declared it? If this is argued, we say no; for there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that "there exist such perfected beings (*siddha*), and having seen [it], they act accordingly."
Therefore, such a place as that simply does not exist.
But surely, it is understood from common worldly usage, from narratives, and from the Veda that heaven is indeed a place of this kind. To that we reply: no.
Because men do not rely upon such a region, their word lacks authority;
even their narrative is to be disregarded because it was composed by human beings.
Even the Vedic narrative concerning heaven is not intended as an injunction;
rather, it exists as a single syntactical unit with another injunction, being intended for praise.
For even if there were such a place as described by a mere account of heaven, [it would still serve that purpose].
Nevertheless, there is no contradiction with the position that [heaven] is non-existent; for the word "heaven" (svarga) denotes the means of pleasure.
Since there is no linguistic usage regarding such a place, how could the word "heaven" be its designator?
When heaven is a substance consisting of pleasure, then we speak thus.
"In the connection of substances with an action, there is a relation as subordinate factors" (PMS 6.1.1).
Here, it is heard in scripture that "a sacrifice is to be performed by one who desires heaven.
In that case, there must necessarily be a relationship between heaven and the sacrifice.
In this context, that which is already existent (bhūta) is the substance (dravya),
and that which is to be brought into being (bhavya) is the action (karman).
And it is logical that the existent has the purpose of the yet-to-be-brought-into-being, because its purpose is perceptible.
But the state of being an accomplished entity does not belong to that which is yet to be accomplished;
for in that case, it would be merely an auxiliary.
How, then, is it understood that the sacrifice is enjoined as something to be performed?
If it is argued that from this sentence the duty to pursue desire is also understood, we reply:
the duty to pursue desire follows from the sentence only if the duty to pursue the purpose [of the Veda] is more powerful than the sentence itself, as established by direct revelation (*śruti*).
Therefore, this is the meaning:
"One who desires heaven should perform the sacrifice," or "The sacrifice must be performed by one who desires heaven."
That which brings happiness is to be done;
that which brings suffering is not to be done.
And he says of it: "It is to be done."
Therefore, sacrifice will have happiness as its fruit;
it is understood that it is accomplished for one who desires it, and not for anyone else.
Consequently, the desire for heaven is subordinate to the sacrifice.
In every action, there is a desire for a substance, which serves as a subordinate factor;
indeed, one strives to procure that substance by means of this very [desire].
But here, it is specifically the desire for the substance designated as "heaven" that is being regulated.

Just as that desire for heaven (svargēcchā) is attained as a subordinate factor (guṇabhūtā), so too, being thus, it is regulated by means of a visible door, not by an invisible benefit. Therefore, the desire for heaven, having become a subordinate factor, will exert itself toward the substance of heaven in order to accomplish the sacrifice.

Moreover, even if it is unseen, there is still no fault; this is merely an excessive display of pride. Once it is understood that [the Veda] possesses fruitfulness, who would concern themselves with such [objections]? Thus, this is the proper method of inquiry.
However, if there were no fruitfulness, inquiry would be untenable.

And if, in this way, the fruit is understood through words denoting desire (*kāma*), then the discussion in the section on the meaning of verbal roots (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, 2.1.2) arises: whether words denoting action (*bhāva*) are connected with the fruit, or whether it is words denoting substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*). Following that, the discussion concerning the *apūrva* (the unseen potentiality) follows.
Then follows the extended application (*atideśa*).
And regarding the existence of the fruit, there is the inquiry as to whether it is "characterized by an injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*), because that [injunction] is the governing topic (*adhikāra*).
This indeed is the occasion for this chapter.

How so? This is precisely the occasion for the inquiry as to which person is qualified for ritual acts (*karma*), based on the distinctions of difference and non-difference, the relationship between the subordinate and the principal, the instigator and the non-instigator, and the application of such sequential order. [The objection that] the Bhāṣya statement, "Is heaven subordinate and the ritual act primary? is improper, is incorrect.
If the word "heaven" (svarga) is connected with the verb, it is not connected with the word "desire" (kāma);
if it is connected with the word "desire," it is not connected with the verb. By the word "desire," which is expressed by its own term, its connection is established through direct audition (śruti).
Because it is already conveyed by another word through the verb, it constitutes a sentence;

and direct statement (śruti) is stronger than syntactical connection (vākya). Therefore, since the word "heaven" is exhausted as a qualification of the person, it cannot enter into a relationship with anything else.

By which [word], the agent distinguished by the royal caste is enjoined as the means for the Rājasūya, or the Rājasūya itself—as in the case of "by this" (*etena*)—is neither the goal nor the means; likewise, it is not so with heaven. Therefore, the agent qualified by the word "heaven" is connected to the action.
If this were so, doubt would be untenable.

Furthermore, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), the agent is indicated as being subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the sacrifice.
Just as in the case of "Devadatta cooks," the cooking is not for the sake of Devadatta, so too here the agent is perceived as being entirely subordinate.
It is said:
it is not an absolute rule that what is primary becomes subordinate; even the primary element can become subordinate in an action, as in the expression, "One who is dirty should bathe."

Doubt is indeed appropriate here. When the meaning of the word has been understood, and the meaning of the non-word (the sentence-meaning) is yet to be determined, the sentence-meaning follows at a later time.
In that regard, if the word "heaven" (svarga) denotes a substance, then that [substance], being desired as a means, is connected to the sacrifice precisely as a means.

Now, its pleasure (prīti) must be denoted; therefore, that [pleasure], being desired as something connected with the undertaking, is expressed by the word "heaven" (svarga). Subsequently, when it is intended through sacrifice, it is connected solely as the aspect of the goal to be accomplished (sādhya).
The sacrifice, however, is subordinate.
Thus, when there is a twofold desire, a doubt arises as to whether heaven is subordinate or primary;
therefore, the words, their meanings, and the sentences must be determined.
Nor can it be accomplished by the mere fact of being a king, for caste is not necessarily connected with desire. There are two types of prima facie arguments (pūrvapakṣa).
The agency for the sacrifice belongs to one who is qualified by the desire for heaven; the sacrifice is not to be performed by one who is not so qualified.
Just as the Rājasūya must be performed by one qualified by the royal caste (rājajāti) and not by one who is not so qualified, so it is here as well.
If this is so, then a pleasing substance need not necessarily be accepted;
rather, the desire for it will be beneficial by way of its being an object of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
From the passage in the commentary at the end of the first sūtra, "Even if [the benefit comes] through the unseen, there is still no fault," this second position is inferred.
And the prima facie view is based on the word and the thing (meaning "by means of direct statement and indicative mark"). How so? Because of the suffix in the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice).
He states that the very thing which is heard as being for another's sake must be performed according to that scriptural injunction.
Furthermore, because the sacrifice is not yet accomplished, it possesses the status of an end to be realized (bhāvya);
and whatever is to be realized comes to be understood as something to be performed.
That which is already accomplished, such as a sickle and the like, is capable of functioning as an instrument (*karaṇatva*).

In this manner, it is the sacrifice that is to be brought into being (*bhāvyamāna*), not heaven. Moreover, since in common usage the word "heaven" (*svarga*) denotes a substance consisting of pleasure, it is therefore desired as a means to achieve that [pleasure].
"Whatever substance is accompanied by pleasure, that is designated by the word 'heaven' (*svarga*);

for example, [the term] 'staff-bearer' (*daṇḍin*). This is the connection of this text, even though it is established [in a specific order]: namely, "for example, 'staff-bearer'... [up to] 'the word heaven'; whatever is accompanied by pleasure... that is designated by the word 'heaven'. Here is the text: [tadyathā daṇḍī ityanena 'asya granthasya saṃbandho vyavasthitasyāpi (tadyathā daṇḍī...svargaśabda iti, yadyat prīti... tattat- svargaśabdenocyate iti krameṇa). atra granthaḥ].

"Even if such a place were to exist for the sake of denoting heaven alone, nevertheless, there would be no contradiction with the position that [heaven] is non-existent, because heaven is the means to pleasure. Since there is no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) with respect to that place, how could the word 'heaven' be its designator?
For one [the Siddhāntin], pleasure is the denotation of the word 'heaven'; for the other [the Pūrvapakṣin], it is the substance possessing pleasure.
The specific location is inexpressible for both [the universal and the particular].
What is the reason? Because it is not perceptible, there is an absence of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).
Due to that absence of linguistic usage, there is an absence of formal application (*prayoga*).

However, since the pleasure is that which is to be accomplished and the sacrifice is its means, and yet that [pleasure] is not experienced by him [the agent], it is postulated— even though it is denotable—
by the force of the purpose, just like the *apūrva*.
But surely, even in this world, such pleasure can be experienced?
[It is obtained] by means of sandalwood ointments and the like.
Why? Because immediately thereafter, pleasure is obtained—namely, this pleasure derived from food and so forth.
This [joy] is momentary.
However, the joys resulting from actions that are small, middling, or great are themselves small, middling, or great.
Among these, that joy which is unsurpassed can only be experienced by one who experiences it in a place free from the dualities of cold, heat, and so forth.
In this world of mortals, even a hundredth part of a moment is free from the pairs of opposites;
therefore, the section concerning those desiring heaven is established for the sake of experiencing unsurpassed bliss.

In the section concerning those desiring heaven (*svargakāmādhikaraṇa*), the location is specified. As for the pleasure produced by sandalwood and the like, it is sandalwood and such things themselves that are its causes of production, not the sacrifice.
And in this place, everything from the moving beings down to the paths and so forth experiences pleasure and pain;
yet those [beings] have not performed actions in this place.
Therefore, that which consists of common pleasure and pain is produced by their own nature.
Furthermore, it is because of the actions performed by them in another birth that they experience joy;
just as they do not perform all [actions] in this birth, so it is in another birth.
And yet, they experience all [the results] as joy.
Therefore, if this [heaven] were produced by karma, it would be experienced only by some;
if it were not produced by karma, there would be no such fault.
Consequently, pleasure is the denotation of the word "svarga."
And since that [bliss] cannot be experienced in a specific location,
a specific location is inferred.
This passage— "even though it is [attained] through the hearing of mere bliss"— is stated as a concessive argument (*abhyupetyavāda*).
Since the word "heaven" (svarga) denotes a substance,

although you postulate a specific place by the force of [the word's] denoting pleasure (prīti), nevertheless, that substance characterized by pleasure is sublated as the means to that [heaven], because the word *bhāvanā* necessarily implies being employed for a human goal (puruṣārtha).
Furthermore, when distinct meanings of the suffix arise, mutual expectations are produced.
In that case, if the human purpose (puruṣārtha) presents itself in the first instance and the sacrifice (yāga) in the second, then which word's [meaning] has been sublated?
Alternatively, if the sacrifice presents itself in the sense of "what" (kim-aṃśa), then the power of the suffix, which necessitates a specific purpose, is sublated.
Furthermore, there would be the futility of ritual actions.
Therefore, sacrifice is the instrument by virtue of both the word and the object;
or else, the status of sacrifice as an instrument is established in another manner.
How so? One who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) is designated as such because heaven is sought after as something connected to the self.
That person, desiring heaven, then seeks the means to attain it.
Therefore, because these two are inseparable, the word "desirer of heaven" (*svargakāma*) is capable of indicating its means through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, by means of the scripture, sacrifices and the like are enjoined as the means (*upāya*) therein.
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): "Therefore, the word 'one desiring heaven' does not enjoin its own meaning.
What then? It is merely pointed out (*uddiśyate*)."
"Thus, the word *svargakāma* does not enjoin its own primary meaning"—
this means that it is denoted [by the injunction].
By this passage, the author states that the word *svargakāma* has the purpose of indicating the means (*upāya*).
Commentary: In that case, from the sentence, the necessity of performing the desire is understood, as well as the instrumentality of the sacrifice.
And thus, there will be no contradiction with perception regarding the necessity of performing the sacrifice.
Therefore, "there would be an instruction for action" (the portion of the sūtra); action is enjoined with respect to heaven, not heaven with respect to action.
What follows if heaven is not taught [as the result]? This follows from it: for an untaught purpose cannot possess the status of a valid means (*prāmāṇya*) as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*).
Therefore, heaven is primary and the ritual action is subordinate.
Moreover, he for whom heaven is desired would perform the sacrifice; in this way, desiring one thing while performing another would be a contradiction.
Now, if it is thought that this is understood from the connection [implied by the statement], "From that, heaven arises," we reply:
for those who take scripture as their authority, nothing is to be understood apart from the scripture itself.

We understand this relationship solely from this sentence; for example, if one were to say, "One desiring to fetch wood should go to the forest," one might then say: "It is observed there through other means of knowledge that the capacity to fetch wood exists in going to the forest."
Now, if it is thought that [the teaching] must not be purposeless and therefore its meaning will be implied by the context,
it is said in reply: this is not the capacity of the teaching to avoid being purposeless.

If the result of the sacrifice were understood to be pleasure even without a statement of the result, then let it be that this [statement] is purposeless; its capacity [to convey meaning] is never produced [by such a statement].
For the taking up of water by one desiring to burn does not produce the power to burn simply because it is purposeless in the absence of burning.
Alternatively, its purposefulness will be established by resorting to another position, namely, that the sacrifice is enjoined for one who desires heaven (*svarga*).

"Or rather, from that [sentence], the duty (*kartavyatā*) of the desire understood through the sentence is apprehended, as well as the instrumentality (*karaṇatā*) of the sacrifice"—this is the first statement of the division of the earlier commentary (*pūrvabhāṣya*).

"Alternatively, by adopting another position—that the sacrifice is enjoined for one who desires heaven—its purposefulness will be established"; this other position is expressed as "one should perform the sacrifice" (*yāgaṃ kuryāt*), meaning "one should effect [the result] by means of the sacrifice" (*yāgena kuryāt*).

Alternatively, the phrase "of one desiring heaven" (*svargakāmasya*) should be understood as "therefore, for one desiring heaven. This is because no other supporting argument has been stated. The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): But surely, even in the other view, the sacrifice is enjoined for one desiring heaven, not that heaven [arises] from the sacrifice.
This is not so.
Indeed, in that view, there is no fault, because the performance [of the act] is restated with reference to heaven being sought, and the sacrifice is enjoined as its means.
If it is argued that there is no statement that "that performance is for the sake of heaven," [we reply: this performance occurs for the sake of this object [heaven].
And for one who desires heaven, heaven is the desired object.
Thus, the specific mention of the person desiring heaven is nothing other than the specific mention of the performance of that [sacrifice]; this is faultless.
Therefore, there must be an instruction regarding the sacrificial act for one who desires heaven.

Therefore, since heaven is primary and the ritual action is secondary, the statement "one who desires heaven should sacrifice" (yajeta) is established as having the character of an *adhikāra* (qualification for entitlement). Dhuṇḍi: "But even in the other view, it is the sacrifice that is enjoined for one who desires heaven, not heaven [resulting] from the sacrifice. What is the intention here? Since the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the meanings of its constituent words, if one were to hear "heaven [is attained] by means of the sacrifice," then there would be the relation: "this is the goal (*sādhya*) and this is the means (*sādhana*). However, one does not hear "heaven [is attained] by means of the sacrifice."
Therefore, the previously mentioned fault remains exactly as it was.
This is not so;
for indeed, in that position, having referred to the performance of one who desires heaven, the sacrifice is [prescribed] as its means.
Thus, there is no fault.
One who desires heaven, by virtue of its connection with that [result], also desires the means;
for there is no end to be attained without a means.
Therefore, the word *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven) is capable of indicating the means [to that end] through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And that [means], having been so indicated, is enjoined as the means.
The specific sacrifice is supplied by another word.

Therefore, the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the meanings of its constituent words. Consequently, since ritual actions possess results, it is appropriate to begin the section defining the qualified performer (*adhikāra*).
A "qualified performer" is one who stands above the ritual actions; that is to say, he is the master (*svāmin*).
Śālikanātha: "Now that the performance [of ritual] has been thus defined by means of characteristics such as difference and so forth, it is currently being deliberated: who is qualified for this?"
However, by way of an introductory summary, this is first investigated:
Is the person, as an agent, qualified for ritual actions or not?

In such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," it is considered whether or not a person possesses *adhikāra*—that is, ownership or the status of being the enjoyer of the fruit produced by the ritual act. To that end, this is deliberated: regarding this *bhāvanā* (productive operation) which is to be prompted, is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) alone the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) and thus primary, while heaven and so forth are subordinate as means; or rather, is heaven and so forth, being what is desired, itself the object to be accomplished, and the meaning of the verbal root the means to that end?

From this, the following must be discerned: regarding the relationship here between the action and the person desiring heaven who is the agent of that action, is the action primary and the person secondary, or is it the reverse?
Furthermore, this is also considered: does the word "heaven" (svarga) denote a substance or does it denote pleasure?

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is as follows: "By the direct Vedic statement (*pada-śruti*), it is understood that the meaning of the verbal root itself is that which is to be accomplished (*bhāvya*)."
Indeed, the sentence [teaching] heaven and so forth is weaker than the Vedic revelation (śruti);
and the established substance, such as the word "heaven," is taught for the sake of the action to be accomplished (bhavya),
not for its own sake as an established entity, for the instruction of action is directed toward that which is to be accomplished.

This being the position reached, it is replied: "Indeed, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is constrained by the more powerful injunctive word (*vidhiśruti*), which is stronger than the nominal stem (*padaśruti*);
it is not capable of taking the sacrifice and so forth as its end (*bhāvya*). Heaven and the like, because of their connection with desire, are understood solely as the fruit (*phala*)."
For the desire of men indeed has its scope in the fruit [of action].

Soma—the meaning of the aphorism is as follows: when substances such as heaven and so forth are heard to be enjoyed through ritual acts (*karma*), because these substances possess the capacity to produce the act, they are connected [to it] as subordinate factors (*guṇa*).
Vi— "Is there an entitlement to perform the act for the agent, or not? No, because of the direct scriptural statement (*padaśruti*)."

Because the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is that which is to be brought into being (*bhāvya*), and because the enjoyment of the fruit is to be abandoned, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) here is constrained by a more powerful injunctive revelation (*vidhiśruti*). Heaven (*svarga*) is the object to be brought into being because it is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) and because of its connection with a desire (*kāma*); therefore, it belongs to this [action].
Bhaṭṭa: Thus, having defined the procedure as that which is to be employed, the qualified person (adhikārī) is now defined therein.
In this context, "qualification" (adhikāra) is agency (kartṛtva) co-located with the status of being an enjoyer of the fruit (phalabhoktṛtva).
The two qualifiers are included to exclude the qualification of ancestors and the like in rites such as the Śrāddha, as well as the qualification of officiating priests (ṛtvij).

Nor should it be argued that there is no entitlement for the father because of the absence of enjoyment of the fruit of the birth; for even though [the rite] is not performed, since the performance [of the rite] has the son and so forth as its result, it lacks the result of the destruction of sin. This is because what is intended is the state of being a non-agent (akartrtva) which resides in the same locus as the desire for the fruit that motivates the engagement [in the action].

In rites such as the *jāteṣṭi*, even though the fruit belongs to another at the outset, there is no obstruction to the qualification [for the rite] because the desire for that fruit resides in the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Even in the case of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), since their desire—"May the fruit accrue to the sacrificer"—is co-located with their own status as agents (*kartṛtva*), they likewise attain the qualification.
Therefore, the aforementioned objection is refuted.

Because the very desire, "May the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) accrue to me," is what generates the activity of the officiating priest (ṛtvij), it lacks the aforementioned distinction [of being the motivator of activity].
Since it does not serve as the cause for engaging in activity,

this entitlement (adhikāra) is established by the authority of the injunction (vidhi), because it consists in the state of being desirable due to the force of its being achievable by one's own effort, which is co-referential with the capacity [to produce the result] based on the injunction.
This very [section] is called the "rule of qualification" (*adhikāravidhi*).

In that regard, since qualification consists in having a result consisting of a desired form of activity, it is first investigated whether or not that very result in the form of a desired object belongs to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).

In this context, because the productive operation requires an object to be produced (*bhāvya*), the meaning of the verbal root alone is everywhere the object to be produced by virtue of its proximity in the word (*padaśruti*), and not heaven or other such things; rather, those are merely its means (*sādhana*) due to their suitability.

Just as in the case of [words like] *pakṣa* (wing), the word *svarga* (heaven) also denotes a substance, because of its usage in such expressions as "sandalwood is heaven" (*candanaṃ svargaḥ*). This is because [the word] does not grasp the sense of denoting a specific place characterized by easily obtainable objects of enjoyment; rather, it has another purpose. The word *kāma* (desire), however, is a restatement of the desire for acquisition.

Alternatively, the compound *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven) enjoins a specific agent as the performer of the sacrifice, and thereby enjoins the qualifying desire as well as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that [action]; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Furthermore, in this context, there is no arrival of [the injunction] being manifested through the hearing of the injunction, because it is the nature of the injunction to produce activity that must be expressed, and not its connection with the fruit; for even in the absence of activity, the injunction remains like a staff standing in the forest.
This is the section concerning one who desires heaven (*svargakāmādhikaraṇa*).
In the section concerning one who desires heaven...
This is because it is logically established that [the Veda] generates activity.
For the capacity to generate activity directed toward a result is not the meaning of an injunction; for even when an injunction is heard, some people are not seen to engage in activity.
Precisely for this reason, it is not authoritative to claim that an injunction implies that its object is a means to a desired end.

If, however, it is suspected that the sentence would be rendered purposeless by the mere statement of its fitness for inducing activity (*pravṛtti*), then—even though the sacrifice is understood as the end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) through the direct syntactic connection (*samānapada-śruti*)—since the quality of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) alone is implied among the common causes of activity (which include error), and since activity is established even from a mistaken cognition of being a means to a desired end, the sentence does not imply [the truth of] being a means to a desired end.
Alternatively, let the desire for heaven itself be the occasion (*nimitta*) for action, just as in the case of the injunction: "One who desires a woman should perform penance."

Furthermore, when there is a cause (nimitta) for the performance of a contingent rite (naimittika), there is merely an absence of [other] notions regarding its performance; however, nothing desirable is actually achieved through that performance.
Since the engagement of the person is established simply by the absence of such notions when there is non-performance, there is no pointlessness of the injunction either.

In any case, because the sacrifice itself is the end to be accomplished (bhāvya) and lacks the status of being a means to a desired object, there is no establishment of entitlement (adhikāra)—which consists in the agent's identity residing in the same locus as the fruit produced by the object of engagement that motivates the activity.
This being the case, the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) is not merely the suitability for the performance of an action, as that would result in its redundancy.

Nor can the inference of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) be considered an error; for since cognitions are intrinsically valid (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), it is impossible for them to be erroneous in the absence of a sublater (*bādhaka*). Therefore, in order to investigate whether validity—which is established by default—is indeed present, the fact that the sacrifice is a means to a desired end must necessarily be the object of consideration. Consequently, within the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), the state of having a desired end as the goal (*bhāvya*) and the sacrifice as the instrument (*karaṇa*) is already established.
