As for the claim that, having accepted desire as the *nimitta* (occasioning cause), the injunction (*vidhi*) functions as an instigator by implying the sin (*pratyavāya*) resulting from non-performance—therein, although desire may generate activity, there is no evidence for its being the *nimitta*.

Even in cases such as "one desiring a woman" (*strīkāmaḥ*), desire does not function as the *nimitta*, because if it were, it would follow that a different suffix (*pratyaya*) would be required for the performance of the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*).

Rather, [the suffix] merely indicates the locus of the cognition produced by the desire established through other means of knowledge; thus, even in those cases, the injunction functions solely by implying that the act is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).

For this very reason, in all cases involving occasional (*naimittika*) rites, since the non-performance would otherwise entail a lack of justification, the injunction (*vidhi*) implies by parsimony (*lāghava*) nothing other than that [the act] is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). Consequently, it is established that the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) has a desired object as its goal (*iṣṭabhāvyatva*). And how, under such circumstances, the occasional rite has the destruction of sin as its goal is explained in the *Yāvajjīvādhikaraṇa* (2.4.1). Furthermore, that desired end—such as heaven, sons, and so forth—is presented by words like "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), because of their semantic fitness and their connection with the word "desire" (*kāma*).
Desire also [aims] at the fruit by its own nature, whereas [desire] for a substance is merely figurative.

For this very reason, even the word *svarga*—according to the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Purāṇa*, and so forth—denotes either a specific region suitable for the enjoyment of pleasure unmixed with suffering, or, according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* (1.3.9), it denotes such pleasure alone; it does not denote sandalwood and the like, for in that case the contemporary usage would be merely figurative.

For this very reason, even the word *svargakāma* (desirous of heaven) refers to heaven through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and the nominative case-ending signifies the status of being the object; thus, since this is logically consistent with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), there is no suspicion that heaven cannot be connected [to it] because it is subordinate to something else. Some maintain that the person desirous of heaven is connected as the qualified agent (*adhikārin*), and therefore heaven is not connected [to the productive urge] unless one supplies a second-case word denoting heaven. However, in that case, since the requirement for a result comes first, and since secondary indication is simpler than the assumption of an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), [the former view is preferable].

And thus, since it is understood that heaven and so forth alone are the *bhāvya* (the end to be achieved) by following the more powerful scriptural injunction (*vidhiśruti*), it is established that the procedure (*paddhati*) operating in a general manner indicates, through secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*), that the sacrifice and so forth possess the status of the instrument (*karaṇatva*). This concludes the section on qualification (*adhikāra*). Furthermore, it should be understood here that qualification (*adhikāra*) consists in being the agent (*kartṛtva*) with respect to a result that is co-referential with either the desire for the result or the result itself (i.e., co-referential with either the desire for the result that motivates activity or the result produced by the object of that activity).
Therefore, even though the desire for the destruction of sin is not the motivator for activity in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya-sthala*), there is no impairment of eligibility (*adhikāra*).
Maṇḍana [says]: "Heaven and so forth are the fruit of sacrifice and the like.
Śaṅkara [says]: "Heaven is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), not the means (*sādhana*)."
The Section on the One Desiring Heaven (*svargakāmādhikaraṇa*).

(The nature of the reasoning: Since that which is desired cannot be devoid of a fruit, when the word "desire" (*kāma*) is attached [to a term], the word "one desiring cattle" (*paśukāma*) refers to the fruit, according to the established conclusion of the *svargakāmādhikaraṇa* in the rule: "But it is not the means, because it exists for that purpose" (6.1.2). (As in: "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā [offering]. )
Su. Pṛ. 415, *Svargakāmādhikaraṇa*.

(The nature of the argument: In an injunction for an independent ritual (*svatantra-karma-vidhi*), if the word "desire" (*kāma*) were not intended to denote a result, the injunction would be purposeless due to its fruitlessness; yet, even if it is intended to denote a result, since the result can be established through the *Jyotiṣṭoma* itself, the term "one who desires cattle" (*paśukāma*) does not establish cattle as the specific result [of that particular act]. Pṛ. 415, in the *Svargakāmādhikaraṇa*, because the result has been stated as the objective to be aimed at (*uddeśya*), its status as a cause of differentiation (*bhedahetutva*) is possible.

Page 498: Having introduced [the topic] with "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā," it is not correct to say that this is merely a restatement (anuvāda) of the acquisition of wealth, drinking liquor, and so forth; for its status as a restatement was established in the *Svargakāmādhikaraṇa*.
[This refers to] the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*).
Because this will be refuted in the section concerning those who desire heaven (*svargakāmādhikaraṇa*).
Nor should it be argued that the status of the root-meaning as the instrument (*karaṇatva*) was stated in the section concerning the bhāvanā (*bhāvādhikaraṇa*).

Even for this [view], in the *svargakāmādhikaraṇa* (6.1.1), it was previously raised as an objection that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), by virtue of being in the same syntactical word, is the result (*phala*) and not heaven (*svarga*) and so forth; this was established based on the fact that [the result] is the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Consequently, according to the logic of the *svargakāmādhikaraṇa*, because [the result] is that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*), the discussion regarding the "bringing into existence" (*bhāva-adhikaraṇa*) proceeds immediately after the discussion on performance (*prayukti*). (Ku. 3.2.136) [In the case of] "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā," the word "one desiring cattle" (*paśukāma*), by the logic of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the *svargakāmādhikaraṇa*, refers to one who possesses [cattle] through acquisition and so forth, and thus it is not the fruit of the sacrifice.

"For the animal sacrifice cannot be performed by one who merely desires an animal, because the sacrifice is already known [and thus cannot be the object of an injunction]; it is therefore a restatement (anuvāda) of the sacrifice."

PMS 1.4.3, p. 328: Since the person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) and so forth is obtained through the implication of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), it is understood that the substance [denoted by] "desiring heaven" and so forth functions as a qualifier, like the "red turban" (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*) and other examples. Consequently, there arises a doubt as to whether the heaven and so forth included therein are connected to the sacrifice as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) or as the primary factor (*pradhāna*). In the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the *Svargakāmādhikaraṇa* in the first section of the sixth book, the sūtra states: "When substances are related to an action, they are connected as subordinate factors" (6.1.1.9). According to the maxim, "When an accomplished entity (*bhūta*) and a thing to be accomplished (*bhavya*) are mentioned together, the accomplished entity is taught for the sake of the thing to be accomplished," it will be explained that the word "heaven" (*svarga*), being an accomplished entity, is connected as a subordinate factor to the action, which is the thing to be accomplished. Thus, from the word "desiring cattle" (*paśukāma*), it is understood that the cattle are the means (*sādhana*).

Su. p. 415: The concluding sūtra of the section on the one desiring heaven (*svargakāmādhikaraṇa*) states: "But [the action] is not the means [to that], because it is for the sake of that" (6.1.1.2). The meaning of the sūtra is this: if the connection with the word "desire" (*kāma*) did not establish [heaven] as the fruit, the ritual act would be devoid of being a means to it, since human effort is directed toward the attainment of a fruit.
Su. p. 421: The existence of a self distinct from the body is established by the scriptural mention of "one desiring heaven," and so forth.
Maṇi, p. 54. The principle of the sentence concerning one desiring heaven (*svargakāmavākyanyāya*).

In the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), once the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) has been understood through the injunction, two aspects of that which is to be produced by the efficient force (*bhāvanābhāvya*) are apprehended: its state of being an objective (*sādhyatva*) and its being the object of desire (*icchāviṣayatva*).
Among these, heaven’s status as the object of desire is [established] by the word.
However, that which is to be brought about (bhāvya) is implied by the purpose (artha), because there is an absence of desire once [the goal] is established;
but when there is desire, neither of these two [conditions] applies.

Therefore, transcending mere desires, it is precisely that which bestows heaven (svarga) which is accepted there as the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*), preceded by the expectation of a specific desired end.

And although the state of being the thing-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatva*) is presented in the sacrifice (*yāga*), nevertheless, since its status as the means to heaven—whether in a secondary or primary sense—is not established prior to its connection with that [desire], it too is not understood there as the object to be accomplished.
— *Ābharaṇa*.

Brahmasūtra 3.4.15–24: Like the words "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth, the term *svargakāma* (one who desires heaven) serves to designate a specific type of person; that very individual who desires heaven for his own sake is the referent of the word *svargakāma*, and no other. Somaśambhu-paddhati 6.1.1, p. 445: Regarding the two—heaven and hell—since they consist of unsurpassed pleasure and pain respectively, they are to be experienced in another location or in another birth and do not constitute [independent] distinct rituals (*karmāntara*). (Therefore, it must be stated that it is indeed the *apūrva* [unseen potency]). This will be explained in the section on the alternative view. Vākyapadīya 2.1.2.15, p. 397: Heaven and hell.

For heaven and hell are not, by their very nature, states of unsurpassed pleasure and pain, nor are they specific locations that could not be experienced in this very life; for it is impossible to attain the means for the avoidance or acquisition of things that are beyond the world of experience. (This is the view of the author of the *Śāstradīpikā-khaṇḍana* and other commentators).
2|1|2|15, p. 393: It is certain that the fruit of heaven belongs to the hereafter.
Vi. 4|3|129: "And no obstacle whatsoever follows here for one whose fruit is heaven;
for an action that has one fruit cannot produce a different fruit."
In the *Gautamīya* as well, that [is established] with respect to the excellence of its accompaniment.

In the *Ślokavārttika*, in the section on the refutation of the "throwing of the dice" (*citrakṣepaparihāra*), it is stated: "The word 'heaven' (*svarga*) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for supreme pleasure; however, when applied to substances such as sandalwood, it is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*).
It is also [used] for a particular region."

VI. 6|1|1: The fruit is indicated by the word "heaven" (*svarga*), because in the expression "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*), it is understood as that which is to be accomplished through the performance of ritual action. 10|2|121:
In the *svastyayanī* sacrifice, they have protected the offering with the two *ājyabhāga* portions [reciting]: "O Agni, protect us from distress... and "O Soma, you protect us from all sides... etc.
Āśvadhau 2.10.5: "The principle is that mental states flash forth when the mind is healthy.
When the mind is overcome by anxiety, the bodily constituents (dhātus) increase; when the mind is lost, the constituents go to destruction.
Therefore, the mind must be protected in every way. When the mind is healthy, mental modifications (vṛttis) flash forth.
[The term] *sāhasī*. 136. *Svādhyāya*:

By accepting the word *adhyāya* as denoting a scripture through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) based on the object (*karman*)—namely, that which is studied (*adhīyate*)—*svādhyāya* is [defined as] one's own scripture (*sva-śāstra*) and its chapters (*adhyāya*).

Thus, from hearing this analysis (*vigraha*), the establishment of the various stages of the scripture and so forth is achieved through the injunction for private Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) alone.

(Su. pṛ. 991). The injunction "The Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*) is scriptural (*śrauta*). (Bāla. pṛ. 39). The injunction is "The Veda is to be studied. (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ* iti vidhiḥ).
The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that the injunction prescribes the study of the Veda for the sake of heaven and other such rewards;
therefore, since the fruit of heaven is accomplished by mere study alone, one need not remain in the teacher’s house for the purpose of an inquiry into Dharma.

The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the injunction prescribes study for the purpose of attaining knowledge of the meaning of the sentences being recited, up to the point of grasping the syllables and so forth; and since that [knowledge] is impossible without investigation, one must remain in the teacher’s house for the purpose of an inquiry into Dharma.
This is the first section. Vaidyanātha:
111–119. By the injunction, "The Veda is to be studied," the cultivation of the act of studying the entire Veda is prescribed.

In this regard, when the question arises as to what one should bring about (*bhāvayet*), "study" (*adhyayana*) presents itself; however, since the injunction (*vidhi*)—though it has arrived—is incapable of impelling a person [toward that end] because study is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), its capacity to impel toward the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is precluded.
Consequently, by way of non-contradiction, [the injunction] enters into the instrumental role (*karaṇa*) along with the prohibition, such that [the meaning becomes]: "by means of study.
This concludes the section concerning the connection with the master (*svāmī-yuktādhikaraṇa*).
Are they, moreover, for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the principal?
What, then, is the prima facie view? It is established by the previous reasoning that they are for the sake of the subsidiaries and the principal.
This being the case, we reply:
This is joined with the Lord;
therefore, it belongs to the Pradhāna.
Why? Because of the connection with the fruit.
This is the relationship between the person and the sacrifice:
the sacrifice is the giver of the *apūrva*, and the person is the recipient.
But is there not yet another relationship?
The sacrifice is that which is to be accomplished, and the person is the accomplisher.
It is for this purpose—that there shall be a connection with the fruit—that the person is mentioned in the scripture;
for he does not bring the sacrifice into existence.
The sacrifice is said to be performed by sentient beings.
Why, then, is it said that the fruit arises for one who brings it about?
Furthermore, it is said that the formative forces (saṃskāra) perform the formation.
Whatever the purpose of that refinement (saṃskāra) may be, it produces capacity for that end.
And the purpose of the person is to obtain the fruit, not to bring about the sacrifice.
Therefore, those refinements of the person render the person capable of receiving the fruit, not capable of accomplishing the sacrifice.
He asks: "If they do not produce capacity for the accomplishment of the sacrifice, how then are they properties of the sacrifice? It is replied:
They exist to assist the sacrifice as it accomplishes its own purpose.
And what is its own purpose? That to which the agent is connected by means of the fruit.
Therefore, the purificatory rites for the master (the sacrificer) are for the sake of the primary act.

Regarding the sūtra: "But those [rites] pertaining to the sacrificer are for the sake of both the subsidiary and the primary, because he is the principal agent, as in the case of the ritual act" (3.8.4.4), it has been established by this section that certain rites belong to the sacrificer. Now, do these rites serve the purpose of both the subsidiary and the primary through the sacrificer's aspect as the *kartṛ* (agent), or do they serve the primary alone through his aspect as the *bhoktṛ* (enjoyer)? What is the prima facie view? That they serve all purposes, according to the preceding section.
For when the sacrificer is present for all purposes, [the priests] are able to assist everyone;
moreover, there is no cause for their being occupied elsewhere.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"By the very same reason that their dedication to the owner is certain,
it is equally clear that they serve the primary purpose [of the sacrifice].
For if these [animals] were to fall under the category of being for the sake of the agent, then they would be understood as serving all purposes."
They reside in the aspect of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtvāṃśa*);
for that [aspect] is not possible without them (the remainder of the sentence is: because it is threefold precisely by way of having the nature of an enjoyer).
However, how agency (*kartṛtva*) occurs even in the absence of those [faculties] is evident to the perception of all the world.

Furthermore, since that [agency] is possible for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) as well, there would be no exclusion of them. Moreover, this [term] requires the imposition of fitness upon what is intended, and where such fitness has not yet arisen;
however, the essential nature of the agent is not what is intended for the sacrificer.
Nor is it the case that [the capacity] was not already established prior to those [actions];
rather, actions which impart this capability are called "formative forces" (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, they partake in the state of being an enjoyer.
And as for the fruit of an action which is enjoyed by the sacrificer, those [subsidiaries] are able to assist that very [action] and not another;
the fruit of the primary [act] is enjoyed by persons, not by the subsidiaries, because they exist for the sake of the sacrifice.
Therefore, the subsidiaries belong to the primary alone.
He said:
"If they do not fall within the portion that brings about the cessation [of the action], then they would become a constituent part of the result itself.
This is not a fault.
For this indeed is the primary benefit to the principal [sacrifice]: that the agent is rendered fit for the reception of its fruit.

Consequently, just as other subsidiaries whose purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*) also produce fitness for the fruit—though they do not bestow it directly because they are merely subsidiaries—so too should these purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) belonging to the sacrificer be understood.

The practical application (*prayojana*) is that, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), shaving and other such rites are subsidiary to the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice and others, and thus follow it when it is modified.
The preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as shaving and the like, would pertain to both the subsidiary and the principal acts—this being the prima facie view—it is replied:
"Because the status of being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is primary and because it is not perceived [as a result of the rites], the preparatory rites are subordinate to that [status].
However, the status of being the agent (*kartṛbhāva*) is subordinate and is perceived [as a result] from other sources."
The connection [of this section] follows from the preceding discussion on *soma*.

The purpose is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), those [rites] would apply to the *nirūḍhapaśubandha*—which is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *agnīṣomīya-paśu*—whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), they do not.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: shaving, the application of oil, and so forth, when connected with the owner, are the attributes (*dharma*) of the primary sacrifice; because of the connection with the fruit, that is, because of the connection with the status of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) characterized by the possession of the fruit.
Regarding the assistance provided by acts such as sowing and so forth, does it pertain to both the primary and the subsidiary elements therein?
It pertains only to the primary; let it belong to both, however, because of their status as complete agents.
It is logical that the scriptural consecration belongs to the primary element, which is the enjoyer of the fruit.

Even in the absence of a refinement (*saṃskṛti*), agency is observed; however, that [refinement] does not exist there. That assistance produced by acts such as shaving and so forth does not exist in that form of agency. In the Bhaṭṭa view, regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices, acts such as shaving the hair and beard are for the purpose of refining the person engaged in the ritual (*kratukṛt-puruṣa-saṃskāra*), and are not indirect auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*). This is because in injunctions such as "he shaves his hair and beard," "he clips his nails," "he cleans his teeth," "he bathes," "he anoints himself," and "he rubs oil on himself," the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) indicates that these are for the benefit of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
The section on the agent joined with the action: for when the fruit of the action goes to the agent himself, the *ātmanepada* suffixes are used, provided the agent is equal to the master.

However, since the assistance provided is remote, the fruit thereof—the excellence of the sacrifice (*kratusādguṇya*)—does not pertain to the commencement [of the action] by virtue of the sacrifice itself.
That which is an intermediate unseen result (*avāntarādṛṣṭa*) is not the fruit of the action.

Even though here the fruit belongs only to another who enjoys the auxiliary of the sacrifice, nevertheless, because the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is observed in the Veda, and because when a meaningful purpose is possible, it is improper to assume the purpose is merely grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), there is no fault in accepting that the fruit of the action accrues to oneself, having postulated its non-restriction through the rules such as "svarita" and so forth.
Similarly, in expressions such as "he cleanses his teeth" (*dato dhāvate*), the fact that the teeth are the object of refinement (*saṃskārya*) is understood through the accusative case;
in "the milk-vow of the Brāhmaṇa" (*payovrataṃ brāhmaṇasya*), it is understood through the genitive case;
and in the case of bathing, it is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that its purpose is the removal of impurities.
In the same way, it will be stated regarding austerity (*tapas*) as well.

Ultimately, where there is nothing that serves as a restraint (*dama*), [the result follows] from initiation (*dīkṣā*) alone, because [initiation] brings about the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person suitable for undertaking restraints (*yama*) and so forth.
And the person’s utility for the sacrifice (*kratu*) is either by way of being the agent (*kartṛ*) or by way of being the enjoyer of the fruit produced by the sacrifice.

In this regard, when considering whether the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are useful for the aspect of agency (*kartṛtva*) or for the aspect of enjoyership (*bhoktṛtva*): if they were for the sake of enjoyership, there would be the consequence of equal primacy [between the agent and the enjoyer], which would result in the subversion of the connection with the sacrifice as understood from the context. Therefore, they are for the sake of agency.

Since acts such as cleaning the teeth are for the purpose of purifying the body, and since that body is of no use for being an enjoyer of results in the next world, they are likewise [for the sake of agency].
Consequently, because the purificatory rites primarily serve the purpose of agency, they too are of that same nature.

This being the case, since agency arises even apart from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) associated with the body and so forth, it is more appropriate [to regard the self] as a mere enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) in the form of the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Furthermore, this is because the state of being an enjoyer is more fundamental than the state of being an agent.
Moreover, the utility of the body and other factors for the state of being an enjoyer remains unimpeded, as they are designated as distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) which they delimit.

Nor does this result in the [saṃskāras] becoming the primary element; for just as the preparations of the field are for the purpose of sowing the seed, so too the preparations of the self are logically subordinate to the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*), as they produce the fitness for the receptacle of the fruit generated by the sacrifice.
Therefore, that [fitness] is produced collectively by all the saṃskāras through their respective intermediate unseen effects (*adṛṣṭa*).

Alternatively, it is the very fruit of the primary sacrifice that is attributed to the self; thus, the saṃskāras have that [fruit] as their purpose, not the subordinate acts themselves, because that fruit belongs to the sacrifice.

However, where the utility for agency is established either by direct perception or by the explicit statement of the text—as in the case of the various recitations for initial purification, or in such passages as "Those wearing golden garlands proceed"—the quality of being plural serves a purpose for the agency itself; therefore, it pertains to both the subsidiaries and the primary rite.
For this very reason, in such instances, that [quality] is extended to the modified forms of the subsidiaries (aṅgavikṛti). (Mīmāṃsākośa 569)

Maṇḍana: "The primary meanings [of the terms] are the master and the consecrated. Śaṅkara: "[Also] the fruit, the purpose, the speech, and so forth. In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are equal to the master.
Regarding this, one should consult the discussion in Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 12.5.0: "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the priests [are] equal to the master," where the governing principle (*adhikaraṇa*) is to be seen:
"The priests are equal to the master because of the commonality of their ritual function."
It was stated previously that "the officiating priests [are those] of the assembly" (*ṛtvijaḥ sadasaḥ*).

Regarding this, when the question arises whether the *sadasya* (the member of the assembly) belongs to the assembly or whether it is the *gṛhapati* (householder), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—based on the fact that the *camasa* (cup) and the formal appointment (*varaṇa*) exist [only for the former]—is that the *sadasya* belongs to the assembly. This being the case, the following sūtra presents the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
"The officiating priests have been declared to be seventeen; they should be accompanied by the master."
"Those for whom the Lord is the completer of the total number twenty;
the meaning is that He would be the master of their assembly.
Why? Because of the commonality of action—that is, because of the commonality of sacrificial rites."
That which is the *camasa* and that which is the *varaṇa* belong to the *brahman* alone and are not separate from him;
however, the author of the *Bhāṣya* maintains that there is no *sadasya* other than the *brahman*.

The author of the *Vārttika*, on the other hand, considers the *sadasya* to be distinct from the *brahman*; nevertheless, his view is that the status of being the *sadas* belongs to the master (*svāmin*).

The statement regarding this is as follows: "Because it is said that 'the Sadasya also performs the sacrifice through supervision,' he is included by the force of the scriptural statement itself; however, no specific ritual act (padārtha) could be designated for him according to that logic.
Furthermore, there is no distinct ritual act called 'supervision' (pratyavekṣaṇa), by which his status as an agent might be restricted by any means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa).
Therefore, since the Sadasya is indeed present, it is rightly said that 'there are seventeen masters'."

Thus [it is said]. Herein lies the point of interest: in another treatise (*śāstrāntara*), however, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) of the assembly (*sadas*) are enumerated within the statements concerning initiation fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra "On account of the designation in the case of the cups" (3.1.7.22), the following injunction (*praiṣa*) is recorded: "Let the Hotṛ’s cup go forward; let the Brahman’s go forward; let those of the Udgātṛs go forward; let that of the Sacrificer go forward; let those of the Sadasyas go forward."
Consequently, the repeated performance of the sacrifice and the consumption of the Sadas-cup by the members of the assembly certainly do exist.
Therefore, this section should be understood as concerning other sacrificial halls (śālās).
Thus it is said.

Regarding the statement, "The master is equal to the [other] priests because of the commonality of their action" (3.7.18–38), it will be explained that according to the view of Svāyaṃbhuva, the patron (yajamāna) also possesses the status of a priest (*ṛtvik*), just like Brahmā and the others. This is the equality of the master with the priests. 4482. [End of section]. The doctrine of Svāyaṃbhuva will be stated [further on].
Vārttika 3.1.12.1, p. 965: "The state of being both master and priest [belongs to the sacrificers] because of the commonality of the action" (3.1.18.8).

In the *sattra* sacrifice, regarding the statement "those who are the sacrificers are the priests," there is first of all no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the two nominative terms through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by taking the sacrificers' role as both agent and performer of the priestly function; for this would result in the redundancy of the sentence, as it would already be established by the principle "the state of being both master and priest.
(Bhāṭṭa 6.6.3).
In the case of a sacrificial session (*sattra*), one who acts as a representative in the place of the master does not possess the status of a master.

(Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 6.3.1.23–25). See the relevant section in the Mīmāṃsākośa, page 4109, under the entry: "In the case of a sacrificial session (*sattra*), [the rule] regarding one acting as a representative in the place of the master."

In a sacrificial session (*satra*), when there is a substitute for the master (*svāmin*), the purificatory rites such as shaving the hair (*vapanādi*) are performed according to the characteristics of the master.

(Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 6.3.1.26). See the relevant section in Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 4109, under the heading "In a sacrificial session, when there is a substitute for the master, the status of the substitute possesses the characteristics of the master.
This is the opinion of Svāyaṃbhuva.
Regarding the difference and non-difference between cause and effect: in that context, after the *vivici* has been offered,
the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice with the utterance of *svāhā* occurs in the case of offerings made with a wooden ladle (*darvīhoma*).
Bhāṣya 10.8.20–22: "He performs the *svāhākāra* offering.
This is the name of the action of the fifth *prayāja*.
Vi. 10.2.7: Food is offered to the gods either with the *svāhākāra* or with the *vaṣaṭkāra*.

"The oblation is offered to the gods either with the utterance of *svāhā* or with the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*.

8|4|121: Darvihomas are conjoined with the utterance of *svāhā*.
In the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the Soma sacrifice, however, the *vaṣaṭ* call is prescribed.
The purpose of the *svāhā* utterance is restricted to the archetype (*prakṛti*), and does not apply to the *ariṣṭha* oblations or the *pārthana* oblations.

8|4|121. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that in cases where the *svāhākāra* (the utterance "svāhā") is employed before mantras such as "svāhā vāce, svāhā vānaspataye," it does not serve the purpose of an oblation (*homa*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because speech (*vāk*) and the others are understood to be deities by virtue of their being in the dative case, and because the capacity to manifest the meaning of an object remains unchanged regardless of the position [of the mantra], these utterances indeed serve the purpose of offering (*pradāna*).
Saṃkarṣa. 2|4|17 states that the purpose of the *svāhākāra* is offering in instances such as "pṛthivye svāhā" and "antarikṣāya svāhā."

Even when the deity is remembered by means of a mantra beginning with *svāhā*—that is, the invocation mantra—there is a further remembrance for the purpose of offering (*dānārtha*) by means of a mantra beginning with *svāhā*.
(Bhaṭṭadīpikā 10.9.9, p. 205).
The rule regarding *svāhākāra* is: "Svāhā to Agni, Svāhā to Soma," and so forth.

The repeated mention of the *svāhākāra* (the utterance "svāhā") in certain *darvihoma* offerings does not serve to incorporate the *svāhākāra* that is taught [only] in connection with the non-commencement [of the sacrifice].
See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2015; the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) regarding the repeated mention of the *svāhākāra* in some *darvihomas* should be consulted there.
A mantra that has the utterance of *svāhā* at its beginning is also an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the act of oblation (*homa*).
This point is to be seen in the section [of the Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa] stating: "In an oblation, even a mantra with *svāhā* at the beginning is an instrument" (Saṃkarṣa.
2.4.17). [However], the fifth *prayāja* (the *svāhākāra*) does not exist in sacrifices such as the piling of the fire-altar (*cayana*).
Bhāṭṭa 4.27:

In the context of the *svāhākāra* sacrifice, which is enjoined for the purpose of bestowing wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth during the *cayana* rite, there is an injunction for the *svāhākāra* in those offerings where it has not been previously prescribed.
The word *svāhākāra* (the final *prayāja*) denotes a sacrifice, just as the *samidh* and other *prayājas* do.
Bhāṣya 10.17.14. The *Sviṣṭakṛt* fire is indeed distinct from the *Āhavanīya*; it is not the *Āhavanīya* itself.
And that other [fire] is the Gārhapatya.
Saṃkarṣa. 4.2.9–10: The Sviṣṭakṛt fire, when being raised, is not for the purpose of the oblation itself, but rather for the purpose of conveying the offering.
4.2.11: The Sviṣṭakṛt fire is indeed a specific deity presiding over the Gārhapatya.
*Saṃkarṣa.* 4.2.10. See *Mīmāṃsākośa*, p. 19: "Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the presiding deity of the Gārhapatya fire. This section should be consulted.
In the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-paśu*), the Sviṣṭakṛt offering is to be performed with three portions from the remnants of the intestines (*aniyāśeṣa*).
10.3.10–11. See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 124, regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering in the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*mīḍhuṣīya-paśu*). The relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted there.
The *sviṣṭakṛt* in the *anuyāja* offerings is a purificatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*).
The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering should be included in the *anuyāja* because it serves a purpose through its connection with the meaning of the mantras.
Regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the third *anuyāja* is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*).
The established conclusion is that it is an act of ritual preparation (*saṃskārakarma*).

To explain its purpose, he says: in the *anuyāja* sacrifice, the *Sviṣṭakṛt* Agni who is cooked in the third *anuyāja* mantra would be *āvāpika* (pertaining to the insertion), not one who is grasped as part of the insertion itself.
The place for insertion (*āvāpasthāna*) is between the *Ājyabhāga* and the *Sviṣṭakṛt*.
In that context, "āvāpika" refers to what belongs to the insertion (āvāpa). That which exists outside of it is "bāhya.

In the *anuyāja* offerings, the *āvāpika* *sviṣṭakṛt* rite possesses a purpose; it has a visible result and, by way of following the principal fire-offering (*pradhāna-homa*), it possesses the result of being a purificatory act (*saṃskāra*).

Because remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) are connected to the purpose of the momentary ritual service within the context through general application (*prakaraṇa*), whereas direct auxiliaries (*saṃnipātin*) are connected to their purpose for the sake of refinement (*saṃskāra*) by means of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and so forth; and because direct auxiliaries possess greater force than remote auxiliaries,

it is therefore established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the recitation of the *sviṣṭakṛt* formula at the *anuyāja* offerings is a refining act (*saṃskārakarma*) belonging to the *āvāpika* (inserted) category.
The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering should be made from the northern portion.
Bhāṣya 3.5.4.17 states that in a group of animals dedicated to a single deity, such as those belonging to Prajāpati, the *sviṣṭakṛt* is performed by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*).

Bhāṭṭa 5.2.6: The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering exists in the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice. Since it is stated there that "the *ājyabhāga*, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and the *bhakṣa* [are to be performed]," these must indeed be performed therein.
Vi. 10.1.50: The *sviṣṭakṛt* [is prescribed] for the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.
In the case of the *māsāda*, that which is performed is a gift for the deity; it is not a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the deity.
When there is a change in the deity in the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, [the original term] ceases because of the presence of that specific word.
In the *saumika* purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), it is heard in the scripture: "One sacrifices to Agni and Varuṇa as the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
The term *sviṣṭakṛt* is a designation for Agni;

however, Agni and Varuṇa are distinct from a deity consisting of a single [individual] name, because they possess the nature of a deity that functions through a collective application (*vyāsajyavṛtti*).
Therefore, since Agni and Varuṇa are distinct deities, the word *sviṣṭakṛt*—because it is a term for them and denotes Agni and Varuṇa—is excluded.
The meaning is that the qualification "the *Sviṣṭakṛt* of Agni and Varuṇa" should not be applied.
Consequently, one should not say, "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni-Varuṇa-Sviṣṭakṛt," but rather, "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni and Varuṇa," and so forth.
Thus is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa).
Alternatively, there is a conjunction [of the two deities] due to the necessity of the expression, because the naming arises from the action.
In the Soma sacrifice, regarding the Avabhṛtha bath, it is heard in the scripture: "He sacrifices to Agni and Varuṇa as the Sviṣṭakṛt."

In this regard, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position—that the term *sviṣṭakṛt* should be employed—is established by the Sūtra; however, the author sets aside that view with the word "or" (*vā*) and states the final conclusion (siddhānta):
there should be a connection between the term *sviṣṭakṛt* and the term *agnīvaruṇa*.
The meaning is that the formula containing the term *sviṣṭakṛt*—such as "Recite for Agni and Varuṇa, the two *Sviṣṭakṛts*"—should be performed.

"Because of the implication (arthāpatti): because Agni and Varuṇa take the place [of Agni]—that is, because they obtain his position—in the archetype (prakṛti), wherever Agni Sviṣṭakṛt occurs, there at the Avabhṛtha bath, Agni and Varuṇa obtain that position; therefore, the two [deities] must be performed as possessing the designation 'Sviṣṭakṛt'. This is because the designation is produced by the action: since the designation 'Sviṣṭakṛt' is based on the performance of a well-offered sacrifice (*sviṣṭaṃ kṛtavān sviṣṭakṛt*), it is caused by the act of performing a well-offered sacrifice."
Sviṣṭakṛt (486): The section on Sviṣṭakṛt.

Regarding the cake-offering (*puroḍāśa*) of the animal sacrifice to Agni-Soma, it is heard [in the scripture]: "He sacrifices to Agni. In that case, the omission of the qualifying attribute (*guṇalopa*) should be applied to all *sviṣṭakṛt* invocations (*nigama*), not to the sacrifice itself.
10.4.18.36-37. At the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one cuts off two portions of the oblation for the Sviṣṭakṛt.
There should be a prohibition of consumption regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering because the reason is the same.

When the *sviṣṭakṛt* is heard of in the context of the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice in the injunction, "He sacrifices to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," there should be a prohibition of consumption—that is, a prohibition against eating. And this would constitute an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) regarding the consumption of the remnants of other offerings.

Because the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the consumption [of the portions] share the same cause—that is, because the reason for their existence, namely the purpose of consecrating the remnant (*śeṣa-saṃskāra*), is identical—it follows that the *sviṣṭakṛt* serves as an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the other subsidiary rites involving the remnant; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Alternatively, there would be no prohibition, since such a practice is observed in the case of the *idā*.
The word "vā" (or) serves to negate the established conclusion.
There is no prohibition regarding the consumption of the remnants; that is, there should be no prohibition, because it is observed in the case of the *iḍā*.
The statement, "He invokes the *iḍā*," is applicable only if there is consumption; it does not apply when there is none. Therefore, it is a prohibition.
Since the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice possesses the preceding [elements], this is considered a hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtvā-cintya*).
Or rather, it is a prohibition, because it is seen to be preceded by a rule.
The word "or" (vā) sets aside the prima facie view. There would be a prohibition of other remnants-eatings [by the priests] by means of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
However, there is no fault here because it is seen to be preceded by a formal injunction (*vidhi*).

First, there is a cognition based on the general rule of the *codaka* scripture regarding the disposal of the sacrificial remains (*haviḥśeṣa-pratipatti*). Then, the exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) distinct from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is a restatement (*punarādivāciḥ*) for the purpose of permitting the disposal of what is other than itself; it is not a means of bringing about something otherwise unobtained (*netara-prāpaka*). This is the sense. Thus, in this case, a permission (*abhyanujñāpa*) preceded by a formal injunction is observed here.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering serves as an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyāpaka*) for the other [remnant-offerings].

In the section [of the *Tantravārttika*] titled "The *Sviṣṭakṛt* should be an exclusion of the consumption" (10.7.11), regarding the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice where the *sviṣṭakṛt* is an exclusion, it is demonstrated that the statement "he performs the two *ājyabhāga* offerings"—which functions as an indicator of restriction—serves to exclude other sacrifices of the same class as the *ājyabhāgas*, while the *sviṣṭakṛt* itself, being distinct from those, serves as an indicator of restriction that excludes other secondary rites (*śeṣakārya*) [such as consumption].
This is the *Parākrama*.
Just as there is a division of portions in the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, so too there is no division of portions in the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings.
Bhaṭṭa 4.1.14. The Section on the *Sviṣṭakṛt*.
Because there is no specific purpose [to serve as a restrictive factor], the subsidiary rites should be performed from one [offering], since the remainder is subordinate.

The Commentary: There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices. In them, there are subsidiary rites such as the *iḍā*, the *prāśitra*, the *vaṣaṭkāra*, and those performed with the sacrificial food (*auṣadha*).
Regarding this, a doubt arises: should these be performed from every offering, or from only one offering?
What is the conclusion? Because they are not the motivators, the ritual acts should be performed from one [portion].
The subsidiary acts for the remnants are not the motivators of the oblations.
If they were motivated by the subsidiary acts for the remnants, then all [oblations] would be motivated, and thus the acts would be performed from all of them.

However, these [rites] have other purposes; they are not to be employed for the subsidiary acts (*śeṣakārya*). Because of their proximity, they should be performed from whatever source is available, for the subsidiary is merely a means for them.

Or rather—when the remnant of the oblation has been disposed of by being cast into the Āhavanīya fire, it is then deliberated how the subsequent rites, such as the Sviṣṭakṛt offering and others, should be performed.
Regarding this, considering it to be for the sake of the purpose, he says: "from one."

(Regarding the commentary beginning with "yadi śeṣakāryaiḥ" as explained by the passage beginning with "satyapi"): Even though there is oneness [of the deity], if these substances were produced solely for that purpose, then—just as in the case of the animal sacrifices—all would be accomplished even from a single one, provided there were the possibility of all being used; thus, a connection with all [substances] would be established for the sake of the sacrificial remnants (*śeṣakārya*).
However, that is not the case, because they are not the primary motive (*aprayojakatvāt*).
Therefore, their accomplishment occurs only through their status as auxiliary contributors (*upakārakatva*) via the third [case-ending].
And because it has already been consecrated (*saṃskṛtatvāt*).

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: "Since the primary substance (*pradhāna*) has already been consecrated by such a subsidiary operation (*śeṣakārya*) performed once, it need not be performed again for another [substance].

Or rather: that consecration which belongs to the primary substance itself—being based on a single material and so forth—is established through the subsidiary operations and does not require another material.
And the word "once" (*sakṛt*) intends a single cutting.

Otherwise, however, because the performance would be by way of a *tantra* (simultaneous application) even if all were taken, the completion of the whole would be possible. Alternatively, the subsequent rites for the remnants would be performed from all [the portions] if they were purificatory acts; but these are not purificatory acts.
Why? Because it has been refined by another refinement (such as parvan-making and so forth).
If it is argued that this too is not contradictory because it pertains to the object [of cognition], [we reply: no.
In this regard, this is the meaning of the Sūtra: because the sequence of consecration (*saṃskāra*) has been transcended.

As long as a substance has not yet fulfilled its purpose, it requires consecration; however, once the primary rite (*pradhāna*) has concluded, the purpose of the consecrations has already been served, and thus there is no occasion for further consecrations.
Alternatively, [the consecration applies] to all [parts], because there is no distinction in their causal status and because the consecration is intended for that purpose.
The Commentary: The ritual acts with the remnants (śeṣakāryāṇi) should be performed from all the oblations (havirbhyaḥ).
Why? Because there is no difference in the reason.
Whatever is the reason for not performing the ritual acts with the remnant of one oblation is the same for all.
For that which remains must be established;
if it were not established for someone, that person would be excluded from that refinement.
Therefore, [the rites] should be performed for all.
Or rather—by the rule "That by which a substance is intended to be prepared" (Pāṇini 2.1.18), these are understood as preparatory acts (*saṃskāraka*).
Even there, they are to be understood as *pratipatti* (dispositional acts) according to the rule "In the case of production, that with which [the substance] is connected" (Pāṇini 4.2.1.19).
And all of them are required because there is no difference in their having fulfilled their purpose.
Even though these [subsidiary rites] do not employ substances directly, nevertheless, because they are employed by means of the substances themselves, their scope extends to all [the substances].

Furthermore, when the primary rite has ceased, since there arises the expectation, "What shall be the disposal (*pratipatti*) of these [substances] that still belong to it?", a rule for their disposal can be prescribed.
This is also because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).

The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) states: An indicative mark (*liṅga*) is also observed: "The gods said to Sviṣṭakṛt, 'Carry our oblation. He replied, 'I choose a boon; let there be a portion for me. They said, 'Choose it. He said, 'O gods, from each subsequent [portion], let the powerful Sviṣṭakṛt take a cutting. This observation of repetition (*vīpsā*) shows that the cuttings are to be made from all [the portions]. Therefore, the rites are to be performed from all.

Furthermore, the repetition in the expression "once each" (*sakṛtsakṛt*) regarding the cutting for Sviṣṭakṛt is appropriate only if the cutting is made from all [the portions] or if it pertains to the refinement (*saṃskāra*); it is not otherwise possible.

Thus, having first explained the sūtras according to the Bhāṣya by treating them as pertaining to specific topics (*adhikaraṇa*), [the author notes that] regarding such a subject matter, the understanding is to be established precisely in the second quarter (*pāda*) of the fourth chapter, since otherwise there would be the fault of redundancy (*paunaruktya*). Furthermore, the Bhāṣya explains the sūtras for the purpose of stating the utility (*prayojana*) of the preceding topic, beginning with the words "as the utility" (*prayojanatvena*). The utility here is this:

even if, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the subsidiary rites (*śeṣakārya*) are indeed to be performed for this [offering], what then is the purpose of this investigation? [This is the question.]
In this regard, the Sūtra should be applied to those very points previously stated by us as follows:

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the sacrificial oblations (*havīṣi*) do not serve as the motivators for the subsidiary rites (*śeṣakāryāṇi*); therefore, they should be performed separately. Furthermore, because the primary act (*pradhāna*) is accomplished by force from these [oblations], and because it is said that "when it is done once, it is all done," the purification (*saṃskṛtatva*) being established, the rites must be performed even from one's own portion.
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, since there is no distinction in the fact that all [the offerings] are equally the motivators (*prayojaka*), [the rites] are to be performed for all.
Furthermore, the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the placement [of the offering] upon the full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsa*) as its locus—illuminates the established conclusion.

Śābarabhāṣya: When a remnant exists, there arises the inquiry whether the subsidiary rites (*śeṣakārya*), such as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and others, are to be performed from one oblation (*havis*) or from all of them.

In this regard, since the purpose of the scriptural injunction "the *sviṣṭakṛt* [offering] is from one remnant" has been fulfilled by a single remnant, the rites should be performed from that one alone and not from all of them.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
if the subordinate qualities of the remnants were intended for the sake of the principal rite, then it would indeed be so.

However, regarding the remainder, which is scattered and whose disposal is required, this rule for disposal is prescribed. For that very thing for which it is not performed, there would be a deficiency due to the omission of the rule for disposal.
Therefore, the disposal must be performed for all of them.
Soma: [The connection is established] because it depends on what precedes it;
this is the specific point.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: the subsidiary rites (śeṣakāryāṇi) should be performed from only one [substance], because the subsidiary substance (śeṣa) is subordinate with respect to the subsidiary rite, and thus lacks the capacity to be the motivator (prayojaka) therein.
Vi— "But as for the *iṣṭakṛt* [offering], it should be performed from one [portion] or from all;
the fulfillment of the scriptural purpose is achieved from all, because the refinement (*saṃskāra*) is identical.

Bhāṭṭa—In this regard, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that since the subsidiary rites (*śeṣakārya*) are for the sake of the substance itself, those rites should be performed from only a single offering-remnant (*haviḥ*), established instead that they are acts of disposal (*pratipatti*) and concluded with the final position (*siddhānta*) that they should be performed from all [the remnants].

The Vārttikakāra explains that these sūtras are intended to state the purpose (*prayojana*) of the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), because if one were to apply the same understanding to such a subject in the fourth [section], it would result in redundancy since the matter has already been established.

If, in the preceding section, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) had maintained that the subsidiary rites (*śeṣakāryāṇi*) do not imply the offering of the oblation (*havistva*), then the purpose [of this section] would be self-evident.

However, when the preservation of the remnant is for the sake of subsequent rites (*śeṣakārya*), then—even though those rites are not the motivators (*aprayojaka*) because they depend on a substance employed for another purpose, and even though there is a third-case ending (*tṛtīyāpaka-pālatva*) due to their being a single object—since the remnant is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), it is illogical to conclude with the end of the primary [rite] merely to follow its subordinates. Furthermore, because it is intended that the conclusion occurs at the end of that [subordinate] as a specific point of completion, the performance of the remnant rites must be done from only one [remnant]. As for the specific scriptural statement, "once each" (*sakṛtsakṛt*;
Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.6), this refers to a different performance, just like the rule "on every fourth day of the *anyahīna* sacrifice."

In the Siddhānta, however, because there is a remainder present, and since the disposal (*prati-patti*) is possible according to the logic of the fourth book (*cāturthika-nyāya*), the performance [of the disposal] is from all [the portions], in accordance with the requirement of the action which does not take into account the specific number. Furthermore, the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is more appropriate. As Maṇḍana says: "The disposal of the remnant is indeed from all the sacrificial oblations."

Śaṅkara says: "There should be no performance of the search for a single [verse]. In the case of the omission of the explanatory statement regarding the Sviṣṭakṛt, there is an absence of reciting it again.
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad)

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the *sviṣṭakṛt* portion must first be taken from the *āgneya* cake and then from the *sānnāyya*; this is because the order of performance (*pravṛttikrama*) is more authoritative. In the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice, everything from the *sviṣṭakṛt* onwards should be performed exactly as prescribed. (Tup. 5.4.2.2–4).

Regarding the statement "In the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice, only that which is explicitly prescribed should be performed," the relevant section (adhikaraṇa) should be consulted. [This concerns] the Sviṣṭakṛt and other such rites; the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation is part of the primary injunction. [Section 4490: The Hanti-piṣya-adhikaraṇa].
The *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation must be performed from the remnants of all the sacrificial offerings (*havis*), and not from the remnant of any one of them alone.

(3|4|19) In the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation pertaining to the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for Agni-Soma, because the word "Agni" is mentioned alone [in the mantra], the term *sviṣṭakṛt* should be omitted; only the word "Agni" should be uttered.
