6|7|145. Regarding the statement "in the Viśvajit sacrifice, there is the giving of everything that exists," one should consult the *adhikaraṇa* on page 3689 of the Mīmāṃsākośa. This is the *haṃsakānyāya*.
This is composed in the form of a verse (*śloka*).
For it is said: "The foolish travel with hundreds of elephants and horses, while the virtuous move on foot;
even a flight of crows perched upon a mountain peak meets only with royal swans that have come to the riverbank."
Thus [it is said]. This is the *sāhasī* [section], 991. The maxim of the swan and milk (*haṃsakṣīranyāya*).
This very [maxim] has the same meaning as the maxim of the swan and milk.

Inferential knowledge (*anumānajñāna*), arising by the force of the mark (*liṅga*) through the power of the non-cognition of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), arises as having only the specific pervader (*vyāpakaviśeṣa*) as its object, according to the maxim of the swan and milk (*haṃsakṣīranyāya*). (Tautā. 1|3|1|133). The maxim of the swan and milk:
even when milk is mixed with water, the swan takes only the milk therein and not the water.
In the same way, within worldly discourse that is mixed with both the real and the unreal, one perceives only the real and not the unreal.
This is the analogy of the swan and the water.
It applies to a case where there is public ridicule of a person who speaks the truth regarding an excellent object that has been described by an authoritative source (*āpta*).

"Who are you, O red-eyed one with a red face and feet? From where have you come, from Lake Mānasa? Is there a grove of golden lotuses, water that is ever pure, heaps of jewels, golden creepers, and sprouts of lapis lazuli? Are there even frogs there? Having heard this, the cranes let out a cry of "Hīhī! *Tathatā* (Suchness): "Who are you, O red-eyed one with a red face and feet? From where have you come, from Lake Mānasa? Is there a grove of golden lotuses, water that is ever pure, heaps of jewels, golden creepers, and sprouts of lapis lazuli? Are there even frogs there? Having heard this, the cranes let out a cry of "Hīhī!"
"Thus, I have been explained through the fivefold discourse in the form of the dialogue between the *haṃsa* and the crane (*baka*).
As it is said: 'The *haṃsa* is white, the crane is white; what is the difference between the crane and the *haṃsa*?
In the separation of milk and water, the *haṃsa* is truly the *haṃsa*, and the crane is truly the crane.'"
Thus it is explained by some.
*Sāhasī* (75). *Haṭha*: This refers to green matter that has long covered the water of a pond.
Even when being cleared away, it repeatedly covers the water again from beneath its clear surface.
Thus, any other independent action is well known as *haṭha*.
Vākyapadīya 1.4.12, p. 324. The section concerning "beating and grinding" (*hantipiṣyadhikaraṇa*):

In the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) are directly contributing auxiliaries (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) and are prompted by the transcendental result (*apūrva*).
For those engaged in the formative acts (*saṃskāra*), it would be prompted by that [act], because it is for the sake of that. 1.1.12. Section 1.

The Commentary states: Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), they prescribe: "One threshes with the mortar and pestle that have been sprinkled" (*prokṣitābhyām ulkhalamusalābhyām ahanati*) and "One grinds with the *havaṣat* and *upalā* stones that have been sprinkled.

In this regard, there arises a doubt according to the followers of the Sāṃkhya school: Is the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) connected to the acts of threshing and grinding, or is it prompted by the transcendental result (*apūrva*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Since the sprinkling is employed for the purpose of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of threshing and grinding, it must be prompted by those purificatory rites.
For the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are the agents of killing and grinding. Why is this so? Because they are employed for that purpose (*tatprayuktā*).
For whatever is to be performed by something, that thing is the instigator (*prayojaka*) of it.
If it is performed for the sake of the *apūrva*, then the *apūrva* is its motivator; if it is for the sake of the acts of threshing and grinding, then those two are the motivators.

Furthermore, from the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is understood that it must be performed for the sake of the *apūrva*, whereas from the syntactical connection (*vākya*), it is for the sake of threshing and grinding; and the syntactical connection is more powerful than the context. [Objection: But the acts of threshing and grinding will serve the purpose of producing the *apūrva*; in that case, both the context and the syntactical connection will be upheld.
It is said: it is not possible to favor both.
Merely by virtue of a common context, this [text] is not understood to be recited for the sake of that which possesses the context.
From the commonality of context, there is syntactic unity with that which is under discussion; from that, its purpose for that end is understood.
But here, the syntactic unity of the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is with the two [verbs] "strikes" (hanti) and "drinks" (pibati), which are directly perceived.
That—
It would sublate the indirect syntactical unity with the subject matter at hand.
Furthermore, there cannot be syntactical unity with both simultaneously;
for when there is syntactical unity with one, then that which has its requirements fulfilled by that one is not conceived to have syntactical unity with another as well.

Therefore, since there is no syntactic unity with the subject under discussion, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) does not serve an unseen purpose (*apūrva*). [The opponent] says: But surely the acts of striking (*hanti*) and grinding (*piṣi*) do serve an unseen purpose; therefore, the sprinkling is for their sake.
Therefore, it is said that [the sacrifice] assists through the *apūrva*.
It is replied:
it does indeed assist by way of a mediated sequence (*praṇāḍyā*).
That is not previously enjoined.
For an auxiliary (aṅga) assists another auxiliary in two ways:

some [auxiliary] is connected with that specific auxiliary by virtue of being its cause for the sake of the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), while some is connected as a cause by its very nature, without even requiring the status of being an *apūrva*.

When a collection of ritual properties (dharmajāta) is connected with another particular [element] by taking as its basis a previously unestablished relationship of causality, that is "prompted by the apūrva" (apūrvaprayukta). Such [a property] must be modified (ūhitavya) in a modification (vikṛti) when it has been transferred to another purpose that takes over its function. On the other hand, where the intrinsic form (svarūpa) of the subsidiary (aṅga) is the cause for its connection with the ritual properties, that is "prompted by the intrinsic form" (svarūpaprayukta).

In that case, although an unprecedented result (*apūrva*) is accomplished by that [action] possessing the property (*dharma*), at the time it is being accomplished, the property does not serve as the cause for its application, nor is it produced by its application; since its own nature is already established, the property is not applied.
Consequently, in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*), because that form is absent, modification (*ūha*) is not possible for another purpose.
This being the case, the determination is based on the sentence.

If the sentence declares that the *apūrva* is the cause, then it is prompted by the *apūrva*. If, however, it declares that the subsidiary (*aṅga*) is the cause, then it is prompted by the subsidiary.

And that [sprinkling] would be prompted by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) according to the previously stated method; however, from the syntactical connection (*vākya*), it is prompted by the subsidiary act (*aṅga*).
Therefore, the sprinkling is prompted by the acts of striking and pounding.

"Wherever the acts of killing (*hanti*) and grinding (*piṣi*) are employed, there they possess such a nature. [Objection: But surely, since it has been established below that "the *dharmas* have the *apūrva* as their purpose," the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is merely an application of the acts of killing and grinding; thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is simply a matter of performance. [Reply: True; however, the prima facie proponent argues through three sections (*adhikaraṇa*)—namely, by means of sentence (*vākya*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and direct statement (*śruti*)—thinking that those *saṃnipātinaḥ* (auxiliaries directly connected to the sacrifice) cannot possibly have the *apūrva* as their purpose. This is indeed logical.

In this regard, it is rightly raised as a doubt whether the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is prompted by the mortar and pestle, or rather prompted by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result); it is not, however, prompted by the acts of striking (*han*) and grinding (*piṣ*).
Why? Because we hear the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the word "sprinkled" (*prokṣitābhyām*), derived from the root *ukṣ* with the prefix *pra*.
And the past passive participle is applicable in the sense of the object (*karman*).
And the object is that which is most desired to be reached.

Therefore, just as in the case of "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), where the sprinkling is for the sake of the rice-grains, so too here, because of the mention of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), the sprinkling is for the sake of the mortar and pestle themselves (and they are not to be struck). This is said in reply.

In the injunction "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), the sprinkling is for the sake of the rice-grains. For in that case, there exists the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) expressed by "he sprinkles," and that [force] must have something to be brought about (*bhāvya*). In this regard, one thing may be the object to be brought about by way of being produced (*kriyamāṇatayā bhāvya*), as the rice-grains are for the efficient force of threshing; another may be so by way of being refined (*saṃskāratvena*), as the rice-grains are for the efficient force of sprinkling; another may be so by way of being generated (*utpādyatvena*), as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is for the efficient force of kneading; and another may be so by way of being obtained (*prāpyatvena*), as the milk is for the efficient force of milking the cow in the expression "He milks the cow for its milk."

In the statement "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), because of the connection with the accusative case—which expresses that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*)—the rice-grains are what are to be brought about.
By what means? By the act of sprinkling.
(Regarding the present topic: however, at the end of a verbal suffix denoting completion (*niṣṭhā*), there is no productive urge (*bhāvanā*).

Because that [the object] is absent, even that which is to be brought about (*bhāvyamāna*) is absent. (Now, one might argue that since the accusative case expresses "objectness" (*karmatva*), it would express that which is to be brought about; to this he says: Even though there is "objectness," who has said that the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is [performed] "by means of the mortar and pestle"? (If it is argued that it is by the accusative, he says in response: When the accusative and the dative exist within the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), they both effect an action for its own sake (i.e., the meaning of the verbal root) through a relationship established by a single *bhāvanā*. As for the instrumental and so forth, it is indeed true that they likewise effect an action for its own sake through that same *bhāvanā* (by means of it).

Alternatively, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) expresses an action (*karman*) whose capacity is manifest (*udbhūtaśakti*), whereas the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) expresses one whose capacity is latent (*nyagbhūta*).

How is this known? To this he says: "In this context, the mortar and pestle are the objects (*karmabhūte*). And these two factors (*kāraka*) are seen to be joined with another factor, as in the expression "by means of the mortar and pestle" (*ulkhalamusalābhyām*).
Furthermore, a case-factor ending in the second case (accusative) does not connect with another case-factor, because its own capacity has already manifested.
Therefore, that case-factor whose capacity has manifested governs the action, but one whose capacity has not manifested does not, precisely because its capacity is unmanifested.

Moreover, if it were otherwise, the verb *han* (to strike) would have to be uttered for the sake of establishing a connection between the mortar and pestle and the sprinkling; in that case, there would be an excessive syntactical complexity (*vākya*).
Therefore, [the question is] whether the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is for the purpose of killing, and not for the sake of the mortar and pestle; this is the deliberation.

Now, he says that this deliberation is conducted without even abandoning the purpose of the mortar and pestle, nor is that [purpose] served by this [sprinkling]: "Alternatively, having referred to the mortar and pestle—which are obtained as instruments (*karaṇa*) either through another sentence or by implication—the two subordinate factors (*upasarjana*) are enjoined [as the objects of the sprinkling]. (The sprinkling is for the purpose of killing.)

On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is as follows: sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is for the purpose of the act of killing and pounding according to the syntactical connection (*vākya*), whereas it is for the sake of the transcendental result (*apūrva*) according to the context (*prakaraṇa*). And syntactical connection is more powerful than context. Therefore, because of its connection with the sacrifice through that purpose, there is the possibility of the ritual duty (*dharma*); thus, it must be prompted by the sacrifice, since the refinement (*saṃskāra*) is for the sake of that [sacrifice].
The Commentary: The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position. It is not the case that sprinkling is connected with the acts of killing and grinding.

Rather, because the connection with the transcendental result (*apūrva*) arises through that purpose—namely, through the act of killing or grinding—therefore, the sprinkling is connected to that [purpose].

The connection with the act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is brought about by a specific means for producing an unseen result (*apūrva*), not by the authority of the acts of threshing and grinding (*hanti-piṣi*).
Why? Because the acts of threshing and grinding would be purposeless [if they were not themselves means to an end].
If the sprinkling were prompted solely by those two acts, then that [sprinkling] too would be purposeless.
Therefore, it is not prompted by that. He says:
"The acts of killing and grinding are auxiliaries to the *apūrva*; they are not purposeless."
It is said:
there is no connection whatsoever for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) with the *apūrva*.
If the sprinkling were not performed, the acts of striking and grinding would not attain the status of being means for the *apūrva*.

Therefore, although the acts of threshing and grinding are auxiliaries to the *apūrva*, nevertheless, when they are connected with those two [acts], the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) would indeed be purposeless.

If it is argued that "the threshing and grinding, for whose sake they are undertaken, are capable of performing their function only when connected with the sprinkling, and not otherwise," it is replied:
"There is no such word as that.
To this, he replies: "This very word expresses this very meaning."

How so? [One might argue: "He kills with the two [grains] that have been sprinkled; he grinds with the two that have been sprinkled. Thus, whatever is done in the acts of killing and grinding is done with those two things connected to the sprinkling; it does not mean "with those two [grains themselves].
To this it is replied: This is not so.

If that which is performed by means of the *hanti* and *piṣya* [actions] were connected with the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), then there would be no connection for the sprinkling at all; for it is already brought about by those two. What else, then, could that sprinkling bring about?
Now, if the connection is that "something unprecedented (*apūrva*) is produced by means of the two sprinkled [grains]," then they are not connected with the acts of killing or grinding.
If it is argued that their connection is also being stated, then the sentence would suffer from syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to having multiple connections.
Therefore, the sprinkling, while being connected with the acts of killing and grinding, is linked to what precedes it through the context (*prakaraṇa*), namely, that Prajāpati created them.
[Objection: In that case, the relationship between the act of striking and the act of grinding would not be possible. [Response:
We say that it is indeed possible. How so? Here, for one who exerts effort toward threshing, two things are accomplished: the form of the act of threshing itself, and the production of rice grains.
And through the channel [of the ritual], there is a specific *apūrva* (unseen potency) produced by the cultivation [of merit].
For the production of rice grains is indeed the assistance rendered by the *apūrva*;
that [assistance] is manifested by the act of threshing.
Therefore, the sprinkling is connected [to the threshing].

Although there is a direct connection (*śruti*) with the sprinkling when it is related to the act of threshing, nevertheless, because that would serve no purpose, only indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is resorted to.
For indirect indication is directly perceived [as the only viable option].
That [act] brings about the unperceived (adṛṣṭa) through its conceptualization;
yet threshing does not bring about the unperceived as a remote auxiliary (ārādupakāraka).
Rather, it is understood that while performing a visible benefit, it makes it perfect by means of an unperceived capacity.

And even if one were to produce [the result], nevertheless, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*)—which is not connected with the benefit [of the threshing]—would be entirely purposeless by virtue of its connection solely with threshing (*avahanti*).
Therefore, its connection is with a specific benefit indicated by the threshing.
Consequently, it applies even to one who does not thresh.
Since it has entered into that function, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) indeed occurs there,
just as in the case of the nails when the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) is split by them.
Therefore, a duty (*dharma*) of this kind is motivated solely by the *apūrva*.

On this point, some explain the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) as follows: if the syntactical connection (*vākya*) were accepted, it would result in the consecration (*prokṣaṇa*) being rendered meaningless.
Therefore, the syntactical meaning is set aside;
in that case, the consecration, which is not connected with other words, is linked with the transcendental result (*apūrva*).

Furthermore, that which is unprecedented (*apūrva*) and formless (*amūrta*) cannot be sprinkled. Therefore, [the injunction] is by way of the rice-grains (*brīhi*). And the word "rice-grains" (as in the statement "one sprinkles the rice-grains") follows the same logic as the statement regarding the mortar and pestle. How so? Sprinkling is connected to the unprecedented result, and like the *prayāja* offerings, it would follow that it is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*).
In that case, how is it to be understood that "this..."?
Indeed, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position regarding the taking [of the pestle and mortar] is possible here.

However, since the threshing (avaghāta) is already established by another injunction, one must— by way of a restatement (anuvāda)— enjoin the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) with respect to the pestle and mortar, even though their existence is not directly witnessed, by virtue of their prior occurrence and by means of a further injunction of qualification that specifies them as the objects of the sprinkling.

Consequently, an inquiry must be made as to whether the status of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatā*) belongs to the mortar and pestle as such, or rather as means for producing the *apūrva* (the unseen spiritual result).
That inquiry, moreover, would only arise if the injunction for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) were not common to all the vessels used for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
But this is not the case, because that [sprinkling] is already established by another injunction: "He sprinkles the vessels with their openings facing upwards."

In the Mīmāṃsaka view, there is no absence of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the vessels used for the *puroḍāśa* offering; rather, there is an absence of the mantra. For it is precisely the absence of the mantra that is established in the third book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras].

Therefore, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a matter already obtained through another means, intended for the purpose of the injunction regarding the mortar and pestle (*ulūkhalamusala*) by way of conferring excellence (*abhyudaya*).
Furthermore, because it is included within a compound, the fact that there is only a single thing to be enjoined (*ekavidheyatā*) does not constitute a fault.

Therefore, the following investigation must be stated: by the very injunction for sprinkling the vessels, the sprinkling of the mortar and pestle is also established; and that [sprinkling], according to the logic of the preceding section, is indeed a *prayojaka*—a term synonymous with being the motivating cause—for the purpose of serving as the limit (*avadhi*) desired for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), which is a constituent part of the sacrifice. This [sprinkling] resides in the mortar and pestle. However, it is only the status of being the desired limit that constitutes its being a *prayojaka*.

In this regard, for the purpose of avoiding an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), there arises a deliberation as to whether the delimiters of the instrumentality (*sādhanatā’vacchedaka*)—such as the sacrifice (*yāga*), the *puroḍāśa* cake, the threefold nature, or the act of sprinkling (*avaghāta*)—are also intended to be expressed, or whether only the instrumentality consisting merely of the operation (*vyāpāra*) is intended. Upon consideration, because of the lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanā’bhāva*) similar to that which applies to the operation, the delimiters of the instrumentality must also be intended; otherwise, an over-extension would result in cases such as the *kūṭa* (the wooden ring).

Alternatively, it is that very [property] which is intended [as the definition], because it is impossible to specify a delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of being a means (*sādhanatā*); it is not the operation (*vyāpāra*), since even without that, being a means can be specified as such.
Consequently, since there is no threshing (*avaghāta*) on the fingernails, there is no sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).

And thus, although the directly mentioned mortar-stone (*ulūkhala*) and so forth might appear to be exhausted [in their purpose] by being defined as the means to the *apūrva*, nevertheless, the intention to include intermediate delimitors of being a means—such as the sacrifice itself and so on—is unavoidable.

This being the position reached, in order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the causality defined by the state of having an effect residing in the *apūrva*, there is an intention to specify only that operation which, by virtue of its intermediate status, presents itself immediately upon the existence of the operation; however, there is no such intention for the delimitator of instrumentality (*sādhanatā’vacchedaka*), because its causality is not established prior [to the result], as in the case of cattle and so forth.

For this very reason, where there is no intermediate operation—such as in the sacrifice (*yāga*) itself—there is an intention to specify the causality itself by direct apprehension (*śṛṅgrāhikayā*), and not its delimitator, due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*).
This has been established at length by Maṇḍana in his *Kaustubha* within the section concerning the purpose (*arthādhikaraṇa*) of those [subsidiary acts].
Therefore, since the nature of threshing and so forth is not intended to be expressed [as a universal rule], the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is established as being applicable even to nails.
Maṇḍana states: "The sprinkling is not restricted to that which is subject to threshing."
Śaṅkara states: "The status of being a supplement to what precedes the place [of the mantra] in the Vedic text.

7. *Haya*: a specific breed of horse used as a vehicle for the gods, as in the passage, "Having become a horse, he carried the gods" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.1.2). Vi. 9.4.2. The carrying away of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is performed with the mantra, "The carrying away of Bṛhaspati."
VI. 9|1|21. But in the case of the *haraṇa* (carrying away), because of the commonality with the act of *juhoti* (offering) and because substances are subordinate to a purpose, [it is a disposal].
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "He throws the *prastara* (grass-bundle) along with the *śākhā* (branch) into the fire.
*Praharati* means he casts it into the fire.

Regarding this, when the doubt arises as to whether the throwing of the *śālā* (the hall) is a disposal (*pratipatti*) or a purposeful act (*arthakarma*), the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of the sūtra.
By the use of the word "this" (*etad*), which serves to exclude other alternatives:

since it is stated that "one throws the *prastara* (grass-bundle) along with the *śākhā* (branch)," when the throwing of the *prastara* is thus enjoined, the *juhoti* (offering) of the *śālā* must also be understood as being a mere *homa* (oblation).
The meaning is that just as the throwing of the *prastara* grass-bundle is purposeful, so too is the throwing of the *śālā* (house) purposeful.

This is because of the commonality of application (*yogasāmānyāt*), since the connection—the application in the form of the act of throwing, which is synonymous with the oblation—is identical for both the *prastara* and the *śālā*.

Although the word "with the branch" (*śākhayā*) is in the instrumental case and "the *prastara*" (*prastaram*) is in the accusative case, nevertheless, the relationship in the act of throwing is exactly the same for both.
And because substances are subordinate to the purpose.
By the word "purpose" (artha), the sacrifice intended to be performed through its production is understood.

The status of the hall, the prastara-grass bundle, and so forth as being subordinate to the purpose is like that of the limbs of the sacrifice, according to the principle: "That which has already come into being is taught for the sake of that which is yet to be brought into being."

Therefore, the throwing of the branch (*śākhā-praharaṇa*) is a primary act (*arthakarma*), or rather, it is a secondary act of disposal (*pratipatti*), because the word [in the scripture] has that as its primary sense.

Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, where it is heard in the scripture: "He throws the *prastara* [grass-bundle] along with the branch," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that the throwing of the branch is a primary act—is reached by means of the Sūtra; then, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In the act of striking, the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is the primary element (*pradhāna*), and the hall (*śālā*) is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the *prastara*; in that case, there would be no equal connection (*tulyayoga*) between the hall and the *prastara*.

Therefore, like the throwing of the *prastara* grass-bundle, the throwing of the *śālā* (branch) is also merely a *pratipatti* (disposal rite), not a *arthakarma* (primary ritual act).

In this regard, there arises a doubt: whether the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* sacrifice follows the procedure (*vidhvant*) of the *āgneya*, and the sacrifice dedicated to Śuci follows the procedure of the *agnīṣomīya*; or whether it is the reverse. To address this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) states:

in a group of oblations (*havirgaṇa*), such as those in the *adhvarakalpa*, the final one dedicated to Śuci should be a modification (*vikāra*) of the latter—the *āgneya*—and the one following that, the *agnīṣomīya*.

Thus, the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* [offering] should be a modification (*vikāra*) of the preceding *āgneya* [offering], because of the commonality of position; that is to say, because of the commonality of sequence. In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *āgneya* is first; here, the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* is first.
In the archetype, the Agniṣomīya is the second; here, however, the one dedicated to Śuci is the second.
Therefore, due to the similarity of position, by means of an indicative mark (liṅga), there is a modification of the latter—the first—of the former.
Furthermore, it should be restricted by the deity, because [the deity] is expressed by the word, whereas the other is not explicitly heard in the scripture.
The word "or" (vā) sets aside the prima facie view.
Here, there is no restriction based on the commonality of place;
rather, it should be restricted by the deity.
"Because it possesses a word," that is, because it possesses a word denoting a deity, as in "to Agni-Viṣṇu" or "to Agni Śuci.

However, for the other [factor], namely place (*deśa*), there is no scriptural mention (*aśruti*), meaning there is an absence of a word denoting place. This is the intended meaning: in an injunction for ritual action (*karmacodanā*), the deity is invariably proximate.
However, because of the commonality of location (*deśasāmānyāt*), the view that [the order] is determined by priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) is set aside as extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*).

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *Āgneya* [offering] applies to that dedicated to Śuci, and the procedure of the *Āgnīṣomīya* applies to that dedicated to Agni-Viṣṇu.

In the case of the *tantra* (the common procedure), those ritual acts which precede the offerings to Prajāpati for the fire and the cow—such as the five-fold cutting (*pañcālmam*), the *āśruta* and *pratyāśruta*, and the mantra beginning with *avaidagbhiḥ*—if these were performed at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the section ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire) would not have been concluded.
Now, if it is argued that they are performed during the *brahmasāman* so that this fault shall not occur, even so, how does the reversal come about?
It occurs by performing those acts which ought to be done before the *agnigava* after [the *brahmasāman*].
Therefore, there is no exclusion [of the original order].

And furthermore, as for this case of the dual number used for "fire" (*agni*) and "cow" (*go*), namely in the statement "bring forward the commencement," it expresses that which is to be performed when its time has arrived.
If it were uttered at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), then because the time for the ritual act (*padārtha*) has not yet arrived, it would be ineffective.

Regarding these, is the invocation of the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation), which is obtained through the *codaka* rule, a single performance (*tantra*) common to all, or is it to be repeated separately at each pressing?

Similarly, in the Vājapeya, when one begins with the animals dedicated to Prajāpati (*prājāpatya*) and the seasonal animals (*ṛtupaśu*) together, and having performed the ritual cooking and release of the *prājāpatya* animals, one seizes them at the time of the *brahmasāman*, then is the invocation of Agni and the cow—which was performed at the time of the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) at the start of the seasonal animals—a single performance also for the *prājāpatya* animals, or must it be performed again at the time of the *brahmasāman* because they are specifically *prājāpatya*?

Likewise, regarding the passage, "One should sacrifice a black-necked animal to Agni, a brown one to Soma, and a black-necked one to Agni," when the offering and the cutting of portions (*avadāna*) are performed separately for the two black-necked animals, there arises a deliberation: is there *tantratva* (single performance) of the *anvākhyāti* and the *manotā-mantra*, or is there repetition? In this inquiry, because these [mantras] are not directly productive (*asaṃnipātin*), there is *tantratva* in order to favor the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*). The statement "he will perform" (*kariṣyad-vacana*) refers to the performance of the action following the utterance of the *vyāhṛti*s. § The maxim of the *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of the hand (*hastāmalakanyāya*).

Just as an *āmalaka* fruit held in the hand is seen without doubt, so too the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), when freed from the obstacles of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of agency and objecthood, produce a knowledge capable of manifesting reality directly (*aparokṣa*) regarding that reality, whereas previously it was revealed only in a mediated (*parokṣa*) manner. This is the intended meaning. And it has been said in the *Pañcadaśī*: "When [reality] is manifested through direct perception by means of the sentence, it arises as something immediate, like an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of the hand."
Thus [ends] the *Sāhasrī*.
For the hand gesture (*hastasaṃjñā*) indicates the convention in this way: "When this meaning is intended by me, then this [hand] must be struck by me."

When he moves his hand again in that same manner, then, recalling the previously acquired linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), the listener understands the specific intention—that is, the meaning—of this hand-gesture once more.
The hand-gesture is merely an adventitious condition (*upādhi*).

Regarding the doubt: although where the scripture mentions both the casting off (*hāna*) and the taking up (*upāyana*) of good and evil deeds, or where it mentions only the taking up, the latter is independent as it forms a single syntactical unit with the former; nevertheless, the Commentator has stated that even in the case of the knowledge of the attributeless (*nirguṇa-vidyā*), where only casting off is heard—as in "shaking off evil like a horse shakes off its hair"—the term *upāyana* is to be connected with that knowledge for the sake of attaining a higher degree of praise.

In the subsequent section (*adhikaraṇa*) concerning the means of abandonment (*hānopāya*), the authors of the *Bhāṣya* have stated the excellence of the praise as a secondary purpose (*ānuṣaṅgika-prayojana*), but not as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the act of "drinking" (*pāyana*). A means of knowledge is indeed necessary there: first, because there is a requirement for the means of abandonment based on the principle that "whatever is diminished by something else attains [something else]"; and second, because there is a requirement for a substratum (*āśraya*) for even those good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*) that have been diminished, since they require one in order to produce their fruit—it is precisely these two requirements that constitute the "ornament."

Regarding the injunction, "One desiring long life should offer a *caru* oblation of gold weighing one hundred *kṛṣṇalas* to Prajāpati," the scriptural text specifies that the sacrificial material (*havis*) is gold of an unspecified quantity measured by *kṛṣṇalas*. That gold possesses the characteristics of clarified butter (*ājya*), because [the procedure] follows the rule for the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice involving clarified butter.
This is the principle of the "holding of gold" (*hiraṇyadhāraṇanyāya*).

That which has the properties of clarified butter (*ājya*) is *ājyadharma*. The suffix *anic* is applied as a compound-ending (*samāsānta*) by the rule "after *dharma*, [the suffix] *anic* [is added] when it stands alone" (Pāṇini 5.4.124).
Why? Because of its luminosity (*tejastva*).
Gold is the luster (*tejas*) in this [offering]; clarified butter (*ājya*) is the luster of cows—meaning it is their essence.

Alternatively, gold is radiant, and clarified butter also produces radiance. Therefore, the sacrificial horse consisting of one hundred *kṛṣṇalas* possesses the ritual characteristics (*dharma*) of the *upāṃśuyāja*; such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
And because of the favoring of the properties of the *dharmas*.

In the case of the *prājāpatya* offering consisting of a hundred *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces and a *caru* oblation, the view of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the procedure of the *upāṃśuyāja* applies. This is another reason: since the properties of the clarified butter (*ājya*), such as inspection and so forth, are favored in the gold, whereas the properties of the grain-offering (*auṣadha*), such as threshing and so forth, are abandoned, only the properties of the clarified butter should be adopted.
Or [it is] "vegetable" (auṣadha) because of its clarity.

this belongs to vegetables; thus it is "vegetable" (auṣadha).

Therefore, such a thing is a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*).
Now, it is deliberated whether the *śruti*, *liṅga*, and *vākya* studied within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*) enter into conjunction with that context or not.
Regarding such passages as "Therefore, gold is to be worn; [thereby] his rival becomes ill-favored," there is doubt.

Is it that, in connection with ritual acts, the holding of gold and the wearing of beautiful clothing are enjoined as mere qualities, or is it rather that a permanent duty for the person is enjoined by way of a qualified injunction?

In this regard, since various distinct forms of ritual acts involving gold and clothing are restated (*anuvāda*), and the qualities of being "excellent" (*suvarṇa*) and "beautiful" (*śobhana*) would otherwise follow [as mere descriptions], it is stated that this is a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*).
Why? "Gold and clothing, being non-dharmas, would be purposeless;
furthermore, no authority is found for their connection with the ritual action.
For this is precisely the purpose of the context (prakaraṇa): namely, to make known how [these items] constitute subsidiaries (aṅga) of that [action].
If even that which is studied within a specific context were to be an injunction for ritual action (*karmadharma*), then it would become purposeless due to that very context.

However, since the Veda itself has made the distinction between what belongs to the context and what belongs to the person (*puruṣadharma*) by means of the context, it is understood that those things studied within a context are indeed qualities of the person.
Because it lacks both a material substance and a deity, it would be a subsidiary act (*śeṣa*).
[Bhāṣya: The word "but" (*tu*) serves to set aside the previous position. It cannot be a duty pertaining to the person (*puruṣadharma*).
It would be a subsidiary part of the Agnihotra and other such rites.
Why? Because it lacks a material substance.
For here, neither a material substance nor a deity is mentioned in the scriptural text.

Upon hearing that [word], it might be conceived as "belonging to the wife" (*bhāryam*) or "belonging to this person" (*yad-yam*). However, in the absence of a connection between a substance and a deity, this case-ending is understood as denoting "holding"—that is, it is designated as a *saṃskāra* (consecration)—because it is subordinate (*śeṣabhūtatvāt*), and not otherwise.
Therefore, it is a subsidiary element (*śeṣa*) of rituals such as the *Agnihotra*.
Thus, [the injunction] "one should be well-dressed" is as follows:
even if it were indeed a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), it would still be merely a subsidiary part of the ritual action (*karmaśeṣa*).
Otherwise, a separate result (*phala*) would have to be postulated.
But surely, even the connection with the season must be postulated?
True; however, that postulation is supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And when there is a general expectancy for a purpose regarding an action, it is that very action itself which presents itself [as the object].
Therefore, its connection [with the result] is supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whereas its connection with heaven is not.

And he thinks thus: just as nothing other than sacrifice, gift, or oblation is established as a primary action (*pradhānakarman*), and since there is no sacrifice or the like here due to the absence of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
Therefore, by virtue of its innate status as an auxiliary, it constitutes a remainder of the ritual action.
Alternatively, this "holding" is what is heard in the scripture;
and because it possesses the nature of dharma, it is a subordinate element precisely in relation to what follows.

Nor can the worldly [act] be subject to refinement (*saṃskāra*) because it serves no purpose; therefore, this is an injunction regarding the cloth and gold which have become constituent parts of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*). Alternatively, precisely because of the various defects [of the alternative view], and since [the primary sense] is possible, the injunctive power is forcibly transferred to the subordinate quality (*guṇa*); thus, having referred to the wearing of gold as enjoined by such sentences as "Gold is in the hand, then he takes it," "Having handed over gold into the hand, they chant the *ṣoḍaśin*," the quality of being gold (*suvarṇatā*) is what is enjoined.
And in the injunction "he puts on a garment," there is the quality of being beautiful [implied] regarding that garment.
Thus, this very point is the basis for the technical definition (paribhāṣā) of the Sūtra-writers, namely, "by the word *hiraṇya*, gold (*jātarūpa*) is understood.
Otherwise, since the word *hiraṇya* would be common to both silver and gold, some other basis for restricting it to one or the other would have to be postulated.
And regarding the phrase "because of the absence of substance" (*adravyatvāt*) in the Sūtra: here no substance is being enjoined; rather, this is an injunction of its specific quality alone.
Therefore, wherever there is a substance, one must proceed by means of this [quality].
Furthermore, as for the mention of the deity (*devatā*) made here by the author of the Bhāṣya:
That [position] is contrary to the Sūtra and improper, for even recitation (*japa*) and the like are indeed primary;
since we observe that even those which are not sacrifices can be primary, there is nothing [to be gained] by the mention of "deities.
This is because of their connection with the Veda.

Commentary: The connection with the *adhvaryu* [is established] through the Veda; it is appropriate for that which is subordinate (*śeṣabhūta*). For it is by the *adhvaryu* that the subordinate element is performed; it is not a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*).
Indeed, the *adhvaryu* is the performer of the rites such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) along with their constituent parts.
Therefore, for this reason also, such [acts] are indeed properties of ritual action (*karmadharma*).
Furthermore, if this action is a constituent part of a ritual (*karmāṅga*), the designation *ādhvaryava* (belonging to the Adhvaryu) will serve as its applicator;
if it were a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*), that designation would be contradicted.

Even if, by way of restating the *hiraṇyadhu* (golden vessel), its nature as gold is enjoined, nevertheless, because that injunction is subordinate to the action, the name (*samākhyā*) is not extended to it; thus, the meaning is "connection with the Veda" due to the commonality of being Vedic.

By this, even one who might argue that the wearing of garments and the holding of gold are already established for the world at large, and therefore an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) could be made even by way of restating those, is refuted.
Furthermore, this is because the passage has the substance itself as its primary referent.

Commentary: Here, the reference is directed toward the substance (*dravya*), because of its connection with the accusative case in the expression "gold is to be worn" (*suvarṇaṃ bhāryam*). An action that consecrates a substance is purposeful under the view that it is subordinate to the sacrifice; it is useless as a duty pertaining to the person (*puruṣadharma*).
Or rather, it was previously established that wearing [the gold] is inherently a consecration (*saṃskāra*) itself.

Now, in that very context, because [the word *hiraṇyam*] is designated as an object (*karman*) due to its being a cause for accumulation and so forth, there arises the misconception that this is an accusative case—just like in the example *vrīhīn*—on account of the observation of the suffix *-am* (in *hiraṇyam*) and the statement in the Bhāṣya, "due to connection with the meaning of the second case.
However, since the [object] is already expressed by another [grammatical element], the accusative has not been produced here for the sake of the object; rather, this is simply the nominative case.
The second meaning, however, is that it is "the wife" (bhāryā), as stated by Utpalī; thus, there is a designation of [the term] being directed toward the substance (dravya).
For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya also states: "The principle of wearing gold [is applied] to the meaning of the accusative case."
It was stated [in the sūtra] "from conjunction" (*saṃyogāt*). Otherwise, one would have had to say simply "from the second conjunction" (*dvitīya-saṃyogāt*).
Therefore, because it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*), retention (*dhāraṇa*) is a subsidiary element of action (*karmaśeṣatva*).
"There may be a connection of this [act] with the fruit, like that of conjunction; therefore, it is an action," says Ātiśāyana.

The Bhāṣya states: "There may indeed be such a connection with the fruit for those of this kind; the meaning is that it is a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*). If it were a property of gold or cloth, it would be purposeless."
[Objection: But surely the ritual act will be accomplished by means of refined cloth.
[Reply: This is not so;
for gold is a constituent part [of the vessel], and it cannot assist the ritual act [directly].
And because there is an absence of an injunction (*śruti*), [the passage] is a subsidiary element of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*).
Therefore, by such statements as "his rival becomes ill-favored," there is a connection with a result for those [passages] of this kind.
But is this not a statement of present fact (*vartamānāpadeśa*)?
This is indeed true.
To avoid the charge of meaninglessness, a connection with an injunction of result must be sought.
And between that which must be sought from elsewhere and this [connection] residing within the same sentence, the modification of the latter is the simpler course.
Why? Because [the former] is perceptible through its syntactical unity with that [word], while [the latter] is imperceptible through another.
Furthermore, there is a transformation of the present tense, which is not intended to be expressed;
and the determination of the intended meaning rests upon the relationship [between the words].

Therefore, there would be an instruction regarding this as a primary action, just as there is a connection with a fruit for the Prajāpati-vows in the statement, "For by this much he becomes liberated"; it should be understood in the same way here as well.
Consequently, such a thing is a duty of the person.
Or rather— the connection with the ritual action is not established by anything [else];

for every statement not introduced as a specific context (anārabhyavāda) enjoins an auxiliary either through syntactical connection (*vākya-saṃyoga*) or through some non-deviating indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Thus, the analogy of the hidden treasure of gold (hiraṇyanidhinyāya) [is established]. Section 4510: The Topic of the Gold Fragments (hiraṇyaśakalādhikaraṇa);
the analogy of the hidden treasure of gold.
Just as knowledge does not arise when there is an obstruction—whether of the past, the future, or the present—of any one of these three types;

for example, those walking back and forth over a hidden treasure of gold might not find it even while passing directly above it, so too all these creatures go day after day to that world [the sun], yet they do not find this world of Brahman. This is the summary.
(Sāhasrī 455). The word *kṛṣṇa* denotes a measure of gold.
Bhāṣya: The wearing of a golden garland in the Vājapeya sacrifice belongs to all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), not to the Adhvaryu alone.
See the section titled "The Section on the Red Turban" (lohitoṣṇīṣādhikaraṇa) at Gīko, page 3389.
The section concerning the gold fragments (*hiraṇyaśakala*);
the principle of the *vetasa* branch;
and the single performance of the two options regarding sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) in the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*).
The ritual procedure for the fire-altar (*agnidharma*) applies to each individual brick because it is a composite whole, just like the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*).
Commentary: There exists the fire-altar (*agni*) [prescribed] by the text, "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar.

In that context, it is handed down as follows: "He sprinkles the fire-altar with a thousand pieces of gold," "He sprinkles the fire-altar with curds mixed with honey," and "With a branch of reed-grass, he sweeps the *avakā* plants over the fire-altar."
"He drags [the bricks] with the names of frogs.

Regarding this, there is doubt as to whether the dragging and the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) should be performed for each individual brick, or whether they should be performed only once for the entire collection (*citisamudāya*).

This is how it is deliberated: if [the action] pertains to the collection, then, since no distinction can be perceived among the bricks piled therein, the sprinkling and the dragging must apply to all of them.
And when [the word "fire"] refers to a distinct substance, then it applies to each deity simultaneously.
What is the conclusion? It applies to every brick. Why? Because the word "fire" (agni) denotes the aggregate.

How is this understood? Because of the absence of any other substance. For if there were another substance, what else would exist that could be designated by the word "fire," or in what would it be deposited?
But how is it not thus?

Just as in the case of a single cognition, even when there are differences in place, time, and so forth, [the cognition] establishes the existence of an undifferentiated whole (avayavin) without being sublated.
And that [reason] exists here as well;

furthermore, since attraction is not observed even in trees and the like despite their being composed of parts, it follows that [the reason] is present even where there is composition of parts. Moreover, because it is doubtful, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to cloth and other such things.
Therefore, by the force of perception, even when there is a connection with many [bricks], the fire exists as a composite whole; thus, its sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) should be performed only once.

In the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), it was deliberated whether the Jyotiṣṭoma is prompted by the individual substances or by the collection [of those substances]; following that discussion of the collection, the sprinkling is now deliberated. This is the incidental (*prāsaṅgikī*) connection [to the subsequent section]. Soma: But surely, just as the sprinkling is not performed for each individual grain of rice, so too, even though the bricks are denoted by the word "fire," the sprinkling should not be performed for each individual one.
Therefore, do not say that this is untenable.

For the purpose of the scriptural injunction (*śāstrārtha*) is connected with the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). And the purpose of the scriptural injunction regarding rice grains (*vrīhi*) is as the material cause of the oblation (*havis*), because they constitute a single means of accomplishment when cut and measured out in four handfuls, not individually. Consequently, in that case, there is no sprinkling for each individual grain. However, in the case of bricks, since the purpose of the scriptural injunction in passages such as "he lays down the *vajriṇī* [brick]" is expressed through distinct units, the sprinkling is performed separately for each intended object (*uddeśya*), just like the wiping (*saṃmārga*) of the cups (*graha*).

Furthermore, there is a disparity: according to the scriptural injunction "one should sacrifice with rice-grains" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*), many [grains] possess the status of being the means (*sādhana*); however, in the present case, it is the plurality of the means themselves that is intended.

Moreover, although grammarians record the root *ukṣ* in the sense of "to sprinkle" (*secane*) without exception, its usage in common worldly practice is restricted solely to the contact of water with a single part [of the object].

Since it is impossible to effect the contact of water with every single grain individually, the connection with the rice-grains must be understood as occurring collectively, because this is required by the remainder of the injunction (*vidheya-anuśeṣāt*).

Just as the number eleven follows from the collective wisdom [of the fires], furthermore, if sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) were performed on each of the three rice grains individually, there would be a lack of suitability for threshing due to the contact with water; this would contradict the primary purpose. However, in the case of the bricks, because it serves to ensure the firmness of the union, sprinkling is indeed conducive; thus, it is logical that the sprinkling should be performed once for each primary element (*pradhāna*). This is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The meaning of the first *sūtra* is as follows: the ritual properties of the fire (*agni*), such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth, should apply to the individual [fire], because the word "fire" denotes the aggregate itself, just as in the case of the injunction, "One should touch the full moon with the *Caturhotṛ* formula. The meaning of the *sūtra* is: the ritual properties of the fire, such as sprinkling and so forth, should apply to the individual, because the word "fire" denotes the aggregate itself, just as in the case of the injunction, "One should touch the full moon with the *Caturhotṛ* formula. [Vṛtti: "The acts of drawing out (*vikarṣa*) and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) are to be performed according to the opinion of Pradīdhaka."

[The opponent argues: "The first [alternative] is that [the word *agni* refers to the bricks] by virtue of being a constituent part (*avayava*). [The Mīmāṃsaka replies: Let it not be so, because of the existence of the location (*bhūdeśa*). Bhaṭṭa: Regarding such scriptural passages as, "He sprinkles [it] with a thousand pieces of gold," we must consider whether by the word *agni* only the bricks—which serve as the means for a specific configuration—are denoted, and the sprinkling is for their sake; or whether, since they are indeed parts (*avayava*), the word *agni* denotes the state of being a constituent part itself, and the sprinkling is for its sake."

In this regard, the admission of a distinct composite whole (*avayavin*) occurs only where there is syntactic unity such that other [parts] are subordinate, or where no joint (*saṃdhi*) is perceived—as in the case of a body or a jar.
However, here, when one brick is pulled, others are not pulled; furthermore, the joint of even those bricks covered by mortar is indeed perceived through inference.

Therefore, due to the absence of the pervading conditions [for a composite], and because of the statement of Kāśyapa that "another substance arises through conjunction with fire," there is no proof for another constituent part; thus, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is solely for the purpose of consecrating the bricks.

Therefore, by the word "also" (api), the status of being a means to the *apūrva* is indicated as being co-referential precisely with the nature of being a brick (*iṣṭakatva*). Consequently, since that [status] belongs to each individual [brick], it is established that the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) applies to every jar.
Nor does this imply that the same would apply individually in cases such as the sprinkling of rice-grains or vessels;
for although that would follow from logic, it is not so perceived there due to the force of the plural number employed in the mantra: "I sprinkle you, who are dear to Agni; be pure."
In the present case, however, since such [an effect] is absent, [the whole] must be considered as nothing more than its individual parts.

This being the position reached, we reply: the pulling of one part does not entail the pulling of the other parts, nor is there a failure to perceive their conjunction; for there are counter-examples in the case of trees, cloth, and so forth. Therefore, the acceptance of a "whole" (avayavin) occurs only where there is a cognition of a single form.
Otherwise, there would be no evidence for the acceptance of even a brick as a distinct entity.
The statement of the Kāśyapīyas, however, is to be disregarded because it contradicts the fundamental doctrine (*mūla*).
In the case of "the forest" and so forth, the cognition of a single form is sublated;
therefore, since the word "fire" denotes the whole (*avayavin*) itself, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is for that very purpose.

And because that [altar] is a single entity, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is performed all at once. Nor does it follow from this—that the sprinkling of gold fragments and other such ritual properties would be redundant with respect to the nature of the individual parts—due to the absence of a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the *uttaravedi* as the locus of the fire which serves as the means to the *apūrva*. This is because the specific substratum delimited by a particular unseen merit (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) is denoted by terms such as *uttaravedi*, since the word "fire-altar" (*agni*) applies to a specific worldly location where bricks and so forth are prepared, through its primary sense (*mukhyārtha*).
And in that case, since there is no lack of purpose, there is an absence of even the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) [of the word] as being a means to an unprecedented result (*apūrva*).

Therefore, the properties of the fire-altar (*agni*) and the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) do not apply; for this reason, the *Hiraṇyagarbha* [mantra] is the locus for the gold fragments (*hiraṇyaśakala*).

This would result in confusion (*sāṃkarya*). Nor is it the case that, as stated in the *Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa* (4.3.14), there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the properties of the *uttaravedi* to the fire; this is the principle of the *Hiraṇyagarbha-mantra*.
The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the *garbhamantra* is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the preceding substrate (*adhāra*), but rather of the subsequent one.
Ke.: This mantra, "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre," which refers to Prajāpati, has been demonstrated by the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) to refer to Indra.
Bhā.

In the case of the Vāyavya animal sacrifice, because the *hiraṇyagarbha* mantra is indicated by the *uttarārdhapūrva-dharaṇī* (the northern part of the eastern hearth), there is no sublation of the original [mantras] for the intermediate [hearths].
Bhāṣya 10.3.12–12. This is the principle of the *hiraṇyagarbha* mantra:
the *hiraṇyagarbha* mantra is to be applied to the *uttarārdhapūrva-dharaṇī* in the Vāyavya animal sacrifice.

"Hiraṇyagarbha" [is the mantra] for the first [offering], because of the indicative mark (liṅga) of the mantra. Commentary: There is an animal sacrifice dedicated to Vāyu, [stated as]: "One desiring prosperity should offer a white animal to Vāyu. In that context, it is heard: "With the mantra 'Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre,' he performs the Āghāra libation. In this matter, the following point has been established: since the Āghāra libation is already established [by another rule], this [mantra] is an injunction regarding a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi).
This, however, is considered: is this an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi) regarding the former fire-altar, or regarding the latter?
What is the prima facie view? "Hiraṇyagarbha" [is the deity] of the former, because of the indicative mark (liṅga) in the mantra;
this is an injunction of a subordinate quality for the former fire-altar.
Why? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra.
The meaning of the mantra is as follows:

regarding the injunction, “He offers the *āghāra* oblation with the mantra ‘Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre...’,” there is this statement within the mantra: “In the beginning, the one Lord of what has come into being was.”
"One" is a designation for Prajāpati;
for he is understood to be endowed with the number one prior to the production of progeny, due to the possibility of the origin of progeny. This very mantra is capable of denoting Prajāpati.
The first *prājāpatya* is the primary substratum;
in that case, this [quality] is capable of accomplishing the task, but not in the latter.
Therefore, it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) for the former.
Ṭup: The prima facie view is based on the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra.
Bhāṣya: By the principle "as in the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*), there will be no obstruction of the extended injunction (*codaka*), because the mantra for the latter base (*ādhāra*) is not displaced.
Otherwise, the mantra "ūrdhvo'dhvaraḥ" would have to be removed.
Therefore, for this reason as well, it is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) for the preceding [rite].
Ṭup—This is a supplementary sūtra stating "because of being like the archetype" (prakṛtitvāt).
(And as for what was cited [in the sūtra], namely) “because of the obstruction of the natural state” (*prakṛtyuparodhāt*),
that too serves merely to establish the reason for the subsequent inclusion (*anvācaya*). Or rather, because the latter [mantra] possesses the meaning of a mantra.
The Commentary states: It sets aside the Vāyavya section; it is not an injunction of a quality for the preceding [section].
What then? A quality is enjoined for the subsequent one. Its meaning pertains to the mantra, not to the preceding one.
How so? It is thus recorded in the sacred tradition: "He offers the Āghāra-libation with the verse, 'Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning...
What is the meaning? One recites this Ṛc-verse during the Āghāra-offering. When recited, it produces a specific scriptural knowledge that serves as an auxiliary (aṅga).

Regarding the phrase "To what god shall we offer worship with oblation," the meaning is "to one god. Through the elision of the letter 'e' and the recognition of this word, the understanding of its meaning arises: that the oblation is to be given to one god.
Furthermore, in the preceding substrate (the *ādhāna* rite), there exists no scriptural cognition (*śrauta-vijñāna*) that serves as a subordinate member (*aṅga*).
In that case,
one might suppose that the Vedic knowledge (*śrauta-vijñāna*) serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*).
However, there is no authoritative basis for the assumption that this [knowledge] must be performed by means of the verse "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre."
For this sentence is an injunction for a specific function of a mantra, not a restrictive rule for the general function of a mantra.
The general function of a mantra is only occasional.
If it is argued that this is an injunction for a specific [function] within that occasional function of a mantra:

[Otherwise there would be] pointlessness and the acceptance of a non-existent alternative; for the instruction possesses purpose because it concerns the *jauhava* and the *āghāra* offerings. Therefore, the subsequent [text] is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).
As for what was said—that this mantra, being addressed to Prajāpati, will be unable to address Indra—[that is incorrect].
This is not so.

For just as Prajāpati is praised as being "one" because he possesses the designation "Prajāpati," it is understood that "there was one Prajāpati" in the sense that he was alone prior to the production of creatures.
In the same way, Indra as well [is capable], because the word *indra* signifies sovereignty;
he is fully able to produce everything.
"Who indeed would praise you? Who would satisfy you? Who would sacrifice, since you are fierce and protect us at all times?"
"As if striking two feet, he makes the former the latter by his powers.
Likewise: "Who among the ancient seers has reached the limit of your entire greatness?"
"Those whom you, O Mother, and Father, brought forth together—[those] most excellent [ones] of your own [lineage].
"Who would praise him? Who would satisfy him? Who would sacrifice to him? Because of this statement in the *aindra* hymn, it is an *aindrī* verse.
He instructs everyone, saying: "Who is able to praise him? Or who gives to him? Or who sacrifices to him?
He alone performs all this.
Just as someone walking places one foot forward and then the other behind it.
In this way, he performs all this.
If it is the case that he performs everything, then prior to the performance, he is one.

Likewise, [in the verse] "Who indeed can reach the limit of your entire greatness?"—who, even among the ancient seers (*ṛṣi*), is able to reach the end of this whole majesty? Since you brought forth even your mother and father from your own body, you were prior even to them; how much more so than any other person? Thus, the oneness [of the Self] is established.
That [Self] also existed prior to all creation.
Therefore, there is another *ṛc* regarding Indra and the others.

Therefore, there is no contradiction. [The *Ṭupṭīkā* states: Because both are based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), they are equal for both [options]; [thus] neither one becomes the sole authority. And the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is likewise [equal].
And the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is indeed equal, according to the principle that will be stated in the *Bhāṣya*.

What follows from this? (This results from the following: In the archetype (*prakṛti*), when the constituent elements (*padārtha*) are being carried forward, the four means—namely *brāhmaṇa*, *pada*, *sūtra*, and *upadraṣṭṛ*—are applicable everywhere.
Consequently, in the subsequent substratum (*ādhāra*), by virtue of the authority of the *mantra* (*mantrānmāna-sāmarthyāt*), the others are excluded.
Since there is no *mantra* in the former (substratum), those very same means (*brāhmaṇa* and so forth) apply there.
In the case of the vikṛti as well, it is the same: the former [rite] is accompanied by a consecration formula (*abhimantraka*), while the latter is accompanied by a mantra.
This being so, only a specific mantra will be prescribed for the latter;
otherwise, both the general and the specific mantras would have to be prescribed for the former [base rite].
(To the question "How so?", he says: The remembrance of the specific (viśeṣasmaraṇa) is enjoined;

Since simplicity is apprehended by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is inappropriate to assume a different basis for its specific instance;

for if one were to postulate that Hiraṇyagarbha alone is the deity in the subsequent fire-installation (*uttarādhāra*), there would likewise be a lack of parsimony (*gaurava*). Furthermore, even regarding the former installation (*pūrvādhāra*), since it has been stated in the fifth [book] (sūtra 119) that where mantras are absent everywhere, the Brāhmaṇa portion serves as the reminder, and since the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is governed by the Brāhmaṇa, the injunction of this mantra is justified simply by its being the generator of that merit; thus, there is no difference in parsimony.

Nor is there any deviation of the mantra with respect to that unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); for there is no deviation even with respect to the respective unseen forces that serve as the means (*sādhana*) according to their respective ritual manuals (*kalpa*), since the mantra is the cause of each of those. Otherwise, even in the view of the mantra itself, such deviation could not be prevented.

This being the position reached, however, where the efficacy of the mantra is already established, its application occurs only in the primary substratum (*dharādhāra*), because of the parsimony (*lāghava*) involved in enjoining the specific mantra.

In reality, however, regarding the original model (prakṛti), the statement "He does not perform [the rite] with 'svāhā,' nor does he recite the mantra" is merely a restatement of a constant rule (nityānuvāda) intended to exclude the application of mantra-simulacra precisely because the mantras are absent; thus, it serves to establish the non-Vedic character of the *hiraṇya* mantra. Consequently, there is a sublation of the original mantra in the subsequent fire-altar (uttaravedi), but not of the original Brāhmaṇa passage in the prior fire-altar (pūrvādhāra).

Therefore, this is a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*) which, by having the result of an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) regarding the *hiraṇyagarbha* mantra in the first installation, leads to the injunction of that very mantra for the second installation alone.

Furthermore, since that [injunction] involves the conceptualization of Hiraṇyagarbha as the deity based on the wording of the mantra, the sublation of the natural deity Indra at the second installation is also not improper.

Or let it be so: because of the sense of the supplementary passage, "He who is indeed Prajāpati, he is indeed Indra," one should abandon the conventional (rūḍhi) meaning of terms such as Hiraṇyagarbha and accept their referent as Indra solely through etymological derivation (yoga). Furthermore, in the word "kasmai," by supplying the vowel *e*, it means "to him alone" (*ekasmai*), that is, to him who is unique and not shared by others; for otherwise, if the word *ka* were to refer to Prajāpati, its status as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) would be untenable.

In this regard, the following statement of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) has been stated: "In the injunction regarding a mantra, a restrictive unseen merit (*niyamādṛṣṭa*) must be postulated; otherwise, since the recollection of the ritual purpose could occur even through the Brāhmaṇas, Kalpasūtras, or the words of observers, the restriction to the mantra would lack its purposeful efficacy.

Furthermore, that restrictive unseen merit is not established in the original fire-laying (*pūrvādhāra*), because that rite is performed without a mantra. Thus, there can be no injunction for a mantra in the original fire-laying."

The principle of the *hiraṇyagarbha* mantra and the principle of the *hṛdaya* and other [limbs] must be inferred; however, it is already established in the case of the subsequent substratum (*uttarādhāra*), because that too is accompanied by mantras in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Therefore, since the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the restriction is already established, the injunction of the specific mantra alone is simpler; thus, the injunction of the mantra is properly placed in the subsequent substratum (*uttarādhāra*).

And so it is said in the *Duṣṭīkā*: "In the prior substratum (*pūrvādhāra*), an unseen merit for the restriction of the mantra would have to be postulated; that [unseen merit] is already established in the subsequent substratum, and when that exists, it is not possible to postulate [another].
This is the *Rasāyana*.

Śābarabhāṣya 2.2.6:
The principle of the heart and other [portions].
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, there is an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the others from among the eleven [limbs] regarding the portions to be cut off (*avadāna*).

Since only the heart and other parts of the animal are heard of in scripture as being connected with the act of cutting off by virtue of their status as sacrificial oblations (*havis*), there is an exclusion of the status of being an oblation for the parts other than those.
Because of the diversity of the oblations, there is a repetition of the ritual action; therefore, the cutting off should be performed from those [specified parts].
Commentary: It has been established that the oblation is [to be taken] from the various parts.

Now this is being deliberated: should the sacrifice be accomplished with any part whatsoever as the oblation, or should the portioning be made from all [the parts], or is there an exclusion (parisaṃkhyā) of certain parts? What is the prima facie view? That the portioning should be made from all [the parts], meaning the act of portioning must be repeated for each one.
Why? Because of the difference in the sacrificial oblations (*havis*).

The oblations are distinct, such as the heart and so forth, which are specifically mentioned in the portioning (*avadāna*), as well as the remaining parts determined by the subsequent procedure (*paścākṛti*); from all of these, the portion must be cut off.

For indeed, no specific details are determined by the form of the animal; nor would its status as a sacrificial portion (*avadāna*) be intended if it were not specified. Thus, if it were cut from this limb, it would not be [the portion] defined by the form of the animal, because the animal's status as a sacrificial portion is not delimited by the form of the animal itself.
All specific qualities would be included therein;
however, in that case, the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅga*) would not be established for the animal's form.
For it is only when meat and the like are distinguished by multiple qualifiers that they are brought to the status of a subsidiary, and not otherwise.

For when there is a single oblation (*ekahaviṣya*), since the portions of the limbs are delimited by the form of the animal, the extraction of all the cuttings occurs precisely as prescribed from the source text itself, without repetition.

If the limbs were prepared separately, the extraction from a single limb would cause one to lose certain specific characteristics. However, when the cuttings are repeated, they encompass all the specific characteristics.
Therefore, it must be offered from all [the animals].
He says: But surely, since the specific individuals are defined by the form of the animal and are for the purpose of the sacrifice, the sacrifice would be accomplished by any one of them.
It is said:
This would indeed be established if the connection of the specific qualities (viśeṣas) with the sacrifice were heard [in scripture];
however, it is the form of the animal (paśvākṛti) that is heard.

Therefore, since the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅgabhāva*) arises only when specific details are grasped, for that purpose the specific details are grasped by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*). It is not understood which specific detail has been set aside and which has not;
hence, all are grasped in order to favor the injunction of performance.

And if it were assumed that even without a specific detail that was not grasped, the rite would still proceed exactly as heard in the scripture, then, in the delimitation by the animal's form (*paśvākṛti*), no additional factor would have been accepted as a subsidiary; thus, disregard for that [specific detail] would be adopted.
Therefore, it remains from all [the organs] beginning with the heart.

nor is this a case of exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā).

The syntactical interpretation is not as follows: "There are exactly eleven portions of the animal, no more; those which are the portions, one cuts them twice each.

By prescribing that "these [parts] are to be cut twice each," the word fulfills its purpose once it has enjoined the double-cutting of these;

Therefore, one should cut from all of them.

Otherwise, there would be no performance of the sacrifice for one who has set out to act, and there would be the offering of the entire substance,

For them, the teaching of the scriptures serves as a means of purification, like a ritual effacement for the sake of attaining glory.
Commentary: For this reason as well, it is a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*).

Whether by one part, by all, or by the eleven;
since the sacrifice is accomplished by even one, [yet it is performed] with all the oblations due to their distinctness.

Since their enumeration consists of eleven [factors], one who possesses all three doṣas does not [die] from this, because there is no other possible outcome; thus, vāta alone is declared to be the cause of death.

Therefore, the sacrifice is performed with exactly eleven [parts]. (Bhāṭṭa: It is not just any part whatsoever that constitutes the substance to be offered (*pradeya*). For, since it is impossible for the animal to remain as a single mass while the acts of slaughter and so forth—which encompass the entire purpose—are being carried out, the status of being the means of accomplishment through its own parts must be postulated.
