Therefore, since there is no decisive evidence [to the contrary] and all [the parts] are understood to be means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), they must all be offered.

However, the statements regarding the heart and so forth are intended to prescribe the sequence, according to the principle of the "first among equals" (*ādyanyāya*); for since the act of cutting portions (*avadāna*) is already established as being for the purpose of offering, these [statements] are devoted solely to the order of sequence.

For this very reason, this sequence applies specifically to the eleven [limbs]; for others, however, there is no fixed rule. Alternatively, having stated, "He cuts from the heart first," and so forth, the scripture declares: "There are indeed eleven portions of the animal; he cuts each of them twice. From this, it follows that the double cutting applies to the eleven, while for the others, there is a triple cutting in order to complete the total number of animal portions.
Thus, these [rules] are meaningful; they do not serve to exclude other [options].

For this very reason, even the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) expressed as "one does not cut [the portion] from the shoulders, nor from the head, nor from the spine, nor from the hind thighs" is logically consistent.

This being the case, just as—in accordance with the requirements of the preparatory rites such as slaughter—one assumes that the animal is the material cause (*prakṛti*) of its parts and understands that the parts themselves are directly the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), so too, in statements such as "he cuts off [a portion] from the heart" (*hṛdayasyāgre 'vadyati*), because the heart and other organs are connected to the cutting-off (*avadāna*) which is a preparatory rite for the original oblation, they alone are understood to be the oblation; thus, their status as the material cause is preserved, and not all parts are established as the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

For this very reason, the passages concerning the heart and other organs serve as indicators of the sacrificial oblations (*haviṣyodhaka*) by means of enjoining the purificatory rites known as *avadāna* (cuttings);
this is the principle of the "Heart and Others" (*ita-hṛdayādi-nyāya*). This concludes the section on the observation of reasons (*hetudarśanādhikaraṇa*).
For the purpose of establishing this point:

That is to say, there would be an absence of determination—a lack of restriction—regarding the injunctions, namely the objects to be enjoined such as the wooden spoon, the cooking pot (*piṭhara*), and so forth.

*Ṭup-ṭīkā*, 9.1.9.11, p. 1659: Here, since the substance is indicated by the instrumental case, its status as a means for the *homa* is established. *Soma* 9.1.50: In the passage "Pūṣan has a portion of ground [grain], for he is toothless," the state of being toothless is not the reason for the grinding. This is because, in the *Hetvadhikaraṇa* (1.2.13), it is determined that such a statement of a reason is ineffective.

Or, where there is a statement based on a fallacious reasoning even when it contradicts direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), the performance of that act must proceed from the statement itself; however, the reasoning is not true reasoning but a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), according to the principle of the section on reasons (*hetvadhikaraṇa*)—this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
(Bhaṭṭa 1.1.6).

The Section on the Observation of Causes (*Hetudarśanādhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the immediately preceding Section on the Observation of Causes (*Hetudarśanādhikaraṇa*), [it follows] the Section on the Non-contradiction with the Customs of the Learned (*Śiṣṭākopādhikaraṇa*) and the Section on Expressions Resembling Reasons (*Hetuvannigadādhikaraṇa*). [4523] The Section on the Observation of Causes.

Immediately following the section on *kāraṇa* (the cause), the section on *virodha* (contradiction)—which follows [the section on] *abhyuccaya* (supplementation) at 1.3.2—is intended to demonstrate either the capacity to establish invalidity through the perception of a reason (*hetudarśana*) that serves as a cause for contradiction, or its capacity to do so independently; because it is a subordinate part (*bhakta*) of the section on contradiction, it does not require a separate connection (*saṃgati*).

It impels and inspires you. (Siddhāntakaumudī): Arthavādas, being causes [of knowledge], are authoritative with respect to Dharma by way of praise.

Commentary: Now, those expressions which state a reason, such as "One offers with soup, for by that food is prepared," and so forth.

[The text] indicates that "the non-instrumentality of the ladle is the reason for the oblation being performed with soup.
What is the purpose? It is so that even other instruments, such as the wooden spoon (*darvī*) or the cooking pot (*piṭhara*), which are also non-instruments, might somehow be used for the oblation.
Why? Because even that [substitute] possesses purposefulness in the performance of the action, and it is indeed possible for it to produce food;
for this is what is called "being produced.
Indeed, there is no such thing as a present time for which this substitute would exist.
Furthermore, the goddess Śruti is the word itself, while in the context of praise, it functions through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
If, on the other hand, the ladle, the pot, and so forth were not called "instruments for making food" simply because they do not produce food directly,
then that [definition] would be futile, and the excellent praise would be meaningless.

Or rather, in this context, those words such as "hi" (for) which are stated as if they were reasons (*hetu*) are not actually ultimate reasons; thus, they serve as examples (*udāharaṇa*).
In that regard, if it were the state of being a reason that is being enjoined, then it would already have been covered by the preceding [section].

If its status as a reason (*hetutva*) were with respect to the connection between that [wind] and the oblation (*homa*), then since that [connection] is not enjoined, it does not exist; of what, then, could it be said to be the reason?

It is replied:

The causal status is not enjoined by this very sentence, nor is it a mere restatement of an established fact. Rather, since a reason must be preceded by its own establishment, as long as there is a doubt regarding the establishment of that which has been taught as unestablished, its establishment occurs through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and scriptural statement (*vacana*).
Furthermore, whatever expectation for an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) there may be—namely, "why [is this so]?"—that too is considered to be satisfied by this very reason.

Even if it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), nevertheless, it is understood that its scope applies to all topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) because it serves as the basis for determination within them; consequently, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the reason is the proximity [of the act].
And since the relationship is what is to be enjoined, he states that the homa itself possesses the nature of being the reason.
[The opponent objects: "But surely, when the relation of cause and effect is not well-established..."
Some say:
inference pertains only to cause and effect;
and thus he will also state later, "for one desiring rain and the sense organs," and so forth.
That is not correct;
for even things that do not stand in a cause-and-effect relationship, such as the Kṛttikās and so forth, are observed to be causes for the cognition of Rohiṇī and others that have recently risen.
Therefore, one should consider the relationship of cause and effect to be precisely the relationship between the signifier and the signified.
[Objection: But surely that [relation] too is not a factor, because it occurs subsequent to the inference.
[Reply: True;
however, when another relation already exists, he subsequently puts forward this [relation], which is yet to be established, merely as an illustration of the practice of inference.

When it is intended as a capacity (*śakti*), then causality resides precisely in those two things for which that [capacity] was determined at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by way of the nature of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), since they possess the power to be understood [as such]. And that [connection] is not established; therefore, there is the teaching of a reason (*hetvapadeśa*).

It is true that in common worldly usage, the employment of a reason initially requires the establishment of a relationship through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, in the Veda, since a reason is presented by the word *hi*, one might postulate a statement of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) to express that relationship based on the principle of "otherwise it would be inexplicable" (*anyathānupapatti*), such as: "Whatever is an instrument for preparing food, with that one offers the oblation," and thus the status of being a reason is established.

"What is the purpose?"—if this is asked with the intention that the reason has already been taught; another, however, says: "Once pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established, the *homa* sacrifice, which effects all the constituent parts of the means of proof, becomes established."
"From what?"—
this is precisely the intended meaning of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

But the other says: "Its purposefulness exists in the act of eating; or rather, that much alone will be relied upon.

by that, the intention [of the speaker] is conveyed.

As for the passage beginning with "And the direct statement regarding the cause" (*hetī ca śrutiḥ*), it should be understood in the context of cutting away the fault of connecting unrelated sentences.
"In the case of praise, there is secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).

In that regard, when the statement of the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*), as it was heard, does not establish itself as a reason, it functions toward a purpose consisting in its being a reason for excellence (*praśastya*) which is required immediately thereafter and sought after; for example: "He should sacrifice with rice, because rice is a means of nourishment. But the meaning [of the explanatory passage] exists because it is supplementary to the injunction, just as in common worldly usage. The Commentary states: "Even though the purpose is not explicitly stated, the meaning exists; for that supplementary portion of the sentence is similar to the injunction."

Furthermore, because of the correspondence [with other texts], it is understood as a statement of praise (*stuti*). Just as we know that food is being prepared with a winnowing basket (*sūrpa*), so too it is understood that "food is prepared with a winnowing basket. In that case, it teaches what is not currently occurring as if it were being praised as something currently occurring.
This defect applies to your own position, for whom the logical reason (*hetu*) is the injunction (*vidhi*).
For an injunction is not understood to have a meaning other than [the act itself];
nor can the Veda enjoin a purpose while teaching something that is already present.
In this case as well, this word "other" (para) refers to something else.
Just as in the world, when Devadatta is weak, the term "weak" is not applied with reference to a lion or a tiger, but rather with reference to those who are inferior in strength to Devadatta;
so too,

when it is said "the winnowing basket performs the act of making food," this designation exists because of its superior performance of that act, being made relative to other inferior means of preparing food.

Or rather—on the view that it is non-existent, there exists the status of being the basis for praise (*stuti*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*). For if the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) were to convey even the fact of being made of *parā* grass or the like, then, by the force of another injunction (*vidhi*), it would necessarily have to be a restatement (*anuvāda*); and a restatement occurs regarding something already known.
Therefore, this is merely proclaimed as the very same capacity to produce food (*annakaraṇatva*) that we perceive in the winnowing basket (*sūrpa*) through the word itself;
thus, it is explained by means of this present tense term (*vartamānapada*).
For even in that case, it is said that what has been done or what is about to be done is performed for the sake of praise.

How is there praise? By disregarding the past and the future of all the world, and because of the passion for the present—since the world does not bestow [its favor] upon anything else—it is said that by this very act, affection is produced even at another time.
Alternatively, having figuratively attributed the "presentness" of the act of giving food to the act of eating itself, one praises it.
In that case as well, because people prefer an expression that exceeds their capacity, when it is said "it is performed," it becomes a praise;
it does not [arise] from the mere statement of capacity.
However, in that context, since it is an injunction (*vidhi*), there would be a fault if one were not to grasp the primary status of being the instrument (*karaṇatva*) and the present tense.

What is the reason? For an injunction has as its object a meaning that is entirely dependent [on it]. In that case, to grasp something other than what is heard [in the text] would be without any basis of proof.
This very point he states: "For in an injunction, the meaning of another word is not the purpose."
For the purpose of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is indeed the meaning of the word *para*.

Therefore, in this case, one must either assume that a word denoting a past or future action refers to its own object as having a present action, or that a word denoting a present action [refers to its own object] as having a present action.
When the meaning of the word consists merely of that cause, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is employed to denote the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*).
Furthermore, its being "thus" (as it appears) is not established from any source; thus, it lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).
Now, if it is intended to have a primary meaning, then it is said in reply:
Furthermore, the Veda could not convey a feasible meaning by teaching that which is currently present as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*).

For it is not possible to establish a causal relationship through a winnowing basket (*sūrpa*) or the like, when the action is presently occurring, nor by way of being the most effective means for the act of cooking. Therefore, both [the opponent and the proponent] are in disagreement.
In the case of the view that [the statement] is non-existent, the word "other" (*para*) is employed because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Just as in the world, when one says "Devadatta is strong," the possessive suffix *matup* occurs to denote an excellence of strength over others, and a specific distinction is mentioned, such as "he is stronger than that plowman"; in that case, the word for "strength" is primary in its excellence over all [others], yet it is not possible for it to be so [absolutely] because lions and others are even stronger. Therefore, this is expressed in relation to Devadatta's own inferior strength; likewise, here too, the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) is called the "most effective means" (*sādhakatama*) in relation to other more remote means.

But would it not follow that this usage based on relative dependence (*apekṣā*) is indeed primary? And thus, the application of the word "strong" to Devadatta would not be considered figurative at all.

True, this is so when the term is employed with reference merely to a lesser degree; however, when it is used without distinction, even though there is a greater strength, the cognition of "strength" arises. At that time, that very same word, when applied to something that is inferior in some respect, becomes figurative.

Similarly, if the status of being an instrument for preparing food (*annakaraṇatva*) were restated (*anūdyate*) regarding the winnowing basket (*sūrpa*) by virtue of the injunctive statement, then there would be either a primary status (*mukhyatva*) relative to that which is merely inferior, or a secondary status (*gauṇatā*) because the cognition—having proceeded generally toward the most excellent—would be directed toward the highest degree, since no lesser [degree] is mentioned. That may be so; however, because everything is enjoined as a prior factor (*pūrvavidhāna*), there is no ground for the requirement of something inferior or for secondary status with respect to the action, given that it possesses the state of being an absolute non-effector (*atyantāsādhakatamatva*). Thus, there would be excessive strain [in your position], making it unequal [to ours].
And if it were argued that [the reason] is established because of its mention, and that [the reason applies] by way of generality, then there would be no fixed rule for injunctions.
The Commentary states: Even if the making of food were the reason for various types of implements, nevertheless, it remains restricted to the winnowing basket alone;
for from the word [of the Veda], it is understood that the making of food is the reason [for using the basket].
And the scriptural statement refers to the winnowing basket (*sūrpa*), not to the ladle, the grinding stone, and so forth.
For that [basket] is specifically indicated by the fact that "since food is prepared with the winnowing basket, therefore one offers with the winnowing basket.
Just as when someone says, "My house was burnt because a powerful wind was blowing," it is understood that the fire did not burn it by itself while being blown by the powerful wind.

Now, it might be thought: "By whatever means food is prepared—by the *praṇītā* water, the winnowing basket, or by other means—the oblation (*homa*) is performed by each of those. Thus, there would be a restriction of the injunctions to some specific means;
for instance, "food is prepared by the *praṇītā* water."
In that context, just as it would be said "he offers," so too [it means] "he offers by means of making food.
On the other hand, in the absence of that [primary meaning], the winnowing basket is praised;
for [the statement] "for by it food is made" is a restatement of a well-known fact (*vṛttāntānvā*).
Because it is the cause, its substratum must necessarily be stated as being identical to that [subject];
and due to proximity, it is understood as being delimited by that very [subject].

Furthermore, in common worldly usage, whatever reason is presented after having proposed a particular subject (dharmin), that reason is first perceived precisely as being non-different from the object of cognition itself.

However, because the initiator of that [inference] lacks a connection with the probandum-part (*sādhyāṃśa*) in its universal form, it is determined at the very time of employing the example that it is intended [to function] as a universal. In the case of the causes of the Veda, however, no connection with the probandum is known either in its universal form or in its particular form; therefore, that [connection] must now be postulated by the Teacher.

Since a particular is being introduced there, and since a universal is not established—and thus the grounds for abandoning it are impossible—the impossibility of what is otherwise unaccountable (*anyathānupapatti*), which has been restricted solely to the particular that has arisen, postulates that very [particular] as the example.
For if that [invariable concomitance] were not postulated, the scriptural statement of the reason would be contradicted.
However, if the invariable concomitance between the absence of the status of being a non-instrument (as found in items such as ladles and pots) and the connection with the oblation is not postulated,
then nothing— neither what is heard nor what is seen— would be rendered untenable.
Therefore, one should understand that the statement of an example here—"he offers with this and that"—is intended as a *caru*-offering.
This is an inference based on a specific observation (*viśeṣadṛṣṭam anumānam*).
Even in the world, from seeing smoke from grass, one infers specifically a fire of grass, not merely fire in general.

Just as the act of going (*gamana*), when adopted as the basis for the derivation of the word "cow" (*go*), attains the status of being the basis for that term only because it follows from the cognition of the commonality of possessing dewlaps and so forth—and not merely with respect to any goer—such is the established rule for the word "cow. Similarly, because the instruction regarding the non-making of food (*abhakaraṇa*) is given in reference to the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), it is an instruction regarding the cause residing in the food itself. In this case, the meaning would be this much: whatever winnowing basket is capable of making food, by that alone should one sacrifice; there is no inclusion of the ladle (*darvi*), the cooking pot (*piṭhara*), and so forth.

Just as when fire is said to be the cause of burning, it is that very fire which, when obstructed by a stronger force, does not burn; whereas sound and other such things do not burn because they are obstructed by stronger forces. Therefore, the word "instrument" (*karaṇa*) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already established.
Therefore, it is better that [the passage] is indeed a commendation by virtue of being a cause for food.
Śā—Thus, the *arthavādas* which are the opposites of futility and the opposites of injunctions have been examined. Now, those which are the opposites of reasons are being examined.

Thus it is heard: "One offers with a winnowing basket, for by it food is prepared. In this regard, there is a doubt: when the offering is to be performed with a winnowing basket, is the fact that it is a means of preparing food the reason (*hetu*), or is it an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*)?

In that case, the status of being a reason is understood through the direct hearing of the word (*śabda-śruti*), whereas excellence (*prāśastya*) is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, an explanatory praise is generally devoid of independent purpose.
But the reason (*hetu*) is meaningful. What, then, is the meaning of the reason?
It is that by which food is prepared—whether by a winnowing basket or by other means such as a ladle or a cooking pot—the accomplishment of the oblation (*homa*) occurs through each of those.
The purpose of the reason (*hetu*) is as follows:
how can there be the designation of "reason" when pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established?

Precisely because of this designation of reason—which would otherwise be untenable without pervasion—the statement of pervasion is inferred, such as: "Whatever is used for cooking must be offered as an oblation."
Since that statement, which prescribes all means of making food, establishes that even the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) is an instrument for the oblation,
the phrase "one offers with the winnowing basket" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of its constituent parts.

Therefore, this sentence— composed of one part that is directly heard and another part that is inferred— establishes that the winnowing basket is an instrument for the oblation on the grounds of its being a means of making food.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the offering should be made with a winnowing basket or whatever else is an instrument for preparing food.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: by virtue of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-śruti*), the winnowing basket is understood to function as the instrument; it cannot be treated as an optional alternative to the ladle, the cooking pot, and so forth, which are known only through inference.

Furthermore, the status of the winnowing basket as the means of the oblation, being declared by the Veda itself, does not require a logical reason (*hetu*) as its basis, since the Veda alone is the authority in this matter; rather, it requires only an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
Because it serves the purpose of providing an incentive (*prarocanā*),
it is therefore an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). And thus, there will be no need to assume the status of a statement whose logical concomitance (*vyāpti*) is not well-established.
Furthermore, the use of the present tense in the expression "it is being done" (*kriyate*) is appropriate when it serves the purpose of persuasion (*prarocanā*).
For there is no such delight in what has already occurred or what is yet to come as there is in the present;
therefore, the use of the present tense is justified by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the sake of generating interest.
If, however, they were intended as injunctions (*vidhi*), one would have to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) without any basis in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, they are merely explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
Soma [says]: "As for what was stated—that all interruptions of injunctions serve the purpose of praise—that is incorrect."
In some cases, there are "injunctions of reason" (*hetuvidhi*) because they proceed by way of a brief reference to what was stated in the previous section.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: the statement "for by that food is prepared" would be an injunction of reason; for if that were so, even ladles and other such items would be purposeful as means for the oblation, and the word "for" (*hi*) would be logically justified.
[The Vṛtti says: "The statement 'for by that food is prepared' is declared to be a reason."
Therefore, the status of being a cause is not lost; hence, both the winnowing basket and other means are valid instruments.
The status of the winnowing-basket as the instrument is based on direct Vedic revelation (śruti); it cannot be set aside by non-revealed means.
Therefore, the reason [cited] is useless; consequently, praise is what prompts action.
This concludes the section on "Statements Resembling Reasons" (hetuvannigadādhikaraṇa). False reasons (hetvābhāsas):

Bhaṭṭa: In the Cāturmāsya sacrifice, after the injunction "He offers with a winnowing basket" (*śūrpeṇa juhoti*) has been heard regarding an oblation performed by means of a winnowing basket, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "For by that food is prepared" (*tena hy annaṃ kriyate*) does not employ figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the purpose of praise.
Rather, with the status of being a means to the oblation as the thing to be established (*sādhya*), the fact of being a means for preparing food is enjoined as the reason (*hetu*).
For here, unlike the previous case, there is nothing to be assumed as a goal (*bhāvya*); rather, the word *hi* itself expresses the state of being a reason.
Furthermore, a logical reason (*hetu*) is untenable without pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Therefore, it implies a statement of pervasion such as: "Whatever is an instrument for offering oblations must be used for that purpose.

Consequently, since even winnowing baskets, ladles, cooking pots, and so forth are understood to be means for preparing the sacrificial food (*bhisa*), the mention of the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) in the injunction is either an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of all such instruments or a restatement of their constituent parts (*avayavānuvāda*).

Alternatively, since the word "that" (tat) refers specifically to the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), the reason for its being the instrument for preparing food is its very nature as such. Consequently, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be conceived as residing in that specific [instrument] alone; thus, even if the capacity to prepare food excludes other winnowing baskets, the injunction does not apply to the winnowing basket in this context. This is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: because of the use of the present tense ending in the word *kriyate* ("is being done"), the state of being in the present time must be stated as the reason.
Furthermore, it is not possible for the act of preparing food to occur at the time of the *homa* (oblation).
Therefore, even for you, the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) must necessarily be understood as indicating the past or future through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Although this [indication] is also necessary for me, by way of constituting a quality that serves the purpose of indicating excellence (*prāśastya*), nevertheless, because it functions as a restatement (*anuvādaka*) and generates that excellence, there is no fault; for without the mention of the present tense, that excellence would not be perceived.
Furthermore, since it is possible for [the passage] to have as its purport the praise required [for the injunction], it is not proper to assume that its purport is a cause that is not so required.
Therefore, it is established that all arthavādas possess authority by way of being corroborative (sādhaka).
Maṇḍana [says]: "In the case of the winnowing basket, the praise consists in its being the cause of food."
Śaṅkara: "There is no injunction of a reason (hetuvidhi) in the case of the winnowing basket (śūrpa).

The section concerning that which is stated as a reason (hetuvannigada-adhikaraṇa) is merely a supplement to the section concerning explanatory passages (arthavāda-adhikaraṇa). [Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 93]. An injunction of a reason is an explanatory passage—as in: 'The clarified butter is taken four times; for he is about to perform the after-offerings (anuyāja) here.'"
*Bālakrīḍā*, p. 52: A mantra expressing a logical reason (*hetuvidhi*)—“For Indra indeed follows Vāyu.
*Bālakrīḍā*, p. 62: A mantra in the form of a logical reason (*hetuvidhirūpa*)—“The twelve-spoked [wheel], for it does not decay.
*Bālakrīḍā*, p. 62: Generally, when there is a reversal of the cause (*hetuviparyaya*), a reversal of the effect (*kāryaviparyaya*) is observed.
Or: Vārttika 2.4.2.11, p. 636.
An injunction [is expressed] by means of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) for the cause and that which possesses the cause—as in "If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice. Bālakrīḍā, p. 29.

Fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsas*). A fallacious reason is a defect residing in the probans (*hetu*), which is the mode of a true cognition that is the counter-positive of an absence constituting the cause of inference.
And there exists the absence of cognitions such as those of the unestablished (*asiddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and the sublated (*bādhaka*).

It functions as an instrument of inference by way of being the absence of an impediment (*pratibandhaka*). The status of being an "unestablished" (*asiddha*) reason and so forth consists in their being causes for the cognition of that which is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of that [absence]. Therefore, a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is a defect residing in the reason.
In short, it is the state of being that by virtue of which a true cognition having such a qualified object becomes an impediment to inference.

Alternatively, it is the state of being the object of such a valid cognition. (In place of the word "therein," [one should read] "by that"). A fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is a reason that is defective by virtue of that [invalidity].
The term "corresponding to reality" (*yathārtha*) is included in order to exclude errors such as the misconception that "smoke deviates from fire."
The term "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is used to exclude adventitious conditions (*upādhi*).

Since the knowledge of an adventitious condition is not a direct impediment [to inference], the absence of such a condition is not the cause of inferential cognition; therefore, these are pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
These [pseudo-reasons] are threefold: the unestablished (*asiddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and the contradictory (*bādhaka*).

In that regard, non-establishment (*asiddhi*) is fivefold: non-establishment of the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*), non-establishment of the relation (*saṃbandhāsiddhi*), non-establishment of the negative concomitance (*vyatirekāsiddhi*), non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), and non-establishment of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*).
Among these, non-establishment of the reason itself is non-establishment of the essential nature, as in:
"Buddha is a knower of *dharma* and *adharma* because he is omniscient."

In this context, omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) is an unestablished reason (*hetu*). According to the system of Akṣapāda (Gautama), "unestablished nature" (*svarūpāsiddhi*) is the absence of that which is intended as the pervader (*vyāpaka*) within the subject (*pakṣa*). However, since existence is established for Īśvara, there is no deficiency in the case of Buddha, because that [omniscience] is absent in him. "Unestablished relation" (*saṃbandhāsiddhi*) is the absence, in the subject, of the intended pervasion through the relation that serves as the delimiting factor of the reasonhood (*hetutvāvacchedakasambandha*).
"Fire is a burner because it is cold.

[In this case], when there is no difference between the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) and the reason (*hetu*), there is a failure to establish the negative concomitance (*vyatirekāsiddhi*).
For example: "The word 'cow' denotes that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, because it is the word 'cow'."
The followers of Akṣapāda maintain that this is the uncommon inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason.
This very quality of occurring only in the subject (*pakṣamātravṛttitva*) is what constitutes the uncommon [reason].
Here, the seed of its defectiveness lies in its incapacity to establish either the probandum or the absence of the probandum, and thus its inability to serve as the basis for inference.
The non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is the non-establishment of the subject (*pakṣaprasiddhi*).
For example: "Space is eternal, because it is a partless substance.
This constitutes a non-establishment of the locus for a Sautrāntika (Buddhist), who maintains that space does not exist.
That [non-establishment] is also the non-existence of the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).
For example: "The mountain made of gold possesses fire.
Fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*): 4928. These are the types.
The non-establishment of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) occurs when the reason exists only in a portion of the subject (*pakṣadeśa*).
For example, the logic of Heramba and Narasiṃha:
"Heramba, Narasiṃha, wind, and space are material (*mūrta*), because they are air (*anila*). [In this case, the reason "air" applies only to some of the subjects.]

The non-establishment of the delimiting property of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) in the case of the probandum, or the non-establishment of the delimiting property of the reason (*hetutāvacchedaka*) in the case of the reason, constitutes "unestablished pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*).
For example: "It possesses fire made of gold, because it possesses smoke made of gold.

Likewise, in cases such as "because of blue smoke," since the property of being blue smoke (*nīladhūmatva*) is too cumbersome (*gurutā*) to serve as the delimiting property of the reason, that too is "unestablished pervasion."
Thus say the followers of Akṣapāda:
"An inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason is one that generates doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).
And the state of generating doubt arises both from the cognition of its connection with the absence of the probandum and from its being the subject (*pakṣatva*)."
For example: "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal.
Here, incorporeality, because it is the locus of non-eternal action, generates doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).
Likewise: "Air is imperceptible because it is a substance devoid of color," and "Air is perceptible because, while possessing magnitude, it possesses manifest touch."

In this case, because both [reasons] possess equal strength, they produce doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*). Regarding the state of having a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*), the followers of Akṣapāda maintain that there is a mutual obstruction of inference due to the cognition of the pervader of the absence of the probandum; it is not an inference in the form of doubt.
Here it is said:

Just as there is doubt in the form of perception regarding the cognition of what is pervaded by both "being a post" and "being a person," so too, even when there is a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*), let there be an inference in the form of doubt.
Where the observation of the pervader of one side is stronger, there is no doubt because the stronger force prevents the apprehension of the second side.
And by the force of the result (*phala*), the state of having a superior or equal strength [of the opposing cognition] is to be postulated.
Here, an objection is raised:

"In this case, for the cognition that the existence-part of that absence is pervaded by that absence, the very fact of being a cognition produced by ordinary sense-contact (*laukikasannikarṣa*) is the delimiting factor of its status as an inhibitor; therefore, there can be no inference in the form of a doubt," and so forth.
The subverting [reason], however, is that which establishes the absence of the probandum;
this is the "contradictory" (viruddha) [reason], according to the followers of Akṣapāda.
For example: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced."
In this case, the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), which is pervaded by impermanence (*anityatva*), subverts permanence (*nityatva*).
This is called "that which establishes the opposite of the generality of the probandum" (*sādhyasāmānyaviparyayasādhaka*); such is the direction [of the argument].
"One should sacrifice with the Sākamedha rites during the winter" [is said] regarding the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
This is the Bhāṣya's "Heramba-Narasimha maxim."

The Rāmānujīyas argue that just as the nature of an elephant or a lion may exist in one part of Heramba or Narasiṃha while being absent in another, there is no contradiction due to the difference in location; therefore, since non-existence and other attributes can coexist in a single object of the Arhat, there is no logical inconsistency in describing it as "non-exclusive" (anekānta).
[Sāhasī.
707] This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding such matters as "the Agnihotra sacrifice must be offered" and "the Agnihotra sacrifice must not be offered."
Bhāṭṭa 10.8.5:

At the Kuṇḍapāyināmayana sacrifice, during the measurement of the sacrificial post (yūpa), the Hotṛ should perform the *karaṇa-mantra* of the Adhvaryu, while some other person belonging to the Hotṛ's group should perform the *hotṛ-mantra*, or perhaps someone who is an outsider (*bahiraṅga*).
Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 3.8.10–21.
The *hotṛ* is the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).

Regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), in the *iḍā* offering, [it is said]: "The two *adhvaryus* bring [the portions] to the *hotṛ*. By this, the *hotṛ* receives the instruction from the *adhvaryus*; the others receive their respective shares of the *iḍā*.
The *hotṛ*, standing in front of the *gārhapatya* fire and behind the *āhavanīya* fire, reciting the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, is called the performer of the sacrifice (*yāgakartṛ*).
Bhāṣya 1.2.1.10.5. The *hotṛ* is the first class of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
This Pūrṇa receives a sacrificial fee consisting of twelve cows.
(Vi. 3.7.17) The Hotṛ recites the Prātaranuvāka.
Bhāṣya 3.7.12.2:
Regarding the alternative verbal formulae "O Hotṛ, recite the offering prayer (yaja)" and "O Praśāstṛ, recite the offering prayer," the established procedure is as follows:

After the Adhvaryu and others have offered with the Hotṛ’s yājyā together with all the *camasa* cups, they then assign the *camasas* of those among them who perform the duties in the middle (*madhyataḥ-kārin*), such as the Hotṛ and others, elsewhere. Then, having again drawn Soma into the remaining *camasas* that still contain remnants, they offer it in sequence with the yājyās of the Maitrāvaruṇa and other specific Hotṛs. This is the settled rule.

Furthermore, in that context, regarding the *mantrita-homa*, within the series of directions (*preṣaṇa*) performed by the *adhvaryu*, two directions are heard: "O Hotṛ, sacrifice! (*hotaryaja*) and "O Praśāstṛ, sacrifice! (*praśāstaryaja*). Therein, by the word "Hotṛ," only the Maitrāvaruṇa is meant;

for according to the statement, "In the Soma-sacrifice, the ritual performance of which is the Adhvara, the Hotṛs offer the *vaṣaṭ* call facing eastward," he too has the authority to perform the *yājyā*.

The Commentary states: "In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the selection of the Hotṛ is prescribed as: 'Agni, the divine Hotṛ, shall sacrifice to the gods.
That [selection] is extended by the rule of transfer (*codaka*) to the iṣṭi-type rites associated with the Soma sacrifice, such as the Agniṣṭoma.
However, there is also the selection of the Hotṛ priest in the Soma sacrifice, as it is said: "Agni is the Hotṛ; he is my Hotṛ; O Hotṛ, you are my Hotṛ," and thus one chooses the Hotṛ.
In this regard, a deliberation arises: should the selection of the Hotṛ belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa be performed in the iṣṭi-type rites, or not? What is the prima facie view?
"It should not be performed.
Why? First of all, the act of choosing [the priests] would be purposeless;
moreover, the Hotṛ priest has already been engaged by the choosing performed for the Soma sacrifice.
Since the purpose of bowing has already been fulfilled by the act of making Soma complete,
it need not be performed.
This being the position reached, we reply:
"Because the choosing has already commenced, the choosing of the Hotṛ is performed for each individual ritual system.
This is not so; [one might argue] that 'the choosing pertaining to the Soma sacrifice will accomplish the purpose of the Darśapūrṇamāsa through incidental application (prasaṅga).
[But this is incorrect because] since the choosing has already commenced—that is, since the ritual action has already begun—the choosing pertaining to the Darśapūrṇamāsa is performed."
Therefore, that is not purposeless;
what then? It is merely the performance of the ritual act.
For if it is not performed, there would be a deficiency in the quality of the rite.
Therefore, it must be performed separately for each ritual action.
[Objection: "But what about the Brahman priest?"—the Commentary says:

If you think that because the choosing (*varaṇa*) occurs at the commencement [of the rite], the choosing of the Hotṛ priest must be performed separately for each ritual action, then the Brahman priest is also chosen once the ritual action has commenced.
At the conclusion of the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* waters,
therefore, the choosing (*varaṇa*) of that [officiant] as well is merely a ritual duty (*dharma*).
Therefore, that too must be performed for each individual ritual action,
or else a specific distinction must be stated; for it is not prior to the restrictive rule, as that [rule] is for its purpose.
Commentary: The selection of the Brahman priest need not be performed.
What is the reason? "Prior to the restriction," meaning prior to the selection. True; the selection of the Brahman occurs once the ritual action has already commenced.

Prior to the formal selection (*varaṇa*), there is no such thing as the office of the Brahman priest. After the selection, however, the Brahman performs his ritual duties; therefore, the selection is for the sake of those duties.
Consequently, it is not a mere ritual act (*dharma*).

For what purpose, then, [is it performed]? It is simply for the sake of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*). Since he has already been invited by the Soma-related selection (*varaṇa*), the Brahman-selection need not be performed.

If it is argued that [the rule] refers to what has been specifically prescribed—the Bhāṣya states: "It would be applied; for on the day of the fast (aupavasathya) during the new moon (amāvāsyā), the preparation of the altar (vedikarma) is specifically prescribed by the text: 'On the previous day, on the new moon, he prepares the altar.
In that case, the demarcation of the altar (vediparigraha) is performed by the Brahman priest."
"Therefore, Brahmā also is included in the selection [of officiants].
"No, because it is not heard in the scripture.
Commentary: On the day before the new moon, the construction of the altar (vedi) is prescribed in the scripture, but not the formal enclosure (parigraha), because that is not heard [in the text].
The formal acceptance of the Brahman priest shall be performed at the very time he is appointed, because the act of appointment serves the purpose of the ritual function.
There is no prior acceptance before the construction of the altar;
even in that case, the Brahman must be granted leave to depart.
Commentary:
This, then, is another resolution. In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the construction of the altar is prescribed after the covering of the sacrificial oblations (havis).
The selection of the Brahman priest also occurs at the time of carrying forward the *praṇītā* waters, prior to the commencement of the Brahman’s duties;
because it serves a visible purpose, its immediate sequence [is established].
This being the case, the construction of the altar on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is taught by a direct scriptural injunction.

When that [the *praṇayana*] is being removed, the selection of the *parigraha*, the *prasava*, and the *brahmavaraṇa* are also removed, because these are subordinate elements whose proper place and time are determined by the principal act.
This being so, the *brahmavaraṇa* occurs at the time of the *praṇayana* on the full moon day, and on the previous day for the new moon day;
for in both cases, the office of the *brahman* has not yet been undertaken.
Therefore, there is a requirement for gratification in both cases.

Consequently, the selection (*varaṇa*) of the Brahman priest need not be performed separately for each ritual action, because the Brahman is already gratified by the very selection belonging to the Soma sacrifice.
If it is argued that this applies only to the Hotṛ priest—

Commentary: If you view it thus— that although the choosing of the Brahman occurs once the ritual action has commenced, and there is no prior action on the part of the Brahman before that choosing, therefore the Brahman is not one who chooses after the action has commenced—
it is because of the Hotṛ’s [precedent].
Even for the Hotṛ priest, there is no ritual act whatsoever prior to his formal selection (*varaṇa*);
and his selection is not merely a duty,
because it is not connected with any [other] ritual act.

Commentary: Prior to his formal selection (*varaṇa*), the Hotṛ priest has a connection with the *sāmidhenī* ritual, as stated in the injunction: "He recites the *sāmidhenīs* for one who is about to sacrifice" (*avataḥ sāmidhenīranvāha*).

Therefore, the selection of the Hotṛ serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Consequently, it must be performed in the sacrificial rites such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others. On the other hand, the selection of the Brahman priest serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*); since that has already been accomplished by the Soma-related rite itself, it need not be performed again.

Śabara: There arises a doubt as to whether the selection (*varaṇa*) of the *hotṛ* priest should not be performed because it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), or whether it should be performed. Since the selection is proximate [to the sacrifice], and since the act of propitiation (*ānati*) is already accomplished through the selection pertaining to the Soma-sacrifice by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it should not be performed. In response to this, [the established conclusion is: the selection already in progress cannot in any way serve a visible purpose.

For the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇādāna*)—even though it is yet to come—becomes the cause for propitiation, as is observed in common worldly practice; however, propitiation does not occur through a future selection. Therefore, [the selection] has an invisible purpose.
The selection of the Brahman priest (*brahmavaraṇa*), however, is performed while the Brahman is not yet engaged in his duties.
Regarding the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), there is no dispute that it is indeed performed while he is still unengaged.

On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) as well, the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), being drawn forward on the preceding day, draws along with it the selection of the Brahman for the sake of accomplishing the *upavasatha*, which is an integral part of the rite.
Therefore, because its object has not yet been set in motion, the selection (*varaṇa*) of the Brahman priest serves a visible purpose.
Consequently, the selection of the Brahman priest need not be performed.
[Objection: Even though the Soma-consumers have not yet completed their task, their selection is said to have its purpose fulfilled due to its immediate proximity; this is the connection.
Vi— "In these [Soma-aṅga-iṣṭis], there is either no choosing (*varaṇa*) of the Hotṛ, or there is an absence of the non-performance [of that duty].
It does not exist, because, like the *anvāhārya* fee, it is performed due to its ritual character; thus it would be like a regular sacrifice (*aiṣṭivat*).

Bhaṭṭa—The choosing of the Hotṛ pertaining to the Darśa sacrifice is not recognized as being accompanied by the mantra during the choosing in the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites within the Soma sacrifice, because in the archetype (*prakṛti*), that [choosing] serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

For when certain elements have already commenced, the selection of the *hotṛ* priest is subsequently prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) by the mantra, "May Agni, the divine *hotṛ*, worship the gods," and so forth. Therefore, since that [selection] has already commenced, it is impossible for it to serve a visible purpose; consequently, it is determined to serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Thus, because it is not included within what has not yet commenced, there can be no fulfillment by extension (*prasaṅga*) through the Soma-related rite which serves an invisible purpose. Nor can it be argued that even though it has commenced, its serving an invisible purpose is possible—just like the selection of the *brahman* priest—since the selection of the *brahman* priest also...

It should not be argued that [the *brahmavaraṇa*] is performed on the previous day even though it was intended for the authorization (*abhyanujñāna*) regarding the construction of the altar (*vedi*), because it is performed prior to the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* waters; for in the case of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), since the construction of the altar occurs after the covering of the oblation (*havirabhivāsana*), it does not belong to the time of the previous day. Furthermore, since the selection of the *brahmā* priest at the time of carrying forward the *praṇītā* waters takes the form of an authorization for what has not yet commenced, its purpose as a visible utility (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) is established. Likewise, in the case of the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*), even if the construction of the altar is brought forward, the selection of the *brahmā* can also be brought forward by overriding the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*) through the order of meaning (*arthakrama*), as it serves the purpose of authorizing a subordinate part of that [altar construction]; thus, its purpose as a visible utility is established, being in the nature of an authorization for what has not yet commenced.
Nor does it follow that the choosing of the Hotṛ priest (*hotṛvaraṇa*) must also be performed before the *sāmidhenī* verses on the basis of following the order of meaning (*arthakrama*),

because the supplementary statement to the injunction for choosing the Hotṛ— namely, "He recites the *sāmidhenīs* for one who has chosen" (*avataḥ sāmidhenīranvāha*)— functions as an exception to the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*). For this [supplementary statement] is an independent exclusion of the choosing [of the Hotṛ] in relation to the *sāmidhenīs* alone.
In this case, there is no displacement [of the *nivid* mantras] prior to the *varaṇa* (selection) mantras;
rather, the purpose is merely to set aside the order of recitation in order to achieve syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).

Therefore, since such displacement is untenable, and because it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) by way of being an invocation (*abhyardhana*), there is no *prasaṅga* (extension of application).
However, there is a disparity [between the two cases], because the selection (*varaṇa*) of the Brahman priest has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) precisely at the time it occurs.

Nor should it be argued that, even though the activity consists of appointing someone, just as in the world a laborer who has already begun some work might have his status determined by a supervisor (*niśāyaka*) or similar authority due to greed despite initial doubt—so too, even if there is doubt regarding the selection, the appointment of the Hotṛ priest midway through the *sāmidhenī* verses is justified as having a visible purpose due to his own greed. This cannot be maintained.

For one who proceeds with doubt, there might occasionally arise the contingency of the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*) being performed by the same agent; therefore, the sacrificer must necessarily employ some worldly means—such as solicitation—prior to the *sāmidhenī* verses. Consequently, this Vedic selection (*vaidha-varaṇa*) must necessarily have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). For this very reason, the meaning of the term "unselected" (*avṛtaḥ*) is precisely "one devoid of the Vedic selection. Thus, it should also be understood that in the case of the selection of a wife for a sacrifice, the fact of being "already selected" (*vṛtta-varaṇatva*) is the cause for its having an invisible purpose, and not the fact of its serving to prevent [worldly] solicitation.
And this being the case, there is no consequence of the word "varaṇa" (choosing) being used figuratively with respect to the choosing for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthaka*),
because it is precisely the act of requesting (*prārthana*) that is denoted by that term.
Therefore, it is established that by means of the Soma-related choosing, only the choosing of the Brahman priest (*brahmavaraṇa*) is entailed, and not the choosing of the Hotṛ priest (*hotṛvaraṇa*).

In reality, however, because the selection (*varaṇa*) pertaining to the Soma sacrifice— just like the archetypal selection— is a refinement of the agent and thus serves both the subsidiaries and the principal, and because there is no factor to establish that it serves the principal alone (as there is in the case of the sacrificial fee), it follows that the selection of the Brahman priest from the model sacrifice is indeed sublated;
however, there is no extension (*prasaṅga*) to the selection of the Hotṛ priest.
However, it should be understood that even for one who is ill, that [selection] does not occur.
Furthermore, in this view, the connection with the chapter is established.
Maṇḍana states: "In this case, the selection of the Hotṛ priest should be that pertaining to the Full Moon sacrifice."

Because the *homa* consists of an action (*kriyātmaka*), it is understood as something to be assisted by the "manner of the primary" (*pradhānakathaṃbhāva*)—that is, as being "thus"—and not so [understood] in the case of a substance (*dravya*).
