Since there can be no performance of a Homa without a deity, [it is established]. (Su. p.
457) Homa consists of the aggregate of the dedication to a deity, the renunciation of the substance, and its casting into the fire.
Page 621: Homa is manifested by the act of casting [an offering] into the fire, characterized by the relinquishment of a substance intended for a deity.
Page 1629: Homa is a sacrifice (yāga) distinguished by the pouring [of the oblation].
Bhāṣya 4.2.1328: Homa is the primary element; the taking up of the clarified butter (ājya) is the subordinate element.
VI. 4.12.7. Regarding the *homa*: "In the sentence stating the result, the connection of the root *yaj* alone is clearly heard;
because it is recited in proximity to that [root], the connection of the root *hu* is not known."
Or [it may be argued]: 3|4|14|1, p. 982, *homa*.
Sacrifice (*yāga*) is the primary element, whereas that which is the casting-in (*prakṣepa*, i.e., *homa*) is merely an auxiliary (*aṅga*).

But as for those [acts] which are prompted by the injunction to offer (*juhoti*), in them the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), even though it occurs earlier or later, will either constitute the commencement or, alternatively, they too will have sixteen [components]. (2.1.4.14, p. 983). Regarding the oblation (*homa*) stated as "he offers with the sun" (*sūryeṇa juhoti*) in the Varuṇapraghāsa rites of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, it is prompted by the transcendental result (*apūrva*) and not prompted by the status of the sun and so forth as a cause. (Bhāṣya 9.2.15.11). The oblation is a matter of established practice (*sadācāra*).
Vārttika 3.2.13, p. 205: The *homa* of the *soma* takes place on the *uttaravedi*.

Vi. 3.5.11: A *homa* is a sacrifice characterized by the addition of pouring (*āsecana*) and throwing (*prakṣepa*); it is not merely a sacrifice (*yāga*) in general. Su. p. 1428: An *iṣṭi*-sacrifice is that very same *homa*, with the addition of pouring.

Bhāṣya 6.8.17: Sacrifice (*yāga*) is the relinquishment of a substance with reference to a deity (in the form "it is not mine"); and *homa* is the throwing of that which has been relinquished into the fire. Sacrifice consists merely of relinquishment; *homa* is characterized by the addition of throwing. Vi. 4.12.2: Sacrifice is merely the relinquishment of one's own ownership with reference to a deity.
"Homa is the offering of a substance intended for a deity.
(Vārttika 3.4.14.1, p. 981). "Alternatively, sacrifice (yāga) and oblation (homa) are not distinct from one another;
for they are similar in their prior and subsequent stages, like [the two halves of] Narasiṃha."
3|4|14|1, p. 983. The *homa* offerings must also be performed even when there is an over-extension [of the ritual]:
*homāḥ* 4533; [they are established] by means of both the *homa* and the pressing (*abhiṣava*).
Bhāṣya 6.5.11.40: The oblations connected with ritual acts, such as the *jayas* and others, are the examples. [Sūtra 4534]:
"By means of the oblation and the pressing [of Soma]. This is the definition of an oblation (*homa*).
The *nimitta* is applied to that which is not subject to decay (*acyuta*),
nor is it [applied] to that which is called "the undecaying" (*acyutamasa*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that both together constitute the *nimitta*.
There is no such designation [for him].

Nor does he generally possess the status of being the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer. Who, then, is the performer of the oblation and the pressing? He is the one who, as the agent of the oblation and pressing, is entitled to the consumption [of the soma]; thus, the repetition of the oblation in the *darśa* and other rites is not observed due to the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the breaking [of the vessel] and so forth.
Because it was not previously established, it is enjoined by the rule: "Having offered [the oblation] with the *prāvah* verses in the *havirdhāna* shed into the *āhavanīya* fire" (Vi. 6.2.9).
This is like the case where the ritual procedure (*tantra*) applies to both the offering and the non-offering (Vi.

6.4.7). When a single *kapāla* vessel is broken simultaneously, the status of being a cause for consumption (*bhakṣaṇa-nimitta*) belongs to the offering and the crushing (*miṣava*) together, not to each individually.

Or, just as there is a dependence on the *tantra* (the ritual framework), so too would there be the consequence of a dependence on speech and the jar (*ghaṭa*). Bhaṭṭa 5.2.2; 6.4.7. There is a displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the oblations (*homa*), gifts (*dāna*), and cooking (*pāka*) when they occur at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*). [The displacements] caused by the oblation, the pressing of Soma, and the *vaṣaṭ*-call are the remaining [cases]. Mīko., p. 2108: "And in the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is a displacement of the initiation."

And these [rites] are not to be performed, but rather they are to be preserved; the section concerning the "superiority even of the Agnihotra and other rites" (Bhāṣya 10.2.12.129) should be consulted here. In the case of the oblation and the cooking, the sequence is established by the purpose (*arthataḥ*).
VI. 5.1.2. The presentation of the consumption [of Soma] caused by the *homa* (oblation) and *abhiṣava* (pressing) is the *Jyotiṣṭoma-homapāda*.
Saṃkarṣa 2.4.2–30.
Bhāṣya 3.5.1.132, p. 1009: When merely the *homa* is enjoined, one who has studied the Veda is capable [of performing it]; likewise is the consumption following the *homa* and *abhiṣava*.
It is performed by one who is learned, not by one who is ignorant.

Regarding the action prescribed for the sake of a fruit in the form of a mere oblation (*homamātra*), there is no contradiction in the case of the *agnihotra* between the materials and so forth, the pouring out with the *prāva* ladles into the *havirdhāna*, and the taking [of the offering] in the *āhavanīya* fire.
Su. Pṛ. 777: "Having offered the *prayāja* oblations, they shall consume the portions in the assembly after death"—this is the definition of the *homa*.

Consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) is explicitly heard in the text. In that context, both the consumption and the *homa* are mentioned; since each is separately stated, the *juhoti* (the act of offering) must involve the addition of pouring (*āsecanādhika*).
"The occasion [is] as in the case of the five dishes, where each oblation is a separate act" (4.2.1.38).
He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "the occasion is likewise.
And regarding the oblation (*homa*), the commentary says: "Now, what is the defining characteristic of the act of offering (*juhoti*)?"

In that [context], the terms *homa* (offering) and *āmiṣava* (pressing) are mentioned. That which is connected with both offering and pressing is "connected with offering and pressing. If the root *hu* (to offer) is heard in connection with such a purpose, it refers to that which exceeds mere pouring.
Therefore, it is so designated.

The consumption [of the offering] combined with the oblation and the meat is indeed the sacrifice of the oblation and the meat; it is called *juhoti* because it involves the act of pouring (*āsecanādhika*).
The term "consumption" is derived from the sense "that by which something has been offered" (*hutam anena*), following the analogy of compounds such as *śākapārthiva* (the king who loves vegetables).
Similarly, in common usage, there are forms ending in the suffix *vakan*.
In the Veda as well, the meaning is that what is enjoined by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is [equivalent to] giving (*rāti*).
By the word "and" (*ca*), the connection with the illustrative example is stated.
It restates [the matter] by means of the root *hu* (to offer).

"One should cause a warrior to sacrifice with the *Caturhotṛ* [formula], or indeed with both; for there is no *Dharmaśāstra* (legal code) governing those two. "Having made the *Caturgṛhīta* [oblation] ready, one should apply the *Caturhotṛ*; with the former, there is the oblation and the consumption; with the latter, for each respective occasion, one should offer with the *Graha* for the sake of the purpose. Thus, while the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that it is a case of giving—is reached by the Sūtra, the author refutes it incidentally (*prasaṅgena*) and establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) characterized as follows: [The text continues: "It is characterized by the mark of being a ritual act (*karmalakṣaṇaka*). **Sanskrit Input:** saṃgrāmimaṃ caturhotrā yājayet, ubhābhyāṃ vā, na hi tayordharmaśāstram | caturgṛhītābhyam kṛtvā caturhotāraṃ nyāyacchīta, pūrveṇa homaścābhakṣaṇe homaśca abhyava pratyekaṃ nimittaṃ graheṇārthe juhuyāduttareṇārtham iti | atha dadātiḥ iti pūrvapakṣaṃ sūtreṇa prāptaṃ prāsaṅgena nivārayan siddhāntalakṣaṇaka iti | **English Translation:** "One should cause a warrior to sacrifice with the *Caturhotṛ*, or with both; for there is no *Dharmaśāstra* for those two. "Having prepared the *Caturgṛhīta*, one should apply the *Caturhotṛ*; with the former, there is the oblation and the consumption; with the latter, for each respective occasion, one should offer with the *Graha* for the sake of the purpose. Thus, while the prima facie view—that it is an act of giving—is reached by the Sūtra, the author refutes it incidentally and establishes the final conclusion characterized as follows: "It is characterized by the mark of being a ritual act (*karmalakṣaṇaka*)."
The exclusion of one's own ownership (*svatva*) belongs to oneself, while that of another belongs to both;
thus, the connection with ownership as the occasion (*nimitta*) occurs only through the combination of both the *homā* (offering) and the *abhiṣava* (pressing).

If the *yajati* (sacrifice) and the *tadāhuti* (that offering) were to include all [actions] for the Hotṛ, then there would be the consumption of Soma; it is not the case that each [action] individually serves as the occasion.
The two are similar in this regard.

Therein, with respect to the *yajati* (sacrificial offering) and the *juhoti* (libation), there is merely a designation [of the deity] and so forth; however, there is no scriptural injunction (*śāstra*) for the ritual rules (*dharma*) of the libation or the consumption [of the soma]. Furthermore, the act of *dadāti* (giving) does not exist at all as a connection with another's ownership preceded by the relinquishment of one's own.
If the ritual rules were enjoined for those two, then "the libation and the pressing" would constitute their specific distinction.
If "pradhānam" (the principal) were the act of eating, then the subordinate element (*guṇa*) would differ with each principal.

However, on the other hand, in the treatises of Śabara, Kumārila, and Bhaṭṭa, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is included within the preceding section, wherein the eating is enjoined by both causal factors (*nimitta*).
In that injunction being established, [the present point is subsumed].

A single purpose is established; therefore, it is a single sentence. Regarding this, Maṇḍana states: "The act of sacrifice (*yajati*) mentioned in the context of throwing [the oblation] is indeed the *homa* (offering).
It culminates in renunciation (*tyāga*). [And it is said: "Having inferred [the procedure], having offered, they shall consume [the remains]."
And giving (*dāna*) is the appropriation of another's property. The definition of *homa* (4535). The section concerning the *holākā* sacrifice.
Śaṅkara: "And indeed, it is the very definition of *homa*."
The characteristics of giving,
distribution, and the arrangement of recitation are also found here;
for instance, the Gautama-gobhila [sūtra] is also present herein.
The *prayoga* (ritual application) consists of sacrifice (*yāga*) and oblation (*homa*).
It is distinct from [the mere mention of] substance and deity,
and it is accepted specifically by the followers of the Sāmaveda.
The *Vāsiṣṭha* [Kalpa] is for the Bahvṛcas alone; it consists of a sacrifice (*yāga*) and an oblation (*homa*), with the addition of pouring (*āsecanādhika*).
And that which was spoken by Śaṅkha and Likhita is for the Vājasaneyins, like the *Āpastambīya* *Homa*.

Regarding the disposal (*hyavadāna*) being a consecratory act (*saṃskāra*) like the oblation (*homa*), since this is accepted by the Taittirīyas themselves in the *Baudhāyanīya*, one might ask: "Since each [text] is a *Gṛhyasūtra*, why should there not be a separate performance (*anusamaya*) for each? If this is asked, the answer is no; for even though a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) for each is admitted, having shown this, it must be investigated—does it involve a combination (*sāhitya*)? (Bhaṭṭa 5.2.7). Are those [texts] authorities only for those [respective schools], or are all [authorities] for all? Should the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) and others be considered as optional alternatives (*vikalpyante*) with the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) as the means of the oblation, or should it be understood that a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) applies according to the textual recitation (*pāṭhataḥ*)?

For it is not the case that, having enjoined elsewhere "one offers with a winnowing basket," the reason "for by it food is prepared"—which is established as a *liṅga* (indicative mark)—is inferred to apply elsewhere because the word "reason" (*hetu*) provides the justification; such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). [The opponent argues:
"Reason" (*hetu*) has the sense of purpose (*artha*), and thus it is not an inference (*anumāna*); rather, it is the *liṅga* itself that is being expressed.

Having observed that this [the injunction] is already established, the statement "praise is useful for incitement" implies that it is merely laudatory; therefore, the conclusion is that the sentence—"for by that [praise], food is indicated, let it be understood right there"—is either an injunction or a prohibition. (Vi. 1.2.3). For it is not indicated elsewhere.
In this context, the *holākā* is a spring festival (*vasantotsava*). (Vi.

1.3.8) Based on the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the practice of others, when [the Vedic text] is lost, injunctions and prohibitions regarding that [practice] can be inferred, but not those pertaining to anything else. The *holākā* is a duty for all people; it is only with respect to that subject that [injunctions and prohibitions] can be inferred, and not otherwise.
Why? Not only for those situated in the east.
"Others maintain that this very [object] is a different house existing here and now;
because of the establishment through inference, the means of knowledge would be connected with that."

It is certain here that what is not perceived is not cognized; for those for whom initiation (*upanayana*) and the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) are prescribed, it is understood from inference—that is, from Smṛti and established custom (*ācāra*)—that the injunctions for the Agnihotra and other rites indeed exist. The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): From inference, from Smṛti, and from customs, the authority [of the Veda] is understood, and thus the injunction for the Agnihotra and so forth is apprehended.
And just as the *ṇya*-suffix is desired [in the sense of "fit for"],
by that very same reason those established customs— such as distinctions of caste and family laws— are established;
in that same way, they deserve to be authoritative for their respective regions.

Therefore, rites such as the *holākā* should be performed by the Easterners (*prācya*) alone; thus, there will also be a systematic distinction regarding *dharma* and other matters. If it were otherwise, then rites such as the *ahīnaibuka* would belong to the Southerners (*dākṣiṇātya*) alone, and rites such as the *uddacyabhayaśā* would belong to the Northerners (*udīcya*) alone, because of the restriction of injunctions and prohibitions to their respective regions. Custom (*ācāra*) is likewise [to be understood] in the same way.

Just as it is established for Śilāka that "some [hold] three śīlas, some five śīlas," because of the impossibility of a single fixed cause for such distinctions, so too regarding the conduct prescribed in all the treatises on the subject:

having cited the local customs (*deśadharma*) practiced by men of various capacities in all regions, such as the performance of the *agnihotra* and the study of the Vedas, this is now being investigated.
"But he who performs that [action] according to its application— that is established.
Is the state of being all-encompassing (sarvadharmatā) for these [actions] established at the end of the root?"
Therefore, there must certainly be some Vedic text that prescribes these very [acts];

for all prohibitions here have the purpose of negating an action and are marked by the avoidance of such activity, and this is understood through the principle of "otherwise it would be inexplicable" (anyathānupapatti). Thus, the Vedic text is inferred.
The examples of what is to be adopted and what is to be rejected have been set forth in detail;

by means of that [explanation] and through the logical impossibility of the contrary, it is determined right there that those which the virtuous practice and those which they avoid are to be followed.

It is considered whether these [practices] were taught for those very people, or for all people; for this local custom, or this text concerning the cheeks and so forth, would otherwise be inexplicable.

Thus, some among the Southerners, the Westerners, and the Northerners [hold such views]. If there is no basis in the Śruti, then another basis must be postulated. Therefore, that [basis] should be determined as being established according to specific regulations.
And so it has been said:
"In that same way, all those modes of conduct are to be investigated;
[the author] points out the primary Sūtra if a reason is conceived."
"Whatever two-fold performance of sacrifice there may be, let this be considered here:
the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) is prescribed as the means for the *gṛhya* rites according to Gotama;
therefore, it follows that this [basket] alone constitutes the entire range of applications, including the arrangement of the sacrificial threads (*sūtra*) and so forth."
One might even imagine an illustration from the Purāṇas, Mānavas, or Itihāsas:

if a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) used in a sacrifice were offered by that very [instrument], then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of that rule to the *dharmasūtras* composed by Gautama, Vasiṣṭha, Likhita, Hārīta, and Āpastamba, as well as to the *gṛhya* manuals and the *prātiśākhya* grammatical treatises.
Having observed that [the world] is thus established through local customs everywhere,
it is logical to assume that the Vedic revelation has those [customs] alone as its object, being rooted in them.
Because inference is established through the restriction of place and other factors,
the Vedic word connected with that [inference] would be the means of valid cognition here; thus,
the entire dharma is based on the Veda, because the injunction follows that principle.
Commentary: The word "api vā" (or rather) serves to set aside the previous position.
Every such dharma would be of this nature.
Why? Because that is the principle governing the injunction.
That by which something is enjoined is an injunction (*vidhāna*), namely, the word;
that [word] is inferred from the traditional scripture (*smṛti*).
And it is not logical for it to denote a class-form (*ākṛti*), nor is it logical for it to denote an individual (*vyakti*).

There is no word whatsoever that expresses a single universal common to all universals, which could then be inferred. Therefore, the nature of being a property (dharmatā) must apply to all things. Why? Because there is authoritative evidence for the fact that "objects of words" are what are to be accomplished (*kartavyatā*), whereas there is no authoritative evidence for any restriction.
Or rather—[it is said] here as a reply to the [objection] that "it might apply to all dharmas":
"Because that is the principle for the injunction; the qualification belongs to whoever possesses the capacity.

In this context, when the root *śruti* (Vedic texts) is inferred from the *smṛtis*, which are themselves observed to have a basis, one must infer the injunctions regarding the specific procedures (*itikartavyatā*) for the various means such as oblations, sacrifices, and fasts—which lead to results such as heaven—by means of the principle governing causal injunctions. That is to say, one must infer those injunctions whose causes correspond to the effects being observed, and which are characterized by the non-distinction of the mental dispositions (*bhāvanā*) expressed as "thus" and "in this manner."

Even though [the agent] is thus to be excluded, in the worldly activities involving the body, senses, and objects of pleasure, there must necessarily occur an inference that establishes the prohibition of the prohibited action and its resulting fruit, such as hell. However, since this inference has only "fitness" (*yogyatva*) as its object, it does not yield a certain understanding restricted to a specific agent defined by particular directions, locations, or qualifications.
Why? Because: "The agent is known specifically in three ways according to each case.
Therefore, in this context, [the agent is understood] through the qualifiers of fitness, non-prohibition, and specific [qualification].

In this context, the fitness for the performance of prescribed duties is characterized by being distinguished from those residing in all other [countries] outside [Āryāvarta], such as the *dhigvaṇas*, *rajaputras*, and *dhmakas*.

Furthermore, the fitness for avoidance is understood through observation to apply to those not connected with even two, three, or four castes and stages of life (*varṇa* and *āśrama*), or—by inference from the evidence—to apply to all *mlecchas* and others beyond that.
However, there is no such qualifying term here that does not follow established custom.
One might infer a specific agent observed in a particular location;
yet even those residing in other regions who are prohibited [from acting]—
no word expressive of them can possibly be inferred.

"Even though eligibility (*adhikāra*) applies without distinction based on general capability, it may be specified by some particular term, such as 'the king [is eligible] for the Rājasūya' or 'the Vaiśya for the Vaiśyastoma. However, in this case, it is impossible to conceive of even a single word denoting one who performs the *hṛdayamāna* sacrifice. Why? Because every nominal word is based upon either a genus (*ākṛti*) or a configuration (*vyakti*); whatever might otherwise be inferred would not even have a single referent."

First of all, no such genus as "easternness" (*prācyatva*), "southernness" (*dākṣiṇyātva*), and so forth, is possible, which—by excluding individuals from the west, north, and so on—would reside in all easterners and others, and whose mention would justify an investigation into the *Holākā* section. As for those genera such as "humanity" (*manuṣyatva*) or "Brahminhood" (*brāhmaṇatva*), they are indeed present in all individuals; however, since they are not distinguished by any specific individual, they are not known to have the capacity to serve as qualifiers corresponding to [specific] practices.

"But a name that denotes a specific individual (vyakti) applies to only one [individual], like Devadatta and others; therefore, unity of locus is not established [for it]. Since a single substratum is not possible for the various cognitions belonging to different persons—whether taken individually or collectively—due to the impossibility of their experiencing a common object, [the opponent's position fails]."

By this, the claim that [words] denote individual persons qualified by qualities, actions, or universals is refuted. For no quality, action, or universal whatsoever can be conceived as being capable of characterizing individual persons established in various locations,
because in every case— even in those instances— there is no difference in their exclusion (vyāvṛtti).
"A category (padārtha) that is not perceived through its individual instances (vyakti), configuration (ākṛti),
or class-characteristic (jāti) cannot serve as the basis for a qualification of the person entitled to perform a rite.
Demonstrating this very point, the author of the Bhāṣya says:

When a specific injunction that has begun its application is restricted by a qualifying term—even one whose capacity is merely inferred—it is not logical for that term to denote either a genus (*ākṛti*) or an individual (*vyakti*). For these practices of the *holākā* do not subsist in any genus, nor do they subsist in an individual; indeed, it is impossible for even a single person among all those in whom these practices are established to encompass them through a designation.

For some, it would be logical that [the word] expresses the class (*jāti*) and not the individual (*vyakti*); such is the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*) found in the texts. Just as the author of the Sūtras, in the aphorism "But Bādarāyaṇa [holds there is eligibility for all] because there is no distinction" (6.1.8), will declare—on the basis of the capacity [of the word] that the term *svargakāma* (desiring heaven), though etymologically [denoting a male], refers to the entire human class (*manuṣyajāti*) since the qualification of masculinity is possible in the case of one being addressed, and since it is appropriate [to include all] who seek the fruit; likewise here too, because it conveys the status of being an agent and the desire for the fruit, in all local duties (*deśadharma*), the human class is entitled [to perform them].

Furthermore, someone might explain the meaning of the word *akhyāti* while refuting this reading of the text, even though it was already established previously; and failing to perceive the distinction between the pain produced by the word *dhāraṇa* as found in the Sūtra and its manifestation, he might—out of fear of the Yoga system which extends to the definition of the nature of both [perception and non-perception]—destroy the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the Ācārya’s section, or perhaps [he would do so] according to his own duty through the traditional scriptures, saying:
"It is not like the form of the cognition of a word."

Therefore, when someone desiring to know the true nature of the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-pratyaya*) asks, "What, then, is this *bhāva* and what is *bhāvanā*?"—in response to him, [the following] is explained by means of this [verse]: because there is no observation of the usage of a suffix alone, apart from its being expressed by a word, [it is understood] merely by the utterance of the rule beginning with "of the agent who expresses identity with the meaning of all roots" (*sarva-dhātvarthātmatva-vacana-kartuḥ*), that one should act; the meaning is "one should produce a word. Is every meaning being expressed expressed in the form of a universal (*ākṛti*), or is it something that transcends the domain of both individual (*vyakti*) and universal? Since it lacks any such means of expression, its meaning is "inexpressible" (*anākhyeya*).
Indeed, this very point was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya in this text as well:
"It is not logical that it should denote the configuration (*ākṛti*), nor that it should denote the individual (*vyakti*).

For the word *vidhāna*, which was previously introduced in the Sūtra, is referred to by the pronoun *tat* (in the compound *tad-vacanatā*) and thereby excludes both denotation of the individual and denotation of the configuration.
"For when it is said, 'One should do,' one understands, 'I am doing.
That [understanding] is neither the injunction nor the productive urge (bhāvanā), for it consists of both the universal and the particular.

This [objection], being impossible and logically untenable, has been applied to its own destruction by one who—relying on the mere similarity of the word "sat" and disregarding the intended meaning of the author of the commentary, which is supported by both scripture and reasoning—rejects that very meaning and displays instead the play of his own wit.

This treatise has the purpose of establishing the practice of all dharmas according to local customs; if it is explained by means of a prior commentary as having the nature of a refutation of established arguments, then it accords with the explanation of this Sūtra according to the path of reasoning already stated. However, if it is explained by abandoning that [prior commentary] on the grounds that the meanings of verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta-pratyaya*) are not expressible (*anākhyeya*), and thus its meaning is devoid of both individual manifestation (*vyakti*) and generic form (*ākṛti*), then it would be entirely unacceptable, as its meaning would be disconnected from reality, illogical, and unprovable.

For instance: "Since the word denoted by a verbal suffix (ākhyāta) does not denote either the individual (vyakti) or the form (ākṛti), it is a wonder that the derivative (taddhita) [suffix] should have all things as its object. If indeed the verbal suffix, the nominal suffix (liṅga), or the optative (vidhi) were to denote either the individual or the form, then rituals such as the *Holākā* would be restricted to the customs of specific regions; however, since [the optative] is inexpressible even when devoid of both individual and form, it must therefore concern an object beneficial to all, and thus be a duty for all persons—this is how the meaning should be understood, and this interpretation alone would be the most authoritative in the given example.
"Having stated that [the ultimate] is inexpressible (*anākhyeya*), he has provided a subsequent explanation (*anvākhyāna*) using synonyms of his own fabrication;
and this contradicts what was said previously.

For, by superimposing upon the words *vidhi*, *upadeśa*, *kartavyatā*, *bhāvanā*, and *śabda*—which are in fact absolutely non-existent—the synonymous nature of being extensively spoken and proclaimed, he himself has established, as it were, their very state of being inexpressible."

Even if the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) were to express merely the state of being an agent—as in "because of being an agent" and so forth—nevertheless, because it is delimited by the specific action of "placing" (*upadadhāti*), as in the case of "the Brāhmaṇa is the sacrificer," it conforms to the status of the *śadīna* class and so on; thus, the determination of its eligibility (*adhikāra*) does not depend upon an investigation into whether it denotes an individual (*vyakti*) or a generic form (*ākṛti*).

How much more so when it remains established solely as the state of being the first [to act] and so forth, which is understood through the injunction (*vidhi*) independently of the expression of the agent?

If this much alone were the cause for being a *dharma* for all people, then it would follow that sacrifices such as the *rājasūya*, the *aśvamedha*, and the *iṣṭi* would also be *dharmas* for everyone, because there is no difference in their being enjoined by verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta-pratyaya*) of that nature. Now, if you argue that those [sacrifices] are not *dharmas* for all because they are enjoined by verbal suffixes whose meanings are restricted, yet are limited to specific persons due to the presence of qualifying terms (*upapada*) such as "king" (*rājan*),
then the same must be maintained in this case as well by one who asserts that [the practice] is not a *dharma* for all.
Furthermore, it must be refuted by the statement beginning with "all phenomena" (*sarvadharmas*).
And that [refutation] is for the sake of the self, because [the opponent's position] consists in speaking of individuals and forms in accordance with conventional practice.
Alternatively, it is already refuted by the fact that one understands the scope [of the term] as referring merely to the human form.

For instance, subsequent sūtras such as "And because of the absence of gender [it is] eternal" and "For the name [is applied] due to connection with a place," which are intended to reject the application of secondary suffixes (*upapada*), are collected here.

Therefore, even for those duties (*dharma*) recorded in the *Dharmasūtras*—which are established according to specific regions, customs, and local practices through the rule of universal authority—the status of being "all-encompassing duty" (*sarvadharman*) applies.
This is the injunction regarding the performance of sacrifices and other rites.
It may be so.

The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) states: "Now, as for what was said—that the lineage (*gotra*) is established just as a stone remains fixed—this is clearly seen through the analogy of the stability of a stone. Or rather: 'That which infers a rule that is not established, like caste, family, lineage, or dharma.'"

"In that case, there would be a restriction regarding the performance of seeing [the deity] and so forth, based on the fixed rule for those denoted by a single term—such as *jāti* (caste) and the rest—just as in the case of the *kātr̥* [priesthood]. Just as, for example, the five-fold portion (*pañcāvatta*) belongs to the Bhrgus, and the second fore-offering (*prayāja*) belongs to Vasiṣṭha and the Kātris, while it is not for others; and since such a restriction is possible through differentiation from others and through indicative marks (*upalakṣaṇa*), it is understood as having a restricted scope. In the same way, [the rule] is restricted to those who do not belong to one's own lineage (*gotra*)."

In the section concerning the Holākā rite, there is the possibility of inferring specific established rules such as those found among the Triśillakas and Ekaśilās; thus, there is a disparity with the example [cited] in the *Arthavāda* section. Furthermore, because there is an absence of a probans (*liṅga*), there can be no eternal [rule].
Commentary: This sūtra follows certain words.
Which are those words? Furthermore, why is there no fixed determination based on gender (liṅga), as in "the white cloth" (*śukle drote*)?
There is no such permanent gender for these [words] that would follow according to observation.
Even those who are dark-complexioned, large-bodied, and red-eyed do not all perform the Āhīnaibuka and other such rites;
moreover, they practice even without the specific marks [of their class].
Therefore, there is no fixed restriction.

"Let the Hotṛ priest [be one who is] fair-complexioned"—this is a direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣā śrutiḥ*). Or rather: "When the individual (*vyakti*) and the form (*ākṛti*) have been rejected as the denotable objects, and the qualifiers [such as caste] have been dismissed, now other marks such as 'red-eyed' and the like are likewise refuted."

Anticipating the objection that—even in the absence of a word denoting a genus (*jāti*) or an individual (*vyakti*) as a subordinate term (*upapada*)—the restriction of qualification will still be established by indicating specific qualities such as the physical form and complexion residing in the agent, just as one speaks of "one who wears black hair," this is refuted: "And because there is no indicative mark (*liṅga*), there is no qualification of the eternal agent; for the eternal agent is indicated only by a fixed indicative mark."
That which is considered auspicious for Southerners, such as red eyes and so forth,
is seen even among others who practice those same customs.
And this practice is observed even among those who wear green [clothing] as their mark;
therefore, the eligibility established by the marks is specified.

However, for one who considers the word *nitya* to be a qualifier of *liṅga*, there would follow the contingency of an "unintegrated compound" (*asamartha-samāsa*), because it depends upon the gender (*liṅga*) which has become a subordinate element (*upasarjana*).

[Objection: But surely, since the word *liṅga* is always dependent [on something else], there is no destruction of its semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) due to its connection with another [word] implied by its own meaning; therefore, a compound must indeed be formed here, just as in the case of "Devadatta’s teacher’s family" (*devadattasya gurukulam*). [Reply:
This is not equal [to that example], because in this case, a connection with an intervening term is intended.
It does not constantly depend upon gender, just as a teacher [does not depend on the gender] of Devadatta.

For the word *guru* acquires its meaning only in relation to a disciple; thus, since it does not exceed the scope of the object already conveyed by the word *devadatta*, there is no consequence of obstructing the capacity of its own primary meaning through dependence on something else. As for the view that "here the status of being an indicator (*liṅgatva*) is understood in dependence upon the indicated (*liṅgin*), and yet the indicated is not apprehended as eternal"—this is what is [being addressed].

"Even though this term *liṅga* functions when there is a relationship between the indicator (*liṅgin*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*), nevertheless, in the case of relationships such as teacher and disciple or father and son, it is well known that the word [for the relationship] has its basis of application dependent upon that [relationship].
The possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) always depends upon the mark because it is a derivative word (*yaugika*);
the word *liṅga*, however, requires nothing other than the meaning of its verbal root."

For although the word *liṅga* is said to be "that by which something is marked" (*liṅgyate 'nena*), and thus its designation as a "mark" (*saṃjñin*) is based on its connection with an action, nevertheless, it does not abandon its dependence on other factors of action (*kāraka*) inherent in that action; thus, [the definitions] such as "the perception of the mark of the possessor of the mark" (*liṅgino liṅgadarśanam*) would be incorrect, and this would constitute a failure to avoid the fault [of over-extension]. Furthermore, since the eternality of the definition consists in its dependence on the object and the mark, and this is presented as a property of that [definition], the consequence of incapacity (*asāmarthya*) cannot be avoided when discussing that relationship.

Therefore, because there is no specific mark that indicates either a particular qualification—such as being characterized by a fixed sign—or a fixed agent, or a permanent entitlement, it is not possible to establish the injunction for the *holākā* and other rites as being restricted by a specific accompanying word (*upapada*) denoting such [an agent or entitlement].
For a name (*ākhyā*) arises from a connection with a place.
The Commentary: Now, why is there no restriction based on a name?

Those who are designated as "southerners" will perform the Āhīna, Aibuka, and other such rites; those designated as "northerners" will perform the Uddaṣabha sacrifice and others; and those designated as "easterners" will perform the Holākā and others—just as in the case of the statement, "The king [should sacrifice] with the Rājasūya.
This is not so.
A designation arises from connection with a country.
One who has come from the southern region and is situated either to the east or to the north certainly performs the Āhīnaibuka and other such rites;
likewise, those from the northern region perform the Udvṛṣabhayajña and others in another region, while those from the eastern region perform the Holākā and others.
Furthermore, one who has gone to another country does not necessarily perform the duties of another region;
therefore, there is no fixed rule [based on location]. However, in the case of "The king [should sacrifice] with the Rājasūya," the caste (jāti) is indeed fixed.
Or rather: "But now, as for that conduct which one follows most intensely, even the designation of 'teacher' and so forth is merely an additional qualification applied to it."

"For all regional customs (deśācāra) are performed by men designated as Easterners, Southerners, and so forth; yet they are not found among those very people who bear such designations. Therefore, because the specific designation is inferred from the injunction, the position that the authority [of the Smṛti] is connected to that [injunction] is indeed superior. To this, the following is the resolution:
"For a designation indeed proceeds from association with a place;
therefore, the rule for practices is understood as being qualified by the specific region."
And a place would be distinguished by its direction, yet the nature of direction is unstable;
moreover, the practice [of conventional usage] does not persist through a connection with that place.
Even when [the performers] have departed, because it is observed,
the Holākā section should be performed; [this is so] because of its being seen.
As for the name (*samākhyā*), it has no other cause than the location; its essence consists solely in following the connection with that location, as established by specific injunctions.
However, since both [the name and the location] are subject to deviation, they are logically consistent only when qualified by the specific name whose cause is the location.
If it is argued that this would not apply in other locations—

Commentary: If you hold this view—that if a name were derived from conjunction with a place, it would not apply to one residing in another place—yet it does apply to one residing in another place, as in the case of "Māthura," even for one who was not previously designated by that name because of Mathurā.
Therefore, the name is not derived from conjunction with a place.
Or—having established his own position through this very same reasoning, the opponent, standing in opposition, says: "If it is argued that [the name] would not exist in other places.
[The author replies: "If the objection regarding the name being caused by place has been refuted by me, then it is possible for me to state once again that it is caused by something else."
If its cause were the location, it would not exist in other locations;
therefore, there must be some constant factor such as a universal (*jāti*) that serves as its basis.

Or let it be that [the practice] distinguishes [itself] even without a specific cause; nevertheless, for us who have already obtained the cause in the form of established conduct, what need is there for another cause?

When it is argued that "its status as a cause for designating a location of deviation must be inferred from its designation as 'impermanent' (anityā), which is established by its specific additional quality," the following is replied:
"It would indeed be a designation based on connection (yoga), like [the name] Māthura.
The Bhāṣya states: "Even when a designation is caused by connection with a location, it is not contradictory for one who has departed from that location to still bear that name."
Since this designation "yogin" depends solely upon yoga and not upon a connection with the past, present, or future,
we observe that one who has set out for Mathurā is called a "Māthura," as is one who is currently living in Mathurā or has departed from Mathurā.
However, one who lacks any such connection to it is not a Māthura.

Therefore, the determination [of the origin of a text] is not established by name alone. Or rather: "Indeed, a regional designation (*deśa-samākhyā*) proceeds on account of many connections, such as being born in that place, residing there, or having come from there."
"Thus, its designation [as a place]—such as 'one who resides there,' 'one born there,' or 'one come from there'—never occurs by abandoning these etymological grounds.

Nor does this designation deviate from connection with the region; nor does custom follow it, because some inhabitants do not practice it, and because even among those who have long since departed, such as sons and grandsons, the practice continues in other regions. Therefore, the establishment of a fixed rule cannot be achieved through mere designation."

As for what the Commentator stated—that one who has set out for Mathurā is called "Māthura"—that should be understood as referring to a messenger (*dūta*) according to the rule *tadgacchati pathi dūtyoḥ*, or else it should be disregarded because the suffix is applied to a trustworthy person (*pratyayita*). For even when everyone has set out, there is no such designation [based on the destination]. Or rather, it is a property of the action (*karmadharma*), like the term "inclined" (*pravaṇa*).

Commentary: Now, why is place not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the ritual action? For example, [the status of] Mathurā for one residing in black soil, as in the case of the *Āhīnaibuka* sacrifices and others; or as in the injunction: "One should sacrifice with the *Vaiśvadeva* on ground sloping toward the east.
Or rather—[it is argued that] it is now unassailable by inference because it is the qualificand of an injunction that qualifies the agent.

Considering that the possibility of inference arises from the injunction regarding the eastern direction and so forth, which constitute an integral part of the ritual action (*karma*), he says: "Or it is a property of the action, like a slope. "Just as a place that slopes toward the east or north becomes an integral part of the ritual action, so too should the eastern direction and the rest [be understood]."
"Thus [it is said]. But it is equal with respect to the property of the agent.

The Commentary states: "Just as a characteristic established in the agent, such as being dark-complexioned and so forth, does not enter into correspondence with the ritual objects, for that characteristic is established solely in relation to that person's location."
Even in a place consisting mostly of black clay, some do not perform [the rite], while others perform it even on ground marked by other sectarian signs;
therefore, there is no restriction based on location. However, the rule that the Vaiśvadeva must be performed on ground sloping toward the east is fixed by the Vedic scripture.
Or rather: "But [the inference] is equal [in strength] to a property of the agent"; for that sign is unstable, due to its deviation from such things as direction, black clay, and so forth.
For that which is the eastern region for some is the southern path for others;
likewise, it is perceived as northern or western according to their respective forms.
Even a mark such as clay and the like is the same whether it is there or elsewhere;
therefore, the Holākā and other rites are also distinguished by that very mark.
Conduct is not observed even in that person with respect to his own nature;
yet it is seen in others as well. Therefore, even one's country is not the cause [of conduct].
Thus,
having established the validity or invalidity of the Smṛtis and the Ācāras based on their consistency or inconsistency [with the Vedas].
The independence of the Smṛtis has already been refuted.
Now, it is considered whether certain customs and Smṛtis are restricted in their application or not.
For practices such as the Holākā are performed only by certain people who identify themselves as Easterners and so forth, and not by everyone.
These Gadyāṇis and other Smṛtis are recited by only some individuals and not by all;
therefore, disregarding these Smṛtis and customary practices, they are investigated.
Are these [authorities] restricted to those specific [Smṛtis] alone, or do they apply to all?
Furthermore, can it be assumed that this [Smṛti] is the foundational source for them, having a restricted scope, or is it common to all?
In this regard: "The indicative mark attains its restriction through the restriction of the indicative mark."
For where there is smoke, there alone is fire; it is not perceived elsewhere.
The Vedic revelation (śruti) is not directly perceived, but is inferred through the signs of tradition (smṛti) and conduct (ācāra).
And that sign is observed only in certain instances.
Therefore, the Śruti can be inferred only by its extent;
for there is no proof that it has all things as its object,
since Smṛti and custom are also logically consistent even when their scope is restricted.
Furthermore, if the Vedic revelation were common to all, then the Smṛtis and practices rooted in it would also be accepted by everyone.
For if the non-performance of others were due to causes such as laziness, then a common inference might indeed be possible.
However, the fact that those who identify with the Easterners and others perform certain acts while others do not, does not allow for such a common inference.
Therefore, their status as *dharmas* is established.
This being the position reached, it is replied: "All this [status] is well-known merely by the absence of distinction;
however, the establishment of distinctions would require a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*), and that is not possible here."

As for what was said—that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the state of being all things—that is incorrect. For one who asserts that everything is [all things] need not put forward a means of valid cognition;
because, in the absence of the adoption of a specific qualification, the state of being all things is established by a rule that is already established for both parties.
However, one who maintains the doctrine of systematic restriction (vyavasthāvādin) must state the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for such a distinction;
and that does not exist.
For instance, the Smṛtis enjoin [rites] in a general manner, and thus there is no mention of specific Vedic schools (caraṇa) in them.
And since the assumption of a Vedic text is based precisely on the recollection [of it], that too is a common [principle] and thus logical.
However, the restriction regarding the recitation [of specific verses] arises from the author's school (caraṇa).
For the author, being a Chandoga, taught his own students, who were also Chandogas, this work.
They [the Chāndogyas] likewise [refer] to other Chāndogyas; this is the reading of the *Chāndogīya*.

Similarly, [the reference] to the *Taittirīyas* for the *Āpastamba* text, and so on for the *Gṛhya* texts, renders the claim that these have as their subject matter duties restricted to specific groups (*vyavasthita-dharma*) devoid of authority. Regarding customs (*ācāras*), however, there exists no distinction—whether pertaining to all practitioners or non-practitioners, or consisting of genus, individual, quality, configuration, and so forth—that could serve as a basis for specifying the eligibility (*adhikāra*) for each particular group.
Likewise, even designations such as "Eastern" and so forth are inconsistent, because some people born in those regions do not practice [the tradition],
and because [the tradition] is practiced by sons, grandsons, and others who have long since departed from that region, even in the absence of such a designation.
Therefore, in the absence of a qualification, it is established that the status of being "all dharmas" applies to both the *ācāras* (customary practices) and the *smṛtis* (traditional codes).

Soma [states]: The connection [of this section] is justified because, by purifying the subject matter, the authority (*prāmāṇya*) therein is firmly established; and because if there were no lack of independence regarding authority, an investigation into the determination of limits (*vyavasthā*) would be untenable.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: since the indicator (*anumāpaka*) is restricted, the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the form of Śruti must be inferred as being connected precisely with that restriction.
[The opponent asks: "Is there a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) regarding the *Holākā* festival and so forth, or is there universal applicability (*sādhāraṇya*)? [The answer is:

The former, because it is observed according to different regions; and there is equality [of authority] due to the similarity of the source, since the Vedic text associated with terms such as 'Easterners' (*prācya*) is inferred from the [Smṛti] word."

If it is argued that [the Smṛti] lacks authority because its meaning is not understood, we say no, because [its meaning is established] through inference based on general principles (*sāmānyānumāna*).

The Bhaṭṭa [responds]: Now, in cases where there is a restriction regarding the recitation in Smṛtis—such as those belonging to Gautama being for the Chandogas alone—or where there is a restriction regarding the performers of practices (*ācāra*), such as the *Holākā* and others being for those who identify with the Easterners and so forth; in those instances, since the inferring [Smṛti] has a restricted scope, the corresponding Vedic text (*śruti*) inferred from it must also have a restricted entitlement (*niyatādhikārikā*), and thus it should not be performed by others.

This being the position reached, [we reply]: even if the inferring [Smṛti] has a restricted scope, it is nevertheless impossible to attribute a specific qualification such as "being an Easterner" to the Vedic text that is to be inferred.
For that which is called "easternness" (*prācyatva*) cannot be defined by genus, individual instance, configuration, or the like, as it does not pervade all conduct;
for even among those residing in that region, [the practice] is not observed, while it is observed even among sons and grandsons who have long since departed from that land.
Therefore, due to the absence of such specific characteristics, it has universal scope.

In the case of Gautama’s *Mīmāṃsā*, there is no recourse to the authority of the *Chāndogas* (Sāmavedins), by which it might be connected to that specific Vedic recension (*śruti*). However, their mere inclusion in the text is justified because they belong to the same Vedic school as the author of the *Smṛti*. For the author, being a *Chāndoga*, taught this work to his own students who were also *Chāndogas*.
They too read it thus: "It is established in that alone"; therefore, even there, it refers to all objects. Maṇḍana [writes]: "'The Holākā rite is to be performed without restriction.

'Holākā rite' means the performance of customs such as the Holākā festival; 'without restriction' means by way of being common to all people, due to the absence of a fixed limitation of scope; 'is to be performed' means it ought to be done—this is the construction."
Śaṅkara: [Regarding] the lack of uniformity concerning the Holākā and other such practices.
This is the section on the Holākā.
There is the custom among Southerners to abstain from eating meat, whereas among Easterners and others, there is the practice of eating meat.
The practice of the *hautra* mantras:

In that regard, the inference of a Vedic text (*śruti*) based on both types of practice would occur only in a general sense, because the postulation of qualifying terms such as "Dākṣiṇātya" (Southerner) or "Prācya" (Easterner) has been refuted in the *Holākā* section.

The *holādhikaraṇa-nyāya*. *Sāhasī.*, 899. There is a doubt as to whether customs such as the *holākā* (spring festival) are the duty of the Easterners alone, or rather of all people; the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that they belong to all.
The *Holākā* customs are recorded in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa* and other texts (Bhāṣya 13.7).
According to the *Sudhā* (p. 189), the cause for the regulation of the *Holākā* customs is specifically the particular agent (*kartṛ*), not the region (*deśa*).
Su. Pṛ. 257: Festivals such as the Holākā are authoritative as right conduct (*sadācāra*) because they are the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).
Vi. 1314, Section 3: The restriction of duties is established by conventional designation (*samākhyā*), namely *hautra*, *ādhvaryava*, and *audgātra*.
Vi. 1316: By the designations *hautra*, *ādhvaryava*, and *audgātra*, the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Udgātṛ are respectively connected with those specific ritual acts.

1316|13. See the section titled "The Section on Designation" (*samākhyādhikaraṇa*) on page 419 of the *Mīmāṃsā-kośa*. From the observation of the cognition "this is the *hautra*," it is understood that the word *hotṛ* functions as an explanatory derivation (*anvākhyāna*) meaning "this is the work of that [person]. Vārttika 3.1.9.140: Because the designation "*hautra*" is meaningful, the *hotṛ* is the performer of the *hautra*.
Bhāṣya 12.4.14.135: Actions designated by the technical name *hautra* are to be performed by the *hotṛ*.

3.1.6.13: Regarding the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*), the *hautra* liturgy dedicated to Viṣṇu is handed down [in the Veda] as follows: "Viṣṇu strode across this," and "Viṣṇu is praised for that heroic deed."
Thus [it is stated]. 10|8|1|5|3. The *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest) must be performed by the Hotṛ;
however, the various *hautra* rites are optional because they serve a single purpose.

Regarding the *hautra* formulas—those mantras to be recited by the Hotṛ priest for the purpose of erecting the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) or for the purpose of leading it around—the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that because they serve a single purpose, that is, because they perform a single function, they should be used as alternatives (*vikalpena*).
However, there is conjunction (*samuccaya*) rather than alternation, because they are recitations accompanying an action (*kriyamāṇānuvāditvāt*).
There is no alternation; rather, there must be conjunction of the *hautra* mantras.
Because they are reciters of what is being performed (*kriyamāṇānuvāditvāt*). They are called "reciters of what is being performed" because they recite what is being done by the *adhvaryu*.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhāntaḥ*).
And it demonstrates their combination.
The indicative mark (liṅga), such as "He recites the first [verse] three times, the last [verse] three times," demonstrates the combination of the mantras belonging to the office of the Hotṛ.
What is the Ṛgveda? It is that which has the Hautra-pravacana as its source.
There is a combination of the *hautra* mantras;
however, the *hautra* [mantras] are used by way of option (*vikalpa*), because they serve a single purpose.

The Commentary states: However, those *hautra* mantras which are for the raising of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), such as "Be raised up, O Lord of the Forest" (*uccrayasva vanaspate*), or those intended for the carrying around of the post (*yūpapariṇaya*), such as "Young, well-clad" (*yuvā suvāsāḥ*), these would be optional alternatives (*vikalperan*).
Why? Because they have a single purpose (*ekārthatvāt*).
These [mantras] serve a single purpose, being expressive of both the act of raising and the act of carrying around.
And each one of them denotes that [object] in dependence upon the others;
therefore, there is either an option (*vikalpa*) or a combination (*samuccaya*), because they are restatements of what is being performed.
Commentary: Or rather, there is a combination of the *hautra* (recitations by the Hotṛ priest). Why? Because they are descriptive restatements (*anuvāda*) of actions that are being performed.
It has been stated that there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding ritual acts.
And these [other factors] are not instruments (*karaṇa*).
They are merely restatements of what is being done.
What, then, is the distinction between these two? Instruments produce the cognition "I am doing" in this way.
It is precisely for the purpose of restating what is being done—namely, "it should be done in this way"—that it is asked, "How is it to be done? It is said in reply:
For the Adhvaryu, the purpose is served by the cognition "I am doing it.
If the Hotṛ were absent, the action itself would not even proceed.
And this condition occurs when the preceding condition exists;
for he who thinks, "This must be done by me," performs it.
Furthermore, the *anuvādins* repeat the action being performed by the *adhvaryu*, as in: "The seekers of the gods anoint you at the sacrifice."
The Sixteenth Discussion: The Adhvaryu’s memory constitutes his essential nature as an agent;
and because he is required for that ritual action, these [mantras] are understood to be for the purpose of recollection.

By the power of the traditional transmission (*āmnāna*) of a mantra intended for recollection, that which has been recollected becomes equivalent to what has been performed, just like an act performed according to a formal instruction (*praiṣa*).
But surely, O Lord, for the mantras of the *hautra* [recited by the Hotṛ priest], the recollection of the words of injunction is even more minimal.
True; it follows from the force of the injunctive word as well. It also arises from the mantra.
Because of the mantra’s own inherent capacity, the action must be performed with the mantra.

And since there is a need for a continuous stream of memory (*smṛti-saṃtāna*) regarding extensive ritual acts, even a mantra that recites what is being performed (*kriyamāṇānuvādī*)—though it may belong to multiple [verses]—is possible within a single performance. Therefore, because they recite what is being performed, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of these [mantras]. And the scripture shows this combination:
the Bhāṣya states, "He recites the first verse three times; he recites the last verse three times; he should recite the *jyotiṣmatī* verses."
In the case of multiple conjunctions, this [principle] applies first; thus, it is called "superior" (*uttama*). Therefore, there is a combination (*samuccaya*).

Śā—Regarding those *hautra* mantras that follow the action, such as "O Lord of the Forest, rise up" (*uccaiḥ sya vanaspate*), since they, like the instruments of action, have a single purpose, a state of optionality (*vikalpa*) would result; therefore, it is stated [as follows].
For the instruments (karaṇas) serve as the means for the performance of the ritual action by producing a memory that exists in the moment immediately preceding [the action].
Since the purpose is accomplished by one [instrument], there is no need for another; thus, an option (vikalpa) regarding them is logical.
However, those which follow the action being performed (kriyamāṇānuvādinas) are intended to prevent the loss of memory of the ritual action being performed by the Adhvaryu priest.

And since the interruption of mindfulness is required at the end, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of all [the mantras]. Why? Because of the objection that, just as with the *prathana* and other mantras prescribed for the Brahmins, there might be an option (*vikalpa*) even regarding the *hautra* mantras; thus, the connection is made through this illustration. Vi: "In the case of 'udvice' and 'uccaisvasva', there is either an option or a conjunction."
Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises from the identity of the recollector, while the last [alternative] arises from the difference in the substratum (*ākāśa*).
Because it conforms to the mode of recollection—namely, "one performs what is to be done"—and because there is no identity of the action, there is a combination (*samuccaya*).
He formulates the second section: "Is there an option (*vikalpa*) between *uccair asva*, *samiddhaḥ*, *cetā*, and so forth?"

Alternatively, there may be a combination (*samuccaya*). Since they serve the same purpose, the first [view] holds that there is no recollection of what has been performed (*asmṛtavedanti*). The Bhaṭṭas: As for those *hautra* mantras which are recited as a restatement of what is being performed (*kriyamāṇānuvādinaḥ*), since their status as having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*)—by virtue of generating the recollection of the action being performed—was established in the *Mantrādhikaraṇa* section of the *Kaustubha*, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between them just as with the instrumental (*karaṇa*) mantras.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the reply is: because the recollection generated by the instrumental mantra produces the performance [of the rite], once the task is accomplished by one, the other would be rendered useless; thus, there is an option.

In the present case, however, since the Adhvaryu must remember again and again—due to the interruption of memory—the ritual action he performs, which spans many moments, it is logical that there should be a combination (samuccaya) of multiple mantras, as it is appropriate for each to recall its respective preparatory stage (*āpādārtha*). Furthermore, because there is no possibility of the fault of "defective option" (*aghaduṣṭavikalpa*), such a combination is indeed justified. For this very reason, indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as "he recites the first verse three times," "he recites the last one three times," and "one should recite the *jyotiṣmatī* verses," are also consistent with this view.
Maṇḍana [says]: "The *hautra* mantra should indeed be used in combination."
Śaṅkara: [This refers to] those [mantras] which describe an action as it is being performed;
[this is] the "Collection" (Samuccaya);
[it is] the chapter on the duties of the Hotṛ priests (Hautraka-adhyāya).

The Logic of the Fish and the Pond (Hradanaka-nyāya): Just as a fish and a pond, when separated from one another, are susceptible to being seized by a fisherman, whereas when joined together they provide mutual assistance and become invincible, so it is in the present case as well.
(Therefore, this logic applies to the relationship between the protected and the protector.)

The *sāhasī* is the most excellent *gāyatrī*. There are six, six, and seven syllables in its quarters. For example: "preṣṭhamu priyāṇām" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 8.10.3.10), or alternatively, seven, six, and six.
For example: "Indra, [the best] of the givers of thousands" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā).
